Introduction
Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
The Oxford Handbook of Tantric Studies is designed to explicitly address some of the 
obstacles to the study of tantra; to facilitate scholarly discourse; to address the problems 
of category, definition, and origins; and to facilitate collaboration between scholars 
working on different forms of tantra.1 For this reason, instead of employing sectarian, re­
gional, or disciplinary categories, this Handbook is organized topically. Thus, rather than 
viewing tantra as a subset of Śaiva, or Śākta, or Vaiṣṇava, Jain or Buddhist traditions, the 
chapters demonstrate how tantra can be autotelic—​located within these traditions in 
complex symbiotic relations, practitioners pursue their own ends, interacting with the 
thought and practice of the tradition with which they are affiliated. At the same time, the 
Handbook views tantra as a religious phenomenon best studied from multiple disciplinary 
perspectives, using different strategies of interpretation. Crossing the boundaries of lan­
guage and religious culture, the tantric traditions that extended from South and Southeast 
Asia, through Central/​Inner Asia and East Asia, today constitute part of the global reli­
gious culture. The range of academic specializations involved—​sectarian, linguistic, tex­
tual, and cultural—​has required input from scholars working in several different fields of 
scholarship, and who offer a plurality of perspectives on the shared object of study.2
The editors have divided the Handbook into eight sections. The categories and 
themes that structure the collection emerge directly from the content of the tan­
tric traditions themselves, rather than imposing any of the more typical academic 
structures, such as regions, historical periods, textual genres, or sectarian categories. 
In tantric traditions, all the topics discussed in the first seven sections are intercon­
nected with one another. Many traditions are characterized by transformative actions 
grounded in gendered notions of cosmology, by complex dynamics involving extraor­
dinary beings, or by the efficacy of extraordinary language—​often in some combina­
tion. These characteristics are in turn creatively expressed through visual and sonic 
art forms and through a great variety of literature and linguistic devices, supported 
by—​and given legitimacy through—​a range of social organizations and institutions. 
Finally, the eighth section addresses both the historiographies of modern scholar­
ship as well as the traditional notions of time sequences based on divine revelation 
and lineages of great teachers and disciples. More specifically, these sections allow for 
an expansive and systematic approach to the study of tantric traditions, starting with 
dialectical reflections on the concept of action (part 1) and the goals of transformation

--- PAGE 17 ---
xvi      Introduction
 
(part 2), which themselves are contextualized by concepts of gender, cosmogony, em­
bodiment, and power (part 3), as well as by beliefs in extraordinary beings (part 4). 
Next are representations in imagery and architecture (part 5) and language and sound 
(part 6), followed by considerations of the social order and institutions (part 7) that 
maintain and perpetuate all of the above. In the last section we consider the complexity 
of the subject overall by exploring etic and emic understandings of the histories of the 
traditions (part 8). This structure works to reflect what is important for members of 
the traditions themselves and places what scholars expect (e.g., contextualizing histor­
ical location) last, thus highlighting the contrariness of tantra for being understood in 
Western religious studies.
Part I. Action
Engaging in significantly transformative action—​broadly conceived—​is one of the 
most prominent features of tantra. Action may involve any of myriad possibilities: 
performing a ritual, practicing meditation, chanting, embarking on a pilgrimage, or 
reenacting moments from a sacred text. The goal of any action is not only to confirm 
the actor’s current place in the cosmos, but more importantly to connect and embed 
that actor within a larger soteriological framework. The practitioner’s location in this 
larger framework has cosmological, epistemological, sociological, psychological, and 
political ramifications. To explore these topics, the opening section includes chapters 
on initiation ceremonies, devotional practices at home and in temples, connections be­
tween thought and practice, and the importance of offertory fire rituals. This section 
also includes a chapter on how ongoing studies in neuroscience help us to understand 
the dynamics of tantric practices.
Part II. Transformations: Soteriology, 
Astrology, Alchemy, and Healing
Essential to tantric traditions is some form of transformation, which may also be 
considered the raison d’être of many philosophies or religions. The chapters in this 
section examine the cosmology, esoteric physiology, soteriology, embryology, al­
chemy, and magical processes of transformation. Tantra offers to transform human 
experience, consciousness, or existence into transhuman, transcendent, or cosmic 
forms, as well as having manifest effects in the world. There are almost limitless var­
iations on this foundational tantric process, expressed in diverse systems of thought 
(philosophical, literary, soteriological, epistemological, cosmological) and action 
(ritual, yoga). These chapters provide details and examples of these important tan­
tric endeavors.

--- PAGE 18 ---
Introduction      xvii
 
Part III. Gender, Cosmogony, 
Embodiment, and Power
In addition to valorizing the human body, tantra is also notable for its complex and pro­
found embrace of gender and sexuality—​and the resultant implications, consequences, 
and iterations. Cosmic power is both an embodied and gendered power, and there are 
distinctive expressions of both male and female sexual power, resulting in intriguing 
ritual, symbolic, conceptual, and textual traditions. The numerous goddess traditions 
central to much of tantra are perhaps the foremost example of this development. This is 
also closely integrated with conceptions of esoteric physiology and the various cosmic 
energies that circulate in the body, connecting it to the wider cosmos. Such gendered 
cosmophysiologies are, however, subject to external forces of control and subjuga­
tion, and thus techniques are developed to protect the body and consciousness of the 
practitioner. This often involves powerful protective female divinities, and the help of 
transgressive female beings such as yoginīs and ḍākinīs. Finally, the active domains of 
consciousness can range well beyond that of humans and other creatures, extending to 
the liberation of plants and trees. Thus, cosmogony, gender, embodiment, and power 
constitute a wide range of tantric concerns and practices.
Part IV. Extraordinary Beings: Deities 
and Founders
Extraordinary beings of many types play a key role in both tantric cosmology and soteri­
ology. Rather than being dualistically either good or evil, as tends to be the case in mon­
otheistic traditions, the extraordinary beings of the tantric cosmos are polyvalent. These 
run the gamut from cosmic deities, such as Śiva, to local and territorial deities, to humans 
who attain extraordinary status during life (founders, gurus, thaumaturges, siddhas), to 
those who become extraordinary after death (spirits), to astrological, calendric, and direc­
tional deities, and to guardians and wrathful protectors. Chapters in this section explore the 
roles of goddesses, founders of lineages, and complex figures who straddle the worlds of the 
human and divine as they reveal, disseminate, and protect essential tantric teachings.
Part V. Imagery: Art, Architecture, and 
Visual Expressions
While the trope of sacred sound, expressed in chants, mantras, and literature, is found 
throughout tantric traditions, visual imagery is just as essential to the tantric path. Also,

--- PAGE 19 ---
xviii      Introduction
 
the comparative study of aesthetic programs, symbolic systems, and architectural styles 
has provided an important new perspective on the historical relationships connecting 
the entire span of tantric Asia. Tantra incorporates complex traditions of temple archi­
tecture and ritual settings, as well as precise cosmological diagrams and designs known 
as “mandala,” “yantra,” and other terms.3 These forms relate to visualization, which is 
a major cognitive pathway of the transformative cosmological processes of tantra. To 
explore these areas, this section includes chapters on art history and architecture, along 
with specific essays on image consecration and tantric diagrams, and a theoretical dis­
cussion of the cognitive functions of such imagery.
Part VI. Language, Literature, Words, 
and Metaphor
Tantric literatures, produced in a wide variety of Asian languages, employ metaphors 
and other linguistic devices, often in complex and intertwined fashions. And the inter­
pretation of texts often depends on whether they are to be understood as metaphorical 
or literal, or more specifically contexts for such understandings. Much of the literature is 
oriented toward the performance of rituals, and does not reflect the categories of scrip­
ture, narrative, and doctrinal exegesis expected of religious literature as understood in 
Western religious studies.4 Also distinct from the understandings of Western religious 
studies are tantric conceptions of the power of extraordinary language, such as mantra 
and dhāraṇī. These ideas are widely found in Indic religious culture, but also spread via 
tantra to Central/​Inner, Southeast, and East Asia. This section provides chapters on the 
uses of metaphors and conceptual blending in ritual texts, the importance of mantras 
and phonemes as cosmological devices, overviews of Jain and Tibetan tantric literature, 
and a focused study of a particular Buddhist tantra, the Cakrasaṃvara.
Part VII. Social Organization and 
Institutions
Although the history of tantra is replete with solitary practitioners performing 
austerities and engaging in psychophysical techniques, the development and dissemina­
tion of tantra has generated a wide variety of social organizations and institutions—​from 
small groups of teachers and students, to larger public assemblies, as well as monastic 
institutions. Perhaps the most important social aspect of the tantric tradition involves 
the initiation of novices into a teaching and practice lineage through the efforts of an ex­
perienced and qualified master. Known by a variety of terms such as abhiṣeka, dīkṣā, and 
so forth, this process is most often deemed necessary to allow the individual to progress

--- PAGE 20 ---
Introduction      xix
 
along the tantric path. Not all tantric groups are secret, and some that begin secret 
evolve into public institutions. Other tantric institutions have always been public, such 
as those associated with kings or emperors. And in other cases, the socially marginal 
status of tantric practitioners, such as eunuchs (hijṛā), long kept them out of public—​or 
at least scholarly—​attention. This section includes chapters on the complex dimensions 
of social organizations in medieval India, the geopolitical dynamics of the formation of 
tantric traditions in Nepal, soteriological functions of monasticism in Buddhist tantra, 
oral traditions in contemporary Bengali tantric communities, and the emerging roles of 
gender fluidity in modern Assam.
Part VIII. History and Historiography: 
Events, Memory, and Recollection
Only in recent decades have scholars been able to construct some basic academic 
histories of the major tantric traditions, as such efforts can require extensive language 
skills, access to surviving manuscripts and oral traditions, and successful fieldwork. As 
discussed in Chapter 1, there is still debate about the exact historical origins of tantra—​
although recent scholarship demonstrates that the earliest texts likely emerge from Śaiva 
Hindu ascetic communities. Beyond these larger issues, scholars have revealed impor­
tant historical developments involving tantra and specific sociopolitical complexes, 
especially during the dynamic medieval phases of Asian history.5 But beyond these 
excellent histories and historiographies, which operate on what might be termed the 
ordinary level, we find within tantric traditions very different kinds of histories, time 
and event sequences, and types of recollection and reenactment. Both categories receive 
their own chapters in this section, with essays on more traditional historiographies, the 
chronology of the textual corpus of Buddhist tantra, as well as commentarial traditions 
and revelatory texts. This section concludes with an exploration of the transformation of 
tantra in the modern world as “Neo-​tantra.”
Notes
	1.	 As noted below in Chapter 1, we are using the lowercase form “tantra,” as opposed to the 
uppercase “Tantra,” as the latter suggests some underlying unity and essence, or a singular 
transcendent entity. We prefer the former as there are so many variations of the category 
that any monolithic or essentialist view tends to obscure more than it reveals. This volume 
itself illustrates some of the many manifestations of tantra throughout South, Central/​
Inner, Southeast, and East Asia—​as well as in a global setting since the nineteenth century. 
In explaining the traditional etymology of “tantra,” André Padoux (2017, 7) notes that from 
“the verbal root TAN, which means ‘to extend,’ ‘to spread,’ hence ‘to spin out,’ ‘weave,’ ‘dis­
play,’ ‘put forth,’ and ‘compose’ [the term comes by extension to mean] ‘system,’ ‘doctrine,’ or

--- PAGE 21 ---
xx      Introduction
 
‘work.’ A Tantra is thus a work, a text—​any text.” Hence we find the subsequent meanings of 
a discourse “woven” with the “threads” of words and thought.
	2.	 This is conceptually congruent with Peter Sharrock’s notion of a “coherentist hermeneu­
tics.” This is the use of complementary sources of evidence, as is intended by the multi-​
faceted nature of this collection. See Sharrock 2006, 287.
	3.	 Since Sanskrit terms such as maṇḍala and yantra have become commonplace in English for 
some time, in this volume we will not use the diacritical marks on these widely used terms.
	4.	 Although not addressed directly in this collection, one of the problems for tantric studies 
generally is the ephemeral nature of ritual manuals used in daily practice. Bibliographers, 
librarians, and collectors—​both in Asia and the West—​did not recognize the potential his­
torical importance of such works, and consequently an unknown number have been lost. In 
this regard the Tenri collection discussed by Payne in his chapter seems fairly unique in its 
collection of ritual manuals.
	5.	 The usage of “medieval” does not identify a single historical period across the entire range 
of cultures discussed in this collection. Likewise, use of the term should not be taken to 
imply equivalence, either chronological or cultural, with the European medieval period. It 
is intended to suggest a period of cultural florescence created by urbanization and trade, but 
prior to the conjoined rise of mechanized manufacturing, colonialism, and capitalism.

This volume was conceived in 2019, just prior to the outbreak of COVID-​19, and the 
structure and basic table of contents were developed as the world went into lockdown. 
Lives were upended by the virus and its many consequences, including the teaching, 
research, and travel plans of many possible contributors—​not to mention the lives and 
health of so many. Numerous colleagues who had hoped to contribute to the volume 
were thus unable to dedicate the time to crafting chapters, as others somehow found 
some solace in developing the chapters that you now have before you. Our editor at 
Oxford University Press, Robert Repino, was gracious, understanding, and patient 
throughout this process, as we of necessity had to keep extending the deadlines for 
drafts and revisions. Victoria Harris and Olivia Kier were the development editors for 
this project over several years, and managed the day-​to-​day work of moving chapters 
from the editorial to the production phase.
This effort is thus a pandemic book in so many ways. We wish to thank the many 
contributors, as well as those who were unable to complete submissions, for their resil­
ience and support for what we hope is a generational collection of tantric studies. Some 
of the intended sections developed in ways alternate to our original plans, but in the end 
we feel that our goals have been suitably met.
As Volume Editors, we are also grateful for the superb efforts of our colleagues who 
served as an advisory board for this project: Gudrun Bühnemann, Paul Donnelly, 
Sthaneshwar Timalsina, and Loriliai Biernacki. Each of them helped to review and shape 
the numerous chapters in this volume, sharing their own expertise in areas outside our 
own specializations. In addition, several scholars kindly reviewed sections or versions, 
providing additional perspective and helping us to avoid errors or oversimplifications. 
These include Ronald Davidson, Shaman Hatley, Tony Stewart, Bruce Sullivan, David 
White, Paul Hackett, and Charles Orzech. William Phipps, from Parsons School of 
Design, The New School, provided invaluable guidance in early stages of the cover de­
sign process and with other graphics.
We are indebted not only to the several dozen scholars whose fine work appears in this 
volume, but also to their own social networks of friends, families, and colleagues who in 
turn supported them as the pandemic unfolded. Many traditions of tantra emphasize 
the dynamic and often turbulent forces of the cosmos and its iterations in human na­
ture. But it also teaches about the human ability to master and perhaps overcome those 
very profound forces. In some small way, we feel that this volume might express our own

--- PAGE 23 ---
xxii      Reflections, Acknowledgements, and Collective Efforts
 
contemporary engagement with such larger forces, and hope that it contributes to the 
ongoing development of tantric studies.
In these first decades of a new millennium, tantric studies can offer a useful field for 
considering a fuller range of human experiences and formations of identity found by 
expanding the study of religion, ranging from the cognitive to the behavioral, from the 
individual to the social, across the complete range of gender identities, through creations 
of visual, sonic, architectural, and literary art forms, to speculations on ontology, episte­
mology, and soteriology. Tantra may have developed more than a millennium ago, but 
its content—​and the informed study of that content—​can help us to reappraise our own 
current situations as human beings.

Chapter 1
Tantric Studies
Issues, Methods, and   
Scholarly Collaborations
Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
“Tantra” identifies a category of religious thought and practice originating in early 
medieval India, which has spread throughout Asia and in the modern era globally. It 
was influenced by many concepts and techniques from diverse yogic, ritual, political, 
sociological, artistic, intellectual, and cosmological traditions found in the Indian sub­
continent during the first millennium ce, including the Vedic ritual tradition even then 
dating back more than two millennia. Drawing on that religious culture, the early me­
dieval period saw the creation of sets of practices and teachings that were increasingly 
textualized and codified into sectarian forms. Looking at this variety, tantra is extremely 
complex and requires a variety of methodologies for its study. At the same time, how­
ever, as this volume demonstrates, intriguing underlying themes and common concerns 
emerge when an academic perspective is taken. One of the persistent concerns of schol­
arship results from the quest for origins.
To what degree do the themes and concerns shared by the complex variety of tan­
tric traditions reflect a unitary common source? Or are these similarities due to older 
and deeper shared influences, or to borrowing between traditions, or perhaps to some 
other historical or cognitive process(es)? Scholars have thus had lively debates re­
garding the category and historical origins of tantra,1 as well as the many dimensions 
and interpretations of tantra as it developed into Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain forms in the 
subsequent centuries. Tantra continues in lived traditions throughout Asia, and since 
the nineteenth century, it has also appeared in numerous global contexts, especially in 
the prolific modern yoga movements. These topics are all addressed by the authors of 
the chapters in this volume.

--- PAGE 27 ---
2      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
Academic Debates on Origins and 
Interactions
Along with the growth of the field of tantric studies over the past several decades (see 
Appendix), dynamic academic debates have developed regarding the possible origins 
and earliest forms of tantra. One approach involves what some scholars regard as non-​
sectarian “pre-​tantric” influences that existed across South Asia early in the first mil­
lennium ce. For example, recent research by Davidson, Acri and Rosati, White, and 
other scholars2 suggests that, prior to the development of tantric traditions within 
Śaiva Hinduism and Mahāyāna Buddhism, there was an extensive range of popular 
“pre-​tantric” beliefs and practices. These included rituals to the autochthonous serpent 
spirits (nāga) seeking rains, cemetery practices, skull carrying, raising the dead, fer­
tility, and other magical practices. Although evidence is difficult to evaluate, many of 
these rituals were likely associated with very ancient shamanistic traditions, local and 
rural cults, and other popular “folk traditions.”3 These scholars argue that such “pre-​
tantric” influences played a major role in the subsequent development of Hindu and 
Buddhist tantric traditions. Other scholars, for example, Alexis Sanderson (1995, 2001) 
and Dominic Goodall (see chapter in this volume), would not agree that later Hindu 
and Buddhist tantric traditions originate from diffuse non-​sectarian magical practices 
and folk traditions.
Davidson argues for a socio-​political influence behind the development of sec­
tarian tantric Buddhism, with the “pre-​tantric” era of magical and divinatory practices 
at the end of and following the decline of the classical era of the Gupta-​Vākāṭaka age, 
which had lasted from approximately 320 to 550 ce.4 Sanderson (2009), however, has 
demonstrated the gradual formation of sectarian tantra among Śaiva Hindu ascetics, 
who transformed the system of the Atimārga (“the path beyond”) into the tantric system 
known as the Mantramārga (“the path of mantras”).5 The key issues under debate here 
involve the creation of specifically tantric texts, among which communities, and when 
they were written. Sanderson and his colleagues have argued that the first tantric texts 
were composed by Śaiva Hindus between the mid-​fifth to sixth centuries and subse­
quently exerted a pronounced influence on the development of Buddhist tantra, as is 
most clearly evident in the case of the Yoginītantras (see Hatley 2016a, 2016b; on the 
chronology and categories of Buddhist tantras, see Dalton 2004 and 2005).6 Reflecting 
a different point of view on these important matters, Davidson (2002) challenges these 
early dates and the direction of influence. Among the Indian Buddhist Mahāyāna mo­
nastic communities, Davidson (2017b) argues that the challenges of interacting with 
surrounding lay communities and polities led to the development of new genres of texts 
dealing with empowered spells known as dhāraṇī. As Davidson observes,7 “from the 
fourth to the seventh century, dhāraṇī Buddhist texts constitute our best record con­
cerning the involvement of Buddhist monks and laity with the spectrum of Indian ritual 
systems.” Jacob Dalton has resuscitated the category “proto-​tantric” by emphasizing the

--- PAGE 28 ---
Tantric Studies      3
 
ritual use, rather than conceptual significance, of dhāraṇī (2016, 200). His argument 
may be taken to support our problematizing of the sharp distinctions some historical 
analyses have attempted to impose.
These major developments in both Śaiva Hinduism and Mahāyāna Buddhism would 
lead to what scholars now call “Hindu tantra” and “Buddhist tantra,” although it must be 
emphasized that the details are contested by different schools of scholarship, as we have 
seen. Tantric ideas and practices also interacted with the Jain tradition, an influence that 
continues into the present (Gough, 2021 and this volume; Chapple, this volume).
Sanderson has established an influential body of scholarship related to the historical 
origins of tantra (particularly important instances are 1995 and 2009, and Goodall 2015). 
The central focus of his research has been the textual record of the Śaiva traditions. 
Extensive and nuanced, Sanderson’s work is effectively impossible to summarize 
here. The impression that many scholars seem to have been left with, however, is that 
tantra begins within the Śaiva tradition and that the early history of tantra is bounded 
by the corpus of Śaiva texts. On this basis, the rise of other forms of tantra, such as 
Buddhist, has been interpreted to be derivative—​a consequence of borrowing, adapting, 
appropriating, and renaming. Often presented in abbreviated form, this impression has 
been further propagated by other scholars as well (e.g., English 2002).
The specific understanding that Śaiva tantra has this originary status has, how­
ever, been challenged by several scholars, perhaps most consistently and effectively by 
Davidson (2017a, 2017b, 2021, 2023). In contrast to an elite, literate, and already sectarian 
tradition, Davidson has pointed to sources outside defined sectarian categories as im­
portant contributors to the early history of tantra. Davidson also calls into question the 
impression that the influence has been unidirectional—​from Śaiva outward to other 
traditions. Similarly, Gudrun Bühnemann has demonstrated that the Hindu tradition 
borrowed deities and mantras from the Buddhist (1999, 2000).
Perhaps unsurprisingly, such divergence of scholarly opinion has created sev­
eral contesting narratives, and not a little scholarly opprobrium. In his study of early 
Buddhist tantra, for instance, Christian Wedemeyer has strongly rejected claims 
of sources outside literate, elite, and monastic traditions (2013).8 This in turn has not 
gone unchallenged, with several scholars weighing in to highlight a more complex and 
extended context not only in the high-​Sanskrit cultures of medieval India but in the 
broader religious cultures of South and Southeast Asia (Acri and Rosati 2023).
Recent scholarship by Sanderson, Goodall, Isaacson, and others argues that among the 
Śaiva Mantramārga schools, the earliest known tantric text is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā 
(“compendium on principles of exhalation”), portions of which they have dated to the 
mid-​fifth to sixth centuries and likely no later than the seventh century (see Goodall, this 
volume).9 This dating, while somewhat uncertain, is contested by other scholars, such as 
Bakker (2014, 9, n. 30), who believes that the earliest material developed in the sixth 
century. The dating of early Buddhist tantric texts is also vigorously debated. Davidson 
(2011, 23) suggests that the earliest datable Buddhist tantric text is the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha 
(“collection of magical spells”), which, based on Chinese court records, dates to 654 ce. 
Davidson believes that this text, however, clearly relies on even earlier material. Another

--- PAGE 29 ---
4      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
early text identified by Davidson (2011, 24) is the Amoghapāśamahākalparāja, which is 
largely a compendium of ritual practices (sādhanas) and precepts (vidhis), itself based 
on the Amoghapāśahṛdaya, which was translated in 587 ce by Jñānagupta (Meisezahl 
1962). All of these early Buddhist tantras feature magical systems and describe the ac­
tivities of supernatural beings (vidyādharas), and they also reflect the “pre-​tantric” 
influences of the earlier dhāraṇī texts. Finally, other scholars of early Buddhist tantra 
also cite the Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka, estimated to date from the early seventh century, while 
the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi tantra is more definitely dated to the mid-​seventh century 
(see Sugiki, this volume; Gray 2016, 2023). Textual chronology remains an essential area 
of inquiry. Despite the importance of this line of scholarly inquiry, however, the long-​
standing idea of a specific original text (Urtext), whose primacy gives that hypostatized 
text authority, is now largely outmoded by more complex understandings of textual 
development. Looking beyond texts, the historical record also includes archeological, 
epigraphic and art historical sources (see the chapters in Part 5 of this volume). To sum­
marize, the earliest history of tantra remains indeterminate due to the lack of surviving 
evidence and the ambiguities of the evidence that does survive.
Another point of contention among scholars of tantra involves the possible mutual 
interactions between early Hindu and Buddhist tantra, as well as the directions of these 
influences. Sanderson’s painstakingly detailed and compelling argument (2001) is that 
specific Vajrayāna works (such as the late 8th or early 9th century Cakrasaṃvara tantra 
in particular) silently incorporate text from known Śaiva tantras. Davidson, however, 
argues against interpreting this to mean that Buddhist tantra is derivative from Śaiva 
tantra: “One line of argument has been that tantric Buddhism is ‘Śaivized Buddhism’, 
meaning that the rituals and practices of Śaivism were taken over into Buddhism with 
little change, yielding tantric Buddhism” (Davidson 2021, 5; see also Davidson 2017a, 
2017b; Slouber 2023). Davidson (2021, 5) argues for a more cautious approach here: 
“Without contesting that both tantric Śaivism and Brahmanical ritual were very im­
portant in the maturation of tantric Buddhism, it may be observed that the early ar­
chive has not been explored to date, so that it appears premature to posit such sweeping 
conclusions.”
We are left then with multiple and conflicting academic perspectives on the historical 
origins of tantra, the composition and circulation of texts, and the directions of influ­
ence.10 Stepping back, it is perhaps inevitable—​and a sign of growth—​that such dynamic 
debates have been happening in the field of tantric studies. It is possible that ongoing 
discoveries of early Buddhist tantric texts in Tibetan, Sanskrit, Chinese, or Japanese 
archives may challenge the supposed dominant influence of Śaiva Hindu tantra upon 
Buddhist tantra—​or perhaps not.11 The religious communities in the Gupta and post-​
Gupta periods were very dynamic, and along with the possible influence of diverse “pre-​
tantric” beliefs and practices, it is likely that various Hindu and Buddhist practitioners 
were in constant interaction, negotiating with each other and producing hybrid and syn­
cretic results. Much of this exciting research remains to be conducted, and it promises to 
expand the field of tantric studies going forward.

--- PAGE 30 ---
Tantric Studies      5
 
Matters of Category and Terminology
One of the major issues facing the field of tantric studies remains the very category of 
“tantra.” At the first conference of the Society for Tantric Studies in 1987 (see Appendix), 
the participants gathered for a “brainstorming” session, seeking to clarify the category; 
and a version of those results was eventually published in Douglas Renfrew Brooks’ 
study of Hindu Śākta tantrism.12 Following Jonathan Z. Smith’s discussion (1982, 4; em­
phasis in original text) of a “polythetic mode of classification,” Brooks argued that the 
term “tantra” may also be considered “polythetic” in that it has many different char­
acteristics, but specific manifestations of “tantra” may only have some (but not all) of 
the total number of characteristics. Among the ten characteristics identified by Brooks 
(narrowed down from perhaps twenty-​five or more at the conference) included an 
“extra-​Vedic” character; special esoteric forms of cosmophysiology and yoga, spanning 
both theism and philosophical nondualism; valorizing sound and mantras as soterio­
logical devices; and employing symbolic visual designs such as yantras and mandalas. 
Payne has argued, however, that not only is there no single defining characteristic of 
tantra but polythetic attempts to list characteristics often disagree, reflecting the idio­
syncratic orientations, interests, and judgments of the scholar compiling the list (2006; 
see also Hatley 2020, 2–​3).
When asked about these issues, our colleague Tony K. Stewart reflected on the episte­
mological aspects at some length. Because of the clarity and cogency of his response, we 
quote it in full here.
Rather than working from a fixed definition, which can have the unintended effect 
of essentializing tantra, one might be better served to examine what it is that tantra 
in any specific historical context attempts to accomplish. The a priori determinations 
of a formal definition impose constraints on the perception of the scholar attempting 
to interpret the phenomena of tantra as they appear on the ground or in texts, for it 
leads one to look for preconceived salient features that may well obscure what any 
particular historical form actually reveals. At times tantra can manifest independ­
ently, creating its own autotelic universe. It may also be present parasitically, de­
pendent on some preexisting tradition, but not recognized by it. In other instances 
it can function in symbiosis to a tradition, offering an embedded alternative path 
of religious experience within a mainstream doctrine and practice, or even repre­
sent the esoteric pinnacle of a tradition—​a realm of discipline reserved for the adept 
practitioner. Because few of these tantric turns will furnish a comprehensive state­
ment of intent, and because tantra often only sparingly reveals its ultimate trajectory, 
even to the point of adopting strategies of overt secrecy and disinformation, the her­
meneutics of this exercise depend on abductive reasoning (see Douven 2021). The 
scholar must draw out critical features of that particular religious expression from 
what can be known through text and ritual, and then attempt to fit those elements 
into a comprehensible image of practice and/​or doctrine that fills lacunae with 
reasonable prospects. All the while, the scholar knows that the interpretation can

--- PAGE 31 ---
6      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
never be absolute, but is instead a plausible understanding within a range of pos­
sible interpretations. The set of issues particular to any given form of tantra, in turn, 
dictates the pragmatic interpretive strategy, an approach which most of the essays in 
this volume have implicitly adopted. However tempting it may be to compare dif­
ferent strategies to develop a composite approach, the result of the comparison will 
not constitute a definition. On the contrary each example remains unique to its par­
ticular historical configuration.
(personal communication, April 22, 2023)
In addition to unique historical configurations being an obstacle to efforts at definition, 
the complexity of the historical origins of tantra makes the entire project of defining 
tantra problematic.
The historical origins of tantra are not only complex and obscure, but the plurality 
of contributing sources makes for additional problems. Instead of a single unitary or­
igin, the wide range of pre-​sectarian sources means that diversity of beliefs and practices 
is an inherent characteristic of the traditions retrospectively grouped together as “tan­
tric.” Historiographies that presume a diffusionist model in which a single original form 
diverges into different forms over time, or more narrowly unilinear and unidirectional 
development of influences and borrowings are inadequate to the study of the subject. 
Tantra is simply far too complex and diffuse to be treated as a unitary phenomenon. 
Our goal in this volume has instead been to allow an understanding to arise from 
the materials presented—​though such an approach will no doubt be dissatisfying to 
scholars accustomed to beginning from clear definitions.
A comprehensive review of recent scholarly definitions of tantra is beyond the scope 
of this volume. Many of them seek to be descriptive definitions, and, given the com­
plexity of tantra, such approaches are ultimately less than useful for our purposes 
here. However, in the foundational anthology Tantra in Practice (White, 2000), David 
Gordon White provides a representative “working” definition of tantra which identifies 
some important aspects:
Tantra is that Asian body of beliefs and practices which, working from the principle 
that the universe we experience is nothing other than the concrete manifestation of 
the divine energy of the godhead that creates and maintains that universe, seeks to 
ritually appropriate and channel that energy, within the human microcosm, in crea­
tive and emancipatory ways.
(p. 9)
White notes that this definition would need to be modified depending on the pre­
cise context of a tradition. And, indeed, it has been seen by some critics as a highly 
constricted “definition” that reflects only one strain (Shaman Hatley, personal commu­
nication, April 10, 2023). For just one example, “divine energy of the godhead” is prob­
lematic for Buddhist and Jain tantric schools. But White’s working definition can be 
seen as representing work within the parameters of the polythetic approach suggested

--- PAGE 32 ---
Tantric Studies      7
 
by Brooks. At the end of the day, however, there is frankly no single “definition” that can 
serve as a useful hermeneutic for our study of tantra. Approaches and strategies other 
than definitions may be more valuable for delineating the subject of study.13
Perhaps the one clearest marker is bibliographic, that is, the existence of texts called 
“tantras,” which constitute the textual corpus to which adherents of the traditions refer. 
Describing tantra by reference to a bibliographic category does not create a definition 
with sharp, absolute boundaries but rather itself points to the fuzziness of historical 
realities (see Burchett 2019, 30).14 For the historiography of tantra, however, it is im­
portant to emphasize that texts are not fixed, unitary, homogenous, or unchanging. 
Philological studies reveal that, despite our efforts as scholars—​such as the editing of 
critical editions—​texts are unstable, malleable, blended, and contingent. Employing 
bibliographic categories is more suggestive than definitional. For example, the term 
“tantra” was applied to texts outside the religious usage, and many clearly tantric 
traditions, such as the Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās of Bengal (see Hayes chapters, this volume), 
produced a large number of texts without specifically referring to them as “tantras.” 
Other bibliographic terms used for what are reasonably considered tantric texts include 
kalpa, āgama, and saṃhitā. In the Buddhist tradition, some texts are categorized both as 
sūtra and as tantra.
These considerations regarding texts, taken together with the controversies described 
above, indicate that the search for an adequate definition that would clearly delimit the 
complex histories and ranges of tantric traditions is itself problematic. Examining the 
category “religion,” Talal Asad has argued, “that there cannot be a universal definition of 
religion, not only because its constituent elements and relationships are historically spe­
cific, but because that definition is itself the historical product of discursive processes” 
(Asad 1993, 29). Even a cursory glance over the definitions of tantra proposed in the 
last century and a half by modern academic scholars demonstrates that they are them­
selves “the historical product of discursive processes” (Asad 1993, 29). The same applies 
equally to the much longer history of definitions offered by sectarian scholars. The dis­
tinction between academic and sectarian scholars is itself fuzzy, and is more appropriate 
to identifying different contexts and purposes of scholarship than individual scholars.
Since the earliest encounters between tantric traditions and Western scholars of reli­
gion, tantra has posed a challenge. As detailed by Hugh B. Urban (2003, 3) in his useful 
study of the “complex genealogy of the category of Tantra in the history of religions,” ini­
tial colonial Western encounters with tantra tended to regard it as obscene and depraved, 
an abhorrent distortion of the more philosophical interpretations of Hinduism and 
Buddhism just being discovered at the time. In 1817, for example, the Baptist missionary 
William Ward argued that tantric rituals involved the obscene worship of the naked fe­
male body, in which men “behave towards this female in a manner which decency forbids 
to be mentioned.”15 The representation of tantra, whether in Bengal, Tamilnadu, Tibet, or 
Japan, has tended to emphasize the antinomian, decadent, or demonic aspects, which, 
as attention-​grabbing as they were for audiences in the West, created a one-​dimensional 
understanding and hampered the academic study of the field for more than a century.16

--- PAGE 33 ---
8      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
Being the object of disdain also contributed to different traditions in different cul­
tural and linguistic regions being academically isolated from one another. Because of 
these academic divisions, someone working, for example, on Sanskrit literature may 
not readily encounter the work of a specialist in vernacular Assamese tantra, work that 
might shed light on otherwise obscure aspects of the literature they are studying. The 
detriments created by academic specialization are well known and not peculiar to the 
study of tantra but are no less detrimental for that reason. In many cases, the spread 
of tantra has been invisible because scholars have often understood tantra simply as 
a degenerate form of more positively valued traditions, and therefore something to 
be ignored—​or, lacking familiarity with the tradition, fail to recognize it when they 
see it. This relative valuation has been reinforced by Western scholars automatically 
privileging doctrinal studies (at times interpreted, for example, as philosophy or psy­
chology) and the study of doctrinal texts. Consequently, the study of practice and lived 
religion have frequently been marginalized. An example of the detrimental effects of 
this intellectual history, along with historical, political, and academic reasons, is that 
until only recently this preconception obscured the importance of tantric Buddhism 
and Hinduism in both Southeast and East Asia.
Being dominated by doctrinal studies, the Western study of religion has frequently 
simply replicated sectarian boundaries between different tantric traditions. Research 
tends to be sequestered according to different schools of South Asian, Central/​Inner 
Asian, and East Asian tantric traditions, as well as from across “Monsoon Asia” (Acri 
2023, 6). Thus, for example, specialists working in the Śaiva Siddhānta or Śākta or 
Vaiṣṇava form of tantra may not actively engage across those sectarian boundaries. 
Similarly, scholarship on the various Hindu forms tends to be separated from both 
Buddhist and Jain forms. More broadly, specialists in South Asian forms may have no 
venue in which to encounter the work of specialists in Central/​Inner or East Asian 
forms. Similarly, textual scholars may not be familiar enough with the methodologies 
of archeological, and art historical studies to include them in their work. In addition to 
these artificial academic boundaries, traditions that emphasize practice, such as ritual, 
meditation, breathing, visualization, and yoga, have tended to receive less attention than 
those which give doctrine primacy. Even within tantric traditions, study has often been 
focused on forms that have substantial doctrinal treatises.
Women, Gender, and Tantric Studies
Tantric studies is an important area of the modern academy not only because it explores 
the many traditions and themes found across tantra, but also because it is an important 
corrective to the hegemonic narratives of orthodoxy and orthopraxy which tend to be 
generated by and for male actors. Women and gender are central to many traditions of 
tantric praxis and ideology, not only as participants in ritual and social organization, 
but also as representing various forms of goddesses. In Tibet, women also established

--- PAGE 34 ---
Tantric Studies      9
 
tantric lineages of practice and founded tantric monastic institutions (Diemberger 
2007; Harding 2013).
It has long been recognized that goddess figures were important as symbolic 
embodiments of fertility and power in the civilizations of the Indus valley and elsewhere 
in Asia. However, with the rise of tantra in the early first millennium CE, goddesses 
gained new status. Scholarly attention to the development of tantric goddesses as cen­
tral figures in these Indic traditions has been late to develop. This belated recognition 
reflects that male academics have historically dominated the study of religion. This 
domination began to shift in the twentieth century, with increasing numbers of female 
scholars addressing the topics of women and gender within religious practices. The late 
twentieth century brought with it numerous studies of the importance of women in reli­
gious traditions across Asia, and of the roles that goddesses play in Indic and some other 
traditions beyond the subcontinent.17
Being an important subset of Asian religions as a whole, comparatively less study 
has been given to women and ideas of gender within tantric traditions. Earlier studies 
include Judith Simmer-​Brown (2002; see this volume) on the ḍākinī figure; Serinity 
Young’s 2004 study of sexuality and gender in Buddhism; Miranda Shaw’s (1995) pro­
vocative, if controversial, work on women in Buddhism; Loriliai Biernacki (2007) on 
conceptions of women and speech in Hindu tantra; Judit Torzsok (2014) on female 
spirits, women, and goddesses; Shaman Hatley (2016b) on yoginīs in tantric texts; and 
David Gordon White (2006) on the yoginī rituals and traditions. Gudrun Bühnemann 
has explored the iconography of Hindu and Buddhist tantric deities, many of whom 
are female (1999, 2000, 2000–​2001, 2016), and of ritual diagrams (mandala, yantra) in 
her edited volume Maṇḍalas and Yantras in the Hindu Traditions ([2003] 2007). Madhu 
Khanna wrote her doctoral thesis on the Śrīcakra Śākta diagram and the tradition of 
its worship (1986) and, more recently, a study of ritual manuals from the Mahāvidyā 
goddess traditions (2013). Tantric themes in Buddhist embryology have been explored 
in Central/​Inner and East Asian Buddhist traditions (e.g., Sanford 1997; Andreeva and 
Steavu 2015; Garret 2008). Indic tantric goddesses also were deployed for imperial 
purposes in medieval China (Rothschild 2021). The last several decades have also given 
us explorations of twentieth-​century tantric praxis in works by Neela Bhattacharya 
Saxena (2004) and June McDaniel (2002), in Holly Gayley’s 2016 study of a twentieth-​
century female Tibetan teacher, and in Corinne Dempsey’s 2005 work on a tantric Śrī 
Vidyā temple located in New York State.
These studies of the feminine in tantric traditions have gradually led us to where 
we are now in tantric studies: with an increasing number of both female and male 
scholars exploring myriad issues that reveal the dynamics and importance of women 
and goddesses in the history of tantra. This new research promises much insight as 
scholarship on these topics moves forward. This volume aims to augment this research 
with several chapters included here which consider the complexity of gender dy­
namics in domestic, social, political, and religious contexts. (See especially the chapters 
by Golovkova, Simmer-​Brown, Slouber, and Borkataky-​Varma.) As the chapter on 
eunuchs (hijṛās) by Borkataky-​Varma in this volume suggests, the full range of gender

--- PAGE 35 ---
10      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
fluidity that has always been part of our collective human history is now being acknowl­
edged and addressed by contemporary scholarship.
Ethnography, Lived Tantra, and 
Tantric Studies
Most of the research in tantric studies over the past decades has generally focused on 
the study of texts and textual traditions. Such an emphasis on historical texts and their 
ongoing interpretive schools and lineages is understandable, given the centrality that 
Western religious studies scholarship has historically given to sacred texts. The im­
portance of the Vedic texts and traditions, which is contested and even rejected not 
only by the Jain and Buddhist traditions generally but also by much of subsequent 
Hindu tantra, must be understood as a major context for the development of tantric 
ritual, cosmology, sociology, and soteriology. Within Buddhist tantric traditions, the 
legitimizing role of canonical texts was supplemented by new genres of Mahāyāna 
texts, beginning with dhāraṇī and other ritual texts, then the early tantras, and later 
compilations of extended Vajrayāna texts (Dalton 2016; Gray 2023). In Jainism, many 
key tantric beliefs and practices are expressed in major Jain texts, and they continue to 
hold authority in both tantric and non-​tantric Jain lineages. But such a valorization of 
textuality across Asia has also been reinterpreted through a Western lens, privileging 
it over questions regarding what tantrikas actually do. As suggested by Schopen 
(1991), this tendency of Western scholarship to seek an authoritative “sacred text” may 
be traced, in large part, to the influence on religious studies of a Protestant worldview. 
The primacy of orthodox belief for Protestant soteriology was reconstituted as the 
central concern for religious studies when the field was formulated in the nineteenth 
century. A focus on doctrine led to a focus on doctrinal texts, on those portions of 
texts that could be interpreted as doctrinal, and on doctrinal interpretations of ritual 
and devotional practices.
The problem with this privileging of textuality is that it has limited the study of 
tantra in significant ways. This is especially the case with contemporary communities 
within which a vibrant “lived tantra” is practiced without reference to doctrinal texts. 
And it is also true historically for communities that depended on oral and non-​literary 
traditions and for those outside the Vedic and mainstream institutions of legitimation. 
While recent decades have seen expansions into a variety of methodologies that com­
plement textual studies, we focus here on the much welcome growth in ethnographic 
studies of tantra. This growing trend has culminated in works such as The Ethnography 
of Tantra: Textures and Contexts of Living Tantric Traditions (2023), edited by Carola 
Lorea and Rohit Singh. Growing out of cultural anthropology, folklore, and other 
forms of fieldwork, these diverse ethnographic studies of tantra complement, ex­
tend, and in some cases can correct the insights of the dominant textual approaches

--- PAGE 36 ---
Tantric Studies      11
 
and methodologies. Some notable uses of ethnography and fieldwork-​based anthro­
pology of religion include Stan Mumford’s study of lamas and shamans in Nepal 
(1989), Jeanne Openshaw’s study of the Bāuls of greater Bengal (2004), Patricia Q. 
Campbell’s study of the ritual practices of two tantric centers in Toronto (2011), June 
McDaniels’ studies of Bengali popular religious traditions (1989, 2004), Cody Bahir’s 
several publications on modern Taiwanese tantric groups (2013, 2018, 2020, and 
others), and Jeffrey Lidke’s study of goddess traditions and mandala in Nepal (2017). 
Sthaneshwar Timalsina (2011) explores cross-​cultural aspects of tantric studies, while 
Sukanya Sarbadhikary (2015) combines fieldwork with textual studies in her exam­
ination of Vaiṣṇava traditions in Bengal, including groundbreaking interviews of 
members of contemporary tantric communities. Lorea (2017, 2018) uses fieldwork to 
raise issues regarding secrecy and textuality. The late Jarrod Hyam (2019) conducted 
fieldwork among indigenous healers in India, Sikkim, and Nepal for his doctoral dis­
sertation, while further fieldwork in Himalayan communities has been carried out 
by E. Halperin (2019) and Arik Moran (2018, 2021). Moran also helped to produce 
documentaries on Himalayan rituals and communities in the films Chidra (Moran 
and Harel 2018) and Avatara (Moran and Harel 2020). Anway Mukhopadhyay (2018) 
used fieldwork to examine the role of the goddess as a corpse in tantric traditions. 
Sravana Borkataky-​Varma (see ­chapter 39, this volume) has conducted extensive 
fieldwork among tantric communities in Assam, as has Hugh Urban (2018, 2019, 
forthcoming). These are indeed exciting times for such rich academic encounters with 
lived tantra as such studies promise to complement the many textual and historio­
graphic studies that have come before them.
Cognitive Approaches: Conceptual 
Metaphors, Neuroscience, and  
Other Recent Trends
Since the 1980s, very interesting methods for studying language, metaphor, and concep­
tualization have been developed within the field of cognitive linguistics, most notably 
the conceptual metaphor theory first proposed by George Lakoff and Mark Johnson 
(1980).18 Johnson (1987, xiv–​xv) argues that conceptual metaphor may be
conceived as a pervasive mode of understanding by which we project patterns from 
one domain of experience in order to structure another domain of a different kind. 
So conceived, metaphor is not merely a linguistic mode of expression; rather, it is 
one of the chief cognitive structures by which we are able to have coherent, ordered 
experiences that we can reason about and make sense of. Through metaphor, we 
make use of patterns that obtain in our physical experience to organize our more ab­
stract understanding.

--- PAGE 37 ---
12      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
Metaphor theory helps us consider the nuances and deeper meanings of tantric lan­
guage, as well as the embodied experiences of ritual practices expressed in such lan­
guage. In a number of works over the past several decades Glen Hayes (2003, 2005, 
2006, 2014; chapter 30 in this volume) has used conceptual metaphor theory to ex­
plore subtle-​body systems and cosmologies in Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā ritual manuals. 
Conceptual metaphor theory was further developed into conceptual blending 
theory by Gilles Fauconnier and Mark Turner (2002), and Hayes has explored the 
application of this methodology to the study of tantric texts (2012b; chapter 30, this 
volume).19 Sthaneshwar Timalsina has used methods and concepts from a range of 
cognitive studies in his several recent works (2005, 2007, 2012a, 2012b, 2015a, 2015b, 
2016, 2020). Timalsina has also made innovative use of recent “attention theory” in 
the study of tantric visualization and meditative practices (this volume, ­chapter 29). 
Cognitive linguistics grew partly out of the “cognitive revolution” of the later twen­
tieth century (countering B. F. Skinner’s strict behaviorism) and the larger interdis­
ciplinary fields of cognitive science.20 Collaborations with anthropology, religious 
studies, and other disciplines led to the modern cognitive science of religion;21 and 
it is likely that we will see more cognitive studies being used by scholars in tantric 
studies in the future.
Neurobiology and neuroscience contribute another critical dimension to the 
recent cognitive science of religion.22 Many of these works come from the arena 
of the laboratory and “hard science.” Bringing these discoveries over into the 
humanities and social sciences is still in its early stages.23 Geoffrey Samuel and 
Maria Kozhevnikov (­chapter 7, this volume) exemplify how tantric studies is leading 
the way in bridging the natural sciences and the humanities. Patrick McNamara’s 
work in neuroscience (2001, 2009) partly inspired an essay by Hayes (2014) using 
neuroscientific concepts in the study of Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā texts. McNamara’s work 
was also the focus of an excellent symposium featuring Ann Taves, Jared Lindahl, 
Travis Chilcott, and Kelly Bulkeley (Taves et al. 2011). This dialogue, featuring 
four scholars who are doing groundbreaking work in the cognitive science of reli­
gion, illustrates some of the dynamics emerging as scholars of religious studies en­
gage with neuroscientists such as McNamara. Taves (2009) has also suggested new 
methods and perspectives for studying religious experience.24 Travis Chilcott (2015, 
2016) has used cognitive approaches to understand the dynamics of perception and 
self-​identity in Hindu devotionalism. Kelly Bulkeley (1994, 2004, 2005, 2017) has 
made extensive studies of dreams and the dream process, which can be applied to 
cognitive studies of religion. Loriliai Biernacki (2023) explores issues of conscious­
ness and panentheism in the work of Abhinavagupta, including tantric perspectives 
on information systems.
As with any dynamic growth of scholarship, there are many new publications and 
collaborations in the field of the cognitive science of religion, which we do not have time 
to fully survey here. At noted learned societies there are now established program units, 
such as the Cognitive Science of Religion Group at the American Academy of Religion

--- PAGE 38 ---
Tantric Studies      13
 
and smaller societies, such as the Society for Tantric Studies, have included panels on 
the cognitive science of religion in recent conferences. Readers could certainly add their 
own examples to this list.
There are a number of excellent academic journals dedicated to the cognitive science 
of religion, such as the Journal of the Cognitive Science of Religion, Journal of Cognitive 
Historiography, Journal of Consciousness Studies, Journal of Cognition and Culture, 
Religion, Brain, & Behavior, and the International Journal for the Psychology of Religion. 
Of special note is a recent issue of the Journal of Cognitive Historiography (Vol. 7, No. 1–​2, 
2022). This included an essay by Jed Forman (2022) on examining yogic perception and 
extramission using cognitive science; a study by Roman Palitsky, Isaac F. Young, and 
Ben Williams (2022) on applying cognitive insights from the renowned Śaiva polymath 
Abhinavagupta (ca. 950–​1016 ce) to an understanding of dramaturgy; and a study by 
Jared Lindahl, Willoughby Britton, and David Cooper (2022) on developing a cogni­
tive model of meditation and its associated emotions. These are just some of the many 
intriguing results of the collaboration between cognitive science, religious studies, and 
tantric studies.
Although intended for a general audience Niki Clements’ Religion: Mental Religion 
(2016) brings together many scholars of cognitive science and religious studies. 
This collection provides us with a good “snapshot” of the state of the field as of 2016, 
with chapters devoted to evolutionary psychology, cognitive linguistics, conceptual 
blending (Hayes 2016), neuroscience, entheogens, theory of mind, and dream states. In 
2018, an important volume on the study of religious language using a range of cogni­
tive approaches, Religion, Language, and the Human Mind, Paul Chilton and Monika 
Kopytowska, eds., was published, including an updated version of Hayes 2006 as well as 
chapters on metaphors in a range of world religions.
These developments and collaborations, including the chapters in this volume, dem­
onstrate that the broad range of cognitive studies of religion is indeed a promising 
avenue for emerging scholarly inquiry in the field of tantric studies. Incorporating cog­
nitive studies into tantric studies is based on this simple premise: some of the most in­
teresting domains of human experience can be investigated and analyzed using insights 
and methods from cognitive linguistics and cognitive science.
The tantric traditions are daunting in their complexity, posing a challenge to re­
search. Interdisciplinary methods and multidisciplinary projects are, therefore, not 
simply a nicety but instead a necessity. The cognitive study of religion exemplifies the 
benefits that an interdisciplinary approach to the study of tantra can yield. Even more 
broadly, philological studies—​long dominant in the study of Asian religions—​can no 
longer be relied upon as the sole method for the study of tantra. The complexity of 
the object of inquiry requires an equally complex approach, including ethnographic, 
ritual, art historical, architectural, genre, gender, sociological, medical history, psy­
chological, and economic methods. Such wide-​ranging inquiries will enable the field 
of tantric studies to continue to grow and develop with the vitality that the subject 
matter deserves.

Appendix
 Institutions and Collaborations for  
the Study of Tantra
Much of the inspiration for this volume can be traced back through the decades to 
fruitful interactions and collaborations with colleagues at numerous conferences and 
on publication projects. Following the growth of tantric studies in the latter half of the 
twentieth century, the Society for Tantric Studies (STS) was formed in the 1980s by 
James Sanford, Charles Orzech, and Glen Hayes (see Hayes 2011, 2012a; Payne 2004) in 
order to provide a collaborative venue for scholars of different tantric traditions (e.g., 
Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain), geographical regions (South, Inner/​Central, East, and 
Southeast Asia), and disciplines (e.g., history of religions, philology, anthropology, and 
sociology). As noted in an early draft of the bylaws from 1985 (Hayes 2011, 224),
The goal of the Society for Tantric Studies is to deepen the understanding of the his­
tory, nature, and dynamics of the tantric traditions, and to share this knowledge 
with academic colleagues. To accomplish these aims, the society shall: disseminate 
information and stimulate discussion by sponsoring or participating in appropriate 
panels and conferences; distribute to members such materials as membership lists, 
panel and/​or conference papers, and a bulletin; and in general further the interests of 
this field of study.
Beginning with the first conference in 1987 and continuing every few years down to the 
present time (2019 being the most recent as of this publication), the STS has allowed 
scholars from around the world to gather in order to share their individual research, 
debate matters of category, explore major issues in the field, and consider emerging 
methodologies and topics.25 These academic trends also led to the creation of tantric 
studies program units within the American Academy of Religion (AAR), beginning first 
with separate panels in the late 1980s and 1990s, leading to a seminar in tantric studies 
from 1995 to 2000, and eventually to an ongoing tantric studies program unit (recently 
renewed until 2027).26
For more than seven decades, the Institut Français de Pondichéry27 and École 
française d’Extrême-​Orient in Pondicherry,28 spearheaded by Jean Filliozat and now 
directed by Dominic Goodall, have made important contributions to tantric studies. 
These include enormous contributions by Pandit N. R. Bhatt and Hélène Brunner in the 
earlier decades of the institute’s history. The Collection Indologie book series29 is one of 
the most important resources in Hindu tantric studies.
Colleagues in Europe and elsewhere have also created invaluable venues and 
associations for collaborating on tantric studies. Beginning in 1995, the Asiatica 
Association in Italy published the International Journal of Tantric Studies, with Enrica 
Garzilli as the editor in chief. This journal ran to ten volumes, the last volume being 
2014.30 Also in 2014, the first issue of the journal was made available in both print and

--- PAGE 40 ---
Tantric Studies      15
 
Kindle formats on Amazon.31 The journal’s statement of its “aims and mission” specifies 
that “[p]‌articular attention is paid to the Trika schools of Kashmir.”
The University of Hamburg has established the Centre for Tantric Studies, under the 
leadership of Harunaga Isaacson.32 The teaching program of the Department of Indian 
and Tibetan Studies began offering courses of instruction on topics related to tantric 
studies in 2007; its doctoral program has resulted in many high-​quality theses in tantric 
studies. The center also makes e-​texts available online, which includes both Śaiva and 
Buddhist materials in the collection.33 Several conferences, as well as workshops have 
been organized by the center, and it actively maintains a number of research projects on 
topics such as the early history of tantra and specific texts.
The Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna has been a hub for research on 
Vaiṣṇavism, led by the late Gerhard Oberhammer and his former doctoral students. 
The academy publishes the ongoing project Tāntrikābhidhānakośa (“A Dictionary of 
Technical Terms from Hindu Tantric Literature”), co-​edited by Marion Rastelli and 
Dominic Goodall, which includes entries on key terms, written in English, French, and 
German, from a range of Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva tantric literature.34
Also in Vienna, there is the Arbeitskreis für Tibetische und Buddhistische Studien 
(Association for Tibetan and Buddhist Studies), which is located in the Institute for 
South Asian, Tibetan and Buddhist Studies at the University of Vienna.35 Although 
tantra is not the central focus of the center, in its publication series—​Wiener Studien zur 
Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde (Vienna Series for Tibetan and Buddhist Studies)—​
it has published several volumes on topics related to tantric studies.36
In London, the School of Oriental and African Studies has the Centre for Yoga 
Studies,37 which has supported tantric studies through efforts such as the Hatha Yoga 
Project,38 organized by James Mallinson, Jason Birch, and Mark Singleton. The Oxford 
Centre for Hindu Studies,39 led by Gavin Flood, offers a variety of programs, confer­
ences, and projects dealing with tantric studies, among other subjects. Alexis Sanderson, 
now emeritus from All Souls College at Oxford, has for several decades produced foun­
dational works in the field, especially on Śaiva tantric texts; and his doctoral students 
have become leading scholars in the field. His successor, Diwakar Acharya, continues 
with important research and publications in tantric studies. In Paris, the École française 
d’Extrême-​Orient has supported major research in the field, especially that of Dominic 
Goodall, who contributed a chapter to this volume.40 These superb programs have de­
veloped many fine scholars of tantric studies who continue to support the growth of 
the field.
Another important area of development which supports tantric studies involves 
the preservation of manuscripts and making them, as well as translations, avail­
able on online databases. The Nepal German Manuscript Preservation Project has for 
decades microfilmed and later digitized many tantric texts found in Nepal.41 Other no­
table efforts include the Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages, 
which has many texts in Sanskrit and other languages, including many tantric texts;42 
the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, which has been instrumental in 
making available editions of Śaiva tantras and transcriptions of unpublished tantric

--- PAGE 41 ---
16      Richard K. Payne and Glen A. Hayes
 
manuscripts;43 the Buddhist Canons Research Database, which offers complete bib­
liographic information for the roughly five thousand texts contained in the Tibetan 
Buddhist canon;44 the 84,000 Project, which is undertaking translation of the Tibetan 
Buddhist collections known as the Kangyur and Tengyur;45 and the BDK International 
Tripitaka project, which is making available translations of this core collection of 
Buddhist texts.46 The latter two efforts are perhaps the greatest translation efforts in the 
modern period—​analogous to the Buddhist translation efforts from the fourth to the 
twelfth centuries but in a much narrower time frame.
Scholarship in tantric studies has also been nourished in a variety of other academic 
settings around the world, including, but not limited to, the following institutions: 
the University of California in Berkeley and Santa Barbara; the University of Virginia; 
Harvard University; the University of Chicago; the University of Pennsylvania; 
Columbia University; the University of Washington; the University of Colorado, 
Boulder; the Naropa Institute; Oxford University; the University of Hamburg; the 
University of Vienna; the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, Paris; and the 
École Pratique des Hautes Études, Paris. There are likely others (and apologies for any 
which we have missed), which we hope to learn more about. These institutions have 
offered courses, and in some cases specific programs in tantric studies; have faculty who 
are specialists in tantric studies; and have graduated students who have subsequently 
contributed to the field. All of the above scholarly efforts demonstrate that the field of 
tantric studies has found an enduring and important place in the modern academy and 
suggest that the future is most promising. We hope that this volume also contributes to 
the growth of the field and that it resonates with many of the exploratory efforts begun 
among an informal group of friends and colleagues back in the 1980s.

	1.	 We are using the lowercase form “tantra,” as opposed to the uppercase “Tantra,” as the latter 
suggests some underlying unity and essence. We prefer the former as there are so many var­
iations of the category that any monolithic or essentialist view tends to obscure more than it 
reveals. This volume itself illustrates some of the many manifestations of tantra throughout 
South, Central/​Inner, Southeast, and East Asia—​as well as in a global setting since the nine­
teenth century. In explaining the traditional etymology of “tantra,” André Padoux (2017, 7) 
notes that from “the verbal root TAN, which means ‘to extend,’ ‘to spread,’ hence ‘to spin 
out,’ ‘weave,’ ‘display,’ ‘put forth,’ and ‘compose’ [the term comes by extension to mean] 
‘system,’ ‘doctrine,’ or ‘work.’ A Tantra is thus a work, a text—​any text.” Hence we find the 
subsequent meanings of a discourse “woven” with the “threads” of words and thought.
