Chapter 2
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in 
Indian Buddhism
Ronald M. Davidson
Abhiṣeka is a technical noun derived from the verbal root √sic-​ “to pour out” with the 
prefix abhi-​, which marks direction, “to or toward,” usually taken in the sense of pouring 
some liquid onto a person or image. In its pragmatic employment, abhiṣeka covers a va­
riety of meanings, uses, and ritual events, both before the advent of systems eventually 
identified as specifically tantric and later within self-​consciously tantric traditions, al­
though there are certainly functions common to both. In its most basic sense, abhiṣeka 
denotes the sprinkling of an item or person with water or some other viscous liquid, 
sometimes mixed with other materials employing the liquid as a solvent, whether this 
is performed in fact, in visualization, or in metaphor. In the Indian context, abhiṣeka 
brings to bear powerful symbols and systems of meaning that convey to the person and 
the surrounding community a sense of purification, transformation, or vivification of 
the entity/​person involved. However, neither the agent nor the object of the rite is im­
plied by the term, so it may designate self-​consecration, aspersion by another person, 
a divinity, or some other theological agent. This indeterminacy of agency and signifi­
cation allows the terminology and accompanying ritual to be employed by a variety of 
schools, traditions, and lineages for a range of purposes. As exercised especially by not 
only Buddhists, but also Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others, abhiṣeka was ritually invoked 
to proclaim the empowering of a person into a position of authority and authenticity 
within the specific sectarian system involved. This chapter examines the ritual from the 
perspective of Indian Buddhist texts, including factors that contributed to their forma­
tion in tantric Buddhism. The distinctive use of abhiṣeka in Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and other 
tantric traditions is outside of the purview of this investigation, as is the development 
of abhiṣeka in Tibet, China, and Japan, all of which are complex and in need of sep­
arate treatment.1 Instead, this essay outlines the precedents to abhiṣeka in India and 
Indian Buddhism in a manner not entirely explored before and outlines the two primary 
metaphors employed in abhiṣeka, which have not been well expressed previously. It 
also organizes and presents material found in disparate sources with the goal of having

--- PAGE 55 ---
30      Ronald M. Davidson
 
an overarching presentation of the basic systems and problems associated with Indian 
abhiṣeka rituals.
Primary Metaphors of Aspersion
Given the rich associations of liquids in Indian religious and intellectual history, we 
should not be surprised that the process of sprinkling has both literal and metaphor­
ical significance. The semantic associations of the verb employed—​√abhisiñc—​or its 
semantically related roots and their consequent nominal forms may be understood to 
denote primary varieties of meaning and central metaphors: purification and invigora­
tion. These metaphors change over time.
a.	 Purification or cleansing metaphors, generally associating abhiṣeka with the terms 
√(vi)śudh-​ or √avadā-​, are particularly important to those in South Asia, who have 
made personal hygene a cultural function without parallel in human history. The 
act may also be signified with the verbs √prokṣ-​ or √snā-​, whether this indicates the 
sprinkling of oneself or some other person or object in an act of sanctification. The 
astonishing varieties of cleansing in Indian religion confirms that no other great tra­
dition has accorded such ritual importance to the process of personal cleanliness. 
Cleanliness here is not exclusively physical, although we cannot discount the phys­
icality of Indian religion. Rather, cleanliness is also both spiritual and metaphysical, 
so that the person may be cleansed of transgressions or cleansed of pollution from 
death or disease or other problem conditions by means of bathing, snāna, usually 
at some specific holy bathing site (tīrtha). In some contexts, such as the bathing of 
an image in Matsyapurāṇa 267, the terms snapana and abhiṣeka have both been em­
ployed, so that there is decidedly a semantic intersection between them. So powerful 
is bathing in the Brahmanical system that the five greatest sins, the mahāpātakas, 
may be purified in the case of one undergoing a period of penance followed by a ritual 
bath, especially at sacred places like Vārāṇasī or Rāmeśvaram. Cleansing by water 
or bathing also marks ritual or existential transitions, notable in the rites of passage, 
as when a boy completes his study of the scriptures or his time of internship for a 
trade by taking a ritual bath. Gobhilagṛhyasūtra 3.4.10 requires the teacher to sprinkle 
the graduating student (samāvartana) with warm waters decocted with herbs and 
fragrances (sarvauṣadhiviphāṇṭābhir adbhir gandhavatībhiḥ śītoṣṇābhir ācāryo 
‘bhiṣiñcati), an early invocation of abhiṣeka as a rite of passage. In the Buddhist in­
stance, most hagiographies of the Buddha mark the birth of the bodhisattva by his 
being ritually bathed by the gods Indra and Brahmā.
b.	 Invigoration by water is sometimes overlooked, but the explicit similes of infusion 
and growth employing liquids are not lost on anyone spending time in the subtrop­
ical environment of the Indian plains. Particularly during the monsoon season, 
which follows the hot, dry period, the sudden appearance of water infuses the land­
scape with life and vitality, evident for both plants and animals. In Vedic texts, the

--- PAGE 56 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      31
 
verb most closely associating abhiṣiñc-​ with these meanings is √sū-​, indicating the 
vivification, quickening, or invigoration (Gonda 1965, 12), and some have noted the 
emphasis on varcas, power or splendor associated with Indra (Tsuchiyama 2005; 
Geslani 2018). In the Rājasūya rite in the Taittirīyasamḥita (1.8.14.f-​g), the abhiṣeka of 
the king invokes the gods, particularly Varuṇa, lord of the waters:
varuṇo devā dharmasuvaś ca ye | te te vācaṃ suvantāṃ te te prāṇaṃ suvantāṃ te te 
cakṣus suvantām te te śrotraṃ suvantāṃ somasya tvā dyumnenābhiṣiñcāmy agneḥ || 
tejasā sūryaṃsya varcasendrasyendreṇa mitravāruṇayor vīryeṇa marutām ojasā
Keith (1914, I.125-​26) translated this:
f.	 Soma, king Varuna, and the gods which instigate righteousness, may they insti­
gate thy speech, may they instigate thy breath, may they instigate thy sight, may 
they instigate thine ear.
g.	With the glory of Soma I besprinkle thee, with the brilliance of Agni, with the ra­
diance of the sun, with the power of Indra, with the strength of Mitra and Varuna, 
with the force of the Maruts.2
Earlier Buddhists had discussed the infusion of vitality from master to disciple, with the 
metaphor of water from one vessel into another, or the transfer of vitality in the teaching 
of Mahāyāna texts like the Suvarṇabhāsottama (pp. 70, 75 dharmaśravaṇasalilodaka-​
dharmāmṛtarasena . . . divyātmabhāvān mahātaujasā vivardhayet). In this regard, the 
invigoration of vitality via abhiṣeka probably informs the translation of the term into the 
Tibetan dbang-​bskur, often translated “empowerment,” rather than the sprinkling on the 
top of the head, as in the Chinese translation term guàn-​dǐng (灌頂).
Employment of Abhiṣeka in 
Pretantric Texts
a. The most important aspect of abhiṣeka was in the unction rites of kingship, where 
a king is first coronated (mahābhiṣeka) through being sprinkled by water and other 
substances—​especially ghee, curds, honey, liquor, barley, grasses, and later mud, 
milk, and others—​with priests invoking the gods in imitation of Indra’s coronation as 
the divine king, ladling the liquids from a camasa square wooden cup filtered through 
udumbara branch (Aitareyabrāhmaṇa viii.17-​18: Tsuchiyama 2005). The king is re­
peatedly likened to a tiger and sits on a tiger’s skin on a throne of udumbara wood, 
receiving by abhiṣeka the infusion of dominion and authority. The ritual is attested as 
a stand-​alone rite, but later folded into a soma ritual in the śrautasūtras as the “Royal 
Creation” or “Royal Birth” (rājasūya) rite. In this manner, the rite is interpreted as 
involving the birth of the king as either the son of the priests or the incarnation of 
Indra (Law 1919; Heesterman 1957, 117–​119; Gonda 1969, 18, 87–​96). Abhiṣeka is also

--- PAGE 57 ---
32      Ronald M. Davidson
 
conceived as a continuing event (punarabhiṣeka) in the life of the king, whether annu­
ally or even daily in some texts, although most, like the Nilamatapurāṇa or the Viṣṇu­
dharmottarapurāṇa, afford a specific ideology of the annual renewal (Inden 1981). 
Perhaps most interesting, the Aitareyabrāhmaṇa depicts the king first coronating 
himself in this annual rite before receiving it from the Brahmans (Aitareyabrāhmaṇa 
viii.5: sūyate ha vā asya kṣatraṃ yo dīkṣate kṣatriyaḥ san sa). This practice of repeated 
abhiṣeka, along with self-​consecration, is carried over in some Buddhist traditions, 
where abhiṣeka may be enjoined as a daily event or in the case of the violation of 
vows. Over time, the three-​fire soma or śrauta rite gave way in some traditions to a 
domestic-​type ritual (gṛhya-​vidhāna) that required only one fire and was much more 
modest in its implications (e.g., Ṛgvidhāna 4.106-​110; Baudhāyanapariśiṣṭa 1.23). 
Most tantric rituals that employ homa fire rituals are patterned on single-​fire rites, 
and this is no exception.
b. In both their cleansing and invigorating functions, abhiṣeka or other unction rites 
were extended throughout the domestic ritual syllabus, particularly noticeable in the 
later gṛhyasūtra, vidhāna, or pariśiṣṭa literature. So, the Ṛgvidhāna 1.89 declared that 
the verses ambayo yanti from Ṛgveda 1.23-​16-​2 also may be applied to the purposes 
of extending life, cure from disease, and the release from sin (āyuṣyās tāḥ pariproktā 
bhaiṣajyāḥ pāpamocanīḥ). This extension explains the application of abhiṣeka to 
the purification or invigoration of everything from ritual implements to medical 
procedures to domestic animals (Kauśikasūtra 64.27, 66.11-​20; Gonda 1965, 91, 96–​101; 
Mānavagṛhyasūtra 2.6; Baudhāyanapariśiṣṭa 1.14.1).
c. As a consequence of this general use of aspersion, abhiṣeka also becomes employed 
as a term denoting a variety of meanings: infusion of vitality from gods of the directions, 
the apotheosis of anyone receiving unction, acknowledgment of authority, honoring of 
the person/​divinity/​implement, and others (Davidson 2010; Tsuchiyama 2005). Because 
of these manifold uses, and in association with the increasing emphasis on personal 
gods in the post-​Vedic period, the kalaśa pot from which aspersion is done becomes it­
self a representation of divinity. It largely displaced other aspersion implements like the 
camasa, praṇītā, ghaṭaka, or prokṣaṇī, although its eminent position would be shared 
with the kumbha, with which it is sometimes equated.
Pretantric Buddhist Abhiṣeka Ideology
Central to the early Buddhist cultus practiced by both laity and clergy was the sprin­
kling of the bodhi tree, especially in festivals of the bodhi tree (bodhimaha). Legends of 
Aśoka include him vowing to anoint the tree, in part to revive it from the curse brought 
on by Tiṣyarakṣitā, his jealous queen (Aśokāvadāna, 93–​94), and the reputation of his 
behavior doubtless assisted the popularity of the practice among Buddhists. Anointing 
the bodhi tree extended to festivals associated with the Buddhas of the past as well, 
and there is mention of fragrant water offerings (gandhodaka) made to shrines of the

--- PAGE 58 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      33
 
previous Buddhas once these figures became popular in the Buddhist landscape. In this 
vein, offerings of water were sprinkled at the bodhi tree festival of Padmuttara by the 
Thera Gandhodaka and at the bodhi tree festival of Vipaśin by Thera Bodhisaññaka and 
others in the Apadāna (I.105-​6, 131, 249, II.391).
In their articulation of the bodhisattva path, Buddhists included the royal con­
secration as both an acknowledgment of the authority of the bodhisattva who had 
advanced along the path and an appropriation of the royal rite as a mythic event to 
be performed by Buddhas of the ten directions. In the first instance, the Mahāvastu 
includes the idea that, in a previous existence, Śākyamuni had received the prophecy 
for his eventual Buddhahood and at that time became recognized as a “crown prince” 
(yuvarājye cābhiṣikto; Mahāvastu I.2; Davidson 2010). The Mahāvastu also articulates 
an abhiṣekabhūmi, a level at which the bodhisattva can be assured his awakening, but 
in that case it is the entrance into the activity of his final birth (Mahāvastu I.142-​193). 
This is distinct from the usage of the Daśabhūmikasūtra, which articulates an elab­
orate scenario in which the bodhisattva becomes affirmed in the tenth level of the 
bodhisattva by all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, who confer on 
him the Coronation of Great Gnosis (mahājñānābhiṣeka) by rays of light that enter 
the crown of his head (Daśabhūmika 181–​187). The Daśabhūmika is explicit that this 
is a Buddhist version of the coronation of a king, who will then go on to become a 
Universal Ruler (cakravartin) once he has performed all his acts; similarly, the tenth-​
level bodhisattva will go on to become Saṃyaksaṃbuddha once he performs the acts 
of the Buddha.
Documents in Sanskrit and Chinese from Central Asia and North China reveal yogic 
practices associated with meditative anointing by a range of figures, including by one­
self, by divine women, by the Hindu gods Brahmā, and others.3 In many instances, the 
anointing is by milk and suffuses the body with well-​being while dispelling diseases, 
afflictions, and defilements:
Tato ‘sya karunārtasya bhruvor madhye kṛṣṇataptaṃ piṭaka(m utpadyate) . . . 
mūrdhano niḥsṛtā strī kṣīradhārābhiḥ śarīram a(vasiṃcati) [y]‌āvad vedanopaśāmyati | 
tasmāc char(i)[rā]t kṣīradhārābhiḥ sarvasatvāsamudraḥ plāvyate |. . . . (tato 
naśyamānāṃ sarvasat)[v](ā)[n](āṃ) [ś](ā)r[ī]ramānasaduḥkhāṃ paśyati |
(Yogalehrbuch §148V1-​2)
Then [the yogin] oppressed by compassion [feels] a hot, black boil arise in the middle 
of his brow. . . . And from his head emerges a [mystical] woman who anoints his body 
with streams of milk until the feeling is pacified. Then from his body, the streams of 
milk emerge and inundate the ocean of all beings . . . so that the yogin see the physical 
and mental anguish of beings being thus destroyed.
The diverse nature of these meditations, as well as their richness and the explicit process 
of streaming into the fontanelle down to the base of his body, indicates a highly creative 
meditative tradition. The meditations doubtless stem from the subculture of the yogācāras, 
monks who were specialists in these practices in Gandhāra and Kaśmir, for they are

--- PAGE 59 ---
34      Ronald M. Davidson
 
mentioned in the surviving Sanskrit text, and the practices build on the analogous practices 
seen in the earliest Yogācārabhūmi, attributed to Saṃgharakṣa (Demiéville 1951). The visu­
alization of streaming of milky fluid through the body became a hallmark of the perfection 
process (niṣpannakrama) in eighth-​ to ninth-​century tantric Buddhism, even if the nature 
of the relationship between the Gandhāra yogācāras and the later tantrikas is as yet unclear.4
Pretantric dhāraṇī texts also employed abhiṣeka as rites of both purification and in­
vigoration, especially in the pacification (śānti) of problems, whether in the anointing 
of sites, persons, or implements in the Mahāyāna maṇḍalas. The Amoghapāśahṛdaya 
presents one early version of this ritual action:
Sarvakalikalahavivādābhyākhyāneṣu udakaṃ parijapya mukhaṃ prakṣālayitavyaṃ |  
parivi(ṣ)aya-​rājyarāṣṭropadravarakṣāsu pūrṇṇakalaśaṃ sthāpayitavyā śucinā 
śucivastraprāvṛtena mahatīṃ pūjāṃ kṛtvā vācayitavyaṃ mahāśāntir bhavati |  
tena codakena sektavyaṃ | sarvasatvānāṃ (rakṣā k)ṛtā bhavati | sarvety 
upadravopasarggāḥ praśāmyanti |. (Meisezahl 1962, 325–​326)
In the case of every discord, strife, dispute or calumny, having mantrified water 
(with the Amoghapāśahṛdaya), [the ritualist] is to purify his face [with the water]. In 
the case of protecting a kingdom surrounded by other polities or an impoverished 
kingdom, set up a kalaśa pot filled with water, the pure ritualist is to put on pure 
clothing, make a great offering and recite (the mantra) and [the danger] will be 
pacified. Then the area is to be sprinkled with that water and the protection of all the 
people will come to pass.
This was to prove to be an enduring ritual action, and the purification or pacification of a 
person in an earlier dhāraṇī text may be reinterpreted in later tantric exegesis as invoking 
the tantric initiatory process. In most of these early rituals, the emphasis in the rite was 
the abhiṣeka, not of the disciple, but of the master, who then performed the purification of 
others. The *Mūlamantra, said to be translated in the Liang Dynasty (502–​557 CE), attests:
復次當知其諸物等應入壇者香花飮食果子衣服。乃至灰土水火一切等物。皆
以此呪呪水灑上
(T. 1007.19.668a8-​10)
Moreover, you should know that all of the things brought into the altar—​the in­
cense, flowers, drink, food, small fruit, clothing, even including the dust and earth, 
water and fire—​each of these things, all of them are to be sprinkled on top with this 
consecrated water while reciting the [abhiṣeka] mantra for each.
Thus, abhiṣeka in the later dhāraṇī literature sometimes begins with the self-​
consecration of the master, then to the other accoutrements of the mandala, and finally 
to those guests or disciples who may wish to participate. This is actually in accord with 
the Aitareyabrāhamṇa (viii.5) section, mentioned above, in which the king consecrates 
himself first in the annual consecration and is only afterward consecrated by the purohita, 
and we see residual traces of a similar procedure much later in the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi

--- PAGE 60 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      35
 
(T. 848.18.6b7), the Hevajratantra (I.iv), and the Vajrāvalī (§ 44.2). Yet the abhiṣeka section 
in the *Mūlamantra will, by the time of Amoghavajra’s translation in the eighth century, be 
reinterpreted as an initiatory rite (T. 1005a.19.628a18-​24).
An anomalous abhiṣeka ritual found in an eponymous Chinese apocryphal work, the 
Consecration Scripture (Fóshuō guàndīng qīwàn èrqiān shénwáng hùbǐ bǐqiū zhòujīng; 
T. 1331) has been investigated by Michel Strickmann (1990), who argued that it was a 
fully tantric rite as it invoked the issue of the consecration of a disciple in the manner of 
a king. Consequently, he believed, it should be considered as a predecessor to the later 
tantric rituals. The text portrays the rite as like a king, it is true, but the goal is not—​as in 
normative tantric rituals—​the introduction to a mandala, but instead the transmission 
of the text of the apocryphal scripture. The ritual is short:
佛言若有受此護身神典者. 
先當禮敬十方佛. 
次禮經寶次禮聖僧. 
次禮度經之師. 
皆當專心一意. 
偏露右肩長跪合掌. 
師當右手持文. 
弟子以右手受之. 師以左手持法水灌弟子頂上. 阿難以是因緣故名灌頂章句. 
所以然者如王太子紹王位時. 法應以水灌其頂上. 然後統領治國之事我法亦爾.
(T. 1331.21.497b5-​12)
Buddha said, “If there one who is to receive this body-​protecting spirit scripture, then 
first he makes obeisance to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Then he pays homage 
to the jewel of this scripture (representing the Dharma) and then the Ārya Saṃgha. 
The he pays homage to the master of this perfection scripture. Then he should en­
tirely compose his mind into a single point. He bares his right shoulder, kneels down, 
and puts his hands together. The master then takes the text with his right hand, and 
the disciple also holds the text with his right hand. Then the master with his left hand 
takes the sanctified water and sprinkles it on the head of the disciple. Ananda, for this 
reason it is termed the Abhiṣekaparyāya. The reason is this: as when a crown prince 
is being transmitted the kingship, the ritual is that his head should be sprinkled with 
water, and then he is able to govern the affairs of state—​my ritual is like that.”
While this ritual is interesting, the taking of the text by the right hand in its transmis­
sion and the idea of sprinkling water with the left are anomalous by Indian standards. It 
appears that a Chinese author learned of the coronation rite from some source, written 
or oral, and elected to employ it as a vehicle for the transmission of a Buddhist text. So 
far as they are retained, Indian rituals operate in a substantially different manner, so it is 
doubtful that this anomalous tangent stands in a line from early rites of abhiṣeka and the 
full rituals of esoteric Buddhism.
Early Tantric Buddhist Abhiṣeka Rites
The transition between earlier dhāraṇī and later tantric uses of abhiṣeka in fact effected 
the transition between the mandala as a vehicle for the invocation and worship of the

--- PAGE 61 ---
36      Ronald M. Davidson
 
Buddhas and a mandala as a vehicle for the abhiṣeka as a gateway rite of the newly 
emerging esoteric Buddhism. The difference was not, in the earlier instances, the nature 
of the mandala itself. Rather, it was the fact that the mandala was suddenly to be hidden 
from anyone who had not received the abhiṣeka, so that access to and entrance into the 
esoteric system was limited by those who could receive the new rite. Abhiṣeka had effec­
tively transformed a purification ritual ensuring that anyone coming to the mandala did 
not bring defilement with them and from there turned it into a ritual that restricted who 
could see the mandala diagram and with whom they could discuss it. Because it was 
based on the political ritual of coronation, the tantric initiation brought with it oaths 
of loyalty between master and disciple—​as employing the abhiṣeka to mediate loyalty 
between feudal lord and his vassals was one of its uses—​and specific vows of behavior 
were then invoked. These vows were quite different from those employed in the trans­
mission of either the early Vinaya system or of the bodhisattva vows, meaning that the 
new abhiṣeka rite was the moment in which new vows were taken and, as a consequence, 
a new community was formed. Essential to the new vow structure was the invocation 
of secrecy, so that the “secret mantras” were analogous to the state secrets of the medi­
eval world, both designated guhyamantra. As a gateway rite to esoteric Buddhism, the 
abhiṣeka now gave access to not only the mandala of the tradition, but also the newly 
secretive literature of that tradition. Under the umbrella of secrecy, diverse tantras could 
form in a dynamic and extraordinary manner. All of this was made possible by the 
change of the significance of the abhiṣeka rite.
Arguably the earliest surviving tantric Buddhist work is the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha (T. 
901), and its compilation and translation in 654 CE is attributed to Atikūṭa, a monk 
from Bodhgayā. The three most important abhiṣeka rites in that text are two focused on 
Tejorāśi Śākyamuni from the Uṣṇīṣa ritual system and a long abhiṣeka of Avalokiteśvara 
very similar in organization to that of Tejorāśi. Two of these have been studied in detail, 
the shorter early rite of Tejorāśi (Davidson 2012) and the much longer and more impor­
tant Tejorāśi ritual occurring toward the end of the text (Shinohara 2014, 205–​225; T. 
901.18.885b21-​890c14).
The longer ritual lasts seven days and nights, beginning with preparatory rituals 
of candidate selection and site preparation. As is usual in Buddhist abhiṣeka rites, the 
mandala preparation and construction take up the majority of the time: laying out the 
borders, digging out polluted elements from the ground, sanctification by water, and 
more. However, the mandala is envisioned on a grander scale than most, with different 
sizes dependent on the level of the patron, from 120 cubits for a king, down to 1 cubit 
for the least important persons, although at one point 12 or 16 cubits are mentioned; 
the recitations are sometimes similarly dependent on the status of the patron and 
candidates. At the gateways are lengthy banners with images of the Divine Kings on 
them. The candidates are interrogated as to their commitment to the procedure. At this 
point, the Four Divine Kings, Hayagrīva, Kuṇḍalin, and other protectors are invoked to 
protect the site.
The third day, the mandala is laid out with the usual string that is sanctified, and 
seven precious objects—​from gold to beryl—​are buried, marking the sacred status of

--- PAGE 62 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      37
 
the space, which is now the vajradhātu, and all the Buddhas are established there in the 
place where the Wheel of the Mahāyāna will be turned. The fourth day, the construc­
tion of the pavilion continues, with pillars and poles, and two subsidiary mandalas—​
a four-​cubit white mandala to the northeast and a four-​cubit abhiṣeka mandala to the 
southwest—​are constructed as well as a homa kuṇḍa to the southwest. The adornment 
of the main mandala is extraordinary and employs multiple large banners of different 
colors in the different directions.
The fifth day is devoted to marking off the specific sections within the principal man­
dala, sanctifying the space, and establishing the perimeters and gates. The sixth day is in­
volved with both the preparation of the candidates and the further ornamentation of the 
mandala, now sanctified by the recitation of Hayagrīva’s mantra. The candidates again 
are investigated as to their commitment, and each is investigated for positive omens 
by chewing willow branches that are deposited on the ground. They are also instructed 
to record their dreams for omens, which are interrogated the next day. Application of 
the powders to the mandalas where the deities are marked out—​with Tejorāśi in the 
center—​is finished and protected by the Kuṇḍalin’s rite.
Day seven is the time of the abhiṣeka per se. During the day, offerings are placed; 
Kuṇḍalin and Hayagrīva are invoked; deity and the abhiṣeka pots are prepared, the 
latter numbering one for each candidate; and the deities are invoked. In the night, the 
candidates are examined again, sanctified and enveloped with protective rites while 
musicians play. The eyes of the candidates are covered with yellow cloth, a flower is 
placed in their hands, and they are individually led into the mandala, where the flower 
is thrown, to land on a specific deity, which is recorded. The master then takes the cen­
tral deity’s pot and consecrates himself with it, using the abhiṣeka mantra and man­
dala. Each candidate is given a separate pot, from which he is given the abhiṣeka of 
the deity on which his flower landed. After the abhiṣeka proper is over, then a homa 
ritual is performed, featuring offerings to Prajñāpāramitā, Hayagrīva, eleven-​headed 
Avalokiteśvara, Vajragarbha, and others. Finally, there are the expiation for the 
committing of errors in the ritual, protection of the disciples, distribution of gifts, and 
final worship of the deities of the mandala. The mandala is then destroyed.
By the end of the seventh century, a need seems to have been felt for a synthetic ritual 
manual, and two were composed, albeit differently and probably independently at ap­
proximately the same time. The Guhyatantra identifies itself as the synthesis of 3500 
mandalas (D. 141a5; T. 897.18.760c13), doubtless a hyperbolic number but one that 
gestures at the explosive development of esoteric Buddhism in the seventh and early 
eighth centuries. Similarly, the Susiddhikāra proclaims that the scripture is the accom­
plishment of all of the mandala rituals of the three families (tathāgata, padma, and vajra) 
and all the three tantric karmas (śāntika, pauṣṭika, abhicāra; T. 893.18.603c4-​13). In both 
texts, there are four abhiṣekas, even though their typologies are different.
The Susiddhikāra articulates the abhiṣeka on the rite of anointing an image of the 
deity (T. 893.18.620a12-​28; Giebel 2001, 223) which is infused with power and efficacy 
in the process, and Śubhakarasiṃha’s translation makes this the model of the disciples’ 
consecration (T. 893.18.623c3-​5; Giebel 2001, 253). The rite for abhiṣeka into a mandala

--- PAGE 63 ---
38      Ronald M. Davidson
 
then has the ācārya consecrate himself, having constructed a main, three-​tier mandala 
between five and eight cubits, along with a half-​size separate abhiṣeka mandala at the 
west portal, which is the one gate to be open. A homa altar is also constructed, to the 
south of the west entrance. Flasks should be placed at the corners of the mandala and 
in the center, in the deity’s place, as well as at the entrance for the protector Kuṇḍalin. A 
homa is performed, directed to the goal of the abhiṣeka—​whether śāntika, pauṣṭika, or 
abhicāra. Curiously, the Susiddhikāra does not mention throwing a flower into the man­
dala in the abhiṣeka rite, but at the end, there are four abhiṣekas with four flasks, begin­
ning with that of Kuṇḍalin, in which the ritual assistant to the master actually performs 
the rite (T. 893.18.624b; Giebel 2001, 256–​257).
The fourfold abhiṣeka system in the Guhyatantra is different from that of the 
Susiddhikāra in that there are four purposes for candidates receiving the abhiṣeka, in 
some way similar to the statement by the Ṛgvidhāna above, that abhiṣeka may extend 
life, release from disease, and cure sin. However, the text also foreshadows some of the 
development of varieties of abhiṣeka seen in the later tantras, as mentioned below.
lha yi rigs rnams mthong ba las | dbang bskur ba ni rnam pa bzhi |
bla ma mnyam par gzhag pa yis | de dag shes nas ci rigs bya |
slob dpon go ‘phang thob pa’i phyir | dang po yongs su bsgrags pa yin |
rig sngags rnams ni bsgrub bya’i phyir | gnyis pa legs par bshad pa yin |
bgegs rnams rab tu gzhom pa’i phyir | gsum pa rab tu bsgrags pa yin |
bzhi pa ‘byor pa thob pa’i phyir | cho ga rgyas pa de bshad do |
Through seeing the families of gods [in the maṇḍala], there are four varieties 
of abhiṣeka; the master knows which is applicable based on his deep medita­
tion. First is the widely proclaimed abhiṣeka, to obtain the position of ācārya.  
Second is well explained as the abhiṣeka to practice the mantra rites.  
Third is well known for the purpose of defeating the obstacles (vighna).
Fourth is explained as the extensive rite to gather wealth.
(Guhyatantra D. 806.166a5-​7; T. 897.18.772a6-​8)
The Guhyatantra goes on to dispose of all but the ācāryābhiṣeka quickly, then dwelling 
on the circumstances for obtaining the level of the ācārya, whose qualities the text had 
dwelt on right at the beginning in detail. Here the issue is not the qualities of the ācārya, 
but the ritual systems under which one gains that lofty position and the benefits to be 
accrued to one who does so, as well as the penalties to a teacher who has not received 
the specific validation. The Guhyatantra states that, while initiation into the padma or 
vajra families allows one to be an ācārya of one or both, it is really abhiṣeka into the 
tathāgata family that allows the master access to the entire spectrum of rituals. The text 
also warns that, at one time, only one disciple should be consecrated in this manner, 
even if other disciples are consecrated for other reasons. (D. 806.167a5; T. 897.18.772c7-​
8). The text had already briefly discussed the ritual, which seems to employ a single pot 
for the abhiṣeka of however many disciples are allowed, so it differs from the other texts 
in that regard.

--- PAGE 64 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      39
 
The penchant for abhiṣeka classification extended to the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, 
which mentions three types:
灌頂有三種　佛子至心聽　　　　
若祕印方便　則離於作業　　　　
是名初勝法　如來所灌頂　　　　
所謂第二者　令起作衆事　　　　
第三以心授　悉離於時方　　　　
令尊歡喜故　如所説應作　　　　
現前佛灌頂　是則最殊勝5　
There are three varieties of abhiṣeka, so the disciple should ardently listen. The first 
is conferred by means of mudrās without any other rituals or tantric karmas; it is 
the highest variety, the abhiṣeka bestowed by the Tathāgatas. The second is done 
by rituals and tantric karmas. The third is that received mentally, without regard to 
place or time. Because it pleases the teacher, then the abhiṣeka should be performed 
as taught. Then the abhiṣeka received is (as if) directly from the Buddha; this is the 
superior variety.
The Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi thus picks up a theme that has been hovering about since 
the visualized texts of central Asia and the Daśabhūmika-​sūtra: the Buddhas will 
confer the best abhiṣeka based on the nature of the disciple and how advanced he 
may be.
The abhiṣeka rituals provided in these early texts, most of which call themselves 
sūtra but were later classified as tantra (the Guhyatantra is an exception, as it is clear 
that is part of its name—​jùxì tándànluó 瞿醯壇怛囉; T. 897.18.770b5), reflect an ex­
traordinary variation that runs like a thread through all the abhiṣeka rituals known 
to me. The elaborate directions in the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha describe the elements of a 
temporary construction, similar to that invoked in the śrauta and soma rituals, al­
though it incongruously includes elements of permanent buildings, and Shinohara 
correctly suggested (Shinohara 2014, 206) that the text may have been adapted to 
reflect the actual abhiṣeka that Atikūṭa performed in China for his patrons, so that 
the text includes how that specific performance proceeded. The other works are less 
baroque and, as is usual in Indian works, make allowances for those who cannot af­
ford the gold-​silver-​copper vessels that are ideal, yielding to the reality that some, 
at least, of the ritualists may be impoverished; for them, even the roughest clay pots 
might have been difficult to obtain. Consequently, the abhiṣeka cannot be said to 
emulate exactly the coronation rites of medieval kingship, at least as found in the 
purāṇas or the gṛhyavidhāna literature. Instead, it is an image, a mirage, an aspira­
tion of kingship.
In the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha we see that each candidate is accorded a separate pot, but 
royal abhiṣeka is done with multiple pots for a single royal person. The approximately 
contemporary Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa, for example, indicates that following the 
homa, the priest performs the multiple abhiṣekas of the king with mud, the five products

--- PAGE 65 ---
40      Ronald M. Davidson
 
of the cow, and water from the four various rivers and impregnated with herbs and other 
sources (Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa II.21; Inden 1981). The employment of a single pot 
for a single person may represent a temporary or idiosyncratic moment in the ritual 
because it is not normative for later rituals, which follow more closely the brahman­
ical procedures. The Susiddhikāra, for example, observes some comprehension of that 
program, with four pots for each candidate, as does the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, which 
consecrates the disciples with the four flasks of the bodhisattvas (T. 848.18.23c19-​24a20). 
But the Guhyatantra is less profligate, with the abhiṣeka seemingly employing a single 
pot for all the persons, even if there are others scattered about in the doors and corners 
of the mandala.
Another factor seen for the first time in the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha is the employ­
ment of possession (āveśa) as a vehicle for religious experience. Buddhists had been 
dealing with the issue of possession for centuries since it is ubiquitous in the Indian 
environment, as is well known. The older dhāraṇī texts, like the Saptabuddhaka and 
the Mahādaṇḍadhāraṇī-​śītavatī (Davidson 2014a, 2014b; Krug 2019), recounted 
episodes in which monks would become possessed and how the dhāraṇī spells would 
counteract that limitation. Then there is the well-​known employment of possession 
in a young girl to foretell the future (Subāhuparipṛcchā T. 895.18.741c24-​25; D. 805, 
131a7-​132b3). What is different in the Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha is the positive invocation of 
possession as a soteriological aid, first through the mantras associated with the pre­
vious Buddha Vipaśyin and the deity Indra (T. 901.18.799a8-​16), and later in mantras 
attached to Vajragarbha (T. 901.18.845a17), Vajraśṛṅkhalā (T. 901.18.846a6-​7), and 
Cāmuṇḍā (T. 901.18.883b11-​12, 883c3). This employment of possession is augmented 
in the Uttaratantra section of the Chinese translation of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, 
with the appeal that the Buddha’s gnosis enter the person (sarvatathāgatajñānaṃ me 
āviśatu; T. 848.18.46b17; Giebel 2005, 237). This latter appeal found its way into the 
act of abhiṣeka, as found in the early sections of the Sarvatathāgata-​tattvasaṃgraha. 
There the master binds up the mudrā of the Adamantine Being (sattvavajrimudrā) 
and pronounces:
ayaṃ tat samayo vajraṃ vajrasatvam iti smṛtam |
āveśayatu te ‘dyaiva vajrajñānam anuttaraṃ ||
This is the pledge, the vajra, understood as Vajrasattva.
May it cause the highest adamantine gnosis to possess you just today!
(Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha 69; Giebel 2001, 76)
Possession during the process of abhiṣeka was to go from a marginal moment in the 
system into a major factor in the later tantric rituals.
By the mid-​eighth century, items that had been employed in the abhiṣeka were now 
being accorded their own abhiṣekas, even if they did not center on the performance of 
sprinking with pots. These were initially to be grouped into fives, following the iden­
tity of the five Jinas (Vairocana and the rest) or the five forms of gnosis (ādarśajñāna,

--- PAGE 66 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      41
 
etc.) (Isaacson 2006, 264). The most enduring group is reflected in the Bhagavan-​
Nīlāmbaradhara-​Vajrapāṇi-​tantra (fol. 166a7):
	
i.	 The udaka-​abhiṣeka, the water consecration from the kalaśa vase that is the most 
basic form of the aspersion ritual and was the primary focus until the mid-​eighth 
century.
	
ii.	 The mukuṭa-​abhiṣeka, the crown consecration, in which a crown is tied onto the 
disciple’s head by the master, signifying that the disciple has become the righteous 
king of the mandala, a term also signaling the political arrangement of medieval 
India (Davidson 2002).
	 iii.	 The vajra-​abhiṣeka, the scepter consecration, so that the disciple receives the 
scepter of Vajrapāṇi and, before him, of Indra, whose first abhiṣeka established 
the model for coronation in India, as we have seen.
	
iv.	 The ghaṇṭa-​abhiṣeka, the bell consecration, so that the disciple can ring the vajra-​
handled bell at the appropriate junctures in the performance of sādhana, the 
ritual invocation of the deities of the mandala.
	
v.	 The nāma-​abhiṣeka, the name consecration, reflecting the new name and identity 
of the disciple who has now been coronated.
These items had been part of the standard abhiṣeka ritual as it had developed in 
the early eighth century, and most of them appear in the list of mantras in the 
Sarvadurgatipariśodhana (pp. 150, 168, 190, 258, 270) for example, but were not 
identified as discrete members of an abhiṣeka grouping. The choice was selective, as 
there are many other items mentioned in these earlier tantras that were not immedi­
ately identified with a specific abhiṣeka, such as the wheel (Sarvadurgatipariśodhana 192: 
oṃ vajracakrābhiṣiñca huṃ bhrūm), or the gem, the lotus, the garland, and so on. As 
time goes by, however, some of them become identified as having their own abhiṣeka, 
and the entire category of abhiṣeka changes in the process, from a ritual of unction and 
aspersion to a ritual of the infusion of power and authority, passing from the master to 
the disciple, so that the liquid element becomes extended into a fluidity of power/​know­
ledge/​deity entering the candidate’s body.
Later Tantric Buddhist Abhiṣeka Rites
The development of later tantric Buddhist abhiṣeka rituals was generated through 
a number of factors, of which the circumstances are still obscure. Some may be 
surmised as derived from spirit cults, some from the magical traditions of medieval 
India (Davidson 2017), while others may be derived from sectarian systems, perhaps 
Śaivism or other systems. Irrespective of the sources, the development is best under­
stood to reflect inclusion of sacramental forms of sexuality, in which the sexual fluids are

--- PAGE 67 ---
42      Ronald M. Davidson
 
ingested and in which sexuality is ritualized in the consecration rite. The consequence of 
enumerating “lower” versus “higher” (or exterior vs. interior) forms of consecration is 
that the earlier forms became more formalized, so that the two systems were arranged in 
a hierarchical pattern, in which the now lower tantras were granted initiation through a 
specific program of ritual.
Generally it is accepted that the Guhyasamāja’s supplemental chapter (Samājottara), 
now often numbered ­chapter 18, articulates the inclusion of new forms of abhiṣeka and 
signals some of the issues that remained unresolved through much of the rest of tantric 
Buddhist history (Dalton 2004, 25; Isaacson 2006, 265):
abhiṣekaṃ tridhābhedam asmin tantre prakalpitam |
kalaśābhiṣekaṃ prathamaṃ dvitīyaṃ guhyābhiṣekataḥ |
prajñājñānaṃ tṛtīyaṃ tu caturthaṃ tat punas tathā ||
(Guhyasamāja 18.113)
Abhiṣeka is a three-​fold division, as set forth in this tantra.
The first is the flask abhiṣeka. Second is the secret abhiṣeka.
Third is the insight-​gnosis abhiṣeka. And the fourth is also like that.
The reality that the text unambiguously contradicts itself within three lines certainly 
signals that there was some uncertainty as to both the nature and the number of the 
new abhiṣeka typologies, and these were not entirely resolved through much of the sub­
sequent history of the tradition. In reality, while there are abhiṣeka chapters to many 
tantras, the rituals followed generally become those described in the texts discussing 
correct abhiṣeka practices (abhiṣekavidhi, maṇḍalavidhi), which proliferate from the 
late eighth century forward.
a. Lower Initiations. In the four-​fold division expressed in the Guhyasamāja and ac­
cepted in some form in the later tantric literature, the earlier abhiṣeka systems were 
categorized into the external or vase consecrations kalaśa-​abhiṣeka, the abhiṣeka 
employing a pot or flask for the anointing of the disciple. In some texts, this is referenced 
as the vajraśiṣya-​abhiṣeka, that is, the abhiṣeka by which the disciple is engaged, perhaps 
reflecting a division of motivation of those taking the consecration. Beyond the five­
fold division already seen, the kalaśa consecration includes other kinds of consecration, 
depending on the text. The Sekoddeśa, based closely on the Kālacakra-​tantra, articulates 
seven varieties of abhiṣeka to introduce the immature (8ab: ādau saptābhiṣeko yo 
bālānām avatāraṇam): abhiṣekas of water (udaka), diadem (mukuṭa), hero’s silk fore­
head band (vīrapaṭṭa), vajra, bell (ghaṇṭā), great askesis (mahāvrata), name (nāma), 
and permission (anujñā). The primary purpose of these seven is the purification of the 
potential disciple, and purification is a theme through all the descriptions of abhiṣeka in 
the Sekoddeśa (vv. 12–​17). However, the text does not classify these as among the kalaśa/​
kumbha-​abhiṣeka, which it includes in the four higher initiations (v. 15), making eleven 
initiations total.

--- PAGE 68 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      43
 
Most Yoginītantra tranditions have a menu of abhiṣekas, and eleven is the number 
sometimes provided for the lower initiations alone, as in the Abhiṣekaratnāloka of 
Prajñāśrīgupta, which survives in Tibetan:
Chu dang dbu rgyan rdo rje dang | dril bu ming dang de lnga dang | rigs gsum dam tshig 
yod pa ni | dbang ni brgyad du gyes pa gsungs | brtul shugs lung bstan skyabs sbyin ni | 
de dag gcu gcig gcig yin no |6
Water, crown, vajra, bell, name, these five, and the sacramental commitments (samaya) of 
the three families make eight, it is said. With the practice (vrata), prophecy (vyākaraṇa) 
and support (āśvāsa), together these are the one group of eleven.
While it seems that the number eleven was somehow important, after the five already 
mentioned that are ubiquitous, the rest are constituted by different items, which may 
reference abhiṣekas using flowers from garlands (mālābhiṣeka), nonregression on the 
path (avaivartikābhiṣeka), permission to teach (anujñābhiṣeka), prophecy (vyākaraṇa), 
and so forth in some combination and different order, although they tend to conclude 
with either prophecy or permission to teach.
The Vajrāvalī—​a later synthetic work of Abhayākaragupta from approximately 
1100 CE—​distributes consecrations even more widely, beginning with the conse­
cration of the statue as if it were a disciple (§§ 16–​17), which is similar to the rite in 
the Susiddhikāra, as mentioned above. Following this, there is the preparation of 
the area and the disciple, the entrance of each into the mandala and the disciples’s 
possession by Vajrasattva (§§ 20–​22), and then the consecrations of the actual dis­
ciples. They begin with the blindfolded disciple throwing the flower in the mandala 
to select the appropriate Buddha family of affiliation, then revealing the mandala by 
taking off the blindfold (§ 23 mālābhiṣeka). This is followed by the sprinkling of the 
disciple from the kalaśa vase (§ 24 udakābhiṣeka); placing a crown on the disciple’s 
head (§ 25 mukuṭābhiṣeka); touching the disciple’s heart, throat, and head with the 
vajra and placing it in his right hand (§26 vajrābhiṣeka); placing the bell in his left 
hand (§ 27 ghaṇṭābhiṣeka); conferring on him a name based on the place in the 
mandala that the flower fell (§ 28 nāmābhiṣeka); conferring the three commitments 
as part of the ācāryābhiṣeka (§§ 29–​30); showing a mirror and explaining that 
elements of reality are like reflections (§33 darpanābhiṣeka), all of which are sealed 
by the casting of six ritual arrows—​four in the cardinal directions and one up and 
one down (§ 34).
The many abhiṣeka manuals we have emphasize the relationship of the elements of 
these various kinds of abhiṣeka with the five Victors (pañcajina): Vairocana, Akṣobhya, 
Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, who symbolically preside over the 
Buddha families in the mandala, irrespective of whether they are included in the specific 
mandala into which the disciple is consecrated. The rituals are in each instance filled 
with Buddhist explanations featuring the relationship of the five Victors, the five forms 
of gnosis starting with the mirror, and the five aggregates, so that they may be collectively

--- PAGE 69 ---
44      Ronald M. Davidson
 
termed the “wisdom consecration” (Hevajrasekaprakriyā 25: ebyir abhiṣekaiḥ pañcabhir 
ādarśādijñānaviśuddhyā vidyābhiṣeka ity ucyate). By the time of the Vajrāvalī, these col­
lectively were a method for ensuring the transmission of the teaching, so that most often 
the six consecrations following that first five either included or were collectively termed 
the “master’s consecration” (ācāryābhiṣeka).
b. Higher initiations. The higher initiations were something quite different, for three 
of them may have involved sexual activity, and two certainly did so. If the vase consecra­
tion (kalaśābhiṣeka) was included in the higher initiations, which was unusual, it could 
mean presenting an available girl of twelve to twenty years of age to the teacher, who 
fondled her breasts (Sekoddeśaṭīkā 98). The guhyābhiṣeka—​the secret consecration—​
required the disciple to provide a willing young girl of the same age range, who would 
agree to copulate with the master. Following the copulation, the master was to ejacu­
late (or transfer the ejaculate) into the mouth of the disciple, with the understanding 
that the ejaculate was the physical “thought of awakening” (bodhicitta) that was being 
transferred to the disciple. Thus, the process sacramentalized both sexuality and its 
physical residue, so that the initiation required sacramental sexuality.
The prajñājñānābhiṣeka (consecration by the gnosis from the “insight” [a term for a 
woman]) is described as a ritual in which, under the guidance of the master, the disciple 
copulates with his consort while envisioning himself and her as indistinguishable from 
the divinity to which he is being consecrated. On ejaculation into the vagina of the con­
sort, the disciple licks the resulting fluids as the physical “thought of awakening.”
The “fourth consecration” is difficult to evaluate, not only because of the dispa­
rate descriptions of the ritual, but also because even its legitimacy is contested. Most 
consecration manuals, however, do acknowledge the rite, but very tersely. The 
Hevajrasekaprakriyā, for example, says: “After that (the prajñājñānābhiṣeka), having 
obtained the fourth consecration from the instruction of the teacher, one should give 
a gift again according to your ability” (Hevajrasekaprakriyā 31: tadanu gurūpadeśāc 
caturthasekaṃ labdhvā punar yathāśaktito dakṣiṇāṃ dadyāt). In the instances it is 
described, the language is philosophical and redolent of nondualism, so that the prajñā-
jñānābhiṣeka ritual is to be subsequently understood as an enactment of the nonduality 
of ultimate truth.
Controversies Concerning the Later 
Tantric Abhiṣekas
Given the extraordinary direction taken in the higher initiations by the yoga-​ and 
yoginītantras, it is not surprising that many controversies arose. Even then, with respect 
to these higher consecrations, three primary areas of disagreement occurred. First, and 
most obvious, was the question of sexuality, and these discussions focused on a single 
problem: Buddhist monks and nuns are forbidden to have sexual activity of any variety,

--- PAGE 70 ---
Initiation (Abhiṣeka) in Indian Buddhism      45
 
although the lay participation was not uncomplicated, given the statements in the 
earlier texts on wholesome sexual conduct for upāsakas (laymen). Some of the rituals 
are explicit that the master is a layman, and he is to preside over the gathering along with 
his consort (saprajñaḥ), so that the culture bearers of Buddhism are now envisioned as 
laymen, a direction already apparent in the sixth century. But this did not settle the issue 
for Buddhist monasteries, which relied on the goodwill and financial investiture from 
those in the environment for their survival. The tantric antinomian practices threatened 
that survival. Isaacson (2006, 264) was doubtless correct that the sexual ritual circulated 
separately prior to its inclusion as a rite of consecration, as we find an early version of 
guhyābhiṣeka ritual in the eighth chapter of the Guhyasamājatantra, but with no con­
nection to abhiṣeka (Guhyasamāja, Matsunaga 1978, 24–​26). We can, however, also 
postulate that these rituals depended on at least two factors: the Indian medical under­
standing of the attributes of semen and the much older rituals of spirit seduction, in 
which a yogin can perform a rite and seduce a female spirit, which yields both personal 
satisfaction and overlordship of the celestial sorcerers (vidyādharacakravartin).
Engaging this controversy concerning sexuality, five solutions were fielded in the lit­
erature. First, there is the claim that ritual sexuality is not the same as other forms of sex, 
which are the topic of the Vinaya; thus, the prohibition does not apply to tantric sexu­
ality (e.g., Vajrāvali § 20.2-​3). Second, some authorities stated, as did Atiśa, that monks 
were still forbidden to engage the higher initiations as this is a violation of the monastic 
rule; consequently, they are allowed to practice all the meditations and yogic systems 
with having received only the lower initiations (Davidson 1995). Third, others demure: 
Tantric sexuality is a question of a specific population; those who are advanced may do 
so, but we see no persons now who are so well authenticated (Szántó 2015). Fourth, the 
issue is one of interpreting coded language; the discussion about sexuality is primarily 
for the purpose of ridding the disciple of clinging to words (Wenta 2018). Finally, a few 
authorities temporize: Visualization of the act with a visualized consort (jñānamudrā) 
rather than a physical consort (karmamudrā) was occasionally conceived as a way to 
satisfy the performance but without the debilitating consequences to monks of its phys­
ical performance. Consequently, we get a sense that the Buddhist tradition in India was 
involved in an internal conflict concerning sexuality overall, with these rituals being 
hallmarks of the change in approach to liberation. Whereas in the past sexuality had 
been understood as a catastrophic impediment, suddenly the forces of sexuality appear 
to have turned the tides, albeit in a manner that was both questionable and, in some 
sense, irresponsible, as it opened a door with few safeguards for the unwary.
The second primary controversy was the issue of yogic practice, particularly with ref­
erence to the “insight-​gnosis consecration” (prajñājñānābhiṣeka). This consecration, 
like the guhyābhiṣeka, was initially sacramental, so that the transfer of fluids was the pri­
mary purpose. But the Hevajratantra I.10 emphasized an interior yogic system, with four 
moments of experience (kṣaṇacatuṣṭaya) and the four blisses (caturānanda) that proved 
very influential. Two issues, however, immediately arose. First, how is it that many of 
the other yoginītantras did not have these yogic systems, given that the Laghusaṃvara 
and other previous scriptures also required this consecration? Second, given that there

--- PAGE 71 ---
46      Ronald M. Davidson
 
was some uncertainty in the order of the four moments and the attendant four forms of 
bliss, what was the proper sequence (Onians 2003, 331–​338; Hevajratantra, introduction 
32–​39; Isaacson and Sferra 2014, 97–​111)?
Finally, there was the question of the “fourth consecration” (caturthābhiṣeka): Was it 
actually discussed by the Buddha, and, if it was, what was its nature? It was evident from 
the confusing and contradictory statement in Guhyasamāja 18.113, quoted above, that 
the fourth consecration “and like that” description was not sufficient to understand any­
thing about it. Consequently, there were positions put as to whether there even was a 
fourth consecration, and, if it was necessary, what did it constitute? Seemingly, it began 
simply as an instruction of a teacher about the meaning of the others, but it took on 
a ritualized mandate over time, so that the fourth consecration had to be something 
communicable (Isaacson 2006, 268–​271; Onians 2003, 345–​347; Tattvaratnāloka vv.15–​
16; Abhiṣekaratnāloka 300a3–​303a4; Vajrāvalī § 44.1.6). These are but the most impor­
tant questions of ritual and yogic practice that were to consume the ritual manuals and 
the commentaries on the tantras for much of the balance of the history of Buddhism 
in India.
Conclusion and Contribution
The abhiṣeka as a gateway rite to the tantric Buddhist system was inaugurated in some 
measure to offset the perception that Buddhists were not going to offer rituals reso­
nant with the larger Indian world, which had become obsessed with politics and power. 
Abhiṣeka covered both, but also allowed Buddhist leaders to formulate a ritual system 
that integrated both politics and power into selected Buddhist communities. While the 
ingress was initially slow and emphasized purity, over time it mutated and turned into 
something different under the same name: a hierarchy of indelible authority surrounded 
by a mythology and cosmology of divine investiture. Added to this was the invocation of 
secrecy that built on the political model of state secrets, and the model could be brought 
to a rolling boil with the employ of sexual yoga, which it did from the eighth to the elev­
enth centuries.
This essay contributes to the understanding of abhiṣeka in Indian Buddhism by 
outlining the precedents to abhiṣeka in India and in Indian Buddhism in a manner not 
entirely explored before and by delineating the two primary metaphors employed in 
abhiṣeka, which have not been well expressed previously. It also organized and presented 
material found in disparate sources with the goal of having an overarching presentation 
of the basic systems and problems associated with Indian abhiṣeka rituals. It integrated 
a study of disparate documents from the dhāraṇī and Mahāyāna archive and placed 
them in a ritual frame of reference, for both what they said and what was not indicated. 
The essay also integrated recent work on abhiṣeka in Indian Buddhist studies, as well 
as discussed significant but understudied documents and how they configured them­
selves. Finally, it outlined significant areas of disagreement in late tantric Buddhism.

Chapter 3
The Inner and  
Outer Worship
The Rhythms of Domestic and  
Temple Practice in Nepālī Tantra
Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
Introduction
Nepālī Tāntrikas perceive themselves as abiding in a geopolitical territory that is 
enlivened with the energies of a host of gods and goddesses that dwell at once in the 
land itself, the temples that punctuate that land, the many shrines within the homes 
of the faithful, and, ultimately, within the bodies of the faithful engaged in worship 
(Dyczkowski 2004). Indeed, dating back to King Māṇadeva (464–​506 ce) the land of 
Nepal has been referenced by Nepālīs themselves as Nepāla-​Maṇḍala, a term that is rich 
with theological and ritual significance (Lidke 2017; Slusser 1982). Dating back to the an­
cient hymns of Ṛg Veda, mandalas have been identified as the sacred territories that arise 
from and are sustained by ritual practice, primordially by the gods themselves who set 
the paradigm for human behavior. Translated into the political sphere, mandalas were 
the regions of those righteous kings whose lands were viewed as extensions of their own 
beings (White 2000, 25). As a mandala in such a fashion, Nepal is a land whose history, 
politics, culture, and current religious practices are punctuated by the understanding 
that ritual practice is that which sustains the land, the nation, and its inhabitants.
In this chapter, our focus is on outlining the network of domestic and temple ritual 
practice detailed in the Kaula Tantric liturgical texts of the Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tra­
dition, as well as by the living adherents of these texts. Textual sources and living 
adherents alike understand ritual practice as a central means means by which one can 
come to experience one’s own consciousness as coexistent with the consciousness of 
the supreme goddess herself, Parā Śakti, who manifests not just in the singular but

--- PAGE 79 ---
54      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
as a multiplicity of gods and goddesses associated with the various regions, energies, 
elements, and powers of the cosmos (Timalsina 2007). This supreme goddess expresses 
herself as creation through the outward projection of her inner being. From the per­
spective of this tantric tradition, there is nothing actually outside the being of the 
Goddess. In reality, her outward expression is a projection within the expanse of her 
own infinite consciousness (cf. White 2003, 179–​180). That which is singular takes on 
the appearance of multiplicity by projecting outwardly into its own being at the time of 
creation. Conversely, dissolution, or the ending of creation, is the process by which the 
appearance of multiplicity, as the mandala-​of-​creation, is reabsorbed by the goddess 
back into a state of singularity. Ultimately, “inner” and “outer” are but relative terms. 
All is within the being of the goddess, whose internal being subdivides into an infinite 
array of beings who are all outside each other yet all within the being of the goddess 
who abides within all as the self-​of-​all (cf. Dyczkowski 1989, 2004, 2009; Sanderson 
1986, 1995). Conventional terms are used to make sense of a process by which creation 
arises and appears as somehow distinct from or outside the goddess, who in actuality 
gazes inwardly at the creation inside of her while beings within creation who look out 
into the expanse of space are looking from within the being of a goddess who is simul­
taneously said to dwell within all being as their inner nature. What, therefore is “inside” 
(antar) and what is “outside” (bahir)?
The Dialectic of Inner and Worship in 
the Domestic and Temple Rituals
Inspired by the nondual awareness of the goddess herself, the logic of Nepālī tan­
tric ritual practice is grounded in the understanding of a relative distinction between 
that which is “inside” and that which is “outside.” At a basic level, Nepāli tantric prac­
tice divides into two basic categories of domestic practice, which is labeled “internal 
worship” (antar-​yāga), and temple practice, which is labeled “external worship” (bahir-​
yāga). However, the dichotomy of domestic and temple worship is demarcated by a 
very thin, permeable line, such that the principles, deities, liturgies, and benefits of each 
impacts and mutually informs the other in an ongoing dialectical fashion.
Indeed, the Sanskrit terms antar (inside) and bahir (outside) can and are used var­
iously based upon their application in distinct contexts. In terms of distinguishing 
broadly between domestic practice engaged privately at home versus public practice en­
gaged in a temple, festival, or other shared social space, Nepālī Tāntrikas designate the 
former as “internal worship” (antar-​yāga) and the latter as “external worship” (bahir-​
yāga). However, the distinctions between these terms are not easily maintained. For 
example, although private practice done within one’s home is broadly categorized as 
inner worship (antar-​yāga), there are aspects of such practice that are drawn from the 
external worship (bahir-​yāga) liturgies. Similarly, although temple practice is generally

--- PAGE 80 ---
The Inner and Outer Worship      55
 
labeled bahir-​yāga, elements of such practice are drawn from the procedures for antar-​
yāga practice. For instance, a priest engaged in practice inside the temple, behind closed 
doors, will integrate elements of antar-​yāga into his private worship of the temple icon 
in preparation for the practice done outside the temple, before a viewing audience, ac­
cording to the procedures of bahir-​yāga.
With regard to tantric spiritual practice (sādhana), the internal mental practice is 
generally termed “internal worship” (antar-​yāga) while the visible worship or practice is 
termed “external worship” (bahir-​yāga). Whether in domestic practice or at a temple, a 
complete practice is one that integrates both antar-​ and bahir-​yāga. As temples are often 
considered places of power, doing practices in its premises is believed to increase the ef­
fectiveness of all the tantric practices engaged within the sphere (mandala) demarcated 
by the network of temples in the region. People may seek to engage in yogic practice 
(sādhana) at a temple, but with the frequent visits of devotees to temples, the necessary 
individual concentration, contemplation, and isolation needed for practice and growth 
are hard for practitioners (sādhakas) to achieve.
Figures 3.1 and 3.2 illustrate the difference between the features of practice at home 
and that at temples. In figure 3.1, we see the respected Teacher of Tantra (Tantācārya), 
Vidyānāth Upādhyāya Bhaṭṭa, together with his wife, engaged in the practices of internal

Professor Vidyanath Upadhyaya Bhatta, together with his wife, Annapurna Upadhyaya Bhatta,

--- PAGE 81 ---
56      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
worship (antar-​yāga). Antar-​yāga practices are categorized by an internal, inward, medita­
tive focus grounded primarily in posture (āsana), breath (prāṇāyāma), internal muscular 
locks (bandhas), concentration (dhyāna), repetition of power-​syllables, (bījamantra-​
japa), and visualization (dhāraṇā) (Flood 1993, passim; Lidke 2005, passim).
Typically—​although not exclusively—​engaged in the privacy of one’s home, antar-​
yāga practices are designed to direct the individual’s consciousness inwardly toward the 
presence of the worshipped-​deities of tantric practice which are understood to reside 
within one’s own subtle body system (sūkṣma-​śarīra). Through this inward-​focused 
practice, one learns to harness the powers of the body and direct them toward desired 
outcomes in the context of one’s spiritual practice (sādhana).
While antar-​yāga practices are typically done privately in domestic spaces, with the 
eyes closed and the gaze directed inwardly, the practices associated with external wor­
ship (bahir-​yāga) typically occur in public spaces like temples and are conducted with 
the eyes open, engaged in practices that require the activation of the sensory organs—​
sight, smell, taste, touch, and hearing—​in conjunction with the tantric rituals designed 
to invoke, install, feed, and honor the deities of the location in which one is worshipping. 
As seen in figure 3.2, the priest of Sarveśvara-​Kumbheśvara Temple, Madhav Shyam 
Sharma, engages the worship of the temple icon with his eyes open and all senses fully 
engaged, focused outwardly. In other words, whereas the directional flow of one’s con­
sciousness is inward in antar-​yāga practices, the directional flow of one’s conscious­
ness in bahir-​yaga is outward. And while antar-​yāga is predicated on the withdrawal 
Figure 3.2.  Temple practice: Priest Madhav Shyam Sharma Rajopadhyaya doing pūjā, 
Kumbheśvara-​Sarveśvara Temple, Patan. Courtesy of Shivesh Sharma Rajopadhyaya.

--- PAGE 82 ---
The Inner and Outer Worship      57
 
and internalization of the sense capacities (pratyāhāra), bahir-​yāga is predicated on the 
outward expansion of the sense capacities through engagement with the tools of ritual 
practice. As seen in figure 3.2, the eyes focus on the image (mūrti) of the deity. The nose 
smells the aromatic senses from the incenses (dhūpa) used in worship. The tongue tastes 
the food and drink offerings made first to the deity and then consumed as a blessing 
(prasādam). The ears hear the bells and mantras that reverberate through the air while 
the hands touch the various objects of one’s worship. Through this open-​eyed, fully sen­
sual engagement with the embodied deity, one seeks to invite into the ritual space the 
presence of tantric deities, thereby establishing it as a power-​seat (śākta-​pītḥa). As a 
power-​seat, the space—​typically a temple—​thus becomes filled with a blessing power 
that benefits all those who come into contact with it.
However, this does not mean that temples are not appropriate for deep spiritual 
practice (sādhana) and that homes are; certainly, even at one’s own home there can 
be hindrances that make the practice difficult. So, both at home and in temples, doing 
sādhana may not be appropriate at all times due to different kinds of disturbances and 
hindrances. This is one of the reasons that, even when priests do have the privilege of 
doing their practice in private with the temple door closed, there is either a distinct 
tantric-​house (āgama-​ghāra) or a special tantric shrine room (āgama-​koṭa) into which 
no one except initiates is allowed to enter at any time. In these designated domestic wor­
ship spaces, the initiates engage the liturgies of both the antar-​ and bahir-​yāgas, under­
standing that both forms are necessary for the completion of tantric sādhana. Indeed, 
these inward-​gazing and outward-​gazing practices are understood to mirror the dyadic 
expression of the supreme goddess herself, who brings creation into being through the 
opening of her eyes only to withdraw creation again at the time of cosmic dissolution 
with the closing of her eyes. And yet here again what is “inside” and what is “outside”? 
That which the goddess projects is done so not outside herself but rather within herself 
as there is nothing that is outside that supreme consciousness which is the ultimate iden­
tity of the goddess. From the perspective of the goddess, all that is projected “outside” as 
the universe is in fact an unfolding of her own being within herself. Within the context 
of a nondual reality, inside and outside are just conventional terms. Nepālī Sarvāmnāya 
Tātrikas seeking the ultimate attainment of spiritual freedom (mokṣa) engage in “in­
ternal” and “external” ritual practices with the aspiration to see as the goddess does, in a 
nondual state in which the distinctions between “inside” and “outside” collapse into the 
singularity of nondual consciousness that is at once within oneself and also manifest ex­
ternally, not just in the tools of worship but the world at large.
Evoking and Installing the Deity
One of the prime differences between practice at home and at temple involves invoking 
(āvāhana) and installing (pratisthā) the deity for the specific practice (yāga). In home 
practice, āvāhana and pratisthā are done in the beginning and then at the end will be

--- PAGE 83 ---

“sky of consciousness” (cidākāśa). This process is not undertaken in temple practice be­

to provide an ideal space for devotees to receive spiritual blessings and make progress in 
their respective sādhanas. Table 3.1 further clarifies the breakdown and overlap of prac­

the Śākta temples in Nepal. Indeed, animal sacrifice is an essential component of

A Union of the Left-​ and  
Right-​Handed Paths
Yet, as a Kaula tantric tradition, one finds that there is flexibility in terms of the use of 
both literal and symbolic sacrifice and offerings in both domestic and temple practice. 
Many Nepālī Tāntrikas integrate both literal and symbolic elements to their practice. 
For instance, in Table 3.1, Dr. Jagman Gurung illustrates one of several ways that Nepālī 
tantric practitioners offer the five forbidden substances (pañcamakāra). In the bamboo 
tray (nāṅglo) one finds rakṣi, a local alcohol made from millet and corresponding to 
madya (typically identified as “wine”), as well as three more of the transgressive 
substances, including red meat (māṃsa), fish (matsya), and pounded grain (mudrā). 
Each of these four substances is literal and is offered by Gurung during his worship. 
However, the fifth element, “sexual union” (maithuna), is not literally present but rather 
is symbolically represented by an egg, the yellow yoke of which is “female” while the 
white outer layer is “male.” Additionally, the fruit on the tray represents the phallus 
(liṅga) while the flower represents the vagina (yoni). In this way the ritual combines 
the actual offerings (pratyakṣa) of four of the forbidden substances together with both 
the symbolic (anukalpa) and actual (pratyakṣa) of sexual union (maithuna) which, in 
addition to its symbolic representation through egg, fruit, and flowers, is embodied in 
literal form with the presence of Gurung’s wife. A Kaula tantric practitioner must have 
an actual consort and therefore literal ritual intercourse (pratyakṣa-​maithuna) typically 
occurs in private. Hence, it is not just in vain that it is said that a Kaula must be married.
