As is written in the Vivekavyākhyā of Tantrāloka (29.96), “Just as a Vedic practitioner 
must be with his wife in Vedic yajña-​yāga, so must he be a Kaulacārya with his wife in 
Kaula practice.”3
Daśain: The Preeminent Tantric 
Festival of Nepal
Additionally, it is important to see how the other communities of Nepal, beyond the 
Newārs of Kathmandu valley, operate and practice tantra in their respective temple and 
domestic lives. Doing so, one recognizes, for example, that the rhythms of domestic and 
temple practice observed in the village of Yāngjākot, where Jagman Gurung performs 
tantric worship (yāga) as the commander-​in-​chief (mir-​umarā-​mukhiyā),4 are structur­
ally similar to the ritual observances found in a majority of villages throughout Nepal.5 
One prime example would be the yāga practices associated with the festival of Daśain.
The festival of Daśain, which includes both the “nine autumnal nights” (śāradīya-​
navarātra) together with the “great victorious tenth day” (vijayā-​daśamī), is not only 
the most significant festival of Nepal but also the most important time for the worship of 
the tantric goddesses (śakti -​upāsanā). Consequently, each year, Jagman Gurung travels 
from Kathmandu to his village to lead the most important ritual sacrifice of the annual 
tantric ritual cycle, the sacrificial worship of the goddesses (śakti-​pūjā-​yāga) of Daśain 
as well as his ancestors (see fig. 3.5).6
A day before the first day of Daśain, on the dark moon night (auṃsī), as head of the 
village, Jagman Gurung engages first in the worship of musical instruments (nagarā-​
pūjā) at his home. Next, an assembled band (nagarcī) takes those instruments to 
the temple at the fort (koṭa) and then, while playing the instruments, circumam­
bulate the village informing everybody that the time of the great festival of Daśain 
has come. At night, Jagman Gurung sows barley (jamarā) in a soil kept on a tray 
made from the leaves of a Sal tree (shorea robusta); this barley grass is then used for 
the worship of the sacrificial animals (bali-​pūjā) on the eighth day (aṣṭami), called 
kālarātri, but mainly on the ninth day (navamī) at the Fort Temple of Goddess Durgā 
(koṭa-​durgā-​maṇḍir).
On the first day of Daśain, called the Establishment of the Water Pot (ghaṭa-​
sthāpanā), Jagman Gurung initially sows the barley to be used on the culminating 
tenth day (vijayā-​daśamī) for the blessing of all the villagers. He also establishes three 
main ritual vessels (kalaśas), respectively, for the goddesses Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, 
and Mahāsarasvatī, with an additional two kalaśas, one on each side for subsidiary 
deities to the right and left (aṅga tathā pārśva devatā). On the seventh day (saptamī), 
he establishes the goddess Durgā (Durgā-​sthāpanā) by placing large, decorated swords 
in the same place where the barley is kept and uses a copper utensil (pāthī)—​inscribed 
by the Kings of Nepal with special authority given to the forefathers of Jagman

--- PAGE 88 ---
The Inner and Outer Worship      63
 
Gurung—​for the worship of the sword (khaḍga-​pūjā) and the attainment of the 
sword (khaḍga-​siddhi). On the eighth day, a goat is sacrificed and meat from the same 
sacrificed goat with wine is served to all those who have come to Jagman Gurung’s 
house for singing the Garland of Auspiciousness (mālaśrī7) hymns from the beginning 
day of the dark night of the moon (auṃsī).
On the ninth day, all the swords and ritual barley grass are taken to the fort-​temple 
(koṭa-​maṇḍir) from the fort-​house (koṭa-​ghar) of Jagman Gurung (see figs. 3.4, 3.5). 
Upon arrival a Brahmin of the Lamichhane family within the Garga Gotra lineage 
invokes an intention-​mantra (saṃkalpa-​mantra), establishing the aims of the worship. 
A Gurung (either Jagman Gurung or his son) from the indigenous community serves 
as the head of the village and as the officiant (kartā) of worship (yāga) who is holding 
the water in his hand in order to firmly establish the intention of the ritual (saṃkalpa). 
Metal smiths (kāmī) and musicians (damāi) from an occupational community (śilpī) 
come to contribute to the festival by sharpening the sword and playing the music. Both 
the ash-​gourd (anukalpa) and a literal (pratyakṣa) buffalo sacrifice are performed. 
Music is played and villagers gather to celebrate. In this way, the ritual integrates mul­
tiple ethnic identities in a shared celebration of the tantric goddesses that combines both 
Sanskritic and vernacular interpretations (Gurung 2010; Timalsina 2006).
On the tenth day (vijayā-​daśamī) a bullet is fired into the air and blessings with tika 
powder on one’s forehead and a jamarā on one’s head are received from Durgā Bhavānī 
and respected elders.
Within the Sarvāmnāya sequence of worship (sarvāmnāya-krama-yāga) associated 
with Durgā, there are two systems of ritual order (pūjā-​krama). The first ritual order 
consists of the following ceremonies: (1) Ekākṣarī Durgā, (2) Aṣṭakṣarī Durgā, (3) 
Jaya Durgā, (4) Navārṇa, and (5) Pañcadaśī. The second ritual order system includes 
(1) Mahākālī, (2) Mahālakṣmī, (3) Mahāsarasvatī, (4) Ugracaṇḍā, and (5) Pañcadaśī. 
Combined together, the entire system is called the Great Perfected Sequence (mahā­
pūrṇakrama).8 Jagman Gurung, who is an initiate (adhikārī) in the practices of Durgā 
from his earliest childhood understands Durgā to be the supreme goddess of the 
Total Revelation (sarvāmnāya-parādevī), especially in her form as Mahālakṣmī.9 The 
Puraścaryārṇava identifies Durgā as “she who is to be worshipped by all the revelations” 
(sarvāmnāyaprapūjitā)10 while the Hāhārāvatantram claims that she is the “great reve­
lation” (mahā-​āmnāya).11
The Three Modes of Tantric Worship
In addition to all the ritual activities of Daśain detailed in the previous section, Jagman 
Gurung additionally engages in the worship of his ancestors (kula-​pitṛ-​pūjā) as well as 
his tutelary deity (kula-​devatā), Śrī Jñāna Caturbhuja Mahākāla, a Buddhist form of Śiva 
specific to his tradition (see fig. 3.6). These rituals are typically conducted on the sev­
enth and eighth day (māhāṣṭami) and are done specifically according to the traditional

--- PAGE 89 ---
64      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
Gurung family method of practice.12 In this context, there is again the incorporation 
of both the symbolic and literal use of the five forbidden substances (pañcamakāra), 
reflecting again that Nepālī tantra is grounded in the Kaula tradition, which integrates 
both the literalism of the left-​handed way together with the symbolic interpretative 
tradition from the right-​handed way. Moreover, the ritual is engaged with an under­
standing of the important tantric concept of the three states of being (tri​bhāva) asso­
ciated with tantric worship. These three existential states are those of a fettered beast 
(paśubhāva), the hero-​state (vīrabhāva), and the divine state (divyabhāva) (Gupta, 
Hoens, and Goudriaan 1979, 72–​73).
Figure 3.6.  Jagman Gurung doing ancestor worship. Courtesy of Jagman Gurung.

--- PAGE 90 ---
The Inner and Outer Worship      65
 
In paśubhāva, the sacrifice (yāga) is done with the mental attitude of duality 
wherein one sees oneself and the deity as distinct beings. In this mode, with de­
votion and discipline, one looks for the grace (anugraha) of the deity so that one 
overcomes the eight impediments of the bound condition (aṣṭapāśa)—​hate (ghṛṇā), 
doubt (śaṅkā), fear (bhaya), shyness (lajjā), abhorrence (jugupsā), clan (kula), ethics 
(śīla), and caste (jāti). In the paśubhāva, one is considered unqualified for the use of 
the literal (pratyakṣa) substances of the pañcamakāra and should only use the sym­
bolic (anukalpa) representations of the five forbidden substances. The emphasis at 
this stage of tantric worship is on the establishment of a high morality (śīla). Indeed, 
one of the most frequently consulted texts in Nepal, the Kulārṇava-​Tantra, warns 
that one must not smell, look at, touch, or eat and drink any meat or wine in the 
paśubhāva stage.13
Only when one is free from the eight impediments (aṣṭapāśa) is one qualified 
(adhikārī) to do the worship in a “heroic-​temperament” (vīrabhāva). In the heroic state, 
the pañcamakāra are utilized in both their literal (pratyakṣa) and symbolic (anukalpa) 
forms. Further, these substances are identified as establishing the seeds for bliss and 
enlightenment.14 In vīrabhāva, the temperament is that of duality-​within-​nonduality 
(dvaitādvaita) affirming both the dualistic and nondualistic perception of reality. In this 
state, the practitioner sees themselves in a nondual relationship with the deity, yet dis­
tinct from others. Indeed, the most predominant bhāva that one sees in Nepālī tantra is 
that of vīrabhāva.
In the highest stage of tantric worship, termed the “divine state” (divyabhāva), even 
the experience of “I” as a deity that distinguishes oneself from others does not remain. 
Instead, there is only the nondual (advaita) perception that everything is nondual and 
perfect in its essence (sarvaṃ sarvātmakam pūrṇah). There is neither necessity nor re­
striction of pañcamakāra in divyabhāva.
The practice of all these bhāvas in Nepal is exhibited in figure 3.7, a photo of the well-​
known practitioner and reputed master of all three bhāvas, Mohani Prasad Koirala, 
affectionately dubbed Viṣṇu Guru by his devotees (at right, with a ritual wine bottle in 
front of him). Specifically, the paśu-​bhāva is demonstrated through the focused med­
itative attention of the practitioners as they gaze into the fire and utter their mantras. 
Vira-​bhāva is represented by the incorporation of symbolic ritual elements such as the 
flowers and ritual vase. And the divya-​bhāva is represented by the literal (pratyakṣa) 
presence of the bottle of wine, highlighting that Koirala is in the highest state of aware­
ness and capable of integrating the literal five forbidden substances into his practice. 
In the state of divya-​bhāva, Koirala integrates both internal meditative practice (antar-​
yāga) with external worship (bahir-​yāga) to achieve the nondual state in which the 
distinctions between “inner” and “outer” collapse as the worshipper becomes the deity 
worshipped.
The practice of the three tantric states of consciousness (tri​bhāvas) in association 
with the five forbidden substances (pañcamakāra) is directly linked to the impor­
tance of the five elements (pañca-​tattvas), which are earth (pṛthvī), water (āpas), fire 
(agni), air (vayu), and space (ākāśa) (Woodroffe [1929] 2009, 553–​607). In the context

--- PAGE 91 ---
66      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
of tantric ritual practice, in which the practitioner seeks to experience his own body 
as a microcosm of the cosmos itself, which is composed of nothing more than the 
five elements, a correspondence (bandha) is set up between each of the five forbidden 
substances and each of the five elements: meat (māṃsa) represents earth (pṛthvī), fish 
(matsya) represents water (āpas), wine (madya) represents fire (agni), bread made 
from pounded grains represent air (bārā for Newārs sel-​roṭī for Gurungs), and finally 
the egg or fruit and flower are used as a symbol for sexual union (maithuna) which 
represents space (ākāśa). The practice of the pañca-​tattva with the direct usage of 
pañca-​makāra within one’s own body (which is made of pañca-​tattva itself) is foun­
dational for the establishment of the nondual state that is the highest aim of Nepālī 
Sarvāmnāya tantra. Further, it is precisely in this practice that kuṇḍalinī-yoga is highly 
developed in Nepal (Sapkota 2022; Lamichhane 2018).
The Fivefold Sequential Worship
Fundamental to all of these tantric practices, the fivefold system of practice (pañca-​
krama-​yāga) in Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra is given a high significance. In fact, in the 
system of practice associated with Kālī, the Kālī-​Kula, it is of utmost importance. As 
one of the most predominant texts in Nepālī tantra, the Mahākāla-​Saṃhitā15 says of 
Guhyakālī: she is nondual (advaitāṃ), supreme bliss (paramānandāṃ), eternal (nityā), 
Figure 3.7.  Viṣṇu Guru (on right) with disciples at Guhyeśvarī temple. Courtesy of 
L. S. Akshunna.

--- PAGE 92 ---
The Inner and Outer Worship      67
 
pure-​absolute (śuddhāṃ), and immaculate (nirañjanām). She is the Secret Kālī, 
Guhyakālī, nondistinct from the Supreme Goddess Parā Devī, having the nature of cre­
ation (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti), destruction (saṃhāra), inexpressibility (anākhyā), 
and bhāsā (immeasurable potentiality) as her nature. She is understood to reside at 
the center of the fivefold process of creation (madhyastha-​pañca -​krama) (see fig. 3.8). 
Further she is identified as the essence of the Five Great Statements (pañcamahāvākya) 
of nondual Vedānta: i) “the supreme reality is all that is” (oṃ tat sat), ii) “I am that ul­
timate reality” (so’ham asmi), iii) “I am Brahman” (ahaṃ brahmāsmi), iv) “I am this 
truth” (tat sat ahameva), and v) “I am all this” (ahamevedaṃ sarvam).16 The Mahākāla-​
Saṃhitā17 further states that these great sayings (mahāvākyas) are the means for instil­
lation of the deity (nyāsa) and that this nyāsa is itself the means of worship (yāga). In 
other words, the essence of the practice is to achieve through direct bodily experience 
the perception of nondual awareness that is captured in the mahāvākyas themselves.
While engaging in the fivefold sequential worship, the Nepālī Sarvāmnāya Tāntrika 
seeks to cultivate qualities like integration (samanvaya), harmony (sahacāra), and com­
passionate equitability (samabhāva) in both domestic (antar) and temple (bahir) forms 
of practice. Nepal’s domestic and temple yāga practice bases its experiential rhythms on 
these five prime processes discussed above. Table 3.2 provides a summary of Nepālī yāga 
practice.

L. S. Akshunna.

The Integration of Kālī and 
Tripurasundarī in the Tantra of 
Nepāla-​Maṇḍala
With the prominence of Kālī-​Kula discussed herein, it would be inaccurate to assume 
that the Śrī-​Kula has no space in Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantric practice. Indeed, the 
traditions of Śrī-​Kula, also known as Śrī Vidyā, are equally prevalent in Nepal and are 
so intimately integrated into Kālī-​Kula that for the majority of Sarvāmnāya Tāntrikas 
Kālī and Tripurasundarī are understood as just two names for one supreme god­
dess (Dyczkowski 1989; Lidke 2017). The Vaḍavānala-​tantra, for instance, states that 
there is no difference between Caṇḍayogeśvarī (Guhyakālī) and Mahātripurāsundarī, 
and that one who differentiates them will go to hell.18 In fact, even in the Parātantra, 
a recognized Kālī-​Kula text, the designation of “total revelation” (sarvāmnāya) is 
given to the goddess Mahātripurāsundarī of the Śrī Vidyā above all other deities. The 
reason for this is that Mahātripurāsundarī is identified with the Upper Transmission, 
the ūrdhvāmnāya, which is the scriptural transmission associated with the upper face 
or īśāna-​mukha of Lord Paśupati. The mantra of Īśāna can be rendered as “the lord 
of all knowledge, beings, study, and devotion”—​in other words it is the lord of all the 
āmnāyas (sarvaāmnāyaīśvara).19
At the Paśupatinātha temple, daily worship is conducted by the main Bhaṭṭa priest 
who uses blessed sandalwood to draw the preeminent symbol of the Śrī-​Kula, the 
śrīyantra—​identified as the supreme body (parārūpa) of Tripurasundarī (Brooks 
1992, 115)—​atop the formless īśāna-​mukha (upward face) of the five-​faced icon of Lord 
Paśupati (paśupati-​pañca-​mukhaliṅga). As it is strictly prohibited to take photos within 
the Paśupatinātha temple, figure 3.9 presents a photo from the Sarveśvara-​Kumbheśvara 
temple in Patan. In the photo, we see the placing of a copper śrīyantra cap upon the 
upper face (īśāna-​mukha) of the śiva-​liṇga. While this śrīyantra is not inscribed in san­
dalwood, as at Paśupatinātha temple, the ritual intention and statement here are the

same. The point is to demonstrate that the Śrī-​Kula is to be identified with the Upper 
Transmission of the Sarvāmnāya system. The important ritual text, the Meditation on the 
Great Lord of the Beasts (Mahāpaśupati-​dhyāna), clearly states that the worship of the 
upward face of the śivaliṅga is to include the placing of a śrīyantra for its completion.20 
This practice of the Śrī Viydā tradition involving the śrīyantra is prevalent throughout 
Nepal, with its origins in the western region of the Khas kingdom and its roots deeply 
established in the Kathmandu valley (Lidke 2023; Maskarinec 1999). Indeed, the sixty-​
four-​fold initiation sequence (krama-​dīkṣā) practices of Śrī Vidyā are foundational to 
the entire system of Sarvāmnāya tantra.21
Conclusion
The interwoven rhythms of domestic and temple practice in Nepal operate under an in­
digenous logic of unity-​within-​multiplicity (bhedhābheda-​vāda), grounded in the the­
ological perception that one supreme goddess has manifested herself as an embodied 
cosmos (kula), replete with a multiplicity of tantric gods and goddesses who in turn are 
embedded in the lands, shrines, and homes of Nepāla-​Maṇḍala. Just as that Goddess 
projects creation internally onto the screen of her own being, thus playfully exhibiting 
Figure 3.9.  Śriyantra on the Ūrdhvāmnāya of the śivaliṅga of Sarveśvara (Kumbheśvara) 
Temple, Patan. Courtesy of Shivesh Sharma Rajopadhyaya.

--- PAGE 95 ---
70      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
that “inside” and “outside” are mutually interwoven, necessary, relative, and comple­
mentary facets of divine consciousness, so Nepālī tāntrikas intertwine internally fo­
cused meditative and visual practices (antar-​yāga) together with externally oriented 
liturgical exercises (bahir-​yāga) in both their domestic and temple contexts. Whether 
inwardly focused or outwardly focused, and whether in the privacy of their home 
shrine-​rooms or in public display in a temple courtyard or other communal ritual con­
text, these tantric practitioners—​be they lay adepts or temple priests—​share a common 
caste-​transcendent identity as adherents of Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra, the Tantra of 
the Total Revelation, being the composite revelatory system of the six transmissions 
(ṣaḍāmnāya) associated with the six faces of their Lord Paśupati.
This historically grounded tradition is not simply the collection of texts at Nepal’s 
National Archives but a coordinated system of practices that interweave private 
and public ritual cultural patterns, enabling its adherents to perceive themselves as 
participants within a larger mandala of shared meaning—​one in which each of them is 
trained through ritual practice to recognize the essential teachings prescribed through 
the revelations found in their respective scriptural sources.
Nepal provides for scholars of tantra an invaluable opportunity to not just read care­
fully preserved manuscripts but also to meet, observe, and learn from living adherents 
of a genuine, fully developed tantric system. In Nepal, one finds initiated, informed 
tāntrikas engaged in a network of domestic and temple practices and committed to the 
preservation of their tradition, not just by passing it on to their own sons and daughters, 
but also to non-​Nepālīs who have sincere interest in the tradition. Just as the Supreme 
Goddess Parāśakti abides in a state of being transcendent to the dualistic ideologies that 
distinguish “internal” from “external,” so Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas today recognize 
that the preservation of their cultural mandala necessitates the bringing of the inside out 
through the allowing of the outside in.
