Chapter 4
On the Union of 
Emptiness and Bliss
Buddhist Thought and Tantric Practice
Paul B. Donnelly
What Is Buddhist Thought?
Buddhism thrived in India for more than a thousand years before its demise in the 
fourteenth century. By that time, it had spread to most of the surrounding countries 
of Central, East, and Southeast Asia. A body of thought, practice, and institutions 
that endured over such a long period of time and geographic and cultural expanse ob­
viously evinced a great deal of evolution and variety from its earlier forms, which are 
themselves more diverse than later tradition and modern understandings are often ac­
knowledged.1 The final major developments in India established tantric Buddhism, or 
the Vajrayāna, as the pinnacle of Buddhist thought, practiced by wilderness-​dwelling 
yogis and monastery-​dwelling scholar monks alike. While authoritative Vajrayāna texts 
and teachers would typically assert that these new doctrines and practices were as much 
grounded in the teachings of the Buddha as more familiar doctrines such as dependent 
origination, the Four Noble Truths and selflessness, even a cursory reading of the tantras 
and their attendant commentaries and practice manuals reveal a Buddhist worldview 
that can seem to the outsider difficult to reconcile with such core teachings.
In order to engage in an examination of Buddhist thought and tantric practice, we 
need to first establish a working sense of what these two elements, familiar Buddhist 
doctrines and less familiar tantric teachings, mean. Tantric practice is quite di­
verse across different tantric cycles and meditative systems such as Mahāmūdra and 
Dzokchen (rdzogs chen), not to mention unique lineages of teachers and subsequent re­
vealed teachings such as “treasure texts” (gter ma). We will have more to say about tan­
tric practice later, but for now it suffices to note that late Indian Buddhism and Tibetan 
Buddhism came to accept the complex yogas of the Highest Yoga Tantra consisting

--- PAGE 101 ---
76      Paul B. Donnelly
 
broadly of techniques to cultivate purified states of subjectivity such as the visualiza­
tion of oneself as an awakened tantric deity and techniques that meditatively worked 
with the subtle body consisting of “winds” or energies (prāṇa) in order to produce a 
blissful nondual subjectivity that takes the ultimate nature of things as its object and 
leads quickly to full enlightenment. The Mahāyāna path to Buddhahood is tradition­
ally said to comprise two components, method and wisdom, and these practices are the 
method side of this system.
The second component, wisdom, is the realization of ultimate truth, the direct gnosis 
of reality as it is. That which the mind of great bliss knows in nondual gnosis is what is 
taught in the numerous sūtras and śāstras of the Mahāyāna. In order to examine the re­
lationship between Mahāyāna Buddhist thought and tantric practice, we first trace the 
stages by which Mahāyāna thought developed, and the different ways of interpreting 
those developments.
Mahāyāna Thought
By the early centuries of the common era, numerous new texts (though their proponents 
would assert that they were not new) were circulating in the Indian Buddhist world. 
While accepting the Four Noble Truths, and so on, as legitimate as far as they went, there 
were now texts that asserted that those teachings were in fact a lesser vehicle or path 
(Hīnayāna) that were surpassed by new teachings that were greater–​the Mahāyāna.2 
This Mahāyāna, it was said, was the ultimate Buddhist path, the one that Śākyamuni 
himself tread and that took him to complete, perfect awakening. Many pages have been 
filled attempting to define, delimit, and explain what this greater path is and how it came 
to be, both in Buddhist texts and in modern works in Buddhist studies. Paul Williams’ 
volume (2009) is an authoritative and accessible overview of the modern scholarship 
on this very broad topic, but for our purposes I offer Joseph Walser’s (2018) concise set 
of themes typical of Mahāyāna thought: “there is a limited set of themes that recur in 
different combinations across time and space, coalescing around the term ‘Mahāyāna,’ 
namely: 1) emptiness, 2) mind-​only, 3) non-​discriminating or non-​cognizing awareness, 
4) ‘perfection of wisdom,’ and 5) bodhicitta” (Walser 2018, 10).
The five themes suggested by Walser are a good place to start in presenting, admit­
tedly briefly, core teachings of the Mahāyāna, which are considered to be fundamental 
to the Vajrayāna. Not all of them are pervasive through the major Mahāyāna Sūtras, or 
even the Perfection of Wisdom corpus itself, but between those sūtras, the Madhyamaka 
śāstras, the fundamental sūtras associated with a Yogācāra, the Dharmas of Maitreya 
(byams chos sde lnga),3 and their commentaries, they lay out and extensively develop 
these themes.
The well-​informed reader will likely notice that Walser does not include a few concepts 
that many introductory books on Mahāyāna and practitioner-​oriented works often in­
clude. For instance, there is no mention here of compassion, skillful means, an emphasis

--- PAGE 102 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      77
 
on devotion, and the highly developed system of bodies of the Buddha that arises from 
the Ornament of Realization (Abhisamayālaṅkāra) commentary on the Perfection of 
Wisdom corpus, and Yogācāra texts. The last one will be treated in what follows as it is 
important in Vajrayāna, but the previous ones, although important, will not be given 
much consideration given the time/​space constraints in a chapter of this kind. And, they 
are not as particularly pertinent for the subject matter examined in this chapter.
As tantric Buddhism considers itself to be Mahāyāna, these themes are similarly 
central to its thought and practice, and in a similar move to the Mahāyāna in regard 
to the “Hīnayāna,” Vajrayāna texts will claim to be the pinnacle of Buddhist thought 
and practice. As we will see, there are different strategies for this move: some assert that 
Mahāyāna doctrine is Vajrayāna doctrine (differing only in practice); others will say 
that while Mahāyāna thought is the foundation of Vajrayāna, its ultimate view is actu­
ally higher than Mahāyāna, or requires a unique understanding of Mahāyāna. It should 
be noted here that what follows will privilege the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras that are 
the most important to tantric Buddhism. This leaves out a great many texts that have 
been hugely influential across Asia, particularly East Asia. The Lotus Sūtra, the Flower 
Garland Sūtra, and the Pure Land Sūtras were not accorded a great deal of attention in 
tantric Buddhism, so they are not considered here.
Questions of Origin
As new texts arose, their adherents were in a position to have to defend their authenticity 
to those who did not accept them. The mere fact that they were unknown to most of the 
monks and nuns of the various Buddhist schools needed explaining. As mentioned in 
the previous section, the proponents of these new sutras did not regard them as new 
at all. They asserted that, at least in the case of the most important of these texts, the 
Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras, the explanation was that they were taught by the Buddha 
but fell out of favor due to their profundity and were lost to this world. According to 
Mahāyāna tradition and recorded in the histories of the great Tibetan historians Butön 
(Bu-​ston Rin-​chen Grub 1931, 122–​125), and Tārānātha (1980, 106–​108), Nāgārjuna 
recovered them from the serpentine beings, the nāgas, who had protected them in their 
realm beneath the sea. Not that a belief in the possibility of such things was unknown in 
early-​first-​millennium India, but one could imagine that the story would not have con­
vinced everyone. Modern Western scholarship has not found this explanation compel­
ling either. For the academic field of Buddhist studies finding the Mahāyāna’s origins has 
long been a desideratum, and an elusive one at that. Boucher (2021) noted that the two 
predominant theories are that it originated among lay communities based around tra­
ditional cultic centers or was the produce of monastic communities around particular 
scriptures of teachers.
Walser (2018) tackled this problem, and it is impossible to do the argument justice 
here, but in the introduction the author succinctly stated his thesis. “the Perfection of

--- PAGE 103 ---
78      Paul B. Donnelly
 
Wisdom was probably composed near the royal seat outside of Mathura sometime in 
the latter part of the first century ce by a Sarvāstivādin monk who was born and raised 
a Maitrāyaṇi Brahmin” (9). Walser argues that the puzzling doctrinal assertions in the 
opening verses of the eight-​thousand-​line Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra reflect concepts 
and turns of phrase that were prominent in the thought of that Vedic branch.
Walser has argued in his book and in a number of articles that the idea of “Buddhist 
Brahmins” was not seen as in any way contradictory or problematic in the early 
centuries of Buddhism, only becoming so much later.4 This willingness to push beyond 
the presuppositions held both by Buddhists and much of Buddhist scholarship is ad­
mirable, and hopefully signals a change in the prevailing winds. In his chapter in this 
volume, Payne urges “embracing the methodological orientation in which traditions are 
no longer conceptualized as closed systems, idealized in conformity with authoritative 
doctrine, and selectively represented by instances most closely adhering to that ideali­
zation. Moving away from decontextualized and ahistorical representations means also 
that the study of tantra can engage models of contact, interaction, and change.” This 
applies equally to the seemingly monolithic categories “Hinduism” and “Buddhism.”
Paradigmatic Mahāyāna Sūtras
The Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras became and have remained an important cata­
lyst for much of the subsequent developments of Buddhist thought in India and be­
yond. Conze (1975) established the model for how modern scholarship has seen how 
this corpus developed over time. After the 8,000-​line text, the texts expanded to larger 
versions of up to 100,000 verses and then there was a period of the production of more 
contracted versions from 2,500 verses, down to 300 (The Diamond Sūtra), to 25 (The 
Heart Sutra), all the way down to one syllable (“A”) (Conze 1975, xi). There have been 
some reconsiderations of this history of the corpus, but it still remains largely accepted. 
Conze also asserts that the first forty verses of the text (covering the first chapter 
and beginning of the second chapter) are the earliest portion, with the subsequent 
verses being gradually added later over time. This view too has been revisited but has 
remained widely accepted. New discoveries of texts or epigraphical evidence could of 
course change this.
It is often said that the central teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras is that of 
emptiness. Emptiness is said to be the extension of the non-​Mahāyāna teaching of self­
less to the skandhas that are the basis of the imputation of the putative “self” and further 
even to the dharmas that at least the non-​Mahāyāna Sarvāstivāda school considered to 
be the ultimately existent. They are “empty” specifically in the sense that they lack the 
intrinsic existence or own-​nature (svabhāva) that make them uniquely what they are. In 
Madhyamaka, literally “Middle Way” texts, which are considered to be the philosoph­
ical working out of this concept and which we will consider later, this comes to mean 
that everything, from selves down to dharmas, lack a causally independent ultimately

--- PAGE 104 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      79
 
real existence. As perhaps conceptually challenging as the preceding may be, it is clearer 
than what the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras themselves give us.
Emptiness is certainly expressed, but usually along with signlessness (ānimitta) and 
wishlessness (apraṇihita). That trio constitutes the “three doors of liberation” known also to 
the non-​Mahāyāna. The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines opens with a discus­
sion between Subhūti, who speaks “by the Buddha’s might” and Śāriputra, who speaks from 
the perspective of the Abhidharma traditions of the early schools. Asked by the Buddha 
“what dharma does that word ‘Bodhisattva’ denote?” Subhūti responds “I do not, O Lord, 
see that dharma ‘Bodhisattva,’ nor a dharma called ‘perfect wisdom.’ What Bodhisattva 
shall I instruct and admonish in what perfect wisdom?” After identifying the true bodhi­
sattva as who is not terrified by this truth, Subhūti continues, “When a Bodhisattva courses 
in Perfect Wisdom and develops it, he should train himself that he does not pride himself 
on that thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta). That thought is no thought, since in its es­
sential original nature thought is transparently numinous” (Conze 1975, 83–​84).
In just these few opening verses of this paradigmatic sutra, we can see most of the 
themes that Walser sees as characterizing the Mahāyāna in general. The phrase “form 
is empty” appears later in the first chapter, but as something that the bodhisattva should 
not meditate on. The term “emptiness” does not appear until the second chapter, and 
there only appearing in a long list of ideas on which a bodhisattva “does not take a stand.” 
Three of the remaining four of Walser’s themes are expressed here in these first few verses. 
Subhūti’s not seeing can be understood to be nondiscriminating or noncognizing aware­
ness, perfect wisdom is a “thought that is no thought,’ and it seems that it is related, or 
equivalent to “that thought of enlightenment” (bodhicitta). Furthermore, the reason that 
thought is no thought is that it is “transparently luminous.” Walser translates the Sanskrit 
(prakṛtiś cittasya prabhāsvarā), “The original substance/​nature (prakṛti) of thought is 
clear light,” and observes, that “The introduction of the term prakṛti renders the thought­
less thought to be a kind of ‘original’ or even ‘foundational’ consciousness that is any case 
more fundamental than awareness as it is usually understood” (Walser 2018, 198).
“Mind-​only” is not explicitly stated here, but even the Madhyamaka author Bhāviveka 
presented both Madhyamaka and Yogācāra (sometimes called Cittamātra or “Mind-​
Only”), as grounded in a certain reading of the same core passages of the Perfection of 
Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines (Walser 2018, 116). Anyone acquainted with tantric 
Buddhist thought and praxis will find the term “clear light” or “natural luminosity” 
quite familiar. Though elucidated here, this concept will be greatly expanded on in the 
Yogācāra interpretation of the Perfection of Wisdom corpus, which is central to tantric 
thought and practice.
The other most important Mahāyāna sutra for the development of the Mahāyāna 
thought that undergirds Vajrayāna thought and practice is the Discourse Explaining 
the Thought (Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra). The text was probably composed between the 
second and fourth centuries and was the first attempt to develop a hermeneutic for 
interpreting the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras according to Yogācāra doctrine, which 
perhaps was developed by a community of practitioners particularly dedicated to med­
itation, as the name “Yogācāra” (practice of yoga) implies (Keenan 2000, 1). It has also

--- PAGE 105 ---
80      Paul B. Donnelly
 
been observed that Yogācāra developed against the backdrop of Abhidharmic analyses 
of mind and mental functions (Germano and Waldron 2006).
The Discourse Explaining the Thought is a relatively brief and systematic text that 
clearly demonstrates a self-​awareness of the novelty of Mahāyāna thought in the 
Buddhist world and explains exactly how and why the Buddha deployed different 
teachings over time to lead his followers stepwise according to their preparedness for 
the highest view. The Pali Canon sutta in which the Buddha teaches the foundational 
teachings of the Four Noble Truths Path is entitled The Setting in Motion of the Wheel 
of Dharma,5 and this metaphor of turning the wheel is found throughout Pali texts. In 
the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the gods exclaim that the Perfection 
of Wisdom teachings are a “second turning of the wheel of doctrine” (Conze 1975, 150–​
151) which, in typical Perfection of Wisdom style, the Buddha negates. Nonetheless, the 
Discourse Explaining the Thought assumes this and takes it further, saying that the first 
two Turnings of the Wheel were provisional and delivered for specific purposes, but 
that the Discourse is the Third Turning and is the final definitive teaching of the Buddha 
(Powers 1995, 139–​140; and Keenan 2000, 49).
Central to these assertions is the traditional division of the scriptures into those that are 
definitive (nītārtha) and those that are provisional (neyārtha). The Discourse Explaining 
the Thought says that the First Turning was given by the Buddha for those Aryan disciples 
on the Hearer (śrāvaka) vehicle. These teachings were “wondrous” but were in need of 
further elucidation (neyārtha) and could serve as a source of misunderstanding and dis­
pute. While they taught selflessness, they did not go far enough. From the Mahāyāna per­
spective these teachings could lead to an overly realist understanding of the fundamental 
constituents of the phenomenal world, the dharmas. The Second Turning, which includes 
the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, was for Mahāyāna disciples. It was “more wondrous still,” 
but though it taught the emptiness of all dharmas, their being unarisen, unceasing, and 
naturally in the state of nirvāṇa, it too was in need of clarification (neyārtha). From the 
perspective of this text and the Yogācāra tradition, the problem with the Second Turning 
teachings was that there was the risk of overnegating and falling into nihilism, thus pro­
viding an easy target for refutation. The Third Turning was “exceedingly wondrous” and 
for those of all vehicles. It included all previous teachings but made fine distinctions that 
clarify them and established their definitive meaning (nītārtha) and could not lead to 
disputes. The Discourse itself is of course, in this category, but subsequent traditions would 
place other teachings into this category according to their doctrinal stance.
The teaching that is presented as definitive is a clarification and refinement of the 
statements about emptiness in the Second Turning that save those teachings from 
accusations of nihilism and truly lead to Buddhahood. This is the doctrine of the “three 
natures.” The first aspect, soteriologically but not ontologically, is the imagined or 
conceptualized nature (parikalpitasvabhāva). The world of experience consisting of 
subjects and objects is in fact constructed and imputed by conceptual thought. These are 
in fact “only perceptions” (vijñaptimātra). The dualistic, putative world of subjects and 
objects does not exist, but this does not mean there is literally and ultimately nothing at all.
Both the constructing, imputing perception, and its objects arise from the nondual, 
dependently arisen causal flow of dharmas. This is the second nature, called the

--- PAGE 106 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      81
 
dependent (paratantrasvabhāva). It is both “what remains” after the meditatively 
realized emptiness of the imagined nature is seen and the dependently arisen ground 
from which both bondage and liberation arise. It can’t be said to be “existent” or “nonex­
istent” (or anything else) as such dichotomous concepts are nothing but constructions 
of perception. The dependent nature tends toward the generation of ignorance and suf­
fering of the beings in it due to their ignorance of the true nature of things, but it also 
makes possible the eradication of ignorance and suffering through the realization of the 
absence of the imagined nature in the dependent nature. This absence, or rather its re­
alization, is said to be the perfected nature (pariniṣpannasvabhāva). It is emptiness. Put 
another way, the imagined nature and the perfected nature are the two possible experi­
ential orientations on the dependent nature. The ordinary experience of the dependent 
nature through the erroneous constructions of the imagined nature is saṃsāra, while 
the nondual experience of the flow free from those constructions, the perfected nature, 
is nirvāṇa. This idea of a nondual ultimate ground, along with the related Yogācāra idea 
of a storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), is further developed in the śāstra texts, 
and is fundamental to much of tantric Buddhist thought and practice.6
The Treatises of the Two Openers of 
the Great Chariot Way
While the Mahāyāna Sūtras discussed previously were seen as the canonical texts 
establishing the core Mahāyāna doctrines in late Indian scholastic Buddhism and 
Tibetan Buddhism, these have nearly always been approached through the two exeget­
ical traditions of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra. These two textual traditions are frequently 
referred to in Tibetan Buddhism to this day as “the two traditions of the great chariot”; 
that is, the Mahāyāna and the two founders of these traditions are revered as almost 
as highly as the Buddha himself. The first, whom we have already encountered in the 
mythical origin story of the discovery of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras is Nāgārjuna. 
Nagārjuna’s treatises and their commentaries form the foundation of the Madhyamaka 
philosophical tradition.7 The other is Asaṅga. Asaṅga is the author of several seminal 
Yogācāra works but traditionally, he is even more important for his part in the revelation 
of the teachings of the future Buddha Maitreya, known as the Five Dharmas of Maitreya.
Nāgārjuna and the Madhyamaka 
Treatises
In addition to his legendary retrieval of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras from the nāgas, 
Nāgārjuna (second century ce) composed a number of texts that have been hugely in­
fluential across the Mahāyāna Buddhist traditions. According to Tibetan traditions,

--- PAGE 107 ---
82      Paul B. Donnelly
 
Nāgārjuna’s texts can be grouped into three collections: the collection of argumentative 
texts (rigs tshogs), the collection of advice (gtam thogs), and the collection of hymns (bstod 
tshogs).8 While the latter two are highly regarded by tradition and have attracted some 
modern scholarly attention, it is the argumentative works that are regarded as expressing 
the heart of Madhyamaka thought and have attracted extensive attention in modern 
scholarship. Among the argumentative works, it is the Root Stanzas on the Middle Way 
(Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, or MMK) that is generally regarded as Nāgārjuna’s mas­
terwork.9 The text is extant in Sanskrit, and was translated early on into Chinese and 
Tibetan. The opening salutary verse of Root Stanzas announces the text’s purpose:
I salute the Fully Enlightened One, the best of orators, who taught the doctrine of 
dependent origination, according to which there is neither cessation nor origination, 
neither annihilation nor the eternal, neither singularity nor plurality, neither coming 
nor going [of any dharma, for the purpose of nirvāṇa characterized by] the auspi­
cious cessation of hypostatization. (Siderits and Katsura 2013, 13)
The Root Stanzas consists of twenty-​seven chapters, each examining a core Buddhist 
doctrinal concept. In every case, the concept under consideration is assumed to be ul­
timately real by some rival Buddhist school, but it is revealed by Nāgārjuna’s argument 
to be without reality in any ultimate sense, being in fact nothing more than a conceptual 
construction. By revealing that each concept only exists dependently, it is declared to 
be empty (śūnya). The world appears to the senses and the mind as composed of real, 
independent entities, but although this might be true from the conventional perspec­
tive (samvrtti), it is revealed to be ultimately (paramārtha) false. Nāgārjuna states that 
distinguishing between these two modes of knowing is crucial to understanding the 
teachings of the Buddha and for understanding what Nāgārjuna is doing in the Root 
Stanzas. Realizing ultimate truth is what brings the attainment of nirvana.
Several of the early commentaries on the Root Stanzas were by important masters 
traditionally understood to belong to the Yogācāra school, so the very idea of exclu­
sive, competing philosophical schools should be treated cautiously.10 Only a few of the 
commentaries, however, endured and influenced the development of Madhyamaka 
schools of thought in China and Tibet. The extant Sanskrit text is embedded in 
Candrakīrti’s seventh-​century commentary, which was translated into Tibetan in the 
eleventh century. In Tibet, and in much of Western scholarship, Nāgārjuna’s text has 
been seen through the lens of Candrakīrti’s interpretation and frequently through the 
further interpretative lens of the commentaries of the Geluk sect of Tibetan Buddhism, 
though this is beginning to change with recent works on Madhyamaka as understood by 
important figures in Sākya, Kagyü, Nyingma, and Jonang orders.11
The final verse of an Indian treatise of this sort can also conclude or restate the pur­
port of all that came before it. Though the two major Indian commentators, Bhāviveka 
and Candrakīrti, take the current twenty-​seven-​chapter version of the MMK to be 
entirely composed by Nāgārjuna, some modern scholars have asserted that the final 
two chapters were later additions by another author. If this were so, the final verse of

--- PAGE 108 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      83
 
chapter twenty-​five, “An Analysis of Nirvāṇa,” should be expected to tell us about the 
intent of the work. “This halting of cognizing everything, the halting of hypostatizing, 
is blissful. No Dharma whatsoever was ever taught by the Buddha to anyone” (Siderits 
and Katsura 2013, 304). This verse clearly echoes the dedicatory verse, though the 
translation here obscures this slightly in that the same phrase (prapañcopaśamaḥ 
śivaḥ) appears in both verses. In the dedicatory verse, it is translated “the auspicious 
cessation of hypostatization.” This attainment of the blissful nonconceptual reality is 
nirvāṇa. Subsequent developments in Mahāyāna thought will elaborate on this idea, 
as will the Vajrayāna.
As we continue to establish the foundations of Mahāyāna thought upon which Vajrayāna 
thought and practice build, we can profitably return to Walser’s five themes to see which 
are developed in Madhyamaka, and specifically in the Nāgārjuna’s Root Stanzas. The reader 
will recall that “emptiness” is not treated in any developed way in the earliest portions of the 
Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, but it is certainly consistent with Subhūti’s 
not seeing the dharmas “Bodhisattva” or “Perfect Wisdom.” It is pervasive in the Root Verses 
and the other argumentative works of Nāgārjuna that the Mahāyāna concept of emptiness 
takes on its fully developed sense. Nondiscriminating or noncognizing awareness seems to 
be expressed in Nāgārjuna’s praise of the Buddha as having taught the “auspicious or blissful 
halting of hypostatization.” Neither “perfection of wisdom” nor “bodhicitta” is discussed, or 
even mentioned in the Root Stanzas, and not surprisingly, “mind-​only” is never mentioned. 
More positive representations are found, however, in the texts in the collection of advice 
texts and the hymns. But these are not the texts that are most celebrated or most influential 
in most late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism. These traditions typically look to the teachings 
of the Five Dharmas of Maitreya and the commentaries (śāstras) of Asaṅga where these 
other, complementary themes are developed.
Asaṅga and the Five Dharmas  
of Maitreya
Like the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras, the teachings that are the foundation of Yogācāra 
thought were held by their proponents to be “word of the Buddha.” Unlike in the case 
of the “rediscovery” of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras from the Nāga realm, the Five 
Dharmas of Maitreya were not taught by the Buddha Ṡakyamūni but rather the fu­
ture Buddha Maitreya. In the widely known legend, Asaṅga longed to meet the future 
Buddha Maitreya in order to learn the teachings of the Mahāyāna, so he entered a cave 
to meditate. Not having had a vision after many years, Asaṅga gave up, but when he was 
overwhelmed by compassion for a suffering dog along the road, the dog was revealed 
to be Maitreya himself. Asaṅga’s perception had been purified by this act of kindness. 
Maitreya took Asaṅga in Tuṣita, where he was taught the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras, 
the Foundation for Yoga Practitioners (Yogācārabhūmi), and other Mahāyāna sūtras.

--- PAGE 109 ---
84      Paul B. Donnelly
 
He then asked Maitreya to compose a treatise to reveal the meaning of these texts, so 
Maitreya taught him the Five Dharmas.12
Butön’s fourteenth-​century account further says that at the time of the birth of Asaṅga 
(and his half-​brother Vasubandhu) the dharma was under attack in India, so their 
mother resolved to have sons to defend and spread it. The dharma in question is specif­
ically said to be “the Abhidharma which is the foundation of the teaching.” Tārānatha’s 
seventeenth-​century account does not foreground Abhidharma as explicitly but does 
say that his mother, because of her past life as a scholar monk, knew and understood the 
sūtras and Abhidharma and urged her son(s) to spread the doctrine. Asaṅga studied 
and understood the sūtras of the three piṭakas and most of the Mahāyāna sūtras but 
found it difficult to understand the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras. His quest for a vision 
of Maitreya was specifically to know the meaning of these texts. In Tuṣita, he learned the 
“real significance of the whole collection of sūtras,” culminating in the Five Dharmas of 
Maitreya.
European and American scholarship on Yogācāra has lagged behind that on 
Madhyamaka and the two schools of thought have largely been seen as rival Mahāyana 
movements, though this has begun to change in the last few decades.13 In East Asian 
scholarship, Yogācāra has received significantly more scholarly attention and has 
been seen as more continuous than discontinuous with Madhyamaka.14 Consistent 
with what traditional accounts suggest about Yogācāra, modern scholarship has 
largely contextualized it as being responsive to Abhidharmic and Madhyamaka 
developments, as well as systematizing a Mahāyāna path system and developing notions 
of Buddhahood. (Waldron 2013).
The heart of the revelation of the bodhisattva Maitreya to Asaṅga is considered by 
the Tibetan traditions to be the Five Dharmas (byams chos sde lnga).15 These traditions 
agree on the five texts that make up this corpus, but there are significant differences 
in how they fit together and what their final intent is. The idea of the “Five Dharmas” 
seems to have been established by the sixth century in India and to have taken root in 
China by that time, though with only partial agreement with the Tibetan traditions 
on which texts constituted the collection (Turenne 2015). Though it appears that 
only three of the five texts were known in Tibet by the end of the early propagation of 
Buddhism,16 the established collection of five was known early in the second propaga­
tion, was included in the Tibetan collection of the śāstras, the Tengyur (bstan ‘gyur). 
It became the topic of extensive discussion as to whether they formed a single work, 
they shared a common intent, and how they should be understood to be ordered 
(Turenne 2015).17 These texts are the Ornament of Realization (Abhisamayālaṁkāra), 
the Ornament of Mahāyāna Sūtras (Mahayānasūtrālaṅkāra), Distinguishing be­
tween the Middle and Extremes (Madhyāntavibhāga), Distinguishing Phenomena from 
their True Nature (Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga), and Distinguishing the Jewel Lineage 
(Ratnagotravibhāga), which Tibetans more often refer to as the Supreme Continuum of 
the Mahāyāna (Mahāyāna Uttaratantra).18
The Ornament of Realization is understood to be an explication of the hidden meaning 
of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras by way of elucidating eight topics, which describe the

--- PAGE 110 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      85
 
Mahāyāna worldview with an emphasis on the path (Dreyfus 2003, 174–​182). While the 
contemporary curricula of the Nyingma, Kargyu, and Sakya sects include all five of the 
Maitreya texts,19 the Geluk sect studies only the Ornament of Realization.20 Furthermore, 
Tsongkhapa Lobzang Drakpa (tsong kha pa blo bzang grags pa, 1357–​1419), the founder 
of the Geluk (dge lugs) sect, accepted Haribhadra’s eighth-​century commentary as au­
thoritative, while most earlier Indian Buddhist scholars and the great scholars of the 
other Tibetan sects accepted the commentary of sixth century of Ārya Vimuktisena.21 
Makransky (1997) sees this rift as reflective of two different approaches to the Ornament 
of Realization and other Maitreya texts. The commentary by Vimuktisena, and those 
who follow in his way of thinking, is informed by what Makransky calls a “nondual 
yogic-​attainment perspective” while Haribhadra’s approach assumes an “analytical-​
inferential perspective.” Makransky argues that Ārya Vimuktisena reads the Ornament 
of Realization and the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras through Yogācāra doctrines, and 
more importantly praxis, while Haribhadra reads it through Madhyamaka, specifically 
a Madhyamaka that had been informed by the logico-​epistemological developments of 
Dignāga and Dharmakīrti.
The concept of an analytic and a yogic perspective (whether contrasting or comple­
mentary) is well-​known in traditional Tibetan Buddhist scholastic literature. The great 
nineteenth-​century Tibetan polymath Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Tayé (‘jam gon koṅ sprul 
blo gros mtha’ yas, 1813–​1900) reports that there were two distinct lineages of the trans­
mission and practice of the Maitreya texts, one in accord with the common philosoph­
ical tenet systems (grub mtha’) and one “uncommon philosophical tenet system,” which 
remained with supreme disciples, who transmitted it orally (Koṅ-​sprul Blo-​gros-​mtha’-​
yas 2007, 250). The former was known as the “the tradition of hearing and reflection.” It 
was first associated with great translator Ngok Loden Sherab (rngog blo ldan shes rab, 
1059–​1109), and was carried on by Tsongkhapa and the Geluk sect.
The latter was known as “the meditative tradition.” It was passed down through the 
translators Zu Gawé Dorjé (gzus dga’ ba’i rdo rje) and Tsen Khawoché (btsan kha bo che, 
b. 1021) and further elucidated by the Third Karmapa Rangjung Dorjé (rang byung rdo 
rje, 1284–​1339), Longchenpa Drimé Özer, (klong chen pa dri med o zer, 1308–​1364), and 
others who “clearly maintained that this view was the final definitive meaning” (Koṅ-​
sprul Blo-​gros-​mtha’-​yas 2007, 396, n. 811). Kongtrul is appealing here to the authority 
of “hearing, reflection, and meditation,” which is a traditional Buddhist framework (e.g., 
Vasubandhu 1991, 911–​912 and Powers 1995, 183–​184) for arranging the three progressive 
ways that the dharma is to be understood, ascending from conceptual to nonconceptual 
realization.
Though many Tibetan scholars saw the Ornament of Realization as in accord with 
the Madhyamaka, since it is self-​evidently a commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom 
Sūtras,” Makransky argues that, “it functions like a grid to map a Yogācāra model of en­
lightenment on the Prajñāpāramitā sutras” (1997, 8). The Ornament of Mahāyāna Sūtras, 
Distinguishing between the Middle and Extremes, Distinguishing Phenomena from their 
True Nature all evince Yogācāra doctrines such as the three natures, the “transformation 
of the basis” or “fundamental transformation” (āśrayaparāvṛtti), and most importantly

--- PAGE 111 ---
86      Paul B. Donnelly
 
for the purposes of this chapter, the “three embodiments” (trikāya) of Buddhahood. The 
Supreme Continuum stands out among the Maitreya texts in its teaching of “buddha na­
ture” (tathāgatagarbha). The “nondual yogic-​attainment perspective” of these teachings 
was held to be central to tantric thought and practice by much of the late Indian and sub­
sequent Tibetan traditions (Makransky 1997, 365–​367). We turn now to a discussion of 
these last two crucial developments in Mahāyāna thought.
The Dharma Body
In the non-​Mahāyāna Sarvāstadādin Abhidharma texts, it is stated that the Buddha in 
whom Buddhists take refuge is not the physical body or mind of the Buddha (rūpakāya) 
but rather his undefiled, fully accomplished qualities (anāsrava aśaikṣa dharmāḥ). 
For the Sarvāstivādin abhidharma in particular, dharmas, the irreducible ultimate 
components of experience, were held to possess their own unique essence or identity 
(svabhāva) that defined them. The list of which qualities (dharmāḥ) those were varied 
for different Nikāya schools, but it appears that the collection of those qualities was un­
derstood to constitute what made a Buddha a Buddha. It was sometimes referred to as 
his dharmakāya. These qualities, since still conditioned, continue until that awakened 
being in question attains final, formless liberation (nirupadhiśeṣa nirvāṇa), at which 
point the awakened being passes beyond all conditionality and future birth into an eter­
nally liberated unconditioned state (Makransky 1997, 25–​28).
The Mahāyāna notion of the final awakened state expressed in the Perfection of 
Wisdom and other Mahāyāna sūtras is radically different than the nirvāṇa of the non-​
Mahāyāna. Makransky (1997, 85–​109) argues that the development of trikāya doctrine 
can be seen as a response to the problematic notion of nonabiding nirvāṇa (apratiṣṭita 
nirvāṇa), that is, the paradoxical notion that although nirvāṇa is an unconditioned 
state, it was to be attained for the purpose of acting in the conditioned world for others. 
Buddhahood seems to have both an unconditioned and a conditioned aspect, and the 
development of trikāya doctrine, with an ultimate, unconditioned embodiment in 
dharmakāya and two embodiments (sāṃbhogikakāya and nairmāṇikakāya) that con­
tinue to engage with sentient beings in the world, explains how that can be.
The term dharmakāya rarely appears in the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtras, and when 
it does, it means something quite different from what is assumed in abhidharma. 
Perfection of Wisdom sūtras declare that the dharmas that abhidharma traditions hold 
to ultimately exist and possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that makes them what they 
are, are in fact only conventional and thus ultimately empty. That emptiness is said to 
be the true nature of dharmas (dharmatā), and of course all the conceptually fabricated 
phenomena that they constitute. This realization is the perfection of wisdom, and is the 
ultimate defining quality of a buddha. The Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom 
says, “But, monks, you should not think that this [physical] body is my actual body. 
Monks, you should perceive me through the full realization of the body which is dharma

--- PAGE 112 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      87
 
(dharmakāya). And one should see that this, the actual body of the Tathāgatas, is brought 
about (prabhāvita) by the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭiḥ), i.e., the perfection of wisdom” 
(Makransky 1997, 31). Makransky (1997) nicely summed this up: “The ultimate defining 
principle of a Buddha, whether referred to as ‘Tathāgata,’ dharmakāya, tathāgatakāya, 
‘enlightenment’ etc., is identified both with the perfection of wisdom and with the object 
it knows nondually (dharmatā, śūnyata, tathatā, bhūtakoṭi, dharmadhātu, etc.)” (38).
Makransky (1997) later says, “Buddhahood, as complete ultimate transformation 
(āsrayaparāvṛtti), is expressed through either one, or both, of the terms: nonconceptual 
gnosis (nirvikalpa-​jñāna) and purified thusness (tathatā-​viśuddhi, dharmadhātu-​
viśuddhi, or their equivalents)” (76). These two refer to a “subjective” and an “objective” 
pole of the experience, though this is understood to be a concession to our ordinary 
epistemological framework and means of expression. Ultimately, concepts and language 
cannot reach here. The preceding is drawn from the Ornament of Realizations, which 
many Tibetan scholars understood to be aligned with the Madhyamaka view. The other 
four of the Five Dharmas evince a Yogācāra orientation, and emphasize the innateness 
of this ultimate reality with the teaching of tathāgatagarbha.
Tathāgatagarbha
The doctrine of the three natures and the dharmakāya established the notion of a fun­
damental ground that is the ultimate source of Buddhahood and the phenomenal world 
of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra. The meditative stages of the Yogācāra serve to completely 
transform this base (āśrayaparāvṛtti) from a saṃsāric perspective to a nirvāṇic—​
from a bound sentient being to a Buddha. Whereas most of the Maitreya texts and the 
commentaries by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu are careful to point out that emptiness/​
nonduality does not itself possess svabhāva, some tathāgatagarbha texts use much more 
positive imagery and language, emphasizing the innate purity of sentient beings known 
as the tathāgatagarbha.22 This term literally means “womb or embryo of the tathāgata,” 
but “buddha nature” has come to be a common translation in English.
The earliest known text laying out this doctrine is the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra. The rel­
atively short text teaches nine similes. In the first, the Buddha manifests the miraculous 
appearance of huge lotus flowers in the sky. In the calyx of each was a radiant seated 
Buddha. Then, all the petals of the lotuses became putrid and disgusting, but the radiant 
Buddhas were still seated there. The audience was somewhat puzzled, but the Buddha 
explains the meaning of this vision was the main message, which is summarized in an 
early verse. “Son of good family, the True Nature (dharmatā) of the dharmas is this: 
whether or not tathāgatas appear in the world, all these sentient beings contain at all 
times a tathāgata.” The foul, withered petals are the defilements and impurities of sen­
tient beings that obscure a fully awakened, perfect Buddha. The Buddha says that he has 
taught the Dharma to allow beings to destroy these defilements and reveal their Buddha 
within (Zimmerman 2002, 106–​107).

--- PAGE 113 ---
88      Paul B. Donnelly
 
This teaching of an innate, awakened essence is found in a number of important 
sutras including the Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā (Śrīmāladevīsaṃhanāda Sūtra), the 
Mahāyāna Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra), and the Descent to Laṅka 
Sūtra (Laṅkāvatāta Sūtra).23 The former explicitly equates the tathāgatagarbha with 
the dharmakāya and says that it is in reality permanent and unchanging. It is empty, 
but not in the Mādhyamika or Yogācāra sense of being devoid of an own-​nature. “The 
Tathāgatagarbha is void of all the defilement stores, which are discrete and knowing as non-​
liberated . . . the Tathāgatagarbha is not void of the Buddha dharmas which are nondiscrete, 
inconceivable, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, and knowing as liberated” 
(Williams 2008, 106). These texts even explicitly characterize the tathātagatagarbha as Self 
(ātman). According to the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, “The dialecticians who are confused 
in the thicket / Of consciousness, lack the proper doctrine,/ And wish to propound a self / 
Just keep running here and there.// The self to be realized in one’s personal experience / 
Has the characteristic of purity./ This tathāgata heart [tathāgatagarbha]/ Is not the sphere 
of dialecticians.//... Naturally luminous mind / is the pure tathāgata heart,/ But this appro­
priation of sentient beings / Is free from limit and nonlimit” (Brunnhölzl 2014, 26).
Assertions of this sort led some Indian and Tibetan commentators to relegate sutras 
that utilized this kind of language to be instances of the Buddha’s “skillful means” 
rather than to be taken literally and assigned such sūtras to be of provisional (neyārtha) 
meaning, since “self” is traditionally held to be anathema to Buddhist thought.24 
Others, however, accepted them as definitive (nīthārtha). Regardless, tathāgatagarbha 
thought has been immensely influential in the Vajrayāna traditions of Tibet. As Douglas 
Duckworth (2013) has noted, “Arguably, the underlying philosophy behind the prac­
tice of deity yoga is the presence of buddha-​nature within being(s). That is, buddha-​
nature can be seen as the philosophical underpinning for the practices of tantra” (101). 
Makransky (1997) argued that “tathāgatagarbha thought “was the primary organizing 
perspective of tantric practice traditions of late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism” (366).
As is well known, one of the defining features of Tibetan Buddhism is its emphasis 
on the treatises (śāstra) rather than on sūtras, unlike in East Asian Buddhism. The 
tathāgatagarbha text that has been the most influential in Tibetan Buddhism is thus 
not these sūtras but rather a śāstra, the Distinguishing the Jewel Lineage, one of the Five 
Dharmas of Maitreya. Numerous commentaries on Distinguishing the Jewel Lineage 
were composed in Tibet, evincing various lines of interpretation of the meaning of the 
text and to which doctrinal “school” it belongs.25 Distinguishing the Jewel Lineage teaches 
the same basic ideas as the tathāgatagarbha sūtras and quotes many of them. Specifically, 
it reproduces the nine similes of the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra. As we’ve discussed, the 
Distinguishing the Jewel Lineage, along with the other four Maitreya texts, were under­
stood by Tibetans to have been passed down in two different lineages: an analytic one, 
which generally privileged a Madhyamaka reading of the texts, and a meditative tradi­
tion, which allowed a more literal interpretation.
From the analytical perspective, using terms like “permanent,” “unchanging,” and 
“self” are typically declared to be provisional in order to make these texts consistent 
with a more dialectical approach. From the meditative perspective, these statements are

--- PAGE 114 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      89
 
direct expressions of nondual gnosis, which is not limited by the constraints of logic. 
From this perspective, the analytical approach is a preliminary to realization. It can be 
used to demonstrate that the dualistic world of seemingly real subjects and objects falls 
away under analytic examination. This paves the way for the higher realization of re­
ality itself. Texts that speak from that perspective do not need to be justified in terms of 
logical or doctrinal categories, because they are definitive. This emphasis on meditative 
expression over discursive analysis provides a fertile doctrinal ground upon which the 
Vajrayāna can be justified.
It is not insignificant that the Tibetan traditions hold that the Distinguishing the Jewel 
Lineage was revived in India by the siddha Maitripa (986–​1063) and heads the lineage 
by which it was brought to Tibet. Maitripa is one of the two most important scholar/​
siddha teachers (along with Nāropa) of the tantric Mahāmudrā traditions.26 At this 
time in Indian Buddhism, there were increasing efforts to integrate originally tantric 
teachings into more traditional mainstream Mahāyana thought. By the fourteenth cen­
tury in Tibet, this mutually informing of Mahāyāna (both Madhyamaka and Yogācāra/​
tathāgatagarbha) and tantric thought influenced nearly all of the major developments 
across the sects of Tibetan Buddhism.
Tantric Practice
Various aspects of this subject are covered in several other chapters in this volume: 
Sugiki is a study of the chronology the Buddhist tantras, Gray is an examination of 
the Cakrasaṃvāra tantra, Hackett surveys Tibetan tantric literature, and Gardiner 
discusses the visualizations of the generation stage of tantric practice. Though there are 
unique practice systems such as The Great Perfection (rdzogs chen), Mahāmūdrā, Path 
and Result (lam ‘dras), and so forth, the tantric practices shared by all these systems 
are based in one way or another on the class of tantric texts categorized by Tibetans as 
Highest Yoga Tantras (anuttarayogatantra).
Broadly speaking, the yogas are divided into two sequential stages: generation stage 
(utpattikrama) and completion stage (niṣpannakrama).27 In the generation stage, the 
meditator first dissolves away her ordinary self into emptiness and then engages in elab­
orate visualizations of herself as a fully awakened Buddha and her environs as a purified 
awakened realm. This stage purifies the meditator of coarse conceptual thought and 
identification with the limited putative self. “In the creation phase, one must abandon 
ordinary appearances, fixation, and apprehension of reality; the remedies whose 
features are antidotal are clear image, pride, and the conviction that what appears is 
illusory.” Through such practices, one enters pristine awareness (Koṅ-​sprul Blo-​gros-​
mtha’-​yas 2008, 60). A common feature of this stage is the meditative purification of 
death, intermediate state, and rebirth through identifying them with the three buddha 
bodies: dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya. Generation-​stage practices prepare 
the meditator for completion-​stage yogas.

--- PAGE 115 ---
90      Paul B. Donnelly
 
Though again, there are many variant practices, in general, completion-​stage 
practices work with a concept of a subtle body made up of three channels through 
which subtle energies (prāṇa, rlung) flow. Ordinarily, they flow in way that causes 
us to experience the dualistic world of seemingly real appearances. Having purified 
that way of experiencing the world through the generation stage, meditations are em­
ployed that transform the psychophysical perspective allowing us to experience the 
blissful, nondual reality. “Once we are skilled enough to engage in the completion 
stage practices, such as the inner heat at our navel center, we will be able to bring all 
our energy winds into the central channel and cause them to dissolve in it completely, 
as they do in death. As a result the clear light wisdom of our fundamental mind will 
dawn” (Yeshe 2001, 131).
Note that the dissolving of the energies into the central channel results in a 
nonconceptual reality that is both gnosis and bliss. It is often remarked that this gnosis 
is common to Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna, but the generation of the mind of great bliss is 
unique to completion-​stage practices of Highest Yoga Tantra. Most Tibetan traditions 
are in agreement on this point. The yogas that cultivate this great bliss gnosis are the 
method component of the Vajrayāna path to Buddhahood. But method must be con­
joined with wisdom (i.e., the ultimate true nature of things). For most of the Tibetan 
traditions, that is expressed though the largely coextensive concepts of emptiness, 
dharmakāya, and buddha nature.
Tibetan Systemizations of Mahāyāna 
and Vajrayāna Thought
Tibetan traditions frequently refer to the Vajrayāna as the “resultant vehicle,” meaning 
that practice is undertaken assuming that the goal of the Buddhist path, Buddhahood, 
is already present in the body and mind of sentient beings as buddha-​nature. The path 
serves to uncover or reveal the pure, luminous essence. Every other vehicle is then re­
ferred to as the “causal vehicle” which takes practice to create the aspects of awakening, 
which is as yet still potential. Buddha-​nature resonates with the Vajrayāna rhetoric of 
nonduality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, appearance and emptiness, and so on, and tan­
tric practice with its elaborate visualization of purified realms and oneself as an awe-​
inspiring awakened deity is made possible by the presence of the dharmakāya here and 
now. “The legendary quickness of the tantric path (full enlightenment attainable even in 
one lifetime) has assumed this very understanding, permitting a rapid progress on the 
path by revealing the intrinsic purity of deity and mandala as the actual, primordial na­
ture of oneself and one’s world” (Makransky 1997, 366). The completion-​stage practices 
that bring the vital energies into the central channel bring conceptual thought to a halt 
and reveal a blissful luminous, nondual subjectivity that are capable of fully realizing 
that primordial nature.

--- PAGE 116 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      91
 
“Other Emptiness”
As we have seen, the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras associated with the second and 
third turnings of the wheel of Dharma treat the subject of emptiness in very dif­
ferent terms. The perfection of wisdom sūtras, and even more so the Madhyamaka 
treatises of Nāgārjuna, present an emptiness that is expressed in negative terms such as 
phenomena’s lack of own nature (niḥsvabhāva) or freedom from conceptual elaboration 
(niṣprapañca). The Discourse Explaining the Thought and Maitreya texts also assert the 
emptiness of phenomena, but nuance that by saying that the conceptual overlay that is 
negated transforms, or reveals, the base, which is dependent arising itself. Knowing that 
is the perfected nature, reality, and awakening itself. By the fourteenth century in Tibet, 
the concern to interpret these two themes, as well as tantric practice, seems to have 
reached a critical mass, with several prominent masters, including the third Karmapa 
Ranjung Dorjé (rang byung rdo rje, 1284–​1339), Büton Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen 
grub,1290–​1364), the great Nyingma master Longchen Rabjampa (1308–​1364), and 
Dolpopa Sherab Gyeltsen (dol po pa shes rab rgyal mtshan, 1292–​1361), writing major 
works on this topic.
These figures either knew each other or shared many of the same teachers and disci­
ples and all were deeply involved in the practice and teaching of the Kālācakra tantra. 
It is Dolpopa who was arguably the most influential. He developed a radical and influ­
ential reinterpretation of Mahāyāna thought that “contains the most controversial and 
stunning ideas ever presented by a great Tibetan Buddhist master” (Stearns 1999, 2) 
and established a distinct scholastic tradition and esoteric lineage transmission, known 
as Jonang (Jo nang). The order thrived and spread for several centuries and formed 
institutional relations with the Sakya (Dolpopa’s own primary tradition), Kagyü, and 
Nyingma sects.28
The Mahāyāna textual sources that form the basis of this system of thought are 
the sūtras of the Third Turning of the Wheel of Doctrine, the Maitreya texts, and no­
tably, the corpus of hymns of Nāgārjuna, particularly the Praise to the Dharmadhātu 
(Dharmadhātu Stava).29 As mentioned earlier, there were two traditions of the inter­
pretation of the Maitreya texts that are held to be themselves explications of the hidden 
meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras. In the analytic tradition founded by Ngok 
Lotsawa, the emptiness asserted in those was a nonaffirming negation arrived at through 
logical inquiry. The other, the meditative tradition founded by Tsen Khawoché, was said 
to have been preserved and transmitted orally. This lineage took the positive statements 
about ultimate reality literally and as definitive. Sheehy and Mathes note, “The partic­
ular transmission linked to Sajjana via Tsen Khawoche interprets the Five Maitreya 
Works positively, emphasizing the effulgence of luminosity and the buddha-​nature they 
reveal. This became the touchstone hermeneutic for the zhentong (emptiness of other) 
philosophical and contemplative tradition (Sheehy and Mathes 2019, 31). Dolpopa was a 
master of these texts, which clearly influenced him deeply.

--- PAGE 117 ---
92      Paul B. Donnelly
 
Dolpopa was also a fervent practitioner of the Six-​branch Yoga (saḍaṅgayoga) of the 
Kālācakra tradition.30 A strong influence on Dolpopa’s view and one that he frequently 
cites is the Bodhisattva Trilogy which consists of a commentary on the Kālācakra 
tantra, a commentary on the Hevajra tantra, and one on the Cakrasaṃvara tantra.31 
It was during a retreat on the Six-​branch yoga that he had the realizations that led to 
his unique views of emptiness and Madhyamaka, though he waited five years before 
teaching them. What he began teaching was a complete reinterpretation of some fun­
damental assumptions about Buddhist thought, synthesizing texts and concepts of 
Madhyamaka and Yogācāra, and employing the particular vocabulary of the Kālācakra 
system (Dolpopa 2006, 68).
Dolpopa defended his views by relying on the Kālācakra commentary the 
Vimalaprabhā, which utilizes the Hindu concept of four ages (Kṛta, Treta, Dvāpara, 
and Kali). This widely held concept assumes a degeneration of beings and the world 
over time from an original age of purity, the Kṛtayuga, down to the dark Kali age in 
which we now exist. Dolpopa asserted that the pure teachings of the Buddha had been 
revealed in the ancient Kṛtayuga, but those teachings had gradually become tainted 
and misunderstood due to the flawed intellects of ordinary persons over time. The 
Vimalaprabhā says that only the Kṛtayuga teachings should be regarded as expressing 
the final intentions of the Buddha. Dolpopa identified his own tradition with those, and 
regarded many of the mainstream understandings of the Tibetan scholastic traditions as 
flawed and corrupt. The authentic Kṛtayuga teachings was said to include many of the 
highest tantras, the Bodhisattva Trilogy; the Ten Sūtras on Buddha Nature; The Ten Sūtras 
of Definitive Meaning; and the works of Maitreya, Asaṅga, Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, and 
the tantric siddhas Nāropa and Saraha (Stearns 1999, 81). Dolpopa says that the key doc­
trine in these authentic, definitive texts is “emptiness of other” (gzhan stong).
We have here a new (or Dolpopa would say rediscovered) sense of the meaning of 
perhaps the single most fundamental Mahāyāna concept: emptiness. In the argumen­
tative treatises, Nāgārjuna mounts argument after argument proving that any object of 
analysis is revealed to be empty of inherent nature or essence (svabhāva). Dolpopa calls 
this emptiness the “emptiness of self-​nature” (rang stong), which he correlates with con­
ventional truth and accepts that it is indeed true of all conditioned, dependently arisen 
phenomena. Nāgārjuna says that even the Buddha and nirvāṇa are empty of inherent 
existence. As noted previously, in the Maitreya texts’ explication of the Perfection of 
Wisdom sutras, emptiness is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is the 
perfection of wisdom, the perfect nature, the dharma body, the tathāgatagarbha, and so 
on. The nondual realization of this is the very essence of the Mahāyāna sense of awak­
ening. For Dolpopa and other Jonang thinkers, this sublime ultimate reality cannot just 
be the nonaffirming negation of svabhāva.
Dolpopa considered the buddha-​nature to be naturally luminous radiant light, which 
is synonymous with the dharmakāya, and a primordial, indestructible, and eternal state 
of great bliss inherently present as the ultimate essence of every living being. Beings are 
bound in saṃsāra because that essence is obscured by adventitious defilements, which 
are the product of the conceptual elaborations of countless lives in the cycle of birth and

--- PAGE 118 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      93
 
death. Those “stains” are empty of their own inherent existence and the tathāgatagarbha 
is empty of them, but it is not empty of its own nature as described above. It is empty of 
everything other than the luminous buddha-​nature as described above (Stearns 83).
Great Madhyamaka
Tibetan doxographical hierarchies nearly always place Madhyamaka at the top. Tibetan 
doxographers assert that “Madhyamaka” holds emptiness as ultimate truth. Cittamātra, 
or “mind only,” is below it. The term “mind-​only” indicates that this “school” accepts 
that mind is the ultimate truth. Even a brief study of the Maitreya texts and those of 
Asaṅga and Vasubandhu demonstrates that “mind only” does not accurately describe 
their doctrines. The four meditative concentrations encountered in Yogācāra literature 
describe a path that starts with the realization that external objects are actually “mind 
only,” but subsequent stages reveal that since mind depends on cognitive objects (that 
don’t exist), the subject is seen not to exist either. As Makransky concludes in his dis­
cussion of the four stages, “dualistic conception is abandoned, nonconceptual gnosis 
emerges, the nondual realm of reality (dharmadhātu) appears, and he attains the path 
that sees it directly (darśana mārga)” (Makransky 1997, 77).
Dolpopa accuses Tibetan doxographers of denigrating definitive teachings in 
their assignation of the treatises of Maitreya to the school of “mind only.” He says, 
“It emerges from the Kṛtayuga tradition that the three natures are the Dharma tra­
dition of only the Madhyamaka. Therefore, by not understanding that type of classi­
fication, and by mixing it up, the dregs of the view have arisen. Those Madhyamaka 
[treatises] which present the three natures of the fully established, and so forth, have 
been demoted to Cittamātra treatises. The great experts of the Great Madhyamaka 
who taught them have also been demoted to Cittamātra adherents” (Stearns 1999, 90) 
“Great Madhyamaka” (dbu ma chen po) includes Yogācāra, Tathāgatagarbha, and tan­
tric thought and texts, particularly the Bodhisattva Trilogy. This flies in the face of the 
widely accepted hierarchy of tenet systems which consisted of two “lower vehicle” doc­
trinal schools (Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāṇṭika) and the two Mahāyāna schools (Cittamātra 
and Madhyamaka). Dolpopa defended his radical reinterpretation of established tenet 
systems (siddhānta) by saying that Great Madhyamaka is not a tenet system but rather 
a view (darśana) connected to meditative experience and expressive of the awakened 
perspective (Broido 1989, 87).
Furthermore, with the notable exception of the Sūtra Mahāmūdra tradition in the 
Kagyü lineages and some forms of the Nyingma Great Perfection, most of the Tibetan 
traditions were in agreement with Dolpopa that this view and the path that it entails is 
fundamentally tantric. Dolpopa summarizes the essential points of his view:
Therefore, as long as delusion has not ceased it is impossible for the manifestation of 
delusion, the cycle of birth and death, to cease.

--- PAGE 119 ---
94      Paul B. Donnelly
 
As long as this circulation of the vital winds has not stopped, it is impossible for 
this stream of consciousness to stop.
While this stream of mind and mental events has not stopped, it is also impossible 
for this manifestation of delusion, the three worlds, to stop.
Therefore, with the wish to transcend the three worlds, whose nature is suffering, 
if you abandon all distractions and meditate upon the profound Vajrayoga, the sub­
lime nectar from the mouth of the excellent master, this circulation of vital winds 
and mind together will stop.
(Stearns 1999, 101).
Dolpopa is arguably the most influential teacher of “other emptiness.” Jamgön Kongtrul 
cites a few earlier masters as predecessors, such as the Sajjana, Tsen Khawoché, Zu Gawé 
Dorjé and Yumo Mikyö Dorjé (yu mo mi bskyod rdo rje), and claims some of Dolpopa’s 
contemporaries who held “other emptiness” views as well, namely the Third Karmapa 
Rangjung Dorjé and the Nyingma master Koṅ-​sprul Blo-​gros-​mtha’-​yas (2007, 250). 
The next most prolific and influential Jonang teacher of other-​emptiness was Tārānātha, 
whose collected works are contained in twenty-​three volumes.32 The “other-​emptiness” 
view was taken up, qualified, or refuted by the major thinkers of the established Tibetan 
sects.33 The great Sakya scholar Śākya Chokden (śākya mchog ldan, 1428–​1507) also de­
veloped his own unique sense of emptiness, and doxographical hierarchy, indebted 
to but also critical of Dolpopa. The same can be said of several of the major Kagyü 
hierarchs, including the Seventh Karmapa Chodrak Gyatso (chos grags rgya mtsho) and 
the Eighth Karmapa Mikyö Dorjé.34
Not surprisingly, other emptiness views were a source of controversy and incited 
polemic works from many of the most important scholars of the day, all primarily 
associated with the Sakya lineage. Butön Rinchen Drub (bu ston rin chen grub, 1290–​
1364), Gorampa Sonam Sengge (go ram pa bsod nams seng ge, 1429–​1489), Remdawa 
Zhonnu Lodrö (red mda’ ba gzhon nu blo gros, 1348–​1412), and his student Tsongkhapa 
all wrote refutations of Dolpopa and the other emptiness view. As polemics have a 
way of doing, refutations brought responses and other refutations for generations. 
Regardless of who “won” these debates, the matter was effectively settled in the late 
seventeenth century when the now reigning Geluk government, with the aid of an al­
liance of Mongol armies, forcibly converted Jonang monastery and installed a Geluk 
lama as the reincarnation (sprul ku) of Tārānatha, who had died seven years earlier. 
This marked the effective banning of other emptiness doctrine in central Tibet. The 
works of Jonang Tāranātha and Śākya Chokden were also banned at this time (Stearns 
1999, 62).35
Śākya Chokden nuanced Dolpopa’s other emptiness view, bringing it more into line 
with mainstream Sākya views, while remaining unique. Śākya Chokden too accepted 
the teachings of the Third Turning of the Wheel of Doctrine as definitive and included 
its sūtras and śāstras within the doctrinal category of Madhyamaka. He asserted that 
though the view the Dharmas of Maitreya was in agreement with that of the mantrayāna 
(i.e., tantra), “Because they assert that non-​dual primordial mind alone as the object

--- PAGE 120 ---
On the Union of Emptiness and Bliss      95
 
of realization after the apprehended/​apprehender-​phenomena have been realized as 
empty” (Komarovski 2011, 259).
Nonetheless, Śākya Chokden considers Mantra Madhyamaka as a third type, beyond 
that of Nāgārjuna and Maitreya/​Asaṅga. “Pāramitā[yāna] has neither the method of re­
alization nor the object of realization of the uncommon view of Mantra[yāna]—​the in­
nate primordial mind. The mere freedom from proliferations (spros bral tsam) [taught 
by] Pāramitā[yāna] followers is not realized by primordial mind [taught in] Mantra; 
the emptiness realized [the path of] Mantra is subsumed under [the category] of the 
stainless great bliss (zag med bde ba chen po).” The highest view for him is one in which 
conceptual reasoning—​whether related to self-​ or other emptiness—​is not necessary 
to realize primordial mind. Tantric techniques such as the third tantric empowerment 
(shes rab ye shes kyi dbang, prajñājnānābhiṣeka) and completion-​stage yogas are neces­
sary and sufficient cause to actualize the great bliss gnosis (Komarovski 2011, 261). Thus, 
Śākya Chokden holds not just that tantric practice supersedes the preparatory realiza­
tion of emptiness through reasoning but also that the latter is not even necessary.
One can do without the negative reasoning approach of Nāgārjuna’s argumen­
tative works, but the view of the Dharmas of Maitreya is indispensable “because it 
comprises an inseparable part of the tantric view of reality” (Komarovski 2011, 262). 
Śākya Chokden’s formulation of Great Madhyamaka relies heavily and explicitly on 
tantric teachings to validate his inclusion of the view of the Dharmas of Maitreya into 
Madhyamaka (Komarovski 2011, 264). The views of Śākya Chokden were very influ­
ential for the great founders of the revitalization of the ancient practice traditions that 
would come in eastern Tibet.
Great Madhyamaka and other emptiness thought endured through a several 
hundred-​year-​prohibition in central Tibet, largely because of the degree to which they 
had made an indelible mark on the thinking of the non-​Geluk sects. In the nineteenth 
century, there was an efflorescence of scholarly activity across the Jonang, Sakya, Kagyü, 
Nyingma, and Bön orders in eastern Tibet. Emptiness of other and Great Madhyamaka 
came to be regarded as unifying ground for those developments. Deroche, defines the 
Rimé (ris med) movement, or “eclectic movement” as “a transsectarian activity of reve­
lation (gter ma), compilation, and transmission of Buddhist lineages and teachings, led 
by the spiritual trio of Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo (‘jam dbyang mkhyen brtsa’i dbang 
po, 1820–​1892), Jamgon Kongtrul, and Chogyur Dechen Lingpa (mchog gyur gling 
pa, 1829–​1870).” Deroche continues, “the so-​called Rimé (ris med) movement of the 
nineteenth-​century in Eastern Tibet constituted a reaction and a renaissance of the an­
cient earlier orders including the Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Jonang, and Bon” (Deroche 
2019, 323–​324). To accomplish this renaissance, the three great founders of Rimé col­
lected, taught, and preserved the teachings that they felt were in danger of fading 
away in Tibet. To that end, Jamgon Kongtrul composed his monumental Treasury of 
Precious Instructions,36 which details the “eight great chariots”37 that form the distinct 
lineages of spiritual practice that trace back to India. The “eight great chariots” are sys­
tems of tantric practice, unified by the view of emptiness of other and the tantric Great 
Madhyamaka.

--- PAGE 121 ---
96      Paul B. Donnelly
 
Like the great rebirth of the tantric practice lineages in Tibet in the nineteenth cen­
tury, in recent decades Western scholarship has begun to better recognize these 
developments and give them the attention they deserve. Scholarship on Madhyamaka 
has far exceeded that on Yogācāra, and the relationship between these two great chariots 
of the Mahāyāna has tended to see them as more in competition than as complemen­
tary, which has long typically been the perspective of Japanese scholarship. Western 
scholarship on Tibetan Buddhist doctrine has often uncritically accepted Tibetan 
doxographical categories, leading to a reification of conceptual boundaries such as 
“Madhyamaka,” “Yogācāra,” and “tantra.” The boundaries of each of these concepts have 
also largely been informed by the dominant Geluk understandings of them, perhaps be­
cause so many of the Tibetan informants available to scholars were associated with that 
sect. As we have seen, however, the other major sects and practice lineages were intellec­
tually thriving before the ascendancy of the Geluk government and though they some­
times seemed to be in danger of fading away, they endured and were revitalized through 
the extraordinary efforts of the great figures of the Rimé movement.
The sharp division between sūtra and tantra was really only observed in the Geluk 
sect and its monastic educational institutions. Similarly, the nearly exclusive emphasis 
on Madhyamaka over Yogācāra was not the dominant approach in Tibet, as evidenced 
by the centrality of the Five Dharmas of Maitreya among the other sects’ understanding 
of what constituted Mahāyāna thought (Dreyfus 2003, 98–​148). There are encouraging 
signs that our scholarship is evolving to call our received conceptions about these matters 
into question. The recent publication of several volumes of the Treasury of Precious 
Instructions and other works by Kongtrul is a major advance in Tibetan Buddhist studies, 
filling in our knowledge of the full range of Tibetan doctrinal and practice traditions. It 
is hoped that this contribution plays some small part in this direction in our endeavors.
