Chapter 5
Goryū Shintō Goma
Tantric Foundations
Richard K. Payne
Introduction
Over the last half century, scholars have expanded methods for the study of reli­
gious traditions beyond the philological. This expansion of methods simultaneously 
implicates an expansion of theories regarding the object of study.
The idea that a religious tradition can be comprehended adequately solely on the 
basis of authoritative doctrinal texts was in part motivated by the rise of the philolog­
ical method in the nineteenth century when the modern study of religion was initiated. 
More fundamentally, it also reflects the theological idea that authoritative doctrinal texts 
reveal the timeless essence of a religion. These preconceptions have contributed to a his­
tory of the field of religious studies as in many instances being a kind of cryptotheology 
(Payne 2008, 2009, 2012/​2013). The academic study of tantra can, however, avoid that 
fate by embracing the methodological orientation in which traditions are no longer 
conceptualized as closed systems, idealized in conformity with authoritative doctrine, 
and selectively represented by instances most closely adhering to that idealization. 
Moving away from decontextualized and ahistorical representations means also that the 
study of tantra can engage models of contact, interaction, and change. From this per­
spective, traditions are not fixed and rigid but rather constantly changing, constantly 
adapting. In other words, traditions are processes in which practices, beliefs, and rituals 
are all fluid, which is another way of saying that the object of study is the lived tradi­
tion. And, as many scholars have noted, ritual practices are central to the lived tradition 
(Joshi 2006, 51; Magliocco 2014; Strathern and Stewart 2014).
This chapter examines a particular instance of tantric practice, the homa (Jpn. goma 
護摩). The homa is a votive offering that can be traced back to Vedic rituals that were 
transformed by tantric practitioners, probably in the early medieval period. As with the 
Vedic forms, the tantric fire is usually homologized with Agni, who purifies the offerings

--- PAGE 127 ---
102      Richard K. Payne
 
and transmits them to the deities (Payne 2016). Shared by almost all tantric traditions, 
the homa is a singularly important instance of tantric ritual. The theoretical issue 
motivating this study is ritual change, specifically, contributing to an understanding of 
the systematic ways in which rituals change when they are borrowed into a different 
tradition.1 In this case it is the Goryū Shintō tradition of medieval Japan that borrowed 
the tantric Buddhist goma ritual and adapted it for its own use. Pursuit of this under­
standing of the systematics of ritual change in the context of borrowing is initiated by 
adapting concepts, categories, and concerns from contact linguistics.
Methodology: Adapting Contact 
Linguistics to Study Ritual Change
Although he was writing specifically about the sociology of religion, Jens Kreinath’s ob­
servation that the field’s presumptions meant that “the interrelated nature of rituals was 
not recognized as a field or area worthy of study” (Kreinath 2020, 398) is more widely 
relevant. If we take change and interaction as the normal contexts in which tantric 
traditions have existed, then the study of ritual change as a result of interaction provides 
a valuable perspective on the histories of those traditions.
The similarities between ritual and language are extensive, so much so that the 
methods of linguistics have been fruitfully applied to the study of ritual (for an alterna­
tive method, see Dolce 2006–​2007). This does not mean, however, that those methods 
can be applied directly, that is, without methodological adaptation. Instead of taking the 
concepts, categories, and concerns of linguistics as fixed analytics and imposing them 
onto the phenomena of ritual, it is necessary to allow appropriate adaptations of lin­
guistic analyses to be made from the empirical evidence of rituals themselves (Payne 
2021). The linguistic analogy to the study of interaction between different traditions is 
the subfield of contact linguistics (Myers-​Scotton 2002). A useful terminological dis­
tinction made in contact linguistics is between “source language” and “recipient lan­
guage” (Winford 2020, 59; for other terminology for this relation, see Ross 2020, 123). 
We can adapt this to “source tradition” and “recipient tradition.” For our study here, 
Japanese tantric Buddhism, represented by Shingon, is the source tradition and Goryū 
Shintō is the recipient tradition (Gardiner 2018, 2019; Rambelli 2018).
A distinction central to theorizing contact is the question of “agentivity,” that is, 
whether to think about changes resulting from contact as social or individual in char­
acter. As noted by Peter Hans Nelde, it is “speakers or language communities, rather than 
languages on an abstract level, [that] are in contact with one another” (Nelde 2010, 373). 
And, in the same way, it is not religions or traditions or ritual systems in the abstract that 
are in contact but practitioners and groups. Donald Winford explains the emphasis on 
the individual person as the agent of change, noting that linguistically “contact-​induced 
changes originate as innovations in individual speakers’ language use” (Winford 2020, 57).

--- PAGE 128 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      103
 
The very notion of agentivity, however, would seem to privilege exactly the idea that it 
is the individual speaker who is the agent of change rather than change being effected 
within and by a social group. Whereas for this approach to contact linguistics the “ulti­
mate locus of contact” is the individual, ritual praxes are inherently social. This indicates 
one adaptation of contact linguistics needed for its application to the study of ritual. 
In one sense, agents of ritual change are necessarily the individual practitioners who 
decided to use a particular ritual, adapt it in particular ways, and create records of that 
new form, with a few suggestive exceptions, but those individuals may be invisible to 
us today, and in fact for our purposes here need not be identified. However, whoever 
those individuals were, it is an open question as to whether they considered themselves 
to be individual authorial persons (a preconception naturalized in modern individual­
istic societies). Instead, they were acting within a network of relations with both other 
individuals and institutions, a network that supported the adaptation of a ritual, a net­
work of shared ideas and preconceptions, and it is this social network that can be treated 
analytically as the location, rather than agent, of change.
For the social perspective on contact linguistics, change is often understood in terms 
of dominance and power relations between different language groups, relations that also 
change (Winford 2020, 61; see, for example, Langer et al., 2006). Winford distinguishes 
“borrowing” and “imposition” and claims that these two are the “major mechanisms of 
contact induced change” (Winford 2020, 66). He defines borrowing as referring to a
psycholinguistic mechanism by which speakers introduce materials from an external 
language into a language in which they are (more) proficient. In doing so, they tend 
to preserve the more stable (i.e., structural) domains of the recipient language. . . .  
It follows that most borrowings tend to be lexical.
(Winford 2020, 62)
In contrast, imposition involves “transfer from a linguistically dominant first language 
into a non-​dominant second language” (Winford 2020, 64). Winford identifies sev­
eral specific types of both borrowing and imposition. In Winford’s usage, borrowing 
places agency with the recipient language group, while imposition places agency with 
the source language group (Winford 2020, 57). The distinction between these groups 
can be employed for greater precision regarding interacting ritual traditions. As noted 
above, however, ritual change is being treated here as a social process, and therefore an 
additional adaptation of Winford’s formulations is that borrowing and imposition are 
best considered descriptive categories. In this way, they can be uncoupled from the psy­
cholinguistic theorizing that Winford wants to extrapolate from them.
Rather than lexical, Winford defines imposition as the use of grammatical structures 
known from one language in a second language. He argues that this can either be from 
a speaker’s first language to their second, while their first language is still dominant, or 
“backward” from a second language onto a speaker’s first language as the second lan­
guage becomes increasingly dominant. The difference reveals that these are descriptive 
of dynamic situations. Imposition from a first language to a second takes place as skill in

--- PAGE 129 ---
104      Richard K. Payne
 
the second language is developing. Alternatively, a first language may be in decline as a 
second language becomes more dominant, in which case backward imposition is more 
likely (Winford 2020, 66).
While linguistic borrowing may be characterized as involving a “psycholinguistic 
mechanism,” in the case of ritual, borrowing is more explicitly intentional. An ex­
ample of such borrowing is the homa for Jesus and the Saints written by Yogi Chen 
(Payne 2015). In this homa, Jesus and the Saints correspond to semantic elements 
inserted into the structure of a tantric Buddhist homa ritual. Rather than a “chief 
deity” (Jpn. honzon, 本尊) from the tantric Buddhist pantheon, this homa uses Jesus 
as the chief deity. The precise definition of borrowing employed by some contact lin­
guistics theorists can be adapted from being the work of an unconscious psycholin­
guistic mechanism into an intentional act by which ritual elements from one tradition 
are borrowed by members of another. This adaptation from contact linguistics is pos­
sible because the distinction between borrowing and imposition is itself an analytic 
artifact.
The context of the instance examined here is one in which there is a changing power 
relation—​newly institutionalizing Shintō groups gaining social standing and exerting 
greater agency. The Goryū Shintō goma can be understood, therefore, as an instance 
of borrowing. Despite the tantric ritual culture being dominant, ritual practices and 
structures were being actively used by the newly developing Shintō ritual culture de­
veloping within self-​identified sectarian institutions, as distinct from “traditional” local 
kami cult practices (Hardacre 2017, 147–​176). As discussed more fully in the next sec­
tion, medieval Shintō sects were creating both new institutional forms and a new ritual 
culture out of the older, local kami cults. The religious culture, however, was pervaded 
by tantric Buddhist praxis—​both practices and teachings.
Regarding a ritual tradition parallel to the Goryū, the Yoshida Shintō tradition, 
Bernhard Scheid has loosely suggested a linguistic metaphor to the effect that the tra­
dition has a Japanese Shintō phonology, a Chinese Daoist morphology, and an Indian 
Buddhist syntax (Scheid 2001, 184). Although Scheid’s metaphor is suggestive, he 
makes no further theoretical use of it. The linguistic analogy that we are employing in 
this chapter is not only more specific but an explanatory metaphor. The formulators 
of new Shintō rituals are like those employing grammatical structures from what is 
for them a second language in a cultural setting in which that language is dominant. 
Metaphorically, it is like they are speaking tantric Buddhist sentences while using Shintō 
lexical items. In such situations, as indicated by Winford, the use of a lexical item from 
one language in the grammar of another entails morphological and grammatical effects 
as well. Although framed in terms of groups, considerations of agency do enter into the 
choice between borrowing and imposition. Because the newly forming Shintō groups 
were actively creating new ritual forms on the basis of tantric Buddhist ones, the rela­
tionship implied by the category of borrowing is employed in this chapter. Thus, rather 
than treating Scheid’s suggestion as a reified framework, we instead intend here to adapt 
the framework of contact linguistics to ritual and employ appropriately adapted lin­
guistic categories such as lexicon, morphology, and syntax.

--- PAGE 130 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      105
 
Historico-​Cultural Context: The 
Influence of Tantric Buddhism on 
Medieval Japanese Culture
The influence of tantric Buddhist praxis (mikkyō 密教) on the Buddhist traditions of 
Japan is well recognized (Bowring 2005, 135–​152; Taira 1996). The influence of tantric 
Buddhism was not limited to doctrines but included a variety of ritual practices as well. 
The two primary forms of tantric Buddhism in Japan are Tendai mikkyō and Shingon 
mikkyō, known, respectively, as taimitsu (台密) and tōmitsu (東密), and the widespread 
presence of tantric Buddhist praxes throughout Japanese Buddhism can be historically 
traced back to one of these two. However, tantric Buddhist thought and ritual practices 
were also appropriated by the self-​identified Shintō traditions which formed in the late 
medieval period.2
A (Very) Brief History of the Homa: Crossing Cultural 
Boundaries
The history of the tantric Buddhist homa reveals that there has been an ongoing process 
of creativity and change. The earliest source for the Shingon goma practiced today is the 
Vedic tradition of India (Strickmann 1996, 354–​355). Vedic rituals were in turn based on 
earlier, Indo-​European practices, the historical link between the contemporary Shingon 
goma and Greek, Roman, and Persian practices as well (Payne 2002).
The use of three fire altars is normal for Vedic ritual (cf. Dange 1987). The domestic 
altar (gārhapatya) is circular, located at the east end of the ritual enclosure, and as­
sociated with the earth. It is there that the offerings are prepared. The southern fire 
(dakṣiṇāgni) is semicircular and associated with the intermediate atmospheric realm. 
And the offering fire (āhavanīya), located to the west, is associated with the celestial 
realms. It is square, and it is into this fire that offerings are made (Staal 1983, I:44, 1989, 
71–​72). Current research provides few details regarding the historical development of 
tantric homa from Vedic rites. It is, however, plausible that in the medieval period, the 
Vedic pattern of three fire altars became optional. The domestic rituals (gṛhya), such as 
the agnihotra (Payne 2004), use a single altar and may have provided the basis for new, 
tantric forms, which came to be practiced in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist tantric traditions 
(Payne 2016). One of the few factors found in the majority of tantric traditions, or 
lineages of practice—​Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist, nondualistic and dualistic—​the homa 
is also geographically widespread. In Japan, the homa was part of the system of tantric 
praxis that came to pervade Japanese religion in the medieval period.
A predominant portrayal of medieval Japanese religious worldview is that it inte­
grated exoteric and esoteric ideologies (Jpn. kenmitsu shugi). This characterization

--- PAGE 131 ---
106      Richard K. Payne
 
of medieval Japanese religion is the work of Kuroda Toshio (1926–​1993), perhaps the 
most influential historian of Japanese religion in the twentieth century (Dobbins 1996). 
Attention to local praxes from a wider kenmitsu perspective have led to refining this un­
derstanding (Taira 1996, 440–​441).
The history of medieval Shintō is complex, and the identification of specific streams 
(ryū) does not reflect a uniform set of clearly demarcated boundaries. As a general cover 
term, we here follow the terminology employed by Anna Andreeva and refer to “esoteric 
kami worship” (Andreeva 2006, 349). The use of such terminology should help us avoid 
the presumption of two separate monolithic entities—​Buddhism and Shintō—​which 
interacted to create a syncretic or heterodox form. In other words, we are not looking 
at the interaction between two monolithic entities which can be identified in terms of 
a set of essential characteristics. Instead, they constitute sets of praxes—​the dialectic of 
doctrines and practices—​some of which, such as the homa, had been carried from India 
through China to Japan, and which continued to develop in new ways, including being 
reformulated as a ritual for a kami cult. Robert H. Sharf has noted that “for the most 
part, modern studies of medieval Buddhist doctrine [in China] are still framed in terms 
of interrelationships between discrete and autonomous historical entities” (Sharf 2002, 
10). This applies equally well to the way in which medieval Japanese religious praxes 
have been conceived. Consider, for example, Marius Jansen’s description of the status 
of Buddhism at the end of the Edo period: “Buddhism had become almost inextricably 
intertwined with Shinto” (Jansen 2000, 351). This implies that what was pulled apart in 
the Meiji reforms splitting Buddhism and Shintō (shinbutsu bunri, 神仏分離, 1868) was 
actually two different entities that had become entwined over the course of Japanese re­
ligious history. However, a different botanical metaphor, that of hybridization (Kirkland 
2000), provides a more useful way of constructing the discourse.
Modernizing nationalists in the Meiji era (1868–​1912) constructed the idea of Shintō 
as a continuous, primordial, singular, and archetypally Japanese religious tradition. As 
Allan Grapard notes:
[There was no] clear consciousness on the part of the Japanese of the classical period 
that there was a specific entity called Shintō. This does not mean, however, that there 
was nothing at all, for there was the practice of jingi sūhai, “worship of the kami of 
Heaven and Earth,” a matter inextricably linked to politics, court life, and shrine-​
temple multiplexes. (1992, 12)
In the medieval period, esoteric kami worship provided a pragmatic basis for the 
establishment of self-​identified Shintō traditions that did assert separate institutional 
identity. These self-​identified Shintō traditions include the Yuiitsu (or Yoshida), Ōmiwa, 
Sannō, Watarai, and Goryū Shintō lineages (Teeuwen 2000, 112). More generally, Tendai 
mikkyō gave rise to Sannō Shintō, while Shingon mikkyō contributed to the creation 
of “the Shintō of the two realms” (ryōbu shintō, 両部神道), a broad synthesis of eso­
teric Buddhism with the kami cults of the Ise Shrine. The “two realms” refer to the two 
mandalas of the tantric Buddhist tradition of Shingon, that is, the “dharma realm man­
dala” (dharmadhātu maṇḍala, taizōkai mandara 胎藏界曼荼羅) and the “vajra realm

--- PAGE 132 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      107
 
mandala” (vajradhātu maṇḍala, kongōkai mandara 金剛界曼荼羅), which were in turn 
homologized with the two shrines at Ise, the Inner Shrine and the Outer Shrine.
In addition to the ryōbu shintō associated with the Ise Shrine, several other Shintō forms 
were created. These do not adhere to a single, uniform organizing schema but include spe­
cific lineages with centralized authority, that is, the Yoshida (吉田, also known as Yuiitsu, 
唯一), streams associated with a specific temple, such as the Miwaryū (三輪流), and forms 
that appear in several different locations, such as the Goryū (御流) tradition, which claims 
a relation with the Imperial house. Fabio Rambelli has noted that Miwaryū and Goryū were 
the “most influential Shingon traditions within Ryōbu Shintō” (Rambelli 2011, 840). This 
chapter explores one particular ritual, a Goryū Shintō goma, as the site of interactions be­
tween local and translocal traditions, creating a new version of an existing ritual practice.
In medieval Japan, developing ritual practices was an ongoing creative process that 
drew on a shared pool of ritual praxes, some being more inflected as Shinto and others 
being more inflected as Buddhist. Jacqueline Stone has described the type of interac­
tion we are seeing here in terms of “the intersection of Buddhism as a pan-​Asian tradi­
tion with local religious culture” (Stone 2016, 5). Understanding that characterizations 
involving notions of true or authentic Buddhism are rhetorical dead ends, she suggests 
thinking of Buddhism as a “shifting repertoire of resources, one with porous boundaries” 
(Stone 2016, 5). The prominence of Buddhism is, in her view, the result of how Buddhist 
practitioners employ a “conceptual capacity to encompass disparate elements within a 
compelling, if not always internally consistent, ritual program” (Stone 2016, 5). While 
her focus is on Buddhist deathbed rituals, the image of a ritual system as having porous 
boundaries and being adaptable to changing conditions is applicable to the medieval 
Shintō traditions, as well as to tantric traditions more widely.
Relevant to this issue of avoiding outdated conceptions of religions as monolithic 
entities is our knowledge that some of the specific individuals involved in the creation 
of the new Shintō cults were themselves Buddhist priests. For example, along with other 
Tendai priests, Jien, fourth Patriarch of the Tendai sect, played an important part in the 
establishment of the cult of Sannō gongen at Hie Taisha, a shrine on the eastern foot of 
Mt. Hiei (Naumann 1994, 6; also Sugahara 1996). Similarly, the Miwa daimyōjin engi, 
which tells the origin tale of the deity of Mt. Miwa, was compiled by Buddhist priests 
“with a strong interest in esoteric Buddhism and kami worship” (Andreeva 2010, 247). 
Although we do know some of the individuals involved, this does not change the theo­
retical point made earlier that it is social groups that are the location of change—​making 
the distinction between agents and locations.
The Goryū Shintō Goma and the Fudō 
Myōō Soku Sai Goma
The following analysis draws on a published version of a Goryū Shintō Goma manual 
(Inaya 1993, 275–​296). There are many related manuals, including those in the rare book

--- PAGE 133 ---
108      Richard K. Payne
 
collection of the Tenri Central Library, one of which is also referenced at a key point in 
the following discussion. The Shingon ritual manual for the Fudō Myōō Soku Sai Goma 
is the one currently in use for training Shingon priests (Payne 1991).
Sources
The Tenri collection is a very extensive archive of medieval Shintō materials that evi­
dence the nature of the ritual practices in the interface of esoteric Buddhism and the 
newly established or radically revised Shintō institutions. This particular manual is part 
of a complete manuscript that includes three ritual manuals, a grouping that seems to 
have been shared among the Shintō schools. The full manuscript is entitled “Sōgen san 
dan shidai” (宗源三段次第, which can be glossed as “ritual manuals of the primordial 
three stages”).3 In what corresponds to a table of contents, the goma manual is named 
“Goryū Shintō ryōbu shūgō goma shidai” (御流神道兩部習合護摩次第, “goma 
manual of the imperial line of Shintō that integrates both parts”). The phrase “integrates 
both parts” refers to what we can call the interpenetration of the two mandalas of the 
Shingon tradition, the Vajra Realm (vajradhātu) and Womb Realm (garbhadhātu), 
which is the union of wisdom and compassion and at the same time a reflection of the 
honji suijaku theory regarding the relation of the kami and the buddhas (Hardacre 2017, 
158). The text itself is more simply referred to as “Shintō goma shidai” (神道護摩次第). 
There is no colophon, but the condition of the manual and its style of orthography sug­
gest that it is relatively late in the medieval or into the premodern period. For compar­
ative purposes, we also examine another goma manual from the collection of “Shingon 
Shintō” materials published by Inaya Yūsen (1993). This collection includes a goma ritual 
manual, simply identified as “Goryū Shintō goma” (御流神道護摩).
For the scope and intent of this chapter, however, one term of the comparison will 
be the Inaya manual for the Goryū Shintō stream, while the other is the Shingon Fudō 
Myōo Soku Sai goma (Payne 1991). Focusing on one manual from each tradition means 
that each is a representative stand-​in for the practices of the two traditions more gener­
ally. As a more focused study, this examination is able to go more deeply into the analysis 
of similarities and differences, and the import of those, than more general, impression­
istic studies can.
The first step in the following analysis details some of the semantic similarities and 
differences between the two goma. This is not meant to be comprehensive, but, based 
on previous research, is instead the author’s own evaluation as to which items are note­
worthy. Following that is an examination of the organizing structure, or ritual syntax, of 
the two gomas.
Ritual Semantics
The two gomas share a great deal of semantic content. Both the Goryū Shintō goma and 
the Shingon Fudō Myōō goma comprise five sets of offerings. In the course of the larger

--- PAGE 134 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      109
 
ritual, these offerings are made to different deities. If we compare the first of these from 
the Goryū Shintō goma with the first from the Shingon Fudō Myōō Soku Sai goma, sev­
eral similarities can be identified.
Physical Offerings
The same material offerings are made in both rituals, including oil, white rice, a mixture 
of five cereal grains, flowers, and incense. Both manuals refer to the oil as soyu—​which 
is the clarified butter (ghee) used in Vedic sacrifices—​another indication of the histor­
ical continuity from India to Japan. Although no substitute is indicated in the Goryū 
Shintō goma manual, sesame oil (goma abura 胡麻油) substitutes for clarified butter in 
the Shingon ritual.4 White rice is used in both rituals to represent the offering of food 
and drink.
Mudrā and Mantra
As is found throughout the tantric tradition, the Goryū Shintō goma directs the practi­
tioner to perform several ritual hand gestures (mudrā). Some of these have names dif­
ferent from those used in the Shingon goma. However, the Goryū Shintō goma does 
include the Agni mudrā, identified by that name as in the Shingon ritual and described 
in almost exactly the same fashion (for illustrations of the mudrā used in the Yoshida 
Shintō tradition, see Scheid 2001, 177). Although ritual performance of the Goryū 
Shintō Goma (Inaya) employs mudrā, the text includes no mantra. There is also no ref­
erence to visualizing Siddham seed (bīja) mantra, Siddham being the Sanskrit script 
widely employed in East Asian Buddhism for ritual purposes (see, for example, Hidas 
2014; and Robson 2008). Siddham continues to be used for ritual purposes throughout 
Japanese Buddhism. Visualizing seed syllables in the Siddham script is at the core of 
Shingon ritual performance, as seed syllables are identified with, and therefore make 
present, various deities and powers (Payne 2018, 98). For example, such bīja mantra 
visualization is done in the Shingon goma when the practitioner fans the flames of the 
goma fire: “Imagine the syllable haṃ on the surface of the fan; it changes, becoming a 
wind cakra” (Payne 1991, 113, modified). (See Williams, this volume, for Hindu uses of 
phoneme visualization.)
Visualization
Not only are Siddham bīja mantra not visualized in the Goryū Shintō goma, but there 
is no reference to visualization of any kind. Each pūjā offering in the Shingon goma is 
accompanied by a mantra, mudrā, and visualization (which constitute actions of body, 
speech, and mind). The offering of food and drink is an example:
Now taking up the small ladle used for offering food and grain, the practitioner 
scoops up an offering of rice from the closer bowl and pours it into the flames, reciting 
the mantra ON AGYANAU EI SENJIKYA SOWAKA once. He repeats this action 
three times. With the mudrā of Amida’s meditation, he is to visualize this offering as 
going into the mouth of Agni Deva, directly to the upper surface of the lotus in Agni 
Deva’s heart. It there transforms into the most pure and marvelous pūjā offerings. 
These then permeate the whole of his body, and emerge from the hair follicles on the

--- PAGE 135 ---
110      Richard K. Payne
 
surface of his skin as endless clouds and oceans of pūjā offerings which are offered to 
all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas and worldly deities. (Payne 
1991, 299, corrected)
Ritual Identification
Except in some of its earliest stages, ritual identification with the deity, also known 
as “deity yoga,” characterizes Buddhist tantra (Tsongkhapa 2017). Jeffrey Hopkins 
explained the nature of identification in tantric practice, saying that “one learns in 
meditative experience to use the mind ‘realizing’ emptiness and the emptiness—​with 
which it is fused—​as a basis of imaginative appearance, in imitation of a Buddha’s 
ability to do this in fact” (Hopkins 2008, 61). In the Shingon goma, this is a threefold 
identification in which the mouth of the practitioner, the deity, and the altar-​hearth 
are visualized as identical with each other, forming a unitary whole. The flames of 
the goma fire, the digestive “fires” of the practitioner, and the wisdom fire of the deity 
are visualized as identical and are known as the Visualization of Three United (Payne 
1991, 293–​294). This is central to Shingon goma, both in the literal sense that it takes 
place in the third of the five offerings and in the sense that the practitioner becoming 
a buddha is central to the idea of awakening. None of this, however, is found in the 
Goryū Shintō goma.
Kami and Buddhas
It is unsurprising that there is no mention of any buddha or bodhisattva in the entire 
course of the Goryū Shintō goma, references to kami taking their place. This is found, 
for example, in the following comparison of the declarations made when offering 
food and drink. In contrast to the absence of mantras from the Goryū Shintō goma, 
declarations of intent are quite similar to those in the Shingon goma. Continuing with 
the offering of food and drink, the declarations of the two rituals are given here in 
parallel:
Goryū Shintō Goma (Inaya)
Fudō Myōō Soku Sai Goma
By now presenting
By now presenting
this wonderful offering
this wonderful offering
of food and drink
of food and drink
merely desiring the respected kami
merely desiring that Agni
accept this goma, and
accept this goma, and
divinely grant comfort.
perfect all siddhis.
There are two differences between the two declarations of intent: the Goryū Shintō goma 
asks for comfort rather than the perfection of siddhis, and it refers to “respected kami” 
rather than to Agni—​who is the deity evoked in the first stage of the Shingon goma from 
which this version is taken. Here we see what might be described as a “lexical” change—​
from Buddhist deities to kami—​leading to a “cascade” of further semantic changes at 
specific points in the ritual performance.

--- PAGE 136 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      111
 
An interpretative issue worth raising in more detail relates to the references to 
“the Fire God” (Katen 火天) made in both manuals. From the academic perspective, 
such as this chapter, the “Fire God” is the Japanese reflex of the Vedic Agni. However, 
practitioners do not need to understand this equivalence to perform the rituals. For the 
most part, they would no doubt perform these simply as rituals of their own tradition. In 
the present day, however, in addition to ritual training, most Shingon priests do receive 
formal academic education (e.g., at Kōyasan University). My interactions with other 
monks at the temple where I trained in the early 1980s, led me to understand that their 
education included the history of the Shingon tradition and its Indic origins—​so the re­
lation between the “Fire God” they encountered in performing the goma and the Vedic 
Agni would have been evident to them.
Ritual Implements
Material culture, in this case specifically the ritual implements employed, provides an­
other means by which continuities and changes can be identified. Some implements 
are found in both the Goryū Shintō goma and the Shingon tradition’s gomas. The texts 
both prescribe using a pair of ladles, large and small, to make offerings into the fire 
and a wand used to purify the altar-​hearth and offerings with water. In Shingon, the 
ritual implements include beads (nenju) and vajra (ritual implement representing a 
thunderbolt) in three different forms—​one, three, and five pronged—​and a vajra bell. 
The Goryū Shintō manual, however, makes no mention of any implements with vajra 
symbolism.5 One might be tempted to suppose that such symbolism was too strongly 
reminiscent of Buddhist esoteric practice to be employed in a Shintō context. However, 
within the broader range of esoteric kami worship traditions, such vajra implements 
are known. For example, illustrations related to the tradition of Yoshida Shintō 
(Grapard 1992, 49, 51), show vajra implements. Given the variety of esoteric kami wor­
ship lineages, and perhaps even variation from local practices at one shrine to another, 
the specifics of ritual implements and altar decorations may be unique to individual 
settings. Examining such details of material culture may provide ways of tracing his­
torical origins, connections, and interactions that are not otherwise clear from purely 
textual sources. The discussion of the arrangement of kindling that follows in the 
next section, “Scheduling,” is an instance of using material culture to trace historical 
connections.
Scheduling
Shingon practitioners will attend to a calendric pattern based on the Yijing and yin/​
yang principles of systematic change from light, warm, and dry to dark, cool, and 
moist. Each year on Mt. Kōya, an almanac based on these principles is published, and 
many activities are scheduled according to this almanac. This includes such events 
as when to begin a training sequence, as was the case for my own training. Similarly, 
the Goryū Shintō goma manual from the Tenri collection expressly distinguishes be­
tween actions taken on yin days and those taken on yang days. However, Shingon 
ritual manuals do not employ this specific distinction between yin and yang days,

--- PAGE 137 ---
112      Richard K. Payne
 
although practitioners may make choices about scheduling ritual activities based on 
the almanac.
The Kindling
One of the questions regarding the historical origins of the esoteric Shintō ritual 
practices that a detailed study of ritual manuals can contribute toward answering is 
whether the lineage of practice was more influenced by Shingon or Tendai. Both of these 
Buddhist traditions instantiated tantric practices in Japan and could have been influ­
ential in the development of the Goryū Shintō goma. While Shingon is entirely tantric 
(or esoteric, that is, mikkyō, 密教) in nature, Tendai maintains a twofold system of es­
oteric, pairing tantric practice with exoteric practice focused on the Lotus Sutra. Both 
Buddhist traditions have goma ceremonies, and to that extent, either could have been 
the progenitor of the Goryū Shintō goma.
A key detail is the arrangement of the sticks of kindling on the hearth. Gomas 
performed in the Tendai tradition generally use a triangular arrangement of the sticks 
of kindling in the ritual sequence, while Shingon always uses rectilinear arrangements. 
The Goryū Shintō goma manual illustrations show rectilinear arrangements of kindling 
(Inaya 1993, 278, 281, 284, 287, 290).6 These suggest that the primary model for the Goryū 
Shintō goma was the Shingon goma, rather than a Tendai one, a ritual detail answering an 
historical question.
The semantic differences examined here include the physical offerings, mudrā and 
mantra, visualization, ritual identification, kami and buddhas, ritual implements, 
scheduling, and kindling. Although speculative, we suggest that relatively easily made 
changes were used to mark the Goryū Shintō goma as “not” the Shingon goma. Other 
aspects, such as the structure of the rituals, seem to have been more resistant to change. 
We turn now to the issues related to ritual structure, that is, syntax.
Ritual Syntax: Metaphor and Structure
Identifying a basic metaphor employed as an organizing principle of ritual activity is 
one approach to the study of ritual. Identifying a structuring metaphor is of value be­
cause of the metaphoric entailments that follow from its use.
Ritual Metaphor as Basic Organizing Principle
In East Asia, a number of different ritual metaphors were available. One example is 
petitioning the celestial bureaucracy, as found, for example, in Daoist rituals (Lagerwey 
1987, 107).7 Both the Goryū and Shingon gomas share the ritual metaphor of feasting an 
honored guest. This metaphor is Vedic in origin, tracing forward into medieval tantric 
forms, including Buddhist ones, which were then in turn carried into East Asia. The 
Goryū Shintō goma displays the same structuring metaphor of feasting an honored 
guest as does the Shingon goma.

--- PAGE 138 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      113
 
Structure: Five Offerings to Five Deities
Like many contemporary tantric Buddhist gomas in the Shingon tradition, the Goryū 
Shintō goma manual published by Inaya comprises five sets of offerings. Each set is it­
self a (relatively) self-​contained ritual element in which a deity is invited into the altar-​
hearth, offerings are made to the deity, and then the deity departs. Also, like the Shingon 
goma, these sets of offerings are performed within framing actions at the beginning and 
end of the full ritual performance.
The first of the five deities in the Goryu Shintō goma examined is the Fire Deity (Ka 
Ten, 火天) (See Appendix). In the Shingon tradition this is the Vedic god Agni, who is 
almost always the first deity evoked in Shingon gomas. It is unclear from the manual, 
however, whether the association to an imported Indic deity is known or relevant for the 
Goryū ritual. The second deity is Fire Virtue Kami (Ka Toku Shin, 火徳神), the third is 
Wood Virtue Kami (Moku Toku Shin, 木徳神), the fourth is Metal Virtue Kami (Kin 
Toku Shin, 金徳神), and the fifth is Earth Virtue Kami (Do Toku Shin, 土徳神). These 
latter are four of the five phases of Chinese thought, leaving out water—​perhaps under­
standable in a fire ritual. This contrasts with the Indic five elements (earth, water, air, fire, 
space), which is employed in Buddhist contexts, such as the symbolism of five-​cakra 
stupas (Huntington Archive 2022).
In the case of the Shingon goma, the deities evoked are said to come from and return 
to their places in the mandala, which is identical with the actual nature of the cosmos 
itself. Although the Goryū Shintō goma makes no explicit mention of the mandala, the 
invitation and release both refer to the deities’ “original seats,” which in the Shingon 
goma is a reference to their location in the mandala.
Syntactic Diagrams
While ritual metaphors provide one way of examining the organization of rituals, syn­
tactic analysis is a more formalistic consideration of their structure. The idea of a formal 
syntactic analysis of ritual actions derives from the work of Frits Staal. Inverted tree 
diagrams, borrowed from linguistics, provide a visual representation of the organiza­
tion of rituals and can be an effective means of comparing two rituals. While we cannot 
here give complete diagrams of both the Goryū and Shingon gomas for comparison, 
figure 5.1 reveals the relation between the framing activities and the five sets of offerings 
for each of the two goma rituals; it shows the similarity in the structure of the two. In the 
“comparison of overall structures” (fig. 5.1), “offerings” is treated as a “node” for the five 
sets of offerings in each of the two gomas. This is because other gomas can have more or 
fewer sets of offerings placed within the framing actions.
At a more granular level, aligning the actions of the two gomas in the “analysis of first 
offering” (fig. 5.2) provides a preliminary analysis of the structure of the offerings of the 
Goryū Shintō and Shingon gomas.
The lines connecting actions from each list show where similar ritual actions exist. 
Because the level of detail recorded in different ritual manuals varies, in some cases one 
or two actions identified in one manual are identified as several in the other. For example,

--- PAGE 139 ---
114      Richard K. Payne
 
the Goryū Shintō goma simply lists “invitation” as a single action. This corresponds to 
three actions in the Shingon goma: requesting the presence of Agni, inviting the Four 
Embracing Wisdom Bodhisattvas, and again requesting the presence of Agni.
The syntax of the two first offerings reveals two interesting differences. The first is that 
the practical matter of arranging items on the altar comes before the invitation of the 
deities in the Goryū Shintō goma, while in the Shingon goma it comes after. Second, in 
the Shingon goma the kindling is laid and the fire lit before the deities are evoked; in the 
Goryū Shintō goma, the order of these is reversed. These may be incidental differences 
resulting from historical contingences, or there may be some other significance. Further 
research might be able to determine which is the case.
The analysis of ritual change, in this case from one tradition to another, can focus on 
a variety of different aspects. Doctrinal aspects are often at the forefront of such studies, 
a prominence reflecting the presumption that doctrine determines practice. More con­
cretely, however, analysis can focus on specific ritual elements, which according to the 
analogy with a linguistic approach, can be referred to as semantic changes. Semantic 
changes are often accompanied by morphosyntactic changes as well, seemingly driven

Conclusion
There is virtually no trace of esoteric Buddhist ritual practice to be found at Shintō 
shrines in the present day. This results from the extent to which the separation of Shintō 
from Buddhism during the Meiji period was successful. In terms of contact linguis­
tics, this corresponds to a situation in which social dominance of one linguistic group 
over another was suddenly reversed. In the event of this kind of reversal, intentionally 
expunging the linguistic traces of the once dominant group is unexceptional. By analogy 
here, the sudden reversal created by the Meiji reformation raising Shintō to the status of 
a state religion led to intentional expunging of not only rituals such as the goma but also 
of the symbolic universe of Buddhism from now exclusively Shintō institutions. If we go 
back to the medieval period, that is, prior to the rise of neo-​Shintō rhetoric (e.g., that of 
Motoori Norinaga), and examine the origins of the self-​identified Shintō traditions, we 
find that esoteric Buddhist practice was the very basis upon which Shintō practices were 
created.
Esoteric Buddhism transformed Japan’s religious culture, and also influenced 
Japanese culture more generally. I have long held that the extent and importance of the 
role of esoteric Buddhism in the formation of Japanese religious culture has gone un­
noticed for two reasons. First, it was clearly in the sectarian interest of other traditions 
to obscure the role of Shingon in forming their doctrine and practice. The drive for sec­
tarian autonomy was greatly stimulated by the Tokugawa attempts at systematizing and 
regularizing the sectarian nature of Japanese Buddhism. Second, Western researchers 
still tend to be less familiar with Shingon, or with esoteric Buddhism more generally, 
than with other more widely studied East Asian Buddhist traditions, such as Zen and 
Pure Land. To someone unfamiliar with esoteric Buddhism, any influence or appropria­
tion would be largely invisible.
In looking at ritual, the distinction between content (lexicon, semantics) and process 
(syntax) is of heuristic value. While the Goryū Shintō goma may appear very different 
from the Shingon goma when one focuses on some aspects of the content—​for example, 
the deities evoked—​other aspects of the content together with the structure of the ritual 
demonstrate how close the two are to one another. At least three of the Ryōbu Shintō 
lineages—​Yoshida, Omiwa, and Goryū—​created Shintō gomas. An examination of the 
Goryū Shintō goma reveals how extensively this lineage borrowed from Shingon for its 
ritual practice.
The use of the five phases in contrast to the five elements, together with the absence of 
mantra, of visualization of any kind, of ritual identification, and the other distinguishing 
differences between the two gomas, suggests the value that these semantic elements had 
as markers of identity. A plausible explanation is that they were changed as a means of 
transforming the appearance of the ritual performance from a Buddhist one to a Shintō 
one. As a means of semiotically marking the Shintō goma as distinct from a Buddhist 
one, such changes are relatively simple substitutions of elements. Structural changes, 
whether the basic metaphor or the syntax tend to be slower to change.

--- PAGE 142 ---
Goryū Shintō Goma      117
 
A thread that runs throughout this volume, whether explicit or implicit, is the 
question of how we conceptualize tantra. The issue at the base of this is also largely 
the same for Shintō. Mark Teeuwen has noted that “Shinto is not something that has 
‘existed’ in Japanese society in some concrete and definable form during different his­
torical periods; rather, it appears as a conceptualization, an abstraction that has had 
to be produced actively every time it has been used” (Teeuwen 2002, 233). In other 
words, our own scholarly usages in the present are part of a very long line of usages, 
each implicating its predecessors, rather than being marked as distinct from historical 
usages by “insiders.”

Chapter 6
Homa in Jain Traditions
Ellen Gough
Jain Homas as “Tantric,” Not Vedic
Jainism in many ways developed as a rejection of the Vedic fire sacrifice. Many accounts 
in early Jain scriptures place Jain teachings in stark opposition to brahminical ritualism. 
In a famous narrative from the Śvetāmbara canonical text (āgama) the Uttarādhyayana 
(Utt.),1 a group of brahmins insult and encourage the beating of a Jain monk from a low 
birth and only repent and honor the monk after a king’s daughter intervenes, reminding 
the brahmins that the monk, through the power of his austerities, can “reduce the world 
to ashes” (Utt. 12.28, trans. Jacobi 1895, 54). The monk teaches the reformed brahmins 
the true meaning of sacrifice when he explains: “Penance is my fire; life my fireplace; 
right exertion is my sacrificial ladle; the body the dried cow dung; karma is my fuel; 
self-​control, right exertion, and tranquility are the oblations, praised by the sages, which 
I offer” (Utt. 12.44 trans. Jacobi 1895, 56).
Patrick Olivelle has argued that passages like this, which show an internalization of 
the Vedic sacrifice, wherein “the renouncer’s body . . . is equal to the fire altar where the 
Vedic rites are performed,” are more fully developed in brahminical texts than in Jain or 
Buddhist ones, as brahmins wished to show that asceticism emerged not as a rejection of 
the fire sacrifice but as a natural progression from it (Olivelle 1992, 69).
All Indian renouncers, both within and outside the Brāhmaṇical tradition, gave up 
ritual activities. They refused to use fire. It is only within the Brāhmaṇical tradition, 
however, that the renouncer’s abandonment of fire and rites became the focal point 
for the theology of renunciation. 
(Olivelle 1992, 71)
Early Jain texts do, however, focus on the abandonment of brahminical rites in de­
fining their path to liberation. Much of the language, and indeed motivation, for key 
early Jain teachings—​especially nonviolence and celibacy—​emerged directly as a

--- PAGE 151 ---
126      Ellen Gough
 
rejection of the foundation of “Vedic theology: sacrifice and marriage” (Olivelle 1992, 
23). Because of this, the abandonment of fire is a preoccupation in early Jain texts. One 
of the earliest Śvetāmbara texts, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Sū), for example, frames the Jain 
doctrine of nonviolence (ahiṃsā) in terms of the Vedic fire sacrifice. The Sūtrakṛtāṅga 
declares that “earth, water, fire, wind, grass, trees, and corn and the movable beings” are 
all living beings, so when someone injures one of these souls, they “do harm to their own 
souls, and will again and again be born as one of them” (Sū 1.7.1–​2, trans. Jacobi 1895, 
292). The examples of doing harm to these living beings, then, are brahminical rites. To 
show the importance of not using fire, the text explains:
Some leave their mother and father to live as śramaṇas, but they use fire; [Mahāvīra] 
says: “People are wicked who kill beings for the sake of their own pleasure.” He who 
lights a fire, kills living beings; he who extinguishes it, kills the fire. Therefore, a wise 
man who well considers the law should light no fire. Earth contains life, and water 
contains life; jumping (or flying) insects fall in (the fire); dirt-​born vermin (and 
beings) living in wood: all these beings are burned by lighting a fire
(Sū 1.7.5–​7 trans. Jacobi 1895, 56).
At the outset of this passage, the rejection of the use of fire is a way to define who is a true 
renunciant (śramaṇa). A brahmin man who has left his family to enter the third āśrama, 
becoming a forest-​dwelling hermit (vānaprastha) who retains his fire, is wicked. A true 
renunciant—​a Jain mendicant—​does not touch fire. Passages like these abound in early 
Jain texts, showing that the Jain doctrine of nonviolence, the definition of renunciation, 
and the ontology that even the elements have souls emerged in part as a rejection of the 
Vedic fire sacrifice.
It comes as a surprise, then, when some Jain mendicants in the medieval period did 
promote the Vedic sacrifice. Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa (ĀP), a ninth-​century Jain history of 
the universe structured around the life story of the first tīrthaṅkara, Ṛṣabha (Ādinātha), 
is an often-​cited source of the “brahminization” of Jain rites. Multiple scholars have fo­
cused on ­chapters 37–​40, which outline life-​cycle rites (saṃskāra) for twice-​born males, 
all of which include a fire offering (von Glasenapp [1925] 1998, 452–​462; Williams 1963, 
274–​287; Jaini 1979, 292–​304; Dundas 1991, 273, 1998, 35). In Ādipurāṇa 47.351–​352, 
Jinasena even recommends that spiritually advanced lay Jains—​men who have taken 
a vow of celibacy—​daily perform what amounts to a śrauta sacrifice, lighting three 
fires with the same names as the three fires of a Vedic sacrifice—​the householder’s fire 
(gārhapatya), southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni), and offering fire (āhavanīya)—​at the three 
divisions of the day (saṃdhyā)—​morning, noon, and evening (von Glasenapp [1925] 
1998, 452).2 It is unknown, however, how influential this prescription was among lay 
Jains. Although more research needs to be done on Jain adoptions of Vedic paradigms 
from the medieval period to the present day, as of now, we can be sure that most of the 
Jain fire sacrifices that are promoted and performed publicly today do not follow a Vedic 
model, using Vedic mantras, being performed at regular intervals of the day and year, 
and requiring a twice-​born male to undertake the ceremony.

--- PAGE 152 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      127
 
Most medieval-​ to present-​day Jain fire-​offering rites (homa, havana, āhuti, yajña) 
align less with Vedic models and more with “tantric” homas that are performed along­
side, or to conclude, offerings made to ritual diagrams (mandala, yantra). Many Jain 
homas can be called tantric because their ritual structure conforms to tantric Śaiva, 
Vaiṣṇava, and Buddhist fire offerings performed to honor deities who have been invited 
into these ritual diagrams. Charles Orzech (2016, 261) has identified in Bodhiruci’s 
Scripture of the Mantra of Amoghapāśa’s Miraculous Transformations (707 CE), for 
example, an “emerging ritual synthesis” for mandala rites for esoteric Buddhists that 
requires a fire offering to conclude a mandala rite. This text outlines how deities should 
be invited into a mandala by the showing of mudrās, how the body and area of worship 
should be protected and sanctified through the recitation of mantras and the estab­
lishment of containers of water, and how the ceremony should conclude with a fire 
offering.
As we will see, many Jain homas present a similar ritual structure, and they are 
performed for similar occasions as their non-​Jain tantric counterparts. Digambaras 
today cite the Ādipurāṇa as the source of their fire-​offering rites, but the ceremonies are 
not performed by celibate men three times a day, as instructed in Ādipurāṇa. Instead, 
they are performed in the context of mendicant initiations into a mandala, temple 
image consecration ceremonies, and optional ceremonies to boon-​giving deities that 
generate health, wealth, and miraculous powers. For example, in the days leading up to 
their initiations as mendicants, Digambaras from the medieval period to the present day 
have offered coconuts to a ritual diagram called the Ring of Disciples (gaṇadharavalaya) 
constructed out of colored powder into which the mendicant disciples of the twenty-​
four jinas (gaṇadhara) are invoked. To complete this pūjā, the initiands perform a 
fire-​offering ceremony, reciting the mantra to the disciples of the jinas while offering 
camphor into the fire (Gough 2021, 50). Śvetāmbara monks of the highest rank (ācārya) 
also have laypeople perform fire offerings for them as part of their yearly propiti­
ation of the deities invited via mantras into the sūrimantrapaṭa, or the cloth diagram 
of the mantra of the mendicant leader (Gough 2021, 181–​185). In the Buddhist context, 
Tadeusz Skorupski (2016, 115) has explained that after Buddhists rejected homa rites for 
centuries, “with the emergence of esoteric Buddhism, they [were] adjusted and incorpo­
rated into tantric rituals.” The same process occurred in Jainism.
Jain “tantric” fire offerings do, however, differ from their Hindu and Buddhist 
counterparts in a few ways. As we will see, Jains attempt to mitigate the violence of a 
homa. In addition, Jains differ from Buddhists when it comes to the involvement of 
renunciants—​celibate monks—​in fire offerings. Unlike Buddhist mendicants who have 
undergone a tantric initiation, Jain mendicants uphold the earliest Jain definitions of 
nonviolence and renunciation and never perform the fire offering themselves. They 
will recite mantras for the homas while laypeople make the physical offerings. Jains 
also more commonly perform homas not for the supreme objects of worship for their 
tradition—​mendicants, especially the enlightened jinas— but for unenlightened, boon-​
giving deities who need to be pacified or pleased: goddesses, the nine planets, or pro­
tector deities. John Cort (2001, 207) therefore defines havana in the Jain context as a

--- PAGE 153 ---
128      Ellen Gough
 
“fire offering made to an unenlightened deity.” Jain homas are often made to gods and 
goddesses in lay optional rites for health, wealth, and worldly prosperity.
Fire offerings have, however, also been integrated into the Jain path to liber­
ation. Because they are made to conclude the ritual propitiation of a variety of ritual 
diagrams—​including those into which enlightened and liberated souls have been 
invited—​Jain homas are not strictly related to unenlightened deities. They are also not 
solely related to achieving mundane goals and are often part of key rituals of Jain men­
dicancy. The example of the worship of the gaṇadharavalaya in Digambara initiations 
is one such rite in which a homa is performed to honor mendicants and to promote 
worldly detachment. Jain texts on fire offerings take pains to show the ways in which the 
ritual use of fire does not undermine, but instead promotes, Jain teachings about asceti­
cism and achieving omniscience and liberation.
Two modern Gujarati manuals on fire-​offering ceremonies provide a sense of the di­
versity of homas for image-​worshiping (mūrtipūjaka) Śvetāmbaras. The Śvetāmbara 
monk Somasundaravijaya lists the fire pits, or kuṇḍas, required for different fire ceremo­
nies. For the male unenlightened deities Māṇibhadra, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Nākoḍābhairava, 
and Bhomīyājī, a square kuṇḍa should be established, and for goddesses like 
Padmāvatī, Cakreśvarī, Ambikā, Pañcagulī, and Jvālāmālinī, a triangle-​shaped kuṇḍa 
should be constructed. For the three-​day optional ceremony for worldly well-​being 
(pauṣṭikavidhāna), an eight-​cornered fire pit of three levels, in a star shape, should be 
constructed. For the worship of the ritual diagram the nandyāvarta, performed as part 
of image consecration ceremonies, a six-​cornered kuṇḍa should be constructed. To 
make fire offerings to the goddesses of the mendicant leader’s mantra, the sūrimantra, 
triangle-​shaped kuṇḍas should be constructed (Somasundaravijaya 2007–​2008, 80).
Another modern Gujarati Śvetāmbara ritual manual, Ghaṇṭākarṇa-​Pratiṣṭhā-​
Vidhiḥ (GhPV), lists substances that should be offered to different objects of wor­
ship (see table 6.1) (GhPV, 65–​66). This list of substances should in no way be taken 
for hard-​and-​fast rules that all Jains accept. It indicates, however, that Jains make 
offerings to both unenlightened and enlightened souls. The five supreme beings—​the 
five principal objects of veneration in Jainism that are honored in the main mantra 
of Jainism, the Prakrit pañcanamaskāra—​the omniscient souls (arhat), liberated souls 
(siddha), mendicant leaders (ācārya), mendicant teachers (upādhyāya) and ordinary 
mendicants (sādhu)—​are the first objects of worship listed in this table. These two 
modern ritual manuals show that Jain fire offerings are often made for unenlightened 
deities in lay optional rites for mundane aims, but they are also offered to ascetics and 
enlightened souls, required to consecrate images of jinas, and are part of a mendicant’s 
yearly routine.
In this chapter, to provide a limited sense of the ways in which Jain homas, while 
attempting to remain nonviolent, are offered to both unenlightened and enlight­
ened souls, I focus on three Jain homas in which I participated in 2013 in Jaipur and 
Hastinapur. I examine a Śvetāmbara fire offering to the unenlightened deity Māṇibhadra 
and two Digambara homas undertaken to complete the consecration of jina temple

--- PAGE 154 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      129
 
images. These modern Jain practices developed in the medieval period as a response to 
the popularity of non-​Jain tantric rituals, and despite their appeals otherwise, they do, in 
some ways, contradict the fundamental Jain teachings of nonviolence. Because of this, 
several sects of Jainism did emerge in the early modern period to explicitly reject the 
use of fire—​including incense and lamps—​but other Jains have vigorously defended the 
practice, interpreting fire’s ritual use as rooted in early Jain texts and as a means of spir­
itual knowledge, destruction of karma, and progress toward liberation.

130      Ellen Gough
 
The Śvetāmbara Unenlightened Deity 
Māṇibhadra Vīra
In February 2013, as part of a multiday consecration ceremony for a Tapā Gaccha 
Śvetāmbara temple in the Jawahar Nagar neighborhood in Jaipur, Rajasthan, I 
participated in four different fire-​offering ceremonies to goddesses and three pop­
ular protector deities: Bhomiyājī, Ghaṇṭākarṇa Mahāvīra, and Māṇibhadra Vīra. 
Here, I focus on the fire offering performed for Māṇibhadra Vīra, the protector deity 
(adhiṣṭhāyaka) of the Śvetāmbara monastic lineage the Tapā Gaccha since the early 
modern period. Like the mustached, bow-​yielding Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Māṇibhadra is under­
stood as one of the fifty-​two “heroes” (vīra), or protector deities, of the Tapā Gaccha 
(see item 13 in table 6.1), and both these deities are often found flanking the entrances 
to modern Tapā Gaccha temples. In typical modern representations, Māṇibhadra 
rides an elephant with seven tusks (airāvata), has a body of a man, either four or six 
arms, and a head of a boar that balances on his snout a Jain temple with footprints of 
the first tīrthaṅkara, Ṛṣabha, which represents the pilgrimage site Shatrunjay (Cort 
2020; Devluk 1997, 210).3 Both Māṇibhadra and Ghaṇṭākarṇa are known to be pleased 
by fire offerings,4 especially at Ghaṇṭākarṇa’s main shrine in Mahudi, in north Gujarat 
(est. 1898), and at Māṇibhadra’s three key shrines in Magarwada, Gujarat, where 
his lower body is established; in Aglor, Gujarat, where his torso is established; and in 
Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, where his head is established (Devluk 1997, 215). The shrine 
at Magarwada remains especially important, with thousands of pilgrims, both Jain and 
Hindu, flocking to the site to participate in a homa on the fifth day of the bright half of 
each month of the Indian lunar calendar, meaning the fifth day of the first half of the 
month, when the moon becomes increasingly illuminated. The largest homa of the year 
for Māṇibhadra is performed not only at Magarwada but at Tapā Gaccha Śvetāmbara 
temples throughout India, on the bright fifth of the lunar month Āśvina (September–​
October), during the festival of Nine Nights, Navarātri. For these homas, pilgrims pray 
for health, wealth, and relief from worldly troubles by offering a coconut to a massive 
fire burning in the pavilion outside the main temple. After taking darśana of the main 
temple icon of Māṇibhadra, pilgrims receive his famous prasāda, the Gujarati sweet 
made from jaggery, sukhḍī.
The sites of Māṇibhadra’s three important shrines, the dates of these fire offerings, 
and the deity’s iconography all relate to Tapā Gaccha narratives that claim that 
Māṇibhadra is the reincarnation of Māṇekcand “Māṇek” Śāh, a lay devotee of Ācārya 
Hemavimalasūri (1463–​1529 CE), the fifty-​fifth leader of the Tapā Gaccha. These 
narratives all emphasize the superiority of the Tapā Gaccha’s teachings and practices 
over those of competing Śvetāmbara Jain monastic lineages. According to a modern 
Gujarati account by the Śvetāmbara monk Ācārya Candrānandasāgarasūri, Māṇek 
Śāh was born into a pious image-​worshiping Jain merchant family in Ujjain, Madhya

--- PAGE 156 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      131
 
Pradesh, in the fifteenth century (Devluk 1997, 193). As a young man, Māṇek became 
convinced by the preaching of a mendicant who followed the teachings of the fifteenth-​
century lay reformer Loṅkā Śāh, who saw temple worship as anti-​Jain.5 Māṇek decided 
to cease worshiping in his family’s temple, to the dismay of his mother and wife, who 
vowed to give up ghee for as long as he would not worship icons of the jinas (Devluk 
1997, 194–​195). Eventually, the monk Ācārya Hemavimalasūri, along with his mendi­
cant disciples, came to Ujjain, and Māṇek became impressed with Hemavimalasūri’s 
teachings. The monk convinced the merchant that image worship (mūrtipūjā) is not, 
as the followers of Loṅkā Śāh suggest, against the teachings of the early Jain scriptures 
(āgama). To show that temple worship is an integral part of Jainism, Hemavimalasūri 
provided a number of examples of Jain image worship from history and Śvetāmbara 
canonical scriptures (āgama), and Māṇek eventually became Hemavimalasūri’s lay fol­
lower (Devluk 1997, 198–​202).
On the morning of the fifth day of the bright half of the lunar month Māgha (Guj. mahā 
sud pāñcam), Māṇek Śāh adopted the twelve vows of a layperson (Guj. samyaktvamūlak 
bār vrat): the five minor vows (anuvrata) of (1) nonviolence, (2) telling the truth, (3) 
nonstealing, (4) chastity, and (5) limiting possessions, and the seven supplementary 
vows (śīlavrata) of (1) limiting action with regard to the directions, (2) limiting the con­
sumption of perishable and nonperishable objects, (3) avoiding unnecessary negative 
thoughts or actions, (4) regular performance of contemplation (sāmāyika), (5) limiting 
the duration of activities, (6) regular fasting, and (7) offering food and other possessions 
to mendicants.6 He also began performing the eightfold pūjā, offering eight substances 
to an icon of a jina, every day (Devluk 1997, 203).7
After Māṇek Śāh became a disciple of Hemavimalasūri, he followed the monk to 
Agra, where they stayed for the four months of the rainy season. During this rainy 
season retreat, in his daily lectures, Hemavimalasūri drew upon the Sanskrit pane­
gyric the Śatruñjaya Māhātmya to focus on the worldly and soteriological benefits 
of making a pilgrimage to Shatrunjay, the famous Śvetāmbara pilgrimage site in 
south Gujarat whose main temple is dedicated to the first jina, Ṛṣabha. Hearing these 
lectures, Māṇek Śāh became inspired to set out, on foot, for this pilgrimage site at the 
end of the rainy season, on Kārttika Pūrṇimā (Devluk 1997, 204–​206). On the way 
from Agra to the sacred hill, Māṇek stopped to rest in the jungle near Magarwada, 
in north Gujarat, with his mind focused on only one thought: “Praise to Ṛṣabha!” 
(Devluk 1997, 206). Thus lost in meditation, he did not hear the demands of money 
from an approaching band of dacoits, who in revenge slashed his body into three 
pieces: the head (Guj. māthuṃ/​mastak), lower body (Guj. pag/​piṇḍī/​ḍīṃcaṇ), and 
torso (Guj. dhaḍ). Because he died meditating on Ṛṣabha and the sacred pilgrimage 
site of Shatrunjay, Māṇek Śāh was reborn as the deity Māṇibhadra, who today bal­
ances a shrine to Ṛṣabha on his nose to represent his steadfast devotion to this jina and 
the pilgrimage site (Devluk 1997, 207).
Modern Gujarati accounts of what happened to Hemavimalasūri and his followers 
after Māṇek Śāh’s death differ slightly, but they all agree that Tapā Gaccha monks were

--- PAGE 157 ---
132      Ellen Gough
 
being tormented to death through the ritual propitiation of the deity Bhairava by 
Jain monks of competing mendicant lineages. According to the modern Śvetāmbara 
monk Pannyāsa Kalyāṇavijaya’s Gujarati account, Śvetāmbara monks from the lineage 
the Kharatara Gaccha worshiped the deity Bhairava, killing about five hundred Tapā 
Gaccha monks (Kalyāṇavijaya 1940, 209). According to Candrānandasāgarasūri, how­
ever, an ācārya of another Śvetāmbara mendicant lineage, the now-​defunct Kaḍavāmatī 
Gaccha, or Kaḍūāmatī Gaccha, became so jealous of Hemavimalasūri’s fame that he 
honored Bhairava with fierce (ugra) austerities; recitations (jāpa); and mantra, tantra, 
and yantra, and Hemavimalasūri and his fellow monks fell ill (Devluk 1997, 212). 
Māṇibhadra quickly arrived on the scene, challenged Bhairava to a fight, and promptly 
defeated him. Bhairava bowed at Māṇibhadra’s feet, devoting himself to the deity and 
promising that in the future, wherever there are worshipers of Māṇibhadra, he will 
be there as well. The ailing Jain monks were cured. Māṇibhadra cried out in praise of 
Hemavimalasūri and told the monk to establish his lower body right there, where he de­
feated Bhairava (Devluk 1997, 212).
On Vasant Panchami, the fifth day of the bright half of the lunar month Māgha, in 
January–​February, Hemavimalasūri established the lower body of Māṇibhadra at the 
spot where the god defeated Bhairava, just outside the village of Magarwada (Devluk 
1997, 212–​213). In 1490/​1491, Hemavimalasūri’s eventual successor, the fifty-​sixth leader 
of the Tapā Gaccha, Ācārya Ānandavimalasūri, commissioned a proper temple for this 
lower body of Māṇibhadra at Magarwada (Devluk 1997, 212). The bright fifth of every 
month, then, when worshipers today visit Magarwada to offer coconuts to Māṇibhadra 
via a homa, commemorates the moment when Māṇek Śāh, Māṇibhadra’s previous in­
carnation, adopted the proper beliefs of image-​worshiping Tapā Gaccha Śvetāmbara 
Jains. It also commemorates the moment when Māṇibhadra defeated Bhairava and 
Hemavimalasūri established the deity’s temple.
Ultimately, Māṇibhadra’s origin story shows that he is linked to fire sacrifice be­
cause he is a Jain response to popular medieval tantric practices, namely, the worship 
of the Śaiva deity Bhairava. Indeed, non-​Jain locals in Magarwada today still insist 
that Māṇibhadra’s shrine was built atop a temple to Bhairava.8 The modern worship 
of Māṇibhadra with offerings of coconuts into a fire should not be seen as an adop­
tion of a brahminical fire sacrifice but of a tantric fire sacrifice to powerful deities like 
Bhairava. To establish the superiority of the Śvetāmbara mendicant lineage the Tapā 
Gaccha over other Śvetāmbara lineages, Tapā Gaccha monks used the tantric ritual 
practices of non-​Jains to develop Māṇibhadra as a Jain equivalent to Bhairava who 
is particularly concerned with the needs of the supporters of Tapā Gaccha monks. In 
Jain ritual culture today, goddesses and gods like Māṇibhadra, who are seen as more 
powerful, pious Jain equivalents of non-​Jain deities, are some of the most common 
recipients of homa offerings. Using mantras and yantras, Śvetāmbara Jains per­
form homas for boon-​giving gods and goddesses at certain times and places linked 
to their origin stories and during image consecration ceremonies that establish their 
presences in temples.

--- PAGE 158 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      133
 
Details of the Homa to Māṇibhadra
The fire ceremony I witnessed for Māṇibhadra in Jaipur in 2013 corresponded in 
many ways to the prescriptions given in the modern Gujarati “Fire Offering Ritual,” 
Āhutividhān, provided in the collection of texts on Māṇibhadra edited by Nandlāl 
Devluk (1997, 561–​571). I observed the ritual along with a few dozen laypeople, but 
the main participants in the ceremony were two lay ritual specialists (vidhikāra), 
a local family that sponsored the ceremony, and a few Śvetāmbara nuns of the 
Tapā Gaccha. In the front courtyard of the temple, between a metal icon of a jina 
placed in a silver replica of the Jina’s Preaching Assembly (samavasaraṇa) and a 
square fire pit, the ritual specialists established an icon of Māṇibhadra, along with 
a metal yantra of him, in a metal plate (thāli) (fig. 6.1). Earlier that morning, the 
ritual specialists had worshiped the metal jina icon following the eightfold pūjā and 
had consecrated the ritual space by establishing a pot (kumbha) and lamp next to 
the icon.
The homa ceremony then began with the lay sponsors, wearing their pūjā clothes and 
crowns to resemble the ideal worshipers of the jinas, the kings and queens of the gods, 
indras and indrāṇīs, performing a ritual ablution of the yantra of Māṇibhadra.9 The lay 
worshipers and fire pit then had to be purified and protected, and Māṇibhadra had to 
be invited to join the ceremony. One ritual specialist, after reciting a Sanskrit mantra 
to ensure the purification of the ground on which the ceremony was to be performed 
(bhūmiśuddhi), recited the Sanskrit Vajrapañjarastotra, which combines the nine lines 
of the main mantra of Jainism, the Prakrit pañcanamaskāra, with Sanskrit pleas to create 
protective wear for different parts of the body (Balbir 2018, 283–​285). As the ritual spe­
cialist recited the hymn, the laypeople in attendance performed corresponding gestures, 
touching the respective parts of their bodies and visualizing the emergence of protective 
coverings. The ritual specialists then invited Māṇibhadra into the ritual space, reciting 
Sanskrit mantras and showing the corresponding hand gestures (mudrā) of invitation 
(āvāhanamudrā), establishment (sthāpanā), placing near (sannidhāna), asking to re­
main (sannirodha), and hiding (avaguṇṭhana) the ceremony from outsiders so that only 
participants are affected.10
After the ritual space was sanctified and the worshipers were protected, it was time to 
make offerings into the fire. The laymen who had sponsored the ceremony offered 108 
balls of dried fruit and herbs into the fire as the ritual specialists and nuns recited nine 
verses that request from Māṇibhadra a variety of benefits, including wealth, children, 
fame, kingship, protection for unborn babies, protection from childhood disease and 
accidental death, the removal of ghosts and malignant spirits, and general peace and 
well-​being (Devluk 1997, 567–​568). The ceremony concluded with the lay participants 
performing ārati by waving a flame in front of the icon of Māṇibhadra and singing a 
praise poem to him composed in 1808/​1809 by the lay poet Mādhavmās Dīpvijay 
(Devluk 1997, 659–​570). To complete the ceremony, the ritual specialists recited two

--- PAGE 159 ---
134      Ellen Gough
 
Sanskrit verses to dismiss Māṇibhadra from the fire pit and to ask for forgiveness for any 
wrongdoings (Devluk 1997, 570).
This homa for Māṇibhadra takes a structure common to tantric homas, which 
involves a deity being invited into a ritual diagram using mantras and mudrās, rites 
of protection and purification using visualizations and the placement of mantras on 
the body, offerings of oblations into a fire that are accompanied by the recitation of 
Figure 6.1.  The icon and yantra of Māṇibhadra Vīra established for his homa in a conse­

February 2013.

--- PAGE 160 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      135
 
non-​Vedic mantras, and the final dismissal of the deity.11 However, the ritual manual for 
Mānibhadra’s homa repeatedly attempts to make the ceremony “Jain” by stressing the 
importance of nonviolence. For example, the wood for the fire, which should come from 
trees that produce a milk-​like sap (see the trees mentioned in table 6.1), should be com­
pletely dry and free from living beings. The fire offerings should also be vegetarian—​the 
108 balls offered into the fire should be made of ground saffron, musk, amber, valerian 
(Guj. tagar), bitter aloe (Guj. agar), camphor, dried rose petals, almonds, pistachios, 
almondette seeds (Guj. cāroḷī), walnuts, cashews, areca nuts, dried coconut, raisins, and 
ghee (in fig. 6.2, the seated, crowned layman in white holds the 108 balls of dried fruit on 
a circular plate (thālī)) (Devluk 1997, 562).
In addition to these nonviolent offerings, the ritual specialists, after establishing the 
fire pit, recited a mantra to ensure that no living beings would be harmed in the offering. 
They first recited a Sanskrit mantra typical to tantric homas that invites the fire deity 
Agni, using Vedic epithets, into the fire pit:
oṃ hrīṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakāryāṇi sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya 
svāhā. (Devluk 1997, 565)12

(Oh, Vaiśvānara! Jātaveda! Come here, come here, Red-​Eyed One! Fulfill all [my] 
actions, svāhā).
The ritual specialists then recited a mantra unique to Jain homas that requests that the 
ceremony not harm single-​sensed living beings (ekendriyajīva):
oṃ

hrīṃ
