(May this homa fire for the Jain tutelary gods and goddesses be here always to burn 
all impurities [and] to illuminate the teachings of the jinas. May there be no harm  
to the single-​sensed souls of the fire. May there be no pain in the worship of the  
gods and goddesses of the teachings of the jinas. May there be no bad karma (pāpa). 
May there be good fortune. May there be no violence here for us in this worship).
Jain ontology places souls (jīva) into a hierarchy of five different categories: those with 
one, two, three, four, and five senses. While humans and some animals have five senses, 
plants and the elements of earth, water, fire, and air only have the sense of touch (Tatia 
1994, 41–​46). This mantra, then, recognizes that homas have the potential to harm not 
only the souls of the plants offered into the fire but also the fire itself. It draws on a long 
tradition of Jains using their words—​recitations—​to offset the karmic effects of their 
actions. If recitations are powerful enough to destroy bad karma, as early Jain texts and 
the main mantra of Jainism, the pañcanamaskāra, proclaim,13 then they should also 
be able to end violence. In this way, by promoting Jain teachings in the narratives and 
worship of Māṇibhadra, Tapā Gaccha Śvetāmbara Jains justify embracing a popular 
practice—​homa—​which is explicitly rejected in early Jain texts but benefits the tradition 
because its perceived ability to grant worldly success can attract lay followers to support 
Jain mendicants.
Fire Offerings for the Consecration  
of a Digambara Icon of a Jina
Digambaras also follow tantric models of homa to honor Jain ideals that have been 
invited into ritual diagrams, and they also attempt to validate the ritual use of fire by 
mitigating violence and interpreting homas as a promotion of Jain teachings. As is 
the case for Śvetāmbaras, modern Digambara image consecration (pratiṣṭhā) cer­
emonies are good places to see different types of homas, since they always involve 
multiple fire offerings. In his manual on image consecration the Pratiṣṭhāsāroddhāra 
(PrS), the thirteenth-​century lay Digambara Āśādhara even recommends that the lay

--- PAGE 162 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      137
 
participants in the ceremony bathe daily and make offerings into a fire, reciting mantras 
for pacification (śānti), to ensure that the ceremony is free from disturbance (PrS 1.140; 
Gulābcandra n.d., 83).
Many of the homas of Digambara image consecration ceremonies were developed 
in the medieval period in response to non-​Jain tantric image consecration ceremonies. 
Today, followers of one of the two main branches of Digambara Jainism, the Bīsapantha, 
adhere to the instructions in Nemicandra’s Pratiṣṭhātilaka, a Sanskrit manual com­
posed in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, around 1200. Nemicandra’s Pratiṣṭhātilaka shows 
great influence from the “tantric” texts on image consecration of the Śaiva Siddhānta 
promoted by the Chola kings ruling at that time and place.14 Like manuals of the 
Śaiva Siddhānta and other tantric traditions, Nemicandra’s Pratiṣṭhātilaka and other 
Digambara image consecration handbooks require the construction of ritual diagrams 
to consecrate different types of temple image—​from deities to images of a liberated soul 
(siddha). To transform the stone or metal images into the sacred beings they embody, 
the qualities of these sacred beings must first be called into a diagram in the presence 
of the image, and the worship of these ritual diagrams concludes with a fire sacrifice. 
For the consecration of a jina, the yāgamaṇḍala must be constructed. Ritual specialists 
recite mantras to invite into the yāgamaṇḍala the seventy-​two tīrthaṅkaras of the pre­
sent, past, and future; the twenty tīrthaṅkaras permanently located on the island of the 
cosmos Videhakṣetra; thirty-​six qualities of a mendicant leader; twenty-​five of a mendi­
cant teacher; twenty-​eight qualities of a mendicant; and forty-​eight superhuman powers 
(ṛddhi) (Gough 2020, 590–​591).
In 2013, I participated in two Digambara image consecration ceremonies that cen­
tered on the worship of a yāgamaṇḍala and concluded with a homa. In January 2013, 
in Hastinapur, Uttar Pradesh, I attended the final two days of an image consecration 
ceremony led by disciples of the nun Āryikā Jñānamatī, a Bīsapanthī. Only a dozen 
laypeople participated in the homa—​the lay sponsors of the ceremony—​along with 
a nun, who did not make offerings but recited the mantras for the oblations. The cer­
emony followed the instructions given in Jñānamatī’s edition of Nemicandra’s 
Pratiṣṭhātilaka, and the concluding homa ceremony on the final day corresponded 
to instructions given in modern manuals on the yāgamaṇḍala like Śītal Prasād’s Yāg 
Maṇḍal evaṃ Pañckalyāṇak Vidhān (Prasād 2019). As is common for the concluding 
fire-​offering rites for the worship of Digambara ritual diagrams made of synthetic col­
ored powder (vidhāna, see fig. 6.3), three fire pits were constructed in a row in front of 
the yāgamaṇḍala: one triangular kuṇḍa, one square one, and one circular one. After 
auspicious and protective invocations were recited and Agni was invited into each of the 
fire pits via mantras, the laymen and -​women who sponsored the ceremony established 
themselves on either side of the kuṇḍas and offered camphor into the fire pits as the nun 
recited sets of Sanskrit mantras outlined below (fig. 6.4).
The following month, in February 2013, just outside Jaipur, Rajasthan, I attended a 
seven-​day festival attended by the monk Ācārya Vibhavasāgara for the consecration of 
a temple of the other main branch of Digambara Jainism, the Terāpantha. The lay ritual 
specialists leading the ceremony followed the instructions in the Pratiṣṭhāratnākara,

tied to their right wrists, performed the eightfold pūjā to the nine supreme entities of 
Jainism (navadevatā)—​the five supreme beings plus right view, knowledge, conduct, 
and austerities—​by transferring eight different substances from one plate to another 
(Gulābcandra n.d., 271–​273).16 The fire offering followed, using seven sets of mantras 
discussed below. With the pronunciation of “svāhā” that concluded each mantra, the 
laypeople would offer ghee and camphor to small individual fires burning in front of 
them. The ceremony concluded with the ritual specialist reciting a Prakrit invocation for 
peace, or pacification of negative influences (śānti): the pañcanamaskāra, the mantras to 
the four auspicious entities inscribed on the vināyaka yantra, plus a concluding plea for 
peace (Gulābcandra n.d., 280).
Both of the homas in Hastinapur and Jaipur, following Nemicandra’s Pratiṣṭhātilaka17 
and the Pratiṣṭhāratnakara, respectively, drew upon the instructions for fire offerings 
given in Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa, the ninth-​century Jain history of the universe mentioned 
earlier. In describing the homa, the compiler of the Pratiṣṭhāratnakara, Paṇḍit 
Gulābcandra (n.d., 86 nn. 1–​2, 88 n. 1, 89 n. 2, 90 n. 1), explicitly references Sanskrit 
verses from ­chapters 38 and 40 of the Ādipurāṇa. The Ādipurāṇa tells the story of the 
first tīrthaṅkara, Ṛṣabha, and ­chapter 38 describes how Bharata, Ṛṣabha’s son and the 
universal emperor (cakravartin), having established himself as king in his capital, 
Ayodhya, lectures his subjects on the proper ritual actions of a lay Jain. In this narrative, 
Bharata insists that a twice-​born (dvija), a term that in brahminical texts designates a 
member of the three higher classes (varṇa) who have the right to perform the fire sac­
rifice, has two births: one from his mother and another from Jain ritual actions (kriyā). 
A true twice-​born performs 108 kriyā: fifty-​three rituals related to birth as a Jain layman 
(garbhānvayakriyā), forty-​eight rituals related to initiation and life as a Jain monk 
(dīkṣānvayakriyā), and the seven acts that occur only because of the fruition of merito­
rious actions (kartranvayakriyā) (ĀP 48.51–​53).18 Padmanabh Jaini (1979, 292), noting 
the brahminical influence on these kriyās, which include most of the sixteen brah­
minical rites of passage (saṃskara), explains that “the five essential elements of Hindu 
ritual—​presence of a deity, availability of a priest capable of invoking that deity, use of 
a holy chant or mantra, ritual offering, and, most important, holy fire—​were all made a 
part of [these] Jaina ceremonies.”
Chapters 38 and 39 of the Ādipurāṇa describe each of these kriyās, which essentially 
outline the Jain path to liberation by tracking the journey of a single soul from concep­
tion as a human to liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The “fruition,” or kartranavaya, 
ceremonies detailed in Ādipurāṇa 39.81–​200 are connected to the so-​called seven su­
preme stations, the saptaparamasthāna, or the stages through which a soul destined for 
liberation will pass:
	
1.	 Birth as a human male in a good family (sajjāti)
	
2.	 Being an honorable householder (sadgṛhitva)
	
3.	 Initiating as a monk (pārivrājya)
	 4.	 Birth as a god (surendratā)
	
5.	 Birth as a universal emperor (sāmrājya)

--- PAGE 167 ---
142      Ellen Gough
 
	 6.	 Achieving omniscience (paramārhantya)
	
7.	 Achieving liberation (parinirvāṇa) (ĀP 38.37)
Chapter 40 details the mantras one should use in each of the kriyās, grouping 
them into seven sets. It is these seven groups of mantras that the Pratiṣṭhāratnākara 
(Gulābcandra n.d., 276–​282), Nemicandra’s Pratiṣṭhātilaka (Jñānamati 2012, 70–​72), 
and the Hindi manual on the yāgamaṇḍala by the ritual specialist Śītal Prasād (2019, 
160–​164) prescribe for their homas. Each Sanskrit mantra ends in “svāhā,” indicating 
that its recitation should accompany an offering.
The seven groups of mantras are:
	
1.	 Pīṭhikā mantras (ĀP 40.10–​26): thirty-​six verbal offerings to Jain ideals, including 
the qualities of the soul (infinite knowledge, perception, power, bliss). These 
“foundation” (pīṭhikā) mantras act as an auspicious invocation and ensure that the 
results of the mantras are pure (Gulābcandra n.d., 86).
	 2.	 Jāti mantras (ĀP 40.26–​31): eight verbal offerings to Jain ideals, including praises 
to the three jewels (ratnatraya) that constitute the path to liberation: right view, 
knowledge, and conduct. The purpose of these “birth placement” (jāti) mantras 
is to ensure that proper thought arises in worshipers (Gulābcandra n.d., 86). 
Padmanabh Jaini (1979, 296), explaining that this set of mantras today among 
Digambaras “is typically recited during the celebration of a Jaina birth-​ceremony,” 
provides a translation of the mantras, which I have modified:
Oṃ, I take refuge in the one who is born [has realized] the truth, svāhā
Oṃ, I take refuge in the one who is born [has become] an arhat, svāhā
Oṃ, I take refuge in the mother [the enlightenment] of the arhats, svāhā
 Oṃ, I take refuge in the sons [the disciples] of the arhats, svāhā
Oṃ, I take refuge in those whose knowledge is infinite, svāhā
Oṃ, I take refuge in those who have reached the incomparable birth [liberation],  
svāhā
Oṃ, I take refuge in the three jewels, svāhā
O Sarasvatī! You who are the correct view, the embodiment of knowledge! Svāhā! 
May the fruits of this ritual the be the attainment of omniscience.19 May it elimi­
nate [the possibility of a] premature death. May it bring about a liberating death 
(samādhimaraṇa), svāhā.
	
3.	 Nistāraka mantras (ĀP 40.31–​37): eleven verbal offerings to Jain ideals, in­
cluding praises to different types of pious people (e.g., Jain laypeople 
[śrāvaka]). The purpose of these “liberating” mantras is to ensure that the cor­
rect thought that has arisen will not be momentary and will remain in the soul 
(Gulābcandra n.d., 86).
	 4.	 Ṛṣi mantras (ĀP 40.37–​47): fifteen verbal offerings to Jain ideals, including the five 
vows of a Jain mendicant and different Jain mendicants, like the disciples of the 
jinas (gaṇadhara). The purpose of these mantras to “sages” (ṛṣi) is to ensure that

--- PAGE 168 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      143
 
laypeople, having adopted the lay vows, will achieve a good birth placement where 
they can take the vows of a Jain mendicant (Gulābcandra n.d., 86).
	
5.	 Surendra mantras (ĀP 40.47–​56): thirteen verbal offerings to Jain ideals, including 
different types of gods (indra). The purpose of these mantras is to ensure that after 
becoming a mendicant, one’s soul is reborn as a god (surendra) devoted to the jinas 
(Gulābcandra n.d., 86).
	 6.	 Paramarājan mantras (ĀP 40.56–​63): nine verbal offerings to Jain ideals, in­
cluding, as in the surendra mantras, an invocation to the twenty-​second jina, 
Nemi. The purpose of these mantras of the “supreme king” (paramarājan) is to en­
sure that one’s soul will be reborn as a king who is devoted to Jainism and achieves 
worldly success (Gulābcandra n.d., 87).
	
7.	 Parameṣṭhin mantras (ĀP 40.63–​73): twenty-​three verbal offerings to the quali­
ties of spiritually advanced souls; the twenty-​first mantra praises the five supreme 
beings (parameṣthin) themselves. The purpose of these mantras is to ensure that 
one’s soul will be reborn as one of the supreme beings, a siddha, or liberated soul 
(Gulābcandra n.d., 87).
Here, we can see the connection between the “seven supreme stations” and each set of 
mantras. When laypeople recite these mantras and make offerings into the fire, Gulābcandra 
(n.d., 86) confirms, they establish the intention (saṅkalpa) that the fire offering will allow 
their souls to pass through these seven stages, eventually becoming liberated.
The Ādipurāṇa explains that the recitation of these mantras should accompany the 
homas and image worship that take place for all the different kriyās (ĀP 40.77). At 
the outset of each kriyā, a twice-​born should establish three fires—​the gārhapatya, 
āhavanīya, and dakṣiṇāgni—​which commemorate the fires that were used in the crema­
tion ceremonies of the tīrthaṅkaras, the disciples of the tīrthaṅkaras (gaṇadhara), and 
the other Jains ascetics who have achieved omniscience (kevalin), respectively (40.82–​
84). A twice-​born should also recite these mantras daily for his fire offering made at the 
three junctures of the day (saṃdhyā)—​morning, noon, and evening (ĀP 40.79).20 The 
man who maintains these three fires in his home, regularly performing this fire offering, 
is called an “āhitāgni” and “agnihotrī” (ĀP 40.85).
Digambara Jains to this day use these same names for the three fire pits established 
for the concluding worship of a ritual diagram (figs. 6.4, Gulābcandra n.d., 89).21 In Śītal 
Prasād’s manual on the yāgamaṇḍala, the Sanskrit mantras to be recited to establish the 
three fires identify them as follows:
	
1.	 Square fire pit: the pit that evokes the cremation of the tīrthaṅkaras 
(tīrthaṅkarakuṇḍa), into which the gāryapatya fire is invited.
	 2.	 Circular fire pit: the pit that evokes the cremation of the disciples of the 
tīrthaṅkaras (gaṇadharakuṇda), into which the āhvānīya fire is invited.
	
3.	 Triangular fire pit: the pit that evokes the cremation of other omniscient souls 
(sāmānyakevalikuṇḍa), into which the dakṣiṇāgni is invited (Prasād 2019, 159).

--- PAGE 169 ---
144      Ellen Gough
 
Prasād (2019, 155) confirms that these three fires should be established for the yāgamaṇḍala 
havana, but he recognizes that individual kuṇḍas (sthaṇḍila) made of earth can be used if 
the number of participants requires it; in the ceremony in Jaipur, this was the case (fig. 6.5).
The description of these fires in the Ādipurāṇa, in the words of Padmanabh Jaini 
(1979, 292), is “clearly brahminical.” Jinasena has defined an ideal Jain layman in essen­
tially brahminical terms, requiring him to undertake nearly all sixteen of the brahmin­
ical saṃskāras. This Jain “twice-​born” should be invested with the sacred thread in the 
fourteenth garbhānvaya ceremony and then maintain three fires in his home, making 
sure not to give the fires to anyone who has not undergone the proper saṃskāras (ĀP 
40.87). Jinasena even names this Jain layman an agnihotrī—​the Vedic term for one who 
performs the agnihotra śrauta sacrifice daily, at the morning and evening saṃdhyās, 
using the three fires22—​and an 1, “the householder who sets up the sacred fires and 
thereby gains access to the transcendent world of śrauta sacrifice” (Heesterman [1982] 
1988, 268).
However, Digambara Jain homas that are performed today do not conform to this 
Vedic paradigm. While Digambaras may have adopted Vedic terminology, they use the 
three fires in “tantric” ceremonies to complete the ritual propitiation of diagrams like 
the yāgamaṇḍala and vināyaka yantra. The laypeople who participated in the homa cer­
emonies were not required to undertake the saṃskāras and sacred thread investiture 
ceremonies. Indeed, unlike Śvetāmbaras, who do not allow female participation in the 
physical offerings, modern Digambaras permit both men and women to make offerings 
into the fire.
Digambara homas have also been made “Jain” in several ways. As in the Śvetāmbara 
homa to Māṇibhadra, the Pratiṣṭhāratnākara emphasizes the importance of nonvio­
lence. Paṇḍit Gulābcandra acknowledges that previous Jain ācāryas have dictated that 
the wood of certain special trees be used to start the fire, but because this pure wood is 
not always available, and living beings (jīva) can be found in some types of wood, the 
fire should be started with camphor to avoid harming any souls (Gulābcandra n.d., 83, 
273). And even more so than in the Śvetāmbara worship of Māṇibhadra, the Digambara 
homas in which I participated in 2013 were committed to promoting uniquely Jain 
teachings. From the spiritually advanced Jain ascetics honored in the vināyaka yantra to 
the connection between the mantras of the homa and the seven stages on the Digambara 
path to liberation, the components of these ceremonies show how Jain homas are 
not solely performed to appease unenlightened deities for mundane ends. Medieval 
Digambara Jains did not simply appropriate the tantric image consecration practices of 
non-​Jains; they integrated them into their path to liberation.
In Defense of Jain Homas
The homas documented in this chapter are, however, only two of the dozens of dif­
ferent types of fire offerings modern Jains regularly perform. Jain homas are much more

--- PAGE 170 ---
Homa in Jain Traditions      145
 
common than the dearth of scholarship on the practice suggests. One might be sur­
prised to know how widespread the ritual use of fire is for modern image-​worshiping 
Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras, since Jainism is known for being based on the rejection 
of the Vedic sacrifice.
Some Jains, recognizing this contradiction, have actively rejected the ritual use of fire. 
One of these reformers plays a key role in the origin story of Māṇibhadra: Loṅkā Śāh, 
the fifteenth-​century founder of the Śvetāmbara mendicant lineage the Loṅkā Gaccha. 
Loṅkā repudiated image worship, arguing that it is not enjoined in the true canonical 
scriptures and contravenes the most fundamental of Jain teachings: nonviolence. Today, 
two groups of Śvetāmbara Jains—​Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs—​remain committed to 
aniconic worship practices and can trace their roots to the Loṅkā Gaccha (Dundas 2002, 
246–​262). In Digambara Jainism, lay reformers in Jaipur in the eighteenth century also 
noted the violence involved in using single-​sensed beings—​plants and the elements—​in 
temple worship and formed a new sect of Digambara Jainism, the Terāpantha, which 
rejected the ritual use of fire, lamps, and incense, among other practices. In his Buddhi 
Vilāsa from 1770, Bakhatrām Śāh, an important Digambara intellectual, documents 
the distinguishing practices of Terāpanthīs, emphasizing that “they do not use flowers, 
cooked food, or lamps when worshiping Jina images in temples, nor do they lustrate 
them” (Cort 2002, 64). Today, when performing the eightfold pūjā, Terāpanthīs transfer 
yellow-​colored coconut pieces from one plate to another to represent offering a lamp to 
the jinas, and they transfer cloves to represent incense.23
However, for as long as fire offerings have been a part of Jain ritual culture, there have 
been Jains who have defended the practice. In his introduction to the Pratiṣṭhāratnākara, 
Paṇḍit Gulābcandra (n.d., 84–​86) provides twelve citations from foundational 
Digambara Jain scriptures attributed to important ācāryas like Kundakunda and 
Pūjyapāda that enjoin the ritual use of incense, lamps, or fire. Padmanabh Jaini (1979, 
297), who notes that “Jinasena seems to have been the first śramaṇa ācārya to elevate 
fire to a ‘holy’ status,” has translated Jinasena’s definition and justification of Jain fire 
offerings in the Ādipuraṇa:
Fire has no inherent sacredness, and no divinity. But because of its contact with the 
divine body of the arhat [at the time of his cremation], it can be considered pure. . . .  
Such worship of the fire, like the worship of places made sacred by a saint’s having 
attained nirvāṇa there, is not in any way blameworthy.
(ĀP 40.88–​89)
For Jinasena, fire is not sacred because it is a deity, but because it is connected to the 
liberation of the enlightened founders of Jainism and thus can inspire Jains to follow in 
these teachers’ footsteps. In this context, fire becomes worthy of honoring not because 
the Vedas enjoin it but because it is connected to “something that is for Hindus ritually 
impure in the extreme: the funeral pyre” (Jaini 1979, 298).
While one might agree with the arguments of Loṅkā, the Terāpanthīs, and other Jains 
who have rejected fire sacrifice due to the violence of the ceremony, one must admit

--- PAGE 171 ---
146      Ellen Gough
 
that Jains have remained firm in their rejection of the brahminical fire sacrifice. Jain ac­
ceptance of homa ceremonies has become a way to recast common tantric practices as 
the promotion of Jain teachings. Therefore, for the many image-​worshiping Digambaras 
and Śvetāmbaras who regularly perform fire offerings without any inhibitions, criticisms 
of the ritual use of fire in early Jain scriptures can be seen less as a rejection of homa, per 
se, and more as a rebuke of brahminical hegemony.

Chapter 7
The Neuroscience of 
Tantric Practice
Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
Introduction: Tantra, Meditation,  
and Neuroscience
The term “tantra” has been used to describe a wide range of practices and texts from 
South, Southeast and East Asia and the Himalayas. Our concern in this chapter is more 
specific, with tantric practice as part of a process of spiritual training or self-​cultivation 
within Buddhist and Hindu religious traditions. To quote Glen Hayes and Sthaneshwar 
Timalsina (2017, 1–​2):
Tantra may be regarded as historical systems of ritual practices in which an individual 
engages with a layered cosmology, utilizing diverse senses, cognitive capacities, and 
sexuality in order to achieve elevated states of consciousness and embodied liber­
ation. There are innumerable iterations of Tantra, ranging from theistic to nonthe­
istic, although most seek to “reverse” the flow of cosmic process and manifestation in 
order to lead the individual to some heightened, typically unitive, state.
This chapter is particularly concerned with Vajrayāna, a tantric tradition practiced in 
Tibet and the Himalayas.1 For Buddhist practitioners in the Vajrayāna tradition, the aim 
of their spiritual training is to attain culturally valued ideals of awakening, Buddhahood, 
and liberation. This is the Buddhist version of the unitive state mentioned by Hayes and 
Timalsina. Vajrayāna practice is thought to give special insight into the nature of reality 
to those who practice it successfully, and also to confer powers and abilities that may 
be used for the benefit of others. It also provides a training for a career as a tantric prac­
titioner. In Tibet, Bhutan, and other culturally related areas of the Himalayas, tantric 
practitioners perform rituals for laypeople or lay communities, intended to bring about

--- PAGE 177 ---
152      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
healing, prosperity, defense against misfortune, and the like. They may act as religious 
teachers and, in some cases, have secular authority within their communities.
Becoming a tantric practitioner does not necessarily involve permanently adopting a 
monastic or ascetic lifestyle, but it does require a commitment to sustained practice over 
many years, including prolonged periods of full-​time retreat, often as part of a commu­
nity of practitioners, and normally under the guidance of a tantric guru (in Tibetan, 
“lama,” bla ma2). A standard introductory retreat period in the Kagyü (Bka’ brgyud) and 
Nyingma (Rnying ma) traditions of Tibetan Buddhism is three years and two weeks (or 
three years, three months, three days) (Kongtrul 1994); full training might involve two 
or three such retreats.3 How does this training equip tantric practitioners for their future 
careers?
Like other forms of tantric and non-​tantric meditation and yoga practices (see, e.g., 
Farias, Brazier, and Lalljee 2021; Newcombe and O’Brien-​Kop 2021), Vajrayāna involves 
a systematic training of mind and body. Alternatively, and preferably, one might speak of 
the unified bodymind, since much of the training works across any imagined boundary 
between the two. Many of these yoga and meditation practices, along with secularized 
versions such as the so-​called mindfulness-​based interventions (Baer 2006; Purser et al. 
2016), have been studied in recent years using the methods of neuroscience as well as of 
psychology and other contemporary scientific disciplines.
One important question is whether, from a neuroscientific perspective, tantric 
practices such as those of the Vajrayāna differ systematically from other forms of yoga 
and meditation, and if so in what ways. The question is complicated by the wide variety 
of practices covered by terms such as “meditation” and “yoga” (see, e.g., MacDonald et 
al. 2013; O’Brien-​Kop and Newcombe 2021, 5–​8). We argue, however, on the basis of 
Kozhevnikov’s neuroscientific research, that the techniques of the Vajrayāna do, in 
fact, differ systematically from non-​tantric forms of meditation or yoga studied by 
neuroscientists. More specifically, the non-​tantric techniques studied so far generally 
involve activation of the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS; the so-​called relaxa­
tion response). Tantric (Vajrayāna Buddhist) techniques involve arousal,4 not relaxa­
tion, and do not primarily engage the PNS. This contrast links to specific features of 
tantric techniques, including their incorporation of physical activity (special types of 
breathing, physical movements) and specific types of cognitive activity, along with mul­
timodal imagery of one’s body transformations and associated emotional components.
Arousal-​based techniques are not unique to Vajrayāna Buddhism. While evidence so 
far is limited, a range of techniques used in Hindu tantric practice also appears to be­
long to this neurologically distinctive class of techniques. So do some Islamic and East 
Asian spiritual and self-​cultivation practices. All this points to a more complex picture 
of Asian meditative and contemplative practices than has been generally recognized.
The following sections of the chapter provide a short introduction to Vajrayāna 
Buddhism and to the experimental techniques of neuroscience. Later sections examine 
the growth of the neuroscientific understanding of meditation and of tantra, including 
the question of nondual awareness. The conclusion considers the current state of our 
knowledge and discusses possible future directions.

--- PAGE 178 ---
The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      153
 
Vajrayāna Buddhism within the 
Buddhist Tradition
In Tibetan Buddhist societies, Vajrayāna (Tibetan dorjé tekpa, rdo rje theg pa) is 
regarded as the primary mode of attaining Buddhahood and other high spiritual states. 
Other Tibetan Buddhist practices, whether or not aimed at attaining Buddhahood, 
frequently incorporate Vajrayāna (tantric) elements (Thurman 1985). However, by no 
means all Tibetan Buddhist practices are classified by Tibetans as Vajrayāna or tan­
tric.5 Vajrayāna practice is the summit of the spiritual path, not its totality. Most Tibetan 
scholastic systems understand it as the final stage of a three-​stage sequence of Hīnayāna 
(“Lesser Vehicle”), Mahāyāna (“Great Vehicle”), and Vajrayāna (=​ tantra). The first two 
stages may also be grouped together as “Sūtra practices.”
These three stages also correspond in general terms to the historical development of 
Buddhism in India; Vajrayāna’s known presence in the human world dates from the later 
stages of Indian Buddhism (ca. 650 CE onward). Tibetan Buddhist practices include 
Hīnayāna6 and Mahāyāna material alongside specifically Vajrayāna techniques.
Vajrayāna practices continue today as a central component of Buddhism in Tibet, 
the Himalayas (including Nepal and Bhutan), and Mongolia. Elsewhere in Buddhist 
Asia, they were also widely cultivated in the past and continue on a smaller scale in a 
variety of Buddhist and Buddhist-​related contexts (e.g., Crosby 2020; Gellner 1992; 
Hooykaas 1973; Orzech et al. 2011). The Vajrayāna is also increasingly popular in North 
America, Europe, and other regions outside Buddhist Asia. Vajrayāna Buddhism is a 
major form of Buddhist practice, understood by many Buddhists throughout much 
of the history of Buddhism as a central and essential part of the Buddhist path, par­
ticularly for serious and committed practitioners. For Tibetan and Himalayan 
practitioners, it remains central but continues to be seen as a difficult, a challenging, 
and an elite form of practice, to be undertaken after a thorough initial grounding in 
non-​tantric practice.
So far, scientific research on Vajrayāna practices has been limited. This is particularly 
true in relation to neuroscience. Kozhevnikov’s own work, which is discussed at some 
length in this chapter, represents the most substantial body of experimental work in 
neuroscience on Vajrayāna, or indeed on any tantric tradition.7 Instead, neuroscientists 
investigating meditation practices have focused on a limited range of non-​tantric 
techniques that originate from the so-​called Theravāda tradition, practiced in mainland 
Southeast Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia) and Sri Lanka, and on the clini­
cally defined mindfulness-​based interventions, such as mindfulness-​based stress reduc­
tion (MBSR; Baer 2006). In Tibetan terms, these correspond to Sūtra-​type practices. 
In neuroscientific terms, they generally involve the so-​called relaxation response (PNS 
activation, discussed below, also Benson 1976; Benson et al. 1974). We refer to them as 
“relaxation response-​based practices” or “relaxation-​based practices” for short. By con­
trast, central Vajrayāna practices are “arousal based.”8

--- PAGE 179 ---
154      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
Vajrayāna can be subdivided into two main variants, the Old tantra or Nyingma 
(rnying ma) and the New tantra or sarma (gsar ma). Both derive from late Indian 
Buddhism, but the former go back, at least in part, to the time of the Tibetan Empire 
(seventh to ninth centuries CE), while the sarma teachings were introduced from the 
tenth to twelfth centuries. The sarma schools are often subdivided into the Sakya (sa 
skya), Kagyü, and Geluk (dge lugs), the Geluk being the most recent in origin (early 
fifteenth century). The various schools today have individual versions of specific tan­
tric transmissions, passed on through defined teaching lineages and involving subtle 
differences both in practices and in how the aim of the practices is described and under­
stood (see, e.g., Samuel 1993).
The growth of the sarma schools led to further changes and reformulations among 
the Nyingma, much of it mediated through characteristic visionary techniques (Samuel 
1993, 294–​302, 461–​463, 515–​516). The Nyingma also developed a distinct set of practices 
known as Dzogchen (rdzogs chen) (e.g., Studstill 2005, 125–​171). Dzogchen has its own 
techniques and vocabulary, different from those of tantra proper, although it is generally 
undertaken only after extensive tantric training.
Many Vajrayāna practices are oriented to pragmatic ends such as healing, protec­
tion from illness or misfortune, or destruction of hostile forces or beings, reflecting a 
major aspect of the role of the Vajrayāna in Tibetan society. Others are primarily con­
cerned with the practitioner’s progress toward Buddhahood or awakening (Skt. bodhi). 
Although many techniques are shared between these types of practice, and practitioners 
generally learn both, it is the Buddhahood-​oriented practices on which we focus here. 
They form part of the Mahā, Anu, and Ati categories of the Old tantra (Nyingma, rnying 
ma) traditions, and the equivalent Supreme or Unexcelled, la mé (T. bla na med pa) or 
“Anuttarayoga”9 practices of the New tantra, sarma (T. gsar ma), traditions. The earliest 
known written versions of these various practices appeared in India in the eighth and 
ninth centuries CE (Samuel 2008, 229–​338).
Table 7.1 shows the relationship between these categories diagrammatically.
It is worth noting how Tibetan lamas characteristically contrast the Sūtra (=​ Hīnayāna 
and Mahāyāna) and tantric paths to Buddhahood. A typical formulation is that the 
Sūtra path is focused on the renunciation of ordinary life (Skt. saṃsāra, the “relative” 
dimension, “conventional truth”) and its passions (desire, anger, pride, etc.; Skt. kleśa,

2. Mahāyāna

The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      155
 
also sometimes translated as “negative emotions”). Tantric methods, by contrast, make 
deliberate use of the passions to achieve Buddhahood. To quote the late Tibetan lama 
Chögyal Namkhai Norbu:
From the sutra point of view, the relative dimension is an obstacle to be renounced in 
order to realize the absolute level of voidness. But tantra uses the relative to fuel prog­
ress on the path that leads beyond it, and its attitude to the passions renounced at the 
sutra level is expressed in the tantric saying, “When there is more wood (passions) 
there is more fire (realization).”
(Norbu 2000, 49)
This does not mean that the tantric path is one of willful indulgence of the passions but, 
rather, that the passions are systematically employed as part of the practice. The overall 
contrast implied by Namkhai Norbu’s comments fits with the neuroscientific data, ac­
cording to which Sūtra techniques generally involve calming down the nervous system, 
while tantric techniques involve its deliberate arousal and redirection.10 Note too that 
the absolute level is expressed in terms of “voidness” (Skt. śūnyatā, also “emptiness”), 
a mode of engagement with the world which transcends ordinary dualistic thought. 
We will return to the question of nondual awareness, and to the wider question of the 
achievement of awareness and awakening, later in the chapter.
Neuroscience and the  
Relaxation Response
Neuroscientists have used a variety of experimental methods to study meditation. 
Among the most important is electroencephalography (EEG), first developed in the 
1920s to 1940s (Borck 2018). This involves recording the brain’s spontaneous electrical 
activity over time through multiple electrodes placed on the scalp. The most common 
method of EEG analysis used by meditation researchers relies on changes in EEG power 
in specific frequency bands, referred to by the Greek letter names gamma, beta, alpha, 
theta, and delta. Another important measure is EEG coherence, in other words whether 
two or more sensors exhibit similar oscillatory activity to each other. Changes in EEG 
power and/​or coherence in specific frequency bands have been associated by meditation 
researchers with different mental processes involved in meditative and contemplative 
states (e.g., Cahn and Polich 2006, Fell et al. 2010). Electrocardiography (EKG or ECG), 
the recording of the electrical activity of the heart from electrodes on the chest, was also 
developed during the 1920s to 1940s, and it provides further valuable information about 
internal processes related to meditative techniques. For example, heart rate variability 
(HRV) can be used to trace autonomic nervous system (ANS) activation (e.g., Amihai 
and Kozhevnikov 2014, 4–​6; Tyagi and Cohen 2016).

--- PAGE 181 ---
156      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
Further methods were developed from the 1970s onward, including functional mag­
netic resonance imagining (fMRI), which traces blood flow as an indicator of neural 
activity within the brain, along with other new methods such as arterial spin labeling 
and diffusion MRI. These new neuroimaging methods have been used to detect patterns 
of neural activation within the brain, including those associated with various kinds 
of meditative activity. Although, unlike EEG, the new neuroimaging methods have 
high spatial resolution, they have low temporal resolution, limiting their usefulness in 
tracking change over time. Generally, they allow us only to distinguish static patterns of 
brain activation averaged over the duration of an experiment.
It is important to note that data on neural activity alone rarely provide a clear and 
unambiguous view of mental processes. Data require interpretation through cognitive 
models, which are simplified representations of one or more cognitive processes for 
the purposes of prediction and comprehension (Forstmann et al, 2011; Forstmann and 
Wagenmakers 2015; Smith and Ratcliff 2004). Put otherwise, the field of cognitive neu­
roscience is model based.
The primary focus of neuroscience is the nervous system, including the brain. The 
nervous system is traditionally divided into the central nervous system (CNS; brain and 
spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system, the nerves that branch out from the 
brain and spinal cord throughout the body. The ANS consists of neurons from the CNS 
and peripheral nervous system, and it monitors and regulates internal processes that are 
largely below the level of conscious awareness. There is also a close connection between 
the ANS and the endocrine system, and in human beings, at least, both are related at a 
subjective level to our emotions.
Langley (1921) introduced a distinction between two major aspects of the ANS, 
the sympathetic and parasympathetic, and that distinction was elaborated by subse­
quent authors (e.g., Cannon 1932; Hess 1957). Generally speaking, these early scientists 
thought of sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and parasympathetic nervous system 
(PNS) activity as contrasting and complementary. The SNS was understood to accel­
erate the heart rate, constricting blood vessels and raising blood pressure in order to 
enable a quick and mobilizing response, generally as a reaction to an immediate threat 
(“fight or flight,” in Cannon’s terms). The PNS was understood to slow down the heart 
rate, lower blood pressure, increase intestinal and gland activity, and relax sphincter 
muscles, facilitating rest and social interaction in situations that are safe from danger.
This tidy symmetry between SNS and PNS, fight or flight versus rest and relax, 
gave way from the 1980s onward to a more complex picture, to which we shall return. 
However, it provided the basis for the first major theoretical account of meditation prac­
tice; Herbert Benson’s “relaxation response” model was developed in the early 1970s on 
the basis of a study of transcendental meditation (TM; Benson 1976; Benson et al. 1974). 
Benson’s influential work saw meditation as primarily concerned with bringing about 
relaxation through the activation of the PNS. Jon Kabat-​Zinn’s development in the 
1980s of a Buddhist-​derived practice, originally called Stress Reduction and Relaxation 
Program but subsequently popularized as Mindfulness-​Based Stress Reduction 
(MBSR), provided further support for this approach (Kabat-​Zinn 1982; cf. also Britton

--- PAGE 182 ---
The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      157
 
et al. 2014, 65). The dominance of the relaxation-​response, stress-​reduction approach 
to meditation, along with the popularity and convenience of the mindfulness-​based 
interventions as research topics, has meant that most published meditation research has 
been on practices that fitted this pattern.
Alternatives to the  
Relaxation Response
By the 1990s, researchers had begun to appreciate that Buddhist meditation contained 
many different techniques of mind-​body cultivation, even within the more accessible 
versions of Buddhism. Many of these were quite different from the “mindfulness” ap­
proach popularized by Kabat-​Zinn (Purser and Milillo 2015; Samuel 2016a, 2020), and 
none of them appeared to be primarily aimed at stress reduction. On the practical side, 
these techniques started to be used increasingly as a complement or alternative to the 
“bare awareness” practices which dominated the early years of the “mindfulness move­
ment.” All this led to a need for taxonomies to encompass these various new techniques.
These new taxonomies were generally derived in a relatively uncritical way from 
Buddhist classifications or phenomenological research. Thus, one of the most 
widely used taxonomies of meditation practices distinguishes between “two broad 
categories” of meditation, focused attention (FA) and open monitoring (OM) (Lutz, 
Slagter, et al. 2008, 163). This derives from a traditional Buddhist distinction between 
samatha and vipassanā in Pali (śamatha and vipaśyanā in Sanskrit). However, as we 
will see later, we do not find systematic contrasts between practices classified as FA 
and OM either in cognitive neuroscience models of attention or in experimental 
work. Other newly introduced categories, such as LKM (corresponding to metta-​
bhāvanā—​e.g., Galante et al., 2016; Lippelt et al., 2014) or constructive versus decon­
structive (Dahl et al. 2015), suffer from similar difficulties.11 An ambitious typology 
by Antoine Lutz and others involves a matrix within which kinds of meditation 
are located along three axes, object orientation, dereification, and meta-​awareness 
(Lutz et al. 2015). The matrix helps to clarify the phenomenological categories un­
derlying the researchers’ understanding of various Asian practices, and the authors 
also attempt some neuroscientific interpretation in terms of various neural networks 
postulated from fMRI data, but this interpretation still remains phenomenological 
rather than grounded in experimental data.
The fundamental orientation of Buddhism is toward liberation from saṃsāra 
and toward the attainment of awakening (Buddhahood), a state clearly thought 
of as involving high levels of awareness. A key issue therefore is how one might find 
neuroscientific models for this process. The progressive development of a more sophis­
ticated understanding of the ANS and its relationship to brain activity opened up some 
possible answers.

--- PAGE 183 ---
158      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
Arguments along similar lines came both from experimental psychology and neu­
roscience. Scientists began to point to the existence of a more complex and modulated 
response to potentially threatening situations than was allowed for by the simple SNS-​
PNS contrast. Thus neuroscientist Stephen Porges located this more complex and in­
teractive response in a revised understanding of the ANS (e.g., Porges 2011, 20–​51), 
based on the role of the vagus nerve in mediating processes of SNS arousal. He distin­
guished a “freeze” response to threat, which he associated with phylogenetically older 
(reptilian) parts of the vagal system, from a more complex response associated with the 
later, mammalian parts of the system. In this more modulated response, humans and 
other mammals were able to inhibit the basic freeze response of the SNS in relatively safe 
situations and to develop more complex and adaptive forms of interaction, involving 
control of facial expression, vocal tone, and emotional state (Porges 2011, 57). Lazarus 
and Folkman came to similar conclusions through an examination of how human 
subjects appraised complex social situations (Folkman and Lazarus 1988; Lazarus and 
Folkman 1984). “Appraisal” allowed for situations within the subject’s coping capacity 
to be dealt with by a complex cognitive-​emotional response, rather than a simple fight-​
or-​flight reaction of the SNS.12 Both approaches pointed to a third, intermediate state 
between simple activation of the PNS or SNS.
This state, now generally referred to as autonomic arousal (also PNS withdrawal as­
sociated arousal) has by now been the subject of a number of studies (e.g., Aston-​Jones 
et al. 2000; Dosenbach et al. 2008; Kozhevnikov, Strasser, and Abdullah, 2022, 2). It is a 
state of high wakefulness, in contrast to the state of PNS dominance (relaxation), which 
is closer to the state of sleep. Autonomic arousal allows for a skilled and modulated re­
sponse to a complex situation.
These two states, autonomic arousal and PNS dominance, support different kinds of 
alertness. Although mental states during PNS dominance are associated with relaxa­
tion, they are not necessarily characterized by drowsiness and actual sleep and can occur 
concurrently with a specific type of attention, tonic alertness (i.e., vigilance or sustained 
attention of a relatively permanent character). States of autonomic arousal, however, 
are accompanied by a contrasting form of attention, phasic alertness, which implies the 
deployment of focused (selective) attention and occurs in response to arousing stimuli 
(Petersen & Posner, 2012). It is phasic alertness that allows for the complex, modulated 
response to events described by Porges (2011) and Folkman and Lazarus (1988).
Britton et al. (2014) suggested that, in emphasizing the importance of relaxa­
tion, researchers might be missing the point of Buddhist meditation practices. These 
practices were in fact aimed at the cultivation of tonic alertness, through developing 
a special state of relaxation during which a person remains alert. This changed focus 
would bring our understanding of meditation more into accordance with the Buddhist 
goal of awakening (Britton et al. 2014). In fact, the combination of alpha and occasional 
theta activity noted in Benson’s initial studies of TM and found in most EEG studies 
of meditation (Lomas et al. 2015) is a characteristic EEG marker for tonic alertness 
(Sadaghiani and D’Esposito 2015).

--- PAGE 184 ---
The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      159
 
These studies had however almost all been of relaxation-​response meditation 
techniques. Phasic alertness, the form of alertness associated with autonomic arousal, 
would seem a better basis for developing the wakefulness and fluid responsiveness asso­
ciated with Buddhist awakening. Were there other forms of meditation that were aimed 
more at cultivating phasic alertness? Specifically, could Tantric meditation be directed at 
the development of phasic alertness? In fact, there was already some evidence pointing 
in this direction.
Kozhevnikov’s Research on Vajrayāna
When Kozhevnikov published her first neuroscientific study of deity yoga in 2009, there 
was little substantial research on any Buddhist tantric practices; almost all the research 
had been on non-​tantric practices, including the mindfulness-​based interventions 
and various modernist Vipassanā practices. There had, however, been a number of 
small-​scale studies of Hindu tantra from the 1950s onward.13 In retrospect, some of 
these suggest what we might now interpret as autonomic arousal. They include studies 
by Das and Gastaut (1955)14 and Wenger and Bagchi (1961), each involving some re­
search subjects undertaking Kriya and similar tantric-​affiliated practices, and a third 
study which examined a breathing and mantra practice from the Ananda Marga, a 
modern group whose practices are also in part tantric-​derived (Corby et al. 1978). 
One early study of Tibetan Vajrayāna practice pointed in a similar direction. This had 
been carried out by Herbert Benson on the practice known as tummo (inner heat),15 
later studied by Kozhevnikov (2019). Benson’s initial study of tummo was primarily 
concerned with changes in body temperature (Benson et al. 1982, Benson and Proctor 
1985), but on a subsequent visit he collected EEG data from three monks in Sikkim. His 
data clearly showed increased SNS activity during tummo, though since this did not fit 
the relaxation-​response model he was unable to make much sense of his observations 
(Benson et al. 1990).
Kozhevnikov’s research on Vajrayāna was to take the “arousal” model much further. 
Her work grew out of a wider research agenda on neural mechanisms of visual cogni­
tion (see Kozhevnikov 2019). Motivated by the description of Vajrayāna practices in the 
texts as enhancing the mind and leading to states of high wakefulness, Kozhevnikov 
hypothesized that tantric practices generate the state of arousal and associated phasic 
alertness (focused attention), as contrasted with the “mindfulness” practices, which 
generate the relaxation response and tonic alertness.
Her Tibetan Vajrayāna studies have involved practices from the Kagyü and 
Nyingma traditions, which form part of the sequence of practices oriented to awak­
ening or Buddhahood. This sequence has a similar form in the two traditions, 
commencing with the visualization of a mandala of tantric deities and with self-​
identification with the central deity (yidam, yi dam).16 This stage is referred to in

--- PAGE 185 ---
160      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
English as the generation (also creation or development) stage, in Tibetan kyerim 
(bskyed rim), and it is followed by a second stage, the completion or perfection stage 
(dzogrim, rdzogs rim).17
The completion stage itself consists of two phases: (1) a series of practices working with 
the flow of an inner breath or lung (rlung =​ Skt. prāṇa) through an internally visualized 
network of channels and cakras, followed by (2) other less conceptual practices.18 In the 
Nyingma tradition, these two phases are called “with characteristics” (tsenché, mtshan 
bcas) and “without characteristics” (tsenmé, mtshan med) (e.g., Kongtrul 2007, 69). 
Here tsen19 implies conceptualization, reification, or mental labeling, and the aim is to 
go beyond the conceptual practices (tsenché) to the nonconceptual awareness of the 
tsenmé practices. Practices “with characteristics” in Nyingma tantra include tummo 
(gtum mo, see below).
Once the generation and completion stage practices are mastered, they are performed 
consecutively. Thus, the practitioner might typically perform a generation-​stage prac­
tice involving deity yoga, proceed to completion stage practices “with characteristics” 
such as tummo, and then undertake a practice “without characteristics” involving 
nonconceptual awareness, such as Mahāmudrā or Rigpa (table 7.2). The completion 
stage is the context for the achievement of the nondual awareness which is the insight 
into reality. This, as Elio Guarisco and Ingrid Mcleod note, following Jamgön Kongtrul, 
is “not a new state of mind developed through practice, but one already fully present in 
the mind stream of every being: the pristine awareness of luminous clarity, the union of 
bliss and emptiness” (Guarisco and McLeod 2008, 15).
Could tantric meditation be seen as enabling and facilitating this state of high aware­
ness? This is an issue that Kozhevnikov’s research has progressively explored, initially 
through studies of deity yoga (yidam practice), a central technique in the generation 
stage (Kozhevnikov et al. 2009) and of tummo (gtum mo) meditation, the well-​known 
“inner heat” completion-​stage practice on which Benson had done some preliminary 
research (Kozhevnikov et al. 2013). Kozhevnikov demonstrated that deity yoga brought 
about a dramatic, if relatively short-​lived, increase of visuospatial processing due to 
enhanced capacity for focused attention. She also showed that tummo practitioners 
were indeed able to generate an exceptionally high level of arousal, enabling control over

This is consonant with the Tibetan understanding of the purpose of these practices as 
part of a larger process and indicates that with practices such as deity yoga or tummo we 
need to look not just at what state of awareness is achieved in the practice itself but also 
at what the practice may enable the meditator to do in subsequent practices.
Kozhevnikov’s next study looked at this sequencing of practices directly, showing, 
through a study of deity yoga followed by rigpa (rig pa, a completion-​stage-​type practice 
“without characteristics”), that deity yoga generated a state of arousal (and high wake­
fulness), which was later employed in rigpa meditation. The research was carried out 
with nine long-​term Vajrayāna practitioners from Shechen monastery in Nepal, and ten 
long-​term Theravāda-​style practitioners from a temple in Bangkok. It used a four-​way 
comparison between the two Vajrayāna practices and two Theravāda practices (Amihai 
and Kozhevnikov 2014). See Table 7.3

the Theravādin practitioners going from rest to kasiṇa practice to vipassanā.
The EKG results confirmed that, while both Theravāda practices elicited the state of 
relaxation, both Vajrayāna practices brought about autonomic arousal. The EEG results 
for the Theravāda practices were typical of Sūtra-​type practices, and consonant with 
a relaxed state of tonic alertness, whereas those for the Vajrayāna practices indicated 
arousal, not relaxation. In a following series of visual tasks, the Vajrayāna practices led 
to a dramatic if short-​term boost in cognitive performance. On the basis of the EKG

data, Kozhevnikov concluded that this was indeed phasic alertness, as opposed to the 
tonic alertness brought about by the Theravāda practices, and that it was enabled by the

A further aim of the study was to show that the “relaxation response” and the FA/​OM 
taxonomy could not accommodate tantric practices. Kasiṇa meditation, as a samatha 
practice, is classified as FA, while vipassanā is OM. These were compared with Tibetan 
deity yoga (classified as FA), and rigpa (classified as OM). If the FA/​OM distinction 
were really to be valid across all meditation practices, one would expect to see similar 
contrasts between the FA and OM practices in the Theravāda and Vajrayāna cases, This, 
however, was not found, implying that the FA/​OM distinction did not hold up at the 
neurological level.
Overall, the four-​way study suggests the need for a substantial reconceptualizing of 
meditation. It establishes that the relaxation response is by no means universal, and that 
the FA/​OM contrast also cannot be assumed to be generally valid (see also Amihai and 
Kozhevnikov 2015).
Achieving Nondual Awareness
Rigpa, the Tibetan “OM-​type” meditation from the Nyingma-​Dzogchen context used 
in the four-​way study, is generally regarded as a form of nondual awareness (NDA; Lutz 
et al. 2007). Another form of NDA, Mahāmudrā, or chagchen in Tibetan (phyag chen), 
has a similar role in the New tantra (sarma) system (Dunne 2011; Jackson 2011). As noted 
above, these modes of awareness are believed to arise when the conceptualizing activity 
of consciousness is quieted, and to represent insight into the true nature of the mind and 
reality. NDA rose to prominence in the meditation research community through a se­
ries of articles by Zoran Josipovic, who had been involved in Kozhevnikov’s deity yoga 
study. Commenting on the FA/​OM distinction, Josipovic noted that
Both focused attention and open monitoring styles of meditation contain an essen­
tially dualistic orientation of “subject-​observing-​object.” Yet, there is another group 
of meditations that do not employ this strategy, but instead rely on accessing a level 
of awareness that is inherently free from this dualistic subject-​object construct. This 
non-​conceptual awareness has sometimes been termed nondual awareness, open 
awareness or open presence,
(Josipovic 2010, 1120)
NDA is a complex term to operationalize. There are many kinds of unitive awareness, 
theistic as well as nontheistic, described in the literature and aimed at by meditators 
(see Josipovic 2010, 2014, 2019, 2021, for further discussion). However, there is no doubt 
that NDA is significant within both Vajrayāna and Mahāyāna Buddhism, and that clas­
sical descriptions of Rigpa and Mahāmudrā place both in this category. Kozhevnikov’s

--- PAGE 188 ---
The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      163
 
most recent research (Kozhevnikov, Strasser, McDougal et al. 2022) has focused on 
Mahāmudrā, the New tantra version of NDA.
In the New tantra tradition in eighth-​ and ninth-​century India, the state of NDA 
known as Mahāmudrā was initially evoked through (physical or visualized) sexual 
practice, with the nonduality of male and female, and of “male” and “female” aspects 
within each individual, as an explicit model. These practices were not accessible to cel­
ibate practitioners, and a non-​tantric mode of access to Mahāmudrā, attributed to the 
Indian guru Maitrīpa (Kragh 2015; Mathes 2021), was developed in the eleventh cen­
tury. This practice (often known as “Sūtra Mahāmudrā”) was transmitted to Tibet and 
passed down among the new monastic lineages of the Kagyü and Geluk (e.g., Jackson 
2019; Rheingans 2017). In modern times, the sexual practices are rarely undertaken lit­
erally, being replaced by symbolic equivalents, so “Tantric Mahāmudrā” is available to 
both monastic and nonmonastic practitioners. However, the Vajrayāna traditions of the 
New tantra in Tibet have maintained both tantric and non-​tantric (Sūtra) routes to the 
achievement of Mahāmudrā.
Kozhevnikov designed an experimental procedure to examine whether the states 
associated with tantric and non-​tantric types of Mahāmudrā differ in terms of their 
neurophysiology. The research involved sixteen highly experienced Vajrayāna 
practitioners from several retreat centers in Bhutan, working under the guidance 
of H. E. Gyeltshen Trulku Rinpoche, a retreat master in the Drukpa Kagyu (Śākya 
Śrī) lineage. The practitioners performed Mahāmudrā meditation after a rest period, 
then undertook deity yoga, followed by a second Mahāmudrā meditation. This was 
followed by tummo for ten members of the group who were also experienced in this 
practice. The intention was to contrast the first Mahāmudrā period, undertaken di­
rectly from rest, with the second, which had been preceded by the “arousal”-​type 
practice of deity yoga. Kozhevnikov assumed that this might replicate the difference 
between tantric and non-​tantric Mahāmudrā practice and show whether they in fact 
involved neurologically similar states. This study showed clearly that the two forms 
of Mahāmudrā had quite different neurological signatures (Kozhevnikov, Strasser, 
McDougal et al. 2022). This implies that these two “NDA practices” involve different 
cognitive processes, and that NDA cannot be treated as a unitary category. The study 
also has consequences for the discussion of attention and its relationship to arousal 
(see Timalsina, this volume), though a consideration of these aspects would take 
us beyond the scope of this chapter (see Kozhevnikov, Strasser, and Abdullah 2022; 
Kozhevnikov, Strasser, McDougal et al. 2022).
Conclusion
Overall, Kozhevnikov’s research so far provides compelling evidence for tantric med­
itation forming a distinctive class of practices, based on the sequential use of specific 
techniques to achieve a degree of control over the ANS. More specifically, they involve

--- PAGE 189 ---
164      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
the creation and maintenance of autonomic arousal and facilitate high levels of phasic 
alertness. The ability to access such enhanced awareness might well be of practical use 
for tantric practitioners making decisions on behalf of clients, and needing to see com­
plex situations clearly and objectively.
At the same time, it is clear that there are many aspects of tantric practice we cannot 
yet model through the experimental techniques of cognitive neuroscience. Consider, 
for example, the so-​called subtle body,20 the complex internal “physiology” of channels 
and wheels or junction points (nāḍī and cakra in Sanskrit) through which flow inner 
air or breath and energetic substances (prāṇa, bindu in Sanskrit), which forms a cen­
tral part of tummo and other completion-​stage practices (see also Hayes, this volume). 
Hindu versions of this “subtle physiology” of tantra have been familiar in Europe, North 
America, and English-​speaking circles in India from the 1920s onward through the 
work of Sir John Woodroffe (e.g., The Serpent Power, first published in 1919; Woodroffe 
1974). More recently, Glen Hayes has described the related subtle body concepts of the 
Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā textual corpus (2012, 2014). Similar procedures and ideas are found in 
many other spiritual traditions, Asian and Western (e.g., Pati and Zubko 2020; Samuel 
and Johnson 2013).
The possibility of a relationship between the internal “subtle physiology” of tantric 
yoga and the structure of the ANS, and so of a neurological interpretation of tantra, was 
already raised in the 1920s by the Indian scholar Vasant Rele in the context of Kuṇḍalinī 
Yoga, a Hindu tantric practice with close similarity to Vajrayāna completion-​stage 
techniques such as tummo (Rele 1931, xiii), and it has been suggested by a number of sub­
sequent writers (e.g., Loizzo 2016; see also Hayes 2014, 692). Both Hindu and Buddhist 
versions of these practices work with a similar visualized internal structure of channels, 
cakras, and flows. The flow through these channels, prāṇa in Sanskrit or lung (rlung) 
in Tibetan, is related to the breath, semen, and menstrual blood. In the Vajrayāna case, 
these male and female sexual substances are also homologized with bodhicitta, the fun­
damental altruistic motivational state that drives the attainment of Buddhahood.21
However, although we can certainly speculate about ways in which such concepts and 
the associated breathing techniques might help to focus mental visualization and facil­
itate control over the ANS (cf. Kozhevnikov et al. 2013; also Minvaleev et al., 2014), at 
this point we do not have concepts or models within the field of neuroscience which we 
could relate to the existence of chakras and channels.22
Future research might also develop a finer-​grained analysis of specific techniques. 
For example, there are many forms of deity yoga, both in the Buddhahood-​oriented 
practices and in those with more pragmatic purposes such as healing. They differ greatly 
in the appearance, color, attributes, prescribed emotional mood, and so on, of the deity, 
and the structure, complexity, and appearance of the mandala or mandala-​s. We are 
not yet in a position to evaluate the effects of these differences, but they are certainly 
regarded as significant within the tradition.
We should also consider the strong affective and devotional component to the 
training, beginning with the religious life most practitioners have experienced in 
families and village communities before entering tantric training, and explicit within

--- PAGE 190 ---
The Neuroscience of Tantric Practice      165
 
the ngöndro (sngon ’gro) practices which are an essential preliminary for Vajrayāna 
practice. Although such factors cannot easily be incorporated into our current exper­
imental methods, there may be ways in which we can gradually work toward neuro­
science models that can incorporate them more fully. The connections between the 
ANS, the endocrine system, and the emotions (cf. Epel et al. 1998), for example, might 
provide ways to build in some of the affective dimensions of the practice situation. The 
latter might be particularly relevant if we are interested in possible applications of tan­
tric processes to promote good health through self-​regulation of physical and psycho­
logical processes. We are all limited by the neural habits we have acquired in the course 
of our lives; tantra may offer an opportunity to balance and restructure some of these 
habits.23 A significant direction for further research might be to examine some of the 
Vajrayāna practices oriented toward pragmatic goals such as good health and vitality 
(Samuel 2016b).
There are many other aspects that might be incorporated into a more developed 
analysis. Practices such as the tulkor (’phrul ’khor) exercises, which involve physical 
movements, breathing, and the directing of consciousness and provide a necessary 
preparation for advanced Vajrayāna practices, surely make an important contribution 
(Baker 2013; Chaoul 2007; Loseries-​Leick 1997). The elaborate monastic dances or cham 
(’chams) performed in many of these communities also contribute to the shaping and 
training of the practitioners’ body techniques and experience (Samuel and David 2016, 
13–​15).
Overall, it is evident that we are still in the relatively early stages of understanding 
tantric processes in neuroscientific terms. As with all research on Buddhist medi­
tation practices, there is a complex relationship between what we can measure, what 
participants experience, and what the practices are intended to bring about according to 
Buddhist sources. Applying the methods of cognitive neuroscience to the study of med­
itation will be a valuable development, among other reasons because it both enables and 
requires researchers to be more explicit about whether and how they are incorporating 
the experience of tantric practitioners and the purpose of the practices. Explicit models 
make it possible to go beyond simply measuring the changes in neural activity during 
different meditative practices, and allow us to begin to understand these changes within 
the parameters of the model.
To formulate such models, researchers need to work closely with practitioners to for­
mulate meaningful hypotheses about the neurophysiological and cognitive processes 
involved in tantric practices, which are aligned with contemporary cognitive psy­
chology and neuroscience theories on the one hand and Buddhist accounts on the other 
hand. We do not have direct access to the practitioner’s subjective experience, though it 
is possible that microphenomenological studies based on careful and detailed recording 
of meditators’ accounts of their subjective experience might take us somewhat further 
in this direction (cf. Bitbol and Petitmengin 2017), and so help meditation researchers to 
build more informed neuroscience models of meditative practices.
As for the purpose of the practices, the central goals of Vajrayāna as of other tantric 
processes can be represented only very approximately within English and other modern

--- PAGE 191 ---
166      Geoffrey Samuel and Maria Kozhevnikov
 
European languages. However, we can start building neuroscientific models of the 
practices, within which we can specify in scientific terms what the practices and states 
might achieve. For example, tummo practice, in this model, could be seen as a practice 
that ideally leads to a full conscious control over the SNS, and therefore over the ANS as 
a whole. This already offers potential connections to, for example, Tibetan descriptions 
of awakening in terms of gaining control over the inner winds of the subtle body 
(cf. Samuel 2019: 780–​781, citing Yangönpa 2015, 73, 78).
Further work on Hindu forms of tantra is also clearly desirable. There are close his­
torical connections between Hindu tantra and Vajrayāna, and similarities between 
many of the practices. Thus various kriya practices described and taught by various 
modern teachers of tantric yoga such as Swami Satyananda (Satyananda 1985) or Swami 
Yogananda (Stevens 2013; Yogananda 1930) have resemblances to tulkor and completion-​
stage practices in the Vajrayāna. Much of this material probably goes back in some form 
to the period when Hindu and Buddhist tantric practitioners were part of a shared ascetic 
milieu in India. However, it is probably more difficult to find the kind of widely shared 
and clearly structured practice regimens available in Tibetan and Himalayan regions 
within the Hindu context. Charismatic twentieth-​century teachers such as Yogananda or 
Satyananda have generally put together their own systems on the basis of material from 
a variety of sources. However there are certainly Hindu practitioners in India and Nepal 
who have attained high levels of competence in tantric practice, and it would be good to 
know more about how their modes of practice compare with those of the Vajrayāna.24
To conclude, the neuroscience of tantric practice is still at a relatively early stage, but 
some significant and important results have been achieved which illuminate not only 
tantric practice in South Asia and the Himalayas but the wider field of meditation and 
mind-​body training processes in many cultures. It is already clear that the methods of 
neuroscience are a valuable complement to the more traditional textual and ethno­
graphic approaches to tantric practice, and that there is the potential for a close and mu­
tually enriching relationship between these different approaches. It is to be hoped that 
the traditional boundaries between academic disciplines do not obstruct the flourishing 
of such a relationship.
