The structure and functions of the subtle body of the AR, reflecting the diverse traditions 
and texts available in seventeenth-​century Bengal, provide us with a quite distinctive 
and transgressive model of the subtle body. As with the models from the Pāñcarātra 
traditions, they demonstrate the richness of esoteric physiology in Vaiṣṇava tantra. This 
chapter now turns to the consideration of the subtle body in Śaiva and Śākta tantric 
traditions, which have their own diversity and complexity.
Subtle Body Systems in Śaiva and 
Śākta Traditions
There is a substantial history of development and variation in the subtle body systems 
within tantric Śaiva and Śākta traditions. Although the well-​known model of the six cakras 
plus the thousand-​petaled lotus appears by the time of the Kubjikāmata-​tantra (ca. eleventh 
century), there are numerous iterations of the subtle body found in the earlier mainstream 
Śaiva Siddhānta, as well as in the Trika and Pratyabhijñā schools of nondual Śaivism. We 
also find extensive systems of the subtle body in later Śrīvidyā and Śākta schools. Alexis 
Sanderson has commented upon these complex layers of subtle body systems (1986, 164):
In fact it [the system of six cakras] is found in none of the early traditions mentioned. 
Instead we find there a great variety in the division of the vertical line of the cen­
tral power (suṣumṇā). There are six “seasons,” five “knots” (granthayah), five voids 
(vyomānī) nine wheels (cakrāni), eleven wheels, twelve knots, at least three sets of 
sixteen loci (ādhārāḥ), sixteen knots, twenty-​eight vital points (marmāni), etc.
The renowned polymath Abhinavagupta (ca. 950–​1016 ce), in his voluminous works 
such as Tantrāloka and Tantrasāra, incorporates ideas from earlier texts and describes 
highly complex subtle body systems involving numerous deities, mantras, and bodily 
regions. It is important to remember, however, that all these systems represent the 
entextualization of the body, as all these are tradition-​ and text-​specific bodily systems.29
Flood discusses an interesting anonymous text belonging to the Krama tradition, 
the “Hymn to the Circle of Deities Located in the Body” (dehasthadevatācakrastotra).30 
This text presents the goddesses of the senses making offering to Śiva, who is described 
in sexual union with Śakti as Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī. Of note is that this 
text, which describes a complex esoteric physiology, provides a visualization sequence 
in the context of a standard daily ritual. Many deities are placed on the circle, most no­
tably the eight mothers of Kaula tantric tradition, who also represent the senses.31 Flood 
observes (2006, 156) that “we see that the body becomes the text upon which the deities 
of the tradition—​the goddesses of the senses—​are inscribed. The body is inhabited by the 
circle of deities; this pantheon animates the body, which becomes the mandala wherein 
they reside.” Thus, we have another instance in which esoteric physiology is essential in not 
only entextualizing the hymn but homologizing the body with the cosmos and deities. The

--- PAGE 232 ---
Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems      207
 
“circle” (cakra) here is not so much a bodily center but rather the pantheon of deities as the 
“clan” (kula), a term with great significance in subsequent centuries with Kaula traditions.
Tracing the history of the uses of the term cakra for a subtle body center is difficult, 
but White (2003, 224–​225) notes that the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (ca. 900 ce) mentions six 
“places” (sthāna): navel, heart, breast, root of the palate, between the eyebrows, and the 
cranium.32 Although the Śaivasiddhānta traditions mention different kinds of centers, 
as noted by Sanderson, these are “almost never cakras” (White 2003, 225). White 
argues that perhaps the earliest use of cakra specifically as a subtle body center is in the 
Kaulajñāna-​nirṇaya (KJnN), which lists eight cakras, each of which conveys magical 
powers (siddha) as they are visualized. He notes (225) that “we find in this source a juxta­
position of (1) the locations of the cakras; (2) the use of the term cakra; (3) a description 
of the cakras as being composed of spokes and leaves (but not petals); and (4) a portrayal 
of color-​coded divine maidens as dwelling in or on the spokes of these cakras.”
White (2003, 226) and others have shown how Abhinavagupta synthesizes structures 
from the Kaulajñāna-​nirṇaya as well as the ca. 800–​850 ce Netra Tantra (NT) in his own 
descriptions of the subtle body. His disciple Kṣemarāja composed a commentary on this 
material. In his comments on the seventh chapter of the NT, Kṣemarāja identifies two 
types of subtle body systems in the NT “as belonging to the ‘Kaula’ and “Tantric’ liturgies 
respectively” (226). White argues that, taken together:
The two systems presented in the text and commentary appear to be more direct 
forerunners of the later haṭha yoga system of Gorakṣanātha than do the KJnN and 
other works attributed to Matsyendranātha, who was Gorakṣanātha’s guru, ac­
cording to Nāth Siddha tradition. The Netra Tantra’s presentation of yogic practice 
combines breath control, meditation, “the piercing” of knots and the central channel, 
the raising of the “Śakti who is filled with one’s semen” the length of that channel, 
and the internal production of the nectar of immortality. At the same time, the Netra 
Tantra agrees with the KJnN on a number of subtle body locations.”
White concludes that many of the details of the subtle body from the KJnN are taken up 
by the very influential Kubjikāmata tantra (KM), which we now consider.33
Mallinson and Singleton’s comprehensive Roots of Yoga (2017) discusses the 
connections between the six-​cakra subtle body systems of the KM and later texts in 
the Śrīvidyā, Nāth Siddha, and haṭhayogic traditions. The KM is a foundational text of 
the Western Transmission (paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śaivism, focusing on the manifes­
tation of Śakti as the hump-​backed goddess Kubjikā. It is this system which becomes 
dominant (but hardly universal) after the fifteenth century and eventually popularized 
by Woodroffe into today’s version. This KM model consists of the mūlādhāra, 
svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddhi, and ājñā cakras, to which the subsequent 
sahasrāra of one thousand petals is added. Mallinson and Singleton summarize the his­
toric trajectory of this basic system (2017, 177):
Its six-​cakra system is subsequently found in texts of the Southern Transmission 
(dakṣināmnāya) of Kaula Śaivism associated with the cult of the goddess

--- PAGE 233 ---
208      Glen A. Hayes
 
Tripurasundarī, which later became known as Śrīvidyā. The Śrīvidyā Śivasaṃhitā 
provides very long and detailed descriptions of the lotuses . . . These connections 
enabled the subsequent popularization of the Kubjikāmatatantra’s system, because 
India’s two best-​known ascetic yogi lineages, those of the Nāths and Saṃnyāsīs, 
inherited the yoga traditions of the Western and Southern Transmissions respec­
tively. The popularity of the Kubjikāmatatantra’s six-​cakra system was subsequently 
reinforced by its ubiquity in modern representations of tantric and yogic eso­
teric anatomy, beginning perhaps with Arthur Avalon’s 1919 English edition of the 
sixteenth-​century Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (“The Description of the Six Cakras”), a text 
of the Southern Transmission of Kaula Śaivism (Avalon 1919; see also Taylor 2001), 
whose detailed descriptions of the cakras resemble those of the Śivasaṃhitā.
When considering these historical transformations and continuations of the six-​cakra 
systems, it is important to keep in mind Flood’s hermeneutic of the entextualization of 
the body. All these Kaula, Śrīvidyā, and other texts presented subtle body systems that 
reflected the respective contexts of their scriptures: cosmological, epistemological, on­
tological, and soteriological. However, Csaba Kiss (2009) has identified an increasing 
tendency, by the time of the thirteenth-​century Matsyendrasaṃhitā, to deemphasize 
the sectarian nature of subtle body systems “that eventually produced the well-​known 
cakra-​centered haṭha-​yogic traditions devoid of any definite claim to belong to any early 
tantric cult” (22).34 This tendency, only strengthened by the twentieth century, as well 
as Woodroffe’s publications and the growth of global yoga movements, has resulted in 
the perception of the cakras as discrete ontological objects, separate from the texts and 
traditions that originally generated them as ritual practices.35 The actual supposed loca­
tion of the cakras may not be important at all, and the decoupling of the subtle body from 
specific traditions may not only account for this modern fixation on the six-​cakra system 
but also help to explain why there have been myriad systems over the centuries. Since the 
premodern subtle body systems emerged from textual and tradition-​specific contexts, it 
follows that there would be as many variations as there have been lineages and traditions. 
There indeed may be deeper cognitive forces supporting the basic wheels and channels 
of the subtle body (see “Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending in Vaiṣṇava 
Sahajiyā Texts” Hayes, this volume), but historical forces have likely led to both the com­
pression and differentiation of models of the subtle body. We must now turn to a consid­
eration of the networks of channels (nāḍī) that connect the bodily centers, as well as the 
energies (kuṇḍalinī-​śakti, prāṇa) and fluids (bindu) that move through the networks.
Channels (nāḍī), Serpentine Energy 
(kuṇḍalinī), and Fluids (bindu)
In another chapter in this volume, I discuss the underlying metaphorical processes that 
may be at play in the creation of the subtle body systems, using insights from modern

--- PAGE 234 ---
Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems      209
 
cognitive linguistics. The wheels and other bodily centers function as “containers” for 
the subtle body, while the channels serve as “conduits” that connect the centers to the 
other parts of the body and, indeed, the cosmos. There is general agreement across many 
traditions that there is some form of a central channel, such as the suṣumṇā-​nāḍī, based 
upon the spinal column.36 There is also typically the belief in two side channels, the 
left (iḍā) and the right (piṅgalā). But beyond this, there is great variation concerning 
the total number of channels, with a frequent total of 72,000 being found.37 In systems 
using fluid-​based dynamics, such as the Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās (see previous section), we 
more often find the channels described as “rivers” (nadī), and the central channel as the 
“Crooked River” (bāṅkānadī). The function and nature of the channels thus depends 
upon the overall structure and dynamics of the overall system, which will be text-​ and 
tradition-​specific. However, in the majority of systems employing wheels and channels, 
it is energy and breaths that move along the nāḍīs, especially the “coiled energy” of 
kuṇḍalinī.
White notes that the Kubjikāmata tantra mentions a coiled female serpentine energy, 
but variations of the term as kuṇḍalī (“she who is ring-​shaped”) appear even earlier, 
in the ca. eighth-​century ce Tantrasadbhāva Tantra (White 2003, 230). However, he 
identifies perhaps the earliest use of the actual term kuṇḍalinī in the tenth-​ to eleventh-​
century Jayarathayāmala, in which it is related to the origin of mantras emanating from 
the supreme god Bhairava (a manifestation of Śiva). This early form of kuṇḍalinī is pri­
marily a phonemic entity (White 2003, 232):
Māyā is the mother of the phonemes and is known as the fire-​stick of the mantras. 
She is the kuṇḍalinī Śakti, and is to be known as the supreme kalā [goddess of time]. 
From that spring forth the mantras as well as the separate clans, and likewise the 
Tantras.
Abhinavagupta and other nondual Śaiva philosophers developed this phonemic sense 
of kuṇḍalinī into a two-​phase process of the descent of a cosmogonic energy into the 
human microcosm, and the subsequent ascent of consciousness to a transcendent state 
of union with Śiva. Hatley (2022) points out the threefold scheme of distinguishing 
kuṇḍalinī employed by Abhinavagupta: (1) śaktikuṇḍalinī, the cosmogonic creative 
power; (2) prāṇakuṇḍalinī, the vital energy of living beings; and (3) parākuṇḍalinī, the 
ineffable power of the divine. With Abhinavagupta, we find another version of the model 
identified by Flood: an emanationist cosmology which is in turn retraced via the subtle 
body as a “reversal” of the cosmogony. Kuṇḍalinī exists in union with Śiva in the “point” 
(bindu) as creation commences, with the generation of the tattvas (ontic levels), and her 
descent results not only in the cosmos but also in the phonemes of the Sanskrit alphabet, 
which result in the salvific sets of mantras.38 Hatley (2022, 3–​4) nicely summarizes the 
ascent through the wheels:
At the level of the root chakra (mūlādhāra), the Word (vāc) exists in transcendent 
form (parā vāk) as undifferentiated phonic energy, containing the essence of

--- PAGE 235 ---
210      Glen A. Hayes
 
language. With kuṇḍalinī’s imperceptible ascent to the navel chakra, sonic vibra­
tion reaches the incipient stage of differentiation—​language in inchoate, potential 
form (paśyantī vāc). At the level of the heart chakra, this becomes particularized in 
intermediate form (madhyamā vāc) as the unexpressed inner dialogue of thought. 
Reaching the chakra of the throat, the Word attains expression as verbal utterance 
(vaikharī vāc), completing its movement from unmanifest to manifest.
In the Kubjikāmata tantra, kuṇḍalinī is identified with the central goddess of the text, 
Kubjikā, the “hunchbacked one.” Kuṇḍalinī continues to be a major feature of the subtle 
body in haṭhayogic and especially Śrīvidyā traditions, often viewed as the coiled fe­
male serpentine energy located at the base of the spine, in the root cakra, or in a “bulb” 
(kanda; Mallinson and Singleton, 2017, 178). She is coiled three and one-​half times 
around the “point” (bindu) of Śiva in the lowest wheel, her head blocking entry into the 
central channel. Using breath control (prāṇāyāma), mantras, and other forceful yogic 
means, she is eventually awakened and rises upward. Accounts of this process can vary, 
but the ascent of the kuṇḍalinī through the wheels, piercing the “knots” (granthi) is often 
extremely detailed. Hatley (2022, 6) provides a concise summary of the ascent in the 
seventeenth-​century Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, which became influential due to Woodroffe’s 
publications:
Kuṇḍalinī reposes in the basal lotus (ādhāra-​ or mūlādhārapadma) of four 
petals situated between the anus and genitals at the root of the suṣumnā nāḍī. 
Downward facing, its four red petals have inscribed the Sanskrit syllables VA-​
ŚA-​ṢA-​SA in gold, and enclose a golden square in which the syllable of the earth 
element (LAṂ) is written in white. Presiding over the chakra are Brahmā, with 
an elephant as his vehicle, and the goddess Ḍākinī. In the center is a down­
ward triangle with the icon (liṅga) of Śiva known as Svayambhu in the middle. 
Radiant like lightening, the serpentine Kulakuṇḍalī coils around him three and 
a half times like the spiral of a conch, her gaping mouth covering the entrance 
to the suṣumnā nāḍī and the even subtler channels therein. With the mūlādhāra 
begin a series of lotuses or wheels: the svādhiṣṭhāna at the base of the penis (male 
anatomy is presupposed), maṇipūra at the navel, anāhata at the heart, viśuddha 
in the throat, and ājñā between the eyebrows, with a seventh lotus of a thou­
sand petals (sahasrāra) above, the pinnacle of the yogic body and abode of the 
supreme deity, Śiva. One established in the disciplines of yoga may awaken the 
serpentine śakti, “attacking with the vital air and fire” the liṅga around which she 
slumbers and causing her to enter the medial channel (v. 51). Ascending through 
the six chakras, piercing liṅgas in the heart (anāhata) and forehead (ājñā) and 
drawing the life-​essence (jīva) upwards with her, she unites with Śiva in the lotus 
of one thousand petals (sahasrāra), engendering the highest ecstasy. As kuṇḍalinī 
returns to the basal lotus she releases a flood of divine nectar. Perfected in this 
process, the yogi may attain liberation.
Among the many interesting details of this process, which are replicated and modified 
in myriad ways in modern yogic traditions (see Leland 2016), the concept of the descent

--- PAGE 236 ---
Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems      211
 
of kuṇḍalinī resulting in a flood of “nectar” (amṛta) is noteworthy. Such fluidic imagery 
exists alongside the energetic and respiratory imagery. The dispersion of nectar leads to 
the experience of bliss (ānanda), and is a liberating experience. It parallels the Vaiṣṇava 
Sahajiyā notions of vastu, yogically reversed sexual fluids noted in the previous section. 
As far back as the Mahābhārata, we find the trope of collecting and preserving semen in 
a supposed reservoir in the cranium (Mallinson and Singleton 2017, 180). The goal was 
to prevent the emission of semen, as keeping the reservoir full guaranteed male vitality, 
a general concern found throughout South Asian history.39 Mallinson and Singleton 
discuss the importance of the fluidic imagery of seminal fluid as well, but the soteriolog­
ical status of the fluid is quite different to amṛta or vastu. In later haṭhayogic texts such 
as the Amṛtasiddhi,40 instructions are given to prevent the loss of bindu, including a type 
of urethral suction (ūrdvaretaḥ) which, combined with breathing exercises, prevents the 
“falling” of the vital seed into the lower fires of the sun, drying them up and lessening 
vitality (Mallinson and Singleton 2017, 181). In these haṭhayogic systems, the network of 
channels is still involved, but in this case they are conveying a substance, not an energetic 
breath. Thus, the subtle body continues to be used by tantric systems to entextualize spe­
cific traditions and texts, varying as the historical and cognitive situations vary. The next 
section finishes the survey of subtle body systems by considering their appearances in 
Buddhist tantric traditions.
Subtle Body Systems in Buddhist Tantra
The history of esoteric physiology in Buddhism, at least in its earliest stages, varies from 
the development of subtle body systems in Hinduism. Part of this is due to the relative 
lack of influence on Buddhism of Vedic and Upaniṣadic beliefs and practices, especially 
involving the ritual sacrifices (śrauta), caste, and ritual purity. But the central impor­
tance of meditation practices in Buddhism, as well as an awareness of the imperma­
nence of the body, led to techniques involving the body either directly or as a tool for 
achieving higher states of consciousness. As the body serves as the basic “location” of 
meditation (leading to higher/​inner states), it is not surprising that we find interesting 
developments leading to subtle body systems in later Buddhism.
In discussing the later importance of tantric rituals for the purification of the elements 
within the body (bhūtaśuddhi, dehaśuddhi), Flood (2006, 106–​108) argues that one pos­
sible origin may be early Buddhist meditation exercises (Pali: kṛtsna; Sanskrit: kasiṇa), 
connected to (107):
the cultivation of the meditative sign (nimitta) that leads into meditative absorption 
(dhyāna/​jhāna). Indeed, it is possibly here that we find the origins of the visualiza­
tion methods that were to become so important in the tantric traditions, both Hindu 
and Buddhist. These exercises are ten among forty objects of meditation objects 
described in Buddhaghosa’s Visuddhimagga, although they also occur in the Pali

--- PAGE 237 ---
212      Glen A. Hayes
 
canon itself. The kasiṇas comprise the five elements and the five colours, focusing 
upon which leads into the higher levels of meditation. For example, the earth kasiṇa 
is a clay disk, an object that is concentrated upon until the image is internalized 
within consciousness without external support. In this way the kasiṇa is akin to the 
internally arising sign (nimitta), like an afterimage, which leads into jhāna. Traces of 
these practices can perhaps be found in the bhūtaśuddhi.
Although we will not find specific Buddhist systems of wheels (cakra) and channels 
(nāḍī) until the eighth century ce and the Caryāgīti and Hevajra tantra (White 2003, 
224), these objects of meditation41 require the body to be recognized as necessary and 
useful for achieving higher states of consciousness.42
Samuel (2008, 271) observes that “a striking innovation in both Śaiva and Buddhist 
traditions in the eighth to tenth centuries was a new series of yogic practices and 
techniques based on a subtle anatomy of the practitioner’s body.” White notes that the 
Caryāgīti and the Hevajra tantra both envision four wheels at the levels of the navel, 
throat, heart, and head. He notes (2003, 224) that these
cakras are identified with four geographical sites (pīṭhas), which appear to corre­
spond to points of contact between the Indian subcontinent and inner Asia: these 
are Kāmākhyā (Gauhati, Assam), Uḍḍiyāna (Swat valley?), Pūrṇagiri (Punjab?), 
and Jālandhara (upper Punjab). This tradition is repeated in numerous sources, in­
cluding those of the Nāth Siddhas, whose twelfth-​century founder Gorakṣanātha 
identifies the same set of pīṭhas with sites aligned along the spinal column within the 
yogic body.
The subtle body system in the Hevajra tantra includes thirty-​two channels and four 
wheels: the mahāsukha-​cakra at the head, the saṃbhoga-​cakra at the throat, the dharma-​
cakra at the heart, and the nirmāṇa-​cakra at the navel. (Samuel 2008, 285–​286). These 
are based on the ascending hierarchy of the “bodies” (kaya) of the Buddha, a concept 
that could only enhance notions of esoteric physiology in Buddhist history.43 In place 
of the term kuṇḍalinī, which we find in Śaiva and Śākta systems, the term used here is 
caṇḍalī (“fierce goddess”), although it functions in a similar way.44
There were major developments in Buddhist tantric textual and practice traditions 
occurring after the eighth century.45 Samuel notes (2008, 286):
There appears to be a gradual evolution from the tantras classed by the later tra­
dition as kriyā and caryā, which are primarily about “external” ritual practices, to 
the yogatantra (c.700-​c.750 CE) where the emphasis becomes much more on the 
achievement on inner purity, and we first find the identification of the practitioner 
with a tantric deity, a form of the Buddha.
Dalton (2004) has studied this gradual interiorization of Buddhist rituals, and the de­
velopment of the anuttarayoga tantra in the ninth century, including the Cakrasamvara

--- PAGE 238 ---
Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems      213
 
tantra (see Gray, this volume) and the Hevajra tantra. Dalton (2004, 2, cited in Samuel 
2008, 286–​287) notes:
The tantric interiorization of Buddhist ritual was not a rejection of
ritual. Nor was it a psychologization [ . . . ]. This shift took place in the
physical realm. Its beginnings can be traced to the first half of the eighth
century, and the ritual technologies it spawned continued to develop
through the ninth century. By the end of these two crucial centuries,
a new ritual discourse of the bodily interior was in place. The tantric
subject had become the site for the entire ritual performance; the body’s
interior provided the devotee, the altar, the oblations, and the buddha to be
worshipped.
An intervening tradition of Buddhist tantra, the mahāyoga, appeared briefly between 
the early yoga and later anuttara (unexcelled) tantras (Dalton, 2004, 3). Dalton argues:
These works presented for the first time the ritualized sexual
practices for which tantra has since become so notorious. They focused
on the body’s interior, on the anatomical details of the male and female
sexual organs and the pleasure generated through sexual union. In this
way, three periods can be discerned in the development of tantric ritual,
each of which focused the Buddhist subject’s attention further inwards,
first from the external altar to himself, then to his physical anatomy
and embodied experience, and finally to the subtleties of his internal
physiological processes.
During this interstitial period, we find a number of transgressive practices, such as the 
ritual consumption of male and female sexual fluids, presented in mahāyoga (great 
yoga) tantric texts such as the Guhyasamāja and Guhyagarbha tantras. As discussed 
by Dalton and others (Davidson 2002), this involved a secondary “secret initiation” 
(guhyābhiṣeka) where the initiate consumed a drop (bindu) of the intermingled sexual 
fluids of the master and his consort (or of his own and his consort’s), assisting with the 
achievement of enlightenment. The sexual fluid is identified with the “aspiration to en­
lightenment” (bodhicitta), generating Buddha bodies out of the transformed seed.46 
Such transgressive ritual practices were thus grounded within a larger cosmological and 
physiological system.
As summarized by Dalton (2004, 7–​21), we find a range of elaborate ritual processes 
described in some of the mahāyoga texts unearthed in the Dunhuang cave complexes 
in inner Asia,47 a development that would prefigure the eventual Buddhist systems of 
wheels and channels. The ritual consisted of two stages: development and perfection. 
During the first, based on earlier yoga tantras, the practitioner visualizes an inner man­
dala, with himself at the center (eventually identifying with the deity and emptiness). 
It is during the perfection phase that the transgressive consumption takes place. In

--- PAGE 239 ---
214      Glen A. Hayes
 
versions where the practitioner is engaged in coitus reservatus with a female partner, he 
is instructed to maintain a drop of semen at the tip of the penis while he visualizes an­
other mandala and Buddhas. Then (2004, 10):
The practitioner is then instructed to worship the mandala, using the
blissful sensations flowing through his body. Such instructions seem to
reflect an early prototype of the subtle body systems that were articulated
in more complex forms in later works. The later systems involved
intricate arrangements of cakras and energy channels mapped across the body’s 
interior. In the early Mahāyoga texts, however, the technologies
are simpler, the descriptions limited to the energies associated with sexual
pleasure which rushes through the practitioner’s torso.
The ritual then proceeds, including visualizations, consumption of sexual fluids, and 
manifestations of Buddhas. The conclusion involves forms of blessing, and the dissolu­
tion of the visualized mandala. However, at the very end it seems that the practitioner 
applies the sexual fluids to the body. Dalton (2004, 16) notes:
The theory that the practitioner conferred his own sexual fluids upon
himself at the end of the perfection stage is made even more explicit in
yet another Dunhuang manuscript. Here the practitioner is engaged in the
sexual practice when he is advised:
	 At the time of practicing the samādhi, do not practice apart from the vajra emana­
tion. When the bodhicitta falls, say, “a la la ho,” imagining that the goddess is pleased. 
From between the vajra and the lotus, with the ring finger of the left hand, take the 
dew of the lotus, and offer it to the noble ones. Then oneself and the consort also 
receive the sacrament.
The Tibetan use of the Sanskrit term śākta (shad ta pa; 11) in the Guhyagarbha is unu­
sual, but suggests some early influence from Hindu tantric traditions. Dalton (2004, 11) 
concludes:
It would appear to reflect an early phase in the development
of the technologies of the subtle body that later became widespread
during the ninth century. No mention is made of the complex systems of
channels and energies that dominate later discussions of the perfection stage. The śākta 
of the Dunhuang manuscripts seems to be of an earlier
and more rudimentary variety, a raw physical force that is used to worship
and energize the buddhas.
There was obviously a dynamic situation within Buddhist traditions of yoga, 
mahāyoga, and anuttara tantra from the eighth through tenth centuries, one which 
would only later result in the development of full systems of wheels and channels in texts 
like the Hevajra tantra. Samuel, having discussed a range of sexual practices in India and

--- PAGE 240 ---
Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems      215
 
China, speculates on these new systems and possible interactions with China in the pro­
cess (2008, 289):
One could read the development of the new system in either of two ways, as an indig­
enous inspiration suggested by continued yogic practice in mahāyoga style, or as a 
set of concepts and processes incorporated from another source into the more basic 
sexual yoga discussed here. To me, the second alternative seems more likely, espe­
cially given the presence of such ideas in the cognate Chinese practices. If Buddhist 
practitioners were already employing sexual yoga of the kind suggested here, the 
cakra systems would provide both a structure to aid practitioners in directing their 
sensations, and a grid through which associations could be built up with other 
elements of the symbolic world within which the practice was taking place.
The interactions between early Buddhist and Hindu tantric traditions remains an active 
area of ongoing scholarship,48 and the intricacies and varieties of subtle body systems 
illustrate the richness of those interactions.
Although it remains to be fully studied, esoteric physiology also developed with Jain 
tantra, as systems of bodily purification (bhūtaśuddhi) were developed to support Jain 
methods of meditation. Gough (2021) has examined these processes of purification, 
as well as some Jain subtle body systems (see, e.g., 111–​143), for example, in the tenth-​
century Tattvānuśāsana of Rāmasena, where we read about meditation diagrams 
sharing features of Hindu and Buddhist models (127):
An eight-​petalled lotus resides in the heart [of the meditator], situated in the middle 
of a four-​sided earth maṇḍala. On each petal the letters of the eight classes of the al­
phabet are inscribed. The pericarp has the name of the omniscient ones (arhats). It 
contains the Ring of Disciples (gaṇabhṛdvalaya) and is encircled three times by the 
seed syllable hrīṃ. It should be worshipped and meditated upon.
Although Rāmasena is presenting a specifically Jain subtle body segment here, it 
illustrates the cosmophysiological usefulness and efficiency of subtle body concepts. 
As Gough notes, much more research on Jain tantra awaits, and her two chapters in 
this volume (“Homa in Jain Traditions” and “Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess 
Padmāvatī”), as well as the chapters by Chapple and Slouber (in this volume) represent 
promising steps in this direction.
Concluding Thoughts and 
Future Directions
This chapter has examined the importance of esoteric physiology in a range of tantric 
traditions. Such systems—​and within them, the more specific models of the “subtle

--- PAGE 241 ---
216      Glen A. Hayes
 
body,” with wheels, channels, ponds, and rivers—​are a central feature of tantra due, in 
part, to the embrace of embodiment as a vehicle of practice (sādhana) and means of lib­
eration. Due to the complicated history of tantric traditions throughout Asia (and, more 
recently, globally),49 as well as the myriad teaching lineages and textual traditions, there 
have consequently been almost countless variations of esoteric physiology, including 
subtle body systems. While the Hindu tantric models emerged gradually, influenced by 
Brahmanical concepts of the interiorization of the Vedic ritual and philosophy, Buddhist 
models may have emerged from meditation practices focusing on specific objects, as we 
have seen. But from approximately the eighth through thirteenth centuries ce there was 
a proliferation of subtle body systems as Śaiva, Śākta, and Vajrayāna tantras underwent 
innovative and creative expansion. As Flood has argued, subtle body systems emerge 
from specific traditions and texts, so it follows that the medieval expansions of tantra 
would lead to greater diversity of subtle body systems. In this chapter, we have only been 
able to consider a few of these many models.
Beyond the translation and textual study of esoteric physiology that have been 
accomplished over the past century, a number of scholars have recently applied 
methods from the disciplines of cognitive science and neuroscience in the study of 
these systems. My other chapter in this volume has taken methods from contempo­
rary metaphor theory and conceptual blending theory and applied them to the study 
of Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā dehatattva. The chapter argues that there may be underlying 
somatic and cognitive features of subtle body systems that connect them to wider 
and deeper domains of human experience.50 Timalsina (2015a, 2015b, 2016, 2020) has 
also developed innovative methodologies from cognitive science and modern phi­
losophy in his recent studies of the tantric traditions of Nepal and India. Lidke (2016) 
has used concepts from consciousness studies in his exploration of Nepali tantra. 
Samuel and Kozhevnikov’s chapter in this volume uses concepts from neuroscience 
to consider some important aspects of ritual practices and experiences in tantra.
There have also been important developments in the discipline of the Cognitive 
Science of Religion (CSR), although the study of tantra in this field is still in its early 
phases.51 The field of consciousness studies has also been developing, especially 
connected to studies of meditation and altered states of consciousness,52 but again 
specific studies of tantric texts and traditions (apart from Tibetan Buddhism) are 
only gradually emerging. However, the Mind and Life Institute, involving the Dalai 
Lama, has been supporting many innovative studies, and this should result in our 
enhanced appreciation of subtle body systems.
To be sure, the future study of esoteric physiology and subtle body systems 
promises to be fascinating and will contribute to the growth of tantric studies, as 
exemplified by this volume. As noted in the Introduction to this chapter, such study 
raises profound issues about the human experiences of embodiment, imagina­
tion, sexuality, and transformation. The texts and traditions we have considered in 
this chapter have hopefully provided vivid glimpses into these fascinating ways of 
being human.
