Chapter 10
Transforming the Body 
by Mastering 
the Elements, Some 
Tantric Sources
Lubomír Ondračka
The elements (bhūtas), often called the great elements, material elements, classical 
elements, or gross elements (mahābhūtas; in Sanskrit plural mahābhūtāni), play a key 
role in all Indian doctrines that take a realist position, that is, those that consider the 
world around us to be real. According to such teachings, the elements are the basic 
building blocks of the world we perceive with our senses. Most schools assume the ex­
istence of five elements, four of which are universal (earth, water, fire, and air), while 
the fifth element (called “space” or “ether”) often has a special status and properties that 
sometimes exclude it from the list of material elements.
This brief description of the elements in Indian thought must sound familiar to an­
yone who has encountered the basics of ontology in Western philosophy. The notion 
that the elements are the building blocks of the world, their repertoire (fire, air, water, 
and earth), and even the addition of a fifth and always somewhat problematic element 
(ether)—​all these concepts appear already in early Greek philosophy, beginning with 
Empedocles, through Plato and Aristotle, to their followers (Ball 2004, 1–​20). The 
striking similarity between Indian and Western conceptions of the elements naturally 
raises questions about possible common origins or mutual influences (especially since 
the conception of the elements in classical China is different; Ikeda 1966; Mou 2009, 
161–​163), but these questions will not be addressed here. For our study, this similarity is 
simply useful because we do not need to explain in detail the basic principles of how the 
elements function in Indian thought.1
Even though the basic principles of the elemental doctrine in India are relatively 
simple, not all Indian philosophical and religious traditions share the same ontology 
and the same conception of the elements. Among realist schools, we can distinguish two

--- PAGE 251 ---
226      Lubomír Ondračka
 
quite different ontological models, one horizontal and one vertical (Halbfass 1992, 48). 
The horizontal model proposes that there are several independent entities, or distinct 
ontological categories, and that matter composed of the elements is one of these entities. 
The best example of this model is offered by the Vaiśeṣika school; it contains six ontolog­
ical categories (Potter 1977, 86–​91; for greater detail, see Mishra 1936). This teaching is 
shared by Vaiśeṣika’s close sister, the Nyāya school, and it was also adopted (and modi­
fied) by the Mīmāṃsā system, which had different interests and did not develop its own 
independent ontology. The Ājīvikas had a similar concept of elemental atoms (Basham 
1951, 262–​266), but surprisingly the Jains did not. They did not classify atoms according 
to the elements but instead taught that all atoms are of only one kind.
For our study, however, the second, vertical model is more important. In this onto­
logical system, the elements stand at the end of the evolutionary series of individual 
entities produced in the cosmogonic process. The prototypical example of this model 
is presented by classical Sāṃkhya (Larson 1979, 180–​188) and its variant, Pātañjala 
Yoga. The Hindu tantric traditions adopted this concept but had to modify it because 
the initial source of the evolutionary process in Sāṃkhya is primordial matter (prakṛti), 
whereas tantric systems are mostly theistic, so they had to place a deity at the beginning 
of their cosmogonic model. Different tantric traditions have dealt with this in different 
ways, and the process of modifying this model always took some time until the final doc­
trine was settled (Goodall 2016). Fortunately, however, we do not have to deal with these 
historical issues here, because the modifications to the Sāṃkhya model concerned the 
initial levels of cosmogony, whereas its final stage, the five elements, remained mostly 
unchanged.
While these two models, the horizontal and the vertical, are dominant in Indian re­
alist ontologies, they do not exhaust all the ways the elements can be produced. For 
example, the later theistic Vedānta schools combine both models: like Vaiśeṣika, they 
postulate a horizontal set of ontological categories (though their source is the ultimate 
reality, brahman, which is the highest God), but at the same time apply Sāṃkhya’s ver­
tical evolution in which one of the ontological entities is prakṛti, which is the source of 
the material world down to the level of the elements that combine with each other in a 
process called pañcīkaraṇa (literary “quintuplication”) to produce physical matter (see 
Srinivasa Chari 1988, 22–​26, 317–​323 for the Viśiṣṭādvaita position, and Narain 1986, 77–​
86 for the Dvaita teaching). Although the Viśiṣṭādvaita school is particularly relevant 
to the late doctrine of tantric Viṣṇuism because of its gradual fusion with the teachings 
of the Pāñcarātras, for the purpose of the doctrine of the elements we need not concern 
ourselves with it.
To understand how the elements function in tantric Buddhism, however, we must 
concern ourselves with the Buddhist concept of the elements. Unfortunately, unlike 
the realist Brahmanical schools, this doctrine cannot be briefly introduced because 
Buddhism offers a wide range of very different and contradictory ontologies, from realist 
Abhidharma (in which entities that are ultimately real exist) through idealist Yogācāra 
(where nothing exists except mental things) to skeptical Madhyamaka (in which every­
thing is just a conceptual construct devoid of any real essence or intrinsic nature). Even

--- PAGE 252 ---
Transforming the Body      227
 
the concept of the elements in Abhidharma, which at first sight looks similar to the ideas 
of the Brahmanical schools, is in fact quite different, for the elements here are not of 
a substantial nature. This doctrine is rather counterintuitive. The elements are not the 
building blocks of matter or particles, but only a particular occurrence of the inherent 
qualities proper to a given element (e.g., an atom of earth is merely the presence of so­
lidity at a given time in a given place; Siderits 2007, 113–​115). Tantric texts commonly 
speak of four (or less often five) elements, but since their doctrinal position is close to 
Yogācāra or Madhyamaka, their elements cannot be real substances. However, this weak 
ontological status of the elements does not prevent their use in Buddhist tantric rituals, 
where they are quite often invoked.
After this brief introduction, we can begin to explore the role of the elements in tan­
tric rituals. An exhaustive survey of this topic would require a monograph, so here I 
focus only on the techniques in which the elements are directly used for transforming 
the practitioner’s body. There are two such rituals: the purification of the elements and 
the mastering of the elements. I first briefly introduce the much better-​known ritual of 
purifying the elements, and then in the rest of the study I examine the technique of con­
trolling the elements.
The Purification of the Elements
This ritual is part of the preliminary purification techniques that formed over time in 
the Hindu tantric ritual manuals to create the set of “five purifications” (pañcaśuddhi; 
Goodall and Rastelli 2013, 360). Their form, order, and names are not fixed and differ 
not only in Śaiva, Śākta, and Vaiṣṇava works but also within texts of the same tradi­
tion. A typical Śaiva set consists of purifications of one’s self (ātmaśuddhi), the sacri­
ficial place (sthānaśuddhi), all the materials used in worship (dravyaśuddhi), mantras 
(mantraśuddhi), and the image to be worshiped (liṅgaśuddhi). In the Vaiṣṇava var­
iant, the last member is replaced by the purification of the deity image (beraśuddhi, 
bimbaśodhana), and sometimes the purification of the vessels (pātraśuddhi) is used 
instead of the purification of the mantras. This series of purification techniques must 
precede daily standard worship (nityapūjā), and therefore it is a necessary part of the 
regular tantric ritual (Gupta 1979, 134–​138).
There are two ways in which the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) can be 
placed in this set of five purifications. First, bhūtaśuddhi can be understood as a syn­
onym for the purification of one’s self (another common synonym is “purification of 
the body,” dehaśuddhi) or as only a part of the purification of one’s self, which consists 
of several techniques (Ganesan 2009, 70). In any case, bhūtaśuddhi always stands at the 
very beginning of a series of ritual acts.
There is a clear reason for this. Tantric ritual requires the sacrificer to identify with the 
deity to whom the offering is made. As the famous tantric dictum says: “Having become 
a god, he should sacrifice to the gods” (Dviveda 1992). Self-​deification is in fact the main

--- PAGE 253 ---
228      Lubomír Ondračka
 
characteristic that distinguishes tantric pūjā from non-​tantric pūjā (Bühnemann 1988, 
9, n. 14). Therefore, before a tāntrika can perform any proper ritual act, he must trans­
form himself into the deity he will worship. The purification of the elements is instru­
mental to this self-​deification and therefore stands at the beginning of the entire ritual.
The actual performance of the purification of the elements varies considerably from 
a relatively simple act to a very complicated procedure. However, the basic principle is 
common to all variants and is based on a doctrine that sees the cosmos and the body as 
composed of successively emanating planes of reality (tattvas), a teaching adopted from 
Sāṃkhya philosophy. The technique consists of two basic steps. First the material body, 
which is considered impure at that moment, is destroyed through the gradual dissolu­
tion of its constituent elements, and then it is recreated, this time from the purified indi­
vidual elements. The process of divinization is completed by placing deities on different 
parts of the body with mantras in a ritual called “placement” (nyāsa; or more specifically 
aṅganyāsa or dehanyāsa). The whole process is purely mental (although some of the 
actions may be accompanied by hand positions, mudrās). In the tantric worldview, the 
mental plane of reality is higher than the material.
The precise procedure of purification of the elements is rarely described in the re­
vealed tantras (mūlatantras); more detailed instructions are usually found in the ritual 
manuals (paddhatis). There are exceptions though. For example, the Jayākhyasaṃhitā, 
an early Pāñcarātra tantra that is regarded as one of the three most important texts 
(triratna) of this tradition, devotes an entire chapter to this technique (­chapter 10, which 
is more than a hundred verses long), which contains a fairly comprehensive explana­
tion.2 Simply put, the first stage of the bhūtaśuddhi consists of the gradual dissolution 
of one element into another. However, this does not happen directly. The earth element 
is first dissolved in its mantra form (mantramūrti), and this is dissolved into the energy 
of the corresponding subtle element (tanmātra), which is smell. The energy of smell 
(gandhaśakti) is exhaled and dissolved in the next element, which is water. Thus, the 
process continues with the other elements (fire, wind, and space) until finally the in­
dividual consciousness leaves the body. This empty body is then burned, and the ashes 
are washed away in all directions. Then comes the second stage, when the practitioner 
creates from the elements a new, purified body, identical with the supreme deity, into 
which the soul returns.
The Śaiva form of this ritual follows the same pattern (Davis 1991, 52–​60; Flood 
2002, 31–​33). However, its actual performance may be more complex because the 
Śaiva cosmos consists of thirty-​six planes of reality, whereas the Vaiṣṇavas op­
erate with only twenty-​five, and therefore the gradual dissolution of the elements 
into their original source and their subsequent re-​creation is more complicated. 
The Śaivas also tend to have a more complex concept of the yogic body, whose dif­
ferent elements (nāḍīs, granthis, cakras, etc.) can be involved in the performance of 
bhūtaśuddhi. Particularly in more Śākta-​oriented and Kaula texts, the kuṇḍalinī and 
its upward ascent may also play a role in this technique. But otherwise, the principle 
is the same: the sacrificer’s body must be transformed and deified so that he can pro­
ceed to worshiping the deity.

--- PAGE 254 ---
Transforming the Body      229
 
Today, the purification of the elements is part of the sacrifice wherever tantric ritual 
manuals are followed. Sometimes, though, it appears outside the direct tantric context. 
In Bengal, for example, where most Hindu rituals have their roots in medieval local 
Kaula-​Śākta works, some form of bhūtaśuddhi is practiced almost universally. If we 
consult the cheap ritual manuals for worshiping various deities sold in the bazaars of 
Bengal, we find that this procedure is perhaps found in all paddhatis, even those ded­
icated to clearly non-​tantric goddesses such as Sarasvatī. Even strongly anti-​tantric 
Caitanya Vaiṣṇavism has not escaped this influence; the purification of the elements 
occurs in various forms also in its texts and practice (Valpey 2006, 140–​142).
But it is not only in Bengal where bhūtaśuddhi is performed outside the tantric en­
vironment. In neighboring Orissa, which has a similarly strong tantric historical back­
ground, we find this ritual in a rather unexpected place, at the Jagannātha temple in 
Purī, the most famous pilgrimage site in the region. The presence of such a ritual in this 
temple is indeed surprising, as it is a very conservative Vaiṣṇava site with no connection 
to the Pāñcarātra tantric ritual tradition. Moreover, the form of bhūtaśuddhi outlined in 
the ritual manuals used in Purī is quite detailed and elaborate, as described in detail by 
Gayan Charan Tripathi (2004, 150–​172). Interestingly, to justify the tantric elements in 
the worship of Jagannātha, the ritual manuals proclaim that they draw from the works of 
Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra. But this is not true; in fact, the entire pūjā is heavily influenced by 
other tantric works popular in Orissa, such as the Śāradātilaka (Tripathi 2004, 122–​124), 
a rather eclectic Śaiva-​Śākta tantra.
We can conclude this brief introduction to the bhūtaśuddhi ritual by summarizing 
that it is the most common tantric ritual in which the body is transformed through 
mental practice working with the five gross elements. It is described in dozens of texts 
from various tantric traditions and is still practiced in everyday regular tantric pūjā and 
other tantric rituals, but as we have seen, it also appears outside the strictly tantric set­
ting (even in Jaina worship; Gough 2021, 168; see also Gough “Homa in Jain Traditions” 
and “Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī,” this volume). Yet, apart from 
the Jayākhyasaṃhitā, this purification ritual has not been thoroughly studied, so we 
do not know when and where it was formed (it is missing from the early corpus of the 
Śaivasiddhānta texts; Goodall and Isaacson 2016, 7) or the historical process of how it 
developed into its standard form. However, this study focuses on the second technique, 
where the elements are used to transform the body.
Mastering the Elements
The goal of the second technique, which will be explored in the rest of this chapter, is the 
mastery of the elements. As we shall soon see, control of the elements can pursue dif­
ferent goals, and its successful acquisition can have different consequences. I will focus 
on the results that relate to the transformation of the body. In other words, the central 
focus of our attention will be on the various bodily perfections (siddhis) that can be

--- PAGE 255 ---
230      Lubomír Ondračka
 
obtained through this technique. The goal of mastering the elements is obviously very 
different from that of bhūtaśuddhi, yet the two techniques are closely related, as they 
often share almost identical verses describing the basic characteristics of the elements.
The technique used to control the elements is yogic dhāraṇā, a practice that is found 
both in the Pātañjala system of eight auxiliaries (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and in the tantric sixfold 
system (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), so its description is most often seen in the yoga sections of the 
tantras. The term dhāraṇā is usually translated as “concentration,” but here it is better 
to use the more literal meaning of “holding” or “fixation,” as the most common prin­
ciple of this technique in its developed form is to hold the breath or mind (or both) in a 
certain place in the body for a specific amount of time. The doctrinal background is the 
idea that different parts of the body are the domain of particular elements (this concept 
is shared with the bhūtaśuddhi ritual; Davis 1991, 54–​56); therefore, to master a given 
element, one must perform a fixation at a particular place in the body. How the body is 
divided into the domains of the elements varies in different works, but the idea itself is 
common. Since most texts work with five elements, the whole practice is often called the 
“five fixations” (pañcadhāraṇā) by scholars (and in some haṭhayoga works).
There are two main contexts in which the mastery of the elements appears in the 
tantras. First, this technique can stand alone, as one member of a yoga system consisting 
of six auxiliaries (ṣaḍaṅga). This is its common placement (Brunner 1994, 441–​442). 
As shown in more detail later, though, it can also be part of the complex practice of 
mastering all planes of existence (tattvajaya), that is, all thirty-​six levels of the Śaiva 
cosmos. Since the gross elements stand at the end of the evolutionary process in the 
Sāṃkhya and tantric systems, their mastery (bhūtajaya) must stand at the beginning of 
the opposite process, that is, the upward progression through the levels to the original 
source.
Now we can look at how this technique is described in texts from different tantric 
traditions. To get a better idea of how this ritual developed, I will try to proceed chron­
ologically, although it is notoriously difficult to date tantric texts. However, especially 
thanks to Alexis Sanderson’s many years of research, at least a relative chronology of in­
dividual works is largely possible.
Śaivasiddhānta
Śaivasiddhānta literature contains a large number of revealed tantras, commentaries on 
them, ritual manuals, and other works (Sanderson 2013, 12–​29). But as Dominic Goodall 
has shown (1998, xxxix–​xlvii), only a smaller part of the vast corpus of revealed tantras 
belongs to the early (that is, pre-​tenth-​century) North Indian phase of this tradition. 
Since the practice of mastering the elements, as it is known in its classical form in later 
texts, first took shape in these early Śaivasiddhānta tantras, we begin our historical ex­
amination of this technique with texts from this tradition.
The earliest work is Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā. As the title suggests, it is a collection 
(saṃhitā) of several texts (namely, five) that probably took shape between the fifth and

--- PAGE 256 ---
Transforming the Body      231
 
seventh centuries (Goodall 2015, 71–​73). Fortunately, this corpus (apart from a single 
text) has recently been meticulously edited, translated, and annotated, which will 
greatly facilitate my analysis. The earliest piece in this collection (Mūlasūtra) is silent on 
the mastery of the elements, but the very next text, the Uttarasūtra, contains one impor­
tant verse (5.28). Unfortunately, the whole passage is full of ambiguities, and, moreover, 
the part of the manuscript containing this verse is damaged. The editors translate it as 
follows (ellipsis in the original): “Alternatively one should visualise . . . as having the form 
of fire, of wind, of earth, water, ether.”3 The verse is interesting for several reasons. First, 
it is part of a chapter that describes a yogic practice—​meditations on the various levels 
of the cosmos—​but its placement is out of the expected order, and moreover, elemental 
meditation is declared here to be only a variant (athavā) of the practice. Second, the 
verse enumerates five elements, whereas the vast majority of the early Śaivasiddhānta 
texts work with only four elements. Third, the order of the elements is unusual and 
differs from that found in other texts. Fourth, and finally, the term used for the earth 
element, mahendra, is quite rare and does not commonly occur in other texts of this tra­
dition.4 This technique produces quite general results; the following verse (5.29) states 
that the yogin “will be successful” (siddhyate) and “will attain identification with Śiva” 
(śivasāyojyatāṃ vrajet), that is, final liberation.
The next work in this collection, the Nayasūtra, contains a much more informa­
tive passage (3.1–​3.8). It describes a series of visualizations of the five elements (in the 
standard order: earth, water, fire, wind, and space), which perhaps represents the em­
bryonic form of the later classical group of the five dhāraṇās because one important 
characteristic of this developed set appears here: in the standard series of five fixations, 
each element is associated with a bījamantra. Here too a mantra is mentioned for each 
element, but these mantras are not mentioned by name, except the one for space. The el­
ement of space is associated with prakṛtibīja, which is the vowel ū. The editors of the text 
assume that the same mantra is associated with all the other elements (Goodall 2015, 75). 
That may seem a bit odd, but at this formative stage it was certainly possible.
There is one more interesting thing in this passage. In the classical series of five 
dhāraṇās, each element is associated with a particular color. Although this is not yet 
expressed systematically here, the element of earth is described as yellow (3.2c). This 
color is then characteristic of earth in all other texts. While no other element is assigned 
a color here, a few verses later (3.15–​3.16b) the colors are associated not directly with the 
gross elements (mahābhūtas) but with their corresponding subtle elements (tanmātras). 
Smell is yellow, taste is white, form is red, touch is black, and sound is colorless. These are 
the same colors normally attributed to the gross elements in the group of five fixations 
(yellow earth, white water, red fire, black wind, and colorless space).
What are the results of the visualization of each element? Earth brings the immobi­
lization of poisonous creatures and solidity or immobility. Water brings the destruc­
tion of poisonous beings, the absence of all calamities, and also the absence of dāgha. 
The exact meaning of this word is not clear. The translators believe it denotes “fever” 
or “thirst,” but it may also have a more literal meaning, namely, “burning.” Since in the 
previous verse it is said that all the limbs of the yogin’s body will be filled with water

--- PAGE 257 ---
232      Lubomír Ondračka
 
(jalapūritasarvāṃgaḥ, 3.4a), the ability not to be burned would be quite natural. On the 
other hand, in the later texts, this ability is the result of mastering the element of fire. 
Here the result of visualizing fire is somewhat unclear, since it is said that the practi­
tioner “will perform a thousand acts” (kuryāt karmmasahasrāṇi, 3.6c; perhaps “mag­
ical deeds,” as the translators say). The results of visualizing the last two elements are 
similarly vague. The wind brings success or power (siddhi, 3.7d) and amazing feats 
(āścaryakarmma, 3.7d), and space, various deeds (citrakarmāṇi, 3.8d; probably again 
miraculous feats).
This passage on the elements in the Nayasūtra is part of a section on cosmic levels 
and their conquest (tattvajaya). However, there is one more passage in this text de­
voted to the elements (4.115–​4.118), this time included in a comprehensive descrip­
tion of yoga. We learn some important information from these four verses. First, the 
terms used for individual fixations, except for earth dhāraṇā, called here māhendrī, 
are then commonly, almost standardly, found in later texts (vāruṇī, āgneyī, vāyavī, and 
ākāśadhāraṇā). Second, the individual elements are assigned different places in the 
body: wind to the left big toe, fire to the navel, earth to the throat, water to the uvula or 
tonsils, and space to the head. The order of the elements is admittedly strange here (we 
would expect the classical Sāṃkhya sequence beginning with the grossest element of 
earth, which Nayasūtra teaches in verses 2.15–​2.17b), but the very fact that different parts 
of the body are the domain of different elements is important and common in later texts. 
Third, it is possible to deduct from these verses how this technique should presumably 
be performed. Simply put, it is the holding (dhāraṇā) of the breath in a particular place 
of the body that is dominated by a given element. The yogin is to hold his breath until 
he feels asphyxiation, then there will come an “eruption” (udghāta) in which the breath 
rapidly expands into the head and then returns to its original place.5 The number of 
these eruptions is prescribed from one to five, perhaps beginning with one eruption 
during the first dhāraṇā (vāyavī) and ending with five during the last (ākāśadhāraṇā).
The results of successfully mastering the five fixations mentioned here are some­
what lackluster and overly general. There are no specific results assigned to the indi­
vidual dhāraṇās, except for the ākāśadhāraṇā, which is said “to bring all siddhis” 
(sarvasiddhikarī, 4.116b). Then we learn that through these fixations, attachment (rāga) 
and hatred (dveṣa) will disappear, and the yogin will be freed from all sins (sarvapāpāni). 
And that is all.
Skipping the next text, the Guhyasūtra, which has not yet been edited, we can look at 
the last work in the Niśvāsa collection, the Niśvāsamukha. Here we find some verses on 
dhāraṇā (4.57c–​4.61) in the passage describing the ṣaḍaṅgayoga. The practice explained 
here is quite different from the dhāraṇā of the yoga section in the Nayasūtra. First, there 
is no holding of the breath; instead, the technique is purely meditative and consists of 
visualizing the individual elements in different parts of the body. More precisely, the lo­
cation of the elements is specified only for wind (the tip of a toe) and water (uvula). Since 
the order of the first four elements is the same as in the Nayasūtra (air, fire, earth, and 
water), it can be assumed that fire and earth are also to be visualized in the same places 
as in that text. Surprisingly, however, the fifth element, space, is not mentioned at all,

--- PAGE 258 ---
Transforming the Body      233
 
so in this respect the Niśvāsamukha is closer to most of the other early Śaivasiddhānta 
tantras, which teach only four types of dhāraṇā.
Notable, though not entirely clear, are the results of individual fixations. The text says 
that a person who visualizes the elements of air, fire, and water will attain the nature or 
form of that particular element (vāyurūpa, vahnirūpa, and āparūpa, respectively). This 
is highly interesting, but it is not clear what exactly does it mean. Perhaps that the yogin 
acquires the qualities of a given element—​for example, lightness (wind), radiance (fire), 
and fluidity (water).6 Or will his body be made up of that element? Unfortunately, the 
term rūpa used here does not help answer this question because its semantic field is too 
broad. The answer is not to be found anywhere else in this text. Apart from these vague 
effects, meditation on the element of water removes sins.
I introduced the technique of elementary dhāraṇās in the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā to 
show how this practice gradually formed in this earliest collection of the Śaiva tan­
tric texts. Most of the features that characterize fixations in their developed form are 
already present here, but they are not yet combined into a single whole. Although the 
bījamantras, the colors of the elements, the locations of the elements in different parts 
of the body, the retention of breath in these places, and so forth are mentioned here, all 
these features are scattered throughout different passages. Perhaps the best evidence of 
the formative nature of this practice in this collection is the fact that the concept of both 
four and five dhāraṇās is present here. The results of the practice are similarly diverse. 
They tend to be rather general and are only rarely more specific.
While the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā is considered by consensus to be the oldest among 
the early Śaivasiddhānta tantras, the other works in this corpus cannot be dated more 
precisely. However, Dominic Goodall has developed several criteria that allow us to es­
tablish at least a plausible relative chronology for these texts (Goodall 1998, xlvii–​lxxiv). 
I will follow his suggested chronology and discuss the passages on dhāraṇā in these 
scriptures. This time, however, the analysis will be rather selective in comparison with 
the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.
Let us begin with a short passage in the Rauravasūtrasaṃgraha (7.6–​7.10). This text 
teaches four dhāraṇās (āgneyī, saumyā, aiśānī, and amṛtā), but only the names of the 
first two can be clearly associated with the elements. The fiery dhāraṇā is placed in 
the navel and burns the sins. The water-​fixation (saumyā) is located in the heart and 
strengthens (āpyāyana) the whole body.7 Aiśānī dhāraṇā is situated in the head, and it 
brings all siddhis and the rapid attainment of the highest place of Śiva. The final dhāraṇā, 
amṛtā, is placed in the whole body, brings bliss (or Śivahood, śivaṃkarī) and nourishes 
everything with the nectar of knowledge.
The four fixations taught in the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha are very similar to 
those in the Rauravasūtrasaṃgraha, but the passage it contains on dhāraṇās is much 
longer (20.4–​20.26) and describes their intricate mechanism in considerable detail. 
Since the whole technique has been perfectly summarized elsewhere (Vasudeva 2004, 
412–​418), we can focus on the effects of the individual fixations. Āgneyī destroys all sins 
(surprisingly, not only one’s own, but also those of others), removes the feeling of cold, 
and drives away snakes and enemies. Saumyā strengthens (or rejuvenates) and defends

--- PAGE 259 ---
234      Lubomír Ondračka
 
against heat and poison. The only effect of the aiśānī is the attainment of the highest 
place. Finally, amṛtā dhāraṇā gives the nectar of dharma and knowledge, and by it one 
masters both yoga and knowledge. It is worth noting that the technique described in this 
text contains breath-​holding, including eruptions (udghātas).
The Kiraṇatantra also teaches the four fixations in a relatively short passage (58.18c–​
58.26b), but in a different order and using slightly different terminology: vahni, saumyā, 
amṛtā, and parā. In a few places, it lists the same effects as in the previous texts, but 
sometimes it offers something new. For example, water-​fixation brings peace and 
nourishment (puṣṭi, which seems to correspond to āpyāyana in other texts) and 
removes calamities or, more probably, diseases (upasarga). Amṛtā, pervading the head, 
protects life, and the supreme (parā), placed on the forehead, even bestows immor­
tality. Eruptions are again part of this technique; the text defines two types, a general 
(sāmānya) and a special (viśeṣaka) eruption.
The section on the dhāraṇās in the Parākhyatantra is very important, as it teaches 
the five elemental fixations (in the standard order: earth, water, fire, wind, and space) 
in a fairly long passage (14.33–​14.49), where the various characteristics of the elements 
probably appear together for the first time. Each element is assigned a color, shape, and 
a few basic properties. Bījamantras are also mentioned, but these are never specified, 
although it is clear that each element has its own individual mantra (svabīja, nijabīja). 
Surprisingly, the locations of the fixations in the body (ādhārās) are not mentioned 
here, although they are announced in an earlier verse (14.15a). So, we are left uncertain 
as to which of the three systems found in the Saiddhāntika sources is taught here (the 
first dhāraṇā may be placed in the big toe, the navel, or the heart). No specific number of 
eruptions is assigned to each fixation, but at the end of the passage it is said that victory 
over the dhāraṇās can be obtained by performing one hundred udghātas.
As for the characteristics of the elements, earth is described as yellow and square, 
water as white and crescent-​shaped, fire as red and triangular, wind as smoky or dark 
(dhūmra) and round, and space as free from all characteristics. The effects of the 
fixations are related to the properties of the individual elements. Earth causes immo­
bility, water cools and heals, fire can burn anything to ashes (such as an enemy army), 
wind can drive away anyone (demons) or push anything away (trees or mountains), and 
space removes poison and can empty the entire universe. Although not all the details 
in this passage are entirely clear (as the translator’s copious and illuminating notes 
make evident), for the history of the formation of the concept of the five fixations the 
Parākhyatantra is certainly a seminal text.
The Mataṅgapārameśvarāgama, in the chapter devoted to the ṣaḍaṅgayoga, 
teaches four fixations (āgneyī, vāruṇī, aiśānī, and amṛtā) that are similar to those in 
the Rauravasūtrasaṃgraha and Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha, but much more de­
tailed (yogapāda 2.35cd–​2.65). The dhāraṇās are not associated with any color, shape, 
or bījamantra, but their visualizations are described quite comprehensively and some 
of their effects are interesting. For example, the fire-​fixation destroys sins, cold sensa­
tion, obstacles, and so forth, but it can also burn or even kill an enemy, and the amṛtā 
dhāraṇā destroys diseases, aging, and death. Besides this, the fourth and fifth chapters

--- PAGE 260 ---
Transforming the Body      235
 
of the yogapāda deal with the conquest of the planes of reality (bhūtajaya), beginning 
with the five elements, but this visualization practice is not called dhāraṇā here. As a 
result of mastering the elements, the yogin acquires extraordinary physical abilities that 
are associated with the corresponding subtle elements (smell, taste, shape, and touch). 
In addition, mastering the element of earth brings the first of eight classic extraordinary 
powers (siddhis), the ability to shrink to the size of an atom (aṇutva, 4.48c).
The last work in the corpus of early Śaivasiddhānta texts that we will look at is the 
Mṛgendratantra. Its yogapāda, which has just one chapter, contains a description of yoga 
with eight auxiliaries (to the classical ṣaḍaṅgas it adds the repetition of mantras, japa, 
and yoga itself).8 The passage on the five fixations is relatively short (33c–​44b) but infor­
mative. Each element is assigned a color, shape, function, sign, and place in the body (no 
bījamantras are listed). Earth is goldish, square, stabilizing, having a thunderbolt (vajra), 
and located in the heart. Water is white, semicircular, strengthening (or rejuvenating, 
āpyāyana), having a lotus, and located in the throat. Fire is glowing in color, trian­
gular, burning, having a flame, and placed in the navel. Wind is black, round, stimu­
lating, having a dot (bindu), and can be placed in different parts of the body depending 
on which type of breath the yogin wants to control. Finally, space is transparent, lotus-​
shaped, emptying, and characterized by void (śūnya) and can be located anywhere in the 
body where the yogin needs to overcome poison or some other difficulty. The effects of 
the other elements are very simple: the earth-​fixation solves a distracted mind, water-​
fixation quenches thirst, and fire-​fixation helps against weak digestion. The actual per­
formance of dhāraṇā consists of holding the breath in a particular place. In fact, the 
definition of fixation is based on prāṇāyāma: if a yogin multiplies the time the breath is 
held (kumbhaka) by twelve, then it is called dhāraṇā.
We see that the concept of fixations described in the corpus of early Śaivasiddhānta 
texts is very diverse. This can be partly explained by their historical development: these 
works span at least four centuries, and it is apparent that the later the text, the more com­
plex the concept of dhāraṇā becomes. At the same time, however, it seems that there 
must have been parallel different ideas about the practice of fixations in this tradition. 
This is best seen in the number of dhāraṇās. Although four fixations dominate, five also 
appear in some texts (which would later become standard in Hindu tantric and yoga 
works). The actual performance sometimes consists purely of the technique of visuali­
zation, but more often it involves holding the breath at a specific point in the body. The 
results of this practice are similarly diverse. Most often they are different tantric siddhis 
or, generally speaking, various bodily effects.
Non-​Saiddhāntika Śaiva Texts
Although, as we have just seen in the example of the dhāraṇās, the Śaivasiddhānta is not 
a completely unified tradition, it offers a relatively coherent teaching and ritual practice 
compared to the rest of the Śaiva and Śaiva-​Śākta cults, whose doctrines, pantheons, 
and rituals are much more diverse. There are different ways to classify the whole Śaiva

--- PAGE 261 ---
236      Lubomír Ondračka
 
milieu (Sanderson 2013), but I will use the simplest one, which divides Śaiva literature 
into the Śaivasiddhānta and all the rest, the non-​Saiddhāntika traditions. This includes a 
large number of texts, many of which have not yet been edited, so the following analysis 
is very selective and focuses on the most important works and on texts that have some­
thing substantial to say about the technique of mastering the elements.
One of the most popular non-​Saiddhāntika tantric cults was that of Svacchandabhairava. 
The text dedicated to him, the Svacchandatantra, mentions the five fixations in several 
places, but the two most important passages are taken almost verbatim from the Nayasūtra 
of the Niśvāsa collection.9 Therefore, the most detailed and original treatment of the 
mastery of the elements is found in the Mālinīvijayottaratantra of the Trika cult. This work 
was probably not very popular at the time of its composition, but because it was the subject 
of exegesis by Abhinavagupta, its teachings later became influential.
The mastery of the elements is described in the Mālinīvijayottaratantra in the 
chapters on yoga (which, unlike the previous Śaivasiddhānta tantras, are very compre­
hensive) in the sections on tattvajaya and ṣaḍaṅgayoga. The conquest of the levels of 
reality is in fact the core of the practice taught in this work; hence, its description is very 
detailed and takes up five chapters (12–​16). The actual performance is very complicated, 
but fortunately it is thoroughly explained by the translator of this text (Vasudeva 2004, 
293–​365). Tattvajaya naturally begins with the mastery of the five gross elements (in the 
standard order starting with earth). Although the technique used to conquer the indi­
vidual levels of reality is referred to as dhāraṇā, its actual form is much broader, for it 
involves the simultaneous use of other elements of the ṣaḍaṅgayoga system (dhyāna, 
tarka, and samādhi). The resulting complex visualization practice has several stages in 
which the yogin delves deeper and deeper into meditative absorption and which takes a 
very long time to master successfully.10
In the first stage of visualization, the yogin identifies his body with the given element, 
so the text indicates the characteristics of each element (its color, shape, and sign). These 
do not differ much from those found in the other texts. Earth is golden, square, and 
having thunderbolts; water is white, round (not semicircular as is more common), and 
cooling; fire is red, triangular, and having flames; wind is black, round, and having six 
drops; and finally, space is without characteristics. More interesting are the effects of the 
dhāraṇās, which can be quite spectacular. If we limit our focus to bodily effects, we will 
observe that the mastery of the element of earth will remove diseases, make the body 
heavy and stable, and turn it into a diamond body having the strength of nine elephants 
(12.23–​12.24). Conquest of the element of water will remove the diseases caused by the 
fire-​humor (pitta), moisten the body, and cause the hair to darken, which is a sign of re­
juvenation (13.3–​4). Āgneyī dhāraṇā removes the diseases caused by the humors of wind 
(vāta) and phlegm (śleṣma), gives the yogin the ability not to sleep, increases his appetite, 
reduces his excretion, and finally gives him the power to burn anything (13.22–​13.23). 
Mastering the element of air will remove the sickness caused by the humor of phlegm 
(kapha), and grant the ability to move like the wind and the power to move anything 
(13.35–​13.36). Finally, the mastery of the element of space will create protection against 
snake venom and remove all diseases, wrinkles, and gray hair. Later the yogin will

--- PAGE 262 ---
Transforming the Body      237
 
acquire a body that will have the properties of the sky (gagana), making it indestructible 
and able to take on enormous or, conversely, minimal dimensions (13.45–​13.47).
While the dhāraṇās in the tattvajaya practice include meditation and visualization 
but not breath-​holding, the principle of dhāraṇās in the ṣaḍaṅgayoga system is the re­
tention of breath in certain places of the body. The Mālinīvijayottaratantra teaches four 
fixations in a short passage (17.13c–​17.17), but only the first two are related to the elements: 
the fire-​fixation (śikhin) and the water-​fixation (ambu). The remaining two are īśā (or 
īśānī) and amṛtā, and therefore, they form the set we know from the Śaivasiddhānta 
tantras. Holding the breath using a varying number of eruptions should be done gradu­
ally in the navel, heart, palate, and the top of the head. The specific bodily effects of each 
fixation are not listed here.
The comprehensiveness and complexity of the conquest of the planes of reality 
described in the Mālinīvijayottaratantra have no parallel in other Śaiva and Śaiva-​
Śākta works, so there is no need to review them. As for the dhāraṇā, since it is part of 
the yoga system (both ṣaḍaṅga, which is more common in the tantras, and aṣṭāṅga), 
it is often described or at least mentioned in the texts. Sometimes, though listed 
among the auxiliaries of yoga, it is said to be just twelve times longer than withdrawal 
(pratyāhāra), so it is not described further and has no clear relation to the elements.11 
More often we find the set of four fixations known from the Śaivasiddhānta (with the 
first two elemental dhāraṇās), or some variant of it. The Matsyendrasaṃhitā, for ex­
ample, teaches only three dhāraṇās (6.1–​6.17): those of wind, fire, and nectar (amṛta). 
We also encounter redefinitions of dhāraṇā, such as in the Netratantra, where it is said 
(8.16) that dhāraṇā is “the constant holding of the supreme self” and the result is the de­
struction of the bonds of existence. Similarly, the Prapañcasāratantra also completely 
redefines dhāraṇā (19.22ab) in the list of the eight auxiliaries of yoga, but a few verses 
later (19.56–​19.57) it describes the visualization of the five elements in different parts 
of the body (along with their bījamantras) resulting in cheating death (kālavañcana) 
but does not call this technique dhāraṇā. And in the same chapter (19.52c–​19.53), this 
text enumerates the twelve bodily places of breath retention (dhāraṇā) from which 
one can leave the body for a time, enter another body, and return to one’s body again. 
Surprisingly, this list of bodily places is used in the Śāradātilakatantra (25.24–​25.25), a 
text that draws from the Prapañcasāra (Bühnemann 2011, 207–​208), to define dhāraṇā 
in its aṣṭāṅgayoga system, so this work teaches twelve fixations, but which have no re­
lation to the elements. These few examples demonstrate the diversity of the concept of 
dhāraṇā in the non-​Saiddhāntika Śaiva and Śaiva-​Śākta texts, and that the association 
of fixations and elements is not firmly and uniformly established in these works.
Pāñcarātra Tantras
The corpus of the Vaiṣṇava tantras of the Pāñcarātra tradition contains many texts, but 
it is difficult to use them in research on the historical development of some phenom­
enon because most of these works cannot be accurately dated (Sanderson 2001, 35).12

--- PAGE 263 ---
238      Lubomír Ondračka
 
Fortunately, at least a relative chronology of the early texts has been established (Rastelli 
2006, 49–​54). Of these, three works are considered to be the earliest, which have gained 
prestige over time and have been called the “three jewels” (Leach 2014). Therefore, my 
exploration of mastering the elements in the Pāñcarātra tantras begins with them.
The Jayākhyasaṃhitā, which I have already mentioned in the section on the 
bhūtaśuddhi ritual, is considered to be the oldest and is usually dated to the tenth cen­
tury.13 In the first part of the last chapter (33), which is entirely devoted to yoga, dhāraṇā 
is listed among the seven auxiliaries of yoga (the repetition of mantras, japa, is added 
to the usual tantric set of ṣaḍaṅgas), but its explanation is very brief and somewhat un­
clear. The text says: “Then dhāraṇā is to be kept to remove cold and heat; it is fivefold 
as before.”14 Marion Rastelli (1999, 338) believes that the purpose of dhāraṇā here is to 
hold in mind the object of meditation created in the previous step (dhyāna) and that 
the removal of cold and heat is only a side effect of this technique. That does not seem 
very likely. The text apparently prescribes the performance of all five fixations on the 
elements (described earlier in ­chapter 10 in the verses on bhūtaśuddhi), but it states their 
results very elliptically, mentioning only two effects (which are the common results of 
the elemental fixations described in other texts). Interestingly, the later Pārameśvara-
saṃhitā, which draws from the Jayākhyasaṃhitā, in a verse defining dhāraṇā (7.450ac), 
instead of the removal of cold and heat, speaks of the elimination of sins, which, as we 
have seen in the Śaiva tantras, is another common effect of mastering the elements.
The next early work of the “three jewels,” the Sātvatasaṃhitā, makes no interesting 
contribution to our subject, for it contains no chapter on yoga and mentions dhāraṇā 
in connection with the elements only in a brief passage on bhūtaśuddhi (7.17–​7.26). The 
last text of this trinity, the Pauṣkarasaṃhitā, does not bring anything substantial either. 
Although it contains a fairly comprehensive passage on the conquest of the levels of re­
ality (33.87–​33.130), its style differs substantially from the description of the tattvajaya 
in the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. Hence, we do not learn any details about the technique 
(dhāraṇā is not mentioned here), the characteristics of the elements, or the effects of 
conquering each level.
The later Pāñcarātra texts are more informative. An excellent example is the 
Pādmasaṃhitā (composed in the twelfth to the first half of the thirteenth century; 
Schwarz Linder 2014, 31), which is the only one of the edited works that is divided into 
four parts (pādas), following the model of some Śaivasiddhānta tantras. Its yogapāda, 
which has five chapters, contains a fairly detailed description of the yogic body and yoga 
practice. (See also the Hayes, this volume.) The Pādmasaṃhitā teaches the aṣṭāṅgayoga 
system, and its concept of dhāraṇā consists of the five elementary fixations (yp 4.13c–​
4.24). Each element is assigned a place in the body (starting from earth, whose area is 
from the foot to the knee), a color, a shape, a sign, and a deity (different forms of Viṣṇu). 
No bījamantras are listed here.15 The practice consists of holding the breath and mind 
in the place of a particular element for a specific time. The length of retention increases 
gradually, from five ghaṭikās or nāḍikās (twenty-​four minutes) in the case of earth to 
twenty for air (the length of retention for space is not specified). No effects of individual 
fixations are mentioned; only at the beginning of the whole passage it is said (yp 4.14cd)

--- PAGE 264 ---
Transforming the Body      239
 
that dhāraṇā is the means of rescue from the ocean of rebirth. On the other hand, in the 
previous chapter, in the passage on prāṇāyāma, the retention of the breath in various 
places of the body is described (yp 3.23–​3.28), which produces the effects known as the 
results of the fixations of the elements in other texts (e.g., the removal of diseases).
The most mature form of mastering the elements by dhāraṇā present in the 
Pāñcarātra works is contained in the Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā. Unfortunately, there is no con­
sensus on the date of this tantra. It is generally considered to be late, but exactly how 
late is not clear. It adopts verbatim large passages from earlier Pāñcarātra works, and 
the third chapter on yoga is almost identical with the Yogattvopaniṣad.16 Now, this 
longer form of the Yogattvopaniṣad is part of a collection of works that were composed 
in South India by an Advaitin scholar in the first half of the eighteenth century using 
older and shorter forms of the Upanishads and several haṭhayoga texts (Bouy 1994). 
The Yogattvopaniṣad itself draws from three earlier haṭhayoga works (Bouy 1990, 109). 
Consequently, the verses on the five fixations in the Śrīpraśna (3.71–​3.88) can be traced 
to the Yogayājñavalkya and Dattātreyayogaśāstra, via the Yogattvopaniṣad (83c–​103).17 
This passage is quite comprehensive and clearly structured. Various characteristics are 
assigned to the elements (including the bījamantras yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, vaṃ, and haṃ), 
but the most interesting are the effects of the individual dhāraṇās. Simply put, mastery 
of a given element transforms the body so that it cannot be hurt or killed by that ele­
ment. As a whole, these five fixations bring to the yogi an immortality that extends even 
beyond the end (pralaya) of the universe.
Buddhist Tantras
Before concluding this overview of elemental control in tantric sources, I must at least 
briefly mention Buddhist tantras. In the introduction we saw that Buddhist ideas about 
the elements are diverse and differ from the realistic Sāṃkhya-​based model in Hindu 
tantras. However, this does not mean that Buddhist rituals do not involve the elements. 
While the ritual of purifying the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is not found in Buddhist texts 
(Goodall and Isaacson 2016, 7), visualizing the elements along with their characteris­
tics in various places of the body is a common part of meditation practice in tantric 
Buddhism.
Fairly complex ideas about the elements in relation to visualization practice appear 
already in one of the earliest Buddhist tantras, the Mahāvairocanābhisambodhisūtra 
(often called Vairocanābhisambodhitantra), which was probably composed in the sev­
enth century (Hodge 2003, 14). Information about the characteristics of the elements is 
scattered throughout the text, but if we piece it together, we get quite a comprehensive 
picture. The Tantra teaches the four elemental mandalas placed in the body. The earth 
mandala is located in the lower part of the body (between the feet and the abdomen), 
is yellow, square, and connected to the bījamantra aṃ. In the chest area (from the ab­
domen to the heart) there is a water mandala, which is white, round, and associated with 
the mantra vaṃ. Above it (between the heart and the eyebrows) is a fire mandala, which

--- PAGE 265 ---
240      Lubomír Ondračka
 
is red, triangular, and associated with the bīja raṃ. Finally, at the top of the head is a 
wind mandala, which is dark (or black), semicircular, and associated with the syllable 
haṃ. This pattern of elemental mandalas is quite stable in the later Buddhist tantras, ex­
cept for the bījamantra set (the standard series being laṃ, vaṃ, raṃ, and yaṃ; Goodall 
and Isaacson 2016, 8) and the locations in the body (later tantras often associate these 
mandalas with the four cakras placed in the navel, heart, throat, and forehead; Wayman 
1977, 66–​67).
The Buddhists, however, did not use the elements only in visualization techniques. 
Like in the Hindu tantras, the elements played a role in Buddhist yoga practice. Buddhist 
tantras share the same ṣaḍaṅgayoga system found in Śaiva tantric sources, so their 
practice also includes breath retention and fixation. The first exposition of this yoga 
system appears already in the Guhyasamājatantra, though in its last eighteenth chapter, 
which was added to the text a bit later (perhaps in the second half of the eighth cen­
tury). From the verses on prāṇāyāma and dhāraṇā in this text (18.147–​18.152) and some 
of their commentaries (translated in Sferra 2000, 18–​20) we learn that the five types of 
breaths associated with the five elements need to be restrained, and this technique leads 
to the stabilization of the mind and the dissolution of one element into another, which 
is accompanied by various signs. The actual yoga practice in other Buddhist tantric 
lineages may take different forms, but the connection between breath control, fixation, 
and the elements is quite common.18
Conclusion
This survey of the techniques of mastering the elements in tantric sources,19 although 
necessarily selective, has revealed several facts. First, efforts to conquer the elements 
are present in some form in all traditions and in the vast majority of texts. Second, the 
techniques of mastering the elements formed over several centuries and never achieved 
any unified shape; even within a single tradition, different practices occur. Third, the 
mastery of the elements is most often a part of the yogic practice of a given tradition, 
using the fixation (dhāraṇā) of the ṣaḍaṅgayoga or aṣṭāṅgayoga system to achieve it 
(often in combination with breath control and visualization techniques). Fourth, and 
finally, control of the elements has diverse effects, mostly different tantric siddhis and 
various bodily perfections.
Although several tantras contain quite comprehensive descriptions of the tech­
nique of controlling the elements through fixation, the most mature form of this prac­
tice appears only in the later haṭhayoga works. This fact seems to have been accepted by 
some authors of tantric texts. When Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the learned commentator on the 
Śāradātilakatantra, addresses the verses on the twelve dhāraṇās, he quotes an extensive 
passage on the five breath retentions resulting in the control of the elements (p. 900–​
901). This passage lists their locations, colors, shapes, deities, bījamantras, and various 
effects. Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that it comes from the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā, but it is not found

--- PAGE 266 ---
Transforming the Body      241
 
in the edited text. However, these verses do occur in another early haṭhayoga work, the 
Vivekamārtaṇḍa (69–​75). Or, when in 1820 the Bengali author Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya 
compiled the extensive tantric compendium the Prāṇatoṣanī, on dhāraṇā he quotes 
verses on the five fixations (p. 418) taken from another haṭhayoga work, the Dattātreya-
yogaśāstra (112c–​122b). We have also seen that the passage on the five fixations in the 
Pāñcarātra work Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā also comes from the haṭhayoga texts. Maybe this is 
not so surprising. After all, dhāraṇā is a yogic technique, and it is therefore proper to 
take its practice from the yogic texts.
At the same time, it should be added that the technique of mastering the elements is 
not an innovation of the tantric authors, as it is found in several older sources. The con­
quest of the elements (bhūtajaya) is described in the Pātañjalayogaśāstra (3.44–​3.46), 
where the result is the eight extraordinary powers (commonly known as aṣṭasiddhi) 
and other bodily perfections that overcome the limitations imposed by the elements 
in the material world. Even older is the Buddhist practice of controlling the elements 
(Wilson 2003, 35–​36), which is systematized in Buddhaghosa’s work Visuddhimagga 
(4.22–​4.30, 5.1–​5.11, 5.24–​5.26). The results of the successful conquest of the elements 
described in this text are absolutely astonishing (12.87–​12.101). However, a thorough 
survey of the historical roots of the technique of mastering the elements would re­
quire a separate study.

commentary on them.
	10.	 The complete mastery of the fifteen dhāraṇās takes about seven years (Vasudeva

does not quote Abhinavagupta is (as Alexis Sanderson 2001, 35 rightly points out) not

	16.	 See the list of parallel verses in the Śrīpraśna edition on pp. lxiv–​lxvi.
	17.	 This way of borrowing is evident from the deities associated with the elements. The 
Yogatattvopaniṣad takes verses from the Yogayājñavalkya, including the standard set of the 
karaṇadevatās (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva), while the Śrīpraśna removes 
the Śaiva forms and creates a rather odd set (Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Brahmā, 
and Vāsudeva). This implies that the present form of the Śrīpraśnasaṃhitā could not have 
taken shape before the second half of the eighteenth century. Although this may be dif­
ficult to accept for scholars who tentatively date the text to the fourteenth century, it is 
consistent with the information given by V. Raghavan in the preface to its edition (on page 
H): “I have heard that the Śrīpraśna is a very recent production . . . , is not to be counted 
with the earlier standard Saṃhitās and that its authority had also been some time back 
questioned in a court of law.”
