Chapter 11
Cosmology and 
Embryology in 
Medieval Japan
Anna Andreeva
Embryologic Notions and Metaphors 
in Premodern Asia
The religious traditions of premodern Asia had been attuned to the notions and themes 
of conception and embryological growth since early times. The surviving written 
sources are often fragmentary, and the exact historical pathways of these notions and 
themes across the vast spaces spanning what is now Central Asia, India, China, Tibet, 
Korea, and Japan remain difficult to define with precision. What is clear, however, is 
that for the best part of the past two millennia, the people inhabiting these spaces had 
a profound need for understanding the deeper mechanisms of life and death, and their 
own spiritual experience, in terms of reproductive metaphors and gestational patterns. 
In East Asia, several religious traditions and practices had adopted these metaphors and 
patterns at different times—​as doctrinal, ritual, or visual aids leading to a realization of 
higher truths, construction of distinct cosmologies, or acquisition of divine wisdoms. 
Prominent among these traditions were Buddhism (particularly, its esoteric variety) 
and Daoism, with premodern knowledge on medicine and healing closely following 
both. Medieval Japan serves here as an interesting study case, which brings to light an 
intermingling and mutual influence of several important strands: those of Buddhism, 
Shinto, medicoreligious thought, and literary practice.
Early India and China were both historically important for the development of East 
Asia’s tantric or esoteric Buddhist traditions. Before and during the first millennium, 
the notions of conception and embryological growth had been adopted there into 
a variety of oral and written sources. In India (including Sri Lanka), embryological

--- PAGE 275 ---
250      Anna Andreeva
 
narratives and motives appeared in the Garbhopaniṣad (Kritzer 2009: 73; Kapani 1989), 
the Mahābhārata and other Brahmanic texts (Couture 2009: 16–​19; Suneson 1991), and 
the Jātaka stories and Buddhist sutras spanning the Mahayana and Pāli or Theravāda 
traditions (McDermott 1999; Boisvert 2000; Kritzer 2009, 2014; Sasson 2009; McDaniel 
2009; Langenberg 2017), as well as in later Jain hagiographies (albeit with attitudes 
differing from those found in Brahmanic and Buddhist traditions, De Clercq 2009). In 
these early texts, the embryological metaphors and descriptions of gestational growth 
and death served a variety of purposes—​for example, as stern pedagogical and moral 
admonitions for the proselytization of religious truths, or as cosmological narratives, 
detailing the emergence of the universe and major divine or heroic figures.
In Brahmanic and Jain traditions, one motif that remains noticeable is that many of 
them contain an early Indian embryological theory, purporting that the mother and 
her unborn child are connected through their hearts (the state called dvaihṛdayya): the 
fetus is understood to have a capacity to influence the actions of its mother, although 
not the other way around (De Clercq 2009: 43–​44, 50–​52). Contrastingly, in some of 
the Purāṇic texts (Hara 1980) and early Indian Buddhist philosophical treatises, such 
as Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośabhāsya, Buddhagosa’s Visuddhimagga (Sasson 2009: 
63–​64; LaVallée Poussin 1980; Bhikku Ñaṇamoli 1975) or the Garbhavakrantīsūtra 
(Sutra of Entry into the Womb), the fetus was described as completely dependent on its 
mother, and it was the mother’s behavior and actions that caused the fetus indescribable 
hardships and pain (Kritzer 2014: 51–​74; Langenberg 2017: 65–​69). In their less prescrip­
tive mode, these embryological metaphors and descriptions were adopted by medical 
literati and practitioners into the treatises on women’s health, as in the case with Indian 
Āyurverdic tradition and its most important medical works, such as Suśrutasaṃhitā, 
Carakasaṃhitā, and Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā (Kritzer 2009: 77, 80–​81; Selby 2006: 266–​
271; Wujastyk 2003).
In early China, a separate cluster of such reproductive notions existed, recorded in 
medical manuscripts from Mawangdui 馬王堆, for example, the Taichan shu 胎産書 
(The Book of the Generation of the Fetus, c. 168 B.C.E.; Harper 1998: 372–​384), and 
adopted into medical literary classics, including the Yellow Emperor’s Canon (c. first cen­
tury B.C.E., Unschuld 2003). The early Chinese scriptures, such as Laozi 老子 (late third 
century B.C.E.) and Huainanzi 淮南子 (139 BCE), explained the emergence of the uni­
verse and the human kind through the interaction of yin and yang and circulation of qi; 
the latter, for example, stated that:
The one generates the two;
The two generates three;
The three generates the myriad things.
(Huananzi 7.2; trans. Harold Roth, 
Huainanzi 241; Choo 2012: 182)
Although the quote may appear deceptively simple, the Huainanzi also contained an­
other, more detailed description of human physical development during the ten months

--- PAGE 276 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      251
 
a fetus spent in utero until birth; it described the emerging fetus’s bodily parts and 
organs as linked to external cosmic phenomena, thus emplacing the human body within 
a larger universe as its smaller but complete reflection, a microcosm:
In the first month, the lard occurs (er gao 而膏).
In the second month, a lump develops (er die 而胅).
In the third month, an embryo forms (er tai 而胎).
In the fourth month, the flesh is produced (er ji 而肌).
In the fifth month, the muscles form (er jing 而筋).
In the sixth month, the bones develop (er gu 而骨).
In the seventh month, the fetus forms (er cheng 而成).
In the eighth month, the fetus starts to move (er dong 而動).
In the ninth month, its movements become more pronounced (er zao 而躁).
In the tenth month, the birth occurs (er sheng 而生).
The physical body is completed
And the five orbs (zang 臓) are formed.
(Huainanzi 7.2; Choo 2012: 183).
Translating this and other related passages from Huainanzi, the scholar of Chinese cul­
tural and religious history Jessey Choo has further pointed out that the five orbs (i.e., 
lungs, kidneys, gallbladder, liver, and spleen) were envisioned as “the conduits through 
which the qi of each individual human being is harmonized with the universe” (Choo 
2012: 184–​185). This idea would be further developed in medieval China and Japan.
Some similarly conceptualized ruminations on the origins of the universe and the 
humankind were seen in early Han-​dynasty cosmological scriptures such as Taiping 
jing 太平經 (Great Peace Scripture; Espesset 2016), or later, in meditative Daoist texts 
focusing on the acquisition of immortality (Choo 2012: 189–​190; Katō 2002) and in 
Chinese Buddhist and Confucian texts focusing on filial piety (Andreeva and Steavu 
2016: 19–​26). Both the “ten months” model, typical for early Chinese discourse on gen­
eration and procreation, as well as the week-​by-​week descriptions of pregnancy more 
often encountered in Indian Buddhist sources were known in East Asia. Moreover, the 
Chinese thinkers had developed further avenues of inquiry and imaginative interpreta­
tion, when it came to the ideas of formation of the human body.
For example, the Buddhist scholar Zhiyi 智顗 (538–​597) included the segments 
discussing a meditation on the emergence of a human being and the five viscera (Ch. 
wuzang 五臓, Jp. gozō) as well as their correlations to other pentadically ordered phe­
nomena in the ninth chapter of his treatise On Great Calming and Contemplation 
(Mohe zhiguan 摩訶止観, T. 1911, lines 0121a29–​0121b17; Swanson 2017: 1445–​1446) and 
other texts (Dolce 2016: 274). Zhiyi’s treatises came to be influential both in Chinese 
Tiantai and later, in Japanese Tendai schools of Buddhism. According to the aforemen­
tioned Mohe zhiguan passage, the first aggregate takes place in the womb, the embryo 
is endowed with basic consciousness and is able to generate a single thought through 
the power of past karma. But it is the mother’s conceptualization of colors, substances,

--- PAGE 277 ---
252      Anna Andreeva
 
tastes, and sounds and the mother’s qi which prompts the emergence of organs and 
bodily parts of the growing embryo.
Chinese medical literati of the Sui and Tang periods, including Wang Tao 王燾 
(675?–​770), also described the fetal gestation during the ten months of pregnancy and 
produced complex descriptions of linkages between the Five Phases (wuxing 五行), the 
five major internal organs, the five structural components of the human body (qi, blood, 
skin, bones, flesh), and the five tastes (Choo 2012: 191–​194; ten months of pregnancy in 
Wang Tao’s Waitai miyao 外台秘要, ibid., 215–​221). Similar, but briefer descriptions of 
the ten months of pregnancy and corresponding stages of fetal gestation were incorpo­
rated by the court physician Tanba no Yasuyori 丹波康頼 (912–​995) in Japan’s earliest 
surviving medical compendium, the Ishinpō 醫心方 (Essentials of Medicine, 984), 
which was predominantly (although not exclusively) based on the Sui and Tang Chinese 
medical sources (Andreeva and Steavu 2016: 27–​29; Khan 2016: 166–​185; Triplett 2019: 
78–​84). Separate traditions of embryological discourses and reproductive metaphors 
had been developed by religious and medical practitioners in Tibet (Garrett 2005, 2008, 
2009; Gyatso 2015) and in esoteric Theravāda traditions, for example, in Cambodia 
(Crosby 2000; Bizot 1976, 1992).
These diverse philosophical, religious, and medical texts espoused a variety of 
opinions on how exactly the bodies of the fetus, its mother, or the cosmos were 
connected, and how either of them influenced the other. This is to say that during the 
first millennium C.E., the religious and medical practitioners and thinkers in different 
corners of Asia were exposed to a multiplicity of ideas about gestation and fetal growth, 
not only in terms of cosmological but also physical phenomena, such as reproduction, 
conception, and birth, as well as women’s or children’s health. A more specific survey of 
premodern Asian sources regarding embryology in East Asian religious and medical 
texts can be found elsewhere (Sasson and Law 2009; Andreeva and Steavu 2016: 1–​50; 
Andreeva 2016).
Given these broader historic developments, it should come as little surprise that 
some reproductive metaphors, similar to those seen earlier in Chinese scriptures such 
as Laozi, Huainanzi, or Taiping jing, came to be adopted into the early Japanese cosmo­
logical narratives, known collectively as the “fascicles from the Age of Gods” (jindai no 
maki 神代巻), which survive as the opening chapters to Japan’s earliest mythohistorical 
records from the eighth century, Kojiki 古事記 (The Records of Past Matters, 712; 
Philippi 1968: 37–​38 and 47–​48) and Nihon shoki 日本書紀 (The Annals of Japan, 720; 
Aston [1896] 1972 I:1–​63, esp., I:1–​7). These two compendiums commissioned by the 
eighth-​century Yamato court and composed by Japanese literati also contained a few 
legends referring to fetal life and death (Law 2009: 261–​269). The already mentioned 
tenth-​century Ishinpō adopted a strand of Chinese classical medical writings on em­
bryological growth into its contents; this valuable knowledge on the prenatal stages of 
human life was composed and presented, again, for the imperial court’s consumption. 
However, this was not the only route by which the embryological discourses and re­
productive imagery from multiple continental traditions in Asia had reached Japan. 
Buddhism, with its rich scholastic and ritual customs, played a key role in this process.

--- PAGE 278 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      253
 
Linked to the continent by a conduit of the seas, Japanese isles were the terminus on 
a long-​ and short-​distance maritime and terrestrial routes connecting to the Silk Roads 
of Central, East, and Southeast Asia. Buddhism was introduced to early Japan’s polity 
from the Korean peninsula in the middle of the sixth century. Since then, Japan became 
one of the locations where Buddhist concepts, teachings, and practices found a partic­
ularly fertile ground, interweaving themselves into the domains of politics, economics, 
and cultural production. This assures premodern Japan’s position as an important 
case study for the dispersal of Buddhist ideas, especially, those of esoteric (or tantric) 
kind. Although the reproductive metaphors were adopted into early Japan’s cosmo­
logical discourses even before the arrival of esoteric Buddhist (mikkyō 密教) ideas and 
institutions in the ninth century, it is through the agency of Japanese Buddhist monks, 
specializing in this new form of Buddhism, that the embryological metaphors found 
their way into multiple discourses and religious practices in medieval Japan, where they 
appeared in a variety of texts, including esoteric ritual manuals, handbooks on child­
birth and women’s health, as well as literary and poetic texts. The next section outlines 
the role of Japanese monks, particularly those who specialized in the study and practice 
of esoteric Buddhism, in the adoption of such ideas.
From India and China to Japan
The Sanskrit terms outlining the key stages of human gestation, the arising of sensory 
faculties, emergence of organs, and different types of consciousness, were found in 
important Indian Buddhist sutras and treatises. These include the already mentioned 
Garbhavakrantīsūtra, the “Manobhūmi” chapter of the Yogacārābhūmi (c. first half of 
the second century) by the Indian scholar Saṃgharakṣa (Demiéville 1951; Schmithausen 
1987: 127–​128; Yamabe 2013), or the “Lokanirdeśa,” the third chapter of Abhidharmakośa 
bhāṣya by Vasubandhu (c. fourth–​fifth century C.E.) (de La Vallée Poussin 1980; Londrö 
Sangpo 2012, vol 2: 971–​972). The embryological terms used in these sources were nec­
essarily linked to the Buddhist philosophical discussions of rebirth, suffering, and 
karmic retribution. As all these important works were translated into Chinese, most of 
them, sometimes in several different renditions, had also reached Japan as a part of the 
broader processes of the transmission of Buddhism (Andreeva and Steavu 2016: 15–​19; 
Dolce 2016: 264–​270).
Some of these embryological notions initially formulated in Sanskrit and later 
rendered phonetically in Chinese, for example, kalala 歌羅羅, “the initial state of an 
embryo shortly after conception,” were known to the monastic community in Japan al­
ready since the eighth century. This was the time when Mahayana and Abhidharmic 
treatises, sutras, and commentaries to them were copied or studied within the scholastic 
seminars at Buddhist temples in Nara (modern Nara Prefecture in central Honshu). The 
monks residing there often combined a study of two or more of the Buddhist scholastic 
traditions. It is not surprising that many of them would have had to read or comment on

--- PAGE 279 ---
254      Anna Andreeva
 
the key philosophical issues discussed in major Buddhist scriptures, such as the Great 
Wisdom Treatise (Ch. Dazhi dulun 大智度論, Jp. Daichi doron, T. 1509), Mahāratnakūṭa 
sūtra (Ch. Da baoji jing 大寶積經, Jp. Daihōshaku kyō, T. 310), Apidamo jushe lun 
阿毘達磨倶舍論 (T. 1558, 1559; 1546) and Chengshi lun 成實論 (Jp. Jōjitsuron, T. 1646).
To give an example of these early engagements with Buddhist embryological dis­
course on a philosophical and scholastic level, let us take an example from one of the 
Japanese scholar-​monks based at Nara’s Daianji 大安寺 temple, Anchō 安澄 (763–​
814). He combined the study of Madhyamaka thought with esoteric teachings (mikkyō) 
and recorded personal “Notes on the ‘Commentary to the Madhyamaka śāstra’ ” (Jp. 
Chūronsho ki 中論疏記, T. 2255). This “Commentary” was most likely Jizang’s 吉藏 
(549–​623) Zhongguanglun shu 中觀論疏 (T. 1824), a commentary on Kumarājīva’s 
Chinese translation of Nāgarjuna’s Mūlamadhyamaka kārika (Ch. Zhongguanlun 
中觀論, Jp. Chūkanron), the first and most influential of the “Three Treatises” (Ch. 
Sanlun 三論, Jp. Sanron). Anchō’s “Notes,” cited below, quoted a slightly amended and 
shortened passage from another extensive Mahayana source with esoteric flavor, the 
Great Assembly Sutra (Sk. Mahāvaipulya mahāsaṃnipāta sūtra, Ch. Da fangdeng daji 
jing 大方等大集經, Jp. Daihōdō Daijikkyō, T. 397, lines 0169a29–​0169b07). The orig­
inal sutra passage found in the beginning of the twenty-​fourth fascicle, translated by 
Dharmakṣema, is considerably longer. It described the process of conception and emer­
gence of consciousness during an initial stage of embryonic development and followed 
by subsequent stages until birth. Its overall focus was on the idea of birth as a form of 
suffering.
The Great Assembly Sutra says: “Complying with the workings of cause and effect, 
[when] father and mother merge amicably, first, the consciousness is received. 
During the stage of kalala (initial stage of embryo’s formation shortly after con­
ception), its body now settles into forming an embryo. It does not inhale or exhale 
yet. Neither it has any cognisance of suffering or joy. It is not suffering, neither it 
experiences joy. It is separated from its previous material existence. Its later physical 
form is not yet provided. It does not exercise power, neither it has any desire. It does 
not manifest any vigour. It does not manifest any pride. The mind [which] first enters 
the embryo is called consciousness.
Anchō, “Notes on the ‘Commentary to the Madhyamaka śāstra’ ” 
(T. 2255, lines 0239c24–​28).
Anchō here seems to be interested in the ideas regarding the karmic predispositions 
and mechanisms of transmigration of souls, as he follows up this quotation by an ex­
planation of another key term, often seen in the Buddhist discussions of embryolog­
ical themes. This term, antarābhava (Ch. zhongyin 中陰, Jp. chūin), represents a state 
of “intermediate being” or an intermediate form of existence which takes place in be­
tween the moment of death and rebirth as another form of being. Although the source 
which Anchō quotes, the Great Assembly Sutra, contains tantric incantations (dhārāṇī 
陀羅尼) and has been described by modern scholars of Buddhism as fairly esoteric in 
character, no particular evidence has yet been seen of engaging the embryological ideas

--- PAGE 280 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      255
 
and metaphors within ritual practice at the Nara Buddhist temples during that stage 
(Mochizuki 1931–​1937, vol. 4: 3419–​3423).
This situation gradually begins to change from the ninth century onward. This was 
the time when the esoteric scriptures, translated by Chinese monks and containing 
discussions on the emergence of human consciousness, begin to be adopted and their 
knowledge systematized by scholar-​monks directly engaged in further constructing 
Japan’s own esoteric Buddhist traditions. Two such traditions, Tendai and Shingon, 
were established, respectively, by Saichō 最澄 (767–​822) and Kūkai 空海 (774–​835) in 
the early decades of the ninth century. As noted by multiple scholars, this was a process 
which often took place in circumstances of religious and political competition (Groner 
1984; Abè 1999; Chen 2009; Bogel 2009).
One important example here is Yixing’s一行 (683–​727) “Commentary on the 
Mahāvairocana sūtra” (Ch. Da Piluzhena chengfo jing shu大毘盧遮那成佛經疏, Jp. 
Daibirushana jōbutsu kyō sho, also known as Ch. Dari jing shu 大日經疏, Jp. Dainichi 
kyō sho, T. 1796). It was studied, copied, and lectured on at major esoteric Buddhist 
temples in Japan, especially those of the Shingon School, as the cornerstone of eso­
teric Buddhist teachings. Many minute details or notions appearing in this founda­
tional scripture subsequently took up particular cultural or religious significance in 
esoteric temple milieu of premodern Japan (for one example of the “human yellow,” 
Ch. renhuang 人黄, Jp. ninnō, a magical substance thought to be contained within 
a human head, see Iyanaga 2016: 344–​346; on another practice, “visualization of the 
five syllables on the practitioner’s body,” Jp. goji gonshinkan 五字嚴身觀, see Dolce 
2022: 284).
As part of the fundamental discussions on the arising of life, the abovementioned 
term kalala, together with other similar terms, can be seen not only in Yixing’s 
“Commentary” revered by the Japanese Shingon School. It also appears in the 
ninth-​century Japanese Tendai monks’ writings, for example, in the “Abbreviated 
Commentary on the Tantra on for All Wondrous Achievements in All Endeavours” 
(Jp. Soshitsuji katsuma kyō ryakusho 蘇悉地羯羅經略疏, T. 2227) by the founder 
of Tendai esoteric tradition and the Sanmon lineage Ennin 円仁 (794–​864); or in 
the Collection of Doctrines in the Tendai Lotus School (Tendai hokke shū gishū 
天台法華宗義集, T. 2366) by a chief disciple of Saichō, Gishin 義眞 (781–​833). 
Both went to study in Tang China and, subsequently, were engaged in the long-​term 
process of establishing the esoteric Tendai teachings, practices, and institutions in 
ninth-​century Japan. Overall, their aforementioned writings addressed the aspects 
of esoteric ritual practices more straightforwardly. However, the embryological 
themes sporadically seen in these early Japanese Tendai treatises still formed part 
of discussions on the arising of minds and bodies, and, most likely, were not yet 
actualized in ritual practice in any form.
For example, in Gishin’s collection, there is a following exchange on the initial stages of 
the embryo’s formation. The term “stages of name and form” (Ch. mingse wei, Jp. myōshiki 
i 名色位) already occurs in the aforementioned Chinese translations and commentaries 
to the Indian Abhidharmic and Yogacārā treatises, such as Apidamo da piposha lun

--- PAGE 281 ---
256      Anna Andreeva
 
阿毘達磨大毘婆沙論 (T. 1545), Yuqie shidi lun 瑜伽師地論 (T. 1579), Jushe lunji 
倶舍論記 (T. 1821), and Sanlun treatises (Dolce 2016: 262–​270; Licha 2016: 497). In his 
treatise addressed to the Japanese monastic audience, Gishin identified five such stages.
Question: In principle, how many “stages of name and form” (Jp. myōshiki i 名色位) 
are there?
Answer: There are five “seed stages” (goshui 五種位). After depositing itself in the 
womb, [the embryo] transforms itself once every seven days. In the first week, it is 
called kalala. In the second week, it is called arbuda 阿浮陀. In the third week, it is 
called peśī 閉手, and resembles short and small medicine pestle (yakusho 藥杵). In 
the fourth week, it is called ghana 伽耶 [sic], and resembles a warm stone (onjaku 
温石). In the fifth week, it is called praśākha 波羅奢呵, and [has] five blisters which 
open and expand. For thirty-​eight weeks it resides in the mother’s womb (botai no 
naka 母胎中). This time constitutes the “stages of name and form.”
Gishin, Collection of Doctrines in the Tendai Lotus School 
(T. 2366, lines 0273b26–​0273c02)
This passage from Gishin’s Collection may have been one of the earliest ninth-​century 
Tendai sources to act as a precursor for the subsequent development of a medieval 
theory known as the “five stages of embryo in the womb” (tainai goi 胎内五位, to be 
discussed in the next section). A few decades after Gishin’s work, the themes mentioned 
in it were employed by at least one scholar-​monk well-​versed in esoteric scriptures and 
doctrines, to a very different end. For example, the notions and terms associated with 
Buddhist philosophical discussions of arising of life and embryological growth were 
introduced by the ninth-​century systematizer of esoteric Buddhism, the Tendai monk 
Annen 安然 (841?–​880?) to a new form of Buddhist knowledge expertise—​on preg­
nancy, childbirth, and women’s reproductive health.
Embryology and Women’s Health in 
Ninth-​Century Japan
The full details of Annen’s life and thus the attribution of his authorship to certain es­
oteric texts, ritual manuals, and handbooks remain somewhat fragmentary, but 
Japanese and Western scholars agree that his role in the shaping and localizing of the 
ideas and practices of esoteric Buddhism in late ninth-​century Japan can hardly be 
underestimated (Groner 1987; Sueki 1995; Dolce and Mano 2011; Iyanaga 2016: 353–​
356, 393–​394n121, 398–​399 n.140, 400 n.144; Andreeva 2018). The scholar of medieval 
Japanese Buddhism Lucia Dolce has recently investigated Annen’s key role in the for­
mation of exegetical discourse on the Yugikyō 瑜祇經, one of the esoteric sutras, influ­
ential in medieval Japan (Dolce 2021: 5–​10, 22; to be mentioned further). As a scholar 
with access to the latest arrivals of Buddhist scriptures, translations, and ritual manuals

--- PAGE 282 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      257
 
imported from Tang China, Annen would have been in a perfect position to research 
the Buddhist literature arriving to Japan and, when necessary, compile his own treatises, 
ritual manuals, or specialized handbooks. Undoubtedly, among the Buddhist scriptures 
that passed through his hands were the Chinese translations of important Buddhist 
treatises and sutras which contained discussions or descriptions of conception, embry­
onic development, and childbirth, as well as the writings penned by the earlier Japanese 
Tendai school founders.
One of Annen’s most intriguing contributions in this respect was a production 
of a specialized handbook consisting of quotations from esoteric ritual manuals 
and Buddhist scriptures containing medical prescriptions, which was aimed at lay 
practitioners of Buddhism, specifically, high-​ranking aristocratic women of child­
bearing age. Although it is not entirely certain, if his authorship of this handbook 
can be accepted as it was within the Tendai school milieu by the mid-​twelfth century, 
Annen may have been the first to use the embryological ideas found in Indian Buddhist 
treatises and Chinese sutras in his own writings produced for scholastics and possibly, 
individual lay male patrons and their daughters, in ninth-​century Japan. In a hand­
book, titled Collection of Secret Methods on Conception, Pregnancy and Childbirth 
(Gushi nintai sanshō himitsu hōshū 求子妊胎産生秘密法集, Nihon daizōkyō 43: 191–​
198), attributed to him later by the scholar-​monks within the Tendai school, there are 
at least three quotations of earlier Chinese translations of Buddhist scriptures which 
dealt specifically with the theme of embryology. This handbook was arguably the first 
Japanese Buddhist practical treatise written by a Buddhist scholar-​monk for the ben­
efit of elite aristocratic women, with a specific aim of offering them concrete advice 
on ritual and medical matters related to procreation. The embryological sequences 
that Annen used for this first-​of-​its kind handbook derived from one of the Chinese 
translations of the Yogācārabhūmi (Ch. Xiuxing daodijing 修行道地経, Jp. Shūgyō 
dōjikyō 修行道地経, T. 606), the “Sutra of the Five Kings” (Ch. Wuwang jing 五王經, 
Jp. Goōkyō 五王經, T. 523), and the “Sutra on the Topics [of the Meditation on] 
Mindfulness in the Correct Dharma” (Jp. Shōbō nen[jo]kyō 正法念[処]經, T. 721). Two 
of these scriptures, Shūgyō dōjikyō (T. 606) and Shōbō nenjokyō (T. 721), explained the 
mechanics of rebirth, the work of the karmic forces, and the ideas of suffering, which 
were relatively well known already in the ninth-​century Japan as part of more general 
mainstream Buddhist teachings.
The “Sutra of the Five Kings” appears to be a Chinese creation; the precursor 
versions of it may have possibly been produced during the Eastern Jin dynasty (317–​
420 C.E.), but its existence is more reliably attested during the Liang period (502–​557) 
(Lin 2017: 124, 154–​155). This sutra, explaining the nature of the eight kinds of suf­
fering, together with a brief account of conception and gestation, was included in the 
Kaiyuan catalogue of the Buddhist canon (Kiyuan shijiao lu 開元釋教録, 730; T. 2154) 
by the Tang scholar Zhisheng 智昇 (669–​740) and a later revision of it (Zhenyuan 
xinding shijiao mulu 貞元新定釋教目録, 800; T. 2157) by Yuanzhao 圓照, a disciple 
of the prominent Tang esoteric master Amoghavajra (Ch. Bukong 不空, Jp. Fukū, 
705–​774). The “Sutra of the Five Kings” may have been imported to Japan during the

--- PAGE 283 ---
258      Anna Andreeva
 
eighth or early ninth century and so may have been used by Annen during his com­
pilation of his Collection of Secret Methods on Conception, Pregnancy, and Childbirth 
in the latter half of the ninth century. Late twelfth-​century handwritten copies of this 
Chinese sutra, although shorter and somewhat different in contents from the more 
mainstream version now included into the printed Buddhist canon (T. 523), had 
also been preserved in the temple archives of the Amano Kongōji 天野金剛寺 in 
Kawachi Nagano town of modern Osaka prefecture and Nanatsudera 七寺in Nagoya 
(Hayashidera 1989–​1991: 94–​99).
These three sutras had in principle yet little to do with esoteric Buddhist discourses 
being introduced to Japan, but their quotations in Annen’s work present the first 
occurrences of the embryological terms, translated from Sanskrit into Chinese, in rela­
tion to women and women’s health. These terms include the Chinese transliteration of 
the Sanskrit term kalala as well as the Indian ideas of fetal gestation, noted in the two of 
these sources, the Yogācārabhūmi translation (Shūgyō dōjikyō) and the “Sutra of the Five 
Kings,” as “thirty-​eight weeks,” thus presenting the Indian Buddhist ideas on gestation 
to lay patrons in Japan.
On the whole, however, Annen’s handbook dedicated to lay aristocratic women’s 
reproductive health introduced many other important Buddhist scriptures which 
bore the hallmarks of Indian and Chinese tantric or esoteric traditions. One of these 
was the Chinese translation of the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa (T. 1191), possibly the oldest 
Indian sutra containing tantric elements—​specifically, its ninth chapter translated by 
the Chinese esoteric scholar Yijing 義浄 (635–​714) in 703, which circulated in Tang 
China as a separate “Sutra of the King of One Syllable Spells, Among the Store of Spells 
of Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī” (Ch. Manshushili pusa zhouzang zhong yuzi zhouwang jing 
曼殊師利菩薩呪藏中一字呪王經, T. 1182). Different but similar fragments from 
Yijing’s Chinese translation, containing medicinal formulas and rituals for women 
wishing to conceive children, were included by Annen in his Japanese handbook, as well 
as spells and instructions for ritual worship of the esoteric deity Hārītī (Jp. Kariteimo 
訶梨帝母, also known as Kishimo 鬼子母, the “Demon Mother”).
Hārītī, known already in Central Asia, India, and China, was introduced as a 
ritual icon and protective deity to aristocratic women of childbearing age in ninth-​
century Japan for the very first time. Although this otherwise dark and scary ogress 
(yakṣiṇī) was known to snatch and devour other people’ offspring (Iyanaga 2016: 
345, 355), in Annen’s handbook she was portrayed as a “maiden of golden color,” 
wearing beautiful attire and flower garland decorations, holding the auspicious 
pomegranate fruit in her hand, and surrounded by several children. Even though 
at times Annen’s handbook had repeated widely accepted Buddhist views on the 
inherent corruptibility of women’s bodies and on birth as a source of suffering, it 
nevertheless included instructions for esoteric empowerment rituals and offerings 
invoking Hārītī, which were recommended to women who suffered from infertility. 
Moreover, Annen’s handbook promoted the aspirational goal of becoming “compas­
sionate mothers” (jibo 慈母) of rulers and kings to the aristocratic women in ninth-​
century Japan (Andreeva 2018).

--- PAGE 284 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      259
 
Soteriological Possibilities 
for Women in Ninth-​ to 
Twelfth-​Century Japan
It is significant, that along with this process of introducing embryological ideas to a 
very limited audience of aristocratic patrons and their families, another process was 
underway—​that of introducing the Buddhist theories positively regarding the women’s 
bodies, within the same elite social strata. First researched by the Japanese scholar of 
gender and Buddhism Nishiguchi Junko and later translated and studied separately by 
American scholars of Japanese Buddhism Lori Meeks and Heather Blair, the Sutra on 
Transforming Women into Buddhas (Bussetsu tennyo jōbutsu kyō 佛説轉女成仏經) 
was most likely composed in ninth-​century Japan (Nishiguchi 2006, 2009, 2014; Meeks 
2010: 303–​304); in fact, it may have already been in use by the 880s (Blair 2016: 266). 
Although its title incorporates the term tennyo 轉女, literally meaning “transforming 
the female [body into male],” thus referencing an ample body of Buddhist canonical and 
Japanese vernacular literature, this sutra created in Japan focused instead on a rather 
different motif: that of women as the mothers of the buddhas.
The scholar of Japanese Buddhism Heather Blair, who has studied this overlooked 
source and its extant manuscripts in English, has proposed the term “reproductive so­
teriology” (Blair 2016: 275). She has argued that, overall, the Buddhist sources known in 
Japan have propounded at least three positions on the status of women: (1) what she has 
called the “impurity hypothesis,” describing the women’s bodies as inherently polluted, 
(2) the “emptiness argument” appearing in the Vimalakīrti nirdeśa sūtra (Ch. Weimo jing 
維摩經, Jp. Yuimagyō, T. 474, 475, 476), which refutes prejudices against women, and fi­
nally (c) the “polysemic”—​essentially, ambiguous,—​nature of Buddhist sutras, which 
conflate both earlier positions and “demand interpretive work from its lay and ordained 
audience” (Blair 2016: 269). She has argued that the Sutra on Transforming Women into 
Buddhas represented “one viable option among the many scriptural discourses [on 
women’s enlightenment] in the Heian period (795–​1185)” and was possibly created by 
and for elite lay practitioners (Blair 2016: 264, 285).
Indeed, it has often been pointed out that the Mahayana canonical Buddhist litera­
ture, contained multiple, at times conflicting, sources detailing the “transformation of 
women.” One of those most influential in East Asia was undoubtedly the “Devadatta 
Chapter,” the twelfth chapter of the Lotus Sutra, translated by Kumārajīva (Hokkekyo 
法華経, T. 262, lines 0034b23–​0035c26; Watson 1993). Although a detailed reading of 
the Devadatta episode is most likely to produce an ambiguous interpretation, in classical 
and medieval Japan it was often credited with being the very fountainhead of a theory 
urging women to seek enlightenment through a rebirth as a man. Other sutras with sim­
ilar titles, which were included in the Buddhist canon, such as the one on Transforming 
Women’s Bodies (Ch. Foshuo zhuan nüshen jing 佛説轉女身經, Jp. Bussetsu tennyoshin

--- PAGE 285 ---
260      Anna Andreeva
 
gyō, T. 564) attributed to Dharmamitra (act. 400), presented the idea of women’s bodies 
being inherently impure and corrupted to lay patrons even more forcefully (Triplett 
2019: 113–​120). Japanese and Western scholars have pointed out that the ninth century 
was a time when numerous religious traditions, including Confucianism, Buddhism, 
and Daoism, promoted the ideas of social subordination of women (Blair 2016: 267).
By contrast, the Sutra on Transforming Women into Buddhas offered and devel­
oped the idea of the woman’s bodies and their reproductive organs as cosmological 
repositories and matrices (Sk. garbha, Jp. zō 藏) where the buddhas and divine beings 
could be conceived and gestate. In Heian Japan, this idea may have been connected to 
the so-​called tathāgatagarhbha theory, which taught that all sentient beings possessed 
the seeds of enlightenment in the form of the “womb of tathagata” (nyoraizō 如来蔵) 
(Blair 2016: 275–​277; Paul 1979; Zimmermann 2002; Radich 2015). In Japan, this theory 
must have been known from the Sutra of Queen Śrīmālā (Sk. Śrīmālādevī siṃhanāda 
sutra, Jp. Shōmangyō 勝鬘經, T. 353), an early Mahayana scripture which was translated 
into Chinese in 435 (Wayman 1974; Paul 1979, 2004). Aristocratic lay patrons and later, 
the Buddhist monks, engaged with the Sutra on Transforming Women into Buddhas, by 
copying it, mostly for the benefit of the female members of their families (Nishiguchi 
2014: 260–​267; Blair 2016: 264). The proselytization of the tathāgatagarbha thought con­
tinued sporadically in medieval Japan, for example, within the medieval “Commentary 
on the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra” (Shōmangyō gisho 勝鬘經義疏, T. 2185), attributed to Japan’s 
very own Buddhist hero, Prince Shōtoku 聖徳太子 (574–​622) (Dennis 2011).
The increasing significance of esoteric Buddhist ideas, imagery, and practices in 
ninth-​ to twelfth-​century Japan hastened the process of linking them to the local 
realities, including the social and political practices and discourses. The Two Mandalas 
of esoteric Buddhism (ryōbu 両部 or ryōkai mandara 両界曼荼羅)—​the Adamantine 
Vajra Realm (Kongōkai 金剛界) and the Womb Realm (Taizōkai 胎蔵界) described in 
esoteric scriptures—​were understood to express the male and female principles at work 
within the divine cosmos. In Japanese Buddhist literature, the latter principle was some­
times linked to an explicitly feminine imagery, for example, that of the “jewel woman” 
(gyokujo or gyokunyo 玉女), understood to be a soothing consort of a ruling king in 
early medieval Japan. The American scholar of Japanese esoteric Buddhism Brian 
Ruppert has traced several kinds of such imagery, including the figures of female eso­
teric Buddhist divinities, such as Wheel-​Turning Kannon (Nyoirin 如意輪), Kichijōten 
吉祥天, and the Buddha-​Eye Buddha-​Mother (Butsugen Butsumo 仏眼仏母) (Ruppert 
2000: 206–​210; on the latter, see also Abé 1999: 353–​355; Grapard 2002–​2003; Payne 
2022). These female figures may have been understood as what Ruppert has called gen­
erative divinities, expressing and representing parts of dualist esoteric cosmology of the 
Two Mandalas. However, it remains a matter of debate to what extent the worship of 
such divinities had contributed to soteriological theories and practices aimed specifi­
cally at women during that time.
Very generally, although these fragmentary theories and practices often conflicted, 
or superseded one another, they may have been fitting together with the scholastic 
discussions of the esoteric term daihi taizō 大悲胎蔵 (“great womb of compassion”).

--- PAGE 286 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      261
 
This term, which can be linked symbolically to the properties of the women’s bodies, 
is seen in a number of major esoteric sutras and treatises, such as the Mahāvairocana 
sūtra (Ch. Dari jing 大日經, Jp. Dainichi kyō, T. 848), Yixing’s aforementioned 
“Commentary on the Mahāvairocana sūtra” (T. 1796), or the so-​called Yogin Sutra, 
known in Japan as Yugikyō 瑜祇經 (full Japanese title Kongōbu rōkaku issai yuga yugi 
kyō 金剛峰楼閣一切瑜伽瑜祇經, the “Sutra of All Yogas and Yogins of the Vajra 
Peak Pavillion,” T. 867). The latter was an esoteric scripture which may have been com­
posed in China but gained a great popularity and influence in medieval Japan (Vanden 
Broucke 1989–​1990; Dolce 2016: 293–​297; Dolce 2021; shortly to be discussed further). 
The term “great womb of compassion” was invoked and discussed sporadically by the 
Shingon and Tendai scholar-​monks in their commentaries, particularly those focusing 
on the Yugikyō, but these discussions rarely transcended the scholastic circles at esoteric 
temples, populated almost exclusively by men.
All of the above is to say that there were limited developments in ninth-​ to twelfth-​
century Japan, which allow us to trace the first tentative uses of embryological concepts, 
knowledge, and patterns stemming from Buddhist scriptures, some of which had clearly 
an esoteric flavor, or were included in the domain of esoteric knowledge in Japan during 
the Heian period (795–​1185). These introductions were made mostly by a very limited 
number of erudite scholar-​monks who specialized in the study and compilation of eso­
teric and more widely known canonical and extracanonical Buddhist texts. Such learned 
Buddhist figures were therefore able to introduce embryological notions to their elite lay 
aristocratic audience, albeit still along with the views denigrating women’s bodies. In 
other cases, it was the elite lay aristocratic practitioners, who created and copied new 
sutras expounding positive views of women’s reproductive capacities and praised the 
cosmological nature of their bodies.
Embryology and Esoteric Ritual in 
Medieval Japan
Most remarkable developments of the esoteric Buddhist ideas regarding embryological 
growth can be seen in medieval Japan, during the late twelfth to fourteenth centuries. 
The research on this fascinating aspect of medieval Japanese religiosity is still on­
going, with many handwritten manuscripts and previously unknown premodern texts 
resurfacing from Japanese temples, libraries, and private archives.
Japanese scholars of Buddhism have noted the presence of embryological notions 
and metaphors in esoteric Buddhist materials from medieval and early modern Japan 
already in the 1960s to 1980s, particularly, in the primary sources attributed to the 
Tachikawa lineage (Tachikawa-​ryū 立川流; Moriyama 1965; Kushida 1979; Mizuhara 
1981). However, due to the somewhat explicit nature of discussed topics—​for example, 
with male and female sexual organs reinterpreted cosmologically as the vajra (kongō

--- PAGE 287 ---
262      Anna Andreeva
 
金剛) and lotus blossom (renge 蓮華), or a particular ritual implement symbolizing a 
sexual congress or unity between the esoteric divinities Fudō 不動 and Aizen 愛染—​
the ritual materials related to the Tachikawa lineage were often labeled “heterodox” 
(literally, “deviant teachings,” jakyō 邪教) by later commentators, and therefore, were 
considered controversial and little suited for academic scholarship in Japan. The 
first English-​language analysis of the embryological notions and theme of gestation 
appearing in medieval Shingon texts was presented by the American scholar James 
Sanford who also coined the term “foetal Buddhahood” (Sanford 1997). Since then, both 
the Japanese and Western scholars began to draw increasing attention to these themes—​
especially, the notion of the “five stages of embryo in the womb” (tainai goi 胎内五位)—​
as they were discovered to be present more widely, not only within the sources produced 
by esoteric Buddhist temple milieux but also within medieval literary and poetic 
commentaries written by Japanese court literati and lay adepts of esoteric Buddhism, or 
in medieval Shintō texts penned by esoteric and mountain religious practitioners as well 
as Shinto clergy (Klein 1998, 2002; Manabe 1999; Faure 2000; Dolce 2006–​2007: 140–​
143). It was soon pointed out that the controversial Tachikawa lineage might not have 
exactly been as marginal as had been previously assumed (Iyanaga 2006, 2010), and that 
the key historical actors who had given the impetus to the production and subsequent 
spread of esoteric rituals and commentaries imbued with embryological theories and 
metaphors were to be sought precisely within the major Shingon and Tendai temples, 
the very establishments of esoteric Buddhism of medieval Japan.
There has since come a real breakthrough in scholarship, which is still ongoing. This 
breakthrough focuses on the key source for these multiple embryological and sexual 
discourses—​the Yugikyō, one of the major esoteric scriptures revered by Japan’s Shingon 
and Tendai schools. It is now understood that Japanese commentaries on this sutra, 
produced by esoteric scholar-​monks and ritual specialists from the ninth and more con­
sistently, from twelfth century onward, formed a whole indigenous exegetical tradition. 
According to the study of this phenomenon by Lucia Dolce, the aforementioned ninth-​
century Tendai scholar-​monk Annen played a special role in its emergence (Dolce 
2021: 6; 2022: 290–​298). Furthermore, medieval Japanese Buddhists’ search for novel 
ritual techniques for “enlightenment with this very body” (sokushin jōbutsu 即身成仏) 
created a fruitful environment for proliferation and spread of embryological and gesta­
tional metaphors found in the Yogin Sutra and other esoteric scriptures, such as the Sutra 
of Guiding Principle (Ch. Liqu jing 理趣経, Jp. Rishukyō, T. 243) and the “Commentary” 
to it (Ch. Liqu shi 理趣釋, Jp. Rishushaku, T. 1003; Astley-​Kristensen 1991), traditionally 
attributed to the Tang esoteric master and translator Amoghavajra (Ch. Bukong 不空, 
Jp. Fukū, 705–​74).
The Dutch translation of the Yogin Sutra had appeared in the 1990s (Vanden Broucke 
1989–​1990), and the key role of this scripture (particularly of its second fascicle) in the 
emergence of ritual embryologies in medieval Japan soon became briefly acknowledged 
(Sanford 1997: 6–​8; Yamamoto 1997: 86). The more fundamental critical investigations 
of this important sutra and its broader impact, together with other esoteric scriptures, 
on medieval Japan began to take place in the first two decades of the twenty-​first century.

--- PAGE 288 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      263
 
The Japanese and Western scholars of medieval Japanese literature and religions grad­
ually mapped out the networks of esoteric temples and subtemples involved in produc­
tion of the Yugikyō-​related embryological theories, for example, the Shingon temples 
such as the Sanbōin 三宝院 of Daigoji 醍醐寺 or Ninnaji in Kyoto, or the Tendai eso­
teric lineages, such as Anō-​ryū 穴太流 (Itō 2003; Yoneda and Abè 2010; Dolce 2006–​
2007, 2010, 2016, 2021: 6–​10). Ogawa Toyoo, the scholar of Japanese medieval literature, 
and Lucia Dolce, the scholar of Japanese medieval Buddhism, have separately analyzed 
a plethora of ritual, visual, and literary medieval Japanese sources on which the em­
bryological theories of the Yugikyō had a profound effect (Ogawa 2014; Dolce 2006–​
2007, 2010, 2016, 2021, 2022). In medieval Japan, the earliest such commentaries were 
attributed to the Shingon monk Jichiun 實運 (1106–​1160) and the Taimitsu scholar Enni 
Bennen 円爾弁円(1202–​1280), among many others following; the repercussions of 
such medieval exegetical tradition had continued to be seen within local temples until 
the Meiji Restoration (Dolce 2016: 293–​298, 2021, 2022).
Of special significance here were the discourses on the “merging of two drops, red 
and white” (niteki wagō 二滴和合), leading to a conception of an idealized human being 
or an esoteric practitioner-​to-​be, who passed the five ritual stages of gestation in the 
lotus womb (tainai goi), finally emerging to achieve a status of a vajrasattva (kongōsatta 
金剛薩埵) and obtaining the full unity with the cosmic divinity Mahāvairocana 
(Dainichi 大日). These discourses were adopted into a performative context of esoteric 
rituals in medieval Japan. The already mentioned pioneering research by Lucia Dolce 
has shown how the tainai goi imagery and the Yugikyō-​inspired ritual transmissions, 
particularly those focusing on the second, fifth, and seventh fascicles of this sutra, had 
emerged as part of a series of secret esoteric consecrations (Sk. abhiṣeka, Jp. kanjō 灌頂) 
within multiple esoteric and Shinto practices in medieval Japan (Dolce 2006–​2007, 
2010, 2016, 2021: 20–​22, 2022). These activities were not confined only to the scholar-​
monks supremely versed in esoteric ritual theories and secret traditions guardedly prac­
ticed at major esoteric temples. Dolce has shown that ritual transmissions based on the 
Yugikyō were accessible at least to some female practitioners (Dolce 2022: 314). Toward 
the second half of the thirteenth century, even nonelite esoteric practitioners were able 
to learn the less secret contents of the Yugikyō and further transmit them, along with es­
oteric initiations, to others (Andreeva 2020).
The embryological ideas, identical or similar to those linked to the Yogin Sutra 
or Sutra of Guiding Principle, also came to be known to late medieval court literati, 
as they made appearance in Japanese poetry consecrations, known as waka kanjō 
和歌灌頂 (Unno 2022: 417–​419), and the poetic treatises, such as Ise monogatari zuinō 
伊勢物語髄脳 (Klein 1998, 2002) during the Muromachi period (1136–​1573). Similar 
adoption of embryological metaphors and notions can be seen within the initiation 
rituals of the Sōtō Zen school of Buddhism and seasonal rites linked to mountain reli­
gion, Shugendō 修験道, in early modern Japan (Licha 2016; Sekimori 2016). The most 
detailed overview of these many consecration practices in Japan’s esoteric Buddhist 
traditions, including those featuring the embryological, generative, and reproductional 
symbols and metaphors, has recently been presented in a volume of scholarly essays

--- PAGE 289 ---
264      Anna Andreeva
 
edited by the scholars of Japanese medieval esoteric Buddhism Fabio Rambelli and Or 
Porath (2022).
A separate theme in medieval esoteric texts and practices was the emergence of 
human organs, or rather, in the monastic ritual context, a contemplation on the five vis­
cera (gozō 五臓). In addition to the aforementioned discussions by the Chinese Tiantai 
scholar Zhiyi, mentioned in one of the previous sections, Japanese esoteric monks had 
developed their own ritual ideas and strategies. Kakuban 覚鑁 (1095–​1043), the founder 
of the “New Shingon” movement (Shingi Shingon 新義真言), and Yōsai 栄西 (1141–​
1215), the founder of the Japanese Rinzai Zen 臨済禅 school, were among the early 
adopters of this theme and the idea of correspondences between the five Sanskrit seed 
syllables (written in Siddham script, a medieval Indic script now used only in East Asia), 
five elements, and the five viscera, considered to be the vital constituents of the human 
body (Van der Veere 2000; Rambelli 2000; Dolce 2006–​2007, 2016: 273–​275; Yoneda and 
Abè 2010; Yoneda 2015; Kameyama 2020). More remarkably, not only did these ideas 
come to be adopted in medieval Japan, but toward the end of the thirteenth century, 
they also became visualized in a genre of ritual writing now known as the “Mandala 
of the Five Viscera” (gozō mandara 五臓曼荼羅). This mandala and the Japanese 
commentaries to it (gozō mandara waeshaku 五臓曼荼羅和會釋) form a representa­
tion of a micro-​ and macrocosmic realm expressed through the template of the human 
body, which combined and presented in visual format the pentadic correspondences be­
tween the Sanskrit syllables, sensory faculties, viscera, tastes, colors, and the Five Agents 
(gogyō 五行). The earliest example of such a mandala and the commentary to it is dated 
1162 and preserved at Ōsu Bunko 大須文庫 temple archive in Nagoya. Other examples 
of this remarkable mandala had also been discovered at Kanazawa Bunko archive of the 
temple Shōmyōji 称名寺 near Yokohama and Shōren’in 青蓮院 in Kyoto (Dolce: 2016: 
275; Abè 2016). An item conceptually close to it, tentatively titled as the “Mandala of 
the Five Stages of the Embryo in the Womb” (tainai goi mandala 胎内五位曼荼羅) is 
preserved at the temple Amano Kongōji 天野金剛寺 in Osaka Prefecture. The visual 
tropes from the latter seems to have been adopted as a “ten months in the womb” (totsuki 
tainai 十月胎内) trope appearing in broader popular Buddhist discourses on rebirth 
and reproduction and later seen in the Edo-​period woodblock printed texts, such as 
Seika mibungo 生下未分語 and Kumano no gohonji 熊野の御本地 (Nakamura 1990; 
Yoneda 2018). Even the placenta, protecting the gestating fetus in the womb, had be­
come conceptualized as a whole cluster of deities, which were thought to be born to­
gether with the human being and accompany him or her as a kind of protective and 
morally unswayable surveillance deities (Faure 2016).
Conclusion
However difficult it may be to trace the precise pathways of esoteric ideas regarding em­
bryology throughout the vast spans of premodern Asia, the written and visual evidence

--- PAGE 290 ---
Cosmology and Embryology in Medieval Japan      265
 
from medieval Japan shows that the terms linked to conception and fetal gestation 
were adopted as important elements of monastic and secular debates on the nature of 
rebirth and Buddhist enlightenment. Scholar-​monks from varying backgrounds and 
temple affiliations, including those based at Nara, Shingon, Tendai, and Zen temples 
throughout central and eastern Japan, used the notions and imagery related to fetal life 
to explain the mechanisms of rebirth and arising of consciousness as well as posit new 
soteriological ideas and methods in the context of ritual initiations and performances. 
Some of the embryological vocabulary and terms conceptualizing pregnancy and fetal 
gestation, seen previously in Buddhist philosophical and religious treatises arriving to 
Japan as translations from China, were adopted into special handbooks on women’s 
health; cosmological notions, such as the tathāgatagarbha were utilized in locally 
produced scriptures assumed to provide women with equal opportunities for salva­
tion. The deified process of pregnancy and embryological notions deriving from eso­
teric Buddhist scriptures produced in East Asia thus served as conceptual templates, 
which offered an inspiration for constructing the gendered theories of salvation. These 
notions were also employed for creating entirely new indigenous methods for acquiring 
“sudden enlightenment with this very body” (sokushin jōbutsu) by male adepts 
practicing the Tendai, Shingon, Zen, Shinto, and Shugendo traditions in medieval and 
early modern Japan.
