Chapter 12
Astrology and Astral 
Magic in Tantric Japan
Jeffrey Kotyk
Historical Background
The history of East Asian astrology requires that we understand a lengthy web of in­
tegrated elements that incorporate materials from diverse ancient and medieval 
sources. To begin, the astrology of India was originally separate from the systems of 
astrology that emerged in Mesopotamia and Egypt. Ancient Indian astrology was pri­
marily concerned with the movement of the moon relative to twenty-​eight lunar sta­
tions (nakṣatras), the full list of which first appears in the Atharva Veda (Yano 2004: 
333). Falk (2018: 532) suggests that the nakṣatras were originally used to estimate the 
time of delivery of infants, since the moon will pass through a nakṣatra ten times from 
the date of conception until delivery. Personal characteristics became associated with 
each of the nakṣatras and these varying features were assigned to people born under 
them. Another feature of the ancient Indian calendars are the periods of waning (kṛṣṇa-​
pakṣa) and waxing (śukla-​pakṣa) of the moon. Each of these periods comprise fifteen 
tithis (lunar days). Each tithi has its own unique hemerological features, which can be 
either auspicious or inauspicious. This model of lunar astrology did not incorporate 
the planets, such as Saturn, Jupiter, and so on. Astrology as it existed in Europe and the 
Islamic world was largely horoscopy (i.e., the casting of horoscopes). Horoscopes are ta­
bles that indicate the positions of the planets relative to zodiac signs (Aries, Taurus, etc.) 
at a given point in time, such as the time of a person’s birth, from which predictions are 
made, or alternatively to determine the optimal time to carry out an action. Horoscopy 
has its roots ultimately in Hellenistic Egypt, starting from the second century bce. 
Pingree (1992: 560) describes Hellenistic astrology as “a union of aspects of advanced 
Babylonian celestial divination with Aristotelian physics and Hellenistic astronomy.” 
Horoscopy requires not only systematic knowledge of planetary movements but also 
the mathematics to calculate the positions of stars relative to an exact terrestrial latitude.

--- PAGE 299 ---
274      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
Horoscopy was later transmitted to Sasanian Iran and India between the third to fifth 
centuries, although the exact details of how all this unfolded remain unclear in many 
aspects. Indian astrology amalgamated their autochthonous system of nakṣatras with 
the zodiac signs and doctrines of Hellenistic astrology (Pingree 1997).
Turning to China, it had its own unique model of astronomy and celestial omenology. 
Cullen (2011: 218–​223) points out that the Wu xing zhan 五星占 (Prognostics of the Five 
Stars), which appears to date to the Warring States period (475–​221 bce) and was discov­
ered in a tomb dating to 168 bce, “is the earliest surviving Chinese document showing 
clear evidence of systematic consideration of planetary motions.” The significations 
of the motions are also considered in order to prognosticate political and military 
developments. Such an interest in celestial omens fostered the development of astro­
nomical and calendrical sciences in later centuries, which came under the strict do­
main of imperial governments. Celestial omenology in ancient China, we must observe, 
was concerned chiefly with the affairs of state and not individuals, which is in contrast 
to horoscopy and nakṣatra astrology, both of which address the fate and character of 
individuals.
Chinese astronomy was oriented around a system of twenty-​eight lunar sta­
tions (ershi ba xiu 二十八宿) relative to the celestial equator. Although similar to the 
twenty-​eight nakṣatras, a point that has led some scholars to argue for a common or­
igin, these two models were, in reality, separate and developed independent of one an­
other as demonstrated by Pankenier (2014). The Chinese calendar, which should be 
characterized as pan-​Asian in character, follows a sexagenary cycle. This is a repeating 
cycle of sixty terms comprised of the earthly branches (dizhi 地支) and heavenly stems 
(tiangan 天干). This cycle records the passage of days and years. This system was 
utilized alongside a lunar-​solar calendar, which is comprised of twelve lunar months 
(i.e., months defined by lunar phases), recurring intercalary months, and twenty-​four 
solar terms (Wilkinson 2000: 176–​187). The first day of a month falls on the New Moon 
(shuo 朔). The fifteenth day falls on the Full Moon (wang 望). This model was replicated 
in Japan, where it is attested in the Nihon shoki 日本書紀, an early state history which 
was compiled in 720.
In the case of Buddhism, it is clear that, with few exceptions, Buddhists in India gen­
erally held a common belief in astrology, even though the deterministic premise of as­
trology technically contradicts the law of karma (e.g., outcomes are decided by one’s 
actions, not the stars, according to the basic theory of karma). Indian Buddhist litera­
ture in its various historical stages reflects the gradual incorporation and development 
of what were originally foreign astrological concepts, such as the zodiac signs (Kotyk 
2018a). The vinaya (monastic codes), several of which were translated into Chinese, pro­
hibited monks and nuns from practicing astrology, but this was not because of any chal­
lenge to the validity of astrology itself—​the main issue was that it was inappropriate for 
a renunciant to engage in such a worldly art (Kotyk 2017b). Early Brahmins shared neg­
ative sentiments toward astrology. Gansten (2011: 217) explains that “before the accul­
turation of horoscopic astrology proper, introduced from the Greek-​speaking world in 
the first centuries of the Common Era, practitioners of astral divination were described

--- PAGE 300 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      275
 
in not very flattering terms by the authors of religious codes of law.” Gansten highlights 
the Manusmṛti (3.162) and Baudhāyanadharmasūtra (2.2.15–​2.2.16) as texts that regard 
astrologers as lowly persons. The former expressly forbids upper-​caste astrologers from 
joining sacrifices, although divination itself was not regarded as invalid.
Indian astrology was initially introduced to China via translated Buddhist texts, in 
particular the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna, although the astrological elements were relatively 
basic and impractical to implement without recourse to further material or experts, 
particularly since the astrometric definitions of the nakṣatras from India would have 
been alien to Chinese astronomers. The first version was translated by Dharmarakṣa 
(Zhu Fahu 竺法護; c. 239–​316), titled Shetoujian Taizi ershiba xiu jing 舍頭諫太子
二十八宿經 (Sūtra of Prince Śārdūlakarṇa and the Twenty-​eight Nakṣatras), which 
he translated sometime between 307 and 313. The other version is the Mātaṅga-​sūtra 
(Modengjia jing 摩登伽經). This translation is traditionally attributed to Lü Yan 律炎 
and Zhiqian 支謙 in the year 230.1 The style of translation and records in bibliographies, 
however, seem to indicate it was translated some time later, perhaps around the late 
fifth century by Guṇabhadra (Qiunabatuoluo 求那跋陀羅; 394–​468). Hayashiya (1945: 
541) already raised doubts about the traditional dating of the Mātaṅga-​sūtra. This 
point was further taken up by Kotyk (2017c: 28). Zenba (1952) examined the Mātaṅga-​
sūtra in detail and noted a number of anomalous features, in particularly its gnomonic 
measurements which when calculated would give a position beyond the frontiers of 
even northern India, suggesting a point of observation in Central Asia. The text also 
has a number of details and information not found in the earlier version of the Śārd
ūlakarṇāvadāna, such as planetary revolution periods, which indicates that it was 
translated from a significantly revised source text. The Mātaṅga-​sūtra foreshadows later 
practices of stellar worship (i.e., the worship of asterisms). For instance, the nakṣatra 
Kṛttikā (mao 昴) is presided over by Agni (Huo shen 火神) and yogurt (lao 酪) is to be 
offered to him (T 1300, 21: 404c10–​404c12).2 The astrological content of some sections 
in the Mahāsaṃnipāta (Dafangdeng daji jing 大方等大集經) has been examined 
by Zenba (1957) and Mak (2015). Therein the Candragarbha-​parivarta (Yuezang fen 
月藏分), translated by Narendrayaśas (Naliantiyeshe 那連提耶舍; 490–​589) in 566, has 
the Buddha tell Brahma about the planets and zodiac signs, and how he orders them 
to guard over countries and people (T 397, 13: 373a21–​373a29). Buddhist cosmology at 
this point in history was increasingly incorporating an active pantheon of astral deities 
including deified zodiac signs, which was unique to India (the zodiac signs were not 
deified elsewhere in antiquity). This development likely reflects growing interest in as­
trology among Buddhists. Buddhist cosmology, particularly that based on Abhidharma, 
regarded the sun and the moon as discs orbiting around Mt. Meru and the Four 
Continents, all of which was atop a flat disc-​shaped surface. Buddhists in India never 
appear to have adopted spherical-​earth cosmology.3
Although astrology was explained to an extent in some Buddhist scriptures, 
Buddhists did not have a pressing need to study astrology in detail until the advent of 
early Vajrayāna, in which the timing of a mandala and rituals became a key factor, in 
large part perhaps explained by a growing appreciation for astrology in Indian society

--- PAGE 301 ---
276      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
(Kotyk 2018b). The Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, which is an early example of this new system 
of Buddhist practices, dating to around the mid-​seventh century, incorporates some as­
trological lore (Hodge 2003, 14–​15: 88, 409). A copy of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (the 
short title in Chinese is Dari jing 大日經) was acquired by the Chinese monk Wuxing 
無行 (b. 630) and this version was translated by the Indian monk Śubhakarasiṃha 
(Shanwuwei 善無畏; 637–​735) and Yixing一行 (673–​727) in 724 (Kano 2015; Kotyk 
2019e). Yixing compiled a commentary to this text sometime before his death in 727, 
based on the oral testimony of Śubhakarasiṃha. This commentary is titled Dari jing shu 
大日經疏 (Commentary the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi). The text includes a section that 
briefly outlines Indian astrology, primarily for timing the execution of rituals and the 
creation of a mandala (T 1796, 39: 617c22–​618a19), that is, a model of hemerology (the 
practice of selecting auspicious days). Kotyk (2018c) translates this section and argues 
that this explanation reflects the astrological knowledge current at Nālanda, given that 
the outline is likely the voice of Śubhakarasiṃha himself for the most part. The impor­
tance of astrology in the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi therefore highlights the growing incor­
poration of astrological concepts into early Tantric Buddhism.
The Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi came as a package which included a mandala that 
depicted not only the principal Buddhist deities but also the planets, zodiac signs, 
and nakṣatras, albeit as minor figures located on the periphery. There are also unique 
mantras, mudrās, and seed syllables for each of these figures (Somekawa 2013: 170–​
239). These elements were preserved within Mikkyō lineages in Japan (i.e., Tōmitsu 
東密, denoting the “Esoteric Teachings” of Shingon, and Taimitsu 台密, denoting that 
of Tendai). The original icons of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi were preserved in an illus­
trated document titled Taizō zuzō 胎藏圖象 (Icons of the Womb Matrix), which is a col­
lection of illustrations of figures. The postscript explains that the Tendai monk Enchin 
圓珍 (814–​891) copied these illustrations in the year 855 at the monastery Qinglongsi 
青龍寺 in Chang’an in China. The first copy was produced in 1181, and another was 
created in 1194. The Taizō zuzō is therefore the third copy of the original brought by 
Enchin.4 These illustrations are possibly the closest versions we have to the originals 
produced under Śubhakarasiṃha’s direction around 724. The Taizō zuzō includes the 
planets and nakṣatras in anthropomorphic forms, as well as the zodiac signs (Sagittarius 
is a half-​man half-​horse bowman, which is the earliest known example of a creature 
resembling a centaur or satyr in China).5 These astral deities became part of the wider 
East Asian pantheon from this point in history. They became established in Buddhism 
and slightly later also in Daoism (for a discussion of the latter, see Kotyk 2021b).
The pressing need to understand foreign astrology with accessible materials and the 
growing importance of astrology itself for Buddhist purposes were likely the reasons 
underlying Amoghavajra’s (Bukong 不空; 705–​774) creation of the first authoritative 
manual of Buddhist astrology in China. This manual is generally known by its abbrevi­
ated title, Xiuyao jing 宿曜經 (Sūtra of Constellations and Planets). The full title in the 
modern Japanese Taishō Canon can be translated as Sūtra on Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and 
the Sages’ Teaching on Auspicious and Inauspicious Times, Good and Evil Constellations 
and Planets (Wenshushili Pusa ji zhuxian suoshuo jixiong shiri shan’e xiuyao jing

--- PAGE 302 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      277
 
文殊師利菩薩及諸仙所說吉凶時日善惡宿曜經). Although the work is attributed to 
Mañjuśrī, there is little of anything specifically Buddhist in character within the text.
Zenba (1968) surveyed the version of this text in the Taishō Canon (T 1299) and 
pointed out that there is no extant Sanskrit original of it. Yano (2013) has demonstrated, 
however, that the version of this text in the Taishō likely postdates the Tang period, 
given its heavily modified content when compared to extant recensions which date 
back to the ninth century and were preserved in Japan. Yano also points to the monk 
Kakushō 覺勝 (n.d.) from Kōyasan 高野山, who collated the editions available to him 
and in 1736 compiled a critical edition of the Xiuyao jing. This edition is titled Sukuyō 
yōketsu 宿曜要訣 (Essential Key to Sukuyō). It was printed in 1897 by Wakita Bunshō 
脇田文紹 as a typeset edition, Sukuyō-​kyō shukusatsu 宿曜經縮刷 (Typset Xiuyao 
jing). This version was used for the Shukuyōkyō uranai shinden 宿曜經占真傳 (The 
True Transmission of Xiuyao jing Divination), which is the Xiuyao jing with a modern 
commentary, published in 1908 by Wakahara Yukitsune 若原敬經 (1854–​1926).
Amoghavajra and a team of assistants compiled the first version of the Xiuyao jing 
in 759. The preface explains that the text was subsequently revised in 764 to produce 
a version more easily understood by Chinese readers (Sukuyō-​kyō shukusatsu vol. 1: 
4). The first fascicle is the revised work, while the second fascicle is the former version. 
The Xiuyao jing provides a diversity of astrological lore, including material related to 
the nakṣatras, zodiac signs, and seven-​day week, but all of this was conceived within a 
flat-​earth model of Mt. Sumeru and the Four Continents (Kotyk 2021c). The Xiuyao jing 
appears to have been the first manual in Chinese to explain and discuss the seven-​day 
week in detail. The days of the week are given in Chinese, Persian, Sogdian, and Sanskrit 
to facilitate inquiries about the day of the week (the week was observed by foreign peo­
ples but not China at the time), but this also points to the likelihood of multicultural 
materials having been referenced (Yano 2013: 110). Enough information is given in the 
Xiuyao jing so that Chinese monks could determine, using their own calendar, auspi­
cious days to carry out specific types of rituals. The text, however, also introduced natal 
astrology—​that is, doctrines utilized to predict the fate and fortune of an individual 
based on their time of birth. In this case, the techniques do not constitute horoscopy, 
since a birth chart is not described (Kotyk 2018e: 11–​17). Nevertheless, astrology for the 
purposes of prognosticating the future of an individual was novel to China at the time, 
since the ancient form of Chinese celestial omenology was chiefly concerned with the 
state and realm.
Natal astrology prognosticates various aspects in a person’s life, including lifespan, 
misfortune, and hardship. In the decades following Amoghavajra, this concern 
about fate appears to have prompted interest in apotropaic practices to mitigate or 
ward off baneful events or otherwise to enhance longevity. The genesis of the cult of 
so-​called Tejaprabhā (Chishengguang Fo 熾盛光佛) is likely best explained by a 
growing interest in astrology among Buddhists in China. The first text in Chinese 
to introduce this figure is the Da shengmiao jixiang pusa shuo chuzai jiaoling falun 
大聖妙吉祥菩薩說除災教令法輪 (Disaster Eliminating Edifying Dharma-​Wheel 
as Taught by the Great and Holy Excellent Auspicious Bodhisattva), also titled

--- PAGE 303 ---
278      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
Chishengguang Foding 熾盛光佛頂 (*Tejaprabhā-​buddhōṣṇīṣa?). The colophon itself 
does not provide a date or translator but an editorial note in the Taishō text (T 966) 
records written remarks (okugaki 奧書) from the original manuscript. It is said that the 
“Indian monk, Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra from Mahānālanda Saṃghārāma in Central 
India 中天竺國大那欄陀寺梵僧尸羅跋陀羅三藏,” in the year 796 translated the work 
(347, n. 20). This text includes a pūja (ritual), instructions for painting a mandala, and an 
array of mantras to be utilized when facing inauspicious astral omens.
The name “Tejaprabhā” is not attested in any extant Sanskrit source and was, it 
seems, devised by Nanjio Bunyiu (Nanjō Bun’yū 南條文雄; 1849–​1927) based on the 
Chinese titles of texts retranslated into Sanskrit, which he provides in A Catalogue of 
the Chinese Translation of the Buddhist Tripitaka (Nanjio 1883: 222; Kotyk 2019d: 612). 
Mak (2018: 241–​242, n. 64) shows that the typical mantra of this “Tejaprabhā” is re­
corded in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, in which the mantra is called Jvāloṣṇīṣa (Blazing 
Tuft); thus Jvāloṣṇīṣa is possibly the original Indic name of the Tathāgata in question. 
A medieval Japanese source, the Byakuhō kushō 白寶口抄 (Oral Instructions on the 
White Treasure), recorded by Ryōson 亮尊 (taught by Ryōzen 亮禪; 1258–​1341), gives 
lo-​ka-​jva-​la in Siddhaṃ script as the Sanskrit name (TZ vol. 7: 243b23). This might be 
reconstructed as *Lokajvāla (i.e., Light of the World), but this name is not found in any 
other source and could be a translation from Chinese into Sanskrit. Modern scholarship 
in the Anglosphere and Japan continue to use the name Tejaprabhā.
Tejaprabhā became a widely worshipped deity across East Asia. One often cited 
example from the art record is a painting titled “Tejaprabhā Buddha and the Five 
Planets” (熾盛光佛并五星圖), which was painted by Zhang Huaixing 張淮興 (n.d.) 
in the year 897 (Stein no. Ch.liv.007, British Museum 1919,0101,0.31). An important 
ritual text of this cult was the Chishengguang daweide xiaozai jixiang tuoluoni jing 
熾盛光大威德消災吉祥陀羅尼經 (Great Venerable Disaster Eliminating Auspicious 
Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Tejaprabhā), whose translation is attributed to Amoghavajra. Liao 
Yang (2003: 329), however, points out that it does not appear in Tang-​era catalogs. Jōnen 
靜然 in the Gyōrin shō 行林抄 (Summary of a Forest of Practices), compiled in 1154, 
notes that this text was brought to Japan by a Chinese merchant in 907 (year 7 of Engi 
延喜). This date is noteworthy since the text was apparently unknown to the Shingon 
and Tendai monks who collected materials several decades earlier in China (T 2409, 76: 
84b19–​22).
The ninth century saw the translation of horoscopy into Chinese from Indo-​Iranian 
sources. One key Buddhist text in this regard is the Qiyao rangzai jue 七曜攘災決 
(Secrets of Seven-​Planet Apotropaism). This text does not appear in any Chinese canon 
or bibliography but was preserved in Japan and reproduced in the Taishō Canon. The 
Qiyao rangzai jue provides everything necessary to cast a basic horoscope and then in­
terpret it, including ephemerides (tables indicating the positions of planets over periods 
of time), descriptions of planetary orbits, a table of solar terms, and some general as­
trological lore. There is more to the text, however, than only astrology. Mantras for the 
planets are also given, as well as basic rituals with which one can ward off baneful plan­
etary influences. Two sets of planetary icons, which are to be drawn, are also described,

--- PAGE 304 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      279
 
yet these differ entirely from what we observe in the aforementioned Taizō zuzō. One 
set bears close resemblance to depictions of the planets in medieval Arabic and Persian 
manuscripts (e.g., Venus as a lute-​player, Mercury as a scribe, Saturn as an elderly 
hunched-​over man, and Mars as a red warrior). Kotyk (2017a) has suggested an Iranian 
heritage for these icons on the basis of comparative iconographical data, as well as the 
fact that Sogdian loanwords (the names of the planets) are given in the Qiyao rangzai 
jue, although firmly establishing a Sasanian origin is presently impossible due to the fact 
that no known representation of the planets from Sasanian times is extant. The paucity 
is due to the fact that Zoroastrianism viewed the planets as demonic in nature (Panaino 
2015). Kotyk (2017a, 2017c) also pointed out the strong parallels between the astral magic 
of the Qiyao rangzai jue and that of medieval Islamicate and European traditions. The 
same type of astral magic and astrology was adopted by Daoists but modified for their 
own purposes (Kotyk 2021b).
Shūei’s 宗叡 (809–​884) inventory also records one text, grouped together with the 
others related to astral science, titled Duli yusi jing 都利聿斯經. With regard to this text, 
the Xin Tang shu 新唐書 (59.1548), a revised history of the Tang compiled by Ouyang 
Xiu 歐陽修 (1007–​1072) and Song Qi 宋祁 (998–​1061) in 1060, explains that “during 
the Zhenyuan period [785–​805], the duli diviner Li Miqian transmitted it from Western 
India. A certain Qu Gong translated the text 貞元中, 都利術士李彌乾傳自西天竺, 
有璩公者譯其文. The Duli yusi jing is not extant, but Ishida (1950) first identified 
fragments of the text. Yano (2013: 160–​164) proposed that the Duli yusi jing might have 
been a translation of Claudius Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos from the second century ce. Mak 
(2014) convincingly demonstrated, however, that the Duli yusi jing was, in fact, most 
likely based on the work of Dorotheus of Sidon, a first-​century ce Hellenistic astrol­
oger. Kotyk (2018e) further documented some of the specific Hellenistic doctrines that 
are apparent in a variety of Chinese and Japanese sources, which stem from the Duli 
yusi jing.
Several other texts that deal with astral magic were composed during the late Tang, 
many of which were brought to Japan. One of the prominent texts is the Fantian huoluo 
jiuyao 梵天火羅九曜 (*Brahma-​hora-​navagraha), which is attributed to Yixing, who 
died in 727. The Fantian huoluo jiuyao gives mantras for the planets, illustrations, and 
astrological lore. The attribution to Yixing was already questioned by Chavannes and 
Pelliot (1913: 167), who suggested a date of 874 based on data in the colophon of the 
text. Osabe (1963: 256–​261) also questioned the attribution. Mollier (2008: 141), in con­
trast, refers to the Fantian huoluo jiuyao as Yixing’s “outstanding astrological treatise” 
and identifies it as “a synthesis of Chinese and Indian traditions.” Kotyk (2018f: 16–​20) 
argues for the existence of a historical Yixing that must be contrasted to a pseudo-​
Yixing. Various texts, including the Fantian huoluo jiuyao, were attributed to this 
pseudo-​Yixing. In any case, astrologers and clerics in the ninth century utilized this text 
as a means to ward off negative planetary influences, so the attribution was arguably 
only to enhance the prestige of the practice.
The other astral texts attributed to Yixing, all of which were preserved exclusively 
in Japan, include the Xiuyao yigui 宿曜儀軌 (Ritual for the Asterisms), Beidou qixing

--- PAGE 305 ---
280      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
humo fa 北斗七星護摩法 (Homa Ritual for the Seven Stars of the Big Dipper), and 
Qiyao xingchen bie xingfa 七曜星辰別行法 (Special Practices for the Seven Planets 
and Stars). The last one is particularly unique since it illustrates and describes thirty 
spirits which cause diseases on the day of the month assigned to each one. Moreover, 
asterisms are assigned to each of the spirits. The text explains measures to be carried out 
to halt the ill effects of these dangerous spirits. These include, for instance, offerings of 
alcohol and lamps. The names of these spirits in transliterated Chinese are of uncertain 
origin (they are not obvious transcriptions of Sanskrit, Turkish, Persian, or Arabic). The 
illustrations, which are connected to lunar stations, are unlike anything seen elsewhere 
in the earlier extant textual or iconographical record in China. The figures include var­
ious bestial and zoomorphic figures. However, illustrations of jinn, as found in Persian, 
Arabic, and Turkish manuscripts—​such as the Kitāb al-​Bulhān from the fourteenth-​
century example—​are similar to these.6 The figures illustrated in the Chinese text are 
often drawn with nails inserted into them. The text explains this practice as follows:
教人眼見諸鬼形, 於鬼形上下釘手, 明日收禁之. 患人當日差訖. 與出却其釘, 鬼
既得放更不敢到於門焉.
It was taught that if someone sees the figures of spirits with their eyes, they should 
nail the top and bottom of the figure of the spirit, and then the next day bind them. 
The victim will be healed [from the illness caused by the spirit] that day. Having 
removed the nails, the spirit will be released, and they shall not dare come to one’s 
home.
(T 1309, 21: 456c29–​457a2)7
The connections between these spirits and asterisms, as well as the utilization of nails to 
control and banish them, are elements similar to what is found in jinn lore. Omidsalar 
(2000) states that “the jinn are especially afraid of iron, and anyone who manages to 
insert an iron needle in their bodies or clothes, gains control of them because their 
great fear of iron prevents them from pulling the needle out of their persons or attire.” 
Although it is possible that the spirits in the Chinese text are based on jinn lore, their or­
igin remains uncertain.
The Introduction of Buddhist 
Astrology to Japan
The introduction of Buddhist astrology to Japan was preceded in earlier centuries by 
the Chinese system of astronomy (Jpn. tenmon 天文) and the related calendrical sci­
ence (Jpn. koyomi 曆). There appears to have been an earlier autochthonous system of 
timekeeping in preliterate Japan. One Chinese account of Japan from the third cen­
tury explains that the people simply followed a habit of plowing during spring and

--- PAGE 306 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      281
 
harvesting during autumn while remaining ignorant of the seasons as they would have 
been defined in the Chinese system. Tanisaki (2016) theorized that a solar calendar was 
originally used before the adoption of the lunar-​solar Chinese calendar.8 In addition, 
Goto (2021) has surveyed the extensive native star lore of the Japanese archipelago and 
demonstrated that rich skyscapes existed that did not stem from Chinese or Buddhist 
origins. In any case, these indigenous systems did not evidently affect later systems of 
astronomy and calendrical science in Japan in any significant way, which were based 
on the Chinese model (twenty-​eight lunar stations, years comprised of twelve lunar 
months plus intercalary months, etc.) with no reference to an indigenous system, al­
though Japanese names were assigned to the twenty-​eight lunar stations, so there likely 
existed names for some of the constellations associated with the lunar stations before the 
wholesale adoption of the Chinese calendar in Japan. The Wamyō ruiju shō 倭名類聚抄 
(Digest of Classifications of Japanese Words), a Japanese dictionary compiled around 
931–​938 by Minamoto no Shitagō 源順, gives the following definition of the kanji 昴 
(the Pleiades):
宿耀經云昴星六星, 火神也, 音與卯同. 和名須八流.
The Xiuyao jing states that the stars of Mao are comprised of six stars and that it is 
[associated with] the fire god. The pronunciation is the same as mao [Jpn. bō]. The 
Japanese pronunciation is Subaru. (1.3)
Subaru is the Japanese name for the Pleiades, which also is connected to one of the 
Chinese lunar stations. The Japanese appellation Subaru was naturally assigned to it. It 
is additionally noteworthy that the Xiuyao jing had an impact on early Japanese lexicog­
raphy, which demonstrates that the text was read outside Mikkyō circles (i.e., outside 
Shingon and Tendai).
With respect to the introduction of astronomy and calendrical science from the main­
land, the Nihon shoki (vol. 2: 179) records that in the year 602, the monk Gwalleuk (Jpn. 
Kanroku 觀勒) from Kudara (Baekje 百濟) arrived at the Japanese court and presented 
a calendar and works on astronomy. This arguably marks a significant point in history 
from which astronomy and also its associated practices of divination became a known 
part of aristocratic culture in Japan. Later, the Engi shiki 延喜式 (Procedures of the 
Engi Era; 16.4), compiled in 927, describes a vocation titled Tenmon hakushi 天文博士 
(Academician of Astronomy). They were to monitor the heavens for anomalous phe­
nomena. Japan already possessed a grasp of Chinese astronomy during the period when 
Buddhist astrology was introduced.
Buddhist astrology in Japan formally commences with Kūkai 空海 (774–​835), the 
founder of Shingon, when he brought back with him from China a copy of the aforemen­
tioned Xiuyao jing in 806. The text is listed in his inventory of items, which was recorded 
upon returning to Japan (T 2161, 55: 1062a23–​1062a24). We know that Kūkai read and 
understood the Xiuyao jing in detail, in light of an oral explanation of how to approach 
short months (months with twenty-​nine days) and intercalary months in relation to the 
lunar stations assigned to each day of the month. This explanation is preserved in the

--- PAGE 307 ---
282      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
Hino’o kuketsu 檜尾口訣 (T 2465; The Oral Testimony at Hino’o), which was compiled 
by Kūkai’s disciple Jichie 實慧 (786–​847) of Tōji 東寺 (T 2465, 78: 30c13–​30c26).
Not only was the Xiuyao jing necessary for the timing of rituals according to Buddhist 
astrological conventions as laid down by Amoghavajra, but the text also introduced to 
Japan the concept of the seven-​day week. Shingon scholars traditionally credit Kūkai 
with introducing the seven-​day week. The Kōya Daishi go kōden 高野大師御廣傳 
(Extensive Biography of the Kōya Great Master), written by Shōken 聖賢 (1083–​1147) in 
1118, explains that
before the Daidō reign era [806–​810], calendar experts did not know of Sunday. 
This is why there was confusion about astrological auspiciousness and inauspi­
ciousness. People often violated this. After the Great Master [Kūkai] returned to 
court, he transmitted this practice 大同以往, 曆家無知密日, 是故日辰吉凶雜亂, 
人多犯之. 大師歸朝之後, 傳此事.
(Z 8-​2: 661b14–​661b17; Yamashita 1990: 488)
This cultural memory likely reflects the reality that before the advent of Mikkyō, there 
was no compelling reason for Japanese clerics, or the court for that matter, to observe the 
seven-​day week (the civil calendar, in contrast, divides the month into three segments 
called jun 旬, each comprised of ten days). The concept of the week served in religious 
contexts, while the civil calendar based on the Chinese model remained mainstream in 
timekeeping.
Astrology was also important to the early Tendai tradition. Although Saichō 最澄 
(767–​822) does not seem to have taken an interest in the subject, Enchin records the 
Xiuyao jing in his inventory of items from China in the year 857 (T 2172, 55: 1098b8). 
Takada (1992: 40–​56) points out that Enchin wrote some titles related to the Xiuyao 
jing: Sukuyōkyō gishū 宿曜疑集 (Compilation of Concerns on Xiuyao) and Sukuyōkyō 
mondō 宿曜經問答 (Questions and Answers on the Xiuyao jing). Enchin also lectured 
on the Xiuyao jing at the age of thirty.
Astral Magic in Early Heian 
Period (794–​1185)
The inventory of items brought back from China by the Tendai monk Ennin 圓仁 (794–​
864) in 847 includes what appears to be an altar diagram for Tejaprabhā (Shijō dan yō 
熾盛壇樣) (T 2167, 55: 1084c8). Annen 安然 (b. 841) in his Sho ajari shingon mikkyō 
burui sōroku 諸阿闍梨真言密教部類總錄 (Mantrayāna Works of the Ācāryas) records 
that this item was brought by Ennin and lists it under diagrams of mandalas (mandara 
to 曼荼羅圖). The Asaba shō 阿娑縛抄, which is a Tendai compendium of Mikkyō 
practice and lore from the thirteenth century includes what appears to be a copy of this

--- PAGE 308 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      283
 
mandala (reproduced as image plate no. 13, fascicle 58 in Taishō zuzō 大正圖像 edition 
of Asaba shō). The Asaba shō also records that Ennin was responsible for establishing the 
practice of Tejaprabhā in Japan, explaining that in year 2 of Kashō 嘉祥 (849), Ennin—​
named Jikaku Daishi 慈覺大師—​carried out the related rituals at Sōji-​in 總持院 
(TZ vol. 9: 42a6–​42a9). Elsewhere in the Asaba shō we read, “It is said that this prac­
tice is secretly held by the mountain order [Enryaku-​ji]. It is a sacred treasure of the 
state. The [Shijū]chō ketsu states that the Tejaprabhā practice is not cultivated at Tō-​
ji 此法山門之祕揵, 國家之珍重也云々.帖決云熾盛光法東寺不修之云々” (TZ 
vol. 9: 24c3–​24c5). According to this statement, the longer form of the ritual involving 
Tejaprabhā was unavailable to Shingon. See discussion of astral magic in Yamashita 
(1996: 298–​305).
An important manual of astral magic is the Kuyō hiryaku 九曜秘曆 (Secret Calendar 
of the Nine Planets). This text includes both text and illustrations of the planets in both 
anthropomorphic and zoomorphic forms. The illustrations are of particular interest 
and small details can differ in the extant recensions. There is a typeset version with the 
accompanying illustrations in the modern Taishō zuzō (TZ vol. 7: 769–​773). There is also 
a copy by Sōkan 宗觀 (1125) held at the Metropolian Museum of Art, New York (item# 
1975.268.4) (see fig. 12.1). Another is in the ARC Collection, Ritsumeikan University, 
which was copied by Genpō 賢寳 (1333–​1398). Nakano (1969) surveyed a version stored 
at Kanchiin 觀智院 in Kyoto.
The Kuyō hiryaku provides mantras for each of the planets alongside lore regarding 
each of them, which also includes Rāhu and Ketu. The days of the week are discussed, 
as well as the specific activities to carry out or avoid on each one, given that a planet 
with specific characteristics rules over each day (e.g., Venus rules over Friday). Various 
procedures are described for each of the days of the week, in particular wearing 
clothing colored to match the planet presiding over the day. This practice highlights the

importance of the seven-​day week in Mikkyō. The content of the Kuyō hiryaku appears 
to be pieced together from multiple sources, but it is uncertain whether it is a Chinese 
or Japanese composition. Similar content is found in texts from the Tang period. The 
ritual for Saturn in the Kuyō hiryaku is similar to that found in the Qiyao rangzai jue, as 
well as the Daoist Chengxing lingtai miyao jing 秤星靈臺祕要經 (Scripture of the Secret 
Essentials of the Compass Spiritual Terrace). The latter is a fragmentary collection of ap­
otropaic spells to ward off planetary influences. It appears to have been compiled within 
a few decades after 898 (Kalinowski 2004: 337–​338; Kotyk 2021b: 95–​97).
Suffumigations of specific aromatics are utilized in these spells. The longer procedure 
for Saturn in the Kuyō hiryaku calls for burning kokkō 黑香, “black incense” (TZ vol. 7: 
772a28), but the other versions of the ritual give anxi xiang 安息香 (T 1308, 21: 449b2–​
449b12; DZ vol. 5: 30c2–​30c10; Kotyk 2017c: 53–​55). Although anxi 安息 can refer to 
Parthia—​it is a Chinese transcription of Aršak—​in this case it is better understood as 
“the incense which placates.” As to the identification of this aromatic, Laufer (1919: 464–​
465) wrote, “Under the term ṅan (or an)-​si hiaṅ 安西香 the Chinese have combined two 
different aromatics—​an ancient product of Iranian regions, as yet unidentified; and the 
benjoin [tree resin] yielded by the Styrax benjoin, a small tree of the Malay Archipelago.” 
Yamada (1976: 131) later noted the different Sumatran and Thai species. However, the 
resin of the tree Styrax benzoin (commonly called styrax) is indigenous to Southeast 
Asia, not India. When translating Indian sources, anxi xiang refers instead to either 
guggulu or bdellium, which are types of aromatic resins (Kotyk 2020b). As to whether 
styrax or bdellium was available in Japan, the use of imported incense in this context 
would have posed a problem in Japan, since it is uncertain how much of these aromatics 
would have been available. The Hishō mondō 祕鈔問答 (Questions and Answers on the 
Secret Digest) by Raiyu 賴瑜 (1226–​1304), for instance, states that anxi-​xiang is kurara 
久良羅 (T 2536, 79: 468a17–​468a19), which is Sophora flavescens or Sophora angustifolia, 
the shrubby sophora, in modern taxonomy.9 Kurara is unrelated to guggulu and Styrax 
benzoin, but it is a plant native to Japan. It seems likely, therefore, that substitutes were 
used, since the originally prescribed aromatics were largely unavailable in Japan. The 
use of substituted items in Japanese rituals can also be observed in other contexts.10
Another major astral deity in Japan was Myōken Bosatsu 妙見菩薩 (Skt. Sudṛṣṭi 
Bodhisattva), who personifies Polaris, the North Star. Sørensen (2011: 127) remarks:
Although this important astral god would appear to have an Indian identity, he exists 
in a variety of forms, some of which were evidently created in Heian Japan after the 
ninth century. The presence of Sudṛsṭi in China can be documented as far back as 
the middle of the Nanbeizhao, but no icons from this early period have yet been 
identified.
Myōken was more popular in Japan than in China, although Ennin in his travelogue 
to China, Nittō guhō junrei kōki 入唐求法巡禮行記 (Record of Travel to the Tang in 
Search of the Dharma) does record witnessing the painting of this deity in China (B18, 
no. 95: 18a5–​18a6). Aruga (2000) wrote a reliable and detailed study on Myōken.

Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      285
 
Horoscopy and Astral Magic 
in Japan: Sukuyōdō
Genji monogatari 源氏物語 (Tale of Genji), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部 (c. 973–​
c. 1014), is an early witness to the tradition of Sukuyō 宿曜 as an identifiable community. 
They make predictions in chapters one and fourteen (vol. 1: 45; vol. 2: 106). The full name 
for this tradition is Sukuyōdō 宿曜道 (Way of Lunar Stations and Planets), which was 
comprised of astrologer-​monks from various sects. Murasaki conceivably had some con­
tact with these individuals during her life, which would have been an early stage in the 
history of Sukuyōdō. Momo (1969: 410) points out that the Nichū reki 二中歴 from the 
Kamakura period (unknown authorship) lists Hōzō 法藏 (905–​969) as the first Sukuyōshi 
宿曜師 (Sukuyō Master). It is important to note that neither Kūkai nor Enchin is included 
in this list, even though they were the early users of the Xiuyao jing (Jpn. Sukuyō kyō) in 
Japan. Sukuyōdō ought to be treated as separate from Shingon and Taimitsu, since it fell 
under neither sect. In light of this point, it is also a question whether Sukuyōdō would 
fall under Mikkyō. The lines of succession in Sukuyōdō were separate from Mikkyō 
(Kanechiku 1999). There is no consensus on whether Sukuyōdō falls under Mikkyō. There 
is, in reality, comparatively limited modern scholarship on Sukuyōdō, since it has often 
been discussed in its role as a counterpart to the better documented Onmyōdō 陰陽道 
(Way of Yin and Yang), or as a minor element in Genji monogatari and other novels.11
Sukuyōdō was primarily comprised of three aspects: the study of astronomy and 
calendrical science, casting of horoscopes, and practice of astral magic. There was no 
single or uniform calendar for calculating the positions of the planets. The Chinese 
state designed and implemented calendrical reforms, which usually included an adop­
tion of a new calendar altogether. Yixing, for example, compiled the Dayan li 大衍曆, 
which was in use between 729 and 761 in China. This same calendar was used in Japan 
between 764 and 862. There were, however, unofficial or popular calendars produced. 
One of these was the Futian li 符天暦 (Calendar which Tallies with Heaven) by Cao 
Shiwei 曹士蒍 (d.u.). The Xin Wudai shi 新五代史 (58.670), a history of the five post-​
Tang regimes compiled in 1053, records that during the Jianzhong 建中 (780–​783) era, 
Cao Shiwei compiled the Futian li, but that it only circulated among commoners. Cao 
Shiwei sometime thereafter created new material to accommodate Rāhu and Ketu (the 
ascending node of the Moon and, in this context specifically, the lunar apogee both 
treated as pseudo-​planets, although Ketu is normally the descending node of the moon). 
The reason for this was most likely an interest in astrology (Momo 1975: 14–​15; Kotyk 
2017c: 42–​43). Although the Futian li is not extant, Takesako (2016) has reconstructed 
its parameters based on available data from other sources. Also, the ephemerides in 
the Qiyao rangzai jue appear to be derived from the Futian li, based on their epochs 
(Yabuuchi 1982: 5–​6; Kotyk 2017c: 42–​43).
The Futian li is significant to Sukuyōdō because this was primarily the calendar which 
they employed, as already emphasized by Momo (1975: 17). The Futian li appears in

--- PAGE 311 ---
286      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
the Nihonkoku genzai sho mokuroku 日本國見在書目錄, titled Tō shichiyō futenreki 
唐七曜符天曆 (National Diet Library ed., 33). This bibliography of texts available in 
Japan was compiled by Fujiwara Sukeyo 藤原佐世 (847–​898) in c.891. The Futian li was 
therefore available in Japan sometime before 891, although it is uncertain who brought 
this edition and when (Momo 1969: 397). The first known Japanese expert to work with 
the Futian li was the monk Nichi’en 日延 (fl. 953–​957) of Tendai. Nichi’en left for China 
in 953, where he arrived in Wuyue 吳越 and studied the Futian li. He then brought 
this back in 957. He was also responsible for transporting Tiantai texts from Japan that 
had earlier been lost in China.12 His trip is documented in a text Daizaifu jinja bunsho 
大宰府神社文書, which was identified by Takeuchi Rizō 竹内理三 (1907–​1997) in 1954 
at Dazaifu Jinja 大宰府神社 in Kyushu (Takeuchi 1955; Momo 1969).
The aforementioned texts dealing with astrology and calendrical science were nec­
essary for the casting of horoscopes. Sukuyōdō was the exclusive lineage in Japan to 
offer this service. As Momo and Yamashita have explored, the primary sources used in 
horoscopy in Japan included the aforementioned Qiyao rangzai jue and Duli yusi jing. 
The Xiuyao jing was consulted, but since it does not discuss the casting of horoscopes, it 
does not appear to have been the main work used in Sukuyōdō. It is often assumed that 
Sukuyōdō must have been based chiefly on the Xiuyao jing (Sukuyō-​kyō in Japanese).
Shūei brought back to Japan with him copies of the Qiyao rangzai jue and Duli yusi 
jing, as well as ephemerides. Shūei lists these as “miscellaneous books” (zōjo 雜書) and 
comments, “Although they are not Dharma practices, they are held as important by 
the worldly 雖非法門世者所要也” (T 2174A, 55: 1111b20–​1111c1) (Yano 2013: 160). He 
expresses a clear awareness that these texts were not designed for awakening or specif­
ically Buddhist practice, but nevertheless their utility was recognized. Shūei was not a 
known expert in astrology. Sukuyōdō and the casting of horoscopes appears later on 
in Japanese history. Toda (2007: 46) observes that the early references to Sukuyōshi 
and Sukuyōdō in the private journals of aristocrats date to around the early to mid-​
eleventh century. Yamashita (1990: 508) notes that Sukuyōshi, mainly from Kōfukuji 
興福寺, became particularly active among the aristocracy starting from the late tenth 
century.
There are only two extant horoscopes with accompanying commentary from me­
dieval Japan, which were produced for clients born in the years 1113 and 1268, respec­
tively. These documents are titled Sukuyō unmei kanroku 宿曜運命勘錄 and Sukuyō 
go-​unroku 宿曜御運錄. Momo (1990: 131–​151) reproduced these in his volume on ca­
lendrical science but earlier had published a study on them (Momo 1975). The Sukuyō 
unmei kanroku was reproduced in the Zoku gunshoruijū 續群書類從 of the twentieth 
century, but it is beset with typographical errors and Momo’s critical edition is preferred. 
Yano (2013: 188–​197) and Kotyk (2018d: 59–​70) also discuss these horoscopes in detail 
and point out the astrological doctrines which were originally Hellenistic in origin. 
The scientific value of the 1113 horoscope was pointed out by Nakayama (1969: 60). The 
Japanese horoscopes can be further compared to a horoscope from Dunhuang (P. 4071) 
to better grasp how horoscopy was employed in East Asia. The main difference between 
Japanese and Chinese forms of horoscopy from this general period is that the Japanese

--- PAGE 312 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      287
 
used nine planets (the seven visible planets, Rāhu and Ketu), while the Chinese used 
eleven: the aforementioned nine plus Ziqi 紫氣 and Yuebei 月孛.13 These two, like Rāhu 
and Ketu, are immaterial “planets” used for astrological purposes. Ziqi tracks interca­
lary months while Yuebei is the lunar apogee (Kotyk 2018d: 71–​79).
These three extant horoscopes all discuss birth charts with an interest in predicting the 
future of the client in question. Various astrological doctrines are employed toward this 
end. However, the Japanese practice of horoscopy was not limited to prognostication. 
The horoscope of 1113 lists off the asterisms presiding over the chart in various capacities 
and then states, “Prayers and offerings should be constantly made 常可令祈供” (Momo 
1990: 134). This reveals that astrology was connected to a belief in sentient astral deities 
but also that fate could be negotiated through ritual means. Astral magic was clearly 
utilized alongside horoscopy.
Yamashita (1990: 488) observes that the Mikkyō interest in calendrical science 
around the mid-​tenth century stemmed from a move toward stellar worship. Yamashita 
(1996: 307–​308) also argues that increasing engagement in star worship was a response 
to the failing Ritsuryō 律令 (i.e., statist legal) system. This, in turn, led to uncertainties 
for both the ruling aristocracy and the Tennō (Emperor). There was another important 
catalyst which helps explain the development of Sukuyōdō. As Yiengpruksawan (2015) 
has pointed out, the Japanese (and the rest of the world) on May 1, 1006 witnessed one 
of the largest supernovae in history (SN 1006). This subsequently facilitated major cul­
tural and sociopolitical changes. It was within such circumstances that professional 
astrologers would have been especially important, especially if they could offer ritual 
services. Sukuyōdō was active throughout the Kamakura period (1185–​1333). Toda 
(2006, 2007, 2008) and Akazawa (2007) have explored Sukuyōdō and its evolution in 
this period. Sukuyōdō and the associated practice of horoscopy ceased to exist in Japan 
toward the late fourteenth to early fifteenth centuries, which is explained by the demise 
of their patrons (Yamashita 1996: 319–​368).
Astral Iconography
The production of illustrated icons of planets and asterisms were an element of star wor­
ship in Japan. One prominent example is a painting of Saturn (Doyō 土曜) as a single 
deity, held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Saturn is depicted as 
an old bearded Brahmin in sandals and a few layers of robes with a bull’s head for a 
cap (see fig. 12.2). This object dates to the twelfth century. Saturn holds a crook, the top 
part of which resembles a sickle, not unlike traditional depictions of Kronos in Greco-​
Roman antiquity. He holds a text in the other hand. This icon appears to be based on a 
set of Chinese drawings of the planets in anthropomorphic forms, which were devel­
oped based on earlier models. The document Kuyōtō zuzō 九曜等圖像, “Icons of the 
Nine Planets, etc.” held at Tōji (reproduced in TZ vol. 7: 737–​747) includes these figures. 
Saturn and the other planets are similarly depicted in Tangut Xixia representations from

--- PAGE 313 ---
288      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
Khara-​Khoto held in the State Hermitage Museum of St. Petersburg (for a survey, see 
Samosyuk 1997/​1998).
Another form of star worship, which was uniquely developed in Japan, was star 
mandalas (hoshi mandara 星曼荼羅), in which the planets, lunar stations, zodiac signs, 
seven stars of the North Dipper (hokuto 北斗), and/​or thirty-​six beasts (sanjūroku kin 
三十六禽) are depicted. These mandalas were either rectangular or circular in form. 
Aruga (2000: 32) notes that the rectangular originate in Tōmitsu (Shingon) between 947 
and 957, while the circular stem from Tendai between the late tenth and early eleventh

centuries. The foremost study on these is a monograph written by Takeda (1995). Ujiro 
(2012) discusses this form of mandala with particular reference to the examples of the 
Big Dipper. The Metropolitan Museum of Art possesses a circular star mandala (2020: 
391), which was studied by Kotyk (2019c) who argues that based on the irregular config­
uration of planets relative to the zodiac signs that this reflects a horoscope which would 
date to around October 3, 1225, but not all specimens reflect this type of configuration 
and instead simply represent the totality of asterisms (see fig. 12.3 for an example of the 
latter). This would presumably be the time of birth for the patron who commissioned 
the piece. The reason for this configuration was likely to facilitate rituals on behalf of 
the client. Kotyk furthermore points out that the lunar stations depicted therein are the 
Vedic deities (Śiva, Viṣṇu, etc.) traditionally associated with the nakṣatras.
The various astral figures became part of the core of Buddhist iconography in Japan. 
The Butsuzō zui 佛像圖彙 (Collected Buddhist Icons) by Tosa Hidenobu 土佐秀信, 
which was printed in 1690, includes all the asterisms, but caution must be exercised since 
the depictions of the lunar stations ought to be compared to those of the Goma rodan yō 
(Chn. Humo lutan yang 護摩爐壇樣; Fire Altar Specifications for the Homa). This text 
was brought to Japan by the monk Jōgyō 常曉 (d. 867) in 839. It contains a diverse array 
of information including astrological lore (Kotyk 2018e: 14–​16). The illustrations of the 
lunar stations and planets are also important iconographical examples of astral deities, 
with the former being based on Vedic deities (Aruga 2000: 50; Kotyk 2019c).
Later Developments
Although a robust and sizable practice of horoscopy with large texts continued to 
exist in China, none of the works from the Yuan and Ming periods seem to have been 
brought to Japan until the early modern period. Nevertheless, Sinological studies 
can gain much from comparing Chinese and Japanese materials, especially since the 
Japanese faithfully preserved much material—​textual and iconographical—​that was 
otherwise lost in China.14
In modern Japan, there is a popular tradition of astrology called Sukuyō, which is 
based largely on the Xiuyao jing. Following the printed editions of the Xiuyao jing by 
Wakita Bunshō (1897) and Wakahara Yukitsune (1908), there were published various 
explanatory manuals that often also touch on other divinatory practices. For example, 
Wakita Aiyama 脇田愛山 (1915) published Nijū-​hachi shuku kikkyō hōkan: katei 
nichiyō 廿八宿吉凶寳鑑: 家庭日用 (Precious Mirror on the Fortunes of the Twenty-​
Eight Lunar Stations: Daily Household Use). The postwar popular tradition of Sukuyō 
seems to have especially flourished after Komine Yumiko 小峰有美子 published in 
1982 a manual titled Sukuyō kyō nijūshichi suku senseihō 宿曜經二十七宿占星法 
(Divination Techniques for the Twenty-​Seven Lunar Stations of the Xiuyao jing). This 
was followed by a number of other books on the topic by different authors. These were 
published for popular consumption. These authors often trace their art back to Kūkai

--- PAGE 315 ---

and identify with Sukuyōdō, but their practice does not appear to be endorsed by 
Mikkyō lineages. There are no anthropological studies that document modern Sukuyō, 
although it is a noteworthy movement. Sukuyō has also grown on the internet where it 
has a significant presence.
Conclusion
The survey in this chapter has shown the significance of astronomy, astrology, calen­
drical science, and astral magic in the history of premodern Japanese Buddhism, in 
particular Mikkyō, which comes under the umbrella of “Tantric Buddhism” in schol­
arly discourse. Buddhists in India from early on incorporated into their practice some 
amount of native astral lore, which at the time was based on the nakṣatras. Later, as 
Indian astronomy was influenced by Hellenistic sources, Buddhists also adopted the 
zodiac signs and planets, both of which are unattested in early Buddhist literature. 
Following the advent of practices based on mantras or dhāraṇīs, Buddhists in India, 
perhaps following a wider trend, also came to view astrology as an essential component 
in the timing of their rituals.
Astrological lore originating from Indian sources was translated into Chinese in 
various stages from at least the fourth century ce, but it was only with Amoghavajra’s 
Xiuyao jing that the Chinese Buddhist world had access to an authoritative manual 
in Chinese that could be used for timing Buddhist rituals. Unlike earlier models of 
Buddhist practice, the new “tantric model” expressly required observance of astrology 
to determine when it was optimal to carry out the pūjas necessary for rapid awakening. 
The Xiuyao jing, in turn, spurred wider interest in other forms of astrology, especially 
horoscopy, and from this the gates opened to non-​Indian systems. Horoscopy inevi­
tably predicts calamities in a person’s life; hence there was clearly a contemporary in­
terest in any sort of ritual or magical means with which one could avert the disasters 
brought about by the planets.
Japanese monks in the ninth century who sought training in esoteric practices 
brought back with them texts such as the Xiuyao jing, but also other materials related 
to ritual practices directed at asterisms. The Sinicized systems of foreign astrology were 
transmitted to Japan and thereafter implemented relatively quickly, starting from at 
least the time of Kūkai in 806 when he returned to Japan. Astrology in this context also 
included the seven-​day week.
The texts and illustrations related to astrology became foundational for later Japanese 
developments, such as star mandalas, which were used in acts of worship, and extended 
rituals for astral deities, such as Tejaprabhā. The planets as members of the Buddhist 
pantheon also came to have a prominent role in Japan in large part due to astrology. 
In the late tenth century, we see the emergence in Japan of Sukuyōdō, a unique com­
munity of astrologer-​monks, who not only cast horoscopes for their clients but also 
offered guidance on the ritual means with which one could negotiate prognosticated

--- PAGE 317 ---
292      Jeffrey Kotyk
 
fate. Astrology, practiced in both Sukuyōdō and Mikkyō, became a prominent art 
throughout the Heian and Kamakura periods. These developments during the medieval 
period are still relevant today in Japan, although research is required regarding how, for 
example, astral deities are worshipped in modern Mikkyō, and how astrology is treated 
in practice in Shingon and Tendai today.

Notes
	1.	 The Kaiyuan Shijiao lu 開元釋教錄 (Bibliography of Buddhism in the Kaiyuan Era) of 730 
records that in Huanglong 2 (黃龍二年), Lü Yan translated four texts, which included the 
Mātaṅga-​sūtra, in the city of Yangdu 楊都 (T 2154, 55: 487c21–​487c22).
	2.	 For a study on the identification and uses of dairy products in East Asian Buddhism, see 
Kotyk 2021d.
	3.	 For a comprehensive survey of Buddhist cosmology, see Sadakata 1997. For a discussion of 
the celestial deities in relation to flat-​earth cosmology in Buddhism, see Kotyk 2021a. For 
further discussion of Chinese Buddhism and astronomy, see Kotyk 2020a.
	4.	 See E-​Museum Japan, accessed June 30, 2021. http://​emus​eum.nich.go.jp/​det​ail?lan​gId=​
ja&webV​iew=​&cont​ent_​base​_​id=​100​034&cont​ent_​part​_​id=​0&cont​ent_​pict​_​id=​0.
	5.	 See also comparable icons in Taizō kuzuyō 胎藏舊圖樣 (TZ vol. 2: 477–​566).
	6.	 Bodleian Library MS. Bodl. Or. 133. University of Oxford.
	7.	 Read shou 手 as zhi 之.
	8.	 This theory might explain the discrepancies between some regnal years in the Kojiki 古事記 
(compiled in 712) and Nihon shoki. Tanisaki argues that the compilers of these two histories 
likely struggled with converting over the earlier calendrical dates into a new model, fol­
lowing the introduction of foreign calendrical models, particularly starting from the Asuka 
Period (592–​710). This was a time when the Japanese court moved increasingly toward a 
Sinicized form of centralized government.
	9.	 See numerous encyclopedias available on https://​kotob​ank.jp/​.

--- PAGE 318 ---
Astrology and Astral Magic in Tantric Japan      293
 
	10.	 Dairy products were available in Japan from the seventh century but appear to have 
vanished around the late Heian period. Buddhist rituals can call for the use of butter, milk, 
yogurt, and ghee, for which substitutes were used when dairy was unavailable. See Kotyk 
(2021d: 6).
	11.	 Momo (1964), Yamashita (1988), Kanechiku (1999), Toda (2006), Ujiro (2012), and 
Akazawa (2007) have specifically written on the history of Sukuyōdō in Japanese. Kotyk 
(2018d) was the first comprehensive study of Sukuyōdō in English. These studies ad­
dress the lineage development, practice of astrology, and rituals carried out by Sukuyōshi. 
Sukuyōdō has been mischaracterized in the past. Drakakis (2011, 684), for instance, claims 
that “Sukuyōdō intermingled with the already existing forms of Chinese astrology based 
on yin-​yang and five-​agents doctrines, but also with Daoist thought and practices. It is in 
this form that this complex of doctrines and practices was transmitted to Japan, where 
it was further developed.” A survey of the extant literature of Sukuyōdō would demon­
strate that there is little in the way of Chinese metaphysics or patently Daoist elements in 
their texts.
	12.	 For discussion of these Tiantai texts, see Momo (1968), Brose (2006: 53–​56), and Kotyk 
(2020c: 374–​375).
	13.	 For discussion of the Dunhuang horoscope, see studies by Jao (1984), Niu (2016), Isahaya 
and Lin (2017), and Kotyk (2018e: 79–​81).
	14.	 Horoscopy in China evolved, but to a large extent remained rooted in the doctrines that 
were introduced during the Tang period, many of which were also carried over to Japan. 
Reconstructing the horoscopy of the Tang period requires reference to both Japanese and 
later Ming sources. At the same time, grasping the doctrines employed in Japan requires 
reference to the extant Chinese sources in detail. For a survey of the history of horoscopy 
and its doctrines in Classical Chinese, see Kotyk 2018e. For an overview of astrology in the 
Ming period with a comparison to European, particularly English, horoscopy, see Kotyk 
2019a. For a survey of medical astrology in Classical Chinese, see Kotyk 2019b.
