Chapter 14
Śrīvidyā and Goddess 
Traditions
A Critical Historiographic Essay
Anna A. Golovkova
Śrīvidyā as the Object of Study
Śrīvidyā is a tantric (esoteric) initiatory1 ritual system of worship, centered on 
Tripurasundarī, who is seen as the supreme goddess granting the tantric practitioner 
both liberation and enjoyment in this lifetime. The worship of Tripurasundarī has 
been practiced in South Asia since the beginning of the second millennium CE at the 
latest and remains a vibrant tradition today in the Indian subcontinent and the dias­
pora. As the worship of local goddesses has become subsumed under the authority 
of Smārta2 brahmins, Tripurasundarī came to be seen as the esoteric essence of many 
local goddesses (see Golovkova 2012, 817). Śrīvidyā worship has been adopted by the 
Śaṅkarācāryas, leaders of major monastic and teaching institutions (māṭhas), which be­
came the nuclei of mainstream Hinduism. With the strong ties of Śaṅkara māṭhas and 
Śrīvidyā gurus with royal power and relationships of mutual legitimation between reli­
gious leaders and local rulers,3 it is not incidental that Tripurasundarī came to be referred 
to as Rājarājeśvarī (the Supreme Empress; literally the “Ruler of the King of Kings” or the 
“Empress of Emperors”). Furthermore, a widespread popular devotional worship of this 
goddess has emerged based on Purāṇic sources, in which she is often referred to as Lalitā 
(the Playful One). Devotional (bhakti) practice has become well established through 
chanting hymns to this goddess, particularly the Lalitāsahasranāma (One Thousand 
Names of the Goddess Lalitā), the Saundaryalaharī (the Wave of Beauty), and also the 
Khaḍga Mālā (the Garland of Swords)4 both within and outside initiation lineages.
While the worship of Tripurasundarī has been influential for the making of south 
Indian Smārta brahmanism, utilized for royal initiations, and practiced by initiated 
courtiers and literati and has given rise to a significant devotional movement, Śrīvidyā

--- PAGE 349 ---
324      Anna A. Golovkova
 
remains understudied, and the work that was accomplished in the previous century is 
due to be updated. This chapter outlines some of the major advances in textual schol­
arship on Śrīvidyā in the English language within the context of Hindu tantrism and 
goddess-​oriented traditions, beginning with the first introduction of English-​language 
audiences to Śrīvidyā by Sir John Woodroffe (also known as: Arthur Avalon). Woodroffe 
established Śrīvidyā as a sophisticated philosophical and literary tantric tradition 
worthy of Western scholarship, but he also solidified a pattern of tantric apologetics in 
scholarship, presenting a “deodorized” view of Śrīvidyā, which skewed toward the por­
trayal of the elite “high tantra” aspects of this tradition (to use the terms Hugh Urban 
and David Gordon White applied to tantra, respectively) (Urban 2003, 134–​164; White 
1998, 173–​174). The study of the Mahāvidyās is examined next, particularly the work 
of David Kinsley in popularizing scholarship on Hindu goddesses and highlighting 
advances in understanding of Ṣoḍaśī/​Tripurabhairavī within this subfield. The rele­
vant work on the Mahāvidyās accomplished since the publication of Kinsley’s Tantric 
Visions of the Divine Feminine is analyzed next, including Madhu Khanna’s philological 
work on the Śāktapramoda, while also calling attention to areas in need of future study. 
This is followed by examining major advances in textual scholarship on Tantric Śrīvidyā 
by André Padoux and Douglas Brooks, and outlining aspects that require revision and 
updating. In particular, gaps of knowledge need to be filled by studying texts that have 
not previously attracted scholarly attention (such as manuscript sources and texts of 
lesser literary quality that are important for their historical value), and by rereading 
texts that have been studied against the grain, in order to gain a better understanding 
of this tradition as dynamic, changeable, and far from monolithic. Following Alexis 
Sanderson’s seminal “The Śaiva Age” (2009), digitization and other advances made in 
twenty-​first-​century scholarship are examined. Particular attention is given here to 
Elaine Fisher’s consideration of public esotericism in sixteenth-​century south Indian 
Śrīvidyā. Directions for further study and suggestions for the best approaches to study 
Śrīvidyā as a diverse “text tradition”5 with at least ten centuries of history and a unique 
sectarian identity, reflecting on the shift away from Kaula practices to the establish­
ment of the Vedas as a valid source of knowledge, form the conclusion. Although this 
chapter’s primary focus is on textual historical studies, the conclusion of this chapter 
briefly highlights a body of ethnographic scholarship, as well as directions for further 
study through the anthropological lens.
Śrīvidyā, Tradition of the 
Auspicious Mantra, which Worships 
Tripurasundarī
Let us first define what exactly is meant by the term Śrīvidyā, before discussing the 
scholarship and relevant questions for understanding the making of Śrīvidyā as a

--- PAGE 350 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      325
 
Śākta Śaiva tradition. Although previously translated as “Auspicious Wisdom” (Brooks 
1992), “Tradition of the Auspicious Mantra” more accurately reflects the usage and sig­
nificance of the word vidyā in the term Śrīvidyā (Golovkova 2019, 120 n. 1).6 The term 
Śrīvidyā refers to both the tradition and the mantra of this tradition. Although vidyā 
most broadly refers to knowledge in classical Sanskrit, in tantric context it is used as 
a technical term for the mantra of a feminine deity (i.e., the esoteric knowledge of this 
deity).7 The first usage of the term “Śrīvidyā” that I have been able to track occurs in 
the context of the principal mantra in the Saubhāgyasudhodaya (a paddhati, i.e., ritual 
manual) and the Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā (a commentary on the Yoginīhṛdaya tantra), both 
by Amṛtānanda, a south Indian commentator from approximately the fourteenth cen­
tury (see Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava [1988] 2011 and Yoginīhṛdaya, 1988). Furthermore, the 
pride that the Śrīvidyā upāsakas (worshippers)8 take in the complex ritual and mantra 
system of this tradition and the unique form of the mantra, long and nonliteral, support 
a translation that highlights the mantra, i.e., the esoteric knowledge, of Tripurasundarī, 
rather than the generic meaning of “knowledge” for the translation of the word “vidyā.”
With regard to the first part of the compound, “Śrī,” Goudriaan and others have taken 
it to refer to Lakṣmī (Goudriaan 1981, 58). Although Lakṣmī is referred to as “Śrī,” there 
are few similarities and many distinctions between these goddesses, including their di­
vergent qualities, mantras, yantras, association with different consorts, colors, weapons/​
mudrās, and seats. While Tripurasundarī is associated with loveliness and auspicious­
ness, Lakṣmī symbolizes prosperity. Furthermore, their mantras and yantras are distinct, 
as are their consorts (Śiva and Viṣṇu, respectively, although there is also an historical 
association of Tripurasundarī with Kāmadeva, the god of love) (see Golovkova 2020). 
Tripurā is invariably clothed in red, while Lakṣmī usually wears shades of pink, yellow, 
or gold, although sometimes she is depicted in red garments. Tripurasundarī holds the 
goad, noose, bow, and arrows, the weapons of the god of love,9 whereas Lakṣmī’s ico­
nography is less stable. She is depicted holding one or two lotuses, sometimes a pot of 
gold or gold coins, streaming from her hands, a conch, discus or mace, or a combina­
tion of these weapons, associated with Viṣṇu. Lakṣmī’s hands may be forming mudrās 
(ritual gestures, literally “seals”), such as abhaya (dispelling fear), varada (conferring 
boons), or, sometimes, jñāna mudrā (of wisdom). Lakṣmī usually sits on a lotus, while 
Tripurā reposes on the prostrate form of Sadāśiva, which usually rests on the throne 
held up by Brahma, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara. Thus, both the ritual worship of these 
goddesses and their iconography strongly point to significant differences, which makes 
any similarities incidental. Most importantly, Lakṣmī is not the main focus of wor­
ship in Śrīvidyā, although she may be highlighted in a special pūjā (ritual worship) or 
homa (ritual performed with fire) for prosperity. Therefore, following Brooks’s correct 
understanding of “śrī” as an honorific, but reading “vidyā” as mantra, we can translate 
Śrīvidyā, when it refers to the tradition, rather than the mantra itself, as “Tradition of the 
Auspicious Mantra.”
The issues outlined above speak to the need for more depth of scholarship on Śrīvidyā 
and goddess traditions and the curiosity and attention to detail necessary for contem­
porary scholars to question established authorities. With all respect to the giants of

--- PAGE 351 ---
326      Anna A. Golovkova
 
the previous century, no one is immune to inaccuracies or mistakes, and it is only by 
revisiting and revising established information and filling existing gaps that we can fur­
ther the study of this tradition. Moreover, although some important scholarship has 
been accomplished, Orientalist biases have skewed our understanding of Śrīvidyā to its 
more philosophical and high-​brow registers and away from the complexity of its rituals 
and the reading of other types of texts that have not been considered worthy of study. To 
understand Śrīvidyā in its multifaceted complexity, we need more focused scholarly at­
tention and better cross-​pollination of ideas that will result in a more accurate and com­
prehensive body of knowledge.
Orientalism in the Study of Śrīvidyā 
and Tantric Apologetics
Our brief survey of existing scholarship on Śrīvidyā begins with the work of Sir John 
Woodroffe (a.k.a. Arthur Avalon), who was the first to bring Śrīvidyā to the attention 
of the English-​speaking audience. This allows us to examine an important trend for the 
study of this tradition—​that is, an emphasis on philosophical, highly literary texts that 
generally conform to the higher standards of grammar. That emphasis minimizes the 
importance of its ritual practice, particularly those aspects that may take away from the 
image of Śrīvidyā as a sophisticated elite tradition.
The academic study of Śrīvidyā within the context of the broader study of religion 
and Hinduism is a relatively recent phenomenon. The earliest translations of Śrīvidyā 
texts into English were published by Woodroffe at the beginning of the twentieth cen­
tury. Kathleen Taylor (2001) convincingly argues that Arthur Avalon was a kind of “legal 
fiction” behind a close collaboration of two friends and, likely, fellow disciples of a tan­
tric guru: Sir John Woodroffe, an Englishman and a Calcutta High Court judge, and 
Atal Behari Ghose, a Sanskrit paṇḍit and Bengali intellectual. Woodroffe, who began 
lecturing just two years after the publication of the first work under the pseudonym, 
lends the respectability of the British judge to the enterprise of rehabilitating tantra in 
the minds of Western Orientalist scholars and of the Bengali English-​educated public. 
Behari Ghose, on the other hand, provided Sanskrit expertise and deep intertextual 
knowledge that imbued the work published under Arthur Avalon’s moniker (and, sub­
sequently, under Woodroffe’s own name). Woodroffe acknowledged the anonymous 
contribution of Behari Ghose, at least to the work published under the name of Avalon, 
in the preface to Shakti and Shākta, explaining that he used the nom de plume for works 
that were written in collaboration with others, particularly with the help of a friend who 
Woodroffe claimed had insisted on remaining unnamed.10
Woodroffe’s position vis-​à-​vis his material is a fascinating blend of passionate and, 
likely, personal interest combined with the outward demeanor of scholarly detach­
ment.11 This is not surprising, given the harshly critical attitudes, mired in racism

--- PAGE 352 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      327
 
and cultural and religious superiority, toward tantra and Śāktism commonly held by 
early European scholars. Orientalists, who were often colonial officials and Christian 
missionaries who brought to the scholarship their own agendas and biases, overwhelm­
ingly preferred texts that were monistic rather than polytheistic and philosophical rather 
than those emphasizing ritual instruction. It is no wonder then that Arthur Avalon’s 
debut consisted of a translation of Mahānirvāṇa Tantra (1913), a text that eschewed the 
worship of the goddess for that of the parābrahman (the supreme brahman or Self) and 
privileged liberation as the goal of tantric practice. And this Western attitude toward 
texts and traditions, thoroughly assimilated by educated South Asians, has contributed 
to the elevated place Śrīvidyā has come to occupy among tantric traditions. (See Hayes 
chapter on Esoteric Physiology, this volume, on Woodroffe’s influence on the subtle 
body concepts of the six cakras.)
To represent Śrīvidyā as an exemplary tantric tradition, both scholars and 
practitioners overemphasized the importance of its philosophical nondualism and of its 
meditation practices. In addition, they minimized other aspects, both ignoring texts that 
are not particularly philosophical or literary and underemphasizing the ritual aspects of 
the tradition (e.g., the use of rituals for mundane results [prayogas]). To better under­
stand the creative process of the development of this tradition and the canonization of 
narratives about its nature and history, we must engage in careful historicized reading of 
those texts that have so far escaped scholarly attention and also study practices that have 
remained unexamined.12 Furthermore, when we do return to texts that have already re­
ceived some scholarly attention, we must examine the complicated network of agendas 
and biases that has been brought to this endeavor not only by previous and contempo­
rary scholars, but also by the authors, redactors, and commentators of the Sanskrit texts 
themselves.
Woodroffe’s first foray into Śrīvidyā was publishing the translation of Puṇyānanda’s 
hymn Kāmakalāvilāsa with the commentary by Naṭanānandanātha in 1922.13 
Kāmakalāvilāsa (ca. fourteenth century) is a poetic hymn to Tripurasundarī as the 
supreme Śakti, manifesting in the śrīcakra (the principal ritual diagram of Śrīvidyā). 
From Tripurasundarī’s union with Śiva in the innermost bindu (dot) in the center of the 
śrīcakra springs all creation, language, and cognition. Puṇyānanda’s south Indian initia­
tory branch (hādimata)14, whose principal vidyā (mantra of feminine deity) began with 
the phoneme hā, included Śivānanda and Vidyānanda, authors of commentaries on the 
Vāmakeśvarīmata, the earliest extant tantra from within the tradition, and Amṛtānanda, 
Puṇyānanda’s disciple, who frequently quoted Kāmakalāvilāsa in his commentary on 
the Yoginīhṛdaya (see Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava [1988] 2011 and Yoginīhṛdaya, 1988). Like the 
Yoginīhṛdaya and the commentaries of these south Indian authors, Kāmakalāvilāsa 
encodes the manifestation of the goddess and her retinue within the nine levels of the 
Śrīcakra with the philosophical nondualism of Pratyabhijñā.15 The choice of this text 
is not surprising for introducing early nineteenth-​century English-​language readers 
to Śrīvidyā, as it is poetic, metaphysical, and short, consisting of fifty-​five stanzas. 
Kāmakalāvilāsa extols Śrīvidyā mantra and yantra, describing the nature of the god­
dess as consciousness and speech. While the hymn mentions the structures of the

--- PAGE 353 ---
328      Anna A. Golovkova
 
Śrīcakra ritual, its emphasis is on soteriological and nonmundane benefits of worship. 
Particularly in Avalon’s translation, which leaves a lot untranslated and unexplained, 
Amṛtānanda’s language sounds mysterious and otherworldly. Again, this is under­
standable in a translation that seeks to rehabilitate tantra and present it in a way that 
is comprehensible and acceptable for Western readers and Western-​educated South 
Asians. Describing Śrīvidyā by emphasizing the otherworldly, metaphysical, and phil­
osophical aspects of the tradition remained prevalent in the twentieth century. Other 
important features of this earlier scholarship include deemphasizing transgressive 
ritual and presenting this tantric system as not entirely different from the more main­
stream strands of Hinduism, whose practitioners recognize the authority of the Vedas 
as preeminent.
The origins of tantric apologetics with reference to Śrīvidyā reach a lot further back 
than Orientalist scholarship. These apologetics can be seen already in the work of the 
south Indian commentators from the hādimata branch, mentioned earlier (Golovkova 
2017, 121, 128–​130, 134–​137).16 The Vāmakeśvarīmata described a Kaula17 tantric tradi­
tion, whose practitioners were more interested in prayogas (rituals for gaining mundane 
results) than in soteriology. Beginning in approximately the thirteenth century, and with 
the work of Śivānanda, many south Indian commentators preferred interpretations that 
deemphasized antinomian practices. And it is this particular strand of Śrīvidyā texts 
and practices that has received the most scholarly attention to date from both textual 
and ethnographic scholars. While south Indian exoteric Śrīvidyā is an important tra­
dition to study in both its historical and its contemporary settings, the reality is that 
tantric Śrīvidyā ritual has been practiced within diverse initiation lineages in a variety 
of settings and spaces from the North and Northeast to the southernmost tip of the 
Indian subcontinent during the last millennium. It is both esoteric and exoteric, as well 
as transgressive and mainstream. Only by embracing this diversity and variety can we 
come to a more accurate and realistic grasp of this tradition and its history.
A wonderful example of more recent tantric apologetics can be found in 
Shuddhānanda Bharati’s 1954 introduction to Ganesh and Co’.s reprint of Avalon’s trans­
lation of the Kāmakalāvilāsa, printed together with Avalon’s digest of Tantrarāja Tantra 
(Woodroffe, [1922] 1971). Bharati argues against the association of Tantra with trans­
gressive ritual practices, including consumption of alcohol, fish, and meat and the use of 
sex, and advocates for their metaphorical interpretation.
Tantra is wrongly stigmatised as a libidinous phallic necromancy. This is due to 
instances of the excesses of some misguided Vāmamārgins.18 The real Tantrika19 
is neither a cynic nor a cyronic [sic] hedonist. He is rather an eudaemonist than a 
slave to passions. The much-​ridiculed five M’s are only esoteric symbologies. Wine 
is the lunar ambrosia flowing from the Soma20 Cakra. Woman is the Kuṇḍalini 
Śakti21 sleeping in the lower plexus, Mūlādhāra. Matsya is the annihilation of “I” 
and “Mine.” Māmsa is the surrender of the limited human to the unlimited Divine. 
Mudrā22 is cessation from evils. Maidhuna23 [sic] is the union of the Śakti with the 
Śiva in man. In Tantras, woman is not considered as an object of animal passion and

--- PAGE 354 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      329
 
pleasure. Tāntrikas consider woman as Parāśakti.24 She is deified and adored. If there 
is one science that has explored the divine regions of man and woman, in detail, it is 
Tantra. If there is one method that enables man to rise Phoenix-​like from the dead 
ashes of the animal passion it is the irreproachable Tantra.
(Bharati 1954, xvii, in Woodroffe [1922]1971)
Analyzing Bharati’s perspective on tantric practice brings to the fore questions for the 
study of Śrīvidyā and goddess traditions that have not yet received sufficient attention 
and must be asked explicitly. Which Śrīvidyā is Bharati describing? Is it the Śrīvidyā 
tradition of one or both of the texts of the Ganesh & Co. reprint (i.e., Kāmakalāvilāsa 
and Tantrarāja Tantra, which are, in fact, quite different from each other)? Is it the tra­
dition taught to Woodroffe and Ghose by their guru and explicated by means of tex­
tual reading? And what, in fact, was the understanding of Śrīvidyā practice by Ghose, 
whose ghostly presence emerges from letters and other historical evidence uncovered 
by Taylor (2001)? Shuddhānanda Bharati’s passionate rejection of the antinomian ritual 
elements, which connect Śrīvidyā to its Kaula origins, provides a mainstream brahman­
ical perspective. This nontransgressive, ritually pure transmission of Śrīvidyā described 
in Bharati’s introduction is, in fact, similar to Puṇyānanda’s, at least based on the limited 
evidence that we have. It is also similar to the Śrīvidyā that was known to Woodroffe 
and Ghose. However, it is quite dissimilar to the tradition as recorded in other texts and 
commentaries. Asking these questions of provenance and examining the similarities 
and dissimilarities in distinctive texts and works of different authors uncovers a 
nuanced history of this tradition’s development. It is only through a careful study of 
the polyphony of voices from different chronological and geographical locations and 
perspectives that the complex symphony of Śrīvidyā can be elucidated. Bharati’s implicit 
assertion that what he provides is an accurate portrayal of Śrīvidyā at all times and in all 
places is mistaken. As any other religious tradition, Śrīvidyā is diverse, changeable, and 
lacks clear-​cut boundaries overlapping with other traditions.
Informed by historicizing analysis of texts in context, my own reading of Sanskrit 
texts intentionally separates the views of redactors of tantras from those of their 
commentators, as well as those insights that I have gained from the contemporary tra­
dition. However, this approach, which seems commonsensical, is relatively new in the 
study of tantras. While scholars of the academic study of religion have been advocating 
for years that we must consider religious traditions in their historical and geographical 
contexts, the study of Śrīvidyā has been bound up in Orientalist approaches, which did 
not account for changes over time or ask questions about agency and intentionality.
The worship of Tripurasundarī, Rājarājeśvarī, Lalitā, and so on, is distinct from the 
tantric traditions of Krama and Trika. The former goddesses, especially in the later tradi­
tion, are typically portrayed as lovely, beautiful, and benign. Although their descriptions 
are usually devoid of both mortuary imagery of cremation grounds and associations with 
fierce goddess cults, sexuality has played an important role in the development of Śrīvidyā 
and continues to do so now among some practitioners (see Golovkova 2019, 2020). It may 
very well be that the tantric practice of Shuddhānanda Bharati and his lineage excluded

--- PAGE 355 ---
330      Anna A. Golovkova
 
“libidinous” antinomian elements, such as the use of pañcamakāras (i.e., five substances 
and activities normally prohibited to brahmins). However, their use is well documented, 
and in most contemporary lineages minute amounts of alcohol continue to be added to the 
viśeṣārghya (special offering) during Śrīcakra navāvaraṇa pūjā (i.e., worship of the god­
dess within the nine enclosures of the Śrīcakra). Further work on contemporary practices 
of Śrīvidyā beyond south India is needed for a more nuanced understanding of attitudes to­
ward practices that violate brahminical norms of ritual purity and their prevalence (for this 
issue in contemporary Nepal, see Lidke and Akshunna, Chapters 2 and 35, this volume).
An important contribution to the critique of this “deodorized” view of Śrīvidyā has 
been made by David Gordon White. White challenged both historical and contempo­
rary interpretations of tantra. He critiques both the New Age distortion of “tantric sex” 
as well as Orientalist scholars and nineteenth-​ and twentieth-​century Hindu reformers 
who overemphasize devotional (bhakti) traditions. These emphases undermine the im­
portance of tantra on the Indian subcontinent. White argued that “Tantra has been the 
predominant religious paradigm, for over a millennium, of the great majority of the 
inhabitants of the Indian subcontinent. It has been the background against which Indian 
religious civilizations evolved” (White 2003, 3). Sanderson argued that “the early medi­
eval period, from about the fifth century to the thirteenth, saw a decline in the role of 
Śrauta sacrifice in the religious ceremonies undertaken by the Indian rulers” (2009, 41), 
and that this period was characterized by the “preponderance of Śaivism,” which had a 
profound influence on other religious traditions in South Asia (2009, 44). In compar­
ison to Avalon’s tantric apologetics, which minimized practices that transgressed main­
stream brahminical norms, White’s analyses of tantra have tended toward the opposite 
extreme, overemphasizing the importance of sexual practices and the transmission 
of Kaula knowledge by means of offering and consumption of sexual fluids as power 
substances. Viewing Śrīvidyā and Trika through this lens of “hard-​core” and “soft-​
core” practices,25 White characterized their later forms as “high Hindu tantra,” which 
sublimated Kaula practices and integrated “aesthetic and linguistic theory into their re­
interpretation of earlier theory and practice” (White 1998, 173–​174; see also White 2000). 
My research into the early historical development of Śrīvidyā, particularly the compar­
ison of the texts describing the antecedent Nityā cult, the earliest extant Śrīvidyā tantras 
(the Vāmakeśvarīmata and the Yoginīhṛdaya), and the thirteenth-​ and fourteenth-​
century south Indian commentaries on these tantras, supports White’s theory of do­
mestication and sublimation of antinomian elements. However, I believe that White’s 
emphasis on Śrīvidyā as the “high tantra” may have overstated the case. Because his 
analysis of Śrīvidyā textual sources primarily refers to later Vedicized south Indian texts, 
it has obscured the fact that the worship of Tripurasundarī has been and continues to be 
diverse and multifaceted. Furthermore, while Western scholarship on tantric traditions 
was, in fact, disproportionately overshadowed by that on bhakti (particularly, Vaiṣṇava) 
traditions, devotion to manifestations of the goddess has become an integral part of tan­
tric Śrīvidyā practice since at least the thirteenth century CE. I suggest that instead of 
unidirectional exotericization, we consider Śrīvidyā’s development as a complex multi­
faceted process, and its public esotericism (see Fisher 2017, discussed below), i.e., tantric

--- PAGE 356 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      331
 
practices within public exoteric contexts, as a Venn diagram of intersecting Kaula, tan­
tric, Vedic, and bhakti practices. Further research into many more unstudied texts and a 
significant amount of ethnographic scholarship with a wider geographical distribution 
are necessary for a more accurate understanding of this historical progression.
Mahāvidyās and the Popularization of 
Hindu Goddess Studies
David Kinsley’s work from the 1980s and 1990s is important for us to consider because it 
brought the conversations about Hindu goddesses26 into the realm of Western academic 
discourse and college classrooms. Kinsley’s scholarship is also of particular relevance to 
us since his writing on the Mahāvidyās, a group of ten goddesses that became popular in 
Northeast and East India, along a pattern analogous to the daśāvatāras (ten incarnations) 
of Viṣṇu. He synthesized information available at that time on Tripurasundarī, who was 
often referred to in the context of the Mahāvidyās as Ṣoḍaśī. The name Ṣoḍaśī evokes 
the sixteenth-​syllabled mantra central to Śrīvidyā and the age usually ascribed to the 
goddess is, by no coincidence, sixteen. The earlier Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine 
Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition (1986), includes thirteen chapters dedicated to 
different goddesses and groups of goddesses, such as the Mātṛkās and the Mahāvidyās, 
reaching as far back as the Vedic period and even considering the goddesses of the Indus 
Valley. Hindu Goddesses briefly touches upon Tripurasundarī in a chapter titled “Tārā, 
Chinnamastā, and the Mahāvidyās” (Kinsley 1986, 163) and mentions two important 
Śrīvidyā hymns, the Lalitāsahasranāma and the Saundaryalaharī in the section on 
Mahādevī (Kinsley 1986, 133, 137–​143). However, at that point in his research, Kinsley 
was not aware that the hymns actually lauded the Goddess Tripurasundarī, also known 
under her popular Purāṇic name, Lalitā. Although these hymns most certainly depict 
the supreme goddess, without whom even Śiva is unable to act, as the famous first verse 
of Saundaryalaharī asserts, she is hardly the generic Mahādevī, as Kinsley suggests, but 
rather belongs to a specific bhakti (devotional) tradition that intersects with tantric 
Śrīvidyā.
Kinsley’s Tantric Visions of the Divine Feminine (1997) is a more mature work, which 
built upon the advances in the field of goddess studies in the previous decade and ele­
vated Purāṇic and tantric goddesses as worthy of scholarly attention. Unlike the broader 
focus of the Hindu Goddesses, Tantric Visions investigated specifically the Mahāvidyās, 
synthesizing a wealth of information that had not previously been available to a broad 
readership. In Tantric Visions, Kinsley’s understanding of Tripurasundarī has signifi­
cantly deepened. It is evident that Kinsley was indebted for this expanded insight into 
Tripurasundarī to Douglas Brooks’s work, although he does not say so explicitly. The 
fifty-​two endnotes on the short chapter on Tripurasundarī refers to Auspicious Wisdom 
(1992) and other texts cited in that volume twenty-​one times. Despite the expanded

--- PAGE 357 ---
332      Anna A. Golovkova
 
understanding of this goddess in Tantric Visions, the usefulness of information for a 
contemporary reader is limited because it is often presented without clear reference to 
specific historical and geographical contexts. Furthermore, Kinsley relies primarily on 
secondary sources and translations, with only a few references to primary sources and 
interviews with informants, whose background is not explained in detail.
For an illustration, let us look at the first paragraph in Kinsley’s chapter on 
Tripurasundarī and the two sources cited in the endnotes:
Tripura-​sundarī, who also appears in lists of the Mahāvidyās under the names 
Ṣoḍaśī, Lalitā, Kameśvarī, Śrīvidyā, and Rājarājesvarī, is often cited third, after Kālī 
and Tārā. She is also sometimes said to be, along with Kālī and Tārā, ādi (primor­
dial) Mahāvidyā, which suggests that she occupies a high place in the group, that she, 
like them, represents a complete vision of reality.1 According to other sources, she 
represents the penultimate vision of enlightened consciousness, a stage of conscious­
ness suffused with sattvic qualities but lacking the completeness of fully enlightened 
consciousness, represented by Kali, which is beyond all quality and form, nirguṇa.2
1 Rājeś Dīkṣit, Ṣoḍaśī Tantra Śāstra (Agra: Sumit Prakashan, 1991), p. I.
2 Interview with Swami Annapurnananda.
(Kinsley 1997, 112)
On reading this, the following questions arise: what are the sources for (1) the specific 
lists, (2) the description of Tripurasundarī as ādi śakti or “a complete vision of reality,” 
and (3) a characterization of this goddess as one who represents “a stage of conscious­
ness . . . lacking the completeness of fully enlightened consciousness.” Furthermore, do 
the texts on Tripurasundarī herself or the texts on the Mahāvidyās consider this goddess 
to be “a complete version of reality” or is it the view of Rājeś Dīkṣit cited in the first end­
note? Is Swami Annapūrṇānanda, cited in the second note, a devotee of Kālī or is he affil­
iated with the worship of the Mahāvidyās as a group? Similar to Woodroffe and Bharati, 
Kinsley synthesizes important information about the worship of Tripurasundarī, but 
without historical and geographical contextualization this view is flattened and lacks 
nuance. Although there is nothing unusual in this style of writing for the scholarship 
produced during the last century, these questions allow us to understand its limitations 
and consider what approaches may be more productive in the future.
Although much of his scholarship needs to be updated, Kinsley succeeded in laying 
down the groundwork for other scholars to develop the study of Mahāvidyās as a whole 
and of specific goddesses within the group further. Madhu Khanna’s edition and intro­
duction to Raja Deva Nandan Singh’s Śāktapramoda (2013) provides a useful updated 
edition of this fascinating paddhati (ritual manual) for the worship of the Mahāvidyās 
and five other deities. Śāktapramoda includes sections (designated as tantras) on the 
Mahāvidyā Tripurabhairavī and Bālā Tripurasundarī. Khanna’s unpublished doctoral 
dissertation from Oxford University, “The Concept and Liturgy of the Śrīcakra Based 
on Śivānanda’s Trilogy” (Khanna 1986), is another important contribution to the study 
of Śrīvidyā. The three short texts examined in the dissertation present devotional,

--- PAGE 358 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      333
 
doctrinal, and ritual information on the worship of the Śrīcakra as the embodiment of 
Tripurasundarī. It is unfortunate that this work has not been published and is hard to ac­
cess, but it has had an impact on the field.
Jae-​Eun Shin, particularly in her Change, Continuity, and Complexity (2018), has 
done other noteworthy work on the historical development of the Mahāvidyās.27 
Chapters of the Sacred Geography of Goddesses in South Asia (Singh 2010) provide new 
research on Mahāvidyās in specific geographic contexts. The two volumes of Gudrun 
Bühnemann’s The Iconography of Hindu Tantric Deities, which draw on the pantheon 
of the Mantramahodadhi, the Prapañcasāra, and the Śāradātilaka, provide an overview 
of the Mahāvidyās and iconographic descriptions of these goddesses. Further work 
on Tripurasundarī as a Mahāvidyā (i.e., one of the group of goddesses worshipped in 
East and Northeast of the Indian subcontinent in the later medieval period) is certainly 
needed and is a fruitful direction for future research.
Textual Advances in Tantric Śrīvidyā
Continuing the approach established by Woodroffe, late twentieth-​ and early twenty-​
first-​century scholarship on Śrīvidyā by André Padoux and Douglas Renfrew Brooks 
focused on texts of the highest literary quality that emphasized the philosophical, the 
metaphysical, and the otherworldly. In his digest of Hindu tantric literature in Sanskrit, 
Goudriaan (1981) correctly asserted that Śrīvidyā is characterized by an unusually high 
quality of texts within the corpus of tantric literature. Śrīvidyā tantras, unlike the tantras 
of many other traditions, usually conform to Pāṇinian grammar, eschew nonstandard 
aiśa28 (divine, belonging to Śiva) Sanskrit, and have been commented on by such bril­
liant polymaths as Jayaratha, Lakṣmīdhara, and Bhāskararāya. However, not all Śrīvidyā 
tantras or those relevant to the study of this tradition fit into this pattern, and there is 
much to be gained from studying those types of texts that have not yet attracted schol­
arly attention.
In my own work, I am filling the gaps in textual scholarship that has already been 
completed29 to uncover the development of the worship of Tripurasundarī as a late 
Kaula tradition, which followed and superseded the Nityā cult, an earlier and related 
tradition that worshipped Kāmeśvarī with Kāmadeva as her consort (see Golovkova 
2020, 2021). The texts describing the Nityā cult, the Nityākaula, the Siddhakhaṇḍa of the 
Manthānabhairava, and the Ciñciṇīmatasārasamuccaya, are much less polished than 
those typically studied by textual scholars and abound in aiśa Sanskrit. However, their 
careful reading allows us to trace the Kaula elements that are at times harder to discern 
in mature Śrīvidyā by looking in the metaphorical cracks and interstices of these texts.
In the case of the pioneers in the contemporary study of Śrīvidyā, André Padoux 
and Douglas Brooks, it is the texts of the highest literary quality and of philosophical 
and metaphysical bent that have attracted their attention. From Vāc: The Concept of 
the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras (1990) to his French translation of the Yoginīhṛdaya

--- PAGE 359 ---
334      Anna A. Golovkova
 
with Amṛtānanda’s commentary (1994) to the subsequent study of the Yoginīhṛdaya 
translated into English (2013), André Padoux’s scholarship emphasized connections 
between language and consciousness and contemplative practices with soteriological 
aims. For example, in his analysis of the Yoginīhṛdaya, Padoux paid particular attention 
to the understanding of how cosmic consciousness manifests in the Śrīcakra and the 
yogic body and decoded a series of phonic meditations on the seed syllable hrīṃ and 
other kuṇḍalinī30 practices. While Padoux has already accomplished significant philo­
logical work on the Yoginīhṛdaya and its commentary by Amṛtānanda, in my own work, 
I have found it productive to return to this tantra and its commentary in order to ex­
amine the shift in Śrīvidyā toward Śaiva nondualism and how the tradition was con­
sciously shaped by this and other commentators through their interpretative patterns 
and intertextuality (see Golovkova 2019, 112–​118). Padoux’s work is foundational for an­
yone approaching the study of mantras, just as Brooks’s work, discussed below, is foun­
dational for anyone engaging in the study of Śrīvidyā.
Without a doubt, the most important contribution to bringing Śrīvidyā to the at­
tention of scholars and students of tantric studies, has been made by Douglas Renfrew 
Brooks. I will not go into detail in discussing The Secret of the Three Cities (Brooks 1990) 
and Auspicious Wisdom (Brooks 1992). Anyone seriously interested in Śrīvidyā and 
goddess traditions needs to study Brooks’s work for themselves, but I will provide an 
overview and commentary. In his first published book, Brooks translates the Tripurā 
Upaniṣad along with Bhāskararāya’s commentary on this text, which consists of sixteen 
verses, and provides an introduction to the Śrīvidyā tradition, as well as some general 
comments on Hindu tantra and further directions for tantric studies. As an “Upaniṣad,” 
the text is a fascinating blend of Vedic and tantric influences, and Brooks makes a con­
vincing argument for the need for further investigation of this and other relevant textual 
evidence. As a translation and study of a lesser known short work and, thus, more lim­
ited in scope, Brooks’s first book was overshadowed by his second, Auspicious Wisdom, 
which synthesizes, broadens, and updates information on the ritual details of this tra­
dition. Auspicious Wisdom sifts through a mountain of data to present Śrīvidyā ritual 
details and its self-​understanding. Although some of the information, such as, for ex­
ample, Brooks’s early dating of Śrīvidyā, resting on the too-​early date of the Tamil 
Tirumantiram, has been updated since these publications (see Golovkova 2012, 818), 
Brooks’s work remains essential in describing and cataloguing Śrīvidyā ritual structure. 
He also articulates the dynamics between the Vedic and tantric elements of Śrīvidyā, the 
vāmācāra (i.e., left-​handed practice that allows for the use of transgressive substances) 
and dakṣiṇācāra (which does not). Brooks draws on both textual study and interviews 
of south Indian Smārta initiates and gurus for their contemporary explication. His anal­
ysis of the commentaries by the fifteenth-​century Lakṣmīdhara and eighteenth-​century 
Bhāskararāya, in particular, brings these dimensions to the fore.
Brooks’s explicit goal in both of his books on Śrīvidyā was to study texts in light of the 
contemporary tradition. While this is helpful for understanding how Śrīvidyā initiates 
and gurus understand the history and interpretation of their practice, it is some­
what less helpful for the historian of religion, since the differences in how these texts

--- PAGE 360 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      335
 
were received, understood, interpreted, and reinterpreted by the practitioners are not 
clearly articulated. For example, Brooks’s explanation of the ritual structure of Śrīvidyā 
emphasizes nondual understanding of the identity of the three forms of the goddess 
(i.e., physical, mantra, and yantra). However, nondualism, be it Pratyabhijñā or Advaita, 
was not, in fact, characteristic of the early tradition and became part of Śrīvidyā doc­
trine only over time (Golovkova 2019, 111–​112). Viewing the tradition through the lens 
of its contemporary interpreters and applying the characteristics of several texts to the 
worship of this goddess in all times and places creates a flattened, noncontextualized, 
“timeless” view of the tradition, which was, in fact, shaped and reshaped over time by 
real people, whose dreams, motives, and aspirations can be understood from reading 
their work against the grain (see, e.g., Golovkova 2017, 121–​143).
Digitization and “The Śaiva Age”
One of the positive factors in facilitating textual research on tantric traditions in recent 
decades is a greater access to manuscripts and electronic texts, which, in turn, made 
critical editing of key early texts possible. The increase in access to manuscript sources 
through the Nepalese-​German Manuscript Cataloguing Project (formerly Nepal-​
German Manuscript Preservation Project) (see https://​www.aai.uni-​hamb​urg.de/​en/​
forsch​ung/​ngmcp.html https://​sakyar​esea​rch.org/​sour​ces/​94), as well as through other 
initiatives, has broadly impacted textual-​historical research in tantric studies, proving 
that although manuscript work is often slow and painstaking, a study of unpublished 
textual evidence is well worth the effort. Digitized access to manuscripts, which we need 
to continue to develop, advocate for, and support, has also brought home a well-​known 
fact that the majority of textual sources for the study of tantric traditions remain in un­
published manuscript form. This makes engagement with these sources a necessity for 
scholars who work on the history of Asian religions and have the training to access them 
and, in turn, can make them accessible to others through their research. In my own 
work, I have found access to Nepalese manuscripts an invaluable source for the study 
of a Nityā cult, which preceded Śrīvidyā. Although the Nityā cult has died out, its ritual 
system, goals of practices, and descriptions of deities provide important parallels for the 
study of the early development of Śrīvidyā (see Golovkova 2020).
The inflow of manuscripts and the production of critical editions has made historical 
analysis, relative chronologies, and dating of texts and authors more possible than ever 
before. In “The Śaiva Exegesis of Kashmir,” “The Śaiva Age—​The Rise and Dominance 
of Śaivism during the Early Medieval Period,” and “The Śaiva Literature,” as well as his 
lectures, Alexis Sanderson has provided us with a valuable matrix from which to ap­
proach a historical study of Śaiva traditions. Sanderson’s work is dense, not easily ac­
cessible, but full of information that we will continue to unpack in the years to come. In 
his work, Sanderson devotes only a few sentences and footnotes to the discussion of the 
worship of Tripurasundarī and the antecedent Nityā cult within the context of Śāktism

--- PAGE 361 ---
336      Anna A. Golovkova
 
of the directional transmissions (i.e., classifications of late Śākta traditions that called 
themselves Kaula and were associated with the cardinal directions). My work unpacks 
these precious nuggets and investigates the texts relevant to the early history of Śrīvidyā. 
Sanderson’s timeline, which places these traditions within a larger context of Śaiva 
traditions, has also been a helpful starting point for the historical study of Śrīvidyā (for 
a graphic representation of classification of Śaiva doctrines, see, e.g., Golovkova 2017, 
App. A, 147). Furthermore, a close comparative reading of parallel passages, modeled 
on Sanderson’s close textual comparison of Śaiva, Buddhist, and Jaina sources, has been 
productive for my investigation of how Śrīvidyā ritual and exegesis has evolved over 
time in the early stages of its development (see Golovkova 2020, 87–​106).
Śrīvidyā as Tradition: Latest Findings 
and Considerations for Future 
Research
As we examine future directions of study, let us consider how thinking about Śrīvidyā 
as a tradition that was developed over time by human actors, can contribute to a more 
nuanced understanding of its history. The term “tradition” is, of course, ambiguous, and 
its utility here is worth examining. Referring to Hobsbawm and Ranger (1983), Hamsa 
Stainton points out that “Hobsbawm and the contributors to this volume are certainly 
right to chart the ways that traditions seek to manufacture links to the past. . . . At the 
same time, too much emphasis on the “invention” of traditions potentially obscures the 
revitalizing processes of all traditions. As Gadamer, Prickett, and many other scholars 
have discussed, all enduring traditions are dynamic, adaptive, and changing in their own 
ways” (Stainton 2019, 4). Stainton himself, in describing stotras as tradition, emphasizes 
continuity and innovation with which stotras engage with the past and “reform it to 
meet specific needs in the present” (Stainton 2019, 4).
Sanskrit commentaries on Śrīvidyā tantras, even more than other types of literature, 
are fruitful for studying tradition formation. Lawrence McCrea and Parimal Patil (2010, 
4) have proposed that instead of philosophical schools, we should think in terms of “text 
traditions” that share “a set of building blocks and common intellectual resources.” This 
concept of “text traditions” is particularly applicable when analyzing tantric exegesis, 
in which commentators use a similar set of tools, even though the context and the texts 
they are commenting on are distinct from the mainstream philosophical systems that 
accepted the authority of the Vedas. More than simply elucidating scriptural texts, in 
our case, the earliest extant Sanskrit tantras of Tripurasundarī, the Vāmakeśvarīmata 
and the Yoginīhṛdaya, commentators have used hierarchies of texts to establish their au­
thority, demonstrate intellectual belonging, and elucidate their specific locations within 
the broader religious milieu (e.g., Golovkova 2017, 80–​120).

--- PAGE 362 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      337
 
An examination of sources that these commentaries turn to is particularly revealing. 
The textual resources selected by Śivānanda in his Ṛjuvimarśinī (Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, 
[1988] 2011), a commentary on the Vāmakeśvarīmata tantra, in particular, articulate the 
beginnings of a common language for Śrīvidyā, a tantric tradition that is neither static 
and monolithic nor ever completely new and invented. Significantly more so than in the 
case of philosophical treatises, which have had a long and densely populated intellectual 
history, with south Indian commentators of Śrīvidyā texts, one feels at times as if they 
are, indeed, inventing the tradition anew.
A fitting metaphor for these emergent intellectual frameworks is something that those 
of us who have shipped boxes of books from India can relate to. You rip open the cloth 
covering on a box, stitched by a tailor, showing signs of having been on a long journey. 
A fragrant mix of smells overpowered by turmeric wafts from the box. You rejoice at 
seeing your long-​coveted treasures and make room for them on your bookshelves. You 
wonder what happened to the other boxes you shipped at the same time. I get a similar 
feeling when reading the first south Indian commentaries. It seems that their authors 
are improvising with scant resources (a few boxes lost in transit), without the benefit 
of the existing exegetical tradition, unlike the Kashmirian Jayaratha, who effortlessly 
cites from a variety of texts in his library, many of them from within the discourse on 
the Goddess Tripurasundarī, to which south Indian Śivānanda and Vidyānanda do not 
appear to have access. Furthermore, a few details of ritual and some understanding of 
the technical terminology of the Vāmakeśvarīmata seem to have also been lost in trans­
mission. Śivānanda and Vidyānanda are clearly prevaricating in a number of places, in 
which the meanings of verses in the Vāmakeśvarīmata have obviously become obscure.
But how should we think about the formation of a unique sectarian identity and can 
models from other subfields of religious studies be helpful to our understanding? R. A. 
Markus discusses the cumulative nature of the process of identity formation:
a continuous biography is the core of our sense of personal identity. This is true no 
less of a group’s sense of identity. It needs to be able to recognize itself as one and the 
same group enduring through time, the heir of its own past.
(Markus 1998, 85)
Adam Gaiser (2016) provides a useful model to consider. In thinking through the 
intricate ways in which traditions accumulate among sectarian groups, Gaiser (2016) 
suggested that they “resemble (from the outsider’s perspective) an avalanche”:
at the beginning of any given sectarian movement events, passions, doctrines, and 
practices provide an impetuous: [sic] for the movement of the sectarian group down 
the proverbial mountainside of their history. As the movement gains momentum, 
much new material will be picked up along the way and mixed with the older ma­
terial that remains part of the group’s tradition. What began as a movement of rel­
atively modest proportions now carries along with it a tremendous and compelling 
force, but also one that churns and shifts depending on the terrain in which it finds

--- PAGE 363 ---
338      Anna A. Golovkova
 
itself. As such, what constituted this avalanche of tradition at its beginning point 
cannot be said to be the same as what constitutes it further down the slope of history; 
and yet the avalanche is still considered to be the same avalanche.
 (3–​4)
The shortcoming of this model, as Gaiser acknowledged himself, is that it does not 
take into account the agency of religious actors who shape their tradition. As in the case 
of the development of Islamic notions of martyrdom examined by Gaiser, so in the case 
of Śrīvidyā, the tradition itself does not act but is shaped by those who practiced and 
taught it. It is the people (redactors of tantras and later commentators) who molded, or­
ganized, reinterpreted, and codified the ritual, doctrinal, and philosophical knowledge 
of Śrīvidyā, finding meaning, building communities, and creating memories of this 
tradition, modeling it on what was accepted and practiced within their own lineages, 
backgrounds, and texts that were available and important for them. Whereas Śivānanda 
and Vidyānanda’s work had clearly showed the seams between the building blocks 
of their tradition, by Amṛtānanda’s time, south Indian Śrīvidyā acquired some of the 
richness and density that seemed to have been lacking in the earlier transmission. In 
Amṛtānanda’s Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā, this south Indian tradition is well established and 
clearly defined as a distinctly south Indian, tantric, Vedic, and bhakti Śrīvidyā.
Elaine Fisher has written brilliantly about new modes of religious identity in the 
late-​medieval/​early modern Smārta Śaiva religious culture known today as Tamil 
Brahmanism. Examining the work of Appayya Dīkṣita and his grandnephew Nīlakaṇṭha, 
Fisher points out that Smārta Śaivism did not appear ex nihilo, although she argues for its 
early modern origins (2017, 183). My own study shows that the kernels of the early modern 
tradition of Appayya Dīkṣita and Nīlakaṇṭha, a type of public esotericism, which places 
tantric teachings of Śrīvidyā within the context of Vaidika orthodoxy, was already evi­
dent in the exegetical and devotional compositions produced by a cluster of theologians 
within a south Indian guru lineage in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries: Śivānanda, 
Vidyānanda, and Amṛtānanda (see also Golovkova 2017, 11–12, 128–132).
The corpus produced by this influential group of south Indian exegetes includes 
commentaries, devotional compositions, and ritual manuals (paddhatis) and served 
as a vital step in the process of tradition formation, building upon the understanding 
of Śrīvidyā ritual from within their lineage, but also constituting their tradition in in­
novative ways by means of the exegetical process. Whereas in the earlier worship of 
Tripurasundarī, neither its ritual system nor interpretation had anything in common 
with the Vedic corpus or its mantras, Śivānanda, in particular, envisioned and articu­
lated a new tradition of worship, reimagining a ritual system of tantric virtuosos as part 
of an ancient exegetical framework going back to the Vedas, with a devotional, public 
side to complement its esoteric ritualism.
Remarkably, this development in the early south Indian exegesis of Tripurasundarī tantras 
is very much in line with how Śrīvidyā practitioners (upāsakas) constitute their tradition 
today—​as devotional, tantric, and Vedic. Over the years, I have sought out opportunities to 
discuss my understanding of Śrīvidyā history and practice with contemporary gurus and

--- PAGE 364 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      339
 
practitioners who propagate and practice initiatory, popular devotional, and officiant forms 
of this and related traditions in south India and North America. The picture of the earliest 
history of this tradition that arises from the more in-​depth conversations with these diverse 
contemporary informants and their public discourses is remarkably similar, despite their 
various locations within the tradition and a range of attitudes toward ritual purity, eligibility 
for initiation for lower-​caste, dalit,31 and female aspirants. This picture follows the trajectories 
that were already mapped out in the thirteenth-​ and fourteenth-​century south Indian ex­
egesis of Śivānanda and Amṛtānanda but leaves aside an earlier period of development, 
during which the worship of Tripurasundarī had nothing in common with the tradition that 
recognized the authority of the Vedas: not in its mantras, not in  its philosophical orientation, 
which was neither dualistic nor nondualistic, and not in the corpus of sources cited by such 
commentators as Jayaratha. The Vedicization of Śrīvidyā was part of a deliberate process, 
which I have begun to examine, but which needs further investigation.
Given how closely Śrīvidyā has been imbricated with political power and the brah­
manical establishment (from premodern to contemporary south India), it can no longer 
be regarded as wholly marginal, esoteric, or secret. However, despite its mainstream ap­
peal, Śrīvidyā continues to flourish in tantric initiation lineages, some of which break 
with south Indian Smārta exotericism. Given this complexity, I suggest that, instead 
of an ahistorical view, which paints a picture of a monolithic tradition, or even a di­
chotomous approach, which looks at it from two opposite poles of esoteric/​exoteric, 
tantric/​Vedic, and “hard-​core”/​“soft-​core,” we might consider Śrīvidyā as continu­
ously evolving within the context of ongoing tensions between tantrism and Vedicized 
Smārta Hinduism, keeping in mind that even these strands are neither unified nor 
stable. Viewed in this way, Śrīvidyā may be best described as made up of overlapping 
and ever-​changing spheres of tantric and temple ritual and popular practice, a dynamic 
multistranded tapestry that defies attempts to view it as a stable unchangeable tradition 
or its history as unidirectional domestication.
Conclusion
Throughout my work on this chapter, I have been seeing a recurrent image—​a sunlit 
ocean, sparkling with all the colors in the blue-​green-​gold of the spectrum, which is the 
vastness of this tradition; myself—​a figure with a little dipper, measuring its vast space of 
scholarship, texts, practices, memories, narratives, and stories. Other humans have come 
and gone or are laboring at other spots along the shore: Sir John Woodroffe, who brought 
Śrīvidyā to the attention of the English-​language readers ([1922] 1971), and David Kinsley, 
determined to gather all he could on the Mahāvidyās (1986, 1997), so that scholarship on 
Hindu goddesses would flourish. More recently, André Padoux poured out his love of lan­
guage to benefit our understanding of the Yoginīhṛdaya (1994, Padoux and Jeanty 2013); 
and Alexis Sanderson sketched the many-​layered labyrinth of tantric textuality (1988, 
2007, 2009, 2013, 2014), the complex balancing of chronology, with but a tiny double spark

--- PAGE 365 ---
340      Anna A. Golovkova
 
of the Nityā cult and Śrīvidyā twinkling in one corner of its vastness. Madhu Khanna’s 
study of three short works by Śivānanda is also part of this landscape (1986), as is Douglas 
Brooks’s retrospective view of the tradition’s past through the eyes of its contemporary 
practitioners (1992, 1990). David Gordon White’s corrective view of Śrīvidyā unpacked 
the sublimated meaning of sexual rites within such practices as Kāmakalā and painted 
the narrative of domestication of the goddess’s Kaula practices as “high tantra” (1998, 
2003). Elaine Fisher contributed an incisive view at Appayya and Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita’s 
public esotericism (2017). Recently, Silvia Schwarz Linder (2022) published a study on the 
Tripurārahasya, analyzing the role of Tripurasundarī as a tantric and Purāṇic goddess in 
the later medieval period. There are several ethnographers whose contributions I was not 
able to give attention to in this chapter. These contributions include Corinne Dempsey’s 
outstanding account of a Śrīvidyā tantric temple in upstate New York, whose Srilankan 
Tamil founder blends tremendous attention to ritual detail with breaking conventions of 
gender and caste (2006). Jeffrey Lidke’s ethnographic study of Śrīvidyā in Nepal (2017) 
was supplemented with textual and historical research and insights from Sthaneshwar 
Timalsina in the “Preface” (2017). Timalsina also contributed a comparative chapter on 
mantra practice in Patañjali yoga and tantra, the latter including the Yoginīhṛdaya (2005). 
Mani Rao’s contribution on the “anthropology of mantra” in contemporary Andhra-​
Telangana (2019) includes an examination of Śrīvidyā as practiced at Devipuram, a site 
that has also been analyzed by Monika Hirmer (2021) and whose founder was the guru of 
the Rush temple’s founder, examined by Dempsey (2006). In addition, Maciej Karasinski-​
Sroka (2021) provided an exploration of Śrīvidyā as a link connecting tantric traditions 
of modern Kerala (2020), a textual-​ethnographic study of the Bālā cult (Karasinki-​Sroka 
and Sharman 2022), and Śrīvidyā healing practices in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu (2021). I 
am excited about work that is being completed and look forward to future publications 
by these and other scholars, like Sunitha Das (2021) about to take up the work that was 
started by W. Norman Brown (Śaṅkarācārya and Brown 1958) and Francis X. Clooney 
(2005) on the Saundaryalaharī.
With so much work on Śrīvidyā already accomplished, what are we missing? Where 
are the broadest gaps that we must fill in future scholarship? My view is that the gaps 
are relatively vast; we have but scratched the surface in gathering data and analysis. 
Scholars of ethnography have been challenged by difficulties of access, making existing 
studies skewed toward more easily accessible sites, all located either in south India or 
among the south Indian/​Srilankan diaspora. Textual work on Śrīvidyā is painstaking 
and slow, making deeper large-​scope analysis a long-​term commitment. In addition 
to examining published texts, we need to consider more unpublished manuscripts and 
texts that have received little scholarly attention for various reasons (e.g., lack of com­
pleteness or adherence to Pāṇinian grammar), which slows the scholarship down fur­
ther. We need to also continue rereading texts that have already been studied to update 
our analysis and tease apart the views of their redactors and commentators, in order to 
build a more nuanced grasp of the differences between Śrīvidyā as practiced in different 
times and places. We must continue to be aware of our own biases and the biases that 
have distorted our understanding toward a monochromatic view of Śrīvidyā as an elite

--- PAGE 366 ---
Śrīvidyā and Goddess Traditions      341
 
philosophical and literary tradition and have obscured the study of its rituals for mun­
dane results and the use of antinomian practices.
My own research aims to fill some of these gaps by recovering the early textual history 
of the worship of Tripurasundarī, its emergence from the Nityā cult, in which rituals for 
mundane results and sexual attraction predominated, the solidification of the ritual struc­
ture of the Śrīcakra and the principal mantra, and the first two waves of philosophical 
reinterpretation (Golovkova 2017). By approximately the eleventh century CE, Śrīvidyā 
legacy included the worship of the Śrīcakra and an early form of the principal mantra, 
recorded in the Vāmakeśvarīmata tantra. The first wave of philosophical and doctrinal 
reimagining of this ritual system, according to the nondual Śaivism of Utpaladeva, 
Abhinavagupta, and Kṣemarāja, was undertaken in thirteenth-​century Kashmir by the 
author of the earliest extant commentary on the tantras of Tripurasundarī, Rajānaka 
Jayaratha, and was supported by the redactors of the Yoginīhṛdaya, with which the 
Vāmakeśvarīmata is paired traditionally, and by later commentators. The next vital step 
in the development of Śrīvidyā sectarian identity consisted of a step toward public eso­
tericism, in which exegetes like Śivānanda, Punyānanda, and Amṛtānanda reimagined a 
medieval Kaula tantric cult as an esoteric and devotional ritual tradition that aspired to a 
broader influence within the emerging south Indian Smārta Śaivism.
I plan to fill in the gap of knowledge on the early development of this tradition, but 
more work is needed to connect the scholarship on Lakṣmīdhara, Appayya Dīkṣita, 
Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita, and Bhāskararaya (Brooks 1990, 1992; Fisher 2017) and to an­
alyze the arc of Śrīvidyā development in the middle and end of the second millen­
nium. Further work is also necessary to study Ṣoḍaśī and other Mahāvidyās related 
to Tripurasundarī to understand how the initiatory tantric Śrīvidyā intersected with 
the worship of this group of goddesses and the dynamics of tradition formation in 
the northeast of the Indian subcontinent. Further scholarly work is also necessary on 
Śrīvidyā stotras to recover the textual history of bhakti in Śrīvidyā. We must also seek 
out epigraphic and other historical sources through which we can map the development 
of Śrīvidyā onto the dynamics of royal power. The work has but begun, and the sunlit 
shore is open for more dedicated scholars of every background and specialization to 
add their work to the brilliant kaleidoscope of color and motion that is the Śrīvidyā tra­
dition. Maybe besides working harder, we can also work smarter by exchanging ideas, 
sharing resources and expertise, and collaborating to continue the work begun by the 
previous generation of scholars in the twenty-​first century and beyond.
