Chapter 15
The Ḍākinī in 
Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism
Judith Simmer-​Brown
The great nineteenth-​century Tibetan yogin Shabkar (Ricard 1994, 262) recorded an 
important vision that came to him just at dawn, while camping near a high mountain 
at Gongmo La at the Snow Grouse Pass. In the dream, he encountered a decrepit old 
woman lying on the side of the road, unable to move and begging for help. Filled with 
compassion, the yogin gently lifted her head and fed her nourishing tsampa (rtsam pa) 
roasted barley flour, butter, and tea and provided her with clothing. When she asked for 
his horse as well, the yogin also offered his packhorse.
At that moment, she jumped up joyfully and said, “You are said to be the most com­
passionate one of all, so I thought to see for myself. I have no need of a horse or any­
thing of that sort. Don’t you recognize me?” “No,” confessed the yogin. And she sang, 
“If you don’t recognize me, I am the Diamond Sow Ḍākinī. I shall bestow upon you re­
alization. If you have doubts, look at this!” Instantly she transformed herself into the 
blazing red form of the Diamond Sow Ḍākinī with wrathful expression, her flowing 
hair adorned with the small head of a black sow. The ḍākinī was naked and ornamented 
with bone jewelry and crown, garlands of dried and fresh skulls and the implements of 
a wisdom-​ḍākinī—​a hooked knife and a skull cup filled with blood, a khaṭvāṅga staff in 
the crook of her arm. Majestically, she danced. Her heart center emanated rays of light 
that penetrated Shabkar’s heart, bringing a clear and vivid experience of expansive bliss 
and emptiness. Handing him a cloth medicine bag crammed with thousands of silver 
coins, she whispered, “Here is yogic success. Give these coins to worthy beings so that 
they also can fly.” And she flew off into the sky. Astonished, Shabkar discovered he could 
fly. Shortly afterward, he awoke and marveled at the gift of this dream.
The Diamond Sow Vajravārāhī or Dorje Phagmo (rdo rje phag mo)—​aka Vajrayoginī 
or the Diamond Yoginī—​is the preeminent wisdom-​ḍākinī, the most significant class 
of enlightened female figures in Tibetan Buddhism. This recorded encounter is em­
blematic in the lore of the ḍākinī for the lives of Vajrayāna practitioners in Indo-​Tibetan 
tantra, lore that is a treasured account of the spiritual journey, realization experiences,

--- PAGE 373 ---
348      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
and the sacred transmissions of Tantric practice. Within the yogic communities of 
Vajrayāna practitioners, these encounters are considered semiotic, elusive messages that 
could easily be missed, misconstrued, or misjudged by the practitioner. While these ac­
counts emerge in the hagiographies or namthar (rnam thar) of lineage teachers in at 
least abbreviated form, their primary transmission occurs orally from guru to disciple 
in Tibetan Buddhism.
This semiotic quality permeates Western scholarship on the ḍākinī as well, and lack of 
agreement about her meanings and attempts to interpret her according to various biases 
are reminiscent of Shabkar’s mistake. Janice Willis (1987, 57) has observed:
[The ḍākinī] represents one of the most important, potent, and dynamic images/​
ideas/​symbols within all of Tantra. Yet, precisely owing to such dynamism and 
power, and to the all-​encompassing nature of this symbol, it is almost impossible to 
pin it down to or limit it to a single definition.
As a result, studies of the ḍākinī in Western scholarship have been diverse in method, 
focus, and conclusions about meaning.
Ḍākinī is a term originally derived from Indian regional Prakrit or possibly Sanskrit 
(Cape 2020, 354–​355), vulgar in connotation, attributed to a minor female demon in the 
pantheon of deities associated with indigenous pre-​Brahmanical traditions of India. 
Tantra in India had developments parallel with yoginī traditions where the flying 
ḍākinis were sometimes called “filthy birds of the night” (White 2003, 205), “invariably 
malevolent” contrasted with the milder yoginīs (Hatley 2016, 7), or “vampiric female 
spirits” (Hatley 2022, 9). David Gordon White (65) observed, “[T]‌he terms ḍākinī and 
yoginī are nearly synonymous in Tantric traditions, with Buddhist sources favoring the 
former and Hindu the latter.” David Gray (2007, 86) and others noted the first Buddhist 
text to portray ḍākinīs as non-​demonic is Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara, a 
“proto-​yoginītantra” that describes ḍākinīs in a positive light as spiritual beings but also 
retains the older image of them as nonhuman and dangerous (English 2002, 5, 12–​13; 
Hatley 2016, 14; Kalff 1978, 149–​150). The ḍākinī was assimilated to Buddhist Mahāyāna 
and Vajrayāna meanings, with the unlikely marriage of the Prajñāpāramitā formulations 
of the pristine female bodhisattva of wisdom with the transgressive nasty demonness 
dwelling in charnel grounds. Tantric Buddhism in India highlighted the ḍākinī in lore 
and liturgy, and after these traditions reached Tibet in the eighth and ninth centuries 
CE, the ḍākinī eventually became a unified though elusive symbol of realization in the 
Vajrayāna sense, sometimes called the ḍākinī principle (Simmer-​Brown 2001, 45–​53).
Etymology of the word “ḍākinī” is said to have derived from the Sanskrit root dī, to 
fly, translated “she who flies in the sky” referring to the powerful visionary form who 
finds her abode in the vast space of śūnyatā, emptiness of apparent existence. The 
Tibetan term khandroma (mkha’ ‘dro ma) expresses this meaning further: “she who 
enjoys the abode of the sky.” Kha refers again to śūnyatā (tongpa-​nyi, stong pa nyid) the 
nonconceptual realization of the dreamlike nature of all phenomena appearing in the 
skylike mind. In the oral tradition, dro refers to enjoying as the ḍākinī dances in this vast

--- PAGE 374 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      349
 
space. Her constant movement in the sky of experience points out the this nature experi­
entially (Simmer-​Brown 2001, 48–​52).
Orientalist Studies of the Ḍākinī
When Western scholars and spiritual seekers have encountered partial artifacts of the es­
oteric traditions of ḍākinīs, the potential for confusion and projection has proliferated, 
following orientalist habits that appropriate the ḍākinī for Western agendas. Those who 
longed for a sacred feminine seized on the gender of the ḍākinī as being most significant, 
indiscriminatingly appropriating her meaning as a divine savioress or a construction of 
patriarchal fantasy. The earliest gendered interpretations of the ḍākinī were influenced 
by psychoanalyst Carl Jung, who wrote “psychological commentaries” on newly dis­
covered Tibetan tantric texts implying that the ḍākinī is like the anima.1 The overt 
associations between the ḍākinī of Tibet and the Jungian anima were not explicit until 
1963, when Herbert Guenther (1963, ii–​iii) commented on the appearance of the ugly 
hag to the scholar Nāropa, surmising, “all that he had neglected and failed to develop 
was symbolically revealed to him as the vision of an old and ugly woman,” remarking 
in a footnote that “this aspect has a great similarity to what the Swiss psychologist C. G. 
Jung calls the ‘anima’.”
In critique of this depiction of the “fantasy of opposites,” neo-​Jungian James Hillman 
(1985, 7) reflected that there was a rich trade in which “smuggled hypotheses, pretty 
pieties about Eros, and eschatological indulgences about saving one’s soul through re­
lationship, becoming more feminine, and the sacrifice of the intellect” provided fertile 
ground for New Age appropriation of ḍākinīs for orientalist agendas. The most prom­
inent of these came from James Redfield’s appropriation of the ḍākinī in The Celestine 
Prophecy series (1999), where they were brought into service of a New Age movement 
that sports a journal and website linking with ecological, Christian, health, and so­
cial activism issues. When Jungian views combined with Western projections about 
tantric sexuality, ḍākinīs are considered sexually available, wild women with spiritual 
power. “Dakini trainings,” even those offered online, promise Ecstatic Awareness and 
Conscious Intimacy which may qualify one to be a “sexual priestess.” There are ḍākinī 
clothing companies, assuring the consumer that “ḍākinīs are ready for any adventure, 
big or small.”2 Additional appropriation is found in New Age utopian literature where 
there are ḍākinī oracle decks and fantasy novels featuring sexually free powerful women 
as protagonists.3
Building on Jung’s “fantasy of opposites,” orientalist feminist studies of the ḍākinī 
have fallen into two general contrasexual critiques: one extreme identified the fe­
male ḍākinī as a construct of patriarchy drawn by a primarily monastic Buddhist es­
tablishment in Tibet into service of the religious goals of the male practitioner only. 
June Campbell (1996) critiqued Tibetan Buddhist patriarchal monastic and religious 
systems, arguing that the ḍākinī is the secret, hidden, and mystical quality of absolute

--- PAGE 375 ---
350      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
insight required by men, a symbol of patriarchal Buddhism that guards male privi­
lege. Campbell concluded that the ḍākinī is an emblem of patriarchy, inaccessible to 
and even dangerous for the female practitioner, whether Tibetan or Western. German 
scholar Adelheid Herrmann-​Pfandt (1990) wrote a comprehensive study of the ḍākinī 
from South Asia to Tibet, influenced deeply by the Jungian models of contrasexuality 
found in German psychologist Eric Neumann’s work, The Great Mother: An Analysis of 
the Archetype (1983). The scope of her monograph was impressively broad, but her fem­
inist agenda following the reductionistic models of Neumann’s work shaped her orien­
talist conclusions about the ḍākinī, missing the spiritual significance and symbolism of 
the paradigm.
A second feminist perspective identified the ḍākinī as a goddess figure in an Indian 
gynocentric cult in which females were the primary cult leaders and males were their 
devoted students, asserted by Miranda Shaw (1994). She suggested that in India, women 
served as gurus and ritual specialists, but as Buddhism spread to Tibet, this role changed 
and women no longer played ritual or teaching roles. She argued that Tibetan patri­
archy shaped the ḍākinī symbol into an abstract patriarchal ideal which serves the 
spiritual paths of male yogins only, betraying her Indian historical roots. Both of these 
feminist critiques drew from orientalist agendas, seeking a sacred feminine to meet 
Western longings and measuring the ḍākinī against her relevance for the spiritual lives 
of Western practitioners.
Ḍākinī as Polysemic Symbol 
of Realization
Historian Caroline Walker Bynum (1992) cautions the religious studies scholar against 
assuming that a female goddesses or symbols could be interpreted accurately using 
feminist or sociological methods that may be more appropriate for analyzing texts and 
institutional structures. She found in her work on medieval Christian nuns that gen­
dered symbols say nothing predictable about social structures like patriarchy and an­
drocentrism and very little about the actual lives of women and men. She joins previous 
researchers who indicated that where a feminine symbol is lofty and idealized, patri­
archy is often firmly in place in society (Klein 1985b). She also asserts that all humans 
experience things in a gendered way, and that women often interpret symbols quite 
differently from men. In fact, gendered symbols often transmute gender even while 
referring to it (Bynum 1986, 1–​20). Particular nuance, skill in interpretation, and under­
standing of phenomenology of religious symbols as described by philosophers like Paul 
Ricoeur is required. Her observations are particularly helpful for scholars who work 
in tantric traditions of India and Tibet which valorize the feminine in symbol systems, 
preventing methodological mistakes in interpretation that can distort our work in the 
field of tantric studies.

--- PAGE 376 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      351
 
Gender studies perspectives challenge the orientalist assumptions of early studies, 
bringing the scholar to the phenomenological question of the meaning of ḍākinī for the 
traditions in which she is practiced. Janice Willis’s important 1987 essay opens the explo­
ration of the ḍākinī to broader methods of interpretation as she surveys the prevailing 
interpretations in Tibetan Buddhist scholarship, finding them inadequate to the task. 
Affirming the consistent “feminine” manifestation of the ḍākinī, Willis asserts that it 
is a mistake to assume that the ḍākinī is only female; Willis uses female pronouns in 
quotation marks throughout her essay. For Willis (1987, 58) the overall meaning of the 
ḍākinī can best be found as the embodiment of the genderless penultimate realizations 
of Vajrayāna meditation, “the direct, unmediated, and non-​conceptual experience of 
[śūnyatā, tongpa-​nyi] . . . ineffable reality itself.” She concludes her essay (58) with the 
suggestion that the ḍākinī be understood as a “feminine principle” and “the symbol par 
excellence,” suggesting that a full exploration of these seemingly conflicting features and 
their meaning would “require at least a book.”
My own research (2001) took on this task, analyzing the ḍākinī as “feminine prin­
ciple,” a central, polysemic paradigm of spiritual development in Tibetan Buddhism, 
drawing from Paul Ricoeur’s (1986, 9, 237; Gschwandtner 2020, 91–​93) approach to 
symbol, myth, and culture. The intention of this work is to identify the meaning of the 
elusive construct of the ḍākinī for Vajrayāna practice and realization as interpreted 
within Tibetan tantric culture. Drawing on interviews with Tibetan lamas, Vajrayāna 
sādhana and other ritual practices and their commentaries, narratives of ḍākinī lore 
from hagiographies (namthar) of the great practitioners, and iconographic materials, 
this research surveys the varieties of ways in which the ḍākinī is understood especially 
in Kagyü and Nyingma lineages of Tibet and interprets them with the help of a model 
suggested by a Mahāmudrā yogin, Khenpo Tsultrim Gyamtsho (Simmer-​Brown 2001, 
69–​79). This model includes gendered and nongendered expressions of ḍākinī prin­
ciple, closely integrated in their meaning.
Dakini’s Warm Breath followed the construct of phenomenologist Paul Ricoeur 
(1967, 9, 237) who identifies three levels of a symbol, important for interpretations of 
meaning: primary, secondary, tertiary. The primary level is experienced preverbally 
through dreams and visions or through meditative realization and constitutes what 
Ricoeur called symbol. In this, her most essential aspect, the ḍākinī is called the formless 
wisdom-​nature of the mind itself at the heart of all Vajrayāna practice, overtly associated 
with her Indian roots in the Prajñāpāramitā literature. In its “tantric phase” (Conze 1973, 
201), the sūtra called Perfect Wisdom in One Letter distills the entire teaching into the syl­
lable A. This Sanskrit syllable becomes the representation of the formless ḍākinī, called 
by Nyingma master Dodrupchen Jigme Tenpa Nyima (1865–​1926) (Gyatso 1992, 185 n. 8) 
the “empty letter door that displays emptiness.” Sādhanas often invoke this meaning of 
the ḍākinī through the syllable A. Twentieth-​century Nyingma teacher Chagdüd Tülku 
Rinpoche (1930–​2002) explained, “Knowing the nature of emptiness nondualistically 
is liberation. Whether you call it emptiness, the absolute, or the ḍākinī makes no dif­
ference. All are liberating” (Chagdud 1989). On a primary level, ḍākinī also refers to 
the yogic subtle body network of channels and winds activated in the inner practices

--- PAGE 377 ---
352      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
of tantra. The esoteric name for the subtle body is ḍākinījāla, the invisible network of 
the ḍākinīs. Synchronizing body and mind through the subtle body (manomaya-​kāya) 
in tantric meditation generates powerful realization of the true nature (Simmer-​Brown 
2001, 172–​176, 290).
Arising from the experience of the primary, Ricoeur’s secondary level of a symbol is 
found in myth and ritual—​the narrative or poetic expressions or in ritual practice, one 
step removed from nonconceptual experience but often imbued with the power to evoke 
this primary experience. Records of mythic encounters appear in hagiographies or 
namthar like Shabkar’s, above, where she is depicted in a personified manner as an un­
predictable semiwrathful dancing spirit-​woman. Often her appearance is accompanied 
by the bestowal of realization, prophecy, or admonition, experienced somatically by 
the practitioner as nonconceptual bliss and insight. Her demeanor changes in various 
contexts: she may be playful, nurturing, or sharp and wrathful, especially when cutting 
through spiritual arrogance or protecting the integrity of tantric transmission. She is 
also a fierce protector who guards the most private details of the practice, so that only 
those with the purest motivation are able to penetrate their essence (Simmer-​Brown 
2001, 116–​121).
Visionary ḍākinīs also are important meditational deities or yidams (iṣṭadevatā) 
in tantric rituals or sādhanas or drup-​thap (sgrub thabs) that manifest the secondary 
level of the ḍākinī symbol, where they are deities in their own right, or they appear as 
consorts and members of the retinue of male yidams. The most famous of ḍākinī yidams 
is Vajrayoginī, also known as Vajravārāhī, who appeared to Shabkar in the dream above. 
While the ḍākinī counterparts, the wrathful male consort heruka “blood drinkers” or 
trak-​thung (khrag ‘thung) sometimes remain unnamed, all represent the wisdom di­
mension of enlightenment joined with masculine compassion and skillful means. Subtle 
body yoga practices in sādhana practice may include visualizations in deity yoga crea­
tion stage practice (utpattikrama, kye-​rim, bskyed rim), movement of energy through 
the channels of the body in completion stage practice (sampannakrama, dzog-​rim, 
rdzogs rim), and the practice of sexual yoga (karmamudrā, lekyi chag-​gya, las kyi phyag 
rgya) (Simmer-​Brown 2001, 216–​221). Tibetan Buddhism safeguards these aspects of 
advanced meditation, holding them private in the oral transmissions from the personal 
guru; the true meaning cannot be accessed nonconceptually without guidance from 
the guru.4 When ḍākinīs are invoked as deities in ritual practice, they represent the di­
rect realization of the innate wisdom mind, the authenticity of the guru lineages that 
transmit them, the methods of practice—​whether ritual, yogic, or direct—​by which the 
wisdom mind is uncovered.
Tertiary forms of the symbol take the form of theology, philosophical expres­
sion, or societal usages where they are influenced by conventional notions of gender 
imposed by culture. Appellations of ḍākinī status to human women fall into this cat­
egory of the symbol. As contemporary Nyingma lama Dzigar Kongtrul Rinpoche (b. 
1964) cautioned, attributing ḍākinī status to human women is “not really dharma, more 
like folklore” influenced by many factors of culture.5 In traditional Tibet, these women 
were often considered jetsünmas (rje btsun ma), an honorific title signifying powerful

--- PAGE 378 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      353
 
practice, great realization, and exemplary teaching. Whether as the mother, sister, or 
consort of a renowned guru or as a teacher in their own right, these jetsünmas popu­
late the history of the major yogic lineages of Tibet, demonstrating that the essence of 
the ḍākinī can be found in the lives of actual women. Generally restrained by patriar­
chal custom from the full monastic education, public teaching roles, or the recognition 
of being an incarnate tülku, these human ḍākinīs have nevertheless been revered and 
treasured in Tibetan Vajrayāna for the unique ways they have propagated the dharma.
Taken together, honoring the feminine and women are considered foundational in 
traditional Vajrayāna tantric commitments (samaya, damtsik, dam tshig). As patriarch 
Sakya Pandita (1182–​1251) (Willis 1987, 103) described as the fourteenth “root downfall” 
associated with samaya in classic fashion:
If one disparages women who are of the nature of wisdom, that is the fourteenth 
root downfall. That is to say, women are the symbol of wisdom and śūnyatā, showing 
both. It is therefore a root downfall to dispraise women in every possible way, saying 
that women are without spiritual merit . . . and made of unclean things, not consid­
ering their good qualities.
Honoring the ḍākinī paradigm on all these levels connects the practitioner more closely 
with Vajrayāna devotion and realization.
In summary, in Tibetan tantra the ḍākinī principle has at least four polysemic levels 
of interrelated meaning, correlating with various dimensions of transmission, practice, 
and realization. These levels of the ḍākinī symbol relate to the “spiritual subjectivities” 
of women and men, illuminating the intimacy of personal experience in meditation as 
the essence of its meaning. As the ḍākinī paradigm moves from “inchoate symbol to 
narrative myth to explicit articulation of doctrine” (Gschwandtner 2020, 92) diverse 
dimensions of her meaning can easily become confusing and tangled. This perspec­
tive sets the stage for analyzing contributions to understanding the ḍākinī in recent 
scholarship.
Sādhanas, Liturgies, and Teachings
As shown above, ḍākinīs are a primary class of meditational deity (yidam), central to 
ritual practices in which they appear as the primary visualized deity, as a consort, or in 
the retinue of the central deity. The practitioner visualizes the ḍākinī as a self-​ or front-​
visualization in female form as the personification of aspects of the wisdom qualities 
of Buddhahood. Vajravārāhī, the Diamond Sow, is the most famous of these yidams, 
but other deity figures such as the passionate Kurukullā, the wrathful Siṃhamukhā, the 
terrifying protector Ekajaṭī, and the bliss-​granting Yeshe Tsogyal are among important 
ḍākinī yidams. Each of these has their own cycles of sādhanas with detailed mandalas of 
their realms.

--- PAGE 379 ---
354      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
Several studies of the ḍākinī yidams have been published in the last two decades. 
Elizabeth English (2002) deftly translates the eleventh-​century Vajrayoginī sādhana of 
Umāpatideva, one of the collection of the Guḥyasamāja sādhanas, with analysis of the 
ritual dimensions and illustrated with stunning colored plates of Vajravārāhī thangkas 
and statuary. In addition, she briefly places the text in the context of the living cult of 
Vajrayoginī in classical India up to the present day. In a related work, the fine transla­
tion by David Gonsalez (2020) of the collection of sādhana and guru yoga practices of 
Vajrayoginī and the accessible commentaries by influential Geluk master Pabongkha 
Rinpoche (1878–​1941) have contributed to the traditions of Vajrayoginī practice. In spite 
of its title, The Extremely Secret Dakini of Naropa, the book openly publishes diagrams of 
visualizations and subtle body yoga that would be unthinkable in Kagyü and Nyingma 
circles of tantric lamas. Although it is listed as a restricted text, it is readily available from 
both the publisher and Amazon.
Many practitioner-​scholars are reticent to publicly publish translations and especially 
visualized ritual and subtle body yoga details of sādhanas of yidam practices, for they 
are considered esoteric and private, not appropriate for general distribution. Elizabeth 
English (2002, xxiii), for example, noted the “strict code of secrecy in imparting the 
instructions for her actual practice” that kept her from accessing practice instructions of 
Vajrayoginī sādhanas. Nevertheless, important contributions to understanding ḍākinī 
sādhanas continues with lineage blessings without violating secrecy. A precious little an­
thology (Kunsang et al. 2018) of Nyingma ḍākinī treasures and practices entitled Dakini 
Activity is a great example of available resources on the major ḍākinī yidams.
In 1985, Anne Klein (1985a) published a brief study of the sādhana practice of the 
Great Bliss Queen, Yeshe Tsogyal, from the Longchen Nyingthik Dzogchen traditions, 
included as the final chapter of one of her books (1995a, 2008). In the years since this 
essay was published, the renowned Adzom Paylo Rinpoche, one of the most important 
Dzogchen masters in contemporary Tibet, discovered a hidden treasure-​text in a vision 
at Yeshe Tsogyal’s sacred lake, which has become part of his treasure cycle, Luminous 
Heart Essence, Ösel Nyingthik. Treasure-​texts (terma, gter ma), one of two genres of 
source tantric texts, represent fresh revelations from Guru Rinpoche appropriate to con­
temporary changing times and hidden in physical locations or in the minds of realized 
yogins. They are discovered by these visionary yogins, called treasure-​discoverers 
(tertöns, gter ton), often supported by celestial or human ḍākinīs who are said to protect 
the treasures until the time is right. Rinpoche entrusted Klein, aka Lama Rigzin Drolma 
of Houston’s Dawn Mountain Temple, to teach this sādhana and give commentary, 
and she has offered this practice to qualified students.6 In a forthcoming book, Klein 
discusses and translates the two-​part terma—​a ḍākinī foundational practice (ngöndro, 
sngon ‘gro) centered on Yeshe Tsogyal, and a sādhana practice for becoming her. This 
book, part of Wisdom’s new House of Adzom series, unveils the layered richness of the 
sādhana and identifies different dimensions of experience to which the practitioner is 
invited by the practice, such as reflections on the feminine, on gender, and on what it 
means in modern times to have a relationship with the wisdom ḍākinī Yeshe Tsogyal.

--- PAGE 380 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      355
 
Klein’s work comes on the heels of fine translations of major biographies of Yeshe 
Tsogyal, eighth-​century queen of Tibet and the most prominent historical human 
ḍākinī in Tibetan tradition. The two independent namthar of Yeshe Tsogyal appeared 
as treasure-​texts after centuries of appearing as subnarratives in accounts of Guru 
Rinpoche. The treasure of Taksham Samten Lingpa (b. 1655), translated into English 
at least three times (Dowman 1984; Padmakara 1999; Tarthang 1983), depicts Yeshe 
Tsogyal’s miraculous birth, personal obstacles, and auspicious partnership with Guru 
Rinpoche. Drime Kunga’s namthar (Drolma 2017) of Yeshe Tsogyal from the fourteenth 
century is more abbreviated but still depicts her as “not exclusively human,” an emana­
tion of the mahāsattva Sarasvatī, goddess of wisdom (Angowski 2019, 15). In addition, 
a treasure revealed by Nyang Ral Nyima Oser (1124–​1192), entitled “The Questions and 
Answers of the Noble Lady” (Kunsang 1990), is a series of concise teachings given by 
Guru Rinpoche to his consort Yeshe Tsogyal on how to take the teachings to heart, mod­
eling the intimacy between guru and disciple, heruka, and ḍākinī. We are fortunate to 
have such extensive materials on Yeshe Tsogyal as a Tibetan woman from legend and 
history who became a ḍākinī meditational deity with her own cycle of practices.
Sarah Harding has translated the teachings of several revered human ḍākinī lin­
eage holders, contributing richly to understanding their teachings and practices. Her 
guru Kalu Rinpoche (1905–​1989) requested her to collect and translate teachings of 
Niguma, the elusive eleventh-​century Kashmiri genetrix of the Shangpa Kagyü lin­
eage, often referred to as the “secret lineage” because tradition has it that Niguma 
instructed Khyungpo Naljor to give transmission to only one person for seven gener­
ations. Niguma’s treasury of thirteen teachings (Harding 2010) from the Tibetan canon 
include her Six Yogas (Nigu Chödruk) teachings that parallel those of her brother or hus­
band, Nāropa, as well as general practice instructions for Mahāmudrā, sādhanas from 
Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra cycles, and advice for practice in daily life. Niguma’s pre­
cious instructions on subtle body yoga are appropriately entitled “The Ḍākinī’s Personal 
Instructions” (183–​192). Harding’s translation foregrounds an endangered lineage of 
Tibetan Buddhism that has influenced all the other Kagyü schools.
Harding has also translated the treasury of teachings of Tibet’s most renowned 
yoginī, Machik Lapdrön (1055–​1149/​53), entitled Machik’s Complete Explanation 
(Machik Namshe) (Harding 2003). This Tibetan handbook provides the lineage his­
tory, practice, and view of the severance (chöd, gcod), the unique and innovative 
ḍākinī practice that cuts through ego-​clinging and fixations in contemplations of 
the charnel grounds (śmaśāna, turtrö. dur khrod) that invoke the realization of emp­
tiness and compassion. Harding’s additional translation of the fourteenth volume of 
Jamgön Kongtrul Lodro Thaye’s Treasury of Precious Instructions (Harding 2016) is an 
anthology of important source texts for Chöd practice, including rites of initiation, 
empowerments for the practice, and general instructions and guides for the practi­
tioner. With these three translated volumes and their informative and accessible 
introductions, Harding has proven herself to be a pivotal contributor to ḍākinī re­
search in the twenty-​first century.

356      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
Namthar—​Autobiography 
and Biography
With the expansion of Buddhist studies into Himalayan Buddhism in the last twenty-​
five years, methods of research exponentially contextualize understanding of the ḍākinī 
through translation, fieldwork, literary studies, ritual studies, art history, anthropology, 
and women’s studies, redressing the orientalist agendas of the past. Janet Gyatso cautions 
against using ahistorical paradigms to essentialize the female gender in her anthology, 
Women in Tibet (2007, 5–​6), identifying her study as concerned with historical women 
only. When the Tibetan ḍākinī paradigm is appropriated “to further Western feminist 
goals” such as in the assertion that all women are ḍākinī, elements of the ḍākinī are 
essentialized beyond cultural and historical circumstances; this is contested by Tibetans 
themselves who have repeatedly asserted that all women are ḍākinīs, qualifying that 
statement as not ontological and referring to intangible aspects of the nature of mind 
(Simmer-​Brown 2001, 202–​207). Also, as Dzigar Kongtrul reminds us, assertions like 
these are “not really dharma, more like folklore.” These perspectives share with Carolyn 
Walker Bynum the recognition that there is no direct correlation between the idealized 
symbols of the ḍākinī with the lives of Tibetan women specifically, and especially for 
non-​Tibetan women who might be ensnared by the orientalist enterprise.
In 1984, Tsultrim Allione published the first Western anthology of biographies of 
realized Tibetan women, based on the translations of biographies of six women from 
Tibetan lore identified as ḍākinīs; these “rough” translations were motivated by her 
own desire to support her own practice. Since then, Tibetan studies scholars have 
produced polished translations of hagiographies (namthar) and biographies of en­
lightened women, many of whom are identified in their Tibetan communities as incar­
nate ḍākinīs. This work reverses in part what Rita Gross (1993; Miles et al. 2006, 68–​70) 
called the “quadruple androcentrism” of historic Buddhist traditions: not only did in­
itial determinations of what was canonical favor the experience of men, subsequent 
choices of accounts favored hero accounts over those of women. In addition, Western 
Buddhist studies have been dominated by male subjectivity and power, and contem­
porary Buddhism in Asia and the West continues the androcentric habit. In redress 
of these omissions, many contemporary scholars have prioritized the retrieval and 
translation of the lives and teachings of realized Tibetan women, including recognized 
human ḍākinīs.
The sheer vitality of this strain of ḍākinī studies raises important questions about 
traditional Tibetan society, and for the contemporary Tibetans in Chinese Tibet and in 
exile, and their considering some notable women to be ḍākinīs. What does it mean to be 
a human ḍākinī? Does this refer to some innate ontological quality, and how does this 
not reify female sex and gender in ways that offend feminists, scholars, and Buddhists? 
While namthar of the great female practitioners emphasize the special qualities of

--- PAGE 382 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      357
 
incarnate ḍākinīs (zugpe khandroma, gzugs pa’i mkha’ ‘gro ma), born already enlight­
ened with auspicious physical marks, such idealized accounts also raise questions 
about the gap this fosters between ordinary women in Tibetan society and the elevated 
ḍākinī. How are the accounts of Tibetan yoginīs understood and interpreted in modern 
Tibetan society?
Tibetan sacred biographies share features found in exemplar accounts in every reli­
gion, where there is a creative tension between imitability on the one hand and distinc­
tiveness of the exemplar on the other. The body of literature associated with exemplars 
is commonly understood to derive from religious institutions meeting the needs of 
folk religion, animating the efficacy of the spiritual path in dynamic and engaging ways 
through inspiring narrative (Kieckeffer and Bond 1990, viii; Ray 1984, 3–​14). In these 
accounts, conferred sainthood, in order to be inspirational, must represent the lives of 
exemplars as imitable in some way, demonstrating the attainability of the goal. However, 
if these accounts are too ordinary in displaying intractable challenges, they may not suf­
ficiently depict the qualities of realization valued in the tradition. Generally speaking, 
Tibetan namthar locate themselves along a spectrum between these two extremes 
(Gyatso 1998, 105–​107).
Over the span of Indian and Tibetan history, previous lofty and miraculous accounts 
of the lives of ḍākinīs have become more humanized, adorned with personal challenges 
and societal obstacles that these remarkable women have overcome. The early 
biographies are often embedded within the namthar of great male herukas like Guru 
Rinpoche, or as fragments in anthologized namthar in sacred history (chöjung, cho 
‘byung) texts. Independent biographies emerge as terma texts centuries later, indicating 
the increasing importance of the human ḍākinī in Tibetan lore, and these biographies 
include emphasis on imitability. While accounts of ḍākinīs like Yeshe Tsogyal and 
Machik Lapdrön include unique challenges faced by women on the path of dharma—​
overcoming parental pressure to marry, resisting demands of impatient suitors, the sur­
liness of in-​laws and extended families about wifely responsibilities, and the suspicions 
surrounding the ḍākinī’s retreat practice—​there remains strong emphasis on the super­
human births and miracles as well as the remarkable realization of the wisdom-​ḍākinīs. 
The traditional accounts are filled with miraculous elements with rainbows at birth, or­
nate visionary material, auspicious signs on the ḍākinī‘s body, and plenty of flying, and 
so we can conclude that these historic ḍākinī namthar lean more heavily on the distinc­
tiveness of the ḍākinī‘s life than upon her imitability, but that imitable themes remain 
important. Elizabeth Angowski (2019, 300) concludes that these narratives are intended 
less as “proto-​feminist” narrative and more as inspiration for tenacity in one’s practice of 
the dharma.
The stunning translation and study by Sarah Jacoby (2014) of the autobiography of 
the twentieth-​century Sera Khandro (1892–​1940) more explicitly expresses the ḍākinī’s 
human conundrums shared with ordinary women. Sera Khandro’s first-​person ac­
count locates her as an accomplished woman entering a predominantly male religious 
calling, supported by visionary ḍākinīs constantly encouraging and guiding her. Under

--- PAGE 383 ---
358      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
Jacoby’s skillful moniker of “the ḍākinī dialogues” (­chapter 3), Sera Khandro’s autobiog­
raphy juxtaposes her inner human doubts stemming from her “inferior birth” (kyemen, 
skye dman) as a woman with vibrant visionary ḍākinīs who praise her, encourage her, 
and remind her of her ḍākinī destiny. This namthar exemplifies the rich literature in 
visionary ḍākinīs’ support for women’s practice, contesting earlier claims to the con­
trary. The dialogue between Sera Khandro and her ḍākinī mentors becomes what Jacoby 
calls “autobiographical ventriloquy,” which simultaneously affirms her lofty qualities 
and acknowledges the personal challenges she faces as a human ḍākinī. Sera Khandro’s 
importance in contemporary Tibetan renaissance cannot be overemphasized. Tsadra 
Foundation translator Ngawang Zangpo has published a collection of Sera Khandro's 
teachings in Refining Our Perception of Reality (2013), including a short autobiography 
translated by Christina Monson.
Fieldwork research has added a great deal of nuance to the way human ḍākinīs are 
identified and designated in modern and contemporary Tibetan communities. More 
time-​honored criteria derived from analysis of namthar appear to be miraculous 
elements at birth, such as distinctive physical marks or celestial events; personal reali­
zation through tantric practice; serving as a recognized tantric guru; family relationship 
with an incarnate lama (tülku, sprul sku)—​as wife, mother, or sister; and having devel­
oped realization power (siddhi, ngödrup, dngos grub) in a ḍākinī yidam practice.7 Tülku 
incarnations are discovered usually as children, reeducated, and formally empowered to 
continue the work of their former incarnation. Contemporary fieldwork has provided a 
more nuanced study of contemporary namthar with greater contextualization of social 
and historical factors. There appears to be no formal procedure or approval process at 
work; instead, regional male hierarchs or gurus from nearby monasteries develop an 
unspoken consensus in the matter, tying the ḍākinī designation directly to patriarchal 
structures.
In the case of contemporary Tibet, the ḍākinī designation is tied not only to dharmic 
criteria but also to regional and lineage social fabric, to the power of sacred places, and 
to the strength and inspiration of Tibetan dynastic history in a time of cultural and en­
vironmental degradation. The study of Golok’s Khandro Rinpoche (b. 1954) by Sarah 
Jacoby (2015) emphasizes “relational autonomy” in the ḍākinī’s life as her unwavering 
devotion to the dharma emerged in antireligious times during the Cultural Revolution. 
Her siblings and husband were Chinese officials, offering her wealth and status under 
Chinese rule, which she rejected in favor of a life of practice and patronage of Tibetan 
lamas and monasteries. After her first son was recognized as a tülku in utero, she 
contracted a mysterious illness that left her mute and turned her mind to the dharma. 
As she came to be recognized as a wisdom-​ḍākinī, she used her Chinese family contacts 
to finance and support endangered teachings and rebuild monasteries, cementing her 
ḍākinī role as protector and preserver of the teachings. Later in life, her many years of re­
treat in Vairotsana Cave identified her more fully with Tibet’s golden age and revitalizing 
the dharma in Eastern Tibet.

--- PAGE 384 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      359
 
Sexuality and Tibetan Buddhist Tantra
The tantric rite of sexual union has been part of Vajrayāna meditation from tantra’s an­
tinomian roots in Indian circles through its introduction to Tibet in the eighth century; 
it has been a practice associated with subtle body yoga, as harnessing the channels and 
winds fueled by sexual desire has been an intrinsic part of realizing the true nature of 
mind (White 2003, chaps. 3, 4). Compassionate intent has been considered central, and 
motivations for merely personal gratification have always been considered the greatest 
obstacle in the practice. Traditionally, there have been three ways to channel desire in 
tantric meditation. First, in creation-​stage practice, one visualizes the yidam deities as 
yab-​yum in sexual union. Second, one can generate internal heat (caṇḍalī, tummo, gtum 
mo) by moving the winds through the central channel of the subtle body in comple­
tion phase formless meditation. These first two methods are the primary ones practiced 
in celibate monastic communities and by most contemporary Vajrayāna practitioners. 
In a third way, one practices so-​called sexual yoga (karmamudrā, lekyi chaggya, las kyi 
phyag rgya) with a consort. Based on the experience of bliss that can become great bliss 
(mahāsukha, dewa chenpo, bde ba chen po), it is possible to more quickly remove emo­
tional and conceptual obscurations in one’s practice (Simmer-​Brown 2001, 216–​217). 
This third method is rarely taught because the transmissions have been lost in many 
lineages through misuses, societal controversy, and the rarity of its mastery. The ḍākinī 
has always been tied to karmamudrā—​symbolically as the network of subtle channels 
(ḍākinī-​jāla); as seed syllables of the sacred sites of the body mandala; iconically with 
a wrathful male yidam consort in visualizations in sādhana practice; or actually as co-​
consorts with male yogins. Tibetan tantra’s patriarchy has privileged the male perspec­
tive in this practice, often objectifying and denying agency to the female consort partner.
Recent research has shed additional light on the traditional practice of karmamudrā 
and the ḍākinī, showing that even in fourteenth-​century Tibet, it was not without con­
troversy. Kali Cape (2020, 353–​356) summarizes the “taxonomy” of consort types in her 
essay on the fourteenth-​century Dzogchen treasure-​text revealed by Pema Lendreltsal 
(1291–​1315/​17) and expanded by Longchenpa (1308–​1363) and students of the Third 
Karmapa, Rangjung Dorje (1284–​1339). The Ḍakki’s Path and Fruit (dakki lam ´bras 
skor) text is a manual by and for male adepts in heteronormative sexual yoga practice on 
352 variables to consider when choosing an appropriate consort, part of a genre of such 
texts in the corpus. This text warns of the dangers of the choice of an inauspicious con­
sort whose partnership might induce “interpersonal problems, social consequences, ec­
onomic consequences, shortening of one’s life span, grave soteriological consequences, 
and even sexually transmitted diseases” (Cape 2020, 364). Cape contextualizes these 
cautions in a tradition in which the general norm is renunciation of sexuality by 
speaking not only of negative consequences in personal karma and dharmic destiny but 
also of the disastrous social effects of inadvisable consorts. Nowhere are the intentions,

--- PAGE 385 ---
360      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
agency, or consequences for the woman considered, highlighting the patriarchal privi­
lege assumed in the treasure-​text.
Sera Khandro’s experience as a consort figures prominently in her autobiography, 
as she speaks candidly about her intimate relationship with her beloved guru Drime 
Özer as they entered extended retreat together and attained enlightenment through 
karmamudrā sexual yoga practice (chap. 4). She speaks of her final years with her guru 
as “the two, method and insight, actually merging into one taste” (296). Her rare first-​
person account also shows the challenges faced by a noncelibate yoginī in Tibetan 
communities where resisting unwanted advances from unscrupulous lama suitors, en­
during gossip and jealousy in the community, distinguishing between ordinary lust and 
passion that supports one’s practice, and establishing her own agency in her spiritual 
journey figure prominently in her narrative. Jacoby (2014, 191) remarks:
The candor with which Sera Khandro writes about such matters takes consort 
practices out of the distant, abstract, and highly symbolic frameworks in which they 
often appear in prescriptive, doctrinal and ritual Tantric texts and situates them 
within the specific context of twentieth-​century religious encampments in the no­
madic highlands of eastern Tibet.
Sera Khandro clarifies that the three purposes of karmamudrā—​what Jacoby calls 
“soteriological, hermeneutical, and pragmatic”—​apply to both yogins and yoginīs (2014, 
chap. 4). Sera Khandro’s skillful navigation of these perilous circumstances contributed 
greatly to her ascendance as a respected treasure-​discoverer and enlightened woman, 
but the anguish, indignities, and derision she experienced on the way “cast a pall on 
arguments that claim Buddhist Tantra is pro-​woman or sex-​positive” (248).
In these times of the #MeToo movement, fresh scrutiny is being brought to sexuality 
in Buddhist tantra, recognizing that even in Tibet the practice was misused for per­
sonal gratification and that even the most realized women were exploited by immoral 
lamas with libidinous intent, as we have seen with the accounts of ḍākinī Sera Khandro. 
According to Holly Gayley and Somtso Bum (2022), contemporary Tibetan short stories 
depict “fake” lamas who use tantric language as a pretext for taking advantage of young 
women (seduction, assault, or as a rationalization) including references to “secret con­
duct” (gsang ba’i mdzad pa), consorts (rig ma), and in one case ḍākinīs. The stories 
surface in the contemporary social critique of this exploitive behavior with greater com­
passion for women who are victimized than the previous scapegoating and gossip evi­
dent in accounts like Sera Khandro’s. One wonders about the distinction between “fake” 
lamas and any other kind, and how discernment might contrast beneficial engagement 
in secret conduct versus damaging ones.
Sexual abuse scandals have torn Western Vajrayāna communities apart, bringing 
open discussion about the power of the guru, the objectivization or agency of women, 
and the nature of tantric commitments. Holly Gayley addresses contemporary 
controversies about sexual abuse in Vajrayāna communities in light of the consort 
traditions of Tibet, scrutinizing the association between secrecy and sexuality. She notes

--- PAGE 386 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      361
 
that the tradition of the sang-​yum (bsang yum)—​“secret consort”—​privileges those in 
power “by compartmentalizing public accomplishments and private indiscretions” 
(Gayley 2018, 3). She asks whether the “perfect storm” of joining secrecy and sexu­
ality might be mitigated by an ethic of transparency, clearer education about the na­
ture of tantric commitments informed by the gender dynamics of power and privilege, 
and standards for ethical conduct endorsed by gurus and their communities (Gayley 
2018, 17–​18). Controversies like these would benefit from cross-​tradition tantric studies 
discussions, untangling the challenges for channeling desire in tantric practices without 
exploiting women or causing harm.
Ḍākinī Mothers of the Tibetan 
Renaissance
The remarkable work of Holly Gayley (2017, 2019) on a pair of modern renowned 
treasure-​revealers (tertöns) shows how the ḍākinī paradigm is supporting the regen­
eration of dharma on the eastern Tibetan plateau. Her study focuses especially on the 
ḍākinī Khandro Tāre Lhamo (1938–​2002) whose exchange of fifty-​six letters with her 
tantric consort Namtrul Rinpoche (1944–​2011) forged a powerful prophetic legacy 
for healing the damage of Chinese oppression and environmental degradation. Tāre 
Lhamo’s namthar, Spiraling Vine of Faith, depicts her as enlightened before birth, an 
emanation of Yeshe Tsogyal and Sera Khandro, tying her to a distinguished line of 
ḍākinī women, emblems of unmistakable enlightenment, protective care of the tantric 
teachings, and resilience in the face of obstacles. Gayley speculates that her identifica­
tion as a ḍākinī reflects the privilege of her birth into a family of treasure-​discoverer 
tertöns that gave her access to lamas and teachings that supported her spiritual and so­
cial status. Her typical namthar’s features have unique elements coming from the con­
text of the Maoist and post-​Maoist periods of occupied Tibet in which her teachers, 
husband, and three brothers were imprisoned under torture and died, and her only son 
died of illness. While she was condemned to a decade of manual labor, it is rumored that 
her powers as a ḍākinī helped her evade extended imprisonment, even though she was 
likely detained and briefly tortured. Throughout these years she practiced in secret and 
served as a resilient example and inspiration to a devastated community (Gayley 2017, 
38–​45, 2019, 6–​7).
It was here that Khandro Tāre Lhamo’s visionary example assumed a remarkable 
new role. On the heels of cultural trauma and environmental damage inflicted by the 
Cultural Revolution and inspired by prophetic visions, she initiated dynamic corre­
spondence with a young lama, Namtrul Rinpoche, who lived nearby in Golok. In their 
ongoing exchange of what Gayley calls “epistolary courtship,” they exchanged poetic, 
erotic, and prophetic visions for a more optimistic future for a devastated Tibet, drawing 
on inspiration of their past lives together. Their letters conjoined Guru Rinpoche’s

--- PAGE 387 ---
362      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
prophecy, their karmic connection, dharmic inspiration, and the promise of healing the 
damage of degenerate times. Tāre Lhamo (Gayley 2019, 97–​98) wrote:
Now, to obtain the inheritance of Padmasambhava,
The time has come for the entrustment of us pair of friends.
Now if we proceed according to his command, it is good.
In the vast casket of the inner sanctum of the mind
Is the heart certificate of the 100,000 mother ḍākinīs,
Expressly the means to reverse the strife of degeneration.
Motivated by compassion, the two together joined as visionary partners to reveal terma 
that drew on Tibet’s past glory and projected a regeneration in community life, dharma 
teaching and practice, and environmental repair that has been part of what has come to 
be known as the eastern Tibetan renaissance.
The charismatic Khenchen Jigme Phuntsok (1933–​2004) was the most important 
leader of this movement when he founded the Serta Buddhist Institute (aka Larung Gar) 
in 1980 (Gayley 2017, 96–​100, 2021, 17–​36; Germano 1998, 53–​94). His vision of the revi­
talization of the dharma included persuading nomadic herders to give up raising ani­
mals for meat, promoting vegetarianism, and engaging with scientific discourse. He also 
endorsed the uplift of women, encouraging nuns’ education at Larung Gar, and assumed 
ethical reforms for his entire Buddhist community. He died after cardiac surgery in a 
Chinese hospital in Chengdu in 2004. Khandro Tare Lhamo and Namtrul Rinpoche 
were encouraged by Khenchen to support the resurgence of the dharma through 
building monasteries and temples, revealing terma for the future of Tibetan Buddhism, 
and traveling through the region sharing their visionary teachings and inspirations. 
Altogether, their work has brought healing and renewed fervor for the dharma in Kham 
or Sichuan province (Gayley 2017, 221–​226).
Since Khenchen’s death, Larung Gar has continued as a vibrant community in spite 
of continued Chinese harassment, the largest Buddhist institution on the Tibetan 
plateau. Known for its dedicated and brilliant khenmos (mkhan mo), nuns who hold 
the highest monastic degree, new initiatives are contributing richly to the vitality of 
ḍākinī traditions. Motivated to promote the uplift of women in Tibetan communities, 
in 2011 a group of seven Larung nuns under the guidance of Jetsün Ani Mumtso, 
niece of Khenchen Phuntsok, resolved to gather and anthologize Buddhist women’s 
writing and hagiographies. The resulting voluminous text, Ḍākinī’s Great Dharma 
Treasury (Khandro Chödzö Chenmo), was published in 2013 by the Ārya Tāra Book 
Association comprising writings by and about more than two hundred different re­
markable Buddhist women in fifty-​three volumes. By 2016, the association had been 
formally incorporated into Larung Gar as part of its educational division. The in­
troduction to the series supplicated the “vast multitude of mothers (ma yum)” for 
blessing, meaning not only human mothers but the mother ḍākinīs and all Buddhist 
women, all powerful women, and for “future generations of Tibetan mothers and 
daughters” and “all women in the world” (‘Tsho & Jacoby 2021, 219–​221). When asked

--- PAGE 388 ---
The Ḍākinī in Indo-​Tibetan Buddhism      363
 
whether this was a feminist enterprise, the nuns said they didn’t want to debate gender 
equality and only wanted to “take concrete steps to improve women’s circumstances” 
(‘Tsho & Jacoby 2020, 6). To these ends, they prioritized improving the lives of women 
and girls, enhancing nuns’ education, and promoting Tibetan women’s history (‘Tsho 
& Jacoby 2020, 3).
Recommendations for Future Research 
on the Ḍākinī
Research on the ḍākinī has been informed by a variety of methodologies, at first 
dominated by orientalist Jungian and feminist perspectives and then with the methods 
of gender studies and phenomenology of symbols. Over the last three decades, able 
translators have retrieved and made available the biographies, textual teachings, and 
practices of ḍākinīs both visionary and human, further revealing the importance of the 
ḍākinī for Vajrayāna practice and realization. In the last decade, Tibetan-​Himalayan 
area studies have focused on contemporary translations of namthar of Tibetan women 
who have been recognized as ḍākinīs, providing cultural and historical context for 
what it means to be a ḍākinī in contemporary Tibetan society. Modern Tibetan human 
ḍākinīs have revitalized and reinterpreted Vajrayāna teachings for a degenerate time 
under Chinese oppression, serving as charismatic visionaries for personal and social 
awakening and repair of a damaged environment. However, the obstacles in the future of 
the field are evidence of several previously siloed and separated intellectual disciplines 
in religious studies.
For future research on the ḍākinī, three prospective directions would be fruitful. 
First, it is curious that there has been so little ongoing study of the symbolic meaning 
of the ḍākinī in Vajrayāna practice, given the central importance of levels of the symbol 
in Tibetan Buddhism. One of the major interests of contemplative studies as an aca­
demic field within religious studies is the investigation of contemplative practices 
in their cultural and historical contexts, including unpacking the meaning of symbol 
systems that guide them, in conversation with other contemplative practice traditions 
(Komjathy 2018, chap. 3). Contemplative studies valorize first-​person inquiry along with 
other scholarly approaches, validating the lived events of an experiencing subject and 
exploring the discoveries of the inner life. The ḍākinī is above all a unifying symbol that 
ties the realization of the true nature of mind; the integrated enlivening experience of 
embodiment; clarification about the nature of desire; and the visionary world of dream, 
insight, and compassion. Many aspects of the ḍākinī have nothing to do with gender, 
and this in fact informs the experiences of being in gendered bodies for women and men 
in no doubt interesting ways. Engaging in this manner, it would be helpful to explore 
contemplative dimensions of the ḍākinī symbol, discovering the relationship between 
creation stage and completion stage practices in ritual practice, including visualization,

--- PAGE 389 ---
364      Judith Simmer-Brown
 
subtle body yoga, breath, and formless practices and their integration through the 
symbol of the ḍākinī. The application of a gendered symbol as a guide has interesting 
parallels across traditions, as we have seen in the work of Carolyn Walker Bynum, and it 
would be fruitful to identify how women and men experience gendered symbol systems 
in their practice.
In the current research in Tibetan studies, it has been fruitful to include fieldwork 
research that investigates the experiences of contemporary Tibetan women as context 
for the translations of modern autobiographies of Tibetan women ḍākinīs. This corrects 
some of the exclusions generated by quadruple androcentrism of the tradition. However, 
insistence on historical women within Tibetan studies has sometimes focused research 
on the relationship between the ḍākinī paradigm and the struggles of women in patri­
archal society to the exclusion of other concerns. Within this focus, how has the reli­
ance on the ḍākinī paradigm changed over the history of Tibetan Buddhism? How is the 
current renaissance reformulating the ḍākinī paradigm in unforeseen ways? How is the 
ḍākinī understood in diaspora communities, and how does this relate to perspectives in 
Chinese Tibet? A priority of Tibetan studies is translating into Western languages the 
Ḍākinī’s Great Dharma Treasury compiled and published by the Larung Gar nuns of 
the Ārya Tāra Book Association as well as financially supporting the dissemination 
of the Tibetan anthology to Tibetan communities in China and diaspora. It will also 
be fruitful to listen deeply to these communities identifying the unfolding meaning of 
these ḍākinī treasures for their own lives.
A third priority for research is the collaboration of scholars working on tantric 
materials across cultural settings and religious traditions. Given the antinomian Indian 
origins of tantra and the diverse developments and appropriations of tantric contem­
plative, ritual, and textual traditions, the historical navigation of elements that societies 
often have considered degenerate could inform scholarly methods and attention to phe­
nomena that may otherwise be suppressed, ignored, or discounted. Tantra stimulated 
great creativity and innovation in cultures throughout Asia, and its gifts can be more 
fully appreciated and understood when scholars step out of the narrowness of their 
specializations and collaborate with others. The living, dynamic traditions of the ḍākinī 
hold splendid promise for revealing the contemplative depth, narrative wealth, and so­
cietal implications of a tantric vision.
As we have seen, the traditions of the ḍākinī are alive and well in contempo­
rary Tibetan Buddhism, both in Chinese-​occupied eastern Tibet and in diaspora 
communities, adapting and changing throughout history. They are especially playing 
a significant role in the revitalization of Buddhism in contemporary China for both 
women and men. In a place beyond time, ḍākinīs are said to have sworn on a visionary 
level to protect and sustain the dharma, extend the lives of the teachers, and inspire sin­
cere practitioners in dealing with obstacles on the path. Perhaps as with Shabkar, in 
these degenerate times the visionary Diamond Sow ḍākinī is favoring these leaders with 
magical pouches of silver to share realization with their devotees while gifting them 
with the ability to fly.

Chapter 16
Three Shades 
of Tantric Yoga
Chapter 20 of the Netra Tantra
David Gordon White
An important document for the history of “tantric yoga,” the ninth-​century Netra 
Tantra’s twentieth chapter (NT 20) on “threefold yoga” has received relatively little 
scholarly attention to date. This notwithstanding, its content may be viewed as an im­
portant corrective to widely held views concerning the nature of yoga itself, in both its 
tantric and non-​tantric iterations. The earliest scholarly account of NT 20’s content fig­
ures in Hélène Brunner’s (1974: 183–​187) pioneering survey of the entire work. More re­
cently, Somadeva Vasudeva (n.d.) has referenced the chapter’s ten opening verses in an 
unpublished paper;1 and both Olga Serbaeva Saraogi (2010: 72–​76) and myself (White 
2009: 162–​164) have interpreted selected verses (NT 20.27–​35) in earlier publications. 
Independent of its quite original content, the NT’s treatment of what it calls the three­
fold yoga (trividha yoga) is significant for the fact that it classifies these three dis­
parate bodies of tradition and practice as forms of “yoga.” As I will show, the NT’s 
“supreme yoga” (parayoga) closely resembles the “violent consorting” (haṭhamelaka) 
of tantric adepts with Yoginīs as documented in earlier tantric works, while its “subtle 
yoga” (sūkṣmayoga) is an elaboration on the technique of entering a foreign body 
(parakāyapraveśa) for the purpose of initiation or for more nefarious ends, and its dis­
cussion of “gross yoga” a guide to sorcery and countersorcery.
Supreme yoga is supreme in the sense that the total transformation the Yoginīs ef­
fectuate on their target is unequivocally salutary, regardless of the fact that it entails 
the death of their target’s body. In this respect, as the text relates, its effect is identical 
to that of tantric initiation. While its internal procedures are comparable to those of 
initiation, the NT and its commentary equivocate with respect to the effects of subtle 
yoga: when practiced for the good, it assures its target’s virtual salvation; when prac­
ticed to evil ends, the yogi or Yoginī turns their target into a sort of slave or involun­
tary “psycho-​mental organ donor.” Gross yoga generally involves external techniques

--- PAGE 395 ---
370      David Gordon White
 
that serve to manipulate and harm a target when used to evil ends, or to protect 
against the same when used for the good, in the practice of countersorcery. In su­
preme yoga, the Yoginīs internalize their victims by eating them; in subtle yoga, yogis 
and Yoginīs transform their targets from within; in gross yoga, good and evil Yoginīs 
and practitioners transform their targets from without. In all three cases, “yoga” is 
presented in the literal sense of “yoking,” which denotes one or another type of posses­
sion. This tantric usage of the yoga signifier was not unusual for a period in which the 
concept of yoga was very much in flux.
“Haṭha” and Aṣṭāṅga Yoga in the NT
Like many tantric scriptures, NT 20 is a shaggy dog of a text whose uneven prose; fre­
quent shifts in gender, number, and person; and occasional nonsequiturs show it to be 
more a compilation of fragments than a single cohesive composition. It nonetheless has 
a structure that, based on the core dynamic of “yoking” (yoga), subdivides the chapter 
into four parts: a general introduction, which provides the nondualist metaphysical 
context for what will follow, and three sections devoted, respectively, to para, sūkṣma, 
and sthūla yoga. This triad reprises a classificatory system introduced earlier in the 
work: the NT’s sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters are devoted to supreme, subtle and 
gross “meditation” (dhyāna), introduced in the opening verses of chapter six. Here, after 
announcing that he is about to reveal a secret teaching (rahasyam), and evoking the var­
ious ills that afflict humanity, Śiva explains
how all are saved, my darling, from the cruel conditions I mentioned earlier. Now, 
it (i.e., the secret teaching) is threefold, and its strategies the gross, the subtle, and 
the supreme. The gross [strategy involves] sacrifice, fire offering, the repetition of 
spells (japa), meditation together with seals (dhyānam samudrakam), devices for 
perplexing [demons], and the like. The King of Mantras forcefully effects [this]. 
The subtle [strategy] is effected [through] the yoking (yoga) of the cakras, etc., and 
by the rise through the channels (nāḍīs) of the phonematic particles (kalās). The 
supreme [strategy], which is, moreover, universally applicable, is Mṛtyujit, the 
bestower of liberation. (NT 6.6–​8)2
Mṛtyujit, the “Death-​Conqueror,” is the vibratory essence of the supreme deity of the 
NT, Amṛteśa, the “Lord of Immortality,” a form of Śiva popular in medieval Kashmir 
(Sanderson 2004: 240). It is He who, in His mantric form of OṂ JUṂ SAḤ, governs 
the motley assortment of beings, practices, “sealing techniques” (mudrās) and “spells” 
(mantras) that populate this sprawling treatise. As Brunner (1974: 127, 138) has noted, the 
NT is a heterogeneous compendium whose original “clusters” of instructions—​which, 
taken together, comprised a technical manual for the various optional (kāmya) rites 
of healing and magic practiced by tantric specialists (sādhakas, ācāryas, mantravids,

--- PAGE 396 ---
Three Shades of Tantric Yoga      371
 
daiśikas, etc.)—​“appear as so many brightly colored stones” held in place by the “grayish 
cement” of the all-​powerful Mṛtyujit-​Amṛteśa. As a tantric manual, the NT in its earlier 
redaction(s) was dualistic in its metaphysics, with a bright line separating the Creator 
from His creatures, to say nothing of the demonic beings that tormented and preyed 
upon them. In the work that has come down to us, however, all of these are shown to 
be internal to the universal Mṛtyujit-​Amṛteśa. It is this nondualist metaphysics that 
constitutes the work’s “grayish cement,” which, while providing a modicum of cohe­
sion to its variegated parts, requires no small number of philosophical pirouettes (if not 
contortions) on the part of its compilers to gel. Appearing in particularly high relief in 
the opening verses of ­chapter 20, this nondualist gloss is a leitmotiv for both the text and 
for Kṣemarāja’s learned eleventh-​century “Netroddyota” commentary, to which I will 
refer frequently, albeit not slavishly.
In addition to the divine person of Amṛteśa-Mṛtyujit, the semantic glue that holds 
this chapter together is its explicit usage of terms derived from the verbal root √yuj 
(yoke), which generates many of the nominal (yoga, yogi, Yoginī, yojanam, prayojanam) 
and verbal forms (niyukta, viyukta, upayukta, yojayanti) found therein. There can be no 
question that the expressed topic of NT 20 is yoga, or a triad of yogas, but as its accounts 
of them show, these “yokings” have virtually nothing in common with yoga as we know 
it, whether “classical,” haṭha, or otherwise.
With this in mind, I turn to the NT’s seventh chapter, as its contents offer a glimpse 
into the emerging subtle body systems that would begin to coalesce, two centuries later, 
into what is known as haṭha yoga (Birch 2011, 2019). To begin, the chapter opens by 
announcing that its teaching concerns “subtle meditation”—​or to use Gavin Flood’s fe­
licitous translation, “subtle visualizing meditation”3—​rather than the “subtle yoga” that 
will be described in NT 20. However, it is here, under the heading of sūkṣma dhyāna, 
that terminology denoting the components of the subtle or yogic body and the med­
itative raising of energy, consciousness, and the nectar of immortality is extensively 
employed.
The chapter’s opening verses (NT 7.1–​7.2) define sūkṣma dhyāna as a visualizing med­
itation on the six cakras, three objects (lakṣyas), five voids (vyomans), twelve knots 
(granthis), three Energies (śaktis), three domains (dhāmans), three channels (nāḍīs), 
and so forth. While the names of some of these are common to several contemporary 
and later texts and traditions, others—​beginning with the six cakras—​are not (NT 
7.28b–​7.29b). Named “birth” (janma), “illusion” (māyā), “tantric practitioner” (yogi), 
“cleaving” (bhedana), “splendor” (dīpti), and “mild” (śāntam),4 and situated in the 
“circle of channels,” navel, heart, uvula, the “place of the drop,” and “[place of the] rever­
beration,” respectively, these have little in common with what has come to be considered 
the canonical system of seven cakras as illustrated in Sir John Woodroffe’s The Serpent 
Power (1950: 317–​431).5 In fact, in my research on the topic, I have identified some forty 
different systems of “cakras” or “centers” from across Hindu, Buddhist, Sufi, and Jain 
sources. Of these, seven are four-​cakra systems; five are five-​cakra systems; twelve, like 
the NT, are six-​cakra systems; four are seven-​cakra systems, six are nine-​cakra systems; 
with the remaining eight featuring ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, and more.6 As for the

--- PAGE 397 ---
372      David Gordon White
 
names and locations of the individual cakras, these too are variable. To summarize: the 
names and locations of the NT’s six cakras are in no way nonstandard, because there 
never has been a standard system of cakras.
The seventh chapter’s treatment of subtle visualizing meditation comprises 
a set of instructions for the yogi to vividly cultivate the experience of rising 
through the yogic body, an ascent simultaneously realized on three registers: vi­
bratory (involving mantras), fluid (involving the generation of nectar, amṛta), and 
gnoseological (issuing in the gnostic realization of his identity with Śiva-​Amṛteśa-​
Mṛtyujit) (NT 7.50–​7.51). Many of the signal elements of haṭha yoga are present here: 
the identification of the practitioner as a yogi; the practice of breath control; the 
central suṣumnā nāḍī as conduit for the raising of consciousness, energy, and fluids; 
the identification of internal Energy as “She Who is Ring-​Shaped” (kuṇḍalā) (NT 
7.21b); the identification of various centers as the abodes of the high gods of Hindu 
theism (NT 7.26); the dynamic of “piercing”; the frequent recourse to lunar meta­
phor; the evocation of the “aviator’s seal” (khecarī mudrā) (NT 7.37a); and the ulti­
mate goal of immortality.
However, as the text declares, these are not instructions for the practice of subtle yoga 
but rather for subtle visualization meditation. Which begs the following question: if 
this chapter insists on referring to haṭhayogic body mapping and techniques as sūkṣma 
dhyāna, what account does the NT give, if any, of the meditative system of so-​called 
classical pātañjala yoga? The answer is provided in ­chapter 8, which, devoted to para 
dhyāna, “supreme meditation,” identifies its practice as the eight-​part yoga (aṣṭāṅga 
yoga) (NT 8.9). Nearly all resemblance to the Patañjalian system ends here, however, 
as the NT’s accounts of yama, niyama, and so forth generally deviate significantly from 
their descriptions in the Yoga Sūtras.7 So, for example, its description of āsana (pos­
ture), the third part of aṣṭāṅga yoga, has nothing to do with seated postures. Rather, the 
text declares that “taking refuge in the middlemost breath and holding both it and the 
indwelling Energy of Gnosis within the path [taken by] the in-breath and out-breath, 
one shall succeed in [the practice of] āsana” (NT 8.11). As we will see, dhyāna and 
dhāraṇā, the sixth and seventh parts of the eight-​part yoga, are brought into play in NT 
20’s treatment of “gross yoga,” while the Energy of Gnosis plays a crucial role in its ac­
count of “subtle yoga.” That chapter is the focus of this study.8
NT 20.1–​20.10: Introducing the 
Threefold Yoga

hear [something else]. This is the doubt remaining in my heart.
