21.	 The wise ones know that killing [by the Yoginīs] is actually a bound person’s 
(baddhasya puruṣasya) disconnection (viyoga) from a body, even when its 
fetter (pāśa) is massive, fully grown.17
In these two opening sections, NT 20 addresses a conundrum central to all monotheistic 
traditions. Theodicy, or the problem of evil, may be described as follows: (1) God alone is 
God, and He is wholly good and all-​powerful; (2) yet evil exists in the form of creaturely 
suffering, death, and so forth. Therefore, either (3) God is not alone, not wholly good, or 
not all-​powerful, or (4) the same all-​powerful God nonetheless allows for evil to exist 
in the world. The premier theodicy of the South Asian religious world is the doctrine of 
karma, which maintains that while God’s creation is good and perfect, any evil suffered by 
creatures is of their own making, the outcome of evil acts committed in past lives, or due 
to nescience in their present life. One can escape this trap and accede to liberation and re­
lease from suffering by leading a life (or several lives) of righteousness through devotion 
to a powerful, grace-​granting God; through the gradual attainment of gnosis; or through 
recourse to powerful expedients. The mṛtyuñjaya mantra is the preferred expedient of 
the NT, as its mention of aṣṭāṅga yoga in chapter eight makes clear: “Thence [through the 
practice of supreme meditation on Mṛtyujit, the yogi is] immediately liberated, and he 
shall not suffer rebirth; but he attains [that liberation] through the eight-​part yoga, and 
not otherwise.” However, the three yogas of the NT’s twentieth chapter (or, at least, the first 
two) may also be viewed as alternate means to the transcendence of the human condition.
Embedded in the broader Trika tantrism of medieval Kashmir, the nondualism 
championed in the NT’s final redaction further complicates the metaphysics of the­
odicy, inasmuch as it also maintains that the God who created the universe is the entire

--- PAGE 400 ---
Three Shades of Tantric Yoga      375
 
universe, and that every being, process, and apparent conflict within the universe is 
internal to Him (or, more properly speaking, to His consciousness of the universe 
as Himself). This is the issue that these verses of NT 20 seek to resolve. The chapter’s 
opening statement of the problem and proposed solution was significant enough for 
it to be taken as a proof text by Abhinavagupta, the great eleventh-​century polymath 
(and guru of Kṣemarāja, the commentator of our text), for the justification of sac­
rifice, the offering of one of God’s creatures, a part of God himself, to that same God. 
Abhinavagupta’s treatment of the issue, like that of the Vedic apologists before him, 
has a casuistic ring to it.18 Reducing the problem of evil to the problem of sacrifice in 
a nondualist Śaiva context, Abhinavagupta’s defense of tantric sacrifice, part summary 
part paraphrase of NT 20.1–​20.21, reads as follows:
This (i.e., sacrifice) is a great assistance to the sacrificial victim, though it appears to 
be disagreeable at that time. In this context the utilization of [caustic] medication 
and a [harsh] regimen in order to destroy disease can serve as an illustration. And 
it is taught in the venerable Mṛtyuñjaya [i.e., the NT]: When its bonds have been 
sliced off, a body does not grow back for the victim due to its unyoking from the 
three impurities (malas). It is agreed that the body falls away when the burden of 
[karmic] righteousness and unrighteousness has been sliced off. Therefore this is not 
killing but an extraordinary initiation. For killing is the disconnection of the vital 
energies from a person’s body, even when its fetter has fully grown, but this [sacrifice] 
is the conjunction of a bound person in the act of worshipping God.19
Abhinavagupta’s use of this passage notwithstanding, sacrifice is not so much the issue 
here as it is a rationalization for the underlying issue, which is, once again, the problem 
of evil. This is what the Goddess clearly states in the question she poses to Śiva, her sole 
contribution to this “semi-​dialogue”: What (or whose) purpose is served by killing? 
The Goddess’s turn of phrase is important here, because the agents of death, the beings 
that “drain another [creature’s] body of its vital breaths,” are identified as Yoginīs, 
Mothers, and Śākinīs. In the NT’s preceding chapter (NT 19) and elsewhere throughout 
the text and medieval South Asian tantra and demonology in general, these and other 
demonesses of their ilk are identified as the primary causes of virtually all untimely 
death and human suffering, and not merely death by sacrifice.20 Furthermore, whereas 
Abhinavagupta appropriated these verses to justify all tantric sacrifice, both animal 
and human, verse 21 of our chapter refers to the victim of the Yoginīs, Mothers, and 
Śākinīs as a puruṣa, a human person. In other words, these introductory verses are not 
merely referring to victims of animal (and in rare cases, human) sacrifice; rather, their 
referents are all humans as potential victims of the diseases, afflictions, and deaths that 
occur when Yoginīs prey upon them. However, as its discussion of supreme yoga makes 
clear, because the Yoginīs are “in no way separate from” Śiva, their yoking and eating 
of their victims is not killing but rather a means to liberation, which in this nondualist 
context connotes the realization, by those victims, of their intrinsic identity with Śiva, 
the sole being in the universe He created. As such, their yoking has the same salvific

--- PAGE 401 ---
376      David Gordon White
 
effect as tantric initiation, in which the guru, after fusing the channels (nāḍīsandhāna, 
nāḍīsaṃghaṭṭa) of his disciple with his own, ensures the former’s liberation.
How this is possible is explained in verse 18’s discussion of the “triad of impurities” 
(malatraya). According to Śaiva metaphysics, the three malas, which are also identified 
as the “fetters” (pāśas) that bind victims to suffering existence, are what differentiate 
Śiva (pati) from his creatures/​victims (paśus).21 With the removal of these impurities 
cum fetters, creatures realize their ontological identity with Śiva. According to the 
Mālinīvijayottara Tantra (MVUT 1.23b, in Brunner, Oberhammer, and Padoux 2000: 
182), the fundamental nature of the first of these malas is nescience (ajñāna), which is, 
as the following section of our chapter proclaims, overcome by the Yoginīs by virtue 
of their Energy of Gnosis (jñānaśakti). According to the dualist metaphysics of the 
Śaivasiddhānta school of medieval Śaivism, the destruction of the malas transforms a 
person into a second Śiva; that is, one becomes like Śiva, but because this is a dualist 
system, only Śiva can be Śiva. Not so in the nondualist contexts of the MVUT and our 
text, where those persons whom the Yoginīs yoke “have in fact become Śiva.” Once 
again, in a universe in which all is Śiva, it would be impossible for a being to not be Śiva.
Furthermore, as verse 16 proclaims, initiation and supreme yoga—​being eaten by 
Yoginīs—​are the prime means to that Self-​realization. This concept appears in a number 
of earlier tantric sources, which have been brilliantly analyzed by Olga Serbaeva Saraogi 
(2010, 2013, 2016). On the one hand, in tantric initiation, called yojanikā (yoking) dīkṣā 
in the Bhairava tantras,22 the guru’s actions are virtually identical to those of Yoginīs 
in subtle yoga (see below). In both cases, these active agents manipulate consciousness 
from inside the disciple’s or victim’s body with the same term, paśu, being applied to the 
passive targets of both of these interventions.23 However, the terminology found in these 
earlier sources differs from that of the NT: instead of para yoga, these favor the term 
haṭhamelaka, a tantric practitioner’s “violent consorting” with the predatory Yoginīs. 
Parallels between the two processes include (1) “possessing” the paśu’s body by entering 
into it and manipulating its channels in order to transform (or destroy) it from within; 
(2) the use of a series of specific mantras and/​or “hypnotizing or possessing” mudrās, 
which in these contexts refer to “complicated acts of mental concentration accompanied 
by particular body positions or movements . . . believed to provoke a modified state of 
consciousness in the practitioner himself or in another person, often without the agree­
ment of the latter” (Saraogi 2010: 68); (3) the ultimate transformation of the paśu into 
Śiva or Bhairava; and (4) a conceptual link between these practices and the special case 
of the “seven-​times born” paśu.24
NT 20.22–​20.37: Subtle Yoga
In drawing her parallels between tantric initiation and haṭhamelaka, Saraogi reads the 
following section of the NT, on “subtle yoga,” to be an account of the same, with the vam­
piric Yoginīs being the active agents of this “yoking” practice. NT 20.1–​20.21 appears

--- PAGE 402 ---
Three Shades of Tantric Yoga      377
 
to support her interpretation. The Goddess’s queries and Śiva’s responses all appear to 
single out the Yoginīs as the agents of the threefold yoga; and the introductory verses 
(22–​27) to this section, which presuppose the nondualist metaphysics of Śiva’s teaching 
on supreme yoga, specifically identify the Yoginīs as its agents. Yet, verse 10 gives pause: 
“[It is] by means of supreme [yoga] alone (pareṇaiva hi), or (tu) by means of the triad 
[i.e.,] by means of [supreme,] subtle, and gross [yoga that] they yoke with their power; 
but in no way do they kill.”25 Are the Yoginīs the actresses of the threefold yoga, or only 
of supreme yoga? Bearing in mind the NT’s composite nature, and in light of the fact 
that the agent of subtle yoga is always given in the masculine gender in the instruction 
portion of this section (vv. 28–​37), one might argue that these instructions on subtle 
“yoking” were originally intended for use by a male yogi.
	
20.22.	 Supreme [yoga] has thus been elucidated, and now subtle [yoga] is also 
proclaimed. Gnosis is subtle, comprised of Energy. Indeed, it is obtained by 
means of the Energy of Gnosis.
	
23.	 The airborne [Yoginīs] partake of that gnosis which, in conformity with 
the sonority of the sound (rāva) [produced] by a sonorous female being 
whose sound is not a sound, affords supernatural perfections (siddhis) to the 
Perfected Ones (Siddhas).

impurity, but those goddesses overcome that [nescience] with [their] pris­

of] someone who is asleep, [moving it] every which way, [or] in quite the 
same way that a drunkard can amuse himself, no matter where he is, by 
drinking liquors . . .
	
26.	 . . . or [in the same way that] a young child, due to his lack of autonomy [in

	 29b–​30.	 Attacking that [vital principle] which is verily situated in the heart, via its

37a.	 The connoisseur of yoga will instantaneously obtain all of that by means of

The rather cryptic language of verse 23 (“the . . . female being whose sound [or cry: rāva] 
is not a sound”) is a reference to an encoded vidyā, a “female” spell that quickens the 
Yoginīs.29 Kṣemarāja’s gloss qualifies this as a “simultaneously arising sound, a reflec­
tion of the primal vibration,” a description that could apply to both mantras, which are 
“male,” and to female vidyās. In fact, NT 15.26a declares that mantras are “embedded 
in the Energy of Gnosis” referenced in both verse 22 and in this verse (“the air­
borne [Yoginīs] partake of that gnosis”). Elsewhere, in his commentary on verse 39, 
Kṣemarāja, quoting the Vyomakuṇḍalinī, evokes another such spell, identifying it as the 
cry (rāva) uttered by the Yoginīs when they devour their victim.30 In their accounts of 
haṭhamelaka, the Tantrasadbhāva Tantra (TST), Jayadrathayāmala (JY), and other early 
sources identify a number of these unarticulated sounds with the cries of great birds 
(cillarāva) and jackals (śivārāva),31 and so one would expect Kṣemarāja’s reference to be 
of a similar sort, casting the Yoginīs as birds and beasts of prey. The identification of their 
cries with the howling of jackals is particularly intriguing, inasmuch as the term used for 
these creatures is śivā, the feminine form of the name of God. Given that the Yoginīs are 
identified in the NT and other works as “possess[ing] the state of oneness [with Śiva]” in 
the form of His Energy,32 jackals constitute their ideal mammalian form. Jackal behavior 
further supports this identification: they feed on their victims in packs (kulas) and are 
notorious for their howling (rāva). This is attested in several tantras, as well as in tantric 
art, including a medieval sculpture from central India, which depicts two jackal-​headed

--- PAGE 404 ---
Three Shades of Tantric Yoga      379
 
Yoginīs feeding on chunks of flesh.33 This notwithstanding, Kṣemarāja internalizes the 
same sky-​faring (khecaryaḥ) Yoginīs as “goddesses who move in the sky of conscious­
ness.”34 Once again, this is of a piece with the nondualist hermeneutic already observed. 
Saraogi (2016: 59, 63) offers a concise summarization of this process:
The fact that the JY links melaka with the mudrās makes it an important step in the 
process of interiorisation of the melaka: a process already embryonic in the TST, and 
which goes on to become a self-​evident reality in the works of Abhinavagupta . . . 
In becoming a practice for the expansion of consciousness, the melaka loses its vi­
sionary external tantric character and becomes rather a non-​dualistic philosophical 
expression of a quasi-​absolute state. . . . I would tentatively suggest that the haṭha 
variety of melaka can be defined as that mode of unity of consciousness between two 
beings in which one is sucked/​transported/​extracted and absorbed into the other; 
precisely the varieties of practices referred to in the Urmikaulārṇava 2 and NT 20.
As for the Siddhas referenced in the latter half of verse 23, Kṣemarāja identifies these 
as “the venerable Lord of the Birds (khagendra), etc.” Khagendra[nātha], “Lord of the 
Birds,” is also the name of the first of a group of four Siddhas, revered as the Kaula mas­
ters of the four ages (yuganāthas). The last of these, Matsyendra[nātha], is featured 
in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya, in which two passages describing the relationship between 
the Yoginīs and Siddhas appear to be addressing the same concept as that found here: 
the Kaula gnosis, which came naturally to the Yoginīs, was transmitted by them to the 
Siddhas through inarticulate sounds.35 The same gnosis (jñāna) affords the Yoginīs 
total control over their victims whose inherent gnosis is clouded over by nescience 
(ajñāna), by virtue of which they are able to manipulate them in the ways metaphori­
cally described in verses 24 to 27.
With verse 28, however, the perspective shifts, as the agent of subtle yoga is given in the 
masculine singular and called a yogi. In his commentary on this verse, Kṣemarāja relates 
it to a passage from the NT’s second chapter, concerning the “most excellent” (paramam) 
Death-​Conqueror mantra.36 It is this embodied mantra, as a source of “supreme strength 
comprised of consciousness,” that empowers the yogi to practice subtle yoga.37
Unlike its account of supreme yoga, the NT’s treatment of subtle yoga does not explic­
itly identify its outcome as identical to that obtained through tantric initiation. However, 
that initiation ritual as presented in the Svacchandabhairava Tantra (SBhT) and other 
earlier tantric texts serves as the blueprint for the sequence of actions the yogi will per­
form here; in fact, this and the eight verses that follow draw upon those prior sources 
more or less directly (Saraogi 2010: 69–​72).38 In his commentary, Kṣemarāja glosses 
“having entered” (praviśya) as “having co-​penetrated” (samāviśya), a term frequently 
employed in the tantras to denote the dynamic of initiation. In the oft-​referenced Śaiva 
initiation ritual called nirvāṇadīkṣā (Davis 1991: 99–​100), the guru penetrates the initiate’s 
body, drawing the latter’s soul into his own body. Following this, he raises their conjoined 
souls along the central channel up to the dvādaśānta located twelve finger-​breadths 
above his fontanel.39 This is the abode of Paramaśiva, with Whom the guru unites the 
initiate’s person, ensuring his release from the fetters that had previously bound him to

--- PAGE 405 ---
380      David Gordon White
 
suffering existence, and thereby ensuring his virtual identity with Śiva. In its discussion 
of the Cause Deities, the SBhT identifies the highest of these—​the para kāraṇa referenced 
in verse 30—​as none other than Paramaśiva, situated in the dvādaśānta.40 So, whereas 
the subtle yoga practiced by the Yoginīs, Mothers, and Secretive Ones issues in the direct 
subjugation of their victims (v. 27b), that of the yogi or initiating guru, detailed in verses 
28 through 36, requires a sequence of steps, and follows a more circuitous path.
Kṣemarāja’s commentary on verses 29 and 30 is also highly instructive, inasmuch as 
it describes the means by which the tantric guru is able to enter into and make his way 
through an initiate’s body. Here, citing the Tattvārthacintāmaṇi of Kallaṭa, he describes 
the “globule practice” (golakābhyāsa) by which a yogi concentrates his vital principle, 
fluid essence, volition, and consciousness into a single subtle droplet, by which he enters 
into his victim’s heart via either the fontanel or toes. Then, quoting from the Āmnāyadṛṣṭi, 
he goes on to describe how, lodged in his victim’s heart for the period of 100 measures and 
activating his breaths,41 the yogi is able to possess another body. So, even as the yogi’s sub­
sequent manipulation of his target’s body imitates that of the Yoginīs, its ultimate effect is 
salutary, the raising of his target’s vital essence or person up to God:
He sets the other person in motion. “The very thing that I do, this one (i.e., the other 
person) shall do that very thing.” Having realized identity with him, the one who 
is overpowering such a person “may overpower his autonomy,” [which means] “he 
shall hold back the one who is intending to go, he shall cause the one who is standing 
still to move.” Gradually, he shall make him dependent upon the movement of his 
own limbs. This has been said by the preceptors: “Stationed there [in the heart of the 
other], he shows himself to be a yogi when the result of his action—​total simultaneity 
of movement—​has been realized, whether he be eating, drinking, moving, standing 
or sleeping. After that, he may fetch him [to himself], let him go, bewilder him, open 
him up, enclose him completely, or cause him to reach the most excellent abode.”42
Kṣemarāja’s commentary (Shastri 1939: 230) on the mudrās evoked in verse 36 is also 
worthy of note, inasmuch as its set of five (karaṅkiṇī, krodhanī, lelihānī, khecarī,43 and 
bhairavī) is the same as that employed by the Ūrmikaulārṇava for both tantric initiation 
and the killing of a paśu (Saraogi 2010: 78). The first of these, the karaṅkiṇī (Skeletal 
Female), appears in the JY in the context of a specific melaka called the cillāsaṃyoga. In 
this practice of “consorting with the cillās,” the Yoginīs appear before the solitary practi­
tioner in the form of female kites (cillās), to whom he offers an oblation cut from the left 
side of his own body.44
NT 20.38–​20.66: Gross Yoga
Kṣemarāja’s commentary notwithstanding, NT 20.36–​20.37 clearly identifies the prac­
titioner of subtle yoga not as a female Yoginī but rather as a male yogi or “connoisseur

--- PAGE 406 ---
Three Shades of Tantric Yoga      381
 
of yoga” (yogavit). Now, as noted above,45 it may be that these verses are employing the 
masculine in order to denote either a male or a female agent, or that “yogi” was tan­
tric shorthand for Yoginī. More cutting and pasting appears in our chapter’s opening 
statements on gross yoga, with the agent of verse 38 being given in the singular and 
verse 39 in the plural. The language of the NT’s discussion of “gross yoga” appears to 
further show the hand of the work’s final redactors, who sought to decant three dis­
tinct bodies of practice—​involving human yogis, superhuman Yoginīs, and malevo­
lent beings, both human and superhuman—​under the single heading of a practice of 
yoga as undertaken by the Yoginīs alone. This is the gist of verse 40, whose second pada 
may be compared to NT 20.2a, in which it was the Śākinīs who were characterized as 
“proud of their powers.” As such, it would appear that the Yoginīs evoked in this verse 
are not supernatural embodied Energies of Śiva but rather malevolent human witches 
or sorceresses, in which case their victims are not liberated, freed from their existential 
fetters, but rather simply slaughtered. Referring back to verse 16, Kṣemarāja’s commen­
tary to this verse appears to support this distinction, referring to these female beings as 
flesh-​eating “mistresses of yoga” (yogeśīs), a term reserved for human witches in other 
medieval works.
As Brunner (1974: 185) has noted, verses 38 and 39 in fact comprise the entirety of 
the chapter’s account of gross yoga, which Kṣemarāja glosses as “this or that vengeful 
act [accomplished] through assorted vile tricks, poisoning, and so forth.” The sole form 
of gross yoga actually mentioned by name in these verses is the charnel ground-​based 
sorcery known as the “dust practice” (pāṃsava), for which our commentator provides 
a description based on revelations made by Śiva in the Gupta Tantra (Shastri 1939: 233):
O my darling! At daybreak on the dark seventh of the lunar fortnight, the Yoginī, 
who, whether she be skillful or not, is empowered by the application of mantras, shall 
always choose her target; firstly, [the corpse of] a woman who has come into view, as 
well as [that of] a man. Taking the left and right feet of these with her left and right 
hands, and removing the dust that is on the right foot of the man together with the 
dust of the left foot of the woman, she may always kill in my [i.e., Śiva’s] world.
The mention of dhyānayoga in verse 39 reopens the question of the applicability of the 
terminology of six-​ or eight-​part yoga to our text. If we are to follow Kṣemarāja once 
again, these have little in common, since he reads the term as referring to a Yoginī’s “ex­
traction of the five nectars” (pañcāmṛtākarṣaṇa) of her victim, a practice referenced 
above in verse 27 and dramatized in Bhavabhūti’s eighth-​century Mālatīmādhava.46
As Kṣemarāja indicates, verses 41 to 43 are devoted to the protection of potential 
victims from supreme yoga, and verses 44 and 45 for the protection of potential victims 
from subtle yoga. He then introduces verse 46 by noting that it and the verses that 
follow will treat of the release of a person who has been possessed (mudrita) through 
the workings of gross yoga. When his adversaries are employing supreme yoga, the tan­
tric practitioner must combat them through supreme yoga, that is, by deploying the 
Death-​Conqueror mantra. Once again, one cannot help but observe that there is an

--- PAGE 407 ---
382      David Gordon White
 
internal contradiction here, since it is the Yoginīs’ supreme yoga precisely—​which verse 
20 of our chapter characterized as effecting their victims’ “release from suffering exist­
ence”—​that the connoisseur of spells (mantravit) is called upon to counter here. The 
same conundrum obtains when our text sets out to describe the defense of potential 
victims from subtle yoga, in verses 44 and 45. Its not altogether satisfactory solution is to 
qualify its agents—​both male and female, human and superhuman—​as wicked (duṣṭa) 
and injurious (hiṃsaka). This is at variance with verse 6, in which Śiva had declared 
that the Yoginīs, Mothers, and Śākinīs “do not [slaughter] out of confusion, nor for the 
sake of injury, nor indeed out of a desire to slay.” Verse 66, which concludes this section, 
comprises a weak attempt to resolve this contradiction.
The final twenty verses on gross yoga provide a general description of the tantric 
specialist—​variously referred to as a mantravit, mantra master (mantrin), mantra 
master cum connoisseur of yoga (yogavinmantrin), or local practitioner (daiśika)—​and 
his practice.
	
37b.	 Subtle yoga has been fully recounted: gross [yoga] is now declared.
	
38.	 By means of it, one shall assuredly draw the target’s indwelling self toward 
one’s own body through the expedient of mudrās and mantras, as well as by 
means of the dust practice.
	
39.	 By the sole power of [their] “yoking meditation” (dhyānayoga47) targeting 
bodily features—​hidden markings, etc.—​they undoubtedly destroy the 
fleshly fortress of their victims.48
	
40.	 When the Yogi[nī]s who are proud of their powers49 wish to slaughter by 
means of the threefold yoga, O Goddess, then the Death-​Conqueror shall act 
in a way conducive to [their targets’] welfare.
	
41.	 The nature of supreme [meditation] is its pervasiveness. By means of that 
alone, the connoisseur of spells (mantravit) knows the Death-​Conqueror 
(Mṛtyujit) [mantra to be] the excellent immortal god (Amṛteśa) who has 
faces in every direction.50
	
42.	 The mantra master (mantrin), recognizing that (i.e., the Yoginīs’ wish to 
slaughter) to be supreme yoga shall, [by] pervading the [body-​]fortress of 
their [potential] victim, [and] standing guard over [it] with his Energy of 
Desire, defend the good life of [all] creatures.51
	
43.	 O glorious One! The mantra master cum connoisseur of yoga 
(yogavinmantrin), recognizing the subtle [yoga] of both [evil] yogis and all 
the aforementioned injurious ones (i.e., evil Yoginīs, Śākinīs, etc.) on the

	 44–​45.	 . . . shall, by the piercing of the aforementioned knots [and by] energetically

is never otherwise. Endowed with the powers [accrued] through the yoking

Coda: NT 20.67–​20.75
The two Kathmandu manuscript witnesses to this chapter are more or less consistent 
with the Kashmir edition I have used here. However, those manuscripts end at verse 64, 
with their final two verses being absent from the Kashmir edition. While the final verses 
of the Kashmir edition, given below, provide further data concerning the mighty female 
beings that are the agents of gross yoga, they do not treat of gross yoga itself, nor do they 
provide any new information. They are little more than an encapsulation of NT 19.12–​
19.30, in which it is Śiva himself who recounts the events described here. It is for that 
reason that the discourse shifts from the third person to the first person between verses 
67 and 68. All that remains is for Śiva to declare, one final time, the irresistible power of 
the Death-​Conqueror mantra, which He does.
	
67.	 In a former time, they were commanded by me through the use of mudrās 
and mantras. They do not seek to destroy for their own individual sake. For 
that reason they are declared to be powerful.60

	 74b–​75b.	 And by virtue of that (i.e., His virility), it is called the Death-​Conqueror,

Conclusion
As is the case with the nondualist Hindu tantras in general, the NT is a gnostic system, 
with the attainment or realization of gnosis (jñāna)—​transformative esoteric insight 
triggering a sudden expansion of consciousness—​tantamount to the transcendence of 
the human condition. In these traditions, however, the attainment of said gnosis is less 
often realized through philosophical analysis than through active ingestion of either a 
Yoginī’s sexual or menstrual emission or the caru, a mixture of prohibited or polluting 
human bodily emissions; or through the penetration, even violation, of a passive body 
either by an initiating guru or by a Yoginī. This can take the form of possession, benign 
in the case of a guru but maleficent in the case of an evil yogi. It can also take the form of 
the total or partial consumption of one’s body by Yoginīs. Here, gnosis is weaponized, as 
it were, and wielded like a tooth, a claw, or a scalpel. In all cases, gnosis effects a sudden 
transformation of consciousness in its passive target, even if such can sometimes prove

--- PAGE 411 ---
386      David Gordon White
 
fatal. As Brunner (1975: 435) has opined, the sadhaka of our text would have been the 
direct descendent of “popular magicians versed in the sciences of spells . . . herbal 
concoctions, metals, and so forth.” Clearly, the NT’s twentieth chapter on the threefold 
yoga is a record of that legacy.
But what does that legacy have to do with yoga? Can the activities of the NT’s yogis 
and Yoginīs, figures whose names would indicate that they were the prime agents or 
practitioners of yoga, be reconciled with yoga in the proper sense of the term? Which begs 
the question: what is the proper sense of the term “yoga”? Contemporary scholarly con­
vention and popular opinion maintain that the Yoga Sūtras have defined “classical yoga” 
for some 1,500 years, with all that has followed tributary to Patañjali’s system. Compiled in 
the ninth century ce, the NT’s account of the threefold yoga dates from heart of the period 
in which the Yoga Sūtras were enjoying their greatest pre-​twentieth-​century popularity in 
India and the wider world (White 2014: 159–​171). Yet, as we have seen, even in the rare cases 
in which the NT references the Yoga Sūtras, its account of the work and the eight-​part yoga 
differ wildly from their referent. This tendency is not unique to the NT or to either tantric or 
non-​tantric scripture and commentary in general. Time and again throughout history, the 
Yoga Sūtras have been invoked only to be misrepresented. How are we to explain these per­
ennial uses and abuses of Patañjali’s so-​called foundational work?
A comparison with the role of the Veda as a touchstone of Hindu self-​identity may 
help to resolve this conundrum. As Brian K. Smith (1987: 45) has noted,
the great paradox of Hinduism . . . is that, although the religion is inextricably tied 
to the legitimizing authority of the Veda, in post-​Vedic times the subject matter of 
the Veda is largely unknown by those who define themselves in relation to it . . . The 
Hindus, it would seem, use only the “outside” of the Veda, oblivious to its “inside.”
In other words, the Veda, the language of whose mantras is incomprehensible to the 
Hindus who identify it as the foundation of their religion, is an empty signifier. The yoga 
subculture’s elevation of the Yoga Sūtras to the status of divine revelation (śrūti) on a par 
with that of the Veda has the same implications (White 2014: 212–​215). No matter that its 
aphorisms are incomprehensible to virtually all gurus and practitioners of postural yoga 
and only distantly related to their practice, it is the authority of that work that legitimizes 
their contemporary practice. As such, the authority of the Yoga Sūtras is for them an ar­
ticle of faith. While believers are entitled to their beliefs, scholars are not. The embrace 
by scholar-​practitioners of the yoga subculture’s contemporary belief system, over and 
against the historical record, is unacceptable.

against those same spirit beings when they attack creatures (especially those belonging

Chapter 17
Generative Buddhahood
Enlightened Plants and Trees in Japanese 
Tendai Esoteric Buddhism
Matthew D. McMullen
Becoming a buddha, the goal of Buddhist soteriology, is fundamentally a cognitive pro­
cess. Therefore, one would presume that sentience is a necessary component of enlight­
enment. But what about living things such as plants and trees, which are traditionally 
not considered to have sentience, or are marginally sentient?
The topic of the enlightenment of plants and trees, or that of enlightened plants and 
trees, is often discussed in the context of buddha-nature thought, and for good reason. 
The question of what is buddha-nature and to what extent it permeates sentient beings 
and the world around them is treated extensively in Chinese and Japanese Buddhist 
sources. Rather than add to an already extensive body of scholarship on the connection 
between buddha-nature and the sentience of plants and trees in East Asian Buddhism 
(see, e.g., Rambelli 2001; Sueki 2015), I would like to propose an alternative explanation 
that positions the development of this concept within the framework of Buddhist cos­
mology and the generation of buddha lands.
The view of the cosmos in Buddhism is complex and diverse. Because heavens, hells, 
and multiple rebirths in a variety of supernatural worlds were largely assumed as a part 
of the broader ancient Indian worldview, there is no definitive representation of the 
cosmos even in the earliest Buddhist sources (Gethin 1997, 186–​187). In China, Buddhist 
cosmology was fused with indigenous notions of the afterlife (Teiser 1994, 11–​20). In 
Japan, buddhas and other members of the Buddhist pantheon were paired with local 
deities, creating networks of sacred and celestial spaces, which included geographic 
formations such as mountains and waterfalls (Teeuwen and Rambelli 2003, 29–​30). 
However, despite this diversity of philosophical and cultural conceptions of the cosmos, 
Buddhist scholastics have tended to draw a parallel between the structure of world sys­
tems and abstract doctrines concerning the path to liberation.
This chapter examines an early and influential version of the discourse on the 
Buddhahood of plants and trees found in the writings of Annen 安然 (841 to 889, or

--- PAGE 421 ---
396      Matthew D. McMullen
 
915), a ninth-​century scholastic monk in the Japanese Tendai school and patriarch of 
Tendai esoteric Buddhism. Annen’s discussion of vegetal Buddhahood expanded on 
previous writings in Chinese Buddhism on the buddha-nature of plants and trees and, 
by extension, insentient objects.
In addition to addressing the classical discourse on the buddha-nature of things as 
inherited from his predecessors, Annen devised his own interpretation by situating 
the proposition that plants and trees can become buddhas within the cosmogony of 
buddha lands. This fusing of the path to becoming a buddha, which is a cognitive pro­
cess requiring sentience, with a cosmic typology, which is essentially spatial and mate­
rial, was fundamental to Annen’s notion of esoteric Buddhism.
Buddhist Cosmogony and the 
Generation of Buddha Lands
Among the Mahāyāna sutras, perhaps the most comprehensive and fantastic view of 
buddha lands can be found in the first chapter of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra. Unlike sutras 
such as the Sukhāvatīvyūha, which focus on the teachings of a single buddha in a partic­
ular buddha land, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra proposes a general theory of how buddha lands 
come into existence (Sadakata 2009, 113–​116). In the first chapter of the sutra, an at­
tendee named “Accumulator of Jewels” (Baoji 寶積) addresses the Buddha, asking him 
to explain how a buddha land is purified by a bodhisattva (Taishō no. 405, 14:538a15–​
14.538a18; McRae 2004, 75–​76). In his response, the Buddha explains how buddha lands 
are generated, stating that a bodhisattva obtains a buddha land according to the needs 
of the sentient beings who will occupy that land. Specifically, a bodhisattva purifies a 
buddha land depending on the discipline, wisdom, and faculties of the sentient beings 
they are assisting. Therefore, the generation of a buddha land is always contingent upon 
the interaction between sentient beings and the bodhisattva. The Buddha elaborates on 
the symbiotic nature of buddha lands, explaining to Accumulator of Jewels that these 
lands are the space in which a bodhisattva fulfills his vow to save sentient beings. Just 
as the teachings are adapted to the needs and capabilities of the individual, so too is the 
space in which these teachings occur. The lands are simply reflections of the sentient 
beings who are to be reborn in them (Taishō no. 405, 14:538a21–​14:538a23).
Although the Buddha explains buddha lands as a space for saving sentient beings, 
these lands are not necessarily located in a distant corner of the cosmos. Rather, they are 
the by-​product of the bodhisattvas’ perfection of their practices and vows. The Buddha 
tells his assembly that a bodhisattva purifies his land by cultivating a sincere and pro­
found mind, proclaiming:
Accumulator of Jewels, you should know that a sincere mind is the bodhisattva’s pure 
land. When a bodhisattva becomes a buddha, sentient beings who are not deceitful 
will be reborn in this land. A profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land. When a

--- PAGE 422 ---
Generative Buddhahood      397
 
bodhisattva becomes a buddha, sentient beings who are replete with merit will be re­
born in this land. Accumulator of Jewels, the types of sentient beings are the buddha 
lands of the bodhisattvas. Why? Because bodhisattvas obtain buddha lands in ac­
cordance with the sentient beings they transform.
(Taishō no. 405, 14:538b1–​14:538b4; McRae 2004, 76)
In other words, when bodhisattvas direct their minds toward the attainment of 
Buddhahood, they generate lands in which sentient beings can also develop minds to­
ward awakening. The Buddha continues to detail how bodhisattvas can purify their 
lands and become buddhas by cultivating a variety of Mahāyāna practices. The point 
of this passage, of course, is that cultivating these practices will assist sentient beings 
by causing them to be reborn in the appropriate buddha land where they, like the 
bodhisattvas, can perfect these practices under the guidance of a buddha.
For Chinese and Japanese exegetes, this brief passage in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra was 
central to how these lands function as loci for the path toward becoming a buddha. In 
the earliest commentary on the sutra, Sengzhao 僧肇 (384–​414), a member of the team 
that translated the Vimalakīrti Sūtra into Chinese, explains buddha lands as imperma­
nent mental constructions that are conditioned by the beings who reside within them, 
thus concluding that the distinction between buddha lands is completely subjective. A 
buddha land arises in response to the actions of sentient beings; it does not exist inde­
pendently (Taishō 38:327a27–​38:327b5; Chappell 1977, 22–​53; Sharf 2002, 37).
Sengzhao’s commentary inspired further exegesis of the buddha land passage in the 
Vimalakīrti Sūtra. The great Chinese scholastics of the sixth century, Jingyingsi Huiyuan 
淨影寺慧遠 (523–​592), Jizang 吉藏 (549–​623), and the founder of the Tiantai school 
Zhiyi 智顗 (538–​597) each developed complex taxonomies of buddha lands based on 
the above passage from the sutra (Mochizuki 1942, 107–​111). Zhiyi’s twenty-​eight fas­
cicle commentary on the sutra, the Weimojing Wenshu 維摩經文疏, is perhaps the most 
extensive treatment of the buddha land concept (Ōkubo 2004, 107–​127). According to 
Zhiyi, the sutra explains the circumstantial causes for attaining Buddhahood, rather 
than the direct causes—​such as practice, precepts, wisdom, and so on—​that must be cul­
tivated by the individual to attain rebirth in these lands. Therefore, not only do one’s di­
rect actions determine rebirth, and ultimately liberation from it, but the environment in 
which these actions occur also conditions the results. The world in which one inhabits, 
its contents (climate, vegetation, landscape, etc.), and the buddhas and bodhisattvas that 
share this space are an essential factor in attaining liberation.
Although buddha lands are theoretically infinite in number, Zhiyi, in typical scho­
lastic fashion, nonetheless takes it upon himself to categorize these infinite lands into 
four types. Although later commentators expand on his four-​part taxonomy (Chappell 
1977, 32–​36; Oda 1954, 749–​750), the basic model prescribed in the first fascicle of the 
Weimojing Wenshu can be summarized as follows:
	
1.	 Lands where worldlings and sages both reside (fansheng tongju tu 凡聖同居土) 
consist of both impure lands, like our Sahā world (the buddha land of Śākyamuni), 
and pure lands such as Amitābha’s Sukhāvatī, the difference being that the former

--- PAGE 423 ---
398      Matthew D. McMullen
 
includes the evil destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, whereas pure lands 
do not (Shinsan dai Nihon zokuzōkyō 27:864).
	
2.	 Lands of skillful means for those with remaining attachments (fanbian youyu 
tu 方便有餘土) are occupied by the “nonreturners” (buhuan 不還) specified in 
the Abhidharma treatises and bodhisattvas of the lower stages of the Mahāyāna 
path who have yet to eliminate all of their attachments to ignorant views and 
perceptions (Shinsan dai Nihon zokuzōkyō 27:864).
	
3.	 Lands of true reward without obstacles (shibao wuzhangai tu 實報無障礙土) are 
where advanced bodhisattvas become buddhas. Ignorance and obstacles are com­
pletely eliminated, negative actions cease, and, as a result, the bodhisattva attains a 
new body with all of the marks of a buddha (Shinsan dai Nihon zokuzōkyō 27:864).
	 4.	 The land of eternally quiescent radiance (chang jiguang tu 常寂光土) is the 
most abstract of these lands and, subsequently, it became the focal point of eso­
teric conceptions of buddha lands. In the third type of land the advanced bodhi­
sattva exits the cosmological structure entirely, becomes an awakened being, and 
generates a new buddha land. This land, however, is unoccupied, no one can be 
reborn in this land, and there is no mental activity. Zhiyi calls it the “nature of the 
Dharma as it is,” “the essence of the Buddha without form or land,” “the aspect that 
preaches through a body and in a land, but is neither the body nor the land.” In 
other words, “lands of eternally quiescent radiance” denotes the spatial dimension 
in which the path toward Buddhahood is complete and the entirety of the cosmos 
is comprehended from the perspective of a fully awakened buddha (Shinsan dai 
Nihon zokuzōkyō 27:865–​27:866). The form of the buddha abiding in the land of 
eternally quiescent radiance is typically referred to as the dharmakāya, or body of 
the Dharma.
Although somewhat recondite in detail, taxonomies of buddha lands such as the one 
outlined above are not merely scholastic wordplay. Rather, they have a soteriological 
objective. Zhiyi stipulates that there are two ways of understanding rebirth in the var­
ious types of buddha lands. The first is a hierarchical interpretation: as one perfects the 
practices of generosity and precepts, they are reborn in a pure land where they can fur­
ther advance the practices that will inevitably lead to being reborn in the third category 
of land where they finally attain Buddhahood. The second is a lateral interpretation; one 
can be reborn or become a buddha in any land depending on the vows and intention 
of the bodhisattva who generated that land at the moment of enlightenment (Shinsan 
dai Nihon zokuzōkyō 27:869). In the first interpretation, enlightenment depends on the 
cognitive activity and moral actions of the individual, but, in the latter, the land and 
its material content define the conditions by which its inhabitants attain Buddhahood. 
This two-​part hermeneutic is again based on the first chapter of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra in 
which the Buddha explains that the practices of generosity, precepts, and so on deter­
mine the structure, inhabitants, and environment of the bodhisattva’s purified buddha 
land (Taishō no. 405, 14:538b; McRae 2004, 76–​77). Zhiyi concludes that it is possible to 
be reborn in any of the lands because they are all generated from the awakened mind of

--- PAGE 424 ---
Generative Buddhahood      399
 
the Buddha. Therefore, from this perspective, the land of eternally quiescent radiance is 
none other than our Sahā world (Shinsan dai Nihon zokuzōkyō 28:1).
Mantra and Cosmogony in Japanese 
Esoteric Buddhism
Cosmogony also factored into how esoteric Buddhism was interpreted in Japan. 
Esoteric Buddhism in East Asia is difficult to define in simple terms. In the broad 
sense of involving rites concealed from the public or transmissions of teachings whose 
methods were closely guarded, the term “esoteric” can be applied to most religious 
traditions. However, if we limit the scope of usage, it specifically concerns the practice 
and transmission of reciting secret incantations. Therefore, simply put, in the Japanese 
context esoteric Buddhism denotes ritual, doctrinal, textual, and institutional traditions 
that take the recitation of mantra (shingon in Japanese) as their primary religious ac­
tivity (Matsunaga 1989, 15).
Defining mantra and their soteriological purport, however, is itself a rather complex 
issue and has been the topic of scholastic writings for a millennium. Interpretations of 
mantra are frequently associated with Kūkai 空海 (774–​835), the revered founder of the 
Shingon school who returned from China in 806 claiming to have been initiated into a 
lineage of Buddhism that he cryptically referred to as the “esoteric treasury” (mitsuzō 
密藏) (Takagi and Dreitlein 2010, 200–​201). In his catalog, the Shōrai mokuroku 
将來目錄, Kūkai links this esoteric treasury to translations and commentaries 
composed by Amoghavajra (705–​774), the Chinese-​born tantric master and pro­
genitor of his lineage. In particular, he highlights Amoghavajra’s translation of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and its ritual manuals, collectively known as the Vajra 
Peak Sūtra (Jingangding jing 金剛頂經), which were new to Japan at the time. In his 
catalog and later works, Kūkai presents these texts, their associated rituals, and, in par­
ticular, their enclosed mantra as an esoteric form of Buddhism, which he distinguishes 
from the dominant Mahāyāna schools (Abé 1999, 180–​184).
Kūkai’s signature claim regarding the esoteric treasury, which later became the pri­
mary doctrine of the Shingon school, was that the teachings constituting the esoteric 
sutras, the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and Mahāvairocana Sūtra, were originally 
expounded by the dharmakāya. On the one hand, this is a radical claim when con­
sidering that it was made in the context of a scholastic Buddhist tradition in Nara that 
traced the Buddhist teachings to various moments in Śākyamuni’s lifetime (Abé 1999, 
10). By definition, the dharmakāya is void of speech and mental activity and abides in 
a constant state of quiescent bliss (i.e., the fourth type of buddha land in Zhiyi’s par­
adigm). In other words, the dharmakāya was conceived of as the embodiment of en­
lightenment. Suggesting that it preaches, or even has the capacity to preach, negates the 
conventional notion that the dharmakāya as inconceivable to sentient beings. On the

--- PAGE 425 ---
400      Matthew D. McMullen
 
other hand, the fact that the buddhadharma originates with the dharmakāya, or is the 
teaching of the dharmakāya, is obvious. If one assumes that the words preached by any 
buddha are true regardless of the time, place, or form of the Buddha who preaches them, 
then these words must be from the dharmakāya (McMullen 2016, 3); or, as Kūkai states 
in his catalog, “The Dharma is originally beyond words, but without words it cannot be 
revealed” (Takagi and Dreitlein 2010, 12).
In his writing on sound and syllables (Shōji jissōgi 聲字實相義), Kūkai elaborates on 
this association between language and the dharmakāya. According to Kūkai, language 
consists of three components: (1) sound caused by vibrations in the air; (2) syllables that 
signify sounds; and (3) reality, which Kūkai equates with the dharmakāya. Language 
is the result of differentiating sounds, syllables, and reality to create meaning (Takagi 
and Dreitlein 2010, 84). Put another way, syllables are derived from differentiating 
sounds, and words are created by the arranging of syllables. The individual sounds and 
syllables themselves do not inherently have meaning, and the reality to which sounds 
and syllables point are the fact that they are empty of any inherent meaning. In Kūkai’s 
theory of language, this emptiness is personified by the dharmakāya. Thus, language, as 
a system of sounds and syllables, forms a “cosmic text,” which “is the ultimate scripture 
of emptiness” (Abé 1999, 15). This “scripture of emptiness” has been transmitted to our 
Sahā world in the form of mantra.
In contrast to Kūkai’s hermeneutics of mantra, which was intended to complement 
the scholastic schools in Nara (Abé 1999, 189), the Japanese Tendai school situated 
the esoteric teachings of mantra within the Tiantai/​Tendai doctrinal system. In this 
system, first proposed by Zhiyi and gradually systematized by subsequent generations 
of Chinese scholastics, the differences between multifarious teachings, sutras, practices, 
and buddhas only exist to the extent that they are adapted to the needs and capabilities 
of the individual. Therefore, for a bodhisattva with advanced abilities to comprehend 
the totality of the Buddha’s teachings, the teachings are ultimately identical; in the 
Tendai tradition this is called the “perfect teaching” (engyō 圓教) (Swanson 2018, 2030). 
However, Zhiyi and the Chinese patriarchs were unfamiliar with the esoteric teaching of 
mantra as expounded in the Mahāvairocana Sūtra and Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, 
and, as a result, they were not included in the classical Tiantai taxonomies of teachings. 
What distinguishes the Japanese Tendai school from its Chinese counterpart was an ef­
fort to incorporate the esoteric teaching of mantra into the Tendai system, which came 
to be known as the perfect-​esoteric (enmitsu 圓密) teaching. The person primarily re­
sponsible for this integration was an unrenowned Tendai scholar monk named Annen 
of Godaiin 五大院.
Unlike his predecessors in the Tendai school such as Saichō 最澄 (766–​822), Ennin 
圓仁 (794–​864), and Enchin 圓珍 (814–​891), Annen left behind few disciples to docu­
ment his biographical details. Based on the limited records available, he seems to have 
been rather isolated on Mt. Hiei and was not involved in the political jockeying for rank 
that was typical of scholar monks at the time. According to his biography in the Genkō 
shakusho 元亨釋書 (Dai Nihon Bukkyō zensho 101:183–​101:185), a fourteenth-​century 
collection of eminent monk biographies in Japan, Annen was in the lineage of Saichō

--- PAGE 426 ---
Generative Buddhahood      401
 
and studied under Ennin. He was consecrated as an ācārya in 884, probably under the 
tutelage of the famed Tendai ritualist and poet Henjō 遍昭 (816–​890). Despite the lack 
of historical information about Annen’s life, his writings were foundational to the de­
velopment of a Tendai esoteric tradition. His extant works include catalogs of imported 
esoteric texts and ritual implements, summaries of esoteric rites and their respective 
lineages, and doctrinal writings on the esoteric teaching of mantra (Dolce and Mano 
2011, 768–​769; Sueki 1995, 42–​63).
Unlike Kūkai’s view of esoteric Buddhism that emphasizes sound and syllables as the 
primary components of mantra, Annen situated mantra within the Tendai taxonomical 
system of teachings and practices to create a comprehensive interpretation of mantra 
and esoteric Buddhism. By Annen’s definition, the esoteric teachings are the culmina­
tion of all teachings preached by all buddhas in all conceivable locations throughout the 
past, present, and future (Taishō no. 2396, 75:374a). Thus, Annen applied Zhiyi’s four-​
part model of buddha lands to explain how the esoteric teaching of mantra is universally 
accessible to all beings in all buddha lands, including plants and trees.
The problem for Annen was not only that Zhiyi did not account for the esoteric 
sutras in his doctrinal system but that the esoteric sutras do not fit neatly into the 
buddha land paradigm. The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, for instance, states that 
Mahāvairocana preaches to an assembly of all tathāgatas (sarvatathāgata), who in turn 
consecrate the bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi (Taishō no. 848, 18:207–​18:208; Giebel 
2001, 19–​25), and the Mahāvairocana Sūtra simply opens by stating that the Great 
Sun Tathāgata (Dainichi Nyorai, 大日如來, i.e., Mahāvairocana) preaches to a group 
of bodhisattvas and vajra-​wielding beings (Taishō no. 848, 18:1). Most sutras identify 
their location in the opening lines, which is set within Śākyamuni’s biography. Thus, 
the vast majority of sutras claim to have been preached in our Sahā world sometime 
during Śākyamuni’s lifetime. Although the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha takes place 
in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the highest meditative state in the realm of form), the sutra 
does not situate the Buddha’s teaching within a particular buddha land (Taishō no. 865, 
18:17a). Both texts describe Mahāvairocana as traversing conventional notions of past, 
present, and future. Therefore, the opening scenes of the esoteric sutras are, literally, 
not of this world.
To make sense of the esoteric sutras and their teachings, Annen employed Zhiyi’s 
four-​part buddha land paradigm. First, he uncovered two references to the land of the 
esoteric teachings. In the commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, the land in which 
Mahāvairocana preaches is identified as the buddha land of Secret Adornment (miyan 
fotu 密嚴佛土) (Zoku Tendaishū zensho 1:76b). This land is described in a relatively ob­
scure sutra by the same name, which describes this land as a land of “unlimited radi­
ance” and “has as its characteristic the adorning of all other buddha lands” (Taishō no. 
681, 16:723c8–​16:723c13). Applied to the taxonomy of buddha lands, this passage would 
suggest that the land of Secret Adornment is a title for the land of eternally quiescent 
radiance in Zhiyi’s typology. However, a passage in the Putixinlun 菩提心論, an au­
thoritative esoteric treatise translated by Amoghavajra, the land of Secret Adornment 
is where a bodhisattva is reborn before immediately attaining Buddhahood “without

--- PAGE 427 ---
402      Matthew D. McMullen
 
having to get up from his seat” (Taishō no. 1665, 32:574c19–​32:574c20). This description 
in the treatise suggests that the land of Secret Adornment is a land of true reward (i.e., 
the third type of land in Zhiyi’s paradigm), because it is the location in which a bodhi­
sattva becomes a buddha before generating a new buddha land.
This contradiction regarding the buddha land of Secret Adornment as the location of 
the esoteric teachings required explanation. Annen’s solution was that the land in which 
Mahāvairocana preaches the esoteric teachings is actually both types of land. Thus, the 
land of “the aspect of the Buddha that preaches through a body and in a land, but is 
neither the body nor the land,” that is the dharmakāya, is accessible in the land of true 
reward (Taishō no. 2396, 75:427c13–​75.427c16; no. 2397, 75:480b18–​75.480b24; Ōkubo 
2022, 87). Mantra are the language of the dharmakāya as manifested in lands inhabited 
by sentient beings. Therefore, Annen concludes, the mantra teachings of the esoteric 
sutras are the preaching of the dharmakāya.
Making a similar deduction to Kūkai’s theory of sound, syllable, and reality, Annen 
proposed that the preaching of the dharmakāya in the form of mantra is found in the 
various buddha lands. However, unlike Kūkai, his theory was not premised on the dif­
ferentiation of sound. Rather, according to Annen, the way in which this preaching is 
accessed depends on the conditions of the buddha land.
In a dialogic exchange in his compendium on the mantra teachings (Shingonshū 
kyōji gi 眞言宗教時義, or commonly known as the Kyōji mondō 教時問答), Annen 
addresses a question regarding the correlation between buddha lands and mantra 
from Ennin’s commentary of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the Kongōchō daikyōō 
kyōsho 金剛頂大教王經疏. In his commentary, Ennin attempts to explain how the 
teachings of this esoteric sutra came to be documented in a written text if they were 
preached by the dharmakāya to the bodhisattvas. He reasons that these teachings only 
find their way into speech, and then written text, because in the Sahā world, our own 
buddha land, this is the primary form of communication. Then he writes:
In general, if words have sound, then they can be called mantra. In some cases, there 
are lands where one attains the path [to becoming a buddha] if touched by the di­
vine garments. In some cases, one attains the path upon seeing the radiance of the 
Buddha. In some cases, one attains the path by quietly discerning the mind without 
words. In this way, the fragrant lands take aroma as the deeds of the Buddha.
(Taishō no. 2223, 61:11a16–​61.11a20)
Annen poses the quote from Ennin’s commentary as a question, inquiring as to how 
there could be mantra in such lands in which sound is of less importance than our 
world. He responded by redefining mantra not just as oral utterances but as any perceiv­
able object.
Alluding to Kūkai’s theory of language in the Shōji jissōgi, Annen proposed that 
mantra have three components: (1) syllable, (2) sound, and (3) meaning. If any 
one of these elements is present, then it can be defined as mantra (Taishō no. 2396, 
75:417a19–​75:417a21). Therefore, even if there are no sound or written syllables,

--- PAGE 428 ---
Generative Buddhahood      403
 
mantra can be said to exist in that land if their meaning is accessible through some 
sensory means (Ōkubo 2022, 92).
Both Kūkai’s sound-​based theory and Annen’s application of buddha lands to the her­
meneutics of mantra have been consequential to the cosmogonic function of language. 
Kūkai’s theory of cosmic generation via the differentiation of sound harkened back to 
an ancient notion of language as progenitor of the cosmos found in the Vedas and, later, 
in Indian tantras (Payne 2018, 90). Annen’s model, however, went beyond language to 
include all phenomena as conditioned by the genesis of a buddha land. Sound is not the 
only vehicle for transmitting the esoteric teaching of mantra. Any of the senses can per­
ceive a mantra, and any object can transmit it: even plants and trees.
Esoteric Interpretations of Buddha 
Lands and Their Inhabitants
Annen formulated his discussion of the enlightenment of plants and trees as a re­
sponse to a question in a series of letters composed a generation earlier. In 844, 
Tokuen 徳圓 (b. 785), the interim abbot of Mt. Hiei and head of the Tendai school 
in Japan, sent a letter consisting of ten questions regarding esoteric Buddhism to the 
Chinese Tiantai master Zongying 宗頴 (d.u.) in the Tang capital of Chang’an. One 
of these questions concerned the possibility that insentient plants and trees could 
attain Buddhahood. In his letter, Tokuen asks, “Is it because the mind [seeking en­
lightenment] pervades [the space of] insentient objects that plants and trees become 
buddhas? Or, must plants and trees themselves cultivate the conditions to become 
buddhas? Or, is it because the direct reward [of becoming a buddha] encompasses 
the circumstantial reward [of generating a container world]” (Nihon daizōkyō 78:218–​
78:219)? In other words, Tokuen asks if plants and trees become buddhas on their 
own, which would require sentience, or if they become buddhas as a consequence of a 
bodhisattva generating a buddha land.
As with many of the other questions in Tokuen’s letter, Zongying never provided a 
direct response to his question. Rather, Zongying cited the opening chapter of the 
Vimalakīrti Sūtra in which the Buddha explains to the Accumulator of Jewels that 
all buddha lands are pure according to the purity of the mind of the bodhisattva who 
generates it (Taishō no. 405, 14:538c4–​14:538c5; McRae 2004, 78). Therefore, Zongying 
claims, the mind of the bodhisattva-​cum-​buddha and the land are ultimately indistin­
guishable. Referencing the sutra, he explains to Tokuen the purport of the buddha land 
doctrine, writing, “You should know that when an enlightened mind realizes [that the 
land and mind are the same], among all phenomena there is nothing that has not awoken 
[as a buddha].” Therefore, according to Zongying’s reckoning, the notion that plants and 
trees cultivate the necessary practices to become buddhas is absurd. One is deluded, 
he exclaims, if they seek to understand how plants and trees cultivate the practices

--- PAGE 429 ---
404      Matthew D. McMullen
 
necessary to attain Buddhahood in the Sahā world “like a man with poor eyesight trying 
to see fruit blooming from flowers in the sky” (Nihon daizōkyō 78:218–​78:219).
Annen’s theory of the enlightenment of plants and trees was an extended response to 
Tokuen’s inquiry. However, unlike Zongying, he did not merely dismiss it as a misun­
derstanding of Tiantai/​Tendai teachings. Rather, he situated this concept within Zhiyi’s 
taxonomy of buddha lands.
As previous scholarship has pointed out, Annen’s essay on becoming a buddha in 
one’s current body, Sokushin jōbutsu shiki 即身成佛私記, was seminal to the develop­
ment of the enlightenment of plants and trees discourse in Japan (Rambelli 2007, 31–​
32; Sueki 2015). In this essay, Annen frequently refers to Zhiyi’s taxonomy of buddha 
lands when discussing the structure of the Buddhist path. Those at the lower stages 
are rewarded by being reborn and dwelling in lands where worldlings and sages both 
reside, either the higher stages in the impure lands or in a pure land (i.e., type one of 
Zhiyi’s taxonomy). Those in the middle level of the path are rewarded by being reborn 
in lands where worldlings and sages both reside (type two). Those at the higher levels 
of the path are reborn in lands of true reward without obstacles (type three). Finally, 
ultimate awakening occurs when all people dwell in the land of eternally quiescent ra­
diance (type four). Thus, one’s stage on the path determines the type of buddha land 
into which they will be reborn. Universal Buddhahood is achieved when all beings 
become buddhas in the land of eternally quiescent radiance, which, as a result, means 
all phenomena—​including plants and trees—​likewise become buddhas. At the end of 
the essay, Annen asserts that if one grasps the teachings of the Lotus Sūtra, the primary 
scripture in Tendai, then one will understand that plants and trees become buddhas as a 
circumstantial result of these teachings. Like Zongying, he claims that it is not the case 
that plants and trees become buddhas on their own (Dainihon Bukkyō zensho 24:216). In 
other words, plants and trees are not in themselves sentient beings, nor do they have the 
capacity to become buddhas through their own efforts. Rather, they become buddhas as 
a by-​product of the Buddhahood process.
Although he relies on the same sutra passages as Zongying, Annen goes a step further 
than his Tiantai predecessors on the question of vegetal Buddhahood. Annen concludes 
his essay by asserting that one obtains “inconceivable” awakening by contemplating the 
“inconceivable” space of the fourth type of land, the land of eternally quiescent radi­
ance (Dainihon Bukkyō zensho 24:200a). According to Zhiyi’s paradigm, this land is 
uninhabited and lacks mental activity; hence, it is “inconceivable.” Annen, however, 
proposes that this land is conceivable. Moreover, it is accessible from within our own 
Sahā world, because “Sahā is identical with the land of eternally quiescent radiance” 
(Ōkubo 2022, 90).
Annen further developed this argument in his compendium on the awakened mind, 
the Bodaishingishō 菩提心義抄, which is ostensibly a commentary on the aforemen­
tioned Putixinlun. He first notes that, according to the Abhidharma treatises, a buddha 
body is generated when the container world becomes a buddha land. The buddha land, 
and the Buddha who governs it, are determined by the positive actions of sentient 
beings and the vow of the bodhisattva who generates this land. Annen then offers four

--- PAGE 430 ---
Generative Buddhahood      405
 
interpretations of how sentient beings and insentient objects, specifically plants and 
trees, become buddhas (Taishō no. 2397, 75:484b26–​75:484c27).
The first interpretation is a standard axiom in original enlightenment thought. 
Namely, because the container world was generated by the awakening of a buddha, all 
sentient beings in that world have the ability to become buddhas. Therefore, cultivation 
of a mind toward becoming a buddha depends on the internal processes of one’s own 
mind. In other words, when one commits themselves to positive actions, they set in mo­
tion the eventual result of liberation.
The second interpretation directly references the taxonomy of buddha lands. Annen 
argues that just as sentient beings become buddhas as a result of cultivating the path to 
enlightenment, all material contents of the buddha land become buddhas as an indi­
rect or circumstantial result of the enlightenment process. For example, he notes that all 
plants and trees become the body of the Buddha at the moment of Śākyamuni’s enlight­
enment. Citing a passage from the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra (Taishō no. 310, 11:150a7–​11:150a14), 
Annen asserts that “all mindless grasses, trees, and forests can generate the body and 
marks of the Tathāgata and preach the Dharma.” Therefore, cultivation of a mind toward 
becoming a buddha also depends on processes external to the mind, which is the gener­
ation of a buddha land and its inhabitants.
In the third interpretation, Annen argues that, in some cases, if a bodhisattva 
contemplates the nature of a buddha among plants and trees, these insentient objects can 
become sentient. In other cases, buddhas or bodhisattvas transform or guide plants and 
trees to become buddhas. In other words, the distinction between sentience and insen­
tience is determined when a bodhisattva generates a buddha land. However, depending 
on the vows of a buddha or bodhisattva, plants and trees may also become buddhas in 
order to assist sentient beings in those lands. Therefore, cultivation of a mind toward 
becoming a buddha depends on both the internal processes of one’s own mind and the 
external assistance of a buddha or bodhisattva (Taishō no., 2397, 75:484c12–​75:484c21).
Finally, in the fourth interpretation, Annen concludes that buddhahood can only be 
achieved when one realizes that there is no difference between the internal cognitive 
process of the path to liberation and the structure of the external cosmos. He states that 
the nature of the buddha is neither internal nor external, nor does it have a center or pe­
riphery; it exists in all places just like empty space. Therefore, it is not the case that sen­
tient beings independently possess the nature of a buddha within their own minds, nor 
is it the case that plants and trees exist as independent external manifestations of the na­
ture of a buddha. Furthermore, the nature of a buddha is not contingent on the fusing of 
the internal processes of sentient beings and external manifestation of insentient objects 
but pervades all cosmological space (Taishō no. 2397, 75:484c21–​75:485a5; Ōkubo 2022, 
62–​67). Like Zongying, Annen based his analysis on a passage from the Vimalakīrti 
Sūtra, concluding that the awakening of grasses and trees, like all phenomena, occurs 
when the bodhisattva purifies his mind and generates a buddha land (Taishō no. 2397, 
75:487c2–​75:489; Taishō no. 405, 14:547c20–​14:547c22; McRae 2004, 127).
Annen also accounts for how the teachings of a buddha may differ depending on the 
buddha land. In his other major compendium on the mantra teachings, the Shingonshū

--- PAGE 431 ---
406      Matthew D. McMullen
 
kyōji gi, he alludes to a passage in the tenth chapter of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra. This chapter, 
“The Buddha Accumulation of Fragrances,” begins with Śāriputra asking Vimalakīrti a 
practical question about lunch and how he intends to feed the assembly of bodhisattvas 
that have gathered to hear him preach. Admonishing his guest for invoking such a 
worldly desire as eating while he is trying to preach the dharma, he nonetheless fulfills 
Śāriputra’s request and vows to present him with a nutritious meal, which of course is 
the Buddhist teachings. This meal, however, is located in a distant buddha land called 
“Host of Fragrances.” In this land, the Buddha of Fragrances preaches to his assembly of 
bodhisattvas not in words but through the power of scent (McRae 2004, 149–​150).
Applying this episode from the sutra to the buddhahood of plants and trees, Annen 
implies that plants and trees do not inherently have minds or sentience themselves. 
Rather, they become sentient only in an alternative buddha land in which the bodhi­
sattva who generates this land in his mind determines to preach to the inhabitants of 
that land by means of plants and trees. He paraphrases the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, stating, 
“Some buddha lands generate the deeds of the Buddha through light. Some buddha 
lands generate the deeds of the Buddha through scent. Some buddha lands generate 
the deeds of the Buddha through taste. Some buddha lands generate the deeds of the 
Buddha through speech. Our Sahā world generates the deeds of the Buddha through 
speech” (Taishō no. 2396, 75:408c24–​75:408c27; Ōkubo 2004, 157).
For Annen, a mantra can be any manifestation of the buddhadharma and is not 
merely aural. In a buddha land that privileges smell, mantra is the preaching of the 
dharmakāya as scent; in a buddha land in which taste is the primary form of commu­
nication, mantra is the flavor of the buddhadharma. Therefore, it is possible to con­
ceive of a world in which the buddhadharma is transmitted via taste or smell rather 
than sound or written text (McRae 2004, 59). In such a world, one might find that 
the sutras consist of fragrant and tasty foods and begin with the savory expression of 
“Thus have I eaten.”
Conclusion
In this chapter, I have situated Annen’s theory of the enlightenment of plants and trees 
within a Buddhist cosmological framework. Specifically, I argue that the notion of 
buddha lands in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra and Zhiyi’s taxonomy of these lands in his com­
mentary informed Annen’s interpretation of Buddhahood and how plants and trees 
may obtain liberation. Rather than a statement on the ontological status of Buddhahood 
or an epistemological claim regarding insentient objects, Annen simply used the phrase 
“plants and trees” to denote the material world and all phenomena comprised within 
it. When a bodhisattva generates a buddha land as stated in the sutra, all beings and 
objects in that land become or potentially become buddhas. The logic behind this 
claim, as Zongying asserted in his response to Tokuen, is that the land and the mind are

--- PAGE 432 ---
Generative Buddhahood      407
 
indistinguishable. Therefore, buddha lands are cosmic spaces in which even plants and 
trees can reach liberation.
