Introduction
The Buddhist Monk Jien, the Gukanshō, and Buddhist 
Ritual Practice
The Buddhist priest Jien (1155–​1225) is known as an exemplary literary figure of medi­
eval Japan and a prolific composer of waka 和歌, a form of Japanese poetry most com­
monly consisting of five lines to express feelings of the poet and reflect on the beauty 
of the natural world. Jien is particularly renowned for his composition of shakyōka 
釈教歌, a genre of waka that poetically expressed the Buddhist teachings (Tsukudo 
1942; Ishikawa 1998; Yamamoto 1999; Robert 2008; Ishikawa 2015; Yamamoto 2016). 
His most well-​known work, the Gukanshō (literally “Jottings of a Fool,” 愚管抄), is 
considered one of the first historical treatises that incorporated a Buddhist lens into its 
interpretation of Japanese history (Brown and Ishida 1979; Brownlee 1991; Hambrick 
1978; Marra 1985; Ozaki 2004; Fukazawa 2006). In writing the history of Japan, Jien 
carefully suggests that it is not enough to highlight the glorious past of the imperial 
family of Japan and brings the reader’s attention to how the rising military power of 
the Kamakura Shogunate poses a threat to the existing structures of authority held by 
the imperial and aristocratic families of the Heian capital. Jien carefully addresses the 
realities of the decline of imperial authority through the application of the notion of 
the Three Ages of the Dharma, which sees a deterioration of the Buddhist teachings 
across three periods: the True Dharma Age, the Imitation Dharma Age, and the Last

--- PAGE 435 ---
410      Eric Haruki Swanson
 
Dharma Age (Marra 1985). According to Jien, the gradual, yet dramatic shifts seen 
in political stability starting from the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156 were indications that 
Japan had entered the “Last Dharma Age” (mappō, 末法; Marra 1985). In composing 
the Gukanshō, Jien suggests that in order to counter the inevitable reality of the “Last 
Dharma Age,” it is necessary to reenvision a governing structure that is in accordance 
with the Principles (dōri, 道理) of the Buddhist teachings (Hambrick 1978; Marra 1985). 
While the Gukanshō is known today as a historical work, it is important to recognize 
how Jien’s presentation of history reflects his motivations as a Buddhist priest. In fact, 
Jien was an active practitioner of Buddhist rituals throughout his life, and served in 
the highest levels of administrative duties at Buddhist temples belonging to the Tendai 
school. By Jien’s time, the Tendai school, established by Saichō (767–​822), had devel­
oped into two rivaling factions, the Tendai Mountain Lineage (sanmon ha, 山門派) and 
Tendai Temple Lineage (jimon ha, 寺門派). The Mountain Lineage traced its group to 
Ennin (794–​864) and Enryakuji Temple 延暦寺, a monastery located on top of Mount 
Hiei, and the Temple Lineage traced theirs to Enchin (814–​891) and Onjōji Temple 
園城寺‎, located at the base of Mount Hiei (Adolphson 2000; Dolce 2012; Gardiner 2018; 
Groner 2000, 2002). Jien belonged within the Mountain Lineage, and this institutional 
rivalry between the two groups is clearly reflected in his written work, which often 
presents the Mountain Lineage in a more favorable light (Taga 1980, 95). Jien served 
four times as the abbot of the Tendai Mountain Lineage, overseeing institutional affairs 
at Enryakuji on Mount Hiei. In addition to his administrative duties, Jien performed 
various Buddhist rites for members of the imperial and aristocratic families of the Heian 
court, such as Buddhist rituals for the safe birth of a child of the imperial ruler and his 
consort. He established a particularly close relationship with Retired Emperor Gotoba, 
the de facto ruler of Japan, serving as his personal “protector monk” (gojisō, 護持僧) 
and performing rites at times when he fell ill (Taga 1980, 215–​227). In addition to his role 
as a practitioner of Buddhist rituals that supported the well-​being of members of the 
aristocracy, one of Jien’s greatest achievements was the construction of a ritual center 
at Sanjō Shirakawa bō 三条白川坊, present day-​Shōrenin Monzeki 青蓮院門跡 in 
Kyoto, a project that involved establishing an elaborate ritual program based on Tendai 
Buddhist rituals already in practice on Mount Hiei (Taga 1980, 147). This included 
reinterpreting existing rituals with strong associations to the Mountain Lineage, such 
as the Rite of Radiant Light (shijōkōhō 熾盛光法), which had already been viewed as 
effective rites to pray for the emperor’s longevity and, by extension, the protection of the 
state (Dolce 2012). In establishing his new ritual program, Jien reformulated the Rite of 
Radiant Light, renaming it the Rite of Great Radiant Light (dai shijōkōhō 大熾盛光法) 
and presenting this as a ritual effective specifically for the subjugation of vengeful spirits. 
Furthermore, he grounded this reenvisioning of the rite in a further articulation of the 
role of the practitioner’s body in these efforts to restore order in the world. Treatises 
composed by Jien, such as the “Origins of the Main Deity” (honzon engi, 本尊縁起) 
and “Questions and Answers Regarding the Commentary on the Main Deity” (honzon 
shaku mondo, 本尊釈問答) illustrate how Jien reinterpreted the relationship between 
the practitioner’s body and the enlightened figures of buddhas, bodhisattvas, and

--- PAGE 436 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      411
 
vidyarajas (myōō, 明王; wisdom kings). In fact, upon close analysis, these treatises illus­
trate a concern of the future trajectory of imperial authority and its seemingly inevitable 
decline, which went hand in hand with the claim of the necessity of the intervention 
of Buddhist ritual practice in mitigating the further dismantling of the social order. In 
other words, whereas Jien’s Gukanshō presented a vision of history that explained the 
process in which society was falling into disorder, the Buddhist ritual program that Jien 
constructed at this site can be seen as an example of a concrete solution that would ad­
dress this problem. In explaining why imperial authority was experiencing decline in 
the Gukanshō, Jien suggested through his retelling of the imperial history that there was 
an underlying “principle of vengeful spirits” (onryō no dōri 怨霊の道理) at work that 
plagued the capital, and claimed that only the “principle of the buddhadharma” (buppō 
no dōri 仏法の道理) would be able to restore order.
Jien’s Ritual Project and the Problem 
of Vengeful Spirits
Jien’s envisioning of the ritual practitioner as seen in his writings should be viewed within 
the larger historical context in which they were presented. Jien’s project of establishing 
a new ritual center in the proximity of the Heian capital was an undertaking that took 
over two decades. In 1202, Jien first obtained permission to build two structures as offi­
cial prayer centers for the imperial family at the location of Sanjō Shirakawa, just to the 
east of the Heian capital. The structures built at these locations were collectively called 
the Temple of Great Repentance.
It is important to note that Jien’s ritual program at this new location was largely based 
on Buddhist rituals that were already in practice at Enryakuji, the headquarters of the 
Tendai school. Enryakuji was located on Mount Hiei northeast of the capital, the direc­
tion known as the “demon gate” (kimon, 鬼門). According to yin-​yang cosmology the 
demon gate was understood as the direction from which malevolent spirits entered the 
space of the capital. Rituals performed at Mount Hiei were presented as a form of pro­
tection for the capital, and the rituals established at Jien’s Temple of Great Repentance, 
following the model of those practiced on Mount Hiei, were also designed to fulfill the 
same purpose of providing protection for the capital, although now these rituals were 
performed in its immediate proximity. Interestingly, changes could also be seen in what 
were envisioned as the causes of the disorder, particularly as it pertained to the concerns 
felt by those involved in the politics of the Heian court. When Jien started the construc­
tion of his new ritual center in the proximity of the capital in 1206, he composed the 
“Articles Regarding the Establishment of Temple of Great Repentance,” which included 
a prayer in the form of a ganmon (願文), a liturgical genre of writing that poetically 
expresses one’s intentions and are dedicated to buddhas and kami as the recipients of 
their stated vows. In this short piece, Jien specifies vengeful spirits as the cause of the

--- PAGE 437 ---
412      Eric Haruki Swanson
 
problems of disorder that plagued the capital (Zen 2012) and emphasizes the necessity 
for the collaboration between the Imperial Court and Buddhist institutions: “ever since 
the Hōgen Rebellion [of 1156] until this day, it has been chaotic times. The vengeful spirits 
have permeated Heaven, and the dead soldiers occupy the four seas. I have yet to hear of 
a virtuous form of governance that can help to liberate [these beings from their suf­
fering]; there is also no sign of a revival of court ceremonies. In spring dreams, crimson 
tears flow down to my sleeves and in autumn slumber, my bare heart enflames my chest. 
The only thing that can liberate these vengeful spirits and bolster the Court is the Power 
of the Buddha Dharma” (Taga 1945, 841; emphases added).1 In addition to the general 
term used for the deceased, vengeful spirits (onryō, 怨霊) and “dead soldiers” (bōsotsu, 
亡卒), Jien specifies two historical figures, Emperor Sutoku (崇徳天皇, 1119–​1164) and 
Fujiwara no Tadazane (藤原忠実, 1078–​1162), who was, notably, Jien’s grandfather. Jien 
suggests that one of the main purposes of the Buddhist rites established at his new ritual 
center is to assist these two spirits toward liberation (Taga 1945, 841). The use of the term 
“vengeful spirit” here is significant.
When Jien pointed to vengeful spirits as the cause of social disorder in the capital, he 
was engaging with precedents set in the development of a larger discourse on vengeful 
spirits and court politics that dated back to the eighth century. In fact, stories of vengeful 
spirits in Japan arose in popularity alongside the development of the ancient capitals of 
Nara and Heian. As populations became more dense in these urban spaces, epidemics, 
as well as rumors of ill intent among members of the aristocracy were more easily 
spread among the populace. This, in combination with the heightened rivalry between 
competing aristocratic families, led to the popularization of the notion that natural 
disasters, and epidemics, were caused by the vengeful spirits of deceased members of the 
aristocracy and imperial family who had experienced untimely deaths as a result of po­
litical discord and exile from the capital (Kobayashi 2010; Stockdale 2015; Yamada 2014).
What was specific to Jien’s contribution to this discourse, however, was the way he 
incorporated these narratives of vengeful spirits into his retelling of history and made 
them a central concern for the ritual program he established at the Temple of Great 
Repentance. His claim, in other words, was that his Buddhist ritual program would pro­
vide a means of salvation for the vengeful spirits who haunted the capital and, through 
the liberation of these vengeful spirits, could restore order to it (Zen 2012). Importantly, 
both of the two aforementioned historical figures passed away at the location of their 
exile in the aftermath of the Hōgen Rebellion (hōgen no ran, 保元の乱), a political up­
heaval that occurred in July and August 1156. The conflict was between two factions 
within the imperial court, divided between Emperor Go-​Shirakawa (後白河院, 1127–​
1192) and the aforementioned Emperor Sutoku, over the question of succession to the 
throne and the extent to which the powerful aristocratic family of the Fujiwara clan 
exercised control as hereditary imperial regents. The conflict was brief and ended with 
the defeat of Emperor Sutoku, who was exiled from the capital. After his death, he came 
to be viewed as a vengeful spirit who caused strange misfortunes to happen in the capital 
as a form of revenge on his political enemies. Significantly, it was during this period of 
internal strife of the imperial court that samurai warriors were enlisted to help resolve

--- PAGE 438 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      413
 
the conflict. In Jien’s view, the growing reliance on the warrior class to ensure social sta­
bility was a troubling sign that imperial authority was on the decline, and the emergence 
of the idea of the vengeful spirit of Emperor Sutoku was an ominous sign of growing 
disorder. The recognition of the untimely death of the historical figures in the aftermath 
of the Hōgen Rebellion and the claim that the purpose of the Buddhist rituals at this 
site was to liberate the spirits of the dead illustrates the way Jien’s understanding of the 
purpose of his ritual center was deeply intertwined with his retelling of history, as artic­
ulated in his Gukanshō.
The Gukanshō and Jien’s Discussion of 
the Principle of Vengeful Spirits
The Gukanshō was written around the year 1220, just before the advent of the Jōkyū 
Disturbance of 1221, in which Retired Emperor Gotoba famously attempted to over­
throw the Kamakura Shogunate. At this time, the forces of Retired Emperor Gotoba 
clashed with those of the Hōjō Clan, who were the regents of the Kamakura shogunate. 
Retired Emperor Gotoba’s forces were quickly quelled, and he was banished to the Oki 
Islands, from which he never returned. The repercussions of these actions by Retired 
Emperor Gotoba were harsh, with many of his family members also banished from 
the capital. The timing of the writing of the Gukanshō has led scholars to conclude that 
one of the driving motivations for composing a historical narrative was to try to con­
vince Retired Emperor Gotoba not to rise up against the military class. According to 
this view, Jien is portrayed as the “rationally minded” Buddhist historian who, with his 
extensive knowledge of past events, attempted to prevent the inevitable defeat of Retired 
Emperor Gotoba (Ozaki 2004). While this may have been part of Jien’s intentions in 
composing the work, this explanation does not take into account the extent to which he 
wove vengeful spirits into his historical narrative as agents who precipitated the decline 
of imperial authority. Jien begins his discussion of the history of Japan with the claim 
that the “period of the military class” (musha no yo, 武者の世) began with the advent of 
the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156 and points to this event as a turning point in which violence 
and disorder started to be seen occurring in the immediate proximity of the Heian cap­
ital. To explain how this unfortunate turn of events occurred, he suggests that there are 
both “good” and “evil” principles that govern the world. According to Jien, just as there 
is a principle (dōri, 道理) underlying good governance, there is also a principle behind 
the evil present in the world. He explains that vengeful spirits are an example of this evil 
principle and have a natural propensity to cause disorder. Importantly, the evil principles 
that cause disorder can be countered through the principles of the Buddhist teachings, 
which Jien describes as “extirpating sin and giving rise to goodness” (metsuzai shōzen, 
滅罪生善) and “removing evil and grasping the good” (shaaku jizen, 遮悪持善). This 
language found in the Gukanshō is similar to what is seen in the “Articles Regarding the

--- PAGE 439 ---
414      Eric Haruki Swanson
 
Establishment of Temple of Great Repentance” that Jien composed in 1206, indicating 
that the issue of the growing presence of vengeful spirits was an underlying theme across 
his writings. In the Gukanshō, vengeful spirits appear at certain points in Jien’s telling 
of imperial history as the result of the feelings of unresolved conflicts that occur as per­
sonal issues among members of aristocracy. Jien points to a number of historical figures 
who he claims have become vengeful spirits, including Fujiwara no Motokata, Fujiwara 
no Akimitsu, the Buddhist priest Raigō, and Emperor Sutoku, who are all members with 
close ties to the aristocratic society of the Heian capital. The ramifications of these his­
torical figures becoming vengeful spirits is that they, although in very subtle ways, neg­
atively impact the trajectory of history, as indicated in the decline of the effectiveness of 
imperial authority. Significantly, Jien stresses that if negative feelings that have arisen 
from these instances are not sufficiently addressed through the practice of Buddhist 
rituals, they will not only come to haunt the members of the families involved in these 
past instances but also eventually bring disorder to the entire capital. While natural 
disasters, such as droughts, fires, and earthquakes, that appeared after the exile of a po­
litical figure were viewed as a result of an unappeased spirit, Jien further emphasized 
that unresolved personal conflicts of individuals could have a continued influence on 
the actions of those in the present, with dire consequences to the future of the capital 
if they were left untended. The role of Buddhist ritual practice, in other words, was to 
subjugate harmful, vengeful spirits as a means to restore an ordered society governed 
with good principles supported by the Buddhist teachings. In other words, Jien effec­
tively drew attention to the lingering anxiety among members of imperial and aristo­
cratic families caused by their memories of past political conflicts such as the Hōgen 
Rebellion so as to highlight the necessity of Buddhist principles and ritual practice. Jien 
claimed that the Buddhist rituals at his center had the power to dissolve the negative an­
imosity associated with the conflicts of the past and would restore peace for the future of 
the capital.
This claim that Buddhist rites should be viewed as the solution to the problem of 
vengeful spirits continued to be central to Jien’s ritual program, even under the drasti­
cally changing political climate following what came to be the most dramatic political 
upheaval of his own lifetime, the Jōkyū Disturbance of 1221 (Taga 1980, 296). In 1222, just 
a year after the drastic turn of events of the Jōkyū Disturbance that ended in the defeat 
and exile of Jien’s main patron, Retired Emperor Gotoba, Jien composed another prayer 
that was dedicated to the buddhas and kami: “today, the disruptions in heaven are the 
same as they were in the past. Strange apparitions reveal their hidden forms. Is this not 
due to the lack of prayer? How is this not a sign of envy? How much more do we need the 
efficacious activity of the Radiant Light [shijōkō, 熾盛光]? In order to provide protec­
tion in these times of the Latter Dharma, we must remove the evils of the world through 
the merits of the Wondrous Lotus Sutra” (Taga 1945, 862; emphasis added). Here, Jien 
clearly states how he views his ritual program as contributing to restoring order. In 
this vow, he reiterates many of the points seen in his previous vows, emphasizing that 
“strange apparitions have revealed their hidden forms” and that both exoteric and eso­
teric rituals need be performed to provide protection in chaotic times. Jien also lays out

--- PAGE 440 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      415
 
in more detail the content of his ritual program, referring to the two structures as the 
Exoteric Teaching Hall (kengyō dō, 顕教堂), built for the practice of the Rite of Lotus 
Repentance (hokke senpō, 法花懺悔), and the Mantra Hall (shingon dō, 真言堂), for 
esoteric rites such as the Rite of Great Radiant Light (daishijōkō hō, 大熾盛光法) and 
goma fire rituals. (See table 18.1.)
As for the purposes of these two categories of Buddhist rites that Jien specifies, he 
states that while the exoteric rites help to alleviate the suffering of the vengeful spirits 
and hungry ghosts, the function of the esoteric rites is to incinerate the obstructions 
and wipe away the influence of the harmful spirits on the Law of the Buddhadharma and 
the Law of the Emperor. Jien’s newly established ritual center exhibited an extensive 
exoteric-​esoteric ritual program that incorporated rites that were based on those al­
ready practiced on Mount Hiei (Dolce 2012; Fujii 1998; Stevenson 1986). An impor­
tant difference, however, is that Jien reconceptualized the purpose of these rites and 
presented the rituals as actions to be performed in the proximity of the capital in order 
to pacify not only evil spirits in the abstract sense but also, importantly, the individual 
spirits of historical figures who had passed away as a result of violent political clashes 
and remained embedded in the collective memory of the members of the Heian court. 
These included, as stated earlier, not only the soldiers who had died as a result of polit­
ical conflict that occurred in Jien’s own lifetime but also specifically the spirit of Retired 
Emperor Sutoku, who had been exiled in 1156 as a result of the Hōgen Rebellion. It is 
not hard to imagine that Jien, who had been the personal protector monk of Retired 
Emperor Gotoba, viewed Gotoba’s recent exile as a result of the Jōkyū Rebellion of 1211 
as resonating in ominous ways with the exile of Retired Emperor Sutoku in 1156. In other 
words, the historical reality of the Heian court and Jien’s own reflection on the history

of the political affairs of the capital can be seen as informing and reforming the raison 
d’être of the Buddhist ritual practice of the Tendai school at the turn of the 13th century. 
It is within the broader discussion of the recognition of social disorder, the vengeful 
spirits as perpetuating the negative trajectory of history, and the call for the practice 
of Buddhist rites in order to restore order in the Heian capital that we see innovative 
interpretations of the function of Buddhist deities, as well as a reenvisioning of how 
these deities were embodied within the body of the practitioner through ritual practices.
Reinterpreting the Function of 
Buddhist Deities
A short text titled “Commentary on the Fifteen Deities of the Hall of Repentance” 
(senpōin jūgo son shaku 懺法院十五尊釈, hereafter “Fifteen Deities”), provides 
commentaries on the fifteen Buddhist figures who occupied the ritual space of the 
Great Repentance Hall at Jien’s ritual center. This short text is found in the fourth sec­
tion of the Monyōki 門葉記, which compiles records of ritual services. The Monyōki is 
a collection of temple records regarding rituals practiced at the Shōrenin temple from 
the 12th to 15th centuries. Although the authorship of “Fifteen Deities” is not specified, 
the short work contains themes and word uses that resonate with Jien’s other work and 
was likely composed by him around the time of the temple’s reconstruction efforts 
in the year 1222, when he composed “Vows for the Rebuilding of the Temple of Great 
Repentance.” As indicated in Jien’s dedicatory prayers introduced earlier, an integral 
part of his ritual program included the daily “eye-​opening” (kaigen, 開眼) ritual for 
the fifteen Buddhist deities. Although lacking in detail as to the actual ritual proce­
dure, “Fifteen Deities” provides interesting explanations of how the function of the 
Buddhist deities were reconceptualized to fit the goals of Jien’s ritual center, specifi­
cally how these deities might contribute to dealing with vengeful or malevolent spirits 
and help in efforts to reestablish political and social order. The short text begins with 
a list of the dates to which each of the fifteen Buddhist deities are allocated within the 
time period of a month. According to this text, the practitioners at this temple cycled 
through these fifteen Buddhist deities every month, with the eye-​opening for each 
deity performed on specific dates. (See table 18.2 for a list of the deities and the dates 
associated with each.)
In providing a description of each of these Buddhist figures, the text follows a two-​part 
structure, beginning with a brief explanation of the deity through the lens of the theory 
of the “three bodies [of the buddha]” (Sk. trikāya, Jp. sanshin 三身): the “truth body” 
(Sk. dharmakāya; Jp. hosshin 法身), the “reward body” (Sk. saṃbhogakāya; Jp. hōshin 
報身), and the “transformation body” (Sk. nirmāṇakāya; Jp. keshin 化身; Williams 
2008, 173–​186). This is followed by an explanation of how each deity may assist in 
reaching the goal of restoring order in the world and, in some cases, the goal of pacifying

--- PAGE 442 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      417
 
vengeful spirits. A prime example of this is the description of the Immovable Wisdom 
King (Fudō Myōō, 不動明), a prominent wrathful figure in Japanese esoteric buddhism 
(Faure 2015; Payne and Witzel 2015). The text begins by listing the basic characteristics of 
this figure, as described in other esoteric Buddhist scriptural commentaries, as endowed 
with the ability to subjugate both inner and outer obstructions, and by referring to 
the recitation of his mantra as a method of realizing the enlightened mind (bodaishin, 
菩提心). These commonly seen attributes of Fudō Myōō are followed by a description 
of how the features of this deity’s ability to eliminate obstructions within the mind of the 
practitioner as described in the esoteric Buddhist scripture could also be applied to ad­
dress the problem of vengeful spirits:
because the eyes of compassion of the manifested form [of Fudō Myōō] sees all sen­
tient beings as equal and like his only child, he saves vengeful spirits and the souls of 
the dead by including them as equal to his only child. . . . This subjugation of the evil 
demons of the vengeful spirits ultimately leads them toward the path of enlightenment, 
and through this it is possible to destroy the delusions of the land. It will certainly open 
the gates to Virtuous Governance. . . . The merits obtained through the sword and rope 
[of Fudō Myōō] is “removal of evil and maintaining good” [shaaku jizen, 遮悪持善]. 
It is the prayers of the lords, ministers, and the people that will bring forth victory in 
the present and future. The function of the wisdom king [myōō, 明王] is to remove

both inner and outer obstructions. The praises [for Fudō Myōō] twice a month is 
what all sentient beings should depend on.
(T. zuzō 12:29a–​b; emphasis added)
The text not only claims that one of the prime functions of Fudō Myōō to “subjugate 
evil” (gōma, 降魔) is applicable to the goal of pacifying vengeful spirits but also suggests 
that it is precisely the removal of the “evil demons of the vengeful spirits” that will lead 
to the restoration of a virtuous governance (tokusei, 徳政). The text also comments that 
the iconographical features of this deity, that is, the sword of wisdom in his right hand 
and the rope in his left, are visual expressions of the idea of “the removal of evil and 
maintaining good” (shaaku jizen), a term Jien specifically highlighted both in his his­
torical work, the Gukanshō, and in the dedicatory prayers he proclaimed at the time of 
the rebuilding of the Temple of Great Repentance. Furthermore, the section in “Fifteen 
Deities” concludes the commentary on Fudō Myōō by suggesting that this figure is the 
very embodiment of the “principle of the buddhadharma,” which Jien understood as 
the necessary antidote in countering the negative influence of the “principle of vengeful 
spirits.” In other words, an examination of this short commentary on Fudō Myōō reveals 
an attempt to reinterpret the iconography, functions, and activities of this deity in such a 
way as to address the specific problem of pacifying vengeful spirits. The explanations of 
all fifteen deities indicate how each offers specific methods to effectively counter, pacify, 
and ultimately liberate vengeful spirits as a way to restore order in the world.
Another underlying theme seen across Jien’s writings is an emphasis on the mutual de­
pendence of imperial authority (ōbō, 王法) and the buddhadharma (buppō, 仏法). The 
late historian Kuroda Toshio has argued that the political ideology of the mutual depend­
ence of imperial authority and buddhadharma occupied a central position in the medieval 
system of state and religion, allowing temple-​shrine complexes to assert their own polit­
ical autonomy and power. Kuroda has also noted that Jien’s Gukanshō was the first work 
to put forth a systematized treatment of the notion of this mutual dependence, suggesting 
that Jien played a crucial role in shaping the political ideology of religious institutional life 
in medieval Japan (Kuroda and Stone 1996, 279–​280). Discourse on this mutual depend­
ence is also provided in “Fifteen Deities,” articulated perhaps most clearly in the discussion 
of the deity Uṣṇīṣavijayā (sonshō, 尊勝). The text explains: “through the merit [attained 
through this figure], the evil thoughts of the vengeful spirits will be dispelled immedi­
ately, and the liberation of the dead soldiers will easily be achieved,” and the empower­
ment from the Victorious Buddha-​Crown Dharani (sonshō darani, 尊勝陀羅尼) will 
“remove the erroneous thoughts of the vengeful spirits . . . and realize peace in the land.” 
The text also emphasizes that the recitation of the Victorious Buddha-​Crown Dharani not 
only will ensure the removal of the erroneous thoughts of vengeful spirits but also will as­
sist in establishing peace in the land (T. zuzō 12:27b, 31c). Furthermore, in discussing the 
Thousand-​Armed Avalokitêśvara (senju kannon, 千手観音), a Buddhist deity associated 
with a universal compassion to save all sentient beings, Jien concludes his description of this 
figure by stating: “all the evil demons and vengeful spirits who obstruct the Buddhadharma 
and Imperial Law will be beckoned by the call of Avalokitêśvara and enter into the gate of

--- PAGE 444 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      419
 
the universal teachings.” In terms of the connection between the pacification of vengeful 
spirits and the emperor’s role in restoring peace in the capital, this is most clearly articulated 
in the description of Ekâkṣara-​uṣṇīṣacakra (ichiji kinrin, 一字金輪): “a shallow interpre­
tation understands the Wheel-​Turning King of the Buddha Realm as the Wheel-​Turning 
King of the Human Realm. The profound secret is that they are [both] the bodies of the 
Buddha’s skillful means to bring benefit to all sentient beings . . . through the virtue of the 
Seven Treasures of the Wheel-​Turning King, the vengeful spirits and dead soldiers of this 
world will be healed and saved” (T. zuzō 12:26c; emphasis added). In this passage, the com­
mentary introduces the notion of the cakravartin, the ideal universal ruler in buddhism 
who is said to rule ethically and benevolently. By revealing the unity of bodies between the 
“wheel-​turning king of the human realm” and Ekâkṣara-​uṣṇīṣacakra, Jien suggests that the 
liberation of the vengeful spirits depends on the realization that the imperial body serves 
as an integral node in the soteriological activities of the universal buddha. This point is 
emphasized again in the commentary of the same figure in another section of the text:
the external manifestation of [the Universally Shining Tathāgata] is the position of 
the emperor. The bodhi of inner realization is the manifestation of the One Letter. 
Currently, prayers for [maintaining the balance of] principle and chaos in the land 
of Japan is done through the wheel-​turning king, and the activities of the Heian cap­
ital are done by the people. . . . If the Lord of the Buddha Realm does not assist the 
lords and ministers of the human realm, the beings of the human realm are unable 
to attain the benefits of the Buddha realm. Who will uphold the three jewels? Who 
will have faith in the Buddha’s words? Principles are necessary. I pray that there is no 
mistake in this.
(T. zuzō 12:30c–​31a)
As indicated here, Jien understood that the balance between order and chaos lay in the 
hands of the emperor of the Heian capital, and recognized that the maintenance of this 
social order depended on a collaborative relationship between the ruler and his subjects. 
The commentary highlights the importance of the emperor setting a clear example of 
the principles of the buddhadharma so that the benefits of its practices would spread 
across the capital and beyond. Furthermore, the notion seen here that the figure of the 
emperor serves as an integral node from which the soteriological activities of the uni­
versal buddha manifests can also be seen in how the relationship between the different 
bodies of buddhas and bodhisattvas are articulated. The idea of the interpenetration of 
the bodies of all Buddhist figures is seen most clearly in a discussion in the section on 
Śākyamuni Buddha, the first in the list of the fifteen deities. The short commentary for 
Śākyamuni Buddha offered here is based on an exegesis of a passage from the Parable 
Chapter of the Lotus Sutra:
Now this threefold world is all my domain,
And the living beings in it are all my children.
Now this place is beset by many pains and trials,
I am the only person who can rescue and protect [them]. (Watson 1993, 69–​70)

--- PAGE 445 ---
420      Eric Haruki Swanson
 
The commentary on this short passage divides this verse into three sections. The first line 
is interpreted as expressing the principle of the dharma-​body, the unchanging, eternal 
body of thusness (dharmakāya). The second line is seen as an expression of the wisdom 
of thusness that is in accordance with various capabilities and associated with the re­
ward body (saṃbhogakāya). The third and fourth lines are described as reflecting the 
benefits gained from the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). Using the three-​bodies 
theory in the interpretation of this short passage from the Lotus Sutra, the commentary 
suggests that Śākyamuni Buddha is none other than the omnipresent, single dharma 
realm, while the various forms of all buddhas and bodhisattvas are distinct expressions 
of this single dharma that appear in various ways to address the different needs of those 
who are on the path to salvation. Referring specifically to the teachings of Godaiin 
Annen (五大院安然, 841–​889?)—​“one buddha as all buddhas” (ichibutsu issai butsu, 
一仏一切仏)—​the text presents Śākyamuni Buddha as the single, underlying unity of 
all buddhas and bodhisattvas. The distinct bodies of all other buddhas and bodhisattvas, 
including the other fourteen deities covered in this text, are understood here as none 
other than the distinct expressions of a single, universal truth-​body that subsumes all.
This vision of the mutual interpenetration and unity of all bodies of buddhas and 
bodhisattvas is also mentioned as a key feature of a ritual exegetical treatise composed by 
Jien, titled “Questions and Answers on the Commentaries of the Main Deity” (honzon 
shaku mondō 本尊釈問答). Here, Jien suggests that this vision of the interpenetrating 
bodies of all buddhas and bodhisattvas is also extended to the body of the ritual practi­
tioner. In other words, the practitioners of Buddhist rituals must view their own bodies 
as also inseparable from the interpenetrating bodies of all buddhas and bodhisattvas 
and understand that they, too, are part of the expansive network of nodes through which 
Buddhist salvation manifests in the world. Jien explains: “now, the body of the mantra 
practitioner is the body of the manifested form of Mahāvairocana Buddha. Is this any 
different from what you see in the ritual right in front of your eyes? The shallow and pro­
found understanding with regard to this awakening is clear. To enter into the profound 
interpretation and to closely observe this contemplation is what makes one a practi­
tioner of the Shingon Esoteric Teachings” (Abe 2019, 132; emphasis added).
According to Jien, the realization of the practitioner’s body as another node through 
which the buddhas and bodhisattvas are able to act is what distinguished the esoteric 
Buddhist methods of practice from other forms of Buddhist practices. To put it differ­
ently, the realization that the esoteric Buddhist practitioner embodies the vast network 
of the interpenetrating bodies of all buddhas and bodhisattvas was necessary for the 
practitioner to channel the salvific actions of enlightened figures and what allowed the 
ritual practitioner to successfully subjugate the obstructive vengeful spirits so as to re­
store order in the world. For the ritual practitioner, the embodiment of the universal 
Buddha Mahāvairocana and the participation within the vast network of buddhas and 
bodhisattvas was the meaning of “attaining enlightenment in this very body” (sokushin 
jōbutsu, 即身成仏), one of the defining doctrinal positions of esoteric buddhism as it 
developed in Japan (Hakeda 1972, 87; Yamasaki 1988, 106; Sharf 2003; Payne 2022). As 
articulated in these texts composed by Jien, it was through the embodiment of buddhas

--- PAGE 446 ---
Embodiment and Subjugation      421
 
and bodhisattvas that ritual practitioners were able to channel their salvific activities 
to pacify vengeful spirits and restore order in the world, and this assertion supported 
his claim for the necessity of the mutual dependence of imperial authority and the 
buddhadharma to ensure a stable future for the Heian court.
Conclusion
Reflecting upon the great political turmoil and the uncertainties of the future at the 
turn of the 13th century, the Buddhist monk Jien established a new ritual program with 
the support of Retired Emperor Gotoba. At this time, major Buddhist rites of Jien’s tra­
dition were transported from the mountainous regions in the outskirts of the capital 
to an urban space in close proximity to the imperial quarters for the purpose of pro­
viding protection to the state. In his efforts to establish this new ritual center, Jien ac­
tively reconceptualized the purpose of these ritual practices and its underlying Buddhist 
theories to address what he claimed was a burgeoning threat to state affairs caused by 
the malevolent influence of vengeful spirits that plagued the capital. The construction 
of a new ritual space in the proximity of the Heian capital provided Jien with the op­
portunity to bridge together various aspects of medieval religious culture: an ongoing 
concern with the pacification of vengeful spirits to maintain peace in the land and a 
reenvisioning of the relationship between imperial authority and the buddhadharma. 
Jien’s writings examined here illustrate the extent to which Buddhist deities were crea­
tively reimagined so as to respond to the social realities and deepening anxieties of the 
Heian court in 13th-​century Japan. A consideration of Jien’s articulation of the purpose 
of Buddhist rituals and his description of the relationship between the practitioner’s 
body and the Buddhist figures that occupied the ritual space of his temple illustrates the 
process by which buddhas and bodhisattvas were understood to act within the world 
and, importantly, how the body of the practitioner was viewed as the site through which 
the buddhadharma would be enacted to maintain social order in medieval Japan.

Chapter 19
“Hard-​Core” Tantric 
Traditions and the Cult 
of Bhairava in Java
Andrea Acri
Introduction
The etic umbrella term “hard-​core tantra” (White 2000, 6–​7, 31–​32; 2003, 13–​16), roughly 
corresponding to the emic Indic category of “left-​hand” or antinomian ritual practice 
(vāmācāra), includes the traditions stemming from the scriptural corpora of the Śaiva 
Bhairavatantras (the male-​oriented Mantrapīṭha and the Śakti-​oriented Vidyāpīṭha) 
and Kaulatantras, the (largely nontextual or scantily documented) Śaiva traditions of 
the Lākulas and Kāpālikas, as well as the Buddhist Yoginītantras/​Yoganiruttaratantras. 
These texts and practices may be contrasted to those of “soft-​core tantra,” corresponding 
to the “right-​hand” or orthodox ritual practice (dakṣiṇācāra) of the mainstream (and 
to various extents Brahmanized) Śaiva tantra, like the Śaivasiddhānta, or to main­
stream monastic Theravāda and Mahāyāna Buddhism and their textual canons. Here 
I define hard-​core tantric traditions as initiatory systems that tend to share a common 
emphasis on transgression of social norms and Brahmanical or monastic rules of pu­
rity, quick empowerment toward obtaining mundane and supramundane goals through 
magico-​ritual means (often including sexual elements), ontological and epistemolog­
ical nondualism (or nondualism in ritual practice, i.e., advaitācāra, rejecting the main­
stream Brahmanical opposition between pure and impure), worship of demonic and 
wrathful hypostases of Śiva (i.e., Bhairava) and the goddess, as well as transactions with 
ambiguous demonic entities inhabiting such inauspicious places as charnel grounds.1
Even though hard-​core tantric tradition occupied a relatively marginal position in 
the religious landscape of the Indian subcontinent throughout the post-​Gupta or medi­
eval period, they formed important realities at a regional level (for instance, in Kashmir, 
Odisha, Bengal, Assam, etc.), and contributed in various ways to the development of

--- PAGE 453 ---
428      Andrea Acri
 
Indic religious as well as cultural imaginary and ritual practice at both the elite and 
popular levels. Increasing evidence suggests that various traditions of hard-​core tantra 
reached Southeast Asia and contributed to shape local cultures through texts, icono­
graphic motifs, and magico-​ritual practices. As suggested by textual, archaeological, 
and art historical vestiges, hard-​core tantra played the role of a marginal undercur­
rent in Central Java from ca. ninth to tenth century, while in East Java, from ca. elev­
enth to fifteenth century, it became more prominent and widespread at the level of both 
the urbanized political elites as well as the religious communities in the countryside. 
After the rise to dominance of Islam from the late fifteenth century onward, motifs 
and behaviors associated with hard-​core tantra survived, in a vestigial form, into the 
nineteenth century and beyond as a radically monistic undercurrent in the doctrines, 
mythology, and textual sources of modern Javanese mysticism, as well as within an anti­
nomian group of performers at the Islamic court of Surakarta.
The Rise of Bhairava Cult in East Java: 
ca. Tenth–Mid-​Thirteenth Century
Most of the (rare) texts, inscriptions, and art historical remains dating back to the 
Central Javanese period reflect a mild form of mainstream, soft-​core tantric religi­
osity revolving around the benevolent masculine aspects of the Godhead—​Sadāśiva/​
Mahādeva for the Śaivas, and the Buddha Śākyamuni and/​or Vairocana for the 
Buddhists. The Śaiva speculative religious texts and ritual manuals in Sanskrit and Old 
Javanese that have survived and that might have been in circulation in some form in 
the Central Javanese period appear to have been based on the pan-​Indian mainstream 
Saiddhāntika corpus.2 However, it is likely that the practices and beliefs associated with 
adepts of hard-​core tantric traditions (whether real or imagined, for instance, through 
Brahmanical stereotypes associated with them) were part of the collective imaginary of 
the cultural and religious elites of that period, for we find rare references (often stereo­
typical, and formulated from the critical point of view of the mainstream or “orthodox” 
elites) to them in pre-​tenth-​century textual sources (see Acri 2022). These traditions 
would only become prominent in the later period, when the center of political and cul­
tural power shifted from Central Java to East Java in the tenth century, probably as a re­
sult of a natural catastrophe.
Although there is no incontrovertible evidence that the Kāpālikas themselves, or 
Kāpālika-​influenced traditions of the Bhairavatantras, reached Java by the ninth cen­
tury, there is no reason to assume that they did not either. But firmer evidence dates 
from a slightly later period: witness, for instance, a prob. ninth–​tenth-​century bronze 
skullcap unearthed in Central Java,3 as well as the brief references to adepts adhering 
to Bhairava and Kāpālika observances found in prose Sanskrit-​Old Javanese literature 
probably written in East Java between the late tenth and early eleventh century, shortly

--- PAGE 454 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      429
 
after the shift of political power from Central to East Java. For instance, the Udyogaparva 
(45.4) glosses the Sanskrit half-​verse (uttered by Yudhiṣṭhira) vayaṃ vadhena jivāmaḥ 
kapālaṃ brāhmaṇe vṛtam (“we live by murder; the skull-​bowl is the conduct of the 
Brahmins”) as “like if our food was a warrior dead in battle, that is called food and drink; 
when a Brahman adhering to the observance of the Kāpālikas begs what is used as his 
food [i.e., human flesh]” (45.4),4 thus reflecting an association between Brahmanical 
adepts carrying out the anthropophagic observances stereotypically associated with 
the Kāpālikas in Sanskrit sources from the Indian subcontinent. The Agastyaparva 
(385.7) defines the highest goal (muktapada) of the way of Bhairava as “the endless par­
amount [sexual?] bliss” (anantaparamānanda ṅaranya ri saṅ bheravamārga), and an 
analogous expression, “endless paramount bliss is the way of the illustrious Bhairava 
[practitioner]” (anantaparamānandana ṅaranira de saṅ bhairava), is found in the 
Sanskrit-​Old Javanese Buddhist manual Saṅ Hyaṅ Kamahāyānikan (Advayasādhana), 
b45, p. 51. While in this context the sexual connotation is not clear,5 it is still possible that 
this might reflect the trope of Bhairava-​worshiping Kāpālikas and Kaulas having a fe­
male consort, just like Śiva is accompanied by or (sexually) united with Umā.6
A clearly antinomian imagery is found in four stanzas (7–​10) of a long Sanskrit hymn, 
preserved in Balinese manuscripts, entitled Śivastava (Goudriaan and Hooykaas 1971, 
290–​293). The stuti refers to transgressive behaviors of Śiva that would also be ap­
propriate for a Kāpālika or Bhairavika devotee acting like his elected deity (“He Who 
performs all these acts is Mahāśiva” [etāni sarvakarmāṇi, yaḥ karoti mahāśivaḥ]), 
namely, eating what cannot be eaten (abhakṣyabhakṣaṇaḥ), intoxicated by liquor 
(surāpānamadānvitaḥ), enjoying young women (yuvatīratisaṃyuktaḥ), singing, making 
noise and dancing (gītaṃ dhvanir nṛttam), and using sperm combined with phlegm, 
fat, excrement, and urine (kaphamedayutaṃ śukram, purīṣamūtrasaṃyutam); the final 
stanza declares that a person, whether impure or pure, and even when full of desires, 
should meditate on Īśāna (i.e., Śiva), thereby becoming pure outwardly and inwardly.7 
This passage calls to mind a Kaula ritual practice; indeed, the final verse adumbrates 
the analogous discourses on the enjoyment of impure/​forbidden substances as well as 
the practice of sinful behaviors by the adept, known in some traditions as svecchācāra, 
found in South Asian Śaiva and Śākta Sanskrit sources.8 Similar passages referring to 
a practitioner mastering the esoteric knowledge (niṣkalajñāna) as acting according to 
his own will (yathecchā) and performing both good and bad actions are found in the 
Sanskrit-​Old Javanese Śaiva text Bhuvanakośa (8.35–​8.36, 11.67–​11.70, 84–​86), a scrip­
tural source mainly reflecting a Saiddhāntika context. While both the Sanskrit hymns 
from Bali and the Bhuvanakośa preserve material of remarkable antiquity that may 
well go back to pre-​tenth-​century Central and/​or East Java, they are difficult to date 
firmly, and therefore a later East Javanese or Balinese origin for these passages cannot 
be ruled out.
What may be a turning point in the history of Java in terms of royal support to hard-​
core, Bhairava-​focused tantric traditions is the reign of King Bāmeśvara (ca. 1117–​1135) 
of Keḍiri. Albeit little is known about this sovereign, it appears that the candrakapāla 
motif, a representation of a skull eating a half-​moon that we find depicted on a number of

--- PAGE 455 ---
430      Andrea Acri
 
East Javanese monuments and statues from the early Kaḍiri period onward, constituted 
his official emblem. It is attested for the first time, both iconographically and textually, 
in two inscriptions of 1117 and 1120 ce from the early reign of this king (Brandes and 
Krom 1913, 159) and is also depicted on the four corners of a stone “bathtub” or sarcoph­
agus dating to the same period (1118–​1119), now preserved in the Airlangga Museum at 
Kediri (figs. 19.1a and 1b). If this imposing artifact is a bathtub (as suggested by the hole 
on the bottom), it could have been used for (royal?) consecration rituals; if it is a sar­
cophagus, it could have hosted the corpse of a prominent religious master, as in Hindu-​
Buddhist Java inhumation was reserved to saintly persons only.9 The candrakapāla has 
been interpreted as a Śaiva symbol connected with the gradual growth in popularity 
of Bhairava cults in East Java since that period (Hadi Sidomulyo in Robson and Hadi 
Sidomulyo 2021, 150–​151). This popularity is also attested by the earliest epigraphic men­
tion of a Bhairava royal priest (paṅajyan śrī mahārāja) “follower of the Nyāyadarśana, 
producing prosperity, following the way of the Bhairavas, leader among yogins”10 in the 
stone inscription of Ngantang dated to 1135 ce, at the beginning of the reign of Jayabhaya 
Dharmeśvara, Bāmeśvara’s successor. The royal priest, called an instrument or cause of 
prosperity (samṛddhikāraṇa), is mentioned after the king, suggesting that he retained a 
prominent role in the court.
While literary sources datable to this period are lacking, the kakavin Ghaṭotkacāśraya 
by Mpu Panuluh, ascribable to the reign of Kṛtajaya (1194–​1205 ce), is remarkable from 
the point of view of religious persuasion as it attributes a prominent position to Durgā 
in the narrative. It even devotes its hymn of praise (canto 31), proffered by Abhimanyu, 
to Durgā in her manifestation as Bhairavī, conceived of as the highest immaterial 
being and source of life for all beings. Just like other divinities of the Hindu pantheon, 
Durgā in the East Javanese period often takes on a demonic quality accentuating the 
fierce and bloodthirsty aspects known from the forms of the goddess, such as Kālī,

known from hard-​core tantric traditions of the Indian subcontinent.11 In canto 30.8 
of the Ghaṭotkacāśraya, Durgā partakes with excitement of the offering of human 
flesh brought by her devotee Karālavaktra; the goddess’s abode up on the mountain is 
characterized by a cremation ground ambiance (30.6cd). This passage contains echoes 
of the trope, found in Sanskrit literary sources, of the adept (usually a Kāpālika) offering 
human flesh to Bhairava or the Goddess in a charnel ground at night.12
A significant landmark in the religious iconography of East Java is the depiction of 
skulls (in relief) on the pedestal of the so-​called Boro Gaṇeśa statue from Blitar, which 
also holds a skull-​cup in his left hand; the statue is dated by an inscribed chronogram that 
can be interpreted as yielding a date between 1219 and 1259 ce, that is to the Kuṭa Rāja/​
early Siṅhasāri period (Edi Sedyawati 1994, 116). It is still debated whether the skulls 
carved on the pedestal of this icon are coeval with the icon itself,13 as statues belonging 
to the type “Gaṇeśa with skulls” can be mainly traced back to the reign of Siṅhasāri King 
Kṛtanagara (r. 1265–​1292 ce) of the Rājasa dynasty and its aftermath (figs. 19.2a, 2b, 
and 2c). However, this iconographic detail might very well have originated from 
the period preceding Kṛtanagara: if we match this visual evidence with the above-​
mentioned inscriptional and textual evidence, it does not seem unreasonable to 
assume that hard-​core tantric traditions revolving around the cult of Bhairava, and in­
spired by the “charnel ground” religious culture, existed as esoteric palatine religious 
undercurrents in that period, and influenced elite expressions of visual and literary

culture. Indeed, the Mūla Maluruṅ inscription issued by Viṣṇuvardhana in 1255 ce 
(Hadi Sidomulyo 2010, 107; plate III.b.3) mentions, apparently in a position of promi­
nence at court, the “great priest of the Bhairava religious denomination” (sthāpaka riṅ 
kabhairavan) Ḍaṅ Ācārya Astrarāja Patipati.
East Java: Siṅhasāri and Majapahit 
(ca. 1265–​Fifteenth Century)
Icons of Bhairava are found in East Java from the thirteenth century onward, in con­
comitance with the explosion in religious iconography of horrific aesthetic motifs asso­
ciated with the “charnel ground culture” of the Śaiva Bhairavatantras and the Buddhist 
Yoginītantras, as well as a progressive demonization of visual representations of divine 
figures in East Javanese art (figs. 19.3a, 3b, and 3c). The expansion and wider application 
of a demonic and transgressive set of iconographic features becomes dominant during 
the reign of Kṛtanagara, a sovereign of cosmopolitan outlook that was known to em­
ploy foreign (i.e., Newar and Eastern Indian) artists, as suggested by the inscriptions in 
Indian script engraved on several statues as well as their Indian/​Nepalese iconograph­
ical influences. The full manifestation of this peculiar iconography under Kṛtanagara 
may be due to reasons that may be mainly political in nature—​namely, his initiation into 
hard-​core currents of Buddhist and Śaiva tantra and the dissemination of statues across 
his reign (even as far as Central Sumatra) as a reaction to the diplomatic and military 
confrontation with Mongol Emperor Kublai Khan of the Yuan dynasty.
Among the statuary attributed to Kṛtanagara, some of the deities hosted at the Śaiva 
Candi Singhosari stand out for their exquisite craftmanship and their characteristic 
pedestals surrounded by eight skulls. Skulls are found in abundance especially in the 
icons of Bhairava (figs. 19.3a, 3b, and 3c) and Gaṇeśa (figs. 19.2a, 2b, and 2c)—​on hands, 
ear, and body ornaments: diadems, garments, and headdresses. Similarly, skulls are 
carved on several other statues of the Siṅhasāri and Majapahit periods, like the demonic 
guardians (dvārapāla) of Candi Singhosari and Candi Panataran, the colossal statue re­
ferred to as Totok Kerot, the Rāmāyaṇa reliefs of Candi Panataran, as well as some Kāla 
heads of East Javanese temples, such as Candi Singhosari, Candi Jago, and Candi Lima 
near Trowulan. Symbolizing death and the fear of death, as well as the wider religio-​
cultural complex of the charnel ground, the skull in India is considered inauspicious and 
impure, and yet powerful. Even if such pervasive depictions of skulls have few (if any) 
close parallels in the medieval art of the Indian subcontinent,14 the decorative use of 
skulls is a characterizing feature of the Bhairavatantras and the Buddhist Yoginītantras, 
like the Cakrasaṃvara, where it also symbolizes the mastering of death and the tran­
scendence of the mundane world (Gray 2005, 25). Thus, the flourishing of this peculiar 
iconography reveals an affiliation to transgressive, hard-​core tantric currents through a 
pervasive application of themes linked to the charnel ground culture and an associated

--- PAGE 458 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      433
 
ideology of power. Kṛtanagara’s conscious association with this ideology and ritual prac­
tice is further suggested by the fact that the Sanskrit inscription of Wurare dating from 
the late period of his reign (i.e., 1289), engraved on a statue of Mahākṣobhya (possibly 
representing the king himself: see Sinclair 2022), mentions the installation of this statue 
on the homonymous charnel ground (śmaśāne vurarenāmni, v. 13), which was already 
associated with the āśrama of the powerful royal guru and siddhācārya Mpu Bhāraḍa 
nearly three centuries before.15 From an impure and terrifying locale, the charnel ground 
of Wurare is here praised as an important seat of the sacred royal geography of East Java 
from the eleventh throughout the thirteenth century (see Chemburkar, this volume).
Besides reflecting these tantric ideals (and perhaps also resonating with local/​
indigenous belief), Kṛtanagara’s ideology and ritual praxis also had an eminently

practical function (i.e., the protection of the state).16 This ideology and ritual practice, 
emphasizing protective and/​or aggressive violence, were the hallmarks of hard-​core tan­
tric traditions of the late phase of tantric Buddhism and were closely intertwined with 
the troubled political situation of the period. It needs, therefore, to be contextualized 
against the background of the coeval adoption of state-​protection tantric magic in many 
contemporary Asian kingdoms. Association of monarchs with antinomian and martial 
forms of tantric Buddhism was common from the twelfth to the fourteenth centuries 
and beyond across the Buddhist world.17 Various sovereigns appear to have been eager 
to be initiated into tantric systems dominated by wrathful and martial esoteric Buddhist 
deities like Mahākāla or Heruka/​Hevajra, which were worshiped as the protectors of 
various kingdoms and as powerful icons ensuring success on the battlefields.18
As argued by Hadi Sidomulyo (2010, 98), the major shift in religious orientation de­
tectable after Kṛtanagara’s accession to the throne noted by Hunter (2007, 38) “should 
probably be linked in part to the threat posed by the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan in the 
last quarter of the 13th century.” This concern is hinted at in passages of the Deśavarṇana 
(Cantos 42 and 43) by Mpu Prapañca, which praise the sovereign as “more and more 
energetic in his policy” (makin atiyatna riṅ naya) in view of the difficulty to protect the 
world in the age of Kali (kevәh iṅ bhuvanarakṣaṇa gavayәn i kālaniṅ kalī), as a result 
of which “he held fast to esoteric doctrines and observances” (nimittaniran aṅrәgәp 
samaya len brata) of the Buddhists (Robson 1995, 155). Kṛtanagara was deemed a “god-​
king” (devaprabhū), “very energetic in the rites for application of magic” (mahotsāheṅ 
prayogakriyā, 43.4).
Further evidence of Kṛtanagara’s eclectic adherence to both Śaiva and Buddhist tan­
tric systems for political purposes, and his interest in “war magic,” is provided by textual 
and epigraphic references. The Deśavarṇana makes clear that the fear-​inspiring “divine 
embodiment” of Kṛtanagara (kadevamūrtin, probably a statue of the sovereign, or a ref­
erence to his own persona as a “divine incarnation,” 41.5)19 was instrumental in the defeat 
of the Malay kingdoms of Sumatra (malayu). The Sukhāmṛta copper plate inscription 
(1296 ce; Poerbatjaraka 1940, 33–​49) mentions the manifestation of Kṛtanagara’s “divine 
nature” (kadevātmakan) as a powerful means to terrorize and subdue his enemies, and 
mentions an ācārya whose consecration name (mapuṣpapāta) was astrarāja (“Chief of 
Weapons”), which suggests that his duties included war rituals (Jákl 2020, 36).20 The 
same inscription refers to the special patronage accorded by Kṛtarājasa (aka Raden 
Wijaya, r. 1293–​1309) to Ḍaṅ Hyaṅ Astrarāja’s son, Mpu Kapat, a bhujaṅga priest of Śaiva 
persuasion (bhujaṅga śaivapakṣa) adhering to the Bhairava observance (bhairavabrata) 
bearing the court name (pañji) Patipati, whose father already served Kṛtanagara in the 
same capacity. Hunter (2007, 35–​36) argued that Kṛtanagara may have patronized the 
family of Patipati because of its role as instructors in Bhairavika Śaivism, which assisted 
the ruler in the art of warfare.
Another association with martial magical empowerment is suggested by an unu­
sual iconographical feature of the statues of deities facing the main directions at Candi 
Singhosari (i.e., Nandīśvara and Mahākāla [east], Durgā [north], and Gaṇeśa [west]—​
the ascetic Agastya [south] being the exception), namely, the short sleeveless “military

--- PAGE 460 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      435
 
jacket” (kavaca), which according to Stutterheim (1936, 308–​309), has a magically 
protective function. An analogous martial character may be detected in the Cāmuṇḍī 
group probably originating from Candi Singhosari, now preserved at the Trowulan 
Museum. This badly damaged group is interesting for preserving a Sanskrit invocation 
in Devanāgarī script identifying the deity as Cāmuṇḍī (instead of the more common 
form Cāmuṇḍā), one of the “Eight Mothers” (aṣṭamātṛkās) worshiped by Hindus in me­
dieval Northern India and Nepal, which is otherwise scantly attested in Javanese art; 
for including among the retinue of the central figure of the goddess what look like min­
iature replicas of the Singhosari Bhairava and Gaṇapati; and for a unique depiction of 
the guru Matsyendranātha, a figure associated with the Nātha-​Siddha lineage as well 
as Kaula Śaivism (Lunsingh Scheurleer 2008, 292, n. 21). Hariani Santiko (1997, 217), 
having noted that in Bengal Cāmuṇḍī was associated with vaśīkaraṇa (“subjugation”) 
rituals aiming at defeating enemies (śatrubali), hypothesized a connection between 
this sculptural group and analogous rituals directed toward Kṛtanagara’s archenemy 
Kublai Khan. Although speculative, this interpretation would not be out of place given 
the link between the religious and political sphere in Kṛtanagara’s milieu. Invocations to 
Cāmuṇḍā also occur in mantras associated with the tantric magical acts of vaśīkaraṇa 
and uccāṭaṇa (“expulsion”) in the Saṃvarodaya, a Buddhist tantra belonging to the 
Cakrasaṃvara cycle, in a context belonging to the cult of śmaśāna containing an invoca­
tion to the wrathful Mahākāla (Tsuda 1996, 102).21
Kṛtanagara and Kublai Khan may have been engaged in a ritual war that extended 
beyond the one they fought on the battlefields in the final years of their reigns. Kublai 
Khan received initiation into the Hevajratantra and other transgressive tantric sys­
tems revolving around wrathful deities associated with state-​protection Buddhism, 
and equated himself to one such fierce martial deity, for instance a form of Mahākāla 
(possibly a precursor of Gonpo Gur/​*Pañjaranātha) transmitted by the Tibetan Sakya 
Pa order. Kṛtanagara is likely to have received initiation into similar systems. The im­
portance of Mahākāla in the Buddhist system adhered to by Kṛtanagara is evidenced 
by a colossal statue found at Padang Roco in Central-​Western Sumatra, which has pre­
viously been regarded as a Bhairava or a “Buddhist Bhairava,” but which most likely 
represents a form of Mahākāla with some Śaiva iconographic contaminations (Acri and 
Wenta 2022). Having been associated with the Sumatran king of East Javanese pedi­
gree Ādityavarman (fl. ca. 1320–​1378), who consecrated an Amoghapāśa statue sent to 
Padang Roco by Kṛtanagara, it may be rather connected to Kṛtanagara himself in view 
of the iconographic resemblances with similar statues produced in East Java during 
the Siṅhasāri period.22 This icon, presenting some iconographic features that prefigure 
those of the “deification statues” of elite persons in the Majapahit period, might rep­
resent an early example of such statues, representing Kṛtanagara himself. The sover­
eign was also represented, postmortem, as a deified Śiva-​Buddha at Candi Siṅhasāri 
(Deśavarṇana 43.5), as a Buddha (jina) at Sagala, and as an Ardhanareśvarī-​cum-​
Bajradevī and Vairocana-​cum-​Locanā, and possibly also at Candi Jawi while he was 
still alive, as the Deśavarṇana (56.1) appears to say that he himself was embodied there 
in material form (sirāṅadhiṣṭita śarīra tan hana vaneh).23 The “syncretic” Candi Jawi,

--- PAGE 461 ---
436      Andrea Acri
 
where both Śaivas and Buddhists used to worship during Kṛtanagara’s reign, indeed 
hosted a Śiva statue with an Akṣobhya icon in the headdress above the crown, just like 
the Mahākāla of Padang Roco.
Old Javanese poems composed in the East Javanese period betray an interest in deities 
and motifs associated with hard-​core tantric traditions. A description, recalling the 
above-​mentioned episode of Karālavaktra and Durgā-​Brairavī in the Ghaṭotkacāśraya, 
of the Buddhist goddess Bhairavī/​Vidyutkarālī appearing to Prince Sutasoma 
meditating on corpses in a charnel ground is found in passage spanning cantos 9.5–​12.4 
of the Buddhist kakavin Sutasoma by Mpu Tantular, composed between 1365 and 1389 
ce. References to the fierce and demonic aspects of the goddess are occasionally found 
in Sanskrit stutis preserved in Balinese manuscripts. The Aṣṭakamantra/​Durgāstava, 
an impressive twenty-​four-​verse-​long Sanskrit hymn of antinomian character divided 
into three parts, is entirely dedicated to the fear-​inspiring manifestation of the Goddess, 
who is addressed as Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kālarātrī, Kāpālinī, Karālī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Durgā, 
among other appellatives. While the hymn cannot be dated with certainty, it may be ei­
ther a product or an import of the Siṅhasāri-​Majapahit period.
The demonic form of Durgā is displayed in the reliefs of two temples built in the 
Majapahit period, Candi Tegowangi (Ni Wayan Ariati 2016, 120–​144) and Candi Sukuh, 
as well as in a small number of free-​standing statues, such as the one from Candi Rimbi 
(Lunsingh Scheurleer 2000, 197), and the one now kept at the Rijksmuseum Amsterdam 
(Lunsingh Scheurleer 1998, 421; fig. 7). The above-​mentioned reliefs are connected to the 
Middle Javanese text Sudamala, focusing on purification and exorcism (ruvat)—​a ritual 
practice that has survived in Java and Bali to today. In the story, Umā is cursed by Śiva 
for having committed adultery; having become the demonic Durgā, she was called Ra 
Nini and sentenced to reside in a cremation ground for twelve years along with her ret­
inue (Ni Wayan Ariati 2016, 130). Ra Nini may be a “localization” of one of the terrifying 
forms of the goddess known in Indian tradition: indeed, the mention of a twelve-​year 
expiation period is reminiscent of the twelve-​year funerary penance carried out by the 
Kāpālikas to recast the same observance performed by Bhairava to expiate the sin of 
Brahmanicide resulting from the cutting of Brahmā’s fifth head. Furthermore, the name 
of Ra Nini’s follower, Kālikā, corresponds to that of the manifestation of Durgā known 
from South Asian Sanskrit literature and may have been inspired by a Śākta, Bhairavika, 
or Kaula milieu. The figure of Kālikā conforms to that of a practitioner assuming the 
traits of its demonic iṣṭadevatā, having traits in common with a yoginī/​ḍākinī/​bhaginī 
type known from Sanskrit literature. In the Middle Javanese Calon Araṅ (ch. 3, p. 121), 
we find a description of a wild dance performed in a charnel ground by the witch Calon 
Araṅ and her disciples, along with a ritual in which she brings a corpse back to life. The 
witch washes her hair with the blood of the corpse and fabricates a necklace and caste-​
cord with its intestines of the corpse, then she cuts its head and offers it to the goddess 
(bhagavatī) to provoke an epidemic in the kingdom. These actions are reminiscent of a 
tantric black magical procedure (abhicāra).
Bhairava is a well-​codified figure in the East Javanese literary landscape. Kakavins 
often equate demons to Bhairava(s)—​using the adjectival or verbal form (m)abhairava,

--- PAGE 462 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      437
 
which according to Zoetmulder (1982, 249) means “frightful, terrible, terrifying”—​
and sometimes associate them with martial activities and war dances.24 In the 
Buddhist Sutasoma kakavin, Bhairava and his devotees are stereotypically linked to 
anthropophagic practices. For instance, the text characterizes the villain called Poruṣāḍa 
(the worldly counterpart of the Śaiva Mahākāla) as follows: “He grew more and more 
like a Bhairava as he devoured human beings and became king of the great demons” 
(makin ta ya mabhairavān maṅan ikaṅ nara makaratuniṅ mahāsura, 22.9b). In canto 
38.8, such practices as ritual worship and yoga, good and bad behavior (or pure and im­
pure practices, aśubhaśubhapravṛtti), along with the pure (or: purifying?) observances 
of the religious denomination adhering to the “Bhairavahood” (pakṣa bhairavatva), 
cause rebirth.
While the Sutasoma, loosely based on the Buddhist jātaka tale of the conversion 
of Poruṣāda, presents a moral and social critique of (stereotyped) hard-​core tantric 
practices involving cannibalism, violence, and so on, it also praises the ascetic and med­
itative practices carried out in charnel grounds.25 Its descriptions of those fear-​inspiring 
loci, like the one found in Canto 9.5bcd–​9.8ab, share the tropes that are commonplace in 
tantric sources from the Indian subcontinent, viz. practitioners meditating on Bhairava 
or Bhairavī amidst the remains of dismembered bodies and the wild animals feasting 
on them.26 Another passage of the same text (125.8–​125.11) describes the meditation of a 
Mahāyāna adept in a battlefield using a vividly gruesome imagery. This passage seem­
ingly hints at the tantric practice of vetālasādhana, namely, the supernatural power to 
resurrect corpses to use them as servants, as well as at the Buddhist practice, described 
in Sanskrit sources, of aśubhabhāvanā or “meditation on impurity,” to be conducted 
in the charnel ground (śmaśāna) by heroic renunciants (Gray 2006, 23). The monk’s 
sādhana is “not because he wishes to devour human flesh, not because he wishes to sat­
isfy himself with food and drink: his greatest concern is the oneness of the mind [ . . . ] 
his mind did not deviate as he waited for Lord Heruka to descend on earth.”27 The men­
tion of Heruka is noteworthy, as this wrathful deity—​emanating from Akṣobhya, and 
popular in the Cakrasaṃvara cycle—​is poorly attested in the Old Javanese corpus.
Besides the reference to a “religious official of the Śaiva order [following] the Bhairava-​
observance” (bhujaṅga śivapaksa bhairavabrata) in the above-​mentioned Sukhāmṛta 
copper plates (1296 ce) issued by Krtarājasa, other epigraphical and textual material 
suggested that the alliance between the political power and Bhairava priesthood con­
tinued from the Siṅhasāri to the Majapahit period. Interestingly, a religious official of 
the Bhairava denomination, Saṅ Ārya Vaṅśādhirāja, erected and consecrated a statue 
of Mañjuśrī in East Java (probably at or in the vicinity of Candi Jago) in 1343 ce (Kozok 
and van Rijn 2010, 142). Three religious figures, Ḍaṅ Ācārya Śivanātha,28 Smaranātha, 
and Agreśvara, are mentioned in the Manah-​i-​Manuk charter, issued under the reign of 
Hayam Vuruk (Śrī Rājasanagara, r. 1350–​1389), as being “of the Bhairava denomination, 
fully competent in the sciences of logic and grammar” (bhairavapakṣa nyāyavyākaraṇa-
śāstraparisamāpta; Pigeaud 1960, 104–​107).29
The popularity of the Bhairava cult is still detectable in the late Majapahit period 
and beyond. In the Koravāśrama (6, p. 60.33), an Old Javanese text probably composed

--- PAGE 463 ---
438      Andrea Acri
 
between the fifteenth and early sixteenth century, the Bhairava denomination is 
mentioned alongside boddha (Buddhism), sridanta (Śaivasiddhānta),30 maguru (=​ 
mahāguru?), and mahāpuṣpita, which I take to be a corruption for Mahāpāśupata, a 
term occurring in Sanskrit sources from the subcontinent as a synonym of Kāpālika, 
Kālamukhas, or Lākula Pāśupatas practicing the mahāvrata (Lorenzen 1991, 19, 107, 
151).31 The Tantu Paṅgәlaran, our best source of information on the Bhairava cur­
rent in Java from the fourteenth to the fifteenth century, documents an efflorescence 
of Bhairava cults that may have been the expression of the rural, noncourtly religious 
communities of the hermitages-​cum-​scriptoria known as mandalas and kabuyutans 
located in mountainous areas of Java.32 The text narrates that Śiva/​Bhaṭāra Guru 
manifested himself in the form of Mahāmpu Palyat, a bhujaṅga of the Śaiva denomi­
nation, who carried out tapas in a charnel ground in Kalyasәm on Mt Hyaṅ “according 
to the Bhairawa order, eating the corpses [of people]; he kept them cool and damp, 
and in the middle of the night he ate them.”33 Mahāmpu Palyat’s party meets the king 
of Galuh, carrying human meat: “The skull of people they used as a drinking cup, 
and bowls [ . . . ] served as their containers for keeping the corpses cool and damp.”34 
Disgusted by this view, the king vomits, and a priest of the king’s entourage advises 
him to put Mahāmpu Palyat to death, for “a wiku like that looks like a case of what 
is called brahmālokasanghāra, destruction of the realm of Brahmā.”35 But the ascetic 
reveals himself to be none other than God, and the king’s emissaries become his dis­
ciples. A similar episode is recounted with respect to the king’s elder son, who hears 
of a Brahmin of clerical rank (bhujaṅga) called Mpu Barang, following the Bhairava 
way, who eats corpses and drinks from people’s skulls in the Kalyasәm charnel ground 
(Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 53). The mention of the eating of human meat and 
drinking of human blood (among other impure bodily products) at night in a charnel 
ground is attested in Śaiva and Buddhist tantric sources from the Indian subconti­
nent as part of the “nocturnal-​vigilance” (niśāṭana or niśācāra—​the latter being also 
the name of a category of demonic beings, which were arguably “emulated” by the 
practitioners). Imaginal elements aside, these accounts agree remarkably well with co­
eval epigraphic evidence, and Hadi Sidomulyo sees them as preserving elements of his­
torical truth about the adoption of Bhairava traditions by the Javanese royalty from the 
Keḍiri period onward (Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 150–​151).
A visual and architectural expression of the same local reconfigurations of the 
Bhairava cult that informed the Tantu Paṅgәlaran may be the graphically erotic and 
transgressive fifteenth-​century Candi Sukuh and Candi Cetho on Mount Lawu on the 
border between Central and East Java (fig. 19.4). Both complexes are characterized by 
statues and reliefs of demons as well as deities—​Bhīma, Garuḍa, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and 
so on—​displaying demonic traits and a charnel ground ambiance (Duijker 2010, 219), 
as well as scenes based on the Sudamala and Calon Araṅ stories. This strikingly horrific 
iconography constitutes a unicum in Javanese art, and it probably reflects the icono­
graphical and architectural project of the temple, which revolves around the concept of 
purification and empowerment.

--- PAGE 464 ---
