Diagnostic of a “localized” Bhairavika Tantrism may also be the “Bhīma cult” that 
flourished in Java (and Bali) in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Stutterheim (1956, 
117–​118) identified the figure of Bhīma as a conflation between the demonic, skull-​
bearing ascetic Bhairava (of identical meaning, “the terrible/​frightful”) and the popular 
Pāṇḍava hero of the Mahābhārata.36 Bhīma is the protagonist of a cycle of ca. fifteenth–​
sixteenth-​century Middle Javanese narrative-​cum-​philosophical texts narrating his 
Figure 19.4.  Candi Sukuh, Central-​East Java, temple (top left) and details of reliefs.
Photo: author.

--- PAGE 465 ---
440      Andrea Acri
 
mystical journey toward self-​purification and enlightenment, such as the Navaruci 
(and the related Bhīmasuci) and the Bhīmasvarga (Aditia Gunawan 2019). This cycle 
constitutes a common plot for old as well as modern puppet (wayang) narratives and 
performances. In Javanese literature and wayang lore, Bhīma is associated with features 
that are remindful of demons in general, and of Bhairava in particular: for instance, he 
indulges in drunkenness and sexual promiscuity; he eats anything without discrimina­
tion; he speaks only the low register of Javanese language; he is said to have stayed in the 
Gaṇḍamayu cemetery, the abode of Durgā; his behavior is inclined to violence and rage; 
he wears snake-​bracelets and sports an erect penis (Stutterheim 1956, 124). A passage 
from the Navaruci describes the incarnation of Bhaṭāra Guru—​who is later revealed 
to be no one else than Bhīma indeed—​as having similar characteristics, for example, 
paying no attention to his diet, laughing violently, eating his own body, and drinking 
his own blood.37 The references to Bhīma as paying no attention to his diet—​veiledly 
hinting at anthropophagy—​and also practicing self-​anthropophagy call to mind the no­
torious dietary habits of the Pāśupatas and Kāpālikas.38
Vestiges of Hard-​Core Tantra in Early 
Modern Javanese Texts and Practices
The key themes of hard-​core tantric traditions discussed above, including transgres­
sion, power, and nondualism, were deeply engrained in Javanese society, in both the 
countryside and the centers of political power, so much so that they did not disappear 
after Islamization but survived as an undercurrent, in a reconfigured manner, through 
the Islamic period to the present. Even the symbolical association of the “left-​handed” 
(kiwa, pangiwa) with “bad, wicked, sinister, inherently condemnable” (as well as the 
pre-​Islamic, Hindu-​Buddhist order), as opposed to “right-​handed,” tĕngĕn, panĕṅĕn, 
associated with “good, virtuous, praiseworthy” (as well as the Islamic order: see Arps 
2019, 315, 317, 327) that is still recognized in Modern Javanese culture could ultimately 
reflect a convergence between the Indic dichotomy of vāma and dakṣiṇa, which is also 
applied to “left-​hand” and “right-​hand” tantric practices and an ancestral dualistic out­
look widespread among Malayo-​Polynesian language-​speaking societies of insular 
Southeast Asia.
Nineteenth-​century suluk mystical texts in Modern Javanese attest to the trope of 
mystics “acting like Bhairava” (mañjing ambirawa), that is, engaging in radical and an­
tinomian behaviors transgressing moral, social, dietary, and religious rules; behaving 
like madmen or ill-​mannered children and consuming forbidden foods; and upholding 
unorthodox monistic views, thereby becoming “one with Bhairava” and identifying 
with God (Acri 2019).39 Although these views do have counterparts in the Sufi traditions 
that influenced Javanese mysticism, they are too specific to constitute direct borrowings 
from Sufism and are rather to be viewed as survivals of pre-​Islamic tantric currents

--- PAGE 466 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      441
 
(Acri 2019; Zoetmulder 1994). Indeed, the form ambhairava is attested in Tantu 
Paṅgәlaran 118.11: ambhairava ta sira, siṅ paṅan tan ana linivatan denira, “He [the master 
Mpu Baraṅ] followed the way of life of a Bhairava (or: of the Bhairava sect), eating an­
ything without passing it over” (Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 284). It is also used 
in another premodern Old Javanese source, the Tutur Raṇayajña (probably composed 
or recompiled in Bali and containing material on rules of conduct and observances of 
men of religion), to describe an ascetic devoted to Bhairavī (viku bheravi) as “one who 
takes up/​behaves like one of the Bhairava denomination within the Buddhist religion” 
(ambhiravipakṣa kabhudayan [=​ kabuddhan?]), who performs a war-​dance (aśrama) in 
a charnel ground (śamasana) (p. 24). The expression mabharawa (=​ mabhairava) was 
still recorded by Lovric (1986, 73) to be in use in late-​twentieth-​century Bali to refer 
to the high level of spiritual elevation of a pedanda Siwa (Śaiva high priest) who took 
on “terrible and demonic powers” and reached the “transcendence of human nature, 
needs and motivation.” Such pedanda,40 before being ordained, had allegedly lay in a 
graveyard at night, assuming the form of the evil witch Rangda, and consumed a corpse, 
without fear. According to another source, a pendanda “had pursued the ‘left-​hand’ path 
(pangiwa) and had become bharawa, but had not deviated to the dangerous path of de­
struction” (Lovric 1986, 73).
The Tantu Paṅgәlaran may have played the role of a textual bridge between the Hindu 
and Islamic traditions in Java, for it contains various motifs that appear to have been 
reused in modern Javanese Islamic texts. These “threads of information” may “help us 
to establish a line of continuity, linking the age of the Hindu-​Javanese mandala with that 
of the early Islamic period” (Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 77–​78). For instance, 
the text relates the story of a certain Aji Uṇḍal of Daha who, refusing to acknowledge 
the authority of his religious superior, one night initiated a pupil, unaware that the cer­
emony was witnessed by a group of slaves accompanied by a black dog (note that the 
black dog is the vehicle, and symbol of, Bhairava). Each one of them, including the dog, 
became at once a devaguru, with the right to establish their own religious communities. 
The newly ordained vikus then “proceeded to attract disciples indiscriminately, 
imparting the message: ‘Do whatever you want; eat anything without exception; take a 
wife; there is no necessity to make offerings, to worship or fast, to know the scriptures 
or to be taught about anything, just think of yourself as the Lord’ ” (Robson and Hadi 
Sidomulyo 2021, 77).
The hedonistic and at the same time radically monistic message of the passage quoted 
above is in harmony with analogous teachings attributed to Kāpālikas and Kaulas 
practitioners in India, whose classical descriptions usually included derisive expositions 
of hedonistic doctrines “more suitable for a Cārvāka or Lokāyatika than a Kāpālika” 
(Lorenzen 1991, 47).41 It also echoes similar passages contained in the Old Javanese 
Śaiva text Dharma Pātañjala, where they represent the false teachings of an opponent 
(pūrvapakṣa). The opponent, introduced by the Lord as a teacher whose doctrines 
cause one to fall in hell, upholds the monistic position that any persons—​including 
those who fabricate liṅgas, build temples, organize assemblies, or organize food-​ and 
drinking-​feasts—​are the loci where the Lord in his manifest form resides, and death

--- PAGE 467 ---
442      Andrea Acri
 
equals liberation; this view causes one to transgress the customary rules of conduct.42 
Other passages of the same text relate a materialistic doctrine prescribing the enjoy­
ment of food, riches, and women as a mark of “purity,” as well as the abandonment of 
observances.43 Such materialistic and hedonistic doctrines are labeled the “knowledge 
of Kāla”—​Kāla being the fierce, Rudra-​ or Bhairava-​like embodiment that the Lord takes 
up when He destroys the universe. Indeed, the text adds that the appearance of religious 
men teaching such a doctrine in the future will be a sign that the time of the great cosmic 
dissolution is approaching.44 This view can be compared to the above-​mentioned viku 
brahmālokasaṅhāra, the cause of the destruction of the realm of Brahmā, in the Tantu 
Paṅgәlaran.
As noted by Hadi Sidomulyo (in Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 77), the Aji Uṇḍal 
episode in the Tantu Paṅgәlaran “points to the presence of a heterodox current, which 
ran counter to accepted norms and probably aroused a measure of disapproval from 
the Hindu-​Javanese religious establishment” and finds an intriguing parallel in the 
doctrines and activities of the controversial sixteenth-​century Islamic saint known as 
Siti Jĕnar or Seh Lĕmah Abang, whose radically monistic teachings—​which bear traces 
of Indian influences (Zoetmulder 1994, 306–​307)—​were held in contempt by the court 
of Demak. Siti Jĕnar was regarded as having deemed himself God (i.e., adhered to a doc­
trine proclaiming the identity between man and God), and as preaching that heaven and 
hell are already here and now, that there is no recompense in a future heaven, and that 
prayer and ritual are useless. These views which again call to mind similar views upheld 
by Indian materialists, who denied karmic retribution and the effectiveness of religious 
undertakings.
Siti Jĕnar himself, like Aji Uṇḍal in the Tantu Paṅgәlaran, is regarded as having been 
accidentally initiated during the ordination ceremony of Sunan Kalijaga by the saint 
(wali) Sunan Bonang, and transformed from a worm to a human being “upon inad­
vertently gaining access to the ‘Great Mystery of the Supreme Being’ ” (Robson and 
Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 77). Also worthy of note is the fact that one of the two demons 
escorting the functionary Ki Kabhayan-​panglayar to the former hermitage of Mpu 
Baraṅ, who is later initiated by the former as he obtains divine favor and spiritual power, 
and is referred to as the “Lord Guru”, is called (Ki) Lĕmah-​bang, just like Lĕmah Abang/​
Siti Jĕnar (Robson and Hadi Sidomulyo 2021, 54). Furthermore, Siti Jĕnar is sentenced to 
death by a synod for his heretical, radically monistic doctrines (as well as for having re­
vealed them indiscriminately), but his corpse transforms into a reddish/​brown dog and 
manifests itself as a multicolored light representing God,45 thus revealing that Siti Jĕnar 
was in fact God; this echoes the passages of the Tantu Paṅgәlaran related above about 
the death sentence issued by the king against Mahāmpu Palyat, who reveals himself to 
be God, as well as the episode of the bhujaṅga Mpu Barang following the Bhairava way 
who is also sentenced to death by two Buddhist monks, and who revives each time, in 
the end revealing himself to be Parameśvara.
This motif also finds a counterpart in the story, narrated in the Islamic Sĕrat Cabolek, 
around the (likely fictitious) character of Ki Bĕbĕluk, who was sentenced to death 
during the kingdom of Pajang. According to Soebakin Soebardi (1975, 30), this character

--- PAGE 468 ---
“Hard-Core” Tantric Traditions and the Cult of Bhairava      443
 
provides an “archetypical continuity” between Seh Siti Jĕnar and two other antinomian 
figures, Pangerang/​Sunang Panggung (also known as Malang Sumirang), and Haji 
Mutamakin. The former, as narrated in the Babad Jaka Tingkir, is followed by his dog 
everywhere, even in the mosque, which provokes a stir;46 attended by his dog during his 
trial and execution, Malang Sumirang writes his testament in the midst of the fire, that 
is, the eponymous antinomian suluk, which is carried in the dog’s mouth from the fire.47 
The latter, Haji Mutamakin, is a quintessential “heretic” described in the Sĕrat Cabolek 
(1.2) who, just like Siti Jĕnar, “disclosed esoteric knowledge, and revealed the secrets of 
the Science of Reality” (Soebakin Soebardi 1975, 66), for which he is executed, and who 
also breeds dogs, naming them after prominent Ulamas.48
According to Soebakin Soebardi (1975, 38), Mutamakin is related to the figure of Ṛṣi 
Visrava, a pre-​Islamic ascetic who, as recounted in the Modern Javanese Sĕrat Suluk, 
“was cursed by the gods because he drew aside the [Divine] veil and proclaimed himself 
to be God.” Indeed, while these heterodox Islamic characters and their teacher Siti Jĕnar 
have often been linked to the radical doctrines expounded by Sufis, and in particular 
the Persian mystic al-​Hallaj, who was executed for blasphemy, the idea of a direct link 
with, and influence by, al-​Hallaj’s theology (and, possibly, even his biography) has been 
persuasively problematized by various leading scholars of Javanese Islam (Feener 1998; 
Headley 2006; Zoetmulder 1994). These figures admit a more nuanced interpretation, 
presenting as they reflect striking continuities with pre-​Islamic heritage and themes 
associated in the Javanese imaginary to the same constellation of ideas representing 
the continuation of a resilient tantric ideology grounded on transgression and radical 
monism (converted to pantheism), which is associated with Rudra-​ and Bhairava-​
worshiping practitioners in the Indic imaginary.
Nonliterary evidence of the existence and survival in Java of Kāpālikas are the myste­
rious canthang balungs, a category of antinomian, low-​status functionaries observed at 
the court of Surakarta in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, who Brandts 
Buys (1933, 259) described as “degenerate Brahmans” (gedegenereerde Brahmanen). Their 
name, meaning “rattling bones,” could be a “survival” pointing to their ancient status of 
Kāpālikas, who were indeed wearing ornaments made of bones and carrying musical 
instruments made of the same material.49 The canthang balungs worn strings of flowers 
adorning their naked bodies—​being reminiscent of the garland of flowers offered to 
the gods (nirmālya) worn by Pāśupata ascetics; performed dances and buffooneries; 
emitted dog’s cries (and imitated their mating), nonsensical interjections, and vehement 
laughter; superintended female dancers (taledhek) who also doubled as prostitutes, 
and engaged in obscene acts on stage during their plays; indulged in drinking liquor 
on stage; held a staff or a pike; executed mudrās during their performances; and origi­
nally possessed seals of office depicting a phallus (a liṅga?) inside a heart-​shaped vulva, 
which are remindful of the heart-​shaped pubic plaques worn by ascetics in East Javanese 
art—​a motif that is also represented at Candi Panataran/​Singhosari and at Candi Sukuh. 
The canthang balungs’ most un-​Islamic and highly transgressive practices, as well as 
their Indic insignia, all conspire to identify them as localized Javanese “descendants” of 
Kāpālikas or Kāpālika-​like groups.

	 5.	 Although in nondualist Śaiva (as well as Buddhist) traditions release can be conceptualized 
as a state of supreme bliss, the erotic connotation (ānanda in Sanskrit can also mean ‘sexual

(Ullāsa 8) mentions paramānanda in the context of the gaṇacakra (“tantric feast”), in 
which sexual rituals took place. See also Lorenzen 1991, 47, paraphrasing Ānandagiri’s 
Śaṅkaradigvijaya: “the joy (ānanda) of sexual union is the true form of Bhairava”.
	 6.	 This can also be evinced from one of the Kāpālikas’ denominations (i.e., Somasiddhāntins),

umā),” also implying that the Kāpālikas’ ultimate goal was conceived as the union between 
the liberated adept (identified with Śiva) and Umā (Lorenzen 1991, 82–​83, 90). Törzsök 
(2020, 34) considers this interpretation rather forced, while admitting that “it is possible 
that the Kāpālikas themselves intended to make full use the natural polysemy of the word 
Soma, although it is less likely that such polysemy was intended from the very beginning.”

	21.	 One of the transmitters of the Cakrasaṃvara according to the Indo-​Tibetan tradition was 
Matsyendranātha, who was equated to the Buddhist Lūyipa (Mallinson 2019, 272 n. 35; 
White 2007, 106–​107). The Cakrasaṃvara, dominated by Heruka, betrays a characteristic 
“bricolage,” incorporating as it does Śaiva deities, including Cāmuṇḍī (alias Cāmuṇḍā). 
For the form Cāmuṇḍī (rather than Cāmuṇḍā), see also the Buddhist Ḍākārṇava (a prob. 
tenth–​twelfth century Eastern Indian or Nepalese Tantra; Sugiki 2018, 81), and the Śaiva 
Mahāgaṇapatividyā (Sanderson 2007, 199–​200 n. 16).
	22.	 This form of Mahākāla may have been introduced to East Java by one of the Buddhist mas­
ters who traveled from the Indo-​Tibetan and Himalayan regions to China and vice versa, 
like Gautamaśrībhadra, an Eastern Indian paṇḍita who was active in Tibet and China, 
where—​as an initiate in the Kālacakra and other tantric traditions—​he influenced the reli­
gious paradigm at the court of Kublai Khan. Gautamaśrī left an inscription in the Karimun 
Islands off Sumatra in the second half of the thirteenth century, to record his passage 
(Sinclair 2019); although we do not know his destination (either China or India), he or one 
of his followers might very well have visited East Java, a major political, cultural, and reli­
gious powerhouse of the time.
	23.	 My interpretation differs from that of previous translators, who read aṅadhiṣṭhita in

appointed; superintending,” but uniquely on the basis of this passage and a 1360 ce in­
scription), while I interpret it as having a meaning akin to that of the Sanskrit adhiṣṭhita, 
“inhabited,” as well as the cognate Old Javanese aṅadhiṣṭhāna, inadhiṣṭhāna, “(intr.) to 
take one’s place in st. material, embody os. in; (tr.) to give a material support to, make 
st. enter into st. material, give a visible form to”; paṅadhiṣṭhānan, “that in which st. is 
embodied or made visible.”

Chapter 20
Timeless Symbolism
An Early Dzogchen Patriarch’s Hagiography 
and Scriptures
Georgios T. Halkias
Introduction
In the Tibetan contemplative traditions of the Nyingma and Bön schools, the 
teachings of the Great Perfection or Dzogchen (Skt. Mahāsandhi; Tib. rdzogs chen) are 
considered the pinnacle of all instructions that lead to liberation.1 The arcane concepts 
of the Great Perfection are commonly traceable across two overlapping geograph­
ical regions: Uḍḍiyāna for the Buddhists and Zhang Zhung for the Bön. Apocryphal 
Tibetan narratives describe the supramundane origins and spread of Dzogchen often 
in symbolic terms, including hierophanies and kratophanies that we discern in an­
cient Mediterranean mystery cults, Neoplatonic, Kashmiri Śaiva, and other esoteric 
fraternities active along the ancient routes of communication and trade, the Eurasian 
Silk Routes.2 Despite similarities in the view and methods of Dzogchen in the Nyingma 
and Bön schools and the intersecting geography of Uḍḍiyāna (Swat valley) and the 
kingdom of Zhang Zhung extending to the northwest of the Indian subcontinent, each 
school features its own unique lineages of transmission formed in different historical 
periods and by different people. Theologically speaking, such competing claims are in­
consequential since both schools concur that Dzogchen is not the creation of a human 
founder or the outcome of an internal development within a philosophical tradition. 
Rather, the Great Perfection is the expression of the intrinsic nature of our mind (sems 
nyid) which has always been in a state of perfection or completion (rdzogs pa). When 
recognized for what it is, it becomes the basis of liberation (grol gzhi) from samsara. In 
the Nyingma School, the soteriological potential of this nature is known as “basis” or 
“ground” (gzhi) and is symbolized by Buddha Samantabhadra (Kun tu bzang po) who 
is set free in the recognition of the inner radiance of the ground prior to any distinction

--- PAGE 479 ---
454      Georgios T. Halkias
 
between buddhas and sentient beings. The default mode of straying into confusion 
during the presencing of the primordial basis (gdod ma’i gzhi) is the basis of illusion 
(’khrul gzhi) that obscures the recognition of phenomena that arise from the ground as 
self-​appearing.
In the early history of the Nyingma School, Śrī Siṃha occupies a central position be­
cause of the succession of his Indian and Tibetan disciples who brought the Dzogchen 
scriptures and practices to Tibet. According to the authoritative and often cited 
Extensive History of the Great Perfection of the Seminal Heart (Rdzogs pa chen po snying 
thig gi lo rgyus chen mo),3 the source of the Great Perfection lineage is Samantabhadra, 
followed by Garab Dorje (Dga’ rab rdo rje), the first human representative of the lin­
eage. Garab Dorje was succeeded by Mañjuśrīmitra, Śrī Siṃha, Jñānasūtra, and 
Vimalamitra.4 From Mañjuśrīmitra who was a Buddhist scholar of Brahmin origin, 
Śrī Siṃha received the entirety of the Great Perfection instructions arranged in three 
classes. He in turn transmitted the first two classes to his Tibetan disciple and translator, 
Vairocana of Pagor: the Mind Class (sems sde), which features the earliest Atiyoga texts 
dating back to the late eighth century (or later), and the lesser known contemplative 
practices of the Space Class (klong sde). He passed on the Pith Instruction Class (man 
ngag sde), the highest-​order commentary on Dzogchen philosophy, to Vimalamitra and 
Padmasambhava. The two principal hagiographical sources of the Great Perfection’s 
Seminal Heart (Snying thig) tradition, the Seminal Heart of Vimalamitra (Bi ma 
snying thig) and the Seminal Heart of the Ḍākinīs (Mkha’ ’gro snying thig),5 concur that 
Vairocana, Vimalamitra, and Padmasambhava, received the lineage of the Great 
Perfection from Śrī Siṃha.
The Narrative Appearance of a Mystic
Śrī Siṃha’s Tibetan hagiographies are post-​imperial texts shaped by esoteric Buddhist 
precepts and practices. They are not meant to be actual biographical accounts. They date 
several centuries after the latest period assigned to Śrī Siṃha as the teacher of the illus­
trious master Nubchen Sangye Yeshe (Gnubs chen sangs rgyas ye shes, c. ninth century) 
with whom he collaborated in the Tibetan translation of six Dzogchen texts.6 These 
hagiographies are commonly structured around pivotal events and contain hermetic 
archetypes and formulaic motifs that recur in the life stories of the early patriarchs of the 
Great Perfection. Common to these Great Perfection traditional narratives are: a) the 
centrality of charnel grounds as ideal places for meditation and for engagements with 
other-​worldly beings; b) encounters with celestial bodhisattvas and ḍākinīs who aid the 
yogis in their quest to find a teacher; c) the concealment, discovery, and reconcealment 
of esoteric scriptures; and d) striking photophanies that manifest during the passing 
away of the patriarchs who posthumously reappear in a luminous body to deliver final 
instructions to chosen disciples. Although some of these features are known from 
the life stories of accomplished Indian tantric masters,7 the distinct manner in which

--- PAGE 480 ---
Timeless Symbolism      455
 
the early patriarchs convert their bodies into light would appear unique to the Great 
Perfection narratives.8 These visible bodies of light (’od sku) attained through the ad­
vanced contemplative methods of tögel (thod rgal) contribute to the development of 
an embodied mythos and serve as a trademark of the wisdom-​tradition of the Great 
Perfection.9 Just as unusual is the symbolic mode by which these mystics impart to their 
chosen disciples their final instructions enclosed in miniature caskets made of precious 
jewels. These wisdom relics contain their quintessential teachings, their last testaments 
or zhelchem (zhal chems).10
The Life of Śrī Siṃha
According to the Extensive History (folia 110–​19), Śrī Siṃha was born in the town of 
Sokyam (So khyam) in China, fathered by Gewe’i Yitsen (Dge ba’i yid can) and mothered 
by Nangwa Selwa Raptukyenma (Snang ba gsal ba rab tu mkhyen ma).11 From the age of 
fifteen to eighteen he studied the five major fields of knowledge (Skt. pañcavidyāsthāna; 
Tib. rigs gnas che ba lnga)—​logic, medicine, arts and crafts, language, and religious or 
inner knowledge—​under the guidance of master Hastibhala (alias Haribhala). Attaining 
proficiency in these subjects, he sets out for Suvarṇadvīpa (Gser ling), the Land of Gold 
in the west.12 On his way to Suvarṇadvīpa, he has a numinous vision of the bodhisattva 
Avalokiteśvara who appears before him predicting that he must go in India to practice 
at the charnel ground of Sosadvīpa (So sa ling) in order to attain awakening in this life­
time.13 Śrī Siṃha decides instead to train in the tantras and heads for the Five Peaked 
Mountain (Ri bo rtse lnga).14 For seven years he studies the outer and inner doctrines of 
Vajrayāna under the tutelage of the outcast master Bhelakīrti. He ordains as a monk and 
observes the monastic discipline for thirty years. Again, Avalokiteśvara appears before 
him in a vision and repeats his past prediction before vanishing into space. To endure 
the strenuous journey to India, Śrī Siṃha commits to three years of intense yogic prac­
tice and attains the body of an awareness holder (rig ’dzin) and facility in speed walking.15
At the charnel ground of Sosadvīpa he meets his root-​teacher Mañjuśrīmitra who 
instructs him for twenty-​five years on Dzogchen before passing away in an extraor­
dinary display of light. Stunned by this event, Śrī Siṃha faints and falls to the ground. 
When he regains consciousness, he looks up and sees his master in a radiant sphere of 
energy. He weeps in distress: “Oh, alas, if my teacher, the light of the vajra, goes out who 
will remove the darkness of the world?” Mañjuśrīmitra stretches out his right hand and 
places in Śrī Siṃha’s hands a casket made of precious stones the size of a fingernail. 
It contains his last testament known as the Six Meditation Experiences (Sgom nyams 
drug pa). Thereafter, Śrī Siṃha gains irreversible confidence in the unchanging nature 
of reality.
Following Mañjuśrīmitra’s attainment of a body of light, Śrī Siṃha goes to Bodhgaya 
and extracts the Great Perfection teachings, which had been previously hidden by 
his teacher in a boulder and brings them to the Bodhi Tree in China. He arranges

--- PAGE 481 ---
456      Georgios T. Halkias
 
the teachings of the Pith Instructions, in four sections: outer (phyi), inner (nang), se­
cret (gsang), and utmost secret (gsang ba bla na med pa). He collects the outer, inner, 
and secret sections and conceals them in a copper box in the fourth pillar of the Bodhi 
Tree Temple. Following the advice of the ḍākinī Nampar Rolpe’i Gyen (Rnam par rol 
pa’i rgyan) he hides the utmost secret teachings (final order commentary on the Great 
Perfection), at the Chinese Temple of a Thousand Auspicious Gates (Bkra shis khri sgo). 
He seals them with supplications that they be rediscovered in the future and entrusts 
their guardianship to Ekajaṭī (Ral gcig ma), the fierce female protectress-​deity of the 
Secret Mantra. For the remaining days of his life, Śrī Siṃha goes on roaming around the 
cremation grounds where he assumes a multitude of guises and forms. Some of his disci­
ples see him riding naked on a tiger and a buffalo, covered in fat and blood and uttering 
different sounds, with loose matted hair carrying a sword in his right hand and a blood-​
filled skull in his left.16
Śrī Siṃha’s Indian and Tibetan Disciples
The lives of Śrī Siṃha’s two main Indian disciples, Jñānasūtra (Ye shes mdo) and 
Vimalamitra (Dri med bshes gnyen), are dealt with in the next section of the Extensive 
History (folia 119–​29). Here we read that in a prophetic vision, Buddha Vajrasattva 
appears before Jñānasūtra and Vimalamitra and explains to them that even though 
they were reborn as paṇḍitas during the last five hundred lifetimes, they have failed 
to realize the supreme goal of tantra. To do so, they must travel to the Chinese Bodhi 
Tree shrine and request teachings from Śrī Siṃha. Vimalamitra travels from India to 
China to study the Great Perfection corpus and stays there for twenty years. Upon his 
return, he persuades Jñānasūtra to embark for China to study with the master and he 
goes on to spend thirteen years in Tibet translating scriptures and teaching the precepts 
of the Great Perfection.17 Jñānasūtra received the highest Dzogchen initiations, for he 
served as Vimalamitra’s teacher bestowing on him his last posthumous testament, the 
Four Methods of Meditation (Bzhags thabs bzhi pa).18 Śrī Siṃha confers the transmis­
sion of all four sections of the Pith Instructions to Jñānasūtra before transforming his 
five aggregates into light, just as the previous Dzogchen patriarchs have done before 
him. The earth beneath him trembled and Jñānasūtra beheld Śrī Siṃha in a resplendent 
sphere of radiant light. Realizing that his teacher had passed beyond our phenomenal 
world, Jñānasūtra regains his senses and weeps, “Alas, alas, if my teacher the light of 
lamp goes out who will dispel the darkness of the world?” In his luminous form, Śrī 
Siṃha urges Jñānasūtra to go to the One Thousand Gates to retrieve the scriptures of the 
utmost secret essence and delivers in a jeweled casket his final testament, the Seven Nails 
(Gzer bu bdun ma).19
The trials of Śrī Siṃha’s two Tibetan disciples, Vairocana of Pagor and Legdrup 
(Legs grub) of Tsang, are also narrated in the first treasure-​text hagiography of 
Padmasambhava, the Copper Island Chronicle (Zangs gling ma).20 This text, redacted

--- PAGE 482 ---
Timeless Symbolism      457
 
by Nyangrel Nyima Özer (Nyang ral nyi ma ’od zer 1124–​92), details Vairocana’s and 
Legdrup’s long and perilous journey to India following the order of the Tibetan Emperor 
Trisong Detsen, in the latter half of the eighth century, in search of Buddhist teachings. 
In India, they inquire who was the most learned master of Dzogchen and they are told 
to find Śrī Siṃha. At Dhahena assembly hall (Dha he na ku sha ’du khang), Śrī Siṃha 
agrees to teach them and imparts two sets of texts, the twenty-​five tantras (rgyud nyi shu 
rtsa lnga) and the eighteen texts of the Mind Class (sems sde bco brgyad).21
In a later work, the Great Image: The Liberation Narrative of Vairocana (Be ro tsa na’i 
rnam thar ’dra ’bag chen mo),22 we read a similar account: because the Indians were 
possessive of their teachings, Śrī Siṃha instructs the Tibetans under the cover of night 
and in utter secrecy on the eighteen texts of the Mind Class that had been previously 
retrieved from Bodhgaya. On his way back to Tibet, Legdrup dies at the age of forty-​
four, but Vairocana stays behind and receives additional teachings, including the White 
(dkar po), Black (nag po), and Variegated (khra bo) instructions of the Space Class.23 
After completing his training and having mastered the siddhi of “swift-​footedness,” he 
returns to Tibet in seven days only to be discovered back in India that he had defied the 
king’s orders and stole their precious Great Perfection teachings.
In the Garland of Precious Jewels: History of the Seminal Heart of the Ḍākinīs (Mkha’ 
’gro snying thig gi lo rgyus rin po che’i phreng ba) Padmasambhava, the famous eighth-​
century tantric master from Oḍḍiyāna, is listed as Śrī Siṃha’s disciple, though he is com­
monly associated with the transmission of the Mahāyoga tantras. Padmasambhava, 
instructed by the wrathful Vajravārāhī, arrives at the charnel ground Parūṣakavana 
(Rtsub ’gyur tshal) where he meets Śrī Siṃha and receives instruction in all three classes 
of Dzogchen (Mind, Space, and Pith Instructions) and in the eighteen Dzogchen tantras 
that Śrī Siṃha had previously obtained from Garab Dorje at the Śītavana charnel ground 
at Rājagriha.24 Padmasambhava and Vairocana conceal the teachings they received as 
treasure-​texts with a prophetic mandate of their future rediscovery.25
Śrī Siṃha: The Scholar Author
There is little that can be said with certainty regarding Śrī Siṃha’s life. However, given 
the diverse number of texts attributed to him as author and co-​translator with Vairocana 
and Nubchen Sangye Yeshe, there is no reason to doubt his overall historicity. The pro­
cess of identifying his extant Tibetan works across various Tibetan collections is chal­
lenging given the different names and variant spellings he is listed by in the colophons.26 
Moreover, works attributed to him are not gathered uniformly across these collections. 
The following assessment of his works is based on a survey of the digital editions of the 
Kangyur (Bka’ ’gyur), the Tengyur (Bstan ’gyur), the Mtshams brag and Gting skyes 
editions of the Collected Tantras of the Ancients (abbr. NGB =​ Rnying ma rgyud ’bum), 
the Collected Tantras of Vairocana (abbr. BGB =​ Ba’i ro rgyud ’bum), and the Extended 
Teachings of the Nyingma (Rnying ma bka’ ma rgyas pa).27

--- PAGE 483 ---
458      Georgios T. Halkias
 
Three distinct texts composed by Śrī Siṃha are found only in the Tengyur. Two of these 
are of philosophical-​cum-​doctrinal interest: The Lock of the Awakened Mind (Thugs kyi 
sgo lcags), an early doxographical treatise divided into ten sections commenting on the 
nine Buddhist vehicles, and a tantric interpretation of the Heart Sūtra, a Commentary on 
the Secret Mantra Explanation of the Heart Sūtra (Sher snying ’grel pa sngags su ’grel ba). 
The third text, the Upadeśa on the Secret Mantra Sādhana of Uṣṇīṣavijayā (Uṣṇīṣa sngags 
kyi man ngag gi bsgrub thabs), offers apotropaic instructions for protection against sor­
cery, pandemics, hail, obstacles, and demonic influences in three ways: through the real­
ization of the view (non-​conceptual emptiness and the visualization of specific deities); 
through auspicious materials (mandalas made of rare substances and installation of 
ritual daggers); and through the writing and incantation of wrathful mantras.
In the Tengyur, there are also nine short texts of the Great Perfection authored by Śrī 
Siṃha. These works are grouped in two cycles: Cutting the Root of Saṃsāra (’khor ba 
rtsad nas gcod pa), which contains five Dzogchen texts cross-​listed in the BGB, and the 
cycle of Dharmadhātu (chos kyi dbyings), which features four texts included in the BGB 
and the NGB (Gting skyes edition).
In the Tengyur alone, Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana feature as the translators of two works: 
the *Ākāśasamadarśanatantrapañjikā (Lta ba nam mkha’ dang mnyam pa’i rgyud kyi 
dka’ ’grel rin po che sgron ma ’bar ba), a commentary on the Great Perfection by the 
first Dzogchen Patriarch Garab Dorje, and a short commentary, the *Nyāyasiddhyāloka 
(Rigs pa sgrub pa’i sgron ma) on pramāṇa by the late seventh-​century Indian layman 
scholar of Mahāyāna Candragomin. Furthermore, there are four Great Perfection 
commentaries attributed to Garab Dorje in the Tengyur and the BGB, which are 
translated by Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana.
Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana also feature as translators (or somehow involved in the 
transmission) of sixteen Dzogchen texts in the Collected Tantras of the Nyingma (Gting 
skyes edition) which are not found elsewhere. Furthermore, there are eighteen works 
listed in the Collected Tantras of the Nyingma and in the Collected Tantras of Vairocana: 
twelve texts translated by Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana and six by Śrī Siṃha and Nubchen 
Sangye Yeshe who is mentioned under his secret initiatory name Dorje Yang Wangter 
(Rdo rje yang dbang gter).
A total of twenty-​nine Dzogchen scriptures are attributed to Śrī Siṃha in the Gting 
skyes edition of the NGB. These have been grouped in categories devised by the NGB 
editors: eighteen texts of the Mind Class (sems sde’i skor), four texts of the Space Class 
(klong sde’i skor), and seven texts of the Instruction Class (man ngag sde phyi nang skor, 
spyi ti’i skor, & yang ti bram ze’i skor).28 Thus far, five unique texts have been identified 
(where each one is divided in several chapters) that are located only in the eighteenth-​
century edition of the NGB discovered at Tsadrak monastery (Mtshams brag dgon pa) 
in western Bhutan.
The BGB lists four texts not found in other collections. According to the colophon of 
the Precious Light of Wisdom Tantra (Ye shes rin po che ’od kyi rgyud, vol. 3, tsa, 309–​64), 
this work was translated by Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana at the Dhahena Assembly Hall. A 
second work authored by Garab Dorje and Mañjuśrīmitra, Practicing the Wheel of the

--- PAGE 484 ---
Timeless Symbolism      459
 
View (Lta ba spyod pa’i ’khor lo, vol. 5, kha, 155–​68), Śrī Siṃha translated in Tibetan with 
Vairocana. Vairocana and Śrī Siṃha participated in the transmission of a third BGB 
text, the Stirring the Pit of Samsara Tantra: Essence of all Tantras (Rgyud thams cad kyi 
snying po ’khor ba dong dkrug gi rgyud, vol. 6, ka, 1–​18). A fourth scripture on divination, 
the Instructions on Ground Drawing and Pebble Cycle (Sa ris dang rde skor gyi man ngag), 
lists Śrī Siṃha both as the author and co-​translator along with Vairocana.
Śrī Siṃha and Vairocana are acknowledged for their translation of the fundamental 
Dzogchen tantra of the Mind Class staged as a dialogue between Buddha Kunje Gyalpo 
and Sattvavajra. Known in brief as the All Creating King (Kun byed rgyal po), the full title 
of this work is given as All Creating King: The Mind of Awakening in the Great Perfection 
of all Dharmas (Chos thams cad rdzogs pa chen po byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po). 
This seminal work is found in all known editions of the NGB and is the only Dzogchen 
text known to me that is listed in the Derge Kangyur (vol. 97, 4–​173).29
This preliminary survey confirms Śrī Siṃha’s range of scholarship and his Tibetan 
legacy as the most important of all patriarchs of the Great Perfection. Moreover, his 
influence extends beyond the scriptures we have just surveyed. In the early and later 
traditions of revealed scriptures of the Treasure tradition, there is a wide selection of 
Dzogchen texts attributed to Śrī Siṃha by some standing figures of the Nyingma tradi­
tion: Nyangrel Nyima Özer (Nyang ral nyi ma ’od zer, 1124/​1136–​92/​1204), Longchenpa 
(Klong chen pa, 1308–​64), Rigdzin Gödem (Rig ’dzin rgod ldem, 1337–​1408), Chogyur 
Lingpa (Mchog gyur gling pa, 1829–​70), and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo (’Jam dbyangs 
mkhyen brtse’i dbang po, 1820–​92). In 1848 an apparition of Śrī Siṃha on a rock near 
Dzogchen monastery prompted Gyelse Zhenpen Taye Özer (Rgyal sras gzhan phan 
mtha’ yas ’od zer, 1800–​55/​1869) to build on the same spot the famous Śrī Siṃha College.
Śrī Siṃha: Where and When?
Śrī Siṃha’s place of origin has been the subject of debate, alternating for the most part 
between India, Central Asia, and China.30 The Extensive History situates his birthplace 
in China and this account is repeated in several works of a later date, like Padma Karpo’s 
History of Buddhism (Chos ’byung padma rgyas pa’i nyin byed; Pad ma dkar po 1527–​
92), Dudjom Jigdrel Yeshe’s History of the Nyingma School (Rnying ma’i chos ’byung; 
Bdud ’joms ’jigs bral ye shes 1904–​87), and more recently Nyoshul Kenpo’s History of the 
Great Perfection (Rdzogs pa chen po’i chos ’byung; Smyo shul mkhan po 1932–​99). But Śrī 
Siṃha is not the only early Dzogchen patriarch with ties to China. In a later edition (bka’ 
ma version) of the Great Image, we read that Vairocana went to China and met nine­
teen masters inquiring about their views on Dzogchen, however as noted by Karmay 
(2007: 28) all the Chinese masters bear Sanskrit names and there is no mention of a 
single Chinese place name. Moreover, tantric lore has it that after Vimalamitra attained 
the rainbow body (’ja’ lus) he decided to remain at Wu tai shan Mount in Eastern China 
for as long as the teachings of the Buddha endure. He promised to return to Tibet as

--- PAGE 485 ---
460      Georgios T. Halkias
 
an emanation once every one hundred years to expound the Seminal Heart teachings 
(Dudjom Rinpoche 1991: 555).
Sino-​Tibetan exchanges were commonplace at the times of the Tibetan empire 
(eighth to ninth centuries). Tibetans sought out Chinese Buddhist teachers and the im­
perial catalogue from the royal Palace at Phangthang lists eleven Chinese sutras and 
seven Chinese commentaries on the sutras that were translated from Chinese to Tibetan 
(Halkias 2004: 90). Moreover, the religious landscape of the Tibetan empire witnessed 
a sizable population of Chinese monks at Tibet’s first Buddhist monastery of Samye, 
and saw the popular rise of Chan orientations in Central Tibet and at the borders of the 
Tibetan empire in Dunhuang. While Tibetan polemical scriptures highlight the inferior 
position of Chan and stress its philosophical affinities with Dzogchen to tarnish the au­
thenticity of the latter, the question of influence between the two has occupied contem­
porary debates and discussions.31
In the Great Image and in the hagiographies of Vimalamitra compiled from the twelfth 
to the fourteenth centuries, Śrī Siṃha’s life is firmly rooted in India. Well-​known sources 
such as, Nyangrel’s Copper Island Chronicle, Longchenpa’s History of Buddhism (Klong 
chen chos ’byung), and both of the Deü Histories of Buddhism (Lde’u chos ’byung), make 
no mention of Vimalamitra ever traveling to China to meet Śrī Siṃha (Gruber 2016: 
419). In the colophons of the Tengyur and the Collected Tantras of the Ancients, Śrī 
Siṃha is consistently listed as an Indian scholar (rgya gar gyi mkhan po), and Dargyay 
([1977]1998: 19) rightly notes that the name Śrī Siṃha in all its variants can hardly be 
a Chinese name that has been Sanskritized. Furthermore, Śrī Siṃha’s teachers bear 
proper Sanskrit names and should any of them have been among those Indian masters 
who sojourned, or were active in China, we would have expected some mention in the 
Chinese records. The evidence is inconclusive. Śrī Siṃha was either an Indian master 
residing for some time in China proper or Central Asia or, as claimed by Germano 
(2002: 239), the Chinese story is a deliberate fabrication that originated in the Seminal 
Heart chronicles of the twelfth century. It was concocted as a defense against criticisms 
launched by the New Schools of Tibetan Buddhism that Dzogchen lacked an authentic 
Indian Buddhist source and therefore by implication, its doctrines did not reflect gen­
uine Buddhist teachings.32
Dating Śrī Siṃha is equally challenging. The timeline of the Great Perfection 
patriarchs is beset with a number of contradictions and difficulties (Hanson-​Barber, 
1984: 35–​38; Prats 1984; Germano 2002). Van Schaik (2004: 198) notes that the lineage 
arrangement of the early Seminal Heart teachers in the Collected Tantras of Vairocana 
is “awkward” and that it has been difficult to deal with it in the Great Perfection tradi­
tion which has invariably omitted some names and included others. Nevertheless, we 
can venture to speculate on Śrī Siṃha’s chronology by relying on Nyingma sources that 
enlist him as the teacher of Padmasambhava, Vairocana, Vimalamitra, and Nubchen 
Sangye Yeshe. The exact dates of his last identifiable Tibetan disciple and co-​translator 
of Dzogchen texts, Nubchen Sangye, are difficult to establish with certainty (Esler 2014: 
6–​7), but given that he was born in the Water Male Mouse Year this could refer either to 
772 or 832 according to Dudjom Rinpoche, or to 784 or 844 according to Rigdzin Padma

--- PAGE 486 ---
Timeless Symbolism      461
 
Trinley who gives the Wood Male Mouse Year as the date of his birth. It fits to accept an 
earlier birthdate for Nubchen Sangye, such as 772 or 784, for it supports accounts of his 
sojourns to India and Nepal where he could have plausibly met Śrī Siṃha during the 
reign of Emperor Tri Tsugdetsen (Khri gtsug lde bstan, reign c. 815–​38). It seems reason­
able to assume 838 as the latest date we can assign for Śrī Siṃha’s reported engagement 
with the Tibetans. Though there is a fair amount of uncertainty as to Vimalamitra’s actual 
dating and his alleged two visits to Tibet, his meeting with Śrī Siṃha could have taken 
place prior to the years 794–​96, for according to the Zha Lakhang (Zhva’i lha khang) in­
scription (Richardson 1985: 44), these are the dates that Vimalamitra was invited by the 
minister Nyang Tingdzin (Myang Ting nge ’dzin) to Tibet and later served as his teacher. 
Based on the above we could venture to date him between 750 and 840 C.E.
The Seminal Heart of the Ḍākinīs relates how Garab Dorje used secret symbols to 
transmit to Śrī Siṃha the essential meaning of the 6,400,000 tantras of Dzogchen. If 
their meeting is not a later interpolation inserted in the narrative, or a didactic account 
of transhistorical transmissions transpiring through pure visions (dag snang) between 
individuals who are centuries apart, it would imply that Śrī Siṃha and Garab Dorje were 
in fact contemporaries. Some western and Tibetan scholarship situates Garab Dorje as 
early as the first century C.E. Hanson-​Barber (1986) attempted to correct his dates by 
placing Garab Dorje in the mid sixth century, but this date is still too early to accord 
with Śrī Siṃha’s chronology based on the dates of his disciples.
The inconsistencies that plague these Tibetan sources are by no means conclusive 
that the Tibetans fabricated the Great Perfection lineages any more than the absence 
of Sanskrit Dzogchen texts proves that they were Tibetan concoctions of a later date. 
It is true that with the exception of Mañjuśrīmitra’s Meditation on Bodhicitta (Byang 
chub sems sgom pa)—​an early text of the Great Perfection preserved in the Tengyur 
(P. 3415) and listed in the Denkarma and Phangthangma Catalogues (Lalou 1953: 609/​610; 
Halkias 2004: 72)—​no other Great Perfection text seems to be included in the imperial 
records of imported Buddhist texts. Their omission is not unexpected given the pro­
hibition against the open translation and distribution of Tantric works in the earlier 
dates of the imperium. We know that separate lists were kept for the Tibetan translation 
of the inner tantras (sngags nang pa) (Halkias 2004: xx). Perhaps, we will never know 
if these “separate lists” were kept at Phangthang, or some other long-​forgotten place 
that housed the indices and the originals of the inner tantras. For Esler (2005: 45–​46), 
those casting doubts on the non-​Tibetan provenance of Dzogchen seem to ignore the 
fact that the Great Perfection teachings were transmitted orally in a constrained and 
secretive fashion prior to the eleventh century. The mention of Dzogchen texts in India 
and in China in the hagiographical narratives fuels an unsettled quest for discovering 
Sanskrit sources of Dzogchen, either because the Dzogchen teachings and instructions 
for practice were originally transmitted in a language other than Sanskrit (such as those 
languages in circulation in Uḍḍiyāna and Zhang Zhung) and in some scriptural form 
which is no longer extant, or simply because there never existed any systematic scrip­
tural collection of Dzogchen literature prior to its transmission, translation, and system­
atization in Tibet.

--- PAGE 487 ---
462      Georgios T. Halkias
 
The Symbolic Transmission of 
Awareness Holders
The Nyingma School asserts six major transmission lineages (brgyud pa) to account for 
the origins and spread of their secret teachings. The first three kinds of transmission 
are theoretically linked to the trikāya doctrine and the last three to the short transmis­
sion of treasure literature (nye brgyud gter ma).33 The semiotic order for the transmis­
sion of esoteric gnosis begins with the Wisdom Mind Transmission of Conquerors 
(rgyal ba dgongs brgyud pa). This is understood as a mind-​to-​mind transmission 
which, in the first instance, takes the domain of awakening as its own experience. It 
transpires in the identification of the wisdom mind of the Teacher with a retinue of 
disciples who are self-​arising reflections of his own realization. In the second instance 
of this transmission writes Tulku Thondup (1984: 5), the students who are not iden­
tical with the teacher “become ‘inseparable in mind’ from the Teacher by means of his 
blessings.”
The Wisdom Mind Transmission occurs in the timeless awareness of the dharmakāya, 
the mind’s own intrinsic nature, just as the Symbolic Transmission of Awareness holders 
(rig ’dzin brda brgyud pa) transpires during the outer radiance of the mind’s clarity in­
dicated by the saṃbhogakāya. Symbolic Transmissions express gnostic events that take 
place between awareness holders and bodhisattvas whose minds are inwardly clarified 
during the self-​arising nature of their own awareness (rig pa rang sar). The third mode 
of transmission transpires during the Oral Transmission of Individuals [passed on] 
Through Hearing (gang zag snyan khung brgyud pa). The Oral Transmission occurs at 
the time of the nirmāṇakāya and for Tulku Thondup (1984: 12), it depends on the “ap­
pearance of disciples rather than the actual nature of the transmitters” who may also in­
clude buddhas, bodhisattvas, and masters like Garab Dorje and Padmasambhava.
The next three transmission lineages are hidden teachings revealed in scriptural form 
or beheld through pure visions by mystics and visionaries, the treasure-​revealers (gter 
ston). The Transmission Empowered by Aspiration (smon lam dbang bskur gyi brgyud 
pa) is held by treasure-​revealers who redact teachings according to the wisdom-​intent 
of Padmasambhava. The Transmission of Words on the Yellow Scrolls (shog ser tshig gi 
brgyud pa) refers to previously concealed treasure teachings in the form of script on 
yellow paper. The last of the three, the Transmission of the Ḍākinī’s Seal of Entrustment 
(mkha’ ’gro gtad rgya’i brgyud pa) is a lineage of secret teachings kept under the protec­
tion of the sky-​walkers (Skt. ḍākinī; mkha’ ’gro ma) and guardians of the Dharma (Skt. 
dharmapāla; chos skyong).
The recorded history of the Great Perfection begins with the lineage of Symbolic 
Transmissions (brda brgyud pa).34 This descent is distinguished from the Wisdom Mind 
Transmission where the Great Perfection precepts are effortlessly communicated be­
yond time, place, and language by Buddha Samantabhadra to Buddha Vajrasattva who 
is identical in all aspects to himself. According to the Extensive History, the Dzogchen

--- PAGE 488 ---
Timeless Symbolism      463
 
transmission through symbols was revealed to humanity by Vajrasattva with the aid of 
the ḍākinīs.35 For the duration of the Symbolic Transmission, the teacher communicates 
gnostic events through indication, by means of visual forms and gestures (mudras), or 
through the utterance of sacred syllables (mantras).
In the teachings of the Great Perfection, the ritual use of symbols fulfills a vital 
gnoseological function. For example, it is common during traditional Dzogchen 
initiations for the teachers to use a mirror or crystal and a peacock feather as cere­
monial symbols. The mind’s nature accommodates all kinds of thoughts and emotions 
and is symbolically compared to a mirror or crystal which can reflect all sorts of 
appearances without being altered at their core. Likewise, the rings of five colors in the 
peacock feather symbolize the five aggregates manifesting in their most subtle form 
as kāyas of light and as expressions of the wisdoms of the five buddha families (Skt. 
pañcakula; rigs lnga).
In the Threaded String of Pearls (Mu tig phreng ba brgyud), a Great Perfection com­
mentary to the Blazing Lamp Tantra (Sgron ma ’bar ba’i rgyud), it is stated that “the se­
cret key point of secret mantra is realized on the basis of symbols.” It further explains 
that “in this way, since all names, syllables, and so on are designated in symbols, they do 
not transcend symbols. Since all appearances arise as symbols, everything arises as an 
intimate instruction on the meaning of symbols. Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are realized in 
their entirety to be mere symbols” (Smith 2020: 56).
The gnoseological deployment of symbolic language in tantric literature serves a so­
teriological purpose. In the following extract from the Extensive History [smad cha, folia 
85–​88] we read an emic account on the hermeneutics of symbolic transmission.
(folio 85) Symbols (brda) are described in terms of their essence (ngo bo), defini­
tion (nges tshig), and types (dbye ba). Essence is understood as arriving at the key 
meaning of a symbol like the swift blazing of a fire. Its definition is just words used, 
ordinary sounds approximating the symbol, supports for ascertaining the nature 
of reality (chos nyid). The varieties of symbols are innumerable and are subsumed 
under natural symbols, those abiding naturally as descriptive symbols, and as those 
indicating a reason (folio 86). Furthermore, symbols are divided into body-​symbols 
(lus kyi brda) and mind-​symbols (yid kyi brda). Body-​symbols include deliberate 
hand gestures (Skt. mudrā), written syllables (bris yi ge), and representational or 
form-​based symbols (gzugs brnyan).
Buddhists understand hand symbols, but not others [outsiders], and since they 
are the cause for spiritual attainment individual sections of the tantras explain their 
practice. Written syllables vary and by depending upon them on attains freedom 
from self-​arising phenomena (folio 87). Relying on purifying syllables (dag bye yi ge) 
one attains untainted liberation from the three realms. By means of the transforma­
tive syllables (sgyur byed yi ge) the hidden reality becomes utterly evident even if it 
is not known to everyone. Through the purification of the syllables of gods, ḍākinīs, 
nāgas, Brahma, garudas and others, one understands the meaning, but not others. By 
connecting strings of syllables, one becomes proficient in the critical way of reciting 
mantras. Men and women rely on sense impressions for image symbols such as, brass 
butter lamps, and so forth, which produce certainty.

--- PAGE 489 ---
464      Georgios T. Halkias
 
Empowering blessings, feast gatherings and bali offerings (gtor ma) depend upon 
the teacher’s authentic realization and become mind symbols. With a mind of de­
votion and awareness they are liberated in a state of nondual union. This is the key 
point of fusion. These mind symbols (folio 88) arise from the teacher’s intrinsic real­
ization. The meaning of mind symbols is understood as those symbols which are not 
apparent.
Descriptive symbols (brjod pa’ brda) are of three kinds: those which arise from 
scriptures; those which arise from a yogi’s experiential understanding; and those 
intentionally caused during a definite time. Descriptive symbols in scriptures start 
with one’s set of precepts or samaya in respect to individual secret tantras which are 
unintelligible to others as if they were a foreign tongue. Those symbols which arise 
from a yogi’s experiential understanding produce liberation from the sufferings of 
others –​ interdependent origination, the fusion between cognition and phenomena, 
and so forth, are experiences joined with the field of conduct in oneself fall within the 
range of mahāsiddhas. Those symbols intentionally caused during a definite time are 
those expressed during a feast offering, or an empowerment, or the feast of ḍākas and 
ḍākinīs. Those are not dependent upon external elaborations but directly arise from 
within as the nature of reality.
 (folio 89) All these symbols are crucial for generating the experiences of tögel. 
Thus, comprehend the nature of the symbols, enter reality itself as they cut through 
the proliferation of words and letters.
If one was to ask how are we to understand this lineage of transmission?
It is the transmission lineage from Garab Dorje’s emanation.
By whom? It is the transmission of (Buddha) Vajradhara.
How does it operate as a path and means?
This transmission lineage relies upon all the symbols of the Secret Mantra.
What is a simile for this transmission lineage?
It is like pouring water from one full vase to another where neither are full nor 
falling short of water.
What is the purpose for this transmission lineage?
To make ultimate truth known to worthy individuals in the future.
What is the aim of this transmission lineage?
It is unmistaken buddhahood which is beyond imputation, speculation, and any 
kind of conceptualization.
Parting Reflections: The Invisible Visible
The hagiographies of the early Great Perfection patriarchs stem from a historiomythical 
tradition that relies on a lifeline of awakened mystics and their uninterrupted lineages 
of transmissions. Śrī Siṃha’s transhistorical apotheosis belongs to a symbolic kind of 
understanding supporting the Great Perfection’s grand teleology: self-​dissolution in 
a body of light. As stated in the previously quoted passage from the Extensive History 
(folio 89), symbols “cut through the proliferation of words and letters” and “are crucial

--- PAGE 490 ---
Timeless Symbolism      465
 
for generating the experiences of tögel” and “entering reality itself.” The primacy of 
figurative language is echoed in an episode from the life of the Indian mystic Saraha. 
Upon meeting his tantric teacher, the mahāsiddha Saraha asked if she is a fletcheress. 
She replied, “Noble son, the intent of the Buddha can be understood through symbols 
and actions, not through words and texts” (Schaeffer 2005: 21). Śrī Siṃha’s life story can 
be read not only as an idealized narrative of tantric life but as an interpretation on the 
prevalence of symbols as gnoseological methods at the service of the Great Perfection’s 
soteriology.
