Chapter 21
The Twin Miracle
The Two-​Headed Aizen Myōō [Ryōzu Aizen] in 
Exorcistic Shugendō Practice at the Japanese Tantric 
Buddhist Complex of Kōyasan
Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
Ryōzu Aizen
Ryōzu Aizen 両頭愛染 is a tantric deity unique to Japanese Shingon Buddhism. This 
deity has destructive characteristics and appears to have been employed in possession 
and exorcism rites. Since its founding in the ninth century, Kōyasan 高野山 has been 
one of the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism. The thirteenth century was a period of 
conflicting claims there, and such rites were instrumental in assertions of legitimacy. 
During this time, Shugendō 修験道 mountain ascetic practice (lit. “the way to achieve 
miraculous powers through practice”) was at a height at this site, and its influence is ev­
ident in Ryōzu Aizen as well as in texts produced by one Shingon branch particularly 
engaged in claims to legitimacy, the Chūin branch (hereafter “Chūin-ryū”). To demon­
strate the meanings of Ryōzu Aizen at Kōyasan at that time, this chapter discusses the 
development of the icon and gives illustrations from a text produced by the Chūin-​ryū 
after one particular, and violent, instance of conflict.
There are two Wisdom Kings, Aizen Myōō (愛染明王; Skt. Rāga-​vidyārāja, lit. 
“Wisdom King Dyed in Lust,” hereafter Aizen) and Fudō Myōō (不動明王; Skt. 
Acalanātha–​vidyārāja, lit. “Immovable Wisdom King,” hereafter Fudō), that had been 
linked as a pair since the end of the Heian period (794–​1185). By at least the close of the 
twelfth century their identification was well developed in the Ono lineage (Ono-​ryū) of 
Shingon, especially in the Sanbō’in branch at Daigō-​ji in the Kyoto capital (Dolce 2006–​
2007; Faure 2015, 199–​234; Trenson 2018). Far less common, or still largely unknown, 
was a version of Aizen as a single-​bodied, two-​headed version: “Ryōzu Aizen.” This icon 
is a combination of Aizen and Fudō. Jitsu’un (實運 1105–​1160) of Daigō-​ji, who gave the

--- PAGE 498 ---
The Twin Miracle      473
 
first description of Ryōzu Aizen in his twelfth-​century Genpishō 玄秘抄), noted that its 
form is similar to that of Kongōsatta. He also noted that one of the faces of the icon is 
white, which symbolizes compassion, and the other red, symbolizing anger. There may 
be an even earlier origin. Kakuzen (覚禅 1142–​1213) mentioned in his late twelfth-​ to 
early thirteenth-​century Kakuzenshō 覚禅鈔, a text that focuses on the teachings of 
the Ono lineage, that Shōbō (聖宝 832–​909), founder of Daigōji and of the Ono lin­
eage, had described a statue with one body and two heads (Dai Nihon Bukkyō zensho 51; 
Goepper 1993, 52). Shōbō had identified the head on the left as that of Fudō and the one 
on the right as that of Aizen and stated that therefore Fudōō and Aizen were nondual. 
The Kakuzenshō also contains the earliest known image of Ryōzu Aizen. By the end of 
the Heian period, Fudō and Aizen had become paired and identified with the Womb 
and Diamond (kontai 金胎) realms of principle and wisdom (richi 理智). In around the 
thirteenth to fourteenth centuries, the fully nondual body in the form of Ryōzu Aizen 
emerged, a form of Fudō and Aizen that was now expressive of extreme violence and of 
explicit sexuality.
As a fusion of two Myōō, this icon has, then, largely been taken to be a sexual (and 
even heretical) icon. Jitsu’un’s description of Ryōzu Aizen is found in a section of the text 
with the title “the human-​shaped vajra” ningyō-​sho 人形杵: “This is the samaya form 
of the body of Aizen bosatsu. The form is one body with two heads” (Taishō 78, 390). 
This vajra, a tool used in ritual for purification, is also called a “vajra of sexual union,” 
wagōshō (和合杵). It is not “two headed” in the way that Ryōzu Aizen is, though the 
concept seems to be the same. It comprises opposing yet conjoined forces in the form 
of a five-​pronged vajra, which has the conventional appearance of such a tool with the 
“heads” of the vajra at each end but is made of two interlocking parts that can be de­
tached from each other. Since the vajra is specified as (being similar to) a “human form,” 
its construction is meant to symbolize sexual intercourse. The doubled bija “hhum” is its 
vocal-​sonic equivalent. There is also a “five-​pronged” mudra that similarly symbolizes 
intercourse and a mandala connected to the Tachikawa branch of Shingon that shows 
a human male and female connected in the same position as that represented by the 
vajra form. Both the vajra and the Ryōzu Aizen icon represent nonduality. In theory, this 
was meant to be that of Dainichi Nyorai (大日如来 Skt. Mahāvairocana), the central 
esoteric Buddha that unifies the Diamond and Womb realms, and from whom, it was 
understood, all phenomena emanated.1 As explained by Jitsu’un, Aizen as a one-​headed 
icon already had a samaya (symbolic) form as the anthropomorphic vajra, so the fact 
that his description of Ryōzu Aizen is found in this textual context suggests that Ryōzu 
Aizen is a full expression of Aizen in its symbolic form and carries his connotations.
Moreover, Aizen had long been used in rituals for attracting an object or person 
desired. He was already understood as embodying the resolution of the dichotomy of 
enlightenment and destructive afflictions (Skt. klesa; Jpn. bonnō 煩悩), especially those 
of desire in its general sense. This was an expression of the principle bonnō soku bodai 
(煩悩即菩提 “transgressions [worldly desires] are [identical to] enlightenment”), 
discussed below. When the icon became double, the seed-​syllable also did, into hhūm, 
which requires an elongated inhalation and exhalation.2 In its form as a written and

--- PAGE 499 ---
474      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
visualized Siddham syllable, it extended vertically and comprises several extra brush 
strokes. Another version of the dual, palindromic textual, verbal, and breath forms of 
these sounds is found in early names for Ryōzu Aizen, such as “Aizen Zen’ai.” It is much 
like the mantra hamsa, which expresses nondualism in the form and enunciation of its 
“imaginary syllables” aham sah (“I am Him”) and so’ham (“He is me”), which constitute 
an in-​breath and an out-​breath (Padoux 2017, 109–​110). The same concept is expressed 
eidetically in the flashing back and forth between Aizen and Fudō that is required in 
their use in ritualized visualization (discussed below). This dissolution of difference is 
expressed in a mid-​thirteenth-​century Kōyasan Chūin-​ryū text: “Fudō is Aizen, Aizen 
is Fudō” (Abe 1983, 107).3 There is a prominent sexual element, which Lucia Dolce 
highlighted when she wrote that the process of Aizen and Fudō’s embodiment of “dif­
ferent stages of the union of opposites . . . was explicated by using other sets of opposites 
[like] . . . sexual elements such as the interaction between man and woman” (Dolce 
2006–​2007, 122). Both internal and external transformations functionally coexisted, 
and in ways that didn’t have only sexual meaning: Shingon exegeses and the rituals re­
lated to it emphasized “internal” (psychophysiological) change, but the possibilities 
offered by ritual actions of exerting external effects, including violence or exorcism, on 
the environment or on other beings, human or spirit, were by no means denied, as will 
be discussed below.
The Kakugen kudenshō is a collection of commentaries on the Yugikyō sutra (瑜祇経 
Taishō 867)4 from Kōyasan scholar monks Kakukai (覚海 [1142–​1223] of Daigō-​ji and 
Yūgen 融源 [1169–​?]) of Denbō’in. They commented that the form of Ryōzu Aizen is 
(equivalent to) the “the myōe in one body” (myōe ittai 冥会一体). This term can be 
found in a four-​part compound signifying the “profound state of unified mind,” the 
shinkyō myōe 心境冥会 used in a poem by Shingon school founder Kūkai (空海 774–​
835) (Shingon shū zensho 42).5 Like “the profound unity in one body,” this phrase, myōe 
ittai, is another expression of nonduality that was materially represented in Ryōzu Aizen.
There is, though, also an inner-​outer dynamism exhibited iconographically by Ryōzu 
Aizen and in the icon’s sexual aspects. These suggest the nondualism as well as an inner-​
outer conjunction that resonates with paradigms of possession and exorcism (Iyanaga 
2022, 17:n52).6 Similar views are found in the Henmyō’in Daishi Myōjin Go-​Takusen-​
ki (遍明院大師明神御託宣記 Record of the Oracle of Daishi Myōjin of Henmyō’in 
[Cloister]) (hereafter Takusen-​ki) (Abe 1983), a collection of “secret teachings,” and 
another Chūin-​ryū text concerned with the nature of nondualism, Niu Kōya Ryōsho 
Daimyōjin Hyōhyaku (丹生高野両所大明神表百; Invocation and Statement of Ritual 
Purpose to Niu and Kōya Ryōsho Daimyōjin) (Kōyasan monjo 3:453)7 written in 1319 by 
Kakuwa (覚和 c. 1260–​c. 1324).
Each of Ryōzu Aizen’s four hands grips a vajra and a bell, an arrow and a bow, and 
Fudō’s grasp his customary sword and lasso.8 These are paired and displayed as illustra­
tive examples of compassion/​principle and wisdom/​meditative concentration, aligned 
with the Womb and Diamond aspects of Dainichi Nyorai in the esoteric Buddhist tra­
dition. Here, the aspiration for the balance of these two might be understood as being 
neither so much for the enhancement of perception nor for the attainment of cognitive

--- PAGE 500 ---
The Twin Miracle      475
 
accuracy, but for ends more closely related to exorcistic procedures that drew as much 
on Shugendō practice as on Daoist yin-​yang principles and their balancing functions 
(Hori 1966, 1). Ryōzu Aizen’s attributes reflect the principles of duality-​nonduality al­
ready observed in Aizen (as embodiment of bonnō soku bodai). However, the tools 
in his many fanned-​out hands are arranged into six pairs, one of which in each set 
represents an active, forceful, outwardly projected energy (vajra, arrow, and sword) that 
corresponds to wisdom, and the other a receptive and yielding energy (bell, bow, and 
lasso) that corresponds to compassion.
Shingon, particularly from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, gendered the 
wisdom-​compassion binary, and the Chūin-​ryū monks at Kōyasan especially embraced 
this paradigm. They also frequently applied the “active energy/​passive energy” par­
adigm, which has both sexual and gendered aspects to it. The dynamic interplay be­
tween the two parts of the binary is most vividly represented by sexual union, but also 
suggests the attraction (inward force) and destruction (outward expelling force) that 
inform Aizen and Fudō’s functions (desire and destruction) as well as the process by 
which those functions are affected. This is expressed in the Takusenki. During a discus­
sion about suijaku and honji (an avataral system in which a kami [pre-​Buddhist deity] 
is understood to be the “manifest trace” of an “original ground,” that is, a Buddhist di­
vinity), the interlocutors of the 1251 oracle were informed—​following a passage that 
identified Fudō and Aizen with the Diamond and Womb worlds and introduced, in 
connection, the Kōyasan mountain goddess Niu Myōjin 丹生明神9 as the Womb—​that 
“the objects held by the two Myōō (bow and arrow and sword and lasso) are active en­
ergy and passive, holding energy” (Abe 1983, 107).10 Directly following is the statement: 
“Outside, [they] remove calamities, inside [they] obstruct and eliminate the hindrance 
[caused by] passions.” It is not that the objects are just sexualized; rather they represent 
“energies,” of which sex (as both biological condition and act) is one example. There 
then follows an explanation of the union of psychophysical energies as the very char­
acter of the manifest (suijaku) world of samsara:
Suijaku is the expression of the world of the manifest world [表世間 omote seken; 
literally “surface” world]. Also, [it is expressed] that, in terms of people of the world, 
men and women together maintain that world. Women are great sadness [pathos/​
compassion]; men judge right and wrong. The suijaku of the two [i.e., the Myōjin] 
are the expressions of this.
(Abe 1983, 106)11
The conjoined energy is here divided into emotion and reason (or judgment), which 
are respectively embodied by women and men. This appears to reflect a Daoist under­
standing of the world, particularly its yin-​yang principles. This was a worldview that 
had been absorbed into Shugendō or had perhaps been one of its original sources. It 
would have emerged from there into esoteric Buddhism since the incorporation of kami 
into the tradition included their associated yin-​yang principles (Dolce 2006–​2007, 119–​
150, 120). The objects held by Ryōzu Aizen that depict examples of “powers that push

--- PAGE 501 ---
476      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
outward” and “powers that pull inward” are also illustrations of his function, of what 
he promises to his patron. For the targeting of a desired person, the forces of attrac­
tion and subjugation (“binding”) are called for. The attraction is represented by the in­
ward pull or receptivity of the objects that Ryōzu Aizen holds. For destruction of a target 
(for which Aizen was also ritually used), the forces of ejection (also involving subjuga­
tion/​binding) are necessary. This is represented by the outward force of the objects that 
Ryōzu Aizen holds.
In general, esoteric Buddhism in the medieval period was marked by a strong in­
terest in dualism and its transcendence, and Shingon Buddhism favored in particular: 
“the imagery of the unity of opposites that draws from the fundamental Tōmitsu12 idea 
of the interpenetration of the two mandalic realities” (Dolce 2006–​2007, 120). But the 
explanations in the Takusen-​ki regarding dualism (e.g., among numerous examples, the 
aforementioned discussion of honji and suijaku) employ language that suggests “inner” 
(or “inward”) and “outer” (or “outward”). These describe a binary that is dynamic 
rather than static. A similar view of dualism as not purely binary is found in an invo­
cation text: Niu Kōya Ryōsho Daimyōjin Hyōhyaku (丹生高野両所表白) by Kakuwa. 
Kakuwa was also a member of the Chūin-​ryū, and in his text he employed the meta­
phor of a box (interior) and a lid (exterior) to explain a series of dualisms. The mani­
fest world itself—​suijaku—​as described in the Takusen-​ki, is the world of the surface, 
of that which is exposed, visual, and tangible. Kakuwa’s text explains honji-​suijaku at 
Kōyasan. The honmon 本, or “honji gate,” is given as Taizōkai, and the shakumon 迹門, 
or “suijaku gate,” as Kongōkai. Thus, the “origin teaching” is the Womb World, and the 
manifest teaching is the Diamond World. This makes the two worlds (two mandalas) 
a honji suijaku construct. However, in Kakuwa’s text, these two worlds are then called 
naishō (内証; the inner realization of enlightenment), and this inner realization is 
further termed shōchi hōmi 聖智法味 the “taste” of the sacred and wise Dharma. The 
accompanying geyō (外用; outer action, or actions that manifest inner enlightenment) 
are equal to Niu and Kōya Myōjin. The harmonious fusion, or interdependence (wagō 
和合) of these is likened to a box and its lid, an internal and an external.
The emphasis on the transcendence of duality is readily seen in much Aizen-​related 
iconographical art at Kōyasan of this period, such as the sanzon (triptych of devotional 
icons) depicted on (and in) reliquaries, small cabinets (zushi 厨子), and paintings. The 
production and use of these flourished between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. 
With its bicephaly, the new variant of Aizen, Ryōzu Aizen, represents a peak in the 
expression of this doctrine. The original single-​headed Aizen, in being bright red 
from head to foot, was already an immediate embodiment of the identity between 
transgressions and enlightenment. Aizen was enlightened even while thoroughly “dyed” 
with the origin of all destructive mental afflictions. Ryōzu Aizen, the two-​headed form, 
expressed duality even more forcefully by virtue of having a greater number of dualisms 
symbolically invested in and visually represented on it, but it varied from the original 
form since the flip side of desire/​attraction—​destruction—​was heightened through the 
fusion of Aizen (already possessing destructive powers) together with another Wisdom 
King, Fudō.

--- PAGE 502 ---
The Twin Miracle      477
 
Aizen and Fudō in Rites of 
Demonization and Exorcism
From early on in his employment in Japan, Aizen had been used for worldly and de­
structive ends within the realm of political machinations (and the link between tantra 
and state protection is common across pan-​Asian tantra), and demonology is also found 
in the form of subjugation and expulsion rites. He was brought to Japan by Shingon 
monks, including Kūkai (who also brought from China the Yugikyō, which describes 
Aizen [though as a single-​headed icon]). Aizen gained fame in elite circles after having 
been employed by Shingon priest and Ono lineage founder Seison (成尊 1012–​1074) to 
bring about the death of Emperor Go-​Reizei (後冷泉天皇 1025–​1068) (Hayami 1987, 
136–​139). Seison became the new emperor’s official “protector-​monk.” Subsequently, 
Aizen ritual performances became the domain of Ono-​ryū monks and were carried out 
for the purposes of the emperors and elites—​a prestigious and profitable monopoly.
Fudō, like Aizen, has destructive characteristics and demon-​subjugating powers. 
Conventionally, Fudō holds a sword in one hand and a lasso in the other, purportedly 
symbolic of his ability to slay (“cut” through) ignorance and to hurl a lasso around the 
existential drifters of the world. He is depicted as dwelling in the mountains, but he also 
has links with water, waterfalls, and serpentine nagas (Kurikara, a naga wound around 
a sword, is one of his forms). His pedestal is either a mountain or a rock surrounded by 
a stormy sea, representing Mount Sumeru, the divine axis of ancient Indian cosmology. 
Because of these dual meanings, he is the icon used in the mountain and waterfall ascetic 
practices of the Shugenja across Japan and is the tutelary deity in Shugendō. The demon-​
subjugating powers of Fudō are evident in his probable ancestry, and these merged with 
the work of the Shugenja/​monastic exorcists (genja/​geza 験者). In contrast to the ob­
scurity of Aizen’s origins, Fudō’s are clearer, but they also connect him to destruction of 
demons. Fudō has Indian roots. It is possible that he originated in Śiva in terms of shared 
epithets descriptive of “immovability” as well as iconographical connections (including 
the lasso, the coiled snake, and the production of fire) or Candamahārosana (Payne 1988, 
6–​14). He may also be a transmutation of Vajrapāni (“Vajra Holder”), who had once been 
a yakśa, a demonic nature spirit. Fudō was, then, originally a demonic spirit, converted 
into a protector (goho 御法, “Dharma Protector”). Fudō is specifically thought to be the 
(converted) wrathful form of Vajrapāni, Guhyapati Vajrapāni, “The Lord of [esoteric 
Buddhist] Secrets” who, like his Japanese descendent, is blue-​black in color.13 Vajrapāni’s 
attributes vary, but he often holds a lasso, an additional iconographical link with Fudō. 
Another of Fudō’s distinguishing features is his seat, which is a stylized heap of rocks 
(an abbreviated mountain) that appears in many examples to be a pile of colorful bricks. 
Connections can again be found as far back as the 700s in a Kashmiri bronze statue of a 
wrathful Vajrapāni in the collection of the Cleveland Museum of Art. Its stylized brick-​
like seat is narrowed at the center to indicate Mount Sumeru. The presence of mountain 
lions within a cave in the seat gives the meaning of Vajrapāni’s environment: The demon

--- PAGE 503 ---
478      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
slayer has tamed wild beasts, and is even powerful enough to adorn himself with poi­
sonous snakes. Japan seems to have adopted this version of Vajrapāni, and he became 
the central Wisdom King of the “Five Great Wisdom Kings” (Godai Myōō 五大明王). 
Fudō’s function of binding with his lasso is one of the fundamental reasons he is prom­
inent within spirit exorcism practices (mononoke chōbuku no kaji kitō 物の気調伏
の加持祈祷)—​and this is attested to in certain works of art—​because it is a function 
(binding; baku 縛) shared by ally spirits (“Dharma Protectors”; gohō 護法) dispatched 
by exorcists to incapacitate demons inside possessed bodies.14 Historical accounts tell of 
possessed patients being alleviated through the use of Fudō by exorcist monks. Tendai 
priest Sōō (相応 831–​918) released an aristocrat’s daughter from the pain of being pos­
sessed by a demon (Gunsho ruiju 4:530). When priest-​exorcists performed demon sub­
jugation rites, they visualized Fudō crushing the demon’s head with his foot, as Yixing, 
in his Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sutra 大日經疏 described (Taishō 1796).
Shugendō and Kōyasan
In Japan, as noted above, Fudō’s pedestal is either a mountain or a rock surrounded by 
a stormy sea and because of these dual meanings, he is the Shugendō icon used in the 
Shugendō mountain and waterfall ascetic practices. The halo of flames that surrounds 
him is sometimes pictorially indicated by a single flame flickering in the waterfalls used 
for ascetic Shugendō practices. Shugenja robes, and the rope tied around the waist of 
the practitioners, represented Kurikara. On completion of extreme practices, they 
considered themselves to have been reborn as a living Fudō.15 In addition to his signif­
icance in Shugendō at Kōyasan, one specific icon, Namikiri Fudō (the “wave-​cutting 
Fudō”) accrued, in the thirteenth century, fame and site-​specific significance to salva­
tion of the realm after repelling an invading foreign force.16
At Kōyasan, there was a rich Shugendō culture in the medieval period (Yamamoto 
2010, 78).17 Primarily a tradition of ritualized ascetic practice in the mountains, the es­
tablishment and development of the Kōyasan community in this environment made the 
character of its Shingon distinct from that of the important urban Shingon temples of 
the time based in the imperial capital, such as Tōji and Ninnaji. The boundary between 
Shugendō culture and that of the Buddhist institution was porous for much, if not all, 
of Kōyasan’s history. The Chūin-​ryū was deeply involved in Shugendō during the thir­
teenth century, and of this the texts and the visual materials produced by them provide 
ample evidence (Tinsley 2019, 196–​249, 326–​371). It was also from the latter part of the 
thirteenth century that the performance of ascetic practices in the mountains for the 
specific purpose of attaining supernatural powers truly flourished (Castiglione, Roth, 
and Rambelli 2020, 2). It is highly likely that Shugendō beliefs and practice played a part 
in the formation of Ryōzu Aizen. Without discounting the way in which the combina­
tion aligned with pre-​established systems of nondualism (including the system of honji-​
suijaku) that were being developed in high scholastic theory, Fudō—​a central object

--- PAGE 504 ---
The Twin Miracle      479
 
of worship for the Shugendō practitioner as well as the exorcist (the roles overlapped 
since Shugenja performed exorcisms)—​was also likely conjoined with Aizen to 
create the form of a deity for the power of the icon provided in the Shugendō system 
of praxis. Aizen and Fudō were gohō, necessary for these practices, as discussed below. 
Exorcistic-​possession practices, descriptions of which are found in the Chūin-​ryū’s 
Takusen-​ki,18 were used for the expulsion of enemies, whether those be spirits, states of 
mind, living beings, or environmental threats—​all understood as obstacles to mental 
or physical health or to political or personal advancement.19 In short, the Chūin-​ryū’s 
self-​legitimation involved Shugendō exorcistic methods. That these were familiar with 
them is quite evident in the production itself of the Takusen-​ki text, which originated in 
a spirit-​possessed child and that is also replete with descriptions of other possessions 
and exorcisms.
Ryōzu Aizen as icon and in ritual was first transmitted exclusively between the 
Daigō-​ji temple monks in the capital, Kyoto (then Heian-​kyō). It was taught to 
Kōyasan monks and became particularly popular for a time there as indicated by ex­
tant commentaries along with fine iconographical works made for the Kōyasan com­
munity, including an early Ryōzu Aizen statue dated to between the Muromachi 
(1392–​1573) and Edo (1603–​1868) periods and that had been transferred from Amano-​
sha (Kōyasan’s protective shrine where its kami were enshrined) and a painted work of 
the Kamakura period (1192–​1333). It has been suggested by historians of Asian religions 
that Ryōzu Aizen has no direct Chinese or Indian precedents and even to have been 
an entirely Japanese creation (Trenson 2018). Kagiwada Seiko proposed that the ritual 
and iconography of Ryōzu Aizen were probably developed by Japanese monastic 
ritualists (gyōja 行者) (Kagiwada 2012, 615). It is likely that the influence of Shugendō 
mountain practices in the tantric tradition played a part in this, especially those 
practices related to healing, spirit possession, and exorcism that were central to it, and 
to the practitioners who performed these rituals. These had emerged from another 
Shugendō-​rich and mountain-​based Shingon Buddhist culture at Daigō-​ji in the Kyoto 
capital, from which Kōyasan had received Ryōzu Aizen teachings, and they had de­
veloped within the Shingon of thirteenth-​century Kōyasan, where Shugendō practice 
was on the verge of forming into a discrete tradition. Connections between Daigō-​ji 
and the Chūin-​ryū, as well as with key Chūin-​ryū figure Dōhan 道範 (1179–​1252), and 
the Chūin-​ryū’s project of lineage maintenance may explain the significance of Aizen, 
Fudō, and Ryōzu Aizen to the Chūin-​ryū.
The Chūin-​ryū Legitimation Project
References to a fused form of Aizen and Fudō are found in the Takusen-​ki, and the de­
velopment of this variant Wisdom King may be understood as part of the Chūin-​ryū’s 
larger project of the time. It was within one of their other prized texts, the aforemen­
tioned Kakugen kudenshō, a collection of commentaries, including those of a past

--- PAGE 505 ---
480      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
luminary of their own line, Dōhan’s teacher Kakukai of Daigo-​ji (and later Kōyasan), 
that the following information regarding the combination of Fudō and Aizen appears:
[I]‌t is true that in the Dainichi-​kyō there is no line that combines Fudō with Aizen’ō 
and explains their interconnection. Hence, this [combination of Fudō and Aizen] is 
the exclusive, ultimate secret teaching of our own school, the Shingon School.20
The combination of the two Wisdom Kings is not found in the Japanese tantric tradition’s 
canonical text, the Dainichi-​kyō (大日経; Skt. Mahāvairocana sūtra). But in this case, 
the Chūin-​ryū found no contradiction between the matter of correct transmission and 
that of allegiance to what they believed Kūkai had taught, and the absence of the com­
bination from the sutra appears only to have made it more special, for it proved that it 
was the “exclusive, ultimate secret teaching of our own school.” The school was Shingon, 
but the presenters of this claim included a master of the Chūin-​ryū. The Chūin-​ryū were 
an offshoot of the Daigōji Ono-​ryū, the lineage that had early on monopolized Aizen 
ritual for the state and that first described Ryōzu Aizen. The Chūin-​ryū’s branch main­
tenance and dominance at Kōyasan depended on the reinforcement of its connection 
to several of the most important patriarchs of Shingon and its branches, among these 
Kūkai and his Chinese master Keika (恵果 746–​805). They named themselves after the 
cloister believed to have been occupied by Kūkai (Chūin, the “Central Cloister”) and 
then by representatives of the branch as it developed in distinction to others within the 
originally unified community at Kōyasan. The branch also emphasized their ostensibly 
direct and authentic connections to the local Kōyasan mountain kami Niu Myōjin and 
Kōya Myōjin. These connections were naturally drawn since, with a unique claim to 
dharma lineage descent, including the transmission of teachings from Kūkai (from 
which they deemed others to have strayed), Kūkai’s relationships with the local deities 
were also their inheritance. These connections buttressed this branch’s practical legiti­
mization strategies, aided in the reformation and recreation of narratives concerning its 
origins and lineage and even aided its land expansion efforts. Thus, rewritten legends 
(and reformed iconography) concerning the early ninth-​century origins of the Buddhist 
community at Kōyasan and the relationship necessitated by shared occupancy be­
tween the new mountain residents and the old were produced by the Chūin-​ryū, and 
they emphasized in them their own branch leaders’ links to the local deities (Abe, 1983). 
This is exemplified in the sudden claim, in the thirteenth century, to the kami Daishi 
Myōijn 大師明神, who appears to have been a newly formed deity comprising the 
spirits of Keika, Kūkai, and the two mountain kami (Tinsley 2019, 250–​284). This amal­
gamate deity channeled via a possessed child the series of oracular pronouncements 
transcribed by Dōhan in the Takusen-​ki, who was the head of a cohort of scholar monks 
of the Chūin-​ryū and at that time the deputy head of Kōyasan. The Takusen-​ki became a 
prized Chūin-​ryū text, its own shōgyō (sacred text) and kept exclusively at Henmyō’in, 
the temple at which the possession had occurred, with the sole exception of borrowing 
rights for Dōhan. The text represented—​or proved—​their legitimacy as legatees of every 
sacred component of the Shingon school at Kōyasan, from patriarchs to local deities.

--- PAGE 506 ---
The Twin Miracle      481
 
The text opens with an account of a sectarian conflict that had taken place nine 
years previously. In 1242, a faction led by Dōhan set fire to the residences of their 
rivals, the monks of Denbō-​in cloister, who posed a threat to Chūin-​ryū dominance. 
In a bold statement to their community issued by the priestly fire starters on return 
from an exile imposed on them by the bakufu government as punishment for the act, 
the flames of the fire ritual for “Aizen-​Ō” were described as being “the body of the 
living-​body of the [two] Myōō” (Abe 1983, 107),21 indicating a familiarity with Ryōzu 
Aizen ritual. Furthermore, those whose property had been razed, it relayed, had been 
the very objects of the goma ritual, and they deserved nothing less than death. “The 
Denbō-​in [cloister] monks on this mountain, despite having had these particular de­
lusional attachments, are referred to at other places as ‘Kōya hōshi.’ Therefore, they are 
not entirely evil. Because we forgive [them], since this evil deserves a death sentence, 
shouldn’t they kill themselves?” (Abe 1983, 104).22 So suggested returnee priest Dōhan 
some nine years after the event, in the Takusen-​ki description of what had transpired 
that night. By explaining the arson attack as being connected to a goma (Skt. homa; fire 
ritual), the Takusen-​ki’s account lifts the 1242 incident and consequent punishment of 
the exiles from the level of the mundane and resituates them on that of the sacred. It is 
also presented as an example of ritual power, prowess, and efficacy: Regardless of the 
resultant exile, the ritual itself had been a success since total subjugation had indeed 
been achieved. The Denbō’in monks left the mountain as a group to settle elsewhere, 
expelled much like an invading army or a political rival.
The ritual performed was an “Aizen-​Ō goma” but the Aizen that features throughout 
the Takusen-​ki is almost always coupled, at times ritualistically interchangeably, with 
Fudō. In another description of a ritual that may be the same ritual as the one described 
in the opening of the text, a visualization carried out as part of the ritual requires the 
attributes of the two Wisdom Kings to repeatedly merge with each other, dissolving the 
reality of the other:
The flames of Fudō are Aizen Myōō. The fire of the wisdom of the Myōō burns 
the defilements and sins of sentient beings. Or, the flames are Fudō, and the body 
is Aizen. At such a time, the sword becomes an arrow, the lasso becomes the bow. 
And also, the sword becomes the bow, the lasso becomes the arrow. And also, the 
lasso becomes the arrow. Regarding the two ends of the lasso, one is a one-​pronged 
vajra, and one is a three-​pronged vajra. When Aizen becomes Fudō, the bow is the 
lasso, the arrow is the sword. Also, in the teaching of the one body when they are two 
Myōō, the bow is Fudō and the arrow is Aizen. Thus, the flames are the body of the 
living-​body of the [two] Myōō. In one teaching the five colors are used. However, 
practitioners of Shingon, when they face the fire [performing the ritual], they must 
dwell in this visualization.
(Abe 1983, X)23
The reference to “the teaching of the one body when they are the two Myōō” (ittai no 
narai ni oite ni Myōō no toki 於一体習二明王之時) is probably synonymous with isshin

--- PAGE 507 ---
482      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
ryōzu 一身両頭, the “single body with two heads [of Fudō-​Aizen]” that, according to 
the Kakuzenshō, was first articulated by Shōbō.
The Chūin-​ryū and Possession-​Exorcism
Anna Andreeva’s observation that “Buddhist clerics based at local temples in Kantō, Ise, 
and central Japan, as well as their itinerant counterparts, hijiri and shugen practitioners 
travelling from one cultic site to another, shared the same body of concepts fusing eso­
teric deities, visual symbols, relics, and omnipresent kami” (Andreeva 2017, 240) is ap­
posite in explaining the spirit-​possession/​exorcism rites employed by medieval tantric 
Japanese monks. “Interpenetration” (nyūga ganyū 入我我入), for example, which is the 
core accomplishment of esoteric Buddhist rituals as a form of purification and means of 
“enlightenment in this very body” (sokushin jōbutsu 即身成仏), also characterizes the 
fusion of priest-​exorcist and powerful deity (the gohō or gohō zenjin 護法善神 “Dharma 
Protector Good Spirit”), which empowers the priest to invoke an attendant being to 
control and expel the invasive spirit (Iyanaga 2019, 1–​20; 2022, 12).
Dōhan himself noted in his commentary to the Yugikyō (Yugikyō kuketsu, in 
Shingon shu zensho 5, 129a12-​15) that “the method of the genja is said to be the method 
of the āveśa” (possession) (Iyanaga 2022, 4). Dōhan also described the functions of 
it, which include the elicitation of knowledge of “The Triple World of Three Times 
[Past, Present and Future]).” This is precisely how he and his cohort had made use 
of the possessed acolyte whose channeling originated the Takusen-​ki (Tinsley 2010, 
152–​153). In other words, these possession practices were known at Kōyasan, and the 
distinction between āveśa and genja-​led exorcisms was understood, but the methods 
were deemed equivalent. That Aizen is first described in the Yugikyō sutra about 
which Dōhan was commenting is significant, as is the fact that instructions for exor­
cism also appear. The syllables that punctuate the end of the longest Aizen dharani,24 
“jaku un ban koku” (Skt. jah hūm vam hoh) correspond to the Four-​Syllable Mantra 
(or the mantra of the Four Gathering Bodhisattvas), that is used in the twelfth to early 
thirteenth-​century Genja Sahō 験者作法 avesa ritual to bring the gohō into a child 
medium’s body for the purposes of diagnosing and healing a person afflicted by de­
monic possession (Iyanaga 2022, 11, 17:n52). Each sound expresses the tools of cap­
ture required to shift the demon from a deluded state to an awakened one: a hook 
(to capture), a rope (to haul in), and a chain (to bind). Texts that provided healing 
ritual instructions that employed the method of spirit possession (and concomitant 
exorcism) were “probably composed by some Shingon monk around the end of the 
twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth century” (Iyanaga 2022, 5) (al­
though it seems these had their oral origins in the Tendai school). These texts written 
or transmitted by Shingon monks broadly bracket the period in which Dōhan and 
his community of Chūin-​ryu members at Kōyasan were active. The texts Iyanaga has 
examined were of this period, suggesting a flourishing adoption of the rites during

--- PAGE 508 ---
The Twin Miracle      483
 
that time. In these ritual instructions, a gohō would be employed by the empowered 
priest-​exorcist to attend to the business of relocating the possessing spirit to the body 
of a medium and “binding” it so it could be cast out.
Dōhan and, later, his famed scholarly branch successor Yūkai (宥快 1345–​1416) were 
central in the project of dominance at Kōyasan, and both had an interest in Ryōzu Aizen 
concepts and worship. Descriptions of images of Ryōzu Aizen are found in several texts, 
including an iconographical scroll and three Daigō-​ji texts from the late thirteenth and 
early fourteenth centuries, roughly corresponding to Dōhan’s time (Andreeva 2017, 
138:n100; Goepper 1993, 48–​50). A rare ritual manual (shidai sho 次第書) for Ryōzu 
Aizen kept at Jimyō’in cloister at Kōyasan bears Yūkai’s name, although it accompanied 
a much earlier single-​headed Aizen Myōō icon of 1256,25 closer to Dōhan’s time, and 
has not been studied or dated yet. At Kōyasan, there were “secret” commentaries on 
the Yugikyō, including one attributed to the aforementioned Jitsuun (Yugikyō hiketsu 
(瑜祇経秘訣 “Secret Instructions on the Yugikyō”) as well as Dōhan’s own (Yugikyō 
kuketsu 瑜祇経口決) “Oral Instructions on the Yugikyō,” which contains the remarks 
on possession quoted above. It is possible that Dōhan developed the combinatory 
(Ryōzu?) Aizen goma and visualization described in Takusen-​ki based on the Yugikyō 
transmission he had received from Jikken at Daigōji. Indeed, he composed it in around 
1249, the year of Jikken’s death, and two years before he produced the Takusen-​ki.
Ideological Background
Although the imagery of aggression and related ritual for subjugating ends (chōbuku-​
hō or gōbuku-​hō) are far from unusual in the world of tantric Buddhism, the violence 
and sexual impulses embodied by the furious Aizen are, in scholastic tantric theory, 
the ones that could most effectively be transmuted into the state of enlightenment. 
This theory is encapsulated in the phrase bonnō soku bodai (“transgressions [worldly 
desires] are [identical to] enlightenment”). This famous phrase, while representing a 
Mahayana principle, is arguably the most representative of the esoteric Buddhist tra­
dition.26 It expresses the idea that the very suffering (caused by the “transgressions” or 
“defilements” (i.e., greedy, angry, or delusional motivational mental states; bonnō)—​
so-​called in Buddhist parlance as they impede the progress (i.e., make “impure”) of 
the development or emergence of Buddha consciousness; bodai)—​is itself a route to 
enlightenment. The phrase bonnō soku bodai has been understood as a radical expres­
sion of emptiness (Skt. śunyata; Jpn. kū) and of the overcoming of dualism. In fact, the 
tripartite phrase itself deftly also represents this. The transcendence of dualism was 
particularly characteristic of Shingon during the period in which the events examined 
in this chapter took place.27 Certainly, exorcistic practice was part of Aizen and Fudō 
worship from early on in Japanese history (Payne 1987, 53–​55). It was by the end of the 
Heian period that Aizen and Fudō were paired; it was also by the end of this period that 
exorcistic practices focusing on Aizen flourished (Faure 2015, 186). Although it had been

--- PAGE 509 ---
484      Elizabeth Noelle Tinsley
 
mainly Ono-​ryū branch Aizen rituals that were practiced in connection to exorcism in 
the Heian period, exorcistic practices flourished during the medieval period. Percival 
Lowell’s observation in 1894 that there “proved to exist a regular system of divine posses­
sion, an esoteric cult imbedded in the very heart of the Japanese character and instinct” 
(Lowell 1894, 13) may hold true: The system seems to have pervaded society and culture 
beyond any particular religious group and was, arguably, the soil into which esoteric 
Buddhism took root.
Reflections on Issues of Tantric Studies
The relationship between tantra and state protection has long been recognized, but its 
links with exorcism have been less studied, especially in Japanese Buddhism, although 
the work of Komatsu Kazuhiko (1994), Michael Strickmann (2002), Bernard Faure 
(2015), and Nobumi Iyanaga (2019, 2022), among others, is significant. As suggested in 
this chapter, Shugendō, along with Ono-​ryū teachings (which may have been among 
those later deemed heretical by Kōyasan scholar monks), may be a key factor here, espe­
cially in the formation of Ryōzu Aizen with the addition of Fudō, its powerful demon-​
quelling tutelary deity. Violence and exorcistic practices have never been very unusual 
and may fall into the category of transgressive and antinomian acts that characterize 
Indian tantric Buddhism—​which are found in even very early (exoteric) Buddhist 
scriptures: Antinomian acts could provide mundane benefits and protections for people 
of both high (royal) social status and lower (Wedemeyer 2013, 186–​187). However, the 
role of Ryōzu Aizen has not been fully recognized in this way, so there is room for reas­
sessment of the icon.
Also, the subject of duality is raised by the very nonduality of this icon. Certainly, 
charges of (“un-​Buddhist”) violence exemplified by transgressive acts, such as that of 
the ritual-​arson attack, could potentially be resolved with a philosophical explana­
tion such as bonnō soku bodai. Wedemeyer noted that tantric Buddhist professionals 
involved with goma rituals, for example, were “confronted daily with the inherent 
problematic of attempting to reach an ultimate non-​dual goal by discursive, dual­
istic means. Incorporating a visceral reminder of nonduality and transcendence 
of convention into their otherwise dualistic rituals provided a means to digest 
performatively the anomaly of such a highly ritualized mode of Buddhist practice, 
so as to allow the maintenance of such a complex ceremonial without obvious self-​
contradiction” (Wedemeyer 2013, 191). More broadly, on tantric war in Indian tantric 
Buddhism, Iain Sinclair noted that “magical slaying, along with other transgressive 
acts enjoined in the higher tantras, can be sanctioned insofar as it is a manifestation 
of transcendence” (Sinclair 2016, 19).
The practice of the goma that is interiorized or inwardly directed (内 Jpn. nai-​; Skt. 
antar-​) and that which is exteriorized or outwardly directed (Jpn. 外 ge-​; Skt. bāhya-​)

--- PAGE 510 ---
The Twin Miracle      485
 
is one example of the dualism of ritual (transgressive or not). A similar approach was 
taken to the problem of exorcising demons in the medieval period. From the perspective 
of the Buddhist teachings regarding the core problem of suffering, they were considered 
as akin to spiritually deluded beings and treated with compassion (Iyanaga 2022, 522). 
They were (ideally) incorporated into a conventional Japanese Buddhist interpretation 
of a world inhabited by spirits and kami and thus were “purified”—​but they were also 
violently cast out.
The specific deities and motives of the monastic figures involved in the 1242 at­
tack are situated in written account as a case of “sacred violence.” The text as a whole 
provides a worldview since it is made up of various secret teachings about Kōyasan 
and thus a specific cultural context for the attack. A further step for tantric studies 
more broadly may be to trace various similar uses of attacks in cultural context across 
Asia in order to discern the nature of the different uses of exorcism in tantra and the 
transmissions and developments of the deities involved leading to a deeper under­
standing of Ryōzu Aizen.
