Chapter 22
A Dharma Protector in a 
Transcultural Tantric 
Buddhist Context
Vesna A. Wallace
Introduction
In Mongolian Buddhism, Jamsran is popularly known as a Red Protector (Ulaan 
Sakhius) and is included in a group of ten fierce Dharma protectors (Tib. chos skyong, 
Mong. choijin)—​Yamantāka, Vajrapāṇi, Yamarāja, six-​armed Mahākāla, Śrī Devī, 
Vaiśravaṇa, Brahmā, White Mahākāla, and four-​faced Mahākāla. In both Tibet and 
Mongolia, he is addressed as Begze Brother-​and-​Sister, or Yakṣa Brother-​and-​Sister 
(Yagchis Egch Düü), Red Yakṣa (Tib. Gnod sbyin dmar po; Mong. Ulaan Yagchis), the 
Red Lord of Life (Tib. Srog bdag dmar po; Mong. Ulaan Aminy Ezen), Vajrabhairava, 
and so on.1 In various texts, he is given the epithets “lotus dancer” and “murderer of 
the Ten Bodhisattva Grounds” due to having attained the Tenth Bodhisattva Ground. 
As a result, he also bears the name Dharmamega, the traditional name for the Tenth 
Ground (Skt. dharmameghā) or the “Clouds of Dharma,” which designates the apex 
of an attainment on the Bodhisattva path.2 He is also known for accomplishing the 
decrees of various other fierce deities, which are also the tenth-​stage bodhisattvas: 
Hayagrīva, Yamāntaka, Black Yamarāja, Mahādeva (or Maheśvara), and Ekajāti (or 
Mahācīnatārā), a protectress of secret mantras and Buddhist tantric teachings. In 
the Tibetan Sakya, Kagyu, and Nyingma traditions, Jamsran is the main protector of 
the Hayagrīva cycle of practice; this association with Hayagrīva also extends to the 
Mongolian Gèluk tradition. In the Gèluk tradition, he is most commonly associated 
with Yamāntaka and Mahākāla. As a result, many texts dedicated to Jamsran from 
Mongolia begin with an homage to either Hayagrīva or Yamarāja. These are found in 
a minor collection of works dedicated to Jamsran known as the Jamsran Beübüm (Tib. 
Lcam sring be’u bum).3

--- PAGE 515 ---
490      Vesna A. Wallace
 
The popularity of Jamsran as a Dharma Protector in both Tibetan and Mongolian 
forms of Buddhism is evidenced by the preponderance of prayers, sādhanas, and ritual 
texts related to this fierce deity. Such texts are found in the collected works (Tib. gsung 
‘bum; Mong. sumbum) of Mongolian and Tibetan authors of all the schools of Tibetan 
Buddhism, as well as in the above-​mentioned minor collections (Tib. be’u bum; Mong. 
beübüm) of works dedicated to Jamsran. A version of the Jamsran Beübüm published in 
Ulaanbaatar by Shambhala in 2005 contains forty-​seven texts in the Tibetan language, 
and fifty-​seven in Modern Mongolian.4 When compared with a Tibetan-​language ver­
sion reproduced in the Kyi monastery in Spiti, Ladakh, which contains forty-​two texts, 
the Mongolian collection appears larger and significantly different from the one from 
Spiti. Only three texts with the same title are found within both collections: (1) A Fierce 
Method of Accomplishing Yakṣa Lcam sring Together with Essential Exhortation (Gnod 
sbyin lcam sring gi sgrub thabs drag po gnad bskul dang bcas), which also bears the 
title A Mantra of the Red Lord Prāṇātma5 and is attributed to the fourteenth-​century 
Tibetan Sakya master Palden Senge (Dpal ldan Sengge); (2) An Exhortation to the Nine 
Divisions of Assassins (Shan pa dgu skor gyi bskul byang);6 and (3) The Essential Advice 
on the Red Protector Deity (Sgrol gying dmar po’i gnad).7 Special copies of the Jamsran 
Beübüm were traditionally kept in a sealed box, while the others were wrapped in 
cloth and sealed with three “seals,” marked at the end of the text with three symbolic 
syllables, rgya rgya rgya, and called “the seal of entrustment” (tushaakh tamga), “the 
seal of concealment (nuukh tamga),” and “the seal of disguisement” (daldlakh tamga) 
(Bayasgalan 2011, 364). The sealed collection is orally transmitted from a teacher to 
only one trustworthy disciple. As indicated by the colophons to nearly all the texts 
contained in the Jamsran Beübüm, these were received through oral transmission (lung 
thob) due to their secret nature. However, only some colophons to the texts inform us of 
the lineages through which they were transmitted. Some texts trace their transmissions 
all the way back to Padmasambhava, Marpa Lotsawa, and others. Two versions of the 
same text titled A History of the Red Yakṣa (Gnod sbyin dmar po’i lo rgyus) contained 
in the aforementioned copy of the Jamsran Beübüm tell us that the secrecy of these 
texts is due to the power of sādhana practices on Jamsran and his companions, which 
gives to the practitioners the ability to kill others by merely glancing at them or by 
getting angry at them. For instance, the Indian, non-​Buddhist master of evil mantras, 
ācārya Nyima Dragpa (Tib. Nyi ma Grags pa; Skt. Candrayaśas/​Candrakīrti), is said to 
have killed others in an instant by merely looking at them.8 Similarly, his son Paṇḍita 
Dawa Nagpo (Tib. Zla ba nag po; Skt. Kṛṣṇacandra) killed others in an instant by 
merely getting angry at them. In later years, one Nyang Lotsawa became renowned for 
the same ability, due to meditating on the assassins, or butchers (shan pa), of the Red 
Prāṇātma (Tib. Srog bdag dmar po; Skt. Lohitaprāṇātma), a protector of the assistants 
of the four-​faced Mahākāla. After several generations, the ācārya Deva (a teacher of 
non-​Buddhist heretics, who knew many heretical evil mantras), practiced the instruc­
tion of the above-​mentioned masters and transmitted it to one Deu (Tib. Mde’u). Then, 
the transmission passed to Tibet, culminating with Nyangchul (Gnyang chul) Lotsawa, 
who also became renowned for evil mantras (see Gnod sbyin dmar po’i lo rgyus 2005,

--- PAGE 516 ---
A Dharma Protector      491
 
325–​325 and 330–​331). We see here a concern that powerful ritual practices related to 
Jamsran may fall into the hands of non-​Buddhist heretics; Buddhist tantric masters 
were instructed to pass that knowledge only to initiates whose intention, we are told, 
was to save sentient beings, especially at the time of decline of the buddhadharma and 
to prevent the prevalence of those inimical to the Dharma. The secret nature of the 
Jamsran Beübüm is also emphasized by the assertion that it dwells hidden in the heart 
of Red Mahākāla (Bayasgalan 2011). In Mongolia the Jamsran Beübüm circulated in 
different versions, some larger than others.
Legends and Oral Accounts about the Origin of Jamsran
The existence of different accounts of Jamsran’s origin indicate his disparate identities. 
In one legend, he was already a tenth-​ground bodhisattva, who originally dwelt in 
Tuṣita heaven before being birthed from a red egg. According to another legend 
given in the History of the Red Yakṣa (Gnod sbyin dmar po’i lo rgyus), contained in the 
Jamsran Beübüm, he came into existence on account of his future parents’ prayers to 
Maheśvara and Ekajaṭī, for he is also considered to be the accomplisher of the decrees 
of these two deities. The legend says that at the time Jamsran was to descend from the 
Tuṣita heaven into his land of Maruce, the two eggs—​one coral and the other agate—​
appeared, from which two children were born to their father yakṣa, a fierce nature 
spirit, and mother demoness. Begze emerged from the red coral egg, whereas his sister 
came from the agate egg (Gnod sbyin dmar po’i lo rgyus 2005, 330–​331). Due to the 
fierce nature of his parents and the corresponding redness of his egg, his manifesta­
tion became that of a fierce, red yakṣa.
In another legend, A Legend of the Liberating Assassin, The Red Lord of Life (Shan pa 
sgrol byed srog bdag dmar po’i lo rgyus), also included in the Jamsran Beübüm, we find a 
somewhat different version of his origin. According to this version, a long time ago, the 
father yakṣa with copper hair and the bloody mother demoness were unable to control 
the eggs that soared to the sky and tamed the eight deities in the heavens and the eight 
planets in the intermediate directions. Then leaping downward, they pacified the eight, 
great nāga spirits of the earth. In fear, the father prayed to Maheśvara and Ekajaṭī. After 
Maheśvara and Ekajaṭī tamed the eggs, Jamsran emerged from the coral egg, and from 
the agate egg emerged a red-​faced girl. Maheśvara and Ekajāṭī then questioned Jamsran 
concerning his emanation, his name, his abode, and his share of food. Jamsran replied: 
“Mahādeva, I am an emanation (sprul ba) of Yamāntaka’s speech. My name is Man with 
The Color of Power (Skyes bu dbang gi mdog can), Red Prāṇātma (Srog bdag dmar po), 
and Red Yamshü (Yam shud dmar po). My abode is the palace of Maruce of the red, 
copper plain in the northwestern direction. As for the share of my food, they say, it is 
‘the fields of destruction.’ ” The red-​faced daughter answered the same questions posed 
to her by Ekajaṭī, saying: “Great Mother, Ekajaṭī, I am an emanation of the speech of a 
mātṛkā (Tib. ma mo), a fierce mother deity. My name is Red-​faced Daughter of an Ogre, 
Red-​faced Rigpey Lhamo (Rig pa’i lha mo), a powerful lady of a secret dance (Gsang

--- PAGE 517 ---
492      Vesna A. Wallace
 
mtshan gar gyi dbang phyug ma). My abode is in the northeastern direction; as for my 
share of food, it is the flesh, blood, and vital force of those hostile to Buddhism.” After 
that, Ekajaṭī bestowed empowerment on those two, offered her heart’s blood to each 
of them, and extracted an oath from them to protect the Buddha Dharma. From then 
on, they have protected the Dharma in India and in the countries of Ha shan and Li.9 
Protecting the teachings in India, they transformed into yakṣas; in the Ha Shan country 
of China, they transformed into war deities, and in the country of Li, they turned into 
the bodyguards of the cycle of teachings. Indian masters (Tib. slob dpon, Skt. ācārya) 
who held tenets different from those of the buddhadharma, and who intended to bru­
tally harm others, hid this in an Indian terma (Tib. gter ma), or “hidden treasure.” After 
this account, the text describes the powers of the previously mentioned, heretical tantric 
masters, Nyima Dragpa, his son, and others (Shan pa sgrol byed srog bdag dmar po’i lo 
rgyus 2005, 340–​342).
The Mongolian folk tradition contains different oral accounts concerning Jamsran. 
According to one account, Jamsran and Rigpey Lhamo (Mong. Regviilkham) are 
said to be each other’s consorts and the parents of the eight red assistants, who follow 
Jamsran in every battle. Another account tells of Rigpey Lhamo taking Sokdag (Mong. 
Srodag) as her consort during the time of Jamsran’s absence. Having discovered this 
betrayal through his clairvoyance, Jamsran punished Sokdag by making him ride a 
mad wolf, and he punished Rigpey Lhamo by making her ride a mad bear (Bayasgalan 
2011, 377). According to yet another Mongolian oral account, Jamsran was initially a 
harmful war deity imbued with the power and ability of shamans and shamanesses. 
Although subjugated and converted into a Dharma protector, his power did not di­
minish. In accordance with his vow to protect the buddhadharma, he passes through 
three thousand lands within a single moment, making the earth shake with his feet, 
terrifying enemies with his roar, and causing thunder, lightning, and hail with his 
wrath (Bayasgalan 2011, 347).
Jamsran’s Transcultural Identities 
and Functions
In a text contained in the Jamsran Beübüm titled The Exhortation of the Essence of a 
Retinue of the Red Prāṇātma10 (Srog bdag dmar po ‘khor bcas kyi gnad bskul), Jamsran is 
described as a transcultural deity that manifests with different identities and carries out 
different tasks in different regions of Asia. In this text, he is invoked in all the aforemen­
tioned forms: as a transgressor spirit (Tib. dam sri mdzad) of India; a war deity of the 
land of Hashan; a protector of the gods of Maruce; a great guardian spirit of the Dharma 
in the country of Li; a military officer of the mātṛkās of Tibet; a minister of the legion of 
a thousand yakṣas, the chief of all yakṣas; and a yakṣa with a copper ritual dagger (Tib. 
phur pa). With a sword in his right hand, he destroys the life of those who violate their

--- PAGE 518 ---
A Dharma Protector      493
 
religious pledges. He is exhorted in a prayer to follow the instruction of Mahādeva and 
accomplish the work of Yamarāja by cutting the aorta of those violators. On the right 
side of Jamsran is Lohitaprāṇātma, who is similar to Jamsran in appearance as a warrior 
wearing an armor and riding a rabid wolf. Prāṇātma holds a lasso and the head of an ad­
versary in his left hand, and with his right hand he holds a spear.11 In this and other ritual 
texts and sādhanas as well as in iconography, Jamsran is visualized and iconographically 
represented as having a red body and a red face, with three eyes spinning and blazing and 
a mouth showing four fangs. His head is decorated with five human skulls. He wields a 
fiery sword with his right hand, and with his left hand he holds the bow and arrow. He 
carries a victory banner under his armpit. He wears armor on his chest, a nine-​layered 
ceremonial scarf (Tib. kha btags) on his body, and a rosary made of fifty skulls around 
his neck that trickle blood. He is standing on a lotus supported by a sun disc in the center 
of an ocean of fire. He tramples with his feet the corpses of a human and a horse. Day 
and night, he watches the entire world in a mirror. When he finds an enemy antagonistic 
to the Dharma, he expels the enemy and cuts off their life. On the left side of Jamsran 
is his sister, Rigpey Lhamo, riding a mad bear. Her body is dark blue, and her red face 
has three eyes and a semiopen mouth with the four fangs. She wields a scorching sword 
with her right hand and with holds a ritual dagger in her left hand. On the right side of 
Jamsran is Sokdag, similar to Jamsran’s appearance of an armored warrior. While riding 
a rabid wolf, he holds a lasso and the head of an adversary in his left hand, and with his 
right hand he holds a spear.
Jamsran is also accompanied by eight assistants who carry daggers and twenty-​one 
assassins who wear the wet skin of their enemies. The assassins wield a dagger in their 
right hand, and with their left hand, they hold the enemy’s liver, heart, lungs, spleen, 
eyes, marrow, and scalp (with hair). They perform grisly tasks, including the unraveling 
of the enemy’s intestines, tearing off the enemy’s skin and flesh, trampling the ground 
with their feet, and jumping and leaping as they dance.
Numerous armies also accompany Jamsran. According to a short text titled A History 
of the Red Lord of Life, A Liberating Assassin (Shan pa sgrol byed srogs bdag dmar po’i 
lo rgyus), also included in the Jamsran Beübüm, Jamsran’s immense army consists of a 
thousand evil spirits who race in front of Jamsran and hurl red lassos at the enemy. On 
his right side are a thousand black demons who cut the enemies whose tantric pledges 
deteriorated. On Jamsran’s left side there are a hundred thousand mātṛkās, who give 
blood diseases and the like to the enemy. Behind him there are a thousand crawling 
assassins who cut off the life of the enemies of Dharma. Around him in the ten directions 
are a thousand yakṣas who take the life of hostile yogīs, while the billions of divisions of 
his murderous devils display various supernatural powers and disturb the three worlds. 
Together with their messengers and others, they all squash the enemies of Dharma. 
They wield fiery swords with handles in the shape of scorpions, and they hold the esoph­
agus and the heart of the enemy.12
These terrifying images of Jamsran, his army, and his realm of Maruce, which are 
visualized by the yogī who invokes Jamsran and his army and incites them to violent 
action, empower the yogī to overcome external enemies, whether ritually or in an actual

--- PAGE 519 ---
494      Vesna A. Wallace
 
battle. For such a yogī, the described images are not simply a metaphor for the elimina­
tion of negative mental states but also a conduit to victory over the external enemies of 
Dharma. As an archetype of a mighty and fierce warrior who can also be compassionate 
to his worshippers and to those who keep their pledges, Jamsran is put into both mili­
tary service and the service of accomplishing the various other tasks of a protector deity. 
Some of the duties assigned to him are those of protecting the worshipper from common 
dangers and are thus similar to those given to other, fierce tantric deities, like Vajrapāṇi 
and Bhairava. For example, in a short and untitled text composed by the Sixth Panchen 
Lama, Lobsang Palden Yeshe (Blo bzang dpal ldan Ye shes 1738–​1780) at the behest of the 
Venerable Zangpo Tenzin (Tshe dan ldan pa, Bzang po Bstan ‘dzin),13 there appears an 
abbreviated version of the offering of a so-​called golden drink (Tib. gser skyems, which 
is often an alcoholic drink in the offerings to a fierce deity) to Jamsran. In this text, the 
Panchen Lama addresses Jamsran as a devourer of the three worlds and commands him 
and his companions to smash a gang of bandits and create favorable conditions, such as 
freedom from the dangers of humans and nonhumans, famine, epidemics, and so on 
(Shashnyg Khamgaalach Nomyg Tetgeegch, Ulaan Sakhius (Beübüm) 2005, 374).
The fierce nature of Jamsran and his assistants, and the violent tasks that they are ex­
pected to perform are reflected not only in their described appearance but also in the 
violent nature of their rituals. These incorporate mantras of killing, as well as fierce 
offerings such as tormas (Tib. gtor ma, a sacrificial dough offering) containing the blood 
and the flesh of a goat, a dog, a fox, or whatever else being one finds. Moreover, Jamsran 
and his wrathful army can also grant blessings, as seen in Jamsran’s Benediction (Lcam 
sring gi bkra shis) composed by the Second Dalai Lama, Gendün Gyatso (Dge ‘dun rgya 
mtsho, 1476–​1542), where Jamsran is identified with Mañjuśrī:
May there be blessing of the assistant Sokdag (Srog bdag) and his majestic, su­
preme consort (Rig pa’i lha mo), the eight dagger wielders, twenty-​one assassins, 
demons, yakṣas, rākṣas, mātṛkās, and others, accompanied by their retinues of their 
attendants! (v. 3)
May there be blessing of the Dharma protector Jamsran and his retinue, and of the 
ocean of the oath-​bound guardians of teachings, who with powerful lightning crush 
the rocky-​mountains of obstructive spirits, enemies, and hindrances! (v. 4)
May there be blessing of the Red Yakṣa Beg tse, who manifests a fierce appearance in 
order to tame the vicious, Mañjuśrī, the embodiment of wisdom and compassion of 
all the sugatas of three times! (v. 5)
May there be blessing of the Red-​faced goddess, who has a fierce appearance in 
order to cut the aorta of the vow violators, the Red-​faced emanation of Ekajaṭī! (v. 6). 
(Shashnyg Khamgaalach Nomyg Tetgeegch, Ulaan Sakhius (Beübüm) 2005, 371–​373)
Viewed as an emanation of Yamāntaka, who is a fierce aspect of Mañjuśrī, Jamsran is 
also recognized here as an emanation of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. As we will see below, 
he is also praised as an emanation of Amitābha by ways of being also the emanation of 
Hayagrīva, who is a fierce aspect of Amitābha.

--- PAGE 520 ---
A Dharma Protector      495
 
The Worship of Jamsran in Mongolia
In works composed by Mongolian authors, we encounter Jamsran as a tertiary man­
ifestation of the Buddha Amitābha by virtue of being an emanation of Mahākāla, yet 
another fierce aspect of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and ultimately of the Buddha 
Amitābha. In the Saγang Sečen’s chronicle, the Precious Summary (Erdeni-​yin tobči 
1662), we read that when the Third Dalai Lama Sönam Gyatso (Bsod nams Rgya 
mtsho, 1543–​1588) was on his way to Kökenuur to meet with Altan Khan (of the Tümed 
Mongols) and Qutuɣtu Sechen Qung-​Taiǰi (of the Ordos Mongols) in 1576/​1577, he made 
a torma, offering to “the very powerful Begze Mahākāla, who listens to the commands of 
Hayagrīva.”14 Reminding him of his duties as a Dharma protector, and instructing him 
to follow the Dharma, the Dalai Lama dispatched him to corral and subjugate the deities 
and nāgas of the Mongol lands. That night, when the Dalai Lama arrived at the banks of 
the Gün river, all the spirits, deities, nāgas, demons, and ongods (Shamanic spirits) of 
the Mongol land were brought under his control. At that time, the Dalai Lama bound 
them all with a vow to serve the Dharma. Then, while Qutuɣtu Sečen Qung-​Taiǰi and 
Dayan baɣši, accompanied by three thousand people, were welcoming the Dalai Lama 
and making him many, costly offerings, the Dalai Lama appeared as the four-​armed 
Avalokiteśvara to Qutuɣtu Sečen Qung-​Taiǰi. The next day, while the Dalai Lama was 
traveling on his horse, the six syllables (oṃ mani padme hūṃ) of the mantra of compas­
sion appeared on the stones of the path trod by the Dalai Lama’s chestnut horse. Seeing 
this, everyone present developed great faith.15 This passage from the Precious Summary 
shows the Third Dalai Lama, considered by the tradition as a peaceful, earthly ema­
nation of Avalokiteśva, interacting with a deity that is a fierce emanation of the same 
Avalokiteśvara, and exerting authority over Jamsran by means of reverential offerings, 
and then employing him to tame the indigenous Mongolian deities and spirits that 
could be inimical to the spread of Buddhism in the Mongol lands.
It must have been under the influence of the Third Dalai Lama that Abatai Sain Khan 
(1554–​1588) of Khalkha began to worship Jamsran as his protector and Vajrapāṇi as his 
tutelary deity (yi dam) in Baruun Örgöö (Western Palace), which became a central fire 
hearth (gal golomt örgöö) palace of the Mongolian state that has its origin in the time 
of Chinggis Khaan (Bayasgalan 2011, 237–​238). During Abatai Khan’s rule, Mongolian 
officials and nobles swore an oath to Jamsran every year. After Abatai Khan’s time, the 
tradition of worshiping Jamsran was passed to the First Jebtsundampa, Öndör Gegeen 
Zanabazar (Blo bzang bstan pa’i rgyal mtshan, 1635–​1723), and sequentially to his later 
incarnations, such as the Eighth Jebtsundampa (Ngag dbang blo bzang chos rje nyi ma 
bstan ‘dzin dbang phyug, 1870–​1924), the religious and secular leader of the autono­
mous Mongol state. Soon after the establishment of the autonomous Bogd Khaan state 
in 1911, the Eighth Jebtsundampa, together with his queen Dongogdulam (1874–​1923), 
lit the ceremonial fire on the morning of first day of Mongolian New Year (Tsagaan Sar) 
in Baruun Örgöö. It was there, in front of the image of Jamsran, that state ministers,

--- PAGE 521 ---
496      Vesna A. Wallace
 
officials, and noblemen took an oath to wholeheartedly serve the Mongol state. Likewise, 
in 1903, at the establishment of the thirtieth division (aimag) of Ikh Khüre dedicated 
to the queen Dongogdulam and known as Ekh Dagini’s division, an image of Jamsran 
was placed in the queen’s temple for her protection. Among the thirty divisions of Ikh 
Khüree, all seven monastic colleges (datsan, Tib. grva tshang) that belonged to the 
seven divisions of Ikh Khüree—​including Ekh Dagini’s division—​worshipped Jamsran 
as their protector. Among these seven divisions, those that are worth mentioning are 
Tsetsen Toyin’s division, which was established between the seventeenth and eighteenth 
centuries; Dashdarlin (Tib. Bkra shis bstan dar gling) division, which was established in 
the late nineteenth century; Mahamaya (Tib. Ma-​ha ma-​ya) division founded by the fa­
ther of the Second Jebtsundampa; Puntsogtechenlin (Tib. Phun tshogs theg chen gling) 
division; Saingai division; and Namdolin (Tib. Rnam grol gling), also known as Dashilin 
(Tib. Bkra shis gling), division.
On November 20, 1919, at the time when Ikh Khüree was occupied by Chinese repub­
lican forces, Mongolian state officials, including the Minister of Finances, S. Danzan and 
others, swore an oath in front of Jamsran to fight for the independence of the country. 
A year later, they again swore the oath. From 1919 to 1924, the Mongolian Ministry of 
Defense worshipped Jamsran, until the Mongolian People’s Revolutionary Party joined 
the Communist International (Comintern). Worshipped as a war deity with the ex­
traordinary power and ability to terrify the enemy and offer help to all beings, Jamsran 
become a protector of the Mongolian Ministry of Defense (Tsergiin Yam) and was 
summoned, appeased with offerings, and asked to secure the peace of the country and 
subjugate the enemy causing obstacles to the state.
Jamsran’s activities in Mongolia also played out through his medium, a renowned 
military general and leading figure in Mongolia’s fight for independence from the Qing, 
Khatanbaatar Sanagdorjiin Magsarjav (1878–​1927) from Sain Noyon Khan Province 
(aimag). Prior to leaping into battles, Magsarjav entered into a trance and brandished a 
gun and a sword. Within this trance state, his sword is said to have leaped out from its 
scabbard by itself, and bullets would leap out from their compartments. Having thus 
transformed into a ferocious warrior endowed with siddhis and gaining knowledge 
when and how to launch the offensive, he instilled confidence in his soldiers and was 
successful in every battle he waged. In 1912, together with other two military leaders, 
Manlaibaatar J. and Damdinsüren, S., Magsarjav led an army of more than two thou­
sand men (according to some accounts, five thousand men) into the city of Khovd, the 
last bastion of the Qing army. Prior to entering battle, he offered his large standard to 
Rashaant Mountain while a certain Dörvöd epic singer played his two-​stringed lute 
(tovshuur) and sang a heroic epic called Hundred Thousand Jewels (Bum Erdene). There, 
together with Jalkhanz Khutagt (whose current incarnation is considered Jamsran’s 
oracle) and his disciples, Magsarjav meditated on fierce activities, and in order to in­
cinerate the demons of foreign enemies, he participated in the ritual of exorcism, in 
which a model of a human skull made out of dough was placed on a pyramid-​like 
structure made of stalks of grain, to which were attached red, jagged, paper streamers 
representing the flames.

--- PAGE 522 ---
A Dharma Protector      497
 
From 1912 until 1921, Magsarjav fought some thirty battles, including those against 
Chinese incursions in Inner Mongolia and Chinese Republican forces under General 
Xu Shuzheng that occupied Ikh Khüree, and after joining the Mongolian People’s 
Revolutionary Party (MPRP) in 1921, he fought White Russian troops led by ultra­
conservative monarchist Baron Ungern (Roman von Ungern-​Sternberg, 1886–​1921), 
who used intimidation and brutality toward revolutionaries. Due to his bravery and 
victory in battle against the Qing forces and Chinese troops, Magsarjav received the 
honorary title of “Strong Hero” (khatanbaatar) from the Eighth Jebtsundampa and 
the rank of a beis, or a prince of the fourth rank. A year after joining the Mongolian 
revolutionaries, in 1922, he was appointed to the positions of Minister of the Western 
Frontier and then as the Minister of Defense. In 1924, he became an official member of 
the MPRP.
According to one account given by partisan Ts. Dovdoi, who fought along Magsarjav 
in Sülinkheer, on one occasion when Magsarjav sent some of his men to spy on a Chinese 
military encampment, a soldier returned unnerved by the size of the Chinese troops. 
Because of that, Magsarjav entered a trance, and while in trance, he beat his soldiers 
with a whip. After the trance, he instilled confidence in his men by recounting his vision 
of Chinggis Khan in a trance and assuring them that Jamsran was watching over them. 
In another account written by Khorlogiin Choilbasan (1939–​1957), a leader of the MPRP 
and a Marshal of Mongolian People’s Army from 1930 until 1957, Choibalsan wrote 
about Magsarjav, describing Magsarjav’s dealings with a killed enemy.16 After beheading 
the enemy, cutting his chest open, and taking out the enemy’s heart, Magsarjav 
worshipped his flag with the enemy’s heart and had his soldiers taste the blood drip­
ping from it. Magsarjav’s flag was decorated with a triple spear on the top, a skull with 
black tassles, and a ceremonial scarf (khadag). Prior to worshipping the flag, he installed 
it in the ground and tied it with ropes on three sides to balance it (Myagmarsambuu 
2011, 11–​12, 32–​39). When J. Boldbaatar wrote about Magsarjav in 1999, he tried to ex­
plain Magsarjav’s violent actions in a way similar to those in which the fierce deeds of 
Jamsran are justified in various works by stating: “Khatanbaatar Magsarjav was a tal­
ented general. During the war, he would remain in meditation internally, while exter­
nally manifesting ferocity, strengthening his soldiers, and providing the soldiers’ minds 
with great capacity to summon the good fortune” (Boldbaatar 1999, 33). Magsarjav built 
a monastery, between 1919 and 1920, that had about a hundred lamas, two monastic 
colleges, a large assembly hall, and a temple dedicated to Jamsran as the monastery’s Red 
Protector (Ulaan Sakhius). The monastery continued its prayer service to Jamsran until 
1930, when public ritual performances and tantric initiations were still possible before 
their prohibition by MPRP.
Jamsran has also been the object of ritual worship in Mongolia at various mountain 
sites, ovoos (stone cairns), and monasteries. One monastery famous for its ritual wor­
ship of Jamsran and for Jamsran mask dances (tsam, Tib. cham) was the large monastic 
center, Khüree of Erdene Khamba, which was located in a region now known as Khishig 
Öndör district in Bulgan Province. The monastery had four divisions (aimag), a large as­
sembly temple (tsogchin, Tib. tshogs chen), many smaller temples, a woodblock printery,

--- PAGE 523 ---
498      Vesna A. Wallace
 
and more than a thousand monks. According to Bayasgaalan, it belonged to the non-​
Géluk, “Red Tradition” (Bayasgalan 2011, 376). Jamsran also played a part in ritual mask 
dances held at other monasteries, such as Khamar Khiid in Ömnövgovi Province, Ikh 
Küree, the seat of the Jebstundmpas, and others. A Jamsran mask, which was used in a 
mask dance performance in Ikh Khüree held in the early 1930s, was made of approxi­
mately six thousand coral beads and weighing seventy kilograms at the end of the nine­
teenth century by a well-​known artist of Ikh Küree named Puntsog Osor (Bayasgalan 
2011, 381–​382).
Moreover, Jamsran, together with Mahākāla and Śrīdevī, was also worshipped as 
one of the three protectors of Usan Züil Khüree, located in the region now known as 
Govi-​Altai Province. When the Badam Yoga monastic college reopened in Geser (Tib. 
Gesar) temple in Ulaanbaatar in 2001, an image of Jamsran as a protector was placed 
in the temple to replace a human-​size statue of Jamsran, which had stood there be­
fore the ravages of the communist revolution, when it was destroyed. The association 
of Jamsran’s image with Geser temple, known also as Guandi temple, is based on the 
Mongols’ view of the epic hero Gesar (Tib. Ge sar) as an emanation of Jamsran, which 
is based on the Qing’s worship of the Chinese god of war, Guandi, as an emanation of 
Jamsran and a protector of the Géluk tradition.
Nowadays, in addition to various, smaller temples across Mongolia, Jasmran is 
worshipped at two mountain sites, one situated in the Büren district (sum) of Central 
Province (Töv aimag) of Mongolia; and he also continues to be worshipped at Khognu 
Khan Mountain, located in Bulgan Province.
Jamsran in Mongolian Writings
Various texts related to Jamsran, such as supplicatory and confessional prayers and 
eulogies and ritual texts of exorcism, as well as related commentaries on such works, 
continued to be produced in Mongolia until 1921. The aforementioned Öndör Geegeen 
Zanabazar, the First Jebtsundampa, composed a versified prayer of offerings to Jamsran 
in the Tibetan language, titled The Offering of Requisites, together with Offering Verses, to 
the Ferocious Dharma Protector Lcam sring (Chos skyong dregs pa lcam sring gi chas ‘dbul 
mchod ‘phreng bcas).17 In this prayer, he addresses Jamsran as a fierce deity arisen from 
the dance of gnosis of the greatly powerful Buddha Amitābha. Thus, Jamsran is here 
not a mundane deity converted to Buddhism but a manifestation of a buddha. There 
is also an extensive commentary on Zanabazar’s prayer, titled A Coral Necklace, the 
Ornament of Supreme Realization: A Commentary on the Offering of Requisites together 
with Offering Verses to the Ferocious Spirit Lcam sring, a Dharma Protector (Chos skyong 
dregs pa lcam sring gi chas dbul mchod phreng dang bcas pa’i ‘grel ba dam pa’i dgongs 
rgyan byi ‘ru’i do shal), which also begins with an homage to Amitābha. It was com­
posed by a monk named Nomgoni Dar Ekh Lam Agvaantsültemjamts, who was a great 
devotee of Zanabazar, and whom he extolls as “the essence of the Three Jewels, supreme 
refuge, and all pervading-​lord.”18

--- PAGE 524 ---
A Dharma Protector      499
 
Moreover, in his prayer to Jamsran, Zanabazar offers Jamsran a mighty sword 
(representing the blazing fire of gnosis); a bow standing for a sublime method and sim­
ilar to a vajra rock; an arrow of wisdom; a victory flag; an ocean of nectar of stainless 
gnosis; the offering substances, ornaments, and garments of pure ethical conduct; a 
coat of mail representing fearless patience; boots representing indefatigable effort; and 
a cushion of a corpse representing unwavering meditative concentration. To the the 
goddess “Great Consort” (Rig pa’i lha mo), he offers a blazing ritual dagger of meteoric 
iron, which cuts the enemies and destroys obstacles, and he offers her a fast-​running 
bear. To Red Sokdag, he offers a mad wolf that leaps swiftly like lightening, a copper-​
colored banner, and a red lasso that abolishes the hordes of māras. While weaponizing 
these three deities for the destruction of outer enemies, Zanabazar also sublimates their 
weapons in accordance with Jamsran’s ultimately sublime nature, one that can purify 
Zanabazar from his mental afflictions. Each verse of Zanabazar’s prayer is followed by 
a refrain that begins with “if you accept it” and ends with his command to this oath-​
bound protector to carry out all these tasks—​namely, to cut, pierce, and disperse those 
who scorn the Buddhist teachings and holders of the teachings, to vanquish Zanabazar’s 
own mental afflictions and obstacles, to expand Buddhist teachings in the ten directions, 
to increase the happiness of all beings, and to bestow good fortune to teachers like him­
self, disciples, and patrons—​so that they all may effect their own wellbeing and that of 
others. It is evident from the words of this prayer that Zanabazar was familiar not only 
with iconographical representations of Jamsran but also with the symbolic meaning 
of Jamsran’s implements. Like the authors of works contained in the Jamsran Beübüm, 
Zanabazar presents his offerings to Jamsran in a reciprocal or transactional manner. If 
Jamsran, as an oath-​bound protector, accepts the offering, he is, in turn, expected to 
follow the given injunctions in the same manner as nature spirits, nāgas, and the like. It 
is through both prayer and offerings that relationship with Jamsran is sustained.
Like Zanabazar, the Fourth Jebtsundampa (1775–​1813, Blo bzang thub bstan dbang 
phyug ‘jigs med rgya mtsho dpal bzang po) worshipped Jamsran and composed a eu­
logy to him, titled The Hero’s Roar: A Eulogy to the Dharma Protector, a King of Ferocity, 
with His Consort (Chos skyong dregs pa’i rgyal po stod ‘phrin chen po yum bcas kyi bstod 
phrin dpa’ bo’i nga ro). In this work, he calls upon Jamsran as “a powerful deity, akin to 
Amitābha, endowed with eight qualities of mastery” (dbang phyug brgyad ldan ‘od mtha’ 
yas ba’i lha dbang gi skyes bu lcam sring), to arise from the powerful, Fiercely Wrathful 
cremation ground (drag tu rgod pa).19
In various Mongolian prayers, we find statements that appeal to the previously 
mentioned two aspects of Jamsran’s nature and activity. For instance, in the following 
verses composed by Badamjalbuuzal, who calls himself “a yogī of Hayagrīva,” he 
describes Jamsran and his companions as blood thirsty warriors in this way:
I praise you, the one who seizes the lives of the adversaries and hindrances,
Who strikes a thunderbolt on the heads of those with deteriorated commitments,
And who grants the accomplishment of the supreme and ordinary siddhis
To those who merely recite your name! (v. 2)

--- PAGE 525 ---
500      Vesna A. Wallace
 
I praise you, military general and hero,
Who wages a war and flies a [victory] banner,
Who partakes of the lungs and hearts of the saboteurs in his mouth,
And wields a greatly blazing, copper knife against the adversaries. (v. 4)
I praise the ocean of beings who keep their oaths, who listen to the ordinance,
Who, liberating, support the actions of a yogī,
Who with delight ingest the blood and flesh of the adversary,
And manifest various, frightening, and magic manifestations! (v. 6)
You all, together with all your retinues,
Turn into dust the malevolent enemies of ours!
Please bring under my power
All the glory of the three worlds! (v. 7)20
On the other hand, Badamjalbuuzal also refers to Jamsran as an emanation of 
Hayagrīva’s mind, which accomplishes Hayagrīva’s decree, and as a tutelary deity (yi 
dam) of yogīs, who grants the accomplishment of the supreme and ordinary siddhis to 
those who merely mention his name. When summoning Jamsran, Badamjalbuuzal puts 
out this request:
Jee! Please come here from the upper realm, the primordially pure dharmadhātu,
Manifesting in a fierce appearance to accomplish the tasks!
Please partake of the bali offerings, tea, vodka, and the like, presented to a
Greatly ferocious demon from among the quarreling demons and devils. (v. 9)
This juxtaposition of Jamsran as both a deity abiding in the primordially pure 
dharmadhātu, who descends to the earth in order to carry out a requested task, and a 
greatly fierce spirit that dwells with quarreling demons and devils in the land of Maruce 
remains unexplained in this prayer. Badamjalbuuzal, like some other authors, seems to 
take for granted that Jamsran’s nature and activities should be understood from an ul­
timate point of view that breaks down dualities and negates all conceptions, a view in 
which there is no real difference between a yakṣa spirit and a highly realized bodhisattva.
This juxtaposition that we see with regard to Jamsran’s identity also appears in icon­
ographic images and textual references to Jamsran’s abode in the land of Maruce. He is 
depicted as dwelling in a quadrangular palace with four gates made of human skulls. The 
palace rests in the center of the terrifying land of Maruce, which is located northwest of 
Jambudvīpa. In this land, the sky is covered by red clouds of copper color, from which 
emerge the roaring sound of dragons, flashes of lightning, and showers of blood. In ad­
dition, the sounds of the strikes of raining iron spears and swords reverberate, blows 
that smash the skulls of the enemy. The copper mountains of Maruce are filled with the 
internal organs of oath-​breakers and are surrounded by the ocean of blood formed from 
the blood of enemies and animals. This is a place where dreadful and inauspicious birds, 
such as owls and the like, fly across the mountain valleys, and whose wings produce

--- PAGE 526 ---
A Dharma Protector      501
 
a frightening sound (see Bayasgalan 2011, 347–​349). Due to the fierce and red aspects 
of Jamsran’s body and Maruce, the best place for a meditation retreat on Jamsran is 
considered to be a land that has a red color or a mountain with red rocks.
This reference to the presence of owls in Jamsran’s Maruce land is also a reason for 
which the owl became associated with esoteric rituals related to Jamsran in Mongolia, 
and why thirteen owls are included in the ritual offerings to Jamsran. In some Jamsran-​
related rituals, the red torma and red, poisonous arrow sprinkled with blood are deco­
rated with feathers of an owl in order to increase the ferocity and efficacy of the ritual. In 
other secret rituals, the heart of an owl, referred to as a “liberating owl,” is placed into a 
black skeleton that is later destroyed at a burial ground while the antagonistic mantra is 
being recited (see Bayasgalan 2011, 377–​379).
Maruce is also home to red, blazing storms that can bring the entire world into tur­
moil. However, as previously noted, Jamsran’s abode is also the upper realm of a pri­
mordially pure dharmadhātu. This suggests that the dreadful land of Maruce—​just like 
Jamsran himself—​is understood as nothing more than a mere appearance, devoid of 
substantiality. From this perspective, there is no contradiction with regard to Jamsran’s 
dual identity or that of his dwelling place. Until Jamsran is invoked and summoned in 
prayers and rituals, he remains a mere potential for violence and anticipated possibility 
of victory over the enemy. But when he is ritually invoked, internalized through medita­
tion, and incited into an action, he is a powerful ally who can take on the form of a yakṣa 
spirit or be embodied in a human warrior.
In Mongolian works, Jamsran is most fierce of the yakṣas, whose anger causes thunder, 
rain, and hail; whose voice makes enemies’ hearts tremble; and who makes the entire 
earth shake when stamping the ground. As such, he pacifies the harmful demons, eight 
nāga kings, and oath-​breaking enemies. In an anonymous Mongolian prayer to Jamsran, 
titled The Offering to Red Protector (Ulaɣan sakiɣus-un takil-ɣa), Jamsran is summoned 
in his yakṣa form and told to come quickly in accord with the command of Victorious 
Vajradhara.21 It appears that Jamsran never acts on his own initiative but performs 
the tasks of an oath-​bound Dharma Protector through persuasion, summoning, and 
offerings, or when impelled by the mind of other Dharma protectors and Buddhas. 
Hence, Jamsran can be summoned and brought forth in meditation or in prayer in dif­
ferent ways. In the Jamsran Beübüm, there appear two common methods of summoning 
Jamsran; one is by summoning him directly from the land of Maruce, whereas the other 
involves bringing him forth from the heart of Hayagrīva into one’s own heart in med­
itation. Likewise, in correspondence with the red, blazing color of Jamsran’s body and 
his land of Maruce (which indicate his power of subjugation), a meditation on Jamsran 
is said to have the best results if practiced in the red region or in a place where there are 
red stones on a mountainside. But it can also be practiced in a crematorium or burial 
ground; at the confluence of rivers; or in a temple, a monastery, or a palace.
In addition to performing the activities of expelling demons, nāgas, land spirits 
(Mong. savdag, Tib. sa bdag), and enemies of Dharma, Jamsran is also deemed capable 
of performing other types of activities that support tantric yogīs, such as tantric rites for 
pacification and prosperity or long-​life rituals. The latter is accomplished by Jamsran

--- PAGE 527 ---
502      Vesna A. Wallace
 
warding off 404 diseases and inauspicious signs of untimely death, granting the attain­
ment of siddhis, and so on. According to a short, Mongolian text titled The Abbreviated 
Torma Offering to Jamsran (Jamsrang-​un baling ergükü tobči quriyaɣsan), composed 
by Mergen Gegeen Luvsandambijaltsan (Tib. Blo bzang bstan pa’i rgyal msthan, 1717–​
1786), after one summons Jamsran, displays on the altar an image of him, and makes 
the inner torma offering consisting of the red drink containing blood and flesh, one 
asks Jamsran to consume the offerings and to accomplish the given tasks in return. The 
prayer reads:
I pay homage to you, fierce yakṣa, who has the fierce, wrathful body, a command that is 
the sound of a fierce mantra, and a fierce mind free from conceptualizations.
I worship you and pray to you, O Protector. Be a safeguarding friend, protect me, 
and avert the demons of obstacle!
Thoroughly accomplish the tasks, especially the mentioned [tasks]! Purify the 
adverse circumstances and grant me the appropriate siddhi!
Glorious, precious guru, tutelary deity, ḍakiṇī, Dharma protectors, and great yakṣa, 
due to your kindness, may the Holy lama live longer, may the Dharma of the three 
Vehicles spread, and may my life and virtue increase!
May there be abundant blessings!22
In his poem called He (Tere min-​u), the famous Mongolian yogī of the nineteenth 
century by name Danzanravja (Bstan ‘dzin rab rgyas, 1803–​1856, the fifth incarnation in 
the line of Noyon Khutugtus of Gobi), who became an orphan in his early age, praises 
Jamsran as a deity that supports orphans, treats them with compassion, and can pre­
vent theft. The versatility of Jamsran’s activities reflects the condensation of the authors’ 
needs into a single deity. Part a yakṣa spirit and part divine, Jamsran embodies this mul­
tifaceted nature, while ultimately not being established anywhere.
Conclusion
In conclusion, Jamsran is a tantric deity with diverse origins. He represents emanations 
of different fierce deities worshipped in different Tibetan and Mongolian tantric 
traditions. These can be grouped into two main categories: a converted yakṣa deity 
and the fierce emanation of Amitābha. A precise answer to the question as to how 
and when this dual nature came about is difficult to determine. The question of doc­
trinal support for Jamsran’s simultaneous mundane and enlightened identities and 
activities is answered implicitly in texts that suggest that both of Jamsran’s identities 
can coexist because they lack a reified ontological basis. It seems that this lack of in­
herent nature allows for Jamsran to be culturally and religiously adaptable to different 
pragmatic roles—​social and religious—​assigned to him in different circumstances by 
Tibetan and Mongolian Buddhist tantric adepts. Jamsran’s dual identity seems to be

--- PAGE 528 ---
A Dharma Protector      503
 
programmatically re-​created in order to accomplish two types of activities—​one that is 
suitable only for a fierce, mundane deity that can intervene and rearrange social events 
and circumstances with any means necessary and the other that is compassionate and 
supportive of those in need.
As revealed by various ritual texts dedicated to Jamsran, in accordance with the dual 
aspects of his identity and the two, corresponding types of his activities, the frightening 
aspect of Jamsran’s image is at times interpreted semiotically, as a representation of one’s 
own, inner exorcism, in which, the enemy’s heart held in Jamsran’s hand is interpreted as 
one’s own ego-​grasping and mental afflictions. As we saw, at other times, Jamsran’s harsh 
activities are taken literally, especially in the ritual context of exorcism. His cruel deeds 
are justified in two ways. One is that he harms sentient beings in order to help sentient 
beings, for which reason he is called the “lord of life,” and the second is that his harsh 
deeds are justified by the idea that those sentient beings upon whom he inflicts harm or 
even death become purified from their negative karma and, as a result, obtain a favor­
able rebirth.
