Chapter 23
The Goddesses of 
Jaina Tantra
Michael Slouber
Jainism is typically regarded as an ascetic religion, centered on a series of twenty-​four 
austere spiritual warriors of the past (jina, tīrthaṃkara) and those renouncers who 
follow in their footsteps. As is well known, nonviolence (ahiṃsā) is the central principle 
of the religion and one that renouncers uphold with remarkable dedication.
As for the religious paradigm we call tantra, it has been understood to refer to a wide 
variety of religious expressions, from pragmatic magical rites aimed at controlling and 
sometimes harming other people, to transgressive rituals involving sexuality and con­
sumption of impure substances, and to lofty philosophical insights into the nature of self 
and reality.
Last, regarding goddesses, India is unique in the world for preserving contin­
uous traditions of the feminine divine from prehistory down to the present. While 
conceptions of Indian goddesses are diverse and have varied a great deal over time, two 
popular motifs for the past two millennia pose goddesses as either fearsome, weapon-​
wielding warriors whom one might fear as much as admire or as beautiful, full-​bodied 
maidens or mothers who allure and nourish as representations of fertility and abun­
dance. Both types of goddess, and tantra in general, seem, on the face of it, to be “strange 
bedfellows” with Jainism. In fact, their union is ancient and natural, to the extent that we 
can bring nuance to preconceived notions of each topic, and examine more deeply the 
meaning of their convergence.
The Blurry Boundaries of Jainism
A central debate among scholars of Jaina traditions is the nature of the relationship be­
tween the ideal of Jaina renouncers and the lay community that supports them. Lay

--- PAGE 533 ---
508      Michael Slouber
 
Jainas take on few of the restrictions observed by renouncers and go about life in similar 
ways to their non-​Jaina neighbors. So what makes a layperson Jaina? Given that the lit­
eral meaning of Jaina is one who affiliates with Jinas, a starting point is to say that a Jaina 
is someone who venerates the Jinas and Jaina renouncers. Or, one can identify a Jaina 
by observance of vegetarianism, required of all laypeople in the community. But many 
non-​Jainas also venerate renouncers and observe a vegetarian diet. Internally, a Jaina is 
someone with a correct understanding (saṃyagdṛṣṭi) of the nature of existence and the 
detrimental role of violence in perpetuating our entrapment in the cycle of suffering. 
However, as nonrenouncers, lay Jainas may often value different things. They may be 
more concerned with health, wealth, and family and less with ultimate freedom from 
the bonds of karma. But does that mean laypeople are “less Jaina” than renouncers? 
Should scholars of Jainism focus less on what Jainas (lay or renouncer) do and more 
on the ideals espoused by the religion’s intellectual leaders? Scholarship on Jainism has 
tended to give much more attention to said ideals, whereas the past several decades 
have involved a broadening of this gaze to attend to beliefs and practices that were long 
obscured in normative accounts.
A related question is how one should understand the interrelationships between 
Jainism and other Indian religions (especially Hinduism). Some scholars focus on 
specific Jaina sources that are demonstrably based on Hindu exemplars. At its best, 
this approach can illuminate the context and methods of specific instances of bor­
rowing. Alexis Sanderson’s research into the Śaiva source of the important Jaina tantric 
ritual text Nirvāṇakalikā, attributed to Pādaliptasūri, demonstrated that the majority 
of it is copied, with minimal changes, from the twelfth-​century Śaiva ritual manual 
Siddhāntasārapaddhati, ascribed to Bhojadeva (Sanderson 2015). Knowing this is essen­
tial for anyone who seeks to understand the Nirvāṇakalikā in its historical context.
Focusing on Jaina incorporation of other religious traditions has, however, also been 
criticized in recent scholarship. Jonathan Geen, in his article “Jainism and Hinduism” 
in Brill’s Encyclopedia of Jainism, points to the 2,500 years of a common religious culture 
shared by most inhabitants in the region and how “crisp and consistent definitions of 
Jainism and Hinduism are problematic and elusive” (Geen 2020, 305). Likewise, Ellen 
Gough has cautioned that such a focus on Śaiva influence might lead to inattention to 
the ways particular groups modified the material to make it specific to their sect (Gough 
2012). Building on that point, consider the case of Sarasvatī (alias Śrutadevatā) in Jaina 
traditions. While most scholars think of Sarasvatī as “Hindu,” John Cort pointed out that 
her oldest known statue is Jaina (Cort 2020, 160). It would be erroneous to dismiss an in­
stance of a particular goddess as merely a Hindu or Buddhist borrowing, as Jae-​Eun Shin 
did concerning several Jaina mahāvidyā goddesses in her recent study of this goddess 
type in eastern Indian Śākta traditions (Shin 2018, 130–​133). Robert Zydenbos pointedly 
critiqued this sort of facile equivalence, saying: “All such explanations suffer from the 
same shortcomings on the part of their authors: insufficient familiarity with the mate­
rial, a disregard of the theological context and a desire to take intellectual shortcuts with 
regard to what is actually a highly intricate and subtle subject” (Zydenbos 1994, 136–​137).

--- PAGE 534 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      509
 
Rather than think of Jainism, Hinduism, and Buddhism as neat and tidy boxes into 
which we can drop particular deities, the evidence demands a more nuanced approach.
What Makes a Goddess Jaina?
Clearly defining the boundaries between divine identities is challenging. Given the 
thousands of years that Lakṣmī, for example, has been simultaneously a Buddhist, 
Jaina, and Hindu goddess, one needs to ask: Are we dealing with one goddess who takes 
multiple forms, or three (or more) goddesses who happen to share a name and sev­
eral attributes? The fact that Jainism has generally existed as a minority religion does 
not mean that Jainas always passively absorbed elements of the supposedly dominant 
Hindu religious cultures. Many Jaina goddesses seem to have been assimilated from 
pan-​Indian categories that pre-​date classical Hinduism, such as yakṣiṇī (nature spirit) 
and vidyā (spell goddess). Therefore, calling them Hindu is not only oversimplifying the 
matter, but also anachronistic.
Serious scholars would do well to tread cautiously through this complex terrain. The 
starting point should be that any goddess whom Jainas worship is, in some respect, a 
Jaina goddess. From this baseline, one can categorize the depth and nature of a given 
goddess’s Jaina identity based on her history and unique characteristics and the extent 
to which her devotees’ practices are tailored to the Jaina context. Granted, such an ap­
proach is not accepted by all scholars. Nalini Balbir described family or clan deities 
(kuladevatā) as well as the local goddesses known as mātās as not part of the Jaina pan­
theon, despite the fact that they are “elements in the lives of many Jains” (Balbir 2009). 
Her rationale is that “they are not given places in the Jain universe,” but I would point 
out that the theoretical structures that supposedly exclude these classes of deities were 
created by intellectuals before the categories in question (kuladevatā and mātā) even 
became current. Cort drew on a traditional tripartite hierarchy of goddesses—​which 
is probably what Balbir had in mind—​to structure his 1987 article on Jaina goddesses: 
Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī as existing in an “upper realm,” the vidyādevīs (spell goddesses) 
in a “middle realm,” and the śāsanadevatā (“deities [who protect] the teachings,” usu­
ally referring to yakṣiṇī/​yakṣī) as existing in a “lower realm” of the Jaina universe (Cort 
1987, which influenced Sanderson 2009, 243). However, scrutinizing the history of 
Jaina goddesses makes clear that vidyādevī and śāsanadevatā are categories with many 
shared members and much overlap. In a recent article, Cort presented a more grounded 
framing of the categories, explaining how “the categorization of nonliberated deities . . . 
is of very limited use in understanding the many roles of these deities in the daily life and 
annual ritual cultures of most Jains. When worshiping a nonliberated deity, only a small 
minority of Jains would be able to identify that deity according to the cosmographical 
schema” (Cort 2020, 143). So again, the boundaries one needs to navigate when thinking 
about this subject are significantly more blurry than one might initially expect.

--- PAGE 535 ---
510      Michael Slouber
 
How Jaina Are Goddesses?
Goddesses with strong connections to nature, fecundity, and motherhood appear to be 
a legacy of prehistory, as archeological records from the Indus Valley Civilization and 
elsewhere prolifically attest (e.g., Bose 2018, 2–​3; Tiwari 1989, 16). The earliest and most 
prominent Jaina example is the case of Ambikā, a yakṣiṇī nature goddess whose name 
literally means “mother” (not “little mother” as scholars have frequently mistranslated 
it).1 Ambikā is regularly depicted with children and sometimes shown with an expan­
sive midsection indicating pregnancy (Figure 23.1). Maruti Nandan Prasad Tiwari 
pointed out that the earliest sources referred to her as Bahuputrā or Bahuputrikā, 
names meaning “lady with many children.” She appears in Jaina statuary from Gwalior, 
Madhya Pradesh, from as early as the first century before the Common Era and was the 
most popular divine female in early Jaina literature (Tiwari 1989, 11–​19). Ambikā has 
continued to be popular to the present, particularly in northern India. In the south, she 
is known as Kuṣmāṇḍiṇī, and since the medieval period her role in Jaina ritual culture 
has increasingly had to be shared with other goddesses, such as Padmāvatī, Jvālāmālinī, 
and Cakreśvarī.
Fecund nature goddesses like Ambikā are part of a class of such non-​Vedic spirits 
(yakṣa-​yakṣiṇī) whose shrines were favored sites for Pārśva, Mahāvīra, and Gautama 
Buddha to frequent, stay at, and teach at. As Cort put it, these enlightened figures 
considered the worship of yakṣas to be a normal part of everyday religious practice (1987, 
241). While some modern scholars and community leaders seem to struggle with how 
to reconcile these goddesses as Jaina (or Buddhist as the case may be), by all accounts 
the ancient founders of these renunciation-​focused religions were content to assimi­
late them through narratives of conversion and protection and as symbols of the auspi­
ciousness of the enlightened beings they came to be associated with. If the renouncers’ 
emphasis on celibacy and cutting ties with family appears to be in contradiction to the 
prolific sexuality and maternity of Jaina goddesses, we can understand it as a testament 
to the practicality of the founding Jinas: They gave up sex and family themselves, but 
were levelheaded enough to realize that the majority would not. In that context, it makes 
more sense to orient such powerful forces toward supporting their transcendent goals 
and not to wage a battle that is doomed to fail by attempting to suppress them.
In terms of the incorporation of goddesses into Jaina cosmology and practice, it 
seems to have been a very gradual process that started in the early centuries before the 
Common Era. As noted, the first surviving Jaina statue of Bahuputrikā dates to the first 
century before the Common Era. The first reference to the Jaina yakṣī cult in south India 
is found in the Tamil classic Cilappatikāram, which mentions a yakṣī shrine associated 
with Jaina ascetics on the outskirts of Madurai (Desai 1957, 88; Parthasarathy 1993, 155).
Another very early set of references involves the category of goddesses known as 
vidyā, vidyādevī, or mahāvidyā, which, as mentioned above, include many goddesses 
who are also referred to as yakṣiṇīs. One of the oldest—​perhaps even older than the

--- PAGE 536 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      511
 
Cilappatikāram, but likely composed in northern India—​is the Vasudevahiṇḍī, a Jaina 
adaptation of Guṇāḍhya’s lost Bṛhatkathā epic. Most of the Jaina studies scholars whose 
works I reviewed date the Vasudevahiṇḍī to ca. 500 or 600 CE; however, a thorough 
evaluation of archaisms and other linguistic features by Ludwig Alsdorf (1936) pointed 
to it belonging to an era several centuries earlier. Following Alsdorf, Shaman Hatley and 
Andrew Ollett cited it as belonging to the early centuries of the Common Era (Hatley 
2007, 95; Ollett 2017, 70). The Vasudevahiṇḍī is significant because it not only refers to 
Jainas performing daily worship of Vidyādevīs (Jhavery 1944, 175), but also describes 
prototantric practices that are remarkably consistent with later tantric rituals. Hatley 
Figure 23.1.  Ambikā, sixth–​seventh century, Bihar, Shahabad District. Currently housed at 
the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
Image is in the public domain.

--- PAGE 537 ---
512      Michael Slouber
 
described how worship of spell goddesses (vidyā) in the Vasudevahiṇḍī narratives 
requires initiation, making offerings, and reciting the spell a large number of times to 
perfect it. The terminology for these practices is also identical to terms later used for the 
same rituals in classical tantra (Hatley 2007, 97–​98).
Many scholars assert that vidyās were originally thought of as impersonal spells, 
and over time they increasingly became understood as goddesses themselves (Cort 
1987, 239). This may be true, although vidyās are already referred to as goddesses one 
propitiates in the Vasudevahiṇḍī, which is as old as later sections of the Śvetāmbara 
canon, which was first written down in the fifth century of the Common Era. The 
earliest surviving canonical work from the Digambaras is also of similar antiquity to the 
Vasudevahiṇḍī (Balbir 2020, 759). Not surviving are the earliest body of fourteen exten­
sive scriptures of the Jainas, called the Pūrvas. According to lists of their contents, the 
entire tenth Pūrva was dedicated to the subject of vidyās (Balbir 2020). So the evidence 
is mixed on this question of how the vidyā goddesses were popularly understood be­
fore the early centuries of the Common Era. What we can assert with confidence is that 
both the yakṣiṇīs and the vidyādevīs became increasingly central to Jaina cosmology 
over the course of the first millennium. Several stories involving named vidyās in the 
context of Jainism are found in Vimalasūri’s Paümacariẏa, a Jaina retelling of the epic 
Rāmāyaṇa, dating to 473 CE (Cort 1987, 239; Dhaky 1997, 46). It is not until the age of 
early tantra in the seventh and eighth centuries that the set of sixteen mahāvidyās are 
named in Jaina sources, and the yakṣa-​yakṣī pairs come to be referred to as protectors 
of the Jaina teachings (śāsanadevatā) (Shah 1947a, 116–​119; Tiwari 1989, 11). By the tenth 
century, pairings of the yakṣas and yakṣīs with particular Jinas had become popular in 
the artistic record, and around the same time evidence of independent cults of the most 
popular goddesses like Cakreśvarī, Ambikā, Padmāvatī, and Jvālāmālinī began to sur­
face (Tiwari 1989, 11).
The Blurry Boundaries of Tantra: 
What Makes a Goddess Tantric 
in Jainism?
We now come to the third element of the nexus of Jaina tantric goddesses: tantra. At the 
outset, it is important to understand that the use of the word “tantra” in the sense of a 
discrete religious formation is a modern academic construct. It is a helpful neologism, 
but should be used self-​consciously and in a well-​defined manner. Sanskrit sources from 
this religious formation most commonly use the word tantra to refer specifically to tan­
tric scriptures, and never—​in the early medieval period at least—​to refer to the system 
as a whole. Sources like Abhinavagupta’s famous Tantrāloka should be translated as 
“Light on the Tantras,” not “Light on Tantra” as scholars continue to mistakenly render 
it.2 Moreover, these scriptures are not only called tantras, but also just as often other

--- PAGE 538 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      513
 
names like āgama, saṃhitā, mata, sāra, kalpa, and so on. The modern use of the adjec­
tive “tantric,” by contrast, is less distant from original usage since it is comparable to the 
most common meaning of tāntrika in tantric era Sanskrit.
When scholars of Jainism define goddesses and texts as tantric, they do so with a va­
riety of meanings in mind. Some regard any magical rites or supernatural powers as 
“Tantric,” including Umakant Premanand Shah and Jae-​Eun Shin (Shah 1947b, 840; 
Shin 2018, 130–​132). Similarly, Cort glosses Jaina mantra science (mantraśāstra) as “the 
main Jain variant of Tantra” (2020, 143). While magic, mantras, and powers are a prom­
inent component of many Jaina and non-​Jaina tantric texts, they certainly pre-​date the 
era in which the word tantra was associated with such things, so it is preferable to avoid 
the anachronism; in pretantric sources the most commonly used sense of tantra was as 
a generic word for “book” or “treatise,” as it is used, for example, in the titles of partic­
ular early Āyurvedic volumes. This generic meaning is essentially what the word con­
tinued to mean well into the tantric era. It was only with the astounding proliferation of 
thousands of such works that the word started to carry the more specific connotation of 
what we now mean by a “tantric” treatise, and later to refer to the whole gambit of topics 
taught in such treatises.
Since the 1980s scholarship of Alexis Sanderson, tantric studies scholars have gener­
ally understood tantra as the type of Śaiva esoteric literature (and associated religious 
patterns) called the Mantramārga in the earliest Sanskrit sources that are representative 
of this tradition and also to refer to its aftermath. The development of the Mantramārga 
is a circa fifth-​century landmark that involved the expansion of liberation-​granting 
Śaiva initiation to include laypeople. The earliest surviving Mantramārga/​tantric text 
is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, which was the first to introduce the core religious patterns 
that grew into a huge array of early tantric literature over subsequent centuries. In my 
use of the term, tantra refers to any such literature affiliated with Mantramārga Śaivism, 
or any traditions that grow out of it, are inspired by it, or are copied from it. This includes 
a huge array of primary sources from Śaiva, Śākta, Saura, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, and Jaina 
traditions. Even though these types of sources cross religious boundaries, they are tied 
together by various shared ritual systems, specific varieties of mantra and vidyā, unique 
deity iconographies, worldviews, and technical vocabulary—​most of which cannot be 
found before the advent of Mantramārga Śaiva traditions. To be clear, pre-​Mantramārga 
Jaina traditions do have magic, ritual, and mantras/​vidyās; however, the character of this 
early Jaina tradition shifted to adapt to the new Mantramārga norms that were rapidly 
colonizing Indian religions in the latter half of the first millennium.
Already in 1944, Mohanlal Bhagwandas Jhavery defined tantra as a rather broad cat­
egory, over the course of several pages, in a manner that is in harmony with my own 
use of the term. To paraphrase, he said that it includes all manner of common beliefs 
and doctrines, myths about the origin of the world, natural laws, medicine, yoga, 
mantra, and more in texts called by various names and belonging to various schools 
and religions. Tantras (by whatever name and belonging to whatever religion) in­
clude common practices such as mantras, seed syllables, magical diagrams (yantra/​
cakra/​mandala), visualization of mantra deities in the body (nyāsa), rites to purify the

--- PAGE 539 ---
514      Michael Slouber
 
elements (bhūtaśuddhi), construction and consecration of temples and divine images, 
and practical magic (Jhavery 1944, 49–​51). I consider these broad characterizations of 
tantra as a whole to be useful and roughly accurate. However, I think it is more compel­
ling to link all of the aspects to the origin and spread of Mantramārga Śaivism, rather 
than pose it as a complex of shared features without reference to historical context.
In recent publications, Ellen Gough sought to deconstruct scholarly use of the termi­
nology “tantra” and “tantric”: “Jains have no category of scripture called tantra. There is 
no text within Jainism that can be identified as wholly ‘tantric,’ and there is no consistent 
definition of ‘Tantra’ in Jainism, or in any religion” (Gough 2020, 567). As explained 
above, the term tantra as referring to a religious movement is a scholarly construction, 
so in this sense Gough was correct on the first point, that Jainas have no such category. 
But, neither did any other religious group in premodern India. Again, the word tantra 
was originally used most often in the sense of a treatise and was interchangeable with 
the wide variety of other words for tantric scriptures, including kalpa, which is preferred 
in the titles of many Jaina texts of tantric character. As an artificial language in contin­
uous use for thousands of years, Sanskrit words very often have multiple meanings. V. S. 
Apte, in his The Practical Sanskrit-​English Dictionary, counted no less than thirty-​four 
separate meanings of “tantra,” which is not at all unusual in the Sanskrit lexicon (Apte 
1957, 759). Therefore, it makes little sense to insist that no religion has a consistent def­
inition. The meaning of a word has to be deduced from its context. Gough’s claim that 
there is no text within Jainism that can be called wholly tantric is confusing since she 
goes on to reference D. T. Shah’s estimate of five hundred such Jaina works (Gough 2020, 
568). Some of the early sources of this type that I reference in more detail below—​the 
Jvālāmālinīkalpa, Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, and Vidyānuśāsana—​are all wholly tantric, 
following Gough’s own definitions, as well as my own given above (material that is either 
based on or inspired by Mantramārga Śaivism in some identifiable way).
Art historians studying Jaina goddesses have used various criteria to classify a figure 
as tantric. As mentioned already, the prolific scholar U. P. Shah seemed to loosely un­
derstand (or rather misunderstand) anything having to do with magic as tantric (Shah 
1947b, 840). Another quality often associated with tantra is eroticism; Tiwari called 
erotic carvings at Jaina sites a gross violation of Jaina tradition and cited tantric influence 
as the cause (Tiwari 1989, 6). Eroticism in Indian religious statuary certainly predates 
the tantras, so attributing it to tantric influence is an oversimplification. Eroticism does 
have a notable place in some tantric sects, but it is in no way definitive or a signature 
of tantric influence. For example, the dozens of tantric medical texts I worked with for 
Early Tantric Medicine (2017) have no erotic content, with only a few exceptions.
Tiwari also links the feature of his subject (Ambikā) having more than two arms as 
indicating a tantric form (Tiwari 1989, 26). It is an intriguing theory that deities with 
multiple arms are a tantric innovation. Of course, there is precedence for divinity having 
multiple arms (and other appendages) in the famous Puruṣasūkta of the Ṛgveda and in 
Kṛṣṇa’s divine form revealed to Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gītā. However, these pretantric 
textual references do not seem to have significantly influenced the art historical record. 
It is only after the advent of Mantramārga Śaivism that we begin to see depictions of

--- PAGE 540 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      515
 
deities with multiple arms proliferate. Therefore, in this case Tiwari’s idea appears to be 
well founded.
What makes a goddess tantric in Jainism will depend on how one understands 
tantra. Certainly we would be misled to follow Shah and others in characterizing any 
goddess associated with ritual and magic as tantric and portraying the Veda and early 
Buddhism and Jainism as part of the tantric tradition because they include ritual and 
magic. Likewise, eroticism is no reliable marker of tantric influence. Instead, we must 
turn to the primary sources of Mantramārga Śaivism and traditions that grew out of it 
to determine whether particular features of iconography, ritual, mantra, and lore owe 
to its influence or not. The following two case studies focus on early sources from the 
Digambara tradition. The Śvetāmbara community has its own traditions of tantric and 
nontantric goddesses that have been less well studied.
Case Study 1:  Jvālāmālinī in the 
Jvālāmālinīkalpa
Perhaps the oldest Jaina text that is thoroughly tantric is the Jvālāmālinīkalpa (The 
Ritual Manual of Jvālāmālinī), a work in Sanskrit compiled in the Digambara com­
munity of southern India. Its date depends on the date of the original author, a figure 
named Helācārya or Elācārya, who may belong to the ninth century or possibly earlier; 
Shadakshari Settar believed Helācārya must pre-​date the Aihole image of Jvālāmālinī, 
which he dated to the eighth century. Therefore, he said Helācārya probably lived earlier 
than the seventh century (Settar 1969, 320). The received form of the Jvālāmālinīkalpa 
tells us that the work was originally taught by Helācārya and was handed down through 
a lineage of disciples,3 becoming corrupt (kliṣṭaṃ granthaṃ) in the process, and then 
fully restored and rendered in āryā meter by the monk Indranandin in Karnataka in ca. 
939 CE (1.22–​1.27). Notably, the published edition by Chandra Shekhar Shastri (1964) is 
itself full of corruptions, most likely because it was based on a single faulty manuscript; a 
new edition based on as many manuscripts as possible would be an important contribu­
tion to the study of early tantra.4
Helācārya is referred to as the leader of the Drāviḍa Sangha, an obscure and now ex­
tinct sect of Digambara monks purportedly founded by a monk named Vajranandin in 
Madurai in the fifth century (Dundas 1992, 105). The little that we know of this group, 
aside from what can be deduced from the Jvālāmālinīkalpa itself, comes from a ninth-​
century critique by Devasena, in which they are reviled for their supposed sedentary 
lifestyle and lax dietary practices (Dundas 1992, 105). One should not, however, too 
quickly accept allegations from a rival sect as fact.
Jvālāmālinī was evidently a local non-​Jaina goddess located on the Nīlagiri hill 
mentioned in the text (Dundas 1992, 1.10). Settar tentatively identified Helācārya’s 
village, called Malayahemagrāma, as the village now called Ponnur (1969, 310) in the

--- PAGE 541 ---
516      Michael Slouber
 
Tiruvannamalai district of Tamil Nadu. An inscription dated 1733 CE at the Ādinātha 
temple there specifies that its Jvālāmālinī image is to be taken in procession to the nearby 
Nīlagiri hill every Sunday when Helācārya is worshiped (Desai 1957, 47; Settar 1969, 
310). This hill may have been named after the famous Nilgiri Mountains in the Western 
Ghats. Aaron Ullrey discussed Nandi’s alternate identification of Malayahemagrāma as 
a village in southern Karnataka, to the south of Mysuru (Ullrey 2016, 373–​374).
That Jvālāmālinī was originally non-​Jaina can be deduced from two aspects of the 
text. First, the narrative at the beginning describes how Helācārya sought out the 
goddess’s temple in desperation; his learned female disciple Kamalaśrī was suffering 
from a dreadful case of possession by a malevolent spirit, and he did not know how to 
help her (Jvālāmālinīkalpa 1.9cd: “vyākulito ‘bhūt tatpravidhānakartavyatāmūḍhaḥ”). 
If the goddess was Jaina and known for healing possession, it does not make sense that 
Helācārya would have been confused about what to do. By contrast, if we assume that 
she was a non-​Jaina goddess, the narrative justifies Helācārya’s action by underscoring 
his desperation and compassion for his disciple.
The second aspect of the text that points to a non-​Jaina original context is that the vast 
majority of the mantras and ritual actions associated with the goddess in this source 
are plainly Śaiva and Śākta, with many specifically drawn from the Bhūta tantras and 
Kaula scriptures. Mantras to Khaḍgarāvaṇa—​a form of Śiva invoked in the Bhūta 
tantras to control or drive out evil spirits (Slouber 2007, 2017)—​are important parts of 
several chapters. The so-​called five arrow mantras (pañcabāṇa) of Kāmeśvarī from the 
Kaula Nityā sect abound in ­chapters 3 and 6, sometimes combined with Khaḍgarāvaṇa’s 
mantras. Moreover, a series of stanzas in the third chapter openly promote incorpora­
tion of Śaiva rituals and mantras, suggesting that one should simply replace the non-​
Jaina deity’s name in the mantras with that of the twenty-​third tīrthaṃkara Pārśvanātha:
Whatever the wise one thinks, let him make that authoritative in his realm. If a 
rite is not taught here [in Jaina sources], but is taught in full in the [Śaiva] Gāruḍa 
Śāstra, the mantra-​reciter who finds a difference should [know that] whatever 
words one says become a mantra. Whoever might be the object of worship, the 
mantra-​reciter should say it is to Pārśvajina himself. Observing the speech of an 
adept, whatever words he says are the mantra. Cutting, burning, dispatching, split­
ting, beating, binding, etc.—​if you say it is for Pārśvanātha, whatever words you 
say become a mantra.5
Aside from the centrality of exorcism in the Jvālāmālinīkalpa, and the corresponding 
popularity of the goddess and this text, we can also observe, following Panduranga 
Bhimrao Desai, that many inscriptions from medieval southern India refer to a teacher’s 
expertise in mantra and/​or exorcism. For example, Desai cited an inscription at 
Shravana Belagola about a teacher named Kalyāṇakīrti who was credited as “unrivaled 
in the art of exorcising the evil spirits like Śākinī” (Desai 1957, 74).
Cort proposed that evidence of her non-​Jaina origin can be deduced from the nar­
rative at the beginning calling her Vahnidevī (fire goddess), a name he suggested

--- PAGE 542 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      517
 
represents her non-​Jaina identity, whereas elsewhere in the text this name is not re­
peated and Jvālāmālinī (flame garlanded) is preferred (1987, 247). In fact, she is called 
synonyms of Vahnidevī, such as Śikhidevī and Śikhimaddevī, throughout the text. The 
use of closely related names with the same or similar meaning was most likely done to 
conform to the requirements of the meter and perhaps also for variety.
The Jvālāmālinīkalpa makes little reference to what later became the standard 
categories the goddess is said to belong to: śāsanadevatā/​yakṣa or vidyādevī. The terms 
Yakṣa/​yakṣī are mainly mentioned among a series of beings who possess people and in 
so doing become the targets of Jvālāmālinī’s spells. In only one place is she referred to as 
aṣṭamayakṣeśvarī, which probably means “eighth Yakṣa Queen” as the Hindi commen­
tary renders it and alludes to her association with the eighth Tīrthaṅkara Candraprabha 
that became standard in later sources. The Jvālāmālinīkalpa does not describe her as a 
vidyā, mahāvidyā, or vidyādevī; it uses the word vidyā to refer generically to any of the 
scores of spells (mantra/​vidyā) taught in her manual. The word typically used to refer to 
her is simply devī (goddess).
Jvālāmālinī’s appearance is described briefly (3.18–​3.21): One should visualize her in 
the middle of a lotus, surrounded by the eight Brahminical mothers (mātṛ); she bears 
the Jina Candraprabha with devotion on her head, resting on her diadem; she has a light, 
lotus-​like hue to her body, rides astride a water buffalo mount, wears shining ornaments, 
has three eyes, and is fearsome with her flame-​haloed body. She displays eight things 
in her eight hands: a lasso, trident, bow, arrow, salt,6 metal discus, fruit, and the boon-​
granting gesture.
The oldest art historical evidence for Jvālāmālinī is the statue in the vestibule of the 
Gaurī temple at Aihole (Figure 23.2). Settar spent much of his article analyzing every 
feature of this statue and its context. The seated Jina depicted on her crown makes her 
unambiguously Jaina, and most of the attributes she holds in her eight hands tally with 
those described in the Jvālāmālinīkalpa. The presence of flames arising from either 
side of the crown, as well as her buffalo mount, sealed the identification of the image 
as Jvālāmālinī for Settar (1969, 314), as well as for the present author. Settar praised the 
craftsmanship as among the finest examples of early Chalukya work and pointed out 
that the image was likely moved from its original temple, as the Gaurī temple where 
it is currently placed is of later construction. He also argued that this Jvālāmālinī and 
the male yakṣa figure in the nearby Jaina temple were originally housed together and 
“cannot be later than the eighth century [CE]” (Settar 1969, 320). A tourist booklet 
on Aihole published by the Department of Archaeology Museums and Heritage 
in Mysore mentions the Jvālāmālinī yakṣī as dating to the eleventh century along 
with the Gaurī temple itself (Betsurmath 2015, 51) but did not take into account her 
separated pairing with the Jaina yakṣa image or the possibility that she was moved 
as the result of a misidentification of her as a Hindu goddess (which persists to the 
present among locals who regard the image as representing Gaurī). If we accept that 
Helācārya was the first to bring Jvālāmālinī into the Jaina sphere of worship, he should 
pre-​date the Aihole statue.

--- PAGE 543 ---
518      Michael Slouber
 
Other, later, texts and oral lore about Jvālāmālinī exist, and some include 
narratives about her. Shadakshari Settar points out that Puranic literature in 
Kannada, such as the Candraprabha Purāṇa, includes vivid portrayals of Jvālāmālinī 
(Settar 1969, 317). Zydenbos also summarized several popular stories about her in his 
1994 article, including two narratives about her previous life as a Jaina woman. Ellen 
Gough briefly pointed out how Śvetāmbaras also adopted her worship, pointing 
to the undated Jvālāmālinīstotra from the Śvetāmbara community as an example 
(Gough 2020, 573).

The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      519
 
Case Study 2:  Padmāvatī in the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa
Padmāvatī, known as the queen of snakes, is the most popular Jaina goddess today and 
seems to have held this position for most of the past 1,000 years (Figure 23.3). Cort captured 
her importance when he said that one can easily identify a Padmāvatī shrine by the rush 
of worshipers and the abundance of coconut offerings in front of it (2010, 2020, 149–​150). 
Her popularity even eclipses that of the Jinas at many Jaina sites, such as in the Digambara 
Lāl Mandir temple complex in Delhi, where crowds throng to have darśana (an auspicious 
sight) of her icon (Sethi 2020, 459). As Manisha Sethi explained, goddesses like Padmāvatī 
intervene in worldly affairs, which is something the Jinas cannot or do not do (2020).
The precise beginning of Padmāvatī’s rise to fame is difficult to pin down. Images of 
Pārśva with a multihooded cobra protecting him are found as far back as the first or 
second century before the Common Era. However, the earliest written sources do not 
refer to the male snake king as Dharaṇa or Dharaṇendra (Shah 1997, 35). By medieval 
times the story of Pārśva taking compassion on a pair of snakes was well known, and the 
snakes become identified as Dharaṇendra and his queen Padmāvatī (Shah 1997, 33–​34).
A female figure with serpentine associations begins to be found in proximity to statues 
of Pārśva in southern India as early as the seventh century (as in Figure 23.4). Dhaky had 
no qualms about identifying such figures as Padmāvatī; he noted that the Śvetāmbara lit­
erature has no mention of her until the early eleventh century, which indicates her origin 
in the southern Digambara tradition (1997, 66n22). On the other hand, Shah pointed out 
that Padmāvatī is not mentioned at all in canonical lists of the wives of Dharaṇendra and 
is not labeled as Padmāvatī until the tenth century before the Common Era (Shah 1975, 
80). He thought the female figures with Pārśva before 900 CE should rather be identified 
as another goddess associated with snakes, the mahāvidyā named Vairoṭyā (Shah 1975, 
80). By the tenth century, the inscriptions in southern India increasingly record ruling 
families styling themselves devotees of the goddess Padmāvatī (Desai 1957, 171). Cort 
reasonably interpreted this to mean that she may have started as the patron goddess 
(kuladevī) of particular powerful families who supported Jainism (1987, 243).
The earliest long work on Padmāvatī is Malliṣeṇasūri’s Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 
(“Fierce Padmāvatī’s Ritual Manual”), which dates to around the middle of the eleventh 
century.7 In her chapter in this volume, Ellen Gough objects to scholars who have posed 
the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa as important or central to Jaina tantric ritual traditions. 
Yet, as the first work dedicated to Padmāvatī and among the very earliest Jaina works 
heavily influenced by Śaiva-​Śākta tantras, it is in no way insignificant. The text opens 
with some verses praising Pārśvajina and asking for Padmāvatī’s protection. The third 
verse lists six names of Śaiva-​Śākta tantric goddesses, particularly affiliated with the 
Gāruḍa and Traipura traditions—​Totalā, Tvaritā, Nityā, Tripurā, Kāmasādhinī, and 
Tripurabhairavī—​and asserts that they are actually names of Padmāvatī. This verse

--- PAGE 545 ---
520      Michael Slouber
 
should be understood as setting forth the same principle as the verses I translated above 
from the earlier Jvālāmālinīkalpa: Readers may wonder about the propriety of non-​
Jaina spell goddesses and lore associated with a Jaina goddess, but that it is actually not 
a problem; Padmāvatī is their true identity. The author thus justifies the adaptation of 
non-​Jaina tantric material with the verse.
Over half of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is devoted to coercive rites to control 
lovers (and potential lovers) and conquering enemies; the rest concerns other types of 
magical rites and methods for healing snakebite summarized from the Śaiva Gāruḍa 
tantras. The following are several interesting examples of the subject matter of the text:
To attract the desired woman, the original teachers say to draw a yantra on cloth, a 
skull, or a copper pot with ink made from Datura, betel, poison, etc. Within three 
days it will blaze like the flame of a lamp [and draw her near]. (6.3)8
Figure 23.3.  Padmāvatī statue from Sholapur, 12th century. CC BY-​NC-​ND 2.0.
Photo by Sandeepa and Chetan (https://​san​deep​ache​tan.com/​).

Immediately following is a similar rite to lure an unwilling woman. The instructions read:
[Draw a woman and] inscribe the syllables oṃ hrīṃ and the elephant goad (kroṃ) on 
the lotus of her heart and on all of the joints of the limbs. Inscribe māyā (hrīṃ) on the 
breasts, and yūṃ on the genitals. Surround her with kroṃ syllables, and then provide 
her with a mantra garland on the outside of a Fire maṇḍala, situated on Wind and 
Earth maṇḍalas. After three days, she will be drawn by the flame of the lamp. (6.4)9
Figure 23.4.  Pārśva attended by Padmāvatī or Vairoṭyā and Dharaṇendra. Badami cave temple

In this case, the goddess invoked is Kṛṣṇamātaṅginī. As shown below, goddesses with 
names suggestive of outcaste women are a recurring theme in tantric love magic rites. 
Here is another colorful example from the fourth chapter:
One should write the mantra with sweet smelling substances on a piece of birch bark, 
tie it with a red thread, and put it in an unfired clay pot filled with honey. This will en­
chant the woman. If one draws the yantra in a female skull with hrīṃ in place of klīṃ 
and burns it with khadira wood morning, noon, and night, it would attract the lovely 
woman. If one writes the syllable huṃ in place of hrīṃ, and writes it with a mixture of 
poison and blood on human skin, burning it on an inauspicious lunar day, it would 
cause someone to be repelled. (4.4–​5)10
But what of magic rituals that have an even darker aim than enchanting an object of 
desire? Jainism and ahiṃsā are ostensibly inseparable. Nevertheless, some of the early 
Jaina tantric texts have numerous instances of mantras for killing enemies, driving 
them insane, and so on. The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa’s fifth chapter begins with rites 
of stambhana (paralysis), which refers to immobilizing an enemy. This in itself seems 
mildly violent, but does not, on the face of it, entail loss of life. As the chapter continues, 
a darker side emerges:
One must cover [the aforementioned yantra] with clay from a potter and put it into 
a pot filled with water. One then worships Pārśvanātha on top of it—​this is the best 
procedure for divine paralysis. The syllable ya with the enemy’s name, the syllable ṭha 
with ma, la, va, ra, and yūṃ. Around that, an Earth maṇḍala surrounded by tridents, 
ghosts, and fierce animals. Surrounded by likenesses of the enemy being struck with 
swords in the hands of other enemies. One surrounds the image with the name of the 
enemy, that surrounded by the piṇḍa mantras. One writes the mantra oṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ 
klaiṃ glauṃ svāhā ṭha surrounding the names of the enemies, the horse, and the 
great elephant. (5.14–​5.16)11
The commentator Banduṣeṇa interjected here his extracted version of the mantra to 
recite while surrounding the symbolic victim on the yantra:
Oṃ hrīṃ O Goddess with a fierce form, O fierce wielder of the trident, pulverize the 
enemy’s army, pulverize! Shake! Shake! Split! Split! Eat! Eat! Cook! Cook! Devour! 
Devour! Kill! Kill! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
It does not sound at all like the Jaina way to solve a problem, but the way the passage 
continues suggests an explanation:
After surrounding the diagram with the mantra, one then draws a likeness of the 
enemy in the eight directions outside of an Earth maṇḍala. Alternatively, one can 
draw it on a cloth taken from the face of a corpse in the cremation grounds, or better 
yet, that of a warrior who died in battle on the eighth day of the dark fortnight. One

--- PAGE 548 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      523
 
day later, one should inscribe a strip of cloth carded by a virgin using a pen made 
from the Koraṇṭa plant (syn. vairī =​ enemy) with ink of yellow arsenic, etc. First 
one must fully worship Padmāvatī with yellow flowers, then tie the yantra-​cloth to 
a public pillar. Seeing it from afar, the entire enemy army will be overcome with fear 
and will fall out of their battle array and flee. (5.18–​5.22)12
A redactor’s hand is apparent in this passage. The rite began as one targeting a single 
person: writing an enemy’s name on a diagram and surrounding it with violent mantras 
and images. It sounds like a standard liquidation rite in black magic (abhicāra). But the 
text switches to speaking of multiple enemies and then a whole army that flees. What 
has happened, I assert, is that this passage has been adapted from a Śaiva exemplar and 
changed to lead to a nonviolent outcome: the enemy army fleeing. A possible source 
is the Śaiva rite called “Raising the Flag” (patākocchrayavidhi), which is described in, 
among other sources, the Tantrasadbhāva, an influential Śākta text dating to around 
the eighth century before the Common Era. It follows the same basic outline of the rite 
as described here and includes some details and phrases that are exactly the same. One 
inscribes a yantra on a cloth cut by a virgin, visualizes a fierce goddess on a corpse, draws 
an image of the enemy army in a skull, and recites a mantra with similar imperatives 
for the goddess to break and kill the enemy forces. On seeing this yantra mounted on 
a pole, the enemies lose their courage and are easily conquered.13 Thus, whereas the 
Śaiva version renders the enemy easier to kill, the Jaina redactor uses it to disperse the 
enemy’s army.
Many more interesting examples could be adduced from the Bhairavapadmāvatī- 
kalpa and other early Jaina tantras. In his landmark article “The Śaiva Age,” Sanderson 
pointed out one of the key differences between Śaiva and Jaina tantra: The Jainas incor­
porated the mundane dimensions of tantric traditions and for the most part rejected 
tantra as a new path to liberation. Whereas one might think that Jaina tantra was only 
of concern to laypeople, Sanderson rightly observed that monks produced the manuals 
and aided laypeople, including royalty, who sought to carry out tantric rituals. He said: 
“As in the non-​Jaina tradition the goddesses were put to work to serve the interests of 
rulers” (Sanderson 2009, 244).
Conclusions and Future Directions 
for Research
Academic knowledge about Jaina tantric goddesses is conspicuously limited when 
compared to the extensive archive available and the importance of these goddesses to 
the Jaina tradition. While not exhaustive, my own review of the scholarship turned up 
fewer than twenty secondary publications of direct relevance, and most of these fea­
ture only a few relevant pages or are tangentially related. Of the half dozen or so that are

--- PAGE 549 ---
524      Michael Slouber
 
wholly about Jaina tantric goddesses, several draw heavily on twentieth-​century schol­
arship for the bulk of the information they convey, as the present chapter also does.
In her 2020 review of Jaina tantric literature, Ellen Gough referenced the sur­
vival of some five hundred primary sources on Jaina tantra, most of which would re­
late to goddesses such as the ones discussed here. It appears that only a very limited 
number of these have been made accessible to scholars through publication. Even texts 
that are among the earliest and most extensive Jaina tantras (the Jvālāmālinīkalpa and 
Vidyānuśāsana, respectively) are very poorly edited; one would fare better with a manu­
script because of the large number of mistakes in these printed editions.
Many more sources on Padmāvatī, in particular, also await future study. Jhavery’s 
1944 tome gathers together in numerous appendices various other works, like the 
Adbhutapadmāvatīkalpa, Śrīpadmāvatīpūjana, Raktapadmāvatīkalpa, and others. 
Zydenbos pointed to another category of understudied works like the Kannada narratives 
of Padmanābha’s Padmāvatīmāhātmya, which he called the oldest of its class (1994, 138).
Currently, Ellen Gough is the leading scholar of Jaina tantra and has been engaging 
with a much wider range of primary sources than her predecessors. Her recently 
published book Making a Mantra: Tantric Ritual and Renunciation on the Jain Path to 
Liberation (2021) is the most substantial contribution to the study of Jaina tantra since 
the publication of Jhavery’s Comparative and Critical Study of Mantrasastra in 1944. 
The introduction discusses the scholarly construction of tantra and its application to 
Jaina sources as discussed above and offers the new idea that applying the term “tan­
tric” to ritual traditions is less problematic than speaking of broader traditions in this 
manner (2021, 7, 16–​19). The point is well received since tantric ritual is indeed the area 
most heavily drawn on and developed in Jaina tantric sources and practices. Yet ritual 
does not exist in isolation from other religious elements, such as shared pantheons, ico­
nography, and conceptions of the self, the powers, and liberation. Therefore, I would 
caution readers against assuming that ritual was the only element of the wider tantric 
movement that Jainas adapted. The very centrality of goddesses in Jaina tantric ritual 
texts originated at a time when goddesses were also proliferating in Śaiva-​Śākta tantric 
traditions.
Another methodological issue where I both agree and part ways with Gough’s 
published comments concerns the relevance of, and extent to which, Jaina tantras de­
pend on non-​Jaina sources. Concerning Alexis Sanderson’s work on Jaina tantra in 
“The Śaiva Age,” she remarked: “He has focused on these deities’ similarities to ‘tan­
tric’ Śaiva-​Śākta deities, but while the names and iconographies of these deities may be 
similar, their mythologies, mantras, and ritual diagrams differ considerably from their 
non-​Jain counterparts” (Gough 2020, 573). As I have argued above, even the authors of 
texts like the Jvālāmālinīkalpa and Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa are fairly transparent that 
their material is closely based on Śaiva-​Śākta sources. The epigraphical evidence that 
Sanderson gathered in that article also builds a strong case for his conclusions. Since 
that article he has provided even more evidence: His recorded and publicly available 
keynote lecture at the 2015 Jaina Studies Workshop presented incontrovertible evidence

--- PAGE 550 ---
The Goddesses of Jaina Tantra      525
 
that most of the Nirvāṇakalikā—​arguably the single most influential Jaina tantric 
ritual text—​was copied from a Śaiva exemplar. Downplaying the significance of such 
influence closes the door to understanding specifics in these sources from their orig­
inal context. For example, it is impossible to make sense of the vidyā given in code 
in Jvālāmālinīkalpa 3.41–​3.42 without knowing the Śaiva technical terms for coded 
mantras, the fact that “Khaḍgairāvaṇa” is a mistake for Khaḍgarāvaṇa, the Bhūta tantra 
context of Khaḍgarāvaṇa’s ritual system, and the Śaiva and epic contexts of the reference 
to the legendary Candrahāsa sword in the vidyā. Broad learning that crosses religious 
boundaries and understanding of historical context are both essential for making sense 
of Jaina tantric sources.
Simultaneously, I agree with Gough’s point that it is inadequate and inaccurate 
to characterize the Jaina tantric tradition as a whole as something derivative (Gough 
2012, 4). While parts of the early tradition are derived from non-​Jaina sources, Gough’s 
scholarship has demonstrated the value of attending to particular aspects of Jaina tantra 
across time, the elements of host traditions that were not adopted, and the ways and 
reasons that Jainas actively innovated new mandalas, mantras, and deities over time.
In his 1987 article, Cort observed that, with few exceptions, past scholarship on Jaina 
goddesses has been written by art historians taking an iconographic approach, which 
has resulted in a limited range of questions being asked about the sources. For instance, 
historians of religion would want to know things like who worshiped the goddesses 
and what their motivations were (1987, 235). Scholars studying manuscript cultures, 
mantras, mandalas, medicine, magic, poetry, literature, realia, reception history, re­
ligious institutions, and so forth would all have different questions and would benefit 
from engaging with the prolific archive relating to Jaina tantric goddesses.
The two most promising areas of future growth are increased textual publication, 
translation, and study on the one hand and rich ethnographic accounts of tantric and 
nontantric Jaina goddesses on the other hand. Textual scholars with the requisite lan­
guage skills would do a great service by examining which aspects of pretantric Jaina 
mantra science (mantravāda) influenced tantric-era traditions. Further identification 
of textual dependencies—​both among Jaina tantric texts themselves and with non-​Jaina 
sources—​is critical for understanding the historical context and relationships that in­
form Jaina tantric texts. All such textual work will depend on close study of adequate 
editions and availability of manuscripts.
