Chapter 24
The Tantric Temple
Rule-​Bound Beauty
Libbie Mills
The Tantric Temple
The tantric temple could be delimited in any of three ways: first, as the temple marked 
with a founding inscription that designates it as part of a tantric tradition; second, as 
the temple in which the ritual practice is tantric, that is, as prescribed in the tantras; 
or, third, as the temple that those tantras describe. The first might sound a dry study, 
but see Leslie Orr (2019), where she points out that: “we should think of inscriptions 
as agents, as participants in the experiential and social worlds of temple life” (Orr 
2019: 201). The second is a field with scope for rich work, while requiring caution in 
regard to reading the present into the past (Sanderson 2019: 6), and an awareness 
of distinctions between lay practice and the initiatory practice handed down in the 
tantras. Scholarship, such as that of S. A. S. Sarma (2017, 2019), which combines in­
vestigation of ritual practice alongside the textual record, is particularly valuable. The 
present study, though, chooses to adhere to the third route, to the textual side, in order 
to target the underlying conceptions and intent behind the initial construction of a 
tantric temple. The study will work outward from a single tantra textual account of 
the temple built for tantric practice, using it to set out the temple’s purpose, its design 
and construction, and the ensuing ritual practices and management that concern the 
temple structure itself.
Within the tantra record is a class of treatise that treats pratiṣṭhā, that is, treatises that 
are specifically concerned with the construction, installation, and consecration of the 
tantric temple and the image within it. This material will be the primary focus of the 
study. The text around which the study will be based is a pratiṣṭhā of a relatively early 
date, and, for the purposes of a wider study of the temple, of a usefully mixed pedigree: 
the Piṅgalāmata, a northern, pre-​tenth-​century (Mills 2019) pratiṣṭhā text that is Śaiva, 
but which also acknowledges association with the Śākta-​Śaiva text, the Brahmayāmala.

--- PAGE 559 ---
534      Libbie Mills
 
(The chapter colophons read: Chapter xxx in the Brahmayāmala Piṅ galāmata under 
the authority of Jayadratha.) In using this text, a close watch will be placed on what it 
is that is given in material of this kind that is not treated in building manuals (termed 
śilpaśāstra or vāstuśāstra) outside the tantric traditions. Here in the pratiṣṭhā accounts 
we learn about more than the form of the built structure: we learn how that structure 
is understood and used; what it is about the tantric temple that is more than just a 
building. On occasion, the Piṅgalāmata does not cover a topic that needs addressing 
here. In those cases, other tantras will be drawn from, to complete the picture, and in so 
doing, provide some rebalancing of voice across the tantric traditions.
To be clear, the tantras do not outright state that they describe “the tantric temple.” 
Rather, they refer simply to “the temple.” They are tantric texts, describing the temple 
within that system. The information that they offer on the temple can be used to form a 
picture that holds broadly true across the traditions that fall within the tantra bracket, 
and across time and place. But, of course, there are also differences between the ac­
counts: differences of deities and associated visualizations and ritual methods; dis­
tinctive features associated with region; shifts in practice over time; plus differences 
of detail, of inclusion, and of omission. The texts themselves address their differences, 
warning that one should work within the textual record of a single tradition, without any 
blending (saṅkara) of teachings. As an example, here is the advice of the Kāmikāgama, a 
southern, twelfth-​century text:
One should proceed according to the measurements given in the āgamas that are 
the Kāmika, etc. Among them, if what is to be done is not described in one [āgama], 
[the information should be obtained] from another. And if it is not described in all 
the Siddhānta, then the Garuḍa, etc. [āgamas] should be used. If it is not described 
there either, one should turn to vāstuśāstra. Best is what is taught by a single teacher. 
Middling is [what is taught by] a single tantra. Lesser [is what is taught in] a single 
lineage. And least of all [is what is taught in] a mixture of lineages. If even that is 
lacking, it should be despised. Knowing thus, one may proceed.1
Given that advice, it feels a clumsy thing to try to describe the tantric temple, this subtly 
multiple thing, as a single entity. But there are, nonetheless, some strong commonalities 
that one can discern. The telling of the Piṅgalāmata will be observed for what it holds 
that is general to tantra, and for what is particular to its case. In doing that, the aim will 
be to relate the principles that are held in common, while also indicating the breadth be­
yond them.
From the textual record, one can look at extant temple examples that fit that record 
in terms of design, temples that are beautiful, whether in the simplicity of a minor 
shrine, as seen in figure 24.1, the mid seventh-​century Bōricā Sūrya/​Śiva temple, near 
Porbandar, Gujarat, or the grandeur of an imperial edifice designed for public use, as in 
the twelfth-​century Tribhuvana temple, at Kumbakonam, Tamilnadu, figure 24.2. These 
elegantly composed buildings, shaped to stand apart from what is around them, will 
have always drawn attention, and they retain that impact still.

--- PAGE 560 ---
The Tantric Temple      535
 
The attention of modern scholarship can be traced back to the 1834 Essay on the 
Architecture of the Hindus of Ram Raz, who wrote his illustrated essay to give access, for 
readers in English, to the temple textual record held in four śilpaśāstra building texts (the 
Mānasāra, Mayamata, Kāśyapa, and Vaikhānasa) and, by means of illustrations, to link 
the prescriptions of these texts to the forms of extant temples of Tamilnadu. While Raz used 
the order presented in texts to understand temples on the ground, based on their analysis 
of what they saw on the ground, others ordered them in their own fashion, early examples 
of such orderings coming from James Fergusson2 and Gabriel Jouveau-​Dubreuil.3
More recent work has benefited from the publication of editions of śilpaśāstra and 
tantra manuscript materials, permitting scholarship to return to the mode of Raz, in 
using the order presented in the written prescriptions to understand extant buildings 
and their function. The multivolume Encyclopaedia of Temple Architecture (Meister and 
Dhaky 1983) stands out for its thorough assay of temples, using the technical vocabulary 
Figure 24.1.  The mid-​seventh-​century Bōricā Sūrya/​Śiva temple, near Porbandar, Gujarat. 
Mills 2012.

--- PAGE 561 ---
536      Libbie Mills
 
of building texts that are contemporary with the temples themselves. Adam Hardy 
(2007) offers the reader an essential connection between written record and built form, 
and an understanding both of the manner in which the elements of that built form relate 
to one another, and also of the sequencing of temple series described in the texts.
Beauty and Suitability
The beauty that draws scholars’ attention is spoken of in the tantras, too. Chapter 6 the 
Piṅgalāmata sets out the features of twenty-​six types of temple, regularly distributing 
Figure 24.2.  The twelfth-​century Tribhuvana temple, at Kumbakonam, Tamilnadu. Mills 2019.

--- PAGE 562 ---
The Tantric Temple      537
 
references to beauty to the larger temples at the beginning of the list (Piṅgalāmata 
6.206c–​210). These twenty-​six are: Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Sarvabhadraka, Vimāna, 
Nandana, Nandivṛddhi, Garutman, Siṃha, Kumbha, Gaja, Vṛṣabha, Padma, Caturaśra, 
Aṣṭāśra,Ṣoḍaśāśra, Gvāvṛkṣa, Vardhamāna, Śrivatsa, Bhadra, Haṃsa, Nalina, Śrῑnaga, 
Gṛharāja, Gṛhārdha, Valabhῑ, plus those classified as Miśraka (mixed). The Meru and 
Mandara are “beautified” (upaśobhitaḥ, yathāśobhaṃ prakartavyaḥ), and the Kailāsa 
and Sarvatobhadra are “very beautiful” (suśobhana). After that, the compliments di­
minish in fulsomeness as the temples diminish in size, but discussion of adornment is 
sustained (Piṅgalāmata 6.214–​315).
Thus beauty is noted, but expressions of the artistry of the temple are always couched 
in its purpose: this is an artistry achieved in order to render the building, and each of its 
composite parts, beautiful (śobha) in that it is auspicious and suited to its task (śubha). 
Piṅgalāmata ­chapter 6 makes repeated comment on suitability for the task, from the 
choice of temple location to the final consecration. And that task is twofold. The first 
requirement is that there be a benefit to the patron. The temple is raised to achieve par­
ticular gains, siddhis, for the patron, whether they be in this life or after it, or both. The 
temple design is chosen with his particular goals in mind. A successful construction will 
permit him to achieve his goals, but an unsuccessful one will have a countereffect. This is 
a concern right from the very beginning, from the selection of a location onward:
[The temple should be located] at an auspicious kṣetra, upakṣetra, saṃdoha, 
upasaṃdoha, pῑṭha or upapῑṭha; or on a river bank, on a mountain-​top, at an ocean 
shore; in a city, village or settlement; by an isolated tree; in a cremation ground; or at 
the confluence of rivers; at a place where three, four or five roads meet; in a cave or 
thicket; or in a place suitable to the patron, according to his desire.4
Here we see temple locations that range from auspicious: the kṣetra, upakṣetra, saṃdoha, 
upasaṃdoha, pῑṭha, and upapῑṭha (these are designations of areas of ritual effect around 
a liṅga) and river bank, to inauspicious: the lone tree and cremation ground. The impli­
cation is that an auspicious location is suited to a beneficent purpose such as wealth or 
many children, while an inauspicious one is apt for a maleficent one, like the defeat of an 
enemy. So, the first concern is the requirement of the patron. The second requirement is 
that the temple be a suitable vessel for the deity to inhabit. And it is here that the rules 
begin in earnest.
Order
The rules begin at the site. As the base for a temple in which the deity will take up resi­
dence, the site (vāstu) for the construction should be chosen with care and aligned to the 
cardinal directions. Once the site has been chosen, the preparation of the ground has three 
elements to it. First, there is the preparation necessary for any sound foundation, which

--- PAGE 563 ---
538      Libbie Mills
 
begins with a ploughing up of the land, proceeds to the laying down of stable materials, 
and ends with their compaction. Second, there is treatment of the auspicious and inaus­
picious, with a careful removal from the ground of inauspicious objects, and attention to 
augury events. Third, there is ritual preparation of the site, which is treated as a domain 
inhabited by a human figure, termed the “man of the site” (vāstupuruṣa) and, on top of 
him, a set of deities mapped onto the square site in a grid of smaller squares marked out 
by threads (sūtra). The Piṅgalāmata (Piṅgalāmata 8.44–​73b) gives a vivid account of the 
descent of the vāstupuruṣa: snake divinities (nāga) were terrifying and murdering people 
and other divine beings, who turned to Indra for help. Indra struck the nāgas down in 
battle, and they fell to earth. The earth was overcome and its supports, Śeṣa and others, 
were crushed. They let flow poison, blood, and warm tears. The earth, smelling the poison, 
was overcome and fainted. After just a moment’s swoon, it emitted a great hot wind on 
which the poison rose. There was a great opening full of poison, which was a demon body. 
The body had no fixed edges. It hid the everything on the earth and in the sky. The gods did 
not shine in the sky, and on earth, the sages and deities stopped their rituals. Together they 
went to Śiva, praising him, reciting the Vedas, and asked for his help. Śiva said:
“O gods make firm the ropes!” “Be strong! Strike hard! Then I can control him.” 
Hearing the Lord’s words, all were delighted and eager. Then, through meditation, 
noble Bhairava released the mighty Rudra whose powers of illusion were great. 
Having sought approval, he set to at once. He pulled the great demon’s topknot. 
Pulling his hair, he forced him to his knees before Bhairava. Then, spread out on his 
back, his arms and legs folded, his body was bent to fit into the site and fixed with 
sticks and ropes. Overcome with fear, all the deities took up places there.5
Thus is the upstart demon forced to the ground, with his body bent up to fit the site, his 
head at the northeast, in a position established as early as the sixth-​century Bṛhatsaṃhitā 
52.51. He is tied down, and the deities who had sought Śiva’s help in quelling him take up 
positions over his body, in the sūtra-​marked squares of the site, as the deities of that site. 
I have given this story, long as it is, to indicate the depth of the footing in mainstream 
Brahmanical religion that underlies the tantric temple. There is a long history in this 
deity layout. The formation is, again, at least as old as the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, and is repeated 
from text to text, in building texts of all kinds—​tantric and not—​with minimal varia­
tion, with Brahmā in the center, at the belly of the vāstupuruṣa, and the other deities fil­
ling the grid of the site around him.
From the point of view of the Piṅgalāmata, the deities of the Brahmanical world, care­
fully propitiated, form a plug of safety over the poison of the vāstupuruṣa’s body be­
neath. But it is a plug with a demon fringe, since immediately outside the vāstu area are 
eight demons, stationed in the cardinal and intercardinal directions:
Outside, at the northeast corner, is Carakī; in the southeast is Vidārī; in the southwest 
is Pūtanā; in the northwest is Pāparākṣasī. Outside, to the east is Skanda; to the south 
is Aryaman; moreover, to the west is Jambha; and to the north is Pilapiṃcchaka.6

--- PAGE 564 ---
The Tantric Temple      539
 
These demon characters are fierce: as an example, Pūtanā features as a member of 
Skanda’s troop of grahas, “seizers,” against whom averting remedies are given in the 
medical treatise the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya at Uttarasthāna ­chapter 3, on countering child 
snatchers. So, construction is commenced on a bed of propitiated deities, overlaying a 
vāstupuruṣa demon, and with an outer border beyond which no building should take 
place, inhabited by more demons.
Even within the safety of the site, there are places of danger. The sūtra lines that mark 
out the deities are also the basis for a map of vulnerable points (marmans) in the site. 
Marmans are to be carefully avoided during the site preparation. Any encroachment on 
a marman at the time of preparation for building is harmful to the patron. Piṅgalāmata 
8.30–​40 states the harm to be incurred at each type of marman, ending with the sum­
mary statement:
The breaking of the rules of marman brings all these results. So one should not en­
croach upon a deity or a demon, O virtuous one. If one should occasion to do so, one 
should worship the deities and offer an offering (bali), for the deities that bring good 
and bad are appeased when worshipped. An intrusion always brings great danger 
for the king, the kingdom, the patron and the officiant. So one should not encroach.7
A further vulnerability for the site is impingement by shadows. Certain shadow 
impingements are particularly harmful. I have not found a treatment of this problem 
in the Piṅgalāmata, but it is seen widely elsewhere, for example, at the pre-​mid-​twelfth 
century (Mills 2019: 65–​72) Śaiva Bṛhatkālottara prāsādalakṣaṇapaṭala 132–​133b, where 
we learn that temples should not be impinged on by the shadows of other temples, or 
trees, wells, devotee residences (maṭhas), or monuments (caityagṛhas). Bṛhatkālottara 
prāsādalakṣaṇapaṭala 119 makes clear that temples and so on that are not impinged 
upon do not bring harm. But if they are impinged upon, harm arises for the patron and 
worshipper. Shadow impingement is avoided by building at a suitable distance with re­
spect to height. At Bṛhatkālottara prāsādalakṣaṇapaṭala 118cd, the instruction is to build 
at a distance of twice the height of the object that might impinge.
On this baseline of a secured site, free from impingements, considerable ritual care 
is required before construction can begin. Here, as a pratiṣṭhā tantra, the Piṅgalāmata 
concerns itself with things that śilpaśāstras do not. Piṅgalāmata 6.66–​106 details 
the ritual, from the initial laying of the central support (Ādhāraśakti) through the 
positioning of eight altars (vedī) in the four cardinal and four intercardinal directions 
and a ninth one in the center, and the installation of the Brahma stone, the Śiva Śakti, 
the eight deities of the directions, the three Tattvas and Tattva deities, the many tattvas, 
the four bhāvas and their opposites, the eight mūrtis and mūrtidevatās to the final bali 
offering.8 This last act completed, we are told: “Having offered the bali, the building 
of the temple should go well. Otherwise, vināyaka demons will bring about serious 
impediments.”9
The site ritually prepared, construction itself is described with a careful prescription 
for correct proportions and measurements. The measurements are based on the same

--- PAGE 565 ---
540      Libbie Mills
 
square vāstu site, but with an entirely new set of sūtra divisions, a set for construction 
work as opposed to ritual preparation. From this constructive set of sūtra markings, the 
building rises, with each built part assigned a size by proportion to the whole, and each 
measurement tested by means of āya formulae to ensure that they are auspicious and 
therefore suitable for use.10 The layout for the building is given in a steady sequence, 
first in terms of the plan and then of the elevation. The plan is detailed from the center 
outward; the elevation is given from the bottom up. Every element of the building is 
enumerated, with a limited range of options for variation set out, in order that the re­
sult should be suitable and also beautiful. The alignment to the cardinal directions is 
carefully maintained, and possible materials are listed: wood, brick and stone, coated in 
plaster. Altogether, this is a beauty of safety, order, symmetric balance, and proportion, 
founded on a protected site, bordered by walls, away from impinging shadows, and with 
every part of the building under tight control to ensure benefit.
The precision is clear, and so too is the sense of pattern and flow, expressed by the 
term chandas (meter). Chandas, a word usually thought of in terms of the rhythm of 
verse is instead used here to denote the pulse of a building. The solidly linear sequencing 
that characterizes meter in verse is here conceived of in three-​dimensional architecture 
(see Mills and Scott forthcoming). The pulse of a building will have a voluminous na­
ture. However, the instructions for this three-​dimensional rhythm of form are always 
delivered in planar format, in terms of the rhythm of the plan (talacchandas) and of the 
elevation (ūrdhvacchandas). The plan rhythm waves out from the very center of the 
site, in circuits of wall-​bordered space. The elevation rhythm stacks up from the outer 
walls, narrowing back to the center at the summit. The chandas patterns are analyzed 
into categories. In the case of the Piṅgalāmata, the categories are those of the twenty-​six 
temple types listed earlier, which by implication are regarded as pure (śuddha), as op­
posed to the mixed (miśraka) category, which is labeled according to the nature of the 
jaṅghā, which is the portion of the building from the base of the door to the base of the 
superstructure:
From Meru to Valabhī, [these are the temples], one by one, in terms of name and 
shape. One should apportion everything as has been told from beginning to end. 
And there are mixed (miśraka) temples. Their name[s]‌ come about according to the 
degree of their resemblance to one or the other, or difference. The mixed [temple] is 
named according to the type of its jaṅghā.11
It is important to note that the delivery of these metrics is itself made in metric form, 
since all these architectural instructions come in śloka metric verse, the predictable 
beat of which is suited to ease of memorization and communication. At this point, one 
might want to check in on where this communication is going. The śilpaśāstra materials 
hand down plans for the construction and management of built items, with instructions 
that appear to be directed to the builders themselves, the śilpins, or their supervisor, 
the sthapati. The tantras, on the other hand, are specifically the teachings handed down 
within a ritual tradition, and are directed at the ritual officiants of that tradition. Thus

--- PAGE 566 ---
The Tantric Temple      541
 
the tantric teachings properly focus on ritual activity. However, where that ritual activity 
concerns the installation and consecration of a material item for ritual—​a temple or an 
image—​the officiant will need to know enough about the building of that item in order 
to judge that it is being correctly carried out. Thus the tantras necessarily include details 
on correct construction.
In the initial construction of a temple, ritual officiants will be heavily engaged in 
ensuring the correctness of every step. The textual accounts record the patterned order 
of the construction to raise the temple as a thing of beauty in rectitude. The technical 
vocabulary shifts, somewhat, both from text to text, and also from verse to verse of the 
same text. Here I will give the terms seen most commonly in the Piṅgalāmata treatment, 
with the understanding that there are other possibilities. In terms of basic elements, the 
pīṭha is the base or plinth upon which the structure is built, wider than the temple itself. 
Upon it, the elements of the plan radiate out from the center, which is the locus of the 
temple deity. The deity is installed in the innermost chamber of the temple (garbhagṛha).
In every temple, there is an ambulatory passage around the deity within the 
garbhagṛha. Some temples have a second walled ambulatory, termed the andhāra, 
around the outside of the garbhagṛha. The outer walls (bhittis) are shaped into broad 
convexities, minor offsets on either side of these broad projections, and corner 
elements and recesses, known, respectively, as rathas, uparathas, koṇas, and praveśas. 
Occasionally, concavities acting as water channels (jalamārga) and latticed win­
dows (jālas) are set into the walls. Columns, pillars, and pilasters, collectively termed 
stambhas, serve as supports and ornaments. In the case of northern temples, as is seen 
in the northern Piṅgalāmata record, an outermost wall (prākāra) surrounds the temple 
enclosure. Southern texts describe grand gateways (gopura) to mark the temple entrance 
at plural concentric encircling boundaries of the site. Around the garbhagṛha of the cen­
tral deity, other shrines may be arranged, for further deities. In the pañcāyatana design, 
four peripheral shrines surround the central one (described at Piṅgalāmata 6.173–​176c). 
In the navāyatana one, there are eight peripheral shrines (described at Piṅgalāmata 
6.176d–​177b). Also described is the Aṣṭottaraśata design, of 108 shrines (described at 
Piṅgalāmata 6.177c–​189).
The elevation divides into two parts: the jaṅghā and the śikhara. The jaṅghā is the 
portion of the temple between the base of the doorway and the base of the śikhara. One 
or more pillared halls (maṇḍapas) may adjoin this structure. The śikhara is the super­
structure, a highly peaked roof, over the jaṅghā. The superstructure tapers as it ascends, 
in either a gradually increasing curve or a straight line. The highest point of the temple is 
vertically aligned directly over the deity in the garbhagṛha far below.
As an early and northern tantra, the Piṅgalāmata describes a śikhara of the type par­
ticular to that time and place. Each face of the śikhara is divided into horizontal levels 
(āghāṭa). Arrayed along these āghāṭas there are moldings that resemble miniature 
buildings (bhūmikās). The number of bhūmikās decreases as the āghāṭas ascend and the 
śikhara narrows. At the top, a finial termed āmalasāraka, placed directly above the icon 
at the center of the temple, completes the śikhara. See figure 24.3 for an example of this 
form of śikhara, seen in the early seventh-​century Visāvāḍā Old temple/​Śaṅkha-​dēruñ,

--- PAGE 567 ---
542      Libbie Mills
 
near Porbandar, Gujarat. Later texts, and those based in the south, record śikhara 
arrangements of their region and time period.
In all cases, with its heavy base lidded by a tapered śikhara, the temple building barely 
lets in light. At the center of the temple, the garbhagṛha remains in deep darkness except 
for perhaps once a day, when a low angle of the sun would allow light through an east-​ or 
west-​facing doorway to illumine the deity at the heart of the building. The built form thus 
creates a contrast of light without, and dark within, with accompanying cool and quiet.
Residence
In that dark, the temple building houses the deity in a vessel at the center. The vessel may 
be anthropomorphic or not. It may also be man-​made or not: a distinction is made be­
tween the vessel that comes about by its own accord, as a self-​arisen form (svayambhuva); 
the man-​made (mānuṣya) vessel; and the vessel made by some higher being, whether a 
sage (ārṣa), or a divine being (daiva). The ritual officiant installs the deity into the vessel 
by means of installation (pratiṣṭhā) practice. (See Einoo and Takashima 2005 and Keul 
2017. Keul includes an examination by Marko Geslani of the early presentation of con­
secration given in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, a study of the pratiṣṭhā of the liṅga in the early 
mantramārga by Dominic Goodall, a chapter by Anna Ślączka on Ratnanyāsa in the 
Devyāmata, one by Marzenna Czerniak-​Drożdżowicz on consecration in Pāncarātrika 
sources, and S. A. S. Sarma’s analysis of reinstallation in the ritual literature of Kerala.) 
The Piṅgalāmata details the installation procedure in ­chapter 11. Upon installation, the 
temple becomes a container, a body, in fact, for the deity, as is expressed, for example, in 
the twelfth-​century12 southern, Pāñcarātra Īśvarasaṃhitā:
The image, its pīṭha, the temple and the innermost chamber of the temple, with the 
superstructure over it (garbhamandira): This set of four is (samam) the body of the 
god of gods.13
From there, from that temple body, the deity will exert power over a kṣetra, a range, 
around the vessel. That kṣetra is measurable, and differs according to the nature of the 
icon. According to the Suprabheda, a twelfth-​century (Sarma 2017: 229, n. 7) southern 
Śaiva text, the measurements of the kṣetra around a vessel for Śiva are as follows: “The 
Śiva kṣetra extends 150 hastas on all sides of the liṅga. He who dwells there attains the 
Śivaloka. This is the size of the kṣetra taught for a man-​made liṅga. In the case of a 
svayaṃbhuva one it is 1000 [hastas], and half that in the case of one made by sages.”14
The hasta is a measurement taken from the size of the patron himself, being the dis­
tance from his elbow to tip of his middle finger. The kṣetra extends well beyond the 
temple site, which does not go beyond 50 hastas. The temple, then, animated by the 
deity, forms a hub of sustenance for those within its range, sustenance for other lives. 
Not only is the temple enlivened by its deity, as a permanent resident, it is also alive with

--- PAGE 568 ---
The Tantric Temple      543
 
the comings and goings of other beings, both human and not, benign and not. These 
comings and goings will be the next thing to look at.
Entry and Exit
The temple is a focus of attentive service of the deity from the officiants and devotees 
that it sustains. Ritual—​whether daily, occasional or special; whether of act, sound, or 
mentation—​is maintained within the temple, ritual for which officiants and devotees 
Figure 24.3.  The early-​seventh-​century Visāvāḍā Old temple/​Śaṅkha-​dēruñ, near Porbandar, 
Gujarat.

--- PAGE 569 ---
544      Libbie Mills
 
will require access into the boundaried temple site. Yātrā procession of the deity may 
take place beyond borders of the temple, within the kṣetra range, requiring the deity 
to travel beyond the temple site. (Such processions are seen recorded in southern tan­
tric material, which dates from the twelfth century on, but it is not seen in pre-​twelfth-​
century tantric records. For more on the earliest sources for the Śaiva procession, see 
Goodall 2019.) There is, then, a porosity to the site borders, which means that, besides 
devotees, contaminating factors may enter the temple, too.
To counteract the ill effects that result from the entry of these contaminants, a pro­
cedure for remediation (prāyaścitta) is performed. When it comes to prāyaścitta 
procedure, corruptions in the different parts of the temple plan require different 
levels of remediation. A good account of the matter may be seen at ­chapter 69 of the 
Vimānārcanakalpa. As this is a southern text, it works with a temple plan of multiple 
concentric circuits of wall around the temple, which permits a staged mapping of the 
severity of corrupting events. Here one sees that not only does the nature of the contam­
inant matter, from mouse to criminal, so also does the duration of the contamination 
and its degree of proximity to the center of the temple—​whether the corrupting item 
is outside the temple, or, moving inward, within the third, second or first enclosure, or 
within the garbhagṛha itself, at the very center. Corruptions in these different circuits of 
degree of fault, proximity and duration require different levels of remediation. Lesser 
corruptions, in the periphery, and for a short time, require only a prāyaścitta purifica­
tion process. More serious corruptions at the center, and for a lasting period, require 
purification followed by a major pratiṣṭhā reconsecration, going right back to the very 
beginning, with the initial ploughing of the ground prior to laying a foundation. The 
chapter also details the remediation necessitated by contact with an item that has come 
in contact with a contaminant, and that necessitated by contact with an item that has 
come in contact with that, until, at the third degree of contact, there is no harm from it.
Maintenance
The remediation rules with their graded ranking of peril, whereby the same contami­
nant item causes a greater degree of contamination the nearer it is to the temple center, 
until one reaches the vessel hosting the deity itself, raises the question: What happens 
if even that is entered by a contaminating factor? This question, too, is addressed in 
the tantras, in chapters titled jīrṇoddhāra, which cover all aspects of the maintenance, 
repair, and replacement of the temples and images that are the vessels for the deity, 
when they have become damaged or corrupted, right up to the problem of them being 
squatted in by maleficent beings.
The meaning held by the title jīrṇoddhāra is that of a removal (uddhāra) of what is 
old (jīrṇa). Of course, replacement will follow removal, and much attention is paid in 
jīrṇoddhāra literature to how that is carried out, but it is the removal of the corrupting 
force of an old item that is given principal importance in the labeling of the procedure. 
The emphasis on the removal side of renovation, as opposed to the replacement side,

--- PAGE 570 ---
The Tantric Temple      545
 
holds sense when one reads accounts of the great harm that comes from an old object 
if it is not removed and disposed of. An example of such an account can be seen in the 
Bṛhatkālottara chapter on jīrṇoddhāra at verses 20c–​24b, which explain that malevolent 
entities will enter a worn-​out or damaged liṅga, bringing harm to those who serve it:
The liṅga which is aged or corrupted is considered a domicile for beings (bhūta). 
When malevolent beings (mahābhūtas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas) have taken up 
residence there, there are afflictions of terrible fever, convulsion, etc., famine, pesti­
lence, poor sleep, bad auguries, affliction in children, affliction in pregnancy and af­
fliction of the king, among twice-​borns, and hazard from hurricanes, and high-​winds, 
and snakes etc. arise in the area. Risk of hurricanes, high winds, etc. arises in the area. 
Meteor strike occurs, and there is destruction in every direction all around. These and 
other such evils prevail. Therefore one should remove the old liṅga, with every care.15
Any part of the temple vessel may, through age or damage, become corrupted, and prey 
to entry by malevolent forces, at which point it should be removed. The jīrṇoddhāra 
teachings give instruction on how to avert this harm.16 The temple is the deity’s body, and 
like all bodies, the temple faces decay, requiring ongoing maintenance (anukarman) and 
repair (sandhāna) in order that it remains a suitable vessel for the deity, with occasional 
need for a fuller removal (and ensuing replacement) of what is old (jīrṇoddhāra). The 
topic is covered by the twelfth chapter of the Piṅgalāmata, beginning with an explanation 
that it is the vessel, the body, that is disposed of (and replaced), not the deity within:
Piṅgalā asked: Now, how is [the word] removal (uddhāra) used in association with 
the word old (jīrṇa)?
The blessed Bhairava said: The word “old” or “not-​old” is in regard to the material 
vessel, and not at all about the being [within it]. Nor is the removal of an old material 
item such that any beings die. Just as there is no activity in a corpse, in the same way 
the arrival [of the deity] in the liṅga is unseen.17
The seriousness of the need for repair and the degree of attendant ritual correction cor­
relate to the proximity to the temple center, in a continuation of the pattern that was 
seen in the case of prāyaścitta reparation. A distinction is made between minor defects 
(to plaster, to peripheral parts of the temple, to outer shrines of the temple) and major 
ones (to the entire temple, to the liṅga, image, and pedestal). In the case of a minor de­
fect, there may be a repair with prāyaścitta ritual. But in the case of a major defect, there 
must be a rebuild and a full pratiṣṭhā reinstallation.
Not only must the vessel remain in good order, it must also remain in use, receiving 
worship. Ongoing worship is necessary to safety, as is pointed out by the Mohacūrottara, 
a Śaiva pratiṣṭhā text composed prior to the latter half of the eleventh century (Mills 
2019: 65–​72):
The old, etc. item that is worshipped kills. That which is not worshipped [also] kills.
Therefore he who knows the teachings should remove that liṅga according to the 
procedure.18

--- PAGE 571 ---
546      Libbie Mills
 
When there is a serious fault in a part of a temple, whether of wear or of failed worship, it 
must be removed. The Piṅgalāmata begins by discussing the removal of a faulty image:
The liṅga or piṇḍikā base that is burnt, broken, misshapen, lacking parts, hosting 
something living, too thin, too small, too big, too thick, crooked, ruined, cracked, 
broken, split open, or utterly dreadful: one should fully remove that ruined item. In 
this regard, the same is true for anthropomorphic images. The same is true, too, for 
images that are partially anthropomorphic (vyaktāvyakta)19. [Anthropomorphic 
images] without ears, nose or fingers, or with flawed limbs, are [to be] removed. O 
shapely one! O lovely-​limbed one! Destructive to all who live in the area, to officiant, 
patron and builder, those [images] should be abandoned. There would be great harm 
from their corruption. Therefore one should fully remove them.20
As to the procedure for the removal of unwanted material, most detail is given in the 
case of the removal of the image itself, in particular that of the liṅga which, being heavy 
and embedded in the ground, requires the strength of a bull to heave it out:
[The officiant] should tie [the liṅga] with a golden rope to the shoulders of a bull. The 
officiant, with those in attendance, should then lead it away. He should say: “Let there 
be Śiva.” The removal procedure has been described.21
As to the disposal of the spent material: “One should take [the icon] to the south of the 
city, village, hamlet or settlement. Then one should throw a stone [icon] into water, one 
should smelt a metal one, and one should burn up a wooden one.”22
The removal, then, is a thorough disposal, so that the material may not be reused. 
The same is the case for spent material from a damaged part of the temple. This case is 
discussed next in the Piṅgalāmata:
And when a temple is old, a removal should be performed then, too. [The officiant] 
should carefully transfer into a sword the mantra directed to [the deity] and the 
entire collection of tattvas, and then maintain daily worship. He should establish 
[the sword] to the south of the liṅga, and perform a 1000-​fold fire offering (homa). 
A fine protective cover of wooden boards is placed over the liṅga. The removal is 
[done] gently, O wise lady. One should set down a [first] brick. And, using the same 
measurements and shape as before, one should build using stone in the case of stone, 
and brick in the case of brick. In the case of something made of wood or clay, one 
should use baked brick and stone. It should be made better than before. It should not 
be made worse than before. That made of stone is known to be best and that made of 
brick is middling, my dear. That made of wood is lesser. That made of clay is the very 
least. Wood is a hundred times the worth of clay. The worth of brick is thousands of 
times more. Stone is millions of times the worth of brick. When it is time for [re-​]
entry of the deity into the icon, one should unfasten and take him from the sword. 
An effective pratiṣṭhā installation should be carried out according to the procedure 
given above, granting entry into grahalūla. When the removal of the old is done in 
full, one attains the highest reward.23

--- PAGE 572 ---
The Tantric Temple      547
 
Thus is the deity transferred to a safe location, and the icon protected in a wooden box, 
while the temple is repaired around them. Importantly, from the ritual point of view, 
what is being preserved, even as the temple is repaired or rebuilt, is a proper and uncor­
rupted vessel for the deity. The deity must be permitted to move from a failed vessel into 
a restored or replacement one, just as the soul moves from the dead body into a new one. 
And, for making this transition possible, one is rewarded.
Rule-​Bound Beauty
The reward comes from following procedure. This is a world of order. The temple 
building is, as we have seen throughout this account, designed to achieve a beauty of 
suitability and order; a beauty that comes from a controlled balance between the push of 
its active state and the pull of its boundaries.
The temple makes an active push outward in terms of built form: the structure grows 
out from its center and is often crowded with lively ornament. The form of the temple 
changes over time, too, with a tendency to increase in both size and ornament. Hosting 
the principal deity, plus other deities around that, the temple is ritually alive, with a 
kṣetra of power around it. The temple is also a hub of human activity, and can harbor 
other beings, too, some harmful to those humans.
As a consequence, the temple body requires ongoing attention to protection from cor­
ruption. The pull, back inward, on the temple begins with avoidance of the inauspicious 
and impingement by items at the periphery. The built site is strictly limited, walled away 
from the demons at its edges. Access is restricted—​access of light, of people, and of other 
beings that may or may not meet the temple’s purity gauge. Usage of the temple is firmly 
regulated, in act and sound and mentation. And the temple’s purpose is also under con­
trol. It is built for a purpose, a particular advantage (siddhi), for the patron. Like all living 
things, the temple body faces decay and death, countered by repair and replacement. In 
all these ways is this beautiful vessel for god ordered into shape.
More scholarly work lies ahead, largely in terms of the edition of the many pratiṣṭhā 
tantra texts available to us in manuscript form, and the analysis of what they tell us 
of their thinking about, and proposals for, the temples of their distinct traditions and 
times. This work of opening up the textual tradition to modern scholarship, in associa­
tion with ongoing examination of extant materials—​of temples and the inscriptions that 
mark them, and the practices conducted within them—​will enrich the understanding of 
the tantric temple, and of its role in tantra as a whole.

	8.	 Twenty-​three tattvas (principles) are ritually installed in the stones (PI 6.73–​75b). These 
principles are:

--- PAGE 575 ---
550      Libbie Mills
 
23: buddhi intellect; 22: ahaṃkāra self-​identity; 21: manas mind; 20: śrota ears; 19: tvac 
skin; 18: cakṣus eyes; 17: jihvā tongue; 16: nāsā nose; 15: vāc organs of voice; 14: pāṇi 
hands; 13: pāda feet; 12: pāyu anus; 11: upastha reproductive organs; 10: śabda sound; 9: 
sparśa touch; 8: rūpa form; 7: rasa taste; 6: gandha smell; 5: ākāśa ether; 4: vāyu air; 3: 
tejas fire; 2: ap water; 1: pṛthvī earth. The order from 23 to 1 is sṛṣṭikrama (in the order of 
creation). The order from 1 to 23 is saṃhṛtikrama (in the order of destruction). 1–​5 are 
the 5 mahābhūtas, gross elements. 6–​10 are the 5 tanmātras, subtle elements. 11–​15 are the 
5 karmendriyas, faculties of action. 16–​20 are the 5 buddhīndriyas, faculties of sense. In 
the course of ritual, one sees the 23 tattvas grouped into 3 broader categories which are 
again called Tattvas. I use a capital T for the 3 broader Tattva categories, to distinguish 
them from their constituenttattvas. The three Tattvas are the Ātmatattva, the Vidyātattva 
and the Śivatattva. In the accounts of śilānyāsa given in the texts treated here, the Tattvas 
are assigned tattvas as follows: The Ātmatattva is composed of tattvas 1–​10 (pṛthivī to 
śabda). The Vidyātattva contains tattvas 11–​21 (upastha to manas). The Śivatattva consists 
of tattvas 22 and 23 (ahaṃkāra and buddhi). Each of the three Tattvas has an Īśa (lord). 
Brahmā is the Tattveśa of the Ātmatattva; Viṣṇu is the Tattveśa of the Vidyātattva; and Śiva 
is the Tattveśa of the Śivatattva.
Next (PI 6.76–​78), the set of four bhāvas (dharma, jñāna, vairāgya and aiśvarya and 
their four opposites (adharma, ajñāna, avairāgya, and anaiśvarya) are installed, in the 
intermediate and cardinal directions, respectively. Then (PI 6.80c–​84b), the eight mūrtis 
(forms of Śiva) and the eight mūrtīśas are installed in worshipper, sun, water, air, moon, 
and ether. Their eight mūrtīśas are Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, 
and Bhīma. Finally (PI 6.84c–​85), the guardians of the directions (lokapālas: Indra, Agni, 
Yama, Rakṣeśa, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna) are installed, with their weapons, in the 
eight pots, in the directions, from east to northeast.
	 9.	 Piṅgalāmata 6.104c–​105b:
datvā baliṃ śubhāvāptir bhavet prāsādakalpanā || 6.104cd
anyathā tu mahāvighnaṃ prakurvanti vināyakāḥ | 6.105ab
	10.	 A common presentation is of 6 sets of āyas: āya, vyaya, ṛkṣa, yoni, vāra, and tithi or aṃśa. 
There are twelve āyas in a list of twelve items beginning with siddhi; ten vyayas in a list of 
ten items beginning with śikhara; twenty-​seven ṛkṣas in a list of the twenty-​seven lunar 
mansions; eight yonis in the list of eight that is dhvaja, etc.; seven vāras in a list of the seven 
days of the week; thirty tithis in a list of the thirty lunar days in a month; and nine aṃśas in 
a list of nine items beginning with taskara. In each list, some members are regarded as aus­
picious, some as inauspicious. The measurement to be tested is multiplied by a set number. 
The product of that multiplication is then divided by the number of items in the āya set. 
The remainder is checked against the corresponding āya in the set to determine whether 
the measurement is suitable or not.

	16.	 Valuable work has been done on these jīrṇoddhāra materials by, in particular, Brunner-​
Lachaux (1963, 1968, 1977, 1998), von Rospatt (2013), Tom (2013), Czerniak-​Drożdżowicz 
(2014, 2017), Sarma (2017, 2019), and Colas (1996, 2019). The edition and translation of the 
Somaśambhupaddhati by Brunner-​Lachaux includes analysis of this early Śaiva text’s ac­
count of jīrṇoddhāra. Von Rospatt, in a chapter considering jīrṇoddhāra with regard to 
the Svayambhū caitya of Kathmandu, notes that texts, both across time and also across the 
Buddhist and Hindu traditions present similar instruction on jīrṇoddhāra, with distinctions 
necessitated by differences of deity and associated mantra. Tom looks at jīrṇoddhāra in the 
context of the case of the Chovvallur Śiva temple in Kerala, which in 1997–​2001 under­
went the removal and replacement process using the instructions of the fifteenth-​century 
Tantrasamuccaya. Czerniak-​Drożdżowicz examines jīrṇoddhāra in Pāñcarātra sources. 
Sarma observes the connections between the textual record and the continued practice of 
jīrṇoddhāra in Kerala in the modern period. Colas considers the prescriptions for the man­
agement of the man-​made icon as taught in the Vimānārcanakalpa.

Chapter 25
MANDALAS and Landscape 
in Maritime Asia
Peter Sharrock
Outside India, Buddhist tantra texts and the rituals that evolved from them opened 
new and influential positions to esoteric Buddhists in the courts along the southern 
coast of Asia. Recent archaeological and iconographic evidence points to a direct appli­
cation of Buddhist mandalas in the landscape in ways that were first envisaged in tan­
tric texts but remained mostly at some distance from the royal courts. In the 8th–​11th 
centuries under the Pāla dynasty, when feudalism took on new, decentralized forms as 
populations dispersed, the great monasteries of the Ganges Valley were devising elabo­
rate mandalas of the supramundane sphere of buddhas as key soteriological aids to ac­
celerated access to buddhahood. The mandalas eventually included powerful and fierce 
Heruka forms of the supreme buddhas in the Vajrayāna (“thunderbolt vehicle”), yet the 
monastery leaders did not seize on the similarities of these mandalic structures to en­
gage with the evolving mundane feudal dependencies of the political systems Davidson 
calls “sāmanta feudalism” (2002: 137).1 Their ritual technologies for supernatural effects 
were not put at the service of their royal patrons at the intersection of the religious and 
political domains, as they were by the politically engaged contemporary Śaivas.
But outside the Indian subcontinent, in Sri Lanka, Śrīvijaya, Java, China, Korea, 
and Japan, the early “thunderbolt” technologies were molded into varied platforms of 
“state protection” Buddhism, anchored in two major mandalas that were promoted 
by the widely traveled esoteric Buddhist patriarchs Vajrabodhi from Kāñcīpuram and 
Amoghavajra from Samarkand and their Chinese, Javanese, and Japanese disciples. 
By the 12th century, when the Ganges Valley monasteries faced extinction by Islamic 
armies, the Buddhist masters in the courts of maritime Asia fully adapted the insights of 
the mature Indian monastic vehicle to the language and ritual of political imperialism, 
developing a symbiotic relationship with royal power, as well as with Śaivism.
Sanderson’s seminal 2009 study “The Śaiva Age” traces the steady absorption (and 
direct lifting) of Śaiva and Śākta texts into the esoteric Buddhist Yoginītantras. He

--- PAGE 583 ---
558      Peter Sharrock
 
detects the transfers primarily from Śaiva texts already embedded in Brahmanical 
court rituals:
now, this co-​existence of Buddhism and Śaivism under royal patronage was surely 
facilitated by the fact that the form of Buddhism adopted and developed was one 
that had equipped itself . . . with a repertoire of Tantric ceremonies that paralleled 
that of the Śaivas and indeed had modelled itself upon it, offering initiation by in­
troduction before a Maṇḍala in which the central deity of the cult and its retinue 
of divine emanations . . . through the use of Mantras, Mudrās, visualization, and 
fire-​sacrifice (homaḥ); and this was presented not only as a new and more powerful 
means of attaining Buddha-​hood but also, as in the Śaiva case, as enabling the pro­
duction of supernatural effects (siddhiḥ) such as the averting of danger (śāntiḥ), 
the harming of enemies (abhicāraḥ), and the control of the rain (varṣāpaṇam and 
ativṛṣṭidhāraṇam). . . . The latter is particularly important from the point of view of 
Buddhism’s relations with its royal patrons, since such rituals enabled it to match 
the Śaivas by promising kings more tangible benefits than the mere accumulation of 
merit through the support of the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha.
(Sanderson 2009: 124)
The supernatural powers embedded in mandalas were deployed for leveraging 
intrastate legitimization after regime change as well as interstate confrontations. The 
supramundane hierarchy captured in the mandala proffered weaponized defense 
mechanisms for interstate struggles, which found a more responsive audience outside 
the subcontinent and notably in the conflicts between the neighboring Khmer and Cam 
domains in the 12th century, between China and Java in the 13th century, as well as be­
tween Java and Śrīvijaya in the 13th and 14th centuries. The Buddhist strategists of the 
Pāla dynasty conveyed in texts an aspiration to overlay a Heruka mandala on Śaiva holy 
sites so as to implement a local form of “state protection Buddhism” that would rival the 
hold of Śaivism over the courts, but it only materialized outside India.2
This article brings together the patches of evidence scattered over the wide and varied 
geography of the southern seas to trace this royal rebirth of the Herukas in maritime 
Asia. It attempts to describe the final seaward journey of the history of fierce Buddhist 
deities that Rob Linrothe (1999) traced across the subcontinent. He concluded with 
these notable remarks on the 8-​headed, 16-​armed Heruka “Hevajra”:
if there was a Hevajra cult, it seems to have thrived in Southeast Asia. . . . Seemingly 
removed from his yogic and monastic origins, Hevajra was utilized in the royal cult, 
not as in the Ming court, to improve relations with Tibet, but as part of an attempt at 
local legitimization. . . . It appears that despite the earlier origin of the texts and ideas 
behind the Hevajra imagery, they were not influential enough to generate a lasting 
impact until the 11th or 12th century. By that time, however, the ideas and images 
quickly flowed in eastern, southern and northern directions. Islam alone proved an 
impenetrable barrier.
(Linrothe: 274)

--- PAGE 584 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      559
 
In the 11th and 12th centuries, it is possible to discern a long-​term eclectic strategy 
by Khmer Buddhists to bring the established state Śaivism under a parasol of eso­
teric Buddhism—​perhaps on the model defined in the tantras relating to the Herukas 
Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara, who then first began to figure in Khmer temple iconog­
raphy. In the late 12th century King Jayavarman VII, probably Angkor’s greatest king, 
underpinned this drive for the broader population with a tantric Buddhist triad 
headed by Bhaiṣajyaguru, Master of Medical Remedies, who presided over the world’s 
first state health system in an empire-​wide network of 102 hospitals that were free for 
all. His strategy succeeded in turning the Khmer state definitively to Buddhism. Acri 
observes that parallel Buddhist politico-​religious strategies—​though without the med­
ical innovations—​thrived in their localized adaptations in Java and Sumatra until the 
15th century (Acri 2016: 8).
Traces of such royal Heruka cults in the states of the southern seas have been detected 
for a century, but their major importance to rulers and the ways they were deployed 
is only now emerging more clearly. Few texts have survived in the tropics, so the his­
torical data is much thinner than in China, Korea, and Japan, but some recent icon 
recoveries and close studies of temple ruins have brought some clarity for example to 
a 12th-​century dispute between the Khmer empire and neighboring Campā, as well 
as to interstate confrontations some decades later on the islands of Java and Sumatra.3 
They furnish indications that the Buddhists in the south attempted to replicate the 
system of Vidyāpīṭha Śaivism, whereby Śaiva masters drew authority and supernatural 
powers to support kings from potent, networked holy pilgrimage sites. This is sketched 
in words as an aspirational strategy in two Yoginītantras, where Buddhist Bhairavas or 
Herukas are superimposed on the Śaiva Vidyāpīṭhas in a series of mandalic semicircles 
descending from Mount Kailāsa . (The aim was to create and sustain supramundane 
fields of merit over Buddhist royal domains. The compilers of the Hevajratantra and the 
Saṃvarodayatantra include the maritime polity Suvarṇadvīpa (“Golden Isle,” probably 
Sumatra) in the outer mandalic circle.4
The Hevajra System in Maritime Asia
J. J. Boeles (1966: 26) wrote an influential analysis of two Khmer Yoginī bronzes 
from Thailand and, noting Grünwedel’s (1900: 63) work on Kublai Khan’s Hevajra 
abhiṣeka, joined earlier scholars who pointed to signs of a significant royal role for the 
Hevajratantra beyond the subcontinent: “the cult of Hevajra, though its most impor­
tant rites were secret, was by no means confined to an obscure sect. It must at one time 
have been of great importance throughout the Far East. In 1261 the great Khublai Khan, 
the ruler of most of Asia and part of Europe, was consecrated as Hevajra by means 
of abhiṣeka rites exactly like those expounded in the Hevajrasekaprakriyā [ceremony 
manual]” (see Finot 1934). Heruka icons played a role on both sides of a long dispute 
over Vijaya, a new Cam deep water port and a new capital that the Cams and Khmers

--- PAGE 585 ---
560      Peter Sharrock
 
collaborated in building so both their economies would benefit from the burgeoning 
Song dynasty maritime trade. A Cam prince named Vidyānandana was brought to 
the Khmer court by King Jayavarman VII, who had won his own spurs fighting along­
side a Cam king in Campā for several years in his early life. The martial prowess of 
Vidyānandana emerged when he put down the most serious Khmer insurrection 
against Jayavarman soon after the king seized power in 1182 CE. He was then chosen 
to lead a Khmer army to recover control of the Vijaya port, where a faction opposed 
the Khmer presence. He successfully fought to install a Khmer prince on the Vijaya 
throne and took up a vassal king position further south. When Cam rebels overthrew 
the Khmer prince within a year, Vidyānandana came up to end the rebellion but then 
broke with his patron in Angkor and proclaimed himself King Sūryavarman of Vijaya 
and Pāṇḍuraṅga.5 After defeating another Khmer force sent against him, he erected a 
Buddhist temple to Heruka in 1194 CE at the major Cam Śaiva mountain temple com­
plex of Mỹ Sơn. The Heruka icon is lost, but the 3 × 3 m brick base of his “mansion” 
survives in Mỹ Sơn along with the stela numbered C. 92B by French epigraphy that 
recounts his life. His Heruka jinābhiṣekaḥ presumably transmitted a message of defi­
ance and perhaps respect to Jayavarman in Angkor.
Heruka in the Bayon
Vidyānandana’s defiance was eventually overcome, and he was forced into exile by a 
third Khmer army.6 With Campā again closely aligned with Angkor, Jayavarman raised 
his own 3.6 m Heruka in a sanctuary at the main eastern entrance to the Bayon, ac­
cording to experts now working on the monument. Wear marks from the Heruka’s large 
pedestal have been identified on the sandstone floor. Such findings lend support to a 
claim by Bautze-​Picron that “Hevajra is the protector the State in Cambodia and per­
haps also Campā whereas it is Mahākāla who assumes this role in the Yuan Empire” 
(Bautze-​Picron 2014: 107). After discussing the erection of Heruka statues in war in this 
case, Ācārya Malcolm Smith, at a conference in 2018 on tantra at the Victoria and Albert 
Museum in London, said similar confrontations involving a mix of sacred consecra­
tion and political expediency are known in Tibetan history, when the message was that 
both parties had attained participation in the supreme Heruka/​Vajrasattva state of being 
that was way beyond violence, so this should be reflected in the microcosm between the 
earthly rivals. War often followed, however. Jayavarman’s response was to send a third 
Khmer army over the mountains to Vijaya, which defeated Vidyānandana in 1203 and 
drove him into exile. Raising Heruka in the Bayon could then have been the ceremonial 
high point of Jayavarman’s indrābhiśeka, or second coronation, the Indic consecration 
that confers cakravartin status following a foreign acquisition.7
Reconstructing the great Heruka of the Bayon that countered that in Vidyānandana’s 
Mỹ Sơn mansion has taken almost a century. Some of the difficulty of uncovering the 
story of the statue, which must have been known to all Angkorians in the 13th century,

--- PAGE 586 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      561
 
lies in the absence of a Bayon dedication stela, which may have identified the original 
pantheon of the builder. Plus, the large stone Hevajra was dismembered and some of the 
parts dumped in the forest outside the city. With the scattered pieces mostly reunited, 
Cunin produced a computer simulation of the whole statue as it was erected at the Bayon 
main entrance (fig. 25.1).8
This huge stone Heruka erected in a prominent exoteric position in the state temple 
faced east across the mountains to Mỹ Sơn and Vijaya, where Vidyānanda had raised his 
Heruka. Ācārya Smith took the view that only people initiated into the Heruka would 
thenceforth be allowed to pass into the temple. He suggested a samaya or pledge cere­
mony with water would be required. This could be the explanation long sought by art 
historians for why so many bronze conch-​holders, embossed with the Hevajra mandala 
of the deity in a circle of eight Yoginīs, were discovered in Angkor and reached museum 
collections around the world. At least a dozen are in the material record, and they would 
have more than supplied the samaya needs of the citizens residing around the temples 
Jayavarman built in Angkor (Sharrock 2009: 112).
The bust (see fig. 25.2) was sold to the New York Metropolitan Museum in 1937, and 
the legs, arms, and broken hands were left in the forest. The feet were finally recovered 
from a pond in front of the temple and later identified by Cunin.

[1983] 2004: 16) and the East Javanese King Kṛtanagara both underwent Heruka 
consecrations ahead of Kublai’s eventually unsuccessful seaborne invasion of Java. A

pattern thus emerges in interstate confrontations in which supramundane esoteric 
Buddhist mandalas were invoked to underpin imperial strategies in the mundane 
sphere. I will argue that resurgent Khmer Buddhists of the 11th and 12th centuries cast 
a ritual mantle over the temple landscape that had established a Śaiva state over the 
preceding three centuries, and that this would contribute to a definitive Khmer turn 
to Buddhism. The supernatural powers conceived as embedded in mandalas were 
deployed for leveraging intrastate legitimization after regime change as well as in inter­
state confrontations. The supramundane hierarchy captured in the mandalas proffered 
weaponized defense mechanisms for interstate struggles, and such strategies found 
a more responsive audience outside the subcontinent, where the Buddhists were be­
coming gradually more isolated from the courts and the people. But these mechanisms 
were adopted outside India for direct application in realpolitik—​as may be discerned 
in the conflicts between the neighboring Khmer and Cam domains in the 12th century, 
between China and Java in the 13th century, and between Java and Śrīvijaya in the 13th 
and 14th centuries.

(Photo by Peter Sharrock)

--- PAGE 588 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      563
 
Although these royal invocations of supernatural power were based on metaphysics 
rather than physics, a modern reader may find some value in comparing them with 
the 20th-​century Cold War nuclear standoff between the United States and the Soviet 
Union. Bade (2016: 155) glosses the Kublai-​Kṛtanagara confrontation in these terms: “as 
a technique for obtaining power and control over the world, Tantric Buddhism—​and 
especially its rituals—​came to occupy the same place in 13th and 14th century Asian 
societies that science and technology occupies in our own time. The advocates of sci­
entific method, like the advocates of Tantric Buddhism, have claimed that this method 
alone leads to knowledge and that knowledge is power.” The power of the new technology 
is touched on in the fifth opening line in the Chinese version of the Hevajratantra: “there 
is great power in this learning by which one is capable of various performances, viz. 
subjugating, petrifying, or driving away the army of others” (Willemen [1983] 2004: 35). 
Though a far cry from what is known of early Buddhism and Śākyamuni’s 5th-​century 
BCE call in Magadha for withdrawal from normal family life into a saṅgha focused on 
meditation and study, both contexts shared a claim to breakthrough mechanisms to at­
tain a new, applicable, and efficacious form of knowledge. The later esoteric Buddhist 
state protection mechanisms may seem to run counter to the spirit of Emperor Aśoka’s 
standing down his army after the brutal 261 BCE battle for Kaliṅga, its earth plowed 
with salt, and then governing the Mauryan state through personalized Buddhist edicts, 
administered by civilian envoys (Thapar 1961: 62). But Aśoka’s remarkable accomplish­
ment barely survived his reign, and the saṅgha leaders were soon faced with the return 
of conquering Buddhist kṣatriyas.
The propagation of the mandala knowledge is recorded in the 7th century in the 
journeys of learned and enterprising monks over the land silk routes. It expands in 
the 8th century from the monasteries and courts of south India and Sri Lanka to Java, 
Śrīvijaya, and then Tang China (with disciples later moving to Korea and Japan). The 
texts of the Yogatantras and the Womb-​realm and Vajra-​realm mandalas they defined 
would soon be impacting the design of impressive and unprecedented ceremonial 
centers being built by a series of expanding rice empires in the south, and were captured 
in Chinese translations, conserved in state archives, and reflected in state rituals.9
Sanderson (2009: 125) notes that the “monarch is not mentioned in the 
treatments of initiation given in the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi [MVS] and 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha [STTS], the two great Tantras that were translated into 
Chinese in the early eighth century and formed the basis of the Way of Mantras there 
and in the Japanese Shingon and Tendai sects.” The focus was on soteriology for the 
monastic community. Yet Amoghavajra (Chinese name Bukong), the renowned trans­
lator monk from Sogdiana, who perhaps met his preceptor Vajrabodhi (Chinese name 
Jin’gangzhi) at a young age in Java (Abé 1999: 222–​223; Sundberg, Jeffrey, and Rolf 
Giebel 2011: 30) became deeply involved in imperial state protection through esoteric 
ritual. Amoghavajra’s official biography shows him being called on to resolve crises 
of the Tang emperors—​bringing rain to end droughts, repelling a Tibetan army at the 
border, helping to restore the Tang after the An Lushan rebellion and then consecrating 
Emperor Suzong as cakravartin (Lehnert 2012: 262), and holding extended faith

--- PAGE 589 ---
564      Peter Sharrock
 
propagation ceremonies for thousands of courtiers and army officers.10 Charles Orzech 
(1998: 138) reaches the conclusion that the Buddhists’ “teachings were shaped both by 
their particular religious ideologies and by imperial needs. Chinese Esoteric Buddhism 
in the eighth century was driven by political utility.”
With their entry at court level in maritime Asia, the Buddhists’ teachings in cos­
mology, soteriology, and ritual technology found expression in large royal ceremonial 
centers, the remnants of which form the bulk of the material record that has come down 
to us. In addition, the diaries of traveling Indian, Chinese, and Korean monks open rare, 
illuminating windows into how Buddhist courts and communities along the sea lanes 
were linked into an interactive network.
By the 10th century, images took a tantric turn to represent the fierce protagonist 
deities of the later esoteric Buddhist Yoginītantras, which had developed in Ganges 
Valley monasteries and in Bengal under the Pāla dynasty. By the time the Sena kings 
replaced the Pālas in 1070 CE, resplendent Heruka deities dancing on māra (demons) 
had been erected in monasteries in southern Bengal, Nālandā, Ratnagiri (Odisha), 
and Sarnath. No known inscription, however, links these icons to royal patronage. The 
long infusion of tantric techniques into Buddhist scriptures was manifested in saṃsāra 
terms only in fierce-​eyed deities, carved into monastery walls, with fangs, skull chaplets, 
flourishing vajras (thunderbolt ritual instruments), and grasping khaṭvāṅga (skull 
staffs), like those at Śubhapur (Comilla) and the funerary stūpa at Ratnagiri (Odisha).11 
Sanderson sees the Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara as marking the beginning 
of the full appropriation of Vidyāpīṭha Śaivism into the Yoginītantras.12
First, [the Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara] introduces or brings 
to the fore the cult of the deity Heruka with an iconography inspired by that of 
the Bhairavas of the Vidyāpīṭha with their accoutrements and attributes of the 
cremation-​ground dwelling Kāpālika Śaiva ascetic. According to the visualization 
given by Ānandagarbha he has four faces and eight arms, emerging as the transfor­
mation of a dark blue flaming Vajra, itself a transformation of a dark blue syllable 
HRĪḤ. The central face is fierce (raudram), those to its right and left expressive 
of delusion and erotic passion, and that behind open-​mouthed to devour. In his 
two uppermost hands he holds the freshly flayed skin of Bhairava over his back, in 
the two below a bow and arrows, in the third right in descent he shakes a blazing 
three-​pronged Vajra, and in the fourth a skull-​bowl filled with human blood 
(mahāraktam). In the third left in descent he brandishes the Kāpālika’s skull-​staff 
(khaṭvāṅgaḥ), topped with a three-​pronged Vajra and adorned with bells, and in 
the fourth a skull-​bowl filled with human flesh (mahāmāṃsam).
(Sanderson 2009: 148)
The fierce emanations of the supreme buddhas sharing features with tantric Śaiva-​Śākta 
deities signaled the incorporation into the monastic setting of a range of intense, se­
cret rituals, which included antinomian actions, taboo substances, and sexual yoga. 
Sanderson claims the first monks who specialized in the new rituals had already ac­
quired expertise and practice as Śaiva initiands.

--- PAGE 590 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      565
 
The Khmer Empire
The Yogatantras reached the Khmer domains in the 10th century when the liberal King 
Rājendravarman II returned the capital to Yaśodharapura (Angkor) from Koh Ker. 
This Śaiva monarch permitted a Buddhist revival through his polymath minister-​
general-​architect Kavīndrārimathana, who in c. 953 CE built the Bat Cuṃ shrine at the 
heart of the new city on the eastern edge of Angkor and dedicated it to the Buddha, 
Vajrapāṇi, and Divyadevī (Prajñāpāramitā). Thereafter Rājendravarman’s son and suc­
cessor, the Buddhist King Jayavarman V, financed a string of āśramas for the study of 
the root Yogatantra STTS and Śākyamitra’s learned 9th-​century ṭīkā (commentary). 
Jayavarman’s ācārya (preceptor) Kīrtipaṇḍita had them brought to Angkor after “having 
searched in a foreign kingdom.”13 Jayavarman’s Takeo state temple, however, was dedi­
cated to Śiva, in line with the Brahmanical tradition from the founding of the state in 
802 CE. Religious tolerance and eclecticism seem to have come easily to the Khmers (see 
Sanderson 2004: 233, 435).
Phimai
The closing decades of the 11th century saw religious and political regime change in the 
Khmer domains. The esoteric Buddhist Mahīdharapura dynasty seized power, guided 
by the Śaiva strategist and rājaguru Śrī Divākarapaṇḍita (fig. 25.3), who would crown 
three kings (two Buddhist, one Vaiṣṇava). This religious pivot brought a northern vassal 
ruler to the throne as King Jayavarman VI in 1080 CE (Briggs [1951] 1999: 188). Within a 
century the dynasty would make Angkor one of the largest cities outside China.
In Phimai, Divākarapaṇḍita would have been steeped in both Vidyāpīṭha Śaivism as 
well as Yoginītantra strategies developed in the monasteries of 10th-​ and 11th-​century 
Pāla-​Sena Bengal and Bihar and adopted in the Buddhist revival in Tibet. Davidson 
(2005: 41) sees this in Tibet as a Buddhist counterstrategy that consisted in overlaying 
the Cakrasaṃvara mandala on the established 108 Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha holy sites in India. 
He published a hand-​drawn map titled “Sites of Indian Buddhist Tantric Activity 10th–​
11th Centuries” in which the Heruka emitted by the supreme Buddha Vajrasattva/​
Vajradhara held the center of the mandala on Mount Kailaśa above three concentric and 
roughly semicircular rings of pīṭhas (sacred sites) with eight Bhairavas each (fig. 25.4): 
“adapted from a story articulated in such yoga-​tantra works as the Sarvatathāgata-​
tattvasaṁgraha, Cakrasaṃvara proponents maintained that the eternal Buddha 
Vajradhara emanated a form, Heruka, to control Maheśvara (Śiva) and his twenty-​
four Bhairavas, along with their consorts. Maheśvara was eventually humiliated and 
destroyed, and Heruka took his place on top of Mount Sumeru, with the 24 Bhairavas 
controlling the 24 pilgrimage sites of India” (Davidson 2005: 241). This Buddhist

Interestingly, the pīṭhas targeted by the tantric masters in both of these texts include, 
in the outer ring, Suvarṇadvīpa (“Golden Isle,” for Sumatra or the adjacent Thai/​Malay 
peninsula). “Because of its interest in sacred geography, some Indian masters of the 
Cakrasaṃvara were well aware that sacred sites existed outside India as well as inside 
it, and the list includes Suvarṇadvīpa, a medieval kingdom variously located in Burma 
[probably Suvarṇabhūmi, ‘land of gold’] or Indonesia” (Davidson 2005: 241).14
In the burgeoning Khmer empire of the late 11th century, Divākarapaṇḍita was 
the leading religious advisor (rājaguru) to a Buddhist usurper, who became King 
Jayavarman VI, the founder of the Mahīdharapura dynasty that would, within a cen­
tury, take Angkor to its apogee.15 The young brahman would have been instrumental in 
selecting such a Heruka-​mandala concept of alignment with established major religious 
centers as a means of asserting the new dynasty’s support for the long-​embedded Śaiva 
holy sites of the kingdom. Sanderson records, on the basis of inscription K. 194 (A9–​
B17), how the wealth bestowed on Divākarapaṇḍita for the coronation of Sūryavarman 
II was personally borne by the guru to key religious sites in the form of gifts to Śiva from 
the new (Vaiṣṇava) king:
Divākarapaṇḍita . . . is said to have followed this practice as Vraḥ Guru under 
Jayavarman VI (r. 1080–​1107), Dharaṇīndravarman I (r. 1107–​1112) and Sūryavarman 
II (r. 1113–​c. 1150). We are told that after he had performed the royal consecration 
of Sūryavarman II, given him Śaiva initiation, taught him the Śaiva scriptures and 
other branches of learning, and been invited to perform the Koṭihoma and other 
annual brahmanical sacrifices for him, he was given golden palanquins and many 
other valuables so that he could visit various sacred sites around the kingdom and 
give these to the deities installed there. . . . At each of these he had a water-​reservoir 
excavated, founded a hermitage, gave it slaves and villages and made an endowment 
to provide for worship.
(Sanderson 2004: 420)
The iconography of Phimai, constructed in the reign of Jayavarman VI, is truly note­
worthy. The most striking image is a Khmer Heruka on the eastern lintel that appears to 
be an unorthodox, multiheaded, eight-​armed martial representation of Cakrasaṃvara, 
bursting out of a bloodied elephant hide of illusion and trampling crowned māras 
on the elephant’s head. The elephant hide is key to his identification here. In his 2007 
translation of the Śrīcakrasaṃvara-​nāmā-​mahāyoginī-​tantra-​rāja, or Laghusaṃvara, 
David Gray (2007: 36) translates the name Cakrasaṃvara as “the binding of the wheels” 
of kāyavākcitta (body, speech, mind). As the representation of a spiritual embrace of 
the entire human saṃsāra (“wandering through phenomena”), this could have poten­
tial application in the political world, and perhaps in the manner achieved by Guru 
Divākarapaṇḍita. Divakārapaṇḍita’s plan to extend a new sacred Buddhist geography 
across the sacred sites of the empire was first applied with circumspection. Based in 
Phimai, a traditionally Buddhist region in the northwestern wing of the empire, rather 
than in Brahmanical Angkor, the caution of the king and his guru may have reflected

--- PAGE 594 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      569
 
trepidation at the response of the Śaiva landowning establishment. Angkor remained 
under the sway of Śiva in the stately Baphuon pyramidal temple, set beside the palace. 
It would take another century before another esoteric Buddhist king—​Jayavarman 
VII—​would plant Heruka in the center of Angkor within the first Buddhist state temple. 
Yet religious tolerance was the norm in the ancient Khmer domains. It was possible for 
Divākarapaṇḍita, the most eminent Śaiva master of his time, to officiate over the coro­
nation of two Buddhists and one Vaiṣṇava king, and to do this with the traditional 802 
CE Śaiva cakravartin coronation ritual called devarāja.
In an unpublished lecture at a London colloquium Hiram Woodward observed a 
parallel between the stepped Greek cross base of the Bayon in its early phase (1.13), 
recorded by archaeo-​architect Olivier Cunin (see fig. 25.5), and the stepped base of a 
well-​known gilt bronze Hevajra icon in the National Museum of Cambodia (fig. 25.7). 
The Bayon was built first as a set of sanctuaries around a central tower on a raised base 
in the shape of a Greek cross (fig. 25.5). Giant faces as tall as a person are carved as 
addorsed heads on the stone tower that rises 43 m over the city (fig. 25.6). The bronze 
FIGURE 25.5.  Computer reconstruction of the first phase of the Bayon.
(Courtesy O. Cunin)

570      Peter Sharrock
 
mandala with a stepped Greek cross base is set in a miniature sanctuary (Dalsheimer 
2001: 268), which frames the dancing deity in a circle of his eight dancing Yoginīs 
(fig. 25.7). The bronze Hevajra with 8 yogini dancing around the deity is 20cm tall. 
It has a temple-​like structure set over the figures on a stepped base in the shape of 
a Greek cross. Woodward pointed out that the first phase of building the Bayon, re­
vealed by Cunin, was a central sanctuary bearing giant faces with smaller sanctuaries 
set round it also in the shape of a Greek cross, raising the question whether the Bayon 
is a blown-​up rendering of the supreme Buddha Hevajra/​Vajrasattva in architectural 
form. Bruno Dagens (2003: 243) considered that “it is the invention of the face towers 
that makes architecture slide towards monumental statuary and temples towards di­
vine image.”(my translation). T. S. Maxwell (2007: 86) said the face-​towers turned the

temple into a god: “in terms of architectural theory, the new method of depicting the 
four faces on the towers of Jayavarman’s temples appears to represent . . . a sweeping 
liberalization of architecture and iconography, because this method abandons the ca­
nonical distinctions between vāstu [architecture] and śilpa [sculpture]. . . . The Khmer 
temple was therefore no longer merely a devagṛha, the traditional Indian ‘house of 
God,’ it became itself a God.”
Projecting the mandala of state in architecture was not confined to the capital. The 
first tower with giant faces was constructed at the old Buddhist temple of Preah Khan 
of Kompong Svay, east of the capital. Cunin records 59 face-​towers at the Bayon, after 
he tracked the stones bearing parts of carved faces from the collapsed towers (2005:

83–​85), and 47 at Banteay Chhmar, 110 k northwest of the capital under the Dangrek 
mountains. From the viewpoint of sacred geography, the temples with the face-​
towers fit into a circle centered on Angkor and appearing to define a new Buddhist 
mandala of state (fig. 25.8) that implants the face-​tower deity across the kingdom, 
somewhat in the way Amoghavajra created the state as a field of merit on Mount 
Wutai in 767 (as noted earlier). If the face-​towers project a Heruka mandala over 
the formerly Brahmanical Khmer state, Jayavarman can be seen as maintaining the 
Divākarapaṇḍita strategy.
