MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      573
 
East Java
A political confrontation between Java and China that included “supreme buddha 
consecrations” occurred half a century later when the Siṅhasāri king Kṛtanagara (r. 
1268–​1292 CE) underwent a consecration after receiving and injuring an envoy of the 
Yuan emperor, Kublai Khan (r. 1260–​1294 CE), who had constructed a large fleet and 
was threatening a naval invasion. Thomas M. Hunter’s reading of the Sanskrit inscrip­
tion on the base of the so-​called Joko Dolog statue of the Jina Akṣobhya, now in a park 
in Surabaya, commemorates both the reunification of Java by his father and his own 
second consecration of this image of Akṣobhya in 1289 CE:
this second consecration of the image of Akṣobhya was accompanied by a ritual 
in which Kṛtanagara was initiated according to the rites of Mahākṣobhya. . . . As 
scholars have largely agreed since the idea was first advanced by J. L. Moens (1924: 
544), Kṛtanagara’s consecration into the ritual path of Akṣobhya (and hence the 
Guhyasāmaja Tantra) appears to have been intended to counteract the ritual power 
gained by the Yuan emperor Kublai Khan through his consecrations in 1264 and 
1269 as Hevajra, the central Jina of the Hevajra Tantra. This connects the event with 
Kṛtanagara’s earlier gift to Mauliwarmadewa, for this monarch controlled the Melaka 
Straits, which was the linch-​pin in the all-​important international sea trade, and an 
obvious point that needed to be defended at all costs from the expansionist politics 
of Kublai Khan.
(Hunter 2007: 40)
The Yuan emperor’s empowerment in Hevajra was performed by Tibetan Sakya 
master Phakpa and inaugurated a century of Tibetic Buddhism as the official religion 
of China under Mongol rulers; before the Sakya transmission it was deemed heter­
odox under the Ming (1368–​1644 CE; Elacqua 2017: 1304). David Bade, in his reading 
of the Kublai-​Kṛtanagara confrontation, argues that both rulers turned to the esoteric 
Buddhists for a new vision when they were faced with international issues of a scope 
and complexity unknown in their own cultures. They put their trust in a compelling 
image of a cakravartin at the pinnacle of a mandala that mirrored the organization 
of the macrocosm. Lokesh Chandra (Lokesh Chandra and Sudarshana Devi Singhal 
1995: 156) sees Kṛtanagara’s response as aimed both to arrest the Mongol threat “and 
to pay homage to the Mongol Emperor.” Paying homage seems aligned with Ācārya 
Smith’s view (in 2018, see above) that participation in the supreme Heruka/​Vajrasattva 
state of being took initiates beyond violence and that this should be reflected in mun­
dane interstate actions.
Kṛtanagara was killed in 1292 CE before the huge Mongol fleet landed, but the in­
vasion failed (as the others did in Japan and Vietnam), and the East Javanese dynasty 
“was restored in 1294 CE by [Kṛtanagara’s son-​in-​law] Raden Wijaya, who tricked 
Kubilai’s invading forces into attacking [his rival] Jayakatwang, then turned on them

--- PAGE 599 ---
574      Peter Sharrock
 
and destroyed them as they celebrated victory” (Hunter 2007: 28).16 Hunter attributes 
the ongoing esoteric Buddhist tradition in Java and Sumatra to the lasting impression 
made by Kṛtanagara’s fusion of Śaivism and Buddhism to attain political and spiritual 
unity both in Java and in his growing empire. In 1292 CE Kṛtanagara was enshrined at 
Candi Jawi in a single Śiva-​Buddha image after his “release into the realms of Śiwa and 
Buddha (mokteng siwa-​buddha-​loka)” (Hunter 2007: 41).
FIGURE 25.9.  Ādityavarman’s Bhairava with Akṣobhya above the crown, Jakarta national Museum.
(Photos by Peter Sharrock)

--- PAGE 600 ---
MANDALAS and Landscape in Maritime Asia      575
 
Sumatra
Andrea Acri sees the esoteric Buddhist cults of Jayavarman VII, Kṛtanagara, and 
Kublai Khan as a “second wave” that long remained vital in maritime Asia (2016: 
8, 19–​22). In the early 11th century, the collapsing Pāla dynasty in northern India 
led to an exodus from the Ganges Valley monasteries in Bengal and Bihar. The fu­
ture Tibetan Buddhist patriarch Atīśa (982–​1054 CE) undertook the sea passage to 
Śrīvijaya, where he studied at the feet of the guru Dharmakīrti from 1013 to 1025 CE, 
presumably at the pīṭha named Suvarṇadvīpa (Land of Gold) in the lists cited in the 
Hevajratantra and the Saṁvarodayatantra. Tibetan archives credit Dharmakīrti with 
a commentary on the tantra. Schoterman ([1986] 2016: 115) notes campaigns from 
Kabul in 1018 by Mahmūd of Ghaznī “almost reaching Benares (which he plundered 
in 1033) and attacking Somnāth (Kathiawar) in 1024.” For a time Suvarṇadvīpa 
FIGURE 25.10.  Ādityavarman’s Bhairava with Akṣobhya above the crown, Jakarta national Museum.
(Photos by Peter Sharrock)

--- PAGE 601 ---
576      Peter Sharrock
 
emerged as a haven for Buddhist study. But this was soon to change. The Cōḻa army 
marched from south India to the north and then became the first Indian dynasty to 
expand its empire by sea. In 1025 CE the Cōḻa fleet attacked and largely destroyed 
Palembang and Jambi on Sumatra, as well as Kedah on the Malay peninsula. Months 
before this, Atiśa returned to Bengal to become abbot of Vikramaśīla, before being 
eventually being invited to Tibet in 1040 CE to begin the celebrated reform mission 
of his remaining 14 years.
During the subsequent expansion of the Majapahit golden age under King Hayam 
Wuruk (r. 1350–​1389 CE), celebrated today as setting the bounds of modern Indonesia, 
one of the king’s cousins moved to Sumatra as King Ādityavarman (c. 1347–​1379), 
securing control the gold mines and the trade through the Melaka Straits. He even­
tually asserted autonomy within the now sprawling empire by adding an epigraph 
rededicating to himself the Amoghapāśa stela that King Kṛtanagara had sent to Sumatra 
decades earlier to celebrate a marriage alliance. At Sungai Langsat King Ādityavarman 
raised Indonesia’s largest known statue, a 4.4 m Bhairava with bulging eyes and a 
knife at his chest, standing on a Siṅhasāri-​style skull pedestal and with Akṣobhya in 
bhumisparṣamudrā set in his huge ball of ascetic hair (figs. 25.9 and 25.10). The image 
is quite unlike any made in Sumatra and may one day be identified as King Kṛtanagara’s 
final Śiva-​Buddha image erected in Candi Jawi, his mortuary temple, which is defined 
thus in a courtly poem:
And within there was a splendid Shiva-​image, its beauty fitting, without parallel
(With) an image of Aksobhya above the crown, of that there can be no doubt.
(Robson 1995:131; Deśawarnana [Nāgarakṛtāgama] 56.2)
This brings to an end the overt signs of the long “second wave” of royal esoteric cults 
in maritime Asia. The ritual technology of the Heruka-​mandalas, the fruit of a histor­
ical fusion of Indic tantric Śaiva and Buddhist ideologies, attained its political flores­
cence not in the subcontinent, where its long-​term application was cut short by the rise 
of armed Islam, but in the politico-​religious strategies of the royal courts of maritime 
Asia from Phimai to Angkor to Mỹ Sơn to Singhasāri and Sumatra over more than three 
centuries.

Buddhist Tantras bearing many other names of which the most important are Hevajra and 
Heruka.”

Introduction
Mandala: Origin, Meaning, and Ritual Importance
The idea of a mandala with the central figure representing a supreme deity and di­
rectional figures as subordinate aspects closely reflects the idea of a supreme king 
surrounded by vassals who are expected to play local landlords rather than independent 
rulers (Davidson 2002; Samuel [2002] 2014). This very nature of a mandala serves as 
a perfect hierarchical plan of political and social structure, offering a visual device for 
arranging space, a portable model (Smith 1978: 292) of the perfect world that can be 
used in various contexts and across geographies.
Works on Indian tantric Buddhism have identified the individual practitioner’s 
pursuit of kingship and dominion as the central defining metaphor of the tantric 
literature (Davidson 2002; Samuel ([2002] 2014). From this perspective, mandalas 
symbolize not only spiritual enlightenment but also a model used to realize a polit­
ical ideology. While painted mandalas may normally be used for meditation, they 
also emplace ritual magic serving the sovereignty. How then are ritual experience 
and belief inextricably linked with notions of power and ideology promoted by state 
religion and architecture?
Acri (2016a: 13) sees the construction of several monuments during the 7th to 10th 
centuries across maritime Asia as the “first wave of Buddhism.” These monuments 
embedded the Garbhadhātu, Vajradhātu mandalas or their modified versions in their 
architecture, as seen in northeast India, Bangladesh, Central Java, and Vietnam. They

--- PAGE 607 ---
582      Swati Chemburkar
 
propagated images, texts, and practices associated with deities such as Avalokiteśvara, 
Mañjuśrī, Vajrapāṇi, Jina Buddhas, Vairocana, Tārā, and Prajñāparamitā.
After the sudden decline of royal support around the mid-​9th century, tan­
tric Buddhism gained momentum again in the 11th century and remained in force 
through the next two centuries across maritime Asia. The “second wave of Esoteric 
Buddhism” made way for construction activity in East Java, Sumatra, Thailand, and 
Cambodia (Acri 2016a: 13, 19). These monuments propagated images, texts, and 
practices related to the ferocious forms of Vajrapāṇi, Vajrasattva, Heruka, Saṃvara, 
and Hevajra.
The architectural contexts of monuments across maritime Asia constructed on the 
basis of mandalas has hardly been examined. While textual studies have been pri­
mary, this article focuses on “common architectural language” and linkages between 
monuments built across wide geography as a valid and necessary source of evidence 
and follows a “comparative-​coherentist” approach. It remains attentive to textual and 
epigraphical evidences as well as living traditions of the Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu 
mandalas in Japan and Tibet.
The Architectural and Ritual Elements of a Mandala
The representation of mandalas in various media, especially in paintings (see fig. 26.1), 
is the hallmark of tantric Buddhism. The outer enclosure is normally a circle or a square 
border that encloses the sacred space of a mandala. Demons, snakes, marginal beings, 
a circle of flames, or eight cemeteries marked this border, symbolizing fear of death, 
which the adept has to overcome to be admitted to the center. A T-​shaped gate is placed 
in the middle of each side of the border, and a protecting wall joins all the four gates. A 
canopy protected by marine monsters rises above these gates.
Supreme Buddha sits at the center of a mandala. The other Buddhas and bodhisattvas 
live within the proximity of this center. They assume their positions based on the 
Buddha’s will and through his power of bestowing coronation on them. They reflect 
his entourage in their own segmentary entourages and ultimately dissolve into him. 
Practitioners who receive this coronation gain explicit authority to engage and manipu­
late phenomenal existence. Thus, a mandala represents a spiritual state but also suggests 
its inevitable political application. Davidson (2002: 131) has argued that the distinctive 
use of mandalas in tantric Buddhism is a product of the loss of patronage in medieval 
sāmanta feudalism and the growing importance of the imperial metaphors of the “su­
preme overlord” (rajādhirāja) or “universal ruler” (cakravartin).
When this highly complex symbol in paintings is transformed into architecture, it 
follows a simple iconographical frame. The fundamental design is a fourfold symmet­
rical building with a dominating inaccessible or accessible central structure built on 
receding terraces inside a symmetrical enclosure. The terraces confine circumambula­
tory paths that are often adorned with narrative reliefs. The main deity of a mandala

--- PAGE 608 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      583
 
resides in the central structure like a king or queen, accompanied by subordinate deities 
installed in surrounding shrines.
Mandala paintings have limitations, since they represent a three-​dimensional ob­
ject in a two-​dimensional format, but the painters try to solve this problem by drawing 
a combination of elements in the ground plan and in the elevation perspective, as 
observed by Brauen (1997: 52). The vocabulary to read the painted mandala is related to 
palace construction and not a temple building, making the royal metaphor of a mandala 
clear. The several terms assigned to the residences of the mandala divinities are those

employed for palaces and pavilions in Indian medieval architectural manuals such as 
Mayamata (Dagens 1985: 119, 148, 176, 203).1
The Template in Architecture: Mandala on the Move
Mandalas have a centrally oriented hierarchical relationship between the different seats/​
fields occupied by the Buddhas, and their distance from the center. Buddhas occupying 
different seats are less important than to the central seat itself and its hierarchical re­
lation to other seats. The Buddhas are interchangeable and sometimes accommodate 
non-​Buddhist deities too (Tucci 1961: 35) The theme of the domestication of a deity from 
non-​Buddhist outsider to Buddhist insider plays a major role in the development of the 
mandala. Thus, we find various themes, including: to tame, to subdue, to conquer, to cul­
tivate (waste land?), to civilize (the nation?), to educate, to discipline, and to punish. All 
these terms relate to the Buddhist quest for cultural and religious hegemony, a project 
described in the rhetoric of “cultivation” and “domestication,” serving imperial interests 
in organizing political and social landscapes (Samuel 1993: 218).
The mandala is an abstract topography that can be imposed upon various kinds of so­
cial spaces, acting as a mold for architecture. In considering the role of the Garbhadhātu 
and Vajradhātu mandalas in the Buddhist world, it is crucial to understand how ter­
ritory was transformed into something recognizably Buddhist in order to create 
palimpsestuous architectural landscapes across the Buddhist world.
Earliest Architectural Mandalas in Northeastern India
The strong position enjoyed by Buddhists during the Gupta period (320–​550 CE) in 
India underwent major change during the medieval period. Internal military situations 
and conflicts within India led to new kinds of patronage towards monastery complexes. 
Davidson (2002: 166) sees the new institutional tantric Buddhism creating new termi­
nology in architecture and ritual systems in response to the rise of feudalism in the 7th 
century. The sūtras of Mahayāna tradition were replaced by ritual works or tantras, in 
which the Buddha was depicted as a king wearing a crown and in full regalia; the monks 
received the coronation ritual and became divine in the process, and they presented 
dharma as a means of state protection. They performed the rituals to bring peace to

--- PAGE 610 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      585
 
the war-​stricken lands, wealth to the poor, control from chaos, and destruction to the 
enemies of religion. Here, they envisioned the spiritual state filled with Buddhas and 
bodhisattvas, worldly beings, divine families, and their dwellings, a vision that found 
concrete expression in the form of mandalas.
Around this time, the four Buddhas of otherworldly realms were added to stūpas 
as the feature of Buddhist sites (Chakrabarti 1995: 200). The earliest tantric Buddhist 
mandalas—​Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu—​arranged four Jina Buddhas (Amitābha, 
Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi) around the central Vairocana to 
become the principal pentad of the mandalas. The arrangement of four chapels is 
seen at the 8th ​century Kesariya stūpa/​mandala in Bihar (figs. 26.2–​4) and some of 
the important monastic sites in Odisha. Even though the cruciform arrangement is 
visible at the topmost stūpa level of Kesariya, the exact iconographic program relating 
to any specific mandala is difficult to ascertain given the partly excavated nature of 
the site.2 Along with the four Buddhas, eight bodhisattvas are known to have played 
an important role in the formulation of the Garbhadhātu mandala.3 The standard 
group of eight bodhisattvas was established by the middle of the 7th century in India 
(Tanaka 2018: 31).

pentad of the mandalas into architecture is seen at the Somapura monastery in 
northeastern India.

Founded at the end of the 8th century by the Pāla king Dharmapāla (775–​810 CE), 
Somapura soon became a tantric center (Bhattacharya and Haque 2000: 434; Das and 
Chattopadhaya 1980: 111; Dikshit 1938: 15; Dutt [1962] 2003: 374; figs. 26.14–​16). The 
imposing cruciform brick structure in the center of the monastery is raised on three 
receding terraces with circumambulatory paths and a flight of stairs on the north side.5 
Four shrine halls extend at cardinal directions on the second terrace from a hollow, in­
accessible shaft that probably held the Buddha statues and ritual activities. The shaft 
would have served as a base for the superstructure (Dikshit 1938: 14; Chakrabarti 2001: 
115; Mayer 1961: 30). Hevajra fragments and a bronze Buddha torso were recovered from 
the site (Breuil and Gill 2007: 129), but none of the Jina-​Buddhas of Garbhadhātu or 
Vajradhātu mandalas were found during the excavations. However, two of the four 
Jina-​Buddhas and Vajrasattva were found in the Maināmatī region, which houses 
monasteries with an identical architectural layout.

594      Swati Chemburkar
 
Based on the mandalic ground plan of Somapura, one of the theories developed by 
S. and M. Hoque (2004) is the placement of five Jina-​Buddhas in the central cruciform 
structure of the monument following the Vajrayāna philosophy.
For many years the Somapura stūpa was the only one of its kind known in South 
Asia, but several such structures have since been uncovered at Maināmatī (Salban 
vihāra, Bhoja vihāra, Ananda vihāra, Rupban vihāra), in present-​day Bangladesh, and 
at Anticak (Vikramaśīla mahāvihāra) in North Bihar (Gill 2007: 194; Imam 2000: 133). 
The peculiarity of all these structures is the central stūpa/​sanctuary, with the cruciform 
arrangement of shrine halls, the terracotta reliefs along the circumambulatory path, and 
the quadrangular monk’s cells enclosing the courtyard.
The senior Bangladeshi scholar Imam (2002: 616) commented on these temples: 
“it appears that at one stage the entire architectural concept of a Buddhist temple 
was changed in Samataṭa [present-​day eastern Bangladesh and Myanmar] and the 
cruciform design, probably with terraces, was introduced . . . for their religious 
architecture—​why and how it is difficult to say.” It would not be incorrect to say that 
Buddhist monasteries began to resemble one another much more closely than before 
in their architectural development. The layouts of Nāgārjunakonda, Sānci, Taxila, and 
Ellora show a wide variety of regional architectural forms,6 but the megastructures of 
Somapura, Maināmatī, and Antichak show a remarkable uniformity (fig. 26.17). The 
development at Somapura appears to resemble a Buddhist version of “neoclassical of­
fice building” in its repetitive systematization (Davidson 2002: 107).

left: Salban Vihāra, Ananda Vihāra, and Rupban Vihāra, Bangladesh, 7th century. Bottom row 
from left: Bhārat Bhāyna vihara, Bhasu Vihāra, Bangladesh; Vikramśīla Vihāra, Antichak, Bihar 
(all dated to 7th century). Far right: Somapura mahāvihāra, Bangladesh (8th century).

Mandalas and Monarchs      595
 
Does the similarity in layout indicate the same function? What were these 
monasteries teaching/​propagating? How does one understand the central cruciform/​
fourfold structure and its ritual purpose? Two conditions seem to be necessary, in 
fact, for a new form to arise in religious architecture, which more usually progresses 
by evolution or by borrowing: architectural intention on one hand and symbolic ref­
erence or ritual motives on the other. The conjunction of both of these factors is what 
must be established.
Textual Basis: The Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu Mandalas
Four directional Buddhas and eight Bodhisattvas appear in late Mahāyāna texts, but the 
systematic development of the five-​Buddha-​family and eight bodhisattvas is traced by 
Snellgrove (1987: 189, 198) through the various texts such as the Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa 
(MMK), Susuddhikara sūtra (SKS), Mahāvairocanāsaṁbodhi sūtra or Mahāvairocana 
sūtra (MVS) and Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha (STTS) and through the related bodhi­
sattva rituals by Giebel (2011: 27–​36).
The STTS and its explanatory Tibetan Sarvadurgatipariśodhana tantra (SDPS; 
Skorupski 1983: 32, 174) describe Siddhārtha’s entry into the five-​Buddha family, re­
ferred to as fivefold wisdom, via the process of abhiṣeka. Transforming himself into 
Mahāvairocana using the same process, he then constructs the great mandala with 
the other four Buddhas of the central assembly. Through a series of abhiṣekas, he then 
transforms a number of bodhisattvas—​beginning with Samantabhadra.7 The ritual pro­
cess of abhiṣeka is seen as a reproduction technology for the Buddhas. This is the central 
and defining metaphor for tantric Buddhism, where an individual can assume nondual 
reality —​a union with the ultimate Buddha and exercise his powers. These tantras con­
tain the most explicit references to kingship. Snellgrove’s overall conclusion (1959: 206) 
is that Vairocana, as cakravartin-​Buddha, holds the central position in the mandala 
during this developmental period in Buddhist thought.
The two mandalas, Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu,8 from the middle phase of tan­
tric Buddhism, found their way into the architecture, giving a concrete arrangement of 
deities, on a basic fourfold or fivefold model (figs. 26.18, 26.19): Buddha Akṣobhya to 
the east; Ratnasambhava to the south; Amitābha to the west; and Amoghasiddhi to the 
north, along with Vairocana or Mahāvairocana in the center. Along with this pentad, 
attendant bodhisattvas, offering goddesses, guardian figures, and 1,000 Buddhas of 
the Bhadrakalpa all found their place in the architecture (Snodgrass 1988: 634). The ar­
rangement of eight bodhisattvas inside a square forming a nine-​grid pattern was carried 
via the Vajradhātu mandala to the late Tantric Buddhist mandalas such as Guhyasamāja 
tantra (Tanaka 2018: 37–​39).

In some manner or the other, the mandalic elements of these two mandalas were 
eventually embedded in the Buddhist structures of Southeast Asia.
The Architecture of the Garbhadhātu and 
Vajradhātu Mandalas
The Garbhadhātu mandala represents ultimate reality in this world, whereas the 
Vajradhātu mandala represents reality in the Buddha realm. According to Snodgrass 
(1988: 85), each mandala is powerful in its own right but achieves its zenith when paired 
with Buddha’s compassion and wisdom. The combined interdependence of the two 
mandalas is believed to have been devised in the 8th ​century Chinese capital of Chang’an, 
within the religious circle of the tantric Indian masters Śubhākarasiṁha (637–​735), 
Vajrabodhi (671–​741), and Amoghavajra (704–​774). This triad inspired various interna­
tional pupils and built a strong network of Chinese (Huilang, ?–​781; Huiguo, 746–​806), 
Japanese (Kūkai, 774–​835; Ennin, 794–​864), and Javanese (Bianhong, late 8th century) 
Buddhist monks. They worked on specific texts such as the MVS, SKS, and STTS, their 
commentaries, associated mandalas, and ritual practices which traveled to Southeast and 
East Asia, marking the first wave of tantric Buddhism (7th to early 10th century CE).9
The fundamental pairing of the two mandalas was important during ceremonies 
such as ordination, commemoration, memorial rites, and the initiation of a new 
temple building, which can be seen in the central sanctuary of the early 9th century 
Tōji temple in Kyoto, where two scrolls that were carried to Japan by Kūkai, the dis­
ciple of Huiguo, hang facing each other. The central altar served for the daily fire 
rituals during initiation ceremonies. Around the same time, a somewhat similar ar­
rangement is seen translated in the architecture of the Central Javanese temples of 
Mendut-​Pawon-​Borobudur.
By the 7th century, Java was an important Buddhist center, and there was inten­
sive interaction between the Chinese and Indonesian Buddhists (Miksic 2006: 187). 
Bianhong was already initiated into the Vajradhātu mandala before arriving in China 
(Sinclair 2016: 33–​34), but his particular interest in the tantric initiation systems of 
Garbhadhātu, as well as Saptaratnābhiṣeka (Seven Treasure Initiation), possibly led 
him to Chang’an. Possession of seven jewels by a cakravartin king is not per se tan­
tric, but Sinclair (2016: 53) observes that “particular Tantric means for endowing 
the saptaratna were brand new in the Tang.” News of Amoghavajra’s endowment of 
cakravartirājya-​saptaratnābhiṣeka to the Tang emperor Suzong must have reached 
Bianhong’s homeland (Sinclair 2016: 39). His Ritual Manual for Initiation into the

--- PAGE 624 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      599
 
Great Maṇḍala of the Uṣṇīṣa-​Cakravartin, written in China, demonstrates sound 
knowledge of the twin mandalas and specifically deals with cakravartin initiations, 
following Amoghavajra’s methods.10 Whether he returned or was allowed to travel to 
Java is not known,11 but the late 8th-​ or early 9th century Javanese work Saṅ Hyaṅ 
Kamahāyānan Mantrayana deals with the same subject matter as Bianhong’s manual 
(Sinclair 2016: 49), and the architecture of Mendut-​Pawon-​Borobudur indicates the 
knowledge of the twin mandalas in Central Java.
The First Wave of Tantric Buddhism 
(7th to Early 10th Centuries)
Spatial visualization plays a powerful part in architecture, and the mandalas circulating 
in the Buddhist world would have served as blue prints for the builders to map the ge­
ography. Central Javanese monuments were carefully positioned in the landscape, and 
their architecture was determined by sociopolitical, religious, and economic factors 
(Degroot 2009: chap. 1). Harmony between the human and spirit worlds is created by 
constructing a stone version of the deities’ celestial dwellings. As Bade argued (2016: 
155), “tantric Buddhism, with its imagination of a just and universal world ruler bringing 
about a state of affairs on earth that would mirror heavenly state of affairs—​was not just 
a fantasy world of escape for monks and a useful mask hiding ugly realities for kings; it 
was a powerful motivating force that shaped political and social conditions throughout 
Southeast Asia” and led to construction of some of the Buddhist monuments. The 
temples of Borobudur, Mendut, Sewu, Bubrah, Lumbung, Kālaśan, and Plaosan, as well 
as the Abhayagiri monastery on the Ratu Boko plateau near Yogyakarta in Central Java, 
embedded mandalic elements in their architecture, though it’s sometimes difficult to 
pin them down to a specific mandala.
Central Java and Campā
The fourfold arrangement of Buddhas displaying specific mudrās on the square terraces 
of Borobudur (fig. 26.20) accords with the four Jina Buddhas—​Akṣobhya (fig. 26.21), 
Ratnasambhava (fig. 26.22), Amitābha (fig. 26.23), and Amoghasiddhi (fig. 26.24), of the 
Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu mandalas. The three circular terraces above them house 
72 Buddhas in wheel-​turning (dharmacakra) mudrā inside the stūpikās (fig. 26.25).

604      Swati Chemburkar
 
Based on the geometrical perforations on the stūpikas of the three circular terraces 
of Borobudur and the 504 Buddhas of the square terraces, Chandra argues (1980: 
28) that these are not the five Jina Buddhas but the 1,000 Buddhas of the Vajradhātu 
mahāmaṇḍala: “the Vajradhātu becomes a mahāmaṇḍala because of the thousand 
Buddhas, which is its unique and contradistinctive attribute in the world of Tantric 
maṇḍalas. The Vajradhātu mahāmaṇḍala added to the already existing five forms of the 
Buddhas a sixth one with the dharmacakra mudrā. These six forms of Buddhas were re­
peated 168 times to the auspicious number 1008. That is why there are 504 Buddhas, and 
the niches and stūpas enclosing these 504, symbolically make up the requisite double 
number: 504 x 2 =​ 1008.” Archaeological finds dating from the 9th century suggest tan­
tric practices at Borobudur (Griffiths 2014c: 178).
The temple of Mendut (fig. 26.26), aligned with Borobudur, houses eight bodhisattvas 
on its external walls, along with Prajñāparāmitā, Cundā, and Avalokiteśvara (figs. 
26.27–​37). The arrangement of the triad—​Vairocana, Avalokiteśvara, and Vajrapāṇi—​
in the central sanctuary (fig. 26.38) is typical of the Garbhadhātu mandala along with 
the eight bodhisattvas in Japanese MVS as well as SDPS (fig. 26.39).13 However, as argued 
by Woodward (2004: 338), the mandala described in MVS is far more complex than 
what one sees at Mendut. The bodhisattva arrangement displayed on the external walls 
of Mendut and on the internal walls of Plaosan has parallels in the eight-​bodhisattva 
arrangement of the 7th-​century Aṣṭamaṇḍalaka sūtra, which was translated into 
Chinese by Amoghavajra (fig. 26.40).14 The tantric elements of Mendut need to be 
explored on the basis of a gold foil found at the Plaosan temple (Griffiths 2014c: 164–​
165) containing a section of the Kāraṇḍavyūha sūtra, a prototantric text. The same text 
also represents “Cundā’s spell as a proclamation of the obtaining wisdom,” as discussed 
by Woodward (2004: 337) with respect to the goddess’s image at Mendut. The Śailendra 
inscription does mention the building of Mendut to acquire merit and finally reach 
Buddhahood.15

Pawon falls between Mendut and Borobudur and would have served as a homa

uate the homa smoke (fig. 26.41).17 Homa ritual is a distinctive characteristic of tantric 
Buddhism.

614      Swati Chemburkar
 
An important architectural change occurred in Central Javanese temples during 
the Śailendra period: the transformation of a central sanctuary from a square to a 
cruciform plan (Dumarçay 1986: 20), presumably to follow the fourfold structure 
of a mandala system. Some textual material derived from STTS, likely served to de­
marcate the ground plans of Central Javanese Buddhist monuments (Griffiths 2014c: 
159–​166).
The Śailendras installed Mañjughoṣa at Candi Sewu for the protection, prosperity, 
and welfare of the kingdom.18 Designed as a Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara mandala with 
Mañjuśrī as its main deity, Sewu underwent modifications, probably to accommodate 
the Vajradhātu mandala centered around Vairocana.19 Long’s study (2015: 13) convinc­
ingly correlates the number of niches available for the images at Sewu and the number of 
deities in the modified version of the Vajradhātu mandala. The surrounding shrines in 
the two successive rows (28 +​ 44) of Sewu’s central sanctuary make a total of 72, identical 
to the 72 perforated stūpas of Borobudur (figs. 26.42, 26.43).
Figure 26.42.  Arrangement of 72 shrines around the central sanctuary of Sewu. Drawing by 
author, based on the plan displayed at the site museum.

--- PAGE 640 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      615
 
Figure 26.43.  Seventy-​two perforated stūpikas placed on the circular terraces around the top­
most stūpa of Borobudur.
Drawing by author.
Originally, Sewu had four satellite temples (Bubrah, Asu, Kulon, and Lor) located 
on the cardinal points along with others, such as Lumbung, that possibly displayed 
sections of the main mandala of Sewu. Mañjuśrī would have been installed at Lumbung, 
exhibiting the nature of Trailokyavijaya, “Victor of the Three Realms,” and surrounded 
by the wrathful guardians of the ten directions.20 Based on the arrangement of 11 niches 
in the Lumbung’s central sanctuary, Long (2015: 18) argues that the temple was intended 
to represent a particular section of the Mañjuśrī mandala with Trailokyavijaya as a prin­
cipal deity. The importance of Mañjuśrī in the Javanese political sphere finds a parallel 
in the tantric Buddhism of Chinese Tang and Indian Pāla courts around the same time 
(Miksic 2006; Sundberg and Giebel 2011: 130).
It is necessary to note the evidence of Trailokyavijaya worship in Central Java 
during the late 8th century.21 The origin of Trailokyavijaya is explained in the 
Trailokyavijayapatala section of the STTS (Iyanaga 1985: 633–​745; Kwon 2002: pt. 2, 
chap. 6, 136–​156).

--- PAGE 641 ---
616      Swati Chemburkar
 
Along with the temples, the Śailendras re-​created the Sri Lankan Abhayagiri vihāra 
on Ratu Boko plateau, Central Java. The architecture of Javanese vihāra shared several 
common features with the Sri Lankan one, especially that of a building with raised 
double platforms (Sundberg: 2014; figs. 26.44–​47). The Javanese structure was in­
tended to house tantric Sinhalese Buddhist rag-​wearing monks (pāṃśukūlikas),22 
who were studying Buddhist Yogatantra texts. The structure had an extensive li­
brary of tantras, while mastery of the tantric rituals at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka 
was also undertaken. Sundberg (2014: 104) argues regarding the function of the raised 
platforms: “the only role for this structure that seems plausible to me is that of an 
Abhayagirin consecration platform, either for initiates or for kings. . . . and I consider 
it not implausible that the Abhayagirins conducted rituals for the royalty in much 
the same manner, for example, as Amoghavajra. . . . Indeed, if the Abhayagirivāsins 
consecrated the Śailendra kings as cakravartins as Amoghavajra did for Suzong, there 
is circumstantial evidence.”

618      Swati Chemburkar
 
The Sri Lankan Abhayagiri monks played an important role in state coronation 
rituals, as discussed by Powell (2018: 3): “from the eighth to the eleventh centuries, 
Vajrayāna Buddhism, as represented by the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and 
practices focused on its Vajradhātu-​maṇḍala, was widely practiced and studied in 
Sri Lanka. Consecration rituals featuring pañcabuddha Vajradhātu-​maṇḍalas were 
used to sacralise Buddhist sites as important as the Abhayagiri stūpa, and Sri Lankan 
practitioners were known to be experts in the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha—​so 
much so that Amoghavajra travelled to Anurādhapura, seeking out tantric teachers and 
manuscripts.”23 Column bases with the symbols of five Jina Buddhas and a gold plate 
inscription hinting at the cult of Vairocana are the archaeological finds from Ratu Boko 
(Degroot 2006: 72).
Figure 26.47.  The double platform of Girikaṇḍa vihāra at Tiriyāy in Sri Lanka. A similar one 
would have been built at Sri Lankan Abhayagiri vihāra.
Photo courtesy Sven Bretfeld.

--- PAGE 644 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      619
 
After the intense construction activity in Central Java, nothing noteworthy was 
built. In any case, the mid-​9th to late 10th century has been characterized as a “dark 
age for Buddhism” in China, Tibet, (Matsunaga 1978: viii) and Southeast Asia, with 
the single exception of the Đồng Dương temple in Campā (Woodward 2011: 33). 
Campā provided a stopover for the Indian monks on their long journeys to China 
as the navigation technologies of the period did not make the direct trip possible. 
Javanese and Indian influences were integrated into the distinctly Cam art of the pe­
riod (Schweyer 2009: 312). A 9th–​century An Thái inscription refers to a monastic 
meditation in which Vajrapāṇi is in charge of leading human beings “on the path of 
Vajra, the Vajrayāna” (Schweyer 2009: 314). Three levels (tridhātu) of meditation are 
mentioned in the inscription, along with the three Buddhas—​Vajrapāṇi, Lokeśvara, 
and Vajrasattva. No sculptural or architectural remains have been found to corre­
late the underlying philosophical system of the inscription, but Schweyer (2009: 315) 
argues for the close association of the inscription with the Javanese text Saṅ Hyaṅ 
Kamahāyānan Mantranaya.
A form of tantric Buddhism is evident in the construction of the 9th ​century 
Đồng Dương temple. The ground plan consists of an entrance, an assembly hall for 
congregational worship, a long approach, and enclosure I, which accommodated a 
four-​doored sanctuary and the primary image of the temple (fig. 26.48) (Parmentier 
1918; Baptiste and Zéphir 2005: 212–​232). A colossal bronze Buddha, now on dis­
play at Ho Chi Minh City Museum possibly welcomed the devotees. The head­
less, pendent-​legged Buddha was placed in the assembly hall accompanied by two 
bodhisattvas (figs. 26.49, 26.50). Originally, the temple gates were guarded by fero­
cious dvarapālas much like the gatekeepers of mandala paintings. (figs. 26.51–​53). 
Mahāvairocana in bodhyagrī mudrā was placed inside the four-​doored sanctuary 
of enclosure I (fig. 26.54) (Baptiste and Zéphir 2005: 213; Chuttiwongs 2005: 71, 
81). This mudrā is associated with Vairocana of the Vajradhātu mandala in tantric 
Buddhism. Installation of a female deity—​Lakṣmīndralokeśvara, as a primary image 
in the enclosure I, beyond Vairocana (figs. 26.55, 26.56) indicates the importance 
of goddess cults in Campā and suggests certain tantric practices at Đồng Dương.24 
Seven planetary deities were once placed around the enclosure I (numbered 1 to 7, 
one such example is fig. 26.57).

It’s impossible to identify specific mandalas in this location, but Schweyer (2009: 
319) suggests Borobudur’s influence. The pendent-​legged Buddha along with the 
bodhisattvas of the assembly hall would be similar to the central sanctuary triad of 
Candi Mendut. The epigraphy mentions people from Campā and India visiting the in­
tellectual Buddhist center of Java in the 9th century.25
Śailendra rule ended by the mid-​9th century, and Central Javanese power moved to­
ward East Java, marking the “second wave of Buddhism.” The artistic tradition and cul­
ture between the two regions continued, as is evidenced in the bronze mandala deities of 
this period. The 9th-​ to 10th-​century Surocolo and Ngañjuk bronzes from central and 
East Java are identified as part of large three-​dimensional Vajrasattva mandalas, while the 
East Javanese Ponorogo hoard is associated with the Vajrasattvakula mandala.26 Along 
with these statuaries, the various vajras, scepters, bells, mirrors, mandala statuettes, and 
inscribed foils of the Javanese shipwreck cargo appear to be the ritual paraphernalia typi­
cally used in mandalic initiations (Hall 2010: 15–​45; Miksic 2016: 259–​260).

626      Swati Chemburkar
 
Narratives of the Vajradhātu Mandala and Its Appeal 
to Royalty
Why did these mandala initiations and this mandala architecture become impor­
tant to the ruling elites? The narratives of the SDPS introduce the basic cosmolog­
ical themes describing the way gods too are subjected to the law of karma, when they 
have fallen from heaven into hell. Śākyamuni then elaborates a list of horrific hells and 
rebirths the gods must endure to move toward the heavenly realms.27 So upset are the 
gods upon hearing their fate that they request Buddha to reveal the solution (SDPS 319; 
Skorupski 1983: 26). Buddha then promises that those who hear, utter, and perform the spells 
and enter the mandala correctly will acquire worldly benefits, never suffer the bad rebirths, 
and attain enlightenment in due course. He then prescribes specific homa rituals (SDPS 319–​
320; Skorupski 1983: 32) of pacification, augmentation, subjugation, and execution, associated 
with the specific deities one must invoke in order to climb the ladder to the heavenly rebirth.
Buddhist missionaries could use the ominous threat of a bad rebirth to impress upon 
potential converts the value of apotropaic rites that only Buddhists could provide. The 
Vajradhātu mandala is concerned with rectifying the lives of sinful kings, as is discussed in 
the second chapter of the SDPS. It is claimed that by drawing the mandala of the four great 
kings and performing the Indramahābhiṣeka and Pūrṇamahābhiṣeka, “not being a king (the 
uninitiated) becomes a king, being a king (the initiated) becomes a great king” (Skorupski 
1983: 19–​20). These abhiṣeka rituals are discussed by Thomas (1908–​26: 20). Javanese ac­
counts of mandalic rituals influencing architecture come from the 13th and 14th centuries.
The Second Wave of Buddhism 
(Late 10th to 14th Centuries)
East Java
The majority of the Buddhist structures in East Java are from the Siṅhasāri/​Mājapāhit 
reigns (1222–​1500 CE), when Hinduism and Buddhism merged into one religious be­
lief described as tantric.28 The 14th century Javanese text Deśavarṇana/​Nāgarkṛtāgama 
asserts the divine nature of kings who descended to earth for the prosperity of the 
kingdom and returned to the heavenly abode after completing their tasks.29
The Vajrayāna concept of a temporal king as a potential Buddha had an impact on the 
art and architecture of East Java. Worship of the god in a temple became the veneration 
of the deceased king in his deified form, and the East Javanese temples became ceremo­
nial mandala centers through which the union with the chosen deity was established.
Tantric Buddhism provided a perfect support for the East Javanese kingship, which 
was based on bloody battles of succession. Practices of eradicating all negative karma 
are common in the Buddhist tradition, but the ritual techniques explicitly eliminating

--- PAGE 652 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      627
 
the stain of negative karma are crucial to the tantric tradition. For example, in 
Vajrabodhi’s “Brief Explanation of the Production, Recollection, and Recitation of the 
Yoga of the Diamond Peak Scripture” manual we find, “both World Honoured Ones 
[i.e. Buddhas] and sentient beings who have committed great crimes are to be seen in 
this great maṇḍala of the Diamond Realm. And as for those who enter [this mandala], 
each and every one of all of their crimes and hindrances are removed” (Taishō canon T 
8666.224a3-​15, Trans. Goble 2016: 135).
The East Javanese temple architecture displays two distinct types—​a slender tower 
like the structure of Candi Kidal, Candi Jawi, and the terraced temples of Candi Jago and 
Candi Panataran—​but the cruciform plan for the central sanctuary remained constant 
for both.

634      Swati Chemburkar
 
King Kṛtanagara (r. 1268–​1292) built Jago’s cruciform sanctuary on a terraced struc­
ture (fig. 26.58) to commemorate his father, Viṣṇuvardhana, as Amoghapāśa. The stat­
uary of Amoghapāśa, his four attendants—​four Jina Buddhas and their consorts—​house 
a total of 13 deities of the mandala in the architecture of Jago along with Arapacana 
Mañjuśrī, and Mahākāla.30 (See figs. 26.59–​70) for the iconographic program of the 
temple.) O’Brien’s (1993: 261–​279) study of the temple establishes the four quarters of 
the temple as the quarters of the Jina Buddhas of the Vajradhātu mandala. The texts 
STTS and SDPS, which described the Vajradhātu, have not been found in any form in 
Indonesia, but a small selection of verses from both these texts has been identified in 
the old Javanese Saṅ Hyaṅ Kamahāyānan Mantrayana, indicating knowledge of some 
of the key concepts embodied in these texts (Kandahjaya 2016: 70). The 13 deities of the 
Amoghapāśa mandala seen in the architecture of Jago were replicated in sculptures and 
bronzes of the deity, of which one composite stone sculpture was sent to Sumatra (as 
seen in fig. 26.81).
Along with Jago, there are three other religious establishments associated with King 
Kṛtanagara: the site of Wurare, a cremation ground; Candi Siṅhosāri; and Candi Jawi. 
The site of Wurare is not yet satisfactorily identified, but it is known that here the king 
was reconsecrated as Mahākṣobhya, a tantric form of Jina Akṣobhya, the Guhyasamāja 
tantra’s main deity.31
The cruciform temple of Siṅhosāri was built to serve the living king (fig. 26.71). 
Siṅhosāri images include Nandīśvara, the fearsome Mahākāla, the demonic Durgā, 
the skull-​bedecked Gaṇeśa, a bearded ascetic with a trident (figs. 26.72–​77); and 
an image of Bhairava was found in the vicinity bearing the Devanāgarī inscription 
cakracakra (fig. 26.78).32 The image depicts a naked dancing figure on a skull base 
wearing a skull garland and holding a skull cup and sacrificial knife. Bhairava is 
also represented on the few composite sculptures of Siṅhosāri which have been 
found. It seems that Kṛtanagara paid special attention to the Bhairava priests to 
cultivate the divine aspect of the god,33 useful in the course of military encounters 
and warfare.
Siṅhosāri is often referred to as the abode of Śiva-​Buddha, possibly indicating 
the place where King Kṛtanagara finally attained that dual status before his demise 
in 1292 while performing the tantric ritual. The extraordinary macabre traits of the 
skull decorations and sculptural components of Candi Siṅhosāri reflect the con­
cept of a cremation ground. The temple was rebuilt by the Majapahit prime minister 
Gaja Mada (1290–​1364) and dedicated it to the people who lost their lives during the 
Kings’ tantric ritual involving certain horrific cremation ground rites. (Slametmuljana 
1976: 28–​29).

Wuruk’s grandmother, and Kṛtanagara’s daughter, indicating the merging of the queen

Canto 64:3
Now the procedure for the royal ceremony was the ultimate in worship of the All-​

tric thought. Candi Boyolangu was erected as the deification image of Rājapatnī 
Gāyatrī.37
Sumatra
Kṛtanagara’s composite Amoghapaśa statue replicating the Jago iconographic pro­
gram was sent to Sumatra in 1286 (fig. 26.81), to advance either his expansionist poli­
tics (Kulke 2009: 230) or an alliance with the Malayu king against Kublai Khan’s threat 
(Berg 1965: 99; de Casparis 1985: 247–​248). The motive behind this move is debatable, 
but the statue’s importance is undeniable, as even after sixty years, King Ādityavarman 
(1320–​1378) reconsecrated it as Gagaṇagañja at Rambāhan, Dharmaśraya, one of the 
key sites around the upper Batang Hari river. Gagaṇagañja appears in the Mañjuvajra, 
Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara, and Durgatipariśodhana mandalas (Bhattacharyya 1968: 86–​
87) as well as the Vajradhātu and Mahāvairocana mandalas (de Mallmann 1975: 164). 
The statue was possibly used to legitimize Ādityavarman’s rule by employing Buddhist 
imagery, as the inscription hints at the king being the incarnation of the god. It is impor­
tant to note that the base of the statue is carved with the seven jewels, or saptaratna, of a 
universal ruler.

--- PAGE 668 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      643
 
The statue found at Padang Roco—​a ferocious Mahākāla/​*Pañjaranātha Mahākāla—​
is associated with Kṛtanagara and Ādityavarman (fig. 26.80).38 Klokke (1994) suggests 
that it is a deification statue of Ādityavarman. Reichle (2007: 204–​209) and Kulke (2009: 
247) argue that it served as a symbol of royal political power. Hunter (2015: 308) assumes 
that the statue played a symbolic role in psychosexual rituals. Acri and Wenta (2022: 37) 
argue for the statue being a portrait statue of Kṛtanagara that was once housed in the East 
Javanese temple of Jawi and was possibly repurposed/​reconsecrated by Ādityavarman. 
The “made in East Java” statue was either sent to Sumatra by Kṛtanagara or brought by 
Ādityavarman to his kingdom.39
The extent of Ādityavarman’s political power is not known, but the memory of the 
king’s court was carried by the Minangkabau people for centuries in the west Sumatran 
highlands. A “Si Mandang Giri” dagger from the Minangkabau royal treasury displays 
male (possibly Mahākāla) and female images. Bosch (1930: 214, pl. 49a–​f) compares the 
Figure 26.81.  Amoghapāśa statue that was sent to Sumatra, 1.63 m tall. Seven jewels can be 
seen at the bottom. Museum Nasional Indonesia, no. 6469.
Photo by author.

--- PAGE 669 ---
644      Swati Chemburkar
 
weapon held by the male figure to the Padang Roco and Candi Jago Mahākāla statues, 
suggesting the possibility of its use in the royal consecration rites. Similar weapons are 
also depicted on the reliefs of the Majapahit state temple of Panataran.
Sumatra’s significant place within tantric Buddhism from the 7th century onward 
is summarized by Miksic (2006), but most of the archaeological remains displaying 
fierce deities of later Tantric Buddhism belong to the 10th to 13th centuries. The largest 
concentrations of the remains are at Muara Takus, Muara Jambi, and Padang Lawas.
An inscribed gold disc found at one of the Muara Takus temples mentions how they 
were built by the “Vajradhara” sect in the 11th century (Schnitger 1937b). Two stone 
artifacts bearing Viśvavajra motifs and a mandala-​like diagram of seed syllables (ten­
tative reading by Griffiths 2014b: 236), might indicate tantric Buddhist culture (figs. 
26.82, 26.83). The arrangement of Nāgarī letters on the stone represents deities and their 
consorts. Kandahjaya’s (2016: 88, n. 61) revised reading finds a similar series of seed 
syllables in many tantric texts. Due to the restoration of these temples, the original ar­
chitectural design remains obscure.
Figure 26.82.  Stone with Nāgarī letters and vajra carvings found at Bungsu temple.
Photo: Kern Institute Collection, Leiden University Library, GD 13 1321

--- PAGE 670 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      645
 
Candi Gumpung (built in the 9th to 10th centuries and enlarged during the 11th and 
12th centuries), one of the largest temples of Muara Jambi, is a rectangular cella erected 
on a high plinth with projecting niches. Inscribed gold plates found during excavations 
name the deities belonging to either the Vajradhātu or Trailokyavijaya mandala, clearly 
indicating its incorporation in the temple architecture.40
Material remains of Padang Lawas display tantric Buddhist currents from the 11th to 
13th centuries. Several temples, stūpas, and large altars were constructed, of which Bahal 
I, II, III, Pulo, Si Pamutung, and Aek Sangkilon are the most important.

Mandalas and Monarchs      647
 
All these have suffered irretrievable loss with ruined sanctuaries, mutilated 
sculptures, and poorly preserved artifacts, but the 13th century epigraphy clearly 
indicates the importance of the Hevajra cult.41 Images of Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, 
Prajñāparāmitā, Vajrasattva (Schnitger 1937a: 22), fearful animal-​headed dancing fig­
ures (Berger 1995: 149–​152; Miksic 1992: 75), Heruka (fig. 26.84), and Mahākāla do shed 
light on the tantric background of the site as is highlighted by Bautze-​Picron (2014: 
107): “the images from Padang Lawas are integrated in a network which connects them 
to South Asia, East Java (Singasari), Central Sumatra (Malayu), Cambodia, and Campā 
in the 11th and 13th centuries. Evidence of various kinds is found in all of these regions, 
proving the existence of Vajrayāna in its latest phase as an integral part of the royal 
function: Hevajra is the protector of the State in Cambodia and perhaps also Campā, 
whereas it is Mahākāla who assumes the role in the Yuan Empire.” Despite the evidence 
of Heruka worship in Indonesia, the Padang Lawas statue is his only known image 
from the archipelago. Several 11th​ and 12th ​century images of Heruka and an analo­
gous entity—​Saṃvara—​from eastern Indian monasteries have been found, but there 
is no knowledge of how early the related rituals were exercised within the monasteries. 
The tantric deities worshipped within the Indian monastic contexts clearly found a 
place within the royal courts of Southeast Asia (Davidson 2002: 115; Linrothe 1999: 274; 
Sharrock: 2022).
Cambodia
Khmer monarchs viewed the employment of tantric rituals as a necessary adjunct to 
more conventional means of exercising power. The Buddhist dynasty of Mahīdharapura, 
presumably near Phimai in the Khorat plateau in modern Thailand, included a number 
of usurpers who all excelled at building state ceremonial centers.
One of the earliest examples of the royal worship of a Heruka-​type deity, Saṃvara, is 
seen at the 11th ​ to 12th ​century Phimai temple, the first major Khmer politico-​religious 
center (fig. 26.85).42 The tantric Buddhism of the Mahīdhara king, Jayavarman VI, is 
evident at the temple’s central sanctuary. The lintels showcase deeply carved reliefs 
of Saṃvara, a crowned Buddha under a tree, and a six-​armed, three-​/​four-​headed 
Vajrasattva in dhyāna mudrā seated in a celestial pentad in the center (figs. 26.86–​89). 
All the deities are accompanied by yoginīs dancing on corpses. Scholars have 
attempted different interpretations of the Vajrasattva figure.43 Based on a local Sab 
Bāk inscription (K. 1158 of 1066 CE), Conti (2014: 387) identifies it as the pentad of 
Akṣobhya (as Śrī Samāja): “I identify the central deity as Akṣobhya, with his four 
fellow Jinas. Akṣobhya is the Jina in the center of the Guhyasamājamaṇḍala and 
the supreme ‘deity.’ The Jinas in Prasat Hin Phimai fit the description given in the 
Guhyasamājatantra where they are described in their ‘vajra form’ as ‘three-​headed’ 
with ‘six arms’ and wearing a ‘crown.’ ”

The Khmer part of the inscription mentions the erection of Buddhist images 
on Abhayagiri hill by a tantric practitioner, Satyavarman, for the protection of the 
realm (Estève 2009: 442–​453, 541–​546; Prapadvidya 1990: 11–​14; Skorupski 2014: 
381–​383).
Another inscription (Cœdès 1924: 350) from the Phimai temple mentions the instal­
lation of a Trailokyavijaya image. Though no stone image of the deity has been found, a 
bronze kept at the National Museum Bangkok and one of the Phimai lintels might be the 
representation of the deity (Conti 2010: 9, 23; fig. 26.90).
Discussing the role of tantric Buddhist specialists during the coronation of 
Jayavarman VI at Phimai, Conti (2010: 17) points out a lintel illustrating the aśvamedha 
(horse sacrifice) ceremony, typically performed at the establishment of a new kingdom 
(fig. 26.91). It is difficult to know whether any tantric abhiṣeka was performed at Phimai, 
but a clear expression of the acquired siddhis via abhiṣeka rites is provided by the 11th-​
century Sdok Kak Thom inscription that presents Vīṇāśikha, an early Śaiva tantra text, 
as a key support of the Khmer state.44
Figure 26.90.  Possible depiction of Trailokyavijaya on an outer enclosure lintel.
Photo courtesy Olivier Cunin

--- PAGE 677 ---
652      Swati Chemburkar
 
Another Mahīdhara king, Jayavarman VII, made a greater break with tradition when 
he seized power in a military coup and made Buddhism the state religion for the first 
time in Angkor. His Buddhist creed was based on the Yoginī tantras. Boeles suggested 
(1966: 28) that by the early 12th century, the Hevajra cult had adherents in northeastern 
Thailand and a form of Vajrayāna originating from Phimai might have spread to Angkor. 
The earliest Khmer Hevajra bronze icons at Phimai are from the 11th century, but a large 
number of his images and associated ritual paraphernalia are found in Cambodia from 
Jayavarman VII’s reign. Given the overwhelming art historical evidence, there is no 
doubt that the Hevajra tantra was known to the Khmers.
Hevajra became truly a royal deity for Jayavarman VII. His statue was installed at Ta 
Prohm temple;45 two caitya pillars with Hevajra engravings were erected at the Preah 
Khan temple of Kompong Svay (Baptiste and Zéphir 2008: 441; 2013: 236), and then 
a huge cult image of the deity graced the entrance of the 13th century state temple of 
Bayon (fig. 26.94) (Cunin 2018; Sharrock 2022).
Bayon is constructed as a terraced, cruciform structure with the towering central 
sanctuary housing face towers in its architecture. The central sanctuary stands on a 
circular, lotus-​shaped base surrounded by eight chambers with face towers. The dark 
corridor around the sanctuary has four doorways at cardinal points (fig. 26.92). This ar­
rangement of structures resembles Hevajra mandala (fig. 26.93) and the face towers that 
stare out from the central sanctuary make it look like a multi-​headed icon. (fig. 26.95) 
(Maxwell 2007b: 86).
The close affinity between the temple’s sanctuary and the contemporary Khmer 
Hevajra bronze is remarkable (fig. 26.96). Eight yoginīs surround the deity inside

No specific mandala can be assigned to the Bayon, but the development is akin to that 
of the earlier mandala architecture. It is the only temple of the period with a circular cen­
tral sanctuary, similar to the yoginī temples and yoginītantra mandalas.
Linrothe (1999: 274) argues: “if there was a Hevajra cult, it seems to have thrived in 
Southeast Asia. . . . The transmission of the Hevajra teachings was probably reinforced 
through contacts along the maritime routes from island Southeast Asia and eastern India. 
Whatever the exact route, it clearly had considerable influence in the highest levels of so­
ciety. Seemingly removed from his yogic and monastic origins, Hevajra was utilized in the 
royal cult . . . as part of an attempt at local legitimization.” Hevajra was also important in

--- PAGE 683 ---
658      Swati Chemburkar
 
the 12th century Cam domain when Jayavarman VII’s close aide Vidyānandana celebrated 
the revolt against the king with the construction of the “Lord Heruka mansion.”46 There is 
no recorded precedent in Campā for the Heruka cult, strengthening the possibility that it 
was a direct export from Angkor, and therefore a reflection of Jayavarman’s Hevajra cult.
Banteay Chhmar, another important temple complex of Jayavarman VII, was built in 
northwest Cambodia. It consists of a central temple with three satellite structures at car­
dinal directions (fig. 26.97). The central sanctuary has friezes of the multiarmed Heruka-​
type dancing deities of the late tantric Buddhism, but due to its ruined nature the exact 
identification is difficult (figs. 26.98, 26.99). Along with these friezes, eight multiarmed, 
multiheaded tantric Avalokiteśvaras representing scenes from Kāraṇḍavyūha sūtra 
(Boisselier 1964: 73–​89) and 11–​headed, 22-​armed Prajñāparāmitās carved on the temple 
walls are enough to indicate the tantric features of the temple (figs. 26.100–​105).
Under Jayavarman VII, uniquely Khmer tantric forms of Prajñāpāramitā gained 
prominence (Chemburkar 2022) along with other tantric female images. Several 
bronzes of Vajradhara and Vajrasattva found from the kings’ reign indicate the impor­
tance of the last phase of Buddhist tantra.

Mandalas and Monarchs      663
 
Tantra did influence every part of Southeast Asia at some point in history. The 
ritual appeal of these mandalas attained its apogee in the kingdoms of Central and 
East Java, Sumatra, Campā, and Angkor, where they were embedded within the sa­
cred architecture. To sum it up in Davidson’s words (2002: 168): “it is evident, how­
ever, that the maṇḍalas found in the [Indian] institutional works were accepted 
and supported by monarchs on the Indian borderlands, for they understood that 
Buddhist institutions had provided them with exactly the right combination of polit­
ical and religious authority.”
Conclusion
The pure enlightened world of mandalas served as blueprints for the temple architec­
ture, and as a validating feature to the sovereignty in the organization of the court. The 
correspondences among the mandala diagrams, royal ceremonies, and practices leave 
no doubt that mandalic architectural development must have been for ritual ceremonies 
rather than just worship.
Jñānamitra’s 7th-​ to 8th-​century commentary on Prajñāpāramitānayaśatapañcaśatikā/​ 
Prajñāpāramitānayasūtra/​ Adhrdyaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā (the 150-​line Perfection of 
Insight) provides an interesting mythological account of the preaching of the tantric 
scriptures and their transmission into the kingdom of King Indrabhutī (discussing the 
commentary, Davidson 2002: 243): “[Ācārya] Kukura divided up the queens and the 
court, each placed at physical direction in the maṇḍala. They and the princes and prin­
cesses all took their place on an enormous maṇḍala board, in a physical enactment of 
the Vajradhātu maṇḍala by the members of the court. Jñānamitra [the author of the 
commentary] assures us that, at the end, not only did Indrabhūti become a Vidyādhara 
but so did all the thousand members of the court . . . all became Vidyādharas.” Goble 
(2016: 124) provides an account of a ceremony held in the 11th century during a heav­
enly pacification. The Comprehensive Mirror for Aiding Government, produced by 
the court advisor Sima Guang (1019–​1086), depicts the following scene: “His Highness 
set up a maṇḍala (daochang 道場) in the Triple Hall (sandian 三殿) taking the Palace 
Women (gongren 宮人) to act as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and the North Gate mili­
tary elite (beimen wushi 北門武士) to act as Vajra [pāṇis? -​sattvas?] and divine kings. 
He summoned the Grand Ministers (dachen 大臣) to prostrate to and circumambu­
late them (Zizhi tongjian 資治通鑒 222).” Incorporation of the Vajradhātu mandala and 
other successive mandalas in the construction of the royal monuments was a means of 
bolstering the political agendas of their patrons, particularly in periods of instability. 
Jayavarman VII in Cambodia (r. c. 1181–​1220), Kṛtanagara in East Java (r. 1268–​1292), 
Kublai Khan in China (r. 1260–​1294), and Ādityavarman in Java and Sumatra (r. ?–​1375) 
all followed the militant form of tantric Buddhism in building some of their key ritual 
centers. In the absence of literature on how these buildings were used, architecture 
becomes a common language to understand tantra and its development.

--- PAGE 689 ---
664      Swati Chemburkar
 
For example, no text explains Borobudur’s unique architecture, but its comparison 
to other mandalic monuments of the period provides some clues to the motives be­
hind its construction. Similarly, understanding Indian yoginī temples in relation to 
Śaiva/​Śākta texts has proven difficult, but they can be explained via common archi­
tectural elements.

thet of Trailokyavijaya exhibiting the Trailokyavijaya mudrā. He is surrounded by ten 
wrathful deities of the ten directions. The text also describes another mandala in which 
the central deity, Mañjuvajra, is surrounded by ten wrathful deities. See Bhattacharyya 
1949: 44, 58, 59.
	21.	 The Javanese evidence comes from epigraphic documents such as Ratu Boko gold foil and 
a lead plate inscription found from the west of Borobudur. See Griffiths 2014c: 183–​184, 
2014a: 32 and Acri 2016b: 323–​348. For an in-​depth study of the Trailokyavijaya cult in 
Central Java, see Gauvain 2022: 94–​133.
	22.	 The occurrence of the term saṃgūḍārtha, “tantric concerns/​secret meanings” (?), in both 
the Ratu Boko and Kelurak inscriptions is worthy of a mention. This could point to a tan­
tric Buddhist context. Sundberg (2014 [2015]: 96) aptly regards the Abhayagiri inscription 
as “the textual equivalent of the Barabuḍur stūpa” in that it is “superficially an expression 
of conventional Mahāyāna thought but endowed with a deep esoteric undercurrent.”
	23.	 The stone tablet unearthed from the Abhayagiri mahāstūpa was excerpted from the STTS’s 
second mandala, in which all of the peripheral vajra deities are female. Powell 2018 argues 
that the “practice of tantric Buddhism was anything but peripheral in eighth-​century 
Anurādhapura.”
	24.	 Woodward 2011: 39 suggests: “if Lakṣmīndralokeśvara is really Prajñāpāramitā, on the 
other hand, the Mahāvairocana sutra could indeed be relevant, especially if it is held that 
the text can be interpreted to mean that Prajñāpāramitā in fact belongs in a spot more 
prominent than the one she was given in the Japanese Garbhadhātu.”
	25.	 A 9th-​century Cam inscription (c. 149) records the ministers of the king of kings going 
twice to Java on diplomatic missions. See Huber 1911: 299, Jaques 1995: 273–​285, and 
Schweyer 2009: 316. A Javanese inscription that mentions pilgrims arriving from 
Gurjaradeśa refers either to Gujarat in western India, the Valabhī domain of the Maitrika 
kings, or to the kingdom of the Gurjara Pratihāras in central-​north India. See de Casparis 
1956: 188–​189.
	26.	 Lokesh Chandra and Sudarshana Devi Singhal 1995b: 97–​107 found that the Ngañjuk 
bronzes belonged almost entirely to the Vajradhātu mandala described in the 8th-​century 
STTS and SDPS as well as in the mandala of the Niṣpannayogāvalī. For the Surocolo hoard, 
both 1995b: 121–​147 assigned some statues to the Hevajra mandala. Sundberg and Giebel 
2011: 218, n. 173 argue that the Surocolo bronzes were derived from the Hevajra mandala. 
However, the presence of the drummer Mukuṇḍā in the Ngañjuk hoard is problematic, as 
it is not a part of the Vajradhātu mandala, and the principal deity of the Hevajra mandala is 
missing from the Surocolo hoard. See Woodward 2004: 344. For Ponorogo, see Matsunaga 
2017: 1–​21.
	27.	 The SDPS, an Indo-​Tibetan explanatory text of the STTS, probably originated in Java and 
described the Vajradhātu mandala; Tadeusz Skorupski, personal communication. For the 
narratives, see SDPS: 307, Skorupski 1983: 20.
	28.	 The 14th-​century Javanese text Sutasoma, canto 139, says “bhinneka tunggal ika,” which 
means that Śiva and Buddha are two, but at the same time they are one: see Zoetmulder

--- PAGE 692 ---
Mandalas and Monarchs      667
 
1974: 341 and Santoso 1975: 5, 81. Arjunawijaya equates five Jina Buddhas to five 
manifestations of Śiva, as observed by Zoetmulder 1974: 327.
	29.	 See, for example, Nāgarkṛtāgama, canto 92 (Robson 1995: 93), which describes Hayam 
Wuruk as an avatāra of Śrī Girinātha (Śiva, the lord of the mountain); Pigeaud (1960–​63: 
vol. 3:110; vol. 4: 331, 335). See Kern 1917:219 for the 14th-​century Kubu Rajo inscription I, 
which considers Hayam Wuruk an avatāra of Śrī Lokeśvara.
	30.	 Identified as a Buddhist Bhairava by Bosch 1930a: 212–​213, Schnitger 1937a: 9, Kempers 
1959: 88, Reichle 2007: 198–​200, and Lunsingh Scheurleer 2008: 295. Bautze-​Picron 2014: 
113 identifies it as Mahākāla. The image displays a row of skulls above the head forming a 
crown and possibly carries Akṣobhya, which is now badly ruined.
	31.	 The inscription on the statue mentions that it was reconsecrated with devotion at the cem­
etery named Wurare in conformity with Mahākṣobhya. Kern 1910: 99–​108, Poerbatjaraka 
1922: 426–​461, Nihom 1986: 485–​501, and Chandra 1995a: 161 associate Mahākṣobhya with 
mahāyoga tantras and the deity with Guhyasamāja.
	32.	 Fontein 1990: 162. Scholars have emphasized the difficulty in differentiating between 
Śaivite Bhairavas and Buddhist demonic figures such as Mahākāla. The iconographic traits 
of these two deities are common, making it difficult to determine the identity especially 
during the Majapahit period, when Hinduism and Buddhism were fused in tantrism. 
Reichle 2007: 189 identifies it as Buddhist Bhairava. Hunter 2007: 36 hints the association 
of the cakracakra image to the divine Bhairava aspect.
	33.	 Pigeaud (1960–​63: vol. 1: 104–​107; vol. 2: 135–​136; vol. 3: 152–​153); Piegeaud 1924: 104–​128. 
Haryani Santiko 1995: 58. For a good discussion on the sect see Acri 2019: 285–​307.
	34.	 Reichle 2007, 85–​132 identifies Padang Roco statue as Bhairava. Bautze-​Picron 2014: 113 
identifies it as Mahākāla. While supporting Bautze-​Picron’s identification of the image as 
Mahākāla, Acri and Wenta 2021 associate it with a specific form, *Pañjaranātha Mahākāla, 
but keep the option open of iconographic contaminations from Bhairava. They argue that 
it represented a deified statue of Kṛtanagara, and tentatively suggest that its original lo­
cation might have been Candi Jawi. The Bhairava statue found at Jago was described by 
Schnitger 1937a: 9 as “with skull and dagger in his hands and with an Akṣobhya in his hair.” 
Sadly, the statue was badly broken and only the torso remained on site till 1990s but in 
2004 it was reported as stolen.
	35.	 Nāgarakṛtāgama, canto 43, see Robson (1995: 56) and Pigeaud (1960–​63: vol. 2:59; vol. 3: 
50). Chuttiwongs 2008: 102 argues that the image came from the temple of Jawi.
	36.	 See Nāgarakṛtāgama, cantos 6 and 7. Robson (1995: 27, 28, 99) suggests that the names 
are taken from the tantric system of yoga, while Pigeaud (1960–​63: vol. 3: 7, 8; 4: 542, 543 
discusses them specifically with respect to Kuṇḍalinī yoga. Acri confirms the presence of 
some Śaivite tantric yogic practices; email communication, September 7, 2021.
	37.	 The image was the symbol for the unity of the realm, as is argued by Schrieke 1957: 321, 
n. 32. See Nāgarakṛtāgama 68.5 and 74.1, Robson (1995: 73, 78) and Pigeaud (1960–​63: 
vol. 3: 81, 87).
	38.	 Suggesting its link with the damaged Mahākāla image of Candi Jago, Bautze-​Picron 
2014: 113–​114 argues for the image being of Mahākāla. Though it was assumed to be a 
portrait statue of Ādityavarman, Klokke 1994: 178–​201 has argued for the statue being a 
“deification image” that represents a deified mortal and a Hindu-​Buddhist deity at the 
same time.
	39.	 Based on the iconographic traits of East Javanese icons and the Padang Roco statue, 
Reichle 2007: 187, 191 suspects that it was made in East Java. Kulke 2009: 249 notes that this

--- PAGE 693 ---
668      Swati Chemburkar
 
stone was unknown in the kingdom of Ādityavarman. Moens 1924: 557 questions whether 
it was sent by Kṛtanagara along with the Amoghapāśa sculpture.
	40.	 The letters, inscribed on the gold sheet in Kawi script, appear to be from the mid-​9th to 
early 10th centuries, indicating the deposit as the plan of the original foundation of a mon­
ument that was enlarged later. The 21 inscribed gold plates contain names of 5 Tathāgatas, 
16 Vajrabodhisattvas, and 16 Vajratārā deities. Boechari 1982: 229–​143 had argued for the 
presence of the Vajradhātu mandala at Gumpung. Refuting Boechari, Nihom 1998: 245–​
254 has argued for the material belonging to the Trailokyavijaya mandala.
	41.	 A gold leaf found at Aek Sangkilon is studied by Griffiths 2014b: 228–​229. Reichle 2007: 
142 identifies the inscription with the Yamāri tradition. For a Saruaso inscription from 
Pagarruyung evoking Hevajranityasmmṛti, see Hunter 2015: 324–​327; Suleiman 1977: 5–​6. 
See Reichle 2007: 139, 142–​143, 201.
	42.	 Even though there were earlier smaller tantric Buddhist temples built by the Khmers, such 
as the 10th-​century Bat Cum or Phnom Trap, Phimai celebrated tantrism on a grand scale.
	43.	 Several scholars identify the central image of the pentad as Vajrasattva, while admitting the 
unusual iconographic scheme. See Boisselier 1966: 302; Dagens 1995: 19. Woodward 2004: 
351 sees the Phimai deity as three-​faced, six-​armed Mañjuvajra, a form of Vajrasattva. 
Jacques 2006: 75 sees a possible representation of the five-​Buddha system of the Śrīghana 
sect, which is mentioned in the 9th-​century inscription K. 1001, found during the renova­
tion of the temple, as well as a Sab Bāk inscription.
	44.	 Stanzas 26–​28 of the inscription mentions Hiraṇyadāma revealing a unique siddhi to 
the ruler by showing him the fourfold face of Tumburu to allow the ruler to understand 
the Śiraścheda, Viṇāśikha, Saṃmoha, and Nayottara. Inscription K. 235; see Finot 1915: 
53, Cœdès and Dupont 1943: 56, and Bhattacharya 2009: 123. For the translation of the 
Vīṇāśikha Tantra see Goudriaan 1985.
	45.	 Based on the two hands found by The Authority for the Protection of the Site and 
Management of the Region of Angkor (APSARA) and Archaeological Survey of India 
(ASI) in 2011, holding specific attributes, Olivier Cunin identifies them as a part of a 
Hevajra statue; personal communication on email dated to 6th June 2019. (My sincere 
thanks to him for sharing his 3D scans of the hands.) The statue would have been smaller 
than the Bayon one, based on the smaller size of the hands. Currently the hands are kept at 
the Preah Norodom Sihanouk Museum in Siem Reap, Cambodia.
	46.	 Today a small sanctuary stands at the Mỹ Sơn complex in Ɖà Nẵng. The Mỹ Sơn inscrip­
tion C92 B mentions “paṅap rumaḥ śrī herukaharmya” and provides a clear account of the 
Khmer-​Cam relations during the 12th–​13th centuries and the erection of the temple. See 
Finot 1904: 972 and Jaques 1995: 154.
