Chapter 27
Jain Tantric Diagrams of 
the Goddess Padmāvatī
Ellen Gough
Scholarship on the “Main Tantra” 
of Jainism
In English-​language publications on tantric literature, two Jain texts are repeatedly 
mentioned: Indranandin’s Jvālāmālinīkalpa, completed in 939/​940, and Malliṣeṇa’s 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, completed in 1057 (1937, 1899, n.d.) (1966). Both texts are 
Digambara, come from south India, and describe the propitiation of goddesses using 
mantras and tantric diagrams (yantra) to achieve superhuman powers and worldly 
well-​being. Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta’s important survey of tantric litera­
ture, Hindu Tantric and Śākta Literature (1981), names these manuals as representative 
of Jain tantric literature:
The Jainas contributed to Tantric literature with their Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and 
Jvālinīkalpa. The first text was compiled about A.D. 1050 by Malliṣena of Mysore; 
the second was produced by a monk of the Drāviḍa order from the Rāṣṭrakūṭa cap­
ital Mānyakheṭa. The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, devoted to Padmāvatī who is a Jaina 
pendant of Tripurā, is a digest in 308 stanzas written in a good Sanskrit style of Āryā 
metres predominating. Its main concern is the practice of magic rites with mantras 
and yantras of the goddess.
(Goudriaan and Gupta 1981: 111)
Goudriaan, Gupta, and other scholars highlight the influence of Śaiva–​Śākta 
traditions on these two texts. They focus on the similarities between the main goddess 
of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, Padmāvatī—​the tutelary deity of the twenty-​third 
tīrthaṅkara, Pārśva—​and the principle goddess of the Śaiva Kaula Śrīvidyā tradition, 
Tripurā/​Tripurasundarī (Sanderson 2011: 3–​4; Slouber 2016: 84).

--- PAGE 705 ---
680      Ellen Gough
 
The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa has been promoted in this way in large part because 
of the work of two Śvetāmbara Gujarati men in the first half of the twentieth cen­
tury: Sarabhai Manilal Nawab, the prolific author, publisher, and promoter of Jain 
mantraśāstra, and Mohanlal Bhagwandas Jhavery, the solicitor and scholar. In 1937, 
Nawab’s printing press published the text of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa edited by 
K. V. Abhyaṅkar, along with a premodern Sanskrit commentary by an unknown au­
thor named Bandhuṣeṇa and a Gujarati translation by Nawab. He based his publica­
tion on nine different manuscripts, all found in Śvetāmbara collections in Gujarat: 
in Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara, Limbdi, Patan, and Sinor (Abhyaṅkar 1937: 5–​6). 
Nawab’s press then followed up in 1944 with the publication of Jhavery’s introduction to 
the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, Comparative and Critical Study of Mantrashastra, which 
Jhavery himself admits expanded far beyond “its original purpose of introducing the 
reader to the work” and became “an independent treatise” on an impressive range of 
topics related to mantraśāstra, Jain and otherwise (Jhavery 1944: 1). At the end of the 
book, Jhavery summarizes the contents of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and cites the 
third verse of the first chapter of the text, which names Padmāvatī as Totalā, Tvaritā, 
Nityā, Tripurā, Kāmasādhinī, and Tripurabhairavī, to make the claim that “there 
is no doubt that the author identifies Śrī Padmāvatī with Śrī Vidyā alias Ṣodaśī,” or 
Tripurasundarī (Jhavery 1944: 295).
Jhavery’s extensive, if unwieldy, book went on to define the study of Jain tantric 
practices in English, with influential twentieth-​century European scholars like 
Agehananda Bharati (1965) and Teun Goudriaan (1978) relying on it as the sole source 
for Jain materials in their comparative studies of tantra. Goudriaan and Gupta (1981: 
111) and other scholars of tantra (White 2000: 23–​24) also relied on Ramendra Nath 
Nandi’s (1973: 145–​156) chapter on “The Jaina Goddesses of Tantric Association,” 
which focuses on two texts—​Nawab’s publication of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and 
a manuscript of Indranandin’s Jvālinīkalpa from the Jain Siddhānt Bhavan in Arrah, 
Indore. It is no surprise, then, that the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, the Jvālinīkalpa/​
Jvālāmālinīkalpa, and similar medieval texts on the mantra-​based propitiation of 
goddesses have become understood as the principal Jain texts of the category of scrip­
ture called tantra. Aaron Ullrey (2016: xvii) focuses much of his research on these 
“two Jain tantras.” Travis Smith (2018) explains in his article on “Tantras” for Brill’s 
Encyclopedia of Hinduism that “there are also Jaina Tantras, a series of ritual manuals 
dedicated to the worship of fierce female ‘protector’ deities that attended upon the 
tῑrthaṅkaras.”1 And Agehananda Bharati (1965: 121) calls the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 
the “main tantra” of Jainism.
Jainism, however, has no category of scripture called tantra. As Michael Slouber 
notes in this volume with regard to non-​Jain traditions, “the word tantra was originally 
used most often in the sense of a treatise and was interchangeable with other words for 
tantric scriptures.” But Jains do not commonly use this term for their scriptures. The 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and Jvālinīkalpa/​Jvālāmālinīkalpa are not “tantras;” they 
are two of the dozens, if not hundreds, of Jains texts called kalpa: ritual manual. From 
the medieval period to the present day, Jains of both the main image-​worshiping sects,

--- PAGE 706 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      681
 
Digambara and Śvetāmbara, have composed a variety of kalpa texts that outline the 
ritual propitiation of yantras, or diagrams on which mantras are inscribed, to invoke 
deities and ideals. Some of these kalpas outline rituals that remain hugely popular, for 
example various texts on the mantra that Śvetāmbara mendicant leaders (ācārya) to this 
day recite daily, texts called Sūrimantrakalpa (Jambūvijaya 1969: 1977).
Scholars have not, however, assessed the present-​day popularity of the 
Jvālāmālinīkalpa and the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa. The texts certainly gained some trac­
tion in Jain communities between their compositions in the tenth and eleventh centuries 
and scholars’ promotion of them in the twentieth century. As noted, some manuscripts 
of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa include a Sanskrit commentary by an unknown author, 
Bandhuṣeṇa. In addition, a significant part of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is contained 
in the later Digambara compilation of Jain texts on mantraśāstra, the Vidyānuśāsana, 
which is attributed to an unknown Matisāgara (Jhavery 1944: 303). The modest pres­
ence of the Jvālāmālinīkalpa and the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa in manuscript archives 
also speaks to their influence. In his survey of Jain manuscripts from archives in 
Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Pune, the Śvetāmbara monk Ācārya Jinendrasūri has listed 
at least five copies of texts called Jvālāmālinīkalpa/​Jvālinīkalpa that are attributed 
to Indranandin held at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, and the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is found even more commonly in manuscript collections 
throughout India, both Jain and non-​Jain (Jinendrasurishwarji n.d: 295). Importantly, 
the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa—​a Digambara text from Karnataka—​is quite often found 
in Śvetāmbara manuscript collections in north India—​in Rajasthan and Gujarat—​and 
Nawab, as noted, relied upon these collections for his publication of the text.
In some ways, the movement of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa from a Digambara 
context in Karnataka to Śvetāmbara places of worship in north India follows the same 
trajectory as the goddess Padmāvatī herself. Scholars have conjectured that this god­
dess initially rose to prominence as a kuladevī, or a family goddess, of a series of im­
portant royal families in Karnataka such as the Śīlahāras, Raṭṭas, and Śāntaras (Cort 
1987: 243; Desai 1957: 171). Through these families’ adherence to Digambara Jainism, 
she was eventually incorporated into the Digambara Jain pantheon, becoming the fe­
male attendant (śāsanadevī or yakṣī) of Pārśva sometime in the post-​Gupta medieval 
period (Shah 1959: 141–​143, 1987: 276–​285). Pārśva had been associated with snake 
deities (nāga) since an early period; reliefs of the twenty-​third Tīrthaṅkara from the 
early centuries C.E. from Mathura depict him with cobra hoods above his head (Shah 
1970: 305). Padmāvatī, as a snake deity (nāginī), could then be easily linked to him. 
The Digambara text on the history of the universe, Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa (mid-​
ninth century), provides an early inclusion of Padmāvatī in the life story of Pārśva. 
Here, Pārśva saves a pair of snakes, Dhareṇendra and Padmāvatī, from the fires of 
an immoral Brahmin ascetic, and they are reborn as snake deities who later emerge 
from the underworld to shade him from distractions so he can meditate and achieve 
omniscience (Bollée 2007: 34–​35).2 Though Śvetāmbaras do not include her in their 
narratives of Pārśva’s life, only mentioning Dharaṇendra, by at least the time of the 
Nirvāṇakalikā (eleventh–​twelfth centuries C.E.), they had accepted Padmāvatī as

--- PAGE 707 ---
682      Ellen Gough
 
Pārśva’s female attendant deity (yakṣī), and she is now undoubtedly one of the most 
popular goddesses of both image-​worshiping Jain sects.
We can ask, then: What role has the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa played in defining 
Padmāvatī and launching her to her current exalted status?3 Has the text influenced 
modern Jain worship practices? One way to answer these questions is to determine 
how or if the yantras described in the text are commonly used today. Digambara and 
Śvetāmbara temples today are filled with different yantras, inscribed on metal and 
placed in shrines, painted on cloth or paper and framed on the wall of a temple or wor­
ship hall, or traced with foodstuffs or synthetic colored powder for special occasions like 
the consecration of a temple or a festival (Gough 2019). In pilgrimage sites and cities, 
shops that specialize in Jain ritual paraphernalia sell portable yantras that laypeople can 
establish in their personal shrines; most practicing Jains will have a shrine at home, and 
Jain shopkeepers will often establish metal or paper yantras on a wall or in a shrine in 
their shop. While practitioners can always commission special yantras, the readymade 
ones easily available at shops represent the most recognizable yantras today.
To gain some understanding of the relationship between the yantras of the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and modern yantras of Padmāvatī, then, I will compare the 
eleventh-​century text to yantras available for purchase in two different shops: one 
shop in Jaipur that specializes in both Hindu and Digambara Jain yantras, Jain Yantra 
Udyog, and an online site that sells Hindu and Śvetāmbara Jain yantras run by a Jain 
astrologer in Mumbai, Rajendra Chopra Jain (rajendrachopra.com). I will rely on four 
different versions of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa that include images of the yantras 
described in the Sanskrit text. One of these versions is Nawab’s; he commissioned 
forty-​four images of yantras for his publication. The other versions are Digambara. 
The website of the International Digambara Jain Organization has archived scans 
of two manuscripts of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa from the Sri Dev Kumar Jain 
Oriental Research Institute (also known as the Jain Siddhānt Bhavan) in Arrah, Bihar: 
one of fifty-​two folios and another of twenty-​four. Both manuscripts should not date 
before the nineteenth century, are on paper, and contain the same forty-​four yantras, 
which differ only slightly from the yantras in Nawab’s publication. Another version of 
the text, with forty-​six images of yantras, was published in 1952 by Mūlcand Kisandās 
Kāpaḍiyā and translated into Hindi by Paṇḍit Candraśekhar Śāstrī (Śāstrī 1952). Using 
these images of the yantras as a reference, I will follow the text of Nawab’s edition 
(Abhyaṅkar 1937)4—​including Bandhuṣeṇa’s commentary—​to outline some yantras 
described in the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and then compare them with modern 
yantras of Padmāvatī, both Śvetāmbara and Digambara.5 Much more research needs 
to be done to determine the real influence of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, but the 
examination of these yantras shows that there is little evidence that the text has had a 
profound influence on modern Jain mantraśāstra and on the worship of Padmāvatī. 
While many of the mantras and rituals of the Bhairavapadmāvatikalpa are common to 
the images and practices of Jain mantraśāstra, the text should not be seen as the “main 
tantra” of Jainism.

--- PAGE 708 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      683
 
The Yantras of the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa
The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa contains ten chapters and a little over three hundred 
Sanskrit verses, depending on the manuscript or publication. The first chapter, after 
introducing the goddess Padmāvatī with the epithets discussed above (1.3), outlines the 
contents of the text (1.4–​1.5) and the qualities of a person who can undertake its practices 
(sādhaka or mantrin), which include being devoid of anger and bad karma (1.6–​1.7), 
needing to eat and sleep very little (1.8), having conquered the passions (1.9), and being 
devoted to a guru (1.10). The second chapter describes what it calls sakalīkriyā. The best 
known saklīkriyā/​karaṇa rites are the ones in Śaiva texts in which a practitioner must 
undertake visualizations and placements of mantras on his body to transform himself 
into Śiva before worshiping icons of Śiva (Davis 1992). In the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, 
it is a catch-​all term for the mantra-​based preliminary rites of protection and purifica­
tion a practitioner must undertake before propitiating the yantras described in the sub­
sequent chapters.
After bathing, the practitioner should wear red clothes and sit in a clean space (2.1). By 
reciting the syllables and touching his fingers, he then should place on his left hand the 
syllables hrāṃ, hrīṃ, hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ on his thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring 
finger, and pinky, respectively (2.2). To protect his body, he should touch five different 
body parts and recite an expanded version of the main mantra of Jainism, the Prakrit 
Fivefold Praise (pañcanamaskāra), which honors the five supreme objects of reverence 
in Jainism, the omniscient souls (arhat), liberated souls (siddha), and the mendicants 
on the path to becoming liberated: the mendicant leaders (ācārya), mendicant teachers 
(upādhyāya), and ordinary mendicants (sādhu):
oṃ ṇamo arahantāṇaṃ hrāṃ śīrṣaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā
oṃ praise the liberated souls, protect my head
oṃ ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ hrīṃ vadanaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā
oṃ praise the liberated souls, protect my body
oṃ ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ hrūṃ hṛdayaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā
oṃ praise the liberated souls, protect my heart
oṃ ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ hrauṃ nābhiṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā
oṃ praise the liberated souls, protect my navel
oṃ ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ hraḥ pādau rakṣa rakṣa svāhā
oṃ praise the liberated souls, protect my feet. (2.3–​2.4)6
The text requires the daily performance of this nyāsa, or placement of mantras on the 
body (2.4).
The sādhaka then should recite eight seed syllables to protect his space from ad­
verse influences coming from the eight directions (perform digbandhana; 2.5) and

--- PAGE 709 ---
684      Ellen Gough
 
perform bhūtaśuddhi rites—​visualizations of diagrams and seed syllables—​to purify 
the elements that constitute both the universe and his body. He should imagine a series 
of syllables—​the letter ha attached to each of the vowels (ha, hā, hi hī, hu, hū, etc.)—​
that are golden, standing twenty hands tall (2.6); he should then imagine a moat filled 
with water and the syllable kṣa attached to each of the vowels (kṣạ, kṣa, kṣā, kṣi, kṣī, kṣu, 
kṣū, etc.) (2.7) (see Williams, this volume). After imagining himself seated inside a fire 
diagram—​a triangle in which the seed syllable raṃ is inscribed—​he should imagine 
himself bathed by the mantra of immortality, the amṛtamantra,7 and by milk that the 
gods used to bathe the jina Pārśva on Mount Meru in celebration of his birth (2.8–​2.9). 
From these visualizations, the text claims, the practitioner will not be troubled by various 
potentially malevolent forces, including ghosts and planets (2.10). Seated cross-​legged, 
in paryaṅkāsana,8 having given himself a mark on his forehead (tilaka), with his pūjā 
offerings nearby (2.11), the sādhaka should visualize a red Padmāvatī, with three eyes, 
seated on a lotus, with her vehicle—​a snake with the head of a rooster (kukkuṭoraga)9—​
making a gesture of blessing (varadamudrā) with one hand and holding a goad, a noose, 
and a fruit in her other hands (2.12). Finally, to determine which invocations are effec­
tive for ritual use, the syllables of the names of the sādhaka and a mantra are divided and 
placed in a sequence, with some conferring positive results and others negative (for the 
details, see vv. 2.15–​22).
The Padmāvatī Yantra of Chapter Three
Chapter Three describes the construction of a yantra whose ritual propitiation can allow 
for the “six acts” (ṣaṭkarman) of pacification (śānti), causing enmity (dveṣa), gaining 
control (vaśya), stopping another person (bandha), attracting women (ākarṣaṇa), 
and immobilizing negative forces (stambhana). Which act is undertaken depends on 
a number of factors, including the substance offered to the yantra, the hand gesture 
performed, the sādhaka’s posture, and the color of flowers offered to the diagram (3.1–​
3.12). To construct the yantra, the practitioner, using a golden writing utensil, should 
trace with scented substances a diagram made of three concentric squares, with four 
doors placed in the cardinal directions (3.13). Outside each of the four doors, the fol­
lowing four Sanskrit mantras should be inscribed:
East: oṃ hrīṃ dharaṇendrāya namaḥ
South: oṃ hrīṃ adhacchadanāya namaḥ
West: oṃ hrīṃ ūrdhvacchadanāya namaḥ
North: oṃ hrīṃ padmacchadanāya namaḥ (3.14)
Then, inside the outermost square, in each of the eight directions and above and below 
the yantra, ten Sanskrit mantras should be inscribed to invoke the guardians of the eight 
directions, the dikpālas—​Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛtya, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna—​
and the deities who protect from above and below (3.15–​3.16). Inside the second con­
centric square, in the cardinal directions, praises to masculine forms of the goddesses of

--- PAGE 710 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      685
 
victory, the jayādevīs—​Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā—​should be traced.10 The ordinal 
directions should contain praises to masculine forms of the goddesses linked to the “six 
acts”: Jambhā (“Devourer”), Mohā (“Deluder”), Stambhā (“Immobilizer”), and Stambhinī 
(“Immobilizer”):
East: oṃ hrīṃ jaye namaḥ
Southeast: oṃ hrīṃ jambhe namaḥ
South: oṃ hrīṃ vijaye namaḥ
Southwest: oṃ hrīṃ mohe namaḥ
West: oṃ hrīṃ ajite namaḥ
Northwest: oṃ hrīṃ stambhe namaḥ
North: oṃ hrīṃ aparājite namaḥ
Northeast: oṃ hrīṃ stambhini namaḥ (3.17–​3.18)
An eight-​petaled lotus should sit at the center of the diagram. Each of the eight petals 
of this lotus should contain a mantra praising one of the eight messengers, or dūtikās, of 
Padmāvatī: Anaṅgakamalā, Padmagandhā, Padmāsyā, Padmamālā, Madanonmādinī, 
Kāmoddīpanā, Padmāvarṇā, Trailokyakṣobhinī:11
East: oṃ hrīṃ anaṅgakamalāyai namaḥ
Southeast: oṃ hrīṃ padmagandhāyai namaḥ
South: oṃ hrīṃ padmāsyāyai namaḥ
Southwest: oṃ hrīṃ padmamālāyai namaḥ
West: oṃ hrīṃ madanonmādinyai namaḥ
Northwest: oṃ hrīṃ kāmoddīpanāyai namaḥ
North: oṃ hrīṃ padmavarṇāyai namaḥ
Northeast: oṃ hrīṃ trailokyakṣobhiṇyai namaḥ (3.19–​3.21)
The center of the lotus should contain an image of Padmāvatī or mantras that invoke her 
presence. All the syllables of the Devanagari alphabet should be traced in the pericarp of 
the lotus (3.21). In the four cardinal directions should sit the following mantras:12
East: oṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ padmāvatīdevyai namaḥ
South oṃ hrīṃ kṣīṃ padmāvatīdevyai namaḥ
West: oṃ hrīṃ kṣūṃ padmāvatīdevyai namaḥ
North: oṃ hrīṃ kṣaiṃ padmāvatīdevyai namaḥ (3.22–​23)
This is the key yantra to Padmāvatī in the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa. She sits at the 
center of the lotus, surrounded by lower-​level deities, including her messengers, pow­
erful deities who can effect the “six acts,” and protectors. The text declares that this yantra 
should be worshiped regularly (nityam) and outlines the mantras and breath control 
the sādhaka should use to perform the five upacāras—​inviting the goddess into the di­
agram (āhvāna), establishing her there (sthāpana), having her remain in the diagram 
(sannidhīkaraṇa), having her accept scented substances and other offerings (pūjā), and 
dismissing her from the diagram after the worship is completed (visarjana) (3.23–​3.28).

--- PAGE 711 ---
686      Ellen Gough
 
Five mantras to be used in this worship of Padmāvatī are outlined:
Root mantra: [oṃ] hrīṃ hraiṃ hsklīṃ padme padmakaṭini  [namaḥ] (3.29)
Mantra of six syllables: [oṃ] hrīṃ hraiṃ hsklīṃ śrīṃ padme  [namaḥ] (3.31)
Mantra of three syllables: [oṃ] aiṃ klīṃ hsauḥ  [namaḥ] (3.32)
Mantra of one syllable: [oṃ] hrīṃ [namaḥ] (3.33–​34)
The text confirms that hrīṃ is the symbol of Pārśva and his tutelary deities: ha represents 
Pārśva, ra represents Dharaṇendra, and ī represents Padmāvatī (3.33).
Some Yantras of the Final Seven Chapters
While the elaborate yantra of Chapter Three should be worshiped regularly, the yantras 
of the subsequent chapters should be used in specific circumstances. Chapter Four 
details the construction of eleven13 different yantras, each of which should be worshiped 
for a different result, from deluding another person to ensuring that a woman has 
pleasant speech and actions. Each of these yantras is made up of a twelve-​petaled lotus. 
At the center of the lotus, the name of the person to be affected by the propitiation of 
the yantra should be inscribed in the pericarp. The name is surrounded by the mantra 
kṣmlrvyūṃ and flanked by a pair of seed syllables. What seed syllable flanks the name 
depends on the use of the yantra:
	
1.	 To delude: klīṃ (4.4)
	
2.	 To attract: hrīṃ (4.5)
	
3.	 To repel: huṃ (4.6)14
	
4.	 To create enmity: rya (4.7–​4.8)
	
5.	 To eradicate the bondage of an enemy: yaḥ (4.9–​4.10)
	
6.	 To eradicate the family of an enemy: ha (4.11–​4.12)
	
7.	 To force an enemy to wander the earth: phaṭ (4.13–​4.14)
	
8.	 To suppress an enemy: ma (4.15–​4.16)
	
9.	 To delude a woman: ī (4.17–​4.18)
	 10.	 To make a women lovely: kṣavaṣaṭ (4.19–​4.20)
	
11.	 To immobilize: laṃ (4.21)
In the twelve petals of the lotus, mantras to invoke the jayādevīs sit in the petals facing 
the cardinal directions, and mantras to invoke the goddesses linked to the “six acts” sit in 
the petals facing the ordinal directions:
East: oṃ jayāyai svāhā15
Southeast: oṃ jhmlrvyūṃ jambhāyai svāhā
South: oṃ vijayāyai svāhā
Southwest: oṃ bhmlrvyūṃ mohāyai svāhā

--- PAGE 712 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      687
 
West: oṃ ajitāyai svāhā
Northwest: oṃ mmlrvyūṃ stambhāyai svāhā
North: oṃ aparājitāyai svāhā
Northeast: oṃ hmlrvyūṃ stambhinyai svāhā (4.2)
Each of the remaining four petals contains three seed syllables: whatever seed syllable 
sits at the center of the lotus (klīṃ, hrīṃ, hūṃ, etc.) plus two repetitions of kroṃ. In this 
way, the yantras of Chapter Four do not directly invoke Padmāvatī, and they should be 
constructed for much more specific reasons than the yantra of Chapter Three.
The nine yantras outlined in Chapter Five have an even more specific use: They 
should be propitiated to immobilize (stambhana) adversaries, including water, snakes, 
birds, anger, and armies. The first yantra, which helps extinguish fires, is made up of 
an eight-​petaled lotus, at the center of which the name of the object to be immobilized 
should be inscribed, surrounded by the seed syllable glauṃ. In the eight petals, the fol­
lowing mantras should be inscribed: kṣmlrvyūṃ, mmlrvyūṃ, ṭhmlrvyūṃ, smlrvyūṃ, 
hmlrvyūṃ, pmlrvyūṃ, lmlrvryūṃ, and vmlvryūṃ (5.1). In a circle around the lotus, 
two mantras should be inscribed that invoke the goddess “Fire-​Extinguisher,” 
Agnistambhinī, along with other goddesses whose names confirm that they offer well-​
being: Pañcadivyottaraṇī, Śreyaskarī, Sarvakāmārthasādhinī, Analapiṅgalordhvakeśinī, 
and Mahādivyādhipatā (5.2).
Chapter Six focuses on five yantras that can attract women. Two yantras from this 
chapter stand out in the manuscripts, because they each feature an image of a female—​
the sādhaka’s desired woman. For the first of these yantras, on top of the image of the 
woman, oṃ hrīṃ should be written on her heart, kroṃ16 on her joints, hrīṃ on each of 
her breasts, and ryyūṃ on her genitals. The woman should be surrounded by multiple 
kroṃs, a ring of mantras (oṃ namo bhagavati kṛṣṇamātaṅgini, etc.),17 a triangle, a circle, 
and a square. The text confirms that propitiating the yantra with a lamp or flame for 
three days attracts the desired woman (6.4).
The nine yantras of Chapter Seven aid the sādhaka in gaining control (vaśya) of 
different situations and people, including women and fevers. The first yantra is an 
eight-​petaled lotus at the center of which sits the name of the object to be controlled, 
surrounded by the mantras haṃsaḥ, kṣmlrvyūṃ, and all the vowels of the Devanagari 
alphabet. The petals facing the cardinal directions also contain the mantra haṃsaḥ, 
plus a mantra honoring the omniscient soul, the arhat (arhaṃ): oṃ arhaṃ jhvīṃ kṣvīṃ 
haṃsaḥ svāhā. The petals facing the ordinal directions contain the syllable cluster 
kṣmlrvyūṃ (7.1–​7.2). After this yantra is traced on birch bark with scented substances 
and placed in new pot filled with water, an icon of Pārśva should be placed on top of a 
container of grains on top of this pot. This should allow for fevers to break (7.3–​7.4).
Chapter Eight describes different ways to use mantras to forecast the future, in­
cluding rites that use mirrors and lamps. In these divination rites, only three yantras 
are mentioned. The second one, for example, can be used to determine if the person 
will lose his home. It comprises a triangle surrounded by a circle, with kṣmlrvyūṃ, 
oṃ, fourteen vowels (all but ḷ and ṛ), and the name of a person at its center (8.24–​8.25).

--- PAGE 713 ---
688      Ellen Gough
 
Finally, Chapter Ten, devoted to rituals for controlling snakes and curing snake bites, 
describes three different yantras that can be effective in these pursuits. The key mantra 
of this chapter is commonly found in Jain and non-​Jain texts on controlling snakes 
(gāruḍatantra), “Garuḍa’s five syllables,” or the vipatimantra: kṣi pa oṃ svā hā. The first 
yantra of the chapter, for example, comprises a four-​petaled lotus, and in each of the 
petals of the lotus sit the syllables kṣi pa oṃ svā hā (10.6).18
Each of the yantras of these chapters should be constructed, stored, and propitiated 
in a specific way, and many of the instructions contain elements that starkly contradict 
the nonviolent, monastic teachings of Jainism. Some of the yantras should be traced on 
skulls, for example (4.5), using poison, ash, and even animal blood (4.11–​4.12, 4.15–​4.16). 
The first yantra of Chapter Four is to be traced with scented substances on a piece of 
birch bark, tied with a red thread, and placed in a golden pot filled with liquor. Simply 
doing this will delude the woman whose name is inscribed at the center of the yantra 
(4.4). Because many of these yantras are associated with practices that are banned 
for lay and mendicant Jains alike, one would not expect for them to be commonly 
found in Jain temples, or even commonly constructed by Jains. If one yantra from the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa were to be found in temple and home shrines, it would be the 
elaborate one outlined in Chapter Three, which contains Padmāvatī and her attendant 
deities and is prescribed to be worshiped regularly. However, this yantra is not popularly 
found in temples, home shrines, shops, or modern worship booklets.
Some Modern Yantras to Padmāvatī
In my fifteen years of documenting Digambara and Śvetāmbara yantras in 
temples, homes, and shops in north India, I have not encountered the yantras of the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa in places of worship.19 I have, however, seen dozens of dif­
ferent yantras to Padmāvatī, so it is impossible to discuss every type of Padmāvatī yantra 
used in worship today. Looking at the Padmāvatī yantras for sale in two shops—​the Jain 
Yantra Udyog shop in Jaipur and Rajendra Chopra Jain’s shop in Mumbai—​will there­
fore provide a focus for contextualizing the contents of as least a few of the modern 
yantras to Padmāvatī.
Śvetāmbara Modern Yantras
Astrologer Rajendra Chopra Jain’s online shop sells a variety of ritual objects, many 
of them related to astrology and vāstuśāstra, or the Indian system of creating an aus­
piciously organized space. He lists more than seventy different yantras for sale, made 
of copper or gold, most of which are explicitly Jain, although there are a handful of 
yantras to Rāma and Hanumān without any explicitly “Jain” imagery or mantras. 
Many of his yantras relate to pacifying the negative influence of planets and include

--- PAGE 714 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      689
 
images of the jinas associated with each of the planets (navagraha), but he also sells 
popular nonastrological Jain yantras that are found in Digambara and Śvetāmbara 
temples throughout India, including the Siddhacakra Yantra, Ṛṣimaṇḍala Yantra, 
and the Bhaktāmara Stotra Yantra. The Siddhacakra takes slightly different forms for 
Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras but is named after the liberated soul (siddha) (Gough 
2015). The Ṛṣimaṇḍala Yantra takes the shape of a forty-​eight-​petaled lotus, at the center 
of which sits a multicolored representation of the seed syllable hrīṃ on which images or 
the names of the twenty-​four Tīrthaṅkaras are placed (Gough 2012). The Bhaktāmara 
Stotra Yantra contains forty-​eight different diagrams that are each linked to one of the 
verses of the Bhaktāmarastotra, a medieval Sanskrit praise poem that praises the first 
Tīrthaṅkara, Ṛṣabha (Cort 2005). Jain’s list of yantras for sale also includes ones ded­
icated to Jain deities such as Ghaṇṭākarṇa Mahāvīra (Cort 2000), Nakoḍa Bhairava 
(Aukland 2010), Lakṣmī, and, of course, Padmāvatī.
Two types of Padmāvatī yantra are for sale: the more elaborate “The Great Yantra of 
Pārśva’s Goddess Padmāvatī with 108 Names,” 108 Nāma Yukta Śrī Pārśva Padmāvatīdevī 
Mahāyantram, and the slightly simpler “Great Yantra of the Goddess Padmāvatī, Who 
Fulfils all Desires,” Sarva Manokāmanāpūraka Śrī Padmāvatīdevī Mahāyantram, both 
of which the website confirms are supposed to ensure “health, wealth, fame, [and] love.” 
The more elaborate rectangular yantra that contains 108 names of Padmāvatī is nearly 
identical to a yantra I purchased in 2013 in a shop at the Śvetāmbara pilgrimage center, 
Palitana, in Gujarat (fig. 27.1).
As is quite common for Śvetāmbara yantras, the central images and mantras of the 
diagram are situated inside an auspicious pot (kalaśa). Ribbons are tied to either side of 
the pot, and two eyes emerge from the top of the diagram. At the center of the pot sits a 
four-​armed, ornamented Padmāvatī, holding a noose, a lotus, a goad, and a fruit. Her 
main object of devotion, Pārśva, balances, cross-​legged in a meditative posture, on top 
of her snakehead canopy, signifying that while the goddess is the main object of worship 
here, she still sits below him: she is spiritually inferior to the enlightened teacher. She 
sits in a posture of royal ease (lalitāsana), with her left leg tucked under her and right 
hanging down, on top of her vehicle, a snake with the head of a rooster. Two mantras are 
inscribed in a semicircle that curves over the goddess’s head:
oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ padmāvati padmanetre padmāsane lakṣmīdāyini vāñchāpūrṇi ṛddhiṃ 
siddhiṃ jayaṃ jayaṃ jayaṃ kuru kuru svāhā
oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ dharaṇendrapadmāvatīparipūjitāya śrī śaṅkheśvarapārśvanāthāya 
namaḥ
Padmāvatī! Lotus-​Eyed One! She Who Sits Cross-​Legged! Giver of Wealth! 
Fulfiller of Desires! Grant victory, prosperity (ṛddhi), success (siddhi). Praise 
to Śaṅkheśvara Pārśva, the one who is supremely adored by Padmāvatī and 
Dharaṇendra.
In a ring around Padmāvatī and Pārśva, Sanskrit praises to 108 epithets of 
Padmāvatī—​called the Padmāvatyaṣṭottaraśatanāmāvali—​are inscribed. Here, many

--- PAGE 715 ---
690      Ellen Gough
 
of her epithets indicate that she supports Jain teachings. She is called, for example, the 
goddess who is wholly devoted to Jainism (jinadharmaparāyaṇī) and the twelve limbs 
of the Jain canon (dvādaśāṅgaparāyaṇī), the one who is endowed with the three jewels 
of Jainism that constitute the path to liberation –​right view, knowledge, and conduct 
(samyagdarśanasampannā, samyagjñānaparāyaṇī, samyagcāritrasampannā)—​and 
the one who knows anekāntavāda, the Jain epistemological stance that every ob­
ject can be seen from multiple perspectives (anekāntātmatattvajñā). At the same 
time, she is homologized with non-​Jain, transregional goddesses of India, including

Mahādurgā, Gaṅgā, Kālarātrī, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and four of the five names she

In this way, this popular yantra to Padmāvatī refers to some understandings of the 
goddess found in the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa. Her iconography is similar to that 
in Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 4.12, but here, instead of showing the varadamudrā, 
she holds a lotus.21 This diagram certainly represents the same goddess of the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, but it does not replicate any of the yantras described in 
the text.
Digambara Modern Yantras
Many modern Digambara Padmāvatī yantras share a number of iconographical features 
and mantras with their Śvetāmbara counterparts. In 2013, in a visit to the Jain Yantra 
Udyog shop in Jaipur that specializes in Digambara yantras, I purchased more than 
thirty yantras and took home a list of ready-​made yantras available for purchase. This 
list records 140 so-​called Vaiṣṇava yantras, which really means “Hindu,” since many of 
the diagrams are dedicated to “non-​Vaiṣṇava” deities like Śiva, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and 
Kāmākṣī. It also lists eighty-​four Jain yantras for sale, including many of the yantras 
available at Rajendra Chopra Jain’s Śvetāmbara shop—​for example, the Siddhacakra 
Yantra, Ṛṣimaṇḍala Yantra, and Bhaktāmara Stotra Yantra. It also catalogues two 
yantras specifically devoted to Padmāvatī.
I was able to purchase one of these Padmāvatī yantras during my visit, a 5" x 5" copper 
diagram that contains an image of Padmāvatī, a basic Sanskrit mantra asking for her 
blessings, and a grid containing nine numbers (fig. 27.2).
The yantra depicts a crowned, twenty-​four-​armed version of Padmāvatī who offers a 
gesture that dispels fear (abhayamudrā) and sits on a lotus on top of her vehicle, a snake 
with the head of a rooster. As in the Śvetāmbara diagram with 108 names of Padmāvatī, 
here, too, a small Pārśva sits in a meditative posture on top of the goddess’s head. The 
mantra inscribed below the image of the goddess, in flawed Sanskrit, praises Padmāvatī, 
who transfixes everyone and performs all actions. It calls her the one who removes all 
the suffering and worries of the worshiper and who fulfills all desires.
Next to Padmāvatī sits a so-​called magic square—​a numerical grid in which the sum 
of the numbers in every row, column, and diagonal is the same. In English-​language 
scholarship, the numerical diagram (aṅkayantra) of this Padmāvatī yantra is called a 
“Magic Square of Three”; it is a three-​by-​three grid of the numbers one through nine in 
which the sum of the numbers in each row, column, and diagonal is fifteen (see fig. 27.3).
This square with the “magic sum” of fifteen is often found on modern Padmāvatī 
yantras. Indeed, it is inscribed on the Śvetāmbara “Great Yantra of the Goddess 
Padmāvatī who Fulfils all Desires” from Rajendra Chopra Jain’s shop, where it is called 
the “Fifteen Yantra,” the pañcadaśa yantra.

--- PAGE 717 ---
692      Ellen Gough
 
Magic Squares
Magic squares are not unique to Jain yantras. In India, non-​Jain amulets and diagrams of 
Hindu deities and planets often contain them, and they have been popular in other parts 
Figure 27.2.  A metal Digambara Padmāvatī yantra purchased in 2011 from the Jain Yantra 
Udyog shop in Jaipur, Rajasthan.

figure 27.3.  Magic Square of Three.

--- PAGE 718 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      693
 
of the world for at least two thousand years. A “Magic Square of Three” is discussed in 
Chinese texts as early as the first century C.E. (Hayashi 2008: 164; Cammann 1961). The 
Brahmin astrologer Varāhamihira in his Bṛhatsaṃhitā (sixth century C.E.) provides an 
early discussion of the diagrams from India (Hayashi 2008), and Arabic and Persian 
scholars also began writing about magic squares by at least the tenth century (Cammann 
1968: 189–​190, 1969).
Even so, Jains have become well known for their production of magic squares 
(Vijayaraghavan 1941). A four-​by-​four numerical diagram with the “magic sum” of 
thirty-​four that has been dated between the twelfth and thirteenth centuries is carved 
into the wall at the entrance to the Pārśva temple in Khajuraho (Andrews 1917: 124–​125). 
In 1315, in his text the Gaṇitasāra, the Jain lay scholar Ṭakkura Pherū became “the first 
in India [to treat] magic squares in a mathematical work” when he devoted nine verses 
to different types of magic squares (Hayashi 2008: 1252). And the Victoria and Albert 
Museum in London also houses a magnificent, nearly five-​foot-​tall cloth painting of 
an eighty-​one-​by-​eighty-​one numerical diagram with an elaborate painted border 
populated with deities and other auspicious images (Pal 1995: 225–​226). This painting 
is a so-​called Victory Banner (jayatrayantra) that was consecrated on Diwali in 1447 by 
a Śvetāmbara monk named Jinaprabhasūri.22 This type of yantra is still used in ritual 
today; both the Digambara Jain Yantra Udyog shop and the Śvetāmbara Rajendra 
Chopra Jain sell miniature versions of the Victory Banner.23
A magic square is also outlined in the Śvetāmbara Tijayapahuttastotra (1938), a 
Prakrit hymn that has been classified as one of the Śvetāmbara “Nine Remembrances” 
(navasmaraṇa), or nine powerful recitations that are often grouped together in pūjā 
booklets. The Tijayapahuttastotra contains fourteen verses that outline a five-​by-​five 
numerical diagram whose magic sum represents the maximum number of enlight­
ened teachers of Jainism, tīrthaṅkaras, who can reside in our universe at one time: 170 
(Kapashi 2007: 41). According to the hymn, the diagram is called “auspicious in every 
respect,” the Sarvatobhadra Yantra (v. 6), and when someone traces it with sandalwood 
paste and camphor on a wooden board and/​or one’s door, negative effects from illness, 
the planets, ghosts, enemies, and other malevolent forces are destroyed (vv. 13–​14). 
From top to bottom and left to right, the five syllables of the key Gāruḍa mantra, the 
vipatimantra, fill the squares of the middle horizontal and vertical rows: kṣi pa oṃ svā 
hā. The syllables ha ra huṃ haḥ sa ra su saḥ are repeated twice, from left to right, in the 
remaining squares (see fig. 27.4).
This yantra described in the Tijayapahuttastotra—​the Sarvatobhadra Yantra—​
remains popular to this day and is for sale at the Digambara Jain Yantra Udyog shop 
in Jaipur and by the Śvetāmbara Rajendra Chopra Jain. Not only this yantra, however, 
but the majority of yantras for sale at these shops feature at least one magic square. 
Like a full pot or the other commonly depicted eight auspicious objects of Jainism 
(Shah 1955: 109–​115), these representations of symmetry, balance, and perfection 
create positive changes in the world through their auspiciousness.
Therefore, modern Padmāvatī yantras usually contain at least one magic square, 
an image of Padmāvatī, and Sanskrit praises of the goddess that ask for generic 
worldly prosperity. They do not usually contain the components of the yantras of

--- PAGE 719 ---
694      Ellen Gough
 
the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa. Indeed, the five mantras to be used in the worship of 
Padmāvatī outlined in Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 3.29–​3.33 are not often linked to the god­
dess. In Jain places of worship today, yantras that connect the goddess to hrīṃ are some­
times found (see Coomaraswamy 2003: 50), but due to the influence of the Ṛṣimaṇḍala 
Yantra, hrīṃ is much more commonly linked to the twenty-​four tīrthaṅkaras than to 
Padmāvatī, Dharanendra, and Pārśva. The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa’s lack of influence 
on modern temple images suggests that its audience may have been limited.
Assessing the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa’s 
Influence
In the (nearly identical) Hindi introductions to his publications of the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa (Śāstrī 1952) and the Jvālāmālinīkapa (Śāstrī 1966), the 
Digambara layman and publisher Mūlcandra Kisandās Kāpaḍiyā provides some 
insights into the status of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa (and Jvālāmālinīkalpa) in the 
middle of the twentieth century. At the outset of his introduction, Kāpaḍiyā notes 
that among Jain texts on mantraśāstra, the Ṛṣimaṇḍalastotra, the yantras and mantras 
associated with the Bhaktāmarastotra, and the mantra-​based rituals related to the 
Kalyāṇamandirastotra are well known (Śāstrī 1952: 3). Here, Kāpaḍiyā references 
three famous Sanskrit Jain hymns (stotra) that are accepted by both Digambaras and 
Śvetāmbaras and connected with powerful mantras and yantras. The Ṛṣimaṇḍalastotra 
and Bhaktāmarastotra contain the components of the yantras discussed above, the 
Ṛṣimaṇḍala Yantra and Bhaktāmara Stotra Yantra. The Kalyāṇamandirastotra, 
which praises Pārśva, has a number of mantras and yantras associated with it, in­
cluding forty-​four yantras associated with each of its verses (Kapashi 2007: 171–​174). 
The diagrams associated with these three hymns are often found in Jain homes and 
temples and constructed out of foodstuffs or synthetic colored powder for special 
worship ceremonies.

Kāpaḍiyā notes, however, that the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is not well known, de­
spite its presence in Jain archives (Śāstrī 1952: 3). To rectify this problem and shed light 
on the text, around 1928, when stopping in Delhi on a family pilgrimage from his home 
in Surat, Gujarat, to the Jain pilgrimage site Sammet Shikhar, Kāpaḍiyā met with the 
scholar Paṇḍit Candraśekhar Śāstrī and offered to him for translation into Hindi copies 
of manuscripts he had collected of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, Jvālāmālinīkalpa, 
Ambikākalpa, and Jain texts on the grammar of mantras and meanings of seed 
syllables (bījakoṣa). Śāstrī, having accepted the project, decided to first work on the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, and two years later, they had already printed forty-​eight pages 
of the text when Kāpaḍiyā, realizing that there were a number of impure and violent 
prescriptions in the text, put a halt to the printing. For fourteen to fifteen years, the pub­
lication remained on hold while Kāpaḍiyā consulted with scholars, some of whom ad­
vised him not to publish it, and others who assured him that some impure topics will 
always arise in texts on mantraśāstra, so it was fine to move forward with publication 
(Śāstrī 1952: 3–​5). In 1952, Kāpaḍiyā did eventually publish the whole text, with Śāstrī’s 
Hindi explanation and his own introduction explaining the history of the project. In 
this introduction, Kāpaḍiyā confirms that the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa was not an im­
portant text for lay and mendicant Jains in the first half of the twentieth century. He 
recognizes that other Jain texts on mantraśāstra are much better known and established 
in Jain ritual culture, likely because they, unlike the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, do not 
contain impure, violent, “non-​Jain” elements.
The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa should not, however, be seen as an anomalous text 
whose contents do not represent Jain beliefs and practices. Many of the deities, 
preliminary purificatory rites, and mantras of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa are 
common to other Jain texts and objects of worship. The text reflects ritual trends 
described in Śvetāmbara and Digambara texts that emerged between the tenth and 
twelfth centuries, and many of these trends persist in Jain ritual culture to this day. 
For example, the performance of sakalīkaraṇa outlined in the second chapter of 
the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa—​the use of mantras to place the five supreme beings 
on one’s body to protect it as part of the preliminary purification rites—​is common 
to tenth-​ and eleventh-​century Digambara texts on meditation, like Devasena’s 
Bhāvasaṅgraha (v. 434) and Rāmasena’s Tattvānuśāsana (v. 186 trans. in Dundas 
2012: 156). To this day, both Digambara and Śvetāmbara laypeople and mendicants 
recite mantras to place the five supreme beings on different parts of their bodies for 
protection at the outset of worship ceremonies (vidhāna, mahāpūjana) in which 
they make offerings of coconuts, and so on, to a ritual diagram made of synthetic 
powder or foodstuffs (Balbir 2018: 282–​287). Before they make offerings of vāsakṣepa 
to cloth ritual diagrams—​either the Vardhamānavidyāpaṭa or the Sūrimantrapaṭa—​
Śvetāmbara monks also undertake these purification rites daily, placing the supreme 
beings on the same five parts of the body as outlined in Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 
2.3–​2.4 (Gough 2021: 160–​190).
The snakebite-​curing vipatimantra mentioned repeatedly in the tenth chapter 
of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is found in another tenth-​century Jain text,

--- PAGE 721 ---
696      Ellen Gough
 
Indranandin’s Jvālāmālinīkalpa (5.14–​5.15). It, too, remains popular to this day, being 
inscribed on the Sarvatobhadra Yantra. In addition, the same four goddesses of vic­
tory found in many of the yantras of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa—​Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, 
and Aparājitā—​are quite often invoked in Jain rituals. They are invoked in the mantra 
that promoted Śvetāmbara Jain mendicants to higher ranks, the vardhamānavidyā 
that is outlined as early as the eighth-​ to ninth-​century Mahāniśīthasūtra, and they 
to this day sit at the corners of many different Jain ritual diagrams used in worship 
today, including the Vardhamānavidyāpaṭa and Sūrimantrapaṭa (Shah 1941; Gough 
2021: 190–​195). These four goddesses are most popularly known as the “Sisters of 
Tumburu,” a manifestation of Śiva described in most detail in the seventh-​century 
text the Vīṇāśikhatantra. They are also, however, found in all sorts of other medi­
eval texts—​Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu—​from south, southeast, east, and central Asia 
(Goudriaan 1985: 1–​62). It is not unusual for a Jain text to name these goddesses of 
victory.
It is also not unusual for a Jain text like the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa to discuss 
another popular mantra of Śaiva and Jain texts, the so-​called navātmamantra, 
a mantra with nine syllables that ends in the cluster mlvyū plus an anusvara. 
Medieval Śaiva texts often refer to different forms, and different interpretations, 
of the navātmamantra. Having been mentioned in the earliest tantric Śaiva scrip­
ture, the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā 5.35, the navātman eventually found its way 
into a variety of traditions. In the Śaiva tantric text from about the eleventh cen­
tury, the Śāradātilakatantra, forms of the navātmamantra are associated with 
Tumburu (kṣmryūṃ), Jayā (jmryūṃ), Vijayā (bhmryūṃ), Jayantī/​Ajitā (smryūṃ), 
and Aparājitā (hmryūṃ) (Goudriaan 1985: 20, 50). In the Kaula cult of the goddess 
Kubjikā that emerged around the end of the first millennium, it is the mantra of the 
consort of Kubjikā, Navātma-​Bhairava, and is related to the nine important onto­
logical components of the universe (tattva) (Heilijgers 1994: 26–​27). A key text of 
the tradition, the Kubjikāmatatantra (ninth–​tenth centuries), presents the “most 
common form” of the mantra as shrkṣmlvyū-​auṃ (Heilijgers 1994: 26). Other forms 
are present in other Śaiva texts, including the Svacchandatantra (hrkṣmlvyūṃ) and 
Tantrāloka (rhrkṣmlvyūṃ) (Heilijgers 1994: 27). The Navātmamantra for the goddess 
Tripurasundarī eventually became kṣmlrvyūṃ, the form of the mantra that is quite 
often mentioned in the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa (Padoux 2011: 24).
I have not yet found a Jain interpretation of the syllables of the navātmamantra, but 
versions of the mantra are often found in Jain yantras; they are frequently used to in­
voke the eight goddesses of the classes of the Devanagari alphabet (vargadevī).24 Two 
of the most popular Jain yantras—​one accepted by both Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras, 
the Ṛṣimaṇḍala, and another principally used in ritual by Digambaras, the Kalikuṇḍa—​
contain the same eight variants of the navātmamantra. The Kalikuṇḍa yantra is ded­
icated to Pārśva, and its name references a story in Pārśva’s medieval biographies in 
which an elephant, having honored the Tīrthaṅkara at a lake (kuṇḍa) at the base of a 
mountain named Kali, eventually gains rebirth as a god because of his piety (Bloomfield 
[1919] 1985: 115–​116). At the center of the Kalikuṇḍa Yantra sits either an image of Pārśva,

--- PAGE 722 ---
Jain Tantric Diagrams of the Goddess Padmāvatī      697
 
Padmāvatī, and Dharanendra, or a mantra for an omniscient soul, hrūṃ, surrounded by 
eight lotus petals. In each lotus petal, two oṃs are inscribed, each surrounded by swirls 
(anāhata). Each lotus also contains the same eight mantras that fill the eight petals that 
surround the central hrīṃ of the Ṛṣimaṇḍala:
	 1.	 a ā i ī hmlrvyūṃ u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au ṃ ḥ
	 2.	 ka kha bhmlrvyūṃ ga gha ṅ
	 3.	 ca cha mmlrvyūṃ ja jha ña
	 4.	 ṭa ṭha rmlvrvyūṃ ḍa ḍha ṇa
	 5.	 ta tha dhmlrvyūṃ da dha na
	 6.	 pa pha jhmlrvyūṃ ba bha ma
	 7.	 ya ra la va smlrvyūṃ
	 8.	 śa ṣa sa ha kṣmlrvyūṃ (Varṇī 2002: 349, 350)
Here, the mantra associated with Tripurasundarī that is prominent in the 
Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa—​kṣmlrvyūṃ—​is just one of eight versions of the 
navātmamantra linked to each class of the Devanagari alphabet. While scholars are 
right to note the influence of the Tripurasundarī cult on the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 
(Sanderson 2011: 3–​4), this influence is not prominent today. Tripurasundarī has 
not become intimately linked to Padmāvatī today, nor are the mantras of the cult like 
kṣmlrvyūṃ particularly significant in the most important Jain yantras.
Therefore, although the specific rituals and images of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 
are not commonly found in Jain places of worship today, the text—​especially the first 
three chapters—​is not a complete anomaly. The iconography of Padmāvatī and many 
of the rituals and mantras of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa are common to other Jain 
texts and images; the text is certainly not irrelevant for understanding the history of Jain 
mantraśāstra. The text’s peculiarities, however, do not seem to have influenced other 
texts and practices. There is no evidence that the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa transformed 
Jain mantraśāstra.
Suggestions for Future Research on 
Jain Tantric Practices
I look forward to more research being done on the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa and its 
influence—​Aaron Ullrey’s (2016) continuing work on the text will be of great interest. It 
is quite possible that further study of this text in comparison with other Jain and non-​
Jain texts and research on icons of Padmāvatī and collections of yantras in temples will 
indicate much more influence than this chapter has suggested. As research stands now, 
however, the text should not be introduced as the “main tantra” of Jainism. Rather than 
a continued focus on this text, students of Jainism would be better served by studies and

--- PAGE 723 ---
698      Ellen Gough
 
translations of some of the dozens of overlooked texts on Padmāvatī. A real contribu­
tion to scholarship could be made simply putting the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa into con­
versation with the contents and histories of the thirty-​one texts on Jain goddesses found 
in the appendices to Nawab’s publication of the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa (Abhyaṅkar 
1937).
Jain texts on goddesses, however, are not the only sources of Jain tantric practices, 
which in Jain sources means the ritual use of mantras and yantras to achieve miraculous 
powers and eventual liberation. Padmāvatī, for example, is not found on popular yantras 
connected with recitations like the Bhaktāmarastora and the Tijayapahuttastotra or 
on other yantras commonly found in Śvetāmbara and Digambara temples (e.g., the 
Ṛṣimaṇḍala Yantra). Nor is she found on the main diagrams worshiped by Śvetāmbara 
mendicants, the Vardhamānavidyāpaṭa and Sūrimantrapaṭa.
Tantric rituals have been thoroughly integrated into Jain lay and monastic life, 
so many different types of text—​for example, hymns (stotra, stuti, aṣṭaka), ritual 
manuals (kalpa, pūjana, vidhāna, vidhi), narratives (kathā, carita, purāṇa), and 
texts on lay and mendicant ritual practices (śrāvakācāra, yatyācāra)—​have extensive 
discussions of the visualization of mantras, the purification of the body via mantras, 
and the construction and propitiation of diagrams on which mantras are inscribed. 
Naming only some of these texts—​those on the propitiation of powerful goddesses—​
as “tantras” skews our understanding of the history of Jains’ ritual uses of mantras. 
The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, unlike other Jain texts that contain tantric elements, 
does describe tantric practices in each of its chapters, so naming it as a tantra signals 
the character of the text and puts it into conversation with similar non-​Jain texts. 
However, this text has been privileged for too long in studies of Jain tantric practices. 
To avoid privileging certain types of texts as representative of Jain tantric practices, 
it would be best to avoid calling the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, or, indeed, any Jain 
text, a tantra. The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa should be called what it is: a kalpa, not a 
tantra.
