Chapter 28
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN 
TANTRIC BUDDHISM
David L. Gardiner
Introduction
Both implicitly and explicitly, tantric Buddhist (Vajrayāna, or esoteric Buddhist) im­
agery and its practice embody a powerful critique of dichotomies such as subject/​ob­
ject, self/​world, body/​mind, and female/​male. Moreover, tantric Buddhist imagery use 
functions to proactively replace bifurcated, traumatized experiential frameworks with 
alternative, more integrated structures for living. The holistic worldview expressed 
in writings on Vajrayāna meditation constitutes an intentional assault on the funda­
mental patterns of ignorant self-​absorption that Buddhist teachings assert to be the 
source of sentient beings’ suffering. Central to this meditation practice is the sustained, 
creative engagement with religious imagery through visualization methods. These 
visualizations aim to transform the practitioner’s sense of self, both cognitively and so­
matically. Imagery is thus a central tool in the Vajrayāna Buddhist path to liberation, 
manifest not only in rich iconic diversity but also in sophisticated and sublime contem­
plative exercises that utilize creative visual elements. While the traditions of imagery 
use in tantric Buddhism are worthy of study from a variety of perspectives, their cen­
tral role within a clearly articulated soteriological context warrants particular atten­
tion. The Vajrayāna employment of imagery in both material and cognitive domains 
constitutes an ingenious technology that harnesses intention, imagination, and em­
bodiment in remarkable ways (cf. Timalsina, this volume). Elements of both tantric 
theory and method are consonant with recent insights into the body/​mind problematic 
and can support the development of effective methods of healing in the mental as well 
as the physical sciences. Theories of embodied cognition (or extended mind) find pow­
erful resonance in Buddhist tantric thought, just as discourses in the fields of literary 
theory, focusing on metaphor, poetry and narrative, also shed valuable light on the 
inspired creations of tantric visual practice. (See Hayes and Timalsina, this volume.)

--- PAGE 729 ---
704      David L. Gardiner
 
Studying the role of imagery in Buddhist tantra is a rich, interdisciplinary project that 
warrants multiple approaches.
Some nineteenth-​ and early twentieth-​century scholars viewed Vajrayāna Buddhist 
imagery disdainfully because of the wide and wild range of iconography that in­
cluded expressions of violence and sexuality. The tradition was commonly depicted 
as unethical and licentious and thus understood to be contradicting core moral and 
ascetic principles of the Buddha’s teachings (Lopez, 1999, 35–​38; Wedemeyer 2013, 
43–​50). These evaluations arose in ignorance of the symbolic and often metaphorical 
dimensions of the imagery. Loriliai Biernacki notes that “the topic of Tantra continues 
to elicit derision” due to a “persistent, particularly Western scholarly miasma of mis­
interpretation of Tantric images” (Biernacki 2018, 375). Recent scholarship indicates a 
range of interpretative approaches to the imagery, including “literal, symbolic, ‘higher’ 
literal, and yogic” (Jackson 1992), though scholars differ as to which approach they 
emphasize. At the same time, in popular culture, many self-​identifying Buddhists 
lean toward dismissing literal interpretations of sexuality in tantric texts and images. 
Instead, they favor sanitized metaphorical understandings present in the literature, for 
example, interpreting females as representations of wisdom (insight into ultimate re­
ality) and males as symbolizing compassion (skillful engagement with conventional 
reality). While these metaphorical interpretations have traditional grounding, they do 
not represent the historical breadth of available hermeneutics. Contemporary schol­
arship offers insightful treatment of the various roles images play in Buddhist tantric 
thought and practice (examples include Bühnemann 2005; Germano and Hillis 2005; 
Hatchell 2013; Tsomo 2018).1
The often very detailed and iconographically complex images in Vajrayāna are not 
simply pretty pictures that depict sacred figures or hold symbolic meanings derived 
from doctrine. Nor are they solely inspirational props for meditation. Their functions 
are multiple. Commonly understood to be sacred icons that hold divine powers, they 
also serve as catalysts for profound exercises that engage body, speech, and mind in 
visualization practices that aim to reorient the cognitive, emotional, and somatic 
foundations of a practitioner’s being in radically liberating ways.2 Material images (pri­
marily paintings and statues) are central to the practice because their visual form is 
the basis from which active, three-​dimensional visualized scenarios unfold. However, 
structured visualizations are only one part of an embodied ritual process that includes 
introductory prayers and prostrations to establish intention, preliminary visualizations 
to “clear the field” so the deity image can take center stage, and concluding practices that 
entail dissolving the visualized array into clear light before reciting prayers of dedica­
tion. The whole process utilizes imagery as an essential component of a path of spiritual 
transformation along specific Buddhist lines. Because Vajrayāna practice falls within 
the Mahāyāna Buddhist tradition, both an initial setting of intention and a final dedica­
tion serve to galvanize the practitioner’s compassionate bodhicitta vow to work for the 
benefit of all beings. Sandwiching, as it were, the central visualization between verbal 
and bodily gestures of intention and dedication creates a robust package of religious

--- PAGE 730 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      705
 
practice. The practice incorporates ritualized aspects embracing physical movement 
(e.g., prostrations, gestures of offering, and mudrā) and mantra chanting, along with a 
carefully choreographed visualization process.3
The term “tantric Buddhism” used here is synonymous with Vajrayāna, and this latter 
term finds its place in both the Indo-​Tibetan and the Japanese (Shingon) forms of eso­
teric Buddhism (both of which this chapter addresses). Kūkai 空海 (774–​835), the ninth-​
century founder of the Shingon school, frequently uses the Sino-​Japanese translation for 
Vajrayāna (kongō-​jō 金剛乗) to refer to Shingon esoteric Buddhist practice.
The phenomena surrounding tantric Buddhist imagery can be examined from many 
angles. One might look at sources of their material production; influences from and on 
other traditions; sponsorship of the artistic work; iconographic detail and diversity; 
symbolic meanings; correspondences between written texts and visual images; spatial 
placement in ritual locations; conceptions of images’ divine capacity to serve as agents 
of soteriological as well as of political work; and more. Research in all these directions 
continues to yield rich insights. While acknowledging the value of diverse avenues of in­
quiry, this chapter highlights the relatively less traveled road of investigating the extent 
to which the theory and practice related to imagery in tantric Buddhism offer coherent 
and innovative approaches to human development. Investigating dimensions of tantric 
image practice as being instrumental in a thoroughgoing process of “worldmaking” has 
the potential to reap valuable understandings that shed light on pressing contemporary 
issues, thereby aiding efforts to transcend the rigidity of widely accepted boundaries be­
tween religious and secular worlds. Two key factors are particularly relevant in this re­
gard: Vajrayāna Buddhism’s concentration on harnessing the transformative power of 
imagination and its insistence on fully engaging the body, not just the mind, in spiritual 
work. Imagery operates centrally on both these fronts. Fields of study that stand to un­
pack the complexity and richness of tantric imagery include:
Embodied cognition (and extended mind): focuses on body/​mind relations and 
rethinking structures of selfhood.
Phenomenology: aims to ground accounts of experience in embodied modes of 
perception.
Narrative theory: explores the power of “story” for creating meanings, including myth 
broadly conceived.
Poetics: examines the imaginative landscapes of possibilities provided by creative lan­
guage and imagery.
Contemplative neuroscience: investigates the function of visualization, among other 
processes, for molding new cognitive structures.
Positive psychology: affirms the salutary role of overcoming deficits of self-​esteem 
through creative means, including visualization.
Rather than separately listing contributions from these various methodological 
approaches, we can uncover their promise for studying tantric imagery thematically.

--- PAGE 731 ---
706      David L. Gardiner
 
Worldmaking: The Embeddedness of 
Myth and Narrative
Drawing from the wellsprings of Mahāyāna thought, tantric Buddhist imagery serves 
to frame and to vivify tantric practice. While the Vajrayāna tradition hails itself as of­
fering a more powerful and therefore speedy path to enlightenment (with its literal 
meaning of “vehicle of the thunderbolt or diamond”—​vajra has both meanings) than 
does mainstream Mahāyāna, both its inspiration and structure are firmly grounded 
in the Mahāyāna vision of the bodhisattva path. This path is viewed, or envisioned, as 
being rooted in a profoundly compassionate aspiration to attain perfect buddhahood 
in order to better serve all living beings. Many tantric meditation practices begin with 
the recitation of a standard Mahāyāna verse that says, “I take refuge in the Buddha, 
Dharma, and Sangha. By practicing giving and the other [five] perfections [eth­
ical conduct, patience, effort, concentration, wisdom], may I achieve Buddhahood 
for the sake of all beings.” This recitation is commonly followed, as it is in many 
Mahāyāna liturgies, by additional preliminary practices (there is a standard list of 
seven “branches/​limbs”), which include prostrations, verses expressing offerings to 
all Buddhas, regret for all one’s past harmful actions, praise for the virtuous actions 
of all awakened beings, requests that such beings never let go of their vow to bring aid 
to those still trapped in samsara, and dedicating the performance of these “branches” 
toward the liberation of all beings.4 In this way, the visualization practice that follows 
these preliminary ones is framed by a classical Mahāyāna vision. It is helpful to con­
ceive how such intentional envisioning, grounded in bodily performance, is a form 
of “imagery” in action. It calls to the practitioner’s mind—​to their imagination—​a 
conceptual and even somatic frame for holding onto (or simply remembering) the 
larger purpose of the practice. The practice is thus embraced by a narrative structure 
enlivened by the framework of the bodhisattva path.
Deity Yoga: Arising as an Image of 
Enlightened Being
When one turns to the mechanics of tantric visualization practice, the unambiguous 
manner that the meditation is “brought to life” by imagery is striking. Extensive details 
can be found in multiple sources (McMahan 2004; H. H. the Dalai Lama, Tsongkhapa 
and Jeffrey Hopkins 2016; Gyatso 1999; Yeshe 2014). The summary of key features 
common to many Vajrayāna meditations (sādhānas) presented below relies on these 
sources. This is an account of the “self-​generation” practice, in which one imagines one­
self to appear as an enlightened being, as opposed to the “front generation” practice,

--- PAGE 732 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      707
 
which imagines an enlightened being to appear in front, or outside, oneself. Both forms 
of generation practice are also known as deity yoga.
After reciting the preliminary prayers, one strives to manifest a “wisdom” conscious­
ness, one that knows the ultimate reality of emptiness. This is a profound awareness that 
transcends subject/​object duality by “seeing” ultimate reality directly, unmediated by 
conceptual thought. Achieving such a wisdom consciousness is not the equivalent of full 
enlightenment, but it is an essential component of that attainment. If one has already 
“experienced” it, or achieved wisdom (which attainment marks the sixth but not final 
stage of the bodhisattva path, the “path of seeing”), one accesses or generates that con­
sciousness from memory. If one has yet to reach that state, then one approximates it by 
“pretending” that both self and world have dissolved into the clear light of wisdom aware­
ness. This imaginative act entails generating an image of one’s body and its surroundings 
(gradually extended to include the entire physical universe) as actually dissolving into 
a unified, soft light, one often likened to the texture of skylight just before dawn. This 
dissolution process is aided by chanting the mantra Om svabhāva śuddha sarva dharma 
svabhāva śuddho ham, which means, “My own essence is pure, and all phenomena are 
pure, too.”5 Purity here, as in other Mahāyāna contexts, is synonymous with emptiness 
(Duckworth 2019, 79, 124; Shaw 1995, 184). This open, clear state that encompasses all 
existence is either a simulacrum of the wisdom aspect of a Buddha’s awareness or the 
real thing (fully embodied wisdom), depending on one’s previous attainments.
From within this all-​encompassing clear light (which is understood to be one’s own 
wisdom mind, not separate from anything else in the world), an image of a perfected 
being (buddha or bodhisattva) emerges or “arises.” This occurs in stages, not all at once. 
It emerges from the practitioner’s intention to make the image appear, though perhaps 
for an advanced yogi with extensive experience it might appear relatively spontane­
ously. It is imperative to understand that this image is not external to the practitioner, 
not something one “sees” from one’s seat as if it is seated across from you. Rather, one is 
reimagining or reconstructing the very fabric of one’s entire embodied experience in, 
literally, a new light. Prior to the emergence of the envisioned Buddha or bodhisattva 
(usually referred to simply as the “deity”—​ though not to be confused with a theistic 
entity) –​ one visualizes in the center of this vast field of empty existence the appear­
ance of a single mantric syllable (“seed syllable,” bīja-​mantra), which is understood to 
condense the qualities of the deity involved. For example, for the deity Tara it is Tāṃ 
and for Avalokiteśvara it is Hrīḥ. This syllable is also composed of clear light but in a 
form congealed from the expansive light and recognizable as a syllable. The image of the 
deity’s body then emerges from this “seed.” It, too, is made of clear light, though it is col­
orful and is likened to a rainbow in that one can see through it; it is not solid. Again, this 
image of the deity (as of the seed from which it sprouts) is not something seen as residing 
in front of oneself; it is not a separate entity. Rather, one’s own being—​one’s entire 
awareness—​has now become this light-​filled, enlightened being whose body is adorned 
with unique physical features as well as clothing, jewelry, and possibly implements.
A crucial element of the self-​generation practice is that the practitioner is so fully 
identified with the visualized deity (called yidam in Tibetan) that they should experience

--- PAGE 733 ---
708      David L. Gardiner
 
a “divine pride” that accords with possessing all the noble virtues of a buddha. Such pride 
is not a narcissistic arrogance. Rather, it is a buoyant confidence in the capacity that an 
awakened being possesses to exist completely free of all afflictive emotions and to en­
gage fully and effectively in the work of aiding others. The visualized deity is the mani­
festation of one’s holding firmly in mind (and body) all the positive potential that resides 
subliminally in one’s ordinary state. Some contemporary emic accounts of the practice 
affirm that the visualization can be understood as expressing an archetype of awakening 
that resides within one in embryonic form (Landaw and Weber 2006; Lhadrepa and 
Davis 2017; Yeshe 2014). Such a view, however, does not exclude the belief that the deity 
is also somehow an entity that is not merely symbolic of the practitioner’s potential but 
is an enlightened being in its own right. Thus, holding the symbolic and literal meanings 
together simultaneously is not contradictory: the deity is both an archetype and an 
awakened presence. The practitioner’s identification with it, their divine pride, flexibly 
encompasses both postures.
A final, essential component of deity yoga visualization practice is that the “self as 
deity/​deity as self” identity is not sustained throughout the entirety of one’s medi­
tation period. Shortly before concluding the meditation, one is instructed to allow 
the deity image to “dissolve back into clear light.” The image thus emerges from and 
returns to the clear light of the wisdom consciousness that knows ultimate reality 
directly. This gestural turn in the contemplative practice both represents a somatic 
reminder that all things, including enlightened beings, are ultimately empty of any in­
herently existing nature and serves as a caution against emotionally attaching to one’s 
newly constructed “ego.” It is a built-​in prophylactic to ward off inclinations toward 
megalomania.
Both the merging of one’s ordinary sense of self with the enlightened self-​image and 
the merging of all phenomena including one’s body into a clear light signify a breaking 
down of dualities that are otherwise, according to Buddhist psychology, ignorantly 
assumed to be established. This emphasis on the dissolution of boundaries is intrinsic 
to Vajrayāna thought. Naturally, it is also deeply indebted to Mahāyāna philosophical 
orientations that see all distinctions as, in the final analysis, conventions accepted as 
real only by consensus (and therefore as being ultimately empty). This embracing of 
emptiness (which is not nothingness) as the ultimate reality entails as well the relin­
quishment of taking as absolute the foundational distinction between the domains of 
nirvana and samsara—​of the freedom that awakening brings, on the one hand, and 
the experience of suffering that comes with conditioned, ignorant existence on the 
other. Hence, there emerged an affirmation of the so-​called non-​abiding nirvana as 
an ideal articulation of the Mahāyāna goal (see Makransky 1997, 319–​369). The bodhi­
sattva strives to exist neither in samsara, where suffering based on ignorance prevails, 
nor in a nirvana conceived as being apart from all suffering and thus as aloof. The 
“two wings” of wisdom and compassion preserve the non-​abiding, middle way op­
tion: wisdom frees one from samsara while compassion keeps one from “indulging” 
alone in a reified nirvana. Wisdom also enables one to see that no such nirvana can 
exist as an independent state, nor can an independent, permanent “being” exist there

--- PAGE 734 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      709
 
either.6 The deity that arises in the visualization practice is thus a very complex image: 
entirely free yet fully engaged.
The intricacies of the arisen image in deity yoga are galvanized by the incorporation 
of additional doctrinal elements. These elements are the theory of the Two Truths and 
the theory of bodies of a buddha. The Two Truths (or “realities”) are conventional and 
ultimate. Buddha body theories in Buddhist history are complicated, but a simplified 
version divides them into two: form body (rūpa-​kāya) and truth body (dharma-​kāya). 
A buddha’s form body is their participation in conventional reality, via skillful means, to 
assist beings in becoming free from suffering. This body is primarily understood to be 
the flesh and blood, walking and talking buddha (past, present, or future) who models 
awakened life and guides others toward it. Every buddha has a unique form body that is 
shaped by individual conditions. The truth body, however, is shared by all buddhas, and 
thus has no individuating qualities. The truth body is attained when one has realized 
emptiness (or ultimate truth) so completely that all dualities, all attachment, all igno­
rance and therefore all suffering are entirely uprooted. This is the “body” of complete 
freedom, and all buddhas share in it equally. A form body, on the other hand, is unique 
to each enlightened being, as it manifests in ways that accord, most skillfully, with the 
diverse (conventional) needs of all living beings within its reach.
A buddha’s form body is understood to be an expression of their having perfected 
compassion, while their truth body is a result of their perfect wisdom. In this way the 
two are aligned, respectively, with conventional reality and ultimate reality. This doc­
trinal framework helps galvanize deity yoga practice because the visualized image is said 
to be the product of both wisdom and compassion. The dissolution of one’s ordinary, 
dualistic experience into the clear light (Skt. ābhāsvara-​citta; Tib. ‘od gsal) is understood 
to be a manifestation of the wisdom that cognizes ultimate reality directly. When the 
practitioner rests, as it were, in this state prior to the emergence of the seed syllable (and 
later the deity image), they are partaking in the truth body of a buddha. Then, when the 
deity image arises out of this clear light, in its colored and articulated form, it manifests 
as a buddha’s form body. Significantly, the form body arises from the truth body; it 
is made from the very fabric of clear light. Thus, the visualized image that arises (or 
is constructed) within the practice of deity yoga unites the Two Truths in one entity. 
Ordinarily, the attainment of such a simultaneous union of the Two Truths is said to be 
only possible for a fully enlightened being. Even an advanced bodhisattva practitioner 
who has yet to complete the path to buddhahood must alternate between moments of 
seeing emptiness, or ultimate reality, directly and spans of time engaged as compas­
sionately as possible (but with remnant taints of ignorance) within the conventional 
world. The image cultivated within deity yoga practice thus perfectly replicates, via an 
embodied mimesis, the resultant state of buddhahood as a union of the Two Truths 
(see H. H. Dalai Lama et al. 2016, 62). It is for this reason that Vajrayāna practice is also 
known as the “result vehicle” (phala-​yāna, with phala also translated as effect, goal, or 
fruit) in contrast to the “cause vehicle” of nonesoteric Mahāyāna, also referred to as the 
“vehicle of the perfections” (pāramitā-​yāna), because the latter takes the practice of the 
six perfections (generosity, ethics, patience, effort, concentration, wisdom) as the cause

--- PAGE 735 ---
710      David L. Gardiner
 
for buddhahood. Through creative and intricate work with imagery, the complex visu­
alization practice of tantric deity yoga unites the practitioner’s body, speech, and mind 
with the perfect body, speech, and mind of an enlightened being, Vajrayāna deity yoga 
employs the resultant state of buddhahood as the instrument of the path.
Mandalic Imagery
Central to tantric Buddhist practice is the role of mandalas. The visible mandalas that 
are either painted on cloth to be hung, constructed with colored sand on platforms, 
or comprised of three-​dimensional figures, represent only one meaning of the word. 
The term is also used in Vajrayāna discourse to refer to the vast world of awakening 
that one visualizes in (and can realize through) meditation, as well as to the extensive 
corpus of teachings, written and oral, that convey the details of the practice. Many ex­
cellent studies exist on the iconography, production, and ritual use of material mandalas 
(Brauen 1997; Bühnemann 2005; Leidy and Thurman 1998 Ten Grotenhuis 1999), but 
few focus on the way the term is used to indicate the fantastic world of awakened life that 
one imagines—​so as to catalyze it into being—​within the ritual practice. This visionary 
meaning of mandala deserves study in itself, since it not only represents the primary 
spiritual impetus behind the material instruments, but also expresses powerful elements 
of tantric Buddhist thought in a unique way that highlights the tradition’s emphasis 
on the creative force of imagination and the vital connection all practice has to being 
grounded in the body.
The practitioner’s successful conjuring of the image of self-​as-​deity is not limited 
to their body alone, which has taken on the attributes of their chosen bodhisattva or 
buddha. Since the whole world beyond their body is also included in the process of dis­
solution into clear light, for all intents and purposes the initial arisen deity body is the 
entire world. The details of visualized imagery that follow from this (relatively simple) 
initial image vary greatly from sādhāna to sādhāna, with variations dependent upon 
both the deity in question and the “level” of initiation received. For example, in the 
higher level of “unexcelled yoga tantra” practices, the visualizations enter into processes 
such as untangling minuscule networks of energy channels imagined within the body 
(Wedemeyer 2021, 60–​65). But, in general the visualization practice involves both 
details of (and often within) the deity’s body as well as realms outside the body (Cozort 
1986; Shaw 1995; Thurman 1994). One essential aspect of visualizing domains beyond 
the deity body is to imagine the flow of perfected compassion as leaving the body, 
through every pore, in the form of light rays that touch beings throughout all realms of 
samsara thereby releasing them from suffering. This dramatic imagery represents a core 
function of the “result vehicle”: One is embodying the goal of the path by performing the 
liberative work of a buddha.7
The combined construct of self and world in this vast scenario is referred to as 
the mandala. Mandala in this sense means the idealized vision of a world in which

--- PAGE 736 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      711
 
enlightened beings work tirelessly to help others. The practitioner fully embodies this 
ideal world within the activated visualized image. In addition to visualizing the man­
dala, deity yoga also involves the recitation of mantras and the use of mudrās (ritualized 
hand gestures). The practices of these three are commonly said to represent the enlight­
ened body (mudrā), speech (mantra), and mind (mandala) of the deity. However, the 
boundaries of the three are also commonly understood to overlap, and it is legitimate to 
see the visualized mandala as also the represented “body.” After all, the entire world of 
existing things dissolves into the clear light of wisdom consciousness out of which the 
entire mandala, with the help of mantra, then emerges. Is this all mind, all speech, or all 
body? Since the practitioner is exhorted to cultivate a divine pride in the image of self-​
as-​deity, this pride must extend to the image of enlightened activity manifested in the 
mandala. The explicit aim of the practice is to transform one’s own being into the body 
(and speech and mind) of a buddha, and the envisioned world of light, inside and out­
side, is a vast cosmos of awakened beings, a cosmos that is not separate from one’s own 
physicality. Thus, the practitioner’s felt sense of the mandala as real must also be under­
stood as an aspect of body.
David McMahan recommends understanding aspects of the images employed in tan­
tric practice as a “concretization of doctrine” (2004, 182), He traces the role light plays 
in visualization back to pre-​tantric texts such as the Gaṇḍavyūha, where images of the 
whole world being “flooded with light” symbolize metaphorically the undifferentiated 
field that is the emptiness of all phenomena. He refers to related passages as examples 
of “symbolic visual imagery . . . [that] evoke a sensual presentation homologous with 
a cognitive concept. A specific doctrine or idea is concretized in a visual image.” Such 
concretization brings abstract concepts about how wisdom directly cognizes ultimate 
reality into embodied, perceptual form. He contends that there was an evolution in 
Buddhist thought “that involved a transition from doctrine and metaphor to imagery in 
the Mahāyāna sutras, and then from imagery to ritual in Tantra” (181). He suggests that 
the “construction of a mandala in the imagination” (183) is a ritual transmogrification 
of light metaphors embodied in a structured practice. If an imagined mandala world 
is a vast “body” composed of light tissue, then the entire ritual concretization is also a 
somatization.8
Body Image
Two monastics in the Tibetan tradition, Lama Thubten Yeshe and Matthieu Ricard, offer 
excellent insider descriptions and assessments of Vajrayāna imagery practice. Lama 
Yeshe (2014, reprint) asserts that it is not reasonable to criticize, as some have, the im­
agery of light-​filled space in tantric meditation descriptions as being a misrepresenta­
tion of the Mādhyamaka Buddhist philosophical view of emptiness. He says: “[T]‌his 
is a garbage argument. Why? Because such an intellectual approach to emptiness often 
becomes an obstacle to discovering the actual experience of emptiness.”9 Similarly,

--- PAGE 737 ---
712      David L. Gardiner
 
Yeshe rebuts the criticism that imagining oneself as a deity is pure fantasy. Based prima­
rily on Yogacāra theories of the mind, he argues that ordinary beings are almost always 
“emanating” themselves in one way or another. Visualizing oneself as an enlightened 
being is simply a healthy antidote to our routinely projected self-​images, which tend to 
exaggerate either too negatively or too positively based on a deluded perception of self as 
possessing an enduring, independent essence. He recommends the tantric visualization 
of one’s body being “pure” as an efficacious method to counter, in particular, negative 
self-​image.10
Matthieu Ricard (2006) also presents “the practice of Buddhist mental imagery . 
. . as a skillful means of replacing ‘impure,’ deluded perceptions—​which attach strong 
characteristics to the objects of the phenomenal world—​with a much more ‘fluid’ at­
titude that is attuned to the ever-​changing stream of consciousness” (71). In addition, 
Ricard asserts that training in the sustained practice of complex visualization—​where, 
he affirms, some adept practitioners can hold in their awareness with clarity of detail as 
many as seven hundred deity images in a mandala—​“really helps one to achieve a very 
profound mastery of the workings of the mind” (77). (See also Timalsina, this volume.) 
Both Yeshe and Ricard hold that tantric visualization practice offers a powerful path to­
ward overcoming afflictive states of mind by replacing them with embodied visions of 
healthier states.
Imagining the “body”—​whether just the flesh and blood portion or the full, cosmic 
extension—​in an enhanced state is thus a core element of tantric practice. With ref­
erence to the Cakrasaṃvara genre of tantric texts, David Gray (2021) writes that the 
“re-​imagining of the body as completely pure is strikingly apparent,” adding that in 
this tradition, “the deities of the mandala are mapped to one’s body, with one’s body 
thus visualized as their divine abode” (4). Describing the detailed nature of this map­
ping symbolism, Gray notes that it “represents a somewhat radical contemplative 
exercise, in which some of the most foul aspects of the body, including substances 
often considered impure such as blood, pus, urine and feces, are re-​imagined as pure 
divinities. This, naturally, takes the idea of the innate purity of all things to its logical 
conclusion” (5).
The distinction between purity and impurity of the body is dissolved by engaging 
with images of divine purity (symbolic of the realization of universal emptiness as being 
the ultimate purity). In the same way, the conventional understanding of sexual energies 
as being impure is transcended by symbolic visualizations that transmute carnal desire 
into the pure energy that is its basis and direct this energy to dissolving knots of igno­
rance and attachment at the subtlest levels. This tantric view of sexual desire, represented 
iconographically in images of couples in union (see fig. 28.1), is often explained in tra­
ditional texts as advocating an “alchemical” process of spiritual transformation (Gray 
2021, 7) that undermines the simple logic of duality.11
Nondualism is a steady theme in tantric practice. Moreover, scholars studying 
the visualization practices have noted the way they challenge some of the dualistic 
premises common to certain understandings of religious phenomena. One example 
is the tendency in modern scholarship to perceive an opposition between meditation

--- PAGE 738 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      713
 
(as being a still, quiet, private act) and ritual (as publicly involving voice and ges­
ture). This distinction would seem to follow from a perceived division between mind 
and body (and thus between inner and outer states). However, in tantric visualiza­
tion practice, the act of meditation is replete with imagery, movement, and sound. 
Therefore, some scholars note how textual descriptions of visualization often serve 
to bridge “the categories of ritual performance and meditation” (Sørensen 2022, 
307). Gyatso also urges us to avoid the tendency to “draw a strict line between med­
itation and ritual performance,” and reminds us that the visualizations are them­
selves internalized ritual practices that systematically move through a series of steps 
(Gyatso 1999, 117).

Gender fluidity is another striking feature of the Vajrayāna engagement with im­
agery (Shaw 1995, 186–​187; Tsomo 2018, 35). Both female and male deities are widely 
employed in practice. Prominent female deities include Tārā (especially in her green 
and white forms) and Vajrayoginī (English 2002; Mullin 1983) (see fig. 28.2 and 28.3). 
Male practitioners regularly visualize themselves as Tārā and as Vajrayoginī, just as 
female practitioners employ images of male buddhas and bodhisattvas for their own 
deity yoga practice. There are also deities that embrace both genders. This is not an­
drogyny but rather two bodies together seen as one deity. It is fascinating to note 
that when such an image of male and female united in sexual embrace is used for 
visualization—​such as with Vajradhara, Kālacakra, and Cakrasaṃvara with consort—​
the practitioner uses the image to create a self-​visualization that incorporates them 
both (Simmer-​Brown, 2001, 160). That is, whether the meditator is female or male, 
the image generated to replace their ordinary body/​self is the image of the male and 
female in union.(see fig. 28.4) Not only does this undermine the practitioner’s self-​
identification within a binary gender framework, but it also unsettles the preconcep­
tion of self as being singular.

Healing Imagery
Loriliai Biernacki (2018) writes that “the historical effects of colonialism with its 
Protestant-​rooted moral guideposts condemning India’s vibrant Tantric practice 
as savage, revolting, and impure, have left a debilitating, indelible mark such that the 
Figure 28.3.  Painting of Green Tara, an enlightened female buddha, embodying compassion 
and wisdom.

topic of Tantra continues to elicit derision” (375) While Biernacki is referencing pri­
marily Hindu forms of tantra, she mentions Buddhist ones as well, and her assess­
ment is equally applicable to the Vajrayāna tradition. She urges a powerful revisioning 
of our image of tantric imagery, stressing that our understanding of mental images as 
merely representations “must be revised, fundamentally because the combination of 
memory and visualization makes the visualized deity come alive. It is a new encounter 
Figure 28.4.  Painting of White Tara, a counterpart to the Greet Tara, embodying health and

Artist and date unknown. Used with permission from the author’s personal collection.

--- PAGE 742 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      717
 
and not simply a rote exercise of mental capacity” (375). Such a view of the dynamics 
of Vajrayāna practice goes a long way toward comprehending the power the tradition 
accords itself and why it is called the “vehicle of the thunderbolt.” A radical shift of self-​
identity emerges from the intentional cultivation of a revised mapping of one’s own 
presence. Deity yoga visualization entails a full sensory reboot; it represents a vividly 
imagined somatic fresh start. From the envisioned dissolution of one’s body and its en­
vironment into the clear light of emptiness, the practice entails the “generation of a new 
identity of felt body image” within “visualization practices embedded in rituals where 
meaning is inscribed upon the (enminded) bodily processes” (Duckworth 2019, 119). It 
is no coincidence that capacities for healing are traditionally attributed to such practices 
(Shaw 1995, 106–​110). A revised view of these practices grasps “the role of embodi­
ment in Tantra, and the importance of enaction—​where mental images, body schemas, 
and performed utterances become the means to overcome rigid habits of perception, 
thought and action” (Duckworth 2019, 123). In tantric practice, emptiness “must be 
known . . . dramatically embodied, participatory and performative (not simply prop­
ositional)” (Duckworth, 2019, 125). The emphasis in tantric Buddhist practice on the 
somatic nature of its intended cognitions/​realizations finds resonance in contemporary 
theories of embodied mind, as exemplified in philosopher Mark Johnson’s view that 
“an embodied conception of mind . . . shows how meaning and thought are profoundly 
shaped and constituted by the nature of our bodily perception, action, and feeling.”12 
(See also Hayes & Timalsina, this volume.)
Considering that many Vajrayāna visualizations encompass ritual actions in the con­
text of a mandala of holy beings, it is possible to see the practices enacting what the 
texts describe, which is a “reorientation to a path of liturgical practice in a social space” 
(Orzech 2017, 20). In this way the practices “assume the presence of a congregation 
of vajra beings, Buddhas and other deities” so that the visualization “liturgy acts as a 
script through which practitioners can inhabit different subjectivities” (Orzech, 2017, 
20, 28). Such practice thus demonstrates the flexible nature of individual awareness and 
constitutes a palpable reminder that “subjective identity is not fixed; one’s orientation 
and comportment toward the world is malleable” (Duckworth, 2019, 119).
The mandalic orientation toward the world is a striking and explicit feature of the 
creative use of imagery in Vajrayāna visualization practice. Moreover, the mythical 
nature of the narratives embedded within the series of steps in visualization is unmis­
takable.13 As noted earlier, the ideal of the bodhisattva path frames Buddhist tantric 
practice. In many visualizations, the practitioner imagines themselves at the center of a 
circle of beings, making offerings and promises all expressly understood as productive 
of the practitioner’s progress toward buddhahood. The visualization culminates with 
the practitioner’s own body, speech, and mind imaginatively transformed into a buddha 
who engages in liberative activity aimed at helping others.14 That these imagined actions 
involve images of bodily energies such as radiating lights from all one’s pores that touch 
all beings to relieve them of suffering further testifies to the emphatically embodied 
nature of tantric practice. The visualizations comprise a “somatization of realization”

--- PAGE 743 ---
718      David L. Gardiner
 
(Gyatso 1999, 140). The practices seem to “carry realization into the body, simultaneously 
making the body self-​aware of its ontological emptiness and domesticating realization 
as something habitual, sensual, and lived” (Gyatso 1999, 141). Yet, since the mandalic 
image is not just of the single subject but of the entire expanse of beings partaking in 
a sacred drama of liberation, the embodied nature of such meditative experiences 
serves also to “carry realization into the world, rendering them [the experiences] dis­
cernible, transmissible, and finally intersubjective” (Gyatso 1999, 141). In this manner, 
dichotomies of self/​other and ignorant/​enlightened are dissolved as both the imagined 
ideal body and world are united in one perfected vision (Gray 2021, 13–​14).
The power that positive envisioning can have on the overall health of beings is 
affirmed in a plethora of contemporary medical and psychological research. In partic­
ular, the healing impact of cultivating sustained embodied experiences of well-​being 
has received significant attention.15 While scholarly writings on Buddhist thought and 
practice tend not to use the word “healing” to describe core elements of the ethos of 
the path, there are no solid grounds for avoiding this perspective. After all, the path is 
frequently summarized as targeting the sources of suffering within one’s mind to up­
root them so that freedom from suffering can be experienced. And, not only is the 
Buddha sometimes described as a skillful dispenser of “medicines” in accordance with 
the diversity of diseases, but the foundational teaching of the Four Noble Truths is com­
monly explained using a medical analogy (Gethin 1998, 63). Just as a doctor diagnoses 
the causes of one’s symptoms prior to prescribing a regime for alleviating them, so the 
Buddha identified deep-​seated craving (and the ignorance that supports it) as the chief 
source of sentient anguish and so prescribed a path of practice (encompassing ethical 
conduct, concentration, and insight) to uproot the source. The quandary regarding the 
suitability of seeing Buddhist practice—​the system of “three trainings” of conduct (śila), 
concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā)—​as a path of healing is conveyed clearly 
by Rupert Gethin: “If one were to define Buddhism . . . it would have to be as a prac­
tical method for dealing with the reality of suffering. Asked to define the meaning of the 
word religion, English speakers would probably not immediately suggest ‘a practical way 
of dealing with the reality of suffering’ ” (Gethin 1998, 64). Of course, in the case of many 
contemporary Western Buddhists who do not see their practice as being religious, this 
“practical method” view fits their understanding. Yet, if Buddhism is to be considered a 
religion, our concept of “religion” must expand to include such practical methods and 
their aims. Naturally, Buddhist practices incorporate many elements of devotion, ritual, 
cosmological constructs, institutional frameworks, and more, that bear clear likenesses 
to what is commonly recognized as religious. Still, the tradition’s foundational emphasis 
on the Four Noble Truths provides a template for viewing all these elements, including 
the three trainings, as oriented toward a goal of healing, whether this be understood in 
the more proximate context of easing the pains of saṃsāra or the more ultimate concern 
to uproot them at their source.16
Contemporary Buddhist monastics presenting an emic perspective are likely more 
inclined than are academics to stress the healing function of tantric visualization. Some 
write that it can help to “free your mind from disturbing emotions such as clinging

--- PAGE 744 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      719
 
attachment and anger” (Chodron 2005, 11), while others state that “through creative vis­
ualization, we can call upon inborn forces of healing.”17 And yet, an increasing number 
of Western scholars also emphasize not only this healing potential but, further, the de­
gree to which Vajrayāna theory and practice aligns with recent scientific and medical 
understandings of body-​mind relations (see Samuel and Kozhevnikov, this volume). 
Many psychotherapists are utilizing both the principles and the specific practices of 
Vajrayāna visualization to harness healing processes for patients traumatized by var­
ious ailments (Loizzo, Neale, and Wolf 2017). Emily Wolf writes that the visualizations 
constitute an art of self-​transformation with “profound healing methods,” citing mul­
tiple scientific studies to support her claim (Wolf 2017, 157). She elaborates that tantric 
“[v]‌isualization in the creation stage is a powerful means of regulating affect through 
the symbolically charged content of its imagery. Similar to a schema in cognitive sci­
ence . . . the transformative aspect of Tantric visualization is based on its implicit, depth-​
psychological meaning, which encodes healing insight and emotion through imagery” 
(Wolf 2017, 162). Similarly, writing about tantric imagery and trauma, Pilar Jennings 
states that “the process of evoking and communing with such images can offer another 
method for using one’s imagination and archetypal imprints for healing” (Jennings 
2017, 175). And Joseph Loizzo (who has both an MD degree and a PhD in Tibetan 
Buddhist studies) notes, considering that “embodied approaches to healing and change 
are no strangers to modern psychology,” both modern depth psychology and “Tantric 
science agree that the deepest, subtlest layers of the mind-​brain-​body drive processing 
at higher, coarser levels, and hold the imprints of reactive stress and trauma that con­
dition mental suffering” (Loizzo 2017, 202). Accounts such as these demonstrate an 
emerging scientific paradigm of body-​mind relations that acknowledges the power 
of engaging with positive imagery—​specifically tantric imagery—​for alleviating 
symptoms of traumatic suffering.
This emerging perspective not only appears among psychologists and psychiatrists 
applying Vajrayāna visualization methods in therapy, but derives also from other 
specialists who seek to overcome “the challenges [that] come from mind-​body du­
alism” (Loizzo 2017, 185). Insights from their research indirectly shed a revealing light 
on the wisdom of many of the imagistic elements of tantric practice. A tour de force 
in this regard is The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, Body in the Healing of Trauma 
(van der Kolk 2015). One passage conveys the message clearly: “We can now develop 
methods and experiences that utilize the brain’s own natural neuroplasticity” (van der 
Kolk 2015, 5). Van der Kolk emphasizes bottom-​up methods that allow “the body to have 
experiences that deeply and viscerally contradict the helplessness, rage or collapse that 
come from trauma” (van der Kolk 2015, 5). That deity yoga practice aims to facilitate 
such experiences by nurturing, through creative work with images, a fully somatic sense 
of well-​being is clear from Thubten Yeshe’s account:
The image of being diseased is released from the mind and replaced by an image of 
radiance and vitality. On many occasions this approach has proven effective even 
after doctors have given up all hope. The health of body and mind is primarily a

--- PAGE 745 ---
720      David L. Gardiner
 
question of our self-​image. Those people who think badly of themselves, for what­
ever reasons, become and then remain miserable, while those who can recognize 
and draw on their inner resources can overcome even the most difficult situations. 
Deity yoga is one of the most profound ways of lifting our self-​image, and that is why 
Tantra is such a quick and powerful method for achieving the fulfillment of our tre­
mendous potential.18
Furthermore, van der Kolk’s preface to Stephen W. Porges’s influential The Polyvagal 
Theory: Neurophysiological Foundations of Emotions, Attachment, Communication, and 
Self-​regulation points to yet another approach, emphasizing how Porge’s theory reveals 
that “physiological mind-​brain-​viscera communication is the royal road to affect regula­
tion,” and that it represents a “radical shift in our therapeutic approaches” (van der Kolk 
2011, xvi). He adds that “[t]‌he polyvagal theory legitimates the study of age-​old collec­
tive and religious practices” (van der Kolk 2011, xvii). Citing Porges’s theory, Loizzo also 
affirms the potential that research on the “smart vagus nerve” has for encouraging ther­
apeutic interventions that employ embodied methods as does deity yoga (Loizzo 2017, 
187–​188). Finally, psychologist Rick Hanson19 has explored in multiple publications (and 
workshops) the beneficial health impacts of cultivating embodied states with positive 
affect, with an emphasis on Buddhist meditative techniques (Hanson 2016). Famous for 
his phrase, “from state to trait,” Hanson emphasizes how neuroscientific research reveals 
the transformative power of familiarizing ourselves with positive states: “[T]he brain’s 
evolved negativity bias, which makes it like Velcro for the bad and Teflon for the good, 
creates a kind of bottleneck that blocks the conversion of positive mental states into pos­
itive neural trait” (Hanson 2016). Hanson urges practices that focus on “promoting key 
positive experiences that meet our core needs for safety, satisfaction, and connection 
[and] enriching and absorbing these experiences to install them in neural structure” 
(Hanson 2016). While Hanson’s work does not focus explicitly on Vajrayāna imagery, 
the engagement with nonesoteric Buddhist imagery practices to nurture states of posi­
tive affect is central to his approach.20 (See also Samuel and Kozhevnikov, this volume.)
Deity yoga’s approach to achieving such positive experiences is apparent in 
Wedemeyer’s depiction of the mandalic universe constructed within the imagination 
of tantric practitioners. He writes of the first stage of visualization called “body isola­
tion” that the practice “involves the cultivation of the insight that the entire world is not 
the unenlightened place we think it is, but the unfolding of a cosmic play entirely com­
posed of enlightened beings. Thus, [body isolation] is integral to the esoteric practice 
of the creation stage, that seeks to develop the ‘divine pride’ of oneself as an ‘always al­
ready’ enlightened being” (Wedemeyer 2021, 63–​64). In this way, Wedemeyer holds, the 
ritual practice of Vajrayāna visualization is “oriented toward manipulating the porous 
boundary between quotidian reality and the divine presence” (Wedemeyer 2013, 77). 
Duckworth explains that within this porosity, one sees “appearance not simply as illu­
sory but as divine. Divine pride, identifying with the deity, is the distinctive subjectivity 
taken up with Tantra” (Duckworth 2019, 148).21 Gray’s research on Indo-​Tibetan tantra 
also highlights the centrality of the “envisioning” function of the practice: “The buddha

--- PAGE 746 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      721
 
with whom the meditator in this tradition will identify in deity yoga practices pervades 
the entire universe, collapsing the distinction between self and other, the subjective and 
the objective . . . by portraying the body as a multi-​layered, complex entity that is deeply 
and profoundly interconnected with the universe” (Gray 2021, 8–​9). He adds that, con­
sistent with the nondualist approach of Vajrayāna, the tradition embraces
the notion that there is no essential difference between the deluded and awakened 
state, and the latter can thus be realized in and through one’s body and mind. The 
body is both the starting and end point, and, most notably, the instrument of 
the practice, that which acts and is acted upon. . . . This realization entailed a re-​
envisioning of the body and mind, and this is one of the major goals of [Vajrayāna] 
perfection stage practice, namely, realizing the gnosis of a buddha within our bodies. 
This requires a creative re-​engagement with the body, seeing it ultimately as the 
empty abode of radiant self-​awareness.
(Gray 2021, 13–​14)
Conclusion: Mandala as Body in 
Shingon Buddhism
Vajrayāna practice appeared in one form or another in nearly every land in Asia where 
Buddhism has flourished. In particular, the Shingon tradition in Japan has maintained 
continuous lineages of practice for over twelve hundred years. While some scholarly 
accounts suggest that contemporary Shingon practice does not focus on visualiza­
tion per se, and engages with icons primarily as agents of sacred power that consecrate 
ritual space (Sharf 2002, 119), the writings of the ninth-​century founder Kūkai display 
a steady appreciation for the profound liberative impact that Vajrayāna practice has for 
re-​envisioning one’s body and its place in the world. Both the material painted man­
dala and the imaginatively constructed mandala play central roles in these envisioned 
transformations.22 A few passages from Kūkai’s writings illustrate this plainly. In the 
document he sent to the imperial court upon his return to Japan after studying eso­
teric Buddhism in China, he expressed his view of the power of this new dispensation: 
“Former transmitters of the Dharma [merely] tugged at leaves and swam in tributaries, 
but what I now transmit unearths the root itself, and fully exposes the very well­
spring.”23 Describing the new painted mandalas he brought to Japan, in the same doc­
ument he wrote: “With a single glance [at them], one can attain Buddhahood” (Teihon 
kōbōdaishi zenshū, 1:131).24 However, Kūkai also wrote extensively about the awakened 
state derived from ritual meditation in which a practitioner unites their body, speech, 
and mind with that of the buddha through the “three mysteries” practice, referring to 
this state as the mandala: “The three mysteries of the dharma-​Buddha . . . is the original 
mandala of sentient beings. This is why Buddha Dainichi [Mahāvairocana] taught . .

--- PAGE 747 ---
722      David L. Gardiner
 
. in order to startle sentient beings from their long slumber” (Teihon 3:35). And in his 
Attaining Enlightenment in This Very Body, he expressed his view that the power of the 
three mysteries practice derives from adhiṣṭhāna, translated here as “empowerment,” 
in a startlingly somatic image. In Kūkai’s Chinese, “empowerment” is comprised of 
two words ka 加 and ji持, literally “to add” and “to hold,” as reflected in his individual 
glosses that follow:
“Empowerment” expresses both the great compassion of the Buddha and the faith-​
mind of a sentient being. The reflection of the sun of the Buddha[’s compassion] 
appearing in the mind-​water of a sentient being is called “adding.” The ability of 
the mind-​water of the practitioner to sense this [light of the] Buddha’s sun is called 
“holding.” If the practitioner is able to contemplate this principle, then the three mys­
teries [of the Buddha and of the practitioner] will unite. In the present body one will 
quickly obtain the originally existent three Buddha bodies. . . Just like the everyday 
terms to refer to “at this time” or “on this day,” the phrase “this very body” has the 
same meaning [that is, of immediacy].
(Teihon 3:28)
He adds a rich comment on the theme of embodiment:
“Body” here means my body, Buddha’s body and the bodies of all sentient beings. 
These we call “body”. . . All these bodies are multi-​layered, vertically and horizon­
tally, just like the reflected image of a lamp’s light enters into a mirror. Thus, that body 
is this body, and this body is that body. The Buddha’s body is the body of sentient 
beings, and the bodies of sentient beings are the Buddha’s body. They are not the 
same and yet the same; not different and yet different. All three are thus equal and 
without obstruction.
(Teihon 3:28)
Similarly, he equates this vast interrelated nexus that is “body” with the envisioned/​
realized mandala in his Treatise on the Ten Stages of the Secret Mandala. In this text, he 
establishes ten levels of spiritual attainment, the last four of which represent forms of 
Mahāyāna Buddhism, with Vajrayāna at the top:
The mind of secret adornment [the tenth stage] is to thoroughly awaken to the know­
ledge of the root source of one’s own mind and to realize, as it truly is, the multiplicity 
of one’s own body/​ies. This [abode] is none other than the oceanic assembly of the 
Womb Mandala, the assembly of the Diamond World Mandala, and the Eighteen 
Assembly Mandala of the Diamond Peak [Sutra].
(Teihon 2:307)
Finally, on the occasion of consecrating territory in the mountains designated for an 
esoteric Buddhist compound on Mount Kōya, Kūkai’s votive text conveys his vision of the 
mytho-​historical origins of Vajrayāna. He depicts the emergence of the esoteric teachings

--- PAGE 748 ---
IMAGERY PRACTICE IN TANTRIC BUDDHISM      723
 
as being an eruption into our world of a new mandalic vision transmitted by a lineage of 
holy beings, likening this transmission metaphorically to the “tremble of thunder”: 
“Mahāvairocana Buddha, the great compassionate one, enjoying for himself the taste 
of equality that is enlightenment, was saddened by the plight of the beings in the six 
realms of rebirth. And so it was that the thunder of his wisdom that is one with re­
ality trembled throughout the Dharma realm and the secret mandala was thereby 
transmitted to our world. It was passed on to Vajrasattva, to Nagārjuna and down to 
the present without a break in continuity” (Teihon, 8:177).25
Together with other passages presented earlier, these texts encapsulate a vibrant por­
trait of Vajrayāna Buddhist practice as a method that employs dynamic, embodied im­
agery in the task of liberating beings from suffering, startling them from their slumber. 
They manage to: express an expanded sense of self, as if one’s body is coextensive with 
all other bodies; affirm the possibility of experiencing perfected union with the enlight­
ened state; depict the union in richly somatic imagery of a glowing orb of reflected sun 
that warms and brightens the mind/​body of a practitioner; describe this union in all its 
complexity as a mandala; and narrate the availability of these practices, as well as their 
goal, via an image of a powerful hierophany descending from the highest state of awak­
ening into this world, and thus into our bodies, likening it to a thunderous clap of wisdom 
resonating throughout all space. This is the imagistic, poetic world of Buddhist tantra. It 
is a hopeful vision of the world, one that by multiple accounts has potential for enlivening 
various modern, secular discourses on modalities for healing mind and body.
The phrasing that describes how “the secret mandala was thereby transmitted to our 
world” is pure poesis at work, inviting new modes of understanding via metaphor. So 
also is the image of the mandala as body (or as mind, depending on context), and the 
image of enlightened compassion reflected in the watery mind (body?) of the practi­
tioner. Here we meet not only the language of Vajrayāna texts but the practice itself as 
poetry. In the words of Douglas Duckworth, “it is in poetic and aesthetic theory” that 
we can observe “a resonance with Tantra . . . the generation of a new identity of felt 
body image.” He further muses how it is “with the magic of poetic language and thought 
that we discover the linguistic affordances of creative evocation: of worlds and modes 
of being-​in-​the-​world that destabilize and reenact our orientation as subjects within a 
world” (Duckworth 2019, 119).
A strikingly resonant view of poesis is expressed by philosopher Paul Ricoeur, when 
he says that poetic language changes “our way of dwelling in the world . . . [enabling] a 
new way of being in the world, of orienting ourselves in this world” (1991, 85). Ricoeur 
argues that when we assume that “metaphor reaches reality, we presuppose that we al­
ready know what reality is.” But, when we “assume that metaphor redescribes reality, we 
must assume that this reality, as redescribed, is itself novel reality.” (See also Hayes and 
Timalsina, this volume.) Therefore, he concludes, the strategy of poetic metaphor is “to 
shatter and to increase our sense of reality” (Ricoeur 1991, 85). Notably, we likewise find 
Kūkai also saying that “the mind of secret adornment [perfect enlightenment] is to thor­
oughly awaken to the knowledge of the root source of one’s own mind and to realize, as

--- PAGE 749 ---
724      David L. Gardiner
 
it truly is, the multiplicity of one’s own body/​ies. This [abode] is none other than the oce­
anic assembly of the Womb Mandala” (Teihon 2:307).26 He presents this mandalic image 
as a realizable embodied state, as an attainable “novel reality.”
Susanne Langer’s Philosophy in a New Key urged philosophers in her day to transcend 
the parochial view that all rationality must be “discursive” in nature. She juxtaposed the 
necessarily grammatical and sequential logic of verbal symbolism with the “representa­
tional symbolism” of art and music, emphasizing the immense value to human life that 
nonverbal forms of reasoning bestow: “[T]‌here is an unexplored possibility of genuine 
semantic beyond the limits of discursive language” (Langer 1957, 86 [emphasis in orig­
inal]).27 Regarding visual imagery, Langer wrote:
[V]‌isual forms . . . are just as capable of articulation, i.e., of complex combination, 
as words. But the laws that govern this sort of articulation are altogether different . . 
. visual forms are not discursive. They do not present their constituents successively, 
but simultaneously, so the relations determining a visual structure are grasped in one 
act of vision. (Langer 1957, 93, [emphasis in original])28
Kūkai’s catalog of items he brought back from China, cited above, included in its 
preface wording remarkably like that of Langer’s:
The Dharma is originally without words, and yet it cannot be expressed apart from 
words. . . . The esoteric teachings are very profound, and it is difficult to convey them 
in writing. Thus, they are provisionally revealed to the unenlightened via paintings. 
The myriad forms of sacred deportment and the myriad gestures have their origin in 
great compassion. With a single look [at them], one may realize Buddhahood. . . . The 
root source of the oceanlike assembly [that is, the mandala of deities] corresponds 
just to this.
(Teihon 1:31)
The two nearly identical phrases—​Kūkai’s “with a single look” and Langer’s “grasped 
in one act of vision”—​convey something remarkable about the power of visual experi­
ence: it is both physically and cognitively impactful.
Conjoining the insights of Kūkai’s Vajrayāna vision, Langer’s philosophy of sym­
bolism, and Ricoeur’s poetic sensibility, we can imagine the possibility of a novel and 
potent aesthetic methodology: the somatic-​semantic approach. Tantric Buddhism’s 
employment of visual images deftly straddles the commonly assumed gap between the 
domains of body and meaning. Duckworth’s pithy prose offers a fitting encapsulation of 
the potential for a somatic-​semantic approach to investigating Vajrayāna practice. He 
contends that deity yoga’s paradigmatic engagements with “mental imagery of felt shifts 
in experiential orientation—​that are constructed and dissolved—​offer a unique entry 
point to stage our felt bodily presences in new ways, akin to the ‘interventions’ of art and 
poetry, which can play a role in dismantling our ordinary senses of self and world. These 
practices can serve to rupture habitual patterns of identity by recreating them in delib­
erate and expressive ways” (Duckworth 2019, 123). This is a perfect distillation of the 
“art” of tantric Buddhist imagery.
