Chapter 30
Exploring Metaphors and 
Conceptual Blending in 
Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā Texts
Glen A. Hayes
Approaching the Study of 
the Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās
The term “Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā” refers to a number of Hindu tantric lineages, which have 
often employed transgressive ritual practices, dating back to perhaps the mid-​sixteenth 
century in the region of greater Bengal in northeastern India (modern West Bengal, 
Assam, and Bangladesh).1 They combined antinomian tantric practices and complex or­
thodox Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava2 devotional traditions centered on the god Kṛṣna and his divine 
consort Rādhā. Developing in the religio-​cultural context of deltaic Bengal, an ancient 
center of tantrism, the Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās incorporated an impressive range of beliefs and 
practices from earlier Śaiva, Śākta, and Nāth traditions. They also adapted the aesthetic 
categories and ritual practices of traditional Indian aesthetics (rasa-​śāstra; see Ramanujan 
and Gerow 1974) as interpreted by Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava intellectuals. Developing prima­
rily after the time of the renowned Bengali religious figure Kṛṣna Caitanya (ca. 1486–​1533 
ce), they have throughout their history practiced complex and esoteric forms of sādhana. 
These practices included adulterous ritual sexual intercourse, which has drawn the ire 
of orthodox Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas.3 According to Sarbadhikary (2015), communities of 
modern-​day Sahajiyās continue to practice transgressive rituals, although their current 
texts do not typically refer to the earlier Sahajiyā texts of the seventeenth to nineteenth 
centuries. In contrast to the textual traditions of much of tantric tradition (especially in 
Śaiva and Śākta schools), there are virtually no surviving written commentaries on these 
earlier texts—​if indeed there ever were any.4 Instead, due to the highly esoteric and trans­
gressive nature of these teachings, commentary was probably provided orally by gurus.

--- PAGE 781 ---
756      Glen A. Hayes
 
This is unfortunate for modern historians as most of the remaining vernacular Bengali 
texts, which number in their hundreds, are typically written in an enigmatic style. They 
use an obscure terminology and code-​like language that conceals, but for initiates reveals, 
a fascinating cosmophysiology and ritual system. Translating these curious texts has been 
akin to solving a puzzle, as a conventional literal translation of the mostly uninflected lan­
guage is difficult to understand, and the lack of commentary on technical terms is most 
frustrating. Rather than consigning these intriguing texts to the proverbial dustbin of his­
tory, this has led me to a translation methodology that seeks to identify the underlying 
metaphorical structures as a way to better understand the texts. Engaging conceptual met­
aphor theory was followed by discerning the nuances and dynamics of metaphorical en­
tailment known as conceptual blending. This approach, combining conceptual metaphor 
and conceptual blending, has helped me to better understand the otherwise-​inaccessible 
sādhanas presented in Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā texts.
This chapter explores the vivid metaphorical language and conceptual blending of 
a major Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā text: the Amṛtaratnāvalī (“The Necklace of Immortality,” 
henceforth AR), a treatise on the subtle body (dehatattva) by Mukunda-​deva, also 
known as Mukunda-​dāsa (ca. 1600 ce).5 The term dehatattva, which can be translated 
as “principles” (tattvas) of the “body” (deha), is also examined in a range of tantric 
traditions in Hayes, “Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems” (this volume). To 
give the reader a taste of how seemingly obscure the AR can be and to suggest the utility 
of a hermeneutic based on metaphor and blending, here is a typical passage describing a 
portion of the divine inner yogic body (deva-​deha):6
162.	 The Pond (sarovara) should be visualized as having a pleasing shape.
	
I will tell you about it, so please pay attention!
163.	 That Pond is beautifully adorned with precious gems (māṇika).
	
This eternal realm (nitya dhāma) is inlaid with jewels (ratna).
164.	 In four directions, the four landing-​stairs (ghāṭ) lead to the path of the village 
leader (sarddā).7
	
These landing-​stairs are enveloped by the scents of musk, vermillion, and 
sandalwood.
(AR, vv. 162–​164)8
The subtle body system of the Sahajiyās differs from the better-​known system of 
cakras and kuṇḍalinī typically found in Śaiva, Śākta, and Buddhist traditions (See 
Hayes, “Esoteric Physiology and Subtle Body Systems,” this volume.). Instead of a 
cosmophysiology based on the fiery ascent of energies and vital winds into a network 
of channels and a system of floral wheels, the Sahajiyā system of the AR incorporates 
imagery and symbolism from the surrounding topology of riverine and deltaic Bengal. 
It is thus a hydraulic process of fluids ascending a “crooked river” (bāṅkānadī) within 
the physical body, which flows upward “against the current” (sroter ujāna) into a system 
of stepped ponds (sarovara) with landing stairs (ghāṭ). These are not just naturally 
occurring small bodies of water; landing stairs with steps have been constructed on 
the banks of the pond (as found throughout Bengal). There is probably a clever play on

--- PAGE 782 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      757
 
words here, as the Bengali word ghāṭ, “landing stairs,” is a pun with ghaṭ, “a pot made 
of clay or metal,” which could refer to the organs of the body. Whether deliberate or 
not this pun connects riverine imagery with more traditional yogic imagery.9 As we 
will see in greater detail, the primary underlying metaphor for both Śaiva/​Śākta and 
Sahajiyā traditions is that the subtle body is a container. Drawing upon topographical, 
contextual, cultural, and vernacular imagery produces a quite complex metaphor. For 
the Sahajiyās the subtle body is a watery network of stepped ponds and curving rivers, 
distinct from the network of channels, tubes, and floral circles for Śaivas and Śāktas (on 
the intricacies of esoteric physiology in a range of tantric traditions, see Hayes, “Esoteric 
Physiology and Subtle Body Systems,” this volume). This exploration of the uses of pri­
mary and complex metaphors in the expressions of the subtle body continues below.
In their quest for bodily transformation, the Sahajiyās made use of a wide range of 
practices. These included techniques from Indian alchemy (rasāyana),10 which essen­
tially involved the ritual and magical manipulation of fluids, substances, and fire in 
order to achieve bodily immortality (on alchemy, see Sauthoff, this volume). Also, sim­
ilar to Nāth traditions, they adopted the “practice of reversal” (ulṭā sādhana), in which 
the practitioner attempts to reverse the phenomenal flow of creation and embodiment. 
Reversal uses yogic powers to ascend “upwards against the current” (sroter ujāna) of 
emanation back to the underlying cosmic unity of Sahaja—​the “together-​born” (saha-​
ja) or “innate” unitive cosmic state.11 They also adapted tantric ritual sexual intercourse 
(maithuna), collecting male semen (rasa, śukra, retas), and female vaginal secretions 
(rati). Thus, the Sahajiyā system of dehatattva, based on fluidic metaphors, also assumes 
scatological dimensions by involving the ritual ingestion of the male and female sexual 
fluids.12 But following “reversal practice,” these fluids are believed to be yogically with­
drawn into the male urethra, into the “crooked river,” and on “up” through the stepped 
ponds until the attainment of Sahaja at the upper reaches of the river. It recalls a system 
of locks on a river system, and Sahajiyā traditions employ imagery of boating.13
For the Sahajiyās, once drawn into the rivers and ponds, the sexual fluids become a 
generative cosmic substance called vastu, literally “stuff.”14 The entire expansive subtle 
body is generated (nirmāṇa) from this yogic substance. This also results in the practi­
tioner acquiring incredible yogic power (śakti), and achieving an intense spiritual state 
(mahābhāva). Later, this chapter explores a range of primary metaphors involving the 
container, conduits, substance, and entities. The analysis continues by considering com­
plex metaphors and conceptual blending theory.
Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā Appropriations of 
Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism
As already noted, the Sahajiyās may broadly be considered an interaction of intricate 
transgressive tantric yoga with Vaiṣṇava bhakti devotionalism, resulting in a quite 
distinctive vernacular Bengali tantric tradition. Sahajiyās appropriate and modify

--- PAGE 783 ---
758      Glen A. Hayes
 
classical devotional interpretations of Kṛṣṇa, transforming him from a supreme being 
(as Bhagavān, the “Bounteous Lord,” very distinct from human beings) into the inner 
cosmic form (svarūpa) of every human male. Rādhā is transformed from the milkmaid 
consort and hlādini-​śakti (“bliss emanation”) of Kṛṣṇa into the svarūpa of every woman. 
For Sahajiyās, in other words, the goal is not to worship Kṛṣṇa or imitate Rādhā and 
the cowherd maidens (gopī) in a modified dualistic way as Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas do (di­
vine above human)15 but rather to become Kṛṣṇa or Rādhā themselves, in a monistic 
tantric manner (human and divine together). Sahajiyās also expressed these alternative 
notions of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā in regional vernacular Bengali metaphors, language, and 
verse. They embedded these narratives in specific Sahajiyā teaching lineages, shifting 
the figures of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā even further from the Sanskrit-​based and classical 
formulations into the local cultural and cognitive realities of Bengali men and women of 
the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
Dimock (1966) and Stewart (2010) have shown that narratives involving Kṛṣṇa and 
his erotic encounters with Rādhā would have provided useful tropes for late medieval 
Sahajiyā tantrics to adapt as they sought to express the need to reverse the phenom­
enal flow of creation—​engendered as the “play” of male and female powers—​“upwards 
against the current” (sroter ujāna) back to the unitive state of Sahaja. The popular no­
tion of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava leader Kṛṣṇa Caitanya as himself the dual incarnation of 
both Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, developed by Kṛṣṇa-​dāsa Kavirāja (ca. 1615 ce) in his renowned 
hagiography Caitanya-​caritāmṛta, was also taken up by the Sahajiyās.16 This was subse­
quently appropriated to their own belief that all Sahajiyās must themselves realize male 
and female powers within their own physical bodies. The metaphorical language and 
conceptual integration networks found in Sahajiyā texts are complex not only because 
they blend dualistic bhakti and monistic tantra but also because they orchestrate highly 
complex cosmophysiologies, ontologies, and soteriologies. The power of conceptual in­
tegration and metaphorical language facilitates the central goals of Sahajiyā sādhana.
Sādhana Is a Journey: Conceptual 
Metaphors and Cognitive Domains
Having briefly introduced the importance of metaphorical language and concepts in 
Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā texts, we now more fully explore conceptual metaphor theory. The 
English word metaphor has its roots in the Latin metaphora, “carrying over,” and extends 
further back to the Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), also glossed as “carrying over,” 
“moving across,” and “transferring.”17 Over many centuries, the word “metaphor” has 
acquired a range of rich and complex meanings, as well as myriad usages in systems of 
rhetoric, theology, philosophy, and literature.18 However, the modern sense of concep­
tual metaphor was first fully presented by linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark 
Johnson in Metaphors We Live By (1980) and later works19 and goes much deeper than 
earlier usages. Cognitive linguists and neuroscientists argue that the human brain and

--- PAGE 784 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      759
 
mind organize perceptions, cognitions, language, and behaviors using a vast web of cog­
nitive and neural connections. Conceptual metaphor is one form of such connective 
webs, along with metonymy, counterfactuals, analogies, and categorization.20 Though 
constrained by current limits on neural imaging and scanning technology, detailed em­
pirical evidence for these webs continues to be gathered. It is clear, however, that these 
networks or webs partly function by processes known as “cross-​mapping,” connective 
and associative projections that are established between mental spaces, image schema,21 
and neural assemblies. Johnson (1987, xiv–​xv) argues that conceptual metaphor may be
conceived as a pervasive mode of understanding by which we project patterns from 
one domain of experience in order to structure another domain of a different kind. 
So conceived, metaphor is not merely a linguistic mode of expression; rather, it is 
one of the chief cognitive structures by which we are able to have coherent, ordered 
experiences that we can reason about and make sense of. Through metaphor, we 
make use of patterns that obtain in our physical experience to organize our more ab­
stract understanding.
According to this approach, now known as conceptual metaphor theory (CMT), 
metaphors involve the dynamic interaction between a “target domain” (the abstract 
thing that the metaphor seeks to describe—​such as “life”) and a “source domain” (the 
concrete object or detailed thing providing structure to the abstraction—​such as 
“journey”) from which the target domain’s meanings and entailments derive. This can 
be visualized as two “mental spaces” (Target/​LIFE and Source/​JOURNEY), and the 
cognitive activity involves “cross-​domain mapping” between the two spaces. For ex­
ample, in the basic metaphor LIFE IS A JOURNEY,22 the more concrete experiences of 
journeying along a path, over surfaces, perhaps with companions, and facing obstacles 
may be applied to the rather abstract concept of “life.” We may not be able to fully com­
prehend what life is all about, but using the details derived from the concrete realm of 
journeys helps to make “life” seem less abstract. There is a remarkable complexity be­
hind such a seemingly simple metaphor, which can be discerned by considering the 
“entailments” or semantic implications of the metaphor. Thus, entailments of LIFE IS A 
JOURNEY might be expressed as “My life came to a crossroads,” “The country is going 
downhill,” or “I am on my way to graduation.” As one explores the uses of CMT, the 
entailments—​the nooks and crannies—​of many fascinating metaphors may be found. 
And, for our purposes in this chapter, these remarkable features of conceptual metaphor 
can be found in Sahajiyā and other tantric texts.
Categories of Metaphors
LIFE IS A JOURNEY is both an “orientational metaphor,” as it expresses spatial 
relationships (up/​down, in/​out, forward/​backward), and an “event structure” meta­
phor, expressing temporal and spatial sequences. This connects the journey metaphor

--- PAGE 785 ---
760      Glen A. Hayes
 
to another fundamental metaphor, STATES ARE LOCATIONS (Lakoff 1993, 220–​222). 
This involves projecting details of boundaries and spatiality onto otherwise-​diffuse 
states, such as consciousness, emotion, or transcendence. As one progresses through 
the journey (life), they pass in and out of sequences of bounded regions (life stages). 
Cognitive scientists believe an “event sequence schema” is based upon a very deep net­
work of body schema and prenoetic capacities which may be universal functions of the 
human mind and body. Kövecses (2015, 4) observes:
The system of metaphors called the Event Structure metaphor (Lakoff, 1993) includes 
submetaphors such as CAUSES ARE FORCES, STATES ARE CONTAINERS, 
PURPOSES ARE DESTINATIONS, ACTION IS MOTION, DIFFICULTIES ARE 
IMPEDIMENTS (TO MOTION) and so forth. Remarkably, in addition to English, 
this set of submetaphors occurs in such widely different languages and cultures as 
Chinese (Yu, 1998) and Hungarian
(Kovecses, 2005).
Event structure metaphor23 is clearly expressed in Sahajiyā texts. Some examples in­
clude SĀDHANA IS A JOURNEY, SAHAJA IS A PLACE, and THE SAROVARA IS A 
DESTINATION. We can reflect on Lakoff’s (2008, 30) observation that
primitive image-​schemas (e.g., container, source-​path-​goal, degree of closeness, di­
rection, and amount of force) are computed by brain structures that are either innate 
or form early. Action schemas and frames are structured using such primitive image-​
schemas. For example, putting in makes use of the container schema, the source-​
path-​goal schema, a force schema, a direction schema, and an aspectual schema.
For Sahajiyās, this directly relates to key aspects of sādhana: directing, or putting fluids 
into, one of the sarovaras.
The cognitive and neurobiological foundations beneath metaphor run deep, and in 
many different directions, such as with journeys. In the AR (v. 154),24 Mukunda-​dāsa 
states:
154  The path of sādhana is difficult to traverse, it is near-​yet-​far;
From a distance it seems close, from close up it seems distant.
Here we find an orientational metaphor about sādhana—​SĀDHANA IS A JOURNEY—​
based upon a number of basic metaphors, including PURPOSES ARE DESTINATIONS, 
CHANGE IS MOTION, and STATES ARE LOCATIONS. But this is itself based upon 
a more global metaphor: A PURPOSEFUL LIFE IS A JOURNEY. Lakoff and Johnson 
(1999, 60–​64) unpack some additional dimensions of this metaphor as follows:
A Purposeful Life is a Journey
A Person Living a Life is a Traveler
Life Goals are Destinations

--- PAGE 786 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      761
 
A Life Plan is an Itinerary
This may be applied to many cases of ritual transformation and pilgrimage in the his­
tory of religions, and certainly to Sahajiyā texts; the details may include entailments of 
surfaces, paths, companions, objects, obstacles, and destinations.
Based on the “event-​sequence” schema, there are countless entailments of the journey 
metaphor. For example, in Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā traditions, the guru must first impart the 
initiatory “seed” (bīja) mantras25 to the disciple before the journey can even begin, and 
there are typically three distinct levels of practice, regarded as sections of the path (AR, 
vv. 14–​19): beginner (pravarta), accomplished (sādhaka), and perfected (siddha). The 
journey metaphor connects to the metaphor of destination, and in Sahajiyā texts we 
see many examples of adepts traveling to an inner realm of villages, rivers, ponds, and 
jungles—​destinations that must be reached in order to arrive at the ultimate destination 
of Sahaja. These realms are typically blissful realms of higher states of consciousness, 
where powerful beings and radiant colored lotuses are encountered, and where the ul­
timate state of the Together-​born Inner Being (Sahaja-​mānuṣa) may be attained. In the 
AR (vv. 42–​47) we read:26
42	 This teaching (dharma) is the purest, without division nor lust (kāma).
	
The transcendent realm (dhāma) is beyond the heavenly Virajā river.
43	 Along the far shores of the heavenly Virajā river27 is “The Place” (deśakhāna).
	
A Village (grāma) named Sahajapur is [a place of] eternal bliss (sadānanda).
44	 To the west of that [river] is [a village named] “Orissan Flower Bud” (Kaliṅga 
Kalikā);
	
The female partner (nāyikā) of that place is named “Magnolia Bud” (Campaka 
Kalikā).28
45	 [In that place are] the Tree of Emptiness (śūnya vṛkṣa), and lotuses of one hun­
dred and one thousand petals.
	
“The Place” surrounds that tree and the waters of the Pond (sarovara).
46	 To the north [of the Virajā river] is the Village of Ānandapur (“Place of Bliss”).
	
[In that place are] connoisseurs of love (rasikas), groves of rapture (rasera 
kuñja), and the realm (dhāma) of the god of Love (manmatha, or Kāmadeva).
47	 Forever blissful, forever overwhelmed, forever desirous,
	
the Together-​born Inner Being (sahaja-​mānuṣa) always makes [its] home there.
Reflecting the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava heritage, the text speaks of the need to travel to regions 
similar to Vaiṣṇava realms such as Vraja and Nitya Vṛndāvana—​mythical and celestial 
places associated with the life and loves of Kṛṣna and Rādhā. But the realization of the 
cosmic state of Sahaja is also presented as a destination, framing an otherwise-​abstract 
transcendent state of consciousness spatially and in a sequence. Thus, the transcendent 
state of the sahaja-​mānuṣa is found after taking a journey to the location of the village of 
Sahajapur (“the Together-​born Place”). However, this journey to such a cosmic destina­
tion must be undertaken in a yogic or subtle body, including passage through a series of 
interior bodily containers. The segments and connections of this inner body comprise a

--- PAGE 787 ---
762      Glen A. Hayes
 
crooked river, running “upwards against the current” (AR, v. 180, sroter ujāna) to celes­
tial realms and Sahaja, flowing through a series of connected stepped ponds (sarovara), 
within which are multi-​petalled lotuses. The basic structure is as follows (AR, v. 
97–​98):29
97	 There are the Pond of Lust (kāma-​sarovara) [and] the Pond of Egotism 
(māna-​sarovara);
	
The Pond of Divine Love (prema-​sarovara) [and] the Pond of Indestructibility 
(akṣaya-​sarovara).30
98	 The four Ponds lie within the heart.
	
If you have a body (deha), you can reach the other shore.
Sahajiyās conceive all of these concepts together under the term dehatattva, which 
means “principles of the body.” An understanding of conceptual metaphors can help 
us to better understand these esoteric processes and the cosmophysiology of Sahajiyā 
traditions.
Lakoff and Johnson (1980, 23–​29) have identified a number of categories of meta­
phor used in everyday speech—​most of which occur in Sahajiyā texts. In addition to 
orientational metaphors involving journey and destination, there are also “ontolog­
ical metaphors,” which would apply to entities and substances. Lakoff and Johnson 
(1980, 25) observe:
Spatial orientations like up-​down, front-​back, on-​off, center-​periphery, and near-​
far provide an extraordinarily rich basis for understanding concepts in orientational 
terms. But one can only do so much with orientation. Our experience of phys­
ical objects and substances allows us to pick out parts of our experience and treat 
them as discrete entities or substances of a uniform kind. Once we can identify our 
experiences as entities or substances, we can refer to them, categorize them, group 
them, and quantify them—​and, by this means, reason about them.
As we have seen, much of Sahajiyā dehatattva and sādhana involves the ritual manip­
ulation of powerful substances, such as sexual fluids, and their transformation into 
vastu, the cosmic substance out of which the inner devadeha is generated (see, e.g., 
AR, vv. 35, 114, 208).31 The metaphor allows the practitioner to engage with the ritual 
substances as discrete things, arranging them into a sequence of cosmophysiological 
achievements. The Sanskrit and Bengali term rasa can mean a rapturous religio-​
aesthetic experience, but it can also be semen (śukra), expressed through the substance 
metaphor as RASA IS SEMEN.32 As inherited from the classical tradition of Sanskrit 
aesthetics and writings of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologians, rasa means to “taste” an 
elevated state of consciousness and aesthetic appreciation, achieved through the culti­
vation of various “moods” (bhava). But it is rendered a more immediate thing through 
the metaphor and is seen as experienced in the substance of semen.33 The Sanskrit and 
Bengali term rati also has a range of meanings, including the wife of the god of love, 
a “desirable woman,” sexual intercourse, or absorption of the mind. In the AR, it is

--- PAGE 788 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      763
 
mapped out by the metaphor of RATI IS UTERINE FLUID as ritualized female sexual 
fluid, again using entailments derived from a substance to express the concept of the 
female ritual partner (see, e.g., AR, v. 38).
Beyond metaphors involving substances, we find ontological metaphors involving 
entities. For example, the AR describes various kinds of divine feminine beings and 
powers regarded as “heroines” (nāyikā), arranged on the petals of an eightfold lotus 
flower in the stepped Pond (AR, vv. 239–​243):34
239	 The Pond of Egotism (māna-​sarovara) is located within the heart.
	
The construction of the system [of the Ponds] is [in] the human body (kalevara).
240	 The eight Heroines (nāyikā) were born in those eight petals.
	
They all came together in the limbs (aṅga) of all the gods.
241	 [Their names are:] Sulakṣanā, Sulocanā, Rambhā, Umā;
	
Rukmiṇī, Menakā, Tina-​umā [and] Satyabhāmā.35
242	 These eight Heroines are manifested in the eight petals.
	
Amidst the floating blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses.
243	 Then one gains perception (avagati) [of] the Heroines in the eight petals.
	
The eight Heroines who are in the eight lotuses are the embodiment (rūpa) of
	
the Goddess of Love (rati).36
The heroines are thus entities that embody not only the qualities of the goddess of love 
and wife of Kāmadeva but the more abstract concepts of erotic desire (rati), as in RATI IS 
A BEAUTIFUL WOMAN. The text also describes ascending levels of transcendent con­
sciousness, understood as a type of Being (mānuṣa): the Purified Being (śuddhasattva-​ 
mānuṣa; AR, vv. 149, 176), the Self-​perfected Being (svataḥsiddha-​mānuṣa; AR, v. 181), 
and the Together-​born Being (Sahaja-​mānuṣa; AR, v. 48). Using the entity metaphor 
of MĀNUṢA IS A PERSON, the Sahajiyās are able to facilitate the experience of these 
rarified and abstract states of consciousness.
Ponds and Rivers: Container and 
Conduit Metaphors
Lakoff and Johnson also identify “structural metaphors,” which help to organize and 
arrange our visual fields and experience of objects, space, and relationships. For the 
study of dehatattva, the most important structural metaphors are CONTAINER and 
CONDUIT. Lakoff and Johnson (1980, 29) observe:
We are physical beings, bounded and set off from the rest of the world by the surface 
of our skins, and we experience the rest of the world as outside us. Each of us is a con­
tainer, with a bounding surface and an in-​out orientation. We project our own in-​out 
orientation onto other physical objects that are bounded by surfaces. Thus we also 
view them as containers with an inside and an outside.

--- PAGE 789 ---
764      Glen A. Hayes
 
The container metaphor is perhaps one of the most fundamental of all embodied 
metaphors, as it most directly maps to our own experiences as skin-​bounded mammals. 
We find many less obvious uses of the container metaphor in expressions such as IDEAS 
ARE CONTAINERS, and statements like “He put all of his effort into his thesis,” “She 
is in love,” and “Many things are needed in that career.” But virtually all systems of the 
subtle body in tantra are based upon the metaphor of the cakras, padmas, and sarovaras 
as “containers,” which contain not flesh and blood but “vital breaths” (prāṇa), cosmic 
energy (kuṇḍalinī), or sexual fluids (rasarati). As containers of the subtle body, they 
are “made” of subtle “substances” such as vastu (and even light can be regarded as a 
substance), while they have specific appearances, shapes, colors, and properties. The 
“seed syllables” (bīja) often visualized in cakras or on the lotus petals serve as types of 
containers of attention and consciousness (see Timalsina, this volume). And although 
Lakoff focuses on things outside our skin surfaces, dehatattva is primarily concerned 
with visualized realms within the physical body. In the text we read (AR, vv. 237–​238):37
237	 The Container (ādharā) is the essence of everything, all of the gods, and 
samsara itself.
	
The Pond of Lust is created [by] the essence of lust (kāma).
238	 All of the gods, the Ponds, the God of Love (Kāmadeva), and Goddess of 
Love (Rati).
	
All of the gods are located in the lotus of eight petals.
Thus, the subtle body is a series of connected containers, with the stepped ponds linked 
by the rivers or channels, as one cakra or padma or sarovara leads to the next. Structurally 
and functionally, this of course requires openings in the containers and, importantly, 
connections or conduits leading into and out of each container.38 In the Śaiva and Śākta 
systems of cakras and padmas, these conduits are the nāḍīs (channels),39 a term also used 
in the Sahajiyā systems of tantric dehatattva, existing alongside riverine passageways 
such as the “crooked river” (bāṅkānadī). The floors of a building require stairways to con­
nect the levels and corridors to connect the rooms. In the same way, the channels and 
rivers of the subtle body, which are often said to be innumerable, are necessary to enter 
each sarovara and, ultimately, to achieve the highest state of consciousness in the akṣaya-​
sarovara. Although these ponds are rarified states of consciousness and liberation, the 
pathways connecting them are made a bit more accessible by the metaphors of journey, 
entity, substance, container, and conduit. The text states (AR, vv. 110–​112):40
110	 Within the physical body (śarīra) there are nine [major] yogic channels (nāḍī) 
and thirty-​
	
two crore [minor channels].41
	
Who is able to know where each of these are located?
111	
I will speak about all of these [channels]. Listen, all you devotees!
	
In the Pond of Lust (kāma-​sarovara) there are three kinds of channels.
112	 There are eight meditation huts (koṭā)42 in the eight lotuses.
	
Madanamohana (Kṛṣna) has cleverly concealed the channels and lotuses.

--- PAGE 790 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      765
 
All of these examples of the subtle body in tantra derive from the descriptions of 
visualized imagery in the texts, which raises the larger issue of a “visual field.” Although 
we are talking about an interiorized visual field in tantra, Lakoff and Johnson (1980, 30) 
make the following observation about ordinary visual fields:
We conceptualize our visual field as a container and conceptualize what we see as 
being inside it. Even the term “visual field” suggests this. The metaphor is a natural 
one that emerges from the fact that, when you look at some territory (land, floor, 
space, etc.) your field of vision defines a boundary of the territory, namely, the part 
that you can see. Given that a bounded visual space is a CONTAINER and that our 
field of vision correlates with that bounded visual space, the metaphorical concept 
VISUAL FIELDS ARE CONTAINERS emerges naturally.
At the different stages of Sahajiyā sādhana described in the texts we encounter varying 
scenarios such as that presented in the opening section: stepped ponds, lotus flowers, 
surrounding fields, trees, and beings. We might call this a “visualized field,” within which 
various objects exist and events occur (for details concerning the interplay between vis­
ualization, imagination, and attention in tantra, see Timalsina, “Attention, Memory, and 
the Imagination: A Cognitive Analysis of Tantric Visualization,” this volume). Lakoff 
and Johnson (1980, 30) note that “We use ontological metaphors to comprehend events, 
actions, activities, and states. Events and actions are conceptualized metaphorically 
as objects, activities as substances, states as containers.” Thus, the visualized stage of 
sādhana within a specific cakra or sarovara is viewed as a container, which exists in inner 
space and time, and has well-​defined boundaries. Lakoff and Johnson would regard this 
visualized experience as an instance of a CONTAINER OBJECT metaphor. The met­
aphoric container has within it participants (male and female beings), events like the 
ritualized entry into the realm (a metaphoric object), and the activity of achieving the 
particular cakra or sarovara (a metaphoric substance).
Crooked Rivers and Forest Groves: 
Primary and Complex Metaphors
Primary metaphors emerge from the basic dynamics of human embodiment and our 
experience of the surrounding world.43 Some of the most obvious ones include MORE 
IS UP, KNOWING IS SEEING, and STATES ARE LOCATIONS.44 Lakoff and Johnson 
(1999, 5) illustrate the semantic range of STATES ARE LOCATIONS as follows:
Subjective Judgement: A subjective state
Sensorimotor Experience: Being in a bounded region of space
Example: “I’m close to being in a state of depression and the next thing that goes 
wrong will send me over the edge.”

--- PAGE 791 ---
766      Glen A. Hayes
 
Primary experience: Experiencing a certain state as correlated with a certain location 
(e.g., being cool under a tree, feeling secure in bed).
Examples of many of these primary metaphors can be found in tantric language. And 
to the degree that all humans share roughly similar bodies and cognitive abilities, many 
such metaphors may be close to universal or, more precisely, global. Primary metaphors 
are thus connected to our neural processes and overall life experiences.
The primary metaphor of Sahajiyā sādhana, STATES ARE LOCATIONS, becomes a 
more complex metaphor SAHAJAPUR IS A LOCATION. Built on the primary meta­
phor, Bengali cultural frames and associations, as well as Sahajiyā soteriology, are added. 
For Sahajiyās, the basic MORE IS UP metaphor might be expressed in DEVADEHA IS 
UP, as it enhances the primary meanings of the location of the subtle body, with the 
placement of the stepped ponds not only “within” the physical body, but “upwards 
against the current” along the “crooked river.” It also expresses the verticality body 
schema.45 Keeping in mind the neural and sensorimotor implications of primary meta­
phor, we can appreciate how any tantric sādhana requires much time and effort. Well be­
yond the mastery of life in the ordinary world that children encounter, sādhana requires 
the creation and activation of entirely new and complex neural networks, which we will 
consider in the final section on conceptual blending.
As noted, although primary metaphors provide the basic foundation for the neural 
and cognitive processes, most of the actual metaphors we find expressed in tantric litera­
ture and ritual are “complex” or novel metaphors. Lakoff and Johnson (1999, 60) explain 
that complex metaphors are “built out of primary metaphors plus forms of common­
place knowledges: cultural models, folk theories, or simply knowledge or beliefs that are 
widely accepted in a culture.” Thus, the Sahajiyās combined primary metaphors such as 
THE BODY IS A CONTAINER and MORE IS UP with imageries from the local Bengali 
landscape, both geographical and cultural, to create their elaborate complex metaphors 
of the subtle body with its ascending series of stepped ponds, the crooked river, villages, 
and groves. Complex metaphors are not universal but are context-​specific, in this case to 
Bengal and to the individual histories and lineages of those experiencing the metaphor.
The system of the subtle body in the AR is thus an extremely complex cognitive 
product, fashioned as it is by a blending of primary metaphors such as THE BODY 
IS A CONTAINER, MORE IS UP, and STATES ARE LOCATIONS with imagery and 
concepts from tantric and bhakti traditions, as well as details from deltaic and riverine 
Bengal. It is notable that the system of stepped ponds and rivers is somewhat different 
from the system of cakras and channels (nadīs/​nadīs) found in many Śaiva and Śākta 
tantric systems. The underlying Sahajiyā dynamic involves manipulating fluids into the 
rivers and ponds, while the Śaiva and Śākta systems are based on the movement of ener­
getic breaths and kuṇḍalinī-​śakti. The metaphoric “world” of the Sahajiyās is thus more 
fluid based, while the Śaiva and Śākta systems are more energy based. Also looming 
large in the development of the complex metaphors of the dehatattva are imageries and 
frames from local vernacular Bengali culture and topography.
Different cultural frames might combine with a range of primary metaphors, giving 
rise to specific systems of complex metaphors. Thus, the prominence of footpaths,

--- PAGE 792 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      767
 
lotuses, rivers, stepped ponds, stairs, and boat landings, as well as villages, leaders, snakes, 
bumblebees, groves, and forests demonstrates the vivid nature of complex metaphors. In 
this way, the Sahajiyā system better expresses the realities of local Bengali life and culture. 
Although sharing the pan-​Indian valorization of lotuses with Śaiva and Śākta systems, 
the influence of deltaic and riverine Bengal overrides the drier climes and topography of, 
for example, western India. As noted by Ning Yu: “In other words, the question is how, 
exactly, the interplay between body and culture gives rise to conceptual metaphors that 
are universal, widespread, or culture-​specific” (2008: 248). In tantric studies, one might 
say that within specific teaching lineages (paramparā) there is likely to be a distinctive 
system of complex metaphors, which may share features within regions (e.g., Bengal and 
Assam) and larger traditions (e.g., Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism), but which are not 
global or universal (despite sharing primary metaphors that might be).
Lakoff and Johnson have summarized this complicated process as follows:
Inevitably, many primary metaphors are universal because everybody has basi­
cally the same kinds of bodies and brains and lives in basically the same kinds of 
environments, so far as the features relevant to metaphor are concerned.
The complex metaphors that are composed of primary metaphors and that make 
use of culturally based conceptual frames are another matter. Because they make use of 
cultural information, they may differ significantly from culture to culture (2003, 257).
To be sure, the local culture and community will inevitability filter which bodily 
experiences can be cross-​mapped and projected onto specific target domains. For example, 
Sahajiyās shared many beliefs and rituals regarding Kṛṣna and Rādhā (especially derived 
from the “external practices” or vaidhi-​bhakti, such as communal singing and dancing) 
with Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas.46 However, since the Sahajiyās practiced a transgressive form of 
ritual sexual intercourse with a partner “belonging to another” (parakīyā),47 their practices 
conflicted with those of the orthodox. Thus the Sahajiyā dehatattva ends up using different 
complex metaphors because they were referring to very different experiences of the body 
and human sexuality. Citing Gibbs (1999, 155), Yu (2008, 253) notes that “in short, ‘social 
and cultural constructions of experience fundamentally shape embodied metaphor.’ ” The 
concluding section of this chapter considers these constructions of experience and how the 
resultant complex metaphors may be studied through conceptual blending theory (CBT).
Sahaja and Emergent Structure: 
Conceptual Blending Theory
The process by which complex metaphors are generated is known as conceptual 
blending.48 We have just considered how complex metaphors are generated out of more 
basic primary metaphors, blending in various cultural frames, imagery, and cognitive 
content. Although CMT helps to explore the nuances of complex metaphor, conceptual 
blending theory (CBT) allows us to more fully “unpack” this process on a granular level,

--- PAGE 793 ---
768      Glen A. Hayes
 
identifying the various “inputs” that create the specific and distinct complex (and novel) 
metaphor.
As useful as CMT has been, one of the questions involving the cross-​space mapping 
from Source to Target domains has been why only some aspects and details are projected 
but not others. This and other issues of basic conceptual metaphors led Fauconnier and 
Turner to expand the two-​space model of Lakoff and Johnson’s metaphor theory (target/​
source) to a four-​space (or more) model they called a conceptual integration network 
(CIN).49 (Such networks are often rendered in a graphic chart, as in fig. 30.1.) CBT does 
not reject CMT but rather elaborates upon it, finding added layers of entailments and 
dynamics. In his 2008 essay, Lakoff argues that all complex metaphors are generated 
using conceptual blending of the primary metaphors and other cognitive products. 
Complex metaphors and conceptual integration networks are indeed found in Sahajiẏā 
texts. CBT methodology can help us to better understand their imaginative cognitive 
networks and processes. Fauconnier and Turner devised schematic charts to help us vis­
ualize such otherwise-​abstract cognitive features. We will consider three charts.50
As shown in figure 30.1, basic CBT is visualized using a minimum of four spaces: a 
generic space, which contains a common structure or “frame” (a set of details present in 
all of the input spaces); two or more “input spaces,” which hold the contents and details 
of specific situations or ideas; and a blended or “emergent” space. This blended space 
includes the general structure from the generic space and selected elements from the 
different input spaces, which are cross-​mapped onto this novel space using properties 
called “vital relations.”
Cross-​space mappings and projections (e.g., an inner body of ponds and lotuses) em­
anate from the generic space, which here would be THE BODY IS A CONTAINER,

which implies a bounded region, with conduits and contents. The input spaces are mul­
tiple. These inputs are drawn from a range of traditions, including Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism 
and its aesthetics, Nāth and tantric lineages, and alchemy. The process of blending 
creates an “emergent structure” in the blended space. This emergent structure is essen­
tially the novel and creative end product of the imaginative cognitive process: a cosmic 
body and realms connected to Sahaja. While the root metaphor is common, this new 
structure of cosmophysiology is context-​specific to the Sahajiyās as Bengalis and helps 
the practitioner to conceptualize, and then actualize, the goal of embodied transcendent 
consciousness.
In figure 30.2, the generic space is that of the primary metaphors of the BODY IS 
CONTAINER, and REALITY IS CONTAINER. There are potentially numerous 
“inputs,” but I have chosen just two configurations to present for this chapter. In this 
case, one input involves the concept of the physical body (rūpa), which as we have seen 
may be experienced in tantra as a microcosm—​as an entire “world.” This input also 
involves the male and female, the penis (lingam) and vagina (yoni), as well as the sexual 
fluids (rasa and rati). The second input is that of the concept of the subtle body itself, 
which is experiencing an entire world “as body,” including the inner natures (svarūpa) 
of men as Kṛṣṇa and women as Rādhā, who sport in inner realms of lovely flowers, with 
noisy bumblebees collecting sweet honey (madhu). The cognitive feat of blending uses 
the “vital relations” (see below) of “compressing” together aspects of space, time, iden­
tity, change, and uniqueness to create an entirely new cognitive product: the “blended 
space” or “emergent structure” which is the novel Sahajiyā cosmophysiology. This is the 
blended cosmology of Sahajiyā/​Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava realms (dhāman), the subtle body 
system (dehatattva), and the cosmic substance (vastu)—​all of which practitioners be­
lieve will lead them to liberation in Sahaja.

The Dynamics of “Vital Relations” in 
Conceptual Blending
When we consider the overall forces that propel the dynamics of these cognitive 
processes, Fauconnier and Turner (2002, 101) have identified a number of what they call 
“vital relations.” It is these vital relations that restrict why only some of the details from 
one domain/​input are selectively cross-​mapped to the other domains/​inputs and, hence, 
projected into the eventual blended space. These can include: change, identity, time, 
space, cause-​effect, part-​whole, representation, role, analogy, disanalogy, property, sim­
ilarity, category, intentionality, and uniqueness. Regarding these, they observe:
There are canonical patterns of compression over these vital relations that we will en­
counter again and again. Compression can scale Time, Space, Cause-​Effect, and 
Intentionality. Analogy can be compressed into Identity or Uniqueness. Cause-​Effect can 
be compressed into Part-​Whole. Identity itself is routinely compressed into Uniqueness. 
It is also a fundamental power of the way we think to compress Representation, Part-​
Whole, Cause-​Effect, Category and Role into Uniqueness. (101–​102)
Vital relations help to shape the nuances of our everyday experiences, but they are nei­
ther static nor uniform. Conceptual integration is a dynamic ongoing process that 
compresses and decompresses selected elements, which gives shape to the emergent 
meaning and allows for situational creativity. Compression is the process of combining 
various elements or qualities into one blended space, while decompression is the reverse 
process, selecting out specific elements and then projecting them into another space. 
Certain basic elements of cognitive architecture make blending and compression pos­
sible; for the Sahajiyās, these shape the vivid imaginative realms of Sahajapur, and the 
groves, flowers, and buzzing bees. Conceptualizing these vital relations is instrumental 
to the Sahajiyā ability to experience their human bodies as stepped ponds and villages, 
while they assume identities as characters in the cosmic drama of Rādhā and Kṛṣna, in­
cluding that of the friends of Rādhā, the “maidens” (mañjarī) who assist with her erotic 
trysts in the celestial realms.51 The maidens (mañjarī) and heroines (nāyikā) are female 
beings, seated on the lotuses of the stepped pond, facilitating the journey to the tran­
scendent status of the Sahaja-​mānuṣa, who “resides” beyond the shores of the upper­
most stepped pond, the Pond of Indestructibility (akṣaya-​sarovara). Thus, for Sahajiyās 
the emergent and blended realms of dehatattva, which from the outside of that system 
may seem to be cobbled together from different sources and local imagery, are both co­
herent and profound conceptual integration networks.
Fauconnier and Turner (cited in Lakoff 2008, 53–​54) observe:
Such integration networks are never built entirely on the fly nor are they preexisting 
conventional structures. Integration networks underlying thought and action are

--- PAGE 796 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      771
 
always a mix. On the one hand, cultures build networks over long periods of time 
that get transmitted over generations. Techniques for building particular networks 
are also transmitted. People are capable of innovating in any particular context. The 
result is integration networks consisting of conventional parts, conventionally struc­
tured parts, and novel mappings and compressions.
Sahajiyās have utilized conceptual integration networks from Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, 
Nāth, and various tantric traditions as they expressed their own experiences of 
dehatattva and Sahaja.
Types of Conceptual Integration 
Networks
CBT has identified a number of different types of conceptual integration networks—​
essentially the major configurations of mental spaces, frames, compressions, and 
emergent structure.52 For our purposes, and of greatest usefulness for Tantric Studies, 
we will consider what they call “single-​scope,” “double-​scope,” and “hyperblend/​
megablend” networks. Single-​scope networks are the two-​space models of basic con­
ceptual metaphors in CMT using the TARGET/​SOURCE domains such as SĀDHANA 
IS A JOURNEY, where the organizing frame of just one of the inputs (journey) is cross-​
mapped onto the other (sādhana). This basic metaphor generates source domain 
details, such as stages of practice, necessary companions, pitfalls along the way, im­
portant objects to have, companions on the path, and indices of success, which render 
the abstract nature of sādhana more conceptually concrete. The complex metaphors of 
SAHAJA IS A DESTINATION and KṚṢṆA IS A DIVINE LOVER also adopt powerful 
single-​scope networks, to extrapolate details regarding spatiality and topography onto 
the cosmic state of Sahaja, and anthropomorphic/​sexual/​emotional qualities are cross-​
mapped onto the god Kṛṣna.
The framing inputs of these basic metaphoric networks (e.g. journey, destina­
tion, divine lover) come replete with the practitioner’s cultural inflections, which 
individualizes and complicates the process. Each of the individual blendings often 
expands because several of the inputs may already be blends themselves, what Turner 
calls hyper-​blends (Turner 2014, 145). Reflecting cultural developments and specific 
sociohistorical contexts—​for example, developments in teaching, textual lineages, 
and esoteric language—​ certain advanced blends become entrenched in the cul­
ture of the lineage, always available as a source for new blends as each successive 
guru interprets the sādhana, modifying existing commentaries and composing new 
ones. The power of this cognitive network lies in its ability to evoke “emotions, seem­
ingly anchored in the trustworthy framing input, which feel to us as if they are all-​
clarifying” (Fauconnier and Turner 2002, 129). People can more readily understand

--- PAGE 797 ---
772      Glen A. Hayes
 
the more diffuse concepts of sādhana, Sahaja, or Kṛṣna because they project onto 
them, in the blend, things that are known from the SOURCE domain of framing 
(journey, destination, lovers). Above all, this cross-​mapping of an “inner-​space” re­
lation, “vital relation,” or property in the SOURCE input with the more diffuse or un­
knowable qualities in the TARGET input (sādhana, Sahaja, Kṛṣna) allows metaphors 
to do the cognitive and imaginative “heavy lifting” that they do, ranging from ordi­
nary language (“He tasted the experience.”) to more elaborate metaphors such as THE 
YOGIC BODY IS LIGHT or COSMIC SUBSTANCE IS SEMEN (cf. Fauconnier and 
Turner 2002, 129–​130, fig. 7.3). To Fauconnier and Turner, “this kind of projection is an 
imaginative achievement” (2002, 131).
Such complex forms of conceptual blending are known as “double-​scope” networks 
or “multi-​scope” networks. These have multiple inputs, while hyper-​blends have at 
least one input that is already a blend. According to Fauconnier and Turner, a complex 
blend has two or more or more “inputs with different (and often clashing) organizing 
frames and has emergent structure of its own” (2002, 131). In these networks, there are 
two or more inputs, as well as two or more organizing frames.53 However, only certain 
parts of each frame are “projected” into the blend, leading to a novel emergent struc­
ture or “new stuff.”
At this point, it is important to recognize that a fundamental property of concep­
tual blending, including metaphors, is the ability to render notions of vast cosmic 
dimensions and entities into what Mark Johnson calls “human scale.” This is essential 
for the human experiences of religion, and certainly for tantric beliefs and practices. 
Johnson observes (2014, 180):
The blending hypothesis takes the view that it is our ability for advanced blending 
that gives us the capacity to create vast mental webs with extended vital rela­
tions that are served by, organized by, and held together by blended scenes that 
are themselves at human scale. The scale of the mental web can be vast because 
it is served by a blend that is itself at human scale. The human-​scale blend that 
serves the mental web provides us with a platform—​a scaffold, a cognitively con­
genial basis from which to reach out, manage, manipulate, transform, develop, 
and handle the mental web.
As we have seen, the AR provides many examples of “blended scenes” such as the Ponds, 
Sahajapur, and the celestial realms of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. Sahajiyā sādhana and dehatattva 
may thus be regarded, using Johnson’s terms, as cognitive platforms with scaffolding 
that allow the practitioner “to reach out, manage, manipulate, transform, develop, and 
handle the mental web” (ibid.).
We have considered how Sahajiyās appropriated and adapted the models and 
processes from Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava bhakti for specifically tantric uses. Such adaptations 
and modifications may be found in numerous tantric lineages and textual traditions, be­
cause the conceptual blending that underlies all of these beliefs and practices may itself 
be recursive: the blended cognitive products of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, for example, are

--- PAGE 798 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      773
 
used by Sahajiyās as inputs for their own blending processes. Johnson offers additional 
insights as to how this fascinating process can occur (2014, 180):
It is of utmost importance that once we have achieved a human-​scale blend, it can 
be used as an input mental space to a new blending web. So blending can work like a 
cascade. Achieving a blend at human scale extends our human-​scale knowledge. It’s 
as if we manufacture a stepping stone, place it ahead of us, and then step from where 
we are to that new stepping stone. And we can repeat the procedure, stepping from 
blend to blend. So what counts as human scale can be repeatedly extended, on and 
on. This can give us a cascade or sequence of blends, each depending upon previous 
blends. . . . What was once beyond human scale is now transformed to human scale.
The four ponds of the AR are very much like the “stepping stones” feature described by 
Johnson, as the path of sādhana leads from one Pond to the next, and also the vastness 
of the celestial realms. The hierarchical containers of embodiment, connected by the 
conduits and generated out of vastu, provided Sahajiyās with access to many things pre­
viously beyond “human scale.” In the concluding section, we will consider how the AR 
expresses cascades of blending that bring together the different traditions of bhakti and 
tantra, and how this is accomplished.
Tantra and Bhakti as Cognitive 
Frames for Conceptual Blending
The concept and process of “framing” has been instrumental in the development of cog­
nitive linguistics as an academic discipline. The role of framing is also fundamental to 
language in general, and is essential to the formation of metaphors, conceptual blending, 
and conceptual integration networks. There must be some type of order amidst the soci­
ological, linguistic, biological, and cognitive registers of lived human life. The primary 
metaphor of the body as container is central to the conceptual blending of dehatattva 
in Sahajiyā texts. In brief, this “container” provides the basic “framing” of the “generic 
space” of virtually all metaphors and blends involving embodiment (See fig. 30.2). This 
same approach will also enable us to better understand the blending of the two major 
“inputs” of tantra and bhakti in Sahajiyā texts.
One major problem in the academic study of the Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās is the fact that 
they combine influences from both monistic tantra and largely dualistic bhakti.54 
Their blending of tantra and bhakti is what distinguishes them from most other tantric 
traditions, to the best of my knowledge.55 Thus, as shown in figure 30.3, there are two 
major input spaces: tantra and bhakti. The input from tantra provides the framing of 
the “body as a world,” while the bhakti input contributes “a body in a world” (such as a 
maiden in Vraja or Vṛndāvana). When reading Sahajiyā texts like the AR, one is struck 
by the apparent conflicts between descriptions of the subtle body that reveal a basic

--- PAGE 799 ---
774      Glen A. Hayes
 
tantric structure, such as the ascending series of stepped ponds, and then, a few verses 
later, a structure that is based upon Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava descriptions of the milkmaids 
(gopīs), dancing and beholding the love play of Rādhā with Kṛṣna in the forests—​
reflecting orthodox Vaiṣṇava mañjarī-​sādhana (“maiden practice,” more on this below). 
Instead, if one considers an earlier or later section of perhaps five to ten verses, one can 
discern a deeper metaphorical (not literal) consistency in the way the descriptions are 
progressing. For example, the following verses simultaneously describe ascent into the 
third stepped pond, ritual intercourse, the cosmic substance (vastu), controlling passion 
(rāga) and desire (rati—​as both a female partner and fluid), while also mentioning that 
the pond is where Kṛṣna lives. It blends tantric physiology (body as world) with a devo­
tional view (body in a world) of Kṛṣna (AR, vv. 253–​259):56
253	 That Pond (sarovara) of Divine Love (prema) is limned (khacita)57 with passion 
(rāga).
	
It is the churning of that passion (rāga) that filled the lake with Divine
	
Love.
254	 By adolescence, a girl has transformed into that very ocean of Divine Love,
	
and instinctively knows how Divine Love generates the taste of
	
Kṛṣṇa rasa, that enduring Cosmic Substance (nityavastu).
255	 Rādhikā is the guru of Passion (rāga), which in turn makes her the guru
	
of Divine Love.
	
From the sound of the “r”-​consonant [of Rādhikā] the author writes rati,
	
love’s liquid partner.
256	 That act of churning the liquid love partner (rati), generates the
	
experience of rasa.
	
When she is immersed in that liquid experience of rasa, she is
	
transformed into the image of beauty itself, Rūpavatī by name.

Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      775
 
257	 Kṛṣṇa resides in every single drop of the Divine Love of that pond
	
(sarovara).
	
Kṛṣṇa’s liquid partner (rati) is the feminine (prakṛti) form of the love
	
experience (rasa).58
258	 He churns the partner of love (rati), whose churning generates the refined
	
essence (sāra) of liquid love (rati).
	
Following Passion (anurāga) night and day amazingly relieves grief,
	
vexation, and distress.
259	 Kṛṣṇa is the crown jewel of those connoisseurs of love’s pleasures (rasika)
	
who follow this Passion (anurāga).
	
and, as a result, Kṛṣṇa has remained in debt to the Divine Love of Rādhā.
The two different, yet somehow complementary, structures of bhakti and tantra are thus 
resolved through conceptual blending in verse 257, as cascades of blending are brought to­
gether. The Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā of the bhakti input shift into the male essence (puruṣa) and 
female essence (prakṛti) used by tantra.59 The practitioner initially uses the bhakti imagery 
of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā as a tool, but after Sahajiyā sādhana, the final experience of the reality 
of Sahaja takes place within the body. Conceptual blending aids in the transition from 
the goals of bhakti (e.g., being a maiden in Vraja, a body in a world) to the goals of tantra 
(e.g., entering the devadeha, the body is a world). The external world of rivers and ponds is 
homologized with the interior landscape, and the journey is realized using bhakti and its 
metaphors—​ not by going “somewhere else” like nitya-​Vṛndāvana, but through realizing 
the tantric model of internal consummation and the final unity of the “together-​born” 
state of Sahaja. Human scale is achieved. Spatially, and structurally, the bhakti realms of 
Kṛṣna become connected along paths to the stepped ponds of tantra, and the inner maiden 
(mañjarī) becomes a powerful type of female ritual partner (nāyikā). The rasa to be expe­
rienced as “liquid love” (rati) is connected to the bliss (ānanda) and semen (śukra) of the 
tantric input. The emergent structure of the Sahajiyā dehatattva effectively organizes the 
different frames and details by blending the inputs of both tantra and bhakti. This emer­
gent structure is integrated, combines topology, and is coherent. This occurs due to the 
cross-​mappings and complex projections of the vital relations across the inputs and into 
the blend. There is a compression of identity, uniqueness, and analogy across the two inputs 
into the blend, as vast mental webs are given human scale. There is thus a blending of ap­
parent cosmological, epistemological, and soteriological differences between the basic tan­
tric structure of “the body is a world” and the more dualistic bhakti structure of “the body 
is in a world.”60 That latter world is dominated by the figures of Kṛṣna, Rādhā, the gopīs and 
mañjarīs. We can see these kinds of differences in the following verses (AR, vv. 25–​29):61
25	 At the time one receives the mantra, one also gains the lineage of the guru.
	
You must [however] perform your sādhana according to the instructions of the
	
teaching master (sikṣāguru).
26	 The qualified one (adhikārī) will acquire the finest available body through 
sādhana.
	
Even older men and women can learn the principles of sheltering in love (bhāva).

--- PAGE 801 ---
776      Glen A. Hayes
 
27	 The divine body (devadeha) must be born within the [physical] body.
	
Through what kinds of practices may men and women learn these principles 
of love?
28	 Within the [physical] body there is a divine body (deva-​deha).
	
By [following] the teachings, the principles of the Cosmic Substance (vastu) 
may be learned.
29	 The woman of practice (sādhana prakṛti) will appear within the [physical] body.
	
When one’s inner nature becomes [additionally] that of a woman, then the 
experience of
	
rāga-​rati ensues.
The many meanings of the “woman of practice” reveal these differences (yet now 
connections) between tantra and bhakti. She can be the female ritual partner, a source 
of sexual fluids used to generate the system of ponds, part of the metaphoric struc­
ture of the body as a world. But, as she also appears within the body, she is the inner 
mañjarī, and thus a body in a devotional world. Using the vital relations, the tantric 
and bhakti inputs are cross-​mapped and projected into the emergent structure as a 
coherent blend.
In many tantric traditions, the human body is not just a world unto itself but usefully 
regarded as a mesocosm (an intermediate framing device) providing access to the infi­
nite microcosms within the body, as well as to the vast regions of the outer macrocosm 
of the sun, moon, planets, and stars. Again, blending based on the “body” allows for 
the transformation of vast cosmic dimensions into human scale. This is a quite partic­
ular form of layered cosmological structure, with consequences for epistemology (that 
knowing the body leads to transcendence), as well as soteriology (Sahaja is achieved only 
through mastery of the body). However, in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional practices 
of vaidhi bhakti (external actions such as singing and dancing) and rāgānugā bhakti 
sādhana (“passionate” interiorized visualization), the goal is to ritually fashion the spir­
itual body of a “maiden” (mañjarī), made out of a “particle of light” (jyotir-​aṃśa).62 As 
discussed in detail by Haberman (1988) and Stewart (2010), mañjarī-​sādhana is an elab­
orate Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava process of visualizing oneself as a particular gopī or attendant 
involved in specific romantic interactions between Rādhā and Kṛṣna in the Vraja-​līlā. 
As developed by the intellectual and devotional leaders (Gosvāmin) of Bengal, this 
requires “her” to have a name, an outfit, a family history, and so forth.63 Far from re­
garding the body as a world in the tantric sense, the Gauḍīya view is that the ideal body 
of the mañjarī exists in the eternal realms of Kṛṣna-​līlā, and is just one of many beings in 
that realm. This is a very different cosmology, for which the epistemology requires many 
distinctive procedures, and the soteriology is very much driven by the salvific powers 
of the Divine Love (prema) Kṛṣna and Rādhā feel for each other, and for the mañjarī. 
As suggested in figure 30.3, only in the “blended space” of the “emergent structure” of 
the Sahajiyā dehatattva are these two seemingly incompatible systems brought together, 
using vital relations such as identity, role, representation, and analogy.
From the tantric input we get the system of the ascending stepped ponds (sarovara), 
the crooked river (bāṅkānadī), and the “reversed” (ulṭā) upward flow of the sexual

--- PAGE 802 ---
Exploring Metaphors and Conceptual Blending      777
 
fluids. From the bhakti input we get the visualized narratives of Kṛṣna and the gopīs, 
in the villages of Vraja, and out in the forests, with bees flitting among the flowers.64 
In these devotional realms, the flow is of the pure emotional divine love of prema, not 
bodily fluids. So how are these two inputs projected into the blended spaces, and how 
are these differences conceptually “resolved”? One way is to structurally, almost archi­
tecturally, reformat the spatial dimensions to blend together the tantric ponds and the 
bhakti villages. This would involve horizontal extensions from the ponds (containers) 
along paths (conduits) to Sahajiyā realms such as the Place of the Hidden Moon 
(guptacandrapur) and Sahajapur (containers and destinations). Another way, using the 
vital relations (such as role, representation, similarity, and analogy) in the process, is to 
connect—​via cross-​mapping—​the relationship between the physical body (rūpa) in the 
tantric model with the “inner essence” (svarūpa) in the bhakti model. As we consider 
the different details, such as the poetic Vaiṣṇava imagery, the transgressive Nāth reversal 
concepts, or the Bengali views of rivers and ponds, we can coax out the “vital relations” 
that are in play as these blends are created. And, as we have seen, using metaphor theory 
and conceptual blending can help us as scholars to conceptualize how Sahajiyās and 
other tantric practitioners use such vivid imagery to guide their sādhanas.
Concluding Thoughts
I trust that I have been able to suggest how using the methods of CMT and CBT can 
help in the translation and understanding of the complex sādhanas and dehatattva in 
the Amṛtaratnāvalī and, by extension, in many other tantric texts. Metaphors are not 
just lovely poetic devices; they express fundamental and profound cognitive processes 
that are essential aspects of being human. We envision and imagine ourselves and the 
world partly through the power of metaphors, and we experience the limitless varieties 
of consciousness thanks, at least in part, to the dynamics of conceptual blending. For 
scholars of tantric studies, using CMT and CBT can be challenging, especially when 
crafting the visual blending charts as I have provided in figures 30.1–​3. But, just as Lakoff 
and Johnson’s wonderful approach to metaphors opens up the richness and depth of 
even ordinary language, the fascinating layers and matrices of specifically tantric lan­
guage can be gradually revealed using methods from the conceptual blending theory of 
Fauconnier and Turner. Tantric language wonderfully illustrates the dynamic cascades 
and complexities of conceptual blending, allowing for the achievement of cosmic 
dimensions at a human scale. What I have offered in this chapter is but an initial and 
early step in this methodological adventure. To cite a trope from Zen Buddhism, this 
is an adventure where one always feels like a beginner. Given the accelerating pace of 
discoveries in cognitive science and neuroscience, especially how improvements in 
neural imaging are revealing how our perception, imagination, and process of construal 
work, we are sure to enjoy many new findings in the coming years. This chapter has 
considered how Sahajiyā sādhana is a journey; it is abundantly clear that Tantric Studies

--- PAGE 803 ---
778      Glen A. Hayes
 
itself will also continue to be a journey as well. This volume demonstrates that many 
of us, in our own ways, and in our own fields and areas of study, are fellow travelers in 
this exciting and rewarding academic pursuit. Solid steps have been taken, yet there are 
many more to go.
