goddess in all beings), celebrating the goddess that resides (saṃsthitā) in all beings, 
offering her praise rendered in the feminine dative case (namastasyai). How would 
the Jain goddess, who does nothing more than lift and support, align with the fero­
cious goddess who slays with many weapons? Would this be an instance of conver­
sion as described by Dhaky and Meister (1991; Meister 1998) in regard to the narrative 
regarding the shift of worship at the Osiāñ temple in Rajasthan? This story describes 
the change in veneration of the fierce, flesh-​eating Durgā Cāmuṇḍā Devῑ to the gentle 
“personal goddess (śāsanadevῑ)” Saciyāmātā of the Osvāl Jain community, a goddess 
who receives only “cakes, sweets, camphor, saffron, and other nice things” (Hoernle as 
quoted in Meister 1998, 129). To clarify, Meister stated that “Saciyāmātā . . . has in rela­
tively recent times, changed from being a local personal goddess (śāsanadevī). . . into 
the kul devī [origination goddess] for . . . communities of . . . Jains” (Meister 1998, 133).
In the Jain pantheon, Padmāvatῑ, as an attendant of the Tirthankara Parśvanath, is 
considered a yakṣῑ, a goddess of the earthly realm accessible to human beings (Cort 
1987, 236). She is associated with many families in Karnataka, as well as the South Indian 
pilgrimage site of Śravanabelgola (Yocum 1997; Rao 2020). The Digamabara monk 
Malliṣena wrote a text about her, the Bhairava Padmāvatῑ Kalpa (Manuals of Rituals to 
the Fierce Padmāvatῑ) in Karnataka in 1057 CE, which includes instructions on how to 
gain power over others through pacification, subjugation, immobilization, sowing con­
flict, displacement, or seduction (Cort 1987, 245). None of those qualities seem to be in­
cluded in the text under consideration here.
The 108-​verse praise text to Padmāvatῑ repeats four primary mantras at the start of 
each line (oṃ, āṃ, kroṃ, hrῑṃ), as well as the laudatory syllable śrī in the middle and the 
praise word namaḥ at the end. Dundas described a link between the first syllables of the 
namo kara mantra a/​arhat, si/​siddha, ā/​ācārya, u/​upādhyāya, sa/​sādhu and the process 
of “placing” those initial syllables on one’s own body and the body represented in the 
Jina image (Dundas 1998, 35; see also Gough, this volume and Williams, this volume). In 
other words, one repeats the mantra, touching one’s own body and then the image of the 
Jina as described in the Yogaśāstra of Hemacandra:
One should meditate on the syllable a [from the mantra, a-​si-​ā-​u-​sā], located in 
the lotus of the navel, syllable si in the lotus of the head, the syllable ā in the lotus of 
the mouth, the syllable u in the lotus of the heart, [and] the syllable sā in the lotus 
of the throat.
(Yogaśāstra VIII:76–​76; Quarnström 2002, 163)
Cort noted in his study and translation of Ghaṇṭākarṇa Mantra Stotra that Jain 
mantras allow one to gain powers such as “cures for disease and increasing worldly 
wealth,” and that “Jainism is as much about how to live successfully in the world as 
it is about ascetic practices to liberate oneself from the world” (Cort 2000, 418). The 
Padmāvatῑ text combines repeated bῑja mantras with qualities of the goddess that 
laud both her devotional and worldly accomplishments. Padmāvatῑ displays the

--- PAGE 850 ---
Jain Tantra      825
 
powerful qualities associated with the many Hindu goddesses who are called out in 
the hymn and is praised as adept in the particulars of the process of Jain purifica­
tion. Hence, it can be seen that this 108-​line verse speaks to the ways of the world and 
the path out of the world. In the analysis that follows, three threads of meaning are 
traced: aspects of the text that allude to the more tantric aspects of goddess worship; 
passages that tie Padmāvatῑ to the mainstream worship of the devī; and decidedly 
Jain references.
Perhaps the most obvious tantric signal can be found at the beginning of each line, 
which begins with the recitation of seed syllables oṃ, āṃ, kroṃ, hrῑṃ, and, at the end 
of each line, the word of praise, namaḥ. Unlike the traditional Devῑ Mantra, the final 
word appears as a simple utterance declined in nominative singular rather than in 
the feminine dative as in namastasyai. However, each word before the final namaḥ 
carries the dative marker, whether –​yai or –​ye. One sequence of three lines states: 
“You are Totilā, the eternal, the goddess of the three cities” (Rāj Rājeśvarῑ Māteśvarῑ 
Māṃ Padme RRMMP108, v. 12–​14). The phrase “three cities” carries several possible 
meanings, including the invocation of the realms of earth, atmosphere, and sky (Bhūr, 
Bhuvaḥ, Sva) and the three major subtle breath channels (Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suśumnā), 
as well as the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) and the three moments of time (past, 
present, and future). It is also a possible allusion to the “three cities” tradition of the 
Tripurā Upanisad (see Brooks 1990, 12). Another sequence calls out Padmāvatῑ as a 
“Yoginῑ, a knower of Yoga, not broken by poverty or death, holding an endowment of 
patience (v. 69–​72).
Mainstream worship of the goddess can be seen in the opening six lines that praise 
Padmāvatῑ as beautiful, powerfully strong, and learned. Several verses invoke other 
forms of the goddess, such as Lakṣmῑ, Sarasvati, Durgā, the wives of Śiva, Kālῑ, and the 
river Ganges (v. 18–​20, 24, 45, 48, 50, 87–​90) and ferocious and benign qualities asso­
ciated with Hindu goddesses such as “holder of the magical noose” and “giver of the 
breast” and “wish-​fulfilling cow” (v. 77, 78, 98). Additionally, several universal qual­
ities are listed that pertain to any goddess: “accomplished in desire, knowledgeable, 
giving, the embodiment of perfection, the essence of spring, fearless, warding off sin, 
garlanded, tender, free from constraints, profound, and fascinating” (v. 15, 17, 31, 40, 
47, 74, 75, 96, 105, 106).
The Jain aspects of Padmāvatῑ permeate at least 22 of the 108 lines. The first section 
of five lines announces unambiguously, “You are devoted to the Jina Dharma” (v. 7), 
followed with a trope of four sets of five, starting with the category of five in general, 
associated with five aspects of Brahma (pañca-​brahma-​pada-​ārādhyāya) followed with 
three standard tropes of Jain faith and practice:
  9.  You teach the fivefold (namo kara) mantra
10.  and are endowed with the qualities that arise from practicing the five vows.
11.  You see the five beautiful events (when the future Jina enters the womb, is born, 
renounces the world, gains all knowledge, and eventually leaves the body).

--- PAGE 851 ---
826      Christopher key Chapple
 
The namo kara mantra, delineated above, shows respect and praise for the liberated 
teachers, the liberated saints, the religious leaders, the teachers, and the practitioners: 
arhats, siddhas, ācāryas, upādhyāyas, sādhus. The five Jain vows are nonviolence, 
truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and nonpossession: ahiṃsā, satya, asteya, 
brahmacarya, and aparigraha. The five beautiful events are important memory con­
nection points for observant Jains and in some ways resemble the remembrance of the 
birth of any religious leader, the moment of liberation, the commitment to help others, 
and the eventual death. Though all follow the same general pattern, details are given 
for each of the twenty-​four Tῑrthankaras, though the stories of Ādinath (1), Neminath 
(22), Parśvanath (23), and Mahāvῑra (24) are perhaps the best known and most often 
represented in works of art and literature.
The physical description of Padmāvatῑ can be found in several of the lines. She is 
crowned with a serpent’s hood (v. 26), she wears a tiara that shimmers (v. 27), and she 
rides a magical bird-​like snake, the kukkuṭaroga (v. 29). Repeatedly, she is associated 
with the eponymous padma or lotus (v. 30, 60–​62, 88). Her role of wife is mentioned re­
peatedly (v. 33, 45, 87) and in the first instance in her role as companion and queen with 
King Dharṇendra. She is described as a snake (v. 34, 35) and as dwelling in the serpent 
realm (v. 59).
Padmāvatῑ also keeps august company. Repeatedly the text associates her with the 
Arhats, the liberated teachers, and the wise persons who affiliate with one another as 
spiritual exemplars. The text proclaims: “You abide with the wisdom of the assembled 
Arhats” (v. 21). Another term that is somewhat particular to the Jains is gaṇa, which in 
a sweeping way evokes the abundance of Jina images generally found in contexts where 
it can be translated as “flock.” In this text, gaṇa has been rendered as assembly, giving 
the sense that the like-​minded souls who desire liberation form a sort of club, and that 
the Siddha Loka includes those who have succeeded in attaining the highest goal. By 
placing Padmāvatῑ in their midst, she may be seen as a mediator and, in a sense, as an 
organizing mother figure:
57.   You are part of the assembly [of sages].
58.   You are the governess of the assembled Arhats.
Two additional lines quietly affirm her ability to form a bridge between the realm of 
sorrow and that of freedom:
102.   You watch over the true dharma.
103.   You pacify all sin.
Padmāvatῑ brings purity and safety.
Perhaps drawing a link between Padmāvatῑ and the scholarly qualities of Sarasvati, 
she is said to be the “teacher of all scriptures” (v. 22), and to know all twelve books of 
Jain scripture (v. 37). Additionally, she represents spiritual attainment as outlined in the

--- PAGE 852 ---
Jain Tantra      827
 
Tattvārthasūtra, knowing the fourteen forms of ascent or guṇasthānas that culminate in 
total liberation (v. 38). The text also refers to the ladder used to make this ascent from the 
morass of karmas to the state of liberation:
79.	 You gather the fruit of the ladder leading to karma’s thinning.
Also, from the opening verse of this foundational text, she embodies the three jewels at 
the heart of Jain faith and practice:
52.	 You possess the purity of right view.
53.	 You are the epitome of right knowledge.
54.	 You are endowed with right action.
Through meditating on her form, the devotee places herself or himself squarely within 
the ambiance of the spiritual path, in a sense visiting “all pilgrimage places” (v. 73).
A quietly evocative string of verses emphasizes the significance of Padmāvatῑ’s hands:
80.	 You have hands.
81.	 You have auspicious wisdom.
82.	 You are noble.
83.	 You hold all in your hands,
84.	 hands that bring
85.	 [the gifts of] the goddess of spring.
The gentle, almost haunting repeat of the word hand (hasta) betokens the power of the 
hand to give and to receive, to bless and to offer.
A similarly delicate triplet of lines links the Jain teaching of nonabsolutism (anekānta) 
with contemplative practice (cintitā) leading to the jewel-​like state associated with states 
of absorption or samādhi:
91.	 You know the essence of Self from multiple perspectives.
92.	 You bring the fruit of meaningful contemplation.
93.	 You are the jewel of consciousness.
The text comes to a close with praise of Padmāvatῑ’s qualities as “profound, fasci­
nating, and accomplished,” culminating in a description of her as a medicinal tree, 
Vitex Negundo, whose flowers quell passion and glow with the color purple. Padmāvatῑ 
carries many attributes, including being a snake, the wish-​fulfilling cow, a great teacher, 
a forest goddess, and a healing tree.
In summary, this 108-​line text includes praise of Padmāvatῑ’s qualities, comparing her 
with well-​known Hindu goddesses and their qualities. It also gives summaries of key 
points of Jain philosophy and suggests that by directing one’s devotion to Padmāvatῑ, 
one will gain the benefits that she symbolizes.

Śrῑ Lalitā’s 108 Names
In their comprehensive study of the Śrῑ Lalitā Triśatῑ Bhāṣyam attributed to Ādi 
Śaṅkarācārya, Sunanda and Yajneshwar Shastri include a 108-​verse text in praise of Śrῑ 
Lalitā (Shastri 433–​435). As with the Padmāvatῑ text translated above, each verse begins 
with a mantra (in this case the single syllable oṃ), includes a description of the goddess 
in the feminine dative (indicating that the words are devoted and offered to Lalitā), and 
ends with the word namaḥ, indicating obeisance.
This particular text is wedded closely to Sāṃkhya philosophy, beginning with the 
gross manifestations and ascending from the material to the mental, and from the 
mental to the spiritual, and eventually to the transcendent. Specifically, the first six 
lines address the earth. The seventh line gives praise to the goddess in the form of water, 
followed with praise to fire (v. 8), wind and its qualities (v. 11–​13), light and space. At line 
17, it turns its attention to bodily capacities that receive the elements, starting with smell 
(v. 18–​19), taste (v. 20–​22), seeing (v. 23–​25), touching (v. 27–​28), and landing on hearing, 
sound, and speech (v. 29–​33). The hands are honored as the locus of action (34–​35), as 
are the functions of walking and digestion (v. 37–​38). Through mind, thought, and in­
tention, one obtains all things (v. 42–​44), depending on the disposition of the buddhi 
(intellect) (v. 45) and its expression through the ego (ahaṃkāra v. 46–​47). Everything 
becomes known to consciousness (v. 48–​49) and depends on the guṇas (v. 50–​51). The 
text mentions the subtle elements, the nature of bondage, and Prakṛti as holding the 
power of time and the form of time (v. 56–​58). It invokes the practice of yantra and 
mantra and states that Lalitā takes the forms of Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, the Great Lord, 
the eternal (Sadā) Śiva, eternal life, Śiva, Lakṣmῑ, and all time (v. 61–​70). She contains 
the gross body and the subtle body (v. 73–​74), all that is spoken and can be spoken; all 
that is known and can be known; all that is done and what can be done (v. 75–​77). She 
is the goddess of all truth, the ten sounds, the myriad rivers of energy (nāḍῑs), as well as 
silence (v. 78–​81). She suffuses the knowledge of the Vedas, the Sūtras, the Śāstras, Ayur 
Veda, the Artha Śāstra, the sixty-​four Arts, the Āgamas, and poetry (v. 82–​92). The god­
dess contains the meaning of all that can be spoken (v. 94–​96), and she is of the nature 
of knowledge and all that can be done (v. 97). She has a great heart (v. 102) and can be 
found in light and in darkness (v. 104–​105). She knows the difference between truth and 
untruth (v. 108).
This 108-​verse text serves as a compendium of philosophy and theology, naming the 
creative categories that comprise worldly experience, linking them through the god­
dess Lalitā to an entire pantheon of gods. Like the Padmāvatī text, it combines praise 
and information. Whereas the Padmāvatῑ text intersperses philosophical content in 
clusters interrupted by panegyric, the Lalitā text moves progressively along the archi­
tecture of Sāṃkhya and Vedānta, moving from the gross elements to the senses, from 
the senses to the mind, from the mind to consciousness, and from consciousness to 
manifestations of the divine. The Padmāvatῑ text clusters verses 7–​11, 26–​30, 31–​38, and

--- PAGE 854 ---
Jain Tantra      829
 
52–​59 and individual verses (73, 79, 91) to convey the uniquely Jain aspects of its mes­
sage. Otherwise, the focus remains on the majesty of Padmāvatῑ somewhat without reli­
gious or philosophical specificity.
Sāṃkhya philosophy and Yoga practice hinge on the reciprocal relationship between 
a witnessing awareness (puruṣa) and the creative realm (prakṛti). The mandala provides 
a cosmic map, a yantra that shows the universe emanating from its center or bindu. The 
recitation of mantra brings one into the center point of clear awareness, while elevating 
the movement that radiates around the center. In the case of Padmāvatī, she is at the 
center of an entourage of saints (21) and the “totality of knowledge” (39). In the case of 
Lalitā, her presence evokes all the creative aspects of the body and the external and heav­
enly realms. As described by Vijaya Nararajan, at its core the drawing of rice powder 
yantras known as kolam each morning reminds the artist and the community of this 
relationship between the world of movement and the still center (Nagarajan 2019, 157).
Reflections of Orality, Musicality, 
and Ritual Engagement in Jain Tantra
The texts composed in honor of Padmāvatī and Lalitā were designed to be sung, and 
most likely were composed at least in part proclaiming their qualities out loud. Kofi 
Awoonar, a scholar of oral literature, has written:
In discussing oral literature . . . it must be understood that we are discussing a large 
body of material which can have its total integrity, impact, and realisation only 
with the scope of performance, transmission, and occasion. The performer of oral 
literature gives body to the material, formulates, it, and realises it, within regulated 
and specified occasions. . . . The chant’s basic poetic qualities include repetition 
of lines, digression, word-​picture painting—​use of ideophones and parallelism—​
comparison, simile, metaphor, metonymy, allusions, and epigrams.
(Awoonar 1975, 80)
In this regard, it is important to bear in mind that the two texts we have considered are 
liturgical texts. They are not designed to be read silently but are designed to be chanted 
out loud and to be heard. They exhibit many of the qualities highlighted by Awoonar in 
regard to oral literature. (On the oral dimensions of tantra, see Lorea, this volume) The 
mantras repeat at the beginning. Each line ends with the word namaḥ. Both serve as 
performative book markers announcing the start and the end.
Digression seems to be an important part of the Padmāvatῑ and Lalitā texts. A theme 
mentioned once might be taken up in more detail further in the text. In the case of the 
Padmāvatῑ text, it serves the function of creating a mood of awe by listing various qual­
ities as well, reminding those receiving the text that she exemplifies the ideals of Jain

--- PAGE 855 ---
830      Christopher key Chapple
 
theology. On the one hand, she is linked with universal powers of speech and culture 
and beauty. On the other hand, she communicates very specific Jain teachings. The 
economy of language uses key phrases to remind the listener of her broader narrative 
without filling in the details. The genre of the 108-​text form is to hit points of memory 
and emotionality within a compact space, allowing the allusions to do their magic.
D’Aquili and Newberg (1999) have written that ritual prompts an affective experi­
ence in the participant (89) and that rhythm can be an important contributor to a ritual 
moment:
In the special case of prolong rhythmic stimuli, it appears that the simultaneous 
strong discharge of both parts of the autonomic nervous system creates a state that 
consists not only of a pleasurable sensation but, also, under proper conditions, a 
sense of union with conspecifics and a blurring of cognitive boundaries.
(D’Aquili and Newberg 1999, 90)
Whitney Kelting, in regard to the Jain musical tradition known as stavan, has noted that 
“repetition . . . has the effect of making the stavan . . . chant-​like and hypnotic” (Kelting 
2001, 91). The repetition of the mantras and the syllable namaḥ creates a mood that lends 
itself to religious experiences.
Without doubt, these hymns to Padmāvatῑ and Lalitā, carry an innate musicality. 
Each in their own way carry what might be described as a “recurring pattern of beats,” 
not in a fixed-​line structure, but through the device of an announced beginning and 
end. This suggests a notion of repeated return as defined by Martin Clayton as “cyclicity 
. . . a reconciliation between linear progression and recurrence” (2000, 21). Just as music 
can lead to an experience beyond space and time, so also praise chants, particularly in 
the rarefied atmosphere of a temple and the presence of a visual image to reinforce the 
content, can bring about a state of absorption and enthusiasm, perhaps leading even to 
bliss. Taking darśan of a god, goddess, or guru can engage multiple senses. These praise 
chants demonstrate the power of transformation through the word, music, singing, 
hearing, seeing, smelling, and even tasting. Music, orality, and aurality all play a central 
role in the building of tantra.
Conclusion
Much research needs to be undertaken to more fully understand the many intersections 
between Jain meditation and ritual and tantra. This chapter began with an explication 
of core Jain teachings and the centrality of nonviolence. This strongly held position 
made the Jain an unlikely dialogue partner with tantra, particularly due to tantra’s vi­
olative practices of eating meat and fish, ingesting intoxicants, and engaging in illicit 
sex. Jain thinkers condemned goddess worship and the overall practices of tantra, par­
ticularly Haribhadra Yakini Putra in his Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya (ninth century CE) and

--- PAGE 856 ---
Jain Tantra      831
 
Somadeva in the Yaśatilakā (959 CE). However, tantra could not be ignored. Even the 
Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya makes some concessions, acknowledging the desire of the tantrikas 
to become free and inviting a thought experiment that encourages conceptualizing the 
Jain path to liberation (mokṣa-​mārga) in light of an eightfold goddess journey. In the 
next two centuries, Śubhacandra and Hemacandra fully adapt Śaiva tantra meditation 
techniques, rendering them not only Jain friendly but also, in many ways, Jain essential. 
Jain practice includes syllabic recitation and visualization and, as can be seen in Gough’s 
analysis (2012), representation with temple adornments. The chapter concludes with an 
example of how contemporary worship of Padmāvatī exemplifies Jain tantra.

Chapter 33
Tibetan Tantric 
Buddhist Literature
Paul Hackett
Tantra in Tibet
Since the time of its popular exposure to the English-​speaking world, Tibetan 
Buddhism has mistakenly been taken to be synonymous with tantric Buddhism.1 The 
introduction and growth of the literature in Tibet that promoted that general idea arose 
in several stages over the history of the country of Tibet, from populist social events to 
translation activities and finally to assimilation and localization.
The origins of Buddhist tantra remain shrouded in speculative histories of inter­
religious growth in the early first millennium in India. Numerous scholars have 
identified “proto-​tantric” themes, practices, and imagery in literature and archeological 
sites datable to as early as the fifth century ce.2 Traditional Buddhist historians point to 
the fourth century ce as the advent of tantric Buddhist teachings entering the human 
realm, and assert that those teachings were then propagated in secrecy for roughly three 
hundred years. In terms of extant literature by datable authors, however, it is difficult to 
identify any properly tantric compositions3 prior to the eighth century ce.4 Nonetheless, 
tantric Buddhist imagery can be definitively dated to the early seventh century, when 
a statue of the Buddha Akṣobhyavajra accompanied the Nepalese princess Bhṛkūṭi to 
Tibet for her marriage to the Tibetan emperor Trisong Detsen, whose father unified the 
Tibetan plateau in the early 600s (Beckwith 1987).
It was not until the late eighth century ce, that the Tibetan imperial government 
began a campaign of active patronage of Buddhist figures from then-​contemporary 
India and Nepal, including the sponsorship of textual translation and temple construc­
tion. This period of activity in Tibet corresponded with the semipublic production and 
dissemination of Buddhist tantric literature in the Indian subcontinent. Consequently, 
in addition to discourses attributed to the Buddha Śākyamuni and major philosoph­
ical treatises of the day, core texts of tantric literature also made their way into Tibet

--- PAGE 865 ---
840      Paul Hackett
 
where they were translated, and which, as a result, had a profound effect on the nascent 
Buddhist culture there.
Early Tibetan historical documents, such as the Testament of Ba (Wangdu and 
Diemberger 2000) and others, recount that the populace attributed the arrival of 
Buddhist monks from India and Nepal with precipitating the anger of local spirits which 
manifested as environmental disasters such as hail storms, earthquakes, and the like. 
Consequently, part of the initial appeal of tantric Buddhism in Tibet—​certainly with the 
country’s rulers—​lay with the utility of the mundane magical powers (siddhis) attributed 
to Buddhist monks in direct connection to the need to control environmental disasters 
such flooding, hail, and so on, which were a common occurrence on the Tibetan pla­
teau, and which, in general, were typically attributed to unruly local spirits. In this re­
gard, the eighth century yogi Padmasambhava played a central role in the propagation 
of Buddhism in Tibet, having been regarded by later generations as having subdued the 
local spirits. Some (e.g., Sorensen 2003) have argued that his acts of spirit subjugation 
may have also included instituting water management practices to limit the damage 
produced by annual flooding.
In addition, it should be noted that one of the identified (Thurman, 1997) features of 
Tibetan culture during this time that contributed to the receptiveness of Tibetan so­
ciety to Buddhism was an attitude of cultural self-​deprecation coupled with a valoriza­
tion of the cultural output of India—​exemplified by the identification of India as “the 
land of the Āryas” as it was referred to in Tibet—​as being the products of a higher civ­
ilization. Having already derived their written language from an Indian script, early 
Buddhist proponents in Tibet began an active campaign of formulating a mythology 
that interwove the royal family of first-​millennium imperial Tibet with figures in the 
tantric Buddhist pantheon and recast Tibet from being a remote and barren moun­
tainous region into a Buddhist safe haven intentionally protected and curated by en­
lightened beings for that specific purpose. It was a narrative that appears to have been 
firmly established as early as the ninth century CE, as described in documents such as 
The Red Annals (Tucci 1971) by Paṇchen Sonam Drakpa (bsod nams grags pa, 1478–​1554) 
and others.
The Early History
It is clear that as early as the eighth century, tantric materials were being translated 
in Tibet. In the preface to the ca. 814 ce imperial edict on translation activities, the 
“Glossary in Two Sections” (sgra sbyor bam po gnyis pa), it is stated:
The tantras of the Secret Mantra [class] are to be kept secret in accordance with the 
texts themselves, and it is also not appropriate to explain or teach them to people 
who are not fit vessels [for such teachings]. In the present time, however, it is the case 
that some people have been translating [these texts] and also putting [their contents]

--- PAGE 866 ---
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist Literature      841
 
into practice, but since they were unable to unravel the explanations [given] in a con­
cealed manner [in those texts] and so took them literally, they have engaged in per­
verted conduct. Thus, since it is known that there are cases where [such texts] were 
selected among the Secret Mantra [class of] tantras and were also translated into 
Tibetan, from now on, except for [certain] dhāranīs and tantras that are approved 
for translation by royal decree, it is not permitted to select Mantra [class] tantras or 
treatises on [Secret] Mantra and to translate them.5
In documents such as this, it is recorded that even at the earliest stages of Buddhism 
entering into Tibet, tantric teachings were prevalent, as was the understanding of the 
encrypted presentation of their contents.6 Even if this imperial edict exercised some in­
fluence over the early translation and propagation activities in central Tibet, it was short 
lived, since the central government would collapse in a succession dispute less than 
thirty years later, and it is clear that tantric texts continued to be translated into Tibetan 
during the decades that followed.
By the mid-​tenth century, it appears that precisely the same problem described in this 
early ninth-​century edict—​practices based on a literal reading of the tantras—​remained 
prevalent. In the “ordinance” (bka’ shog) of a tenth-​century king in western Tibet, Lha 
Lama Yeshe Ö (Karmay 1980), the effects of not only literal readings of Buddhist tantras 
but of apparently non-​Buddhist tantras that made no pretense to containing concealed 
meanings as well are explicitly described:
Heretical tantras, pretending to be Buddhist, are spreading in Tibet. . . . These 
practices of those who claim “we are Buddhists”, show less compassion than the 
monster of karma, more avaricious for meat than a hawk or wolf, more lusty than 
even a donkey or an ox, . . . more indifferent to pure and impure than a dog or a 
pig. . . . Worshipping the Three Jewels with meat and urine, ignorant about the con­
cealed intention [of these texts] and therefore practising it literally . . . what strange 
Buddhist would adhere to such practices!?! If practices such as these were to bring 
about Buddhahood, then hunters, fishermen, butchers, and prostitutes—​all of 
these—​would certainly have attained Enlightenment by now.
In addition to his objection to the state of affairs in the late tenth-​century Tibet, the hag­
iography of this king positions him as having a direct role in the remediation of tantric 
Buddhism in Tibet through his invitation to Tibet sent to the great Buddhist master 
Atiśa. While Atiśa did eventually visit Tibet in the mid-​eleventh century and teach on 
tantra, he does not appear to have explicitly repudiated many of these things—​for ex­
ample, sexual practices described in the tantras—​but rather emphasized tantric practice 
in relation to the doctrine of Mahāmudrā or “the Great Seal,” which placed its focus on 
cultivating an understanding of the nature of mind (Apple 2017).
Although the histories covering this era position both Atiśa and the most famous 
of the new era of translators, Rinchen Sangpo, prominently, it is clear that many 
individuals—​both Tibetan and Indic—​were involved in the translation and transmis­
sion of Buddhism at this time in both its tantric and non-​tantric forms. Indeed, from

--- PAGE 867 ---
842      Paul Hackett
 
even a cursory glance at various histories and the colophons to texts in the Tibetan 
Buddhist canon, over a dozen named Tibetan translators worked with Atiśa alone on 
canonical and noncanonical translations of Indic works. Considering just the eleventh 
century, the colophons to canonical texts record close to a hundred individuals from 
India, Nepal, and Kaśmīr working with more than two dozen Tibetan translators, many 
of those works being tantric in nature.
By the eleventh century, major translation initiatives on the Tibetan plateau were well 
under way, as numerous Tibetans with the financial backing of the fortunes of various 
Tibetan aristocratic families that were purposefully directed to the acquisition, trans­
lation, and dissemination of Buddhist philosophy and both exoteric and esoteric (i.e., 
tantric) Buddhist practice. During this period of acquisition of both Buddhist texts and 
knowledge of the practices, such information appears to have been the proprietary intel­
lectual property of several Tibetan clans which demanded, at times, substantial material 
offerings in exchange for access to its content.
The Era of Competing Translations 
and Transmission Lineages
From the tenth to twelfth centuries, Tibet witnessed a wealth of translation activities 
focusing on traditional accounts of discourses of the Buddha (sūtra) as well as their 
nominally derivative philosophical treatises (śastra), but also on texts related to tantric 
practice from core texts (“root tantras,” mūlatantra) to explanatory commentaries and 
practice manuals (sādhana).
In general, all these materials were rooted in the overarching system of Mahāyāna 
Buddhism, which took, as its objective, the emulation of the life of Śākyamuni Buddha, 
with the goal of likewise achieving a state of Buddhahood above and beyond that of 
mere liberation from saṃsāra as an arhat (“one worthy of veneration”) typified by the 
teachings found in the Pāli Nikāyas. In this Mahāyāna system, the basic framework of 
Buddhist practice followed the Buddha’s multi-​life story of perfecting his interactions 
in the world. That model of practice consisted of meritorious and ethical disciplines 
to calm the body, meditative disciplines to calm and focus the mind, and analytical 
meditations on philosophical principles designed to instigate the realization of the na­
ture of reality along with its soteriological effects.
This same basic pattern is likewise found in those tantric texts in which alternate sets 
of practices are presented for the purpose of attaining that same goal of Buddhahood 
more rapidly, and occasionally including an alternate account of the enlightenment 
story of a buddha. In such alternate enlightenment accounts, the process of the attain­
ment of a state of Buddhahood is framed not in terms of the gradual accumulation of 
merit and wisdom over many lifetimes but rather in terms of the emulation of the final 
enlightened state. In this process, the practitioner is told to cultivate causes similar in

--- PAGE 868 ---
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist Literature      843
 
nature to the body of a buddha and to cultivate as different causes, mental attitudes sim­
ilar in nature to the mind of a buddha. This process known as “deity yoga” was argued 
by some Tibetan scholars, such as Tsongkhapa, to be the singular defining feature of 
Buddhist tantra, with all other aspects of popularly imagined tantric practice—​various 
sexual and nonsexual physical yogas, incantations, cultivations of magical powers, and 
so forth—​not being exclusive to tantrism or even Buddhism. Buddhist deity yoga is thus 
presented as a progressive practice in two stages, known variously as “concentration with 
and without recitation,” “yoga with and without signs,” or “generation and perfection 
stages” depending on the type of tantric practice involved, and variously categorized 
into four, seven, or nine classes of tantra, which are then further subcategorized in terms 
of the central deity and types of practice emphasized (Hackett 2012).
Just as in the non-​tantric texts, in which the attainment of different levels of spir­
itual progress is accompanied by the attainment of paranormal abilities (ṛddhi), tantric 
texts also describe the attainment of paranormal abilities. Unlike some non-​Buddhist 
systems in which powers are bestowed by a deity, the ability to attain certain magical 
powers (siddhi) described in the Buddhist tantras is a consequence of different levels 
of spiritual attainment. This attainment is grounded in “divine pride” in one’s self-​
identification with aspects of the enlightened state, with that “divine pride” being the 
conviction that one’s meditational activities are actually efficacious. Indeed, some texts 
focus on one or more specific types of magical powers as aids in support of more ad­
vanced practices on the path to full enlightenment. Such powers are typically categorized 
into four types—​pacification, increase, subjugation, and wrathful activities.7
Similar to the social circumstances of eighth-​ and ninth-​century Tibet, the attainment 
of such magical powers was also at the forefront of activities of tantric translator-​
practitioners in Tibet in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Indeed, because of the 
wealth and prestige associated with knowledge of Buddhist texts, as early as the elev­
enth century significant rivalries between translators jockeying for political (and hence 
monetary) patronage arose, and the attainment of such magical powers played a role in 
those competitions as well. One figure who exemplifies the extreme nature of some of 
these rivalries was the eleventh-​century translator of many tantric works, Ra Lotsāwa 
Dorje Drakpa (Cuevas 2015). Specializing in certain tantras renowned for developing 
facility in “wrathful activities,” Ra Lotsāwa is reported in his biographies to have killed 
more than a dozen rival translators—​all routinely described as acts of self-​defense—​in 
ritual magical combat by means of his superior powers. Nonetheless, figures such as Ra 
Lotsāwa remained revered by the generations that followed him as a prominent figure 
in the transmission of tantric teachings in Tibet. This is because, far outshadowing 
differences in interpretation of Buddhist philosophy, transmission lineages of different 
tantric teachings formed the basis of what would come to be called the various “sects” of 
Tibetan Buddhism.
Although the production of Buddhist texts came to an abrupt end with the Muslim 
invasion of India and destruction of major centers of learning at the start of the thir­
teenth century (Eaton 2000), the translation into Tibetan of Buddhist tantric and non-​
tantric texts already in Tibet and supplemented from sources in Nepal and Kaśmir

--- PAGE 869 ---
844      Paul Hackett
 
would continue for roughly another century. By the fourteenth century, the vast ma­
jority of Buddhist tantric and non-​tantric texts from India had been translated into 
Tibetan, often in one or more translations of varying quality by different translators. 
The result was that efforts began at this time to collect, select, collate, document, and 
edit the various disparate translations into a coherent canon. The role of the tantric texts, 
however, proved particularly problematic in this process since disputes arose over the 
validity of pre-​tenth-​century translations—​predominantly texts associated with the 
Nyingma sect. Since these texts contained purāṇic-​style cosmogonies,8 as well as other 
heterodox features in comparison with later translated texts, some scholars considered 
these texts to be non-​Buddhist in nature or possibly even forgeries—​the latter charge 
being levied against them given the inability of their proponents to identify Sanskrit 
manuscript originals—​and so the vast majority were excluded from what became the 
formal canon. These disparate excluded tantric texts would subsequently be collected 
into their own extra-​canonical collection referred to as the “Hundred Thousand Tantras 
of the Nyingma Sect” (rnying ma rgyud ‘bum). It was this codification of tantric and 
non-​tantric texts into a coherent canon that would lay the groundwork for the growth 
of major educational institutions in Tibet which would typically have one or more sepa­
rate or affiliated tantric colleges, which would be devoted to explicating the minutiae of 
Buddhist tantric theory and practice.
The Early Commentarial and Practice 
Literature and Integration with 
Exoteric Philosophies
With the establishment of the Tibetan canon as a common basis of reference for tex­
tual analysis, disputes over the specific details of the individual tantric texts as well as 
the relationships between texts in the canon as a coherent whole inevitably arose. With 
regard to the tantric texts in particular, many authors of this period wrote detailed 
annotations and general presentations of specific tantric practice traditions that would 
often argue against alternate interpretations by other scholars. One debate in particular 
that arose concerned the role of the tantric teaching in the context of the Mahāyāna 
Buddhist path as a whole, and was, specifically, aimed at questioning whether the tantras 
presented an alternate set of meditational and yogic practices to be paired with norma­
tive Buddhist philosophy, or if they should be taken as presenting an alternate philo­
sophical stance as well. Two individuals who figured prominently in this debate in the 
fourteenth and fifteenth centuries in Tibet were Dolpopa Sherab Gyeltsen (1292—​1361) 
and Tsongkhapa Losang Drakpa (1357–​1419).
In general, the forms of Buddhist philosophy that serve as a foundation for Mahāyāna 
Buddhism fall into two general categories, that of “Middle Way” (Madhyamaka) or 
“non-​entitiness” (niḥsvabhāva) philosophy, and that of “Mind-​Only” (Cittamātra) or

--- PAGE 870 ---
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist Literature      845
 
“Yogic Practice” (Yogācāra) philosophy. Both of these philosophical schools (and their 
sub-​variants) present permutations on three basic notions: objects as being the referents 
of words and concepts; objects existing intrinsically with their own nature; and objects 
existing as separate entities from the consciousnesses apprehending them, thereby 
entailing the existence of an external world. “Middle Way” philosophy is ontologically 
parsimonious, repudiating the referentiality of words and concepts and denying the in­
trinsic existence of objects, and yet nonetheless asserting the existence, in some ineffable 
manner, of an external world.9 “Mind-​Only” philosophy, on the other hand, advocates 
a more consciousness-​dependent reality by repudiating the referentiality of words and 
concepts but also denying the existence of an external world (but not denying the exist­
ence of other continuums of consciousnesses, i.e., other sentient beings), asserting the 
intrinsic existence of objects in the form of moments of consciousness appearing dual­
istically to the perceiver.10 In practice, when meditating on the nature of reality in either 
of these systems, what is being negated is an exaggerated and falsely superimposed no­
tion of the status of phenomena, with their actual true status—​“the ultimate”—​being a 
nonimplicative negation, a mere emptiness that is the absence of that falsely imputed 
status.
By the fourteenth century in Tibet, “Middle Way” philosophy had achieved an iconic 
status as the definitive and authoritative philosophical view of Mahāyāna Buddhism. 
In the works of Tsongkhapa and other institutionally dominant thinkers of his era, 
Buddhist tantric practice was necessarily presented as compatible and interwoven 
with the philosophical understanding of reality according to Middle Way philosophy. 
Consequently, tantric practice was viewed and presented—​and indeed, supporting 
Indian canonical sources systematized—​from this perspective such that tantric practice 
was presented as an alternative to exoteric meditation practices aimed at the same reali­
zation of the nature of reality presented in Middle Way texts. Thirteenth-​century scholar 
Sakya Paṇḍita Kunga Gyeltsen summarized this position in his “Clear Differentiation of 
the Three Vows”11 stating:
There is just one [philosophical] view from study
That is understood by means of explanations.
Nevertheless, the system of secret mantra is distinctly superior
With regard to the method for realizing [that ultimate, which is] free of elaborations.12
In Tsongkhapa’s presentation of Buddhist tantra,13 he likewise adheres to such an under­
standing of the role of tantras in the larger Buddhist enterprise. In his major work on the 
subject, Tsongkhapa engages in a comprehensive overview of the key points of Buddhist 
tantras, while assessing and evaluating the assertions of different Indian authors as re­
vealed in their works preserved in translation in the Tibetan canon, and lays out the 
overall path structure of various Buddhist tantric systems in terms of a hierarchy of 
their practices. Tsongkhapa accomplishes this by first by identifying the distinguishing 
features of tantric practice from non-​tantric practice, as well as those of the different 
classes of tantras and their practitioners. In doing so, Tsongkhapa lays out a detailed

--- PAGE 871 ---
846      Paul Hackett
 
presentation of the practices and rituals of each class of tantras with extensive scriptural 
citations and evaluations of conflicting opinions in the commentarial literature. In no 
part of his presentation, however, does Tsongkhapa argue that the nature of “wisdom,” 
that is, the nature of reality that is realized by means of these esoteric practices, is in 
any way different from what is presented in the Middle Way writings of Nāgārjuna and 
Candrakīrti.
By contrast, the early fourteenth-​century author Dolpopa, in his extensive work, The 
Mountain Doctrine,14 presents a view of Buddhist philosophy and practice that could 
be described as the exact opposite of the more normative view presented by figures like 
Tsongkhapa, Buton, Sakya Paṇḍita, and others. In that work, Dolpopa argued that the 
tantras should not be taken as restricted to meditational instructions but rather should 
contain their own distinct philosophical view as well, and that this tantric philosophical 
worldview was also compatible with all exoteric philosophical presentations. In this re­
gard, Dolpopa is less interested in providing a discrete presentation of Buddhist tantra 
than in presenting all of tantric and non-​tantric practice, and all Buddhist philosoph­
ical presentations as a singular and all-​encompassing system of practice and theory. The 
different philosophical schools represented by the writings of first-​millennium Indian 
Buddhist thinkers found in the Tibetan canon contain statements that are difficult to 
read as anything other than mutually contradictory, and the standard approach to their 
reconciliation in Tibetan academic circles was to separate them into categories forming 
distinct philosophical schools and subschools that were thus coherent and consistent. 
Dolpopa, however, while pointing out the contradictions that occur from taking the 
wide range of statements in the philosophical treatises literally, argued instead, through 
an appeal to the authority of the Buddha, that all such statements as pronouncements 
from an omniscient source must be impervious to contradiction and so proposed that 
another doctrine—​unspoken by any previous figure (including the Buddha)—​must be 
the only way of achieving a systematic unification of all statements and doctrines. Thus, 
Dolpopa proposed that there was, in fact, a unifying set of philosophical assertions that 
could subsume the various individual philosophical systems, and he proposed such a 
system by asserting categories and proposing new terms that were presented by none 
of them. Called the doctrine of “other-​emptiness” (gzhan stong), this unifying philos­
ophy drew equally on statements from tantras and from philosophical texts and, taking 
such statements literally, asserted that the ultimate nature of reality—​rather than being 
a nonimplicative negation, a mere emptiness, as described in canonical Mahāyāna phil­
osophical texts—​was instead only “other-​empty” (i.e., empty of everything other than 
themselves) and in fact possessed a self-​nature.
Both these approaches by Tsongkhapa and Dolpopa can be viewed as very specific 
characterizations of Buddhist tantra aimed at the goal of systematization for the sake 
of consistency and coherency. While Dolpopa’s presentation sacrifices both historical 
and indeed philosophical fidelity to canonical authors in order to achieve a uniquely 
singular presentation of philosophy and practice, his resulting system was deeply prob­
lematic in relation to fundamental premises of Buddhist philosophy since it appeared 
to reintroduce the sort of “self” (atman) that was universally repudiated in canonical

--- PAGE 872 ---
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist Literature      847
 
Buddhist texts, and was thus roundly criticized for doing so. Tsongkhapa, by contrast, 
is certainly faithful to his Indian canonical sources in presenting a complete and co­
herent presentation of Buddhist philosophy and tantric practice and does not shy away 
from pointing out mistakes and inconsistencies in the writings of some Indic authors, 
although in the process it is clear that Tsongkhapa needed to deploy—​at times, seem­
ingly contrived although ingenious—​hermeneutical strategies to achieve his goal even 
with regard to sources and authors that he accepts as authoritative.
In addition, when examined even merely on the level of exoteric philosophy, there are 
Indian Buddhist tantric commentaries that clearly rely upon the vocabulary of Mind-​
Only philosophy in their presentation of tantric practices and textual exegesis. All of 
this would seem to imply that the philosophical dispositions of Indian Buddhist tantric 
practitioners and scholars was likely (and unsurprisingly) far more varied and less ho­
mogeneous than the later traditions might want to present.
Another dispute during this time was over the appropriateness of sexual yogas in 
tantric practice for ordained monks, that is, for practitioners holding vows of celibacy. 
From reading the canonical commentaries and practice texts on the highest class of 
tantras—​the “Unsurpassed” (anuttara) Yoga tantras—​it is clear that at a certain stage of 
advanced practice, one possible form of practice involves the use of a consort. Far from 
providing a blanket license for licentiousness, however, the bar for engaging in sexual 
yogas and related practices as described in the texts is exceptionally high, involving such 
things as the ability to engage in controlled breathing exercises for a twenty-​four-​hour 
period,15 attainment of the stage of “mind isolation,”16 and so forth. Nonetheless, it is 
clear that some individuals in Tibet routinely engaged in tantric practice with a con­
sort, certainly in the imperial era (seventh to ninth century ce) and well after. Even if 
assuming a practitioner had indeed reached that stage of practice, the question of the 
relationship between monastic vows and tantric practice remained hotly disputed.
One of the categories of tantric literature that addressed precisely such issues was 
the “Three Vows” literature. These discussions and presentations framed the issue in 
terms of three types of vows: monastic, bodhisattva, and tantric. In these presentations, 
a common assertion was that because monk’s vows and the bodhisattva vows of 
Mahāyāna serve as their basis, the tantric vows are to be observed in conjunction with 
the other two (Rhoton 2002).
In the lineage following Tsongkhapa, which came to be called the “system of virtue” 
(“Geluk”) because of their strict observance of the monastic codes and the vow of celi­
bacy in particular, it was argued that “higher” forms of practice (including tantra) did 
not supersede monastic vows, and that any individual who perceived them to be in 
conflict had a mistaken understanding of ethics.17 Thus, in the Geluk lineage, a monk 
who had reached the level of practice where a consort would be of use would either re­
nounce their monk’s vows and return to life as a lay tantric practitioner, or would instead 
follow the model set forth by Tsongkhapa himself, by delaying that aspect of practice 
until the time of death, when the sorts of changes in a person’s psychophysical makeup 
that would be induced by a consort would instead occur naturally. In other lineages of 
Tibetan Buddhism, the monastic codes were less strictly observed in relation to tantric

--- PAGE 873 ---
848      Paul Hackett
 
practice, or were deemed to be superseded by the dictates of tantric practice, thereby 
allowing for the possibility of tantric consort practice.
Praxis Literature and Consolidating 
Compendia in the High Classical Era 
of Tibet (ca. Seventeenth–​Nineteenth 
Centuries)
With the growth of large monastic institutions following the fifteenth century, the locus 
of political and financial power connected with tantric knowledge shifted away from 
clan-​based structures toward a more democratized access model via nominally in­
dependent monastic institutions.18 In concert with this, there was a general move by 
Tibetan authors toward the consolidation and systematization of tantric materials as 
part of a larger trend aimed at the formation of standardized curricula for use in the mo­
nastic universities.
In addition to composing topic-​specific tantric commentaries, several authors 
formulated such curricula, and in doing so looked to the genres of textbooks devel­
oped for non-​tantric subjects such as the Perfection of Wisdom commentarial liter­
ature that presented progression on the path to enlightenment in terms of “grounds” 
(bhūmi) and “paths” (mārga). The overarching structure and vocabulary of these ex­
oteric presentations of the stages leading to enlightenment were deployed to a similar 
end for academic introductions to tantra. Hence, the classification of tantras, combined 
with the various descriptions of stages of practice were homologized into a parallel pre­
sentation of “grounds and paths” subsuming the range of different tantras found in the 
canon.19 For example, whereas in graded progression of the stages of the path to enlight­
enment according to the Perfection of Wisdom, advancement was described in terms 
of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, and the direct realization of the nature of 
reality accompanying the progressive diminution of various levels of obstructions to en­
lightenment, in the tantric versions of these types of presentations, these same stages of 
spiritual attainment became mapped to progressive levels of success in the tantric prac­
tice (sādhana) texts. In addition, a great deal of attention was paid to the development 
of ritual manuals containing practical instructions for conferring empowerments, per­
forming tantric offering ceremonies, and the like.
In other less academically oriented monastic centers around Tibet, there was 
the different problem of coping with a plethora of extracanonical tantric texts and 
transmissions. One of the uniquely Tibetan features of tantra during this period was the 
growth of “treasure” (gter ma) literature. Treasure texts are purported to be teachings by 
notable figures in the past that were intentionally hidden—​in physical and nonphysical 
forms—​for the benefit of later generations. Revealers (gter ston) of these treasure texts

--- PAGE 874 ---
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist Literature      849
 
became a fixture in some lineages of Tibetan Buddhism and instigated the formation of 
extensive tantric lineages based upon these recovered texts (Doctor 2013). Consequently, 
in addition to compiling collections of tantras excluded from the canon, this era saw the 
compilation and consolidation of various tantric systems into large collections called 
“treasuries” (mdzod) by individuals attempting to preserve smaller lineages in danger 
of being lost, although in doing so, much of the uniqueness and specificity of these same 
lineages was subsumed into larger generic systems.
Finally, beginning in the nineteenth century, there was a movement toward 
ecumenicism between the various sects of Tibetan Buddhism in which the tantric 
Treasure traditions played a key role. Promoted as a nonsectarian movement, it was 
rather formed predominantly as a political coalition against the dominant Geluk 
sect in Tibet, who were consciously excluded (Gardner 2006). In the mid-​twentieth 
century, following the Chinese invasion of Tibet and genocide during the Chinese 
Cultural Revolution, the resulting diaspora of nearly all major religious leaders and 
hundreds of thousands more Tibetans and their common need for cooperation for 
survival prompted a de facto ecumenism among the major sects, which some have 
used as an opportunity to promote true understanding and reconciliation between 
those various tantric lineages and their theories regarding Buddhist tantra, with 
the effect of spurring on the ongoing production of yet another new genre of tantric 
literature.20
