Chapter 34
The Cakrasaṃvara 
Tantra
David B. Gray
Critical History
The tantric traditions of Buddhism emerged in the eighth century, developing from es­
oteric traditions of magic, ritual, and meditation in Mahāyāna Buddhist communities 
in India. As Jake Dalton (2016) and Koichi Shinohara (2014) have argued, the precursors 
to the tantras were textual collections of spells (dhāraṇī) that described the ritual and 
meditative practices associated with them. Such collections were increasingly produced 
and disseminated throughout East Asia during the first millennium CE and over time 
demonstrated the increasing complexity and systematization that came to characterize 
the tantric traditions. These traditions claim to preserve the secret teachings of the 
Buddhas that enable one to rapidly achieve the supreme accomplishment, awakening, 
and mundane magical abilities, such as clairvoyance, clairaudience, and so forth.
The earliest known esoteric scripture produced by the Indian Buddhist commu­
nity that came to be known as tantra is the Awakening of Mahāvairocana Tantra 
(Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-​tantra), which was composed circa 640 CE and was 
reportedly one of the texts collected by the Chinese pilgrim Wuxing (無行) circa 680 
CE (Hodge 2003, 14–​17). Both Wuxing and another Chinese pilgrim, Yijing (義淨), 
who also traveled to India in the late seventh century, reported the emergence of new 
esoteric teachings in India (Davidson 2002, 118; Hodge 2003, 10). The eighth century 
saw the development of large numbers of tantric texts, as well as the transmission of 
many of them to China and Tibet.
Among the texts produced and disseminated during this period was a collection 
of eighteen tantras, of which there are various reports. The earliest account is found 
in Amoghavajra’s Index of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra Yoga in Eighteen Sections, a text he 
composed after his return to China from a trip to South Asia in 746 CE; a similar list 
of eighteen tantras was also preserved in Tibet (Giebel 1995, Gray 2009, Almogi

--- PAGE 879 ---
854      David B. Gray
 
2014). One of the texts included in these collections was the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-​
ḍākinījālasaṃvara Tantra. This text, dating to the eighth century, was an important 
precursor to the Yoginītantra genre, which is characterized by focus on both female 
deities and transgressive ritual practices involving sexuality and violence. It has been 
characterized as a “proto-​Yoginītantra” and was later added to this genre of texts.1 The 
Cakrasaṃvara Tantra is textually dependent on this text, repeats several verses found in 
it, and also follows several patterns established by this text.
The first and most noticeable aspects of both texts are their unconventional styles, 
at least in the context of Buddhist scriptures. Most Buddhist scriptures, sutras as well 
as tantras, begin with the standard opening background verse (nidāna). Asserting the 
claim that the text is the authentic speech of the Buddha (buddhavacana),2 the standard 
nidāna verse usually begins: “Thus have I heard: at one time” (evaṅ mayā śrutam 
ekasmin samaye), and continues by indicating the setting and audience for the discourse. 
Both the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-​ḍākinījālasaṃvara Tantra and the Cakrasaṃvara 
Tantra open with a more unconventional text that came to be identified as the back­
ground verse (nidāna) of the Yoginītantras. It occurs as follows in the opening verse of 
the former text:
The Hero that is made of all buddhas,
Vajrasattva, the bliss that is supreme,
Always abides in the nature of all,
The secret that’s supreme and delightful.3
An almost identical version of this verse occurs in the first chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara 
Tantra, where it occurs as follows:
The Hero that’s made of all ḍākinīs,
Vajrasattva, the bliss that is supreme,
Always abides in the nature of all,
The secret that’s supreme and delightful.4
Both texts contain significant overlap in the first chapter, indicating that this text was 
one of the sources drawn on by the author(s) of the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra.
In addition to quoting this text, the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra mentions it and sev­
eral other tantric works by name, in verses occurring toward the end of its twenty-​
seventh and thirtieth chapters. The other texts it mentions are the Tattvasaṃgraha, 
Śrīparamādya, Guhyasamāja, and Vajrabhairava tantras.5 Aside from the last, all of 
these texts are included in the Amogavajra’s Index. Therefore, the Cakrasaṃvara must 
have been composed after these texts, which appear to have existed in some form by the 
mid-​eighth century. And it must have been composed no later than 975 CE since it was 
among the texts that the Tibetan translator Rinchen Zangpo (rin chen bzang po, 958–​
1055 CE) encountered when he journeyed to Kashmir in 975 CE, and that he translated 
into Tibetan with the help of the Kashmiri pundit Padmākaravarman.

--- PAGE 880 ---
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra      855
 
However, the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra was probably composed during the ninth cen­
tury, most likely no later than 900 CE. This is because there is considerable textual ev­
idence pointing to its gradual emergence as a composite text, which grew over time as 
new sections were added to it. As Alexis Sanderson has shown (1994, 2001, 2009), much 
of the oldest portions of the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra was drawn from older Śaiva texts. The 
sections drawn from Śaiva sources deal with the clans of the yoginīs, goddesses who can 
assume human form, and the techniques needed to identify them and win their favor. 
As such lore concerning yoginīs and ḍākinīs are a central feature of the Yoginītantras, 
this is a case in which Buddhists relied heavily on earlier Hindu sources for the devel­
opment of a new practice tradition.6 The passages borrowed from Śaiva sources are also 
the sections of the text that relate antinomian content, namely practices involving ritual 
sexuality, violence, and anthropophagy.7 On the other hand, the portions of the text that 
feature distinctly Buddhist terminology—​the opening of ­chapter 10, the end of ­chapter 
50, and ­chapter 51—​appear to be later additions to the text, as indicated by the fact that 
the earliest commentary by Jayabhadra, composed circa the late ninth or early tenth 
century, does not comment on these passages at all (Gray 2012, 9–​10). However, these 
sections are found in Rinchen Zangpo’s translation, indicating that they were added 
sometime during the tenth century.
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra and its associated practice traditions originated in India 
and continued to be practiced among Buddhist communities in South Asia until their 
decline and disappearance during the mid–​second millennium CE. It was preserved 
and continues to be an important practice tradition for Newar Buddhists in Nepal 
(Lewis and Bajracharya 2016, 157–​166). It was also transmitted to Tibet as part of the 
“later transmission” (phyi dar) of Buddhism to Tibet, a process that began with Rinchen 
Zangpo’s tenth-​century journey to India, which led to the translation of this work into 
Tibetan. Over the following three centuries, many more works associated with the 
Cakrasaṃvara Tantra were translated, and it became an important practice tradition in 
the “New” (gsar ma) Schools of Tibetan Buddhism established during this time, namely 
the Sakya, Kagyü, and Geluk schools of Tibetan Buddhism.
Legendary History
Textual history points to the gradual development of the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra over ap­
proximately a century (ca. 875–​975 CE), with a major feature of its development being 
the transformation of Śaiva Hindu texts and practices into Buddhist scriptures and as­
sociated practice traditions. As we will see, this scenario is interestingly paralleled by the 
origin myth for this text and the tradition preserved in Buddhist sources.
The traditional locus of authority in Buddhist scriptural traditions is, naturally, 
Śākyamuni Buddha, the reputed teacher in most Buddhist scriptures. Most Buddhist 
scriptures are traditionally classified as buddhavacana, literally “that which the buddha 
spoke,” and thus are understood to be records of his teachings. Traditionally, Buddhists

--- PAGE 881 ---
856      David B. Gray
 
emphasized the truth of the teachings that persist through time, to be continually 
rediscovered by new generations of awakened ones.8 While this in theory destabilized 
the locus of authority for Buddhist textual traditions, most Buddhists conservatively 
stuck to Śākyamuni Buddha as the awakened one of our age. However, with the rise of 
the Mahāyāna traditions in the first millennium CE, an increasing number of “new” or 
“newly discovered” Mahāyāna scriptures were attributed to other Buddhas, accessed via 
revelatory, visionary states rather than historical lineages (Harrison 1987).
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra, also known as the “Saṃvara Light” tantra (Laghusaṃvara-​
tantra) or the “Discourse of Śrī Heruka” (śrīherukābhidhāna), was a Buddhist scripture 
not attributed to Śākyamuni Buddha, but rather to Śrī Heruka, a manifestation of the 
Mahāvajradhara Buddha, relayed to his consort, the female Buddha Vajravārāhī. The 
short and cryptic Cakrasaṃvara Tantra, being only about seven hundred stanzas in 
length, bears only traces of the conversational style that is supposedly the context for its 
revelation. The main indication of the conversational context in which the scripture was 
believed to have been taught is the first-​person voice in which most of the text’s chapters 
begin. For example, the text opens with the following: “And now I will explain the secret, 
concisely, not extensively” (Gray 2007, 155).
One explanation for the text’s laconic beginning, athātas, “and now,” is that 
the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra was originally revealed as a much larger text, which was 
called either the “Discourse” (abhidhāna), the “Sky-​like” (khasama) or the “Ocean 
of Spells” (vidyārṇava), a title that was mentioned in the text itself.9 The length of 
this extensive text (mahātantra) is variously described as being either one hundred 
thousand stanzas, three hundred thousand stanzas, or even one hundred thousand 
chapters in length (Gray 2017, 33–​34). The current text, also known as Saṃvara Light 
(laghusaṃvara) as a sign of its abridged status, was shortened to a much more manage­
able seven hundred stanzas for the sake of beings of the current kaliyuga age, who lack 
the long lifespans that the study of such huge texts would necessitate. The authors who 
make these claims thus evoke the old myths of massive revelations followed by loss 
and partial recovery of the lost texts that have been advanced by tantric communities 
from the very beginning of the revelation and recovery of these traditions, going back 
to the seventh century CE.10
Several Buddhist writers, including the Indian commentator Indrabhūti and the 
Tibetan historian Butön Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen grub, 1290–​1364 CE) relate 
the origin myth of this tantra. According to these authors, the Buddha who revealed 
Cakrasaṃvara Tantra was Mahāvajradhara Buddha, and the revelation occurred on Mt. 
Sumeru, either during the past dvāparayuga or during the current kaliyuga ages (Gray 
2017, 39–​40). Indrabhūti’s account, which seems to be the oldest source for this legend, 
relates that the scripture originated with Mahāvajradhara Buddha in the Akaniṣṭha 
heaven and was related to Vajrapāṇi bodhisattva. The trigger for its revelation was con­
cern about the activities of two Hindu deities, Bhairava and Kālarātri, who along with 
their divine, semidivine, and demonic followers, seized control of Mt. Sumeru as well 
as twenty-​four sacred sites scattered across the subcontinent. To deal with this problem, 
Mahāvajradhara and his consort assumed Śaiva guise, manifesting as the deities of

--- PAGE 882 ---
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra      857
 
Śrī Heruka and Vajravārāhī and taking on the appearance of the Hindu deities whom 
they then subdued, Bhairava and Kālarātri. The others in their retinue manifested in 
the twenty-​four sacred sites, subduing their Hindu counterparts and restoring “order” 
to the universe, while at the same time manifesting the Cakrasaṃvara mandala in the 
world.11
While Indrabhūti identifies Vajrapāṇi as the interlocutor whose questions triggered 
the initial revelation of the scripture, some other commentators, such as the tenth-​
century commentator Bhavabhaṭṭa, assign this role to Vajravārāhī (Gray 2007, 32). 
Reconciling these claims, the Tibetan historian Zhönnu Pel (gzhon nu dpal, 1392–​1481) 
claimed that there were two distinct revelations of the scripture, by Vajravārāhī to the 
Mahāsiddha Lūipa and by Vajrapāṇi to the Mahāsiddha Saraha, leading to two distinct 
lineages of the text and associated practices (Roerich 1976, 380–​397).
Interestingly, the traditional accounts acknowledge the debt Buddhist traditions owe 
to rival Śaiva traditions. However, they account for this borrowing as an act of skillful 
means, initiated so as to convert “immoral heretics” to Buddhism. The myths them­
selves, along with associated iconographic art, feature and depict the subjugation of one 
tradition’s deities by another’s. These contentious narratives and iconography point to 
the fierce competition that existed between these traditions in South Asia during the 
early medieval period.
The Textual Corpus
By itself, the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra is a short text that alludes to, but does not relate 
clearly or completely, any of the elements of tantric practice. Key rituals, such as the 
production of the mandala made with strings and colored powders as the site for the 
consecration rituals (abhiṣeka), are described in the text, but incompletely, with some of 
the details of practice presented out of order. Details of the iconography of the deities, 
needed for creation stage (utpattikrama) visualization exercises, are related in a sporadic 
and incomplete manner, and the advanced perfection stage (niṣpannakrama) practices 
are not described at all, except via hidden allusions noted by astute commentators. The 
text thus requires commentary, and hence a larger textual corpus, in order to serve as the 
basis for an actual practice tradition.
Shortly after the composition of the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra, likely within years or 
decades, Indian Buddhists began composing longer scriptures that filled many of 
the gaps left by the root tantra. Among the earliest of the works are the much longer 
“Discourse Appendix Tantra,” Abhidhānottaratantra, the title of which indicates that it 
was understood to be an appendix to the Abhidhāna, in this case most likely the myth­
ical mahātantra, and not the Cakrasaṃvara itself. This is because the work includes 
the Cakrasaṃvara in a list of works to which it claims superiority, clearly indicating 
that it was composed after the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra, and suggesting that its authors 
or compilers intended it to supplant that text.12 It was likely composed during the

--- PAGE 883 ---
858      David B. Gray
 
tenth century. It was brought to Tibet and translated by the great Indian pundit Atiśa 
Dīpaṃkara Śrījñāna (982–​1054 CE), who journeyed to Tibet in 1040 CE.
Ultimately, the Abhidhānottaratantra was classified as an “explanatory tantra” 
(vyākhyātantra) of the Cakrasaṃvara root tantra. The term explanatory tantra refers to 
typically larger works that are thought to fill in the gaps left by cryptic root tantras. They 
are believed to be texts that were revealed by Buddhas. In the Cakrasaṃvara tradition 
there are generally understood to be at least five explanatory tantras.13 Durjayacandra, 
the eighth preceptor of the Vikramaśīla monastic college who met with Rinchen Zangpo 
in the late tenth century, wrote a commentary on the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra that claims 
that there are five explanatory tantras. In addition to the Abhidhānottaratantra, he also 
included the Vajraḍāka Tantra; the “Transit of the Yoginīs” Yoginīsaṃcāra Tantra; 
the “Origin of Heruka” Herukābhyudaya Tantra; and the “Kiss” or Saṃpuṭa Tantra. 
These texts were likely composed during the tenth century since they are mentioned in 
Durjayacandra’s late tenth-​century commentary. Some later commentators added sev­
eral more texts—​“The Kiss of the Four Yoginīs” Caturyoginīsaṃputa Tantra; the “Ocean 
of Ḍākas” Ḍākārṇava Tantra; “The Origin of Saṃvara” Saṃvarodaya Tantra; and/​or 
the “Approach of Vārāhī” Vārāhyabhibhava Tantra—​expanding the list to either seven 
or nine texts. These works were likely composed later, during the eleventh or twelfth 
centuries (Gray 2017, 34–​36).
Several of these explanatory tantras, including the Abhidhānottaratantra and 
Vajraḍāka Tantra, are much longer than the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra and hence do fill in 
many of the details concerning practices that are omitted in the root text. Over time, 
however, many other works were composed by scholars to further elucidate the tra­
dition. There were eleven commentaries on the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra composed by 
Indian pundits and preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur,14 and more were composed by 
Tibetan authors as well.
There were also many practice texts composed by Indian pundits, such as meditation 
manuals (sādhana) and ritual texts for the construction of mandalas (maṇḍalavidhi) and 
the performance of consecration ceremonies therein (abhiṣekavidhi). Particularly influ­
ential among these are those attributed to the greatly accomplished saints (mahāsiddha) 
of the Indian Buddhist tantric traditions.15 These include the “Cakrasaṃvara 
Realization,” Cakrasaṃvarābhisamaya, an influential meditation manual attributed 
to the Mahāsiddha Lūipa, who was generally considered to be a founding figure of 
Cakrasaṃvara practice traditions. The Sanskrit text for this work has survived (edited in 
Sakurai 1998), and its importance is indicated by the large number of commentaries on 
it preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur, including one by Atiśa, which indicates it must have 
been composed prior to his arrival in Tibet in 1040 CE.
Several influential works are attributed to the Mahāsiddha known as Kāṇha and 
also as Kṛṣṇācārya. Attributed to him are several important works that address the 
path of creation and completion stage practice in the Cakrasaṃvara tradition. These 
include his Spring Drop (vasantatilakā), his The Four Stages (olicatuṣṭaya) and its 
autocommentary, and his Light on the Secret Reality (guhyatattvaprakāśa).16 He also 
wrote an influential Cakrasaṃvara meditation manual, the Sanskrit text of which

--- PAGE 884 ---
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra      859
 
has been preserved (Sugiki 2000) and wrote a manual for the rite of fire sacrifice 
(homavidhi; see Gray 2016).
The third mahāsiddha seen as a major figure in Cakrasaṃvara practice traditions 
is Ghaṇṭāpāda, also known as Vajraghaṇṭa. He is the reputed author of an important 
text on practice in this tradition called The Five Stages of the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, the 
Sanskrit text of which has been recovered and edited.17 Two meditation manuals are 
also attributed to him, as well as ritual texts on mandala construction and the bestowal 
of consecrations therein. All of these texts are preserved in Tibetan translation; the 
Sanskrit originals do not appear to have been preserved.
Closely connected to the Cakrasaṃvara tradition are the traditions of practice 
connected with the goddess Vajravārāhī/​Vajrayoginī. As Vajravārāhī she is considered 
to be the consort of Śrī Heruka and hence the central female deity in the Cakrasaṃvara 
mandala. But she is also a very popular deity in her own right, with her own mandala 
and associated practice tradition, which has been particularly popular with female 
practitioners. Many ritual texts focusing on her have been composed, and they remain 
very popular in Nepal, Tibet, and Mongolia.18
Needless to say, in the living practice traditions of Nepal, Tibet, and Mongolia, many 
new practice texts have been composed and are used by contemporary practitioners of 
these traditions. While some of these texts have been translated into English for use by 
practitioners, they are typically not openly published due to the esoteric nature of the 
details of tantric practice. However, there have been some Tibetan lamas who have done 
this recently, relaxing the rules of secrecy in the interest of greater accessibility.19
Distinctive Practice Traditions
Cakrasaṃvara practice traditions were preserved up to the present day by Newar 
Buddhist communities in Nepal as well as the Sarma traditions of Tibetan Buddhism, 
preserved in Tibet, the Himalayan region, Mongolia, parts of China, and ethnic Mongol 
regions of Russia. Both the Newar and Tibetan traditions share common origins, in 
the Indian Buddhist traditions that were transmitted first to Nepal and later to Tibet. 
Indeed, the Tibetans were highly dependent on Nepal as a major locus giving them ac­
cess to Indian Buddhism (Lo Bue 1997). Relatively little is known about Newar prac­
tice traditions since they not only maintain the secrecy that traditionally shrouds 
tantric practice, but also because training in their traditions is limited to the traditional 
Buddhist groups in the Newar caste system, such as the Vajrācārya, Śākya, and Urāy 
caste groups. Partly as a result of this insularity, relatively little has been published on the 
details of practice in Newar Buddhist communities.20
On the other hand, while Tibetan Buddhist communities likewise observed se­
crecy with respect to the details of tantric practice, they tended to be less insular. Many 
Tibetan lamas have engaged in missionary activity, attempting to spread their teachings 
to neighboring regions such as Mongolia, China, and the non-​ethnic Tibetan regions in

--- PAGE 885 ---
860      David B. Gray
 
the Himalayas. Moreover, with the Tibetan diaspora following the Chinese occupation 
of Tibet in the 1950s, numerous lamas have come to serve as spiritual guides for various 
communities around the contemporary world (Zablocki 2009). As a result of this, the 
details of Tibetan Buddhism tantric practice have become much better known, and a 
large number of works dealing with tantric practice have been published, with a con­
comitant disclosure of practice details that were formerly considered to be secret.21
For those interested in practicing in the Cakrasaṃvara tradition, the first step would be 
finding a qualified lama to serve as one’s teacher. Should the lama accept one as a student, 
he or she would likely first have one engage in the “preliminary practices” (sngon ‘gro) that 
are thought to make one qualified, or a “suitable vessel,” for initiation into the practice 
lineage. These are usually divided into two types; one is “ordinary preliminary practices” 
(thun mong gi sngon ‘gro), which are designed to provide one with a good moral and in­
tellectual foundation via introduction to classical Mahāyana teachings. Tibetan authors 
typically recommend as well “extraordinary preliminary practices” (thun mong ma yin gi 
sngon ‘gro), which provide the basis for more advanced tantric practices.
The ordinary preliminaries, or the early phase of tantric training in the Tibetan tra­
dition, are usually articulated in terms of the “three trainings” (bslab gsum) of Buddhist 
practice: moral discipline (tshul khrims), wisdom (shes rab), and meditative concentra­
tion (ting nge ‘dzin). Novice practitioners in Tibetan Buddhism are exhorted to find a 
qualified teacher, under whose guidance they can begin their training. The early phases 
of spiritual training typically involve an introduction to Buddhist teachings in order to 
help the novice practitioner generate a correct understanding of the religion, establish 
a firm moral basis, and engender a strong motivation for spiritual practice, all of which 
are seen as essential foundations for proper spiritual development.
The extraordinary preliminaries include taking refuge in the Three Jewels—​
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—​and generation of the spirit of awak­
ening (Skt. bodhicitta, Tib. byang sems), as well as several contemplative and ritual 
exercises. These exercises include a purification practice that entails focusing on the 
deity Vajrasattva (who is associated with spiritual purification and the overcoming 
of mental obstacles). That involves a relatively simple visualization of Vajrasattva, 
performed while reciting a liturgy that includes the repetition of Vajrasattva’s mantra 
of one hundred syllables. They also include the mandala offering ritual, a simple ritual 
in which one makes an offering of rice or barley, which is visualized as an extensive 
offering made to a vast host of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the gurus of one’s prac­
tice lineage. Another important preliminary is the practice of guru yoga, a contem­
plative exercise in which one visualizes one’s guru above one’s head in the form of an 
awakened being. One takes refuge in one’s guru and the guru lineage that he or she 
represents and recites prayers to one’s gurus. These practices are taught as stand-​alone 
practices for novices who aspire to undertake advanced forms of tantric contempla­
tive practices. They are also commonly embedded in the meditation manuals (Skt. 
sādhana, Tib. sgrub thabs), as preliminaries conducted prior to the actual meditative 
practice (Beyer 1973, 434–​442, and Khetsun Sangpo 1996, 113–​182).

--- PAGE 886 ---
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra      861
 
Once a lama deems that a student is suitably qualified, he or she would be permitted 
to attend a consecration ceremony (abhiṣeka, dbang bskur), an important ceremony 
that initiated the student into the practice tradition and empowers her or him to re­
ceive advanced teachings in the tradition (see Davidson, this volume). Depending on 
the tradition, it takes one to three days to perform. In the ceremony, one is introduced 
to the deity mandala of the practice tradition into which one is being initiated, which 
empowers one to undertake the advanced contemplative practices associated with that 
tradition (see Berzin 1997). Typically, newly initiated students must make a vow to prac­
tice daily according to one of the meditation manuals associated with the tradition into 
which they have been initiated.
Receiving the rite of consecration qualifies one to receive teachings in the advanced 
stages of tantric practice. In the “new” traditions of Tibetan Buddhism, these are twofold: 
the stage of “creation” or “generation” (utpattikrama, bskyed rim) and the stage of “per­
fection” or “completion” (niṣpannakrama, bskyed rim). In the former stage, one engages 
in what is known as “deity yoga” (devatāyoga, lha’i rnal ‘byor). In the Cakrasaṃvara tra­
dition, this entails imagining one’s ordinary identity dissolve into emptiness and then 
emerging as either one of the tradition’s central deities, Śrī Heruka or Vajravārāhī, or as 
the deity couple in inseparable union. This transformed sense of self-​identity is called 
the “divine pride” (lha’i nga rgyal) of oneself as an awakened being. One then imagines 
the mandala as one’s environment, with oneself surrounded by the mandala’s deities. 
One tries to develop and maintain the ability to visualize this in a crystal-​clear manner 
and also to maintain this sense of divine identity existing in a divine abode even when 
one comes out of the meditative state, and engages with the so-​called “ordinary world,” 
retaining the growing sense that one’s perception of it is conditioned and can thus be 
reconditioned and transformed by contemplative practices. Moreover, the beings one 
encounters in the postmeditative state should be conceived as the awakened beings of 
the mandala to undermine ordinary social conceptions (e.g., prejudice) and emotional 
patterns (e.g., lust, hostility, etc.). The mastery of visualization practice is very challenging 
for most people and typically requires a serious commitment on the part of the practi­
tioner. The Tibetan Buddhist practice of going into meditative retreat, ideally for three or 
more years, is designed to enable this kind of accomplishment (Ngawang Zangpo 1990).
While creation-​stage visualization is found in most tantric Buddhist traditions, the 
Yoginītantras feature a special and advanced creation stage visualization practice that 
is designed to segue one into the more advanced perfection-​stage practices. This is 
known as “body mandala” (kāyamaṇḍala, sku’i dkyil ‘khor) practice. As noted above, the 
Cakrasaṃvara origin myth posited a mandala of twenty-​five sacred sites, Mt. Sumeru 
surrounded by a network of twenty-​four sacred sites, which were initially occupied by 
Śaiva deities, but were later overtaken by Śrī Heruka and Vajravārāhī and the twenty-​
four deity couples of their entourage. This outer “map” of sacred sites is represented 
by the Cakrasaṃvara mandala, which centers on the central couple, surrounded by 
the Body, Speech, and Mind Wheels, each of which consists of eight deity couples cor­
responding to eight of the sacred sites. This mandala is also mapped onto the body of

--- PAGE 887 ---
862      David B. Gray
 
the practitioner, which becomes a mesocosm, linking the outer mandala of actual pil­
grimage sites with the inner visualized mandala.
In body mandala practice, one visualizes one’s body as pervaded by the Cakrasaṃvara 
mandala. Each sacred site (sthāna) and associated seed syllable (bīja) is connected with 
a yoginī goddess, associated with various body parts, and their male consorts, who are 
associated with various bodily constituents (dhātu). Interestingly, included in the lists 
of bodily parts and constituents are those conventionally viewed as “filthy” or impure, 
such as the genitals, anus, and feet, as well as substances such as phlegm, blood, and 
feces. Interestingly, the Indian Buddhists who developed this practice drew from lists 
of bodily parts and constituents developed by early Buddhists and found in works such 
as the Scripture on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the pur­
pose of which was to undermine attachment to the body (one’s own or another’s) by 
contemplating its impurity. Here, however, the aim is different—​developing a sense of 
the body in all of its aspects, regardless of their supposed impurity in the conventional 
understanding, as the completely pure abode of the mandala and its deities.22 Moreover, 
the tradition also maps the three wheels of the mandala not only to the three levels of 
the cosmos (triloka) (the heavens, earth, and underworld), but also the three levels of a 
Buddha’s embodiment (trikāya), linking the practice to the ultimate goal of awakening 
(Sugiki 2003, 165–​168).
While body mandala visualization practice is part of the creation stage, it also enables 
the practitioner to transition to the more advanced perfection-​stage practices since 
there is also body mandala practice in the Cakrasaṃvara perfection stage. The per­
fection stage focuses on the subtle body, which consists of channels (nāḍī) and wheels 
or channel nexus (cakra), through which are conducted vital wind (prāṇa) and subtle 
drops (bindu); here the sacred sites of the body mandala correspond to vital points on 
the subtle body to be manipulated in perfection-​stage yogic practices (Gray 2017, 180). 
The ultimate goal of perfection-​stage practice is the achievement of nondual gnosis, 
which is equated with awakening in this tradition (Gray 2021). This is achieved in 
Unexcelled Yoga tantra traditions by opening the lower aperture of the central channel 
of the subtle body and forcing into it the vital winds that normally reside in the left and 
right channels. This purportedly leads to awakening the subtle “Fury Fire” (caṇḍālī, Tib. 
gtum mo), which travels up the channel and melts the subtle “drop” of the brain center, 
whose molten descent down the channel awakens increasingly intense levels of bliss 
(Cozort 1986, 68–​88). The Fury Fire practice, which is analogous to the Hindu kuṇḍalinī 
yoga practices,23 is a perfection-​stage practice that is distinct to the Yoginītantras and is 
linked strongly to the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra tantras.
There were several systems of perfection-​stage practice developed by Indian 
Buddhists. These include the five stages (pañcakrama) system of the Guhyāsamāja 
Tantra, which is attributed to the mahāsiddha Nāropa,24 as well as the six yogas system 
associated with both the Guhyāsamāja and Kālacakra tantras (Tsongkhapa 2013, 4). 
The most famous systems for perfection-​stage practice in the Yoginītantras are the two 
closely related systems of “six teachings” (dharma, chos) attributed to the mahāsiddha

--- PAGE 888 ---
The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra      863
 
Naropā as well as the yoginī Niguma, who was reputed to be his sister.25 These practices 
focus on the subtle body with the aim of opening the aperture of the central channel, 
which reportedly can only be done while dreaming, engaging in sexual intercourse, or 
dying. These practices thus focus on dream yoga, practice with a real or a visualized con­
sort, and preparation for the dying process. Although several texts dealing with these 
sets of six teachings have been translated into English, the details of these practices are 
traditionally considered to be highly secret and thus are typically only revealed by lamas 
who preserve them to students who are considered qualified via being initiated and very 
well trained in the preliminary and creation-​stage practices, typically by successfully 
completing a three-​year meditation retreat.
The Cakrasaṃvara tradition is a living tantric Buddhist tradition that has been pre­
served since its revelation, circa the late ninth century, until the present day. While tra­
dition has been shrouded in secrecy for much of its history, this veil has lifted somewhat 
as both the texts and teachers of this tradition have been widely disseminated around 
the world due to the Tibetan diaspora. It preserves fascinating contemplative practices 
that may be of interest to contemporary individuals interested in meditation and yoga.

Chapter 35
What the Kālamukhas 
Can Tell Us about 
Identity, Institutions, 
and Community in the 
Early Medieval Deccan
Jason Schwartz
The traditions we have variously labeled Kālamukha, Kālāmukha, or Kalāmukha 
have left an outsized material and cultural footprint upon the medieval Deccan.1 And 
yet, scholars of Indian religion and Indology have made only cursory attempts at 
reconstructing their lifeworlds. In the absence of a recoverable scriptural canon, tan­
tric studies tends to treat the Kālamukhas as a black box in our historical record whose 
contents are irretrievable. Either we have presumed that our only access to these 
traditions is through some cursory epigraphy, whose lack of doctrinal specificity un­
problematically indicates consonance with a mainline Brahmanism,2 or else it has been 
suggested that we are encountering “living fossils” perpetuating a pre-​tantric tradition 
of “Rudra asceticism,” whose contours are best gleaned from those rare moments when 
the earliest Śaiva Āgamas deign to represent their formative antecedents (Sanderson 
2006).3
This essay represents an initial attempt to revive the rather moribund study of the 
Kālamukhas by turning to fresh archives and methodologies. Most importantly, the 
evidence in question demands that we overturn our assumption that the Kālamukha 
“tradition” represents a unitary value system primarily articulated in a textual domain. 
As we shall see, the designation “Kālamukha” instead indexes vibrant and internally 
diversified “context-​specific” religious imaginaries. Within these domains, remnants 
of Atimārga praxis, especially from the Lākulas, were blended with the Mantramārga, 
particularly the Dakṣiṇasrotas dedicated to the worship of Bhairava, alongside extra-​
tantric influences (Sanderson 2006).4 Moreover, not only were the corpuses to which

--- PAGE 897 ---
872      Jason Schwartz
 
Kālamukhas lay claim heterogenous and eclectic, but they shared their spheres of op­
eration with other sorts of Śaiva ascetics and ritual specialists. In other words, I assert 
that the very state of ambiguity about the boundaries between the categories Kāpālika, 
Kālamukha, Lākula, and other Śaiva identities that so perplex us when we encounter 
them in the early medieval Sanskrit sources and that have catalyzed our scholarly 
conversations are not so much errors in interpretation as they are candid reflections of 
complex composite contemporary realities.
Given this internal plurality of Kālamukha communities, a strictly philological ap­
proach to the reconstruction of “lost” premodern religions faces certain methodological 
difficulties. However brilliantly executed, such efforts generally proceed by recovering 
a transhistorical canon of fragmentary evidence, in which the inclusion of the relevant 
materials was often originally incidental or served a polemical purpose. On the basis 
of discursive commonalities within this body of evidence, often privileging the most 
archaic materials, scholars then set out to isolate a core essence, inquiring “who were 
the Kālamukhas really and what did they believe?” The aim is to identify a canon of text 
and praxis, disambiguating core theological stances from those of competing strains of 
Śaivas.5 Such an approach presumes, then, that (1) an entextualized doctrine was the 
constitutive feature of religious life, as opposed to one of many conceptual resources, (2) 
that religious identities are static over time and space, and (3) that Śaiva communities 
and institutions were discretely organized according to their unwavering doctrinal 
affiliations. This study suggests the value of reconsidering all of these presuppositions, 
arguing in favor of reembedding texts, whenever possible, within broader lived contexts.
Toward this end, I offer three brief case studies: one purely textual, one concerned with 
visual culture in situ, and one offering regional institutional histories over the longue 
durée. Each of these will speak to the composite nature of Kālamukha imaginaries on 
and off the page, a complexity that generated a certain emic befuddlement within the 
contemporary Śaiva communities of their day. Throughout, I consider how the evidence 
at hand urges us to think more robustly about not merely the content of our sources, 
whether in text or stone, but also their workmanly dimensions. How and why do they 
direct specific messages to discrete audiences? In what contexts do they include or ex­
clude particular types of details? How might questions of form and genre shape what 
can and cannot be communicated in a given register? And finally, how might we as­
semble these intentionally delimited messages in the service of reconstructing a robust 
and multidimensional reality?
They All Look the Same to Me: Or What 
Is a Doxographer to Do?
Written from the perspective of a south Indian living around the twelfth century, the 
Sarvasiddhāntaviveka (SSV), a neglected doxography of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition,

--- PAGE 898 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      873
 
offers us a rare glimpse of tantric imaginaries in all their idiosyncratic diversity.6 Taking 
into account a far greater array of Śaiva and Śaiva adjacent traditions than any other 
work of the genre, the text shows an unusual attentiveness to the incongruity between 
inherited and idealized textual prescription and real world praxis. In places, it even be­
grudgingly recognizes that the type of conceptual clarity that scholars are so inclined 
to prize presents an awkward fit with the messiness of lived realities. At the same time, 
however, what the text offers is not a straightforward snapshot of the religious landscape 
“just as it was” but one person’s perspective. We are encountering a viewpoint shaped by 
the rhetorical and theological agenda of a partisan scholar who, for all his investment in 
verisimilitude, is ardently committed to demonstrating the superiority of his eccentric 
brand of Śaiva Siddhānta above and beyond all other systems.
Far from presenting an obstacle, however, the perspectival nature of the SSV speaks 
volumes concerning the medieval south Indian sociology of knowledge—​that is, who 
had access to what kind of knowledge and under what circumstances? For instance, the 
SSV delineates in some detail that adherents to what it calls the Vāma tradition, which 
scholars today label as belonging to the Kulamārga,7 can be categorized according to 
their chosen philosophical stances, including nondualism, dualism, a peculiar form 
of bhedābheda8 where nondifference with a variety of independent śaktis9 can be 
achieved through possession, and an ontologically pluralist pariṇāmavāda position.10 
Notwithstanding this intellectual diversity on matters of ontology and epistemology, 
however, the author of the SSV presumes that we should speak of the Vāma as a single 
Siddhānta, as these mutually exclusive ideological stances are built on contested readings 
of the exact same sources and entailed the application of many shared practices.11
Even more fundamentally, the SSV cautions us against conflating adherents of Vāma 
traditions with a fixed demography or institutionalized religious community. Any 
person, our author tells us, who has mastered the praxis of a Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, or the 
Bhairava system, once he has been initiated by a sadguru into the Vāma system,12 is ca­
pable of performing the observances of that path and achieving liberation.13 Much as 
scholars today speak of the Mantramārga as organized around a shared ritual grammar 
that crosses the boundary of religious traditions, the SSV speaks to a functional inter­
changeability of all Mantramārga praxis systems, sometimes rendering “doctrine” 
trivial or irrelevant, even when it extends to the workings of such fundamental practices 
as initiation. Perhaps even more significantly, this fluidity suggests a greater degree of 
social permeability within and across religious communities than we have generally 
presupposed, for only in a social world where individual agents frequently crossed such 
boundaries would behavior of this sort not instantly identify a person as a potentially 
disreputable adept of the Vāma.
It is this same portrait of nested religious realities with blurred boundaries, then, that 
characterizes the SSV’s account of pre-​tantric Atimārga traditions. The author takes 
as his point of departure a somewhat familiar inherited schema, the division of reli­
gious traditions into sets of six samayas,14 here further expanded to encompass the ex­
ternal (bāhya) traditions on the one hand (Lokāyata, Buddhist, Jain, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, 
Māyāvāda, and Pañcarātra), and internal (antaḥ) traditions on the other (Śaiva,

--- PAGE 899 ---
874      Jason Schwartz
 
Pāśupata, Vāma, Bhairava, Mahāvrata, and Kālamukha). More remarkably, however, 
he proceeds to discuss at least forty primarily Mantramārga traditions.15 Pre-​tantric 
traditions, in contrast, are effectively subdivided into two interrelated groupings: one 
treating the “Kālamukhas,” “Kāpāla Lākulas,” and “Mahāvratins” as an ambiguously 
interrelated set, while another similarly dissects the Pāśupata landscape. While the 
Pāśupatas in the SSV show very little continuity with the classical sources, our author 
is particularly well informed, it appears, about Kālamukha and Kālamukha-​adjacent 
traditions. Fundamentally, the SSV perceives both the Lākulas and the Mahāvratins as 
successive internal developments emerging out of a baseline Kālamukhamata. That is to 
say, an exceptionally well-​informed Śaiva writing in northern Tamil Nadu believed that 
the Kāpāla-​Lākulas accepted the canonical positions and practices of the Kālamukhas, 
rejecting only those elements conflicting with their own supplementary practices, while 
the Mahāvratins in turn accepted both Kālamukha and Lākula normativities while also 
adopting their own distinctive practices.16
Approaching these transmissions in reverse order, Mahāvratins are distinguished by 
being liṅgadhārins, bearing a portable aniconic liṅga on their bodies at all times and 
supplementing the general reverence of the śivabhakta with a special veneration of re­
ligious authorities called jaṅgamas.17 Doctrinally, they recognize a plurality of souls 
and two of the three canonical forms of mala, but not as an individuated function,18 
while worshipping an immanent and all-​powerful form of Sadāśiva. Sartorially, they 
combine the five signs of a Kāpālika with a sacred thread of human hair, while wearing 
earrings and travelling about with a snake and a great jewel. And yet, apart from these 
emendations, they are quite difficult to distinguish from the Lākulas, the original 
transmitters of the eighteen Pramāṇa scriptures,19 not merely because they are both 
skull bearing ascetics but also because they are supposedly making selective use of the 
very same textual canons.
From the perspective of our author, the skull bearing (kapālin) Lākulas are the 
custodians of the Kāpālasiddhānta, represented as a named canon with titles largely 
corresponding to the Lākula Pramāṇa scriptures.20 This seems to suggest that by this 
period, the “pre-​tantric” Somasiddhāntins have disappeared from the lived religious 
landscape, while the Mahāvratins have evolved into a distinctive community acting as a 
formative antecedent to the traditions of the Vīramāheśvaras, in a manner that demands 
a reworking of stale inherited doxographical categories to bring them into alignment 
with contemporary realities. Despite their given designation, the Kāpālasiddhāntins 
are here seen as yogins who meditate upon the self, adopting attitudes of extreme dis­
passion. Skull bearers who beg and sing for their alms, otherwise consuming no other 
food, they revere Rudra as the lord of the world, while subordinating him to the great 
god (Mahādeva) who dances in the great cremation ground during the cosmic dissolu­
tion. As with the Mahāvratins, they also recognize a plurality of souls, and two forms of 
mala, while maintaining that liberation simply involves becoming similar to Śiva, much 
as a constellation strives to imitate the sun. In contrast to the Kālamukhas, they treat 
the principle of time, and not the ontic category called Dhruva,21 as the causal engine 
generating worldly differentiation and delusion.

--- PAGE 900 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      875
 
As for the Kālamukhas, either strategically or fortuitously, their portion of the 
doxography in the published sources has suffered substantial damage, particularly re­
garding the Kālamukhavrata.22 We are in a somewhat better position, however, con­
cerning the doctrinal dimensions imputed to the tradition. Against the Mantramārga, 
and the proliferation of intermediary demiurgic forces, the tradition seems to ada­
mantly deny any distinction between Rudra and the supreme deity, such that the myriad 
of Śaiva iconographic manifestations are simply perceived to be extensions of this core 
reality. Incidentally, this framework seems to include the Rudrabhaktas themselves 
(rudrāṃśa), whose apparent distinctiveness from the deity is to be seen as no different 
in kind from Rudra’s particularized manifestation as Sadāśiva or Dakṣiṇāmūrti, each 
of which is aligned with expressing a specific function.23 Instead of some strong claim 
about ontology, we encounter a more restricted assertion that all kinds of sanctified 
things partake of Rudra’s nature in precisely the same way.24 Thus, the individual self, 
having arrived at a balance of karmas (karmasāmya), becomes gradually purified of the 
three malas through a practice (anuṣṭhāna) that engenders a conjunction (saṃyoga) 
between Śiva and the Self (ātman), yielding a form of liberation where multiple selves 
shine like constellations reflecting the light of the supreme sun.25
This irenic inclusivism within the Lākula-​Kālamukha-​Mahāvratin continuum, 
however, appears to radically exclude the Bhairavasiddhānta. As depicted in the SSV, 
the Kālamukha perspective emphatically asserts that the Lord manifests directly as 
Mahādeva and Rudra, but not ever as Bhairava (rudra eva na bhairavaḥ). In fact, this ex­
clusion of Bhairava from what constitutes Śaiva knowledge is a conspicuous rhetorical 
choice made throughout the doxography.26 On the one hand, starting from his chosen 
definition of the scope of internal Śaiva knowledge, our author makes copious use of 
inherited material deeply concerned with the Dakṣiṇasrotas. On the other, however, he 
makes an atypically minimal effort to specify the doctrines and praxis of Bhairava re­
lated traditions. In this regard, rather than reflecting lived religious realities—​which, 
as we will soon see, were replete with Bhairava related imagery and praxis—​the SSV 
seems to reflect the particular historical moment within Śaiva Siddhānta discourse out 
of which it emerges. In contrast to earlier generations of less philosophically inclined 
Saiddhāntikas, the SSV seeks to cultivate a “pure” Śaiva knowledge newly segregated 
from proximate “others” it deems somewhat dubious.27 This profound anxiety about 
being conflated with the “wrong” kind of Śaivism finds its clearest expression in a cu­
rious parenthetical aside, inserted between the discussion of the Kāpāla Lākulas and the 
Kālamukhas. The author quips: “how is it that some scholars have imputed the existence 
of a doctrinal unity [ekadeśamatatvena] between the doctrine of the Kālamukhas and 
the Śaivas just spoken of [namely, the Kāpālas]?”28
Once again, through the thickness of his descriptions, our partisan Saiddhāntika au­
thor is offering his reader insights above and beyond his intended purposes. We have 
just seen that the rhetorical distancing of “a pure Rudra asceticism,” whether real or 
imagined, from unsavory and more transgressive forms of religious practice is not 
merely an artifact of modern scholarship, but an apologetics with a deep history. We have 
also learned that many educated people in our author’s day, just as in our own, whether

--- PAGE 901 ---
876      Jason Schwartz
 
erroneously or strategically, readily conflated the Kālamukhas and Lākulas, while 
viewing the Mahāvratins as a closely adjacent phenomenon. The simultaneous existence 
of both perspectives among educated people strongly suggests something fundamental 
and somewhat unexpected about the nature of religion during this period. Specifically, 
in marked contrast to what will emerge with early modernity, it does not entail the public 
performance and publicization of particularized identity. In other words, it was only 
within restricted networks, such as during a learned debate among rivals or a teaching 
session from which nonadepts were excluded, that the specific doctrinal differences be­
tween different types of Śaivas would be aired. Especially if we presume that the lost 
extract on the Kālamukhavrata had also incorporated a skull observance, even when 
one attends with great care to identifying points of contestation, our doxography has in­
advertently elucidated that the distinctions between these communities—​indeed their 
conceptual distinctiveness from other forms of Śaiva thought that elsewhere in this text 
will be associated with different variants on the Siddhānta—​were mostly a matter of the 
narcissism of small differences. In practical terms, someone less savvy than our highly 
learned author, called on to pick a specific subject out of a lineup, would have struggled 
to discern which, if any, of the ascetics on hand was the Kālamukha.
It’s What Is on the Inside That Counts: 
Kālamukhas through Their Material 
Culture
As we are beginning to see, in the decidedly nonconfessional society that was early me­
dieval India, how “religious” communities positioned themselves in relation to the ad­
jacent social worlds of their neighboring “others” was less a reflection of their “deeply 
held beliefs” than it entailed a strategic navigation of competing scholastic, institu­
tional, bureaucratic, and juridical norms. Integral to this process, as in much of India 
today, was the selective representation of communities as they engaged with different 
facets of the legal and political system or represented themselves within specific kinds 
of lived spaces. Even in reference to the very same institutions at a similar moment in 
history, the specificity with which the identities of religious authorities are indicated in 
our documentary records thus says more about the particular bureaucratic practices 
being deployed, as well as the degree of intimacy of the donor with the institution, than 
it does about the ebb and flow of the fortunes of a religious community. Likewise, when 
it comes to treating inscriptions as material objects or visual representations as reflective 
of core community values, specificity of context is everything. With this in mind, I will 
be discussing briefly several institutional spaces often treated as quintessential examples 
of Kālamukha institutional complexes, each of which sheds additional light upon the 
author of the SSV’s deep anxieties about distinguishing an imagined authentic Atimārga 
from the Dakṣiṇasrotas. Succinctly, contrary to our expectations, there is a profound

--- PAGE 902 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      877
 
disjuncture between the Kālamukha imaginaries preserved within of our documen­
tary records when they are treated as texts without context and the portrait that emerges 
when we reembed these supposed messages from nowhere within the relevant material 
cultural landscape.
In Shimoga District in southwestern Karnataka lies Baḷḷigāvĕ, quintessential hub of 
Kālamukha religiosity, home to the lineages of the Śaktipariṣad. Indeed, when our sec­
ondary literature, inspired by David Lorenzen’s (1972) seminal work The Kāpālikas and 
Kālamukhas, generalizes about Kālamukha tradition, it is typically unconsciously re­
fracting its perceptions through the lens of the inscriptional corpus of the Śaktipariṣad, 
concentrated in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Written in a highly Sanskritic and 
formalized register of old Kannada, these documents aim rhetorically to communicate 
the overwhelming erudition of the Kālamukhācāryas of the Śaktipariṣad, their compre­
hensive mastery over the entire spectrum of Brāhmaṇical śāstra, and their habitual suc­
cess in utterly obliterating their opponents, whether Jaina, Buddhist, or Mīmāṃsaka, 
in the context of formal philosophical debates (Rice 1903, 174).29 In fact, it is based on 
this mastery of a primarily Brāhmaṇical canon that Lorenzen dismisses doxographical 
representations of Kālamukhas as antinomian skull bearing tantric practitioners as a 
distortive polemic. After all, who could ever imagine a learned tāntrika!
When we begin to think of texts not as snapshots from the past but as particularized 
and interested strategic interventions into a multifaceted social reality, a markedly dif­
ferent picture emerges. As Shubha Shanthamurthy (2015) has shown, except at the very 
earliest strata of the corpus, rather than representing the concrete accomplishments of 
individual Śaktipariṣad ācāryas, these paeans to the brilliance of the successive heads 
of maṭhas are highly repetitive and standardized. In other words, when we read the 
śāsanas of Baḷḷigāvĕ, we are encountering an iterated scribal formula, analogous to the 
frozen laudatory titles (birudas) used to define a dynasty of rulers, where a tropology 
of conquests in scholarship substitutes for inheriting claims to great-​grandfathers’ 
victories on the battlefield. Just as significantly, these templates do not even originate 
among the Kālamukhas. Rather, they are adapted from rhetoric widely in use among 
Digambara Jains, eager to prove their own uber-​Brāhmaṇical and learned pedigree.30
My point here is not to suggest that this implied erudition is wholly imaginary, but 
rather that its presentation as constitutive of the Kālamukha worldview is not merely 
documentary but served a specific purpose, namely, the cultivation of a rhetorical ef­
fect, directed at both proximate and distant “others.” It creates a public impression that 
the word Kālamukha primarily conveys impeccable participation in the imaginaries of 
the Sanskrit and old Kannada cosmopolises, without specifying the doctrinal and ritual 
dimensions of what it means to be a Kālamukha within the context of multifunctional 
cultural spheres inhabited by diverse social agents. In contrast, when one attends to both 
discursive and physical spaces restricted to Kālamukhas alone and their direct disciples, 
a markedly different set of values, influences, and priorities are in evidence.
A salient example of this dynamic, enacted in stone, is provided by the central ritual 
complex of Baḷḷigāvĕ’s Bhujaṅgāvaḷi Kālamukhas—​the lineage of the snake branch—​
which will prove an apt moniker indeed. Shanthamurthy has suggested that the temple

--- PAGE 903 ---
878      Jason Schwartz
 
of Tripurāntakēśvara, which contains some of Baḷḷigāvĕ’s most spectacular and best-​
preserved material culture, was constructed, or at least substantively revitalized, under 
the direction of Trilōcana Paṇḍita, foremost among the Kālamukhas of his lineage (c. 
eleventh century). (On the lineage out of Tripurāntakēśvara, see Shanthamurthy 2015, 
33–​38.) Where this underexamined site is mentioned at all, archaeological and art his­
torical literature has focused on the exterior of its portico, a multifunctional public 
space where representatives of the Bhujaṅgāvaḷi might well have received their visitors. 
Though apart from a magnificent sixteen-​armed Durgā dancing upon the back of a 
lion, the rest of the exterior of the temple is rather plain, this front porch is replete with 
depictions of secular erotica and kings on the hunt intermingled with episodes from the 
Pañcatantra and Rāmāyaṇa. In short, the whole tableau evokes a common courtly ethos. 
Step inside the structure, however, and the atmosphere instantaneously shifts to reflect a 
rather different visual idiom: the culture of the cremation grounds.
Looming over Tripurāntakēśvara’s first chamber are the leering visages of two im­
mense door guardians (dvārapālas). To the right of the doorway, the more spectacular 
figure (Figure 35.1) has a crown and girdle belt (mekhela) adorned with human skulls. 
The fragmentary remains of a hand seem to shake a broken hand-​drum (ḍamaru) as 
his long dreadlocks (jaṭās) swing wildly about. There is a serpent wrapped around his

throat and an immense five-​headed cobra at his feet. In the next chamber, before the 
garbhagṛha, such ghoulish visages are replaced by an equally immense and exquisitely 
rendered pair of female figures. As inviting as their counterparts were terrifying, each 
stands under a different species of (kula)31 tree encircled by a panoply of serpents and 
nāgas. On the door lintel, Brahmā and Viṣṇu flank the central figure of many-​armed 
Gajasaṃhāramūrti, who unmistakably bears the fanged visage of Bhairava.
If anything, the small figural representations on the pillar inside the second ante­
chamber are even more suggestive. A naked female ascetic, with long dreadlocks, sits on 
a coiled serpent throne (Figure 35.2). While her sword rests upon a severed human head, 
she worships her personal portable liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga). As if to suggest a homology between 
the two figures, directly across from her is a Śākta goddess, plausibly an antecedent of 
the scheduled caste folk deity Maṃchamma (Figure 35.3). Her foot resting on a serpent, 
her four arms, bearing trident, sword, ḍamaru, and skull bowl, mark her as analogous to 
the most common regional iconography assigned to Bhairava. Adjacent pillars display a 
similar pairing of a seated naked male Kālamukha ascetic with long dreadlocks (Figure 
35.4) and a standing Bhairava (Figure 35.5) displaying identical implements.
If Indic texts tend to speak in voices that are prolix and idealizing, then messages 
in stone are blunt yet enigmatic. Is this a pairing of social agents and their respective 
focuses of ritual identification through visualization, or is the female figure also an 
imagined reality? To be candid, we simply do not know. What is clear, however, is that 
the material culture of Baḷḷigāvĕ has integrated images unmistakably saturated with a 
visual idiom derived from Śākta traditions and the Bhairavasiddhānta that must have 
been theologically significant to its inhabitants. And yet, although these features might 
align with specific textual representations, they evidently did not exhaust the conceptual 
resources animating the lived religion of these Kālamukhas. Even within its institutional 
epicenter, Kālamukhas drew liberally upon regionalized vernacular imaginaries, such as 
snake cults, perhaps venerating goddesses such as Mānĕ Maṃchamma. Perhaps it was 
this very synthesis that compelled the residents of Tripurāntakēśvara to self-​identify as 
the lineage (āvali) of the serpent.
The inflection of Tripurāntakēśvara’s visual culture with the visual idioms of Śākta 
and Bhairava related traditions, at least within circumscribed spaces to which di­
verse publics had little access, is hardly an aberration. In fact, these same stylistic and 
conceptual choices are the defining features of virtually all the surviving Kālamukha 
ritual centers that I have visited throughout the Deccan where substantive material 
culture is preserved in situ. A particularly salient case, everywhere evocative of these 
hybrid imaginaries, is provided by the artisan training college and ritual complex at 
Trikūṭēśvara in Gadag. Over a hundred miles northeast of Baḷḷigāvĕ, Trikūṭēśvara has 
been read by scholarship primarily through the lens of a single, rather lucid Sanskrit 
inscription (Hultzsch 1900–​1901, 89–​107). Composed in 1192 CE at the direction of 
the Hoysala King Ballāla, the text praises the preceptor Siddhānticandrabhūṣaṇa 
Paṇḍitadeva of the lineage of the Kālamukhācāryas. He is celebrated extensively 
for renovating everything at the Gadag complex—​apart from the main structure of 
Trikūṭēśvara itself—​and for his integrity and magnanimous charity, which inspired him

--- PAGE 905 ---
880      Jason Schwartz
 
to feed, clothe, and care for desperate people with a resolve more consistent than even 
the ocean tides. Complementing the three stationary liṅgas that provide Trikūṭēśvara 
with its name, this celibate yogin, we are told, is a moving liṅga (jaṅgama) in ceaseless 
union (samāgama) with the goddess who abides at all times as half of his own body.

With a visual style predating the material culture of the reign of the Kalyāṇi Cāḷukya 
emperor Vikramāditya VI onward (r. 1076–​1126 CE), many of these images apparently 
originate from much earlier phases in Trikūṭēśvara’s institutional history. Indeed, in 
both their style and medium of execution, these iconic images (mūrtis) diverge sharply 
from Trikūṭēśvara’s most famous deity, the majestic Sarasvatī (Figure 35.11) who is 
housed within an independent structure incorporated into the monastic complex dedi­
cated to the training of the artisans (śilpins) under Gadag’s Kālamukhas.34

Photo by Jason Schwartz.

EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      889
 
In a testament to the agglutinative nature of these site-​specific traditions, where the 
past is not discarded but habitually incorporated into an ever-​expanding canon of the­
ologically charged possibilities, as the Kālamukhas at Trikūṭēśvara evolved in their 
commitments, they quite literally built on top of older imaginaries without obscuring 
them from view. Such an approach results in the rare preservation of Trikūṭēśvara’s arti­
cles of incorporation in the foundational inscription, literally embedded in the temple’s 
outer reinforcing wall (prākāra; Rao 1986, n. 48). Composed in 1002 CE, a full twenty 
years before our earliest textual records at Baḷḷigāvĕ, and expressed in an archaic and 
irregular register of Kannada, Trikūṭēśvara, at the time of its founding as an autono­
mously administered land grant—​seemingly contemporary with the core of the temple 
and thus the instituting of its liturgy—​was under the direction of a monastic overseer (S. 
maṭhādhipati, or Kannada jīya) named Vākkhāni.35
Figure 35.11.  Sarasvatī maṇḍapa, Trikūṭēśvara, Gadag. Sarasvatī.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 915 ---
890      Jason Schwartz
 
Depicted as “a knower of the kāḷajñāna,”36 Vākkhāni is nowhere identified with any 
specific religious community, whereas Gadag’s later documentary records habitually in­
voke such affiliation. Instead, he positions himself within a specific preceptorial lineage 
(guruparaṃparā), defined in geospatial terms.
Succinctly, he is the disciple of an identically named teacher residing at Kǒppina 
(modern-​day Kopal), who was in turn the disciple of “the scholar at Pūliya” (pūliyapa
ṇḍita).37 Needless to say, this rhetorical choice to privilege place over the names of spe­
cific people renders the correlation of Vākkhāni-​at-​Gadag’s guru with named ācāryas 
at other sites effectively impossible.38 When it comes to questions of place, we are in 
a slightly better position. The town of Pūliya/​Puligere, an alternative designation for 
modern-​day Lakṣmēśvara near present-​day Gadag, as far back as the composition of 
the ninth-​century Kāvirājamārga, has been revered as the “heart of Karnataka,” the site 
of the composition of such literary classics as the Pampābhārata of Kannada’s ādikavi. 
In other words, Vākkhāni’s lineage of ascetics situate their emergence not from the pe­
riphery of the literary and cultural worlds of the early medieval Kuntaladeśa but from its 
very epicenter.39
Though its exterior (Figure 35.12), remains unapologetic in its Śākta-​Śaiva 
commitments (Figures 35.13 and 35.14), the central Śaiva complex at Lakṣmēśvara—​the 
Figure 35.12.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Details of Bhairavas on śikhara.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 916 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      891
 
temple of Somēśvara—​is a composite structure, largely a product of the twelfth and early 
thirteenth centuries. Among the preserved fragments of another early medieval temple, 
possibly a prior incarnation of Somēśvara, and several of the doorway lintels within 
the older portions of Somēśvara itself, the discerning eye will notice the recurrence of 
a figure iconographically identical to the peculiar Naṭeśa we examined at Trikūṭēśvara, 
right down to the mātuluṅga. In one fragment (Figure 35.15) this mātuluṅga-​bearing 
Naṭeśa is even encircled by the deities of the directions, identifying him as the main 
focus of worship of an earlier local liturgy. Such stray relics provide us with clear visual 
indications of an otherwise obscured entangled history.
In other regards, however, there are striking discontinuities. For example, of the 
dozens of seated and standing Bhairavas and Śākta goddesses incorporated into 
Somēśvara’s śikhara, none of them is seated on a serpent; indeed, snake related imagery 
is almost entirely absent from the complex. In its place, we find traces of other highly 
specific extratextual affiliations. Some of these, such as a huge spread-​eagle Lajjā Gaurī 
(Figure 35.16) still under worship, reflect transregional religious focuses long predating 
Mantramārga and maybe even Atimārga traditions, whose popular significance 
demanded they be incorporated into liturgy, independent of the reigning theologies 
of the day.
Figure 35.13.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Details of Bhairavas on śikhara.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 917 ---
892      Jason Schwartz
 
In other instances, however, key extratextual elements stem from roughly recover­
able historical contexts. Such seems to be the case with the central focus of worship 
at Somēśvara, which, in a style and medium utterly distinct from images produced 
in the Deccan, depicts Śiva and Pārvatī riding on a bull (Figure 35.17). Oral tradition 
among the temple officiants asserts that this image (Figure 35.18) was rescued by a cer­
tain Ayya Svāmī from Somanātha in Saurashtra when that famous place was under 
siege, and was then imported by a diaspora of Śaiva ācāryas seeking refuge, from 
whom the current temple managers trace their descent. While the specifics of such 
tales are impossible to confirm, visual representations preserved on a gateway into the 
temple complex (Figure 35.19) indicate that the centrality of the worship of this image 
substantively predates the visual style generally in evidence on Somēśvara’s exterior, 
aligning instead with the sort of figurative representations we find within the old core 
of temple.
In essence, what we are grappling with here is a story of divergent evolution, 
illustrating the plasticity of lived traditions. Sometime within the hundred-​year eviden­
tiary vacuum between the founding of Trikūṭēśvara in 1002 CE and the composition of 
our earliest substantive Śaiva histories in 1102 CE, the authorities in Gadag rebranded 
themselves as descending from an unbroken line of self-​defined Kālamukhas, only 
Figure 35.14.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Details of Bhairavas on śikhara.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 918 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      893
 
subtly inflected by older Kāpālika inheritances. At the same time, the monastic complex 
came to focus on the training of master sculptors and the production of material culture, 
which would define the mission of the institution into early modernity.
Concurrently, the ācāryas at Lakṣmēśvara chose a different path, proudly publicizing 
their primordial status as Mahāvratins. Older points of commonality were rendered 
relics, their places occupied by localized commitments and new site-​specific histories. 
In both trajectories, we see the gradual thickening of ascriptive identities, which 
begins to characterize religious communities by the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, 
prefiguring the formalized sectarianization of early modernity. The labels these 
lineages came to embrace were often as much strategic as they were descriptive, for 
these new identities are hardly exhaustive. Sometimes, indeed, they were barely indic­
ative of the particular practices and commitments that lent these communities their 
distinctive character.

Photo by Jason Schwartz.

Putting It Together: The Āvalis 
and the Tantras
In 1061 CE, while residing with his army in a military camp just outside the walls of 
Puliya, the Kalyāni Cāḷukya emperor Āhavamalla issued a command that a cer­
tain Sōmēśvara Paṇḍita, already recognized as a monastic head and overseer of the 
Nāgarēśvara temple at Sūṇḍi (Figures 35.20, 35.21 and 35.22), be granted an additional 
Figure 35.16.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Lajjā Gaurī.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 920 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      895
 
Figure 35.17.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Śiva-​Pārvatī on Vṛsabha in situ.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 921 ---
896      Jason Schwartz
 
village, so that with the revenue it would provide, he might continue his excellent work 
renovating Śaiva spaces and performing Śaiva pūjās.40 When placed in relation to other 
documentary records preserved in situ from the same period, however, Āhavamalla’s 
beneficence reads less like an act of personal devotion than an exercise in administra­
tive prudence or even restorative justice. Like so much of the central Deccan, Sūṇḍi 
seems to have been heavily impacted by the atypically destructive and deliberately icon­
oclastic invasion of the region by Rājarāja Cōḻa, a cultural calamity that only resolved 
itself when that wildly ambitious ruler was killed in battle in 1052 CE. As a series of in­
triguing but rather fragmentary inscriptions preserved at Sūṇḍi itself makes evident, 
as early as 1050 CE and extending well into the next decade, the imperial court of the 
Kalyāni Cāḷukyas was taking concrete action to contain potential irruptions of social 
disorder. Although we might assume that such actions aimed to legitimate and reaffirm 
Cāḷukya sovereignty over regions that had asserted their independence in a political 
vacuum, these interventions were in fact of a markedly different character. Succinctly, 
our records reveal efforts to reinstate prior statutes and particular regulations, not 
merely as they pertain to specific land grants, but in relation to discrete institutional 
spaces and communities.41 The texts repeatedly assert that the Cāḷukya rulers and their 
Figure 35.18.  Sōmēśvara Temple, Lakṣmēśvara. Śiva-​Pārvatī on Vṛsabha in situ, without 
alaṃkāras.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 922 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      897
 
representatives would continue to protect the specific dharmas of these places in align­
ment with local governing norms. Nevertheless, to affirm the pluralized rights of specific 
preexisting sites and communities required a new kind of taking stock of localized best 
practices. And with this comes a revolution in the expectations assigned to the produc­
tion of documentary records that have specific evidentiary functions. A new emphasis 
is placed on the specification of recipients and other social agents, and more attention 
is paid to how new endowments and acts of institution building might relate to preex­
isting local social realities. In other words, suddenly in the middle of the eleventh cen­
tury, nearly everywhere in the western Deccan where Kannada serves as the language of 
power, it becomes possible to tell much richer and concrete stories about the lifeworlds 
of religious institutions. This fact is less a reflection of transformed religious realities 
than the result of a newly attentive scribal apparatus capturing long-​standing realities in 
a refreshed documentary idiom.
Indeed, as is common with these institutional spaces, the Śaiva presence at Sūṇḍi 
commences with the earliest documentation we have regarding the city. And yet, the 
early tenth-​century sources are not tales of beginnings but highly delimited, virtually 
context-​free fly-​by glimpses of thriving institutions. Thus, for example, we encounter a 
Figure 35.19.  Detail from gateway into temple complex showing image under worship in the 
early medieval period, Lakṣmēśvara.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 923 ---
898      Jason Schwartz
 
certain Mūrtiśivācārya, depicted with traits very often ascribed to Kālamukhas but as­
sociated with no specific temple or monastery, working in concert with the authorities 
of Puli/​Pūliya to feed a thousand ascetics, a state of affairs that presumes that these 
communities were already exceptionally well-​funded, transregionally networked, and 
engaged with substantial publics.42 We generally find such specifics, however, only 
where Śaiva authorities or their direct devotees are the issuing agents. When the royal 
court or its subsidiaries are producing the records, especially if the focus of the grant has 
no connection to Śaiva authorities, representations of Śaiva agents become deliberately 
vague and muted, even to the extent of ācāryas, simply dispensed with as “dēvara,” being 
conflated with the gods they serve.43
With the mid-​eleventh-​century changes in scribal conventions, over the course of a 
decade, our records at Sūṇḍi suggest that Cāḷukya administrators achieved an increas­
ingly sophisticated grasp of on-​the-​ground local realities in accordance with courtly 
priorities. First, in 1050 CE, we find a blanket reinstitution of preinvasion norms, along 
with a delineation of local laws, punishments, and patterns of revenue collection. Then 
three years later, in a document that atypically mimics Cōḻa records in all but its language 
of expression, the Cāḷukyas reinstitute the prior administrative regime governing the 
temple founded by the royal family, which bears the name of the queen Akkā Mahādevī. 
Figure 35.20.  Joḍukalaśa, Sudi,
