This text is so fragmentary that what survives amounts to little more than a partial list of 
proper names and their assigned monetary and real estate allotments. Despite its frag­
mentary condition, we do find specific mention of a certain Viśvaśivācārya as head of 
the institution, and under his purview goldsmiths, cāmara bearers, flutists, and temple 
gaṇikās. Four years after this, the bureaucracy decides to affirm in writing, on behalf of 
the thousand ascetics that make up its constituency, that Akkēśvara will continue to be 
managed according to preestablished rules and norms, and that the Cāḷukyas will con­
tinue to protect the preexisting dharma specific to the community and not, by implica­
tion, advocate for the imposition of some other dharma norms. In other words, it is only 
eight years into an ongoing process of reconstructing a community that the Cāḷukya bu­
reaucracy deigns to acknowledge the numerous other Śaiva and Jain institutions already 
present within the community.
When they do so, their chosen focus is Sōmēśvara Paṇḍita, remembered by his 
successors as the progenitor of the Kālamukha lineage of the Āvalis.44 No such des­
ignation, however, is in evidence in our earliest record. To be sure, much as we have 
seen with the inscriptions at Baḷḷigāvĕ, Sōmēśvara, lord of ascetics (sōmēśvarayati­
patiyaṃ), keeper of the divine vow (divyabratīndrar), whose virtue in austerity is 
exceeded only by his stainless conduct and skill in the domain of learning (ĕṃba 
Figure 35.22.  Joḍukalaśa, Interior garbhagrḥa, Sudi. Image of Kālamukha ascetic.
Photo by Jason Schwartz.

--- PAGE 926 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      901
 
tapōvikhyātiyēnĕṃb’amaḷinacaritrakhyātiyēnĕṃba vidyācaturatvakhyātiyēn), is effu­
sively, albeit formulaically, praised for his excess of erudition. Our ācārya, for example, 
serves as a sun to [open] the lotus of logic (naiyāyikasarasija-​mārttaṇḍa) and an afflicter 
of the bloodlines of the Mīṃāmsakas (mīmāṃ[s]‌akagōtratrāsi). In addition, in more 
pragmatic terms, the Bhaṭṭāraka or dēvara Sōmēśvara, disciple of a certain Vakkhāni 
(vakkhānisūta), whereabouts unknown, is also identified as an administrator, a task that 
entails managing a monastery and governing a temple, here called Nāgēśvara.45
In this latter capacity, our Śaiva ācārya is assigned responsibility for overseeing 
a cornucopia of different varieties of temple dancers, the temple drummer, a stone 
mason, and a flutist. This relatively restricted on-​site staff provides further indica­
tion that the temple, but not necessarily the monastery, that Sōmēśvara is overseeing 
had only been recently institutionalized, a task carried out by a minister of a 
Cāḷukya king named Nāgadēva, who seems to have been Sōmēśvara Paṇḍita’s dis­
ciple. Though the document informs us of a regulation that while gŏravas46 who are 
also Kālamukhas are indeed permitted to stay at the temple, if they indulge them­
selves too much with the temple women, or if students enrolled on site neglect their 
studies, the administrator is required to drive them out. In other words, within this 
text, while Sōmēśvara is implored to manage the behavior of iterant Kālamukhas 
as they pass through the premises, neither he nor his lineage are identified as 
Kālamukhas themselves.
With the passage of a decade, the situation looks very different. Again Sōmēśvara 
Paṇḍita, the beneficiary of a new endowment, seems to have become responsible for the 
management of multiple additional temples, including those whose chief constituency 
comes from artisan, goldsmith, and merchant castes, some of whom seem to be his dis­
ciples, and is now in a position to provide for the mass feeding of ascetics. The passage 
of another year yields even more expanded endowments, incorporating rights to addi­
tional lands, many of them within Sūṇḍi itself. With new resources come new privileges 
and responsibilities. Suddenly, Sōmēśvara, here simply referred to as Munisōma, per­
haps evoking the blurred boundaries between Kālamukha, Lākula, and Mahāvratin we 
have encountered so many times before,47 has both a named successor, Vigrahēśvara, 
and an initiated son, Śrīvallabha, along with a grand disciple, Kalyāṇaśakti. And it is 
only in these later records that our now thoroughly entrenched ācārya, his legacy 
ensured and social position a fait accompli given that he is legally an autonomous agent 
who now owns or has rights to half the facilities in town, suddenly starts presenting 
himself as an incarnation of Lakulīśa, fond of the Lākulāgamas (lākuḷāgamaprasannar; 
Rao 1986, n. 153). In other words, doctrinal specificity has a time and a place, and that 
tends to be when you are in indisputably in charge.
For my purposes, it suffices now to flash forward, to tie this case study together with 
my earlier considerations of how lived Kālamukha religion operates at the confluence 
of the entextualized traditions of the Mantramārga, site-​specific institutional realities, 
and local religion. Serendipitously, to do so requires me to stage a brief encounter with 
one of the most vividly realized personages captured in the documentary records of the

--- PAGE 927 ---
902      Jason Schwartz
 
Deccan, Somēśvara’s great-​grand-​disciple, the Siddha Kaḷēśvara. In a record from 1167 
CE, we are introduced to Kaḷēśvara and his lineage:
among the Kālamukha order of the Nakharēśvara temple at Sudi, by whom the āvalis 
are honored, the firm-​minded, chief munis, Śrī Kaḷēśvara—​the king of those engaged 
in vows—​attained fame. Among the Kālamukhas, honored by the great Sind[h]‌a lin­
eage, the most excellent of ācāryas, Sōmēśvara, had a student Vigrahēśvara Budha 
the learned. His student was Yōgēśvara, the Rājaguru, endowed with a multitude of 
merit. His chief student was Kaḷēśvara, the Saiddhāntika Rājaguru, the sole refuge 
for wise men. . . . Noble Kaḷēśvara has embraced the role of guru of the world
(Desai 1956, 66).48
With the passage of just shy of a hundred years, Sōmēśvara’s tradition has ascended 
to even greater prominence, having served for two generations at least as Rājagurus to 
the Sindha kings. Just as significantly, the lineage is now proudly proclaiming itself to be 
a Kālamukha tradition, with a fixed geographical locus as well as a particular doctrinal 
feature, namely its characteristic honoring of the “āvalis.” At the same time, however, the 
past has not merely been honored, it has also been adjusted. Sōmēśvara’s grand-​disciple 
Kalyāṇaśakti, who appears nowhere in subsequent sources, has been forgotten. Perhaps 
even more significantly, the very nature of the temple headquarters at Sūṇḍi has been 
reimagined. No longer is it Nāgarēśvara, named after a now irrelevant Cāḷukya minister. 
Now it is Nakharēśvara, the collective expression of the Nakharasamūha, in this case 
very specifically, the goldsmiths, responsible for the day-​to-​day administration of its af­
fairs on behalf of the Kālamukha pontiff, who is also their guru. Elsewhere, we learn that 
Kaḷēśvara began his career at Sūṇḍi responding to the needs of these very people. By 1167 
CE, now head of his lineage, he has assumed an even grander office that entails a posting 
out of station, to the great pīṭha of Kukkunūr.
A full account of Kaḷēśvara’s integration into this multifaceted sacred center, 
which has its own recoverable, longue durée history of profound interest to the dis­
cipline of tantric studies, will have to await another occasion (see Schwartz 2023, 
chap. 4). For the moment, I will focus on one rather surprising facet of Kaḷēśvara’s 
tenure at Kukkunūr. Specifically, records point to an undercurrent of frustration 
with the discrepancy between Kaḷēśvara’s personal esoteric religious commitments 
and the understandings held by visiting devotees whose site-​specific religious duties 
he was obliged to accommodate on their own terms. To understand the passage, 
we need to recognize that the Mahāmāyā Temple at Kukkunūr’s garbhagṛha housed 
three deities, each of which had its own distinct mūrti. From Kaḷēśvara’s perspec­
tive, the goddess Kālikā, the mother of the primordial dissolution, and Kapāḷīśa 
Bhairava stood alongside the supreme eldest goddess (jyēṣṭhē) who was none other 
than Siddhayōgēśvarī. Visitors to the shrine, confronted with a material cultural 
representation of the pan–​South Indian goddess Jyeṣṭhā, replete with her crow com­
panion and fan, seem to have seen things rather differently. The resultant tension is 
evoked by a particularly elegant verse:

--- PAGE 928 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      903
 
With her winnowing fan, immediately, swinging [it] delightfully she snuffs out the 
flame of the lamp that is the life of the rogue, who, out of stupidity and blinded 
by intoxication challenges [her]. It’s as if, at that moment, she subjects his body 
to the beak of her frightening crow.
Who would dare say that Jyeṣṭhā is a common [sāmānya] goddess?
What person can survive that great goddess, Mother Māri of insatiable thirst?
She causes lightning to wither as it strikes, and she swallows time and death.
Who is able to evade that goddess Kāḷikā?
(Desai 1956, 66)49
With an exquisite sense of irony, the poet responsible for this portion of our 
śāsana, naturally a disciple of Kaḷēśvara, masterfully captures how initiation into the 
Mantramārga imbued a practitioner with a new perception of old lived realities. 
Whereas ordinary people, concerned with birthing babies, winning victories, and 
warding off misfortune, visited a temple almost transactionally to pay homage to eve­
ryday (sāmānya) pan–​South Indian deities like Jyēṣṭhā and Māri (indeed, the well-​
heeled donor of this record had just such a mission), the people running these temples 
often saw their gods in much grander soteriological, epistemological, and cosmolog­
ical terms, reflecting the entextualized scriptural imaginaries scholars tend to think 
about when they study “classical tantra.” But to be a Kālamukha, however well creden­
tialed, and live in the world among other people, to fulfill one’s transactional duties, such 
understandings had to be selectively invoked, at least in shared spaces, perhaps even 
subjected to self-​imposed acts of epistemological bracketing.
Whenever we have access to thick enough descriptions of institution-​specific values 
and practices, the lived religions of the Deccan offer us both more and less than what we 
might have anticipated. To make sense of the voice of our archives demands that we at­
tend with great depth not only to the careful philological reconstruction of the revealed 
corpuses valued by at least some the social agents we are studying but also to the multi­
tude of extratextual realities that these sources decline to acknowledge. Only in doing so 
can scholars of tantric studies begin to produce maps that more than marginally corre­
spond to the territories we seek to explore.
As a coda, especially for those who discount the value of a dialogical approach 
that takes tantric textuality seriously, I can close by showing what Kaḷēśvara and his 
followers meant when they spoke of their lineage as “honoring the āvalis”: “Kaḷēśvara, 
the disciple of the wise, extracted (uddharisi) his definitive doctrine (siddhānta) from 
the Transmission of the Siddhas (siddhāvali), the Śākta Transmission (dēvyāvali), 
the Siddhānta Transmission ([soma]siddhāntāvali), and the Śaiva Transmission 
(śivāgamāvali) (Desai 1956, 67).”50
Here, beyond any ambiguity, the stories we have glimpsed in stone come into align­
ment with the written record. Within the mid-​twelfth-​century western Deccan, to be 
an illustrious Kālamukha entailed not merely some vague familiarity with incidental 
elements of the Mantramārga, but an encyclopedic command of the entire spectrum 
of Atimārga, Mantramārga, and even Kaula traditions. To be like Kaḷēśvara, guru of

--- PAGE 929 ---
904      Jason Schwartz
 
the world, demanded something more—​not merely the rote mastery of other people’s 
revelations, but the wisdom, learning, and insight to make doctrine own’s one, to craft 
a new Śivasiddhānta and to somehow find the time for such a momentous accomplish­
ment amid one’s worldly duties.
Notes
	1.	 The name Deccan is derived from the Old Kannada Dakkhaṇa, which in turn is a 
vernacularization of the Sanskrit word dakṣiṇa. Taken literally, it simply means “the South.” 
Geographically, it has typically referred to the area of India that is south of the Narmadā 
River. Its southernmost boundary is somewhat more variable, either the far bank of the 
Godāvarī (which would exclude much of southern Karnataka and Maharashtra) or the 
Kāverī River in Tamil Nadu. When defined in linguistic terms, the Deccan encompasses 
most of the regions (present-​day Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, and Andhra) oc­
cupied by mother tongue speakers of Marathi, Kannada, and Telugu, and alludes to their 
intertwined political and cultural histories.
	2.	 Though its core thesis, that the Kālamukhas were a Brāhmaṇical sect that had been er­
roneously conflated with the transgressive Kāpālikas (see, Törzsök 2011) as part of a 
campaign of anti-​Śaiva polemic, has now been disproven, David Lorenzen’s work The 
Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas: Two Lost Shaivite Sects (1972) is foundational to all subse­
quent discussions of Kālamukha doxographic and documentary records. Lorenzen takes 
great pains to translate, periodize and organize many available sources by lineage and 
region. In practice, however, Lorenzen’s mapping of Kālamukha institutional cultures, 
purportedly covering the eighth through fourteenth centuries, artificially distills the 
complex references to distinct guru paraṃparās to focus on two major transmissions, 
the Śaktipariṣad and the Siṃhapariṣad. It is primarily the sixty-​five inscriptions 
produced by the former that provide him with the evidentiary foundation for evaluating 
the tradition as a whole. For more on Lorenzen’s problematic theoretical presumptions, 
see hereafter. See also the work of Vasundhara Filliozat (2001) and Filliozat and Pierre-​
Sylvain (1995, 2012), which draws anachronistically on Vijayanagar era Śaivism in 
reading early medieval Kālamukha religion. Other discussions of Kālamukha traditions 
worth consulting are the Kannada language monograph of Kaṭarāḷa (1955) along 
with some insightful comments tying in the evidence from the Tamil sphere found in 
Ghose (1996).
	3.	 In his masterful reconstruction of the proto-​tantric Lākula Atimārga tradition (on 
which see the next note), Alexis Sanderson (2006) has demonstrated that the numerous 
references to the “Lākulāgama” in Deccani inscriptional records are direct allusions to 
the Lākula Pramāṇaśāstras and that their Mahāvrata observance is documented in the 
Mataṅgapārameśvara. Somewhat more problematically, Sanderson baldly asserts the 
“identity” of this community: “with a tradition of Raudra asceticism known up till now 
almost exclusively from epigraphs . . . the Kālamukhas studied by David Lorenzen” (179). 
Sanderson is almost certainly correct that the Mahāvrata vow in question represents the 
continuation of the skull carrying observance in which Lākula ascetics, rejecting the dis­
tinction between purity and impurity, aspire to see all things as forms of Rudra. What is less 
clear, however, is the evidentiary basis for taking such discrete Lākula informed practices as 
exhaustive of lived Deccani Kālamukha realities.

--- PAGE 930 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      905
 
	4.	 In his most recent work, Alexis Sanderson has provided us an invaluable schematic map­
ping of the tantric traditions that at once offers an account of their historical evolution and 
their doctrinal diversity. In its current form, which draws upon an array of doxographical 
passages in tantric sources, Sanderson’s model proposes that what we call tantric traditions 
emerge out a confluence of two prior religious imaginaries. The first of these, Sanderson 
proposes, is a pre-​tantric “lay Śaiva” tradition of liṅga veneration with its own so­
cial and legal norms, best exemplified by the Śivadharmaśāstra. The second predecessor 
is the Atimārga (the “path beyond”), which is now understood to contain three primary 
divisions, each of which has its own tradition of asceticism. To distill these categories down 
to the essentials: (1) the Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas had as their core surviving scripture the 
Pāśupatasūtra, a work from which the standard features of tantric cosmologies are almost 
entirely absent. These Pāśupatas seem only to have accepted Brahmin males as adepts and 
observed a three-​time daily ash bath as a key component of their five-​stage sādhanā, which 
involved a gradual withdrawal from participation in human society and its norms. In con­
trast, (2) the Lākulas produced a substantial scriptural canon, the Pramāṇaśāstras, which 
seem to supply later tantric traditions with much of their core cosmology and some key 
doctrines. Unlike the Pāśupatas, the Lākulas were heavily invested in the making of explic­
itly Śaiva social institutions. Their core ascetic observance was an occasional practice in 
which ascetics wandered through the world, rejecting normative notions of purity and im­
purity while carrying a human skull. Finally, (3) the pre-​tantric Atimārga Kāpālika tradition 
of the Somasiddhānta, about which we know very little, appear to have venerated emaciated 
goddesses through acts of ritual violence and sexual offerings that prefigure the practices of 
the later Kulamārga. The Kāpālika vow modifies the Lākula skull carrying observance to in­
corporate five additional insignia made from human bone.
	 	   What we now call the tantric traditions begin to emerge in the fifth century, when they are 
known to our sources as the Mantramārga (the “path of mantras”) and encompass a range 
of broadly similar transmissions spanning all of the major religions as well as what will later 
come to be perceived as the main sectarian divisions internal to Hinduism. As we recover 
more fragments from the Atimārga, it becomes increasingly evident that much of what is 
“new” in “tantra” is less a matter of innovative concepts and doctrines than of the emergence 
of a new ritual grammar, a style of textual organization and composition, as well as perhaps a 
model for social organization that actively incorporates nonascetics on a larger scale.
	 	   Though Alexis Sanderson has characterized the early medieval period when the clas­
sical versions of these traditions flourished as “the Śaiva Age,” it is pivotal that we do not 
anachronistically conflate this usage of the term “Śaiva” with a specific doctrinal or phil­
osophical stance, let alone with the programmatic dualistic exegetical approach to the in­
terpretation of a fixed canon of Āgamas proffered by Kashmiris from the ninth century 
onward and then further codified in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in Tamil Nadu. 
For evidence abounds that “Śaiva Siddhānta” in this sense, as a discrete tradition, is a scho­
lastic fiction imposed upon an internally variegated canon of Śivabheda and Rudrabheda 
scriptures that had been previously subject to a wider range of philosophical and the­
ological interpretations by different communities. Indeed “the Śaivism” of the Śaiva Age 
was deeply dialogical, such that virtually all of the scriptural sources incorporate textual 
borrowings from a range of traditions. In particular, what comes to be called Śaivāgama, 
the canon of the Yāmalas, as well as the various Śākta transmissions that coalesce into the 
Āmnāya systems of the Trika, Kubjikā tantras, and Kālīkrama, all draw substantively upon 
the Dakṣinasrotras, whose many traditions of Bhairava veneration are today primarily

--- PAGE 931 ---
906      Jason Schwartz
 
accessible through the Svacchanda tantra. As the present essay makes evident, the cultural 
impact of these Bhairava traditions on the world of the early medieval Deccan has been 
thoroughly underestimated.
	5.	 The writings of the dualistic Śaiva exegetes of Kashmir, particularly Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha 
II, offer substantial scholastic treatments of the philosophical positions ascribed to the 
Kālamukhas by other Śaiva traditions. An unnoticed irony is that these mid-​tenth-​century 
perceptions of Deccani religious realities as viewed from a considerable cultural and ge­
ographical distance predate all but a handful of the earliest attestations of the tradition in 
our documentary records. Succinctly, the Kālamukhas as described by Rāmakaṇṭha II are 
antecedents to most of our recoverable traditions, and thus their values may not accurately 
map onto Deccani institutional histories.
	6.	 Much like the Kashmiri Takṣakavarta’s paddhati, which incorporates substantial extracts 
from otherwise lost classical tantras, including the pre-​ninth-​century Śrīkaṇṭhīyasaṃhitā, 
the Jñānāvaraṇaviḷakkam (Veḷḷiyambalavāṇar 1957–​59) of the seventeenth-​century Tamil 
theologian Veḷḷiambara Vānar Tambirān transmits large portions of unattested Sanskrit 
and Tamil Śaiva texts, including the anonymous Śaiva doxography provisionally titled the 
Sarvasiddhāntaviveka (Nagaswamy 2006). The two most recent works known to the SSV 
are the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā (c. eleventh century) and the Ratnatrayaparīkṣā of Śrīkaṇṭha (c. 
eleventh century), which it twice invokes verbatim. Regarding the latter, the author ambig­
uously writes “ratnatrayādau gurubhiḥ eva hi,” “gurubhir api tathaiva pratipādyate.” Should 
we read this as suggesting that he was Śrīkaṇṭha’s disciple, this would place the work in the 
twelfth century. Regardless, numerous elements suggest against an early modern origin; 
the work’s numerous explications of Śaiva traditions does not incorporate the quintessen­
tial early modern canon of caste-​ and function-​specific Tamil Śaiva identities, and it knows 
a Matsyendranātha-​centric Kaula tradition in which Gorakṣanātha, Siddha, and Buddha 
are explicitly excluded from the core disciples. Perhaps most significant, when our author 
sets out to demonstrate that the Śaiva Siddhānta is the highest form of Śaivism (“śaivaś ca 
siddhāntī para īritaḥ”), the Siddhānta he proposes diverges sharply from the canonical 
tradition as depicted by figures like Aghoraśiva and is utterly dissimilar from the model 
propounded in early modern Tamil Śaiva literature.
	7.	 Following Abhinavagupta and his commentator Jayaratha, who in the Tantrāloka dis­
tinguish between the Tantraprakriyā and Kulaprakriyā, in his most recent publications, 
Sanderson now recognizes the legitimacy of a domain superseding the Mantramārga, 
which he labels Kulamārga. Its defining feature, he proposes, is communal orgiastic modes 
of worship along with, in some strains, a radical rejection of purity that offers an episte­
mological critique of the nature of reality. Sanderson suggests that the Kulamārga emerges 
organically out the pre-​tantric Kāpālika traditions in much the same manner that much of 
the Mantramārga is an evolute out of the Lākulas. In practical terms, however, it is perhaps 
more useful to think of the Kulamārga as a distinctive style of worship, often reserved for 
specialist adepts, that is frequently incorporated, overtly or covertly, within Mantramārga 
ritual. In fact, if we exclude what comes to be called the Siddhānta, the vast majority of 
“Mantramārga” tantric texts, including the Svacchandatantra, come down to us with 
Kulamārga elements already inserted into some chapters.
	8.	 Like “nondual” (abheda) and “dualistic” (bheda), bhedābheda is a doxographical category 
within Indian philosophy that offers an ontological claim about the nature of the universe. 
A very common specific application of such a perspective entails more specifically parsing 
the logic and mechanics of just how humans are connected to higher order realities, such

--- PAGE 932 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      907
 
	 	 as a supreme deity or principle. Variously understood as “difference and nondifference” or 
“identity within difference,” bhedābheda models typically advocate one of two positions. 
Many essentially promote ontological pluralism—​that there are many types of real things 
in the world which both share and do not share a fundamental nature with their source of 
origin and each other. Often this general framework comes paired with the suggestion that 
it is only one specific facet of the individual souls of a discrete set of agents that are iden­
tical in essence with the Godhead. Other more subtle bhedābheda approaches envision 
an ontology where there is only one real thing but it is at once composite and irreducible. 
In much the same way that an egg is made up of complementary but discrete parts, such 
as a shell, a yolk, and embryo, each with its own particular functions and traits, and yet at 
the same time cannot be broken down into “simpler” fundamental components without 
its identity and function as an egg—​and the life within it—​being terminated, this type of 
bhedābheda proposes that everything shares the same nature and that nature is itself varie­
gated in all of its manifestations.
	 9.	 While in Indian philosophy more generally, the word śakti can refer to a principle compa­
rable to force, power, or even potentia, within tantric discourses these abstractions tend 
to be personified, often in the form of at least vaguely menacing female entities. Within 
the otherwise unattested tradition being discussed here, it seems that these different 
individuated śaktis were seen as having their own discrete intrinsic natures which do not 
coalesce into a unified great goddess, nor are they identified with a higher order of reality.
	10.	 The doctrine of change of phase or transformation (pariṇāmavāda) is one of several 
Indian philosophical models that offer an explanation for how causes are logically related 
to effects. In the context of theology, such theoretical models are used to make sense of 
how the ultimate cause, whichever deity that might be, is logically related to the world 
he created as well as the agents within it. Essentially, a doctrine of transformation aims 
to account for the emergence of traits in the effect that were not immediately apparent in 
the cause. In opposition to those who propose that substances and entities from the mo­
ment of their creation have a fixed irreducible nature that cannot change without them 
being destroyed (the position of the Vaiśeṣikas), or that the cause and the effect are iden­
tical and that real change does not exist (the stance of Vivartavāda Vedānta) advocates of 
Pariṇāmavāda positions propose that the substances and agents that make up this uni­
verse can undergo real change and manifest emergent properties, in much the same way 
that milk can go sour, clot, or even change phase to become a solid such as paneer. Often 
the suggestion is that material differentiation proceeds through a kind of curdling of the 
divine nature into less pristine yet palatable forms.
	11.	 Literally “the end of what has been established,” in philosophical discourse the term 
Siddhānta refers both the conclusive position at which the author has arrived as well as 
something like the totality of positions defended by his school of thought. To speak of the 
Vāma, regardless of whether it is dualist, nondualist, or something in between, as forming 
a unified Siddhānta is effectively to say that the cohesiveness of this school of thought is 
defined by a set of shared positions and practices that are more fundamental than mere 
ontology.
	12.	 The concept of the “true guru” (sadguru) is perhaps most familiarly associated with early 
modern vernacular devotional traditions of North India and the Deccan, wherein the 
central focus of liturgical worship shifts from the deity to the embodied human teacher. 
The term’s point of origin, however, as already attested within the Tantrāloka (see for ex­
ample ­chapters 21–​22), is within the Kulamārga. There, alongside the closely related term

--- PAGE 933 ---
908      Jason Schwartz
 
saṃsiddhika guru (­chapter 4,13), it refers specifically to teachers who have the ability to 
directly confer mind and body altering somatic experiences onto their disciples.
	13.	 “Vaiṣṇavādiṣu bāhyeṣu śaivabhedeṣu vā punaḥ /​ bhairavādiṣu bhedeṣu kṛtakṛtyaḥ purā 
naraḥ /​ karmasāmyādisaṃsiddhiśaktipātaviśeṣataḥ /​ vāmatantroktamārgeṇa sadguror 
labdhadīkṣayā /​ caryādīnām [emd. from caryādināṃ] anujñānāt sādhako muktibhāg 
bhavet”; SSV, S-​7.
	14.	 For a learned review of the historical semantics of the lexeme samaya, focusing on its ap­
pearance in early Prakrit sources, see Mette (1991). Often translated as “convention,” from 
its inception the lexeme samaya tends to suggest a special set of context specific rules, 
norms, or circumstances that operate in contradistinction to what is presumed to be the 
“normal” state of affairs. By extension, in a juridical context, it indexes fixed modes of so­
cial relation that fall outside of, substitute for, or even supersede Varṇāśramadharma nor­
mativity. It is from this perspective that we need to reassess the standard designation of 
the entry level initiate to the traditions of the Mantramārga as a samayin. In Dravidian 
languages, as in modern Tamil, an enumerated list of samayas gradually comes to be used 
as something akin to an emic term for “religion” during the early medieval period, eventu­
ally becoming a fixture of inscriptional rhetoric wherein kings and other authority figures 
are called upon and call upon others to protect and preserve either “all the samayas,” “the 
four samayas,” “the six samayas,” or a designated array of the “samayas of the Vaiṣṇavas, 
Kālamukha, Bauddhas, Jinas and so forth.” A similar usage, divided between non-​Śaiva 
and Śaiva traditions, is attested in several Sanskrit Śaivāgamas, seemingly prior to its 
emergence in the Tamil commentarial tradition surrounding the Civañānapōtam. The 
present author is currently at work historicizing its development.
	15.	 “Lokāyato ’tha bauddhaś cārhato mīmāṃsā eva ca /​ māyāvādaḥ pāñcarātraṃ ṣaḍ ete 
samayā bahiḥ /​ śaivaṃ pāśupataṃ vāmaṃ bhairavaṃ tu mahāvratam kālamukhaṃ iti 
khyātam antaḥsamayaṣaṭkakam”; SSV, S-​7.
	16.	 To invoke just two examples of this rhetoric of cumulative inclusion: “atha 
kāpālasiddhāntaḥ kathyate saṃgrahād hi /​ tatkālāmukhasaṃproktam aṅgīkṛtya 
yathocitam”; “atha mahāvrataḥ śaivaḥ kathyate leśataḥ sphuṭam /​ kāpālāgamasaṃproktam 
aṅgīkṛtya yathocitam.”
	17.	 “Liṅgadhārī sadā svasya mastake kandhare ’thavā /​ . . . tathāpi jaṅgame bhaktir viśeṣa 
iti kathyate /​ mahāvratākhyaśāstroktanityakarmāditatparāḥ”; SSV, S.9–​11. On the 
continuities of these materials with early Vīramāheśvara traditions, see Fisher (2021, 
forthcoming).
	18.	 Though they differ in their understanding of the nature of these categories, both the 
traditions of Śaiva Siddhānta and Trika Śākta Śaivism posit that souls are bound by three 
kinds of innate impurity (mala)—​namely, ontic stain related to action (karmamala), 
ontic stain related to māyā (māyīya mala), and ontic stain inherent in the individual soul 
(āṇava mala)—​and that these are the source of suffering and transmigration experienced 
by bound souls. While Diwakar Acharya’s (2014) preliminary periodization of the history 
of ideas about innate impurity (mala) within the Śaiva Siddhānta identifies the seventh-​
century CE Svāyambhūvasūtrasaṅgraha as the locus classicus for the articulation of the 
concept within the Āgamas, he suggests that its antecedents, which identify mala as a facet 
of the fetters (pāśa), most likely emerge within the domain of Atimārga II. The eclectic 
recension of the Kālottara known of as the Jñānapañcaśikā, briefly noted by Goodall and 
Sarma (2007) as teaching a decidedly non-​Saiddhāntika skull carrying vow, provides us 
with additional confirmations of just such a model. For, in addition to retaining an older

--- PAGE 934 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      909
 
Pāśupata model where ontological bondage is ascribed not to a substance but to a “net” 
of causation, somewhat obliquely, the text refers to mala twice. First, in a terse presen­
tation of cosmology, māyā is equated with the will of Śiva, which is responsible for de­
termining the fate of all things (niyama), and the similitude of māyā with an otherwise 
underspecified self-​born innate impurity (sahaja mala) is then suggested. Later, just after 
discussing the dīkṣā ritual, mala is invoked in the context of assuaging doubt or anxiety 
about its continued existence in a state of liberation.
The SSV itself provides additional confirmation that we should seek out the prehistory of mala 
within non-​Pāśupata Atimārga sources, for here all three of our Atimārga traditions incor­
porate a theory of mala into their presentation of the fetters. Thus, for the Kālamukhas, the 
fetters are said to be of multiple types, namely mala itself, māyā (identified with the mate­
rial universe), and some unspecified “other” category, an arrangement perhaps prefiguring 
the threefold mala model. In contrast, in the SSV, though the word mala itself does not 
appear, the Lākulas seem to accept the existence of two types of fetters, karma and māyā 
(here identified not with material reality but with time). Finally, among the Mahāvratins, 
the claim is explicitly made that one of the points that marks their system as distinctive is 
that the fetters of karma and māyā are accepted, but not the concept of an ontological stain 
that is located solely within the individuated soul (āṇava), a formulation that suggests that 
this triadic model was a point of considerable debate within Śaiva communities that did 
not have its origins within the milieu of the Trika.
	19.	 As attested in a range of Śaiva sources, the original Lākula canon is said to be comprised 
of eight Pramāṇa scriptures (Pañcārtha, Śivaguhya, Rudrāṅkuśa, Hṛdaya, Lakṣaṇa, 
Vyūha, Ākarṣaka, Ādarśa), which derive their names from the eight Rudras who revealed 
them. This canon is sometimes expanded to include some supplementary works on ritual 
and, I have argued elsewhere, pratiṣṭhā (the installation of images), associated with the 
Hṛdayapramāṇa, for a total of fourteen Lākula Pramāṇa Āgamas. Of these, only some 
small passages from the Pañcārtha have been identified. The near verbatim adaptation of 
the extant citations into the earliest Trika scripture, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, in its pre­
sentation of what had previously been thought of as our earliest Śākta cosmology, strongly 
suggests that extensive similar textual borrowings have also been incorporated into other 
Mantramārga works.
	20.	 “Pañcārtham ca purākalpaṃ śivaguhyapramāṇakam /​ vyūhamādarśanaṃ caiva 
padmākarakaśailakam /​ nṛttaṃ caiva suduṣprāpaṃ siddhārthaṃ hi caturdaśa /​ kāpālam 
evām ākhyātaṃ lākulaṃ śṛṇu cānagha”; SSV, S-​10. The surrounding passages overlap with 
the decidedly early modern vulgate Dīptāgama, while frequently providing more cogent 
readings.
	21.	 As preserved within the Śaiva canon, for example Niśvāsamukha (4.129) (Kafle 2020), 
Lākula practitioners taught a pre-​tantric cosmological system where the highest reality, 
existing within the pure realm, was equated with the realm of Dhruva, perhaps identified 
with the pole star. In later Śaiva systems, these cosmologies, often mapped vertically onto 
the human body—​with the highest principles placed within or just above the head—​
provided concrete models for ritual practice involving the practitioner visualizing their as­
cent and conquest in ascending order of different planar realms, a task accomplished via a 
confluence of rote actions, the manipulation of various mantras, and control of the breath. 
The direct adaptation of Lākula models into the Svacchanda Tantra of the Dakṣiṇasrotras, 
incorporating such embodied cosmologies, suggests this may also have been a feature of 
Lākula practice.

	22.	 Echoing the calendrical observances of the Śivadharmaśāstra, this vrata is represented as a 
periodic observance performed on Aṣṭamī, on Caturdaśī, and as part of Śivarātravrata.
	23.	 Recent discoveries, both regarding pre-​tantric textual traditions such as the 
Śivadharmaśāstra as well as the rhetorical echoes of older formulations inherited by 
tantric literature proper, have shed some surprising light on the prehistory of devotion 
within Śaiva traditions, especially the emic understanding of Śaiva devotees. In the earliest 
stratum of the literature human Śaiva devotees (rudrabhakta, śivabhakta) seem to have 
been conceived of as partial emanations (aṃśa) or even incarnations either of an aspect of 
Śiva himself or of one of his attendants. The Kālamukhas in the SSV seem to have treated 
most of the iconographically specific forms of the deity associated with specific mythic 
episodes as an analogous phenomenon, expressions of parts of the nature of the Godhead 
as opposed to a manifestation of the whole.
	24.	 “Rudrāṃśena vinā tasya na pṛthaktvena sambhavaḥ /​ tasmād evaṃ mahādevo rudro ’yaṃ 
mūlavigrahaḥ /​ ata eva dakṣiṇāmūrtisvarūpādibahuvigrahaḥ /​ sākṣāt sadāśivo nityaḥ siva 
eva jagatpatiḥ /​ tadbhedo bahudhā proktas tatatkṛtyānusārataḥ”; SSV, S-​9.
	25.	 “Śaktipātānusāreṇa karmasāmye ’pi sambhave /​ tathānuṣṭhānasāmarthyād ātmā śuddho

	26.	 That these omissions are features of the SSV itself and not its selective use by Veḷḷiambara 
Vānar Tambirān himself in his Tamiḷ commentary becomes evident once we recognize 
that Veḷḷiambara Vānar has a positive view of the Dakṣiṇasrotras and makes extensive use 
of the only work of that tradition directly available to him, the Svacchanda tantra.
	27.	 Counterintuitively, the two earliest writings associated with the most famous Śaiva 
Siddhānta lineage of the Mattamayūravaṃśa, namely the Prāyaścittasamuccaya of 
Hṛdayaśiva and the Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya of Vairocana, express a vision of Śaiva 
knowledge inclusive of non-​Siddhānta traditions and practices. So does the key textual 
source for the Somaśambhupaddhati, Bhoja’s Siddhāntasārapaddhati, which makes liberal 
use of Bhairavasrotras materials in a manner that suggests that the typical story about the 
emergence of Śaiva Siddhānta as a knowledge system is in need of revision.
	28.	 “Kāpālīti hi saṃproktaḥ kāpāle sādhakottamaḥ /​ kathaṃ prāguktaśaivasya kālāmukhamatasya

	29.	 “Duṣṭavādiniṣṭhurapaṭiṣṭhaśārddūḷaṃ bauddhābdhibaḍavāmukhaṃ mīmāṃsakadhātrī­

that is the espousers of nonduality, and the third eye of Śiva himself in burning the threefold 
city of the Jain logician Akalaṅka.” The grand irony is that the prehistory of this type of rhetoric 
takes as its focus the eighth-​century Jain philosopher Akalaṅka himself. For a brief discussion 
of the Śaiva adaptation of Akalaṅka-​related rhetoric into their own epigraphy see Gurevitch 
(2022, p. 124).

	31.	 Kula trees appear in the Kaula tantric sources where specific species of trees (Kadamba, 
Tamarind, etc.) are associated with specific deity lineages, mythologies, and systems of

of gift and curse bestowing supernatural entities with trees. See Tantrikābhidhānakośa vol. 
2, pg. 128.
	32.	 Most commonly associated with the goddess Mahālakṣmī of Kolhapur, the object called 
the mātuluṅga or bījāpūra is frequently identified with a citron fruit, either the wild or­
ange or sweet lime. The range of visual representations of this object across regions, how­
ever, suggests a more complex identity than can be accounted for by simple equation, 
incorporating more varied local identifications, including with pomegranate-​holding an­
tecedent Greco-​Roman deities.
	33.	 Within surviving tantric textuality, the worship of Koṭarākṣa Bhairava is entirely de­
pendent upon ­chapter 9 of the Svacchandatantra, where his dhyāna is presented in verses 
9.3–​8. In the seventh paṭala of the Jayadrathayāmala’s third ṣaṭka, Aṭṭahāsabhairava is 
mounted on a snake. His decidedly non-​Śaiva iconography, right down to the śaṅkha, 
cakra, gaḍa, and hala in his hands suggests that this feature reflects his original Vaiṣṇava 
identity as Balarāma.
	34.	 As I will argue elsewhere, a more promising approach to making sense of site-​specific 
Kālamukha normativities is to attend to the specific caste communities (weavers, oil 
makers, goldsmiths, etc.) and social functions (such as whether the institution is also an 
artisan training center) with which a particular complex is aligned.
	35.	 “Agrahāraṃ 
kardugina 
svayaṃbudēvara 
dēgulada 
pūliyapaṇḍitara 
vidyāśiṣyar 
kkŏppina vakkhāṇijīyara śiṣyarappa kāḷagnāni vakhkhāṇijīyarggĕ dhārāpūrvvakaṃ 
vidyādānamāgĕ purigĕṟĕnāḍǒḷagaṇa” (South Indian Inscriptions XI, n. 48).
	36.	 The “knowledge concerning kāla” (Kālajñāna) is an ambiguous compound because kāla 
is a polyvalent lexeme. Although indexing “knowledge of Kālamukha doctrines” in some 
later inscriptions, kālajñāna is more commonly understood as referring to the siddhi of 
knowing the three times (kāla), namely past, present, and future, or, more specifically, to 
the practice of augury.
	37.	 On account of dialectical variation, scribal error, and metri causa, standardization of 
spelling is uncommon in Old Kannada epigraphy. Regarding this site, for example, Puli, 
Pūli, Pūliya, Purigērĕ, and Purĕgērĕ are all attested. Likewise, we find the proper name 
variants Vākhāni, Vākkhāni, Vākhhāni, and Vakkhāni. Determining which of these 
usages is “correct” or even whether they are always synonymous is most difficult.
	38.	 Kǒppina Vākkhāni surfaces again in an inscription from 1179 CE, published in EI 19 
(Sastri [1927–​1928], pp. 228–​232), preserved the city of Rōṇ, in which Kǒppina Vākhhāni 
is treated as the progenitor of a distinct Kālamukha lineage descending from him to 
Rudraśakti, to Jñānadevaśakti, and then to the current authority Gurubhakta, who have 
all been reimagined as belonging to the Parvatāvali line out of Śrīśailiam. This pattern of

--- PAGE 937 ---

the focused forgetting of no longer pertinent pasts and rewriting lineage lists is endemic 
throughout our sources.
	39.	 The highly selective nature of the published inscriptional record from Lakṣmēśvara (all 
which are contained within South Indian Inscriptions [hereafter SII], vol. 20 (Gai 1988) 
with three edited and partially translated in EI, vol. 3 (Hultzsch [1894–​1895], pp. 31–​52) 
poses substantial problems for further contextualization. Of the six major Śaiva temples 
surviving, some with material cultural remnants dating back to the ninth century, only the 
largest complex, Somēśvara, offers us documentary records. In contrast to Lakṣmēśvara’s 
Digambara Jain communities, where we have inscriptions from the early seventh century 
(SII, vol. 20, nos. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 244–​6, 47, 52, 53, 55), our first legible Śaiva sources referring 
to Sōmēśvara (SII, vol. 20, no. 66, 1102 CE) date back only to the twelfth century, though 
significantly, they already presume the preexistence of various institutions including the 
temples of Sōmēśvara and Muddēśvara, and are thus substantively younger than all of 
the relevant material culture. Intriguingly, most of this corpus identifies local authorities 
as belonging to a lineage of Mahāvratins, many with initiatory names ending in Sōma, 
marking them as inheritors of Kāpālika traditions. Our Pūliya Paṇḍita could well have 
been one of the ancestors of these ācāryas, or else been aligned with a maṭha associated 
with one of these other temples.
	40.	 EI, vol. 15 (Thomas 1920), SII, vol. 11, no 95. The epigraphical records discussed in this sec­
tion include: EI, vol. 15 (tenth century); SII, vol. 11 (Rao 1986), no. 87 (1050 CE); SII, vol. 11, 
no. 91 (1054 CE); SII, vol. 11, no. 93 (1058 CE); EI, vol. 15, SII, vol. 11, no. 95 (1061 CE); SII,

	41.	 SII, vol. 11, no. 87, for example, refers to the “śāsanamaryyādĕya,” the “nāḍa maryyādĕya” 
(jurisdictional law), and the “sĕṭṭiyaramarryādĕ” (law pertaining to merchants), treating 
each as a discrete set of norms. For more on the relation between tantric imaginaries and 
community and site-​specific legal pluralism see Schwartz (2019, p. 112).
	42.	 EI, vol. 15, p. 75.
	43.	 The Kannada term dēvara affixes an honorific plural -​ra suffix to the Sanskrit loan word 
dēva. Much like its cognate, Kannada dēvara can refer indiscriminately to a deity, to the 
iconic and aniconic embodiment of the deity on earth, a human king, or to other political 
and sacerdotal authorities. Since in the formal compositional conventions of many land 
grants there is no distinction drawn between the authority acting on behalf of the recipient 
and the intended recipient itself, the result is that in many cases it is impossible to distin­
guish whether a grant is being given to a specific empowered human sacerdotal agent or 
directly to the god.
	44.	 The Sanskrit world āvali literally refers to a row or continuous sequence. In Śākta tantric 
sources, especially associated with the goddess Kubjikā and the Kālīkrama, Āvali becomes 
the proper name of specific lineage transmissions, paralleling the usage in the inscriptions 
we are studying. As the Kālamukha lineage we are studying incorporates into its program 
of worship elements from both the Western transmission and the Kālīkrama, it is likely 
that a specific referent is intended.
	45.	 EI, vol. 15, pp. 88–​89.
	46.	 Of uncertain origin but appearing frequently in Old Telugu and Kannada inscriptional 
records from at least the eighth century, the terms Gŏrava, Gŏraga, Gurava, Gŏrāva, etc. 
refer to a class of non-​Brahmin religious authorities. Primarily Śaiva but occasionally

--- PAGE 938 ---
EARLY MEDIEVAL DECCAN      913
 
Digambara Jain, in the inscriptions Gŏravas often act as the sthānācāryas of a temple com­
plex or are presented as managing a settlement (often called x-​vāḍa or x-​pura) dedicated 
to their specific community. While by the early modern period in the western Deccan such 
terms have become associated with specific caste communities, either, in Maharashtra, a 
Śaiva priestly caste called the guravs, or, in Karnataka, a subcaste of the nomadic Kurubas 
with their own largely Śaiva ascetic tradition, these narrower identifications appear to be a 
subsequent development.
	47.	 Here it is important to remember that both the pre-​tantric Atimārga Kāpālika traditions 
and their tantric successors often referred to themselves as adherents of the Somasiddhānta 
and initiated their adepts into names ending in x-​Soma as well as other semisynonymous 
terms referring to the moon, such as Candra. By identifying here as “Muni-​Sōma”—​the 
Soma Sage—​the Kālamukha Sōmēśvara seems to be deliberately evoking such older 
resonances.

Chapter 36
The Total Revelation 
Tantra
The Geopolitical Origins and Significance of 
the Name, Nepālī Sarvāmnāya Tantra
Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
Introduction
Surrounded by the Tibetan Autonomous Zone of China, India, Pakistan, and Bhutan, 
Nepal is at the historical and cultural heart of the development of Hindu and Buddhist 
tantra. Many of the most significant lineages of tantra have either arisen in or subse­
quently migrated to Nepal, which continues to be home to one of the most vibrant living 
traditions of tantra throughout the world. Known by Nepālī tāntrikas themselves as 
the Tantra of All Revelations (“all”: sarva, “revelations”: āmnāya), Nepālī Sarvāmnāya 
tantra is inherently syncretistic, reflecting the rich history of the development of tantra 
throughout the subcontinent over the last two millennia and into the present. Not only 
is Nepal a repository of many important tantric manuscripts, but perhaps more impor­
tantly, it is home to a number of the world’s most highly educated tantric practitioners. 
Careful study of Nepālī tantra must therefore combine (1) reading source texts in their 
original languages, with (2) studying the many works of secondary scholarship (in­
cluding, particularly, those ethnographies done by Nepālīs themselves), and addition­
ally (3) engaging contemporary practitioners through fieldwork in Nepal. This triadic 
heuristic, grounded conjointly in Indology, ethnography and “indigenous hermeneu­
tics,”1 provides deeper access to the place-​specific patterns of tantric practice in Nepal.
Engaging the field in this interdisciplinary way, one comes to appreciate Nepālī tantra 
as a multileveled, historically-grounded tradition expressing itself simultaneously 
in a plethora of texts, temple complexes, power seats (śākta-​pīṭhas), and a network of 
both domestic and temple practices. The host of liturgical practices use sacred visual

--- PAGE 941 ---
916      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
diagrams (mandalas, yantras), mystical utterances (mantras), body gestures (mudrā), 
the consumption of wine and certain foods, and “coupling” (maithuna), whether lit­
eral or symbolic. Nepālī tantra operates according to a dyadic rhythm of “internal” 
practice (antar-​yāga) and “external” (bahir-​yāga) linking the rhythms of private, do­
mestic practices with temple rituals and public festivals. Sarvāmnāya additionally 
links together the multiplicity of Nepālī castes, interconnecting the various so-​called 
indigenous castes with the many so-​called mountain peoples or Parbatiyas. While the 
Parbatiyas are sometimes viewed as migrants to Nepal, they are in fact as much Nepālī as 
the Newārs, who are typically identified by scholars as the original inhabitants of Nepal 
(Gellner 1992; Levy 1990; Slusser 1982).
Regardless of debates over insiders and outsiders or natives and migrants, it is a mistake to 
assume that the tantra of one caste is in some way fundamentally distinct from the tantra of 
another. Within Nepal, all the tantric traditions operate and coalesce within an overarching, 
integrated system of revelation and practice known as Sarvāmnāya or the Total Revelation 
Tantra. This Sarvāmnāya tantric tradition operates under the logic of bhedābheda-​vāda,2 
or the orthodox ideal of multiplicity within unity—​of the many comprising the One and 
that One being the material and efficient cause of the many. It is a tradition that has arisen 
from multiple regions throughout the subcontinent, including from within Nepal itself, 
and which therefore integrates a plethora of textual sources and related peoples and cultural 
traditions. Embodying a theological presupposition that one supreme Godhead projects 
itself internally onto its own Being as the multiplicity that is creation, Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas 
are called to engage in ritual practices in which they mimic the activity of the Godhead they 
seek to realize. Moreover, they are trained through their practice to see their own geopolit­
ical and cultural landscape as mirroring the activity of that Godhead.
To understand these complex dynamics, we first turn to an important debate within 
the field of scholarship on Nepālī tantra. The debate has unfolded over nearly thirty 
years and is of interest not just to the scholars engaged in the debate but to Nepālī 
tāntrikas themselves who have become familiar with the debate and have taken their 
own stand on the central questions that drive the debate. This stand-​taking sheds light 
on the nature of Nepālī tantra as it is understood and practiced by contemporary and 
past tāntrikas of Nepal.
Not Six but All: The Significance of 
Naming to Nepālī Tāntrikas
The debate at hand is between Jeffrey S. Lidke and Mark Dyczkowski over the correct 
and traditional name for Nepālī tantra. Lidke, based on his research with Timalsina, 
identifies Nepālī tantra writ large as the Tantra of the Total Revelation, “Sarvāmnāya 
Tantra.” Dyczkowski, on the other hand, argues that the proper label is the tantra of the 
Six Revelations, “Ṣaḍ Āmnāya Tantra.” Why does this matter? And what do we learn

--- PAGE 942 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      917
 
from the debate about the tantra of Nepal? First, it matters because Nepālī tāntrikas 
themselves care about the debate. Second, an analysis of the specifics of the debate sheds 
important light on the nature of Nepālī tantra—​light that will be helpful in illuminating 
both the origins and practices of the tradition.
In a relatively recent assessment of the work of Lidke (2017) Dyczkowski identifies the 
Sarvāmnāya system outlined by Lidke as “alien to the Newārs of the Kathmandu valley” 
(Dyczkowski 2009, 2:351).3 However, he does concede that while Newār Kaula tāntrikas 
do not refer to their tradition as Sarvāmnāya, they do uphold the ideal of being “well 
versed in all the āmnāyas (sarvāmnāya-​viśārada)” (Dyczkowski 2009, 2:348). Why does 
Dyczkowski view the tradition described by Lidke as “alien” to the Newār community 
of Nepal even as he acknowledges the importance to said tāntrikas to be well versed in 
“all the revelations” (sarvāmnāya)? His primary objection is to Lidke’s stance that Nepālī 
Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas receive a multiplicity of initiations in the overall context of their 
tantric practice as opposed to one single initiation. His position in this regard is that 
Newār tāntrikas receive only a single initiation which itself provides eventual access to 
all the āmnāyas. In this regard, he seems to be stressing the important notion of a root 
initiation (mūla-​dīkṣā) linked to a single root teacher. However, a number of contempo­
rary Nepālī tāntrikas, Newār and non-​Newār alike, emphasize the necessity of receiving 
distinct initiations into each of the six systems of revelation. Receiving each of the neces­
sary initiations for each of the six āmnāyas makes one “well versed in all the āmnāyas.” 
Since the aim of Nepālī tantra is to achieve the total revelation that comes with initiation 
into all of the āmnāyas, Nepālī tāntrikas tend to use the term “Sarvāmnāya” to identify 
their tradition. Dyczkowski’s ethnographic research was primarily with the late great 
Kedar Raj Rajopadhyaya. In his instruction to Dyczkowski, Kedar Raj seems to have 
deemphasized the term sarvāmnāya in favor of ṣaḍāmnāya and also to have stressed the 
value of receiving a single initiation within a single āmnāya.4
A second reason that Dyczkowski rejects Sarvāmnāya as the universal name of Nepālī 
tantra relates to Lidke’s claim that within the Sarvāmnāya system, the Śrī Vidyā holds a 
special, preeminent position for all Nepālī tāntrikas due to its status as the tradition of 
the Upper Revelation (ūrdhvāmnāya). Indeed, Lidke has claimed that the secret iden­
tity of Taleju, the royal goddess of Nepal, is Tripurasundarī precisely for this reason 
(Lidke 2017, 108–​145). Dyczkowski himself reserves this place of special status for the 
goddess Kubjikā (Dyczkowski 2001, 24–​25), the tutelary deity of the Western Revelation 
or paścimāmnāya, and he is correct in pointing out that Newārs as a whole do not 
view the Śrī Vidyā tutelary deity Tripurasundarī with the centrality that is presented in 
Lidke’s work.
The truth is that Lidke and Dyczkowski are both right and both wrong. In their re­
spective studies, both scholars were viewing the Sarvāmnāya system through a par­
ticular point of focus. Lidke was focused on the Upper Revelation while Dyczkowski 
was focused on the Western Revelation. As a result, both scholars failed, at least ini­
tially, to recognize that each and all of the āmnāya systems are operating by a similar 
“difference-​in-​unity” (bhedābheda) logic of total mutual inclusivity. As Lidke’s work was 
focused on Nepālī Śrī Vidyā, consequently, for those Nepālī tāntrikas with whom he was

--- PAGE 943 ---
918      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
working, Tripurasundarī did indeed embody the highest of empowerment in a special 
way and was therefore associated with the patron deity of Nepal, Taleju. On the other 
hand, Dyczkowski’s ethnographic focus, and access to Nepālī Śākta tantra, has prima­
rily been through the lens of the paścimāmnāya tradition. Therefore, for him, Kubjikā 
embodies the highest state of empowerment in a special way and is in turn viewed as the 
secret identity of Taleju. Neither is entirely wrong.5 Both are providing important schol­
arly examples of how the nondual logic of Sarvāmnāya operates through two of the six 
āmnāyas that comprise Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra. Scholars who plan to do research on 
Nepālī tantra are advised to understand that the tradition is like a six-​sided crystal, each 
side with its own hue. Each side of this crystal is an āmnāya. If you gaze into the crystal 
from the west, then the center of the crystal will be colored by that western hue. Seeing 
it from the north you will see the northern hue, and so on. The key is to view the crystal 
as a whole, to see the center from all the sides and to understand that the tradition itself 
demands this kind of viewing-​from-​all-​sides perspectivalism.
Within the Sarvāmnāya system—​which embraces, is open to, and includes participa­
tion by Newārs, Parbatiyā and nearly all other Nepālī caste groups—​the secret identity of 
Taleju, the royal goddess, is not restricted to a single deity or name. Rather, Taleju, being 
none other than Parā Śakti, the Supreme Power, and Mahā Devī, the Great Goddess, is a 
dynamic, multitiered shifting symbol signifying a non-dual state of supreme conscious­
ness that by nature and definition is beyond labels. What appears as Tripurasundarī 
becomes Kubjikā for another, depending on initiatory context. As Mahā Devī and Parā 
Śakti, the names and revelations of Taleju are multiple. All these names and revelations 
arise from and return to her—​this is the basic understanding of the majority of Nepālī 
tāntrikas, regardless of their caste identification.
In sum, while Dyczkowski claims that Sarvāmnāya is a tantric system “alien to the 
Newārs,” the reality is that a good number of contemporary Newār tāntrikas do in fact 
refer to their tradition by the name Sarvāmnāya. And, indeed, the textual basis for such 
an identification appears to extend back several centuries. The exact origin of this term 
sarvāmnāya is not known, but evidence for its use is abundant in a variety of textual 
sources, ranging from classical pan-​Indic scriptures to the eighteenth-​century Nepālī 
tantric compendium the Puraścaryārṇava to a host of ritual manuals (paddhatis) in 
use by Newārs and non-​Newārs alike.6 It is our assumption that because this term, 
sarvāmnāya, has been in use in the classical tantric sources for at least four hundred 
years the consequence is that over time Nepālīs—​Newār and non-​Newār alike—​have 
come to adopt the term as the name for their distinctive Nepālī Śākta tantric traditions.
A Loss of Meaning?
In his classic study, The Canon of the Śaivāgama, Dyczkowski makes the following im­
portant, understandable yet problematic, statement: “In Nepal . . . the Nepālī . . . aban­
doned themselves to . . . a formal ritualism, which, though charged with meaning, had

--- PAGE 944 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      919
 
lost all significance for them beyond the ritual itself. Thus the Nepālīs, unlike the Kashmiris, 
did preserve the original tantras they made use of in their rituals, but largely failed to see 
anything beyond their immediate content” (Dyczkowski 1988, 12–​13 [emphasis added]).
It is understandable that Dyczkowski came to the conclusion that Nepālī tāntrikas 
had by and large “failed to see” the meaning beyond the immediate content of their re­
spective rituals. Such meaning is not easily found in any written materials. And given 
tantra’s strict hermetic tendencies, no one in Nepal is going to be easily talked into 
conveying cult secrets. Moreover, the kind of deep “mystical” analysis found in the 
writings of the likes of Abhinavagupta is not going to be readily apparent in the everyday 
cultural patterns of contemporary Nepālīs. However, the fact that Nepālī tāntrikas may 
not be talking about the deeper meaning of their ritual practices is not inherent proof 
that they do not recognize the presence of said meaning in the activities in which they 
engage. The truth is that there are tāntrikas in Nepal who do in fact know the esoteric 
meanings of their rituals.
We of course cannot assume that all Nepālī tāntrikas know the deepest meanings of 
their tantric practices, but such is the case with all religious traditions: within a populace 
as a whole the levels of understanding of any given religious community are going to vary 
significantly. Being able to identify exactly what the percentages are in Nepal of tāntrikas 
who know the esoteric meanings of their ritual actions and meditative practices would 
require a careful and comprehensive quantitative analysis that is not only beyond the 
scope of this current chapter but would also would likely be doomed to failure given that 
most tāntrikas are sworn to secrecy regarding the inner meanings of their tradition. That 
no one (beyond Kedar Raj) seems to have shared with Dyczkowski the inner meanings 
of their tradition may simply reflect the fact that in the eyes of most of his informants, 
he was an outsider. To be fair to Dyczkowski, his above comments on meaning were 
published in 1988. Perhaps the landscape had changed by the time Lidke did his exten­
sive field research in the Kathmandu valley in 1996–​1997. At that time, as documented 
in The Goddess Beyond (2017), there were multiple Nepālī tāntrikas who not only clearly 
knew the deeper meanings of their rituals but were willing to speak about them to Lidke. 
And at the time of the writing of this chapter it is certainly the case that there is a high 
degree of evidence that a significant number of contemporary tāntrikas are clearly aware 
of the deeper meaning laden in their respective ritual practices.7
One could further counter that these informed individuals are but a short list of ed­
ucated tāntrikas, but that the majority of the tāntrikas in Nepal do not know the deeper 
meanings of their practice. To such an argument, our reply is twofold. First, we ask, 
how many individuals must know something before we can comfortably claim that it 
is known within the individual’s community? Is there a magical percentage that sud­
denly transforms a society from being generally “unaware of deeper meaning” to “aware 
of deeper meaning”? Second, if the ideal for an “enlightened tantric community” is 
eleventh-​century Kashmir (as Dyczkowski and many other tantric studies scholars—​
Müller-​Ortega, Sanderson, etc.—​seem to think) then are we to assume that just because 
we have the writings of Abhinavagupta and his interlocutors that therefore the majority 
of Kashmiri tāntrikas knew the deeper meaning of their rituals? If a handful of people in

--- PAGE 945 ---
920      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
a community write a few books that last through the centuries and are later “discovered” 
by a foreign scholar, does that therefore prove that those authors were a reflection of the 
general knowledge in their respective communities at the time of their writings? Could 
it not be rather that the authors were members of an elitist literati community and that 
their reflections reflected the exception and not the rule in terms of what was known 
in their community about their practice? Could it not even be that, as White has pro­
vocatively suggested, Abhinavagupta even fabricated the meaning he articulated in his 
numerous works (White 2003, xi–​xvi)? If White’s thesis is correct, then clearly the only 
people who knew Abhinavagupta’s deeper meanings were the very few folks who either 
were initiated by him or read his works or both. Is it not likely the case that those who 
truly know the “deeper meaning” of tantric rituals have always been relatively few and 
far between?
It would seem that we need to revise Dyczkowski’s claim regarding the understanding 
of tantra in Nepal by Nepālī tāntrikas. We do so by putting in writing the fact that today 
in Nepal itself and spread throughout the globe are a number of Nepālī tāntrikas who 
not only know the deeper meaning of their respective rituals but who are actively en­
gaged in preserving and disseminating this understanding, not only within their own 
tightly knit initiation groups, but also together with the international community of tan­
tric practitioners and scholars. Scholars of tantra can never return to eleventh-​century 
Kashmir, but we can be in communication with contemporary Nepālī tāntrikas and we 
can learn from and with them the modes by which their complex ritual system embodies 
and disseminates the esoteric meaning of what White has dubbed “high Hindu tantra” 
(White 2003), both at private and domestic levels.
Paśupati-​Guhyeśvarī as Commingled 
Source of the Six Revelations
A primary reason that Nepal is home to each and all of the six primary tantric systems of 
revelation is because the Paśupatinātha temple (see fig. 36.1), together with the Temple 
Seat (pīṭha) of Guhyeśvarī, has been a magnet for drawing in tantric practitioners from 
all over the subcontinent. Evidence of the existence of Paśupatinātha can already be 
found in the inscription from the fifth century ce (Rājavaṃśī 1989) with local chronicles 
pushing the origins of Paśupatinātha back to the third century bce (Michaels 2008, 10). 
Gautama V. Vajracharya (2021a), a noted historian, traces the antiquity of Paśupatinātha 
to the Vedic era and beyond—​in other words, to before it was formally organized as 
Paśupatinātha itself in the fifth century ce. In reference to the ancient indigenous culture 
of the Newārs, based on what he identifies as Monsoon-​Culture (an ancient culture that 
was based on monsoon weather and rain), Vajracharya argues that initially Paśupatinātha 
was hidden underground as a subterranean sacred watery presence (Vajracharya 2021a, 
2021b).

--- PAGE 946 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      921
 
In Nepal, these national patron deities, Paśupatinātha and Guhyeśvarī, are no different 
than Śiva and Śakti. Appropriately, the most important temple in Nepal is Paśupatinātha, 
which is dedicated to Śiva and includes an important temple to Guhyeśvarī, his female 
consort and source of power, Śakti. The main idol in Paśupatinātha is a five-​faced liṅga 
(pañcavaktra mukhaliṅga), with Tatpuruṣa as the eastern face, Aghora as the southern 
face, Sadyojāta as the western face, Vāmadeva as the northern face, and Īśāna as the 
upward face, assumed but not typically carved into the idol. These five faces of Śiva are 
identified as the five faces of Paśupatinātha in the classic “Hymn to the Five Faces of 
Paśupati” (Paśupati-​pañcāsya-​stava).8
One of the oldest extant inscriptions that mentions Śiva having five faces is a fifth-​
century ce inscription from the Paśupatināth temple. It reads: “five faces adjoined 
together (sa-​pari-​cumbita-​vaktra-​pañca), possessed with all qualities (sarva-​guṇa-​
upapanna), an idol (pratimā) is established here.”9 This inscription echoes the 
Svacchanda-​tantra (8.31)10 which states that in order to disseminate the tantric reve­
lation, Śiva himself became both teacher (guru) and disciple (śiṣya) by unveiling him­
self as five faces (pañcamukhebhyaśca) and giving the teachings of the five āmnāyās 
(pañcāmnāyāḥ), being the paths to liberation (mokṣamārgāḥ) to his five Śaktis.11
Figure 36.1.  Paśupatinātha Temple, Kathmandu.
Courtesy of L. S. Akshunna.

--- PAGE 947 ---
922      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
The Kulārṇava-​tantra (3.7) further states that from its five faces (pañcamukhebhyaśca) 
emerged (samudgatāḥ) the five revelatory systems (pañca-​āmnāyas). Including the 
sixth face, Paśupatinātha becomes the six-​headed (ṣaḍ-vaktra) Mahā-​Paśupatinātha 
and together with his six śaktis reveals sarva (all) ṣaḍ (six) āmnāyas (see fig. 36.2 
and table 36.1).The Kulārṇava-​tantra (3.43–​44)12 further identifies twenty-​four var­
iations of the Western Revelation (purvāmnāya),13 twenty-​five of the Southern 
Revelation (dakṣiṇāmnāya),14 thirty-​two of the Western Revelation (paścimāmnāya),15 
and thirty-​six16 of the Northern Revelation (uttarāmnāya).17 With regard to the Upper 
Revelation (ūrdhvāmnāya), the Kulārṇava-​tantra (3.45) states that it transcends all 
divisions and that through engagement in the practices of this revelation one becomes 
Śiva himself. Nonetheless, we do see in Nepal a great deal of variation in terms of the 
representations of the deity Mahātripurāsundarī. Similarly, although not mentioned 
by the Kulārṇava-​tantra, Vajrayoginī additionally appears in diverse forms within the 
Lower Revelation (adharāmnāya). With all of these revelations and their variations still 
alive in Nepal as living traditions, we come to see why Nepālīs themselves, both Newār 
and non-​Newār like, identify Nepāli tantra as the Tantra of All Revelations (Sarvāmnāya 
tantra).
Figure 36.2.  Sarvāmnāya Paśupati Śiva Śakti.
Courtesy of Vidyanath Upadhyaya Bhatta.

--- PAGE 948 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      923
 
Based on the evidence of the fifth-​century, five-​faced Paśupati liṅga and its associa­
tion with the five Śaktis we can conclude that the krama traditions of the Ciñcinnīmata, 
Siddhayogeśvarī, and Śiraścheda tantras originated in Nepal by the seventh century, 
through the Yoginīkula of Matsyendranātha.18 Indeed, it is not just these key texts but 
their prescribed practices that flourish to this day in Nepal.19 Ciñcinnīmata is the first 
text to provide a fourfold division of the āmnāyas with the Purvāmnāya originating 
from Mīnanātha.20 The fifteenth-​century Parātantra arises out of and aligns itself with 
the older Śiraśchedamata and is undoubtedly of Nepālī origin (Sanderson 2014, 66). 
One could even argue that the seveth-​century Śiraścheda is itself of Nepālī origin. It 
is true that in the Parātantra the goddess of the southern āmnāya is called Niśeśī, not 
Tripurasundarī. However, Parātantra 2.321 identifies this Niśeśī as Raktakālī, which is but 
another name of Tripurāsundarī.22 From this textual and ethnographic evidence, it can 
be concluded that the indigenous Nepālī lineages of the Ciñcinnīmata and Parātantra 
are not in conflict with each other. The Parātantra simply expands the possibilities 
for Tantric practice through the variations (bhedas) it maps out, such as crafting the 
Dakṣiṇāmnāya as a synthesis of the Dakṣinakālī and Tripurasundarī traditions.
Nepal as the Water Pot of Revelations
Yoshizaki provides a detailed description of the imagery of the water pot (kalaśa), 
wherein multiple Buddhist deities are invoked, invited, and enlivened. He extends his 
analysis to claim that the Kathmandu valley is itself such a kalaśa (Yoshizaki 2012).23 
Drawing from this analysis, we argue that the kalaśa is a fruitful metaphor for under­
standing the development and practice of Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra. Certainly, for the 
Śaiva-​Śākta Hindus of Nepal any and all of the āmnāya deities can be and are invited 
into the ritual kalaśa. However, the goddess that abided originally in the “water pot” that 
is Nepal is Guhyeśvarī. Indeed, the “water pot” that is Nepal contains within itself the

waters from a multiplicity of streams that have flown into Kathmandu over the centuries 
and have mingled with Nepal’s own autochthonous scriptural stream, the uttarāmnāya 
or Northern Transmission, which is grounded in the Northern Seat (uttara-​pīṭha), and 
which is both a body of revelation and a geographical region from which that revelation 
arises (Dyczkowski 1988).
Being the origin for the emergence of the Northern Revelation, Nepal is thus the 
Northern Seat. As the Northern Seat, the Nepāl-​Kalaśa has been intermingled with 
the revelations of the multiple revelatory streams (āmnāyas) and sacred sites of power 
(pīṭhas) from the regions at its borders. This fluid intermingling and development 
has resulted in the Sarvāmnāya tantra tradition, which is the dominant tradition 
within Nepal, across Newār, Parbatīyā (pahāḍe) and all other divides, whether they 
be identified as ethnic, linguistic, caste, or cultural. In other words, the Sarvāmnāya 
tantra system, in its comprehensive, historically grounded instantiations, speaks for 
and embodies a country of diverse peoples whose primary religious orientation is 
grounded in the understanding that their religiocultural and geopolitical identities 
resemble the very water pot that is at the heart of the worship of their primary national 
goddess, Guhyeśvarī.
To understand how Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas themselves view their own tradi­
tion, one must take into account the historical assimilation of the multiple revelatory 
streams (āmnāyas) that merged into the waters of Nepāl’s own Northern Revelation 
(uttarāmnāya), and as a result how the Nepal kalaśa became a vessel for containing all 
the streams (nepāla-​sarvāmnāya-​kalāśa) (see fig. 36.3).
The ritual water–pot deity goddess par excellence in Nepal is the Mistress of the 
Secret, Guhyeśvarī. This fact is well documented by the presence of a kalaśa both out­
side the Guhyeśvarī temple’s tympanum (see fig. 36.4) and inside in its main sanctum. 
Guhyeśvarī is a highly venerated goddess by both the Hindus and Buddhists of Nepal. 
For Buddhists she is Vajrayoginī, or more precisely Nairātmyā, while for Hindus she 
is Guhyākālī and at times they overlap each other in people’s practice. For example, a 
Buddhist can at times be seen doing worship to Guhyākālī as Nairātmyā, while simul­
taneously a Hindu Śaiva-​Śākta might be seen chanting a Buddhist Guhyeśvarī hymn 
by Mañjunātha (from the Svayambhū-​purāṇa) or even chanting the verses from 
Māyātantra (Buddhist) which expounds the mysteries of Guhyeśvarī.24
As the goddess of the Northern Revelation (uttarāmnāya), arising out of the revel­
atory scriptural sources and geographical region associated with Nepal (uttarapīṭha), 
Guhyakālī is inseparably bound with the tutelary national god of Nepal, Paśupatinātha, 
who is the composite form of each of the six āmnāyas, which are themselves the means 
for removing all the fetters (pāśa).25 As such, Guhyeśvarī26 is referenced as the Goddess 
of All Revelations (sarvāmnāyeśvarī), and one who is to be “worshipped through all 
transmissions” (sarvāmnāyaprapūjitā).27
The Hāhārāva-​tantra (32a)28 likewise affirms that Guhyākālī is the goddess of all 
revelations (sarvāmnāyeśvarī) while clarifying that this same label can be applied to the 
other deities of all the other āmnāyas, as the principal deity of each are all manifestations 
of the supreme Goddess, Mahā Devī or Parāśakti. Abiding in a recurring logic that 
the one nondual reality (abheda) is manifest in manifold expression (bheda), Nepālī

initiates of Paścimāmnāya similarly understand the Goddess Kubjikā to be the Goddess 
of All Revelations (sarvāmnāyeśvarī). In fact, the Newār Rājopādhyāyas29 often say 
that the paścimāmnāya is both the sarvāmnāya (all āmnāyas) and the jyeṣṭhāmnāya 
(seniormost āmnāya). As such, they reiterate claims made by adherents of each of the 
other five āmnāya traditions within Nepal, as we will further discuss below.
An Account of the Six Revelations (Ṣaḍāmnāya-​Māhātmya), an unpublished manu­
script (ca. eighteenth century ce; see fig. 36.5) from Nepal, states that the one who has 
received full empowerment into either the Southern or Upper transmission is eligible 
for the practice of all the transmissions (sarvāmnāya).30 In Nepal, this principle of eligi­
bility applies to all the āmnāyas. For instance, the Newār Rājopādhyāyas of the Western 
Revelation (paścimāmnāya), upon receiving the final and complete initiation, known as 
the Liberating Initiation of Complete Eligibility into All the Revelations (sarvāmnāya 
sarvādhikāra nirvāṇa dīkṣā), thereby become eligible (adhikārī) for performing and 
imparting each and all of the revelations and related practices of the Six Revelations 
(ṣaḍāmnāya). For this reason, these Rājopādhyāyas refer to the Western Revelation 
(paścimāmnāya) as the Total Revelation (sarvāmnāya). When doing careful, system­
atic fieldwork in Nepal and not limiting one’s focus to just one revelation system, then 
one recognizes that this similar process of full inclusion of all the āmnāyas is also found 
among the practitioners of all the systems of revelations.
Sarvāmnāya as a Krama 
Tantra Tradition with Watery 
Indigenous Roots
To understand the history of Sarvāmnāya tantra in Nepal, it is of utmost importance 
that we understand the history of the krama system of tantra, as Nepālī Sarvāmnāya 
Figure 36.5.  First page of a manuscript named Sadāmnāya Māhātmya, ca. eighteenth century. 
Nepal National Archives.
Courtesy of L. S. Akshunna.

--- PAGE 952 ---

tantra is a krama practice—​one of “systematic order” (krama). The Bṛhad-​vaḍavānala-​
tantra reads, “Sarvāmnāya is prescribed into the krama division of six main vidyās 
(āmnāyas).”31 The Mahākāla-​Saṃhitā in its Kāmakalā-​Khaṇḍa section (8.690) reads, 
“one should do the practice in krama (a systematic order), first by practicing saptadaśī 
(seventeenfold mantra), accepted by sarvāmnāya (all-​revelations).”32 Moreover, the 
fifth-​century ce Śīlavatī inscription,33 which describes the krama system and its god­
dess Śarvāṇī,34 is not only the oldest Śākta inscription in Nepal but in the entire Śākta 
world (see fig. 36.6). The inscription reads: “with full devotion, the goddess of the Krama 
system, Śarvāṇī, is established” (Acharya 1996, 39–​45) (see fig. 36.7).
When discussing the krama system of tantra, one must understand the primacy of 
the Northern Revelation (uttarāmnāya), which emerges from the Northern Power Seat 
(uttarapīṭha). As Rastogi states, “Really speaking Krama is called Uttarāmnāya because 
it arose in and spread out from Uttarapīṭha” (Rastogi 1979, 44). Along these lines the 
Vaḍavānala-​tantra35 reads, “The deities Guhyakālī, Siddhilakṣmī . . .(etc.) are of the 
Northern Power-​seat (uttarāmnāya-​pīṭha) and they are excellent among all vidyās 
(wisdom) which give the caturvargaphala (fourfold-​fruits).”36 The Parātantra (4.1), a 
fifteenth-​century text37 says, “uttarāmnāya emerged from kālīkula.”38 The Mahākāla-​
saṃhitā reads, “among all (sarvāsāṃ) Kālīs, ten-​faces (daśa-​vaktrā) Guhyakālī is the 
principal-​one (mukhyatamā).”39
As noted above, in Nepal, Guhyakālī—​principal deity of uttarāmnāya—​is popu­
larly known as Guhyeśvarī and has her primary temple (pīṭha) near Paśupatinātha 
in Deopatan. The Kubjikāmata (10.22)40 provides the name of Guhyeśvarī as 
Guhyakālī and the Manthānabhairava states succinctly that Guhyeśvarī to­
gether with Paśupatinātha reside in Nepāla.41 The important Śākta text the Śrīmad‌ 
Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa (7.38.11) identifies the seat of Guhyakālī as Nepāla42 
while the Niśisañcāratantra, a text cited by the illustrious Abhinavagupta,43 links 
Guhyeśvarī together with Paśupatinātha as situated in Nepāla.44 Additionally, 
the Tripurārahasya Mahātmya-​khaṇḍa (48.74) claims that Nepāla is “the place of 
Guhyakeśvarī” (nepāle guhyakeśvarī).
