In sum, Nepal is clearly identified as the uttarapīṭha or Northern Seat by a multiplicity 
of central texts, inscriptions, and important architectural structures. Nevertheless, 
Rastogi opines for Kashmir as the true Northern Seat with the sole evidence for his 
case being a single mention of the term uttarapīṭha (in relation to the krama) in 
Tantrāloka-​viveka where it states that Śivānanda (a Kashmirian krama exponent) re­
ceived teachings at uttarapīṭha.45 But this statement begs the question: where exactly 
is the uttarapīṭha? Our position is that the overwhelming evidence is that the original 
seat of the Northern Revelation is Nepal. Moreover, we identify Guhyakālī (Guhyeśvarī) 
as the primary goddess of the Northern Revelation (uttarāmnāya). In this capacity, we 
understand Guhyakālī to have preeminent significance with regard to understanding 
the development and practice of Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra. In her status as the Goddess 
of All Revelations (sarvāmnāyeśvarī), Guhyakālī is to be worshipped through all the 
transmissions (sarvāmnāyaprapūjitā) in Nepal. The Goddess of the Secret abides as an 
indigenous core at the heart of the Nepālī tantric tradition.
But what exactly makes Nepal’s indigenous Northern Transmission tradition 
(uttarāmnāya) distinct from other tantric āmnāyas? To answer this question, we must 
appreciate the degree to which tantric traditions are literally grounded in the lands, 
peoples, and histories from which they emerge and for which they function as living 
expressions of the connection of identity to place. With regard to the prehistory of 
Figure 36.7.  Śarveśvara (a.k.a. Kumbheśvara) temple, Lalitpur.

Guhyeśvarī/​Guhyakālī in Nepal, a thorough study has not been done. However, as noted 
above, one can certainly trace her roots back to the early, pre-​Vedic Monsoon-​Culture of 
Śakti worship in which the goddess was and continues to be associated with water and 
fertility. The modern remnants of this ancient monsoon culture remain prevalent in the 
geographic and cultural landscape of Nepal to this day (Vajracharya 2016).
The Influence of Kashmir, Bengal, 
and South India
With regard to the historical development of Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra, we now note 
the important influence from and integration of the ritual manuscripts (paddhatis) that 
entered Nepal over the centuries from Gauḍa (Bengal), Kerala, and Kashmir. While the 
indigenous roots of Nepālī tantra are rightly traced through her Northern Transmission 
associated with the Guhyakālī, the complete development of the Sarvāmnāya tradi­
tion must be understood as a result of the migration of the important tantric traditions 
that flowed into Nepal from its western, southern, and eastern borders. A significant 
number of ritual manuals (paddhatis) from three regions share a geographic parsing 
of the subcontinent into three central regions. This parsing is consistent with that as 
stated in the Kālī-​khaṇda portion of the ca. seventeenth-​century ce Śakti-​saṅgama-​
tantra (4.3),46 which divides the triangular India (identified as bhāratavarṣa) itself into 
the three regions of Gauḍa (Bengal), Kerala, and Kashmir. It is from the central line of 
the Vindhyāvāsinī/​Vindhyācala mountain ranges that a geographical division is drawn. 
All regions east from the central point of the vindhyācala are Gauḍa, all regions west are 
Kashmir, and all regions south are Kerala. Nepāla is at uttara (north) of Vindhyācala.
As noted above, the cultural and geopolitical extents of Nepal ae not limited to the 
Kathmandu valley but rather incorporate the cultures of the lands at its borders. With 
specific regard to tantric revelation and practices, Nepal has equally integrated Gauḍa 
or Bengali tantra (as seen in the Śakti-​saṅgama-​tantra)47 together with Kaśmirī tantra 
(as seen in the Mahā-​siddhasāra-​tantra)48 and the tantra of South India generally and 
Kerala specifically. Indeed, Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantrics view their land as a sacred hub 
for the paddhatis of the regions of Gauḍa, Kashmir and Kerala (see fig. 36.8). Let us now 
turn to a brief analysis of the influence of each of these three regions.
Bengali/​Gauḍa Influence
In the 1920s, P. C. Bagchi (1934, 1), discovered the original manuscript of the 
Kaulajñānanirṇaya (together with other Kaula texts) in Nepal. This Gauḍa text of 
the Kaulajñānanirṇaya is attributed to Matsyendranātha,49 who is well known to be 
a Mahāsiddha from the Gauḍa region of Assam/​Kāmarūpa-​Kāmākhyā. However,

--- PAGE 955 ---
930      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
Matsyendranātha is nowhere venerated as he is in Nepal. The longest and one of the 
most important festivals of Nepal, the festival of Rāto (red) Matsyendranātha is cele­
brated every year in Nepal. In the festival, Matsyendranātha is brought to Lalitpur 
from Bungamati. The main priests are Buddhist Newār Shakyas under the mentorship 
(ācāryatva) of Newār Vajrācāryas, but the Kaula priests are also necessary to do the 
pūjā of Matsyendranātha in Lalitpur and they are the Newār Rājopādhyāya priests from 
Pūrṇacaṇḍī (Siddhilakṣmī) temple (see fig. 36.9). Nepali tradition believes that the deity 
(Siddhilakṣmī) in this temple is the tutelary deity of Matsyendranātha.
In his Kāmakalā-​Rahasya (1979, 40) Ja.Ba.Rā. goes so far as to state that Nepālī tantra 
is mostly Gauḍa-​influenced, and that a majority of the practices in Nepal’s temples are of 
Gauḍa nature. Indeed, if we look into Kulārṇava-​tantra (ca. eighth–​thirteenth century), 
we find that most of the Nepālī practices resemble its descriptions.
Kashmir Influence
Though not a Kaśmiri by birth, a śaivācārya named Vimalaprabodha (a south Indian)50 
who had studied in Kashmir51, came to Nepal in the thirteenth century ce with a 
Figure 36.8.  Regional division of tantra.

--- PAGE 956 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      931
 
number of books like the Devīdvyardhaśatikā (eleventh century ce) related to Trika 
Śaivism (also known as Kashmiri Śaivism).52 He was a guru who gave the coronation-​
empowerment to Ari Malla (r. 1200–​1216 ce), the first Malla king of Nepal. Inspired by 
his coronation-​guru, Ari Malla centered his political-​religious vision of his kingdom 
(dubbed “the territory of Nepal,” Nepāla-​Maṇḍala) specifically within the Kathmandu 
valley (Nepāla 2005, 136). With Vimalaprabodha, even when his ideas appear inspired by 
Kashmiri sources, his own written “expressions are unmistakably Dravidian, and prob­
ably from the Kannaḍa-​or Tuḷu-​speaking areas of the Deccan,” as Sanderson (2014, 64) 
noted. In other words, for Sanderson, those texts by Vimalaprabodha have their origins 
in the south, not Kashmir. According to Sanderson (2020, 8), the Trika texts that sur­
vive in Nepal are Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Tantrasadbhāva, and Trikasāra. Additionally, 
the Nepālī king following Ari Malla, Abhayamalla (r. 1216–​1255 ce), composed a tantric 
text named Amṛteśvarapūjana (Sanderson 2014, 47) based on Netra-​paddhati (which 
was composed in Kashmir between ca. 700 and 850 ce) (30).
Sanderson (2007, 2014) and Dyczkowski (1988) both identify a significant 
number of texts related to Kashmir Śaivism extant in Nepal. In addition to the 
Kālikākulapañcaśataka and the Devīdvyardhaśatikā, there is a text peculiarly impor­
tant for Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra based on the Kālī tradition (kālīkula) known as the 
Figure 36.9.  Kaula Newār Brahmin priests at Pūrṇacaṇḍī (Siddhilakṣmī) temple, Patan, 
Nepal. Courtesy of Bijaya Sharma Rajopadhyaya. This photo is of Newār Kaula Rajopadhyaya 
priests associated with the temple Pūrṇacaṇḍī (Siddhilakṣmī). Bijaya Sharma Rajopadyaya 
(standing on a lower base), who is associated with this temple, is one of the emerging well-​known 
young Kaula Newār priests, expert both in practice and philosophy.

--- PAGE 957 ---
932      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
Parātantra. This important tantra describes in detail all (sarva) of the systems of reve­
lation (āmnāyas). In its colophon, the Parātantra identifies itself as a tantra under the 
root tantra Śiraccheda.53 Sanderson (2007) writes “the non Saiddhāntika Śaiva exegetes 
of Kashmir are grounded within the Śakti tantra division of the Vidyāpītha, which 
contains texts of the two main divisions of that tradition: the Trika and the Kālīkula, 
rooted respectively in the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and the Śiraccheda” (235). While 
Parātantra mentions Śiraccheda,54 which suggests Kashmir, Parātantra is uniquely 
Nepālī in its composition and authorship. Moreover, while Sanderson states that this 
text is concocted and fictitious (2014, 67), from the emic view of Nepālī tāntrikas it is in­
stead perceived as a legitimate adaptation based on the authentic Nepālī tradition itself. 
Vimalaprabodha (thirteenth century ce), a non-​Nepālī, used a similar adaptive process 
when he came to Nepal and wrote Kālīkulakramārcana as a ritual text (paddhati) for the 
worship of the indigenous Nepālī goddess, Guhyakālī.55 Regardless of opinions on au­
thenticity, Parātantra (5.1) establishes that by the early fifteenth century, Nepālī tāntrikas 
were using the term sarvāmnāya in reference to their own traditions. Today, Parātantra 
remains a root text for the majority of Nepālī tāntrikas.
Keralan Influence
In Nepal, two roots of Keralan influence are noticeable, one in the temple practices of 
Paśupatinātha and a second in the practices of Taleju temples.56 At the Paśupatinātha 
temple in Deopatan, Nepal, the worship of all the revelations (sarvāmnāya-​pūjā) is 
practiced by placing a śrīyantra diagram drawn on the upper face (ūrdhva-​īśānāmukha) 
by the main temple priests, who are of the Bhaṭṭa clan. Though the Nepālī tradition 
holds that the renowned south Indian philosopher Ādi Śaṅkarācārya (ca. eighth century 
ce) himself established this practice here in Paśupatinātha, there is a lack of a sound 
historical evidence for this claim. Nonetheless, south Indian Bhaṭṭas have continuously 
been the priests here since at least 1734 ce, and they perform the pūjā according to the 
Keralan ritual manuals (paddhatis) (Michaels 2008, 23).
Regarding the goddess Taleju and her tradition, Newār Rājopādhyāyas, Karmācāryas, 
and astrologers (jośīs) have maintained her practice. Over the centuries, a number of 
different deities have been integrated into the figure of Taleju. One very popular legend57 
is that Tulajā Bhavānī (a form of Durgā) was brought to Nepal by King Harisiṃhadeva 
(r. 1304 to 1325 ce) of the Karnāṭa dynasty.58 This Tulajā is unique and distinct from the 
Tulajās that are prevalent in India at the moment because this Tulajā, according to the 
legend, has a śrīyantra incorporated within her. This integration is certainly seen in as­
sociation with the Taleju of Nepal. For example, on the tympanum of one of the doors 
of the Bhaktapur Taleju temple there is a goddess with nine heads in three rows. The 
uppermost row has a single head of the Durgā called Tvaritā whose Nature is Śrīvidyā 
(śrīvidyātmaka-​tvaritā59). In the second row there are three heads that represent the 
three forms of Durgā as Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Mahāsarasvatī. Below that, in the 
central row, there is Siddhilakṣmī60 with five heads. The entire composite form is known

--- PAGE 958 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      933
 
as the Tvaritā Durgā Whose Nature is Siddhilakṣmī and Kubjikā (siddha-​kubjikātmaka-​
tvaritā). Here, the śrīvidyātmaka tvaritā component of the images demonstrates the 
historical influence of śrīvidyā coming from the Kerala division of tantra.61 However, a 
prior, perhaps indigenous tradition, can easily be detected in Nepal through the analysis 
of the temples’ existence and practices in place before the start of both the Paśupatinātha 
and Taleju traditions (Bhanī 1984; Michaels 2008). In other words, the texts of these two 
Keralan traditions are integrated and adapted as per the already existing Nepālī tradi­
tion but without significantly altering the original function and meaning.62
The Influence of the Śāha Dynasty
To complete this study on the origins and nature of Sarvāmnāya tantra we must now 
look at the influence of the Śāha dynasty of Gorkha kings. It is through the patronage 
of these kings that the Sarvāmnāya tradition becomes firmly established as the national 
religion of Nepal. A proper early history of the Śāha (family of Gorkha) kings before 
Jaina Khām̐ṇa—​including their territories before they settled in Syāṅgjā—​is unknown 
and their Magar-​origin is controversial.63 However, in Syāṅgjā district of Gandaki 
Province, there is a temple of Śāha’s tutelary deity named Ālama-​devī where a preteen 
Magar boy occupies the role of a priest (see fig. 36.10). In this temple, in place of an idol 
Figure 36.10.  Temple of Ālama Devī, Lasargā, Syāṅgjā.
Courtesy of Ālama Devī Temple.

--- PAGE 959 ---
934      Jeffrey S. Lidke and L. S. Akshunna
 
there is simply a small tree. There is a saying that this goddess, which was brought by 
Jaina Khām̐ṇa, submerged (alapa) underground upon reaching the region. Hence this 
deity is called Ālama-​devī, meaning the “submerged or disappeared deity.”64 However, 
Jagman Gurung claims that the words Ālana (Karnali region), ālama (Gandaki region), 
and alām̐ (in Gurung dialect) are words meaning dhvajā, or flag.65
To identify this Ālama-​devī, the tutelary deity of Jaina Khām̐ṇa, one has to see when 
and how the main pūjā is practiced. The pūjā of the tutelary deity is done here every 
year on the fourteenth day of the bright lunar fortnight of vaiśākha month. According 
to Āgamic tradition,66 this is the day when the pūjā of Siddhilakṣmī is done. So, the tu­
telary goddess of Jaina Khām̐ṇawho disappeared (lost?/​submerged?) here seems to 
be Siddhilakṣmī. However, the disappearance of the goddess does not seem to mean 
the loss of her power, because a descendent of Jaina Khām̐ṇa has even more success in 
getting the kingdom of Kāskī (kāskī-​rājya).
The goddess Guhyakālī (Guptakālī in the local dialect) resides in Kāskī-​koṭa (see 
fig. 36.11). This is intriguing given that Siddhilakṣmī and Guhyakālī are both deities 
of the Northern Revelation (uttarāmnāya) and in one of the krama practices of 
the uttarāmnāya, the practice of Siddhilakṣmī is to be mastered first before that of 
Guhyakālī. It is also noteworthy that King Kulamaṇḍana Khām̐ṇa of Kāskī was bestowed 
with the title of Śāha or “mighty” by the Bādaśāha of Delhi, and since that time Śāha has 
been in use for their surname (Subedi 2003).
Figure 36.11.  Temple palace of Guhyakālī, Kāskīkoṭa.
Courtesy of Dinesh Sharma Marasini.

--- PAGE 960 ---
The Total Revelation Tantra      935
 
From Guhyakālī, Kāskī-​koṭa, one of the descendants of Kulamaṇḍana Śāha went 
to Lamjung and became king there; from Lamjuṅg, their descendent Dravya Śāha 
migrated to Gorkhā and became the first Śāha king of Gorkha in 1559 ce. There is a 
temple of Kālī at the Gorkhā palace (see fig. 36.12) and this deity is often called a younger 
sister of Guhyakālī of Kāskī, so Gorakha-​kālī seems to be another form of Guhyakālī.
Adjacent to the palace is also the Gorakhanātha cave temple. The relationship be­
tween the Gorakhanāthī and the Śāha Kings is well known in Nepal. In the Kathmandu 
valley, both Taleju (as Kubjikā) and Guhyeśvarī (as Guhyakālī) have great authority 
(see fig. 36.13). In the Gorakṣa-​saṃhitā (14.159–​14.167), there is an integrated form of 
Guhyakālī and Kubjikā whose iconography is detailed in fig. 36.14 (Pandeya 1976, 150–​
151). Moreover, the Gorakṣa-​saṃhitā (14.170–​14.171) explicitly states that this form is a 
higher form of Guhyakālī (as Guhyeśvarī).67
The descendent of Dravya Śāha, King Pṛthivī Nārāyaṇa Śāha, is said to have entered 
Kantipur with his military force in 1768 ce upon the occasions of the annual festival 
of Indra-​jātrā. Fearing for his life, King Jaya Prakāśa Malla fled to Lalitpur for asylum. 
Pṛthivī Nārāyaṇa went straight to the living goddess Kumārī, and rather than taking 
control of her, kneeled down and prostrated to her. In response, the Kumārī anointed 
Pṛthivī Nārāyaṇa Śāha as the King of Nepal by putting a ṭīkā on his forehead. This 
shows that the living goddess Kumārī (the embodiment of Goddess Taleju) favored him 
(Gurung 2022; Lidke 2017, 125).68 The Bṛhat Puraścaryārṇava69 says that the kumārī, the 
clan virgin (kulabālā), is herself worshipped by all the āmnāyas (sarvāmnāya-​prapūjitā).

Conclusion
In conclusion, we offer a timeline for Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra in table 36.2, which 
identifies the key sources for the tradition, beginning in the fifth century. We have pro­
vided notation for the purpose of reminding the reader of the specific significance of 
each reference in the table.
What table 36.2 establishes is that the origins of Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra extend 
back to the fifth century with the famous Paśupatinātha inscription identifying the five 
faces of Śiva as the source of the streams of revelation (āmnāya). In this same century we 
find evidence of the presence of the Krama tantric tradition in Nepal, which is signifi­
cant as Nepālī Sarvāmnāya tantra is a Krama system grounded in the revelations that 
arise from the faces of Śiva. Contemporary Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas identify the seventh 
century as the time of the great Nepālī Kaula master, Matsyendranātha. This is also the 
beginning of the composition of important root texts which are not only housed at the 
Nepal National Archives but which likely were composed in or around Nepal. Running 
from the seventh through the sixteenth centuries, these texts include the Ciñcinīmata,

In terms of architectural evidence for Sarvāmnāya tantra, we see the construction of 
the Sarveśvara temple (see fig. 36.7) to the āmnāya-​generating Śiva in the fourteenth 
century, and by the sixteenth century we witness the construction of multiple temples to 
the royal Newār Sarvāmnāya goddess par excellence, Taleju (see fig. 36.16). By the eight­
eenth century we see the composition of the Sarvāmnāya-​tantra, Śakti-​saṅgama-​tantra, 
and Tantracintāmaṇi—​all key texts for contemporary Sarvāmnāya practitioners. It is in 
the eighteenth century that the great Śāha king, Pratāpa Siṃha, composed the Bṛhat-​
Puraścaryārṇava, an invaluable compendium of Sarvāmnāya practice. In the modern 
age, we have the invaluable writings of Dhana Śamaśera and Pt. Kṛṣṇa Prasāda Bhaṭṭarāī 
as well as the scholarship of a host of Nepālī and Western scholars—​scholarship that is 
helping shape and preserve the Sarvāmnāya tradition even as Nepālī culture and society 
undergoes tremendous forces of change.
Today, Newār and non-​Newār Nepālī tāntrikas alike identify their tradition as 
being the tradition that contains the total (sarva) revelation of the six streams of rev­
elation (ṣaḍ-​āmnāya) by naming it Sarvāmnāya tantra (see fig. 36.17). In the course 
of their respective spiritual disciplines (sādhanas), Sarvāmnāya tāntrikas seek in­
itiation into each of the six revelations as it is through the cumulative total of all

Taleju head priest).
Courtesy of Binaya Bikram Shah and Sandip Sapkota.

The Total Revelation Tantra      941
 
the revelations that one achieves the desired status of being “established in all the 
āmnāyas” (sarvāmnāya-​viśaradā). Although no religious populace is ever 100 per­
cent cognizant of the esoteric meaning of its respective religious practices, it is the 
case that in Nepal there are a significant number of scholar-​practitioners who are 
indeed well versed in the deeper meaning of the practices of all the āmnāyas. Given 
that Nepal not only birthed a good number of texts and traditions—​including but 
not limited to the Guhyakālī tradition of the Northern Revelation—​but also has 
functioned to this day as a proverbial “water pot” for the inflow of the streams of 
revelation that came from Kashmir, Bengal, and Kerala, one therefore cannot over­
emphasize the impact and value of the Sarvāmnāya tradition for the study and un­
derstanding of tantra in South Asia.

	2.	 From verbal root bhid “to portion or divide,” bheda implies “diversity,” and its opposite, 
abheda, indicates the absence of diversity or unity. The compound phrase bhedābheda 
literally means “unity-​in-​diversity.” The term has been used by Hindu theologians across 
sectarian lines since the seventh century ce to refer to the panentheistic vision that crea­
tion is God’s emanation. The multiplicity of creation is One. See Nicholson 2010, passim. 
This vision of unity-​through-​multiplicity is in turn translated into the social and political 
logic at the heart of the vision of Nepal as a mandala. See Lidke 2017, 78–​84. Cf. Slusser 
1982, passim.
	3.	 Dyczkowski makes this claim as part of his brief response to an uncited passage from 
Lidke’s dissertation on Śrī Vidyā traditions in Nepal in which the latter summarizes 
the Sarvāmnāya as a progression of Śākta tantric initiations that link the scriptures and 
mantras of the six āmnāyas to cakras within the subtle physiology through the methods of 
kuṇḍalinī-​yoga.
	4.	 This kind of variation in labels and practices is a characteristic of the very nature and, as it 
were, style of Nepālī tantra, with its inclusivist orientation. The ideal of a Total Revelation 
can certainly incorporate the label “Six Revelations.” While some Newārs, like Kedar Raj, 
may teach (to at least some) that there is only one initiation, this does not mean that for 
other Newārs multiple initiations is not the norm. One need not assume, as Dyczkowski 
does, that Sarvāmnāya is a Parbatīyā tradition, alien to the Newārs. Further, it important 
to note here that the term “Parbatīyā” (“of the hills”) is by no means a fixed caste category 
that in each and every case identifies people who are clearly distinct from those who call 
themselves Newār. Relative to the people of India, for example, the entire population of 
Nepal has been labeled “of the [northern] hills.” Relative to the people of the Kathmandu 
valley, everyone outside the valley has been labeled “of the hills,” including, primarily 
those who migrated from India. And within the Kathmandu valley itself some groups ei­
ther self-​identify as or are otherwise labeled as “of the hills” and at times even if they are 
otherwise properly identified as Newārs. In short, the question of what or who exactly a 
Parbatīyā is can be a rich and complicated topic of debate. Indeed, one example of this 
complexity is the fact that Newār Rājopādhyāyas and Parbatīyā Kumāī Brāhmaṇa’s both 
trace their origins to Kannauj in north India (Toffin 2007, 51). Before migrating to Nepal, 
both of these groups likely viewed the land of Nepal as “of the hills” and while today the 
Rājopādhyā may reference his Kumāī contemporary as “parbatīyā” the use of such a label 
does not eradicate the historical fact that they share common geographical and cultural 
roots. In short, whatever conclusions one comes to in the context of this debate, it would 
be a mistake to assume that within the Kathmandu valley particularly, but even Nepal 
as whole, that that which is Parbatīyā may not be Newār and vice versa. Certainly, this is 
true when it comes to the greater system of Nepālī tantric practice. Whether we call that 
system All Revelations or Six Revelations or both, depending on context, it is important 
to understand that the essential components of the practice are shared by tantrics across 
caste categories and boundaries.
	5.	 Indeed, from the Sarvāmnāya perspective, Tripurāsundarī and Kālī are the same deity 
with two aspects. As it states in the Bṛhat-​Puraścaryārṇava: “In accordance with the dis­
tinction as Śyāmā (the dark one) and Raktā (the red one), Kālī is twofold. The dark one 
is called Dakṣiṇā whereas the red one is called Śrī [Tripurā]Sundarī.” Sā Kāḷī dvividyā 
proktā śyāmāraktāprabhedataḥ. Śyāmāra tu dakṣiṇā proktā rakta Śrī Sundarī matā. (Bṛhat-​
Puraścaryārṇava, Part 1, p. 24).

	26.	 The goddess often associated with Kubjikā in Nepal is Taleju, who is said to be the Royal 
Goddess of Malla Kings; however, there is a difference between the royal goddess of the 
Mallas and Kubjikā. One of the reasons Taleju is considered as Kubjikā is because the 
Newār priests who do the worship of her are initiates of pascimāmnāya and do ritual-​
worship according to this āmnāya’s specific conduct and codes. However, to say Taleju 
is exactly Kubjikā and nothing else would be far-​fetched because there are many Taleju 
temples and there is no uniformity in their practice. Even the Kubjikā established on the 
southern door tympanum of Taleju temple in Kathmandu is integrated with Tvaritā (see 
Ja.Ba.Ra. 1979, 151). So, together with Kubjikā, multiple deities including Siddhilakṣmī, 
Ugracaṇḍa, Tripurā, Pratyaṅgirā, and Guhyākālī (all deities mostly from uttarāmnāya) 
are worshiped in the practice of Taleju. Nevertheless, even when Taleju is considered as 
Kubjikā, the importance of Guhyeśvarī is of utmost importance in Nepal. This becomes 
clearer with the jātra (festive-​procession) from Taleju to Guhyeśvarī temple that occurs 
every year on Mārgaśīrṣa-​Daśamī (tenth dark fortnight of the lunar months around 
November–​December) where it is said that the festive-​procession is about the goddess 
Taleju visiting Guhyeśvarī to pay her homage.

that is, sarvāmnāya-​prapūjitā (worshiped by all āmnāyas).
