--- PAGE 978 ---
Chapter 37
The Soteriologies of 
Buddhist Tantrism
Iain Sinclair
Introduction
Soteriology can be defined as the theory and practice of saving living beings from 
suffering in an ultimate sense. If soteriology is at heart concerned with the transition 
from being lost to being saved,1 and with a process of internal transformation, then the 
role of an external savior may be peripheral or altogether unnecessary. Such a notion of 
soteriology has been applied to Buddhist analytical approaches involving the aggregates 
of personality, for instance, and the application of the dialectic of emptiness to the sub­
ject of suffering.2 For Buddhists, what ultimately saves lies within, and dependence on 
an outer, absolute force cannot be reconciled with the agency of the practitioner or with 
nonessentialist Buddhist thinking.
In the classical Buddhist worldview, it is ultimately the attainment of awakening 
(bodhi) that saves from suffering. The associated final state of peace, nirvana, is corre­
spondingly remote and elusive. Nirvana is not, however, the prime goal of the tantric 
practitioner. Buddhist tantrism builds on the soteriology of the Mahāyāna, in which cy­
clic existence, the condition of misery from which beings need to be saved, is under­
stood to be codependent with nirvana (saṃsāranirvāṇavibhāvana). The exemplar of 
salvation, the bodhisattva, hovers in “nonsettled” nirvana (apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa) lifetime 
after lifetime in order to perform altruistic deeds for others. Although the bodhisattva 
ideal continues to be valued in tantrism, it is shaken up by the revelation that awakening 
can be attained “in this lifetime” (iha janmani). The deferred gratification of the bodhi­
sattva, concomitant with belief in rebirth, is no longer central or even relevant. While 
Buddhist tantras put forward a plethora of methods that are claimed to lead to rapid sal­
vation, they were often seen as drastic, unconventional, and especially at odds with the 
rule-​following monastic or layperson, the śrāvaka.

--- PAGE 979 ---
954      Iain Sinclair
 
The conception of tantric Buddhism as a path to salvation distinct from other paths 
is the focus of this chapter. The many and varied means for moving along this path can 
only be mentioned in passing, even if these means are often regarded as integral to the 
salvific process. Nor is there room to go into aspects of Buddhist tantrism such the 
emic classifications of tantras—​which were often correlated to grades of soteriological 
efficacy—​and the evidence for dating individuals, texts and so on.3 What is presented 
here is but a sketch of the progression of tantric Buddhist soteriology, which draws on 
published editions of tantras as well as the renascent scholarship in this field that has 
been stimulated by the Tibetan diaspora, postwar Japanese prosperity, and the improved 
availability of primary sources in the information age. Attention is given to the busiest 
period, spanning the mid-​seventh to the mid-​eleventh centuries, and to South Asian 
and Sanskrit sources, which underpin Buddhist tantrism wherever it manifests.4
Defining Tantrism
Buddhist tantras appeared at a time when religions in South Asia were giving more at­
tention to techniques such as mantric invocation, programmatic visualization, and 
yogas of the body, and to the role of the teacher who knows reality. Such developments 
spread across sectarian boundaries, along with speculation about the nature of the re­
ality that they opened up. However, the teachings of the tantras are not easily reduced to 
one type of praxis. In tantric traditions that urge yogis to remain focused on salvation, 
rather than the specifics of process—​the “practice without elaboration” is discussed later 
in this chapter—​ubiquitous forms of religion such as mantra repetition and the wor­
ship of images are disparaged.5 The supposedly unimpeachable authority of the guru, 
likewise, is sometimes met with criticism and calls for teachers to meet the standards 
set for them in tantric discourse.6 And although it has been noticed since the start of 
the modern era that tantrism is an initiatory religion,7 transmitted by a guru or ācārya, 
much of the behavior that co-​occurs with tantrism—​such as magic, divination, pūjā, 
yoga, pilgrimage, and artistic and architectural creation of certain kinds—​does not need 
to be authorized by a rite of initiation.
Tantrism has been defined both emically and etically by listing its observed features.8 
It is also possible to identify a common tantric culture in instances of intertextuality, 
which express shared ideas about salvation. One maxim, for instance, has been seen as 
typical of tantric soteriology:9
That by which creatures are bound . . . by that itself they are freed from the bondage 
of existence.
This is an example of a principle propounded in a tantric Buddhist context that was 
adopted into Śaivism and its exegesis.10 Tantric soteriology often transmutes the subjects 
rejected by other faiths into an otherwise unattainable experience of the extraordinary.

--- PAGE 980 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      955
 
Tantrism can then be described as a religiosity of the other, of becoming other (para) in 
search of transcendence, which leads toward different soteriological goals in different 
religious traditions. Buddhist tantrism, in the present context, refers to the principles 
and processes of salvation taught in Buddhist tantras and in their exegesis.
The First Soteriological Buddhist 
Tantras
The potential for a “way of mantra praxis” (mantracaryānaya) to reach the endpoint of 
enlightenment, or an equivalent state, becomes a central concern in a revealed scrip­
ture, the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi. Like other texts of the seventh-​century period that 
teach mantric methods for salvation, the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi calls itself a sūtra of 
the Mahāyāna, but is often referred to by others as a tantra.11 Earlier scriptures that re­
vealed mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī), “heart” mantras (hṛdaya), and so on were some­
times claimed to be conducive to spiritual progress, but individual texts of this kind did 
not arrive at a systematic vision of salvation.12 The Vairocanābhisambodhi, by contrast, 
positions its mantric practices both within the bodhisattvas’ religion and as an alter­
native to the “difficult relinquishments” (duṣkaraparityāgāni) that they perform over 
uncountable lifetimes, such as the giving up of their lives and comforts for others. The 
effects of mantras are said to extend directly into the mindstream in the present lifetime:
It is to be entirely realized (abhisambudhyante) by the bodhisattva who practises bo­
dhisattva practice through the gateway of mantra (mantramukhabodhisattvacaryācā
riṇā) that their own mind—​devoid of all existence, dissociated from the aggregates 
of personality, the senses, and their domains, and the perception of subject and ob­
ject (skandhadhātvāyatanagrāhyagrāhaka)—​is, due to its similarity with the non-​
selfhood of dharmas (dharmanairātmyasamatayā), originally unborn, having the 
inherent nature of emptiness.13
The association of mantric methods with the attainment of an essenceless, liberating 
cognition was an important development. The terminology of this passage was incor­
porated into the later Guhyasamāja, and it had lasting significance in the exegesis of the 
Buddhist tantras as a whole.14
Another key proposition of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi is that the state of salvation, 
namely, the realization of the “gnosis of all-​knowledge” (sarvajñajñānam), has compas­
sion as its root (karuṇāmūlam), is caused by the will to awaken (bodhicittahetukam), 
and is brought to a conclusion through skilful means (upāyaparyavasānam). Although 
this is but a restatement of elementary Mahāyāna principles,15 in the tantric context it 
foregrounds the critical role of bodhicitta in the practitioner’s motivation and the ac­
ceptability of means of all kinds. Positioning compassion as the foundation of tantric 
practice harks back to the classical understanding that the Buddha taught in order to

--- PAGE 981 ---
956      Iain Sinclair
 
benefit all beings, and deprecates tantrism practiced for the sole purpose of gaining per­
sonal power or gratifying the deity.
Mantra praxis in this system involves identification with the pantheon of the 
“mandala born from the Matrix of Great Compassion” (*mahākaruṇāgarbhodbha-
vamaṇḍala). The mandala emanates from the cosmic buddha Vairocana, proliferating 
into the tathāgatas of the directions, a host of bodhisattvas and mantra deities drawn in 
part from pre-​existing dhāraṇī traditions, and a conclave of nature spirits, demigods, 
and gods who take their places on the periphery.16 Each member of the mandala can 
be invoked by a variety of means, whether by recalling their physical likeness, forming 
their associated gesture, or reciting their characteristic mantra. Such mandalas and their 
processes of rote yogic identification with its inhabitants comprise a schematic, totalistic 
vision of awakening, which varies according to the particulars of the tantra in which it is 
taught.
The Vairocanābhisambodhi self-​consciously arrives in a crowded religious field in 
which all-​knowledged gnosis “teaches religion to all beings according to various ways, 
various inclinations, various means.” It manifests as “the way of the Śrāvakayāna for 
some, the way of Pratyekabuddhayāna for some, the way of the Mahāyāna for some.” 
The dharma emanating from the Great Vairocana could even be seen to be taught by 
Viṣṇu or Śiva for those so inclined.17 On the other hand, these diverse paths to salva­
tion are not held to be equivalent in their efficacy. For instance, the śrāvakas are only 
taught about gnosis, without the means for attaining it.18 The suite of meditative and 
ritual techniques imparted in the Vairocanābhisambodhi is typical of a new soteriolog­
ical vision of programmatic gnosis. Mantra praxis is presented both as a subsidiary path 
of the Mahāyāna and as the “foremost vehicle” of salvation (agrayāna), rather than as an 
entirely distinct development.
Vajrayāna and the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha
The denomination of Vajrayāna is introduced in the revelation of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, a scripture divided into sections that end with the 
words: “This well-​spoken Sūtra, the diamond-​thunderbolt-​like vehicle (vajrayāna), the 
secret of all Tathāgatas, is an encapsulation (abhisaṃgraha) of the whole of the Great 
Vehicle.”19 Accordingly, Vajrayāna soteriology incorporates pioneering features of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha: the unfolding of a vision of the Buddha pentad united 
by thunderbolt-​like gnosis (vajrajñāna), the routines of mantra-​yogic identification 
with the mandala by means of the Four Seals (caturmudrā) and so on, and the rites that 
authorize their practice and further propagation.
As is the case throughout tantric Buddhism, the formal authorization of praxis 
occurs in a rite of initiation, generically known as “unction” or “anointment” (seka, 
abhiṣeka),20 which forges a compact (samaya) between the initiand and a “deity” 
(devatā) who resides in the mandala.21 The rite of initiation introduces the initiand

--- PAGE 982 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      957
 
to a set of methods for performing yoga, in which the deities themselves are called 
on to grant authorization and ultimately reside in the practitioner’s consciousness 
as Vajrasattva. Although access to initiation is often restricted, in a spirit of univer­
sality the initiation of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha is open to all takers. Its 
yoga is said to offer better prospects of salvation for persons who are not suited for 
non-​tantric Buddhism—​to those who “crave all kinds of things, food, drink and sen­
sual enjoyments,” to those who “dread precepts,” and even to “religious beings” who 
have been worn out by pursuing conventional goals of ethical discipline, meditation, 
and insight (śīlasamādhiprajñā).22 The initiatory processes themselves are, how­
ever, to be kept secret. Some initiands are anticipated to have prior commitments to 
non-​Buddhist religion—​namely, to have “entered the maṇḍalas of other deity clans” 
(anyadevakulamaṇḍalāni praviśanti).
From the start, Buddhist soteriology has aimed to expose and sidestep the pitfalls 
of the ambient socioreligious environment surrounding the Buddha’s path. The 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha narrates a famous episode in which Maheśvara, “con­
ceited with supremacy over the whole triverse,” refuses to enter the mandala that 
distills the “teaching of all Tathāgatas” and imparts the gnosis of all-​knowledge. In an 
angry altercation, he is slain by the mantras of the Buddha’s bodyguard Vajrapāṇi and 
resurrected. Maheśvara then joins the other converted gods as one of the mandala’s 
protectors.23 This much-​discussed Maheśvara subjugation myth asserts the primacy of 
the gnosis attained through the Vajrayāna, while internalizing in pacified form the ex­
ternal reality of hostile theist competition. The forcing of Maheśvara into the fold of 
the all-​knowing Buddha reflects the altruistic concern, expressed in the proto-​tantric 
Kāraṇḍavyūha, that the masses who place faith in Maheśvara will be deprived of a path 
to awakening (bodhimārgeṇa viprahīṇāḥ).24 The subjugation episode further sets the 
scene for the yogin to reenact the suppression of the gods in apotropaic ritual, a topic of 
interest in Buddhist tantras of all kinds.
The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha also asserts that the Vajrayāna is synonymous 
with, or supervenes upon, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattvas. The mandala duly 
sources some of its inhabitants from preexisting Mahāyāna narratives, as had also 
occurred in the Vairocanābhisambodhi and other early tantras.25 However, the model 
renunciant of conservative Buddhism, the śrāvaka, is not mentioned even once in the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. Increasing prominence and centrality is instead given 
to female figures who personify salvific Mahāyāna virtues or acts such as pūjā, as well as 
new tantric concepts such as the Four Secret Seals of the “sex-​thunderbolt” (rativajra) 
and so on.26
Beyond Convention and Conceptuality: The Guhyasamāja
A watershed in the development of tantric Buddhist soteriology is reached with the 
inversion of conventional morality in the Guhyasamāja. The speaker of this tantra,

--- PAGE 983 ---
958      Iain Sinclair
 
Vajradhara, combines the “body, speech and mind of all Tathāgatas,” a typically tantric 
abstraction of Buddhahood. In the tantra’s fifth chapter Vajradhara tells bodhisattvas:
The clans of passion, hate and delusion, becoming intent on nonconceptuality 
(nirvikalpa), can achieve greater success (siddhi) in the highest vehicle, unsurpassed 
. . . the Buddhayāna, this Mahāyāna.27
The path to salvation is now open to groups who would otherwise be hampered by 
their defilements. The goal is no longer awakening or nirvana—​already out of reach for 
most followers of the Buddha—​but its effective equivalent: a state of cognition without 
conceptuality or discrimination, which had been established as a trait of all-​knowing 
gnosis in the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi.28 And the ideal means is not restraint or altruism, 
as advocated in regular Buddhism, but the experiential “proving” or “effectuation,” 
sādhana, of the desired state of mind through special means. A sādhana is applied so­
teriology, shaped according to the situations of its practitioners and of the tradition in 
which it is transmitted. It leads ultimately to the status of adept, siddha, or some other 
achievement tantamount to Buddhahood. The Guhyasamāja’s teaching on sādhana is 
so unconcerned with conventional morality that it causes bodhisattvas to faint in shock:
Beings who kill, who love lying, who delight in stealing others’ possessions, who love 
lust, who make bodily wastes their food (viṇmūtrāhārakṛtyā)—​they indeed are good 
at sādhana.29
Here is a direct inversion of the five precepts of the Buddhist layperson—​namely, the 
precepts to abstain from killing, lying, stealing, sexual misconduct, and intoxicants.30 
The extremeness of the inversion serves to downgrade the idea of regular ethics as re­
flective of reality in any essential way. However, these “perverse” dismissals of conven­
tional Buddhist morality, so called, amount to more than mere verbiage or “hyperbole.”31 
As the tantra turns to other topics, its soteriology continues to hinge on “worshipping 
as one likes with the enjoyment of all desires,”32 and to be expressed in acts involving 
polluting substances and sexual intercourse. This is all positioned as legitimate Buddhist 
soteriology, with the speaker of the tantra being addressed as follows: “O Vajra of pas­
sion, hate and delusion, O Preacher of Vajrayāna . . . Salutation to you, Purified body, 
speech and mind, O Vajrayāna.”33 But insofar as the Vajrayāna is understood to require 
the transgressive behaviors taught in this tantra, its compatibility with conventional and 
institutional Buddhism remains in doubt.
The game-​changing antinomianism of the Guhyasamāja, which moves far beyond 
the reserved transgressive sentiments of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha,34 has not 
yet been located in a particular socioreligious environment or otherwise explained 
as a product of historical circumstances. It has been pointed out that the moral inver­
sion taught in this tantra scandalizes Brahmanical sensibilities even more than those 
of Buddhism—​a reaction that became quite apparent when the tantra resurfaced in the 
nineteenth century35—​and that in so doing it rebels much more against theist hegemony

--- PAGE 984 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      959
 
in South Asia.36 However, the tantra reveals only a “dehistoricized” vision, in which 
known episodes of social stress or crisis are not discernible and non-​Buddhist religion 
is barely noticed, apart from passing references to Hindu gods (or their followers) as 
potential opponents in magical battles.37 While erotic, antinomian rituals were also 
starting to appear in the Hindu tantrism of the Picumata and so on at around the same 
time,38 their rationales are tied to the Brāhmaṇa–​Śaiva milieu to such a degree that they 
do not transfer to Buddhism in any straightforward way.
It is clear that the Guhyasamāja’s message found a receptive audience, as the tantra 
was soon quoted in manuals for initiation, consecration and regular meditation or 
sādhana.39 Its dictates were taken seriously—​if not by the “outcastes, flute makers, 
slaughterers,”40 and other marginalized persons who were excluded from institutional 
Buddhism and who are identified as the tantra’s ideal practitioners, then by a faction 
of the monastic saṅgha. The Guhyasamāja’s injunctions to kill, lie, steal, and fornicate 
were repeated verbatim at initiation ceremonies presided over by saṅgha members. 
One of the earliest practical handbooks in this tradition, the Vimśatividhi, is reli­
ably attributed to the tantric monk Nāgabuddhi.41 Many more monastics followed 
Nāgabuddhi as interpreters and practitioners of the transgressive soteriology revealed 
in the Guhyasamāja. In some traditions, the Guhyasamāja would be held up as the de­
finitive revelation of the soteriology of the Buddha pentad, which corresponds to the 
literary genre of Yogatantra or Mahāyogatantra, whereas for others, the most important 
revelation in this genre continued to be the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha.
The Subaltern Theophany of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga
The growing acceptance of the involvement of women in praxis, and of the body as 
the locus of enlightenment, is apparent in the Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃ-
vara or Sarvabuddhasamāyoga, another influential Buddhist tantra. The practices 
of this tantra are repeatedly said to bring about “equivalence with all Buddhas” 
(sarvabuddhasamāyoga) —​ to emulate or reflect the qualities of enlightened conscious­
ness. Much of this tantra is taken up with instructions for invoking deities with hand 
gestures (mudrā)—​a common element of early Buddhist tantric ritual—​together with 
newer methods such as whole body postures (abhinaya) and tantric songs (vajragīti) 
sung in Apabhraṃśa, a Middle Indic vernacular. Performances of this kind persist in a 
major subculture of tantric Buddhism in which the practitioner manifests the persona 
of the deity with the immediacy of song and dance. The honoring of the samaya in a 
gathering of initiates who embody their respective deities is a related practice, which 
is later standardized as the ritual of the “group circle” (gaṇacakra). It is described in the 
Sarvabuddhasamāyoga in brief and prototypical form:
A well accomplished woman, lovely with her own mudrā and insignia, should 
be imagined as the maṇḍala of the group (gaṇamaṇḍala) by those facing their 
principal deity.42

--- PAGE 985 ---
960      Iain Sinclair
 
There is a consistent emphasis on vocal and bodily performance in this tantra, which 
extends to another form of embodied practice, that of “forceful yoga,” haṭhayoga. The 
Sarvabuddhasamāyoga has been identified as the earliest known tantric source for the 
term haṭhayoga.43 The salvific psychophysical experience of “great bliss,” mahāsukha—​
which had been deified as Vajrasattva in an earlier Buddhist tantra, the Śrīparamādya—​
also receives more attention here. Again, such praxis terms are introduced with 
assurances that they create identicality with all Buddhas.
Although many of the innovations and practices of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga- 
ḍākinījālasaṃvara were absorbed into Buddhist tantrism as a whole, this tantra 
is also known as the progenitor of a distinct and divergent stream of religiosity that 
the later tradition classifies as Yoginītantra. The titular woman of this tantra is the 
ḍākinī, another fringe figure, seen as a “witch or an old woman,”44 a sorcerous female 
type existing outside the Buddhist mainstream. As the ḍākinī masters flight of the 
shamanic or yogic kind, she is identified with the yogic attainment that traverses the 
whole of space (sarvākāśacarā siddhi), a hallmark of the gnosis of all tathāgatas, and 
in this sense she has the status of “universal mudrā.”45 This tantra also nominates as 
a ferocious figurehead the mortuary divinity called Heruka, a kind of successor to 
Vajrapāṇi.46 Heruka is a deity of the charnel grounds where ḍākinīs gather to offer 
flesh and blood, and who is briefly noticed in this capacity in non-​Buddhist tantras. 
He is described as
Immense with a crown of skulls and a great blaze of flaming hair, frightening like a 
charnel ground [made] pitch dark by a great conflagration.47
The elevation of the frightful Heruka and the man-​eating ḍākinīs into figures to be 
adored and imitated on the path to salvation represents another major shift away from 
the benevolent ethos of the buddhas and bodhisattvas. This Buddhist thrust into the 
subaltern territory of charnel-​ground religion led to the advent of the Herukābhidhāna 
(a.k.a. Cakrasaṃvaratantra48), the Hevajra (a.k.a. Dvikalpa) and so on. These 
tantras centered on different sexually coupled forms of Heruka soon supplanted the 
Sarvabuddhasamāyoga itself.
In appraising the position of these Yoginītantras within Buddhist tantrism as a whole, 
it should be recognized that most commentators construed them through established 
Mahāyāna and mantranaya conceptual frameworks such as the gnostic Buddha pentad. 
The Yoginītantras’ objects of devotion, the ḍākinīs and bone-​clad warlocks, were not 
as widely depicted in South Asia as the tantric buddhas, bodhisattvas and deities of the 
“lower” tantras.49 Furthermore, the practices later associated with Heruka, such as the 
previously alien cult of pilgrimage to the goddesses’ power places (pītḥa), received little 
attention from exegetes of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the Guhyasamāja, and so 
on. These foundational tantras remained at the heart of Buddhist tantrism and its inter­
pretative enterprise, even after the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga gave rise to one of its major 
subtraditions.

--- PAGE 986 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      961
 
Pioneering Interpretations of Tantric 
Buddhist Soteriology
Some of the earliest and most influential figures in the exegesis of tantric Buddhism are 
non-​monastic yogīs or yoginīs, according to tradition and internal indications in their 
works.50 They are not known to have belonged to a monastic saṅgha,51 and they inter­
pret the Buddhist tantras without referring to the conventional ethics of the monk or the 
layperson, even though they teach from an otherwise Buddhist standpoint. A seminal 
work from this milieu is the Jñānasiddhi of Indrabhūti —​ apparently a nom de plume for 
a king of a region once known as Oḍḍiyāna. Indrabhūti’s impact was such that Oḍḍiyāna 
was valorized as a tantric Buddhist homeland for many generations; this region has not, 
however, yet been decisively identified with a historical polity in current scholarship.52 
The Jñānasiddhi refers directly to the Sarvatathāgatattvasaṃgraha, the Guhyasamāja 
and its uttaratantra, the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga and so on. Much the same tantric 
corpus informs Padmavajra’s Guhyasiddhi. Then there is the brief Advayasiddhi of 
Lakṣmī, which shares some verses with the Guhyasiddhi. Lakṣmī’s treatise heralds the 
growing visibility of women in Buddhism as authorities on tantrism. These three works 
along with four others in the same vein, all having titles ending in siddhi, constituted a 
mini-​corpus of “seven siddhi texts” (grub pa sde bdun) for the Tibetans who eventually 
received and translated them.53
Much of the Jñānasiddhi, Guhyasiddhi, and Advayasiddhi and so on is occupied 
with paraphrasing or amplifying the doctrines of the Guhyasamāja. Padmavajra and 
Lakṣmī, for instance, both reiterate the tantra’s injunctions to take polluting substances 
as sacraments.54 Indrabhūti, however, often discusses misunderstandings and abuses. 
Even and especially on the path to salvation where anything goes, the cardinal sins of 
disrespecting the guru and the samaya could not represent the only wrong turns. Some 
of the admonitions in Indrabhūti’s Jñānasiddhi were separately reexpressed as a set of 
praxis “downfalls” (āpatti), which were later adopted as formal restraints on the be­
havior of the Vajrayāna practitioner.55 In one long discussion, Indrabhūti is at pains 
to point out that transgressive acts do not in themselves lead to liberation, and that 
nonconceptuality does not warrant immorality:56
Some most idiotic juveniles who do not look at reasoning and scripture say, ‘evil may 
as well be just conceptuality,’ destroying themselves.57
His appeal to the classical reasoning-​and-​scripture dialectic tempers the absolute 
authority of the guru—​often asserted in the tantras—​and helps to establish Buddhist 
tantrism as a principled undertaking rooted in scriptural sources. Although no over­
arching interpretative strategy is put forward at this stage, Indrabhūti and Padmavajra 
pay close attention to certain passages of the Guhyasamāja, and are aware of the

--- PAGE 987 ---
962      Iain Sinclair
 
relatively developed two-​stage system of tantric praxis comprising the stage of genera­
tion (utpattikrama) and the stage of the generated (utpannakrama).58
The seven siddhi texts provide valuable data on the early reception of tantric religi­
osity, which is not always easy to glean from the tantras themselves. One passage in the 
Guhyasiddhi that has excited a great spurt of interest in modern scholarship mentions 
two Śaivite tantras by name.59 Here Padmavajra recommends that the yogī tout copies 
of these tantras to win the confidence of non-​Buddhist outcastes, such that they be­
come willing to offer a tantric consort to the yogī. Yet the explicit references to Śaivite 
scripture, so very rare in Buddhist tantric discourse, are acceptable here precisely be­
cause they portray outcaste devotees of Śaivism as gullible exclusivists who accept “ab­
solutely no other divinity” (naivānyaṃ daivatam), if not as deserving candidates for 
the “web of lies” that the yogī may weave in servicing the samaya.60 For critical con­
text on the acceptability of non-​Buddhist tantrism in this Buddhist milieu, the views of 
Padmavajra’s coreligionist Indrabhūti can be kept in mind. He reminds his audience to 
keep up conventional religion such as feeding and donating to the saṅgha on holy days, 
while warning against “practitioners of false religion” and charismatic preachers of the 
Supreme Spirit (parātma), who are “bound by the noose of Māra.”61
The proliferation of divergent opinions on how to go about practising tantra, which 
nonetheless draw on much the same canonical sources, illustrates the capriciousness 
introduced into Buddhism by “guruism,” a third source of authority accepted alongside 
reasoning and scripture by tantric practitioners. The guru or ācārya is encouraged to be 
seen as identical with Vajrasattva, the personification of the tantras’ ultimate goal. The 
word of the guru allows the norms and interpretations developed in one tantric circle to 
be superseded by contrary advice, at the same level of authority, in another circle.
Contesting Nonconceptuality: The Tattvasiddhi and the 
Sūtakamelāpaka
Śāntarakṣita, a specialist in epistemology writing in the second half of the eighth cen­
tury, examines a vital aspect of tantrism in his Tattvasiddhi. The very title of the 
Tattvasiddhi—​as well as its circumstances of transmission, and its reliance on a common 
tantric corpus62—​may indicate that Śāntarakṣita worked in the same period and milieu 
as the Oḍḍiyāna siddhas. Śāntarakṣita, however, has a monastic background and a more 
theoretical focus, and argues with both formal reasoning and scriptural citations.
The Tattvasiddhi’s author starts by recalling that the mahāvajrayāna or 
vajramahāyāna suits those who are kept ignorant by their conceptualizations, and who 
would not otherwise find the means to be saved from suffering over countless eons. 
The state by which they are saved “in the convenience of this very lifetime” is “the holy 
Vajrasattva-​hood of great bliss” (śrīmatmahāsukhavajrasattvatvam). This “great bliss” 
(mahāsukha) is the transcendent state realized through the conjoining of “insight and 
means” (prajña-​upāya). Śāntarakṣita does not reduce these polysemic, euphemistic

--- PAGE 988 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      963
 
terms to practical or ritual particulars; instead he investigates their general soteriolog­
ical potentials:
Here, the sense-​objects of tangible form and so on, grasped with insight and means 
(prajñopāyaparigṛhītā rūpādayo viṣayāḥ), being transformed into a state of enjoy­
ment, become conveyors of special effects (viśiṣṭaphalāvāhakāḥ). This surely is to be 
admitted by the circumspect, for it is established for all disputants that a totality of 
special [conditions] (viśiṣṭā hi sāmagrī) arises as a quite special effect (viśiṣṭam eva 
phalam).63
The relationship between special effects and special causes occupies the bulk of the 
discussion. Śāntarakṣita argues against the objection that mental defilements and 
latent tendencies, which are particular in nature, cannot be brought to an end by 
nonconceptuality, which is unspecific.64 He concludes that the objects of enjoy­
ment (upabhoga) that characterize the tantras are a valid basis for developing gnosis, 
but this gnosis nonetheless entails conceptuality (savikalpam api jñānam). This is far 
from an unqualified endorsement of the soteriology of Buddhist tantrism as it existed 
in his day.65 Still, Śāntarakṣita establishes the Buddhist tantras as a rational subject of 
inquiry, which can be interrogated with reasoning and brought into conversation with 
Mahāyāna scriptural ideals.
In a rejoinder of sorts to the Tattvasiddhi, deutero-​Āryadeva’s Sūtakamelāpaka—​
also called *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa66—​argues that nonconceptuality proper is attain­
able through tantric practice. The Sūtakamelāpaka does not respond directly to the 
Tattvasiddhi but draws upon it silently, cribbing text blocks and giving lip service to the 
idea of special causes giving rise to special effects.67 The author assumes the identity 
of the classical Mādhyamika theorist Āryadeva, affecting historical and intellectual pri­
ority over Śāntarakṣita. This deutero-​Āryadeva accepts the authority of the sūtras and 
tantras cited in the Tattvasiddhi, and often cites the same passages, but he relegates their 
teaching to a lower level of efficacy. A distinctive practice of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga, 
the theophany of mandala deities in the bodies of the yogī and yoginī, now typifies the 
lower-​grade category of practice with “specificity” or “elaboration” (prapañcacaryā). 
The slightly higher grade of “practice without elaboration” (niṣprapañcacaryā), obtained 
through a six-​month period of cohabitation with a single initiated consort, is the Wise-​
Woman Vow or vidyāvrata described in the Guhyasamāja.68 The Sūtakamelāpaka 
commends the Wise-​Woman Vow with the proviso that it is to be practiced in a nondual 
and aconceptual frame of mind.
For deutero-​Āryadeva, the highest kind of practice, “exceedingly without elaboration” 
(atyantaniṣprapañcacaryā), is exemplified by the Madness Vow (unmattavrata). The 
practitioner of the Madness Vow wanders alone and at will, following no defined path—​
“sometimes laughing, chattering, sometimes standing” like a lunatic. His meditation is 
defined only as “proficiency in the gnosis of clear light” (prabhāsvarajñānakauśalya).69 
However, this Madness Vow is not taught by that name in the Buddhist tantras cited 
by Śāntarakṣita. It had been introduced by Padmavajra as one way of honoring the

--- PAGE 989 ---
964      Iain Sinclair
 
transgressive mandates of the Guhyasamāja. Padmavajra all but admits its provenance 
in non-​Buddhist Pāśupata religiosity.70 And while the Sūtakamelāpaka’s author does 
know of the Guhyasiddhi and refers to it by name, he finds a different source for the 
Madness Vow: a new and ostensibly canonical “explanatory tantra”71 not noticed in the 
Tattvasiddhi. This explanatory tantra, as cited in the Sūtakamelāpaka, twice states that 
the practitioner of the Madman’s Vow is “nonconceptual” (nirvikalpa), as if to hammer 
in that salvation through nonconceptuality is possible in Buddhist tantrism—​against 
Śāntarakṣita’s conclusions—​after all. This is one example of the way in which a soterio­
logical claim is bolstered by grounding it in a previously unknown scriptural revelation. 
Over time this developed into a common exegetical strategy.72
Carnal or Chaste: Monastic 
Receptions of the Guhyasamāja
As tantric practice became more entrenched among monastics, its challenges to con­
ventional morality drew more concerted responses. The prospect of celibate monks en­
gaging in noncelibate behavior, seemingly condoned in the tantras, emerged as a major 
concern for the saṅgha. The rule of celibacy is in general paramount for the monastic 
community. It comes first in the list of prātimokṣa rules for monks, and a deliberate 
breach of celibacy is an offense warranting immediate expulsion (pārājika).73 Although 
a monk or nun who is found to have engaged in sexual activity may not, in certain cases, 
be expelled from the community automatically,74 the exemptions for diminished re­
sponsibility in the monastic code do not apply to monastics who abandon celibacy in 
order to perform tantric practice.
The prospect of prominent, well-​trained monks bound by prātimokṣa norms who 
breached their vows of celibacy for the sake of tantric liberation was then a pressing 
concern. Large monasteries could not afford to ignore persistent allegations of miscon­
duct among the monastic fraternity. They often depended on state support and operated 
in view of pilgrims, non-​Buddhist provocateurs, and Buddhist saṅghas that rejected 
tantrism. A glimpse of a heated situation is given in a letter by the famous monk Atiśa 
calling on the mid-​eleventh-​century Pāla emperor Nayapāla to punish “malfeasant 
monks” (*duḥśīlabhikṣu, tshul khrims ’chal ba’i dge slong) whose misdemeanors are not 
specified.75 As ordinary ethical lapses among the saṅgha should have been handled by 
the protocols of the vinaya, Atiśa must have been referring to monastics who considered 
themselves above the law—​tantric monks. The emergence of a theoretical discourse 
on the interoperability of monastic, bodhisattva, and tantric religiosity then points to 
a growing need to manage different praxis regimes according to common principles, 
without relying too much on a particular individual or tantric tradition.
The notional scenario of magical murder did not attract nearly as much attention 
from the monastic establishment as noncelibate behavior.76 Institutional Buddhism has

--- PAGE 990 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      965
 
tended to turn a blind eye to the dark arts of tantrism. Prescriptions for black magic are 
more widespread and explicit in Buddhist tantras than those relating to sexual yoga. 
Rites for magical slaying were among the few recourses available to monks who faced 
marauding armies, tyrannical rulers, belligerent practitioners of other religions and 
other homicidal threats. The overcoming of an opponent in yogic combat was itself seen 
as a sign of advanced spiritual attainment, if not an act of mercy toward the opponent’s 
future victims.77 An accusation of black magical murder would also be hard to substan­
tiate before the monastic assembly (bhikṣuparṣad), unlike accusations of carnal know­
ledge leading to pregnancy, which are noticed many times throughout the canon and in 
monastic case law.
For observant Buddhist monks, the question of how to perform the sexual yogas 
mandated in the tantras can be reduced to a dilemma. Contact with a flesh-​and-​blood 
tantric partner is either forbidden—​monastic celibacy being the normative position—​
or it is permitted by some authority, theory or strategem accepted by a monastic com­
munity. These opposed standpoints are not only seen in the writings of the period 
spanning the eighth to the eleventh centuries; they are also discernible in period art. The 
art-​historical corpus shows that there were different modes of representing an erotic 
pair of tantric deities. The male deity can be either solitary (ekavīra) or positioned along­
side a female deity; alternatively, the two can be depicted as coital “insight-​and-​means” 
(prajñopāya) couples.78 Many of the former depictions are associated with monastic 
sponsors or sites such as Nālandā and feature deity twosomes, which if visualized from 
texts alone might instead be conceived as sexually united. Such sensual imagery was 
promulgated amid disagreements about the implementation of tantric praxis among the 
saṅgha. The *Mantrāvatāra of Jñānākara, for example, is critical of “initiations which 
involve intercourse with women” and “any action which is preceded by hatred and delu­
sion.”79 Here the Guhyasamāja and its ethos receives criticism from within the broader 
mantranaya. Conservative polemics were not common within Buddhist tantric dis­
course, but they point to the presence of informal pressure to tone down any public dis­
play of sexual imagery or praxis in monastic settings.
Jñānapāda’s School of Guhyasamāja Interpretation
One of the two main traditions of interpretation of the Guhyasamāja condones con­
tact with a woman (mudrā) as a means toward realizing ultimate reality. This school 
is named for Buddhaśrījñāna or Jñānapāda (jñānapādakrama,80 ye shes zhabs lugs). 
Tradition regards Jñānapāda as the first abbot of Vikramaśīla monastery, the center 
for tantric studies established early in the Pāla dynasty. In one of his major works, the 
*Dvitīyakrama, Buddhaśrījñāna sets out a procedure for initiation inspired by the tan­
trism of the Guhyasamāja. In the course of this procedure, the initiate has a scripted 
tryst with a consort provided by the guru. The musings on the selection of the consort 
based on her physical characteristics, as categorized in worldly bedchamber literature 
(kāmaśāstra),81 leave no doubt that this encounter was meant to occur in the flesh rather

--- PAGE 991 ---
966      Iain Sinclair
 
than in meditation. Similarly, this initiation is a prelude to a regime of erotic praxis, 
carried out in the flesh, as mandated in the aforementioned Wise-​Woman Vow, the 
vidyāvrata.82 The flagrant impropriety of carnal rituals in the context of celibate mo­
nasticism is brushed aside with the claim, going back to the Guhyasamāja, that they are 
necessary for salvation: “by no other means is Buddhahood attained.”83
The sexual yoga process described by Buddhaśrījñāna is prefaced with an unusually 
detailed account of his training, as though anticipating that his system needed to be 
vouchsafed with strong credentials. Buddhaśrījñāna attributes his system as a whole to 
the bodhisattva of gnosis, Mañjuśrī. He identifies his human teachers as Vilāsavajra, a 
literate commentator on tantras such as the Guhyasamāja, trained in Oḍḍiyāna; Pālita­
pāda, a specialist in tantric ritual; and, unusually for the time, two women.84 However, a 
key element of the sexual yoga he teaches was known outside this circle. It concerns the 
instruction given to the initiate at the climax of his initiation:
In the middle of bliss and cessation of bliss, the targeted [state] is to be observed and 
made stable.85
Here “the targeted” (lakṣya) refers to the fleeting peak experience of orgasm, which 
exemplifies essenceless or nonconceptual cognition and can therefore justify, in this 
system, ritualized intercourse. The instruction to mark this experience is worded in 
a very similar way in Padmavajra’s Guhyasiddhi.86 Whereas sexual dalliances pose no 
inherent difficulty in Padmavajra’s nonmonastic Buddhist tantrism, they could only 
occur under exceptional (yet unspecified) circumstances in a monastic community 
such as Vikramaśīla’s. The procurement of a consort is another common topic covered 
by Padmavajra and Jñānapāda, but the latter treats the topic more systematically and 
without mentioning non-​Buddhist tantras.
Whether the erotic practices mandated by Buddhaśrījñāna were actually performed 
by him at Vikramaśīla is not known, but his methods are known to have been propagated 
and modified by later generations. His method posed few problems for lay practitioners 
such as Kṣitigarbha—​an associate of the monk Atiśa—​who gives frank instructions for 
sexual yoga.87 The question of whether monks should take initiations involving corpo­
real women was taken up by Vāgīśvarakīrti, a tantric monk active in the late tenth cen­
tury. In his short initiation handbook, the Saṃkṣiptābhiṣekavidhi, Vāgīśvarakīrti allows 
both monks and laypersons to be sexually initiated on the condition that they “develop 
the mentality of the way of mantras” (mantranayacittotpāda).88 However, the mentality 
of the mantric practitioner is neither specified nor tied to the altruism of bodhicitta, 
which might justify the recourse to carnal tantrism for the benefit of all beings. While 
Vāgīśvarakīrti advanced the exegesis of the Guhyasamāja by confronting the problem of 
celibates’ involvement in carnal ritual, the low bar that he set for participation ensured 
that the problem would continue to be investigated.

--- PAGE 992 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      967
 
The Āryas’ Guhyasamāja Exegesis and the Kālacakra
A second school of Guhyasamāja interpretation, that of the Āryas (’phags lugs)—​so 
called because its proponents assume the identities of famed ecclesiastics or āryas such 
as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti—​is ambivalent about the need for initiates to 
experience physical contact with a woman. A defining project of the Ārya school is its six-​
point hermeneutics (ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā) and its allowance for scriptural statements to be 
interpreted as either definitive (nītārtha) or nondefinitive or “indicative” (neyārtha).89 
These multiple levels of interpretation allow scriptural directives to be implemented in 
different yet equally valid ways. The ideal sādhana of this school codified by deutero-​
Candrakīrti refers to the “exterior/​interior consort” (bāhyādhyātmikā mudrā),90 in ef­
fect allowing the parts of the procedure involving a mudrā or woman to be carried out as 
visualizations by a celibate practitioner.
By permitting ethically questionable processes to move into the subjective realm, the 
Ārya exegetes not only condone but also encourage a physically chaste form of praxis. 
Deutero-​Āryadeva tells devotees that “the outer lady” (bāhyāṅganām), that is, a flesh-​
and-​blood woman, is to be put aside when undertaking the aforementioned “practice 
absolutely without elaboration,” which he ranks as the best and fastest path to salva­
tion.91 Operating under cover as they promoted competitive interpretations of the 
Guhyasamāja, the self-​styled Āryas also confected explanatory tantras to give their 
views the respectability of buddhavacana.92 Their tactics counter an unnamed sensu­
alist approach to tantrism by reasserting long-​standing norms of Buddhist chastity. The 
Āryas’ school is understood to have been based outside Jñānapāda’s seat of influence at 
Vikramaśīla, probably at Nālandā monastery.93
The Āryas’ exegesis provided a foundation for the later Kālacakra tantric system, 
which moves beyond the Guhyasamāja and emerges as its own distinct tradition in­
tegrating elements from the Yoginītantras. The chief commentary in this system, the 
Vimalaprabhā, authored by a putative bodhisattva-​king called Puṇḍarīka, gives both 
“indicative” neyārtha and “definitive” nītārtha interpretations of the statements of 
the Kālacakratantra. Often Puṇḍarīka interprets injunctions for transgressive beha­
vior on the “definitive” level as acts of internal yoga that only advanced yogīs can per­
form. Whereas, for instance, killing beings is permissible only under certain extreme 
circumstances in the neyārtha interpretation, in the nītārtha interpretation “killing” 
is allowable in the sense of halting the flow of bodhicitta in yoga.94 The proponents 
of the Kālacakra also urge tantric practitioners to heed the commentaries of the 
bodhisattvas,95 presumably meaning those of the Āryas as well as those produced by 
the Kālacakra insiders. Kālacakra proponents used such hermeneutics to claim that 
celibacy (brahmacarya) can be maintained in yogic practice with women through co­
itus reservatus.96 Yet another approach to reconciling tantrism with monasticism is 
inaugurated here.

--- PAGE 993 ---
968      Iain Sinclair
 
Tantric Praxis as One of Three Ways 
to Salvation
Advanced treatments of tantric Buddhism, developed with access to a mature tantric 
corpus and sophisticated exegesis, return to the idea of tantrism forming a “way” or 
“guiding principle” (naya) rather than a distinct “vehicle” (yāna) of its own. Attempts to 
situate tantric Buddhism in the framework of soteriological vehicles contend with the 
three legacy classifications of Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna. The 
term “Vajrayāna” provides a useful emic designation for Buddhist tantrism, but it has no 
canonicity outside the tantras. Nor did a consensus form on whether transgressive be­
havior is integral and indispensable to Vajrayāna soteriology.
The Kālacakra commentator Vajragarbha states, in this regard, that “Buddhists 
have no fourth vehicle beyond the Mahāyāna.” It is remarkable that Vajragarbha here 
disregards the self-​understanding of tantric praxis as both Vajrayāna (one distinct so­
teriology) and Mahāyāna (the broader soteriology that includes it), which had been put 
forward since the Guhyasamāja. By rejecting the category of a stand-​alone vehicle for 
tantrism and insisting on the primacy of Mahāyāna, Vajragarbha seeks “to arrest those 
who discard charity and discipline”—​two characteristic behaviors of the bodhisattva—​
on the path of tantric practice.97 The designation “way of mantras,” however, overcomes 
the problem of locating Buddhist tantrism within the preexisting set of three yānas by 
affirming its place as a kind of specialty within the Mahāyāna.
The Way of Mantras and the Way of the Perfections
The notion that the way of mantras constitutes a distinct path to salvation, 
complementing the altruism of the way of the perfections (pāramitānaya), is developed 
in the exegesis of Buddhist tantrism. Like mantranaya, pāramitānaya is a canonical 
term. Expressions such as the “way of the perfection of charity” (dānapāramitānaya) 
go back to Mahāyāna scripture such as the Gaṇḍavyūha. The “way of the perfection 
of wisdom” (prajñāpāramitānaya) is a key term of the proto-​tantric Adhyardhaśatikā 
Prajñāpāramitā, although in this work it refers, unusually, to its elementary form 
of mantric practice.98 In general the term “way of the perfections,” pāramitānaya, 
designates the perfection of six virtues of charity and so on over many lifetimes in the 
pursuit of awakening, as well its associated ideology and sources. Tantric Mahāyāna is 
mantranaya; pāramitānaya is non-​tantric Mahāyāna.
Positioning tantrism as a path parallel to the bodhisattva path may imply that the 
bodhisattva’s cultivation of transcendent virtues such as charity and discipline is 
dispensible. The notion that tantric praxis not only supplements but substitutes for bo­
dhisattva praxis is foregrounded in a stock verse that has found its way into many ritual

--- PAGE 994 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      969
 
handbooks. Here each of the bodhisattva’s six perfections is correlated with a different 
phase of mandala-​making ritual:
Charity (dāna) is [giving] cowdung together with water [to purify the site]; moral 
discipline (śīla) is sweeping [the site]; forbearance (kṣānti) is removing tiny ants 
[from the site]; courage (vīrya) is starting up the ritual; meditation (dhyāna) is in­
stantly becoming single-​minded; insight (prajñā) is the brilliance of a fine line. All 
these six perfections are obtained drawing the maṇḍala of the Buddha.99
This is a confident expression of tantric Buddhism as a self-​contained soteriology, in 
which particular praxis forms are substituted for the more arduous tasks of the bodhi­
sattva. At the same time it raises the question of whether tantrism is practised in con­
junction with the non-​tantric Mahāyāna or separated from it altogether.
The Nayatraya Treatises
The modeling of Buddhism as three ways to salvation (nayatraya)—​the ways of 
śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and mantras—​is developed in treatises that seek to clarify 
the place of tantric Buddhism relative to other soteriologies. The Nayatrayapradīpa 
of Bhaṭṭa Trivikrama has been one of the most influential works of this kind. Other 
treatises on the three ways have also come to light among the many dozens of Sanskrit 
works that were conveyed to Tibet but have remained untranslated there. One such 
work, the Nayatrayabheda, is credited to the ācārya Kuśalaśrī, who describes himself as
learned in dependent origination and the import of the [Nobles’] truths (pratītyotpāda-​
satyārtha), the non-​selfhood of dharmas (dharmanairātmya), and mantra.
These three doxa epitomize the three ways to salvation discussed in his treatise.100 Kuśalaśrī 
further refers to the use of mantras by different religious groups: non-​Buddhists, śrāvakas, 
and bodhisattvas.101 In the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, the mantras of śrāvakas and worldly 
deities had been noticed as having different modes of expression, lesser powers, and so on 
compared to those of the Mahāyāna.102 From this standpoint, the mantranaya is a form of 
praxis associated as much with the bodhisattva as with mantras themselves.
Trivikrama’s Nayatrayapradīpa argues for the acceptance of the mantranaya as the 
best of the means at the bodhisattvas’ disposal. In his view, the inverted morality of the 
tantras is encompassed within the broad ideals of non-​tantric Buddhism, as the bodhi­
sattva can transgress conventional ethics in order to bring benefit to others. On the con­
tingency of lying, for instance:
Suffering and so on is taught to be Truth (satyatā) in order to motivate the śrāvakas, 
whereas even untruth [can be spoken] out of compassion, such as the statement ‘a 
soul exists.’103

--- PAGE 995 ---
970      Iain Sinclair
 
The implication that the Nobles’ Truths on suffering are not truthful in the absolute 
sense is further justified by resorting to the Madhyamaka dichotomy of conventional 
and absolute truth.104 Trivikrama is primarily concerned with the Mahāyāna, which he 
positions above śrāvaka and non-​Buddhist religion due to its higher ideals, wider sal­
vific scope, and so on. He proceeds to assimilate the great compassion of the bodhisattva 
(mahākṛpā) to the passion (rāga) sublimated by the tantric practitioner:
The highest beings [i.e., bodhisattvas], belts tightened to save beings in the three 
worlds, who tossed away lives, sons, land, women and riches like grass because of 
pitying [others’ predicaments]—​who else on this earth has a greater acquaintance 
with passion?105
Why, furthermore, would those of great compassion not to wish to take up the 
best available means (upāyāgra) for saving beings106—​that is, the way of mantras? 
Trivikrama then, in this regard, makes his famous assertion about the superiority of tan­
tric Buddhism:
Although the goal [of the two higher nayas] is common, the body of teaching on 
mantra is distinguished by its lack of confusion, many means, lack of difficulty, and 
authority for those of sharp faculties.107
This verse was often quoted by proponents of tantric Buddhism active at the begin­
ning of the second millennium. Among them were Śraddhākaravarman and Atiśa, 
who were both acquaintances of the Tibetan scholar-​translator Rin chen bzang po. At 
this time Buddhist tantrism resumed its spread across the Himalayas aided by the er­
udite support it was receiving in its homeland. Learned endorsements of tantrism also 
occurred in systematic treatments of Buddhism that reaffirmed the validity of mo­
nastic and bodhisattva religiosity. Atiśa, as is well known, argued to Tibetan students in 
his Byang chub lam gyi sgron ma (*Bodhipathapradīpa) that celibate monasticism was 
integral to Buddhism and that celibates could not take tantric initiations involving a 
sexual liaison.108 Here Atiśa nominates the Kālacakra Paramādibuddhatantra as his au­
thority for this prohibition. There is then the implication—​which may have remained 
opaque to most of his Tibetan audience, and to others who lacked access to the elusive 
Paramādibuddhatantra—​that carnal initiations remained open to those who were “celi­
bate” in the tantric sense, as espoused in the exegesis of the Kālacakra.109
Atiśa’s contemporary Advayavajra—​who, like Atiśa, had been part of the South 
Asian monastic system, knew Tibetans, and became a major authority in Indo-​Tibetan 
Buddhism—​also cites the Nayatrayapradīpa to affirm the superiority of the way of 
mantras. Advayavajra, however, teaches from the standpoint of a tantric yogī rather than 
a lifelong celibate. In his Tattvaratnāvalī, Advayavajra puts forward a brief doxography 
of Buddhism consisting of the three yānas—​Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and 
Mahāyāna—​and bifurcates the latter into pāramitānaya and mantranaya.110 Advayavajra 
further positions the two lower vehicles as “stairways” to the Mahāyāna, while adding

--- PAGE 996 ---
The Soteriologies of Buddhist Tantrism      971
 
that the very conceptualization of yāna is lost in the undifferentiated dharmadhātu.111 
For Advayavajra, the mantranaya is epitomized by the Four Seals, which he homologizes 
to the four phases of orgasmic bliss experienced in initiatory ritual.112 Here mantranaya 
has become another designation for the path of sublimated ecstasy, mahāsukha, and in 
this sense it is just as broad as Vajrayāna. In spite of the chronic ambiguity about how the 
way of mantras is practised, which seems to have never been resolved in a definitive way, 
the place of the mantranaya in transregional Buddhism had been secured in learned 
discourse, at least in those monasteries where the Mahāyāna itself was not rejected.
Conclusions
The plurality of paths to salvation in Buddhist tantrism reflects the variety of factors 
bearing on its constitutive processes. From the start, there is an acceptance of dif­
ferent propensities and proclivities among those who are to be saved, which leads to 
an enlargement in the range of soteriological methods. As these methods expand into 
transgressive behavior and liminal experiences—​tantrism proper—​and come to be 
associated with superior results, they challenge established Buddhist norms of ascet­
icism and altruism. The situation of the monastic who faces potential conflicts with 
vows of celibacy or other religious commitments occasions special, elaborate, and 
sometimes circuitous strategies for reconciling tantric sensuality with the morality of 
the Buddhist establishment. Tantrism then has been accommodated within the insti­
tutional religion in ways that reflect the influence of individual teachers, the strength 
of pre-​existing traditions and so on. External inputs resulting from contacts with 
other religions, transregional flows, and changes in regimes and natural environments 
all merit further consideration, but have not been examined here because they have 
only a slight presence in the self-​understanding of Buddhist tantrism, which affects 
timelessness and universality and which persists today as a plural and heterogeneous 
religion.

Chapter 38
Singing Tantra
Aural Media and Sonic Soteriology in 
Bengali Esoteric Lineages
Carola Erika Lorea
Introduction: Towards a Sonically 
Aware Methodology for 
Tantric Studies
A Brahmin, is astonished to witness a man and woman entwined together 
in a single blue garment. [ . . . ] They are singing very tenderly, but many 
more come into view, singing songs of their sect in the vulgar tongue, 
drinking spirituous liquor, and behaving in a very excited and dissolute 
way, their observance involving sex that disrupts correct, Vedic behaviour 
with regard to caste and stage of life.
This translation from the play Āgamaḍambara, composed during the reign of 
Shankaravarman in Kashmir (883–​902 C.E.), is employed by Gavin Flood (2006: 52) 
to show that before 900 C.E., tantric traditions had already achieved a strong degree 
of visibility and development. It can also demonstrate that singing songs “in the vulgar 
tongue” were already a trademark of tantric communities and an important part of their 
practice.
Tantric traditions in South Asia have been predominantly studied through the lit­
erary and philological analysis of (primarily Sanskrit) texts. However, music and dance, 
songs, and sung stories, in a variety of vernaculars, have always represented an impor­
tant component of lived religion in tantric communities. Religiosity in South Asia is 
performance-​centered: holy literatures as “audible texts” (Wilke and Moebus 2011: 12) 
are frequently ensounded, embodied, staged, or sung. The logocentric and nonsensory 
study of tantric texts—​although archaeological sources and iconography have been used 
too—​has covered a hegemonic role in the history of tantric studies, at the expense of

--- PAGE 1009 ---
984      Carola Erika Lorea
 
sensory dimensions other than the visual. This hierarchizing of the media corresponds 
to Western expectations but hardly at all to the actual use of these media in indigenous 
practice (Wilke and Moebus 2011: 4). Attempting to understand tantric traditions solely 
through philology, epigraphy, and iconography will miss out on precisely those sensory 
media and technologies of communication that are often most central to the tantric 
practitioners themselves: the aural, oral, and sonic fields of tantric expression.
This is especially relevant when dealing with Bengali esoteric lineages. Journeying 
across old, middle, and modern Bengali, esoteric poems, in the form of couplets, sung 
verses, and strophic lyrics (dohās, padas, and gān) have accompanied the development 
of the religious history of Bengal, to the extent that the history of Bengali literature is 
largely a history of Bengali songs (Cakrabarti 1990: 13). Besides a few notable exceptions 
(Hess 2015 among others), esoteric and devotional songs are often studied as “poems,” 
that is, as textual objects rather than performative events, although they are frequently 
preceded by an indication of their melodic framework, musical style, and/​or rhythmic 
pattern (rāga, sur, tāl). The semantic dimensions of these lyrics are certainly crucial to 
understand the worldviews of those who composed them. But besides their text, the 
sonic aspects of these events should be considered on their own right as co-​constitutive 
of religious identity and practice. The repetition of precise sound—​comprising the silent 
or sonorous repetition of mantric syllables (mantra japā), the chanting of the name of 
Hari, and songs in congregations (sādhusaṅga) of Bāuls and Fakirs—​acts upon the per­
sonal and the collective self, transforms sensibilities, and shapes ways of thinking, states 
of the soul, and even moral character (Beck 1995: 23).
Sounds have often been treated as ephemeral, ornamental, or secondary in the study 
of religions. However, citing Ruth Illman (2019): “We need to realize that music, and the 
arts in general, are not just ornaments or illustrations of something more profoundly 
important to religion, but they are aspects of religious engagement in their own right” 
(xxx). An emerging group of scholars of religion interested in sensory epistemology and 
sound studies are placing a new emphasis on aural media, encouraging a “sonic turn” in 
the study of religions (Hackett 2012: 2018). This article is theoretically embedded in and 
indebted to this current debate in the academic fields of religion and multisensory re­
search (Van Ede 2009). Such sonically aware methodological underpinning is, I argue, 
particularly suitable for the study of tantric traditions.
In modern Bengal, aural media, oral literature, and tantric religiosity are inseparably 
interwoven. Primarily studied by ethnomusicologists and area specialists, aural–​oral 
aspects of tantric ideologies in Bengal rarely enter wider debates in the field of tantric 
studies. In the nineteenth century, musicology and tantric practice forged an intellec­
tual, aesthetic, and affective alliance. Richard Williams brought to our attention how 
edited collections of Śākta songs in modern Bengal lie upon a tantric musicological 
foundation through a shared assumption in Śākta music-​making that the embodied self 
can be manipulated, transformed, and refined through sound (Williams 2019). Recent 
studies of Bengali esoteric songs offered a tremendous contribution to understand the 
ways in which tantra as a “deep worldview” (Kripal 2012) is enacted in the material and 
aesthetic practice of contemporary lineages (Salomon 1991; Trottier 2000; Openshaw

--- PAGE 1010 ---
Singing Tantra      985
 
2002; Cantú 2019, to name a few). However, these contributions often remain con­
fined to area specialists and rarely attempt to make a broader intervention in the field 
of tantric studies. In this chapter, I hope to demonstrate that we can gain new insights 
by applying a sonically aware methodology to the field of Tantic Studies, and I attempt 
to unravel some of the knotted reasons why aural–​oral media of contemporary lineages 
who ensound their tantric worldviews are left at the margins of tantra scholarship.
	
1.	 In the first section, I address this issue as a problem of terminology involving 
emic-​versus-​etic categories. Living practitioners in Bengal will hardly at all refer to 
themselves as “tantric.” Matters of self-​definition pose a serious ethical and episte­
mological problem to ethnographers. Through historical sources and the evidence 
found in songs, I will advocate for the use of “tantric” as a post-​emic category.
	
2.	 In the second section I explore the possibility that aural media have covered a mar­
ginal role in the study of tantric traditions because of a scholarly paradigm that 
has constructed songs and collective music-​making as the domain of emotional 
bhakti, contrasting them to tantric religiosity as the domain of text-​based ritu­
alism, transgression, and violence.
	
3.	 To problematize the previous point, in the third section I discuss how singing 
features ubiquitously in the history of tantric communities as well as in the 
living practices of contemporary lineages, urging us to take aural media into se­
rious consideration for a fuller anthrohistorical understanding of tantra from a 
multisensory perspective.
	 4.	 In the last section, stepping beyond the semantic significance of songs, I address 
aural media as practices of sonic liberation that are embedded in tantric ide­
ology. Using comparative ethnographies, I suggest that embodied techniques of 
the voice, the dancing body and percussion instruments, produce ecstatic states 
referred to as samādhi. This complex religious acoustemology rooted in tantric 
conceptions of the body and cosmic vibration (nād) can emerge through immer­
sive and long-​term ethnographic fieldwork.
To address these points, I use a multitude of sources. Ethnographic material such as oral 
exegeses and the study of performances through participant observation is drawn from 
an extensive and multisite fieldwork conducted between 2011 and 2019 among diverse 
communities of singers-​practitioners in West Bengal, Bangladesh, and the Andaman 
Islands. The primary sources used for this chapter include: handwritten manuscripts 
from Bengali singers and composers collected during my doctoral research and during 
the digitization of endangered notebooks of songs;1 edited collections of songs; “small 
media” like booklets sold at fairs and festivals; and audiovisual media—​such as my field­
work recordings.
Previous works on sound in Indian thought rely heavily upon tantric texts (Beck 1995). 
Wilke and Moebus’s monumental work on sonic cultural history argues that Sanskrit 
Hinduism provides “the richest source of material on language and sound in India” 
(Wilke and Moebus 2011: 1). While Sanskrit hymns and powerful syllables certainly

--- PAGE 1011 ---
986      Carola Erika Lorea
 
occupy an important place, I wish to emphasize that vernacular traditions, Dalit cultural 
heritage, and low-​caste sonic cultures are equally rich—​although understudied archives 
of sonic cultural history of South Asia. This chapter discusses how tantric conceptions 
of sound and sonic manifestations of tantric ideology are embodied, enacted, and 
performed in living esoteric lineages. In their oral histories, these lineages are only mar­
ginally transmitting a tantric genealogy. In fact, most of the singers-​practitioners I have 
worked with would not like to be associated with anything “tantric,” because of the so­
cially reproachable connotations that the term came to be tinged with (Urban 2003, 
2010). The esoteric literature of Bāul, Fakir, and related lineages seem to have stopped 
referencing a direct tantric heritage since the late nineteenth century. However, this does 
not mean that their texts, ideas, and practices are irrelevant to the field of tantric studies.
The religious history of these various groups is complicated, deriving from a conflu­
ence of Tantric Buddhist, Nāth, Vaiṣṇava, and Sufi religiosities (Dasgupta 1962; Cashin 
1995). I use the broad terms “esoteric” and “heterodox”2 in order to discuss the views of 
predominantly low-​caste practitioners who would define themselves using situational 
and multiple definitions—​Bāul, Fakir, Vaiṣṇava, Sahajiẏā, Matuẏā, Lālan panthī, and 
so on. The lineages often conflate, fluidly overlap, exchange disciples, and participate 
in each other’s ritual occasions. These movements transmit esoteric teachings on the 
human body (dehatattva), based on the assumption that the body as microcosm reflects 
the universe-​macrocosm. They worship the human (mānuṣ), and believe that there is 
nothing higher than a human being in its perfected state.3 Although they live in regions 
that are dominantly Hindu or Muslim, they do not follow the orthodox norms or rituals 
of these religious establishments. Their highest goal is the experience of pure love (prem) 
and the accomplishment of the blissful state of transcendence of all dualities, known as 
sahaja (simple, innate, spontaneous). To purify the body–​mind and reach those goals, 
they employ a set of practices (sādhan or sādhanā) that revolve around the control of 
breath and bodily substances. They all employ music and singing for didactic, ritual, and 
soteriological purposes. Techniques to progress in sādhanā are learned from one—​or 
more—​gurus. Accomplished practitioners are given the honorific epithet of a madman 
(pāgal, khyāpā). Hierarchies and differentiations among human beings based on society 
and religions, such as caste divisions, are scorned and rejected, and so are claims of au­
thority based upon the knowledge of sacred scriptures. Songs, instead, are considered 
the most authoritative repositories of knowledge.4
Tantric as Post-​Emic Category: Duddu 
Shah and the Genealogy of Bāuls
When the Vaiṣṇava Bāul couple Nitai and Shanti5 traveled to Italy for the first time, they 
asked me to write a short introduction to the Bāul tradition in Italian, to help intro­
duce their songs to the unfamiliar audience. Then they looked at my two-​paragraph

--- PAGE 1012 ---
Singing Tantra      987
 
description, and immediately asked me to delete the word “tantric,” which I had used 
in order to locate Bāul ontologies of body and universe. Nitai and Shanti were anxious 
to disassociate from the word “tantric,” because, as they humbly said, “we don’t know 
anything about mantra-​tantra and tantric scriptures.” Historical reasons led the term 
“tantra” in Bengal to acquire suspicious connotations, related to spooky, occult, and 
scandalous practices (Urban 2003). The tantric path came to be seen as incompatible 
with a “proper Vaiṣṇava” (śuddha baiṣṇab) religious self (Lorea 2018b).
I diligently deleted the term. Yet many of the common denominators that char­
acterize tantric traditions6 are definitely shared by performers and practitioners who 
today may reject such legacy according to their lineage and stage of realization. As an 
ethnographer, using the term “tantric” as a descriptive category, when my interlocutors 
do not agree to be identified with anything tantric at all, poses an ethical dilemma, 
which can only be resolved by contextualizing and historicizing such hostility. Esoteric 
movements following tantric ideas on the body and on liberation, opposing castes and 
celibate renunciation (sannyās), worshiping the human (mānuṣ bhajan), and encour­
aging spiritual-​erotic companionship (yugal sādhanā) with a partner came to be viewed 
as heterodox during the articulation of a restored and institutionalized Vaiṣṇavism in 
nineteenth-​century Bengal. Accusations and allegations from the dominant culture 
resulted into a conscious turn away from the nominal transmission of “tantric” heritage 
among practitioners of low caste and class status.
However, Bāul singers and their spiritual teachers often undergo tantric training and 
initiation, especially in the Śākta order, as it is evident from the biographical information 
that we can gather about a number of guru-​composers. The prolific composer Haure 
Gosain of Bardhaman (1202–​1319 BS, c. 1796–​1909 C.E.) received initiation (dikṣā) 
from his mother. Later he received tantric initiation (pūrṇābhiśek) after accomplishing 
textual and experiential training under Swami Vashishthananda. At a later stage, he 
found his śikṣā (teaching) guru in Nadia, Prahlad Goswami, who taught him esoteric 
Vaiṣṇava practices and gave him the name Haure Gosain, which he used in his songs 
(see Bhattacharya 1957: 762; Jha 2009, 547–​548). Raj Kṛṣṇa of Nadia was renowned for 
his cremation ground practices, and for spiritual powers (siddhis) harnessed through 
sādhanā, such as rising up in the air (Openshaw 1995: 139–​140). The famous saint-​
composer Bhaba Pagla was initiated with a Śākta mantra by an itinerant ascetic wearing a 
snake around his neck and carrying a trident; he persisted in worshiping Kālī even while 
professing the uselessness of all exterior rites (Lorea 2016). Despite abundant linkages, 
explicit association with tantric traditions seems to stop, or radically decrease, in the ev­
idence left by Bāuls since the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Concomitantly, 
the intellectual elite that popularized these songs for a bhadralok (upper-​class, high-​
caste Hindu urban) public presented a purged image of the composers, deprived of tan­
tric tones. Perhaps unsurprisingly then, the song of Duddu Shah “Mahānirbāṇ keman 
kare haẏ” (How is the great liberation obtained?), in which Duddu directly mentions 
the teachings of Buddhist tantras, has never made it into a printed anthology. Duddu 
Shah (1841–​1911) was born into a Muslim family in Jhenaidah (now Bangladesh) and is 
possibly the most well-​known disciple of Lalan Fakir (d. 1890), whose songs have been

--- PAGE 1013 ---
988      Carola Erika Lorea
 
studied, translated, and performed internationally. I have recorded this song during a 
sādhusaṅga in Birbhum, at the ashram of Khyepa Baba, a learned tantric guru from East 
Bengal following the lineage of Nityānanda.7

Following the oral interpretation provided by Baba, Duddu is describing the spir­
itual path learned from Lalan as a heritage of the tantric teachings of the Buddha: the 
achievement of nirvāṇa with the acceptance (as opposed to renunciation) of saṃsāra. 
Those then got mixed together with Vaiṣṇava imageries of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa’s love. 
Hence, he said, the song mixes Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava terminology: śunya (void, ulti­
mate reality) becomes a deś (literally “country”), the final stage of Vaiṣṇava progression 
in sādhanā.9 The last stanza exhorts the listeners to acknowledge the value of tantric 
Buddhist revelations.
The song is very unique, and so is its composer. But such an eclectic religious brico­
lage should not surprise us. Duddu was said to be proficient in Farsi and Arabic and 
well-​studied in Sanskrit, and he purportedly knew the Caitanya Caritāmṛta by heart.10 
Moreover, explicit references to tantric texts and a prescription to read them appear in 
at least two songs of his teacher, Lalan Fakir.11 To scholars of Bengali music and pop­
ular religious movements, this genealogy should sound familiar. The Bengali historian

--- PAGE 1014 ---
Singing Tantra      989
 
of kīrtan Hitesh Ranjan Sanyal (1989: 151) states that Buddhist Sahajiẏās in premodern 
Bengal had created a veritable music tradition of their own, and that the success of later 
Vaiṣṇava devotional movements in medieval Bengal was largely due to their ability to 
incorporate and adopt such tantric spiritual-​musical tradition (Chakravarti 1991: 456).
While Lalan’s songs and other sources used by Bāuls12 do not seem to have a problem 
in recognizing a tantric ancestry, Duddu strives to justify the doctrine of the void as a 
respectable and precious teaching, compatible, in fact fused, with Vaiṣṇava devotion. 
Intertextuality can reveal that several songs in Duddu’s oeuvre share this mission, in 
the effort to transmit a lineage history that links Bāuls to tantric Buddhism, while dis­
paraging the bigotry of reformed orthodox Vaiṣṇavas. This effort needs to be under­
stood in the context of the harsh attacks, widespread in colonial and bhadralok sources, 
against Bāul, Darbeś, Sahajiẏā, and various popular religious movements. Gauṛīya 
Vaiṣṇava reformers in the second half of the nineteenth century severely condemned 
Bāuls and cognate lineages both on metaphysical as well as on moral grounds. From a 
doctrinal perspective, they were accused of being “impersonalists,” “voidists,” “tantrics,” 
crypto-​Buddhists, “a-​Vaiṣṇavas,” or straightforwardly “Muslim” disguised as Vaiṣṇavas. 
Their behavior was seen as promiscuous, indulgent, and obscene. Such is the back­
drop against which one should understand Duddu Shah’s historiographic—​or rather 
historiophonic—​project.
