In Bengali esoteric lineages, the aesthetic/​emotional theories of Vaiṣṇava bhakti 
permeated a tantric substratum, but there is no contradiction between the two. Duddu 
outlines a history of syncretic confluence between esoteric Buddhism and Vaiṣṇava aes­
thetic/​emotional theory of bhāb as ecstatic love. As many Bāuls assert up to the present, 
Duddu traced back his lineage history to Nityānanda and his son Bīrabhadra.15 Tantra 
has an explicit presence in such an historical recollection. However, the tāntrika has be­
come a rasika in the process of amalgamation that fused the Śaiva–​Śākta theology of 
union, with the emotion (bhāb) of Rādhā-​Kṛṣṇa love.
The rasik dissolves the boundaries between sacred and profane enjoyment: blending 
aesthetic, spiritual, and musical presuppositions, the rasik experiences and shares the 
emotion of divine love as a form of spiritual practice that is best conveyed through song. 
In bhakti poetry, the rasik modality of religiosity is opposed to the juiceless, dull, and 
sterile modality of yogis and ascetics, “rasa-​less as dried up stem of sugarcane” in com­
parison to the sweetness of singing the names of god (Agradās in Burchett 2019: 235). 
In the code language of Bengali esoteric lineages, rasik is also the practitioner of yugal 
sādhanā who exchanges fluids of pleasure rather than practicing austere abstinence and 
“dry” celibacy, progressing on the spiritual path through regulation and manipulation of 
bodily substance (see also Openshaw 2002: 139).
While practicing body-​centered sādhanā and sustaining a lifeworld where the human 
body is intimately connected to the macrocosm, contemporary practitioners reject the 
tantric label. Discussing the identity of contemporary practitioners and their songs as 
“tantric” does not represent an emic taxonomy. However, the literary heritage as well 
as the ethnography of modern lineages clearly deserve a place in the comparative 
and anthrohistorical study of tantra. This is possible by applying the term “tantric” as 
a post-​emic category: a term that used to appear for definitions of a lineage genealogy 
but has ceased to bring status and prestige because of complex social, cultural, and his­
torical reasons, and thus was substituted by other appellations. Instead of concealing 
this history of erasure, using tantric as a post-​emic category indicates that there are 
textual as well as historical connections between tantra and contemporary lineages. 
The “tantric” category is not entirely an etic fabrication, derived solely from schol­
arly analysis and outsiders’ observations. Linage holders locate their roots in a tantric 
worldview from a diachronic perspective (hence post-​); moreover, direct references 
to authorities, texts, deities, and practices defined as tantric by the practitioners 
themselves are still found in many communities and guru-​disciple circles (hence 
-​emic). The definition of tantric as post-​emic is meant to reflect the ambiguous status 
of the tantric legacy in modern Bengal and its relevance as a controversial yet essential 
backdrop.
Recent studies suggested that since the Delhi Sultanate period, a flourishing devo­
tional religiosity dominated by a Sufi-​inflected Vaiṣṇava bhakti has remodeled the 
Indian religious sphere, at the expense of tantric traditions associated with yoga, as­
ceticism, and ritualism. Patton Burchett (2019) suggests that tantric elements were not 
simply wiped out by the bhakti movement, but rather they shifted out of the public 
sphere and survived in disguise, behind the noncontroversial curtain of bhakti. The

--- PAGE 1016 ---
Singing Tantra      991
 
songs of Duddu Shah are a demonstration of this hypothesis. Highlighting the remem­
brance of a Buddhist tantric past, in the ethnohistory of Bāuls and Fakirs, the songs of 
Duddu retrace the merging of tantric sādhanā with Vaiṣṇava bhakti. While bhakti has 
been often portrayed as antithesis to tantra (and vice versa, tantra as antagonistic to 
devotionalism), this juxtaposition would fail to understand several living traditions16 
and their use of aural media and oral-​performative realms of songs as fundamental 
expressions of tantric ideologies.
Rethinking the Song =​ Bhakti Paradigm
In the history of religions of South Asia, songs have been overwhelmingly portrayed 
as the domain of the bhakti poet-​singer. The songs of Mirabai, Kabir, Surdas, Sant, and 
so-​called bhakti poets are often understood as the outpouring of the poet-​saint’s devo­
tional love to a personal theistic recipient. This modality of worship is contrasted to the 
harsh, virile, heroic path of the ritualistic tāntrika, reiterating Lee Siegel’s assumption 
that “love plays no part in the tantras” (1978: 17). Decades of popular and academic liter­
ature contributed to shaping this dichotomy that essentialized both devotional and tan­
tric phenomena as incompatible. This perspective is of little use for both ethnographers’ 
fieldwork engagements with living communities, who routinely mix devotional and 
tantric elements, as well as the literary study of esoteric songs, which draw from bhakti-​
oriented and tantric-​yogic repertoires of images, ideas, and symbols.
In “Bhakti and Tantra Intertwined,” Karen Pechilis (2016) looks at the insistent crema­
tion ground imagery that appears throughout the poetry of the sixth-​century Tamil po­
etess Karaikkal Ammaiyar. Her poetry suggests “a period of fluidity between the paths 
of bhakti and tantra prior to their overlapping yet contested developments in the medi­
eval period” (1). Pechilis assumes that “deriving meaning from unscripted encountered 
experience is the way of the bhakti poet” while “enacting meaning through scripted ex­
perience is the way of the Tantric ritualist” (7). Drawing from authoritative scholars in 
the field of tantric textual traditions, like Gavin Flood and David Gordon White, for 
her understanding of characteristics deemed tantric, Pechilis writes that Karaikkal 
Ammaiyar’s poetry “does not describe rituals, in contrast to the centrality of rituals in 
tantra, from dīkṣā (initiation) to practices of ritualized sex, which David White (2003) 
considers to be unique to tantra, and to ritual divinization of the body, which Gavin 
Flood (2006) considers to be tantra’s special feature” (7). It is hard to imagine, under this 
light, that a practitioner of tantric rites can also be a poet and an ecstatic singer.
The categorical division of bhakti as qualitatively different and clashing with tantra 
is partly a product of academic ideas on the latter, based upon texts as primary sources, 
and overemphasizing transgressive and violent practices, as markers of authenticity. In 
Burchett’s persuasive history of bhakti, yoga, and tantra after the collapse of the institu­
tionally grounded “Tantric Age” (2019: 30–​64), the dichotomy is reinforced with a so­
ciological explanation. North Indian bhakti is portrayed as “a discourse and sensibility

--- PAGE 1017 ---
992      Carola Erika Lorea
 
spread through the performance of songs . . . in which entertainment, artistic virtuosity, 
aesthetic appreciation, ecstatic religiosity melded in moments of collective efferves­
cence” (181). The joviality of this collective experience of sonic piety is contrasted to an­
tisocial ascetics and yogis who “largely worked for themselves, for their own goals and 
were not particularly interested in diffusing a religious message to a broader public,” 
whereas “bhakti singers and reformers . . . strived, in some sense to work for the ge­
neral good of a larger community” (181). This binary in moral and aesthetic regimes 
is used to reify a tension and a “real difference” (181) between these two styles of religi­
osity. However, such irreconcilable difference can be questioned. There are hardly single 
lonely renunciates but rather organized and connected networks of “sādhu societies” 
(Openshaw 2002: 125–​128). Yogis and Siddhas had obvious interest in sharing their mes­
sage, gathering disciples and generating audiences, which they achieved through the 
performance of songs (Davidson 2002). Songs and dance are forms of worship offered 
in the tantric gaṇacakra rituals. Nāth yogis often were, and still are, bards, performers, 
and entertainers (see Gold 1992; Lorenzen and Muñoz 2011). David Gellner (1992) goes 
to the extent of postulating that “the basis of the cult of tantric deities” in Newar society 
is the use of songs and dance, together with offerings of meat and alcohol (143, 284). In 
the next section I offer a brief outline of how singing features across tantric traditions 
not only as a technology of communication but also as a path to siddhi. What shaped the 
common understanding of tantric religiosity as something at odds with the emotional-​
ecstatic way of the bhakta?
Bhakti poetry insistently preaches the inferiority of rituals, scriptures, and ascetic 
penances, if compared to the blissful way of the devotee intoxicated in the nectar of di­
vine love. To make this point, bhakti composers often address their contempt against 
“tantra-​mantra,” a common compound, often translated as “hocus-​pocus,” referring to 
pragmatic rituals officiated by a specialist, utilizing knowledge of mantras and scriptures. 
Scorn toward mantra-​tantra is a literary topos and a recurrent refrain throughout 
bhakti literature. However, this should not be used to substantiate that bhakti in me­
dieval India constructed itself as distinct from (and superior to) tantric worldviews. In 
fact, the very communities that are often referred to as tantric were equally addressing 
tantra-​mantra in derogatory terms, in their own songs. This is because the rejection of 
scriptures and formal ritualism, and the internalization of all rituals, including mantra 
recitation, is germane to tantric-​yogic formations, particularly of Kaula, Vajrayāna, and 
Sahajiẏā groups. The rejection of mantra-​tantra is already attested in the collection of 
tantric songs known as Caryāgīti (eleventh–​twelfth century): “Of what use are mantras, 
of what use tantras, oh! Of what use explanations of meditation when you are immersed 
in spontaneous bliss [ . . . ]?” (Kvaerne [1977] 2010: 27).
The denigration of mantra-​tantra is pervasive in Bāul, Fakir, and other esoteric 
Bengali repertoires. Adversity to mantra-​tantra is used as a rhetorical device to ex­
emplify the superiority of the sahaja path that subordinates rituals, texts, and exte­
rior paraphernalia, in order to prioritize self-​exploration and self-​transformation 
through the psychophysiological sādhanā learned from a guru. A famous song by the 
saint-​composer Bhaba Pagla, very popular among Bāuls, says: “Singing is the supreme

--- PAGE 1018 ---
Singing Tantra      993
 
sādhanā; it does not require flower offerings or sandal paste: it doesn’t even need 
mantra-​tantra.”17 The composer, however, is known for initiating all his disciples with 
a Kālī mantra, which should be repeated 108 times, at least at initial stages. The blunt 
rejection of mantra-​tantra surely does not mean that Bāuls do not use mantras, do not 
take initiation, or do not learn tantric-​yogic sādhanā.18 Candi Gosain, a Bāul guru of the 
Namashudra caste from Faridpur, makes this point clear. In his songs, mantra-​tantras 
ultimately fall off as the futile reliance upon external devices, which are not needed for 
body-​ and breath-​centered sādhanā:

Formally forsaking mantra-​tantra and pursuing the union (yugal), either within 
themselves or with a ritual consort, esoteric Bengali lineages interweave bhakti-​oriented 
aesthetic-​emotional attitudes with deeply rooted tantric-​yogic worldviews. These fused 
and inseparable elements constitute the foundations of Bengali esoteric lineages. They 
can provide useful evidence to rethink the assumption that vernacular songs in North 
India pertain to the field of Vaiṣṇava bhakti as separate and distinct from tantric re­
ligiosity. Tantric ideas permeate the erotic and ecstatic character of bhakti, particu­
larly in eastern India and Bengal (Flood 2006: 95; Dimock 1966). On the other hand, 
bhakti elements of emotional and participative devotion, to a theistic recipient or to the 
guru, where bhakti represents an active spiritual endeavor (Sharma 1987: 109), feature 
prominently in several tantric traditions. Writing about devotion to Kālī, Patricia Dold 
has argued that “sweetening” and “sanitization” of the Goddess as mother are not only 
later developments of Śākta traditions. Devotional elements appear as co-​constitutive 
of the cosmic mother Goddess tradition since medieval times, yet scholars have often 
overemphasized transgressive and violent elements, neglecting the less exotic/​erotic 
aspects of the Goddess cult (Dold 2005).
Bengali songs of the Śākta poets-​practitioners Ramprasad and Kamalakanta 
(eighteenth–​nineteenth century) are a clear example of the long-​lasting coexistence 
of devotion and tantric yogic practice. Songs provide elements for visualizations and 
veneration of the various forms of the Goddess. A great number of songs describe the

--- PAGE 1019 ---
994      Carola Erika Lorea
 
intricacies of the sādhanā of kuṇḍalinī awakening, employing the yogic jargon of the 
esoteric mapping of the subtle body. However, anthologies of Śākta songs as well as re­
cording studios routinely omit the songs that are overly concerned with tantric-​yogic 
themes (McDermott 2000).
Songs of the Śākta sādhakas (practitioners) are embedded in a rich tradition of 
Bengali spiritual songs connecting premodern esoteric literature with the modern and 
contemporary tradition of Bāul and Fakir performers, who borrow abundantly from 
the śāktapadāvalī repertoire of Bengali songs to the Goddess (Lorea 2016). Bengali 
composers like Ramprasad, Haure Gosain, Duddu, Lalan, and Bhaba Pagla belong to 
diverse lineages and lack a common institution or sacred scripture. Although they are 
not representative of a monolithic genre or of any homogeneous “tradition,” their tropes 
fluidly travel across sects, their performative occasions overlap, lineages cross-​pollinate, 
and imageries mingle freely. They are part of the larger repertoire of ecstatic songs com­
posed by realized “madmen,” often referred to as bhāber gān, bhāb saṅgīt, or sādhanā 
saṅgīt.20 This fluid, open-​ended, and ever-​growing repertoire consolidated only relatively 
recently into discrete communities (sampradāẏa) with separate songs’ canons. For those 
who sing, dance, and listen to them, singing is itself a path toward self-​realization.
Tuning Representations: Songs in, 
Songs as Tantric Tradition
There is no separation between music and tantra: both have the 
same goal.
—​Ramji, interview (Lidke 2017: 137)
In the cultural history of South Asia, singing—​and particularly singing in vernacular 
languages—​has been intrinsically associated with grassroots, socially inclusive bhakti 
traditions. Congregational singing of religious songs in vernacular languages (kīrtan 
and bhajan; see Beck 2018) is often seen as the core feature of a coherent bhakti “move­
ment” which started from the Tamil south and made its way northward, finally entering 
North India and then Bengal. The twilight of the Sultanate period and the Moghul pe­
riod are seen as times of intensification and blossoming of performance-​centered lit­
erary genres in the vernaculars of North India (Orsini 2012). According to Burchett 
(2019), this religious realm of songs contributed to consolidate an aesthetic, emotional, 
and ethical sensibility that has great resonance with Sufism and great dissonance with 
certain “key aspects of tantric religiosity” (86). However, singing and shared sonic 
experiences permeate the history of tantric traditions. Vajrayāna Siddhas were possibly 
among the first practitioners to employ singing and dancing in the acts of offering before 
images (Davidson 2002: 223–​224). Pivoting on vernacular songs as an element of con­
trast between “earlier tantric religiosity” and a Sufi-​inflected bhakti sensibility would 
disregard abundant evidence about the ubiquity of dance and songs in tantric groups.

--- PAGE 1020 ---
Singing Tantra      995
 
Bengali esoteric lineages use singing as a mode of discourse fulfilling several 
purposes. Songs spread the message; their enchanting allegories attract new disciples 
eager to find gurus who might be able to reveal their inner meanings. Their performance 
reinforces the sense of belonging, creating social formations as “communities of sound.” 
Their content reiterates important values and teachings about the body, the cosmos, 
and society. The practice of singing is equated with strenuous yogic practices in that it 
achieves the same results: it is said that one can be born enlightened (svaẏaṃ–​siddha), 
one can become enlightened perfecting the mind–​body complex (sādhan–​siddha), or 
one can accomplish self-​realization through singing songs (gāne siddha). The com­
poser Bhaba Pagla (1902–​1984), whose community I have followed for about four years 
while living in West Bengal, is closely related to Ramprasad Sen in his hagiographies 
(Bandyopadhyay 1985; Cakrabarti 1995). One of his songs says: “I don’t need to concen­
trate or meditate: Songs are my worship and my sādhanā /​ Kuṇḍalinī wakes up, I get 
mad and overwhelmed and I drive the world crazy.”21 In the community of his followers, 
there is no such distinction between bodily and musical sādhanā: both are disciplines to 
control and transform the body–​mind, producing an ascendance through the manipu­
lation of breathing (Trottier 2000: 90–​91).
Singing shapes the gross body, the subtle body, as well the emotional and moral quali­
ties of the practitioners. It is directly compared to the physical and mental effects of yoga 
and meditation. The gurus say that singing naturally brings inhalation and exhalation 
under control. It clears the mind from any outer concern and liberates one from kām, 
selfish sexual desire—​the king of the six afflictions (ripu) which needs to be tamed in 
order to be transubstantiated into prem, divine love. Especially for disciples at initial 
stages, it is important to maintain the practice of singing, no matter if one is out of tune 
or not. In previous works, I have discussed the epistemology of singing among lineages 
whose songs are considered as paramount ways to obtain and disseminate knowledge.22 
Songs are anthropopoietic in that they transmute an unrefined person into a human 
(mānuṣ). This “religion of songs” (gāner dharma, as some interlocutors have called it) 
creates human beings in material, emotional, and moral ways, which is also understood 
as a process of feminization, embracing qualities associated to womanhood (Openshaw 
2007; Lorea 2018: 195–​198).
Such transformation is possible on the basis of a phonocentric lifeworld where 
music is a form of yoga and both the world and the word emanated from primordial 
sound (Wilke and Moebus 2011: 12–​13). Some interlocutors, tackling my questions on 
what singing does to singers and listeners, employ the concepts of universal sound and 
cosmic vibration—​śabda brahman and nāda—​to connect the universe-​as-​sound to the 
power of sound on the human body. When they clarify my doubts about the code lan­
guage of esoteric songs, they trace back the emergence of singing from the embodiment 
of the ultimate reality—​parā—​uttered as perceivable and meaningful sound. These 
understandings are reflected in tantric philosophical formulations whereby cosmic 
sound is generative and pervasive in all layers and levels of the cosmos (Flood 2006: 
65). Both mundane conversations and sung verbal interactions have their origin in the 
hierarchical cosmos pervaded by divine power as sound (Flood 2006). The concept

--- PAGE 1021 ---
996      Carola Erika Lorea
 
of cosmic and cosmogonic sound-​vibration, nāda brahman, developed by the Indian 
musicologist Śarṅgadeva in the early thirteenth century clearly outlines the connec­
tion between tantric sonic ideology and music theories. The tantric text on drumming 
Ḍhol Sāgar analyzed by Andrew Alter (2009) draws connections between drumming 
and tantric sonic cosmology, reflecting the influence of Nath ideas on the contempo­
rary practices of low-​caste communities of drummers in the Himalayas. Passages from 
the text (“In this way Guru Gorakhnath also acknowledges that primordial sound is the 
basis for existence and that this primordial sound emerges from the sound of Shiva’s 
drum—​which is dhauṅ-​dhauṅkār!”) induce Alter to theorize that to understand god 
one must use sound (197). Sound as cosmogonic and salvific is thus a shared symbolic 
capital, historically effective within popular tantric and devotional traditions.
The ecstatic behavior of the tantric practitioner, including songs and dance, is promi­
nent in early Śaiva esotericism and in later Buddhist tantras (Wedemeyer 2013: 157), dis­
tinguishing esoteric practitioners from the code of monastic discipline (Wedemeyer 
2013: 179). Davidson (2002: 223) discussed the employment of songs and dance in eso­
teric Buddhism, particularly as attested in Yoginī tantras, and possibly inherited from the 
Pāśupatas. He outlines a connection bonding Siddha masters, folk poets, and oral litera­
ture: They employed “varieties of language that were inauthentic by any aesthetic standards 
of the day: regional [ . . . ] Sanskrit, Apabrahṃśa, Old Bengali . . . Siddhas spoke in the first 
person, and employed forms of versification most closely allied with folk theater, wan­
dering poets and images of the countryside” (237). Playfulness, comedic expressions, and 
grotesque humor have been observed in Siddha literature (Dowman 2000), together with 
the use of vernacular-​based enigmatic poems and a “secret sacred sociolinguistics” (269) 
that directly ties an aesthetic and expressive continuity between Siddhācāryas, Nāth, Sant, 
and Bāul Fakir literature (or rather, orature, as “audible texts”). Esoteric songs not only 
functioned as a vehicle of worship and spiritual practice, but also laid the very foundations 
for the formation of textual traditions, and consolidated communitas among sectarian 
groups, through the collective dimension of performance participation. Davidson 
suggests that esoteric scriptures arose “as preeminently social events” (238): the new texts 
of the Siddhas, Mahāyoga, and Yoginī tantras are “overwhelmingly dominated by ritual, 
song, dance and story-​telling” and present an extraordinarily “performative nature.” Such 
traditions might have emerged from low-​caste groups of entertainers, itinerant preachers, 
and touring theater troupes, living at the margins or urban society (238).
A comparative overview of the role of singing in the history of Indian religions cer­
tainly encompasses medieval bhakti traditions and underlines a continuity rather than 
a rupture from tantric esoteric groups. In the Hevajra tantra, adepts performed music 
and dance at gatherings with the aim of attaining an exalted spiritual state: “If in joy 
songs are sung, let them be the excellent Vajra-​songs . . . Song symbolizes mantra, dance 
symbolizes meditation, as so singing and dancing the yogin always acts” (I.vi.1O, 14, in 
Snellgrove 1959: 64). Sahaja teachings, singing, songwriting, and tantric sādhanā have 
interconnected histories. Rather than departing from tantric religiosity, bhakti emo­
tional and aesthetic communities intersected with the sonic cultures of living tantric 
traditions, producing fertile terrain for a hybrid religiosity where singing is seen as

--- PAGE 1022 ---
Singing Tantra      997
 
a devotional act (sevā; see Hanssen 2018) but also a path to siddhi in that it mediates 
human and divine spheres.
The “intentional” or “twilight language” (sandhyābhāṣā) of esoteric songs, their par­
adoxical images and enigmatic poetics, constitute a fil rouge that scholars have traced 
to emphasize continuities across sects. The above-​mentioned Caryāgīti is a term used 
to designate a genre of tantric songs in Apabrahṃśa which at one time must have been 
composed in great numbers (Kvaerne [1977] 2010: 7–​8). Composition is attributed 
to the Siddhas, many of whom are also known in Nāth sources. Siddha composers 
of dohās and padas, like Saraha, must have flourished before the twelfth century (5). 
These compositions were intended to be sung, as the name (-​gīti) suggests. A rāga (me­
lodic framework) is indicated for each song in the text of the commentary, and each 
has a refrain (dhruvapada) indicating perhaps that a chorus alternated with a soloist. 
Handwritten note-​books of modern performers also indicate the melody and rhythmic 
pattern before the transcription of the song lyrics (see figs. 38.1a 1b).
(a)

The sung pada has proved to be an extremely popular lyrical form to propagate spir­
itual messages in a form that is accessible, enjoyable, and adaptable to melodic varia­
tions across regions. Probably inaugurated by “Sahajiyā Siddhas, together with the 
Jain Munis,” this malleable format was adopted extensively by later saint-​composers 
like Kabir (Vaudeville 1974: 54). Caryā/​ cacā songs directly connected to the Caryāgīti 
corpus are sung by Newar Vajrācāryas in Nepal (Widdess 2004) to the accompaniment 
of dance and instrumental music. Caryāpada songs translated into modern Bengali 
are currently being sung by Fakirs in Bangladesh, as the result of a revival movement 
initiated by urban intellectuals interested in emphasizing the pre-​Muslim cultural her­
itage of eastern Bengal.23
Singing songs in “the vulgar tongue,” as mentioned in the opening quote of this 
chapter—​including dohās from the Mahāsiddhas, verses sung in offering rituals, 
in initiation, and during worship—​signal intimate and esoteric passages in tantric 
(b)
Figure 38.1a and 1b.  Continued

--- PAGE 1024 ---
Singing Tantra      999
 
literature (Stephenson 2020). In Yoginī tantras and in Śaiva traditions, Goddess songs 
in Apabrahṃśa represent intense, direct mystical revelation by yoginīs. In the Tibetan 
canon, these “songs of realization” (rtogs-​pa brjod-​pa’i mgur) are often sung by yoginīs 
and ḍākinīs during the tantric feast.24 Through metaphorical language and seemingly 
nonsensical questions, they communicate a realm of experience beyond ordinary laws 
of logic (Shaw 1995). Songs create shocking contrasts and disorienting images to give 
a foretaste of nondual truth, conveying the paradoxical ultimate reality of sahaja. For 
such reasons, Kvaerne ([1977] 2010: 63) suggests that tantric songs work as a sort of in­
itiation on their own right, for they reveal the nature of the ultimate state through their 
systematic ambiguity, symbolizing the co-​emergence of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa in the 
state of “great bliss.”
Tibetan yogis adopted this poetic tradition which they refer to as the language of 
mahāmudrā and adapted it to the mgur genre of folk songs (Gamble 2011: 5). Through 
the paradoxical images of these songs, the sādhaka-​singers were able to interrupt the 
audience’s conventional view, prompting an alternative experience of reality. In this 
pedagogical and salvific potential of their “twilight language,” tantric songs’ aesthetics 
share the characteristics of the upside-​down language (ulaṭ bāṃsī) of Kabir (Hess 1983), 
the riddle-​like songs of Jñāndev (Kiehnle 1994), and the symbolic language of Bengali 
esoteric lineages (Lorea 2018c). The “songs of ecstasy” (Bhāber Gīt) of the Kartābhajā 
sect, which emerged out of a Muslim Fakir-​Vaiṣṇava encounter in eighteenth-​century 
Bengal, share an esoteric imagery drawn from Sahajiẏā and other tantric traditions of 
medieval Bengal (Urban 2001: 7). They are intended to generate an experience of gnosis 
and spiritual ecstasy (4) and they are filled with references to tantric subtle anatomy 
and emotional alchemy. While alluding to sexual practices to be performed by a male-​
female couple of practitioners, songs conceal tantric elements behind an elaborate veil 
of coded discourse, thickly embroidered with metaphors (Lorea 2018c).
Scholars of tantric traditions, including Hugh Urban, are interested in song texts and 
their language of secrecy, but not in how nonverbal and multisensory dimensions shape 
the sensibilities of those who participate. Songs are not solely constituted by their se­
mantic content. Their lyrics are often secondary, according to those who sing, dance, and 
hear them. The material and affective qualities of their sound is often paramount. The 
next section explores how such sound, which “awakens bhāb” and “distributes ānanda,” 
in the words of my interlocutors, can transport performers and listeners to higher states 
of realization. The field of tantric studies needs more ethnographic research to grow in 
its comparative and anthrohistorical understanding of how tantric communities use 
aural media, and how such media co-​produce epistemic communities of tantric practice 
that share sonic experiences.
Ethnographers of tantric traditions have suggested that music is widely employed in 
ritual and in everyday life for forging correspondences between microcosm and macro­
cosm and to transform the practitioner’s body into a divine body. Caryā/​cacā songs in 
Nepal are performed in a state of divine possession and are believed to confer esoteric 
powers (Widdess 2004). Rich Freeman (1997) discussed the use of torram songs to enact 
divine possession in Kerala. Singing the song of possession (uccaral torram), a low-​caste

--- PAGE 1025 ---
1000      Carola Erika Lorea
 
dancer “fixes” that state in his consciousness, effecting the deity’s descent as an animate 
and effective presence through songs (Freeman 1997). Freeman suggested that torrams 
fill the same functional roles as stotras, invocation, and meditation ślokas used in high-​
caste tantric rites in Keralan temples. Through immersive and participative research on 
the Tibetan Chöd (gcod) tradition, Jeffrey Cupchik reveals that melodies and rhythms in 
Chöd performance enhance the meditation process by eliciting specific emotions that 
aid the practitioners’ transformative experience. Music in this tantric practice functions 
“not as a secondary aesthetic gesture, a mere accompaniment to written poetry, but in 
fact can be considered a primary text-​and a primary conduit for the participants’ de­
velopment of specific emotional states and visualizations that can lead to meditative 
insights” (Cupchik 2015: 32).
In a different sociocultural constellation, Sukanya Sarbadhikary’s work (2015) on 
musical instruments and low-​caste instrument-​makers in West Bengal portrays tantra 
as a pervasive worldview that imbibes the habitus of performers and craftsmen. In 
Sarbadhikary’s anthropology of Bengali Vaiṣṇavism, the sonorous enactment of devo­
tion is impregnated by tantric ideologies. Vaiṣṇava bhakti in Bengal is suffused with tan­
tric conceptions of polar and gendered oppositions of cosmic principles that in their 
primordial unity exist as erotic vibration. According to Sarbadhikary’s informants, the 
opposite parts of the sacred drum (khol) embody Kṛṣṇa (the black part) and Rādhā. The 
two are struck together, representing the deity-​couple in erotic vibration: “As the khol’s 
edges shiver in sound, the couple vibrates in love” (2015: 212). Partaking the religious 
sound of musical instruments, loaded with affective and soteriological significance, 
practitioners can reach ecstatic stages of bliss and complete absorption in nondual 
reality, referenced as samādhi.
Sonic Soteriology, Ensounded Samādhi
If you attend Matua kīrtan with devotion, then that wind of love can pos­
sess you. . . gradually repeating Hari one can lose consciousness! Is he/​she 
in the realm of humans, or dead? In that time s/​he can talk to God. If you 
can reach that kingdom of bhāb then you find so many things. It is like 
the junction of the Triveni: The union of the three rivers during high tide. 
There is the house of a girl. It is a teaching to look at that girl as a mother, 
with those eyes.
(P. Modal, interview, December 2018)
In modern Bengal, the Matua (Matuẏā) movement continued and renewed the kīrtan 
tradition of sonic liberation, creating new song texts, music instruments, and a distinct 
performance style (Bairagya 1999: 307).25 The Matua religion emerged in the first half 
of the nineteenth century in the Faridpur district of East Bengal (now Bangladesh). Its 
founding prophets, Harichand (1812–​1878) and his son Guruchand Thakur (1847–​1937),

--- PAGE 1026 ---
Singing Tantra      1001
 
rebelled against Hindu casteist norms and created a separate religious identity to em­
power the stigmatized Namashudra caste.26 Imbibed with ecstatic devotionalism, 
Matuas combine a theology of egalitarian devotional love (prem bhakti), with an 
emphasis on remunerative work, disciplined conjugality, and social uplifting (see 
Bandyopadhyay 1997). Placing the human at the very center of their (political) theology, 
Matua members worship people, not in the metaphorical sense but literally performing 
adoration rituals toward other human beings.
Since the second half of the nineteenth century, the Matua religion presented it­
self as a restored and reformed sanātana dharma, with explicit instructions from the 
gurus on how to care for personal hygiene, uphold monogamy, dress, and behave in a 
way congruent to bhadralok expectations.27 Such emphasis on decency and respecta­
bility was partly a response to derogatory caste stereotypes that portrayed low castes 
as dirty, superstitious, and irrational and condemned low-​caste religious movements 
as obscene, allowing for sexual promiscuity and encouraging unproductive idle­
ness, through the use of intoxicants like ganja. The community distanced itself as 
much as possible from any nominally “tantric” path, ritual or textual authority; my 
interlocutors generally react with horripilation when I mention my interest in “tan­
tric” traditions.
A distinctive trait of the Matua style of kīrtan is that it always starts and ends with a 
drumming session led by ḍaṅkā (a large drum struck with two sticks which is said to 
represent the ḍamburu of Shiva), kām̐si (brass gong), siṅgā (buffalo horn), and the in­
cessant repetition of the holy name (haribal), accompanied by a vigorous and ecstatic 
dance. These intense sessions are called mātām.
During mātām, devotees jump, shaking their head up and down rhythmically, with 
arms raised up and repeating incessantly, in a loud voice, or in a panting whisper, the 
sacred sounds of the syllables haribol. The devotees can enter a state of trance called 
bhāber bibhor—​described as a complete annihilation of the ego, when the individual self 
disappears, perception of the outer world ends, and only the incessant interior sound of 
haribol remains. This is interpreted as the instantiation of the Matua ethical precept of 
social equality, because during mātām young and old, rich and poor, men and women, 
all meld undifferentiated in the ecstasy of sacred sound. The entranced is often taken by 
long bursts of uncontrollable crying. Other devotees will help the entranced to slowly 
cool down (or to become ṭhāṇḍā).
In Matua songs, oral teachings, and embodied knowledge, mātām is used as a prac­
tice for self-​realization, bringing one to enlightenment (siddhi); as a form of yoga that is 
ideal for marginalized low castes; and as the most direct method to awaken kuṇḍalinī 
energy and reach the state of samādhi. Matua narratives maintain that the high-​caste 
sages of the past could sit in meditation and repeat the sacred “aum” for twelve years to 
reach enlightenment. But mātām is for householders and working-​class people, who 
cannot afford to sit in an āsana for twelve years. Corroborating ethnographic sources, 
a very informative booklet released by the Matua Press of Thakurnagar explains with 
details the physical and spiritual benefits of practicing mātām (see fig. 38.2).

--- PAGE 1027 ---
1002      Carola Erika Lorea
 
Performers-​preachers of the community, called Pāgal and Gosain, teach how to 
awaken kuṇḍalinī through mātām. This path toward samādhi is simple (sahaja) 
and open to all: it is based on embodied techniques of sound, rhythmic repe­
tition, and dynamic movement. It is considered a superior method, compared to 
the performance of static meditation or exterior ritualism.28 The path of sonic 
liberation is described in the corpus of songs and chanted literature of the Matua 
community:

The embodied performance of mātām constitutes an experiential path to divinity 
through the powerful sound of incessant and intense drumming, rhythmic movement, 
and manipulation of the breath. This possibility is built upon a shared conception of the 
subtle body and the assumption that latent kuṇḍalinī energy can be turned and directed 
upward through sound. The Matua teachings around dehatattva rely upon the subtle 
mapping of a tantric yogic body (see fig. 38.3).
In the Matua community, as hinted at in the initial quotation, salvific sound liberates 
one from kām. Songs of sādhanā narrate equality and respect toward womanhood, 
since all humans come from a mother. Listening to these songs thus delivers one from 
kām and consequently produces a better humanity, where all tyranny, oppression, and 
abuse against women will come to an end.30 A Matua guru eloquently explained that 
kīrtan, through singing and dancing, uplifts the kuṇḍalīni and dispels kām: “If you see 
my guru’s penis, it is so small!” explaining that it reduced in size because of the beneficial 
effects of kīrtan.31
Guy Beck (1995) argued that techniques for the realization of higher truths in various 
paths of sādhanā are significantly centered on exercises involving the transformative 
power of sacred sound —​a characteristic of Indic traditions which he called “sonic the­
ology.” This concept is put to work in tantric traditions, where the material universe is 
an immensely complex web of vibrations and resonances. The integral relation of music

--- PAGE 1029 ---
1004      Carola Erika Lorea
 
and cosmic vibration is essential to Indian views on the soteriological significance of 
sound: as a manifestation of nāda, sacred sound is a mode of access to the highest reality 
(Wulff 1983: 154). Sound and techniques of “deep listening” are so central in the history 
of yoga that Finnian Gerety (2021: 516) proposed a redefinition of yoga as “meditation 
through sound (understood as a technique of chanting that supports contemplative 
Figure 38.3.  Front cover of the booklet “Six cakras and knowledge of sādhana,” authored by 
one of the sons of Guruchand Thakur (Thakur 2009), found at fairs and festivals of the Matuas.

--- PAGE 1030 ---
Singing Tantra      1005
 
states), meditation on sound (as a technique of listening that leads to emancipatory ab­
sorption) and meditation towards sound (as the highest soteriological goal [ . . . ]).”
According to later yoga works like Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā and Haṭhayogapradīpikā (c. 
fourteenth to sixteenth century), concentration on nāda brings about complete ab­
sorption (laya) and samādhi, a state of bliss in which one forgets the ego and can no 
longer hear the individual internal sounds of drums, bells, bees, and so forth, perceived 
in various states of meditation, but only a pure “unstruck” (anāhata) sound (Wilke and 
Moebus 2011: 706). In the Matua community, this state is triggered by the mātām music-​
dance session, at the end of which the sound of the loud drums (ḍaṅkā) and the inces­
sant repetition of haribol are fused with the practitioner’s own pulsation, life rhythm, 
and breath, until all external sensory stimulations stop being perceived.
The central role of sonic mediation in ritual action has been noticed by virtually 
all scholars who use long-​term and immersive ethnographic methods in the study of 
living tantric traditions. Andrew Alter (2019) describes sonic theology as “a notable 
part of Śākta-​Tantra rituals” (322). He studied festivals of the Goddess in the Western 
Himalayas, where drumming, dance, and possession have a crucial role. These ritual 
contexts provide for a material reflection of sonic ideologies through the agency of 
officiates, participants, and most significantly musicians. Andrew Alter (2019) argues 
that in embodied Śākta rituals, the power of sound permits direct association with the 
divine, through the presumption of sound’s divine essence.
These findings are comparable to other ethnographic contexts. In his study of the 
Śrī Vidyā tradition in Nepal, Jeffrey Lidke (2017) has observed that the underlying tan­
tric worldview that appears in sophisticated textual traditions pervades all spheres of 
Nepali society, beyond elite rulers and priests. Shamanic traditions, local healers, and 
musicians equally participate as actors that culturally embody such “Tantric culture” 
(66). Lidke suggests that music and possession are the primary links that tie the center 
and the periphery of tantra into a coherent mandala-​like cultural system. Learning from 
tabla musicians, he noted that the practitioners understand the Goddess as “translated” 
into music and embodied listening, with precise correspondences between rhythmic 
cycles (tāl), mantric syllables, and visual components of the śrī yantra diagram (Lidke 
2017: 78–​81). This comparative framework should be helpful in situating the Matua mu­
sical and spiritual practice of mātām, the drumming-​dancing-​breathing-​chanting com­
plex that dissolves ego identity and mediates the path to divine experience.
Final Remarks: Ensounding Tantric 
Texts, Bodies, and Histories
Case studies drawn upon comparative ethnographies and histories of tantric communities 
in South Asia clearly reveal that sonic media are not solely an accompaniment to more 
significant ritual actions or textual traditions. Far from being mere ornaments or artistic

--- PAGE 1031 ---
1006      Carola Erika Lorea
 
embellishments to something supposedly more relevant and authentic, transformative 
songs and auditory practices are co-​constitutive of many tantric traditions. Religious 
communities create and are created by sonic cultures. This is what Jeffrey Cupchick (2015) 
intended with his provocative title, “Buddhism as Performing Art.”
Singing features ubiquitously in the history of tantric communities as well as in the 
living practices of contemporary lineages, urging us to take aural media into serious 
consideration for a fuller anthrohistorical understanding of tantra from a multisensory 
perspective. I have proposed to employ “tantric” as a post-​emic category to ensure that 
works on heterodox and esoteric Bengali lineages, who do not refer to themselves as 
tāntrikas, can fit into wider interdisciplinary and comparative discussions on tantra. I 
have argued that academic literature has contributed to reproduce a dichotomy between 
bhakti saints and tantric ritualists, whereby songs have been conceived as a product of 
the devotional bhakti movement, and excluded from the territory of tantric studies. A 
comparative overview of the role of singing in the history of Indian religions certainly 
encompasses medieval bhakti traditions and underlines a continuity rather than a rup­
ture from tantric esoteric groups. Performance, music, and dance emerge as central 
components of tantric paths and aesthetic communities.
To conclude, not only are tantric bodies “entextualised” (Flood 2006) following 
tradition-​specific codes, but they are also ensounded. Visual aspects of tantric textual and 
material culture—​the mandala above all—​have been elected as common denominators 
across tantric traditions (White 2000). Sounds lack the historical longevity of texts and 
artifacts, escaping the conventional archives of tantra scholars. However, if scholars 
tune their sensitivity beyond ocularcentric epistemologies and sharpen their ears, sonic 
devices resound throughout the heterogeneous tantric world of South Asia. Mantra and 
speech feature as central subjects in tantric deliberations of a multilayered phonic re­
ality. The agency and sonic efficacy of nonsemantic mantras allows for the manipulation 
of such acoustic power for specific means. However, while mantras have received con­
siderable attention in tantric studies, the application of aural media and sonic efficacy 
encompasses the sophisticated ritual use of mantric and phonetic utterances. Ranging 
from congregational singing to reenactments of the ḍamburu of Shiva, tantric auditory 
practices reflect a complex religious acoustemology. Further research that employs par­
ticipatory ethnography to study local epistemologies of sound will be able to shed more 
light on how diverse communities—​whether explicitly “tantric” or post-​emically so—​
employ aural media to shape aesthetic, spiritual, and ethical realities of the participants. 
A multisensory and multimodal approach could expand the understanding of tantra in 
South Asian religions beyond the overrepresented realm of elite male theologians and 
officiants, to include music-​makers, storytellers, singers, trancers, and healers as pow­
erful and creative agents of tantric traditions.
