Chapter 40
Śaiva Tantra
Toward a History
Dominic Goodall
What is “Śaiva Tantra”? Clearly no such label seems to have been used for the early 
centuries in which what we may now regard as tantric ideas and practices were devel­
oping and circulating. The label “tantra” covers many religious movements spread out 
widely across space and time and is rather wildly used by many today to refer to some 
quite different modern notions. Answering such a question is further complicated by 
the fact that much of the earliest textual evidence has probably been lost.
This chapter concentrates first and foremost on “tantrism” in the first millennium 
of the Common Era, the formative period, in which a school of doctrine and liturgy 
emerged as dominant that was therefore known as the Śaivasiddhānta, “the settled 
view of Śaiva scripture.” A much broader picture of the Śaiva religions is given by the 
numerous invaluable articles of Sanderson, perhaps particularly 1988 (the broadest 
and briefest overview), 1992, 1995, 2004a, 2004b, 2006, 2007, 2009 (the longest, at 
300 pages), and 2014 (a condensed version of which appeared in 2015). This short ac­
count differs in that it focuses on the dominant school between the eighth and twelfth 
centuries.
Philosophically dualist, the Śaivasiddhānta maintained that souls and matter are ir­
reducibly different. Each soul possesses infinite powers of knowledge (jñānaśakti) and 
action (kriyāśakti), but these powers are occluded by three bonds: (1) an innate impu­
rity (mala); (2) the retributive force of past actions (karman); and (3) primal matter 
(māyā), which is the material cause of the universe, in which the nonmaterial souls 
are enmeshed. Each soul is identical to Śiva, except in one particular, namely, that 
Śiva is beginninglessly free of bondage, whereas other souls must be made free. The 
only route to salvation—​consisting in full realization of one’s innate omnipotence and 
omniscience—​is through a ritual initiation.
These tenets were set out at greater length by Sanderson in his article “The Doctrine of 
the Mālinīvijayottara” (1992, 282–​287), in which he demonstrates that even tantras that 
did not belong to the Śaivasiddhānta often shared the same framework. This is contrary

--- PAGE 1061 ---
1036      Dominic Goodall
 
to a widespread notion—​fostered by nondualist thinkers such as the Kashmirian pol­
ymath of the turn of the tenth to the eleventh century Abhinavagupta (see Sanderson 
1992, 281–​282)—​that non-​Saiddhāntika tantras distinguished themselves from those of 
the Śaivasiddhānta in that they taught a higher, nondualist ontology, which Sanderson 
also usefully outlined (1992, 287–​291). Abhinavagupta and his followers, defending what 
has come to be known misleadingly as “Kashmir Śaivism,” sought to demonstrate that 
“the inferiority of the Siddhāntas was proved not only by the less esoteric nature of their 
practice but also, less ambiguously, by the fact that they taught a nonultimate view of re­
ality” (Sanderson 1992, 281).
The Śaivasiddhānta appears in fact to have predominated across and beyond the 
Indian subcontinent, and one of its best-​known theologians, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, also 
lived in Kashmir at the same time as Abhinavagupta. But the label Śaivasiddhānta is 
often wrongly used as though it applied only to a rather different religious tradition 
that developed from it in the Tamil-​speaking south of India after the twelfth century, 
where its scriptures determined the public liturgy of temples and in which a some­
what different soteriology, shaped by the Bhakti movement and by Vedānta-​centered 
philosophizing, developed.1
“Tantrism” avant la lettre?
One of the earliest surviving scriptures that we may regard as a Śaiva tantra is the 
Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā. But that scripture does not refer to itself as a “tantra,” and al­
though it certainly uses that term, the word seems simply to mean “book.” We even find 
it used there to refer to books that are clearly not tantras.2 Furthermore, although the 
Niśvāsa figures in the list of the twenty-​eight scriptures that are said to form the canon 
of the dualist school that came to be called Śaivasiddhānta,3 it contains no allusion to ei­
ther that label or any entity that could be recognized as the school that came to bear that 
label. Instead, the Niśvāsa uses the term Mantramārga, “the path of mantras,” which var­
ious authors hold to be a possible candidate for an emic equivalent of the term tantrism.4 
(The term is used to contradistinguish the new movement from the Atimārga, “the path 
beyond,” an expression used of Pāśupata traditions.5)
Indeed, we find no commitment in the Niśvāsa to the dualist ontology of the clas­
sical Śaivasiddhānta, and its last and longest book, the Guhyasūtra, includes a lengthy 
grimoire of magical rites of the kind that Saiddhāntika theologians tended to ignore, 
deprecate, or eschew. In form and content, these magical recipes are closely paralleled 
in the Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa (Goodall and Isaacson 2016, passim), which belongs to the 
earliest phase of Tantric Buddhism. Moreover, hundreds of verses of the Niśvāsa have 
migrated into non-​Saiddhāntika Śaiva tantras (Goodall and Isaacson 2013, 125–​126). 
So, although it came to be regarded as a scripture of the Śaivasiddhānta, the Niśvāsa 
seems to have come into existence before a separation of Śaiva scriptural revelation into 
different streams, and it shows close affinities with other early tantric traditions. These

--- PAGE 1062 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1037
 
considerations make it a natural starting point for reflections about the history of the 
Mantramārga, and I refer to it often.6
What Are Mantras?
Attempts to define or at least to describe “tantrism” have not been easy,7 but from the 
last decades of research on the subject, it seems clear that what first united the various 
schools of disparate beliefs and practices labeled “tantric” was the notion that all re­
ligious goals could be achieved through the mastery of mantras. Spells had long been 
used to gain special powers: to destroy one’s enemies, to enslave or seduce others, or 
to cross great distances instantly. But the defining claim of the Mantramārga was that 
such mantras could also be used to destroy the bonds of earthly existence and thus 
escape the potentially endless cycle of saṃsāra, the unending sequence of births and 
deaths.8
Tantric mantras broadly conform in shape to two types: bījamantra and 
mālāmantra.9 The first of these, a “mantra in the form of a seed,” consists of a con­
sonant (or group of consonants) followed by a nasalized vowel (or group of vowels). 
A typical bījamantra, for example, is HĀṂ, which is often taken to express the heart 
(hṛdaya) of the god. Sometimes these seed mantras take the form of an almost un­
pronounceable string of consonants with a single vowel, such as HRKṢMLVYŪṂ.10 
These can be represented graphically by writing the successive consonants conjoined 
beneath each other.
The second type, sometimes called mālāmantra, “mantra in garland form,” consists 
of a semantically significant series of syllables. The best known mālamantra, the 
vyomavyāpin, contains eighty-​one syllables.11 A shorter mantra of this type is OṂ 
CAṆḌIKE KRAMA KRAMA SVĀHĀ, “OṂ [O goddess] Caṇḍikā, walk, walk! 
SVĀHĀ!” In spite of its semantic content, this mantra is actually prescribed for a 
catoptromantic process in the Guhyasūtra of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (3.24–​3.27). A 
virgin boy or girl has his or her thumb rubbed with oil impregnated with thousands of 
repetitions of this incantation, and then that innocent child is instructed to stare at the 
glistening surface of the oil and recount what is “seen.”12
Each mantra is conceived as an incarnation made of sound, a sonic body, of a pow­
erful deity, and there are said to be seventy million of them. The central religious fact 
that characterizes all Mantramārga traditions, at least during the early centuries of their 
existence, is dīkṣā, an initiation rite that deploys such mantras to bring about the goals 
of religious aspirants. In translation we call dīkṣā an “initiation” since the term comes 
from Vedic tradition and is originally an initiatory rite that confers the right to perform 
a particular Vedic sacrifice. But it has become much more than that, for, although it may 
function as an introduction to religious activity, conferring on the initiate the privilege 
of being able to use the mantras himself, a full tantric dīkṣā guarantees the initiate’s at­
tainment of ultimate liberation on death. It may, in other words, be itself a salvific ritual

--- PAGE 1063 ---
1038      Dominic Goodall
 
and not merely an initiatory preparation for subsequent religious practice. (Some 
traditions, and not only ones outside the Śaivasiddhānta, allowed that there were other 
paths to ultimate liberation, such as yoga13 or subitist gnosis, which could be transmitted 
through the guru’s gaze or touch, but the view that dīkṣā was an essential prerequisite for 
liberation predominated, so much so that some of these alternative paths became classi­
fied as types of nonritual dīkṣā.14)
The mantras most commonly used in ritual are not so numerous, and the most 
important among them are held to be the sonic forms of the central deity, or of the 
central deity’s heads and “body parts.” In fact, the “central deity,” namely the ul­
timately subtle Śiva, cannot be visualized or conceived of at all, but he adopts, as 
an act of grace toward those who wish to revere and meditate on him, the form of 
Sadāśiva, who is five-​faced and ten-​armed. His five heads—​Tatpuruṣa, Vāmadeva, 
Sadyojāta, Aghora, and Īśāna—​are five mantras that are considered to be Vedic 
and that were already a focus of meditative practice within the Atimārga.15 His so-​
called body part mantras (aṅgamantra) are the heart (hṛdaya); head (śiras); topknot 
(śikhā); cuirass (kavaca, correlated with the chest); weapon (astra, correlated with 
the hands); and, in some cases, eyes (netra).16 Equally important in many rituals is 
a central mantra known as the root-​mantra (mūlamantra) or as the Śiva-​mantra, 
which expresses the divinity as a whole. In some tantras, the root-​mantra and the 
heads and body parts are all of seed-​syllable type, as in the case of the earliest layers 
of the Niśvāsa and in most early recensions of the Kālottaratantra, whose mantra 
system is followed in all extant medieval manuals of ritual (paddhati) bar one.17 
In other tantras, such as the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, the root mantra is the 
garland-​type vyomavyāpin, and the heads and body part mantras consist of small 
sequences cut from the vyomavyāpin.
Given the protracted dominance of the Śaivasiddhānta, one might expect there to 
be many old representations of Sadāśiva, but all seem to belong to recent centuries, 
other than a few eleventh-​ and twelfth-​century sculptures from the Bengali-​speaking 
and Khmer-​speaking regions,18 unless one counts also the famous but contested rep­
resentation in Elephanta on the west coast.19 This paucity might be partly explained 
by Sadāśiva’s relatively esoteric status as the central mantra deity of an initiatory reli­
gion, albeit one that is today regarded as not particularly secretive, and partly by the 
fact that Sadāśiva is primarily a form whose image is to be visualized and projected 
into the liṅga before worship. Any liṅga is thus, from the perspective of an initiate, 
sufficient as a substrate for the worship of Sadāśiva, of whom no graven image is 
therefore required. Aside from the few early figured representations, there are other 
traces of the erstwhile importance of Sadāśiva discernible beyond the Śaivasiddhānta: 
His five-​headedness became generalized for the central deities of other tantric 
cults (Törzsök 2013), and several rival cults incorporate the transcended corpse of 
Sadāśiva in the visualized throne of worship on which their central deity is enthroned, 
expressing thereby both their implicit acknowledgment of the centrality of the 
Śaivasiddhānta and a wish to express transcendence beyond its teachings (Sanderson 
1986; Goodall 2011).

--- PAGE 1064 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1039
 
Growing Social Hierarchy Within 
the Mantramārga
If you have heard the term Śaivasiddhānta, the chances are that you have heard of it as a 
medieval (post-​twelfth-​century) South Indian school of devotion that, though tantric in 
name, can be seen as consistently “right-​handed” in praxis (observant, in other words, 
of widespread conventions of ritual purity), Veda-​congruent in discourse, supportive of 
a monotheistic worldview that must have comforted “the establishment,” and the source 
of a complex courtly protocol of ritual and of calendrical festivals that animated the 
great temple cities of the south, thus shoring up the social status quo.
But when we examine the earliest surviving textual sources, we find no evidence 
of a Veda-​congruent school rooted deeply and broadly in the wider social fabric. The 
more social elements of religious life—​temples; monasteries; public liturgy; festivals; 
and life-​cycle rites marking births, marriages, coming of age, and death—​are ignored 
in the successive textual layers of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (fifth to seventh century), as 
well as in other demonstrably early tantras, such as the 200-​, 350-​, 700-​, and 1,300-​verse 
recensions of the Kālottara. Naturally, this does not mean that such phenomena of so­
cial religion didn’t exist at the time, and indeed we catch glimpses of them in allusions. 
What it suggests instead is that the earliest tantric works were not interested in these 
social dimensions of religion. The Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā reflects rather the concerns of 
specialists wishing to master mantras for “magical” and spiritual benefits. The various 
layers of the text show how “spells” (mantra) are to be propitiated and then put to use 
for achieving either liberation (mukti, mokṣa) or special enjoyments (bhukti, bhoga)—​
often characterized as supernormal powers (siddhi)—​followed ultimately by the attain­
ment of liberation. A prerequisite for the use of mantras is the ritual of initiation (dīkṣā), 
which, by means of oblations into a divinized fire using mantras, at once consumes the 
initiand’s karman—​the retributive force of that soul’s past actions—​that has been or will 
be stored up for consumption one day in the numerous worlds throughout the cosmos. 
But this initiation thereby also gives him (only male initiates are spoken of in this text) 
the authority (adhikāra) to take on mantra-​sādhana, that is to say the pursuit of super­
normal powers (siddhi) by means of propitiation and then ritual deployment of a mantra 
that he chooses (or that is chosen for him) to master (sādhyamantra).
All initiates may be referred to in the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā as sādhakas, in other 
words, aspirants to the attainment of siddhi through sādhana using a sādhya-​mantra. 
(Note that siddhi, sādhana, sādhya, and sādhaka are all terms derived from the same 
verbal root, sādh/​sidh, “to achieve, accomplish”.) Even the guru who performs an in­
itiation may be referred to simply with the word sādhaka, and no other hierarchy 
among initiates is alluded to. What all this suggests is not a vast institutionalized re­
ligious movement, but rather a not-​so-​numerous group of enthusiasts who have 
distanced themselves from societal norms in order to quest for supernormal powers. 
For this they used a largely inherited ritual technology involving the propitiation

--- PAGE 1065 ---
1040      Dominic Goodall
 
of mantra-​deities by making offerings into a sanctified fire to the accompaniment 
of the recitation of mantras, held to be the sonic form of mantra-​deities. The wider 
social aspects of this religious world seem to be so unimportant as to pass largely 
unmentioned.
The absence of a complex social hierarchy in the earliest works is highlighted by 
the gradual emergence in later textual sources of labels, practices, rituals, and ideas 
that clearly do imply a growing social diversity. This is the case even for the more 
power-​oriented, “left-​handed” currents of the Mantramārga. In the Picumata-​
Brahmayāmala, for example, a large non-​Saiddhāntika tantra, which teaches the 
worship of a pantheon of fierce mantra-​deities to be worshipped in a mandala of 
cremation grounds in a manner that involves transgressive sexual rites, there is evi­
dence of a hierarchy within the religion, for we find there different classes of sādhakas 
distinguished, as Csaba Kiss’s work has sought to clarify (Kiss 2015, 35–​53). A social 
hierarchy naturally also emerged in the gradually more orthodox and orthopractic 
Śaivasiddhānta: It is probably in the seventh-​century Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha 
that we find for the first time the four categories of initiate, the lowest being the pre­
liminarily initiated neophyte (samayin) bound to the rules (samaya) of the religion, 
the highest being the guru (ācārya), whose principal disciples (from among whom he 
would choose his successor) were the fully initiated putrakas (the word may have been 
adopted from Dharmaśāstra, where it refers to an “adopted son”). The remaining cat­
egory was that of the sādhaka, the power seeker, which in the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, 
as we have seen, was still a generic label used for all initiates. One implication of this 
hierarchy is that the religion had become centered on households of gurus—​proto-​
monasteries headed by gurus who were waited on by their putrakas and samayins—​
with the sādhakas effectively now liminal figures, pursuing siddhi outside the guru’s 
domain. This adumbrates the gradual marginalization of siddhi and its pursuit within 
the Śaivasiddhānta, which, for instance, Brunner has spoken of in an article about 
the sādhaka as a “forgotten personage” (1975). Concomitantly, the theologians whose 
works have survived seem to have become increasingly uninterested in, even embar­
rassed by, the passages in early Siddhāntatantras that detail procedures for the acquisi­
tion of supernormal powers and pleasures, which they came to regard as the province 
of other traditions of the Mantramārga, whereas the Śaivasiddhānta focused only on 
the loftier goal of mokṣa.
The same four classes of initiates are widely referred to elsewhere, along with 
other sorts of evidence of a growing social scope. In the possibly eighth-​century 
Kiraṇatantra, for example, we find not only a chapter devoted to begging (33), as 
would suit monad sādhakas, but also a passage devoted to communal eating using 
tables (? unless pīṭha here means “stools”) of different heights for each rank of initiate 
(45.7ff.). We also find fairly detailed prescriptions for the creation of a temple (­chapter 
55, edited and translated by Mills 2019), but the text also mentions the installation of 
a liṅga in a large private house (mandire), distinguished from one installed in a public 
temple (51.6).20

--- PAGE 1066 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1041
 
Further Socioreligious Clues
Besides these social clues from what is said about infrastructure, the account that the 
Kiraṇatantra gives of the topic of observance (caryā) is revealing. This term in earlier 
literature typically referred to vrata-​caryā, in other words to the following (by adopting 
a certain dress, diet, and behavior) of a timed religious observance primarily for the 
purposes of propitiating a particular mantra before using it for acquiring siddhi. But 
by the time of the Kiraṇatantra, caryā had evidently slipped in meaning (see Goodall 
2020a, 55–​59) and was now instead applied to the everyday dress and behavior of the 
different classes of initiates. This semantic shift underlines a shift away from the rela­
tively isolated power seekers of the Niśvāsa, toward small communities attached to the 
households of gurus. What is still not in evidence in the Kiraṇatantra’s presentation of 
the religion, however, is any sort of public temple liturgy or any calendrical festivals. 
There are however some life-​cycle rites that appear to emerge in the Mantramārga in 
this period. As part of a generalized diversification of types of initiation, we find the 
prescription of funerary initiations (for a brief account, see Sanderson 1995, 31–​33, but 
for detailed treatment of Śaiva mortuary and postmortuary rituals, including editions 
and translations of primary sources, see Mirnig 2018), somewhat illogically, it seems, 
performed even for those who received a salvific initiation while alive and of forms of 
initiation of the dead performed in the absence of a body, (mahājāla, mṛtoddhāra). 
Moreover, the Kiraṇatantra also adds postfunerary rituals (śrāddha), which, no doubt 
like many death-​related rituals throughout the world, seem doctrinally out of step with 
the soteriology of the religion in which they developed (again, see Sanderson 1995, 34–​
37, and, for greater detail, Mirnig 2018, 189ff.).
One sign of the emerging prominence of Śaiva initiates in wider society is the appear­
ance in literature and inscriptions of individuals bearing initiatory names. Such names 
usually take the form of the name of a mantra followed by a distinctive ending, the most 
common being the ending °śiva; a typical example would thus be Aghora-​śiva, the 
name of the most famous South Indian theologian, whose celebrated ritual manual, the 
Kriyākramadyotikā, was probably completed in 1157 CE, but also a commonly attested 
name in inscriptions (Goodall 2000). Such initiatory names made their first appear­
ance in the epigraphical record in central India in the seventh century (see Goodall, 
Sanderson, and Isaacson 2015, 51–​58); by the tenth century, they had become wide­
spread in Cambodia (Goodall 2015a, 21–​26). We know this because, with its large lists of 
temple personnel, Khmer epigraphy is a rich field for onomastic study. We can also see 
that these Saiddhāntika names gradually replaced anthroponyms that mark Pāśupata 
obedience known from the donors and patrons who figure in seventh-​century Khmer 
inscriptions, namely, ones that begin with Bhā-​ or Bhava-​21 or that end with -​rāśi.22
Over the same spread of centuries, we find also allusions to the tantric initiations 
of kings in epigraphs spread across the entire Sanskrit cosmopolis (Sanderson 2001; 
Goodall 2004; Goodall and Griffiths 2013). This development, a testimony to growing

--- PAGE 1067 ---
1042      Dominic Goodall
 
royal patronage, which was no doubt a factor in popularizing the Mantramārga 
(Sanderson 2013), is reflected in scripture by the provisions of a special “seedless in­
itiation” (nirbījā dīkṣā), which was clearly designed to widen the availability of a sal­
vific tantric initiation to include more than just the power-​seeking sādhakas, who were 
once the focus of the religion as presented in the Niśvāsa. In this newer system, reg­
ular initiands, those judged capable of following postinitiatory observances, received a 
sabījā dīkṣā, a “seeded initiation,” thus making them into putrakas, the “seed” in ques­
tion being the obligation to follow postinitiatory rules (samaya). Those too busy or 
unable to perform postinitiatory observances instead took an initiation in which the 
obligation was removed and thus was called “seedless” (nirbīja). Such an initiation is 
referred to, without such a label, in some pre-​tenth-​century Siddhāntatantras (e.g., 
Kiraṇatantra 6.11; see also Goodall 1998, 363–​365, quoting Sanderson), and the termi­
nology is perhaps first found in the Svacchandatantra (4.88): bālabāliśavṛddhastrībho
gabhugvyādhitātmanām | eṣāṃ nirbījikā dīkṣā samayādivivarjitā, “Children, fools, the 
aged, women, kings, the sick—​for these [there is] seedless initiation, devoid of [the obli­
gation to follow] post-​initiatory observances and so forth.”
As explained above, texts such as the Niśvāsa appear to reflect the ideas and 
practices—​yogic, theological, magical, ritual—​of celibate male power-​seeking ascetics 
on the margins of society who do not appear to cultivate institutional ties. But a reli­
gion consisting only of such persons would surely risk swift extinction. One indication, 
however, that the Mantramārga was already veering toward wider social inclusion at its 
very inception is the inclusion of fire in its rituals. As Sanderson observed (2006, 147, 
192–​193), what we know of the rituals of the early Atimārga groups known as Pāśupatas, 
suggests that no fire was involved, as would be expected of an ascetic tradition, since 
the maintaining of a fire is the prerogative of married householders. The earliest mag­
ical rituals attested in works of the Mantramārga, in contrast, prominently involve 
oblations into fire (see Goodall and Isaacson 2016, 19–​24), unlike those described in the 
Arthaśāstra (as remarked in Goodall, Sanderson, and Isaacson 2015, 82).
The further inclusion of purely salvific and “seedless” ritual initiations for “chil­
dren, fools, the aged, women, kings, the sick,” with none of them regarded as able to 
follow the daily or occasionally obligatory rituals of pūjā (worship) and agnikārya (fire 
oblations), is a marker of a considerable social widening of the religion, even if it still 
remained for a while anchored in small communities grouped around the households 
of gurus. Whether such initiates really had no further religious duties after initiation 
must have varied from one context to another. The tenth-​century Kashmirian theolo­
gian Rāmakaṇṭha, a back-​to-​the-​scriptures fundamentalist whose writings helped to 
standardize Saiddhāntika doctrine, said that such persons could listen to pious tales and 
follow the lay practices taught in texts of the Śivadharma (about which more below). In 
other words, he held that they could be pious but there was no further soteriologically 
significant activity that they could engage in. But it would not be surprising if in fact 
pressure increased to prescribe practices that were tailored to their needs. And indeed 
we find that the Kiraṇatantra, for instance, teaches a procedure for the worship of Śiva’s 
consort Gaurī that was designed to suit the wives of initiates. The suitability of Gaurī

--- PAGE 1068 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1043
 
worship for married women is still more clearly marked in an account of Gaurī wor­
ship given in a chapter of the eleventh-​century Bṛhatkālottaratantra (Sathyanarayanan 
and Goodall 2015, 30–​35).23 There are even allusions in Trilocanaśiva’s twelfth-​century 
manual of expiation to the worship of Śiva by women (Sathyanarayanan and Goodall 
2015, 36–​37). The growing importance of women is perhaps also reflected in a sort of 
“feminization” of the pantheon of worship (Goodall et al. 2005, 25, 149–​151). In all pre-​
twelfth-​century literature, Sadāśiva is consortless, and all the members of his retinue 
of five circles of eight deities are also consortless and masculine, with the exception of 
Gaurī in the second circle and Gadā and Śakti in the fifth and outermost circle, who 
are both personifications of weapons that happen to be grammatically feminine. But in 
some later scriptures, all are visualized with consorts.
Moving back a couple of centuries, the emergence of a body of ritual manuals 
(paddhati) may attest to deepening institutionalization of the religion in the tenth 
and eleventh centuries. The most famous of these is the Kriyākāṇḍakramāvali, best 
known as the paddhati of Somaśambhu, the head of a celebrated and extremely well-​
endowed Śaiva monastery at Golagī (today Gurgi; see Sanderson 2014, 21). That text 
is well known among Indologists today because of the heavily annotated four-​volume 
edition and translation (1963–​1998) of Hélène Brunner-​Lachaux. But it was already a 
somewhat famous and influential text when it was produced in the eleventh century 
and seems to have been disseminated in more than one eleventh-​century “edition” 
(Goodall 2014; Sanderson 2007, 420–​421, fn. 640). The ritual instructions of the manual 
are by default still addressed to individual male initiates or to the guru, but it has been 
plausibly suggested by S. A. S. Sarma (forthcoming) that the will to formulate and then 
disseminate such a standardized Śaiva liturgy might be a natural consequence of the 
flourishing of relatively large monastic institutions, such as the one that Somaśambhu 
himself headed, which was founded by the ninth-​century Kalachuri king Yuvarājadeva 
(Sanderson 2009, 263–​264). The epigraphic record preserves accounts of numerous 
royal grants that resulted directly or indirectly in the creation of Śaiva monasteries (for 
translations of three such grants, including that of Gurgi, see Davis 2000) and that gave 
an exalted—​indeed almost kingly—​status to some Śaiva gurus (see Sanderson 2009, 
263–​273), and the massive stone remains of some of these impressive monasteries still 
stand today (Sears 2014).
No doubt the esoteric speculations, yogic meditations, and (sometimes transgres­
sive) mantra-​based rituals of individual seekers always continued to be practiced 
and to develop, as they do today, but in the background of this new mainstream. But 
within this mainstream the earlier, more ascetic, motive force seems to have been grad­
ually enveloped and then supplanted by a social religion whose expanding embrace 
was marked at first, as we have seen, by the accretion of hierarchical ranks, monastic 
foundations of increasing size, and socially significant life-​cycle rites such as funerals 
and postmortuary ceremonies (śrāddha). To these may be added calendrical festivals, 
which began to make their appearance (again in the Kiraṇatantra) with an autumnal 
rite known as pavitrotsava,24 and then a spring one called damanotsava (Goodall 2019). 
While these festivals may often have had different origins outside Śaivism, to justify

--- PAGE 1069 ---
1044      Dominic Goodall
 
their presence in what was now held to be a widely proselytizing but still narrowly so­
teriological religion, they were treated as expiatory rituals that repair faults or ritual 
omissions that may have occurred over the course of the previous year or month.
But in the Siddhāntatantras produced in South India from the late twelfth century on­
ward, no such quasi-​soteriological justification seems required for the plethora of temple 
processions and festivals described. These scriptures seem to reflect a religion that has 
entirely shifted its focus again, this time away from the salvation of (often wealthy) 
individuals, through expensive initiation rituals, to center instead on the bustling life of 
a South Indian temple city and the communities that kept it alive. Whereas dīkṣā seemed 
earlier always to be the central focus of both the doctrinal and the ritual teaching—​a rite 
of initiation aimed first at enabling control over spells for attaining supernormal powers 
and salvation equally, then primarily directed toward salvation alone—​it came now to 
be seen effectively as a rite of ordination to serve as a priest in temple ceremonies, which 
now became the principal focus of the teaching of the Siddhāntatantras. Those eligible 
to perform these ceremonies were held to belong exclusively to a semiendogamous 
subcaste of Brahmins known as Ādiśaivas or Śivabrāhmaṇas.25
The ritual activities of this class of hereditary priests seem to be the main concern 
of such works as the Kāmika, Kāraṇa, Raurava (trans. Barazer-​Billoret and Dagens 
2000), and Ajitatantra (Bhatt, Filliozat, and Fillozat 2005) and of many other tantras 
that appear to describe South Indian temple rituals, sometimes using distinctively 
South Indian vocabulary (see Goodall 2021), and to have been transmitted only in 
South Indian manuscripts.26 But the rights and duties of members of other communities 
important for public liturgy (e.g., drummers, musicians, dancers, and craftspeople) 
also appear there.27 The earliest labeled and still identifiable quotations from such 
scriptures—​the South Indian Temple Āgamas—​appear in works of the twelfth and thir­
teenth centuries. The majority of them, however, appear not to have been identifiably 
quoted until rather later, in the sixteenth century; this lateness may be partly because 
so very little Saiddhāntika writing in Sanskrit can be firmly dated to the fourteenth 
and fifteenth centuries.28 After intensive production of ritual manuals, theological 
commentaries, and digests in the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries, there seems to 
have been a lull among Śaivas in Sanskrit literary activity in the fourteenth and fifteenth 
centuries (at least by avowedly human authors, for the South Indian Temple Āgamas 
may have been produced in this period), followed by another period of intense produc­
tivity in the Tamil-​speaking south in the sixteenth century.
It should be noted that the gap may be more apparent than real since there may be 
many lost works, or unnoticed surviving works, that belong to this period. Furthermore, 
it is to this period, the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, that most if not all of the 
fourteen theological treatises in Tamil known as the Meykaṇṭacāttiraṅkaḷ belong.29 
These treatises use the terminology of the Siddhāntatantras and their commentators—​
sometimes in the form of words borrowed from the Sanskrit and sometimes in the 
form of Tamil calques—​but in fact teach a soteriology that is different from what was 
defended by the earlier theologians whose works survive, the most famous of whom are 
Sadyojyotiḥ (seventh century), Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha (tenth century), his son Bhaṭṭa

--- PAGE 1070 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1045
 
Rāmakaṇṭha, a certain Bhoja (eleventh century), Aghoraśiva (twelfth century), and a 
disciple of his called Trilocanaśiva. For in these Tamil works, personal devotion to God 
is paramount, ritual initiation is barely mentioned, and the ultimate goal is no longer 
to realize one’s innate powers and to become identical to Śiva, but rather to become in 
some way united with Śiva and yet also not entirely fused within him.
This shift in theology was followed by South Indian Śaivas writing in Sanskrit in the 
sixteenth century. An exception is Jñānaprakāśa of Śālivāṭi in Sri Lanka, who attempted 
to defend the doctrines systematized by Kashmirian thinkers of the tenth century, but 
with an awareness of a now vast body of Śaiva literature that could not easily be brought 
into harmony with it. The vastness of the then-​accessible literature is reflected in the 
tendency in this period to produce nibandha works, or commentaries with a nibandha-​
like quality, that is to say works in which long sequences of illustrative quotations were 
strung together, sometimes only thinly interspersed with explanatory prose or with 
identificatory labels. The voluminous unpublished Sanskrit works of Vedajñāna II 
(whose uncle Vedajñāna I died in 1563 CE) illustrate this tendency.30 We may specu­
late that the growth of institutional monastic libraries may have enabled this style of 
composition.
Once again, we can see the above-​mentioned developments as a reflection of new 
social and theological concerns that had emerged and required discussion and resolu­
tion. For instance, one particular current of thought with which earlier Śaiva thinkers 
hardly engaged had become preeminent in South Indian intellectual life, namely 
that of Vedānta, the body of schools of philosophical exposition of the Upaniṣads.31 
Confronting Vedānta led of course to fresh discussion of old theological issues and 
veering away from the strict dualism of the old Śaivasiddhānta toward something 
resembling the qualified dualism of Viśiṣṭādvaita. Two concomitant further shifts may 
be mentioned, both no doubt also connected to the continued social broadening of 
the religion. One was linguistic, the shift from Sanskrit into Tamil. Some of the earliest 
works of the Mantramārga may already long ago have emphasized that it was not just 
Brahmins who were eligible for initiation, but they are nonetheless full of injunctions 
directed at Brahmin males, who were the addressees by default of their teachings. But, as 
we have seen, an increasing range of actors are taken into account over time, and the use 
of the regional language Tamil is explicitly associated in some of the Tamil works them­
selves with broad accessibility. But the use of Tamil would not have been enough by itself 
to bring Śaiva tantric teachings to the masses because these are verse compositions in an 
elevated literary register, often rendering them actually more challenging to interpret 
than their Sanskrit counterparts. The other shift was religious, namely, the preoccupa­
tion with devotion. In order to understand this shift better, we may step back a moment 
to consider the role of devotion in the Śaivasiddhānta until the twelfth century.
In the early Mantramārga, the conception of mantras as inconceivably powerful 
instruments that could be used not only as spells for wielding supernormal powers but 
also for attaining ultimate liberation from saṃsāra, a goal hitherto typically regarded 
as requiring many lifetimes of toilsome religious endeavor or morally upright be­
havior. But this reliance had led to the view that ultimate liberation was in fact only

--- PAGE 1071 ---
1046      Dominic Goodall
 
possible through reliance on mantras deployed in a particular manner in the context 
of a lengthy ritual initiation involving hundreds of oblations into fire for purging every 
layer of the universe in which the soul would otherwise be destined, because of karmic 
debt, to be reborn. This was the unvarying teaching, over several centuries, of the 
doctors enumerated above, in the period in which the Śaivasiddhānta was still a pan-​
Indian tradition. We know this from the large textual corpus that they have left behind, 
which defends at length a complex cosmography of hundreds of worlds imbricated in 
an intricate ritual procedure of purification by fire oblations that is presented as the 
only path to salvation. Certainly there was religious activity that was enjoined after in­
itiation, notably daily veneration (pūjā) using Śaiva mantras, first internally, which in­
volved first mentally burning away one’s physical body and replacing it with one made 
of Śiva’s mantras, before visualizing the deity Sadāśiva enthroned in one’s heart, and 
then externally, involving visualizing him in (typically) a liṅga, and making offerings 
to him present there and then as present in the fire. But this regular practice involving 
self-​identification with the divine, a sort of prefiguring of the ultimate liberated state 
in which the soul was to realize fully his innate Śiva-​nature, received rather weak 
justifications—​that it was to be practiced in order to ensure the continuity of the re­
ligion, for example (thus Kiraṇatantra 6.13–​6.14), or that it burned off the residue of 
bondage left in place in order to sustain the current birth, since bondage cannot wholly 
be burned away by the mantras in the course of a regular dīkṣā or else the initiate would 
at once drop dead. Such odd justifications were a corollary of maintaining that a ritual 
dīkṣā, if correctly performed, guaranteed liberation.
The result is a somewhat mechanistic soteriology that left almost no place for per­
sonal devotion, and that must surely have been psychologically unsatisfying for some. 
In this dry system, devotion (bhakti) seems to have had no other soteriological func­
tion beyond indicating to the qualified guru that a certain person must be ripe for re­
ceiving a ritual initiation, and the influential exegete Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha accordingly 
gives this lukewarm definition:32 “Bhakti is taught to be a particular kind of know­
ledge that consists in being penetrated by suitability [for initiation and thereby salva­
tion]” (bhaktir yogyatāveśalakṣaṇo jñānaviśeṣa uktaḥ). In other traditions, hymns 
to the divine naturally enough often take the form of emotional poetic effusions, but 
the few surviving pre-​twelfth-​century stotras of the Śaivasiddhānta tend to be pieces 
of dry catechesis, furnishing their users, for instance, with mnemonic versification 
for recalling a sequence of ritual acts (Jñānaśambhu’s Śivapūjāstava), or a sequence of 
visualizations for daily worship (Aghoraśiva’s Pañcāvaraṇastava and Trilocanaśiva’s 
Dhyānaratnāvali33) or exegesis of mantras (Rāmakaṭha’s Vyomavyāpistava). In such 
compositions, we typically encounter neither the elegant wit nor the emotion of, for 
instance, Utpaladeva’s Śivastotrāvali. Knowledge acquired through meditation, moral 
rectitude, piously motivated acts that help others, or any signal manifestation of devo­
tional fervor, including fasting, pilgrimages, participation in festivals—​all these may 
produce merit (puṇya)—​but merit is not salvific for it is ultimately only one ritual, that 
of initiation (dīkṣā), that makes salvation possible. Even though a place is found in the 
Śaivasiddhānta for all the above-​mentioned religious phenomena and activities, their

--- PAGE 1072 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1047
 
importance is inevitably diminished by the soteriology that much of the Saiddhāntika 
literature of the tenth to twelfth centuries was devoted to setting out and defending.
But what, you may ask, about the first-​millennium Tamil devotional poetry of the 
Tēvāram, which celebrates festivals and whose focus was on sacred places, glorifying 
Śiva and his mythological exploits in dozens of Southern temple towns? It is true that 
the devotional hymns of the poet-​saints Appar (also known as Tirunāvukkaracu), 
Ñānacampantar (Sanskrit: Jñānasambha), and Cuntarar (Sanskrit: Sundara) are often 
presented as though they belonged to or helped popularize the Śaivasiddhānta in 
Southern India. But their poems were not in their own time in any sense Saiddhāntika 
compositions and only came to be so regarded centuries later.34 Nor do they exhibit 
any particular leaning toward the Mantramārga. Instead, the hymns refer to several 
groups of Śiva-​worshipping religious professionals, apparently without favoring any 
of them. Among the people thronging the streets of the temple city of Tiruvarur, for 
example, we see mixed together (Tēvāram 4.20.3) ascetics with matted locks, Śaivas, 
Pāśupatas, and Kāpālikas.35 Here, the Śaivas (Tamil: caivar) are probably adherents of 
the Mantramārga and thus perhaps of the Śaivasiddhānta. In other holy sites, we find 
just Śaivas and Pāśupatas presented together (1.66.4), or just Mahāvratins (4.21.1), or 
religious professionals called Rudras (uruttirar, 2.29.4, 2.37.9), who may have been of 
another group who (like the Pāśupatas, Mahāvratins, and Kāpālikas) belonged to the 
Atimārga.36 Similarly, we find the god Śiva himself presented as taking on the dress and 
attributes of these religious professionals: He wears Pāśupata garb in 1.97.6, 6.20.2, and 
6.91.2, but he wears the dress of a Śaiva (caivaveṭaṉ) in 1.53.6 and 1.12.2 and that of a 
Kapāli (viz. Kāpālika) in 1.27.70. Furthermore, we do not find allusions in the corpus 
to details of theology or liturgy that were distinctive of the Mantramārga. Allusions to 
mantras, to bonds and bondage (pācam), and to impurities afflicting the soul (malam) 
are not rare, but they are not particularly distinctive. One clear instance of a distinctive 
piece of tantric terminology does stand out. In a passage alluding to the sage Agastya 
worshipping Śiva, Agastya is said to perform sakalīkaraṇa (cakaḷī ceytu, in 7.65.5), 
which refers to the procedure of laying Śiva’s mantras on his own body as part of his self-​
identification as Śiva (or as a Śiva), which is an essential preliminary to pūjā. To sum­
marize, adherents of the Mantramārga were certainly present in South Indian religious 
life at the time of the composition of such hymns, but they appear to have been just one 
among several groups of co-​religionists, accorded no more emphasis than older groups 
of Śiva-​worshipping religious professionals.
In other words, we should be careful not to read back into this devotional liter­
ature our notions of the preeminence of the Mantramārga. The place of tantrism 
generally, partly because of recent curiosity in the West and because a voluminous 
Sanskrit literature of tantric texts has been transmitted that were the realm of a great 
deal of speculative and esoteric lucubration, may well have been exaggerated at the 
expense of other religious traditions. One useful corrective, arguably, is provided by 
the long-​neglected literature of the Śivadharma corpus, notably what appear to be the 
two earliest texts, the Śivadharmaśāstra and the Śivadharmottara. These two relatively 
staid nontantric Sanskrit treatises of the seventh century encourage pious religious

--- PAGE 1073 ---
1048      Dominic Goodall
 
activity—​foundations, calendrical festivals, copying and keeping religious literature 
(see De Simini 2016)—​under the active patronage of kings and the wealthy. The suc­
cess of the Śivadharma, according to Bisschop (2018a), is to be attributed in part to its 
formulation of a ritual for invoking a pantheon of Śaiva-​aligned deities to promote 
peace (the sixth or śānti-​adhyāya of the Śivadharmaśāstra). Otherwise, these treatises 
appear to promote no groundbreaking doctrines, no radically unfamiliar spiritual 
path, and no paradigm shifts, but instead describe what must surely long have better 
reflected the religiosity of a much larger swathe of people than, for instance, the trans­
gressive Picumata-​Brahmayāmala, with its scatological eschatology (see Hatley 2018 
and Kiss 2015); the Tantrarājatantra and Svacchandatantra, with their complex initia­
tory rites based around an intricate cosmography; the grimoires of sexual or charnel-​
ground rituals aimed at the acquisition of supernatural powers and pleasures that 
we find in, for instance, the Guhyasūtra of the Niśvāsa and in the Vīṇāśikhatantra 
(Goudriaan 1985); or the Saiddhāntika Mṛgendratantra, with its dense, ordered, and 
carefully worded presentation of the theological niceties of Śaiva soteriology37 (or, for 
that matter, than the priestly South Indian Temple Āgamas). In short, all such var­
ious tantric works would probably have been the concern of only a small number of 
individuals at any one time.
The evidence of the Tēvāram and the Śivadharmaśāstra, which document popular de­
votional practices not specific to particular theological schools, underline that festivals, 
temple worship, and other socioreligious phenomena that have come to be associated 
with the Śaivasiddhānta in fact pre-​date the Mantramārga, whose earliest works are in­
stead tightly focused on the individual salvation (mukti) of the sādhaka and his quest for 
special powers (bhukti).
Besides such nontantric sources, for a rounded history of the Śaiva Mantramārga one 
should of course also take into consideration the evidence furnished by non-​Śaiva tan­
tric works. It is clear that Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava tantric systems were not only evolving 
in parallel, but also there was considerable mutual influence between them. Goodall 
and Isaacson (2016) have pointed out shared notions and terminology in the earliest 
surviving texts of these three traditions, for instance, building on Sanderson’s obser­
vation (2001, 38, fn. 50) that “the ritual systems taught in the Śaiva and Pāñcarātrika 
Saṃhitās resemble each other so closely that they have the appearance of two dialects 
of a single ‘Tantric’ language,” as well as on a similar observation of Strickmann (1996, 
24) concerning Śaivism and Buddhism.38 The shared evolution of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava 
(Pāñcarātra) ritual just in the realm of visualization has been demonstrated for their 
“thrones of worship” (Goodall 2011), but a large pool of distinctive shared vocabulary 
for all manner of ritual objects and concepts, particularly in the post-​twelfth-​century 
period of the later scriptures of the Pāñcarātra and the South Indian Śaiva Temple 
Āgamas, is at once evident from perusing any part of the Vienna dictionary of tantric 
terminology.39
This sketch of how we might reconstruct the history of the Śaiva Mantramārga has fo­
cused on the Śaivasiddhānta of the first millennium because we know that this lay at the 
heart of the Śaiva tantric traditions and that the texts that came to be regarded as forming

--- PAGE 1074 ---
Śaiva Tantra      1049
 
its canon constitute a common source (sāmānyaśāstra), a shared doctrinal basis, on 
which other Śaiva schools built. Reflecting the view that doctrinal developments may be 
better understood in tandem with the social background against which they emerge, I 
have tried here to contextualize the evolution of the Śaivasiddhānta with such evidence 
from social history as can be inferred.
