Chapter 41
On the Chronology of 
the Buddhist Tantras
Tsunehiko Sugiki
Introduction
The early medieval age in South Asia1 witnessed the composition of a large number of 
Buddhist tantras, that is, scriptures in Sanskrit and Apabhraṃśa, belonging to tantric 
traditions in Buddhism. Before discussing the chronology of Buddhist tantras, it is nec­
essary to define what the tantra indicates. I use the concept of tantra as an analytical tool 
to define the scope of the research, and that concept must be inherent in the texts in early 
medieval South Asia. From this perspective, it seems best to use the definition proposed 
by Issacson and Sferra, namely, “tantras are defined as scriptures that label themselves 
tantras or that have come to be classified as such by Indian Buddhist authors, starting 
from at the latest about the eighth century CE, even though some of those scriptures no 
doubt were not originally conceived of as tantras”2 (Issacson and Sferra 2015b: 307). My 
analysis of the chronology of Buddhist tantras begins with the Subāhuparipṛcchā and 
several others composed in the sixth or seventh century. Considering the large number 
of tantras, it is impossible to discuss the dates of all of them. However, based on my anal­
ysis and previous studies in recent decades, I wish to cover as many important tantras as 
possible to offer a comprehensive overview of the history of Buddhist tantras. Perhaps 
there is no publication on the chronology of Buddhist tantras that, based on recent re­
search findings, covers more tantras. The “Conclusion” to this chapter presents some 
perspectives for studying the history of Tantric Buddhism in South Asia. I hope that this 
chapter helps students who study the history of Buddhist tantras and serves as material 
for further discussion.
Generally, it is difficult to clarify the precise date of the composition of scriptures in 
South Asia. Buddhist tantras are no exception. This is primarily due to the lack of his­
torical sources, such as inscriptions, and the lack of a sense of historicity in the tantras’

--- PAGE 1083 ---
1058      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
compilers. The compilers are anonymous; they interpret tantras as teachings of timeless 
truth. However, it is possible to determine the approximate time of origin by examining 
the dates of production of the oldest Sanskrit manuscripts of the tantras noted in their 
colophons, the dates of the translators who translated the tantras into Chinese or 
Tibetan, and the references and quotations of the tantras. Different tantras often have 
similar discourses. Comparing similar discourses is also an effective means to clarify 
which tantra was composed earlier.
This study focuses on chronology. I do not examine the places where the tantras were 
compiled, except in some cases where the place of compilation is important to under­
stand the chronology. I do not deal with the concealed root-​tantras (mūlatantra), from 
which the existing tantras often define themselves as having been extracted for author­
ization, because most or all of such root-​tantras are imaginary and do not exist. The 
classifications of tantras are also left undiscussed, such as the classification into kriyā 
and yoga, with which the Indo-​Tibetan exegetical tradition often explains the nature of 
the tantras. These classifications only roughly correspond to the actual chronology of 
the tantras.
Dates of Compilations of the 
Buddhist Tantras
This section analyzes the approximate dates of Buddhist tantras. The tantras are 
listed in a tentative chronological order. However, the order is not chronological in 
part because I have grouped some of the tantras that belong to the same scriptural 
cycle and are closely related. (I have not grouped some of the tantras of the same 
scriptural cycle if the dates of their compilations differ greatly.) In the groups, they 
are listed in chronological order or Sanskrit alphabetical order if the chronological 
order is uncertain.
I have translated all tantras’ titles literally. I often refer to the following two works 
composed in relatively early centuries: Amoghavajra’s (不空金剛) Jingang ding jing 
yuqie shibahui zhigui (金剛頂經瑜伽十八會指歸: “Key Points of the 18 Sections 
of the Yoga of the Vajra Pinnacle Scripture,” T 869) and Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrā
rthāvalokinī (An Explanation of the Meaning of the Name-​mantras) (Tribe 2016: 3), 
a commentary on the Nāmasaṃgīti (Chanting of the Names). Amoghavajra com­
posed the Jingang ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui sometime between 746 and 771 
ce (Giebel 1995: 108–​109). According to Tribe, Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrārthāvalo-
kinī is datable between the second half of the eighth century and the early to mid-​
ninth century (Tribe 2016: 3). The tantras mentioned in the former and latter texts 
were most likely present in some form at the times when the two texts were written, 
respectively.3

--- PAGE 1084 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1059
 
The Guhya (Secret); the Subāhuparipṛcchā (Subāhu’s 
Inquiry); and the Susiddhikara (Bringing Good 
Accomplishment)
Sakai considered the date of compilation of the Guhya,4 the Subāhuparipṛcchā, and the 
Susiddhikara5 to be between the fifth and the mid-​sixth centuries (Sakai [1962] 1973: 
219), and recent scholars, such as Otsuka, dated it between the mid-​sixth and mid-​
seventh centuries before the appearance of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (mid-​seventh 
century) (Otsuka 2013: 731–​778).
The Tibetan translation of the Subāhuparipṛcchā (D 805/​P 428)6 contains treatises 
on antinomian rituals, such as the fire ritual using human flesh that is not included in 
the oldest Chinese translation (T 895) of Śubhākarasiṃha (善無畏) in the first half 
of the eighth century. In his commentary (D 2671/P 3496) on the Subāhuparipṛcchā, 
Buddhaguhya (late eighth century) comments on those antinomian discourses. They 
were incorporated in the Subāhuparipṛcchā by the late eighth century at the latest.
The Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka (Consecration of Vajrapāṇi)
Unlike the three scriptures mentioned above, the Lord in the Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka7 is Vairocana, 
who is also the Lord in the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi and Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. 
Sakai analyzed the date of composition of the Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka to be the early sev­
enth century, after the Guhya, the Subāhuparipṛcchā, and the Susiddhikara and before the 
Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (Sakai [1962] 1973: 219). Otsuka locates the date of composition of the 
Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka roughly in the same centuries when the Guhya, the Subāhuparipṛcchā, 
and the Susiddhikara were composed, namely between the mid-​sixth and the mid-​seventh 
centuries before the appearance of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (Otsuka 2013: 731–​778).
The Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (The Awakening of Vairocana)
Various views have been presented on the date of composition of the 
Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi, such as the mid-​seventh century (Sakai [1962] 1973: 219; 
Matsunaga 1980: 172–​174; Hodge 2003: 11, 14) and the mid-​sixth century (Wayman and 
Tajima 1992: 10). Now, it is almost a common notion among modern scholars that the 
Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi was probably compiled in the middle of the seventh century 
(Yamamoto 2012: 88; Kano 2015: 382). Hodge analyzed it as follows (Hodge 2003: 4–​
14): A Chinese monk Wuxing (無行) had been in India for eight years until he died in 
674 ce. He had gathered Sanskrit manuscripts of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi in India. 
Śubhākarasiṃha and Yixing (一行) found one of them in Hua-​yan Temple in Chang-​
an, and they translated it into Chinese (T 848) in 724 ce. Taking into account some

--- PAGE 1085 ---
1060      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
evidences from Chinese sources regarding the popularity of Tantric practices in India 
at that time, it is most likely that the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi was compiled or gained 
acceptance around the middle of the seventh century, perhaps around 640 ce or a little 
earlier, shortly before Wuxing arrived in India.
The Trisamayarāja (the Triple Pledge King)
The Trisamayarāja is mentioned and cited in Śāntideva’s Śikṣāsamuccaya (Bendall and 
Rouse 1922: 136, 168–​169, 264). The Śikṣāsamuccaya was composed around the first half of 
the eighth century, which is the terminus ante quem of the existence of the Trisamayarāja 
in some form. Trisamayarāja cannot be found in the Chinese Canon. However, it includes 
the two texts (T1199 and T1200) related to that scripture, which were translated by 
Amoghavajra in the eighth century. Sakai pointed out a possibility that the Trisamayarāja 
is older than the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi mentioned earlier.  The Trisamayarāja was one 
of the sources of the Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi (Sakai [1962] 1973: 221; Hodge 2003: 9).
The Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa (Mañjuśrī’s Root Ritual-​Practice)
Using the available Sanskrit manuscripts, Delhey analyzed the title to be originally 
Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa and not Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa (Delhey 2012: 70–​71). The compila­
tion date was obscure. The extant version of the Sanskrit Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa consists 
of fifty-​five chapters. Chapter 9 was in existence in some form before 702 ce. There are 
several Chinese translations of Mañśriyamūlakalpa. The two oldest translations (T 1181 
and T 1182) were produced in 702 and 703 ce, respectively (Matsunaga 1980: 322, and 1985: 
888f). These are translations of ­chapter 9. However, they are not entirely identical to the 
chapter found in the extant Sanskrit version (Delhey 2012: 59). Chapter 53 cannot be earlier 
than the late eighth century because it mentions King Gopāla (750–​775) (Sanderson 
2009: 129, n. 300). The Chinese translation, consisting of twenty-​eight chapters (T 1191), 
was produced by Tianxizai (天息災) in the tenth century ce. The Tibetan translation, 
comprising thirty-​six chapters (D 543/​P 162), was produced by Kumārakalaśa and Śākya 
blo gros in the eleventh century (Delhey 2012: 59). It is the best way to understand that the 
Mañjuśriyamūlakalpa was gradually enlarged and compiled into the extant Sanskrit ver­
sion by different authors over several centuries (Isaacson and Sferra 2015b: 315).
The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (Compendium of 
Truth of All Tathāgatas)
Sakai considered the date of the compilation of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha to 
be the early eighth century (Sakai [1962] 1973: 220). Matsunaga analyzed it as follows 
(Matsunaga 1980: 194–​196): the shorter version of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha,

--- PAGE 1086 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1061
 
which contained only the discourses on the mandala of the vajra-​quality 
(vajradhātumaṇḍala), was translated into Chinese (T 865) by Amoghavajra in 753–​
754 ce. Before that, in 723 ce, Vajrabodhi (金剛智) translated into Chinese a ritual 
manual (T 866) that was written in India based on the shorter or an older version of 
the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. According to the Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu 
(貞元新定釈教目録) (T 2157), a catalog of Buddhist scriptures composed by Yuanzhao 
(圓照), Nāgabodhi (龍智) taught the Vajra Pinnacle Yoga Scripture (金剛頂瑜伽経), 
which was perhaps the older version of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, and gave an 
initiation based on its system (the five-​lineage system) to Vajrabodhi in 700 ce.
The extant Sanskrit Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha is the longer version, corre­
sponding to the Chinese translation (T 882) by Dānapāla (施護) in the early elev­
enth century and the Tibetan translation (D 479/​P 112) of Śraddhākaravarman 
and Rin chen bzang po from the eleventh century. Buddhaguhya (late eighth cen­
tury) composed the Tantrārthāvatāra, a commentary on the longer version of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (D 2501/​P 3324).
From these sources, Matsunaga concludes that the shorter version of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, or the version older than that, which Vajrabodhi 
learned, was in existence in the late seventh century. The longer version of the 
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha was composed before the end of the eighth century.
The Guhyamaṇitilaka: (Secret Gem Ornament)
The Guhyamaṇitilaka is related to the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgaha. Guhyamaṇitilaka 
is also referred to in Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī (Tribe 2016: 376–​379). 
According to Tokushige, the eleventh section of the Vajra Pinnacle Scripture mentioned 
in Amoghavajra’s Jingang ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui possibly indicates the 
Guhyamaṇitilaka, and from its instruction on the deity yoga, the Guhyamaṇitilaka can 
be dated between the second half of the seventh century and the early eighth century 
(Tokushige 2019: 194, n. 1, n. 8). The Tibetan translation of the Guhyamaṇitilaka (D 493/​
P 125), which is the only available text of this scripture, was produced by Sugataśrī and Kun 
dga’ rgyal mtshan in the thirteenth century. This is the terminus ante quem of the entire text.
The Bhūtaḍāmara (Tamer of Spirits)
The Dharmachakra Translation Committee (DhTC) summarizes the teachings in the 
Bhūtaḍāmara as ritual practices that are intended to give the practitioner dominion over 
worldly gods and spirits (DhTC 2020b). Bhattacharyya found that the Bhūtaḍāmara 
was composed in the early seventh century before the Śaiva version of the Bhūtaḍāmara 
(Bhattacharyya 1933: 356). Fujii notes that the compilation of the Bhūtaḍāmara can be 
dated from the 7th to 8th centuries, and points out that the terminus ante quem of its en­
tire text is the tenth century (994 CE), when Fatian (法天) translated it into Chinese (T

--- PAGE 1087 ---
1062      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
1129) (Fujii 2018: 158 and 161, note 1). According to DhTC, ­chapter 8 teaches a visualiza­
tion of Lord Bhūtaḍāmara which contains most of the elements of deity yoga, features of 
the so-​called Yogatantra scriptural class. The Bhūtaḍāmara is mentioned in Vilāsavajra’s 
Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī (Tribe 2016: 376–​379). Based on these two points, DhTC 
assumes that the Bhūtaḍāmara was composed sometime between the seventh and 
eighth centuries (DhTC 2020b).
The Nāmasaṃgīti (Chanting of the Names)
The “Names” in the title of the Nāmasaṃgīti indicate the names of Mañjuśrī. According 
to Tribe, Mañjuśrī is not the personal bodhisattva but the gnosis being (jñānasattva), “an 
entity underlying the very nature of buddhahood.” The “Names” in the title are largely 
articulations of the “myriad ways that gnosis can manifest” (Tribe 2015: 353). Davidson 
found that the Nāmasaṃgīti was composed in the first half of the eighth century. The 
earliest commentator, Mañjuśrīmitra, was from the middle of the eighth century. He 
probably taught Vilāsavajra (Davidson 1981: 5).
The Trailokyavijaya (Conquest of the Triple World); the 
Vajraśekhara (Vajra Pinnacle); and the Sarvarahasya 
(All Secrets)
These tantras, which are closely related to the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgaha, were prob­
ably composed in the eighth century, no earlier than the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃ- 
gaha. The Trailokyavijaya and the Vajraśekhara are mentioned in Amoghavajra’s Jingang 
ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui (Giebel 1995: 111–​112) and Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrārthā
valokinī (Tribe 2016: 376–​379). The Vajraśekhara is frequently cited in Buddhaguhya’s 
Tantrārthāvatāra from the late eighth century (Kitamura 2012: iii, x). The Sarvarahasya 
is quoted in Āryadeva’s Sūtakamelāpaka (Caryāmelāpakapradīpa) (Wedemeyer 2007: 
364, 460) and Candrakīrti’s Vajsasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (Luo and Tomabechi 2009: 24–​
25). According to Isaacson and Sferra, Āryadeva and Candrakīrti flourished in the ninth 
and perhaps tenth centuries, respectively (Isaacson and Sferra 2015a: 476, 2015b: 308). 
From its contents, Wayman considered the Sarvarahasya to have been composed in the 
eighth century (Wayman 1984: 521).
The Sarvadurgatipariśodhana (Complete Purification of 
All Misfortunes)
The Sarvadurgatipariśodhana is closely related to the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgaha. 
The Tibetan Canon includes two versions of Sarvadurgatipariśodhana. Version (1)

--- PAGE 1088 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1063
 
(D 483/​P 116), the old version, was translated into Tibetan in the late eighth century by 
Indian Śāntigarbha and Tibetan Jayarakṣita during the reign of King Khri srong lde brtsan 
(740–​c. 798 ce). Buddhaguhya (late eighth century) composed a commentary on version 
(1). Therefore, it is likely that version (1) already existed in the middle of the eighth cen­
tury. Version (2) (D 485/​P 117), which corresponds to the available Sanskrit version of the 
Sarvadurgatipariśodhana, was translated into Tibetan in the first half of the thirteenth 
century by Devendradeva, Māṇikaśrījñāna, and Chos rje dpal (Skorupski 1983: xvii–​
xviii, xxiv). The Triple Meditation (trisamādhi) section of version (2) seems to have been 
influenced by the triple meditation and other systems of Ānandagarbha (ninth century). 
Version (2) was compiled sometime between the ninth and early thirteenth centuries.
The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā (Perfection of 
Wisdom in 150 Verses)
The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā originated from the scriptural tradition of 
the Prajñāpāramitā-​sūtras. Tomabechi calls the scriptural cycle to which this scrip­
ture belongs the “Paramādya cycle” (Tomabechi 2010: xii). A distinguishing feature of 
this scripture, and the Paramādya cycle as a whole, is the purity (viśuddhi) of sensual 
pleasure, expressed as X-​viśuddhipadam etad, yad uta bodhisattvapadam (The state of 
purity of X, it is indeed the state of Bodhisattva) (Tomabechi 2010: lviii–​lix).
The Chinese Canon includes five Chinese translations of this scripture: the versions 
translated by Xuanzang (玄奘: 660–​663 ce), Bodhiruci (菩提流志: 693 ce), Vajrabodhi 
(first half of eighth century), Amoghavajra (sometime between 763 and 771 ce), and 
Dānapāla (980 ce) (T 220, 240, 241, 243, and 242, respectively). The oldest translation 
by Xuanzang in the mid-​seventh century is a version of the pre-​Tantric stage. The trans­
lation of Amoghavajra in the mid-​eighth century, which is Tantric, is most similar to 
the Sanskrit text and the Tibetan translation (D 489/​P 121, where no translator’s name is 
given) (Tomabechi 2010: xi–​l).
The Paramādya (The Best and First)
The Paramādya (or Śrīparamādya), which belongs to the Paramādya cycle, is an ex­
panded version of the Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā. The former scripture contains 
many discourses on ritual actions and meditations that are more detailed than the latter 
scripture. The Paramādya is referred to or quoted in the several texts composed in the 
mid-​eighth to ninth century such as Amoghavajra’s Jingang ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui 
(Giebel 1995: 111–​112), Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī (Tribe 2016: 376–​379), 
and Āryadeva’s Sūtakamelāpaka (Tomabechi 2010: li–​lii; Wedemeyer 2007: 463–​464, 
466). The Paramādya was translated into Chinese (T 244) by Faxian (法賢 once called 
Tianxizai) in the tenth century (Tomabechi 2010: li), which is the terminus ante quem of 
the basic part of its entire text.

--- PAGE 1089 ---
1064      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
The Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra (Vajra Essence Adornment) 
Also Called Vajramaṇḍalālaṃkāra (Vajra Mandala 
Adornment)
The Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra is another expanded version of the Adhyardhaśatikā 
Prajñāpāramitā (Tomabechi 2010: lii–​liii). It belongs to the Paramādya cycle. In his 
Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī, Vilāsavajra mentions the Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra (Tribe 2016: 
376–​379). Tanaka examined various aspects of the Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra and found that 
it was composed in the second half of the eighth century (Tanaka 2007: 211–​213).
The Guhyendutilaka (Secret Moon Ornament)
The Guhyendutilaka8 is mentioned in Vilāsavajra’s Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī (Tribe 
2016: 376–​379). It was present in some form toward the end of the eighth century. The 
Guhyedutilaka is also cited in several other works composed after the ninth century, 
such as some works of the Guhyasamāja school and Abhayākaragupta’s Āmnāyamañjarī 
(Tomabechi 2017: 112). Despite its popularity, the scripture’s teachings and features have 
been insufficiently researched.
The Māyājāla (Illusionary Net)
Matsunaga pointed out that there were roughly two versions of the Māyājāla. The 
old version was used for the new Tibetan translation (D 466/​P 102) of Rin chen 
bzang po in the eleventh century, and the new version was used for the old Tibetan 
translation (D 833/​P 456) by Vimalamitra and Jñānakumāra in the eighth to ninth 
centuries. The old version of the Māyājāla was composed sometime between the 
appearances of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and the Guhyasamāja. The new 
version of the Māyājāla was produced after the Guhyasamāja was composed and 
before Vimalamitra and Jñānakumāra translated it into Tibetan (Matsunaga 1980: 
240–​244).
The Guhyasamāja (Secret Community)
The Guhyasamāja is the first major tantra in which elements of esoteric eroticism be­
come conspicuous, such as the Buddha or Blessed One preaching scripture in women’s 
vaginas, male deities copulating with their consorts, and the sacramental consumption 
of sexual substances (Tanemura 2015: 326). Several scholars have discussed the date of 
composition of the Guhyasamāja, such as Farquhar (who places the date of composition

--- PAGE 1090 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1065
 
to be the early seventh century), Bhattacharyya (no later than the fourth century), Sakai 
(second half of the eighth century), Wayman (fourth century), Tucci (between the sev­
enth and early eighth centuries), and Hadano (no later than the end of the eighth cen­
tury ce).9
Matsunaga notes that the basic text of the extant version of the Guhyasamāja 
was composed toward the end of the eighth century, particularly in the second 
half of the eighth century. He analyzed it as follows (Matsunaga 1980: 249–​258): (1) 
Amoghavajra’s summary of the Pimijihui yuqie (祕密集會瑜伽, *Guhyasamājayoga), 
the fifteenth section of the Vajra Pinnacle Scripture, corresponds to the contents of 
­chapter 15 of the extant version of the Guhyasamāja. A discourse that Amoghavajra 
referred to as Guhyasamājayoga existed in the mid-​eighth century, and it may have 
been a prototype text from which the tantra titled Guhyasamāja was developed. (2) 
Buddhaśrījñāna, also called Jñānapāda (second half of the eighth century), founded 
a school (the Jñānapāda school) of Guhyasamāja. From comparison with the texts 
attributed to Jñānapāda, it is most likely that the extant version of the Guhyasamāja 
was gradually compiled in the second half of the eighth century. However, according 
to Szántó, Jñānapāda was active in the late eighth to early ninth centuries (c. 770–​820) 
(Szántó 2019: 264).
The extant version of Guhyasamāja consists of eighteen chapters. Matsunaga 
sets forth how the individual chapters of the Guhyasamāja were composed: the 
Guhyasamāja can be divided into three parts: (1) ­chapters 1–​12, (2) ­chapters 13–​17, and 
(3) ­chapter 18. First, ­chapters 1–​12, which contain the elementary discourses of the 
Guhyasamāja and form the oldest part of this tantra, was composed. Next, ­chapters 
13–​17, which are more extensive and contain more teachings on rituals, were compiled. 
Finally, ­chapter 18, which summarizes the discourses in ­chapters 1–​12, was composed 
and added. All these developments took place in the second half of the eighth century 
(Matsunaga 1980: 235–​240).
The Indo-​Tibetan exegetical tradition considers the first seventeen chapters as the 
“root-​tantra” (mūlatantra) and ­chapter 18 as the “continuation tantra” (uttaratantra) 
(Tanemura 2015: 326). The first seventeen chapters and ­chapter 18 are also often called 
Samāja ([Secret] Community) and Samājottara (Continuation of the Samāja or 
Community), respectively.
The Advayasamatāvijaya (Victory of Nondual Equality)
Often regarded as belonging to the Guhyasamāja scriptural cycle, the Advayasamatāvijaya 
was already present in some form in the second half of the eighth century. It is referred to in 
Amoghavajra’s Jingang ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui (Giebel 1995: 111–​112) and Vilāsavajra’s 
Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī (Tribe 2016: 376–​379). Fan analyzed the Advayasamatāvijaya to 
have elements derived from both the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and the Guhyasamāja 
(Fan 2011: 353–​355).

--- PAGE 1091 ---
1066      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
The Sarvabuddhasamāyoga (Complete Union of 
All Buddhas) and the Sarvakalpasamuccaya 
(Compendium of All Rituals)
The Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara (or -​śaṃvara) (hereafter Sarvabuddha­
samāyoga) is the earliest among the major tantras that are generally classified by Indian exegetes 
as Yoginītantras. According to Szántó and Griffiths, Sarvabuddhasamāyoga is probably the 
first Buddhist tantra to use Apabhraṃśa verses (­chapters 6 and 9). It also explicitly introduced 
the practice of gaṇacakra or communal worship (Szántó and Griffiths 2015: 369–​370). Tanaka 
notes that ­chapters 1 and 9 of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga are mentioned in Amoghavajra’s 
Jingang ding jing yuqie shibahui zhigui (Tanaka 2010: 330–​332). Sanderson, Tanaka, and Szántó 
and Griffiths state that the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga existed in some form in the early eighth cen­
tury (Sanderson 2009: 145;Tanaka 2010: 332; Szántó and Griffiths 2015: 367).
The Tibetan translation of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga (D 366/​P 8) classifies itself as the 
uttaratantra (continuation tantra) of the imaginary root-​tantra. The Tibetan translation 
of the Sarvakalpasamuccaya (D 367/​P 9), which is currently the only available text of this 
tantra, classifies itself as *uttarottaratantra (a tantra that is the continuation of the contin­
uation), namely a tantra that is the continuation of the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga. The main 
theme in the Sarvakalpasamuccaya is the encoding of the mantras used in this scriptural 
tradition. According to Tomabechi, the encoding system in the Sarvakalpasamuccaya 
is closely related to that found in the Śaiva Vīṇāśikha-​ or Vīṇāśikhā-​tantra (Tomabechi 
2007). The compilation of the Sarvakalpasamuccaya can be dated after the appearance of 
the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga (eighth century) and before Ānandagarbha (ninth century), 
who wrote a commentary (D 1662/​P 2534) on the former tantra.
In many works, the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga is referred to as Saṃvara (equiva­
lent to Śaṃvara, “Supreme Bliss”), and the Sarvakalpasamuccaya, as Saṃvarottara 
(Continuation of the Saṃvara).
The Vajrabhairava (Vajra Terror)
Vajrabhairava is another name of Yamāntaka (Ender of Yama), who dominates Yama, 
the Brahmanical god ruling the underworld and presiding over death (Siklós 1996: 3). 
Sanderson pointed out that the Vajrabhairava was referred to in Vilāsavajra’s Nāmama-
ntrārthāvalokinī. The Vajrabhairava was present in some form by the time Vilāsavajra 
flourished (Sanderson 2009: 146, n. 337; Tribe 2016: 376–​379).
The Kṛṣṇayamāri (Black Yamāri) and the Raktayamāri 
(Red Yamāri)
Yamāri (Enemy of Yama) is another name of Yamāntaka. Yamāri takes two forms: 
Kṛṣṇayamāri (Black Yamāri) and Raktayamāri (Red Yamāri). In Tibetan, Kṛṣṇayamāri,

--- PAGE 1092 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1067
 
Raktayamāri, and Vajrabhairava are collectively referred to as the “triad of Red, Black, 
and Terror” (dmar nag ‘jigs gsum) (Kuranishi 2004: 61). The Kṛṣṇayamāri was translated 
into Tibetan (D 467/​P 103) by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and Tshul khrims rgyal ba in the 
first half of the eleventh century, and the Raktayamāri (D 474/​P 109), by Candrakīrti, 
Candraśrī, and Grags pa rgyal mtshan toward the end of the twelfth century. These are 
the terminus ante quems of the two tantras. Kuranishi states that the Kṛṣṇayamāri was 
composed sometime between the ninth and tenth centuries under the strong influence 
of the Guhyasamāja (Kuranishi forthcoming: 1). The Raktayamāri is a revision of the 
Kṛṣṇayamāri (Kuranishi 2004: 61–​65, forthcoming: 8).
The Sandhyāvyākaraṇa (Explanation of the Intention); 
the Caturdevīparipṛcchā (The Four Goddesses’ Inquiry); 
the Vajramālā (Vajra Rosary); the Jñānavajrasamuccaya 
(Gnosis Vajra Compendium) and its longer version; and 
the Vajrahṛdayālaṃkāra (Vajra Heart Adornment)
The six tantras presented here are referred to as “commentary tantra” (vyākhyātantra), 
that is, tantras that are commentaries on the Guhyasamāja. The concept of “commen­
tary tantra” was probably first developed in the Guhyasamāja tradition (Isaacson and 
Sferra 2015b: 310).
These six tantras, which are a part of the Guhyasamāja cycle, were written over sev­
eral centuries, beginning around the ninth century. The Sandhyāvyākaraṇa may 
be one of the earliest among them: It contains commentaries only on the first twelve 
chapters of the Guhyasamāja (viz., the oldest part of the Guhyasamāja) and is free from 
interpretations of any particular school (Matsunaga 1980: 236; Tanemura 2015: 326). The 
six tantras were translated into Tibetan in the eleventh century,10 which is the terminus 
ante quem of the final versions of the entire texts. The Guhyasamāja schools developed 
practices that were not explicitly taught in Guhyasamāja. They composed these tantras 
to authorize these practices, and the works of the Guhyasamāja schools were composed 
according to these tantras (Matsunaga 1980: 311; Wedemeyer 2007: 46–​48; Tanemura 
2015: 328).11 The relation to other scriptural cycles is also important. For example, the 
Vajramālā12 contains discourses similar to those in the Mahāmudrātilaka, a relatively 
late tantra belonging to the Hevajra cycle. The discourse on internal fire ritual in the 
Vajramālā (­chapter 60) is a version that seems to have been developed from the ver­
sion of the discourse on the same subject included in the Mahāmudrātilaka (­chapter 11) 
(Sugiki 2016: 172–​181).
The Catuṣpīṭha (Four Chapters)
The Catuṣpīṭha is one of the early Yoginītantras. According to Szántó, it is perhaps 
the second earliest Yoginītantra to use Apabhraṃśa verses. Among Buddhist texts,

--- PAGE 1093 ---
1068      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
Jñānapāda’s Mukhāgama is the first to mention the practice of utkrāntiyoga, or yogic 
suicide. The Catuṣpīṭha is the first tantra to teach this in detail (Szántó 2015a: 320, 323, 
325). Szántó places the probable date of origin of the Catuṣpīṭha in the late ninth cen­
tury. The Catuṣpīṭha and its passages are cited or borrowed in some texts composed in 
the tenth century, such as the Dunhuang manuscript (Pelliot tibétain 849), Jayabhadra’s 
Cakrasaṃvarapañjikā, the Vajraḍāka, and the Sampuṭodbhava (Szántó 2012, vol. 1: 35–​
54) (Szántó 2015a: 320).
The Vajrāmṛta (Vajra Nectar)
The Vajrāmṛta is also an early Yoginītantra. Omi estimates that the Vajrāmṛta was com­
posed sometime between the ninth and eleventh centuries, after the Guhyasamāja 
(or Mahāmāyā) was composed and before Candrakīrti (perhaps tenth century) and 
Ratnākaraśānti (first half of the eleventh century)13 quoted the Vajrāmṛta (Omi 2013: 
35–​36). According to Sferra, the Vajrāmṛta was probably composed sometime be­
tween the end of the ninth century and the beginning of the tenth century. Candrakīrti’s 
Pradīpoddyotana is perhaps the earliest source that cites the Vajrāmṛta (Sferra 2017: 
409–​411).
The Mahāmāyā (Great Illusion)
Omi locates the compilation of the Mahāmāyā between the eighth and eleventh 
centuries, that is, between the periods when the Śākta Devīmāhātmya (which includes 
similar expressions) was compiled and when Ratnākaraśānti wrote the Guṇavatī, a com­
mentary on the Mahāmāyā (Omi 2005: 100–​102). Szántó points out that the Mahāmāyā 
is silently quoted by Bhavabhaṭṭa in his Nibandha commentary on the Catuṣpīṭha 
(Szántó 2012: 102).14 DhTC states that the Mahāmāyā was composed in the late ninth or 
early tenth centuries (DhTC 2013).
The Cakrasaṃvara (Circle’s Saṃvara) Also Called 
Herukābhidhāna (Discourse of Heruka), Laghusaṃvara 
(Small Saṃvara), or Laghvabhidhāna (Small Discourse)
Sanderson pointed out that the Cakrasaṃvara contains many discourses that were 
redactions from the tantras of the Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha cycle, such as the discourse of 
the sacred sites (Sanderson 1995; etc.). The Cakrasaṃvara refers to the titles of some 
tantras, namely, the Paramādya, the Vajrabhairava, the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, 
the Guhyasamāja, and the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga. In his Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī, 
Vilāsavajra mentions an early version of the Cakrasaṃvara or another text that he calls

--- PAGE 1094 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1069
 
Cakrasaṃvara. Davidson estimates the date of origin of the Cakrasaṃvara to be in the 
eighth century (Davidson 1981: 7–​8, 2004: 40; Gray 2007: 11–​14), and Sanderson in the 
relatively late ninth century (Sanderson 2009: 158–​165; Gray 2012: 3–​19).
The extant version of the Cakrasaṃvara consists of fifty-​one chapters, which can be 
roughly divided into two parts: (1) ­chapters 1 to 49 and the first half of ­chapter 50 (–​50.18) 
and (2) the second half of ­chapter 50 (50.19–​) and ­chapter 51. The first part is the ancient 
part of the tantra. Jayabhadra, the earliest exegete, and Bhavyakīrti used some forms of 
the old version (Sugiki 2001: 91–​99, summarized in English in 2010: 509–​510; Sanderson 
2009: 159–​160). The latter part was added to the old part by the time in the tenth century 
when some exegetes, such as Bhavabhaṭṭa, wrote commentaries on the whole fifty-​one 
chapters of the Cakrasaṃvara.
The Hevajra (Hevajra)
A highly influential Yoginītantra, the Hevajra was the first scripture to set forth the 
teachings of the innate (sahaja), the fourfold joy (caturānanda), the subtle-​body system 
centered on the four chakras (cakra), the three main channels (avadhūtī, lalanā, and 
rasanā), and the inner fire called Caṇḍālī. The Hevajra consists of two parts (kalpa) 
called “the awakening of Vajragarbha” (vajragarbhābhisambodhi) and “illusion” (māyā). 
Therefore, the Hevajra is also called Dvikalparāja or “the king [of tantras] in two parts” 
(Szántó 2015b: 334–​335, 339).
Snellgrove believed that the present form of the Hevajra existed toward the end of the 
eighth century because, according to Tāranātha, Kāṇha, who wrote the Yogaratnamālā 
commentary on the Hevajra, was a contemporary of Devapāla (first half of the ninth 
century) (Snellgrove 1959, vol. 1: 14). According to Isaacson, however, this Kāṇha 
or Kṛṣṇa, who is also called Samayavajra or Śāntibhadra, may have been a disciple of 
Ratnākaraśānti in the eleventh century (Isaacson 2001: 458). In his Yogaratnamālā, 
Kāṇha cites the Buddhakapāla (Luo 2010: xxxiii). Davidson states that the Hevajra 
was probably composed in the late ninth or early tenth century (Davidson 2004: 41). 
The Hevajra was not attested in the texts before the tenth century (Isaacson and Sferra, 
2015b: 315).
The Ḍākinīvajrapañjara (Ḍākinī Vajra Cage)
The Ḍākinīvajrapañjara is perhaps the earliest and most influential among the tantras 
belonging to the Hevajra cycle (Szántó 2015b: 339). According to Shimada’s analysis, 
the Ḍākinīvajrapañjara was composed after the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga and before the 
Hevajra. The Ḍākinīvajrapañjara did not teach the fourth initiation ritual or the yoga 
of the subtle body, which the Hevajra expounds (Shimada 1983). Tanaka believed that 
the Ḍākinīvajrapañjara originated after the Hevajra (Tanaka 2010: 351–​352). Yokoyama 
notes that it is difficult to decide which of the Hevajra and the Ḍākinīvajrapañjara is

--- PAGE 1095 ---
1070      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
earlier through comparison of their texts, for both tantras were developed independ­
ently of each other (Yokoyama 2016: 111–​115). The terminus ante quem of its entire text is 
the first half of the eleventh century, when it was translated into Tibetan (D 419/​P 11) by 
Gayādhara and Shākya ye shes.
The Buddhakapāla (Skull of Buddha)
According to Luo, the Buddhakapāla, a Yoginītantra, was composed in the ninth or 
tenth century, and it was very popular in India in the eleventh and twelfth centuries (Luo 
2010: xxxi). It contained some material borrowed from the Guhyasamāja and Hevajra 
and is also influenced by Śaivism (Vidyāpīṭha Kāpālika). As mentioned earlier, the 
Buddhakapāla is cited in the Yogaratnamālā of Kāṇha (Luo 2010: xxxii–​xxxiii). Kāṇha 
was active in the ninth century according to Snellgrove (1959, vol. 1: 14) and the eleventh 
century according to Isaacson (2001: 458).
The Vajrāralli (Vajrāralli)
The scriptural cycle, which includes the Vajrāralli and the Rigyaralli, is often referred to 
as the “Aralli (Ārali) cycle.” The word ārali first appears in the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga 
in the sense of “ḍākinī,” and vajrāralli in the sense of “Vajrasattva.” In the Vajrāralli, the 
main deity is Heruka, who is also called Ārali (or Aralli). The Vajrāralli is mentioned 
in Nāropa’s commentary on the Hevajra, namely, the Vajrapadasārasaṃgrahapañjikā 
(eleventh century). From these sources, Omi concludes that Vajrāralli was composed 
between the ninth and eleventh centuries, after the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga and before 
Nāropa (Omi 2016: 127–​129). The Vajrāralli was translated into Tibetan (D 426/​P 65) by 
Gayādhara and Shākya ye shes in the eleventh century.
The Herukābhyudaya (Realization of Heruka); the 
Abhidhānottara (The Continuation of the Discourse); the 
Caturyoginīsampuṭa (The Union of the Four Yoginīs); the 
Yoginīsaṃcāra (Yoginīs’ Rotation); the Vajraḍāka (Vajraḍāka); 
and the Vārāhyabhyudaya (Realization of Vārāhī) and its 
uttaratantra (continuation tantra)
These tantras, which belong to the Saṃvara scriptural cycle (a scriptural cycle that 
emerged from the Cakrasaṃvara), were most likely composed around the tenth century 
after the old part of the Cakrasaṃvara was composed and before they were translated 
into Tibetan (eleventh century)15 (Sugiki 2007: 1–​17, 19; Sanderson 2009: 158). The 
Herukābhyudaya is perhaps the second oldest among them. Sanderson pointed out

--- PAGE 1096 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1071
 
that the Herukābhyudaya contains a passage that is more archaic than Cakrasaṃvara 
(Sanderson 2009: 213–​214). However, the Herukābhyudaya also contains the instruc­
tion of the root mantra of the goddess Vārāhī (D 374, 6v6–​7r5), which is not found in 
the earlier texts of the Saṃvara cycle. The list of scriptures in the Dunhuang manuscript 
(Pelliot tibétain 849: ll. 21–​37) toward the end of the third quarter of the tenth century 
includes a tantra that may be the Herukābhyudaya (He ru ka a pu tha tan tra or He ru ka 
thams cad ‘byung ba’i rgyud) (Kapstein 2006: 11–​12, 20, n 32).
The Sampuṭodbhava (Emergence from the Union) and the 
Sampuṭatilaka (Ornament of the Emergence from the Union)
The Sampuṭodbhava, often grouped with the Hevajra cycle in Tibetan exegesis, was 
composed around the tenth century, (1) after the appearance of the old part of the 
Cakrasaṃvara (late ninth century at the latest) and before Gayādhara and Śākya ye shes, 
who translated the Sampuṭodbhava into Tibetan (D 381/​P 26), or before Ratnākaraśānti, 
who quoted it in his Muktāvalī (first half of the eleventh century) (Sugiki 2007: 15–​17, 19; 
Szántó 2016: 403); (2) after the writing of the Hevajra (late ninth or early tenth century) 
and before the appearance of the Kālacakra (early eleventh century) (Szántó 2012, part 1: 
50–​51); or (3) after the writing of the Hevajra and possibly before Durjayacandra (around 
1000 ce), who probably quoted a passage from the Sampuṭodbhava (Szántó 2016: 402–​
403). DhTC dates the Sampuṭodhava to the end of the tenth century (DhTC 2020a).
According to Szántó, Sampuṭatilaka may be the first exegesis of the Sampuṭodbhava, 
and it was often transmitted together with the Sampuṭodbhava (Szántó 2016: 403). The 
compilation of the Sampuṭatilaka can be dated after the Sampuṭodbhava was composed 
(tenth century) and before Gayādhara and Śākya ye shes translated the former tantra 
into Tibetan (D 382/​P 27) (first half of the eleventh century).
The Mahākāla (Mahākāla)
According to Stablein, the oldest Sanskrit manuscript of the Mahākāla (Bihar Research 
Society in Patna, a photocopy of the original found by Rāhula Sāṅkrityāyana at the Ngor 
monastery) dates to 1135 ce during the reign of King Madanapāla (Stablein 1976: 84–​85). 
The Mahākāla was translated into Tibetan (D 440/​P 79) by Samantaśrī and Chos rab in 
the early to mid-​ eleventh century, which is its terminus ante quem.
The Kālacakra (Wheel of Time)
The Kālacakra, one of the most influential Buddhist tantras, was compiled in the early 
eleventh century. Traditionally, the Kālacakra is interpreted according to Puṇḍarīka’s 
Vimalaprabhā, a commentary on the Kālacakra. Taking into account the year referred

--- PAGE 1097 ---
1072      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
to in the Kālacakra and the year in which Nāropa, who cited the Kālacakra and the 
Vimalaprabhā, died, Newman estimates that the Kālacakra and the Vimalaprabhā were 
written between 1025 and around 1040 ce (Newman 1998: 343). The year referred to 
in the Kālacakra, according to Orofino and Wallace, is 1026 ce (Orofino 1994: 15–16; 
Wallace 2001: 3). Sferra attaches more importance to the fact that no citation from the 
Kālacakra can be found before the eleventh century (Sferra 2015: 341).
The Rigyaralli (Rigī and Aralli)
In the Rigyaralli, Rigi or Rigī is the main goddess or ḍākinī, equated with Mahāmāyā 
(Buddha’s mother), and so on, and Aralli (Ārali or Āralli), her male consort, defined 
as Śuddhodana (Buddha’s father), is the supplicant. The Rigyaralli uses ten categories 
of sacred sites, such as the pīṭha, which are derived from the ten categories of sacred 
sites inherent in the Saṃvara scriptural tradition. According to Omi, the Rigyaralli was 
composed after the Vajrāralli, and the terminus ante quem is the eleventh century when 
Nāropa cited the Rigyaralli in his Vajrapadasārasaṃgrahapañjikā (Omi 2016: 128–​129). 
Szántó notes that there is no evidence dating the Rigyaralli to any period earlier than 
the mid-​eleventh century. All authors who mentioned this tantra (such as Raviśrījñāna) 
were active between the mid-​eleventh and mid-​thirteenth centuries. The Rigyaralli was 
also translated into Tibetan (D 427/​P 66) by Gayādhara and Shākya ye shes in the elev­
enth century (Szántó 2017: 492–​495).
The Mahāmudrātilaka (Great Seal Ornament); the 
Jñānagarbha (Womb of Gnosis); the Jñānatilaka (Ornament 
of Gnosis); and the Tattvapradīpa (Light of Truth)
These tantras are also part of the Hevajra cycle. The terminus ante quem of their entire 
texts is the late eleventh century when they were translated into Tibetan in the presence 
of Prajñāśrīgupta or by him,16 who flourished in the late eleventh century (Szántó 2015c: 
5). In texts composed before Prajñāśrīgupta, there may be no evidence for the titles of 
these tantras.
It is only the Mahāmudrātilaka whose Sanskrit manuscript is extant (Staatsbibliothek 
zu Berlin no. Hs or 8711), although it is a recent manuscript, copied in the nineteenth 
century. The difference between the Sanskrit manuscript and the Tibetan transla­
tion of the Mahāmudrātilaka is not small. In ­chapter 28 of its Tibetan Translation, the 
Mahāmudrātilaka defines itself as a “continuation tantra” (rgyud phyi ma, *uttaratantra) 
(D 420, 90v5) of the imaginary root tantra. In its colophon, the Jñānagarbha is de­
fined as a tantra that is the continuation of the Mahāmudrātilaka (D 421, 96v6).17 The 
Jñānatilaka refers to the Mahāmudrātilaka and the Jñānagarbha as a continuation 
tantra and a tantra that is the continuation of the Mahāmudrātilaka, respectively, and

--- PAGE 1098 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1073
 
calls itself “a commentary tantra” (bshad pa’i rgyud, *vyākhyātantra) (D 422, 127v1–​v2). 
These suggest that the Mahāmudrātilaka is chronologically earliest among the three 
scriptures.
Szántó argues that the compilation of the Mahāmudrātilaka may be datable in the 
late eleventh century. The Mahāmudrātilaka includes many discourses of the subtle-​
body system that are more elaborate than those in Hevajra. It mentions the titles of the 
Guhyasamāja, Vajramālā, Saṃvara (Sarvabuddhasamāyoga), and Hevajra (Szántó 
2015c: 6, 9, 10). The Mahāmudrātilaka has discourses similar to those found in the 
Vajramālā (Sugiki 2016: 172–​181).
The Ḍākārṇava (Ocean of Ḍākas); the Saṃvarodaya 
(Emergence of Saṃvara); the Vārāhīkalpa (Ritual Practice 
of Vārāhī); and the Yoginījāla (Net of Yoginīs)
These tantras, which also belong to the Saṃvara cycle, share many similar discourses. 
They were composed in the last phase of the history of the Saṃvara cycle, probably after 
the Kālacakra. They contain several teachings that are more developed than those in 
the other tantras of the Saṃvara cycle discussed earlier. Either the Ḍākārṇava or the 
Saṃvarodaya is likely the earliest, and the Vārāhīkalpa and the Yoginījāla are the most 
recent (Sugiki 2007: 17–​19, 110–​113, 257–​282, 316–​330).
The Ḍākārṇava mentions the Vajraḍāka, Herukābhyudaya, and Sampuṭodbhava. 
Although an early version of the Ḍākārṇava or another text that was called Ḍākārṇava 
might have existed in the early eleventh century, the extant version of the Ḍākārṇava 
probably dates from around the early twelfth century. Padmavajra’s commentary on the 
Ḍākārṇava (D 1419/​P 2136), written in the early or mid-​twelfth century, is perhaps the 
first to cite passages taken from the extant version of the Dākārṇava. The Ḍākārṇava 
flourished in Nepal to a certain degree. It was translated into Tibetan (D 372/​P 19) by 
Jayasena (disciple of Padmavajra) and Dharma yon tan in the mid-​ to late twelfth cen­
tury in Kathmandu (Sugiki 2022: 9–​20). Based partially on these two tantras composed 
and/​or flourished in Nepal, the Vārāhīkalpa, and the closely related Yoginījāla, were 
developed. They were not translated into Tibetan (Sugiki 2007: 18; Sanderson 2009: 
177). Most likely the Vārāhīkalpa and the Yoginījāla were compiled in Nepal. Isaacson 
and Sferra note that the Saṃvarodaya was most likely composed in Nepal after the 
Kālacakra (Isaacson and Sferra 2015b: 315). According to the colophon of its Tibetan 
translation, the Saṃvarodaya was translated into Tibetan (D 373/​P 20) by Gzhan la phan 
pa mtha’ yas (Indian) and Rgyus ban de smon lam grags (Tibetan); their translation was 
finalized by Gzhon nu dpal (late fourteenth to fifteenth centuries), who used Vanaratna’s 
(mid-​fourteenth to mid-​fifteenth centuries) Sanskrit manuscript of this scripture. 
Ratnarakṣita, who composed the Padminī commentary on the Saṃvarodaya, was active 
around 1200 ce. After the downfall of Vikramaśīla in the beginning of the thirteenth 
century, Ratnarakṣita came to Nepal (Lewis 1996: 156).

--- PAGE 1099 ---
1074      Tsunehiko Sugiki
 
The Jñānodaya (Emergence of Gnosis)
The Jñānodaya, a short tantra, contains treatises on the yoga of the subtle body that are 
more developed than those found in the tantras of the Saṃvara cycle in the tenth century 
mentioned earlier. The Jñānodaya can also be assigned to the most recent group of tantras 
of the Saṃvara cycle. It is possible that the compilation of the Jñānodaya is no older than the 
Saṃvarodaya and the Ḍākārṇava. The Jñānodaya was composed in Nepal and not translated 
into Tibetan (Sugiki 2007: 17–​18, 170–​175, 257–​263) (Isaacson and Sferra 2015b: 316).
The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Fiery Great Wrathful One)
The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa is of Nepalese origin, most likely of Newar origin. In South 
Asia, the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa is not mentioned outside Nepal (DhTC 2016; Grimes and 
Szántó 2018: abstract). It teaches how to attain the state of Buddha Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa 
through the practice of fourfold joy, and so on (DhTC 2016). Van der Kuijp states that 
Ratnaśrī and Grags pa rgyal mtshan completed the translation of the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa 
into Tibetan (D 431/​P 70) in 1293 or, less likely, 1305 ce (Van der Kuijp 2009: 29). DhTC 
assumes that the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa was composed in the tenth or eleventh century 
(DhTC 2016). Grimes and Szántó point out that there is no certain textual evidence to 
show the existence of the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa before the thirteenth century (Grimes 
and Szántó 2018: 651). Mahāsukhavajra’s Padmāvatī is the only extant commentary. 
Mahāsukhavajra may have been a Nepalese scholar from the thirteenth century (Grimes 
and Szántó 2018: 653). It is uncertain whether the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa was composed 
later than the Vārāhīkalpa, Yoginījāla, and Jñānodaya.
Conclusion
Based on the discussion and overview of the approximate dates of the Buddhist tantras 
in the previous section, I would like to draw attention to three aspects.
First, toward and after the demise of the great monasteries in India in the twelfth and 
thirteenth centuries, Nepal became an important place where tantras were composed. 
This suggests that in India, the great monasteries played an important role in the writing 
of the tantras, including those teaching antinomian practices. The Mahāmudrātilaka 
and the Ḍākārṇava, whose final versions were probably completed in the eleventh and 
twelfth centuries, respectively, list Nepāla (Nepal) in their lists of sacred sites (Sugiki 
2009: 533, 540). Many studies have been conducted regarding Tantric Buddhism in 
India and Tibet. Tantric texts in Nepal should also be more researched attentively.
Second, the history of Buddhist tantras does not advance toward a single goal. It 
has often been said that the Kālacakra is the final tantra that integrates various tantric

--- PAGE 1100 ---
On the Chronology of the Buddhist Tantras      1075
 
traditions. However, it is almost certain that the Kālacakra is neither the final tantra 
nor the only comprehensive one that encompasses and integrates the previous systems. 
The view of diversity that runs through the history of the Buddhist tantras should be 
maintained, even though it can be said that the integrative system of the Kālacakra is the 
most sophisticated among those included in the last Buddhist tantras.
Third, when compiling individual tantras, the diversity of history of the scriptures 
should also be taken into account. Many Buddhist tantras are evolving texts; they were 
gradually compiled, enlarged, and organized by different compilers over decades or 
in some cases even centuries. In this process of compilation, compilers also took ideas 
and texts from other scriptures of the same or foreign traditions and integrated them 
into the scriptures they were working on. Therefore, the final version of a tantra often 
contains both ancient and new elements. It is also common that different versions of a 
tantra were developed separately by different groups of compilers. Although I have been 
able to do it only partially in this chapter, chronological study should also be intended 
to reveal as far as possible the complicated processes of growth and reproduction of the 
tantras mentioned above.

	16.	 The Mahāmudrātilaka was translated into Tibetan (D 420/​P 12) by Prajñāśrīgupta, Chos 
kyi ye shes, and Phyug ’tshams dgra bcom; the Jñānagarbha (D421/​P13) by Prajñāśrīgupta; 
the Jñānatilaka (D422/​P14) by Prajñāśrīgupta; and the Tattvapradīpa (D423/​P15) by 
Prajñāśrīgupta.
	17.	 The text is dpal phyag rgya chen po’i thig le rnal ’byor ma’ rgyud kyi rgyal po’i phyi ma’i 
phyi ma. Literally, it means “[a tantra that is] the continuation of the continuation of the 
Mahāmudrātilaka. However, its correct meaning seems to be [a tantra that is] the con­
tinuation of the continuation [tantra which is] the Mahāmudrātilaka, because the 
Mahāmudrātilaka (its Tibetan translation) defines itself as a continuation tantra.
