Chapter 42
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi 
as an Argument against 
Dharmakīrti
John Nemec
Introduction
It is well known that the Buddhist epistemologist Dharmakīrti figures centrally in 
the philosophical formulations of the nondual Śaiva tantric authors, Utpaladeva (fl. 
ca. 925–​975 CE) and Abhinavagupta (fl. ca. 975–​1025 CE). This chapter illustrates the 
manner in which the same Buddhist author served fundamentally to shape the writings 
of Utpaladeva’s teacher and Abhinavagupta’s great grand-​teacher, Somānanda (fl. ca. 
900–​950 CE). In particular, I here examine what may be found in key passages of his 
magnum opus, the first work of Pratyabhijñā philosophy and one of the earliest nondual 
Śaiva “postscriptural” work of exegesis, the Śivadṛṣṭi (ŚD).1 In particular, I here survey 
arguments found principally the fourth “daily lesson” (āhnika) of this complex, highly 
influential, but still little-​read work, the latter half for which Utpaladeva’s commentary 
is lost (i.e., after ŚD 4.75); and as Abhinavagupta’s Śivadṛṣṭyālocana is entirely lost to 
history, except for a very small number of citations in his Parātrīśikavivaraṇa, we are 
without commentarial resources for many of the textual passages in question. The work 
of interpreting the ŚD is therefore at times exceedingly difficult, though not impossible, 
to engage.
The fourth āhnika marks the point at which Somānanda begins not merely to argue 
against the views of other schools but positively to articulate his own philosophical po­
sition.2 He does so largely by arguing that his opponents’ views can only cohere logically 
if they accept the ontological nondualism for which he argues. And when Somānanda 
comes “positively” to articulate his Śaiva non-​dualism, he does so implicitly and explic­
itly in opposition to Dharmakīrti.3

--- PAGE 1109 ---
1084      John Nemec
 
Somānanda’s Siddhānta
If Somānanda is to speak positively, what, precisely, does he argue? What is his “settled 
opinion” (siddhānta)? First, the view for which he advocates is fundamentally an on­
tological one. The core argument of his text exemplifies this. Without telling us he is 
doing so, he maps his core proposition syllogistically in the opening verses of the fourth 
āhnika. There, he suggests that all things in the universe are in their very nature identical 
with the one and unitary Śiva, who exists in the form of consciousness.
The manner in which he articulates this position is striking. For while it is well 
known that the ŚD is an eclectic and ranging work that mixes tantric and philosophical 
registers, including as it does oblique and explicit references both to a variety of eso­
teric religious traditions and to orthodox Hindu and Buddhist philosophical schools, 
this complex style is perhaps most evident in the passage to be examined next, because 
the language he deploys to claim that all is Śiva uses a terminology that evokes Śaiva 
theological formulations in a manner that simultaneously serves to parry Dharmakīrti’s 
antipersonalist philosophy.
The argument at ŚD 4.1–​5 is structured as follows.
	
(1)	 All phenomena in the world are possessed of Śiva-​nature (this is the pratijñā or 
thesis),
	
(2)	 because all phenomena in the world are possessed of causal efficacy (this being 
the hetu or logical reason).
	
(3)	 Whatever has causal efficacy exists as a power or capacity that is controlled by an 
agent—​what is Śiva-​nature. This is so in the manner that a king directs those who 
serve him, for example, or the god of the dualist Śaivas deploys the power of illu­
sion (moha) and karmic equanimity, respectively, to create the world and to grace 
some among those dwelling within it with liberation. (This is the udāharaṇa or 
example.)
	 (4)	 Since all phenomena in the world are, indeed, possessed of causal efficacy, which 
is the mark of Śiva-​nature (this being the upanaya or application of the universal 
concomitance of the reason to the case in question),
	
(5)	 therefore (the nigamana or conclusion:) all phenomena in the world are powers 
or capacities of one who controls them—​Śiva—​which is to say they are possessed 
of Śiva-​nature.
The claim, then, is this: one sees things appearing in the world having effects, which 
defines them as real, because unreal things cannot do anything, including effecting the 
event of making themselves known in consciousness. Thus, all phenomenal things are 
capable or empowered in the world, at the very least in the sense that they are capable 
of making themselves known to the one who witnesses them. If, moreover, there are 
multiple things in the world which are capable and real, then they must be mutually

--- PAGE 1110 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1085
 
coordinated and structured such that they function in mutual relation. Somānanda 
argues thereby that multiplicity demands—​is the very proof of—​an underlying or over­
arching unity, because a nonchaotic and functioning multiplicity demands the existence 
of a single agent who guides and controls that multiplicity.
As we shall presently see, this syllogistic argument contains within it the seeds of 
Somānanda’s fundamental arguments against Dharmakīrti, all of which aim to prove 
one or another of the following three claims:
	
1.	 All phenomena are causally efficacious, and not just some of them as Dharmakīrti 
claims,
	 2.	 All phenomena are qualitatively mutually identical, meaning it is not the case that 
distinct classes of phenomena exist, as Dharmakīrti claims (principally by distin­
guishing svalakṣaṇas from sāmānyalakṣaṇas); and finally and ultimately
	
3.	 All phenomena are defined by an underlying unity and ontological identity.
And yet, at the beginning of the fourth āhnika, neither Somānanda nor Utpaladeva 
explicitly characterizes the passages there as proffering all the five standard components 
of the well-​known syllogism of the Nyāya,4 as I argue they do. Neither does Somānanda 
in any way make clear he wishes the argument to serve to counter the views of 
Dharmakīrti. Rather, the passage begins in a manner that rather appears simply to fur­
nish a stock Śaiva theological argument. Consider now the entire passage in Sanskrit 
and with the corresponding English translation:
athedānīṃ pravaktavyaṃ yathā [(1) pratijñā→] sarvaṃ śivātmakam |
[(2) hetu→] nāśakto vidyate kaścic chaktaṃ vastv eva te ’pi no  || ŚD 4.1 ||
iṣyante bahavaḥ śaktāḥ sarvasvātantryam āpatet |
athaikasyādhikā śaktir nyūnaśaktinibandhinī || ŚD 4.2 ||
svakāryaviṣaye sarvaḥ śakta eva nibandhanam |
śaktasya śakyate kartum evaṃ cen nānyaśaktatā || ŚD 4.3 ||
[(3) udāharaṇa→] nṛpādisādhanāpekṣā svakarmaphalatā bhavet |
sarvaḥ śakto ’pi sāpekṣa īśavan mohasāmyayoḥ || ŚD 4.4 ||
tasmād [(4) upanaya→] anekabhāvābhiḥ śaktibhis tadabhedataḥ |
[(5) nigamana→] eka eva sthitaḥ śaktaḥ śiva eva tathā tathā  || ŚD 4.5 ||
Next, the manner in which [(1) pratijñā→] everything is of the nature of Śiva is now 
to be explained (by me). [(2) hetu→] Nothing exists that is incapable (of causal ef­
ficacy); (and) that which is capable (of causal efficacy) definitely is a real thing, 
although we certainly do not accept that these many [entities in the world] are them­
selves (individually) capable: that would lead to everything being independent. 
Rather, a superior power of one [capable agent] restrains a subordinate power (of 
the same). Everything(, however,) is fully capable within the domain of its own work; 
(for) the (only) restraining that can be effected belongs to the one [agent] who is ca­
pable. If this is the case, the others are not (individually) capable. [(3) udāharaṇa→] 
The state of being of one who owns the rewards of one’s own actions must depend on 
the means of the king, etc.(, whom one has served). Everything, although capable (of

--- PAGE 1111 ---
1086      John Nemec
 
producing its own effect), is dependent, like the Lord on delusion and (karmic) equa­
nimity. Therefore, [(4) upanaya→] because he remains occupied in various ways with 
the powers, whose natures are multiple, this because he is not different from them, 
[(5) nigamana→] Śiva alone is empowered, he being absolutely unique, one.5
An Argument against the Duality of 
Objects of Awareness
In fact, we here read already Somānanda’s first argument against Dharmakīrti, though 
one imagines it may not yet be obvious given the resonance of the verses in question 
with Śaiva theological formulations. This resonance is particularly evident inasmuch as 
Somānanda says that “real things” (vastus) in the world are “capable” or śakta, the latter 
term of course calling to mind the feminine power or śakti that is invoked across Śaiva 
literatures and in the ŚD itself, as follows for example:
na śivaḥ śaktirahito na śaktir vyatirekiṇī || ŚD 3.2 ||
śivaḥ śaktas tathā bhāvān icchayā kartum īdṛśān |
śaktiśaktimator bhedaḥ śaive jātu na varṇyate || ŚD 3.3 ||
Śiva does not exist apart from śakti; śakti is not different (from Śiva). And Śiva is 
empowered [śakta] to create such entities at will. In Śaivism, no difference whatso­
ever between power and the one possessing the power is described.
Somānanda, however, simultaneously cites the writings of the Buddhist epistemol­
ogist Dharmakīrti and evokes Śaiva theological norms, for in suggesting that nothing 
found in the world is “incapable” (aśakta), ŚD 4.1 clearly draws a contrast with 
the Pramāṇavārttika (PV) regarding the nature of objects of cognition, which for 
Dharmakīrti, as is well known, may be divided into objects that are capable of causal 
efficacy (arthakriyā), on the one hand, and, on the other, what are not real objects, such 
as the floating hair one might falsely sense to be on the eye, since they have no causal 
efficacy.
pramāṇaṃ dvividhaṃ meyadvaividhyāc chaktyaśaktitaḥ |
arthakriyāyāṃ keśādir nārtho ’narthādhimokṣataḥ || PV 3.1 ||
The means of knowledge is two-​fold because the object of knowledge is two-​fold, 
this [i.e., the latter double-​nature] inasmuch as it [i.e., the object] is capable or in­
capable of causal efficiency [arthakriyā]. The hair (one erroneously sees floating on 
one’s eye), for example, is not a real object, because there is no determinate apprehen­
sion of it as such.6
In other words, references in ŚD 4.1cd to a vastu that is either śakta or aśakta may be 
shown to have Dharmakīrti and very possibly PV 3.1 itself in mind, for Somānanda 
denies that any aśakta entity or vastu may exist at all.

--- PAGE 1112 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1087
 
Utpaladeva in explaining Somānanda’s reference to the non-​existence of anything 
that is incapable makes the reference to Dharmakīrti explicit. He does this by speaking 
in the Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti explicitly in terms of the causal efficacy (arthakriyā) of objects. He 
then goes on to describe the nature of the vastu by paraphrasing but reformulating 
Dharmakīrti’s view of the same: the real thing, Utpladeva explains, if it is capable, exists 
in the ultimate sense or is paramārthasat, what is Śiva-​nature itself.7
aśaktaś cārthakriyāyāṃ vidyate ca, ity etāvan nāsti prakhyopākhyākaraṇena tāvad 
avyabhicārāt. śaktaṃ cet, tad vastv eva paramārthasad eva śivarūpam iti .
That which is incapable of causal efficiency and (simultaneously) exists—​there is no 
such thing, because so much [i.e., the nonexistence of such an entity] truly conforms 
with the instrument (of knowing)—​(whether it is) perception [prakhyā] or intellec­
tual reflection [upākhyā].8 If capable, then it definitely is a real thing, it definitely 
exists in the ultimate sense; (thus,) it has Śiva’s nature. This is definitive.
Indeed, though even Utpaladeva’s statement evokes Śaiva theological termi­
nology precisely in referring to the vastu as paramārthasat, it is rather fundamentally 
a reworking of the formulation offered in the NB at 1.14–​15 (tad eva paramārthasat. 
arthakriyāsāmarthyalakṣa​ṇatvād vastunaḥ): “That [svalakṣaṇa] alone is what exists in 
the ultimate sense. This is so because that which is real [vastu] is defined by its capacity 
for causal efficacy.” The argument, then, is crafted in opposition to Dharmakīrti’s two­
fold classification of reality, his distinction of what is the ultimate reality from what is 
merely conventionally real, found in his PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.3 (with PV 3.3ab 
being identical with Pramāṇaviniścaya 2.55ab):
arthakriyāsamarthaṃ yat tad atra paramārthasat |
anyat saṃvṛtisat prokte te svasāmānyalakṣaṇe || PV 3.3 ||
That which is capable of causal efficacy is real in the ultimate sense (paramārthasat), 
here [in the world/​on our view]. What is other is conventionally real (saṃvṛtisat). 
The two are referred to (respectively) as the svalakṣaṇa and the sāmānyalakṣaṇa.
See also PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.54cd:
tasya svapararūpābhyāṃ gater meyadvayaṃ matam || 3.54 ||
It is held (by Dignāga) that there is a pair of objects of cognition, because that [par­
ticular] is understood by its own form (via direct cognition) and by way of another 
form (via inference).
(Translation a slight modification of Franco and Notake 2014, 140.)
This suggests, then, that ŚD 4.1c–​d (nāśakto vidyate kaścic chaktaṃ vastv eva ), what I 
identify as the hetu in Somānanda’s argument, contrasts directly with this position.9
It is for this reason that Utpaladeva repeatedly explains Somānanda’s verses by arguing 
that whatever is found in the world—​whatever is sensible in any sense in consciousness,

--- PAGE 1113 ---
1088      John Nemec
 
including the floating hair—​is real in the ultimate sense, because it does something, at 
the very least causing itself to be known in consciousness. Somānanda, too, is explicit 
in stating as much in what immediately follows what I have identified above as the 
nigamana or conclusion to his syllogism.10 Simply put, according to Somānanda, there 
may be no binary classification of phenomena into qualitatively different classes or types 
of objects of knowledge—​particular, real entities (svalakṣaṇas), on the one hand, and 
conceptual forms, on the other.
An Argument against the 
Nonlinguisticality of Perception
This is also to say that Somānanda rejects the fundamental division of percept from 
concept that is favored by his Buddhist interlocutors. So much is articulated in a diffi­
cult passage of the āhnika (at ŚD 4.81cd–​84ab) for which the commentary is lost. There, 
Somānanda argues in evident consonance with the Mīmāṃsā that the two types of 
objects of which the Buddhists conceive must be mutually integrated in a Śaiva matrix of 
nonduality if his opponent’s position is logically to cohere. For there would otherwise be 
no way for conceptual forms to relate to perceptual phenomena.11
itaś cāsti jagaty aikyaṃ pratyakṣāgrahaṇād12 api || ŚD 4.81 ||
svalakṣaṇena yogitvād vyavahārasya sarvataḥ |
loke cānupapatteś ca pramā vā vyavahāragā13 || ŚD 4.82 ||
bālamūkādivijñānasadṛśī kīdṛśī kriyā14 |
savikalpasya yogitvād yathāvastu grahaḥ katham || ŚD 4.83 ||
tena jñeyam ekam eva vastu bhinne grahaḥ kutaḥ |
And, it is (also) for this (following) reason that there is unity in the universe, be­
cause there would (otherwise) be no apprehension (of that universe) by means of di­
rect cognition, either; (this is so) because discourse/​mundane activity [vyavahāra] is 
everywhere connected with the unique particular in the world, and because it is not 
(otherwise) possible; or, (this is so because) valid knowledge deals with discourse/​
mundane activity. (After all:) Of what kind is the action (of perception) that is sim­
ilar to the awareness of children, mute people, and the like? How(, moreover,) could 
a conceptual cognition accurately apprehend (a svalakṣaṇa, the object of cognition) 
as a result of it being connected (with it,) (if perception and conception were utterly 
divided)? (It cannot.) Thus, one should know the real thing to be absolutely one; if it 
were divided, how could one apprehend it?
One can see that this passage is laden with terminology from the Buddhists—​svalakṣaṇa, 
savikalpa, the vastu—​and Somānanda here clearly cites favorably the Ślokavārttika at 
ŚD 4.83ab. The long and the short of it is that Somānanda agrees that there can be only 
one nature of what is real in the universe. Just as Kumārila accepts a vyakti that is per­
ceivable without conceptualization but also in a manner imbued with the universal, so

--- PAGE 1114 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1089
 
percept and concept, non-​conceptual perception and conceptually imbued cognition, 
cannot by nature be absolutely divided inasmuch as the nature of the object lends itself 
fully to both.
Arguments concerning 
Perceptual Error
Also embedded in the syllogistic logic that opens Somānanda’s fourth chapter is a chal­
lenge to Dharmakīrti’s conception of perceptual error. Simply, if everything in the world 
is Śiva, inasmuch as everything is real, the latter because everything is capable, then 
even what are conventionally understood to be erroneous or illusory cognitions must be 
conceived in the same fashion: everything is real in the ultimate sense (paramārthasat). 
Thus, as I have indicated elsewhere (Nemec 2011, 8 n. 16; cf. Nemec 2012, 233), it is prin­
cipally in the fourth āhnika (though also in the sixth) that Somānanda delivers an argu­
ment for the ultimate reality of apparent illusions, what he promised in the first āhnika to 
explain “later on,” the promise coming in the form of an explicit rebuke of Dharmakīrti’s 
own understanding of the matter:
dṛśyante ’tra tadicchāto bhāvā bhītyādiyogataḥ || ŚD 1.45 ||
tatra mithyāsvarūpaṃ cet sthāpyāgre satyatedṛśām |
By his will, entities are seen here that are associated with fear, etc. If you argue that 
they have an erroneous nature, I will establish the reality of such entities later on.
This passage, as is well known,15 evokes the PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.282:
kāmaśokabhayonmādacaurasvapnādyupaplutāḥ |
abhūtān api paśyanti purato ’vasthitān iva || PV 3.282 ||
He who is blinded by intense desire, by sorrow, by fear, by drunkenness, by dreaming 
of thieves, etc., can see, as clearly as if they were before him, things that, in reality, do 
not exist.16
This denial of the existence of ultimately unreal entities is fashioned in two ways in 
the ŚD corpus. The first, cited here below, is fascinating for dealing with a philosophical 
problem common to other schools of Indian thought, namely, the nature of dreaming 
sleep. Consider Utpaladeva’s ŚDVṛ ad ŚD 4.19-​21ab, which deals with error in this con­
text. There, Utpaladeva argues that even a cognition of something that does not exist 
in the everyday world, such as that of water in a dream, is capable of causal efficacy and 
therefore is real. This is so inasmuch as such cognitions can please the agent who knows 
such cognitions. Causal efficacy is not dependent on the external reality of a cognitive 
experience, then; it may be found even in phenomena that appear only to the internal 
sense organ (the antaḥkaraṇa).17 Thus, the dreamer of the present example may delight

--- PAGE 1115 ---
1090      John Nemec
 
in the satisfaction of drinking water in a dream, the delight being real even while the 
water is merely imagined:18
abhrāntatvād19 vāstavasvapnajalasya pānādyarthakriyā bhrāntāpi syāt, tṛṇnivṛttyā20 
tu tṛptiḥ21 svasaṃvedanasiddhā22 na visaṃvadati23
A causal efficacy—​that of drinking, for example—​must exist (within the dream-​
state) for water that is real in a dream, because it [i.e., the water] is not unreal (in 
the dream), although it [i.e., the causal efficacy] is unreal (outside of the dream); 
and still, with the quenching of one’s thirst (in the dream) there is a satisfaction that, 
having been established in self-​awareness, does not deceive.
What is more, Somānanda may be said somewhat obliquely to make the same claim in 
the passage that Utpaladeva here has explained:24
vyavahārasya bādhā ced vyavahāre yatheṣṭatā |
kvacit satyasuvarṇasya pratyante vyavahāritā || ŚD 4.19 ||
kūṭakārṣāpaṇādau vā vyavahāro ’pi dṛśyate |
tāvatā vyavahāro vā yad ātmāhlādamātrakam || ŚD 4.20 ||
arthakriyāsamarthatvam etad evāsya vāstavam |
Objection: The invalidation is of the mundane activity. (Reply:) The mundane activity 
is as it is wished to be. Somewhere in a bordering country, real gold is the currency of 
trade; but trade [vyavahāra] also is seen in alloyed coins and the like. Alternatively, 
(one may understand the matter as follows:) the mundane activity [vyavahāra] exists 
(only) to the extent that the self is delighted; this alone is the true capacity for the pur­
poseful action belonging to this [object used in mundane activity].
More generally—​this is the second analysis of error—​the ŚD details at length an ar­
gument for the reality of supposedly erroneous perceptions, as I have shown elsewhere 
(see Nemec 2012, 227–​235). Their reality, Somānanda again argues, consists of the very 
fact that such perceptions appear in consciousness. In making this case, he suggests that 
Dharmakīrti can draw a distinction between real and unreal objects of knowledge only 
conventionally, and only by first implicitly accepting the Śaiva view that all phenomena 
are real qua appearing in and as Śiva-​as-​consciousness:
mithyājñānavikalpyānāṃ sattvaṃ cidvyaktiśaktatā || ŚD 4.7 ||
vidyate tat tad atrāpi śivatvaṃ . . . 
Those [perceptions] that could be conceived of as erroneous cognitions are found 
to be capable of manifestation in consciousness. That constitutes their reality; (and) 
that [reality] (in turn) is the Śiva-​nature that exists here [in even these “erroneous” 
perceptions], as well.25
So much effectively claims what Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikās (ĪPK) and 
Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti (ĪPKVṛ) so famously stated at ĪPK 2.4.3a–​d, that all that 
is inexistent must be only that—​totally beyond the realm of the knowable—​while all 
that is existent need do nothing to obtain that existence. Anything appearing in and as

--- PAGE 1116 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1091
 
consciousness is real, existent qua appearing as such; nothing that cannot appear in con­
sciousness may be countenanced at all.
yad asat tad asad yuktā nāsataḥ satsvarūpatā |
sato ’pi na punaḥ sattālābhenārtho . . .
That which is nonexistent is nonexistent; it is not tenable that that which is nonex­
istent has an existent nature. As for that which is existent, by contrast, there is no 
need for it to acquire existence . . . 
Note also the similarity of expression of ĪPK 2.4.3a with ŚD 4.6ab: tathā yatra sad ity 
evaṃ pratītis tad asat katham.26
Endeavoring logically to guarantee this proposition—​that no cognition is 
erroneous—​Somānanda devotes considerable effort to proving that no cognition may 
be said to be invalidated, this—​again—​in an explicit dispute with Dharmakīrti. He 
argues that no cognition or any element of the experience thereof may be shown to have 
been false subsequent to the cognition thereof. None may be contradicted, that is, none 
may be said not to have been real in at least the sense of objects having been caused to 
be known, what is a causally efficacious effect caused primarily by the object itself. Thus, 
the moment of time in which a cognition appeared, the act of its production, the agent’s 
experience thereof, the sense organ that knew it, the relation of the sense organ to the 
object of cognition in question, the activity of seeing erroneously, and the locus where 
such a cognition is said to have occurred all are said not to be impossible to invalidate.27
It is not possible even for a subsequent cognition to contradict a previous one. This 
Somānanda argues by claiming that neither of the two types of contradiction identified 
by Dharmakīrti himself—​mutual nonconcomitancy (sahānavasthiti) and incompat­
ibility (parasparaparihāra)—​validly describe any subsequent cognition that might be 
posited as the invalidator of a preceding one.
sahānavasthitir nāsti virodhaḥ prāgvināśataḥ |
anyonyaparihāro vā jñānājñānātmakaḥ sthitaḥ || ŚD 4.24 ||
The incompatibility that is impossibility of (the) co-​presence (of mutually distinct 
entities) [sahānavasthiti] does not exist (here), due to the destruction in an earlier mo­
ment (of the prior cognition, before the subsequent cognition arises); nor does a mutual 
exclusion [anyonyaparihāra] exist, one of awareness and the absence of awareness.28
There can be little doubt that Somānanda here has in mind the Nyāyabindu (NB) at 3.74–​77.
NB 3.74: dvividho hi padārthānāṃ virodhaḥ.
Opposition between objects is of a double kind.
NB 3.75: avikalakāraṇasya bhavato ’nyabhāve ’bhāvād virodhagatiḥ .
When (one fact that) has duration (as long as) the sum-​total of its causes remains 
unimpaired, and it (then) vanishes as soon as another, (the opposed,) fact appears, it 
follows that both are incompatible.29
NB 3.76: śītoṣṇasparśavat.

--- PAGE 1117 ---
1092      John Nemec
 
. . . just as the sensations of heat and cold.
NB 3.77: parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatayā vā bhāvābhāvavat.
There is also (opposition between two facts) when their own essence consists in mu­
tual exclusion, as between the affirmation and negation (of the same thing).30
Simply put, Somānanda argues that error cannot (ultimately, ontologically) exist, be­
cause no cognition qua appearing in and as consciousness can be invalidated.
Arguments against apoha as Defining 
the Universal (sāmānya)
Still elsewhere (namely, at ŚD 4.68 and following), Somānanda challenges the no­
tion that inference could occur without the existence of a real universal or sāmānya. 
His rationale, elaborated further in the commentary of Utpaladeva (this is one of 
the last passages of the ŚD for which the commentary remains extant), suggests that 
reference to a negative category could not explain the ways in which an entity could 
be positively identified by language. The problem at hand is this: how can categories 
of entities be comprehended or even exist at all unless some essential nature defines 
them as such?
The Buddhist opponent argues that so much results not from the existence of a 
real, universal nature (sāmānya) belonging to various entities, for they deny the per­
manence that the existence of such a nature would presuppose and require. They in­
stead argue that entities of a class, all of which are in reality utterly unique and utterly 
particular in their nature (these are what they refer to as svalakṣaṇas), may only be 
classed contingently, by what makes them relatively speaking mutually similar. The 
relative similarity lies in a similarity of the effects they can have in the world: they 
perform in a manner that is mutually similar and, more importantly, dissimilar from 
other entities. This classing by way of relative capacity or function they refer to as 
apoha, or exclusion. And the Buddhists insist that the similarity is built only on ne­
gation, on the fact of the nonsimilarity of the entities in the constructed category 
with other entities to be found in the world. Something is of a class because it cannot 
be said not to be functionally like others in that class, and because entities not in the 
class can be said not to be functionally like the members of the class in question. In 
this way, entities may be conventionally classed as “of a kind” but without accepting 
they are of some essential or true (and therefore unchanging) nature, such that the 
class may be said ultimately to exist.
Somānanda, by contrast, argues that the quality that defines this contingent classifica­
tion requires there to be something that really is held in common among those entities. 
They must in fact share a common nature or else no similarity even defined on a rela­
tional basis could be identified. In other words, Somānanda argues that the very de­
nial of the real universal nature (sāmānya) of entities for which the Buddhists argue

--- PAGE 1118 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1093
 
implicitly presupposes that that very nature exists. Without the real universal, moreover, 
there would be no way to comprehend or even refer to entities of a particular class.
bauddhasya cen na sāmānyam anumānaṃ nivartate |
yathā suvarṇabhāṇḍeṣu na tathā hematāmrayoḥ || ŚD 4.68 ||
suvarṇam ānayety ukte śūnyatā kiṃ pratīyate |
viśeṣasparśavirahāt kadācid api yujyate || ŚD 4.69 ||
tattvasyaikyaṃ vinā na syād ekasyaiva viruddhatā |
sāmānyena viśeṣeṇa katham ekasya yogitā || ŚD 4.70 ||
If for the Buddhist there is no (real) universal, (then) inference ceases to occur.31 
(When one says “bring the gold,”) (an awareness based on verbal knowledge 
rooted in the universal does) not (arise) with respect to (mixed) gold and copper 
as (it arises) with respect to (pure) gold ornaments.32 Is it absence [śūnyatā] that is 
perceived when one says, “bring the gold,” as a result of the absence of contact with a 
particular (that is not gold)? Is that appropriate somewhere? It could not be so in the 
absence of the unity of reality: (for,) the one [object, e.g., a gold bracelet] itself would 
be (self-​)contradictory. How could the one [object] be connected with the universal, 
(and) with the particular?
Utpaladeva’s ŚDVṛ and ŚD 4.68–​70 reads in part as follows:
atha sāmānyaṃ bauddhasya nāsti, tad anumānaṃ sāmānyaviṣayam abhīṣṭaṃ hīyate. 
tathā sāmānyaṃ vinā yathā suvarṇam ānayety ukte sauvarṇakaṭakakeyūrādiṣv 
artheṣu pratītir na tathā hematāmrayoḥ, tāmrāsaṃsparśena hemna eva pratīteḥ, 
kaṭakakeyūrādiṣu tu na kasyacit parityāgaḥ. anyāpohasyāpi sāmānyatve ’bhyupagate 
kiṃ suvarṇam ānayeti śūnyatā prasajyapratiṣedharūpā pratīyate viśeṣasparśavirahād 
dhetoḥ, api tv asauvarṇavyāvṛttāḥ suvarṇapratyavamarśakāriṇaḥ ta ekatām 
āpādyamānā viśeṣā eveti kadācid api yujyata iti kākvā vyākhyeyam. na kadācid apy 
etad yujyate śūnyatāpi bhātīti. tad etac cittattvasya padārtheṣv aikyaṃ vinā na syād 
ekasyaivārthasya parasparaviruddhatvāt.
If there is no universal for the Buddhist, then he abandons the inference he lays 
claim to, which has the universal as its object. And without the universal, when 
one says “bring the gold” the awareness [pratīti] (that “this is gold” that arises for 
someone looking for gold) with respect to golden objects such as a bracelet or an 
upper-​arm bracelet would not occur as it does with respect to (entities consisting 
of alloyed metal of both) gold and copper, because the awareness of gold only 
[eva] (in the context of both gold and copper) results from the absence of any con­
tact with copper, while nothing at all is left out of (the awareness of those entities 
that are made only of gold,) the kaṭaka and keyūra bracelets, for example. When 
one [i.e., the Buddhist] accepts the exclusion of the other [anyāpoha], for its part, 
as the universal, (then one may ask:) is it an absence the form of which is a pure 
negation [i.e., the total absence of that which is non-​gold] that is cognized when 
one says “bring the gold,” the cause being that there is no contact with a particular 
(that is non-​gold)? Or, (to put the matter in terms of that with which one posi­
tively does have contact,) is it those particulars alone that are (mentally) excluded 
from that which is not made of gold, that (are cognized,) produce the judgment

--- PAGE 1119 ---
1094      John Nemec
 
of gold, (and thereby) receive a unity (as a single class of entities—​as “golden”)? 
[Somānanda] says in a certain tone of voice [i.e., with contemptuous irony] that 
it is this that must be explained (by his Buddhist opponent), viz., whether so 
much is somewhere appropriate; (and so much is not possible, for) this is never 
appropriate—​that absence, for its part, appears. Thus, this [view of the sāmānya] 
is not possible in the absence of a unity of the reality of consciousness in (all) 
things, because (in its absence) there would be a mutual contradiction in the na­
ture of one and the same object.
Utpaladeva here explains the problem of a universal constructed exclusively on ne­
gation in three ways. First, he interprets Somānanda’s reference to the two contexts in 
which a sāmānya may be operative, one where one becomes aware of objects made of 
pure gold after someone issues the order, “bring the gold,” the other where, after the 
same order, one is to be made aware of objects made (if I understand the matter cor­
rectly) of an alloyed metal containing both gold and copper. Utpaladeva notes that 
Somānanda is correct in saying the awareness one might have would not be the same 
in each case, for in the first instance nothing at all is left out of what one sees—​all that is 
present is pure gold, but in the latter instance, one could have an awareness of nothing 
but gold only by way of making no contact with the copper, which would not be possible 
in the instance in question, meaning Somānanda argues that one could not be aware of 
“gold” under such circumstances at all!
Next, Utpaladeva glosses ŚD 4.69. There, Somānanda queries how it is possible that 
an absence or śūnyatā could be perceived when one is told “bring the gold.” The problem 
is as follows: if gold, for example, consists of nothing but not non-​gold, then awareness 
of gold amounts to the absence of an awareness of “not gold”; therefore, Utpaladeva 
suggests, the absence of contact with a particular that is not gold (such as copper, e.g.), 
what is in fact an absence of an awareness of that which is not gold, could lead one to 
have an awareness of gold.
Finally, Utpaladeva queries the nature of exclusion when one cognizes the particulars 
the nature of which is to produce an understanding not non-​x. He asks whether it is 
appropriate for these (unique) particulars, consisting only in the exclusion of what is 
not gold, to lead uniformly to the judgment “gold” and thus acquire a unity. That is, he 
argues that it is difficult for the Buddhists to explain how the particulars themselves that 
are seen (as not non-​x) can lead to an awareness of a particular category of entities neg­
atively so defined: “Or (tu), [to put the matter in terms of that with which one positively 
does have contact,] is it (api) those particulars alone (viśeṣā eva) that are [mentally] 
excluded from that which is not made of gold (asauvarṇavyāvṛttāḥ), that [are cognized,] 
produce the judgment of gold (suvarṇapratyavamarśakāriṇaḥ), [and thereby] receive a 
unity [as a single class of entities—​as ‘golden’]?” Put differently, the previous instance 
involved the production of an awareness of a void, a total absence or prasajyapratiṣedha; 
the present instance understands a cognition of something that is present only inas­
much as what one does contact in the cognition is that which excludes what it is not, or 
in other words is another kind of absence.

--- PAGE 1120 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1095
 
Arguments against Convention 
(saṃketa) Explaining Denotation
Somānanda argues that another consequence of a noneternal universal would be that 
language would lose its denotative capacity. He claims that it is not possible for a theory 
of denotation to rely solely on convention (saṃketa), because the very establishment of 
the convention—​that a word may properly be taken to refer to a particular thing in the 
world—​could never occur in the absence of the existence of a prior and innate connec­
tion of word and thing. A theory of linguistic meaningfulness based on convention, that 
is, presumes the existence of the very possibility of the relation of word and thing that 
it seeks to explain, a connection that Somānanda, like his Mīmāṃsaka counterparts, 
evidently understands to be natural. Yet again, then, Somānanda suggests that his 
interlocutors’ philosophical position is tenable only by way of their implicit acceptance 
of his own: there must be one kind of phenomenon in the universe, and its nature cannot 
be split, the conceptual from the perceptual.
kathaṃ na devadattasya yajñadattavad ākhyayā |
atra saṃketitatvāc cet saṃketenātra kiṃ kṛtam || ŚD 4.78 ||
saṃyogaś cen na dūreṣu mūrtāmūrteṣu yujyate |
śabdasyoccāritadhvaṃsān naṣṭānaṣṭadvaye na ca || ŚD 4.79 ||
vācyavācakarūpaś cet sa eva33 niyamaḥ kutaḥ |
uktasya34 vācakatvaṃ hi vācyatvam aparasya tu || ŚD 4.80 ||
vācyavācakarūpatve vācyavācakatānvayaḥ |
How is one like Yajñadatta not (designated) by Devadatta’s name? (The Buddhist 
opponent’s) Objection: Because of the fact that there is agreement here (regarding the 
one denoted by the name). (Somānanda’s Reply:) What service is done here by the agree­
ment? (The Buddhist’s) Objection: A connection (of the name with the person named). 
(Somānanda’s Reply:) That [i.e., the connection or saṃyoga] is not possible with respect 
to those [entities, i.e., what are denoted and the words that denote them,] which are 
(mutually) distant, which (respectively) have a form and do not have a form; nor, given 
that speech expires after it is uttered, is it (possible) with respect to the pair (in ques­
tion), which (respectively) have perished [viz., the name “Devadatta,” after it is uttered] 
and not-​perished [viz., the perduring Devadatta himself]. (The Buddhist’s) Objection: It 
[i.e., the saṃyoga] exists in the form of designatum and designator [vācyavācakarūpa]. 
(Somānanda’s Reply:) Wherefrom this necessity? For what is uttered [i.e., speech, the 
name] is that which designates, while that which is designated is something different. 
If (you argue:) it [i.e., the niyama or necessity] is (found in) the (very) nature of the 
designatum and designator [vācyavācakarūpatve], (we reply:) there is(, in that case,) a 
definite link of the nature of the designatum to that of the designator.35
The absence of a real—​nonconstructed, substantial—​universal (sāmānya) in the phi­
losophy of the Buddhist epistemologists, Somānanda further argues, would render not

--- PAGE 1121 ---
1096      John Nemec
 
just language but also inferential reasoning impossible. For, he suggests, it is impossible 
for his Buddhist opponent to explain the possibility of inferring the presence of fire where 
smoke is visible (for example), this in the absence of a unity that could guarantee the 
very possibility of associating one svalakṣaṇa (e.g., that of smoke) with another (e.g., that 
of fire), even if the invariable concomitance of the two were apprehended. The reason 
offered to justify this claim is the fact that each svalakṣaṇa, understood by the Buddhists 
to be absolutely unique, would be incapable of effecting a generalized and generalizable 
instance of inferential knowledge abstracted from the unique particulars in question. 
One would have to presume the existence of a generic nature of a svalakṣaṇa to know it.
tathānumānaṃ na bhaved dhūmāgnyor anvaye kvacit || ŚD 4.84 ||
apūrvayor gṛhīte ’pi tatkālaṃ gatayor dvayoḥ |
agṛhīte na gṛhītaḥ saṃbandho ’gniḥ pratīyate || ŚD 4.85 ||
And, no inference could arise anywhere (from a direct cognition, in the absence 
of the existence of a real universal), even if the invariable concomitance of smoke 
and fire(, for example,) were apprehended, the two being unique entities that are 
no longer existent at that time (of the inference). If(, moreover,) that [invariable 
concomitance] has not been apprehended, the relation (between the perception 
of smoke and the presence of fire) is (also) not apprehended; (thus,) the fire is not 
cognized (by way of an inference based in seeing the appearance of smoke).36
Somānanda further argues that no conventional, constructed understanding of the 
nature of the universal could serve to explain how the divide between a truly unique 
svalakṣaṇa and a general characteristic thereof (such as having the nature of “fire,” or 
having the nature of “smoke”) could be bridged, which is indispensably necessary for in­
ferential reasoning. He in fact reasons that it is the Buddhists’ own understanding of the 
universal that proves that no instance of valid knowledge (pramā) could be produced 
thereby.37 Not even a sādṛśya or “similarity” among perceptions of unique svalakṣaṇas 
could explain the same, Somānanda says, because the nature of the sādṛśya by definition 
cannot with any veridicality be associated with svalakṣaṇas when they are in fact unequiv­
ocally and utterly unique. Only by sharing a true, common nature, a real quality—​what is 
impermissible on the Buddhist’s own formulation—​could perceptions of svalakṣaṇas be 
mutually identified or associated.38 In a word, much in the manner of his critique of inval­
idation, Somānanda here exhibits a reliance on a critique of Buddhist ontology to suggest 
that the disparate svalakṣaṇas could never be properly mutually related such that one (ut­
terly unique) svalakṣaṇa could lead to a valid inference regarding the presence of another.
sāmānyam aviśeṣaṃ ced aviśeṣāt kutaḥ pramā |
viśeṣasyāpy apūrvatvāt39 kathaṃ cāsti samanvayaḥ || ŚD 4.86 ||
sādṛśyād atha cen nāsti yāthātmyena samāgamaḥ |
na ca vātrānumānatvaṃ dhūmataḥ kevalād bhavet || ŚD 4.87 ||
Objection (of the Buddhist opponent): There is a universal; it is the non-​particular.40 
(Reply:) How (on your view) is valid knowledge the product of a non-​particular?

--- PAGE 1122 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1097
 
And how, since the particular (according to you) is, for its part, unprecedented, could 
a connection exist (of that unique particular with the aviśeṣa or universal)? Now, (on 
the one hand,) if you argue it [i.e., the connection (samanvaya)] is the result of simi­
larity [sādṛśya],41 (we reply:) there is no conjunction [samāgama] (of the sādṛśya and 
the conceptions it conveys) with the real nature (of the particular). Nor, on the other 
hand, could a legitimate inference (of the fire) arise, here, from (a cognition of) the 
(svalakṣaṇa of) smoke alone.
The Buddhist opponent, that is, must implicitly assume the unity for which Somānanda 
argues in order logically to proffer the very position they claim as true. The division 
of entities into two types, ultimately real svalakṣaṇas, on the one hand, and merely 
constructed and therefore only conventionally real universals (sāmānyas), on the other, 
is, on Somānanda’s view, simply untenable.
Arguments against Momentariness 
Devoid of Overarching Unity
Finally, a similar line of attack is prosecuted, as well, in response to the kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda 
(to which Somānanda explicitly refers at ŚD 4.93c), the doctrine of the instantaneous 
destruction of each momentary svalakṣaṇa.
kṣaṇabhaṅgaparāmarśād apy etad upapadyate || ŚD 4.93 ||
śaktāśaktavikalpair hi dīpajvālādyudāhṛtaiḥ |
sthiratā nopapannā te pratyakṣenāpi ca sthitā || ŚD 4.94 ||
sthiratvaṃ kṣaṇikatvāc42 ca pramāṇāṃ cintayā sthitam |
avisaṃvādirūpāc43 ca viruddhaṃ tat kathaṃ bhavet || ŚD 4.95 ||
yāvan na sarvabhāvānām ekatvena vyavasthitiḥ |
pareṇa kṣaṇabhaṅgasya parāmarśāgamaḥ kutaḥ || ŚD 4.96 ||
tato ’py etac chivātmatvaṃ bhāvānām upapadyate |
This can be rationally justified by a consideration of (your doctrine of the) instan­
taneous destruction (of all phenomena), as well. For, according to you, (real) per­
manence [sthiratā] is not obtained by way of conceptual constructions—​which are 
exemplified by the (apparently perduring) flame of a lamp, for example—​whether 
they are capable or incapable,44 nor is it established by direct cognition, either.45 
Moreover, because the instances of valid knowledge [pramā] are (thus) momen­
tary in nature, their stability is established (only) by way of intellectual reflection; 
and, given that (you maintain that) they are by nature reliable [avisaṃvādi],46 (we 
ask:) how can they be possessed of that [stability,] which is contrary (to their real 
nature)? As long as there is no fixed existence of all entities (in the universe) as a 
unity, how could another bring one to reflect on the instantaneous destruction (at 
all)? It is also for that reason that this, the Śiva-​nature of (all) entities, is rationally 
justified.

--- PAGE 1123 ---
1098      John Nemec
 
Somānanda here argues that the utter uniqueness and momentariness of all phenomena 
would inhibit all inferentiality and even conceptuality. This is so because the very stability of 
any instance of valid knowledge (pramā) must of necessity be, on the Buddhists’ own logic, 
conceptually constructed and therefore self-​contradictory in nature. That is, Somānanda 
argues that a pramā is deceptive (visaṃvādaka) on their own definition, for while it is un­
derstood to furnish valid knowledge, what it offers is a form that in its very capacity to per­
dure is false: it deceptively presents a stability (or nonmomentariness) where none exists. 
This, then, constitutes Somānanda’s critique of inference for oneself (svārthānumāna). And 
in the absence of a unity of all phenomena, Somānanda concludes in a rhetorical flourish, 
the instantaneous destruction of all—​including the instantaneous destruction even of the 
abstract concept or idea of “instantaneous destruction” itself—​would render it impossible 
for the kṣaṇabhaṅga doctrine to be communicated to one by another. So much, then, for the 
Buddhists’ conception of inference for another (parārthānumāna).
Conclusion
The logic of Somānanda’s siddhānta, in sum, implicitly and explicitly challenges the 
notion that causality could function in an impersonal manner and by being grounded 
in an ontology recognizing a multiplicity of phenomena only related by such (contin­
gent) causal events. Indeed, the entire core ontology of the PV is challenged in that 
Somānanda and Utpaladeva reject the notion, expressed at PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 
3.44, that everything that is real necessarily ceases to exist.47 Instead, Somānanda argues 
not only that disparate appearances, disparate capable phenomena, could not be co­
ordinated and could not interact in the absence of the existence of an organizing ma­
trix, directed by an agent who possesses and directs and orders capable phenomena as 
capacities—​and who is identified with them, allowing thereby such coordination and 
direction—​but also that everything is always and ever existent, if not always percep­
tible.48 He argues, in a word, that none of the philosophical positions of the Buddhists 
addressed by him is logically supportable unless a unity as mapped in the syllogism 
found at the beginning of the āhnika, a unity embodied in the person of an ever-​existent, 
power-​wielding god, Śiva, is implicitly assumed to exist. For all of existence in being 
perceivable and experienced is real in that it causes such experience in the first place. 
All is capable. And capable entities can only be circumscribed in their effectiveness by a 
governing power, an agent who controls them. The very multiplicity that Somānanda’s 
Buddhist opponents describe demands a unity and a controlling agent.
With this, one witnesses a relatively early exemplar of the sophistication of the 
“postscriptural” works produced by tantric philosophical authors. In Somānanda’s case, 
the Śaiva scriptural background is rendered relatively indeterminate and, while evoked 
rather clearly, somewhat underexamined by him in the ŚD. But its presence is felt even 
in his turn to arguing about and for a philosophically grounded understanding of di­
vinity and reality that largely characterizes Śaiva postscriptural works. In making such a

--- PAGE 1124 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1099
 
philosophical turn, the authors of the Pratyabhijñā, beginning with Somānanda, devoted 
considerable attention to their Buddhist interlocutors, whose philosophical sophistication 
and influence, in Kashmir of the day and well beyond the valley, demanded nothing less.

	 	   Here, Kumārila explicitly and directly challenges a core assumption of the Buddhist 
epistemologists, namely, that a clear and absolute distinction exists between the object of

moments of awareness, and therefore not truly a perception of the object at all.”

by the knower—​not as something unique, since it does not conceptualize the exclusion of

	32.	 The problem of the inferential nature of language and its dependence on the universal 
is of course well known in the Buddhist epistemological tradition. See, e.g., Dignāga’s 
Pramāṇasamuccaya 5.1 (cited in Kamalaśīla’s Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā and Tattvasaṃgraha 
1514, page 539: na pramāṇāntaraṃ śābdam anumānāt tathā hi tat | kṛtakatvādivat 
svārtham anyāpohena bhāṣate ||. (Cognition based on the word [śābda] is not different 
from inference, for just as (an inferential mark or liṅga such as) the quality of having been

[anyāpoha]), it [i.e., the cognition based on the word] expresses its own object through 
the exclusion of others.) (The translation, excepting very minor modifications, is that 
of Hattori, for which see Hattori 2000, 139; cf. Hattori 2006, 56. Compare, also, with the 
translation of Jha 1937–​1939, 2: 754–​755, noting that Jha counts TS 1514 as TS 1515.)

	35.	 The argument, it is clear, turns on Somānanda applying the very line of questioning that 
was prosecuted by the pūrvapakṣin of the Śābarabhāṣya (ŚBh) to the view of his Buddhist 
opponents. He asks how one can account for a connection or relation of speech, which 
denotes meaning, to the object it denotes, when the two are mutually distinct entities 
situated in mutually differing locations and are of distinct natures, the one (i.e., what is 
denoted; Devadatta, e.g.) having a form and being a perduring entity, the other (i.e., the 
name; “Devadatta,” e.g.) not having form and perishing immediately after it is uttered. 
Somānanda objects to the possibility that the connection is ad hoc, constructed by conven­
tion, because, he argues, there would be no way to account for any necessary connection of 
designatum and designator, unless, that is, the designatum and designator are intrinsically 
connected, are connected inasmuch as it is their very nature to be thus (there must be a 
vācyavācakatānvaya). Put in other words—​and as the Vṛttikāra in the ŚBh argued against 
the pūrvapakṣin, and as Kumārila, following on the ŚBh, did as well in his ŚV—​the relation 
between vācya and vācaka (which are explicitly dealt with in the ŚV) cannot be fabricated; 
it must always have existed. See, esp., ŚV (saṃbandhākṣepaparihāra) vv. 5ff. It is at verse 12 
of the saṃbandhākṣepaparihāra section that an opponent objects to the Mīmāṃsā view of 
the saṃbandha as permanent, arguing instead that it exists as a matter of convention. See 
also Arnold 2006, 461–​467 for a treatment of the issues here at hand and see esp. 462 for 
Arnold’s translation of saṃbandhākṣepaparihāra, v. 12. This may also be compared to that 
of Jha [1900] 1983, 349.

--- PAGE 1128 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1103
 
	 	   Note, however, that although it seems likely the opponent here is a Buddhist, it is at least 
possible that Somānanda here has a Naiyāyika or Vaiśeṣika opponent in mind, for they, 
too, hold that speech is conventional. On the notion that speech is denotative on the basis 
of convention according to the Naiyāyika Vātsyāyana, see NS and NSBh ad 2.1.55–​56, esp., 
NSBh ad 2.1.56. See also, e.g., VS 7.2.15ff., along with Candrānanda’s commentary thereon, 
for a treatment of the conventional nature of denotation according to Vaiśeṣikas, esp. at VS 
7.2.24.
	 	   One must also note that Dharmakīrti grounds his understanding of saṃketa in his 
theory of apoha, which in turn is based on an understanding of causality as that which 
establishes difference, what is not found in Dignāga’s understanding. See Dharmakīrti’s 
Pramāṇavārttikasvopajñavṛtti (PVSV) ad PV 1.72cd (Gnoli 1960: 40): yasya 
pratyāyanārthaṃ saṃketaḥ kriyate, abhinnasādhyān bhāvān atatsādhyebhyo bhedena 
jñātvā tatparihāreṇa pravarteteti. ([A convention is established] so that, when one knows 
that [certain] entities having the same effects are *different* from [those] which do not 
have those effects, one may act [toward the former] by excluding the [latter].) The same 
passage is quoted in Arnold 2006, 441, n. 64. The present translation, however, is that of 
Eltschinger et al. 2018, 84. Compare also the translation of Dunne 2004, 343–​344, cited 
also in Arnold (2006), 441, n. 64.
	 	   For Dharmakīrti, convention is formed on the basis of identifying bhāvas that have 
common effects; yet, as above, the classification of such entities is based on a relative 
basis (measuring the entities in relation to others) and involves identification by way 
of exclusion. The convention, moreover, is precisely that, on Dharmakīrti’s view. See 
PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.171 (note that the edition of Sāṅkṛtyāyana 1953, 264, ll. 8–​
9 reads nirdṛṣṭārthena for nirdiṣṭārthena; Sāṅkṛtyāyana 1938 records what here follows, 
excepting it reads śrutāṃ for śrutau): tasmāt saṃketakāle ’pi nirdiṣṭārthena saṃyutaḥ | 
svapratītiphalenānyāpohaḥ sambadhyate śrutau ||. (Therefore, it is also at the moment of 
(the applicability of) the convention [saṃketakāle] that exclusion of the other [anyāpoha], 
which is connected with an object that is indicated (by the saṃketa), one that itself results 
in knowledge of itself, is joined to what is communicated.) (The same is cited in Arnold 
2006, 444, n. 70.) Cf. Arnold 2006, 445. On ŚD 4.78–​81ab, see Nemec 2019, 253–​258.
	36.	 Note that Kumārila himself made a similar argument, as Taber 2005, 29 indicates. That is, 
he suggested that the viability of inference is directly implicated by the question of whether 
or not conceptual cognition is possible: if the latter is not possible, then inference is also 
not possible. See ŚV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 248cd–​249ab and Taber 2005, 146 for his rend­
ering of the same.
	 	   The only relation recognized by Dharmakīrti is that of cause and effect, what can be es­
tablished by a series of two perceptions and three nonperceptions. (And even this relation 
is ultimately called into question as such, about which see Saṃbandhaparīkṣā 7ff.). Thus, 
the present argument essentially anticipates Utpaladeva’s and Abhinavagupta’s similar 
claim, that a unified knower must connect discrete perceptions, inasmuch as both depend 
on the notion that the cognitions in question are utterly momentary. See, esp., ĪPK 1.2.10, 
where the Buddhist position is articulated: tatra tatra sthite tat tad bhavatīty eva dṛśyate | 
nānyan nānyo ’sti saṃbandhaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvataḥ ||. (This is what is seen and nothing 
else: where one or another entity is present another entity comes into being. There is no 
other relation [saṃbandha] than that of the relation of cause and effect.) (This translation 
is based on the renderings of Torella 1994, 95 and Ratié 2011, 298, n. 85.) The necessity of a 
single knowing agent to establish such a relation is articulated at, e.g., ĪPK 1.7.4.

--- PAGE 1129 ---
1104      John Nemec
 
	37.	 See ŚD 4.86. Unfortunately left out of this argument is any sense of Dharmakīrti’s (well-​
known) response to this concern, namely, that the product of one of the two means of valid 
knowledge—​inference—​is such that it is useful, even if it is the product of what ultimately 
is unreal and, in this sense, erroneous. To this position, an opponent of the Buddhists 
objects by asking how it is that a false apprehension can be a means of knowing. (See PV 
[pratyakṣapariccheda] 3.55: ayathābhiniveśena dvitīyā bhrāntir iṣyate | gatiś cet pararūpeṇa 
na ca bhrānteḥ pramāṇatā ||. (The second [apprehension, namely, that of the particular 
in another form] is considered to be false because it determines [the object] incorrectly. 
[Objection:] If [the second apprehension, namely, inference is] an apprehension [of the 
particular] with another form, [it is false], but a false cognition is not a means of know­
ledge [just like an illusion].) Translation that of Franco and Notake 2014, 141.)
	 	   Dharmakīrti’s reply is that even a false cognition can sometimes offer a valid means of 
knowledge, because it can lead one successfully to engage a causally efficacious action. 
(See PV [pratyakṣapariccheda] 3.56: abhiprāyāvisaṃvādād api bhrānteḥ pramāṇatā | gatir 
apy anyathā dṛṣṭā pakṣaś cāyaṃ kṛtottaraḥ ||. ((Reply:) Even an error is (sometimes) a 
means of knowledge, because the intention (of the one acting on the knowledge produced 
by the error) is not violated [-​avisaṃvāda]. Even an apprehension [gati] that is at vari­
ance [anyathā] is seen (to lead to an object capable of causal efficacy), and this position (of 
the opponent, viz., that inference must apprehend something real) has been answered to.) 
See also the rendering of Franco and Notake 2014, 142 and the notes thereon. The present 
translation is an adaptation of theirs.)
	 	   To exemplify as much Dharmakīrti offers the famous example of two errors, each 
involving a misperception leading to an awareness of the presence of a gem, only one of 
which leads one to grasp the gem. The light of a lamp, seen through a keyhole, could be 
mistaken for a jewel, as could the light of the jewel itself. The latter, if pursued, will lead one 
to acquire the gem, while the former will not. See PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.57–​58.
	38.	 See ŚD 4.87ab.
	39.	 apūrvatvād] TC; apūrvatve Ked.
	40.	 The sāmānya may be said to be related to but different from the unique particulars, the 
svalakṣaṇas. It may be defined by the similarity of effect of the svalakṣaṇas in question, 
which therefore may be referred to by a common term. See, e.g., PVSV ad PV 1.137–​142 (239 
of Pandeya’s edition): evaṃjātīyāś ca sarve samūhasantānāvasthāviśeṣaśabdā ye samastāḥ 
kiṃcid ekaṃ kāryaṃ kurvanti teṣāṃ tatra viśeṣābhāvād apārthikā viśeṣacodaneti sakṛt 
sarveṣāṃ niyojanārtham ekam ayaṃ lokaḥ śabaṃ teṣu niyuṅkte ghaṭa iti. te ’pi sajātīyād 
anyataś ca bhedāviśeṣe ’pi tatprayojanāṅgatayā tadanyebhyo bhidyanta ity abhedāt tato 
’viśeṣeṇa pratīyante. The purpose of this passage of Somānanda’s text, then, is to record the 
pūrvapakṣin’s response to Somānanda’s argument at ŚD 4.84cd–​85. A single word may be 
used to refer to multiple unique things that function in a similar manner to effect a single 
result. A perception (of smoke, e.g.) can lead to a (verbally based) conception that gives 
knowledge of another real phenomenon (fire, e.g.). In a word, Somānanda’s Buddhist op­
ponent claims a cogent explanation for the existence of a constructed, conventional uni­
versal that can effect the kinds of inferential knowledge here in question.
	41.	 I do not think reference to sādṛśya here is simply to the similarity of the perceptual image 
to the empirical object. Rather, Somānanda here suggests that his Buddhist opponent 
cannot argue that similarity (sādṛśya) may guarantee that a particular that is unique may 
be related to a general, universalized (and therefore conceptual) understanding of the

--- PAGE 1130 ---
Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi as an Argument against Dharmakīrti      1105
 
same. He wishes to argue that to thus guarantee knowledge of a unique object there must 
be something categorically real about the object itself that encompasses or guarantees the 
possibility of such similarity. A real sāmānya must properly be associated with the partic­
ular if any similarity is to be recognized at all.
	42.	 kṣaṇikatvāt] conj.; kṣaṇikatvaṃ TKed., kṣaṇitvaṃ (hypometric) C.
	 	   I conjecture that the text should read kṣaṇikatvāt where T and Ked. read kṣaṇikatvaṃ 
and C reads (hypometrically) kṣaṇitvaṃ. It seems possible that degemination led to the 
presentation of an apparently errant form (kṣaṇikatvā, losing the final c before ca), and 
a scribe, seeing the connective ca took both sthiratvam and (he supposed) kṣaṇikatvam 
to be joined thereby, correcting to kṣaṇikatvam ca from what was clearly wrong, namely, 
kṣaṇikatvā ca. I understand ca to be connective with the previous verse.
	43.	 avisaṃvādirūpāc ca] conj.; api saṃvādirūpāc ca T, atisaṃvādarūpā ca C, apy

	 	   I propose a conjectural emendation of avisaṃvādirūpāc ca where Ked. reads apy 
asaṃvādarūpaṃ ca, T witnesses api saṃvādirūpāc ca, and C atisaṃvādarūpā ca. T

and pi and vi are exceedingly similar in the Malayalam script in which T is recorded.
	44.	 Chaturvedi (1986, 162) suggests that śaktāśaktavikalpa refers to two types of conceptual 
construction, one that has the capacity to lead to purposeful action and one that does not. 
Dharmakīrti accounts for both types, the former as represented by the well-​known ex­
ample of the mistaken perception of the reflection of a jewel for the jewel itself, the latter by 
that of the light of a lamp seen through a keyhole (and understood to be the light of a gem). 
The conceptual form of the former, though erroneous, can lead to acquiring the jewel, but 
the latter example is of a conceptual form that will not accomplish the purpose in question. 
See PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.57–​58.
	45.	 I here read the negative particle twice, with both sthiratā . . . upapannā and pratyakṣenāpi

records ca sthitā, T witnesses ca sthitaiḥ, and C reads cāsthitaḥ.
	46.	 Cf. PV (pramāṇasiddhipariccheda) 2.1ab: pramāṇam avisaṃvādi jñānam arthakriyāsthitiḥ 
|. See also Dharmottara’s Nyāyabinduṭīkā, pp. 17–​18, on correct cognition as avisaṃvādaka, 
as follows: avisaṃvādakaṃ jñānaṃ samyagjñānaṃ loke ca pūrvam upadarśitam 
arthaṃ prāpayan saṃvādaka ucyate. tadvaj jñānam api pradarśitam arthaṃ prāpayat 
saṃvādakam ucyate. Ratié (2007, 351, n. 78) translates the passage as follows: (“Right know­
ledge” is a knowledge which is not deceptive [avisaṃvādaka]. And in the world (as well), 
(someone) who makes (us) reach an object that (he) has first shown (to us) is called “trust­
worthy” [saṃvādaka]. Accordingly, the knowledge also which makes (us) reach an object 
that (it has previously) shown to us is called “trustworthy.”) Cf. Ratié 2011, 134, n. 56.
	47.	 PV (pratyakṣapariccheda) 3.44: vastumātrānubandhitvād vināśasya na nityatā | 
asaṃbandhaś ca jātīnām akāryatvād arūpatā ||. (Because [being] real is sufficient to entail
