Chapter 43
Dynamic Manifestations 
of Eternal Divinity
Late Nondual Śaivism on the Emanation and 
Contemplative Reabsorption of Time
David Peter Lawrence
Introduction
There is no time to consider all the important theories and practices regarding time. 
Time has been discussed by many or most Sanskrit and world philosophical traditions. 
Time is often said to be cognized in the sequence of action or change and to be meas­
ured by the regular synchronized repetition of particular actions. Religion and philos­
ophy have often viewed temporal finitude as the central human predicament. Heidegger 
described our limited temporal situation as being-​towards-​death (Heidegger 1962, 279–​
311 and passim). Psychological terror management theory argues that the denial (or we 
may say vanquishment) of death is the foundational human motivation (Solomon et 
al. 2015).
Utpaladeva advanced the initiatives of his teacher Somānanda (ca. 900–​950 CE) 
in creating the originary verses and commentaries of the Pratyabhijñā philosophical 
theology of late nondual Śavism. Abhinavagupta is famous for brilliant and extensive 
commentaries on Utpaladeva’s writings and for the creation of a vast and influential 
corpus of philosophical hermeneutics, itself comprising both a poetics and an exegetics 
of tantric symbolism and ritual.
In nondual Śaivism, as in many Hindu understandings of male deities, the Lord is 
the śaktimān, “possessor of Śakti,” encompassing her within his androgynous nature 
as his integral Consort and Potency.1 According to the predominant nondual Śaiva 
panenthistic cosmogony and metaphysics, Śiva out of a kind of play divides himself 
from Śakti and then in sexual union emanates, embodies himself within and controls the

--- PAGE 1135 ---
1110      David Peter Lawrence
 
universe through her. The basic pattern of return is the recapitulation of the cosmogony. 
Thus, in nondual Śaivism practice the approach to Śiva is through emanatory Śakti. The 
same mythico-​ritual process is articulated in practical, symbolic, and philosophical-​
theological terms.2
The Pratyabhijñā system replicates this modus operandi in śāstraic philosophical dis­
course as the disclosure that one has Śiva’s Śakti (śaktyāviṣkaraṇa) (see IPK and IPV 
1.1.2 in IPV 1:56–​1.59; and IPK and IPV 2.3.17, 2:139–​149). The publicly intelligible in­
ference (parārthānumāna) is: I am Śiva because I have Śakti (Lawrence 1999, 49–​57).3 
The Pratyabhijñā epistemology primarily explains Śakti as the idealistically constitutive 
self-​recognition (pratyabhijñā, ahampratyavamarśa), apprehension with a recognitive 
structure or recognitive apprehension (vimarśa and cognates), and analogous 
recognitive synthesis (anusaṃdhāna and cognates) (on this vocabulary, see Lawrence 
2022, 20–​21). Śakti and its equivalents are also identified with a principle of Supreme 
Speech (parāvāk) derived from the linguistic philosopher Bhartṛhari and are thereby 
articulated in language or “subtly linguistic”—​or “semiotic”—​signifiers (Lawrence 
1999, 87–​90 and passim). Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta further conceived recogni­
tion, and so on, ontologically as universal first-​person agency (uttamapuruṣa, kartṛtva, 
svātantrya) (Lawrence 1999, 2008a, Dupuche 2001; Baumer 2011) constituting reality as 
divine action (kriyā).
In the course of this chapter, I need to introduce a few new terms and concepts. 
Previously, I have etically characterized the overall argumentation of the Pratyabhijñā 
system as a transcendental inference.4 I have also spoken of the late nondual Śaiva 
approach to time specifically as the subsumption of time and sequence (Lawrence 
2008b, 32–​37). At the outset of the present essay, I humbly suggest two more of 
such characterizations: First, the Pratyabhijñā epistemological and ontological 
interpretations of Śakti are what the West since Neoplatonism has described as 
“henological” (see the recent formulation in Macquarrie 1987)—​there is the con­
templation of unities in various domains, as deriving from the nondual Ultimate-​
cum-​Potency.5 The interpretations of Śakti—​in terms of recognition, recognitive 
apprehension, recognitive synthesis, Supreme Speech, relation, action, agency, and so 
on—​all advert to sorts of unity. In the Pratyabhijñā, henology is often articulated within 
an idealistic logic that “to be is to be perceived” (esse est percipi), as worldly unities rest in 
some sort of originary subjectivity.
Second, I suggest that the Pratyabhijñā argumentation may be characterized as a form 
of what C. S. Peirce called “abduction,” for affirming the Ultimate Self on the basis of the 
Ultimate’s potentiality and correlative practical consequences.6 The disclosure of Sakti 
more fully may be understood as the disclosure of the potentiality of a nondual agent, 
for emanating and controlling the various domains of epistemological and ontological 
diversity.
The Pratyabhijñā conceives time (kāla, and sometimes other expressions of se­
quence, though we focus on time) generated by the Kāla Śakti as one of the chief ways 
of explaining the differentiation of Śiva’s totality.7 Paradoxically, this differentiation is 
abductively posited and immediately realized as consisting of modes of dynamic unity

--- PAGE 1136 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1111
 
manifesting the unity and Potency of God. To reiterate, the main objective of this 
chapter is to demonstrate and interpret the nondual Śaiva henology and potentialism or 
abduction that ascribes sequential time to Śiva-​Śakti (paramaśiva) as unity-​cum-​potency. 
The culmination of Śaiva henological and abductive reflections and contemplations is 
the affirmation of the subitist and apophatic realization of pleromatic eternity in the re­
plete present moment.8
Backdrop of Theories and Practices 
Regarding Time and Moments
We first discuss some of the important South Asian backgrounds to the late nondual 
Śaiva understanding of time. An entire section later is devoted to some of the influen­
tial ideas of Bhartṛhari. Scholars such as Mircea Eliade (Eliade 1991) and Ananda K. 
Coomaraswamy (Coomaraswamy 1992) wrote groundbreaking early surveys of time in 
Sanskrit texts. Eliade, in his general theory of religion, contended that the eternal myth­
ical time of the Sacred transcends or sacralizes ordinary mundane times (Eliade 1958, 
388–​409).9 Eliade suggested that in Hinduism and Buddhism, with their individual and 
cosmic cycles, there is also an effort toward a transcendence of time (Eliade 1991).
A dominant, though of course not the only, theme in Hinduism is the assertion 
that an eternal Ultimate, superagent deity, Potency or related aspect of the deity, is the 
emanatory source that “encompasses” or “subsumes”—​and thereby in a sense “stops”—​
time amid worldly actions. A major source for broader henological reflection in 
Brahmanic and Hindu traditions is the Puruṣa Sūkta of the Ṛg Veda, which describes 
the emanation of the world through the sacrifice and dismemberment of an immanent-​
cum-​transcendent “Cosmic Man” (puruṣa) (Rig Veda 10.90); thus, a central theme 
of Vedic and later Hindu praxis is the recovery of the various aspects of the unity of 
God. Whether or not it was influenced by the Puruṣa Sūkta, Atharva Veda XXI 53.1–​
53.8 henologically describes the deity Time (kāla) as intentionally bringing together and 
encompassing things:
He indeed together brought beings; he indeed together went about (pari-​i) beings; 
being father, he became son of them; than him verily there is no other brilliancy that 
is higher (para).
(Atharva Veda 1905, 29.53, 2:988; cf. the rest of 2.53 and 29.54)
There are related ideas of the “reintegration” of the sacrifice in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 
(Coomaraswamy 1992, 173–​174).
In the discussion of time in Maitrī Upaniṣad, brahman is said to have the forms of both 
time and timelessness, described as being with parts (kala) and henologically without 
parts (akala) (Upaniṣatsaṅgraha 1970, 6.15, 185). The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad states that,

--- PAGE 1137 ---
1112      David Peter Lawrence
 
through dhyana and yoga, some have found the divine self’s potency (devātmaśakti) 
ruling over kāla and other causes (Upaniṣatsaṅgraha, 1.3, 135).10 Finally, another early 
deification of time is evinced in the omnipotent Kṛṣṇa’s identification with time in the 
11th chapter of the Gītā (1975, 11.32, 311).11
While not a passage on the eternalization/​deification of time per se, the Īśā Upaniṣad 
takes perhaps a step toward a henological explanation. It describes a sort of religious 
“transfiguration” of temporal change or action as a conjunction of an entry into, and de­
parture from, existence.
He who knows as conjoined [saha]—​origination [saṃbhūti] and destruction 
[vināśa]—​with destruction overcomes death, and with origination gains immor­
tality [amṛta]
(Īśā Upaniṣad, in Upaniṣatsaṅgraha 1970, 14, 1).12
We return to this crucial issue of temporal sequence as the relation of existence with 
nonexistence throughout this chapter.
The Śaivas were also influenced by the classic Yoga and Sāṃkhya position, which 
presents an alternative henological argument to that based on the deification of the 
causal essence of time. Maintaining the preexistence of the effected world in its source, 
these schools assert the constructedness and unreality of time. For these traditions, time 
is a potential or actualized quality (dharma) in the transformation (pariṇāma) of an en­
during, unifying nature (prakṛti) (Patañjali et al. 1998, 3.13–​3.15, 290–​305). Prakṛti does 
not have the variety of potentiality that is agency, associated with conscious intention­
ality. However, for them Prakṛti does have an unconscious potentiality in the form of a 
repleteness for manifestation.
According to Yoga, prakṛti as substratum is actually one with the moment (kṣaṇa), as 
the locus of all change in the world. Yoga thus prescribes a discipline of concentration 
(saṃyama) on the moment (kṣaṇa) within transformation. That discipline creates a re­
versal of transformation and the subsumption of sequence within the present moment 
(Patañjali et al. 1998, 3.52, 383–​390,13 4.31–​4.34). The Yoga discipline was appropriated 
in various nondual and theistic metaphysics and axiologies.14 This practice is also 
discussed further below.
As already mentioned, another important background to the Śaiva philos­
ophy of time is Buddhism. The Buddhist theories of greatest interest to Western 
scholars deconstruct henological and other substantialist notions of the traversal of 
time, with interpretations, sometimes idealistic, of the doctrine of dependent origina­
tion (pratītyasamutpada). Early Abhidharma theories of time and moments (kṣaṇa) 
seem to have developed in close communication with Sāṃkhya and Yoga and con­
ceive kṣaṇa as similar to a quality (dharma), but without an underlying substance 
(Stcherbatsky 1983, 43–​48). Reminding us of Eliade, Steven Collins contended that 
Buddhists understand nirvāṇa as an, albeit often metaphysically aporetic, realization 
that overcomes time (1998, 121–​285).

--- PAGE 1138 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1113
 
Alexander von Rospatt suggested that a theory of universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) 
may have first been popularized by Sarvāstivādins. The Yogācāra of Vasubandhu argued 
for the immediate origination and destruction of phenomena, as can be illumined in 
mindful awareness (see Rospatt 1995; de La Vallee Poussin 1934; Silburn 1955). In the 
Śaivas’s chief opponents and a major appropriated source—​the logical-​epistemological 
tradition of Dignāga, Dharmakīrti, and their successors—​reality is posited as a stream of 
instantaneous, self-​characterized particulars (svalakṣaṇa), unqualified even by sequential 
relation.
Bhartṛhari’s Theories and Practices Regarding Time
The greatest influence on the Śaivas, Bhartṛhari’s linguistic or semiotic philosophy 
of time (ca. 400–​500 CE), advanced earlier Vedic and Buddhist ideas. Like earlier 
Brāhmaṇic or Hindu eternalizations and deifications of time, for Bhartṛhari the Kāla 
Śakti of the unitary and nonsequential (akrama) “Word Absolute” (śabdabrahman) is its 
Potency for the emanation of all sequential diversity (krama). The Kāla Śakti and time 
are summarized near the very beginning of the Vākyapadīya and further clarified in 
later verses from the Kāla Samuddeśa:
The beginningless and endless, Brahaman, the nature of which is Word [śabda], from 
which are the phonemes—​[also] projects [vivartate]15 objects. From that, there is the 
production [prakriyā] of the world. (VP 1966, 1.1, 1:1)
That which has been known through tradition [āmnāta] as entirely one [ekam] is the 
basis of diverse Śaktis. Even though there is no separation, that projects as if separate 
from the various Śaktis [in their emanation]. (VP 1966, 1.2, 1:14)
Resting on whose Time Potency [kālaśakti], to which are ascribed partitions—​the 
six changes, that is, production, and so on [existence, transformation, growth, decay 
and destruction] are the sources [yonayaḥ] of the diversity of entities. [bhāva]. (VP 
1966, 1.3, 1:18)
However, the differentiation of the synchronized [saṃsargiṇām, that is, active 
entities] are regarded as its [measured] specifics. Differentiated by them, time [kāla], 
constructs the differentiation of situations [avasthānām]. (VP 1973, 3.9.8, 3.2)
The Omnipresent, impelling its partitions [kalā] through actions that are like the 
turnings of a water wheel, thus obtains the name time [kāla]. (VP 1973, 3.9.14, 3.2:45)
The action [viceṣṭita] of time is the arisal of the appearance [nirbhāsa] of the universe, 
which is actually sequenceless—​as if it were sequential. (VP 1973, 3.9.46, 3.2:57)16
Anticipating the Śaivas, Bhartṛhari explained (taking the Vṛtti as the work of 
Bhartṛhari) that the Kāla Śakti of śabdabrahman is also its agency:

--- PAGE 1139 ---
1114      David Peter Lawrence
 
Indeed there are all powers, which are heteronomous [paratantra] and have their 
origin—​by means of the agential autonomy [svātantrya] named the Kāla Śakti. 
(VPV 1966, 1.3, 1:18)17
Bhartṛhari additionally theorized that a unitary-​eternal and emanatory Kāla 
subsumes the moments and other temporal divisions that constitute sequential time:
Such enduring [unitary] time [kāla], through divisions by the intellect [buddhi] 
[becomes] the worldy usages of moment [kṣaṇa], yuga and manvantara. (VP 1973, 
3.9.6, 48)18
We again return to the consideration of moments in nondual Śaivism.
In the present context, we recall the passage of a contemplation in the Īśā Upaniṣad in 
which there is a religious transfiguration of temporal change or action as an entry into 
and departure from existence.19 In my interpretation of the underlying concept, in any 
action, there is a combination of continuity and difference, or existence and nonexist­
ence. Amidst differences, one identifies both the continuities of the action itself and the 
acting items in one condition and then another; Bhartṛhari explains this as the Time 
Potency’s employment of allowance (abhyanujñā) and prevention (pratibandha):
There is contrariety within the manifold universe. By means of prevention and al­
lowance, brought about through their discrimination by Śakti, there is the manifes­
tation [of that manifold universe] as if it were sequential. (VPV 1966, 1.3, 1:18–​1.19)20
We will see that the Śaivas further reduced directly to Paramaśiva’s unity, time’s very 
constellation of allowance-​prevention or existence-​nonexistence.
Pratyabhijñā Theorization on Time: 
Explanatory and Contemplative 
Subsumption
Evidently the influence of Bhartṛhari on tantra precedes the Pratyabhijñā. Thus, Pierre-​
Sylvain Filliozat demonstrated the influence of Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of time on 
āgamas such as the Mataṅgapārameśvara and Siddhānta thinkers such as Rāmakaṇṭha 
(2009, 221–​223). Though Somānanda is well known to have had his reservations about 
Bhartṛhari, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta utilized that thinker’s linguistic philosophy 
as a central component of their system (Torella 2008). Bhartṛhari is the primary source 
for their theories of time.
Inspired by Bhartṛhari’s as well as earlier Hindu, Buddhist, and tantric 
contemplations—​Abhinavagupta’s own name as ever-​new (abhinava) and hidden 
(gupta) or eternal, came to epitomize the late nondual Śaiva approach to the moments

--- PAGE 1140 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1115
 
that constitute sequential time.21 Like Bhartṛhari, the Śaivas described temporal se­
quence as characterizing worldly action (IPV 2.1.2).22 Just as the Pratyabhijñā theory of 
the recognition (potency) I call transcendental subverts the Buddhist epistemologies of 
instantaneity, so the eternal Kāla Śakti emanates the flux of time.
Utpaladeva explained Paramaśiva as the Unity-​cum-​Potency underlying all sequence 
and diversity, sometimes quantifiable by synchronous repetition:
It is possible for worldly [laukikya] action to be sequential, due to the [Lord’s] Time 
Potency [kālaśakti]. However, [sequence] cannot belong to the eternal [action] of 
the Lord, just as it cannot belong to the Lord himself. (2.1.2)
Time [in worldly experience] is really [tattvataḥ] nothing but the sequence [krama] 
indicated by movement of the sun, and so on, the birth of various flowers, or hot and 
cold. (2.1.3)
That Lord causes to manifest [ābhāsayati] . . . the sequence of time from the 
manifestations [nirbhāsa] of the diversity of action. (2.1.5) (IPV 2:10–​16)23
In the Pratyabhijñā explanation, there are at least two levels of henology-​cum-​
postulation pointing to the intertwined Action (kriyā) and Time (kāla) Śaktis. First, 
the Śaivas explicitly invoke the recognition (pratyabhijñā) and recognitive synthesis 
(potencies) to account for the uninterruptedness of active entities within temporal 
sequence:
However, from the force of the awareness [prakāśa] of strong recognition 
[pratyabhijñā], there is the experience,“This is that very characteristic form of the 
hand.” In that conception, there is no differentiation of material form [mūrti]. Yet 
different forms appear [bhāti]. Those different forms that cannot exist in that which 
has a single form, are explained to be action, which cannot exist as such because of 
contradiction. He manifests the diversity of that [action] through its recognitive 
synthesis [anusaṃdhāna] as measured [actions such as the going of Devadatta] and 
unmeasured [actions such the repetitive movement of the sun],24 and according to 
emotional proclivities [yathāruci] about what is conceived [carcitena], as the basis 
for the accomplishment of [particular] results. Thus, he manifests that very sequence 
that has the form of time.
(IPV 2.1.5, 2:17)25
At the same level of henology, the Śaivas also asserted the unity of action itself across 
time as the coordination of syntactico-​semantic factors (kārakas, things expressed by 
words declined in what the West calls “cases”) in the sequence of process (vyāpāra). 
Utpaladeva asserted:
The coordination [samanvaya] of the action-​factors [kāraka] is the domain of the 
recognitive apprehension [vimarśa, potency] of action [kriyā].
(IPV 2.2.6, 2:54)

--- PAGE 1141 ---
1116      David Peter Lawrence
 
Abhinavagupta explained the unity in this manner:
Thus, kārakas also have the nature of nothing but relation [sambandha]. . . . A kāraka 
depends on action [kriyā]. That [kriyā] also rests upon kāla, which is the Lord of its 
life [prāṇeśvara]. And that kāla, which through action [kriyā] is the essence of all 
entities, depends upon relation [sambandha].
(IPV 2.2.4, 2:47–​2.49)26
Abhinavagupta also identified the recognitive apprehension (vimarśa potency) of ac­
tion itself (kriyā) as established through the semantic and syntactic relations of the 
kārakas articulated in the epistemic triad (tripuṭi) of cognizer (pramātṛ), means of cog­
nition (pramāṇa), and object of cognition (prameya). (Lawrence 1999, 150–​152)
The Pratyabhijñā thinkers do not conceive that there are emanated unities only 
amidst the temporal sequence of action. At the second level of henology, they con­
template temporal sequence or difference as itself an emanated unity. This builds on the 
understandings of time we examined in the Īśā Upaniṣad and Bhartṛhari, of time as the 
relation of the existence-​and-​nonexistence, or allowance-​and-​prevention of the aspects 
of action. Utpaladeva thus explains temporal sequence in terms of the existence and 
nonexistence of manifestations brought about by the divine:
Sequence has differentiation as its substratum. There is differentiation from 
the existence and nonexistence of manifestations. The existence and nonex­
istence of manifestations is due to the Lord, who is the maker of variegated 
manifestations.
(IPK 2.1.4)27
In this vein, Abhinavagupta interpreted time as a relation between something in the al­
ternate conditions of being with and without, in the course of action:
The extension of one’s [an example such as Devadatta’s] action [kriyā] subsisting ei­
ther as being with or without—​such is time, which is present, and so on [absent].
(IPV 2.2.4)28
Abhinavagupta has explained worldly time as the relation of difference between 
manifestations of something in the course of action.29 He has in effect explained differ­
ence as a kind of emanated unity.30
To repeat, the Śaivas have discovered an emanated unity amidst difference and such 
a unity as difference itself.31 Finally, reminding the reader of the religious context of the 
Śaiva philosophy, the Śaivas distinguish between the unenlightened immersion in se­
quential temporality and the subsumption of it within the eternal:
In all things, the differentiation of manifestations may be the basis for the sequence of 
time for the knower . . . who has a limited light [vicchinnabhāsa]. However, it cannot

--- PAGE 1142 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1117
 
[be the basis for the sequence of time for the unlimited knower], who has manifested 
already and always [sakṛd].
(IPK 2.1.6, 2:20)32
Further Contemplations of the 
Subsumption of Temporal 
Sequence (Krama)
The Krama, “Sequence,” tradition of tantric symbolism and ritual interpreted by 
Abhinavagupta and his commentator, Jayaratha, well illustrates the religious sub­
sumption of immanent time and sequence into the potency of the nondual eternal. 
Basing himself on the Kālīkulapañcaśataka and other āgamas (see Sanderson 2007), 
Abhinavagupta viewed Śakti or Potency as Kālī (TS 6, 45–​4633; cf. Rastogi 1992). In 
Krama, Kālis are commonly differentiated as twelvefold (there are other numerical 
divisions), in terms of knower (pramātṛ), means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and object 
of knowledge (prameya) multiplied by creation (sṛṣṭi), continuation (sthiti), withdrawal 
(saṃhāra), and the inexpressible (anākhyā). These twelve Kālīs correspond to moments 
of sequence in the process of cognition.
Building on the erasure of sequence into the apophasis of the divine, the Kālīs 
are finally dissolved into the Goddess as Kālasaṃkarśinī, “the Retractor of Time.” 
Abhinavagupta explained the underlying consciousness:
Therefore, consciousness [saṃvit], which is entirely unitary, subsists as twelvefold 
in all cognizers. Thus, there is never a specification [niyama] that sequence [krama] 
belongs to it. There is no simultaneity because of the lack of sequence. There is also 
no sequence because of the lack of that [simultaneity]. Because that principle of con­
sciousness [saṃvittattva] has transcended [atīta] talk of sequence and nonsequence, 
it is without taint [nirmala].
(TA 1987b, 4.178cd–​180a, 3:823–​824)
This Krama tantra is reflected in the program of the eleventh-​ to twelfth-​century 
nondual Śaiva contemplative manual, Virūpākṣapañcāśikā. That text advocates the 
contemplative subsumption of sequence discussed by Abhinavagupta. A divine per­
fect egoity (pūrṇāhaṃtā subsumes the limited knower (pramātṛ), knowledge (pramā), 
the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and the object of knowledge (prameya) (Lawrence 
2008b, 32–​37).
I can only mention here the complex schemes of the emanation and reabsorption of 
time in terms of breath [prāṇa] and other subtle physiology, tantric theosophy, cosmic 
cycles, and moments or small portions of ti (tuṭi) throughout the Tantrāloka and partic­
ularly in the discussion of concentration on the place (sthānaprakalpanāī) in Tantrāloka

--- PAGE 1143 ---
1118      David Peter Lawrence
 
6 (TA 19887b, 6, 3:1089–​1291). The basic henological-​potentialist realization regarding 
time is as described:
Supreme Time [the Kāla Śakti] has the nature of sequence and nonsequence and 
subsists in [nondual] consciousness [saṃvid]. The one called Kālī is praised as the 
Supreme Śakti of God.
(TA 6.7, 3:1094)34
Intercultural Reflections
We find numerous other examples of the quest for a unitary and potent, often but 
not always agentive—​Ultimate, generator or creator—​of time throughout the world. 
Henological-​cum-​potentialist reflections aimed at establishing a nondual, eternal, the­
istic, or nontheistic Creative Source are found throughout Western traditions. They 
are paramount in varieties of Platonism and Neoplatonism, though less completely 
expressed in Aristotelianism that has not been influenced by Neoplatonism, as is 
Thomism.
In the Timaeus, Plato suggests that God or the Good somehow emanated the syn­
chronously measured dunamis of this shadowy word:
Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order 
the heaven he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eter­
nity itself rests in unity, and this image we call time. For there were no days and 
nights and months and years before the heaven was created, but when he constructed 
the heaven he created them also.
(Plato, 37d-​e)
However, the schemes of emanation in Timaeus are interrupted ironically by the “sub­
lation” of temporal becoming by being in Parmenides, The Republic, and other dialogs. 
While aporias about the possibility of change preclude a firm understanding of poten­
tiality in Plato, he in any event conceives a likeness to its source in the entire creation as 
mediated through participation in the Ideas or Forms that unify spatiotemporal differ­
ence (e.g., Plato 1989, 1163; Gerson 2004). Victor Ilievski has argued that the sempiter­
nity of cosmic time that qualifies motion is an image of the eternity of God and the Ideas 
(Ilievski 2015).
We may leave aside the question of emanation in Aristotle’s philosophy of the eternity 
of the world. Nevertheless, Aristotle developed profound conceptions of act and poten­
tiality (Dufour 2004), which Plotinus forthrightly appropriated within Neoplatonism. 
Plotinus maintained that a transcendent, eternal One in its potent (whether or not 
agential) and overflowing perfection manifests the immanently actualized world, via 
the Ideas and hypostases. Plotinus says about time and eternity:

--- PAGE 1144 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1119
 
Eternity, we have said, is Life in repose, unchanging, self-​identical, always endlessly 
complete; and there is to be an image of Eternity—​Time—​such an image as this 
lower All presents of the Higher Sphere. . . . Over against that Oneness without ex­
tent or interval there must be an image of oneness, a unity of link and succession. . . 
. Over against the Whole in concentration, there must be that which is to be a whole 
by stages never final. The lesser must always be working toward the increase of its 
Being; this will be its imitation of what is immediately complete, self-​realized, end­
less without stage: only thus can its Being reproduce that of the Higher.
(Plotinus 1992, III.7, 266)
Plotinus describes the contemplation of time: “If, then, the Soul withdrew, sinking itself 
again into its primal unity, Time would disappear” (Plotinus 1992, 3.7, 267).35 Proclus 
explains tersely:
Eternity . . . is indeed measure as unity, but time as number. . . . And the former meas­
ures the [eternal] permanency of beings, but the latter the [enduring or sempiternal] 
extension of generated natures.
(Proclus 2017, 4.189, 499, my bracketed inserts)
There are numerous Jewish, Christian, and Muslim expressions of Neoplatonism in 
which the One that emanates time is identified with the Abrahamic, omnipotent cre­
ator God. Their theologies have encompassed Platonic and Aristotelian immanence 
in the world and time, within a dialectical tension with their religions’ emphasis on 
transcendence.36
Italian, Christian Renaissance Neoplatonist, Marsilio Ficino strongly emphasized the 
older Neoplatonic doctrine of the midpositionality and consequent choice of the soul 
between unitary and omnipotent, divine eternity and mundane temporality (Ficino 
2010, 450).37 Ficino’s Neoplatonism greatly influenced later Romanticism, occultism, 
and German, British, and American idealism. In my understanding, henology is re­
flected in Kant’s “transcendental unity of apperception,” although that thinker greatly 
limited the metaphysical meanings of unity and the transcendental.
This quest for a theistic, dynamic unity was later found in American philosopher 
Charles Sanders Peirce. Peirce was deeply influenced by Friedrich Schelling’s “nature 
philosophy” (Franks 2015, 732–​734; Niemoczynski 2011, 110–​112, 117–​121) and thus in­
directly by Neoplatonism (for the interpretation of Peirce himself as a Neoplatonist, see 
Parker 2001).38 Like Schelling, Peirce described his prospective synthesis of idealism 
with science as “objective idealist.” Various scholars have also characterized Peirce as 
a panentheist.39 Granting his more dualistic proclivities, Peirce sometimes came rather 
close to the Pratyabhijñā philosophy:
And what is religion? In each individual it is a sort of sentiment, or obscure percep­
tion, a deep recognition of something in the circumambient All, which if he strives 
to express it, will clothe itself in forms more or less extravagant, or less accidental, but

--- PAGE 1145 ---
1120      David Peter Lawrence
 
ever acknowledging the first and the last, the [𝚨] and [𝛀], as well as a relation to that 
Absolute of the individual self, as a relative being.
(CP 6.429, 302)
Like Bhartṛhari and the Śaivas on Word or Speech, Peirce also variously described the 
world as a sign, poem, argument, painting, and so on, of God.40
We should recall Abhinavagupta on temporal action as a relation, deriving from 
nondual divine Potency, unifying the syntactico-​semantic factors (kārakas) in which 
action takes place. Introducing a couple of new terms to reconstruct more of Peirce’s 
metaphysics, it is suggested that his henology was articulated in terms of what he called 
synechism. While sometimes claimed to be a regulative principle of reason, this concep­
tion is frequently and ultimately constitutive. Synechism may be viewed as an alterna­
tive to monism/​nondualism in its reduction of everything, including time-​-​to a unitary 
and integral (panentheistic) continuum (on Peirce regarding unification or synthesis 
and its backgrounds in Kant, see Corrington 1993, 53, 93, 180; Niemoczynski, 47; on the 
synechism of time, see Schmidt 2020).
Even more thematically than for the Neoplatonists, for Peirce the unified continuum 
also comprehends what he called an element of tychism, a potentiality that becomes im­
manent as in indeterminacy and chance. Peirce interpreted creatio ex nihilo not prima­
rily in terms of God’s lack of a preexisting material cause, but from his ordering creation 
and time from what in Genesis is called tohu bohu, a state of unlimited potentiality or in­
determinate chaos (CP 6.490, 337; cf. Niemoczynski 2011, 48–​53, 64; Raposa 1989, 70–​71; 
Corrington 1993, 200, with links to Platonism).41 Leon J. Niemoczynski explained this 
primordial condition in a manner reminiscent of the way the Śaivas conceive Śakti:
I begin my project by considering “infinite being” first as an honorific sheer avail­
ability of being: potential or possible being that is the unlimited and supreme power 
behind the divine’s creative becoming. I entitle this creative becoming “the divine 
life,” as it represents the life of possibilities continuous phasing into actuality that 
makes for the evolutionary growth and development of the divine’s created cosmos. 
I then proceed to consider infinite being in terms of how hypothesis-​formation, or 
Peircean “abduction,” may reveal the infinite to be an encompassing reality of nature 
that situates and locates but also sustains what is finite (specifically in this context 
human inquirers, but also other life in a perspectival universe)
(Niemoczynski 2011, 2; cf. Niemocynski 2011, 120).
For Peirce, there was the consequent accumulation in actualized diversity of what 
we could call henological “habits” or unifying regularities grounded in the originary 
synechism-​cum-​tychism.42 These regularities include scientific laws, which Peirce 
described as “ideas or resolutions in the mind of some vast consciousness, who . . . is a 
Deity relatively to us” (CP 5.107, 69). They also include the order of relations in time.
In the temporal-​process orientations of later Peircean pansemiotics and biosemiotics, 
habits also become the unifying information in ever-​evolving, self-​organizing sys­
tems, adjusting to potentially and actually changing circumstances.43 Soren Brier found

--- PAGE 1146 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1121
 
support for this in Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers’s contention (1984) that in the 
big bang of contemporary cosmology “nothing became everything” (Brier 2008, 22). 
In the thermodynamic context, biological as well as cultural evolution are rudimen­
tary unifying or counterentropic “dissipative structures,” developing by tychistic “order 
through fluctuation” (Prigogine and Stengers 1984).
Somewhat like the Īśā Upaniṣad, Bhartṛhari and the Śaivas, Peirce described time as an 
experienced but inexplicable combination of what amounts to existence and nonexistence:
It is simply a unidimensional continuum of sorts of states of things and that these 
have an antitypy is shown by the fact that a sort of state of things and a different one 
cannot both be at the same time.
(Peirce 1908, 1976, 2:611,)44
Peirce is one of the fundamental influences on philosopher and theologian Robert 
Cummings Neville. Somewhat along the lines of Peirce, Neville conceived creatio ex ni­
hilo as the generation of the determinate from a potent, indeterminate source, often pos­
ited with a great deal of apophasis. Surprisingly, he contended that there is creatio ex 
nihilo whether cosmogony is viewed as coming from divine command, “out of thin air,” 
as it were, or from preexistent matter or self-​emanation.45
In Eternity and Time’s Flow, Neville described his position as a form of panentheism 
that views the cosmos as constituted within the immanence of God’s creative, eternal 
unity (Neville 1993, 180). The creative, eternal unity of past, present, and future is the 
henological basis of all sorts of relations through time:
The ontologically creative act is the context of mutual relevance, and only by virtue 
of the eternal unity of this act can there be temporal relations among the creatures 
with changing moments of present existence. Time’s flow is made possible by eternal 
togetherness.
(Neville 1993, 198)
Conclusion: Suppose That the Nondual 
Śaivas Contemplatively Absorb 
Sequential Time Within an Ineffable, 
Transtemporal Now of What They 
Conceive as the Divine Self
In the absorption of sequential time into the divine potency contained in the uni­
tary, transtemporal now, the relation of existence and nonexistence comes to a head.

--- PAGE 1147 ---
1122      David Peter Lawrence
 
As discussed above, long before nondual Śaivism, Yoga also established for South 
Asian traditions that one can realize that all sequence is subsumed within the present 
through concentration on a moment (kṣaṇa). Esteemed tantra scholar and practi­
tioner Hemendra Nath Chakravarty suggested that in nondual Śaiva contemplations of 
the moment (kṣaṇa), through kālasaṃkarśana, one realizes an equilibrium in spanda 
[cosmic vibration, a synonym for Śakti], beyond the gross oscillation of sequential time 
(Chakravarty 1985, 121; my bracketed explanation). Spanda is a nondual, potential “sort 
of” a movement (kiṃciccalana).
Although nondual Śaivas do contemplate the subtle physiology and cosmology 
of temporal intervals or moments [tuṭi], they do not thematize the moment per se as 
extensively as do other varieties of tantra. For them all sequence is subsumed in the 
nondual and replete “eternal present” of Śiva. We find the basis for Śaiva subitism in 
reconsidering Utpaladeva’s statement:
The differentiation of manifestations may be the basis for the sequence of time for the 
knower . . . who has a limited light [vicchinnabhāsa]. However, it cannot [be the basis 
for the sequence of time for the unlimited knower], who has manifested already and 
always [sakṛd].
(IPK 2.1.6, 2:20)46
In a different context, on the basis of self-​luminosity as well as soterific agency or 
grace, Abhinavagupta taught the sudden, present realization of Śiva throughout the 
discussion of the “nonmeans” (anupāya) in the second chapters of the Tantrāloka and 
Tantrasāra. All reality is a nondual and omnipotent consciousness (cittamātratattvva) 
as I. Since the subitist transcendence of all means of attainment includes means of the 
attainment of ordinary cognition (pramāṇa), the discussion of the nonmeans is also rig­
orously apophatic (TA 2, 2:111–​152; TS 2, 9).47
Plotinus articulates a hoary theme in Western culture of a replete eternal now:
We know it as a Life changelessly motionless and ever holding the Universal content 
in actual presence; not this now and now that another, but a consummation without 
part or interval. All its content is in immediate concentration as at one point; nothing 
in it ever knows development: all remains identical within itself, knowing nothing of 
change, for ever in a Now, since nothing of it has passed away or will come into being, 
but what it is now, that is ever.
(Plotinus 1992, 3.7, 255)
From an alternative philosophical perspective, Peirce also agreed that the potenti­
ality of the present moment synechistically and tychistically subsumes the rest of time. 
To further understand this, we need to consider his theory of the nature of moments—​
such as the present—​themselves. Peirce conceived moments as infinitesimals (Raposa 
1989, 49; Levy 1991) that are defined as “less than any finite quality” (Peirce 1976, 3:989). 
He maintained that each infinitesimal contains the entire flow of time (NE 3, 989; cf.

--- PAGE 1148 ---
Dynamic Manifestations of Eternal Divinity      1123
 
Raposa 1989, 49, and Niemoczynsky, 46).48 Neville similarly described a particular tem­
poral moment as “an abstraction from the whole” (Neville 1993, 173). Neville described 
the present moment as the place of “spontaneous creativity” in which temporal change 
takes place (Neville 1993, 86).49 In what we would call their henology and potentialism, 
these reflections are rather similar to the Śaiva disclosure of Śakti in the kṣaṇa.50
Paralleling Abhinavagupta’s reflections on the insolubility of the relation of unity and 
diversity, Peirce affirmed impossibility of the logical-​comprehensibility of the moment 
in his contention that there cannot even be found a pure moment because it would be 
contradictory. As in any action, something somehow becomes something, somewhere, 
or what not, else—​in a moment something would have to be itself and not itself at the same 
time (“The Logic of Time” in Schmidt 2020). Robert Corrington, in formulating his the­
ology of “ecstatic naturalism” on the basis of Peirce, made an interesting comment:
Infinitesimals are not so much discrete units as they are potencies that compel 
continua into being, while, ironically, opening out forms of novelty and chance. The 
ontological status of the infinitesimal is unique. It is neither an order with the world 
nor is it pure nothingness. I suggest that the infinitesimal is a kind of ontological link 
between the depth dimension of nature (the greater nothingness) and the manifest 
world of phenomena. . . . We cannot find an infinitesimal, if by “find” is meant that we 
isolate it as an object of inquiry. However, we can feel the pulsations of infinitesimals 
whenever we see continua grow and, at the same time, allow for diversity.
(Corrington 1993, 188–​189)
We cannot here inquire further into possibilities of mystical experience in Peirce or 
theologians influenced by him. Abhinavagupta was speaking of a subitist and apophatic 
religious realization of nondual and pleromatic Śiva-​Śakti.51 Bringing things together, the 
obscure nondual Śaiva named Nāgārjuna or Nāga states in the text Paramārcanatriṃśikā:
Śiva is changelessly devoid of conceptual constructions [kalpanā] regarding cogni­
tion and object of cognition, and without abode. When one is not very deeply ab­
sorbed into him in a moment [kṣaṇāt], worship [arcana] has no value
(Paramārcanatriṃśikā 10, edited in Kaw 1960, 32).52

	1.	 A higher female deity also often encompasses a male component.
	2.	 Although there are strongly apophatic (nirguṇa) traditions in Hinduism (including in 
nondual Śaivism), Hindu theism often approaches the divine through its (emanated) im­
manent traces or images. Diana Eck has explained that the Hindu divine makes itself pre­
sent through images (Eck 1985, 46, 51), and that “the divine is visible not only in temples 
and shrines, but also in the whole continuum of life—​in nature, in people, in birth and 
growth and death” (Eck 1985, 10). Gavin Flood discussed how the various accoutrements 
of tantric practice contain the immanent manifestations of the divine (2006). On the clas­
sification of nondual Śaivism with Karl Christian Friedrich Krause’s term “panentheism,” 
see Lawrence, 1999, 169. Loriliai Biernacki has creatively explored many aspects of nondual 
Śaivism as panentheism. For a survey of panentheism that includes nondual Śaivism, see 
Biernacki 2013. On the emphasis on the combination of transcendence with immanence, or 
a “vaguely panentheistic ultimate” in the nonaffiliated spirituality movement, see Forman 
2004, 51–​60. John Macquarrie (1987) labeled “panentheism” as “dialectical theism.” (Robert 
S. Corrington proposed the additional alternative of “deep pantheism.”) In the contempo­
rary period, including in retrievals of tantra and nondual Kashmir Śaivism, the Ultimate’s 
panentheistic transcendence-​cum-​immanence has been highly praised as mediating tradi­
tional “other-​worldly” and modern “this-​worldly” values (Lawrence 2001, 2022). I believe 
that panentheism and so on are a matter of emphasis rather than a unique doctrine, and 
that some transcendence and immanence are necessary respectively for its ultimacy and 
expressibility. As John Mbiti’s theological phenomenology, Concepts of God in Africa stated: 
“The transcendence of God is a difficult attribute to grasp, and one which must be balanced 
with God’s immanence. The two attributes are paradoxically complementary: God is “far” 
(transcendent), and men cannot reach him; but God is also “near” immanent, and he comes 
close to men.” (Mbiti 1979, 12)
	 	   What differs are cosmogonic and other metaphysical understandings of transcendence 
and immanence in relation to one another. Panentheism and its relatives emphasize both 
polarities.

“I am this” (aham idam). One more of the diverse Śaiva ontological categories is relation

(sambandha), which includes among its rudimentary forms relations between guru and dis­
ciple, subject and object, word and object, and object and object. All syntactic associations

Cf. the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha, which comprehends nondual Śaivism among its influences: “All re­

	6.	 In spite of the further characterization, I remain unready to induct, deduct, or abduce—​that 
abduction is an entirely separate type of argument from induction and deduction. In any 
event, there is such a practical judgment or argument as has been called abduction. This clas­
sification of Pratyabhijñā argument as abduction accords with (1) the significance of Śakti as 
a Potency, Potentiality, or Capability to effect practical results (arthakriyā), including basic 
epistemological and ontological explicanda, or in the case of Time, sequential action or 
change itself; (2) the system’s stated highest purpose of bestowing on humanity the practical 
benefit (upakāra) of identity with the deity, described as the attainment of all prosperity (this 
interpretation construes samastasampatsamāvāpthetu in the benedictory verse of the IPK as 
a tatpuruṣa; Lawrence 1999, 38-​43); (3) Abhinavagupta’s approach to the arbitration of diver­
gent recognitions or knowledge claims in terms of coherence-​in-​practical utility (nirbādha 
in pursuing arthakriyā; Lawrence 2013); (4) the parāthānumāna’s grounding of an inference’s 
deductive conclusion in pragmatically formulated inductions and deductions (Lawrence 
2022; Lawrence unpublished manuscript); and (5) John Hick’s fallibilistic construal of reli­
gious arguments as demonstrations of the coherence of intellectual options rather than final 
proofs (Hick 1964).
	 	   My interpretation of Pratyabhijñā argument as abduction was developed in discussions 
between Arindam Chakrabarti, myself, and Sean MacCracken, for whose doctoral disser­
tation Prof. Chakrabarti and I were both readers. As I recall, Prof. Chakrabarti was the first 
to discuss abduction in another context. Then Dr. MacCracken was the first explicitly to 
ask whether the Pratyabhijñā inference may be understood as an abduction. Both Prof. 
Chakrabarti and I thought that this accorded with our own understandings of the philos­
ophy. Of course, both Prof. Chakrabarti and Dr. Maccracken may change their minds or 
develop their own understanding of these topics. After completing the present interpre­
tation, I read the somewhat different treatment of transcendental argument and practical 
hypotheses in the completed work of MacCracken in 2021. For Charles Sanders Peirce’s own 
abductive “Neglected Argument” for the reality of God, see CP 6.452–​6.493, 311–​339. See 
the discussion of this argument and its relation to abduction in Raposa 1989, 123–​137 and 
passim. Grounding himself in ideas of Peirce, Robert S. Corrington formulated a theology 
of “ecstatic naturalism” associated with his “deep pantheism” that affirms that the numinous 
presents within nature. For a later expression, see Corrington 2000. Leon J. Niemoczynski 
further built on views of Peirce and Corrington (Niemoczynski 2011).
	 	   We may ponder how many logical problems or paradoxes would be obviated, or at 
least deferred, if we interpreted Śakti as “Potentiality” or “Potency.” We could also speak 
of potencies of recognitive apprehension, self-​reflection, and so on. Arindam Chakrabarti 
agreed with the rationales in support of the present hypothesis and also thought that I 
should continue to engage with questions about it.

	 7.	 The Pratyabhijñā thinkers conceived of at least seven abstract ways of explaining the dif­
ferentiation of Śiva’s totality: (1) The Kāla Śakti, generating the sequence (krama) of time, 
place, form, and so on. (2) The fragmentation (khaṇḍanā), contraction (saṃkoca), and 
so on, of his pūrṇatā, “perfection, completeness or pleroma.” (3) Semantic Exclusion 
and Inferential Noncommitance (apoha), generated by the Apohanaśakti (on the appro­
priation of this concept in debate with the Buddhists; see Lawrence 2018; Pruiett 2019 
correlates construction/​exclusion with time). (4) Fantastic Fabrication (māyā), brought 
about by the Māyāśakti, invoked to explain the epistemology and theodicy of delusion (on 
the relation of the Māyā and Kāla Śaktis, see Torrella’s note to Utpaladeva 2002, 153n39). 
(5) Derivative or emanatory relations between personal pronouns-​cum-​referents: That is, 
from the indexical “I” (aham) emerges “this” (idam), or more fully “you” (tvam) and “this” 
(idam). (6). Derivative or emanatory relations in the semantics-​cum-​syntax and corre­
sponding referents of action and its action factors (kāraka) (kriyākāraka theory): From 
the divine agent (kartṛ) emerge action (kriyā) and other action factors. (7) Diversification 
of reflections (pratibimba; see Kaul 2020; Lawrence 2005) or of entities within a unitary 
manifestation, such as a vista, painting, dancer, river, or ocean.

	30.	 Cf. bhinnatvaṃ sāmānyam (VPP 3.1, 3.1).
	31.	 Abhinavagupta in various places acknowledges the logical problem of reducing diversity to 
unity. He says that the experience of the one-​in-​the-​many is actually logically impossible, 
but that it is also possible within consciousness (cf. IPV 2.1.1, 2:7–​9)! The practical coherence 
of what we experience supersedes a more hypothetical argument. We return to the forthright 
transgression of logic in attempts to reduce time or difference in general to nonduality.
	32.	 ābhāsbhedo’pi bhavetkālakramākaraḥ/​vicchinnabhāsaḥ . . . māturbhāsya no sakṛt. See 
the discussion below of Utaladeva’s allusion here to Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1–​8.4.2. 
On favorable and unfavorable human relations to time, cf. TA, 4.165, 3:795–​796: kartā ca 
dvividhaḥ proktaḥ kalpitākalpitātmakaḥ/​kalpito dehabuddhādivavacchedena carcitaḥ. 
Jeffrey Kripal has described the religious theme of the dual human trajectory toward ei­
ther the worldly or the spiritual, as the human as two (Kripal 2014).
	33.	 kramākramakalanaiva kālaḥ sa ca parameśvara eva antarbhāti tadbhāsanam ca devasya 
kālī nāma śaktiḥ.
	34.	 kramākramātmā kālaśca paraḥ saṃvidi vartate/​kālī nāma parā śaktiḥ saiva devasya 
gīyate. Similar contemplations are found throughout late nondual Śaiva writings. An in­
teresting point in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa is that the adept aspires to a state of the nondual 
anuttara in which there is not even the temporal transmission between the teaching and 
taught (as occurs in the āgamas). Per the Parātrśīkāvivaraṇa Sanskrit in Abhinavagupta 
1989, 34: tad vānuttara-​padaṃ sṛṣṭirityarthaḥ. yadyapi ca sṛṣṭāvapi prāktananayenta

the Prapañcasāra ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya, along with the Yogavāśiṣṭha, also speak of the 
transition to the higher form of nonsequential time through tantric practice. See discus­
sion in Kaviraj 1990, 143–​145).
	35.	 Plotinus, endeavoring to interpret Plato, deplores any person who does not immediately 
trace the reflections in the world to their transcendent source as perishing like Narcissus 
gazing in the water (Plotinus 1992, 1.6.8, 71).
	36.	 Transcendence is traditionally understood in Christianity as evinced in creation from 
God’s command, without preexistent material cause. On what I have labeled a “dialectic” 
in Christianity, see Underhill 1961, 96ff.
	37.	 On Neoplatonic participation in the Forms conceived in Renaissance painting, see

	38.	 Paul Franks maintained that Peirce’s stated heritage in the “monstrous mysticism of the 
East” is more likely about Jacob Boehme’s appropriation of kabbalah than Hinduism or 
Buddhism. Franks also explained that in kabbalah, as in nondual Śaivism, the physical 
world is a sort of contraction of the spiritual world (2015, 745–​751).
	39.	 Charles Hartshorne classified Peirce as a panentheist, albeit decrying his tendencies to­
ward classical theism and the overall coherence of his philosophy (Hartshorne and Reese 
2000, 258–​259, 268–​269). For other classifications of Peirce as a panentheist, see Raposa 
1989, 48–​51; Brier 2008; Niemoczynski 2011, 60, 118.
	40.	 This statement is illustrative:
“The universe is a vast representamen, a great symbol of God’s purpose, working out its 
conclusion in living realities. Now every symbol must have, organically attached to it, its 
Indices of Reactions and its Icons of Qualities; and such part as these reactions and these 
qualities play in an argument that, they of course, play in the universe—​that Universe 
being precisely an argument. . . . The Universe as an argument is necessarily a great work of 
art, a great poem—​for every fine argument is a poem and a symphony—​just as every true 
poem is a sound argument. But let us compare it rather to a painting.”
(CP 5.119, 75–​76)
On the world as God’s icons and symbols, see Raposa 1989, 108–​109.
	 	   I have previously compared Abhinavagupta’s view that recognition should be evaluated 
for truth in coherence (abādhya) in the pursuit of purposeful action (arthakriya)—​with 
the tripartite criteria David Tracy identified in William James—​possibility (which Tracy 
further interpreted in terms of hermeneutic disclosure), coherence and, praxis (see Tracy 
1990; Lawrence 2013). I now believe that James’s criteria have their basis in Peirce’s semi­
otic abuctivism and pragmatism.
	41.	 This tohu bohu corresponds to either the semiotic category Peirce called Firstness or a sort 
of precursor to Firstness.
	42.	 That is, consequent on the interruptive objectivity of “Secondness,” there evolves 
“Thirdness.”
	43.	 See Calcaterra 2012, 415, on the fallibilism provided by Peirce’s union of necessity and 
spontaneity in an evolutionary continuum.
	44.	 Peircean biosemiotic theorists Terrence Deacon and Tyrone Cashman likewise suggested 
that time is the mixture of actuality and its absence: “But what if time [is] . . . but a feature 
of the open-​ended nature of present/​absence relationships compounded on each other” 
(Deacon and Cashman, 2016, 426). Reminiscent of the contention by Abhinavagupta 
that difference is a sort of unifying relation of similarity, Corrington also explained that 
in Peircean philosophy: “Contrast is actually a subspecies of resemblance and functions 
according to the same momentum” (Corrington 1993, 103). Peircean pragmatic pluralist, 
Rosenthal also spoke of the sense of continuity within the process of time as recognition 
(Rosenthal 1994, 69).
	45.	 Neville thus accommodated within his abstract conception of cosmogony—​Abrahamic, 
Daoist, Confucian, Hindu, and Buddhist notions of creation or origination (Neville 1991). 
W. T. Stace observed that many Jewish mystics interpret creatio ex nihilo as creation out of 
the incomprehensible God who is “Nothing” (Stace 1952, 11–​12).
	46.	 This verse is inspired by Chāndogya Upaniṣad in Upaniṣatsaṅgraha 1970, 8.4.2, 79: “This 
world of brahman has at once and always manifested [sakṛdvibhāta].” sakṛdvibhāto

hyevaiṣa brahmlokaḥ. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage is quoted or referred to in nu­

	47.	 In the Tantrāloka, Abhinavagupta discusses haṭhapākapraśamana. See TA and 
TAV 3.260–​3.263, 2:591–​2:594. On the distinction of haṭhapākapraśmana from

	 	   Regarding apophasis, in TA 2.28, 2:59, Abhinavagupta even sounds like a Mādhyamika 
in mentioning a catuṣkoṭi.
	 	   There is not existence [sat], nonexistence [asat], both existence and nonexistence 
[sadasat] or what lacks both [tannobhayojjhita]. For that state is difficult to compre­
hend [durvijñya]. That something is Anuttara samastamidam ekaṃ cinmātratattvaṃ 
kālena akalitaṃ deśena aparicchinnam . . . ākṛtibhiraniyantritam. . . . kālādeḥ 
pramāṇaparyantasya svarūpalābhanimittam ca. . . . tadeva ca aham.
	 	   Although there are roots of such apophasis in the Nāsadīya Sūkta (Rig Veda 10.129), 
the appropriation here of more recent Mahāyāna Buddhism, such as from the streams 
of Prajñāparamita or Mahāmudrā, within Śaiva metaphysics is evident. Sanderson and I 
have thus separately suggested that Krama and nondual Śaivism share common sources 
with Tibetan Dzogchen or Chinese sudden Ch’an (Lawrence 2016).
	48.	 Raposa explained that each individual makes one aware of the continuous whole (Raposa 
1989, 21).
	49.	 Cf. the biosemiotics of Kull 2018: “Semiosis takes place in the Now.”
	50.	 W. T. Stace himself observed that the mystic sees in the moment God immanent at the in­
tersection of the temporal and the eternal (Stace 1952, 75–​80). For corroboration he quoted 
his contemporary T. S. Eliot:
To apprehend
The point of intersection of the timeless
With time is an occupation of the saint.
(Eliot 1943, 26)
	51.	 Notwithstanding the dangers of irrationalism, I suggest that logical puzzles or aporias are 
present in virtually all philosophies. In line with what was said above on Abhinavagupta 
regarding the combination of the one and the many in consciousness—​perhaps disclosed 
or recognized truth claims, along with overall coherence in the practical pursuit of the 
highest felicity, can decide which philosophies are more persuasive (Lawrence 1999, 106; 
2013; cf. the commentary in Hick 1964 and elsewhere)
