Chapter 45
Modernity and 
Neo-​Tantra
Hugh B. Urban
The representation, popular imagining, and practice of tantra have changed dramati­
cally over the last two hundred years, particularly in the context of modernity, globaliza­
tion, and consumer capitalism. Once a highly esoteric tradition focused on awakening 
and harnessing the divine power that flows through the cosmos and human body, tantra 
has increasingly become a popular path focused on the pursuit of sensual pleasure and 
sexual freedom.1 Today, we need only browse the pages of Amazon.com or the shelves 
of Barnes and Noble to find a wide array of books, videos, and products such as The 
Complete Idiot’s Guide to Tantric Sex (Kuriansky 2004) and The Art of Sexual Ecstasy 
(Anand 1990). At the same time, new forms of practice such as “Neo-​tantra” have been 
marketed by global gurus such as Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh (aka Osho), now combined 
with elements of post-​Freudian psychoanalysis, the mysticism of George Gurdjieff, and 
experimental forms of therapy taught at New Age centers such as the Esalen Institute 
(Rajneesh 1980, 1981; Urban 2000, 2016).
So how did this remarkable transformation take place? This chapter retraces the com­
plex genealogy of tantra in the modern context, as it was interpreted, reinterpreted, 
appropriated, and transformed by a wide variety of British, European, American, and 
Indian audiences from the nineteenth century onward.2 For the sake of brevity, I focus 
on six key moments in this genealogy: (1) the largely negative representation of tantra 
in Orientalist discourse and in the works of Hindu reformers of the nineteenth century; 
(2) the positive revaluation of tantra in modern European esoteric groups such as the 
Ordo Templi Orientis and in the works of the British occultist, Aleister Crowley; (3) 
the development of the Left-​Hand Path in modern magic and Satanism; (4) the early 
twentieth-​century American reworking of tantra that we see in Pierre Arnold Bernard 
and the Tantrik Order in America; (5) the development of Neo-​tantra in the movement 
led by Osho-​Rajneesh; and (6) the contemporary marketing of tantra as an “art of ec­
stasy” or spiritual sex in New Age spirituality, where it now circulates globally for a mass 
consumer audience.

--- PAGE 1179 ---
1154      Hugh B. Urban
 
To conclude, I discuss the reimportation of a globalized form of tantra to contempo­
rary India, where it has taken on a number of new interesting forms (though most often 
associated with black magic and sorcery rather than sex). Here I revisit Agehananda 
Bharati’s famous idea of the “pizza effect” (1970) as a way of thinking about cross-​
cultural circulations of ideas and suggest that it needs to be updated a bit to address the 
contemporary global context. Rather than pizza, however, I argue that something like a 
“curry effect” is perhaps a more apt culinary metaphor to describe the complex histor­
ical journey of modern tantra.
“Black Art of the Crudest and 
Filthiest Kind”: Tantra in 
Orientalist Discourse
Much of the modern understanding and interpretation—​or perhaps more accu­
rately misunderstanding and misinterpretation—​is indebted to European and British 
Orientalist literature of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. As scholars such 
as Ronald Inden have shown, most European Orientalist scholars typically imagined 
India as a land of irrationality, sensuality, mysticism, and “disorderly imagination,” set 
in opposition to the rational, orderly, modern “West” (Inden 1990), and tantra was often 
portrayed as the very epitome of that dreamy, irrational realm, as “India’s darkest heart” 
or the “extreme Orient” (Urban 1999, 2003).
Most of the early Christian missionaries and European Orientalist scholars writing 
in India had an intensely negative view of Hinduism in general and of tantra in par­
ticular (Urban 2003). One of the first British authors to write about the religions of 
India was the British Baptist missionary, Reverend William Ward (1769–​1823), who 
described Hinduism as “the most puerile, bloody, and impure system of idolatry that 
was ever established on earth” (1817: 2.lxxvi); meanwhile, he denounced tantra as the 
worst example of this idolatry, involving a “most shocking mode of worship” and 
practices “too abominable to enter the ears of man and impossible to be revealed to 
a Christian public” (1817: 1.247). Ward’s intensely hostile view of tantra was echoed 
throughout Orientalist literature of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, 
where it was widely dismissed for its perverse mixture of magic and sensuality—​for 
example, as “black art of the crudest and filthiest kind” in which a “veritable Devil’s 
orgy is portrayed” (Avalon 1960: 5). As the great British Sanskritist, Sir Monier Monier-​
Williams, concluded, tantra is simply “Hinduism arrived at its last and worst stage of 
medieval development” (1894: 122–​123).
Many Indian authors and Hindu reformers of the colonial era largely accepted, 
internalized, and even amplified this Orientalist view of tantra. Thus, the great Bengali 
reformer Rāmmohun Roy (1772–​1833) described tantra as the clearest example of 
the polytheism, idolatry, and decadence that had corrupted the noble, pure spirit of

--- PAGE 1180 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1155
 
the Vedas. In Rāmmohun’s view, the “golden age of the Vedas” had been replaced in 
modern times by the “dark age” of the tantras, with their “ceremonies utterly subver­
sive of every moral principle” (Roy 1982: 1.9, 2.vii; Urban 2003: 61). Likewise, Swami 
Vivekananda (1863–​1902)—​arguably the most important figure in the articulation of 
modern Hinduism or “neo-​Hinduism”—​was particularly critical of the left-​hand or 
vāmācāra form of Tantric practice with its literal use of sexual rites and consumption 
of alcohol and meat. The degenerate vāmācāra practice, he lamented, was a kind of di­
sease that had gradually infected the marrow of the Indian body politic, emasculating 
and effeminizing this once powerful nation and allowing it to be dominated first by the 
Mughals and later by the British Empire: “Just look to your own province and see how 
this Vamachara (immoral practice) of the tantras has entered into our very marrow. . . 
. We must stem the tide of this Vamachara, which is contrary to the spirit of the Vedas” 
(Vivekananda 1984: 174).
In the early twentieth century, a few brave scholars did attempt to defend and 
rearticulate tantra for a modern audience. Foremost among these was Sir John 
Woodroffe (aka Arthur Avalon), a British High Court judge in India and also a secret 
tāntrika. Woodroffe argued passionately that tantra should be understood as a noble, 
respectable, and philosophical form of Hinduism, comparable to other philosophical 
schools such as Advaita Vedānta and in its ritual practice even not so dissimilar to the 
rites of the Catholic Church (1974: 4; Avalon 1960: 63). He also chastised his countrymen 
for their hypocritical prudishness and suggested that the tantras were perhaps far more 
honest in their views of sexuality than any in the modern West:
There is nothing “foul” in them except for people to whom all erotic phenomena are 
foul . . . [T]‌he ancient East was purer in these matters than the modern West, where, 
under cover of a pruriently modest exterior . . . extraordinarily varied psychopathic 
filth may flow. This was not so in earlier days . . . when a spade was called a spade and 
not a horticultural instrument.
(Woodroffe 1978: 134)
Despite Woodroffe’s efforts, however, tantra continued to be largely associated with 
sexuality, magic, and transgression throughout the European and American popular 
imaginations. Yet ironically, this association with magic, transgression, sexuality, and 
power also helped give birth to a wide array of new religious movements from the late 
nineteenth century onward.
The Ordo Templi Orientis, Aleister 
Crowley, and Sex Magick
One of the first and most important European groups to begin to embrace tantra 
in a more positive form was the Ordo Templi Orientis (O.T.O.) or Order of Oriental

--- PAGE 1181 ---
1156      Hugh B. Urban
 
Templars. Founded between 1895 and 1902 by Karl Kellner and Theodor Reuss, the 
O.T.O. combined elements of Western esoteric traditions such as Gnosticism and 
Freemasonry with aspects of Hindu yoga and tantra (Pasi 2005; Urban 2008). Kellner 
(1851–​1905) was a wealthy Austrian chemist and industrialist who claimed to have been 
initiated into Tantric sexual techniques by a Sufi and two yogis, one of whom may have 
been a Bengali Tantric practitioner (Dvorak 1998; Urban 2008). Meanwhile, Reuss 
(1855–​1923) was an Anglo-​German occultist, Freemason, and journalist who wrote 
widely about both Western sexual magic and tantra, including a large volume on phallic 
worship entitled Lingam-​Yoni (1906; see Howe and Möller 1986).
Calling itself a kind of “neo-​Gnostic” tradition, the O.T.O. strongly condemned 
the doctrine of original sin, which it saw as a corruption of authentic Christian tra­
dition. Instead, it called for the dawn of a “new civilization” based not on repression 
and denial but rather on the open embrace and celebration of sexuality (Reuss 1997: 
227). Indeed, the O.T.O. claimed to possess the deepest secret of all esoteric traditions, 
which lay at the heart of all Masonic systems and ultimately derived from the “Wise 
Men of the East.” According to a publication from 1912, this occult key is none other 
than the secret of sexual magic, which is the original core of all religious traditions, 
both “East” and “West”:
Our Order possess the KEY, which opens up all Masonic and Hermetic secrets, 
namely, the teaching of sexual magic, and this teaching explains, without exception, 
all the secrets of Nature, all the symbolism of FREEMASONRY and all systems of 
religion.
(Reuss 1912: 21)
Much of the O.T.O.’s practice clearly drew on nineteenth-​century Western forms of 
sexual magic, such as the work of the American spiritualist Paschal Beverly Randolph 
and European groups such as the Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor (Deveney 1997; 
Urban 2005). However, it also borrowed heavily from nineteenth-​century Orientalist 
scholarship on tantra to reimagine this as the most profound source of all mysticism 
and religion, one known to the ancient Greek mystery religions, to the early Christians 
Gnostics, and to the left-​hand tāntrikas of India alike. Like most Orientalist scholars 
before him, Reuss identified tantra primarily with sexuality and indeed as “sexual-​
religion,” in which the central focus is on the “principle of generation as it manifests 
in the female energy (Shakti) and the manly energy (Shiva)” (1993b: 71). In his view, 
this Tantric sexual religion was no different from the ancient worship of the phallus in 
the West:
The Eleusinian mysteries were pure Phallus cult. The ceremonies were those of the 
Tantrics. The members of these mysteries partook of such ecstasy that the freedom of 
the senses came to them as a totally natural by-​product . . .
The secret teachings of the Gnostics (Primitive Christians) are identical with the 
Vamachari rites of the Tantrics . . . Phallicism is the basis of all theology and underlies

--- PAGE 1182 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1157
 
the mythology of all peoples . . . The Phallus as a divine symbol received divine vener­
ation for thousands of years in India.
(see Reuss 1993a, 1993b: 71)
Ultimately, Reuss hoped that the O.T.O. and its more wholesome understanding of 
sexuality would usher in a whole new society and a new age of human civilization, one 
based not on denial of physical instinct but rather on acceptance and celebration of the 
divine power of sexuality. By wedding the left-​practices of tantra with his own neo-​
Gnostic spirituality, he hoped to usher in a new era to replace the repressive morality of 
the past: “A new civilization, a new system of morals will arise from the new Christianity 
of the gnostic Templar-​Christians . . . [T]‌he Church of the gnostic Neo-​Christians seeks 
to found communities, existing on a co-​operative basis, i.e., freed from the Nazarene-​
Christian ideas of original sin” (see Reuss 1993a, 1997: 226–​227)
Surely the most influential leader of the O.T.O. was the controversial British oc­
cultist, poet, and novelist Aleister Crowley (1875–​1947). From an early age, Crowley 
was involved with a variety of Western esoteric groups, such as the Hermetic Order of 
the Golden Dawn, and was also one of the first Western authors to begin writing about 
South Asian practices such as yoga, Buddhist meditation and tantra (Pasi 2005; Urban 
2005). After meeting Reuss in 1910, Crowley became closely involved in the O.T.O. and 
was named the “Sovereign Grand Master General of Ireland, Iona, and all the Britons.” 
Crowley actually wrote an entire liturgy for the O.T.O. called the Gnostic Mass, which 
prominently highlights sexual symbolism and the dynamics between the male priest 
and the female priestess. At the same time, he also elaborated the higher grades of the 
O.T.O.’s initiatory structure, which now included eighth, ninth, and eleventh degrees 
(the tenth in Crowley’s system is an administrative grade with no sexual aspect), which 
focused respectively on autoerotic, heterosexual, and homosexual rituals (Pasi 2005; 
Urban 2005).
Crowley’s actual knowledge of tantra does not appear to have been very deep and was 
mostly derived from secondary sources. However, he did discuss the general similarities 
between his own system of sexual magic and Tantric techniques:
Paradoxical as it may sound, the Tantrics are in reality the most advanced of the 
Hindus. Their theory is, in its philosophical ultimatum, a primitive stage of the 
White tradition, for the essence of the Tantric cults is that by the performance of cer­
tain rites of Magick, one does not only escape disaster, but obtains positive benedic­
tion. The Tantric is not obsessed by the will-​to-​die. It is a difficult business, no doubt, 
to get any fun out of existence; but at least it is not impossible.
(Crowley 1969: ch. 30 and 72, 1991: ch. 7)
More specifically, Crowley also noted the similarity between the central importance of 
semen in Tantric sexual practices and its role in the upper grades of the O.T.O.’s sexual 
magic. Many esoteric traditions, he argued, agree on the importance of semen and re­
gard it as a fundamental source of both physical and spiritual potency:

--- PAGE 1183 ---
1158      Hugh B. Urban
 
Like the Jews, the wise men of India have a belief that a certain particular Prana, or 
force, resides in the Bindu, or semen. . . .
Therefore they stimulate to the maximum its generation by causing a consecrated 
prostitute to excite the organs, and at the same time vigorously withhold by will . . . 
Nor is this ever to be lost, but reabsorbed through the tissues of the body. The organs 
thus act as a siphon to draw constantly fresh supplies of life from the cosmic reservoir 
and flood the body with their fructifying virtue. . . .
Initiates will notice also that these heathen philosophers have made one further 
march towards the truth when they say that the Sun and Moon must be united before 
the reabsorption (see almost any Tantra, in particular Shiva Sanhita).
(Crowley 1986: ch. 16)
In many ways, however, Crowley’s use of sexual magic did also depart quite sig­
nificantly from South Asian Tantric practices. Perhaps most important, South Asian 
tantra is for the most part built on a quite heterosexual (indeed, heteronormative 
and quite essentialist) metaphysical system: in Hindu tantra, for example, the entire 
universe unfolds through the interplay of cosmic male and female principles, Śiva 
and Śakti, liṅgam and yoni, and so on. Historically, moreover, the accounts of sexual 
practices outlined in Tantric texts have always been heterosexual, despite their other 
transgressions of class and purity (Urban 2010). Yet Crowley introduced techniques 
of autoerotic and homoerotic sexual magic that were not only quite unlike those of 
any South Asian Tantric tradition but also highly transgressive in the context of early 
twentieth-​century England, at a time when masturbation was widely believed to cause 
insanity and sodomy was illegal. Indeed, a large part of the power of Crowley’s sexual 
magic appears to have derived from its transgressive nature, its use of dangerous 
and impure techniques, and its deliberate violation of social and religious taboos 
(Urban 2005).
While Crowley’s own knowledge of tantra was probably limited, much of the syn­
thesis of Crowleyian magic with tantra was really due to the work of his follower, 
Kenneth Grant (1924–​2011). It was largely Grant who helped revive interest in Crowley’s 
work in the 1960s and 1970s, where it found a happy home among the burgeoning 
counterculture and sexual revolution. At the same time, Grant also developed his own 
system of magic called the “Typhonian current,” which he essentially identifies with 
tantra (Grant 1975: 63). Grant himself claimed to have received full initiation into a 
“highly recondite formula” of the Tantric path at the hands of David Curwen, who in 
turn claimed to have been initiated by a guru in South India. After meeting Crowley 
in 1944, Grant went on to write a series of books on Crowley and magic, which re­
peatedly emphasize the tāntrik nature of Crowley’s work. Thus, he praised Crowley’s 
text, The Book of the Law, as “the New Gnosis, the latest Tantra” and credited Crowley 
with having penetrated the innermost secrets of tāntrik sexual practices (1973: 7). 
Ultimately, Grant also found in the tantras a confirmation of the central tenet of 
Crowley’s teachings—​his law of Thelema (derived from the Greek for “will”), which 
rests on the fundamental belief in the divinity of the individual human will: “Another

--- PAGE 1184 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1159
 
point of contact between Tantra and Thelema is contained in the Thelemic aphorism: 
There is no god but man!” (1973: 127).
The Left-​Hand Path: Radical 
Transgression and Self-​Deification
Grant’s synthesis of Crowley’s magick with tantra has had a lasting influence on almost 
all later forms of occultism and much of New Age spirituality more generally. Today, 
this synthesis is widely known as the Left-​Hand Path (LHP) and has been articulated in 
various ways by a wide range of neo-​pagans, occultists, and modern Satanists (Flowers 
2012; Schreck 2002; Granholm 2012; Urban forthcoming).3
In striking contrast to most Orientalist scholars and Hindu reformers such as 
Swami Vivekananda, Grant saw vāmācāra as the highest form of Tantric practice. 
With its deliberate use of normally impure and forbidden substances such as alcohol, 
meat, and sexual fluids, vāmācāra in Grant’s view aims to achieve the overstepping 
of all taboos and all social boundaries, including the boundary between the human 
and the divine: “the ultimate aim is total absorption in the goddess, and this is some­
times accomplished through sexual union with the priestess who embodies her” 
(1975: 72–​73).
One of the most influential exponents of vāmācāra tantra was the controversial 
Italian scholar and self-​described “Traditionalist,” Julius Evola. In many ways, Evola’s 
embrace of vāmācāra was a part of his larger critique of modernity, which he saw as 
a general decline into moral decadence and spiritual emptiness. In his view, we are 
now living in the last phase of this cosmic cycle (the kali yuga, in Hindu cosmological 
terms), when most religious institutions are in decay and genuine Tradition has been 
displaced by the corrupt forces of materialism, secularism, and democratic political 
systems. In such extreme circumstances, extreme measures are needed, and the most 
viable path is therefore a path of action, virility, and heroic courage that can turn these 
dark forces to a spiritual end. This, for Evola, is the essence of the LHP. His clearest 
articulation of this idea appeared in Lo yoga della potenza (the Yoga of Power), which 
was published in 1949 as a revised version of his 1925 book L’Uomo come potenza (Man 
as Power):
During the last age, elementary, infernal and even abyssal forces are untrammeled. 
The immediate task consists in facing and absorbing these forces, in taking the risk 
of “riding the tiger,” to use a Chinese expression . . . or “to transform the poison 
into medicine” according to a Tantric expression. Hence the rituals and special 
practices of what has been named Left-​Hand Tantrism, or the Path of the Left Hand 
(Vama-​marga).
(Evola 1992: 3–​4)4

--- PAGE 1185 ---
1160      Hugh B. Urban
 
However, perhaps the most explicit turn to the LHP was taken by Anton Szandor 
LaVey (born Howard Stanton Levey, 1930–​1997), the controversial American founder 
of the Church of Satan. Established in San Francisco in 1966—​in the very midst of 
the sexual revolution and the psychedelic movement—​LaVey’s Church of Satan also 
represented the “dark side of the counter-​culture,” as it were. While embracing much of 
the sexual revolution, LaVey also ridiculed hippies, feminists, neo-​pagans, and others 
whom he believed had embraced weakness and a herd mentality rather than strength 
and individualism (Urban 2005: 210–​217).
At least in LaVey’s version of Satanism, “Satan” does not refer to some imagined ex­
ternal being set in opposition to God and dwelling in the underworld; rather, Satan is 
really the symbol of the individual human being, with all of his most physical, sensual, 
sexual, and violent drives and desires. Satan is in fact the embodiment of the left-​hand 
practice itself, as the path of the flesh, the religion of worldly desire and personal gratifi­
cation. As he explained in his first major text, The Satanic Bible:
The Satanic religion has not merely lifted the coin—​it has flipped it completely over 
. . . Satanism is not a white light religion; it is a religion of the flesh, the mundane, 
the carnal—​all of which are ruled by Satan, the personification of the Left-​Hand 
Path. (1969: 52)
The ideal of the LHP was carried over into many offshoots of the Church of Satan, 
including the Temple of Set and myriad others. However, one of the most explicit 
articulations of the Satanic version of the LHP came from Anton LaVey’s daughter, 
Zeena, working together with her partner, Nikolas Schreck. While their positions 
changed significantly over time, the Schrecks’ most extensive discussion of the LHP 
appeared in their 2002 book, Demons of the Flesh: The Complete Guide to Left Hand Path 
Sex Magic. Here, they echo Evola’s emphasis on the inherently elitist and undemocratic 
nature of the LHP. In their view, this path is only for the few and the strong who are ca­
pable of engaging in these dangerous rites, which are neither advisable nor possible for 
the common herd of humankind:
The left-​hand path is closed to the common man and woman, who is regarded as 
little more than a herd-​animal (Sanskrit pashu). The sinister current is considered 
fit only for the temperament of the heroic warrior (Sanskrit vira) . . . The ultimate 
left-​hand path goal of Awakening (Sanskrit bodhana) occurs through exerting a rig­
orous effort against the innate low-​level consciousness which is regarded as the nat­
ural condition of the human animal.
(Schreck and Schreck 2002: 2)
While the Schrecks do want to ground themselves in South Asian traditions of 
vāmācāra tantra, they have also transformed these traditions in a number of signifi­
cant ways. Among others, their version of the LHP is identified first and foremost 
with sexuality, erotic rites, and “sexual exaltation,” and the particular form of sexuality

--- PAGE 1186 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1161
 
emphasized here is radically transgressive, demanding an explicit violation of every im­
aginable social and religious taboo. Beginning with the principle that “SEX IS POWER,” 
Demons of the Flesh promises to unveil the secrets of “Sadomasochism, Orgies, Taboo-​
breaking, Fetishism, Orgasm prolongation, Sexual vampirism, Ritual intercourse with 
divine and demonic entities, Awakening the Feminine Daemonic,” as well as “Erotic 
deprogramming and deconditioning” (2002: back cover). In this respect, the Schrecks’ 
version of the LHP goes well beyond even the most “hardcore” forms of South Asian 
tantra, in which sexual union is typically restricted to heterosexual couples (White 
2002; Urban 2010). Indeed, the vāmācāra use of meat, wine, and sexual union seems 
rather tame compared to the Schrecks’ use of S&M (sadism and masochism), sexual fet­
ishism and vampirism.
The Tantrik Order in America: The 
“Loving Guru,” Pierre Bernard
Meanwhile, in the United States, probably the most important figure in the modern 
reimagining of tantra was Pierre Arnold Bernard (1876–​1955). Easily one of the most 
colorful, elusive, and enigmatic characters in American religious history, Bernard was 
also a key figure in the development of modern yoga and in the general interest in all 
things “Oriental” and exotic. In his own day, Bernard was known in the popular press 
as “the Great Oom” or “Oom the Omnipotent,” while in some modern publications, he 
is even credited as the founder of yoga in America (Lardner 1939; Boswell 1965; Urban 
2003; Love 2011).
Bernard’s biography is a bit difficult to reconstruct due to his own retellings and 
embellishments, but it seems that he was born with the name Perry Arnold Baker in 
Iowa. While just a teenager growing up in Nebraska, he became close friends with a 
young Syrian Indian from Calcutta named Sylvais Hamati. The two shared an interest in 
the occult, and Hamati took Perry under his wing, making him his chela or student and 
teaching him the basics of yoga and vāmācāra tantra. Eventually, the two would travel 
up and down the West Coast teaching yoga and a new sort of Americanized form of 
tantra (Love 2011: 1–​26).
In 1906, now using the name Pierre Bernard, he established his own Tantrik Order 
in America (1906), which published its own journal and also offered its own docu­
ment for initiation into the “Tantrik Brotherhood.” After the San Francisco earthquake, 
he relocated to New York City, where he established an “Oriental Sanctum” in 1910. 
Arguably the first Neo-​Tantric group in the United States, Bernard’s order attracted 
some of the most prominent social figures of the day, including composer Leopold 
Stokowski and members of the Vanderbilt family.
Like his European and British contemporaries such as Reuss and Crowley, Bernard 
saw sexuality as the most fundamental, most powerful drive in human nature and also

--- PAGE 1187 ---
1162      Hugh B. Urban
 
the key to personal and social transformation. As he wrote in his article from 1906, 
“Tantrik Worship,” the sex drive is in fact “the animating spirit of the world”:
The animating impulse of all organic life is the sexual instinct. It is that which 
underlies the struggle for existence in the animal world and is the source of all human 
endeavor. . . . That affinity which draws the two sexes together for the . . . production 
of a new being, that overmastering universal impulse, is the most powerful factor in 
the human race and has ever been the cause of man’s most exalted thought.
(1906a: 71)
In Bernard’s view, tantra is unique among religious techniques because it is the one that 
not only acknowledges the power of love and sexuality but uses these human drives as a 
primary means of spiritual liberation. Indeed, in his Tantrik Journal Bernard spells the 
word tantra in Sanskrit characters comprised of tiny hearts (1906b: 91).
Not surprisingly, Bernard also became an object of intense gossip and scandal in the 
New York press. Known in the popular media as the “Loving Guru,” Bernard was infa­
mous for his Tantric sessions with “Oriental music and women’s cries, but not those of 
distress” (Douglas 1997: 195). As one neighbor who occupied an apartment across the 
way summarized the local grievance: “What my wife and I have seen through the win­
dows of that place is scandalous. We saw men and women in various stages of dishabille. 
Women’s screams mingled with wild Oriental music” (Sann 1967: 190).
Yet despite—​or perhaps because of—​his controversial reputation, Bernard’s 
uniquely American practice has had a lasting legacy and helped redefine most twen­
tieth-​ and twenty-​first-​century versions of tantra. Indeed, there was even a revival of 
Bernard’s group with the formation of a “New Tantrik Order in America” by New Age 
guru, Nik Douglas, in 1996. Through his website “Tantra Works,” Douglas offers an 
updated Tantric initiation now adapted to the sensibilities of a contemporary audience, 
by correcting some of the “rather sexist, obscure and outdated” language of Bernard’s 
original Tantric document and presenting the secrets of tantra for a “new millennium” 
(Douglas 1996).
Osho-​Rajneesh and “Neo-​Tantra”
However, of all the various characters figures discussed in this chapter, arguably the 
most important for the global spread of modern tantra was the controversial Indian 
guru known in his early years as Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh and in his later days as Osho 
(1931–​1990). Today, Osho-​Rajneesh is known to most readers as the “Rolls Royce Guru” 
and “Guru of the Rich” who made global headlines during the 1980s when he estab­
lished a large and briefly very successful utopian commune in central Oregon (see Osho 
2000; Urban 2016). As documented in a recent series such as “Wild, Wild Country” on

--- PAGE 1188 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1163
 
Netflix, this utopian experiment quickly went off the rails and ended in a series of crim­
inal activities, including the largest bioterrorist attack on US soil and the largest immi­
gration fraud and wiretapping conspiracies in US history (Carter 1990; Urban 2016; Way 
and Way 2018).
Yet despite its sordid and often surreal history, the Osho-​Rajneesh movement is also 
critically important for our understanding of the modern development and transfor­
mation of tantra in a global context. Osho-​Rajneesh was in fact the first modern guru to 
coin the phrase “Neo-​tantra” and to explicitly synthesize aspects of Hindu and Buddhist 
tantra with modern psychoanalytic theory and techniques drawn from American New 
Age spirituality (Rajneesh 1980, 1981; Urban 2016).
Born Chandra Mohan Jain (and nicknamed “Rajneesh”) in Madhya Pradesh, he 
claimed to have achieved full enlightenment in 1953 and assumed the title “Bhagwan” 
(meaning “glorious” or “holy,” a traditional name of God). By the late 1960s, Osho-​
Rajneesh had gathered a large and wealthy following in Bombay (modern Mumbai) 
and then established a lively ashram in nearby Poona (Pune). He quickly became quite 
infamous as “India’s most dangerous guru,” known for his irreverent sense of humor 
and his iconoclastic attacks on religious and political leaders such as Gandhi, Nehru, 
and Mother Theresa (Urban 2016). Attracting a growing number of the American and 
European young people then touring South Asia, the Pune ashram became known as 
the “Esalen of the East” due to its rich synthesis of Eastern spirituality with new forms of 
therapy and psychological techniques practiced at New Age centers such as the Esalen 
Institute in California (Urban 2016; see also Kripal 2007).
At the heart of Osho-​Rajneesh’s eclectic, iconoclastic, and often seemingly contra­
dictory philosophy is the ideal of “Zorba the Buddha.” While other religions split the 
material from the spiritual, Osho-​Rajneesh argued instead that a fully realized being 
would combine the sensuous enjoyment and lust for life of Zorba the Greek with the 
spirituality and transcendental insight of Gautama the Buddha: “My concept of the 
new man is that he will be Zorba the Greek and he will also be Gautama the Buddha: 
the new man will be Zorba the Buddha. He will be sensuous and physical, in the body, 
in the senses, enjoying the body and all that the body makes possible, and still a great 
consciousness . . . He will be Christ and Epicurus together” (Osho-​Rajneesh 1982: 15; 
see Urban 2016).
From the outset, Osho-​Rajneesh set out to overturn established ideologies and 
to redefine all previous ways of thinking. Thus, his movement was dubbed a “reli­
gionless religion” that rejected the dogmatism of all existing traditions; his followers 
were called “neo-​sannyasins,” who only “renounced” the idea that sensual pleasures 
or worldly pursuits needed to be renounced; and his meditations were “dynamic” 
sessions that involved not seated contemplation but primal scream and free-​form 
dance. Similarly, Osho-​Rajneesh redefined traditional South Asian tantra, creating 
his own brand of “Neo-​tantra” that focused primarily on sexuality and the transfor­
mation of sexual pleasure into a kind of “superconsciousness” (Rajneesh n.d.). As he 
put it in two lectures from 1980 and 1981, the world today needs an updated form of

--- PAGE 1189 ---
1164      Hugh B. Urban
 
tantra that would transmute the primal power of orgasm into the ultimate source of 
godliness:
My whole effort here is to bring Tantra to the twentieth century and make it Neo-​
Tantra, to bring Tao to the twentieth century and make it Neo-​Tao . . . Neo-​Sufism 
and Neo-​Yoga (1980: 207).
That’s my effort here: to introduce a neo-​Tantra to the world, a new vision of love 
. . . and an insight into the reality of the orgasm—​because orgasm is your greatest 
source of finding godliness, harmony, truth, the universal unity of all life. . . . If you 
can be one with one woman, one man, you have the secret key in your hands. You can 
be one with the whole universe.
(1981: 342; Rajneesh 1974, 1983)
In his understanding of sexuality and his redefinition of tantra, Rajneesh drew heavily 
on post-​Freudian psychoanalysis, and above all the work of the enigmatic Austrian 
therapist Wilhelm Reich (1897–​1957). Like Reich, Rajneesh saw sex as the most powerful 
force in human nature, the cause of most of our social and psychological ills, and also 
the most powerful tool on the path of spiritual liberation. Indeed, Osho-​Rajneesh’s un­
derstanding of kuṇḍalinī as a kind of primal sexual energy latent in the body bears more 
than a passing resemblance to Reich’s notion of “orgone” energy, or the innate sexual 
power coursing through every physical body (Reich 1973).5 Like Reich, moreover, Osho-​
Rajneesh clearly linked sexual repression to social and political repression and therefore 
also identified sexual liberation as the ultimate source of social and political transforma­
tion. As such, he even recognized Reich as a kind of “Western tāntrika” who had discov­
ered the secrets of Tantric sex independently of the Eastern sources:
I will call Wilhelm Reich a modern Tantra master, although he was not aware of it. 
Perhaps in his past lives he may have known the secrets of Tantra—​because his work 
contained the secrets of Tantra . . .
Reich will have a revival because what he was doing was absolutely scientific . . . I 
have so many sannyasins educated in psychology, psychoanalysis, in analytical psy­
chology. . . . He belongs to us. I give him posthumous sannyas.
(Osho 1987: 143)
With its complex synthesis of East and West, Osho-​Rajneesh’s brand of Neo-​tantra 
has had a tremendous influence on virtually all popular forms of Tantric yoga in Europe 
and America since the 1970s (Urban 2016). Not only do many of these popular texts 
directly credit Osho-​Rajneesh as a primary inspiration, but some of the most influen­
tial works on popular tantra were in fact written by direct disciples of Osho-​Rajneesh. 
These include hugely influential best-​selling works such as The Art of Sexual Ecstasy by 
his disciple, Margot Anand (1990), and Tantric Pulsation by Osho disciple and trained 
Reichian therapist Aneesha Dillon (2005). Meanwhile, Osho-​Rajneesh’s own works on 
tantra and Yoga continue to sell widely throughout the globe in an array of books and

--- PAGE 1190 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1165
 
DVDs such as Yoga: The Science of the Soul, Tantra: The Supreme Understanding, The 
Tantra Experience: Evolution through Love and dozens of others (Osho 2012, 2016, 2017).
“Nookie Nirvana”: Tantra, the New 
Age, and Consumer Culture
By the 1980s and 1990s, this popularized form of Neo-​tantra or “spiritual sexology” had 
become a ubiquitous part of the New Age movement and of alternative spirituality more 
broadly. Now mass-​marketed through countless books, videos, and sensual products, 
Neo-​tantra has become in many ways emblematic of New Age spirituality as a whole. 
Today, not only can we browse The Complete Idiot’s Guide to Tantric Sex, but we can also 
easily discover the secrets of Sex Magic, Tantra, and Tarot, American Tantra: A Modern 
Guide to Sacred Sex, and New Age Tantric Yoga, among countless others. Virtually all of 
these popular texts are based on the fundamental equation of tantra with sex, usually 
combined with the erotic positions of the Kāma Sūtra and a healthy dose of the Joy of 
Sex. As Cosmopolitan magazine put it in an article, tantra is nothing less than the art of 
“nookie nirvana” and the secret to “mind blowing sex” (Collins 2000).
Although the term “New Age” is really a rough label that has been applied to a vast 
and diverse body of modern beliefs and practices, many scholars have argued that there 
are at least a few common themes that run through these various forms of alternative 
spirituality. As Paul Heelas suggests, the New Age can be characterized in general terms 
as “the celebration of the self and the sacralization of modernity”—​that is, a belief in 
the inherent divinity of the individual self and an affirmation of basic values of moder­
nity such as “freedom, authenticity, self-​responsibility, self-​reliance, self-​determinism, 
equality, and above all, the self as a value in and of itself” (Heelas 1996).
Contemporary “American tantra” or “Neo-​tantra” is a striking illustration of this 
larger celebration of the self and sacralization of modernity. Throughout popular liter­
ature, tantra is presented as the ultimate path to self-​fulfillment and personal pleasure, 
one uniquely suited to a modern global context in which “East” and “West” are cross-​
fertilizing in powerful new ways.
Thus in the Complete Idiot’s Guide, tantra is explicitly advertised as a “modern” 
practice, especially appropriate for our highly individualistic, materialistic, and 
quick-​fix lifestyle.
Although Tantric practices were developed in the Eastern part of the world, they 
are particularly applicable and appealing to the Western world today. . . .Tantric sex 
promises simple steps and instant results, which are appealing to Westerners who are 
conditioned to “instant” lifestyles (instant coffee, fast food, instant gratification). . . 
. Tantric sex starts with individual practice. . . . This is consistent with the individu­
alism that is the basis of Western society. . . . Tantric sex encourages heightening the

--- PAGE 1191 ---
1166      Hugh B. Urban
 
senses through beautiful clothing, attractive surroundings and stimulation of all the 
senses, which is consistent with Western obsessions with worldly pleasures.
(Kuriansky 2004: 8–​9)
As the modern Tantric guru, Nik Douglas, put it, Neo-​tantra is therefore perhaps the 
quintessential religion for the New Age as a whole—​a more democratic, less elitist and 
popular path open to all spiritual seekers in this dawning Age of Aquarius:
As the New Age manifested, traditional Tantra was transformed into a Tantra for the 
masses, a neo-​Tantric cult of sensual pleasure with a spiritual flavor. . . . In the 21st 
century, Tantra will . . . bless those prepared to deal with the new spiritual reality . . . 
in the flowering of the Age of Aquarius which commenced in 1962.
(Douglas 1997: 17, 345)
At the same time, much of Neo-​tantra also seems to embody what Kimberly Lau has 
called the rise of “New Age capitalism”—​that is, the tendency for alternative spiritual 
practices and exotic “Eastern” traditions to become transformed into commodities 
and marketed to a large new audience of spiritual consumers (Lau 2015; see also Urban 
2003; Carrette and King 2004; Jain 2014). Like Yoga and other spiritual imports from 
Asia, tantra has become a huge commercial industry in the United States, the United 
Kingdom, and Europe, spawning not only books and videos but a wide array of products 
and services. The online Ananda Shop, for example, offers a variety of spiritual-​sensual 
services, such as the “Men’s Tantra Session” ($250), as well as a wide range of products, 
such as the “Couples Tantra Video” ($25), “Coconut Tantric Massage Oil” ($15), and 
a “Pelvic Floor Yoni Egg” ($60) (Ananda Shop 2021). Imagined as the ideal wedding 
of mukti and bhukti, spiritual liberation and sensual pleasure, Neo-​tantra seems to fit 
perfectly with the contemporary consumer mentality; indeed, it might even be said to 
be sort of the quintessential religion of the current form of global capitalism generally 
known as neoliberalism—​a system in which, as David Harvey defines it, essentially 
“everything is a commodity,” including sexuality, the body, and religion itself (Harvey 
2007; Urban 2016).
Conclusions: From the “Pizza Effect” 
to the “Curry Effect”
This chapter has only scratched the surface of many different forms of modern tantra. 
If space allowed, we could also have explored the synthesis of tantra with other es­
oteric traditions such as Gnosticism, Kabbalah, and Tarot (Frater U.:D.: 2002), the 
many LGBTQ transformations of tantra (Urban 2012), and various other iterations of 
Neo-​tantra.

--- PAGE 1192 ---
Modernity and Neo-Tantra      1167
 
To conclude, however, I would just like to make some broader observations on the 
changing representations of tantra in the modern context, not only in Europe and in the 
United States but also in contemporary South Asia. Here I would like to revisit and re­
think Agehananda Bharati’s famous notion of the “pizza effect,” by which he meant the 
ways in which ideas from one culture are transferred to another, undergo profound 
transformations, and then return to the home culture in a new form (1970: 271; see Urban 
2003).6 We can clearly some of this pizza effect at work in figures such as Osho-​Rajneesh, 
who was strongly influenced by Americanized versions of tantra and ideals of sexual liber­
ation that were circulating at New Age centers such as Esalen in California; however, Osho-​
Rajneesh is also an interesting case, insofar as he was as much an exporter as importer of 
modern tantra and also spread his own version of Neo-​tantra to the West (Urban 2016).
For the most part, however, the version of tantra that circulates in the contempo­
rary South Asian imagination is very different from the forms of spiritual sex circu­
lating in the American and European popular imaginations. Indeed, if we look at the 
wide array of Bollywood films dealing with Tantric themes or at the myriad popular 
booklets sold on street corners throughout India, we find that tantra is almost always 
identified with black magic, sorcery, and horror (Urban 2020). The figure of the “sinister 
tāntrika” and black magician is a recurring trope in popular films such as Gerhrayee, 
Sangarsh, or Jaadugar, not to mention low-​budget productions such as Shaitan Tantrik 
and myriad others (Urban 2020). Still today on street corners throughout India, one can 
find countless booklets and cheap paperbacks on Tantric black magic, such as Tantra 
Mantra Maner Icchā Pūraṇ and Ādi Vaśīkaraṇa Tantrasāra. Almost all of these booklets 
have lurid covers featuring sinister tāntrikas who perform dark rituals with skulls and 
corpses in cremation grounds, surrounded by ghouls and terrifying forms of the god­
dess (Śāstrī n.d.; Jaiminī n.d.; Urban 2020).
What we see in the popular image of tantra in India versus “the West” is not so much a 
“pizza effect” but rather what I would call a “curry effect.” By this I mean that the modern 
development of tantra is not so much the story of a dish that travels from one culture 
to another and then back again (like pizza) but rather that of a dish that has a common 
origin but develops in two very different directions in two different cultural contexts 
(like curry). Although there is some debate over the origins of the word “curry,” many 
trace it to either the Tamil or Kannada terms khari or caril, which were then adopted 
into Portuguese and other European languages (Collingham 2006: 115). Prior to the 
sixteenth century and the introduction of chili peppers from the new world, however, 
Indian curry would have been a very different dish than what we find today. After the in­
troduction of chilies brought by the Portuguese from Mexico, South Asian curry quickly 
evolved into a wide array of new kinds of saucy dishes, often with intense spices and 
high heat (Collingham 2006: 49–​73). In the nineteenth century, British colonizers then 
developed their own more homogeneous form of “curry powder” and usually much 
milder curry dishes, and in the twentieth century, Americans developed the sort of 
highly processed and generally bland curries that we can buy canned or frozen at most 
grocery stores (Collingham 2006: 129–​154, 245–​255).

--- PAGE 1193 ---
1168      Hugh B. Urban
 
This culinary narrative is, I think, a better metaphor for the complex development of 
modern tantra in India versus the United States and Europe. Rather than a pizza effect 
and a reimportation of an Americanized tantra to South Asia, we seem to find more of a 
“curry-​style” bifurcation of popular representations of tantra in its modern South Asian 
and Western forms: while the latter generally exaggerates the sexual elements of tantra, 
the former typically amplifies its sinister, sorcerous, and black magic aspects. Both sides 
of this global play of representations and misrepresentations are crucial for our under­
standing of the complex nature of modern tantra.

ways by modern scholars. For the sake of this chapter, I find David Gordon White’s defi­
nition useful: “Tantra is that Asian body of beliefs and practices which, working from the 
principle that the universe we experience is nothing other than the concrete manifestation 
of the divine energy of the godhead that creates and maintains that universe, seeks to ritu­
ally appropriate and channel that energy. . . in creative and emancipatory ways” (2000: 9). 
For other useful definitions, see Brooks 1990; Urban 2010; Padoux 2017.
	2.	 I use the term “genealogy” in Michel Foucault’s sense, as a way of thinking about history 
that examines not so much the smooth historical continuities but rather the ruptures, 
discontinuities, and often complete reversals in the development of broad categories such as 
“tantra.” See Foucault 1984: 76–​100; Asad 1993; Urban 2003.
	3.	 LaVey identifies the LHP explicitly with Satan, understood not as an external being but as 
the symbol of the individual ego: “Satanism . . . is a religion of the flesh, the mundane, the 
carnal—​all of which are ruled by Satan, the personification of the Left-​Hand Path” (1969: 
52). Flowers, on the other hand, defines the LHP more broadly in terms of self-​deification 
and the rejection of all social, moral, or religious norms: “There are two major criteria for 
being considered a true lord (or lady) of the left-​hand path: deification of the self and anti­
nomianism” (2012: 11; see also Urban forthcoming).

characterize the Kali Yuga greatly decrease the effectiveness of purely intellectual, contem­
plative, and ritual paths. In this age of decadence, the only way open to those seeking the

neither are the themes and the works of the tradition which is thought reactionary and 
obsolete. Yet, one and all, they gather momentum and respect through a process of re-​
enculturation. I have coined the facetious-​sounding term ‘pizza-​effect’ for this pervasive 
pattern” (1970: 271). Gavin Flood uses the phrase to describe the larger exporting and re-​
importing of Hindu ideas since the nineteenth century: “elements of Hindu culture, such 
as yoga, bhakti, gurus . . . have been exported to the West . . . where they have gained great 
popularity and then gained popularity among urban Hindus in India as a consequence” 
(1996: 267). On the pizza effect in the specific case of tantra, as it circulated from India to the 
United States and back again, see Urban 2003: 204.

Glossary
This glossary includes technical terms used in the chapters of this collection, that is, it is 
not intended as a comprehensive glossary of tantric terms. (The Tāntrikābhidhānakośa 
(Hélène Brunner et al., eds.; 3 vols. to date, Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences 
Press, 2000, 2004, 2013) is a comprehensive resource for Sanskrit tantric terminology 
with explanations in German, French, and English.) Except for a very few emendations 
by the editors, the English explanations (glosses) of the technical terms included here 
are those of the contributors. Proper nouns and accepted loanwords in English are not 
italicized and are not marked with diacritics. Some of the terms reach across several 
of the chapters, including crossing linguistic boundaries, as indicated by instances in 
which terms from different source languages are grouped together. These are just one in­
dication of the extent to which concepts, categories, and concerns are shared throughout 
tantric culture when understood broadly as this collection does.
Unless otherwise indicated, terms are Sanskrit, and only when needed for clarity are 
marked S. Sanskrit root forms are marked √.
Tibetan terms appear frequently with alternative transcriptions.
